## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE EXISTED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COLLATED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH SEVERAL MANUSCRIPTS, CORRECTED WITH THE GREATEST CARE; CONTINUOUSLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE VERY FULL EDITIONS THAT HAVE APPEARED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME AND EACH AUTHOR OF ANY IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; AUGMENTED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, AND WITH OTHERS POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY EACH FATHER ON ANY TOPIC MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE OTHER OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY EASILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHICH PLACES OF THEIR WORKS, COMMENTED ON THE TEXT OF EACH OF THE BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and above all this collection—unified, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, drawn from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Published under the direction of J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.**

# [The Complete Works of Saint Isidore]

## [Col. 0007]

# Notice of the Editor of the Patrology

When we were seeking a collection of the works of Saint Isidore superior to all others, the first edition that presented itself to us was that of Grial, published at Madrid in 1778 amid the immense applause of scholars. We had already printed the first volume of that recension when the Roman edition of Faustino Arévalo came into our hands—much more recent than the others, more extensive, and indeed more accurate. Accordingly, we rejoiced beyond measure, immediately changed our plan, and, without regard to expense, ordered the work already begun to be sent back to the press, so that we might share this treasure with our reader.

You therefore have, most beloved reader, the complete edition of Arévalo, except that we were compelled to gather into a single body the notes which that most learned man had continuously placed beneath the text of the *Etymologies*. Nor were we able, from the beginning of this volume, to transfer to their proper place certain preliminary pieces that Arévalo had inserted among his Isidorian works—namely, the *Life of Saint Isidore* and several prefaces by Grial. We arranged for these to be separated from the Isidorian works, lest their repetition twice over prove unwelcome.

## [Col. 0009]

# Preface

I wish, benevolent reader, gladly to offer for your benefit and for the common benefit of all the complete works of the most holy Father and most distinguished doctor of Spain, Isidore—all those that survive and that, in the judgment of learned men, are genuinely his productions. Nor do I think that whatever service I may have rendered in preparing this edition will prove unwelcome to anyone. I am sufficiently convinced of this, if for no other reason than that, for nearly two centuries—from the year 1617, that is—no one, so far as I know, has taken care to reprint them.

The universal and illustrious learning of this most noble Author plainly demanded that, just as he is rightly celebrated by all, so his works should long be worn smooth in everyone’s hands, day and night. But how could that happen unless copies were plentiful? Therefore the desire for copies—heightened by the great name of a doctor celebrated throughout the world—was troubling and testing the minds of all learned men, especially Spaniards, urging them toward the preparation of a new and exceptionally accurate edition. Yet no one appeared who would satisfy the public wishes by his labor and industry.

Observing all this, and at the same time fearing that some disgrace might thereby come upon the Spanish nation, I undertook and completed this edition with as much diligence and zeal as I could.

I greatly desired not only to bring once again into public view the works of Isidore long ago printed, furnished with the finest type and with the other embellishments belonging to printing, but also—after collating ancient manuscripts from every quarter—to publish them for the public in a more correct, fuller, and more distinguished form. But the magnitude of the undertaking, exceeding my resources, restrained my courage, as did the fact that the hope of my effort had either already been entirely fulfilled or could be fulfilled only with extreme difficulty.

For no one is unaware how carefully and diligently, under the special command of Philip II, the most august prince of Spain, the most learned men from throughout Spain searched out ancient codices—not only throughout Spain but also through almost the whole of Italy—each weighing the portions assigned to him, until at last they corrected and illustrated with selected annotations all the writings of Saint Isidore that could be found.

From this there appeared in 1599 an edition distinguished by the royal name. The celebrated man John Grial, taking advantage of the labors of others and adding his own, issued it to the public dedicated to Philip III, who was then reigning. Learned men affirm that this royal edition is indeed excellent and preferable even to later ones, but they do not consider it complete in every respect. They cry out that the contest must continue and that new labor must be undertaken, so that Isidore may come forth into public view with the glory and dignity that are his due. But they speak and do not act. Meanwhile Isidore remains almost hidden and is increasingly missed with every passing day.

Therefore I offer what lies within my power and what both reverence for Isidore and love of the public good require of me: I bring once again into public view that same royal edition in its entirety, arranged in a more distinguished format, with more elegant type and bright paper—in other words, conspicuous in the finest typography, which is the printer’s responsibility. Nor should you, benevolent reader, expect anything else from me.

But perhaps, you will say, there are more little works bearing Isidore’s name that you would look for in vain in the royal edition. Some of these have been published here and there by various persons; the rest still lie hidden in church archives or chartularies. They certainly exist, and I now present them to you in the form of an Appendix.

In this matter you have clear testimony that my conjecture has been confirmed by the event itself. Indeed, I spared neither labor nor expense in seeking out everything that might make a new edition more abundant and richer. I therefore received from various places a number of copies bearing the name of Saint Isidore. But when learned men subjected them to examination, almost all were found to be apocryphal. Nevertheless I published them, both for the benefit of students and for the exercise of the learned. I shall therefore set out the series of these works, adding a brief judgment on each.

The first place is occupied by the *Fourth Book of Sentences*, which until now some people, relying on the testimony of certain codices bearing Isidore’s name, had regarded as a genuine work of that holy Doctor. But no one who has carefully read the five books of *Sentences* collected by Tajō, bishop of Zaragoza, and most recently published by the continuation of *Sacred Spain*, volume 31, will doubt that this book must be considered spurious. For this fourth book is excerpted from that work, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. To make this readily apparent, each chapter contains a note indicating from which book and chapter of Tajō it was taken.

Variant readings are also recorded, and in some places the sequence of the *Sentences*, otherwise connected on both sides, is not continuous. All this will greatly contribute to the elucidation of the works of the holy Fathers Augustine and Gregory, from whom Tajō compiled his books.

Two other chapters of *Sentences* follow. The first is drawn word for word from Saint Gregory’s work on Ezekiel; the second from Julian Pomerius’s *On the Contemplative Life*, book III, chapters 3, 4, 9, and 10. (See *Patrologia*, volume XVI.) This work is found among the writings of Prosper of Aquitaine and was attributed to him by very many writers for a long time. Now everyone vindicates it for Pomerius. On this matter see our Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 25, and the distinguished Ceillier, volume XV of his *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, where he discusses Julian Pomerius.

## [Col. 0011]

In third place I appended a little work with the title *An Exhortation to Humility*, which is attributed to Saint Martin, bishop of Braga, and was published among his works in volume XV of *Sacred Spain* by the most learned Flórez.

The sermon that follows, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter*, must likewise be rejected as a work of our Isidore, since it is altogether identical with homily 7 of Saint Caesarius of Arles, *On Easter*. See the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume II, column 277, Paris edition, 1624.

Some poems appended to the *Library of Saint Isidore* are also added. They were published in volume IX of *Sacred Spain* under this heading: “Title of the Library Published by Lord Isidore”; some fragments are added as well, to complete the chapters indicated there.

In sixth place I published the *Explanation of the Mass*. Although it may not seem unworthy of Isidore’s ability and learning, it must nevertheless be removed from him for this reason alone: in Isidore’s time another order and rite of the Mass prevailed in the Spanish Church than the one expounded here, which is altogether identical with the modern Roman rite.

Next I appended nine readings once recited on the feast of the Translation of Saint Isidore. They are taken word for word from the *Acts of his Translation*, published in volume IX of *Sacred Spain*.

Finally, I arranged for chapter XVII of the *Questions on Leviticus* to be supplied from the Albornoz manuscript, transcribed by Don Pedro de Castro. Its copy is preserved in the Flórez Library of the convent of Saint Philip Royal in Madrid, belonging to the Order of Saint Augustine.

I did not add to this edition the *Lament of Repentance*, published in two alphabets, etc., which the distinguished Nicolás Antonio mentions in volume I, book V, chapter 4, page 265 of his *Bibliotheca Vetus*, and which the authors of the *Acts of the Saints*, having received it from that same Nicolás, published in volume I for April, on the fourth day. I was informed of it too late—when the edition was already almost completed.

Nor were the book *On the Order of Creatures*, published by D. d’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, page 225, or the little works published by Abbot Constantinus Cajetanus under Isidore’s name included here, since learned men treat them either as spurious or as excessively doubtful, and they did not seem suitable for insertion here.

You have, therefore, candid reader, the works of Isidore—not illuminated and restored to their native purity with that highest degree of diligence which only the most learned and scholarly men could provide, but nevertheless somewhat more cleansed and more extensive than the royal edition presented them.

Enjoy them, therefore, devote yourself diligently to their reading, and willingly embrace my labor, zeal, and effort. Farewell.

## [Col. 0011]

# To Philip III, Catholic King  
## J. Grial

Many years ago your father, the greatest of the Catholic Kings, after manuscripts had been gathered from all over Spain and Italy, entrusted the works of Saint Isidore—whose lineage you yourself derive from him—to certain select men for correction. Some of these we, though far inferior, have succeeded. For although, on account of the excellence of the Author, almost all the books now being published had remained in circulation and were commonly known, it should not have been allowed, among so many outstanding writers whom the passage of time had injured, that Isidore alone should be exceptional.

The opposite, however, happened. Since his works were worn smooth in everyone’s hands—for there was no name in letters brighter in those times, nor any authority more weighty in ecclesiastical or civil matters—it came about, through the fault of copyists and the misguided diligence of readers, that scarcely any foreign and adulterated material failed gradually to grow in among the genuine and sound works.

Then came a period in which there was no honor for letters and no cultivation of them. We should therefore not so much complain that people disfigured these works as give great thanks that they transmitted them to us in any condition at all.

When literary culture was restored in our own age and light seemed to have been returned to learning, the distinguished labors of the most holy Father nevertheless began to face a greater danger: partly because of the losses we have mentioned, and partly because of the misguided refinement of certain people.

The studies of the more important disciplines and the stricter concerns—those which Isidore undertook either in relation to religion or in forming and shaping morals—seemed sufficiently protected and secure, whether by their own nature or by the very name of so great a pastor, doctor, and legislator.

But those works that concern not so much life itself as the cultivation and adornment of life would plainly have been cast down from their position and retained scarcely anywhere, and certainly with little honor, unless the most powerful king had defended the writings of his fellow countryman as his own offspring.

Delicate men were disgusted by these works and rejected them, as though, after the discovery of grain, acorns were being thrown before them. Now, however, not only will those works that already defended their own dignity sufficiently by themselves be made more illustrious and honorable through this service, but those that might seem exposed and vulnerable to accusation and calumny will henceforth grow accustomed to relying on their own strength and that of others, and to despising the voices of the unjust.

For the works considered lighter and more trivial will receive a substantial share of strength and authority from the more ancient writers. Since certain men entrusted with this care have displayed outstanding industry in the matter, we hope by their example that other men of distinction in learning—both from our own country and from abroad—will likewise join us eagerly, so that they may continue to investigate with their own zeal the most laborious excerpts of the Spanish Doctor and strengthen our resources with their own riches.

As for the fact that this work, undertaken before you were born, could not nevertheless be brought to completion—although your most devout father had greatly desired it—before the beginning of your reign, we regard this as having happened by divine providence. Thus, since your birthday had been appointed on the birthday of Saint Hermenegild, king and martyr of Spain and Isidore’s nephew through his sister, you might assume the government under precisely the same auspices, and from the same quarter of heaven, under which you had consecrated the beginnings of your life.

And just as from the nephew you were to receive an example for establishing religion, so from the uncle you were to receive aids and lessons for defending and advancing it—not merely lessons handed down by your ancestors, or even by such a father, but also lessons conspicuously commended to you by your own conduct, unless you are reluctant to remember yourself.

## [Col. 0013]

# To the Reader  
## J. Grial

More than twenty years ago, the correction of the books of Saint Isidore of Seville—for thus, in conformity with analogy, and following Gregory the Great, we prefer to call him rather than “Hispalensis”—was entrusted by order of His Catholic Majesty to certain men.

They handled the matter in such a way that some considered nothing more important than immediately devoting themselves entirely to this labor; others were very reluctant to be drawn away from their own studies and occupations to this undertaking; and some, while awaiting the correction of the *Etymologies*—a truly substantial work—delayed the matter so long that they died partly with the work unfinished and partly without having even begun it. Thus one person after another had to be appointed, and not just once.

At last, when the king had been informed that there would be no end unless everything that several men had revised, together with whatever still remained to be repaired, were all assigned to one person, I appeared especially suitable for the task—although it was not because I possessed any special ability of intellect or learning beyond others, since I ranked below everyone, but because I perhaps had sufficient leisure from my own affairs to attend to another’s, or at least was certainly sufficiently involved with many others to be caught up in the undertaking, under this condition and omen: that the solid praise for a task well done should return to others, while the sum total of every fault should fall upon me alone.

To prevent this from happening—that is, to prevent all blame from being diverted to me alone—I shall take this precaution: my foremost concern will be that no one be deprived of the testimony properly due to his labors.

I would have done this somewhat more fully if John López Velasco, royal secretary, a most upright man and no stranger to any branch of learning, had not been taken from us just as this work was nearing completion. He alone had nearly supervised this edition from its beginning, with great devotion and unremitting concern.

Because of his death, we were unable to determine with sufficient certainty either the number of manuscript copies or the persons from whom they had been sent. Accordingly, in the work of correction, I shall report as truthfully as possible what each person contributed and how much, insofar as I know and can establish it.

The correction of the *Etymologies* was entrusted to Álvaro Gómez of Toledo, a man of exceptional learning, and a large number of ancient codices was handed over to him. A substantial portion of these was written in Gothic—or, if you prefer, Lombard—characters. After recording the variants, he reported each matter to Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona, and to Pedro Chacón, then residing in Rome.

The king had also charged both of them to collate their own copies and send back to the same Álvaro their judgment on each matter. It is established that all told they used thirty or more manuscript books in correcting this work.

But when they had reached the twelfth book—that is, nearly the middle of the work—death overtook Antonio Agustín, that most holy prelate, whose books were known throughout the world.

Pedro Chacón—for he himself wrote his name in our manner, not “Ciacon” or “Ciaconio” according to Italian usage, since he preferred to be regarded as a Spaniard and a Toledan, which he was, rather than as a Roman and Sabine—had spent many years correcting ancient authors and had made the restoration of this work one of his principal concerns. It is scarcely possible to say how much assistance he provided: he was a man of intelligence, industry, and a singular art of conjecture.

Yet we gave very little weight to the conjectural skill I have mentioned—perhaps less than was fair. We followed the ancient books, which, in proportion as they were the oldest, we found to be less expanded and less corrupted, as well as the sources from which these materials had been drawn and which he himself had largely identified.

Álvaro, therefore, aided by the outstanding work of the two men just mentioned and by the cooperation of others—especially Antonio de Covarrubias, the most learned and elegant man of all our countrymen, past or present, wherever they may have lived—left behind, and then died, a massive body of annotations on all twenty books. He had been strongly motivated both by extraordinary devotion to Isidore and by his zeal to satisfy the Catholic Majesty.

When serious men examined this work, they highly approved, as was just, its zeal and diligence, but judged that the structure and method of the whole undertaking had to be returned to the anvil and reforged. They considered this necessary for several reasons, but especially because, although there was abundant discussion everywhere of the variety of manuscripts and conjectures, he had left the text itself—the very reason for which all the labor had been undertaken—uncorrected.

I was appointed as the farmer to clean and plant this broad estate, so far as this kind of soil would allow. It is unnecessary to speak of my labor. Although I rightly placed great trust in such men, I could not avoid going through the ancient books myself once more and repeatedly hesitating over nearly every individual point.

I shall meanwhile say nothing of what I found through my own—if I may use his expression—sweet labor. Although these discoveries are by no means few, they generally seem to me extremely few when I consider how many things still remain that require some new cultivation.

In the notes, it was not my intention to spin out disputes over the opinions of certain men who were by no means bad, or to heap together from ancient writings a great many statements to the same effect, or to ransack the libraries of those outstanding men in intelligence and learning whom our own age has produced in such abundance. For what limit could there be to exhausting all the libraries of all the arts and disciplines?

Accordingly, whenever we discovered the source from which something had been taken, we scarcely failed to restore it to its original author. Other writers we cited only when necessary, and then rarely and sparingly. We decided that this should not be done as in comedies, where everyone discovers everything everywhere.

Among more recent writers we scarcely named anyone unless perhaps he had applied a physician’s hand to the treatment of some particular passage.

The first book of the *Differences* was corrected by Father Pantinus, royal chaplain, from two manuscript books. He indicated what material had been taken from ancient grammarians or agreed with them.

We thought it appropriate to add the *Differences* from the Paris edition—partly the same, sometimes different, but arranged in no order—so that the condition in which Isidore’s writings existed might also be apparent from that little work.

The later book, *On Theological Differences*, was corrected by Doctor Roland Wicelius, also a royal chaplain, likewise from two manuscript books.

We found the book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to Sisebutus, enlarged with very lengthy scholia by the person to whom it had been entrusted. Since these were of little use for correction, those who were supervising the work by royal command decided to cast them aside and have us revise the book from four manuscript codices, one of which was a very ancient Lombard manuscript from the Church of Oviedo. We also attached notes that would be useful. This was done, and not without reason.

The most distinguished Garsias Loaisa, later tutor of the most serene prince and now most worthy prelate of the Church of Toledo, enriched the *Chronicle*, beyond its correction and the identification of the sources from which it was compiled, with much additional historical knowledge and varied learning.

For this reason, in book V of the *Etymologies*, where the same periods and events are described somewhat more briefly, the entire passage was preserved intact and untouched. No one should be surprised if the description of certain periods occasionally differs: he represented his manuscripts, while we represented the agreement of our own.

The same most illustrious prelate produced the three books of *Sentences*, corrected from thirteen manuscript codices—two of them Lombard—and illustrated with notes. They had previously been printed at Turin rather inadequately; he now issued them much more accurately, and advanced this entire edition through his favor, industry, and generosity.

John Baptist Pérez, later bishop of Segorbe, corrected the book *On Illustrious Men* from seven manuscripts and elucidated certain passages in it.

The same man corrected the *History of the Goths, Sueves, and Vandals*. It is not clear from how many manuscript books. In the passage that we printed under the year 464, the first year of Justinian’s reign, we did not follow the reading that we see pleasing certain very serious scholars—namely, the ninth year of Justin—but rather the ancient copies of this *History* and of book V of the *Etymologies*. These assign Justin only eight years, with great agreement. In either case, however, Amalaric falls in the same year, as those scholars wish.

The same applies to the words concerning Saint Hermenegild the martyr under Era 606:

> “Then he overcame Hermenegild, his son, who was tyrannizing against his rule, after besieging him.”

These words offend some people. We are not troubled by the unusualness of the word *tyrannizing*: Rodrigo of Toledo used the same expression in book II, chapter 14:

> “Then he captured Hermenegild, his son, who was tyrannizing against the imperial authority, after besieging him at Seville by treachery; and because he refused to consent to impious rites, he tortured him with various torments. Finally, after striking him with the sword, the impious parricide consecrated him to God as a martyr worthy of him.”

We suspect that something of this sort concerning his martyrdom is missing in Isidore. For it is scarcely believable that he did not bear the same testimony to his nephew as to his brother Leander. This is all the more likely because Alfonso de Cartagena, in chapter 26 of his *Anacephalaeosis*, used almost the same words concerning the same matter. Thus we have no doubt that both writers copied this account from Isidore.

The same man also collected and corrected the Letters.

Pedro Fontidonius, a canon of Salamanca, left the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* corrected from eight ancient copies. Although certain highly respected men consider the authority of this book doubtful, the testimony of Saints Ildephonsus and Braulio, together with that of Sigebert, ought to have outweighed all their arguments for us, in addition to the agreement of so many of our own and foreign copies.

We received the *Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments* without any certain title. Each of seven manuscript books bore a completely different and wholly unsuitable title, none of which agreed with the Paris edition.

A most learned man had noted and selected certain variant readings throughout this work. But he had been deceived both by certain codices that had not been examined carefully enough and by the misleading edition of Eucherius of Lyon, from which he believed a large part had been taken. On the contrary, we discovered that all of those materials had been transferred from Isidore to Eucherius.

It would have been fairer and more accurate to examine the authors to whom Isidore attributes these materials—Origen, Victorinus, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Cassian, and Gregory—if the task had not involved so much labor and tedium and required a man with much more leisure than that which he plainly possessed.

In this matter we did what we could. By restoring the title, we seem almost to have returned the work, already nearly alienated from its author, to its rightful owner.

A large portion of it—namely, the whole of Genesis and the books of Kings—is read in Eucherius; indeed, the entire work has been attached to the books of the Venerable Bede. But so much material—not merely from Isidore but from other writers as well—has been inserted or, rather, stitched into Eucherius that one is ashamed on behalf of those who presided over the Roman edition.

For—leaving Augustine and Paulinus aside, since others may determine whether Eucherius ever encountered their writings—how could he have named Gregory and Cassiodorus? Was it not negligence—or should I say rather stupidity—not to see this?

An entire work on Solomon’s Temple, whether Bede’s or someone else’s, in which Cassiodorus is cited, has also been thrown into the commentary on the Third Book of Kings.

But it seems that it was the work of someone who wished to join Isidore to Eucherius so that the historical and mystical senses might be present together.

As for Bede—if indeed it is Bede—his purpose was to arrange questions on the Old Testament from various authors, and he did not carry the work beyond the beginning of Exodus. Nevertheless, throughout Genesis, whenever he presents material from this work, he either expressly names Isidore or calls it this “recapitulated underlay.”

Moreover, the title *Questions* is found in one codex of the monastery of Oliva, in which each exposition is preceded by its own questions. I do not, however, think that the questions in this codex are the same as those mentioned by Ildephonsus in his book *On Illustrious Men*. For he nowhere indicates that the work was altered, and it was not necessary for it to be called a *Book of Questions* merely on the example of Jerome and Augustine.

Accordingly, we too were not afraid to retain the title *Questions*. It also appears from Braulio that these questions had been divided into two books. For he says in his preliminary notice:

> “The two books of Questions, whoever reads them, recognizes in them the store of the ancient interpreters.”

He seems to have had in mind Isidore’s own words in the preface:

> “In them the reader will not read our own material, but will read again the material of the ancients.”

The codices that we used were eight: the Palentinus, Valentinus, Complutensis, Guadalupensis, two from Osma, and the Olivensis mentioned earlier. None was so old as to be written in Lombard letters.

Cyprian Suárez of the Society of Jesus left the *Allegories* corrected and furnished with scholia. It is not known how many manuscript books assisted him.

The same man also corrected the little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*. Here too it could not be established how many ancient codices he had used.

But the most learned man did not notice that this treatise had recently been published together with the works of Saint Ambrose, in which so many things differ from our text that we did not think it necessary to report them one by one. We preferred simply to have our text, whatever its condition, read alongside the Augustinian edition, with which it almost entirely agrees.

The fact that this little work was Isidore’s—as he himself left it written—had been made convincing to that excellent man by the codices bearing his name, by the style—which perhaps does not differ greatly from works of similar subject—and by the testimony of Sigebert.

We believe, without concealing our view, that this was the work which in Isidore’s own time circulated under the name of John Chrysostom. For Isidore says of Chrysostom in his book *On Illustrious Men*:

> “There is also found, addressed to a certain noble matron named Gregoria, a distinguished work of his, *On the Conduct of Life and the Formation of Morals*, or *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*.”

We shall therefore attribute the very numerous textual variations to the interpreters rather than to the copyists.

As for the Epilogue, which is shorter in Ambrose, somewhat longer in our copies, and much longer in Augustine, there is no reason for us to labor over it, since it is plainly foreign to the work, no less than the address to Simplician in the Ambrosian edition. Nor should the theologians of Leuven have attempted to infer the author from the addition.

The same man corrected the *Exposition on the Song of Solomon*, found in only one manuscript, from Bede’s commentaries, which he supposed to have overflowed from this small source. He also added the reason why it should rightly be attributed to Isidore.

For he said that he had found in an ancient preliminary notice of Braulio’s *Works of Isidore* the following words, which are generally missing:

> “At the request of Pope Gregory, he abridged the books of the blessed Gregory on morals in concise form; he elucidated the Song of Songs with a fluent exposition; he published a fourth edition of the Psalter; and he labored with no small diligence on an exposition of the books of Moses, the Psalter, and the four Gospels. In Canon and Civil Law as well he composed very extensive instruments.”

Yet even these words do not sufficiently correspond to the very brief exposition. For it is much shorter than the exposition of Justus of Urgell, which seemed very brief to Isidore himself. What if this work were excerpted from Bede?

Because the authorship of these two little books was not sufficiently clear, we placed them at the end.

John Mariana of the Society of Jesus corrected the two books *Against the Jews* from seven manuscript codices and added annotations. He did the same for the book of *Prologues*, from the same number of manuscripts, and for the *Synonyms*, restoring and illustrating it from ten copies.

We have properly, as we hope, restored the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* from the very ancient Albaild manuscript, already made famous by others. It contains several councils and various other materials. Yet even this excellent codex often required assistance from our labor, through the sources of the authors from which the work had been composed, which we sought out.

We also had another copy from the college of Alcalá.

Father Chacón had previously brought the *Rule of Monks*, found in only one manuscript and extremely corrupt, into substantial order by using Smaragdus and the *Book of the Sentences of the Fathers*. After obtaining another codex—also Lombard, though itself badly disfigured by many errors—we advanced his work very considerably.

And this much regarding the individual books. In all of them, however, one must bear in mind that most are excerpts. For that is what the most holy man himself presented them as; and at times he even took care that passages for which the testimony of authors could be adduced should not be attributed under the heading of his own fault. Since that testimony was neither supplied by him as often as would now be necessary, nor by us, nor could it in any way be supplied after the removal of certain authors whom he used, the reader—if he will heed me—will restrain himself, lest, while accusing a most diligent writer of some negligence, he incur the charge of rashness and recklessness, for which he himself might shortly afterward be condemned both by others and perhaps by himself. For there are also passages which he should be thought merely to have set forth, not judged—and this not without, but following, the example of Jerome and others. Such are the matters in the *History* which he narrated from Victor himself concerning the defenders of the Three Chapters: Theodore of Mopsuestia, Facundus, the emperor Justinian, and Victor of Tunnuna. Such, perhaps, were the matters which very grave men noted in the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* as unworthy of Isidore. In that case, another author ought rather to be sought than the book rejected, since it rested upon the authority of Saints Ildephonsus and Braulio. To these one may add, with my consent, what he reports from Marcellinus concerning the death of Hosius of Córdoba. Nor should this seem surprising to anyone who observes that in Book V, the final chapter, of the *Etymologies*, under David, he says that Carthage was founded in the fourth age, and that the same city was founded again many years later under Amasia. On this matter, however, he took precautions in the *Chronicle*. For under Amasia he added: “Some assert that Carthage was founded at this time; others, earlier.”

There are also some other matters of this kind in the *Etymologies*: not indeed of great importance, but at times conflicting even with one another—as when he says that one should write *exsul*, not *exul*, but conversely *exultat*, not *exsultat*. Yet the former may appear to have been taken from Terentius Scaurus and the latter from Velius Longus; that will be sufficient.

We have noted that statements maliciously and impiously added concerning the definition of the last day (*extremae diei*) in chapter 6 of the *Expositions on Genesis* are wholly absent from certain copies and improperly repeated in others. Unless you prefer to regard these also as reported and set forth not from his own judgment but from that of others, together with this most learned man. Yet it would be difficult to find another work of this kind, so that one could traverse all his books without stumbling.

We also suspect that certain passages have been removed, such as what we mentioned shortly before concerning the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild.

It is hardly possible for someone who wore out his life in this single labor and remained perpetually chained to the press to be responsible for all the typographers’ errors. We, inexperienced in this matter and hindered by other difficulties, could do no more than resist them as best we could. As for what remains, we have carefully taken pains to warn you of anything in which you might stumble or become confused, lest any matter requiring greater attention remain unnoticed.

[Col. 0019]

# LIFE OF SAINT ISIDORE, BY A REGULAR CANON OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT ISIDORE OF LEÓN, Perhaps Lucas, later Bishop of Tuy

(Published in the *Acta Bollandiana*, from a manuscript of Toledo submitted by the distinguished man Nicolás Antonio.) (C,S)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0019A]

### 1

The sacred Church throughout the world proclaims in fitting praises the splendid merits of the most blessed doctor of the Spains, Isidore, confessor of Christ, archbishop of Seville and primate of Spain, dearest brothers; and celebrated fame, always and everywhere, commends this man, illustrious in every respect. Yet beyond that common glory of honor, which he won for himself by the greatness of his merits among all the assemblies of the faithful, he is exalted in Spain by special praises, since it has deserved in him another intercessor on earth after the apostles for its faith.

For he is that most radiant ray of the Sun of Justice through whom, Iberia, the light of truth shone especially upon you; and you, who had been led astray by the errors or deceits of the Arians, the Acephali, Muhammad, and other [Col. 0019B] false prophets, through the teaching of blessed Isidore became a guide to righteousness. He is that distinguished shepherd of yours and outstanding pontiff who intoxicated you with such abundant increases of the divine Scriptures that you were to be set above the highest seats and made fruitful with eternal riches.

[Note: [Col. 0019B] Thus, shortly afterward, “divine intoxication” is mentioned. Bede likewise, in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne*, illuminated on 20 March, no. 46, says that Saints Cuthbert and Herebert the priest intoxicated one another with draughts of heavenly wisdom. Galbert, in the *Life of Blessed Charles the Good*, 2 March, no. 47, says that his murderers were intoxicated with anger and fury. Similar expressions occur frequently elsewhere; hence it is clear that *debriare* is understood to mean “to drink” or “to satisfy fully.”]

Thus, with your position transformed into advancement, you are no longer last among the regions but first among the first.

[Note: [Col. 0019C] Lucas of Tuy, in the preface to his *Chronicle of the World*, writes: “Spain, with its position transferred into advancement, is not last in the farthest regions, but first among the foremost.”]

He is the one who, after the most glorious apostle James, bestowed upon you this excellence of grace: that you should be fruitful in peoples, distinguished in religion, and most renowned in triumphs. Indeed, Spain, named from the city of Seville by the most certain foreknowledge of the event that was to follow, you stand forth richer in divine intoxication than in earthly prosperity. Although victorious in trophies, gracious in delights, and having carried the titles of your praise to the boundaries of all nations, it is much more splendid and much more glorious that, with such constant and devoted services—out of reverence for our Savior, the presence of the most glorious apostle James, and also the presence and resplendent teaching of the most upright father Isidore—every form of Christian religion should honor you and flock to you. For, above what chance offered you or the force of nature granted, the dignity of apostolic privilege rightly secured that, just as Gregory succeeded the apostle Peter at Rome by the singular privilege of grace, so in Spain an Isidore, no inferior to Gregory, should succeed James.

[Note: [Col. 0020B] Nicolás Antonio notes the following: Antonius Nebrissensis once held that the name of the whole of Spain was derived from the city of Seville; Florianus de Campo does not reject this in Book I, chapter 16, of his *History of Spain*, nor do the others whom Rodericus Carus cites in Book I, chapter 4, of his *History of the City of Seville, or Its Antiquities*. They followed Saint Isidore, who, addressing his *History of the Goths*—that is, Book II of his *Chronicle*—to King Sisenand, expresses this opinion; although in Book IV, chapter 4, of the *Origins*, he believes that Spain was named after King Hispanus, not after Seville. Lucas of Tuy, in the prologue to his *Chronicle*, gives an entirely different etymology of Spain, unworthy of such a man.]

For the seeds of the Word of God which blessed James sowed, Isidore, like a watchful farmer, watered with the most salutary preaching of heavenly rains; and, by uprooting with the hoe of the Spirit the thorns, thistles, and weeds of evil doctrines sown above them by heretical enemies, he brought them to the cultivation of the fruits of life.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Saint Ambrose used *zizania* in this way in Book VII of his commentary on Luke: “The leaven of wheat is one thing, and the weeds another.”]

The authority of the whole world set Gregory in the primacy of the most blessed chief of the apostles, alike by primacy of place and of merit; but equality of merits caused the judgment of the Roman curia to acknowledge Isidore as another Gregory. To recount individually all that he accomplished—not only by the course of nature but also by divine Providence, which in the miraculous illumination of the Church graciously worked through him in an aging world—exceeds our strength, talent, and knowledge.

Nevertheless, concerning the most holy man, I, a sinner; concerning the greatest, I, a small man; concerning the wisest, I, an unlearned man—of his many miracles I shall touch briefly upon a few, as far as I can, in charity and with the notation of a faithful pen, for the instruction of those to come, lest the works of so great a Father, as the years pass, slip also from the hearts of the faithful. To speak well of such great and such good things concerning so great and good a man must be attributed only to the merits of that same man; and indeed their greatness has grown to such a height that the elegance of speech falls short of the subject, while the subject of truth commends the cultivation of elegance.

## CHAPTER ONE. The distinguished and holy lineage of Saint Isidore.—His instruction in letters

### 2

Therefore, so that the outstanding confessor Isidore might be ennobled by distinguished beginnings, and so that an illustrious origin might foreshadow the illustrious man he would become, Severianus, duke of Carthage and of the province of Spain, offspring of King Theodoric of the Goths, was his father.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] The manuscript reads: “the offspring of the city of Carthage, province of Spain, Severianus the duke,” which seemed capable of being restored to sound sense by correcting the first word and transposing the other. This agrees with Lucas of Tuy, who in the cited preface calls Severianus the Carthaginian duke. Whether he was descended from Theodoric, king of the Goths, or at least was his brother, let others debate.]

His mother was called Turtura.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Lucas of Tuy calls her Theodora in the passage cited. Quintanadvenas makes her the daughter of King Theodoric in the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, his brother.]

They were the parents of men of the highest distinction and learning, confessors of Christ endowed with extraordinary excellence both of character and intellect: Leander, archbishop of Seville, and Fulgentius, the nourishing and most distinguished doctor and bishop who illumined the universal Church with the radiance of the sacred Scriptures and of his works; and of the most holy virgin Florentina, superior of virgins.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] In the Roman Martyrology she is called Florentina; she is commemorated on 20 June.]

Instructed by their most serene teachings, advancing through prayer, handsome in the gravity of his character, he honored his homeland by religion, his father by prudence, his brothers by discipline, his relatives by respect, his peers by favor, his relations by reward, and his neighbors by affection.

[Col. 0021D] The most glorious doctor and archbishop Leander loved the boy as his only child, keeping him as a special consolation while away from his homeland. And because he desired him to be not so much the heir of deceptive riches as the successor to his own happy character, he watched most carefully lest that age which habitually inclines toward evil should find an opportunity to slide into the corruption of sin.

He did not spare the rod, and he was praised in him; he taught him and placed zeal against the enemy, and in the midst of his friends he gloried in him.

[Note: [Col. 0022D] These words differ slightly from the Vulgate edition.]

In his lifetime he saw and rejoiced, and at his death he was not saddened before his enemies. For he left behind him one like himself: a defender of the household against enemies and one who repaid friends with gratitude.

O most holy Father Leander, this venerable boy whom you love, whom you nourish, whom you teach, whom you educate, whom you correct, whom you guard, is the bridesman of the heavenly Bridegroom, the friend of the holy angels, the equal of patriarchs and prophets, a citizen among the apostles, a companion of martyrs, the splendor of bishops, and one to be proportionately compared with all the ranks of the saints. The outcome of events will reveal this at the proper time.

### 3

When he was still a little child, as we read concerning blessed Ambrose, he was being taken by his nurse to a garden. The old woman, overcome by forgetfulness, left him among the vegetables and went away. After several days, Severianus his father, grieving for his son, climbed to the roof terrace; and, sitting opposite the garden, he looked and saw—

[Note: [Col. 0022D] Nicolás Antonio notes the following: Those who have committed Isidore’s deeds to writing for the past two centuries report that this vision occurred to him: Antonius Morales, Book XII, chapter 4; Padilla, century 7, chapter 22; Vasaeus, under the year 649; Mariana, Book VI, chapter 7; Marietta, Book V, chapter 23, *On the Saints of Spain*—all, as we may suspect, instructed by this account. So much for him.]

an innumerable multitude of bees descending eagerly upon the boy with an immense buzzing, and then flying up from there toward the heavens. Astonished, he hurried down to the garden, summoned the servants, and hastened to see the miracle of what had occurred. When they approached, they saw some bees entering and leaving the boy’s mouth, while others covered his face and entire body with coverings of honey and honeycomb. But when the father embraced his son with cries and tears, the bees rose to such a height in the air that they could no longer be seen by bodily eyes. Of the many things that happened to him in this manner, I have set forth only a few, so that the prudent reader may perceive from how great a beginning of virtue he commenced.

### 4

When the venerable boy Isidore had been handed over to the study of letters, and, as it seemed to him, possessed too little intellectual capacity, he was moved by childish fear, dreading the teacher’s blows, and by divine prompting fled not far from the city of Seville. When, exhausted from his journey and thirsty, he sat down beside the rim of a certain well,

[Note: [Col. 0022D] Nicolás Antonio likewise notes that the authors of this event are those whom he praised above, as well as Laurentius de Padilla in the *Lives of the Saints of Spain*.]

he saw an enormous stone pierced through with twisting holes.

[Col. 0022D] Examining it carefully, he began to turn over in his mind who had made these holes and for what purpose they existed. Likewise, at the mouth of the well there was a certain piece of wood, grooved by the continuous cutting of cords used to draw water. While he was silently reflecting on these things, a woman came to draw water. Greatly astonished by the boy’s beauty, she asked what he was doing there, or why such a small boy had come there alone. For he was of wondrous beauty: radiant in face, handsome in form, cheerful in appearance, happy in expression, modest in his gaze, always displaying modesty in his conduct.

The boy turned humbly toward her and said: “O lady, I beg you to explain to me who made the holes in this stone, and for what purpose, or who made the grooves in this piece of wood, and for what purpose.”

The woman replied: “This stone was pierced by the frequent dripping of drops, and this wood was grooved by the frequent drawing of cords in the raising of water.”

The boy, filled with the divine Spirit, came to himself and said: “If the hardest stone is hollowed out by the frequent dripping of soft water, and wood yields when cut by the strokes of cords, how much more can I, a human being, with God’s grace going before me, advance daily through the smallest increments of learning and arrive at an increase of knowledge!”

O venerable Isidore, the thought behind this reflection belongs not to a young boy but to a perfect man and a most wise elder. Who was it that taught you in this way, even before the discipline of letters, in your tender years, if not the Spirit of truth, who, suggesting all things to you, also chose a sanctified vessel to carry the name of the Son of God before kings, princes, and the children of Israel?

After this, the boy returned to Seville with hurried steps and submitted himself with humble devotion to the discipline of his teachers.

### 5

Finally, so much grace was infused into him from heaven that whatever his teachers set forth from the Scriptures, he eagerly retained in his thirsty heart; and, rather than becoming a forgetful hearer, he stored it in the treasury of his memory for the benefit of many of the faithful. He anticipated his teachers themselves, as though with an already foreknowing understanding; and by this astonishing novelty both the teachers and all who were present were struck dumb with wonder.

Thus, inflamed by the divine Spirit, instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, formed in every kind of expression, distinguished in the education of the trivium, perfected in the pursuit of the quadrivium, eminent in the teachings of the philosophers, learned in divine and human laws, sweet in speech, outstanding in intellect, and also, in life and teaching, most illustrious in the admiration of many for his age,

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Nicolás Antonio indicates the following concerning the trivium and quadrivium: The three arts—grammar, rhetoric, and logic—were formerly called the trivium; the other four—arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music—the quadrivium. Together they form the course of the seven liberal arts, as Vossius says in Book I, chapter 26, *On the Vices of Speech*.]

he advanced from virtue to virtue and shone as so exceptional a teacher that, according to the character of his speech, he was suitable in learning to all—Latin, Greek, and Hebrew speakers, the wise and the less intelligent alike—and vigorous in incomparable eloquence.

When blessed Isidore thus surpassed almost all mortals in knowledge of every kind, an unprecedented thing, as we remember, in our own times, he did not, as that youthful age is accustomed to do, embrace the world’s pleasures. Rather, he devoted himself entirely to logical contemplation, to the pursuit of practical matters, or to meditation upon and study of divine theories.

Finally, nature marked him out, grace enriched him, character exalted him, and studies stirred him so greatly that in intellect he followed Plato, in study Aristotle, in eloquence Cicero, in abundance Didymus “Chalcenterus,” in learning Origen, in gravity Jerome, in doctrine Augustine,

[Note: [Col. 0023D] Nicolás Antonio again observes the following: He understands Didymus of Alexandria, the grammarian, who, according to Suidas, was called among other surnames *Chalcenterus*, that is, “of brazen entrails,” on account of his endurance in study and writing. No one else wrote more books, says Fabius Quintilian in Book I, chapter 8, and Isidore himself in Book VI, chapter 7, of the *Etymologies*, if one reads *Chalcenterus* for *Caliterus*—the reading found in the editions printed before the Madrid edition. See Hesychius, *On Illustrious Men*, Suidas, and Saint Jerome. So much for him.]

and in examples, assuredly, Gregory.

When, at the command of his brother and foster-father Leander, he had sent the same blessed Gregory a letter on blessedness, adorned with wondrous diligence both with the opinions of philosophers and with flowers from the sacred Scriptures, blessed Gregory read it through and, admiring both the eloquence of its language, the coherence of its ideas, and its abundance of learning, perceived in spirit what Isidore would become. He is said to have exclaimed: “Behold another Daniel!” And another said: “Behold, here is one greater than Solomon!”

## CHAPTER TWO. Acquaintance with Saint Gregory the Great.—The *Book of Etymologies* composed.—Sacred learning displayed against heresies, especially the Arian heresy

[Col. 0024C]

### 6

From that time, then, blessed Gregory, delighted by his desire to see blessed Isidore, made known by definite indications to the most holy bishop Leander, bound to him by the ties of charity, the wish of his heart.

The cause of this friendship had arisen when Leander, unable to refute the fervor of the Arian heresy at its roots during the time of Leovigild, crossed over to the assembly of bishops at Constantinople to confirm the articles of the holy and immaculate Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0024D] We stated that no council was then held at Constantinople; rather, the true reason why Leander and Gregory met there is contained in the letter of Saint Gregory himself prefixed to his exposition of the Book of Job. This Gregory was called “cardinal” according to the usage not of his own time but of ours. Read more in both *Lives of Saint Gregory*, elucidated for 12 March.]

Gregory was there, then a cardinal acting in place of the Roman bishop. Leander made a pact of friendship with him and asked him to expound the *Moralia on Job* for him, which Gregory later completed with devoted zeal after becoming pope.

When the venerable Isidore learned of Gregory’s desire—an astonishing thing to hear—on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, as the story goes, after the first lesson had been read through in the church of Seville, he went outside the church and, led I know not by whom, arrived at the city of Rome in the briefest interval of time. There he found blessed Pope Gregory singing God’s praise at Matins.

When blessed Gregory saw him, he was exceedingly joyful and immediately recognized him. Giving thanks, he embraced in Isidore his dearest friend Leander. After the Gospel had been completed, he took leave of the saint, went out from the church, and returned to Seville that same night, where he found the clerics he had left celebrating the same Matins.

[Note: [Col. 0024D] Nicolás Antonio notes the following: Some of our writers did not readily approve this miracle, especially Morales, Book XII, chapter 5, and Mariana, Book VI, chapter 7. Others did not even wish to report it: Vasaeus, Garibay, Marietta, and Morgadus in Book I, chapter 9, of his *History of Spain*. But that Isidore went to Rome to see Gregory and be seen by him is more plausible. Although Tamayo de Salazar cites Lucas of Tuy and the very ancient Breviary of Segovia, he nevertheless considers it a mere fiction, together with Quintanadvenas. “It is by no means credible,” he says, “that such an outstanding event would have been passed over in silence by the ancients Braulio and Ildephonsus.” Therefore the author wisely begins with the formula “as the story goes,” relating the matter under doubt, as he had received it.]

Whether this occurred through the intercession of the most holy Gregory, through Isidore’s merits, or in some other way, I confess that I am uncertain. For it is better not to declare great things where one cannot avoid error without the danger of falsehood than to assert the contrary. Yet I firmly hold that the blessed young man undertook many things through his experience of learning and applied them to the usefulness of the Church and the advantage of the faithful.

For he persecuted the advocates of wicked doctrines, the heretics, in many ways, since at that time many heresies arose, demolishing the vineyard of the Lord’s inheritance, namely, the holy Church. We do not doubt that divine Providence brought it about that Isidore should shine at that time, so that he might refute their insolence not only with testimonies from the sacred Scriptures but also nullify it with philosophical syllogisms and arguments.

### 7

For he attained such a height of learning that, as I think, none of the ancient philosophers could be compared with him by a sound judgment. I would pass over this out of caution if it were permitted, lest the studies of the pagans seem in any way either to be preferred to or compared with authoritative teaching. For just as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so our ways are exalted above their ways and our thoughts above their thoughts; and as the spirit surpasses the flesh, reason the senses, faith opinion, understanding faith, the peace of God all understanding, and finally the Creator every creature, so theology surpasses all the wisdom of the world, and theologians surpass the entire teaching of pagan philosophers.

Since Isidore excelled all the more in this respect—perfect in the philosophy of the ancients and supreme in the theology of the moderns—let us nevertheless omit for the present his other exceedingly numerous works, in which he labored with marvelous ingenuity. The book entitled *Etymologies*, filled with everyone’s admiration and worthy of everyone’s acceptance, calls out, bears witness, and exclaims, lest this also be absent from the praises of the most holy and learned man: by this work he was raised to the level to which the foremost and most skilled philosophers were raised, or to which that supremely wise Solomon is shown to have surpassed them all both in knowledge and in excellence. Thus, after the apostles, he was regarded as incomparable among all the children of men for the variety of his learning.

### 8

In this book you will see Isidore endowed with eloquence in the learning of the trivium; here you will admire him perfected in mathematical discipline through the investigation of the quadrivium; here you will find him teaching both theory and practice for preserving and restoring bodily health. Here, by distinguishing methodical, empirical, and logical medicine, you will finally recognize Apollo, Aesculapius, and Hippocrates.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Isidore explains these in Book IV, chapter 4, and calls them the three schools of physicians.]

Here, by reviewing the institutions of Phoroneus, Hermes Trismegistus, Solon, and Pompilius, you will discover him most skilled in law.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] In Book V, chapter 1, he discusses the authors of laws and inserts Lycurgus among them; he is omitted here.]

Here, by introducing rights and laws through edicts and decrees, you will think that he instructed Justinian. Here, by distinguishing ephemerides, epacts, Ides, calendars,

[Col. 0026B] annals, and histories, you will conclude that he had absorbed Pherecydes and Josephus.

[Note: [Col. 0026D] Pherecydes the Syrian, in Book I, chapter 37, is said to have been the first among the Greeks to write in prose; and in chapter 41 it is added that he flourished at the time when Ezra wrote down the law. See Vossius, *On Greek Writers*, Book IV, chapter 4.]

Here, by pursuing chronicle-writing, you will declare that he read Eusebius, Jerome, and Orosius.

And because it is read concerning Solomon that he discussed everything from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows on the wall, so one finds concerning blessed Isidore that he wonderfully treated matters from the First Cause almost to the furthest of creatures. By examining the functions, offices, and modes of every individual thing, and finally describing the nature and circumstances of all things, you will think that he not only drank deeply of Solomon’s knowledge but surpassed him.

Here, by investigating the distinctions among ether, air, waters, and earth, and the natures and names of all living things, you will believe that he consulted the first man. Here you will be astonished to find him delighting entirely in Rachel’s embraces while you see him occupied in the study of the experience of the ancients.

Here, through the fragrance of the mandrake fruit, you will rejoice to see him recalled to Leah’s lap.

[Note: [Col. 0026D] In Book XVII, chapter 9, discussing aromatic herbs, he says that *mandrake* was so called because it has sweet-smelling apples.]

While delighting in love of heavenly things, you will perceive him devoutly absorbed in the fecundity of sacred Scripture. Here you will find him sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet and choosing the better part; here, with Martha, anxious and engaged in frequent service; here, with Paul, carried up as the chosen vessel even to the third heaven; here, with the same Paul, laboring more than all and becoming all things to all people in order to win all.

Here, with Paul resisting Peter to his face when Peter preached circumcision; here, with Peter, after Simon’s death, not fearing even Nero; here, having conquered individually the doctrines of all heretics; here, having received and venerated the four holy councils.

[Note: [Col. 0026D] The councils are mentioned in reverse order; Isidore treats them in the proper order in Book VI, chapter 15.]

Here, with the Council of Chalcedon, he weakens Dioscorus and the heretic Eutyches; here, with the First Council of Ephesus, he shatters the impiety of Nestorius; here, with the Council of Constantinople, he strikes down Macedonius together with Eunomius; here, with the Council of Nicaea, he condemns the most cunning Arius, blinded by every form of madness.

### 9

This Arius was a certain Alexandrian presbyter who falsely asserted different substances within the Trinity and, with shameless falsehood, maintained that Christ was not true God and did not abide essentially in the Father. But because this wretched man was so foolish, and was both a liar and treacherous in his assertion, denying that Christ was true God, therefore, by God’s just judgment, his body burst open at the middle; all his entrails poured out; he fell prostrate on his face; and with the filthy mouth by which he had denied Christ he received from that same God and man, even in this world, a punishment worthy of his impiety. He preceded many of his followers—those corrupted and yet to be corrupted by his criminal error—into the tartarean fire, where he will be tortured eternally.

When the emptiness of this crime persecuted the faithful throughout the whole world with exiles in every land; after the overthrow of the assemblies and the expulsion of his Athanasius; after the mournful lamentations of Italy, when Eusebius, the bishop of Vercelli, had been driven out; after the ruinous disasters of Gaul, when Hilary had been proscribed,

[Note: [Col. 0027D] These champions are commemorated as follows: Athanasius on 2 May, Eusebius on 1 August, and Hilary on 13 January.]

Leovigild, king of the Spains, seduced by the error of this heresy together with almost all the nobles of his kingdom, fell into such madness that, by persecuting the most distinguished bishops of the Churches, learned in the law of God, from the borders of Spain, he drove them into exile. By striking many of them down with the sword, thrusting them into prison, torturing them with hunger, and afflicting them with various kinds of punishment, through his savage madness he consecrated worthy martyrs to God not only in the regions of Spain but also in Gaul and other lands.

And because he was vigorous in arms, he impiously oppressed many peoples subjected to his rule; out of hatred for the faith he persecuted Catholics; he violated the privileges of the Churches; blinded by greed, he condemned the wealthy; and he proved destructive in everything.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Concerning King Leovigild, or Leuvigild, consult the *Acts of Saint Hermenegild*, his son, who, by his command, earned the crown of martyrdom on 13 April.]

Among all the evils he committed, he banished the most holy Masona, bishop of Mérida, into exile.

[Note: [Col. 0028D] Paulus Diaconus of Mérida gives an extensive account, in his book *On the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida*, of the deeds of Saint Masona, who is entered in Tamayo’s *Spanish Martyrology* under the Kalends of November.]

He also expelled from the kingdom of Spain the illustrious doctor and archbishop of Seville, Leander, who was indefatigably devoted to the conversion of the Gothic people, with special zeal against their wicked heresies. After inflicting many injuries upon him, so that the sheep, deprived of their shepherd and surrounded by seducers, might more easily be shut in by the jaws of wolves, Leovigild subjected himself and his princes miserably to the Arian heresy, and, threatening the Roman pontiff, confirmed by an oath that he would come for the destruction of the city of Rome and the demolition of the Church.

### 10

The venerable youth Isidore, learned in all the disciplines of knowledge, kindled by the fervor of martyrdom, ready to die for the defense of the Church, fortified with the weapons of faith, advanced without fear, by Christ’s grace accompanying him, as a most powerful champion against the raging fury of King Leovigild and his princes.

The ministers of the many-formed seducer therefore tried by every means available to turn him from his holy purpose: sometimes soothing him with flatteries, sometimes driving him back with threats, sometimes provoking him with debates, sometimes offering gifts, sometimes imposing tortures. They believed that a great addition would be made to the heap of their doctrines if, after overcoming Isidore—who shone equally in brilliance of knowledge, nobility of birth, beauty of body, gravity of character, and sweetness of eloquence—they could bend him to their assent.

Come, most courageous champion Isidore: behold now the acceptable time. In these days, then, bring forth into the midst the incomparable treasure which, as we have heard, you gathered in childhood, to be opened not for you alone but also for the faithful. It is time to speak and to scatter the stones of divine sayings, so that the foreheads of the obstinate enemies may be crushed and the faith of the Catholic Church strengthened.

For behold, Peter’s little ship is driven on every side amid waves that shake it; the Church of Christ is sinking unless the hand of divine assistance leads it safely into the harbor of its desired shore.

In the midst of these things the most robust champion Isidore rejoiced in his tortures and gave thanks to God, because he was considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of the Lord Jesus. Amid the Arian crowds barking all around him, he was frightened neither by threats nor softened by flatteries. Rather, kindled more and more by the fervor of charity, secure among the swords of the heretics, he fearlessly hurled forth fiery bolts of the divine oracle, issuing both from the thunder of divine sayings and from the lightning of philosophical propositions; by these he darkened the sight of his raging enemies.

As though he were one of the four rivers of paradise, rivers of grace poured forth forcefully from his mouth. By watering the dry ground of the faithful, he brought it to the greenness of faith; and he submerged the perfidy of the heretics, which trusted in the audacity of babbling and loquacity, beneath the waves of eloquence.

The wretched men grow dull and fall silent; they rage and are confounded. While they think they are overcoming the young man, they are shamefully overcome by him; and they grieve each day that the faith of Christ, which they think they are completely uprooting, is flourishing through the young man’s efforts with heavenly growth.

## CHAPTER THREE. Orthodox faith propagated through Saint Isidore.—His cell.—His life in seclusion
11. When the revered doctor Leander heard of the steadfastness of the most courageous young man Isidore [Col. 0028D], he rejoiced in the Lord and prayed to the Lord in continual supplication that he might strengthen with heavenly power what He had wondrously begun in the tender youth of His servant, and might graciously grant His Church the triumph it desired, once its heretical enemies had been overthrown. Accordingly, he sent him a letter in which he warned him that death was not at all to be feared for the Catholic faith.

The blessed young man, strengthened both by the prayers of his superior and brother and by his exhortations and the assistance of his letters [Col. 0029A], was neither broken by adversity nor elated by prosperity; rather, in all these circumstances he appeared joyful and cheerful, as though delighting in a banquet. Having defeated the madness of the Arians, he demonstrated with the clearest evidence from the authority of the holy Scriptures, from the reasoning of the seven liberal arts, and also from philosophical arguments, that the one true God, the Son, eternally remains with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of essence. He urged the faithful peoples to obey the Roman pontiff, appointed by the faithful in the place of blessed Peter, and all the prelates of the Churches sent by that same heavenly founder, confirming his teaching by testimonies from the divine Scriptures.

He also discharged the duties of his superior and brother Leander, lightened his burdens, and adhered so closely to his steadfastness [Col. 0029B] that, scorning the prison, threats, tortures, and sword of his persecutors, he fearlessly approached the presence of the most serene prince Reccared, son of the most impious king Leovigild. By continually offering him cups of the word of God, he recalled him from the Arian heresy and rendered him obedient to the teachings of the Catholic faith.

He strove not only to overcome the arrogance of the fearful king Leovigild, who had enslaved himself to every vice and stopped his ears with the thorns of diabolical error lest he hear what was good; he also provoked against him, by sharpening the sword of the Spirit, the leading men of the entire kingdom, so that, through their persistent perfidy, the most impious father and tyrannical parricide rose up to kill his son, the most devout and serene prince Hermenegild, who had been bound in chains for the Catholic faith and was Isidore’s closest friend—for blessed Leander had rescued him from the filth of the Arian party and confirmed him in the Catholic faith [Col. 0029C]. At the funeral of the most glorious king and martyr, celebrated by angelic ministry, Leovigild acknowledged his manifest crime of treachery by the example of the betrayer Judas—not repentant, but driven by repentance.

For when he came to Toledo, heavenly judgment compelled him: struck by a most atrocious illness, amid torments and groans he miserably vomited out his soul together with his very entrails [Note: [Col. 0029D] Nicolaus Antonius notes that, concerning the death of Leovigild, one should consult Ambrosius Morales, book XI, chapter 11, and the material collected by Bivarius in the *Chronicon* of Maximus under the year of Christ 587. We have touched on some points in the Life of Saint Hermenegild, 13 April.]—as we believe, to be eternally tormented by the most terrible flames and worms. His seducer, the utterly wicked Arius, had gone before him.

12. After King Leovigild’s death, it came about that Spain joyfully welcomed her triumphant Leander as he returned from Carthage; and when the Catholic Reccared, brother of King and martyr Hermenegild, had been installed in the kingdom, Isidore’s courageous victory was restored, with peace announced to the Church amid the rejoicing of the faithful. The Arian perfidy was expelled from the boundaries of the entire kingdom, with the disgrace it deserved [Col. 0029D–0030A].

The exiled governors were recalled, churches were adorned, and the most devout faithful rejoiced with the fathers. The clemency of almighty God was magnificently praised, for He had strengthened Isidore with such steadfastness of virtue.

Blessed Leander devoted himself most earnestly, through works of charity and the word of preaching, to the Christian king Reccared—who had placed that same Leander over him in his father’s place—to the Gothic peoples, toward whom he had always maintained a fatherly affection, and to the people of Seville, whose concerns he watched over with particular care. He did so with the greatest zeal, solicitude, and unfeigned charity. He urged them to believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God: three according to the distinction of persons, but one according to the divine majesty. When they had come to believe, he first established for them precepts and ecclesiastical offices [Col. 0030B].

[Note: [Col. 0029D] He seems to acknowledge Leander as the first author of the ecclesiastical office later used by the Goths, although it is commonly attributed to Isidore. According to Mariana, book VI, chapter 5, it was decreed at the Fourth Council of Toledo: “Let there be one Missal and one Breviary in Spain.” The task of completing this work is believed to have been entrusted to Isidore, who played the leading role in that council. Usage established that the Mozarabic Missal and Breviary—that is, the rites of sacred prayers and of the daily and nightly offices preserved from the ancient custom of the Goths—should be attributed to Isidore, although Leander devised some elements and later generations added more.]

At that same time the Suebi, already washed in the waters of baptism, occupied Galicia [Note: [Col. 0030D] We discussed, under 20 March, the deeds of Saint Martin of Dumio, archbishop of Braga, and showed, on the authority of Gregory of Tours and Saint Isidore, that the Suebi living in Galicia were converted to the orthodox faith together with their king Theodemir. Elsewhere we do not read whether Saint Leander contributed anything to this. He may nevertheless have done so, since, after the Suebean kingdom was destroyed under Leovigild and transferred to the Goths, it continued under the Catholic King Reccared.].

Seeing, therefore, the admirable steadfastness of Isidore shining forth with such great increases of virtue, Leander—whether prompted by some foreknowledge, lest Isidore, once released from him, should go to foreign regions for the sake of preaching or for some other reason; or because, as we believe, Isidore had consecrated himself to the Lord as a virgin in mind and body from infancy, lest amid crowds he be stained even by a slight association with a woman; or lest he, who had proved most courageous in the time of persecution, should, once placed in tranquillity, be broken by the vanity of being lifted up by the light breeze of human favor—confined the young man of excellent character in a cell, said to have been built by Isidore himself.

Both the most devout King Reccared and many prelates of the Churches [Col. 0030C] bore this with distress and endured it with troubled hearts; for they considered it wrong to oppose the wishes of so great a father. The clergy murmured in whispers, and the people protested with loud cries. They complained that the most brilliant lamp, Isidore, ought not to be placed under the measure of a cell, or even of a single city, since by the splendor of his learning and the radiance of his good works he was sufficient to illuminate the whole world. They cried out in plaintive voices that he, who had been tested like gold in a furnace by the blows of punishment inflicted by the impious, ought not to be shut up in a cell but brought forth as a light to many nations.

13. But the revered Father Leander, pressed down by the weight of his gravity, yielded neither to the devout King Reccared, nor to the prelates of the Churches, nor to the princes of the kingdom, nor to the murmuring of the clergy, nor to the voices of the people [Col. 0030D]. For, having himself been anticipated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he knew what he was doing.

In the end, he provided Isidore with highly learned teachers, from whom he could learn by listening and with whom he could also learn through disputation, consultation, objection and response, and questioning; thus, if he had learned anything imperfectly, he could acquire it by correction. A remarkable thing! All those who confidently expected to teach him from their own learning were themselves wonderfully taught by him, and rejoiced all the more abundantly in the increase of their knowledge.

The venerable King Reccared continually sat beside the blessed man’s cell.
