From the nourishing Isidore, through whom the fountains of the Savior flowed forth, he imbibed through the window the faith of the holy Trinity, with devout ears; and, not forgetful of what he had heard, wishing to return a doubled talent to the Son of God, he faithfully poured out upon the peoples subject to him the cups of eternal life that he had received.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] What follows has been transcribed from Isidore’s *Chronicle*.]

He was endowed with religious devotion and was very unlike his father in character: the former was irreligious and exceedingly ready for war; the latter was devout in faith and distinguished by peace [Col. 0031B]. The former expanded the dominion of his people by the arts of war; the latter gloriously exalted that same people by the trophy of faith.

At the very beginning of his reign he embraced the Catholic faith and, cleansing the peoples of the whole nation from the stain of their long-standing error, recalled them to the worship of the true faith. Then he summoned a synod [Note: [Col. 0031D] The Third Council of Toledo was held in the Spanish era 627, in the fourth year of Reccared, that is, in the year of Christ 589.] of all the bishops from the various provinces of Spain and Gaul for the condemnation of the Arian heresy. That most religious prince himself attended the council and confirmed its proceedings by his presence and signature.

Adorned with virtues, he raised to honors all whom he knew to be dear to God; but those whom he found superstitious he rebuked before everyone, so that the others might learn fear. Following not his perfidious father but Christ the Lord, he loathed and detested the Arian madness and disgracefully expelled it from his entire kingdom [Col. 0031C].

He possessed such grace in his face and carried such kindness in his heart that, flowing into everyone’s mind, he drew even the wicked toward affection for him. He was so generous that he restored by their rightful title the privileges and estates of the Churches that his father had attached to the treasury. He was so merciful that he often relaxed the people’s taxes by generous acts of clemency, storing his wealth among the miserable and his treasures among the needy, knowing that the kingdom had been bestowed on him for this purpose: that he might use it beneficially.

This has been said to the praise of our God and of His confessors Leander and Isidore, who deserved to receive such a disciple from the Lord.

## CHAPTER IV. The death of Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, and his written works.—The succession of Saint Isidore.

[Col. 0031D] 14. When the enemy of the human race saw that he and his followers were persecuting the holy confessors through King Reccared, whom he had formerly held subject to himself, he stirred up against King Reccared two men illustrious for wealth and noble by birth but profane in mind and ignoble in character—namely Ganvistan and Vulgernus—together with an Arian bishop named Athalocus [Col. 0032A].

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Gregory of Tours, book IX of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 15, calls him Athalocus, a bishop of the Arian sect. When the flattery of a few people supported him in his attempt to obtain their agreement, he was inflamed with anger, entered his cell, bent his head over his little bed, and breathed out his evil spirit. Ganvislan and Vulgernus seem to have adhered to this bishop, although others do not mention them; and, stirred up by them, the Franks invaded the province of Narbonne, or Gothic Gaul.]

They gathered a multitude of Franks and, in revenge for the Arian madness, devastated the city of Narbonne and the surrounding regions, slaughtering an innumerable multitude of clergy, religious persons, and Catholics. They also tried to seize the kingdom from the most devout King Reccared.

Against them the most glorious Reccared sent Claudius, duke of Mérida, and won a glorious victory [Note: [Col. 0031D] John of Biclaro calls Claudius duke of Lusitania [Col. 0032D]; Isidore calls him Duke Claudius.]. For, after almost sixty thousand of the enemy had been struck down and thrown into confusion [Note: [Col. 0032D] Biclaro says: “He is known to have put nearly sixty thousand Franks to flight and to have slaughtered the greater part of them with the sword.” Isidore says that so many came, adding that no victory of the Goths in Spain had ever been greater or comparable to it.], he returned to Spain with great glory.

After this, when the storms had been removed from every side, the Lord graciously granted His people the peace they desired. While these things were taking place, and, with the Lord’s favor, much tranquility was being restored to the Catholic Church, and the calamity of the Arian heresy was being driven from almost every mind, the city of Seville rejoiced with the most holy confessors over such great tranquility and unceasingly rendered countless thanks to the Lord. At that time the venerable bishop Leander happened to fall ill, the Lord calling him.

When he recognized that the final day of his most blessed labor was soon to come, he brought his venerable brother Isidore out of his cell and asked that he be presented to him, both for consolation and blessing and so that he might commend himself to Isidore’s prayers. When this was reported to blessed Isidore, whose whole mind already clung to heaven and who preferred his little cell to all temporal riches, he sent them away from him, saying [Col. 0032C]:

“Know, brothers, that I shall not leave this cell at all so long as my brother remains alive in the body of this pilgrimage; for he himself has bound me to this purpose by a solemn oath.”

Blessed Leander, having continually fulfilled his pastoral duties, most happily fell asleep in the Lord after receiving the Lord’s body and blood.

I do not think that I should now omit the fact that this illustrious doctor Leander [Note: [Col. 0032D] This account, with a few additions and alterations here and there, has been transcribed from Isidore’s eulogy of Saint Leander in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. From it we have corrected some things improperly written here. We have used those corrections to elucidate the Life of Saint Leander.] was born of the same father, Severianus, as Isidore; that he was a monk by profession; and that, from being a most vigorous monk, he was appointed bishop of the Church of Seville, despite his own refusal, through the strenuous efforts of many people.

He was a man gracious in speech and outstanding in intelligence; in life and teaching alike he shone with the greatest excellence. Through his faith and industry, the people of the Spanish nation, by means of his blessed young brother Isidore—as has been written above—returned from Arian madness to the Catholic faith [Col. 0032D].

During his pilgrimage in exile he composed two books against the doctrines of heretics [Col. 0033A], exceedingly rich in learning from the holy Scriptures. In them he attacks and exposes Arian impiety with vigorous style, showing clearly what the Catholic Church possesses against them and how greatly it differs from them in religion and in the mysteries of faith.

There is also another praiseworthy little work of his, against the institutions of the Arians, in which he sets his responses against their stated propositions. In addition, he published for his sister Florentina a book on the instruction of virgins and contempt for the world, prefaced by divisions of its topics. He also labored with no little diligence over the ecclesiastical offices: throughout the entire Psalter he composed a prayer in a twofold edition; and for the sacrifices, praises, and psalms he composed many pieces in sweet-sounding verse.

He also wrote many letters to Pope Gregory, and one on blessedness. In them he requested from him the archiepiscopal pallium, a book on the exposition of blessed Job, and the book of the *Pastoral Rule*; and he very frequently begged him to intercede with the Lord on his behalf concerning the gout from which he suffered severely. He obtained all these things from blessed Pope Gregory, who loved him most tenderly.

As we mentioned earlier, he sent another letter to his brother Isidore, in which he warned him that no one should fear death. He also issued many personal letters to the other bishops; even if they were not especially splendid in wording, they were nevertheless sharp in thought.

He flourished under the Catholic King Reccared, serving in Spain as the representative of the Roman pontiff. In Reccared’s time he also brought his mortal life to an end [Col. 0033C], on the day before the Ides of March [Note: [Col. 0033D] Rather, on the third day before the Ides of March; we have given his Life under that date.].

15. When blessed Leander had been translated among the angels, the metropolitan city of Seville, deprived of so great a patron, poured out prayers to the Lord day and night, asking that, in His mercy toward His people, He provide them with a most faithful shepherd who would succeed blessed Leander not only in the dignity of the cathedral see but also in holiness of life.

The merciful Lord did not fail to answer their petition; He graciously granted what they requested. The bishops of the neighboring parishes, greatly grieving the death of so great a father [Note: [Col. 0033D] We have noted in chapter 1 that *parochia* is used for “diocese” in the *Lives of the Saints* and in Saint Jerome. The *Capitularies of Charlemagne* likewise prescribe that no bishop may perform ordinations in another’s parish [Col. 0034D].], gathered together with a convocation of the clergy and religious, so that, according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, they might provide for that Church by electing a suitable prelate.

The most serene King Reccared attended to confirm their election [Col. 0033D], together with the princes and noblemen of Spain. But the people of the city, unable to conceal what they had conceived in their hearts, forestalling the votes of their elders, proclaimed meanwhile that Isidore was worthy of the episcopate: in his youthful years he had acted manfully for the Catholic law and had endured innumerable punishments from the impious in defense of that same faith.

The king, the bishops, and the princes all had the same will, the same unanimity, and the same judgment. They declared that Isidore was most worthy of the episcopate, since by the example of good works and by the speech of holy preaching he would teach the whole of Spain [Col. 0034A]. Approaching blessed Isidore with humility and reverence, they made known to him the common will of all and urged him, for the salvation of all Spain, to assume the burden of the archiepiscopate.

But he, who avoided every lofty position no less than he would avoid a precipice, gave no assent whatsoever to their desire. Then the revered prince and the gracious bishops, seeing that their persuasion accomplished nothing, could endure no longer. Calling the citizens together in one spirit, they went to Isidore, prepared to use force.

The people then rushed together and, with an excited cry, broke open the cell of the blessed man. Although he resisted as much as he could, they led him to the Church amid shouts of rejoicing. From a distance the servant of God cried out, wishing to put forward an excuse; but in vain, since the voices of the rejoicing people prevailed over his ears [Col. 0034B].

16. The herald of Christ, realizing that he could resist in no way, yielded under compulsion. He was elected bishop of Seville with magnificent veneration: wholly distinguished, wholly marked out, wholly renowned, wholly beautiful, wholly lovable, wholly desirable.

He was distinguished by ancestry, uprightness, honor, and majesty; marked by nature, dignity, grace, and discipline; renowned for learning, eloquence, rewards, and praise; beautiful in bearing, appearance, judgment, and conduct; lovable in service, conversation, counsel, and protection; desirable in appearance, desirable in goodness, innocence, and justice; desirable in perfect charity.

Such a man was chosen, such a man was selected, such a man was compelled, drawn, and adopted; such a man was invested with the episcopal insignia [Col. 0034C].

Messengers were also sent to the most glorious Gregory, pope of the venerable city of Rome, asking him, once the election had been confirmed, to send Isidore—his very dear friend—the archiepiscopal pallium from the blessing of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Saint Pope Gregory greatly rejoiced at the election of his beloved Isidore, gave thanks to God, and, having received the messengers honorably, confirmed the election. He sent the pallium together with the requested items and also granted him the honor of exercising primatial authority in Spain [Note: [Col. 0034D] The readings are found in the Spanish Breviaries and in the Breviary of Cardinal Quignonius; Gregory sent him the pallium in Spain.].

Once adorned with the episcopal insignia, let a pontiff assert how great he lived and was, how greatly he advanced, and how much he accomplished; let a prelate affirm it, a bishop prove it, and an overseer testify to it. Let virtue declare the pontiff, knowledge reveal the prelate, doctrine acknowledge the overseer, and conduct speak of the bishop [Col. 0034D].

For he was always prudent, always steadfast, always temperate, always just. He was prudent in discerning, prudent in choosing, prudent in loving, prudent in adhering; steadfast in enduring, steadfast in resisting, steadfast in striking, steadfast in pursuing; temperate in desiring, temperate in investigating, temperate in using, temperate in sparing; just in meditating, just in speaking, just in acting, just in persevering.

He was upright everywhere, devout everywhere, useful everywhere, experienced everywhere; ready to begin, ready to obey, ready to act, ready to persist [Col. 0035A]; devout in meditation, devout in speaking, devout in prayer, devout in petition, devout in obedience, devout in obtaining; useful in persuading, in dissuading, in administering, and useful in making restitution; experienced in uprooting and building, experienced in planting.

He always kept before his eyes the sufferings of the Son of God and was not lifted up by empty glory. For, presenting himself as the servant of all, desiring to be loved rather than feared, and preferring to be useful rather than to rule, he showed himself lovable and kind to everyone. He devoted himself to fasts, prayers, and meditation on the holy Scriptures; he took little food, and that from the cheapest fare, not for indulgence but from necessity. He was called sparing toward himself and generous toward others [Col. 0035B]; he maintained the same gravity of character and pursued the same humility as before.

He remained with the utmost steadfastness the same man he had previously been. As his dignity increased, the gifts of the Holy Spirit increased in him. Thus, full of authority and grace, the praise of his holiness was everywhere proclaimed; and the lamp, kindled with unfailing light, was no longer placed under a measure but set upon a lampstand. Its light was carried everywhere in the praises of all, so that even the most brilliant lamps of many teachers, shining with their own splendid light, were kindled more and more from good to better by the gathered fire of the Holy Spirit and became more radiant.

Although he declared himself indebted to all, he possessed, besides the other gifts by which he shone, something that seemed especially his own: namely, to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep [Col. 0035C]. He took upon himself, through devout compassion, the sufferings of the miserable and felt them more deeply than they did; and, out of zeal for piety, relieved them by lavish alms.

He had such abundant means of giving and such continual cheerfulness in distributing them that, to the astonishment of many, no one—not even his own household—could discover where such generosity of revenues came from. How generous he was throughout his whole life is known to God alone.

He had learned the most serene habit of rejoicing more in giving than in receiving. Sparing toward himself and, in a certain sense, frugal, he overflowed toward everyone else and enriched all by his munificence. In prosperity and adversity his face was always the same; preceded by clear cheerfulness, he came to everyone more joyful than they.

Hostile pride did not claim him as its own amid all his virtues [Col. 0035D]. Rather, displaying gentle humility in everything, he was most dear to the powerful and the poor alike. Even when elevated to the highest summit of the apostolate, he had been called not to a chair but to care; not to honor but to burden; not to rule but to serve; not to empty the purses of his subjects but to uproot crimes; not to rest but to labor; not to seek dishes or cups of varied flavors but to demonstrate and commend the divine commandments to the people, and to administer temporal support carefully to the poor of Christ [Col. 0036A]. He showed by his works no less than by his words that he had been called to the dignity of a bishop.

## CHAPTER V. His care for the formation of clergy, monks, and laity.—The journey to Rome.—Rain obtained by prayer.—A dead person restored to life.

17. He was so solicitous for the clergy and students that, because of his intense vigilance over each one, they recognized him as a father. He considered it too little merely to provide for the neighboring clerics and students; he also summoned people from everywhere, so that he might have more persons to whom he could impart his benefits, whom he could teach personally from the pages of the holy Scriptures, and whom he could provide with temporal sustenance.

Clergy therefore flocked to him, eager not only to hear such a great father but thirsting to hear him [Col. 0036B]. He received them most kindly with paternal affection and urged them not to depart from him before they had been instructed in the law of God and had become known as people who would benefit themselves and the Catholic Church.

To remove from them every occasion for idleness, he built outside the city of Seville a monastery of extraordinary beauty. No student was permitted to leave it before four years had passed. Some of them who appeared wealthier and refused to remain in service—although, as the Spirit of truth revealed, he foresaw that they would become powerful in work and speech in the Church of God—he bound in iron fetters, lest, once they had found an opportunity, they should recall their minds from study by meditating on vain matters while wandering about.

From their community shone forth, like Lucifer, the most holy Ildefonsus, and also the glorious Braulius, bishop of Caesaraugusta [Col. 0036C].

[Note: [Col. 0035] Saint Ildefonsus is celebrated on 23 January and Saint Braulius, or Braulio, on 18 March. These matters are treated more fully in their Lives.]

Since he could not always continue teaching them in person, as he wished, because many duties arose, wherever he observed teachers diligent in the law of God and equipped for the battles of spiritual combat, he humbly honored them greatly and begged them to continue their effective work in teaching the students, mindful of the labor he desired.

For he did not think that the wicked heresies could be uprooted entirely from the Lord’s vineyard unless the clergy and all religious persons, by the reputation of their holiness and the persistence of their preaching, applied themselves to the peoples. The source and occasion of every evil and heresy had been the moral failures of the clergy and religious and their sluggish contempt for knowledge of the Scriptures.

He also watched over religious persons—monks, hermits, and those who, according to the rules of the fathers, had renounced the world—with the utmost care [Col. 0036D]. He ensured that none of them was overwhelmed by poverty or, compelled by necessity to seek things in various places, perished from hunger for the word of God; that the stones of the sanctuary were not scattered; that the finest color of gold, namely the purpose of holy men, was not changed; that, through wandering, they did not forget holy conduct; that, enticed and drawn away by desires, they did not become entangled in worldly concerns; and that, having loosened the straps of their rule, they did not submit themselves to the service of the devil.

Like a mother who loves her only son, he was joined to them all in charity and opened to each one the breast of his goodwill [Col. 0037A]. Like a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings, he protected them from the face of evil people, so that, driven by hostile attacks or oppressed by the hardships of poverty, they would not be afflicted outside what the rule required after their paternal protection had been removed.

Like an eagle urging its young to fly, he encouraged them toward heavenly desires with devout admonitions. He himself first clung to heavenly works, flying above them, and followed the example of that most holy apostle Paul, lest he should preach to others without the performance of works and, being judged by the Gospel as one who says but does not act, be found reprobate.

What brother of the holy congregations, pressed by distress of mind or body, became ill without him hastening to provide remedies for health? Who, scandalized by the temptations of the enemy, burned without him pouring down upon him, with pastoral zeal, the water of holy preaching [Col. 0037B]?

He bore the burdens of his subjects, considering it fitting that he alone should be troubled by worldly cares, so that, once disturbance had been removed from the holy men, they might have food and clothing and devote themselves solely to pleasing God. He believed that, through their intercessions, he would obtain whatever he lacked.

Although, for the sake of his own salvation and that of others, he avoided the presence of women as far as he could, he nevertheless revered with extraordinary affection any nuns or religious women whom he saw persevering in the praises of God. He made provision for them through continual gifts, so that they would not lack temporal or spiritual resources.

Throughout the regions of Spain, therefore, he built many large and beautiful monasteries, in which he gathered companies of religious men and women for the praise and glory of the divine name [Col. 0037C]. He also gave them the rule that he himself had composed according to the institutions of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0037D] Saint Isidore’s Rule is extant among his works and separately in part II of the *Codex of Rules* edited by Luca Holstenius. It is cited by Benedict of Aniane, abbot, in the *Concordia of Rules*, and by the monk Smaragdus in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict.]. He adapted it most suitably to the variety of places and the strength of God’s servants, teaching each person to remain in the rank and grace to which he had been called, and, in the occupation he had held in the world—provided it was honorable—to serve humbly in the monastery as well, according to the command of his superior, if necessity required it.

18. Not content with benefiting one province alone—for he believed himself born for the usefulness of all the faithful—he went out through cities and regions. Sounding the sacred trumpets of the New and Old Testament, he stirred the elect to heavenly desires; or, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, he exhorted them to spiritual battles.

Everywhere the trumpet of the Gospel resounded; everywhere Christ was announced; everywhere the praises of the holy Trinity echoed; and no one was hidden from its heat, because the sound of the confessor had gone out into all the earth.

Those whom the presence of his body could not enlighten, he strengthened by sending letters and messengers. Whatever was unbecoming, disordered, deformed, and especially contrary to the law of God he encountered, his eye did not spare. Anxious lest it increase by growing, he strove to destroy and uproot it from the Christian people as quickly as possible by resisting it at its beginnings.

He also established in all the churches of Spain the apostolic decrees, the decisions of the holy Fathers, and especially the institutions of the holy Roman Church. Already a vigorous legislator, he handed down heavenly and human ordinances. He gave laws suited to modesty and uprightness, presenting himself as a consuming fire for burning up the forests of crimes and as the coldest water for cooling the heat of temptations.

In short, what city, what solitude, what *marka*—that is, what borderland [Note: [Col. 0037D] *Marka*, or *marcha*, is commonly understood in the Acts of the Saints as the boundary of a province or an entire border province. Consult what is said on 6 February concerning the metrical Life of Saint Amandus by Milo, chapter 2, letter 6.]—did not experience the benefits of this teacher?

Thus traveling through all the provinces of Spain, the servant of God refreshed the minds of the faithful with the nourishment of the word of God, restored the poor of Christ through almsgiving, and diligently pursued the doctrines of the heretics. He reached the illustrious city of Rome, at the humble request of the supreme pontiff.

It is beyond the capacity of our own powers to describe with what honor and reverence he was received by the Roman bishop and the cardinals; but the reader can easily infer it from the services and loving obedience they showed him. For, while the burden of the whole Church had been placed upon him, they all offered themselves kindly to him as to a devout father—without compromising apostolic dignity—so that, if he wished, men most noble by birth, renowned in character, and eminent in dignity might perform the duties of servants and minister with whatever humility they could.

Those most prudent men considered it fitting that, because Isidore had exposed himself to death for the Catholic faith and the honor of the Roman Church, scorning the tortures of princes, and had proved the Roman Church to be the mother of all Churches by many scriptural testimonies [Col. 0038C], he should be honored by those same Romans with honor worthy of him.

It was also agreed that the prelates of the Churches should assemble in a holy synod [Note: [Col. 0037D] Labbæus states in his *Synopsis of Councils* that two councils were held at Rome in the year 601. He published the one established for monks; the other was directed against Andrew the Greek, an impostor in monastic dress. Why should there not have been some similar synod in the presence of Saint Isidore? It is mentioned in the Spanish breviaries. We do not think, however, that it was a public or solemn council, in agreement with Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 21; Mariana, book VI, chapter 7; Padilla, century VII, chapter 22; and others.], so that, if anything unbecoming or doubtful were found, it might be corrected together with that most holy Isidore.

They would have kept him in the Roman curia with the greatest desire, for its adornment, had they not recognized—at his own indication—that this would result in harm to the Church. Once the synod had been dismissed, he arranged in the Roman curia whatever he wished, and, after sending away all those who were affected with grief, he returned to Spain with the greatest honor and with apostolic gifts.

They had indeed discovered that, among his other virtues, he shone with the spirit of prophecy, and that he spoke so much about future events as though they had already occurred historically; he seemed to evangelize rather than to predict.

When he returned, great joy and celebration took place in the Church of Spain.

19. When the holy doctor was approaching the borders of Gaul, the Lord wondrously magnified His dealings with His saint. For when the provinces of Gaul and Spain were suffering from excessive dryness of the air, and crops, trees, and grasses were withering from lack of rain, while people themselves endured severe bodily distress because of this unseasonable weather, they heard of the holy bishop’s arrival. Joyful and eager, trusting in the Lord’s customary mercy—He who was always working remarkable things through His servant—they came out from each city to meet him with crosses and lamps, asking that he deign to pour out prayers to the Lord on their behalf.

The people of Narbonne, as he drew near, cried out, saying:

“O pious Isidore, doctor of Spain, rescue us from the impending dangers by your holy prayers poured out to the Lord. You have come, long desired; through you, may the Lord everywhere grant His customary benefits.”

But the most blessed doctor, being ready to show compassion, ordered silence and set before the hungry peoples the food of God’s word. He admonished them to invoke the Lord’s mercy together with him and, with faith in the Holy Trinity preceding all else and every hesitation set aside, to ask for the benefits of God’s children.

Then the holy man, raising his hands to heaven, prayed that, for the glory of His holy name, the Lord would deign to grant the people the remission of their sins, bodily health, temperate weather, an abundance of rain, and the desired plenty of fruits.

O wondrous power of the prayers of the saints! For although the sky was excessively clear and everything was parched by the heat of the sun, after sudden thunderclaps and flashes of lightning struck close by, such an inundation of water followed that no one had seen a rain comparable to it in former times. But the blessed confessor, shaken on every side by the blows of the lightning, seemed wholly to be on fire. Everyone else, terrified by fear of death, abandoned the saint and fled to the churches.

Those who had arrived sick, carried on the shoulders of bearers and seeking the help of the blessed father, now forgot their own weakness and, fleeing, outstripped all the others with good reason: through the intercession of blessed Isidore, all had been restored to their former health.

The others, perceiving that God had wrought a miracle in the healing of the sick, took courage and wished to approach the saint; but no one dared proceed beyond the doors, since both the lightning and the flood of rain prevented them. Thus the herald of Christ waited until the rains ceased. Then the whole multitude hurried to him, praising the wonders of our Savior in His saint.

The blessed bishop gently exhorted them, saying:

“Behold, brothers, how much the undefiled faith of the most holy Trinity accomplishes. In the name of the undivided Trinity you asked to be rescued from three or more dangers, and three benefits—and even more—have been conferred upon you by the Lord: namely, bodily health, temperate weather, and an overflowing abundance of crops and fruits. Moreover, if you preserve your faith unstained, you will obtain what is holier and more precious to embrace: the forgiveness of sins and the prize of eternal reward.

“Now therefore, strengthen your hearts in the love of Christ the Son of God, and do not in any way allow yourselves to be deceived by the seducers who have traversed sea and land to make one proselyte, destined to be horribly consumed by eternal flames. They are wolves, exceedingly voracious in their ill-omened greed; they come only to slaughter and destroy. They disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting, and thereby find an easier entrance for deceiving them.”

After delivering this and similar exhortations, the saint went to his lodging to refresh his weary limbs.

[Col. 0040B] Meanwhile, as the people throughout the lanes and streets joined in praising the mighty deeds of our God, they cursed and detested those who denied that the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, was true God—even merely in thought—and that He remained eternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] Some material followed concerning the preaching of Muhammad in Spain and how, warned by the devil of the arrival of Saint Isidore, he was said to have withdrawn to Africa. Nicholas Antonius considers these matters false and spurious. Tamayo discusses them, loudly proclaiming, together with Morales, Padilla, Mariana, and others, an opinion constructed without even a trace of truth. We therefore remove them from this Life, especially since a summary of what is reported here may be read in Lucas of Tuy, *Chronicle*, book III, under King Sisebut and the era 674; likewise in Maximus, *Chronicle*, under the year 606; in Luitprand, under the year 607; and in similar authors recently contrived, as though Spain thereby gained some glory. Nevertheless, why should it be impossible that some sower of Muhammad’s depravity crossed from Africa into Spain in Isidore’s time and, being promptly detected, was forced to seek safety by flight?]

20. When the gracious doctor had drawn near the city of Seville, a multitude of people of both sexes—clergy, students, monks, and laypeople—came out to meet him. They welcomed him with great joy, in hymns and praises, with cries of jubilation and rejoicing.

As everyone pressed forward to touch the fringes of the holy Father’s garments, a pregnant woman was suffocated by the crushing of the crowd and breathed out her spirit. When the Saint saw this, being rich in the bowels of mercy, he wept profusely, silently pouring forth words of prayer to the Lord.

After a short while the woman rose and said in a loud voice:

“Blessed are you, holy father Isidore, and blessed is the word of your mouth! For through your sacred prayers, I and the child whom I carry in my womb have not only been restored to the present life but have also been rescued from the hand of the enemy.”

The people turned to the woman and asked how this had happened to her. She replied:

“As my soul and that of my son, who is in the womb, were departing from the body, a host of demons appeared. They were preparing to drag us by fiery bonds to the places of punishment. But while our glorious father was praying for us, a voice was heard saying: ‘Let the souls of these people return to their bodies, for God’s friend Isidore is praying for them.’ When this was heard, one of the holy angels who are always with the most blessed doctor Isidore restored us to our bodies.”

Then the whole people raised their voices to heaven, sounding praises more loudly to the Most High, and led him into the city.

Through him the Lord bestowed such peace upon the Church and struck all the children of superstition with such terror that, after every heretical depravity had been utterly uprooted from Spain, no one could be found who wished or dared even to name heresy.

And lest the most holy man leave any work of mercy unattempted, whenever a girl from the secular world, driven by poverty, was compelled to lead a dishonorable life, the minister of God intervened with the utmost speed, cutting short her wretched plans and giving her either in marriage or to a monastery, according to her choice.

Whenever he found a layman willing to live according to the law of the Lord, he revered him with extraordinary affection and amicably recorded him among his secretaries.

He freed almost countless people worn down by the squalor of prison or held captive, giving generous gifts; and those entangled in another’s debt he released by paying money to their creditors, making both parties rejoice.

He also took the greatest care to restore peace among those who were at odds. At one time building churches, at another restoring monasteries, and at another repairing bridges, he remained diligently occupied as a worker of truth, often setting before his people the saying of Solomon: “Idleness has taught many evils.”

Kings and princes were bound to him by such affection, because of the apostolic authority he exercised, that they humbly venerated him as their most holy father and carried out whatever he commanded them with the greatest devotion.

Thus one could see monastic obedience flourishing among princes. Whoever had incurred the displeasure of a king or some other prince, and could not be reconciled to him through other means, approached Isidore confidently as a final refuge.

Whoever came to him as a sorrowful or troubled sinner, or pierced by despair, and did not immediately depart strengthened by the words of grace flowing from his honey-sweet mouth, encouraged by hope of pardon and favor, joyful and cheerful, made righteous through heartfelt contrition, giving thanks and filled with blessings?

All who approached him, whatever their profession, through the constancy of seeing him, the practice of conversing with him, and the example of his good works, ceased to pursue temporal ambitions. Enkindled by the light of truth, they burned with desire for eternal light.

But if all the limbs of the human body were turned into tongues, they would not dare proclaim how great he was in virtue and how brilliantly he shone with the signs of miracles.

Moreover, foreseeing the usefulness of future generations, he produced almost countless books distinguished by their maxims and words. It would take too long to enumerate them, but the blessed Braulius, bishop of Zaragoza, lists some of them.

After he had published an alphabet of *papiae judicum* [reading uncertain; Note: [Col. 0041D] “Of the homeland?” Nicholas Antonius notes that this error cannot be corrected, since no one mentions the indicated alphabet.], an alphabet of verbal matters, an alphabet of theological distinctions, and an alphabet of books, he brought his discourse to an end by writing an *Alphabet of Prayer*, lamenting the future errors and downfall of the Gothic nation. In this work he daily sang psalms to the Lord, and we have thought it proper to note it here.

It is exceedingly useful not only to bishops and ecclesiastical persons but also to all who return to God through repentance.

[Col. 0042B] He also issued many letters on numerous questions. Although we have not thought it appropriate to record them in full, we have noted portions of them, so that the Saint’s virtue and power may become known to the world through them and Christ’s faithful may be instructed.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Synod of Seville. A Heretic Converted, a Blind Man Given Sight.—Letters to Various Persons

[Col. 0042C] 27. Let this suffice for the present concerning the almost innumerable matters relating to him. For if we wished to touch in writing upon everything that comes to mind about him, time would abandon us more readily than material would fail.

He exercised himself throughout his life in these holy works, and the fame of his knowledge and virtues filled nearly every region. Many noble and highly learned people, desiring to see the sought-after Isidore and to hear another Solomon’s wisdom, came from the ends of the earth.

Some came to receive salutary instruction from him; others to see him perform wonders in the name of the Lord. The sick came to be healed of their ailments, because the power of God went forth from him and healed all. Others, however, approached as misguided challengers, relying on themselves, to see whether they might perhaps catch him in his speech.

During the time of their wicked rivalry, when the bishops were coming together at Seville for the synod, Gregory arrived [Note: [Col. 0042D] Gregory was a Syrian by nationality and himself a bishop; the history of his faction appears in canon 12 of the said synod.], contrary to the meaning of his name [Note: [Col. 0042D] In Greek, *Gregory* means “watchful” or “vigilant”], a bishop of the Acephali heresy, talkative in speech and eloquent in language, exceedingly ready with paralogical syllogisms and extremely sharp in disputation.

Like a most turbulent river, he tore many of the faithful who resisted him—people who seemed elect—from the garden of the holy Church and dragged them infallibly with him to destruction and death.

For he denied that Christ possessed two substances and asserted that He was not the true God existing from God the Father before the ages, but merely a human being.

When he came to blessed Isidore, he asked that he be granted permission to undertake a contest of disputation with him before a public audience. He hoped that, even if he could not overcome Isidore, he could in no way be overcome by him. If matters turned out as the heretic had anticipated, this would lead to the ruin of many.

But the blessed confessor, foreseeing that the Lord was arranging this for the benefit of the Catholic Church, kindly assented to his requests and appointed a day.

He summoned the faithful, and judges were selected who, after hearing both sides, would pronounce a fitting judgment against the one who was defeated and in favor of the victor.

What more is there to say? The contest began. As testimonies from various Scriptures were brought forward against one another, the heretic yielded to the bishop, for he could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who was speaking.

Amazed, therefore, at the doctrine of the Lord, he did not wait for the judges to pronounce sentence but with his own mouth openly declared himself defeated.

28. As the people, together with the bishops and clergy, were praising God with devout dedication because the plunderer of Christians who had been seducing them day and night had been overthrown, a certain blind man stood nearby, complaining in an importunate voice:

“Alas,” he said, “gracious doctor Isidore, for a long time I have heard of your holiness; but now that I stand here, deprived of your goodness, I am not worthy to see you.”

Gregory noticed him and asked blessed Isidore, who appeared not to notice, to hand him the episcopal glove that he held in his hand.

When this had been granted, Gregory rose confidently in the sight of all. Touching the blind man’s eyes with it, he said in a clear voice:

“May the Lord Jesus Christ, who through blessed Isidore has enlightened the eyes of my heart, deign through his holy merits to enlighten the eyes of your body for the confirmation of the faith.”

When he had said this, blood burst from the blind man’s eyelids, and he recovered his sight. The people immediately cried out in a jubilation of praise.

The blessed bishop, scarcely having obtained silence, taught that Christ Jesus must be worshiped as true God and true man, and that in one and the same person there are two substances, namely divine and human: divine, because He remains eternally coeternal with God the Father; human, because He began to exist from the undefiled virgin mother in the present age.

## CHAPTER IX. The Synod Held at Toledo.—Excellent Preparation during Illness for a Blessed Death

32. Since the glorious doctor Isidore shone with various signs of miracles and the fame of his holiness spread through nearly the whole world, he foretold far in advance to his disciples the day of his death, through the spirit of prophecy by which he shone most brilliantly.

The students raised a cry; the monks’ mourning began; the nuns’ sobs broke forth; and the people’s joy was turned into grief.

The blessed confessor, however, maintaining the same concern for the flock of God’s Church that he had always possessed, ordered all the bishops, abbots, and princes of Spain to be summoned to the synod at Toledo. He earnestly desired that, before he departed from the body, he might leave the clerical order in fraternal concord and the lay order in perpetual peace.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] This is the fourth synod, held under King Sisenand, under whom Isidore himself also met his death, as Ildefonsus indicates. Yet none of the matters subsequently attributed to this synod—specifically, the explicit confession of faith in it—are found there except in different words. The author’s license in this matter is therefore not to be praised, since he preferred to speak in his own words rather than in those of the synod. So Nicholas Antonius; but what is stated more briefly in the Synod of Toledo is explained more fully in the Second Synod of Seville, canon 13.]

When the synod had assembled, he first exhorted them to remain steadfast in faith in the Holy Trinity, setting forth the following distinction concerning the unity of essence and the diversity of persons:

There is one God in essence and nature, indivisible and true, of whom Moses says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” The faithful must in no way divide Him, even in thought, lest they be turned about in the labyrinth of error. He is everywhere wholly and completely, whether by essence or by the presence of His majesty, which is the same thing: within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded; and yet not locally confined.

Although He is utterly simple according to the majesty of His divinity, He is nevertheless threefold according to the distinction of persons: the Father, unbegotten and always almighty; the only-begotten Son, eternally and inseparably born from the Father; and the Spirit of them both, eternally proceeding inseparably from the Father and the Son. Therefore they are one.

Moreover, in the one person of Christ we profess two births and two natures: one eternal, from the Father, according to which He remains equal to God the Father and is immortal and incapable of suffering; the other temporal, from His mother, with a soul assumed, according to which He deigned to suffer and die for us. Thus He is true God and true man in one person.

But if we do not grasp with the bosom of the mind what it means to beget, to be born, or to proceed, let us grasp it with the bosom of faith, and we shall be saved.

Abhorring all wicked heresies no less than his own downfall, he weakened and anathematized them, especially the abominable and detestable sect of Arius, as well as the wicked superstition of the Acephalites. By pursuing them with the swords of God’s word, he expelled them from all Spain and Gaul, with the zealous support of his brother and predecessor Leander, distinguished by holiness and learning; he confounded them and utterly deprived them of strength.

He also proved, by the clearest testimonies of the holy Scriptures, that all the faithful ought to obey the Roman pontiff, who has been placed in the position of blessed Peter the Apostle, since he is the head of God’s Church in matters pertaining to God. By solemnly bearing witness to this, he also forbade that the members should ever separate themselves from their head, pronouncing a curse upon those who dared to presume otherwise.

[Note: [Col. 0044D] The same writer observes that nothing concerning the Roman pontiff is set forth in the said Fourth Synod of Toledo.]

He established laws for kings and princes; handed down the Catholic rule of faith to the priests of Christ’s Church [Note: [Col. 0045D] Some of these matters are found in canons 39 and 40]; explained the duties and ranks of all orders; displayed the rights of sacred offices to the citizens; and impressed the discipline of the Christian religion upon all the household peoples of the faith.

Finally, when all these matters had been approved by everyone, another Moses and a lawgiver for our times continued in a prophetic voice, saying:

“When you remain in these traditions with a pure heart, you shall enjoy peace and good things in the present life, and in eternal glory you shall rejoice with everlasting praise. But when you abandon these precepts, dreadful evils shall seize you, and the Gothic people shall perish through hunger, the sword of enemies, and pestilence. But when you turn back to the Lord your God and seek these things, your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies, and your glory shall be greater than it has ever been.”

After this, having received the Saint’s blessing and bidding him farewell, all returned to their own homes.

33. The blessed Isidore, however, remaining at Toledo for several days, continued tirelessly in the word of holy preaching. Although he had built many monasteries for God’s servants with wondrous workmanship, while he was at Toledo he was content with a very small cell.

From there he returned to Seville. As the nature of his soul subtly foresaw his body exhausted by continuous illness [Note: [Col. 0046D] The material enclosed in parentheses has been added, along with several other passages here and there. What we have enclosed in parentheses appears to have been inserted by the author of the Life while interpolating the original account.], he nevertheless always practiced generous distribution of alms to many people. For six months or more, he distributed alms on successive days in greater measure than usual to monks, students, and the poor, so that from sunrise to evening he remained occupied distributing abundant possessions to the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Here the account of Redemptus the cleric is transcribed—Saint Isidore calls him archdeacon—in his report concerning Saint Isidore’s death, beginning with the following omitted introduction: “It seemed appropriate to me to explain briefly to your holiness how my lord Isidore, of blessed memory, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Seville, accepted penance and made his confession before God and men, and how he migrated from this world to heaven, so that you might know these things through the faithful writing of my account. This matter first compelled me to thank your charity for the concern which, out of love for him, you offer; and then, because I cannot suppress the truth, and because I am compelled to say these things at your prayer, having gathered from many matters the few things I was able to learn about him. While he was already looking ahead, I do not know by what providence, to his end, and while his wearied body…”]

Afterward, weakened by the illness, as the fever grew stronger in his body and his debilitated stomach rejected food—so that he might leave his people an example of repentance—he recovered sufficiently for penance, so that what he had always taught his people in words he might openly fulfill before all also by his deeds, saying with the Apostle: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

Accordingly, he summoned the clergy and all the people and had himself carried by his disciples on a bed to the church. He immediately ordered the venerable Saint John the bishop and the most blessed Epartius, that distinguished man and bishop—men whom the holiness of their lives had bound to him in friendship—to be present.

As he was being brought from his cell to the church of Saint Vincent the Martyr, all the companies of clergy, students, monks, and nuns—whose teacher and supporter the holy confessor had been—and all the congregations of that city received him with cries and great wailing, tearing the hair of their heads and their beards and rending their faces and garments. Anyone who possessed an iron breast would at once have dissolved entirely into tears and lamentation.

34. When he was placed in the middle of the choir of the aforementioned martyr’s church, near the altar screen, he ordered the crowds of women to stand farther away, so that when he himself received penance, only men, and not women, would be seen present around him.

As the bishops mentioned above, together with the others who had gathered for this sad though holy spectacle, were dissolving in inconsolable lamentation, he had himself wrapped in ashes [Note: [Col. 0046D] In the printed editions, one account says that he asked one bishop to place a hair shirt upon him and the other to sprinkle ashes over him. These two bishops were John of Ilipa, now Peñaflor, and Epartius of Italica, commonly called Sevilla la Vieja. Both signed the Fourth Council of Toledo and, after the metropolitan of Seville, were the first according to the order of the sees enumerated by Charles of Saint-Martin in *Sacred Geography.] and sackcloth, and, extending his hands to heaven, began as follows:

“You, God, who know the hearts of men, who deigned to forgive the publican standing far away as he beat his breast, and who willed to receive him into the bosom of the patriarch Abraham, accept this confession of mine and remove from Your sight the sins I have contracted beyond number. Do not remember my evils, and do not recall the offenses of my youth.”

“You, Lord, did not assign penance to the righteous who have not sinned against You, but to me, a sinner who have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea. May the ancient enemy find nothing in me to punish.

“You know that, after I, wretched man, unworthy of having come to this holy Church—rather to bear this burden than to receive this honor—never ceased sinning; instead, I labored to act wickedly.

“But because You have said: ‘At whatever hour a sinner turns from his ways, You will consign all his iniquities to oblivion,’ remembering this command of Yours, I cry out to You with hope and confidence, although I am not worthy to look upon Your heaven because of the multitude of sins that dwell in me.

“Be present and receive my prayer, and grant me, a sinner, the forgiveness I ask. If even the heavens are not clean in Your sight, how much less am I, a human being who drank iniquities like water and took up the barriers [Note: [Col. 0046D] The same source has *colostra*, “sin”; I would rather approve this reading, for *colostrum* is the first milk, and thus the extended metaphor is joined to the preceding one, in which the Saint says that he drank iniquity like water.] of sin.”

When these things had been completed, he received from the bishops themselves the life-giving sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, judging himself unworthy with profound groaning of heart.

35. Then he asked forgiveness from those same bishops, from all who belonged to the clergy, and from all the congregations—offering us in every respect an example of humility—and said:

“I beseech you, my most holy lords the priests [Col. 0047A], and you, holy assembly of clergy and people, to direct your prayer to the Lord for me, wretched and full of the filth of sin, so that although I am unworthy by my own merits, I may nevertheless, through your intercession, deserve to obtain pardon for my offenses by the mercy I have sought.

“Forgive me, unworthy as I am, for whatever I have committed against each of you: if I have despised anyone through hatred, or injured anyone through anger.”

[Note: [Col. 0047D] This observation does not appear in Redemptus, nor do several other passages below, which were probably added by our author, who everywhere employs considerable amplification—unless someone would prefer to say that the Redemptus we possess is merely an abridged version.]

(“You see a model of virtue, upon whom the necessity of all depended with paternal concern, when you see the teacher asking forgiveness from his subjects. This is the more gracious because of the simple affection of those who benefit from fearing that they have offended in some way. Strive with all your strength to imitate and follow the humility of so great a doctor. For the highest form of humility is to subject oneself to one who is inferior; and chaste or holy fear of God, which endures forever and ever, consists in not setting oneself above another with an elevated heart. Then the blessed confessor added:)

“Forgive me now at least, my lords, I beg you, as I earnestly ask—and indeed as I repent—if I have committed any offense.”

While everyone loudly asked forgiveness for him with tears, some objected that he who shone at the summit of holiness was not aided by sinners’ prayers; on the contrary, they were aided through his intercession—he who had consecrated himself to the Lord from early youth in integrity of mind and body.

As everyone recounted the virtues of this exceptional man, he again admonished those standing around him, saying:

“Most holy lords the bishops, and all who are present, I ask and beseech you to show charity to one another, not returning evil for evil, and not wishing to be talebearers among the people. Bound together by the bond of love, do not allow the ravening wolf to find anyone left behind whom he may carry away.”

After he had canceled the bonds and written acknowledgments of all his debtors—which appeared to be almost innumerable and which also added to the evidence of his extraordinary goodness—he began, having recovered his strength through divine power, to partake of the banquets of heavenly nourishment with such abundant devotion and to set before the people such plentiful dishes of the divine mystery, and to announce to everyone with such joy the day on which he was to be born into life, the day on which he desired, with the Apostle, to be dissolved and to be with Christ, that one could confidently assert that he was always present in spirit at the eternal feasts.

Although seized by a grave illness—through which, the weaker he became, the stronger and more powerful he was—he preached in word and example with such constancy, prudence, and abundance that, while he himself hastened toward heavenly things, he compelled those attending him also to hasten.

After these things had been done, he ordered the remaining money to be given immediately to the needy and poor.

(But this also especially heightens the glory of his reputation: as a herald and bearer of the Lord’s peace, he sought to be kissed by everyone and to receive the peace which he proclaimed with his mouth and in his conduct. By giving each person standing around him the kiss, he left them an imitator of the Author, saying:)

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Redemptus has a shorter version: “Meanwhile he sought to be kissed by everyone, saying…”]

“If you forgive from your whole heart whatever adverse or wrongful thing I have hitherto done to you, the almighty Creator will forgive you all your sins, so that the water of the sacred font, which the devout people will receive today, may be for you unto the remission of sins. And may this kiss remain between me and you as a witness for the future.”

When all these things had been completed, he returned to his cell.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Redemptus adds: “And after the fourth day following the day of his confession or penance, he continually fulfilled his pastoral care and completed his end in peace, on the day before the Nones of April, on the nineteenth day of the moon, in the era 674—that is, in the year of Christ 636—when Easter was celebrated on the day before the Kalends of April. It therefore appears that this confession took place on Holy Saturday itself, when the solemn baptism of catechumens was to be celebrated; the immediately preceding words indicate this as well. Thus he must have died during the fourth sequence of Easter week.”]

## CHAPTER X. The Death, Burial, and Epitaph of Saint Isidore; Various Eulogies

36. For three further consecutive days he was likewise brought to the church by the clergy and an innumerable host of the people—which increased in number each day, wishing to witness the holy Father’s departure, lamentable to them but delightful to the heavenly court. There he poured the words of holy preaching into those who thirsted for them and eagerly desired to welcome the Lord returning from the wedding feast, as though he were proceeding to meet Christ and the heavenly court, which invited him to so solemn a wedding, surrounded by a company of bishops, clergy, princes, and peoples.

After the fourth day following his confession or penance, he stood in the church. Having completed his sermon to the people, he extended his hands to heaven, blessed everyone, and commended to God the flock entrusted to him. Then he delivered his holy spirit to the Lord, leaving us the most precious pearl of his body, to be embraced with worthy veneration.

When the people saw the pontiff’s soul released from the body’s sheath, they sent voices and wails up to heaven, mourning the death of so great a Father with the bitterest sobs.

The city of Seville overflowed with tears. Bishops mourned their shepherd, princes their teacher, clergy their doctor, monks and nuns their ruler and supporter, and the poor their father and defender; all, with mournful faces, displayed the bitterness of their hearts and lamented inconsolably.

Not long afterward, mourning was turned into joy, bitterness into sweetness, the voice of those lamenting into praise, and despair into consolation, because the Saint did not allow them to remain sorrowful for long. For such fragrance flowed from his body—surpassing the odor of every spice—that everyone present seemed to enjoy heavenly blessedness.

Sick people suffering from various illnesses gathered, and they were restored to their former health not only by touching the holy body but even by smelling it alone.

To increase and more fully magnify the abundant gifts of the singular man’s merits, the number forty, dedicated by a manifold sacrament, is also introduced. Having lived and died within its span, he clearly demonstrated that the mystical sacrament of this number marked for him the summit of perfection, since the grace of God dwelt and worked in him most fully.

Let the gaze of your charity, beloved brothers, take heed; let it consider how great this Saint was among the holy: how admirable, how praiseworthy, how magnificent, and how glorious.

One saint gives sight to the blind, another cleanses lepers, another loosens the organs of the mute, another restores hearing to the deaf, another strengthens the steps of the lame, another recalls a dead corpse to life, another preserves people unharmed from deadly touch and draught, and another heals those worn down by any disease. For, as the Apostle says, the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good.

To one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of speeches.

But one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things. Filled with His gift, His grant, His grace, His generosity, His prompting, and His inspiration, God’s chosen confessor Isidore shone so fully with all these gifts of grace and endowments of charisms that, when the Apostle described them by enumerating them, he seemed to have directed the gaze of his mind toward Isidore, in whom the gifts of all the righteous who came before were gathered and from whom, passed on to those who followed, they gradually diminished.

37. Blessed Isidore died in the Spanish era 660, in the year 622 from the incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0049D] Above, from Redemptus, we reported the era 574 and the year of Christ 636, which year is soon confirmed from the reign of Chintila.], superior to all in sound doctrine and sound [Col. 0049C] counsel, advanced in good days, and rich in works of charity. His eyes had not grown dim, nor had his teeth moved from their place. Finally, when the holy body was to be buried with due honor, there was one will among all, the same vows, and the same desire. Since the most holy doctor Leander, before departing from the body, had desired that this most blessed brother be buried beside him, and their sister, the glorious virgin Florentina, had ardently desired the same for herself, they honorably placed the tomb of Isidore’s most holy body in the middle, joining it on either side to the tombs of Saint Leander and Saint Florentina, and adorning them with much gold and silver in embossed work.

Meanwhile, several people, illuminated by a divine gift, saw the Saint’s soul borne upward by a multitude of angels [Col. 0049D] amid a voice of praise and jubilation, and saw Christ the Son of God proceeding to meet him with an innumerable company of saints. A certain man also, whose disciplined life seemed sufficiently worthy of imitation and who loved that same confessor above all else, became anxious when an unexpected circumstance arose and excessive grief refused to be consoled. He testified that he had been carried away in ecstasy and confessed that he had seen this distinguished shepherd holding first place among the throngs of the innocent whom Herod slaughtered for Christ’s name, bearing the palm of martyrdom, the aureole of virginity, and the crown of confession. He said that Isidore spoke to him, [Col. 0050A] “For I am ready to bring assistance to all who implore Christ’s help on my behalf.” After this vision he always appeared joyful and cheerful, though he remained somehow continually anxious, sighing for the presence of his father.

But why should I enumerate the miracles of this most perfect man, magnify his virtues, proclaim his knowledge, commend his teaching, or extol his character? For in this apostolic man—indeed, in an apostle of Christ after the Apostles—why should one seek a harmony of virtues when one plainly sees in him Noah’s prudence, Abraham’s fortitude, Isaac’s temperance, Jacob’s justice, and Job’s patience? Why should I praise Isidore’s excellence in knowledge when in him you marvel at the presence of Moses and Elijah? What grace of teaching could you prefer to that in which you will find the truth of the teacher of the nations overflowing, discipline burning with the Spirit, zeal, and abundant knowledge? What glory of character could you celebrate in one in whom you behold Stephen’s sufferings and the steadfastness of the other followers of Christ presiding?

38. But since we must not dwell on these matters at present, lest an excessively prolonged reading produce weariness in the listener, let us return to our subject. Meanwhile there were many highly skilled clerics and scholars in verse and song who recognized the doctor and, in pious affection for the great deeds of the Father from whom they had received their gift, raised his praises. Among them was the honor of the clergy, Blessed Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, of illustrious holiness. He had drunk the purest streams of doctrine from his master’s breast. To honor his master, in the part of the church where the holy doctors rested, he had their deeds painted in remarkable workmanship; and on the silver cross that lay above the monuments of the saints [Col. 0050C] he inscribed this poem.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] Tamajus Salazar published this poem under 21 December.]

### EPITAPH

This venerable cross bears the bodies of two brothers,  
Leander and Isidore, equal in their order as poets.  
Third, their sister Florentina, ever devoted—  
O what a harmonious companion!—rests here worthily.  
Isidore, placed in the middle, separates the limbs of the two.

Reader, inquire in their books what manner of men they were:  
You will learn that they spoke all things well,  
Firm in hope, full of faith, and dear above all.  
You will see that the faithful grew through their teachings,  
And that what impious laws held was restored to the Lord.

And so that you may believe that these lofty men live forever,  
Strive, as you look upward, to see them painted there.

### ANOTHER POEM

[Col. 0050D]

In praise of the Church, to Christ, King of glory,  
Let us continually sing together;  
And to the only-begotten of the Virgin, in a Davidic song,  
Let us solemnly sing.

Let songs resound with the glory of Isidore,  
Mindful of his merits;  
Let the heap of praises grow, let the people rejoice,  
And the angelic choirs.

In our times he shone forth in conduct,  
And in the words of the Lord:  
Faithful, he exalted the faith, and by faith drove away  
The stain of heretical error.

Born at Carthage, from his origin  
Knowing nothing childish,  
He poured out the fountain of wisdom  
Throughout the regions of Spain, performing wonders.

While he presided as chief bishop at Seville, he taught the law,  
A Spaniard teaching Spain;  
Surpassing in doctrine, preaching the Crucified,  
Driving away idolatry [Note: [Col. 0051D] Medieval writers commonly use *idolatria* for *idololatria*.]

Nobly sprung from a distinguished lineage, he stood immovable  
In the great deeds of God;  
Seeking the reward of heavenly joys,  
He despised temporal things.

Through the splendor of his works, a fruitful example,  
He gave himself to the clergy;  
Never deviating from what was certain, wholly longing for heaven,  
He subdued vices;

He more abundantly restored Roman doctrines  
Here through the regions of the world;  
As evening star he adorned the West,  
As morning star, the Church, more brightly.

Orthodox, he confounded Arius, the dreadful adversary,  
By the reckoning of reason;  
Here this hammer struck him down: the bitter enemy yielded,  
Defeated openly.

Let the devotion of the clergy of Iberia, with full joy,  
Honor the father of his homeland.  
Let the regions of the world, contemplating his teachings, praise  
The doctor of the Church.

[Col. 0051C]

The glory of archbishops, the mirror of priests,  
He wrote, skillfully shaping his song,  
Wonderful poems on the Catholic faith,  
Piling book upon book.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Above we rejected some persons’ view concerning Muhammad’s arrival in Spain. Since the author of this epitaph accepts it as unquestioned, he sufficiently indicates that he is much later than Saint Ildefonsus, to whom the first epitaph is attributed.]

The blindness of Muhammad, destroying ruined peoples,  
Unable to refute his miracles,  
Was sorrowful to yield  
To the blameless man.

As he sincerely believed, so sincerely he set forth  
The pattern of repentance;  
Perceptive in learning, effective in examples,  
A teacher of the multitude.

Who could fully bring forth or prescribe  
The titles of his deeds?  
The tongue would not suffice, the right hand would fail  
In writing each one.

Let us therefore entreat him, whose holiness  
Is firmly believed,  
That he may forever defend us from the enemy’s snares  
And from vices.

O suppressor of crimes, reconcile for us  
The Lord by your prayer;  
Nourish us in hope, remove what is harmful,  
Cleanse all our stains.

[Col. 0052A]

Him whom we venerate together with you, your brother  
Leander—we ask for his intercession.  
May he hear our prayers and, hearing, receive them,  
In eternal remembrance.

We wish to remember Fulgentius the Doctor,  
The companion of these brothers;  
Because of his merit in life, we ask that he be mindful  
Of our salvation.

We ask, together with the brothers, for the distinguished virgin  
Florentina, their companion,  
That she may come as a helper and soften the offenses  
Into which we have fallen;  
And may the Lord likewise deign to be appeased—  
Let the clergy sing, Amen.

By the Virgin’s intercession, may he cleanse from the stain of sin  
Those whom sin defiles.

[Col. 0052B]

May that celebrated Virgin intercede for us,  
Driving away the darkness of vices,  
So that he who rules all things with wondrous power  
May place us in heaven.

Amen!

40. The blessed teacher died on the day of the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 0052D] Rather, on the day before the Nones.], during the reign of the most Christian Chintila [Note: [Col. 0052D] Cintila, or Cintilanus, reigned three years and eight months, from 636 to 640.], king of Spain, and of Heraclius [Note: [Col. 0052D] Heraclius was emperor from 610 to 641.], emperor of the Romans—namely, that Heraclius who restored and exalted at Jerusalem the Lord’s cross, which the impious king Chosroes had carried away from its place.

He left no will, because, although rich in resources in Christ, since he was poor in spirit he distributed everything he possessed to the poor [Col. 0052C] and needy before departing from the world. The true love of all toward their father was also shown by this: they placed in hidden places two lamps, almost perpetually burning and nearly impossible to extinguish, said to have been made by him through natural art—one at his head and one at his feet—so that the most holy body might enjoy a nearly continuous light.

41. Meanwhile, dearest brothers, it is fitting that the whole Church should honor this most holy doctor with praises and encomiums, but especially the Churches of Spain, which, more particularly than others, shone with the health-giving light of his teaching. For who could exalt a man worthy of every praise in infancy, worthy of universal veneration in childhood, full of so many virtues in adolescence, conspicuous for such goodness in youth, most renowned for so many miracles in his episcopate, distinguished by such praiseworthy preaching in old age [Col. 0052D], adorned by such an imitable end in advanced age, and glorified by so wondrous a departure at the end?

Who would not proclaim him most acceptable in the sight of the eternal King, since with his life and character he adorned the episcopal office, with virtues his renown, with signs his grace, with progress his learning, with praises his knowledge, with growth his days, and with such great glory his end? Indeed, while the most blessed man was still burdened by weariness with the weight of the body and, thirsting in spirit for the living fountain, desired nothing in heaven or on earth except Him, the whole world learned, through the renewed grace of miraculous powers in his lifeless body, astonishing to every age, how great he had been in the eyes of the divine majesty, how dear to God, how acceptable to angels, how beloved by human beings, how renowned for miracles, how splendid in virtues, how magnificent in signs, how worthy of glorious praise, and how munificent in the abundance of merits before God and conspicuous in the magnificence of gifts among human beings.

For although the earth, mother and nurse of those who pass away, brought forth, cherished, and held Isidore—who nevertheless was wise in nothing earthly or transient, but, to speak more precisely, continually clung to heaven in mind and action—the whole world bears witness to it: heaven testifies, earth perceived it, the air cries out, the usefulness of the waters proves it, and healings reveal it. At the command of the divine will, these, ever reconciled by Isidore’s merits and ready through his prayers, favor the vows and services of those who piously ask, and minister to their needs, for the instruction of the Church and the praise of Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0053D] This work of Saint Braulio appears before the Works of Saint Isidore and is called a preliminary notice of his books by Tamajus Salazar and others under this date; but nowhere in them does it appear so expansively developed as here. It therefore seems not an abbreviation but a paraphrastic elucidation, as we likewise observed above in Redemptus the cleric’s account of Isidore’s death. We similarly enclose in parentheses what seem to have been added by interpolation. For Braulio compressed this entire beginning as follows: “Isidore the distinguished bishop of Seville, successor to and brother of Bishop Leander, flourished in the time of the emperor Maurice and King Reccared. In him antiquity claimed something for itself; indeed, our age imagined in him the knowledge of antiquity. He was formed in every kind of speech, so that he was suitable to the learned and unlearned according to the quality of their discourse, and, with fitting appropriateness to every place, distinguished by incomparable eloquence.”]

### Abbreviation by Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, concerning the life of Saint Isidore, doctor of Spain

42. Isidore, a distinguished man (by nation Carthaginian, born of Severianus, a most noble leader of that homeland), was archbishop of the Church of Seville (primate of Spain, and biological brother of the most holy bishops and confessors Leander and Fulgentius and of the most holy virgin Florentina, superior of virgins), and most holy successor to Saint [Col. 0053C] Leander.

(This most blessed man, devoted from childhood to literary studies, instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, formed in every kind of speech, distinguished in the learning of the *trivium*, perfected in the disciplines of the *quadrivium*, and fully educated in divine and human laws, was sweet in eloquence, pre-eminent in intellect, and most illustrious in life and teaching. He was rightly called by everyone the doctor of Spain. Thus, progressing from virtue to virtue, the outstanding doctor shone forth, so that according to the quality of his speech he was suitable in learning and vigorous in incomparable eloquence for everyone—that is, for Latins, Greeks, and Hebrews, for the wise and for those of lesser understanding. For he attained such an abundant wealth of delight in speaking that the admirable richness of his discourse turned his hearers to astonishment; whatever someone had heard, he would commit to memory without needing to hear it repeatedly.)

43. Now anyone prudent will be able to understand very easily how great he was in wisdom from his various studies and carefully elaborated little works. Finally, of those that have come to our knowledge, I have recalled the following.

He published two books of *Differences*, in which, with subtle discrimination, he distinguished in meaning those things that are expressed confusedly in ordinary usage. One book of *Prefaces*, in which he briefly marked out what each book of Holy Scripture contains. One book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, in which he briefly noted their deeds, dignity, death, and burial in concise statements. To his brother Fulgentius, bishop, he addressed two books *On Offices*, in which, with an interpretive style and not without the authority of the ancients, he elicited the origins of the offices and why each is performed in the Church of God.

Two books of *Synonyms*, in which, for the consolation of the soul and the hope of receiving pardon, he raised up an exhortation through an ordered sequence of reasoning. One book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to King Sisebut, in which, drawing both on the investigation of ecclesiastical doctors and on that of philosophers, he clarified certain obscure matters concerning the elements. One book *On Numbers*, in which, because of the numbers inserted in ecclesiastical Scripture, he touched upon the discipline of arithmetic. One book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, in which he showed what the persons mentioned signify mystically. One book *On Heretics and Heresies*, in which, following the examples of the ancients, he collected at the greatest brevity he could the material that was widely dispersed.

He collected three books of *Sentences*, which he adorned with flowers from Pope Gregory’s *Moral Works*. He gathered one book of chronicles from the beginning of the world to his own time, with extreme brevity. At the request of his sister Florentina [Col. 0054C], superior of virgins, he composed two books *Against the Jews*, in which he established from the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets everything that the Catholic faith believes.

([Note: [Col. 0054D] This little work and the following two are not mentioned in the published editions already cited.] One book *On the Eternal Birth of Christ from the Father and His Temporal Birth from His Mother*, from the testimonies of Isaiah; he abridged the moral works of Blessed Pope Gregory at the pope’s request; he clarified the *Song of Songs* in a second exposition.) One book *On Illustrious Men*.
