Then we suggested the following works to him: one book *The Rule of Religious Life*, which he most suitably adapted to the needs of his homeland and the strength of those living under a rule; one book of histories *On the Origin of the Goths and the Kingdoms of the Suevi and Vandals*; and two books of *Questions*, in which anyone who reads them recognizes the resources of ancient treatises.

(He compiled the *Library*. [Note: [Col. 0054D] The published books do not mention some of the following works.] He published a fourth translation of the Psalter; he labored with no small diligence on a Commentary on the books of Moses, the Psalter, and the four Gospels [Col. 0054D]; and he composed very extensive works on canon and civil law.)

He also produced the *Etymologies*, a codex of immense size, divided by him into titles rather than books [Col. 0055A]. Because he made it at my request, although he left it unfinished, I divided it into twenty books. Whoever reads this work, which embraces every kind of philosophy, with frequent attention will rightly not remain ignorant of divine and human matters. In it the elegance of various arts is enclosed, and nearly everything that ought to be known is gathered in compressed form.

There are also many other books of the holy man, inscribed in the Church of God with much adornment, by which he clearly fortified it. God raised him up after so many disasters of Spain in the final times, I believe, [Note: [Col. 0055D] In the published editions: “To restore the monuments of the ancients … he set up, as it were, a certain *destina*,” that is, a support or column. The word is used in this sense by Saints Augustine, Fulgentius, and Bede together with Arnobius. What follows is found more briefly and vigorously in the published editions: “To whom this philosophical saying is not improperly applied by us: ‘We, wandering and straying in our own city like travelers and guests, were brought home by your books. You disclosed the age of our homeland; the descriptions of times; the laws of sacred things; the offices of priests; domestic and public discipline; the locations, regions, and places; and the kinds, duties, and causes of all divine and human things.’ With what flood of eloquence and with how many darts of the divine Scriptures or testimonies of the Fathers he pierced the heresy of the Acephalites, the synodal proceedings held before him at Seville declare; in them he asserted that truth against Gregory, the bishop of the aforementioned heresy. ‘He died in the time of the emperor Heraclius and the most Christian king Chintila, superior to all in sound doctrine and rich in works of charity.’”] to restore the wisdom of the ancients, which through excessive antiquity had almost disappeared from human minds, so that the Christian people would not grow old any longer through ignorance or rusticity.

Thus he opened up the succession of times and the ages of the world to a people ignorant of them [Col. 0055B]; he displayed the laws of sacred things; he explained ecclesiastical offices and the ranks of every order to priests; he established laws for kings and princes; he prohibited avarice to judges; and he instilled the discipline of the Christian religion in citizens and in all peoples of the household of the faith. By pursuing and eliminating the filth of the Arian heresy throughout Spain with the sword of God’s word, he confounded and destroyed the wicked heresy of the Acephalites. After overcoming Gregory, the bishop of that heresy, and convicting him by the testimonies of the saints and the authority of Scripture, he taught that there are two natures in Christ, namely divine and human.

Finally, by writing, he disclosed the names, kinds, functions, and causes of places, sites, regions, and all divine and human things, as well as whatever was obscure and almost already removed from human minds [Col. 0055C]. He shone forth as one endowed with such an overflowing abundance of knowledge that, not only in our times but from the time of the Apostles and even earlier—excepting the first man and Solomon—we believe that no one surpassed him in the variety of the sciences.

He flourished in the times of Kings Reccared, Liuva, Witteric, Gundemar, Sisebut, Suintila, and Sisinand [Note: [Col. 0056D] These seven reigned from the year 536.], whom he drew out of the madness of Arianism and confirmed in the Catholic faith.

44. Moreover, he was renowned for the spirit of prophecy, generous in almsgiving, distinguished in hospitality, severe in heart, truthful in pronouncement, just in judgment, constant in preaching, joyful in exhortation, diligent in winning souls for God, cautious in explaining the Scriptures, provident in counsel, humble in dress, sober at table, devoted in prayer, distinguished in integrity, always ready to die for the Church and the defense of truth, and conspicuous in every goodness.

Furthermore, he was a father to clerics, a teacher and supporter of monks and nuns, a consoler of the sorrowful, a protection for orphans and widows, a relief to the oppressed [Col. 0056A], a defender of citizens, a crusher of the proud, and a persecutor and hammer of heretics. And what more? He became for the world a mirror of every good thing, and therefore now reigns without end with Christ.

With what flood of eloquence and with what darts of the divine Scriptures or testimonies of the Fathers he destroyed and weakened all wicked heresies, the synodal proceedings held before him at Seville or Toledo make clear. In them he also established, with the clearest testimonies of Scripture, that the Roman pontiff must be obeyed by the faithful, as one appointed in the place of blessed Peter the Apostle, and that the one God must be served in the Trinity of persons.

He died in the time of Heraclius the emperor and the most Christian Suintila, king of Spain—namely, that Heraclius who restored and exalted at Jerusalem the Lord’s cross, which the impious king Chosroes had carried away [Col. 0056B]. Blessed Isidore slept with his fathers in the Spanish era 660, superior to all in sound doctrine and sound counsel, rich in works of charity, and shining with various signs of miracles. In him antiquity claimed something for itself; indeed, our age imagined in him the knowledge and miracles of antiquity. To him, as a kind of appended praise, we may not improperly apply this philosophical saying: “We, like strangers and guests in our own city, were led home by your books, so that at last we might recognize who and where we were.”

He held the episcopate for forty years and was buried in a good old age, accompanied by choirs of angels. The city of Seville was afflicted with weariness and an inundation of grief, being deprived of so great a father and delivered into the lot of the most voracious robber [Col. 0056C].

Meanwhile, dearest brothers, it is fitting that the whole Church should raise this most holy confessor Isidore up with praises, but especially the Churches of Spain, which, more than others, shone with the special and health-giving light of his teaching. For just as Gregory the doctor succeeded Peter at Rome, so blessed Isidore succeeded the Apostle James in the regions of Spain in teaching.

The seeds of eternal life that the most blessed James sowed, this most blessed Isidore sufficiently watered with the word of preaching, as one of the four rivers of paradise, and he illumined all Spain, both by the example of good works and by the reputation of his holiness, like the most brilliant ray of the sun.

Therefore let us earnestly entreat this most holy confessor, that he may stand continually before God as an intercessor for us, wretched sinners, who are still placed amid the dangers of this life, so that we who embrace his sacred teaching with devout love may be delivered in the present from the dangers pressing upon us and, after this life, may through his holy intercessions deserve to reach the fellowship of God’s elect.

[Col. 0057]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT ISIDORE, BY FABRICIUS

*(From the library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

[Col. 0057A]

Isidore of Seville, of Gothic descent [Note: [Col. 0057D] Vossius, *On Latin History*, p. 263.], born to his father Severianus of the province of Carthage, was a distinguished man, inferior to few men of earlier centuries. He was bishop of the Church of Seville after Leander [Note: [Col. 0057D] Blondellus, *On Bishops*, p. 73.], his biological brother, who died in A.D. 600. Formed in every kind of speech and distinguished by incomparable eloquence, his admirable abundance, to use Ildefonsus’s words, turned his hearers to astonishment. He was a necessary grammarian, in the judgment even of those who disparage him [Note: [Col. 0057D] See Thomas Pope Blount, *Censure of Writers*, p. 336.]. He died in the year 636.

I shall say no more about him, since Lucas of Tuy and others speak of him at length in Mabillon’s *Second Century of the Benedictines* and in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, April, IV, pp. 327 ff. and 900 ff. Concerning the death of the holy man, see the account by Redemptus the cleric, ibid., p. 349.

Concerning Isidore’s writings, see Saint Braulio of Zaragoza in the preface to Isidore’s books [Col. 0057B]—which is repeated by the author of Isidore’s Life in volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*, April, p. 351, and which Oudinus prefixed in full to his dissertation on the same works, volume I, p. 1583—Saint Ildefonsus, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9; Sigebert, chapter 55; Honorius, III, 40; the Anonymous of Melk, chapter 26; Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book XXIII, 31; Trithemius, chapter 232; and, among more recent writers, besides Labbe and the Arnoldus Wion cited by him, volume I of the *Tree of Life*, pp. 244 ff., and others, as well as Cave and Oudinus. Above all, Nicolaus Antonius should be consulted, volume I of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book V, chapter 4, pp. 250 ff. I think I would not merely be repeating work already done if I too briefly listed his writings.

Four editions of Isidore’s works have so far appeared: one by Margarino Bignaeus, Paris, 1580; another, much better, from Madrid, by Joannes Grialius, 1599; and a third by Jacobus Breulius, a monk of Saint-Germain of Paris, of the Benedictine Order, Paris, 1601. Colomesius and others complain that the prefaces of the Madrid edition were omitted in it. This edition was reprinted at Cologne in 1617, and I shall follow its order in reviewing Isidore’s writings. The new edition that the learned Jacobus Hommey had announced would be awaited was forestalled by his death.

## 1. The Twenty Books of Origins, or Etymologies

These were preceded by three letters of Isidore to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, and two letters of Braulio to Isidore. After Isidore’s death, Braulio added the final hand to the work and arranged it into books. It is a highly useful work, in which Isidore briefly collected and explained from the best writers—including quite a few ecclesiastical writers—most of what is worth knowing concerning almost every subject, as well as many things of good quality scarcely found elsewhere.

Book I: Grammar.  
Book II: Rhetoric and Dialectic [Note: [Col. 0057D] Hence Isidore’s *On the Art of Rhetoric* appears in Franciscus Pithoeus’s *Ancient Rhetoricians*, p. 356, 358.].  
Book III: The Four Mathematical Disciplines.  
Book IV: Medicine [Note: [Col. 0057D] Nicolaus Antonius, volume I, [Col. 0058D] p. 255, mentions Symphorianus Camperius’s commentary on book IV of Isidore, *On Medical Matters*.].  
Book V: Laws and Times, where the brief chronicle in the final chapter ends in the tenth year of Heraclius.  
Book VI: Ecclesiastical Books and Offices.  
Book VII: God, Angels, and the Orders of the Faithful.  
Book VIII: The Church and Various Sects [Note: [Col. 0058D] Gratian repeats Isidore’s catalog of heresies in part II of the *Decree*, cause 24, question 3. It was also published by Hieronymus Gebwiler, Strasbourg, 1523, quarto, together with Saint Augustine’s *On Faith and Works* and Saint Jerome’s *Against Helvidius and Vigilantius*, and separately by J. Quintinus, a jurist, Paris, 1560.].  
Book IX: Languages, Societies, and Kinship.  
Book X: Vocabulary in Alphabetical Order and Their Origins.  
Book XI: Human Beings and Monstrous Births.  
Book XII: Animals.  
Book XIII: The World and Its Parts.  
Book XIV: The Earth and Its Parts.  
Book XV: Buildings and Fields and Their Measurements.  
Book XVI: Stones and Metals.  
Book XVII: Rural Matters.  
Book XVIII: War and Games.  
Book XIX: Ships, Buildings, and Clothing.  
Book XX: Food, and Rural and Domestic Implements.

Three fragments are also appended on p. 178: *On Weights*, *On Measures*, and *On Various Words*.

In indicating the origins of words, Isidore does not always strike the matter precisely, just as Varro does not among the Latins, nor Plato among the Greeks, nor Philo among the Jews. Hence the harsher criticism of Christoph Becmann, who says that Isidore does nothing but indulge in trifles and provoke laughter, and the criticism of Salmasius, *On the Augustan History*, p. 28, who disapproves of Isidore, in his customary manner, as inept in presenting etymologies. Nevertheless, other learned men have taught that Isidore must be defended in many matters. See Nicolaus Antonius, volume I, pp. 251 ff.

This work of Isidore appeared in Italy [Note: [Col. 0058D] See Gesner’s *Library*, p. 568.] in an old edition without place or year; then at Augsburg in 1472 through Ginther Zainer of Reutlingen, a copy of which is held by our venerable Wolfius; at Venice in 1483; Basel, 1489; Paris, 1509 and 1520; and at Haguenau, through Secerius, 1529. It also appeared with Martianus Capella, from the recension of Bonaventura Vulcanius, Basel, 1577, folio; among Isidore’s works under the care of Margarino Bignaeus, Paris, 1580, folio; and, from the recension of Dionysius Gothofredus, among the writers of the Latin language, Geneva, 1595, 1602, and 1622, quarto. Finally it appeared with the excellent notes of Joannes Grialius, who made use of the observations of Alvarus Gomez, Antonius Augustinus, and Petrus Ciacconius, in the Madrid edition of Isidore’s works, 1599, reprinted at Paris in 1601 and Cologne in 1617, folio. There are outstanding ancient manuscripts at Leiden among the books that belonged to Isaac Vossius.

## 2. *On Differences, or the Proper Meaning of Words*

[Note: [Col. 0059D] See Goldastus on Valerianus, *On the Good of Discipline*, among the ancient paraenetic writers, p. 54.]

Book I, p. 179, drawn from Agraetius [Note: [Col. 0059D] Sigebert incorrectly calls it *On the Property of Things* [Col. 0060D], chapter 55.] and other ancient writers on this subject, whom I discussed in the *Latin Library*, IV, 6. Book II, *On Spiritual Differences of Sacred and Moral Words*, p. 185. He cites Lactantius and Fulgentius as authorities.

A third book, much fuller than the first, arranged in alphabetical order and furnished with learned notes from the Madrid edition of 1599, folio, is entitled *On Differences, or On the Proper Meaning of Expressions*, p. 194. It is preceded by a preface in which Isidore notes that the ancients distinguished words and expressions more subtly, but that, because poets confused the proper meanings of expressions out of metrical necessity, a custom arose whereby most words were accepted indifferently by authors.

“Among the Latins,” he says, “Cato was the first to write about these matters. Following his example, I have published a very few differences, partly issuing them myself and partly drawing them from the books of authors, and I have noted them for you, reader, for your enjoyment.”

This was the very book that Barthius testified he possessed in manuscript and wished to publish, XXXII, 1, *Adversaria*. Add XXXIX, 14. In this book Isidore also cites the grammarians Melissus and Palaemon.

## 3. Two Books of *Synonyms, or Soliloquies*

Page 216, preceded by a letter to Braulio the archdeacon. These are moral meditations and admonitions called *soliloquies*, because a person is introduced as weeping alone with himself or calling his own reason into counsel. They are called *synonyms* because the same matter is repeated and impressed through various and variously worded expressions.

They appeared at Antwerp in 1488, quarto. Nicolaus Antonius, volume I, p. 263, also mentions an Italian translation composed by Joseph Alchainus and published at Venice in 1570.

## 4. *A Little Book on Contempt of the World*

Page 227. Isidore says that he wrote it in imitation of Cicero’s book, namely the one in which Cicero composed his consolation on the death of his daughter Tullia. It had appeared at Venice in 1523, octavo.

## 5. *On the Rule of Life*

Page 230.

## 6. *An Exhortation to Repent*

With consolation drawn from the mercy of God, addressed to the soul that fears future judgments. Page 233.

## 7. *A Lament of Repentance*

Page 234.

In trochaic rhythms and a double alphabet. It begins: “Hear, Christ, the sad weeping and bitter song.” Compare Lucas of Tuy, *Life of Isidore*, chapter 6, volume I of the *Acts of the Saints*, April, III, pp. 340 ff.

[Col. 0059D]

## 8. Prayers

*Prayer for the Correction of Life*, on the continual lamentation of sins, p. 239; *Prayer Against the Snares of the Devil*, p. 244.

## 9. Letter to Massanus, or Masso, Bishop of Mérida

On the Fall and Restoration of a Priest, written in A.D. 609, p. 245. Canisius also published it, volume I, part II of the *Antiquarian Readings*, p. 300 (in the new Basnage edition, volume II, part II, p. 147), as did Octavianus Cajetanus, Rome, 1616, quarto. It also appears in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, April, p. 342. See Nicolaus Antonius, volume I, pp. 263 ff. and 268.

This letter seems entirely fictitious to Joannes Morinus, book IV *On Penance*, chapter 15, § 6; Oudinus proves this at greater length, volume I, pp. 1586 ff.

## 10. *On the Nature of Things*

A book addressed to King Sisebut, p. 246. In the Chronicle of Fontanella this is the *Book of Wheels*; for Trithemius, chapter 232, it is the *Cosmography*; for others, *On the World*, or *Astronomical*, or *On the Stars*; and in the Augsburg edition of 1472, folio, *On the Response of the World and the Ordering of the Stars*.

See Nicolaus Antonius, volume I of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, p. 253. “Certainly,” says Scriverius in his notes on Vegetius V, 11, “it is not a work to be despised and is worthy of a learned man’s judgment.” Many fragments of Nigidius, Varro, Suetonius Tranquillus, and others may be drawn from it.

## 11. Chronicle

From the origin of things to the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius and of the prince Sisebut, with the notes of Garcia de Loaisa, from the Madrid edition.

Wrongly, some have attributed this Chronicle to Isidore of Pax as its author. Its author, however, just like Isidore of Seville in the final chapter of Book V of the *Etymologies*, declares that he follows in the footsteps of Julius Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome, and Victor of Tunnuna.

It appeared in A.D. 1477 under the title *On Times*, and together with the chronology of Gerardus Mercator and Matthaeus Beroaldus, Basel, 1577, octavo, through Thomas Guarinus. In the Vossian manuscript of the Leiden Library it is entitled *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*. On the pages themselves it is called *Image of the World*. The Anonymous of Melk, chapter 26, calls it an *Abbreviation of Times*.

### 12. History, or Chronicle of the Goths

Page 274, from Spanish Era 214 (A.D. 176) until the death of King Sisebut [Col. 0060C], Spanish Era 666 (A.D. 628), with an appendix on the Vandals, which is read almost identically at the beginning of the history of Rodrigo of Toledo, and on the Suevi [Note: [Col. 0060D] Goldastus also has it in *Scriptores rerum Suevicarum*, Frankfurt 1605 and Ulm 1722, folio, p. 3.], p. 277.

It appeared in the second book of the *Chronicle* of Lucas of Tuy, vol. IV of *Hispania illustrata*, and in a fuller form, together with the *Codex*, or twelve books of Visigothic laws, from the library of Pierre Pithou, Paris 1579, folio; and in Andrea Schott’s *Hispania illustrata*, vol. III, p. 847; and with the scholia of García de Loaysa, Turin 1693, quarto; and with the notes of Bonaventura Vulcanius, appended to Jordanes, p. 201, Leiden 1597, octavo; and with Jordanes and Paul the Deacon by Friedrich Lindenbrog, p. 181. Vulcanius, p. 235, and Lindenbrog, Hamburg 1611, also appended a brief *Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings*. That history appears much more accurately corrected and enlarged in Hugo Grotius’s collection *Rerum Gothicarum*, Amsterdam 1655, octavo, p. 707; and in Philippe Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, p. 61ff.; and in Aguirre’s *Councils of Spain*, vol. II, p. 183ff. See Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 256ff.

### 13. Book of Prologues

A book of prologues to the books received by the Catholic Church into the canon: the Old Testament, p. 278, and the New Testament, p. 282.

What the Western Church’s judgment concerning the canon of the sacred books was at that time can be understood well from this and other writings of Isidore, as Richard Simon observed in his *Censure of Dupin’s Ecclesiastical Bibliography*, vol. I, p. 252ff. [Col. 0061A] He also observes, p. 259ff., that the Latin version of the biblical books does not always follow Jerome’s version, but sometimes another; thus, in the Psalms, the Roman or Italian Psalter. On this see Bona, *Liturgical Matters* II, 3, and Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 262.

### 14. Allegorical Commentaries

Allegorical commentaries, resembling those read among the works of Eucherius and Bede, or *Questions and Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments* of the Old Testament. In them the author says that he drew his statements from Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and, in our own notably eloquent times, Gregory.

On Genesis, p. 283; Exodus, p. 305; Leviticus, p. 315; Numbers, p. 320; Deuteronomy, p. 326; Joshua, p. 330; Judges, p. 333; Ruth, p. 336; the Book of Kings, p. [Col. 0061B] 337 (II, p. 342; III, p. 344; IV, p. 345); Ezra and the Maccabees, p. 347, from the Cologne edition of 1530, octavo. The exposition of the Song of Songs is on p. 503.

Sigebert, chapter 55, testifies that Isidore went through the entire Old Testament by giving a straightforward exposition. This is what Isidore himself says when about to provide a mystical exposition: “And since the whole discourse has already been set forth by us according to the literal sense.” But we lack that work today.

### 15. Allegories

*Allegories of the Old Testament*, p. 248, and of the New Testament, p. 351, appeared at Haguenau from the press of Johann Secerius in 1529, quarto. The notes are those of Cyprian Suárez, or Soarius, in the Madrid edition of Isidore’s works, 1599.

In Cotelerius’s manuscript this book of Isidore is entitled *On the Meanings of the Old and New Testament*. See the *Apostolic Fathers*, vol. I, p. 738, and Braulio’s *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*.

### 16. Book on Ecclesiastical Writers

*Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, thirty-three authors, p. 355.

It had appeared together with similar writings by Jerome, Gennadius, Honorius, Sigebert, and Henry of Ghent, edited by Suffridus Petrus, Cologne 1580, octavo; and in García de Loaysa’s *Hispanic Councils*, 1593; and in Andrea Schott’s *Hispania illustrata*, vol. I, Frankfurt 1603, folio; and in Aubertus Miraeus’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, Antwerp 1638, Hamburg 1718, folio; and in Loaysa and Aguirre’s *Hispanic Councils*, vol. III, p. 71.

This book is not different from the *Book on Illustrious Men*, forty-six authors, which appears on p. 511 from García de Loaysa’s *Hispanic Councils*, Madrid 1593, folio, except that thirteen chapters have been added [Note: [Col. 0061D] These thirteen chapters are appended, in the manner of an appendix, to Isidore, Ildefonsus, Julian, and Felix of Toledo in Miraeus’s edition, and in Aguirre, vol. III of the *Hispanic Councils*, p. 84.]: 1. on Pope Sixtus; 2. on the deacon Macrobius; 3. [Col. 0061D] Philastrius; 4. Theodore of Mopsuestia; 5. on Hosius—the first chapter in the *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*; 6. Rufinus; 7. Vergundus or Verecundus; 8. Victorinus the bishop; 9. Idatius, the writer of the *Chronicle*; 10. Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum; 11. Cerealis; 12. Ferrandus the African; 13. Peter of Ilerda; and 14. on Marcellinus the presbyter.

Then chapter 15, on Idatius, the opponent of the Priscillianists, is the second chapter in the *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, and so all the chapters thereafter correspond up to the end, which in both works concerns Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza.

Appended there, p. 519, is Ildefonsus of Toledo’s little *Book on Illustrious Men*, twelve authors, concerning whose other editions I spoke above, vol. III, p. 259.

### 17. On the Life or Death of the Prophets and Apostles

*On the Life or Death of the Prophets and Apostles, or of the Saints Who Pleased God*: sixty-five of the Old Testament, p. 359, and twenty-two of the New Testament, p. 364.

It had appeared in the *Orthodoxographers*, Basel 1569, folio, part II, p. 1736, and from an old quarto edition without place or year; then at Haguenau in 1529, from Johann Secerius, quarto.

Usserius cites a little book on the feasts of the Apostles in the Hieronymian Martyrology, from which, he says, Isidore drew what he wrote about the saints of the New Testament.

### 18. To Florentia, His Sister

*To Florentia, his sister, on the Nativity of the Lord, his Passion and Resurrection, Kingdom and Judgment*, p. 367.

A notable fragment of an ancient Theodisc version from the Colbert manuscript, which the distinguished Baluzius had supplied to him, was published, together with Tatian’s harmony, and enlarged and elucidated with a notable glossary, by the excellent Johann Philipp Palthenius, Greifswald 1706, quarto. It was also reprinted in the celebrated work of Johann Schilter, vol. I of the *Treasury of Teutonic Antiquities*, Ulm 1727, folio.

### 19. On the Calling of the Nations

*On the Calling of the Nations*, addressed to the same Florentia, p. 379.

Together with the preceding work, this completed two books against the Jews: Venice 1483, quarto; or *Against the Wickedness of the Jews*, published by Johann Secerius, Haguenau 1529, quarto; Venice 1584; and in *Occanus of Law*, or the *Treatise of Treatises*, vol. XIV, p. 23.

It is also entitled *On the Catholic Faith from the Old and New Testament*, or *Testimonies Concerning Christ and the Church*. See Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 262.

### 20. On Ecclesiastical Offices

*Two Books on Ecclesiastical Offices*, addressed to Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi, p. 391.

They were first published by Johann Cochlaeus, Leipzig 1534, quarto; then from Cochlaeus at Paris, by Vivant Gautherot, 1542, in a smaller format, and 1564, octavo; and in the *Orthodoxographers*, Basel 1569, folio; and in Melchior Hittorp’s collection of writers on the Catholic offices of the Church, Cologne 1568, folio. There the final two chapters of the second book are missing, concerning “the intercessions of the Church” and “those for whom its intercessions are beneficial.” In their place the following conclusion is read on p. 36:

> These are a few things drawn from many, which we know to have been received from the teachings of reputable men, whose words we recognize as being present in certain places in our own work, so that our discourse may be strengthened by the opinions of our fathers.

These books also appear in the collection of writers on ecclesiastical offices, Rome 1591, folio, and Paris 1610, folio; in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris 1644, vol. X; and in the supplement of 1624. They also appear in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, April, p. 345.

Sayings taken from this work of Isidore occur in the anonymous treatise *On the Blessing of God*, addressed to Bathericus, bishop of Regensburg from A.D. 816 to 842, published by Stevartius, pp. 799ff., and in Basnage’s edition of the *Canisian Sections*, vol. II, p. 38. Isidore’s *Exegesis on the Canon of the Mass* was published at Paris in 1548, octavo.

### 21. To Ludifredus, or Leofredus

*To Ludifredus, or Leofredus, bishop of Córdoba: What the Office of a Bishop and of Others Is in the Church*, p. 413, from Ivo and Gratian. The final part is missing there, though it is supplied from a manuscript on p. 486.

A fragment *On Prelates* was published with Goldastus’s notes in 1601, octavo, together with Valerian of Cemelium’s sermon *On the Good of Discipline*.

### 22. Theological Sentences

*Three Books of Theological Sentences*, largely excerpted from the *Moralia* of Gregory the Great, p. 414, with the notes of García de Loaysa on pp. 427, 452, and 478, from the Turin edition of 1593, quarto.

They contain much erudition. Yet Loaysa shows himself entirely lacking in critical judgment when he writes on p. 483:

> Even in our most ulcerated times, Oecolampadius’s volume against the Sacrament of the Eucharist is attributed to Bertram the presbyter, addressed to Charlemagne; Carolostadius’s work against images to Charlemagne himself; and a certain book of Calvin to Alcuin, Charlemagne’s teacher.

In older editions Isidore’s books are entitled *On the Supreme Good*, because they begin with the words, “God is the supreme good”: Leuven 1486, quarto, by Johann of Westphalia; Leipzig 1493; and without place or year, in duodecimo. See Theophilus Sincerus, *News of Old and Rare Books*, p. 163. It also appeared at Paris in 1519, duodecimo, and in 1538.

This seems to be the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* mentioned by Sigebert in chapter 55. For the work attributed to Isidore under this title in the Paris edition of Bignaeus, 1580, has Gennadius of Marseilles as its author.

Isidore is praised for the Catholic faith by Aeneas of Paris in his work *Against the Greeks*; but he means the book mentioned above under no. 19.

From book I of the *Sentences*, chapters 7, 10, and 38ff., the *Book on Converts to Monks* was taken. Canisius published it as though it were previously unedited, vol. V, part II of the *Ancient Readings*, p. 305 (new edition, vol. II, part II, p. [Col. 0063C] 153), as Constantine Cajetan observed.

### 23. Six Letters

Six letters, p. 486: two to Braulio, one while he was archdeacon and the other after he had become bishop; a third to Helladius and other bishops; a fourth to Claudius the duke; a fifth to Redemptus the archdeacon; and a sixth to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo.

They also appear in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, April, p. 343ff.

The most learned men regard the fifth, concerning the use of unleavened bread in the Western Church, as suspect. See Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 264. Oudinus rejects the fourth and sixth, vol. I, p. 1592ff.; Dallaeus, *On the Religious Worship of the Latins* III, 2, p. 296; and W. E. Tentzelius, *On the Athanasian Creed*, p. 53ff.

### 24. Rule of Monks

*Twenty-three Chapters of the Rule of Monks*, addressed to the Honorian coenobites, p. 490.

It is the same as that in Holstenius’s *Code of Rules*, Rome 1661, quarto, p. 118, and Paris 1663, quarto. The final chapter, *A Sentence on the Rule of Devout Women*, appears in Edmund Martene, vol. IX of the *Ancient Monuments*, p. 160.

### 25. On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues

*Book on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, p. 497. It was read in an inappropriate place among the works of Saint Ambrose, Augustine, and Leo the Great.

See Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 265. He prefers to attribute it to Ambrose Autpertus, as Oudinus also favors, vol. I, p. 1596.

Notes of learned men on Isidore’s works, collected and enlarged by Johann Grial, pp. 523, 618.

### 26. Book of Glosses

*Book of Glosses*, collected from various glossaries circulated under Isidore’s name, pp. 618, 631.

It also appeared together with the Greek-Latin glosses of Philoxenus and [Col. 0064A] others, in the recension of Bonaventura Vulcanius, Leiden 1600, folio; and among the writers of the Latin language reviewed by Dionysius Gothofredus, Geneva 1595, 1602, 1622, quarto; and with the annotations of Jean-Louis de la Cerda in his *Sacred Adversaria*, Leiden 1626, folio, chapter 141, p. 317ff.; and most recently illustrated by the learned observations of Johann Georg Graevius, together with the *Supplement to the Glossaries* and the collections of Theodor Jansson van Almeloveen, and with Matthias Martini’s *Philological Lexicon*, published for the third time, Utrecht 1698, folio. Some copies refer to Amsterdam 1701.

## Writings Missing from the Most Recent Edition of Isidore’s Works

*Brief Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings.* See above, [Col. 0064B] no. 12.

*Sentence on the Rule of Devout Women.* Above, no. 24.

Fragment *On Prelates*, above, no. 21.

*Exegesis on the Canon of the Mass*, above, no. 20.

An anonymous writer of Melk, chapter 26, says that Isidore transmitted to posterity many sermons delivered at different times and written in an excellent style. Johann Stephan Ferrerius saw a sermon for the feast of Saint Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli, in manuscript in the archive of the Church of Vercelli.

*The Life and Deeds of Three Holy Bishops, Lights of the Benedictine Order—Isidore of Hispalis, Ildefonsus of Toledo, and Gregory, Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia—Illustrated with Scholia.* Some little works by the same Isidore, previously unpublished, were added, Rome 1616, quarto, under the care of Constantine Cajetan of Syracuse: namely, [Col. 0064C] a brief sermon for the day of the Nativity of the Lord, and another on the holy angels; fragments of commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, concerning which see Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 268; *On Converts to Monks*, above, no. 3; and a prayer or confession, which Johann Tamaius Salazar published again in vol. II of the *Hispanic Martyrology*.

A double hymn in praise of Saint Agatha appears in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, February 5, p. 596. One begins, “Come, most faithful people.” The other begins, “A notable feast has appeared.”

An *Exposition of the Prophet Daniel* and *On Susanna* exist in manuscript in the Leiden Library. See the catalogue, p. 329.

A commentary on the Song of Songs, read among the works of Gregory the Great, is attributed to Isidore in certain manuscripts.

A *Book on the Order of Creatures*, addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome—that is, Zaragoza—was published by D’Achery, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 268 (new edition, vol. I, p. 225). See Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 266, where he investigates how the name “Zaragoza” could have appeared under the name “Rome.”

A *Book on the Miracles of Christ*: Nicolás Antonio, p. 267, from the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 223.

*On the Holy Trinity*, Trithemius.

*On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, the same author.

Boxhornius promised to publish a fragment *On the Institution of the Lenten Fast* in his notes on Claudius Albinus of Spartianus. But perhaps it was identical with book I, chapter 36, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

*On the Parts of Speech*, manuscript in the library of Charles de Montchal; [Col. 0065A] perhaps not different from certain chapters of the first book of the *Etymologies*.

Likewise, *On Numbers*, which Braulio mentions from the third book, and *On Heresies*, from the eighth book. I also think that the *Book on the Names of the Law and the Gospels* and the *Book on the Mysteries of the Savior* are concealed under nos. 13, 14, and 15.

Pseudo-Luitprand, in his *Adversaria*, p. 486, says that he had seen Isidore’s *Book of Prophecies* written in Latin, Gothic, the Spanish vernacular, and Arabic.

Lucas of Tuy, in his *Life*, chapter 5, p. 340, mentions some *Alphabet of Papias’ Judgments* [Note: [Col. 0065C] Or “of patronymics”?], and an alphabet of verbal and theological distinctions, an alphabet of books, and of prayer.

Braulio and the writer of the *Life*, chapter 9, vol. I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, p. 347, mention a synodal address delivered at the Council of Hispalis in A.D. 636, shortly before Isidore’s death, in which he condemned the heresy of Arius and the superstition of the Acephalites.

It is not sufficiently established that the Missal and Breviary prescribed by Isidore for the Hispanic churches were his work. Learned men also doubt whether the Mozarabic or Mixtarabic liturgy should be attributed to Isidore. Compare W. E. Tentzelius, *On the Rite of Sacred Readings*, § 54.

They also teach that the twelve books of Visigothic laws, published by Pierre Pithou, Paris 1579, folio, in Friedrich Lindenbrog’s *Code of Ancient Laws*, and in the third volume of *Hispania illustrata*, were collected only after Isidore. Compare Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, pp. 269–270.

Concerning the *Collection of Canons, Councils, and Decretal Letters*, still, as they say, unpublished, and certainly different [Col. 0065C] from that of Isidore Mercator, see what I noted in vol. XI of the *Greek Library*, pp. 13ff. and 66, and Nicolás Antonio, vol. I, p. 270ff.

Allegorical commentaries on several books of the Old Testament, and all the literal commentaries, have perished. See above, no. 14.

I ask the indulgence of fair-minded readers if here I place before their eyes the oldest copy of Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies* that I have ever heard of or read, preserved in the Malatesta Library at Cesena. I believe the book was written in the seventh century.

It contains twenty-five books, [Col. 0066A] namely, five more than the number presented by the printed editions. This difference does not arise because anything has been added beyond the printed text, but solely from a different arrangement of the work.

It is arranged as follows. The first four books are as in the printed editions, except that book IV, chapter 13, *On the Beginning of Medicine*, is absent.

In book V, Isidore’s *Chronicle* varies somewhat; in this manuscript it begins, “The order of times.”

The remaining books proceed in step with the printed editions through chapter 26 of book XVIII. But in the printed editions the beginning of chapter 27 is, in the manuscript, the beginning of book XIX.

Then chapter 20 of book XVIII in the printed editions is there book XX. Book XXI begins with chapter 52 of book XVIII. Book XXII is chapter 60 of book XVIII. Book XXIII begins with chapter 7 of book XIX. Book XXIV begins with chapter 20 of book XIX. Finally, the whole of book XXV is joined to book XX [Col. 0066B] of the printed editions.

Those additions which are separately given in the Paris edition of 1601, p. 269, are also found here, though not all are written in the margin, such as “talent,” etc.; “mina,” etc.; “obol,” etc.; “shekel,” etc. These additions are in another and somewhat more recent hand than everything else.

There are some variants of no little importance, which lack of time prevented me from recording with greater diligence. I neglected only one thing. Where the printed edition, book XIX, chapter 19, reads “Canterium, Gallaia, Guvia,” the manuscript has “Cauteria Lingulina.”

Finally, at the end of the book, the following verses are read in the same hand as the rest:

> As it is labor for farmers to cleave the lands with the ploughshare,  
>   
> So my reed pen is for furrowing fallow fields.  
>   
> It rejoices also to behold the roasted harvests,  
>   
> So I too rejoice to bring the chosen verse to its conclusion. [Col. 0066C]

I found the books *On Offices* in another manuscript from Lucca, written in the eighth century, and observed that the final two chapters were missing there as well—the same chapters absent from Hittorp’s edition. There too, in the same words with which Hittorp’s printed edition concludes the entire work, it likewise ends.

Finally, I certainly must not omit that the distinguished Cajetanus Cenni published at Rome in 1741 a collection of Isidorian canons; in the preface, by arguments he adduces, he also demonstrates that it is genuinely the work of Isidore of Hispalis.

[Col. 0065]

## Testimonies Concerning Saint Isidore of Hispalis

### Saint Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza: Preface to the Books of the Lord Isidore

Isidore, an outstanding man and bishop of the Church of Hispalis, successor to and brother of Bishop Leander, flourished during the time of the emperor Maurice and King Reccared. In him antiquity claimed something for itself—or rather, in him our own age imagined the knowledge of antiquity. He was formed in every kind of expression, so that he could be suitable to the unlearned and the learned according to the quality of his speech; and, with an incomparable eloquence appropriate to every occasion and place, he was renowned.

How great he was in wisdom, the prudent reader will readily understand from his various studies and carefully wrought little works. Finally, I have recorded the following works that have come to our knowledge.

He published two books of *Differences*, in which, with subtle discrimination, he distinguished in meaning things that are commonly expressed confusedly.

He published one book of *Prologues*, in which he briefly indicated what each book of Holy Scripture contains.

He published one book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, in which he noted, with concise statements, their deeds, dignity, death, and burial.

To his brother [Col. 0067A] Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi, he addressed two books *On Offices*, in which, interpreting in his own style and not without the authority of the Fathers, he derived the origin of the Offices and the reason why each is performed in the Church of God.

He published two books of *Synonyms*, by which, through exhortation aided by reason, he raised the soul toward consolation and the hope of receiving forgiveness.

He published one book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to King Sisebut, in which he clarified certain obscure matters concerning the elements, both from the investigations of ecclesiastical teachers and from those of philosophers.

He published one book *On Numbers*, in which he touched in part upon the discipline of arithmetic because of the numbers inserted into the ecclesiastical Scriptures.

He published one book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, in which he showed what the persons mentioned signify mystically.

He published one book *On Heresies*, in which, following the examples of the Fathers, he collected at whatever length he could, in concise form, material that was widely dispersed.

He published three books of *Sentences*, which he adorned with flowers gathered from the books of Pope Gregory’s *Moralia*.

He published one book of *Chronicles*, collected with excessive brevity from the beginning of the world down to his own time.

At the request of his virgin sister Florentina, he published two books *Against the Jews*, in which he confirmed from the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets everything that the Catholic faith believes.

He published one book *On Illustrious Men*, to which we added the following.

He published one book, *The Rule of Monastic Life*, which he most suitably adapted for the use of the homeland and for the minds of the weak.

He published one book, a *History of the Origin of the Goths, the Kingdom of the Suevi, and also the Vandals*.

He published two books of *Questions*, in which anyone who reads them recognizes a great storehouse of the ancient commentators.

He published a book of *Etymologies*, immense in size, divided by titles but not by books. Because he made it at my request, although he left it unfinished, I divided it into twenty books. Whoever reads this work, wholly suited to philosophy, with frequent meditation, will rightly be no stranger to knowledge of divine and human affairs.

There an elegant abundance of diverse arts overflows, and he collected in compressed form almost everything that ought to be known.

There are also many other little works by this man, inscribed in the Church of God with great distinction.

When God raised him up in the latter days, after so many disasters of Spain—I believe to restore the monuments of the ancients, lest we grow old altogether in rusticity—he placed him there like a kind of signpost. To him we rightly apply that philosophical saying:

> “We, wandering and straying in our own city like foreigners and guests, were led home by your books, as though to our own house, so that at last we might recognize both who we were and where we were. You have disclosed the age of our homeland; you, the descriptions of times; you, the laws of sacred things; you, the offices of priests; you, domestic and public discipline; you, the names, kinds, duties, and causes of dwellings, regions, and places; you, the names, kinds, duties, and causes of all divine and human affairs.”

The synodal proceedings held before him at Hispalis declare with what torrent of eloquence and with how many darts of the divine Scriptures and testimonies of the Fathers he pierced the heresy of the Acephalites. In that assembly he asserted the truth against Gregory, the head of the aforementioned heresy.

He died in the time of the emperor Heraclius and the most Christian King Chintila, superior to all in sound doctrine and richer than all in works of charity. [Col. 0068A]

### From Saint Ildefonsus, Bishop of Toledo, *On Illustrious Men*

After his brother Leander, Isidore held the chair of the province of Baetica at the see of Hispalis. He was a man distinguished alike by beauty and intellect. For in speaking he obtained such an abundant wealth of charm that the admirable richness of his speech became a source of astonishment to his hearers; once they had heard him, no one commended what he had heard without repeatedly hearing it again.

He wrote works both excellent and substantial, namely: a book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*; a book of *Lamentation*, which he himself called *Synonyms*; two little books addressed to his sister Florentina *Against the Wickedness of the Jews*; a book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to Prince Sisebut; a book of *Differences*; and a book of *Sentences*.

He also collected from various authors what he himself calls *Expositions of the Secret Mysteries*. When these were brought together into one work, the book is called *Questions*.

Finally, at the request of Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, he wrote a book of *Etymologies*. Although he attempted to complete it for many years, he seems to have brought his final day to a close while engaged upon the work.

He flourished during the reigns of Reccared, Liuvanius, Witteric, Gundemar, Sisebut, Suinthila, and Sisenand. He held the honor of the episcopate for approximately forty years, together with a distinguished reputation and beauty of holy learning.

### From Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Illustrious Men*

Isidore the Younger, bishop of Hispalis, wrote many works. [Col. 0068C]

He wrote twenty books of *Etymologies* to Braulio, the bishop.

He wrote a book of *Prologues* on the books of the Old and New Testament received by the Catholic Church into the canon; a book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, addressed to Fulgentius; a book *On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Holy Fathers* who are praised in Scripture; a book *On the Meanings of Names*, addressed to Orosius; and a book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to Sisebut.

He also wrote a book *On Differences of Words*; a book *On the Properties of Things*; a book of *Sermons*; and a book of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

He wrote *Synonyms*, in which two persons are introduced: one a lamenting human being, the other Reason giving admonition.

He also wrote a *Lament of the Penitent*, arranged alphabetically and supplemented with a prayer.

He wrote one book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*; one book *On the Mysteries of the Savior*.

He went through the entire Old Testament by giving a straightforward exposition.

He also wrote other works belonging to secular literature, which it is no concern of ours to enumerate.

### The Death of Blessed Isidore, Recorded by Redemptus the Cleric

It seemed to me that I should briefly explain to your holiness how my lord Isidore, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Hispalis, of blessed memory, received penance and made his confession before God and men; or how he migrated from this world to heaven. I wished to make this known to your affection in the faithful style of my account.

This matter first compelled me, on account of the concern that you offer him out of love, to give thanks to your charity; then, because I cannot suppress the truth, and because, at your request, I am compelled to relate what I have been able to gather concerning him—little from much.

When, by some destiny, he was already looking toward his end, and the nature of his soul subtly foresaw that his body was wearied by constant illness, he distributed to the poor each day for nearly six months, or longer, such a large alms—more than he had been accustomed to give—that from sunrise until evening many remained waiting to receive the assistance.

After this he was struck by a wound, so that while the fever grew strong in his body, his weakened stomach rejected food.

He recovered sufficiently for penance and immediately summoned his fellow bishops, namely the most blessed John and Apartius, to be present.

As he was brought from his cell to the basilica of Saint Vincent the martyr, all the crowds of poor people, clerics, religious persons of every kind, and all the common people of the city received him with cries and great wailing, so that if anyone possessed a heart of iron, it would immediately melt into tears, and he would become wholly lamentation.

When he was placed in the middle of the choir of the aforesaid martyr’s basilica, near the altar rail, he ordered the crowds of women to stand farther away, so that when he himself received penance, only men—not women—would be seen around him.

And when, by the aforesaid priests, one was placing a hair shirt upon him and the other was … [lacuna] ashes upon him, he stretched out his hand toward heaven and began as follows:

> You, God, who know the hearts of men, and who, when the Publican stood far away and struck his breast, deigned to forgive his sins; who, on the fourth day, after the dissolution of the flesh, deigned to raise Lazarus, who was sleeping, from the tomb, and wished the bosom of the patriarch Abraham to receive him: receive my confession at this hour, and remove from your eyes the sins that I have accumulated beyond number. Do not remember my evils, and do not recall the sins of my youth.
>
> You, Lord, did not impose penance upon the righteous who have not sinned against you, but upon me, a sinner who have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea. May the ancient enemy find nothing in me to punish.
>
> You know that after I, wretched man, came unworthily into this holy Church, more as a burden than as an honor, I never allowed myself to sin; yet I labored to act wickedly.
>
> And because you said, “Whenever the sinner turns back from his ways, you will consign all his iniquities to oblivion,” I remember this command of yours.
>
> I cry out to you with hope and confidence, though I am not worthy, because of the multitude of sins that dwell within me, to look upon your heavens. Be present and receive my prayer, and grant me, a sinner, the forgiveness I ask.
>
> But if the heavens are not clean in your sight, how much less am I, a human being who have drunk iniquity like water and swallowed sin like colostrum. [Col. 0069D–0070A]

After these things had been completed, he received the body and blood of the Lord from the bishops themselves, with a profound groaning of heart, judging himself unworthy.

Then he begged forgiveness from those same priests, from all who belonged to the clergy, from the citizens, and from all the people, saying:

> I entreat you, my most holy lords and priests, and you, the holy congregation of clergy and people, to offer your prayer to the Lord for me, wretched and full of every filth of sin; so that although by my own merit I am not worthy to obtain God’s mercy, through your intercession I may deserve to obtain forgiveness for my sins.
>
> Forgive me, I beg you, though unworthy, whatever I have committed against each of you: if I have despised anyone through hatred; if I have wickedly rejected anyone from the fellowship of charity; if I have stained anyone by my counsel; if I have injured anyone through anger. Forgive me now that I ask—indeed, now that I repent.

When all had asked for indulgence for him with one voice, and had remitted to each person the bonds or written obligations of what was owed, he again admonished those standing around him, saying:

> My most holy lords, the bishops, and all who are present: I beg and beseech you to show charity toward one another, not returning evil for evil.
>
> Do not wish to become whisperers among the people. May the ancient enemy find nothing in you to punish. May the ravening wolf not find anything abandoned by you that he can carry away; rather, may the shepherd rejoice to carry the sheep rescued from the wolf’s mouth upon his shoulders back to this fold.

After this confession and prayer, he immediately ordered the remaining money to be given to the needy and poor.

Who could doubt that he was immediately, after every crime had been forgiven, joined to the company of the angels?

Meanwhile, he arranged to be kissed by everyone, saying:

> If with all your heart you forgive the wrongs and evils that I have inflicted upon you up to this time, the Almighty Creator will forgive you all your sins, so that the water of the sacred font, which the devout people will receive today, may be for you unto the remission of sins; and let this kiss between me and you remain as a testimony for the future.

When all these things had been completed, he was led back to his cell. On the fourth day after his confession or penance, he continually fulfilled his pastoral care and completed his end in peace.

Amen.

On the day before the Kalends of April, the nineteenth day of the moon, Spanish Era 674.

[Col. 0070D]

### From the Eighth Council of Toledo, Chapter 2

“Also the distinguished teacher of our age, the final glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him, not inferior in learning, and—what is greater—most learned at the end of the ages, and to be named with reverence: Isidore.”

[Col. 0069]

## J. Grial’s Admonition Concerning the Books of the *Etymologies*
Origins of words, whether they remain within the bounds of grammar, or roam more widely in the pursuit of philosophy, or follow both paths—as Saint Isidore did—deal with a subject full of perilous uncertainty. This has been experienced not only by Plato and Varro and the Stoics (whom we know from Cicero to have been especially devoted to this matter), but also by nearly all the most serious writers among our own people. Yet the fault lies not with them, but with those who have not sufficiently grasped what they intended. The chief point is this: since, as Varro says, every word has two aspects of nature—the thing from which, and the thing upon which, a name is imposed—grammarians concern themselves with the former, while the latter belongs more properly to philosophers. Many who enter upon the first method and devote themselves to this discipline, called ἐτυμολογικὴ, repeatedly show themselves difficult and captious: reducing everything to syllables and letters, they cannot restrain themselves from concealing any slight deviation. Those, however, who propose the other method—which Varro likewise calls περὶ σημαινομένων—while intent on teaching and presenting the things themselves to the eyes, seize only occasional opportunities in words and strive to shed light not so much upon words as upon things: these, because they take little care to appear grammatical, fall under the judgment of the less learned, although for the most part they are far more skillful in this very matter than those who profess this one art, provided only that they apply their minds to the method which they profess seriously to know.

Who could believe that matters obvious to the most insignificant grammarians escaped the parents and discoverers of all the sciences so completely that they so often offered themselves up to be mocked by the most frivolous men? Or will anyone believe that Cicero was persuaded that *tumultus* was “much fear,” that Sulpicius believed *testamentum* to be “a testimony of the mind,” or that Tertullian thought *limus* was “a rich liquid”? Or that anyone would suppose that Sylvester and the Fathers of the Roman synod thought that *curia* was named from blood? It would be superfluous to heap together examples from Plato, Varro, and Jerome. The first two have long been generally discredited on this matter; Jerome, however, acknowledges this fault—if indeed it is a fault—in such a way as to forgive himself, for otherwise he would not so often have admitted it in his own case, assigning Hebrew explanations so violently to Greek and Latin names, to use his own expression.

“Were the most serious men playing?” you will say. I do not deny it. I maintain only that they achieved this: whenever they wished to be thought to have been playing, they appeared to less prudent people to have fallen disgracefully into error. But again, whether one calls these things games or absurdities, I say that they are not without benefit and usefulness. For no fair-minded judge of such matters will deny that they either unravel what is confused, bring what is obscure into the open, or make what is known and manifest more sharply stimulating to the senses.

Isidore says that *mantum*—which Suidas says is a Spanish garment—was so named because it covers only the hands. Our present use of the garment, however, shows that it has become more extensive, since it now covers not only the hands but the feet as well. From his own Servius—for he had worn out no other book by reading so thoroughly—he knew that a *lorica* was a covering made from leather. He preferred to call it “devoid of straps” (*loris carentem*), in order to turn the reader’s mind and eyes away from the *lorica*, which had long fallen out of use, toward armour joined with iron rings. There are hundreds of examples of this kind.

Those who have written about definitions, although they honor as worthy of the name of true definition one definition that comes closest to the nature of the thing, nevertheless do not disdain the others so completely that they fail diligently to seek out their many kinds—for Victorinus and Boethius handed down fifteen, or even more. Why, then, if you ask, do they so strongly reject explanations and descriptions that unravel words? What reason do they give, unless perhaps that they resent such deviations appearing more plainly in the play of words than in the play of things? Yet they appear with less danger, and sometimes with no less profit. If ever this saying of Horace is plainly true, it is true here:

> The ridiculous cuts through great matters  
> More forcefully and more effectively than the sharp.

But let us return to Isidore. Since he had carefully read through every kind of writing, he judged it best to open a short and easy road to all the disciplines for the people of a comparatively unlearned age: to provide at once a knowledge of things and of words, and, wherever possible, to show everything by dwelling upon the words themselves. Nothing seemed more suitable than that, by disentangling the meanings of words, he should display their proper use, while the things designated by those words, once their sound had been heard, should appear before the eyes and remain there like a kind of phantom and image.

In doing this, he certainly took many origins and explanations from ancient writers; but, following their example—for it was advantageous and convenient to him—he did not fear to offer new ones as well, and to play a similar game. I mean the example of those whose negligence he desired to imitate, caring little for the obscure diligence of petty critics. If they had paid attention to anything they might criticize in him, they would have raged against him less often and less boldly. They are plainly ridiculous themselves when they laugh at many things that turn out to have belonged, in substantial part, to the very authors whom they venerate and whom our author used as authorities. I hope that they will now be fairer when they see many things which they used to greet with laughter as “Isidorian” restored to more ancient authors.

If Saint Isidore had either completed this work himself or if later readers had not enlarged it with very great damage, we might perhaps not despair of freeing him almost entirely from blame. The work itself bears witness that it was collected from the recollection of ancient reading; and he expressly declares that he does not wish to answer for the faults of others. But now, since the author’s finishing hand was absent, and Braulio interpolated and arranged the work—as some think—and since readers, believing that this volume contained for their time a sufficiently large and sufficiently elegant store of books, poured into it whatever they could find elsewhere, while scribes, seeing anything written in the margin of the page, each eagerly inserted it into the text as he saw fit, should we exploit so many faults of others to bring Isidore into disrepute? To see what they criticize in him, it will be worthwhile to set out the main charges.

“They assign Greek origins to Latin words and Latin origins to Greek words. They wish earlier forms to derive from later ones. They pay no attention to orthography. They count vowel lengthings of words among stems and roots. In place of certain origins, they arbitrarily substitute other origins that serve their meanings.” I believe all the accusations can be reduced to this summary. Unless I show that these faults are shared by him with the best authors, I shall not plead his cause, and he may bear what he deserves.

I shall not use many examples, since anyone can easily gather an immense forest of them from the places indicated. No one doubts that *ars* and *orator* are Latin words. Yet Festus held that *ars* was ἀρετὴν, “virtue,” and *orator* was ἀρητῆρα, “speaker.” How many things did Varro derive in the same way, even from those which, as he says, “do not creep in both fields”? What of those among our own writers who said that *Jesus* was ἴασιν, “healing,” and *Cephas* κεφαλὴν, “head,” although they knew the certain origins and interpretations of these names from the Gospel? And what men were they!

Isidore derived *quattuor* (“four”) from *quadratus* (“square”), although it seems simple and obvious that *quadratus* comes from *quattuor*. Did Ulpian not similarly derive *ius* (“law”) from *iustitia* (“justice”)? “He pays no attention to orthography.” What of the man who teaches that *hortus* (“garden”) comes from *oriri* (“to rise”), *hedera* (“ivy”) from *edere* (“to eat”), or from *haerere* (“to cling”)? That man is Festus Pompeius.

Who, in this game, did not treat lengthenings as stems, as Sulpicius did with *testamentum* and Aquillius with *postliminium*? I believe there was absolutely no one who practiced this game who did not do so. What can one do with those who object to the substitution of origins when their purpose is to make meanings more evident, except order them to weep among the grammarians’ chairs? For when Servius derives *sinister* (“left”), in relation to augury, and *senator*, in relation to the power of deliberating, from *sinere* (“to allow”), does he not knowingly and deliberately conceal another explanation?

What of the fact that sometimes the nature of the matter itself compels this procedure? Varro denies that *germanus* (“brother”) means “springing from the same germ,” and says that it means “flowing from the same mother.” What if an explanation serves dignity or honor, or suggests something better than the words themselves seem to present? Did the same Varro not know that *culina* (“kitchen”), which he said was located in the rear part of a house, was named from the rear part of an animal? He preferred to derive it from *colere* (“to cultivate” or “tend”) the fire. Was it obscure to Isidore that *medicina* (“medicine”) came from *mederi* (“to heal”)? He turned it away from *modus* (“measure”) so that he might show what its use ought to be.

But they persist in their cries and press the matter: etymologies and veriloquia—expressions of true origins—which are neither etymologies nor veriloquia, should never have been called by those names; and therefore the books should not have been entitled *Etymologies*. As though Galen had not called etymology “the arrogant witness” (ἀλαζὼν μάρτυς ἡ ἐτυμολογία)!

But the most holy man plainly seems to have labored to indicate a work of exceptional usefulness and, for those times, of immense labor in a very brief and, so to speak, meager form. Thus he wished works filled with the learning of many things to be called *Books of Etymologies*, as though they contained only names; or at least, when he had advanced farther, he wrote to Braulio that he was sending him a work on the origin of certain things. What more modest or restrained title could have been devised?

He therefore achieved this: up to the present day, posterity has continually acknowledged and loudly proclaimed that from these books it possesses knowledge not merely of certain things, but, I might almost say, of all things and words.

[Col. 0073]

# The Twenty Books of the Etymologies of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville (C, S)

## 1. Preface

To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio, Isidore.

Here, as I promised, I have sent you a work on the origin of certain things, collected from the recollection of ancient reading and annotated in certain places just as it stands written in the style of our forebears.

# Book One: On Grammar

## Chapter One: On Discipline and Art

[Col. 0073]

### 1

[Note: “Discipline” from *discere*. These are the words of Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 2.]

*Disciplina* (“discipline”) takes its name from *discere* (“to learn”); hence it may also be called knowledge. For *scire* (“to know”) is said to derive from *discere*, because none of us knows except the one who learns.

It is otherwise called *disciplina* because it is learned in full.

[Note: “Because it is learned in full.” There is no force of *plenus* in *disciplina*, since *plina* is merely a lengthening of the verb. But just as such playful explanations do not demand to be commended under the true and sincere name of etymologies, so anyone who immediately rejects them with disdain as entirely foolish or empty would himself be excessively harsh, beyond what is fair and good.]

### 2

Art (*ars*) is so called because it consists in the precepts and rules of an art.

[Note: “Because it consists in the precepts of an art.” It is established that the ancients wrote *artis* for *arctis*. Valerius Probus distinguishes *artus* (“narrow”) from *arctus* (“contracted, bent in the limbs”) solely by inflection. Festus says: “Artisans (*artifices*) are so called because they skillfully join their works together; for this reason they are also called arts (*artes*).”]

[Note: “Others say.” Donatus, in his commentary on *Andria*, and Servius, in the second book of Donatus’s *Art*. Varro, book 4: “Some nouns,” he says, “have roots in both languages, like trees which, growing on the boundary, spread into both fields.”]

Others say that this word was taken from the Greeks, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς, that is, from *virtus*, “virtue,” which they called knowledge.

### 3

[Note: “Between art and discipline.” Aristotle distinguishes art from knowledge in the same way.]

Plato and Aristotle wished there to be a distinction between art and discipline, saying that art concerns things which can also be otherwise, whereas discipline concerns things that cannot occur otherwise. When something is discussed through true demonstrations, it will be called discipline; when something probable and open to opinion is treated, it will bear the name of art.

## Chapter Two: On the Seven Liberal Arts

### 1

There are seven disciplines of the liberal arts.

The first is grammar, that is, skill in speaking.

The second is rhetoric, which, because of the polish and abundance of its eloquence, is considered especially necessary in civil disputes.

The third is dialectic, also called logic, which by extremely subtle arguments distinguishes truth from falsehood.

### 2

The fourth is arithmetic, which contains the causes and divisions of numbers.

[Note: “The causes of numbers.” The Gothic manuscripts correctly read *numerorum causas*; others read *casus*, “cases.”]

The fifth is music, which consists in poems and songs.

The sixth is geometry, which embraces measurements and dimensions.

[Note: “Measurements.” Only two manuscripts from Tarragona have *mensuras terrae*, “measurements of land.” That word is absent from the others. If one considers not so much the etymology as the subject itself, which is more generally applicable, we shall reject it without difficulty. “Geometry,” he says in book 2, chapter 25, “is the measurement of immovable magnitude and of forms,” although in book 3, chapter 10, he gives the true explanation of the name.]

The seventh is astronomy, which contains the law of the stars.

## Chapter Three: On the Common Letters

### 1

The beginnings of the art of grammar are the common letters,

[Note: “Which scribes.” Augustine, *On Order*, book 2, chapter 12, after discussing letters, adds the following: “Thus the usefulness of counting was noticed under great necessity. Once these two things had been discovered, there arose the profession of scribes and reckoners, as it were a kind of infancy of the art of grammar, which Varro calls *litteratio*.”]

which scribes and reckoners follow; their discipline is, as it were, a kind of infancy of the art of grammar. Hence Varro calls it *litteratio*.

Letters are indicators of things,

[Note: “Signs of words.” Jerome, *On Notations*, letter 34: “And signs of words would precede the speed of the tongue.” And letter 47: “signs and thefts of words.”]

signs of words, possessing such power that through them the spoken words of absent people speak to us without a voice.

Do they introduce words through the eyes rather than through the ears?

[Note: “For they introduce.” These words are absent from certain Gothic manuscripts.]

### 2

The use of letters was discovered for the sake of preserving things in memory. For, lest they escape through forgetfulness, they are bound to letters. Amid such great variety of things, not everything could be learned by hearing, nor could everything be contained in memory.

### 3

[Note: “Letters, as it were *legiterae*.” This is not found in any Gothic manuscript, but it occurs in Priscian and Sergius.]

Letters are called *litterae*, as it were *legiterae*, either because they provide a path for readers or because they are repeated in reading.

### 4

Latin and Greek letters seem to have arisen from the Hebrews.

[Note: “Among them ... *Aleph*.” From Epiphanius, *On Weights*, book 1.]

For among them the letter was first called *aleph*; then, from a similar pronunciation, the name *alpha* was taken among the Greeks, and likewise *a* among the Latins. Thus the translator created a letter from a similar sound in another language,

[Note: “So that we may know ... the mother.” These are the words of Jerome, *Commentary on Zephaniah*, chapter 3.]

so that we may know that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages and letters.

But the Hebrews use twenty-two letters according to the books of the Old Testament; the Greeks use twenty-four; the Latins, advancing between the two languages, have twenty-three letters.

### 5

[Note: “The letters of the Hebrews.” The same things are transmitted concerning various groups of inventors of letters; Crinitus reports them in book 17 of *On Honest Studies*.]

The Hebrews’ letters began with the Law through Moses,

[Note: “Here a word in a personal construction seems to be missing. Isidore used this ellipsis more than once, as will be clear to the reader. —Editor.”]

while those of the Syrians and Chaldeans began through Abraham.

[Note: “Hence, since with the Hebrews.” From Jerome, *Galeated Prologue*.]

Hence they agree with the Hebrews both in number and in sound, differing only in their characters.

The Egyptian letters were discovered and handed down to the Egyptians by Queen Isis, daughter of Inachus, who came from Greece into Egypt.

[Note: “Daughter of Inachus.” Isidore followed Augustine, *City of God*, book 18, chapter 3; Augustine followed Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 1. Suidas also testifies in his collections that some Greeks held the same opinion.]

[Note: “Among the Egyptians.” There is no need to introduce here the monstrous Greek letters that appear in the Gothic manuscripts. It should be enough that Antonius, Augustine, Petrus Chacon, and Vulcanius made conjectures in the same way. Especially since Herodotus’s words, which I shall quote from book 2, leave no room for doubt: “The Egyptians use two kinds of letters, and they call some of them sacred and others popular.” See Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 5.]

Among the Egyptians, they say, the priests had one kind of letters and the common people another: the priests’ were called ἱεραί, “sacred,” and the common people’s πανδήμοι, “common to all.”

The Phoenicians were the first to discover the use of Greek letters, and hence Lucan writes:

> The Phoenicians first—if fame may be believed—dared  
> To mark a lasting voice with crude figures.

[Col. 0076A]

### 6

Hence also the headings of books are written in Phoenician color,

[Note: “Cadmus, son of Agenor.” Pliny, book 7, chapter 56. Yet Isidore’s assignment of the letters does not agree sufficiently either with Pliny or with Georgius Cedrenus.]

because the letters had their beginning with the Phoenicians.

Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the first to bring seventeen Greek letters from Phoenicia into Greece:

α, β, γ, δ, ε, ζ, ι, κ, λ, μ, ν, ο, π, ρ, σ, τ, φ.

[Note: “To these Palamedes added three: η, χ, ω.” I would prefer, following Servius on *Aeneid* 2, θ, φ, χ. Pliny also assigns the same three to him, adding a fourth, ξ.]

During the Trojan War, Palamedes added three to these: η, χ, ω.

[Note: “After him, Simonides Melicus.” Pliny likewise says that four were added by Simonides Melicus; his list is ζ, η, ψ, ω. Since P. Chacon saw that Isidore disagreed with Pliny in number, and found three in part of the Gothic manuscripts and likewise three in another part, while Suidas and Eustathius called Simonides “Melicertes” διὰ τὸ ἡδὺ, “because of the sweetness,” he thought that the reading should be *Simonides Melicertes*.]

After him Simonides Melicus added three others: Θ, Ψ, Ξ.

### 7

[Note: “The letter Υ.” From Servius, *Aeneid* 6, on the words “hidden in the shadowed tree,” and so forth.]

Pythagoras of Samos first formed the letter Υ as an image of human life. Its lower stroke signifies the first period of life, uncertain and not yet committed either to vices or to virtues. The fork above begins with adolescence: its right branch is difficult but leads toward a blessed life; the left is easier but leads toward ruin and destruction.

Persius speaks of it thus:

> And the letter that traced the Samian branches for you  
> Showed the rising path along the right-hand road.

### 8

Among the Greeks there are five mystical letters.

The first is Υ, which signifies human life, as we have just said.

The second is Θ, which signifies death. For judges used to place this same letter, theta, beside the names of those whom they condemned to execution. It is called *theta* from θανάτου, “of death.” Hence it has a weapon through its middle, that is, the sign of death.

Of it someone says:

> O theta, letter unfortunate far beyond all others!

### 9

The third is T, showing the figure of the Lord’s cross.

[Note: “Showing the figure of the Lord’s cross.” The most learned men rightly think that for this reason the canon of the Mass begins among the Latins with this letter. Jerome, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 9: “In the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans use today, the final letter *tau* has the likeness of a cross.” Thus Jerome; yet this is not equally apparent in the Samaritan alphabet that is commonly circulated. Ambrose, *On Abraham*, chapter 2: “And when he gained victory with three hundred and eighteen men, he counted three hundred and eighteen, so that you may know that not the quantity of the number but the merit of the election was expressed. For he enlisted those whom he judged worthy of the number of the faithful, who would believe in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Greek letter T signifies three hundred; the sum IH expresses eighteen. The Septuagint translated the word itself *tau* as ‘sign’; Caninius, a respectable authority, translated it as ‘cross’ in his *Institutions of the Syriac Language*.”]

Hence in Hebrew it is interpreted as “sign.” Concerning it the angel is told in Ezekiel:

> Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and lament.

[Note: “Upon the foreheads of the men.” This must certainly be read on the basis of the Gothic manuscripts and the Septuagint, which has ἐπὶ τὰ μέτωπα, “upon the foreheads.” The Vulgate has *super frontes*, “upon the foreheads.”]

The remaining two, the highest and the last, are claimed by Christ.

[Note: “But the remaining two.” From Tertullian, *On Monogamy*.]

For he himself is the beginning and he himself the end, saying:

> I am alpha and omega.

Since alpha moves forward as far as omega, and omega in turn folds back toward alpha, they meet in one another, so that the Lord might show in himself both the course of the beginning toward the end and the course of the end toward the beginning.

### 10

Among the Greeks all the letters both form words and represent numbers. For the letter alpha among them is called “one” in numerical notation; when they write beta, it is called “two”; when they write gamma, it is called “three” in their numerical system; when they write delta, it is called “four”; and so all the letters among them have numerical values.

### 11

[Note: “They do not count numbers with letters.” There was no reason to doubt this reading, found in all the Gothic manuscripts; it is astonishing that learned men hesitated over it.]

The Latins, however, do not count numbers with letters,

[Note: “But they merely form words.” After this, most books add the following: “Except for certain letters which indicate numbers by their form, such as I for one, C for one hundred, D for five hundred, L for fifty, M for one thousand, V for five, and X, which in its form signifies a cross and in number ten.” Yet in the Old Lombard manuscript of the distinguished Garsia Loaisa and in the Roman manuscript only this is read: “Except I, which signifies one, and X, which both in its form signifies a cross and in number demonstrates ten.” It is clear that all of this is foreign to the text. There is no doubt that our books were enlarged by someone who omitted no mark resembling the form of a letter. First, the signs that now appear, or even are letters today, were indisputably not letters in former times, but merely numerical signs; letters were made from numerical signs, not numerical signs from letters. Moreover, the sign assigned to one thousand, if it is T, as all the Gothic books present it, was never used by the Latins. Instead they used CIC, or 81.
