I know nevertheless that the Gothic T arose from the accidental joining of the Latin I and an overlying line by scribal error, since the Romans also signified one thousand with this mark; and it is not plausible that Isidore was unaware of this. Furthermore, since he had just said that T represents the figure of the Lord’s cross, it was inappropriate now to attribute this solely to X, when he had also mentioned T. Lucian indeed also regards T as the figure of the cross, when he makes Σ attack T. I know of nothing reported by any Latin concerning X. Add that these same statements about X, which occur in some Gothic manuscripts in the following chapter, are absent from the others and from all printed books. Finally, this would not amount to counting numbers with letters. Anyone who added this passage seems to have noticed the point. He did not except those letters because numbers were counted by means of them, but because their forms indicated numbers. Otherwise, how could one be counted with I, or one hundred with C, or five with V, or ten with X, or any of the items excepted here be counted as numbers?”]

but only form words.

## Chapter Four: On the Latin Letters

[Col. 0077B]

### 1

The nymph Carmentis first handed down the Latin letters to the Italians.

[Note: “Carmentis, however.” From Servius, *Aeneid* 8.]

She was called *Carmentis* because she sang the future in songs. Her proper name, however, was Nicostrata.

### 2

Letters are either common or liberal.

[Note: “Common or liberal.” That is, *letters* means both the marks and signs of the sounds that are written and read, and the subjects and disciplines themselves contained in writing. Thus in the following chapter he will call grammar the origin of the liberal letters. For the manuscripts that have *artium* at that point, rather than *litterarum*, clearly offer an interpretation; in most and oldest manuscripts *litterarum* is read. Likewise in book 14, chapter 4, and book 3 of *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 13: “Common letters are better,” he says, “because they are simpler and pertain only to the humility of readers.” The same point also seems to belong to what he says below in chapter 9, where he says that some expressions belong to grammarians and others to rhetoricians. So Spaniards speak today when we call people *litterati*: we do not mean those skilled in reading and writing—which the ancients called “knowing letters”—but rather those who are well versed in the higher disciplines.]

They are called common because many people use them in common activities, such as writing and reading. They are called liberal because only those who compose books and know how to speak and dictate correctly understand them.

### 3

There are two modes of letters. For they are principally divided into two parts: vowels and consonants.

[Note: “Vowels are.” Augustine, *On Order*, book 2, chapter 12: “He noticed that some sounds of the mouth, released through a varied but controlled opening, flowed forth from the throat as though disentangled and simple, without any collision; others, produced by a different pressure, nevertheless retained some sound in the mouth; while the final ones could not burst forth unless joined to the first. Accordingly, he called these letters, in the order in which they have been set down, vowels, semivowels, and mutes.”]

Vowels are those which are emitted through a direct opening of the throat, in varied ways and without any collision. They are called vowels because they fill out the voice by themselves and form a syllable by themselves, without any consonant attached.

Consonants are produced by a different movement of the tongue or by pressure of the lips. They are called consonants because they do not sound by themselves but sound together with vowels.

### 4

These are divided into two parts: semivowels and mutes.

[Note: “Semivowels, because they possess something half of the vowel.” From Sergius, on the first book of Donatus’s *Art*: “Because they possess something of the voice.” Terentianus expressed the same point in elegant verse. Priscian is especially convincing to us throughout this matter: “Vowels,” he says, “are so called because they complete sounds by themselves, or because without them a vocal letter cannot be pronounced. Semivowels are so called because they do not have a full sound, just as we speak of demigods and half-men, not meaning those who possess half of gods or men, but those who are not fully gods or men. Many terms are named by comparison with things that sound well, as *informis* does not mean one lacking all form, but one badly formed. So mutes are not called such because they are entirely without voice, but because they possess only a small part of a voice.”]

Semivowels are so called because they possess something half of the vowels.

[Col. 0078B]

[Note: “They begin with the vowel E.” This distinguishes them from mutes because, as Priscian says, letters sound more fully when a vowel is placed before them than when it follows them. A vowel precedes semivowels but follows mutes.]

For they begin with the vowel E and end in their natural sound.

Mutes are so called because they cannot burst forth unless vowels are placed after them.

[Note: “For if you remove from them the final sound of the vowel, the enclosed murmur of the letter will sound.” Some people transmitted these words incorrectly, so that they judged them either to be deleted or transferred elsewhere, namely to the semivowels. “For,” they say, “if mutes are called such because they cannot burst forth unless vowels are placed after them, how will the enclosed murmur sound when the vowels are removed?” The answer may be given as follows: Isidore could scarcely have spoken more suitably. He did not say that it was uttered or pronounced, but enclosed; nor did he say that it was a sound, but a murmur. When he added “will sound,” he either lacked the expression by which he could better state what he intended, or there was no danger that he would fail to make his meaning sufficiently clear, since he had called it, whatever it is, not an uttered but an enclosed murmur. That it is something cannot be denied, since shortly afterward he says that mutes begin with their own sound and end in a vowel; therefore there is something with which they begin before reaching the vowel.]

For if you remove from them the final sound of the vowel, the enclosed murmur of the letter will sound.

[Note: “Sounding, half-sounding, and unsounding.” From Victorinus’s *Grammar*.]

The ancients called vowels, semivowels, and mutes *sonae*, *semisonae*, and *insonae*: sounding, half-sounding, and unsounding.

### 5

[Note: “Among the vowels, however ... i and u.” Everything is taken from Donatus.]

Among grammarians, the letters *i* and *u* have various functions.

[Note: “They have various meanings.” Chacon read *assignationes*, “assignments,” instead.]

### 6

For sometimes they are vowels, sometimes semivowels, and sometimes intermediate.

They are vowels because, when placed alone, they form syllables and are joined to other consonants.

They are regarded as consonants because sometimes they have vowels after them in the same syllables, as in *Iuno* and *vates*, and are treated as consonants.

[Note: “They are regarded as consonants.” Nigidius, in Gellius, book 19, final chapter: “If anyone thinks that V precedes in these words—*Valerius, Vennonius, Volusius*—or I in these—*iampridem, iccur, iocum, iocundum*—he will be mistaken, for when these letters precede, they are not even vowels.”]

### 7

They are called intermediate because by nature, when alone, they have a sound midway between the others, as in *illius* and *unius*. When joined to other letters they sound more fully, as in *Ianus* and *vanus*. Alone they sound one way, joined another.

The letter I is sometimes called double because whenever it is found between two vowels, it counts as two consonants, as in *Troia*. Its sound is doubled there.

### 8

[Note: “The letter U also.” From Sergius.]

The letter U is sometimes nothing, because in certain places it is not a consonant, as in *quis*. It is not a vowel, because it follows I; it is not a consonant, because Q precedes it. Therefore, when it is neither a vowel nor a consonant, it is without doubt nothing.

[Note: “The same letter, and the digamma.” Some wish its shape to be an upright F, which suits its name; others make it an inverted F, such as is also seen on inscriptions. I think this inverted form was introduced by Claudius, although Varro used the digamma itself long before Claudius. Claudius seems to have succeeded in bringing that form into use in his own age, but in later centuries the ancient form was restored. Hence Priscian and Donatus consistently write an upright F for the digamma.]

The same letter is also called digamma by the Greeks when it is joined to itself or to other vowels. It is called digamma because it is double, like the letter F, which has two gammas. Grammarians wished joined vowels to be called digamma by analogy with it, as in *votum* and *virgo*.

[Col. 0080A]

### 9

Among the semivowels, some are called liquids, because sometimes, when placed after other consonants in one syllable, they fail,

[Note: “They fail.” This is what *liquescere* means. The Greeks call them ὑγρὰ γράμματα, “liquid letters,” and Terentianus, expressing the same idea, calls them “wet letters.”]

and are excluded from the meter.

[Note: “And are excluded from meter.” For although consonants divide time—“two consonants,” as Terentianus says, “divide one time”—a liquid placed after a mute does not supply a portion of the time. Terentianus teaches this most elegantly:

> If a vowel has in its middle a consonant and a liquid  
> Following it, two letters cannot harass the first.

He gives the reason:

> For the liquid, running beneath it, helps the middle not at all.]

Of these, two become liquid among the Latins: L and R, as in *fragor* and *flatus*.

[Note: “The remaining M and N are liquids among the Greeks.” So also do many others. Sergius, by contrast, says: “If liquids are preceded by one another, they lose the rights of liquids, as in *Mnestheus*.”]

The remaining M and N become liquid among the Greeks, as in *Mnestheus*.

### 10

The ancient writing system consisted of seventeen Latin letters.

[Note: “Hence they are also called legitimate.” This is the reading of all the Gothic manuscripts. Chacon retained the common reading, “hence also Latin,” from Donatus: “Hence some think that the Latin letters are no more than seventeen.”]

Hence they are also called legitimate, either because they begin with the vowel E and end in a mute sound, as the semivowels do, or because they begin with their own sound and end in the vowel E, as the mutes do.

[Note: “For that reason, namely ... because they begin with E.” Isidore correctly explains why only seventeen Latin letters are called Latin or legitimate, omitting the vowels, about which there could be no dispute. For consonants, he says, either begin with E and end in their own sound, as do all six semivowels—F, L, M, N, R, S—or conversely begin with their own sound and end in E, as do the same number of mutes—B, C, D, G, P, T. See Donatus, *The First Art*, chapter 2, and Sergius, chapter 6.]

11. The letter H was later added solely to indicate aspiration. [Note: [Col. 0080C] Hence by many it is considered aspiration . . . From Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, from *Deuteronomy*.] Hence by many it is considered aspiration, not a letter; and it is therefore called a sign of aspiration, because it raises the voice. Aspiration is a sound uttered with greater force; its opposite is prosody, a sound modulated evenly.

12. [Note: [Col. 0080C] The letter K was first added to Latin by Salvius the schoolmaster. Others read Sallustius. Pliny mentions Salvius the rhetorician in his letters, and Suetonius in his *Vespasian*. But before him there were Fabii named Kaisōn, whose praenomen was marked by K, as appears from the consular lists. Likewise *kalare* and *Kalendae* are found in all the ancient books.] Salvius the schoolmaster first added the letter K to Latin, in order to distinguish in pronunciation the two letters c and q. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0080C] It is therefore superfluous. So Jerome, Donatus, Priscian, and Terentianus. Sergius, however, says: “K and Q, which seem superfluous to some, have this justification: K is placed before a when a follows it. [Col. 0080D] The ancients placed Q before it whenever V followed.” Diomedes says nearly the same, except that he holds that K is placed only before short A.] it is called superfluous, because it is judged unnecessary except in *Kalendae*: for everything is expressed by c.

13. [Note: [Col. 0080D] The letter Q is not sounded even by the Greeks. From Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, from *Joshua*.] The letter Q is sounded neither by the Greeks nor by the Hebrews; apart from Latin, no other language possesses it. It did not formerly exist. Hence it too was called superfluous, because the ancients wrote everything with c.

### 14.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] The letter X. It is established that the letter X was in use before the time of Augustus from the most ancient coins, from Duilius’ Rostra Column erected more than 1,800 years ago, from bronze tables of laws much earlier than Augustus, and finally from Cicero, who says in the *Orator* addressed to Brutus: “How was your *axilla* formed from *ala*, unless by the flight of the broader letter?” Elegant Latin usage likewise removed this letter from *maxillae*, *taxilli*, *vexillum*, and *paxillum*. Nevertheless, Victorinus reports in his *Art of Grammar* that Nigidius rejected it and never used it in his books, following ancient usage. The following words occur here: “And rightly at this time, when the name of Christ became known, that which depicts the sign of the cross is written through it.” Although these words are found in certain Gothic manuscripts, they are absent from the better codices and printed editions and are unworthy of Isidore’s learning; we have therefore not included them.] The letter X was not yet in use among the Latins up to the time of Augustus; instead, they wrote c and s for it. Hence it is also called double, because it is used in place of c and s; and hence its name is composed from those same letters.

15. Latin borrowed two letters from the Greeks, y and z, for Greek names. Among the Romans these too were not written until the time of Augustus; instead of z they wrote two ss, as in *hilarissat*; for y they wrote u.

16. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Three things belong to every letter. From Donatus and Sergius.] Three things belong to every letter: its name, what it is called; its shape, the character by which it is marked; and its power, whether it is regarded as a vowel or a consonant. Some add a fourth, its order: which letter precedes and which follows, as a comes first and b follows. A is first among the letters in all nations because it is the first to open the voice of those being born.

17. The nations gave the letters their names from the sounds of their own languages, [Col. 0081B] observing and distinguishing the sounds made by the mouth. [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Observing the sounds made by the mouth.” Augustine’s words, *On Order* II.12.] For after they had noticed these sounds, they assigned them names and shapes. They formed the shapes partly by convention and partly from the sound of the letters—for example, i and o: just as one has a thin sound, so it has a slender stroke; while the other has a full sound and likewise a full shape. [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Nature gave the power.” So many shapes were needed to mark the sounds. Chacon, however, preferred the Toledo manuscript, in which these words are absent. I too find this highly convincing: they occur neither in the Gothic manuscript of the Oviedo college nor in a consistent position among the books; each manuscript places them differently.] Nature gave their power, and choice gave their order.

18. The ancients distinguished between the shapes of letters and the *apex*. The *apex* is so called because it is far from the feet and is placed at the top of letters. It is a horizontal line drawn evenly above a letter. The shape, however, is the form in which the whole letter is written.

## CHAPTER V. Grammar

1. Grammar is the knowledge [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Of speaking correctly.” Older editions add “and the method of writing”; this is absent from the Gothic manuscripts but is found in Victorinus.] of speaking correctly, and the origin and foundation [Col. 0081C] of the liberal letters. [Note: [Col. 0082D] “Of the liberal letters.” So the ancient codices read, not “of the arts.” Above he divided letters into common and liberal.] It was discovered among the disciplines after the common letters, so that those who had already learned letters might through it know the proper manner of speaking. Grammar derives its name from letters: for the Greeks call letters *grammata* (γράμματα).

2. It is called an art because it consists of the precepts and rules of an art. Others say that the term was taken from the Greeks, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς, that is, “from virtue,” which they called knowledge.

3. [Note: [Col. 0082D] *Oratio*, “speech,” as though *oris ratio*, “the reasoning of the mouth.” Jerome, in Letter 139 to Cyprian, Victorinus, and others played the same word-game with this term.] *Oratio* (“speech”) is so called as though it were *oris ratio* (“the reasoning of the mouth”); [Note: [Col. 0082D] “For *orare* is to speak.” Servius, *Aeneid* X.] for *orare* means to speak and to say. Speech is a connected sequence of words possessing meaning. A connection without meaning is not speech, because it is not the reasoning of the mouth. Speech is complete through meaning, voice, and letter.

4. Some enumerate thirty divisions of the art of grammar, namely: the eight parts of speech, articulate voice, letter, syllable, feet, accents, punctuation, signs, orthography, analogy, etymology, glosses, differences, barbarisms, solecisms, faults, metaplasms, figures, tropes, prose, meters, fables, and histories.

## CHAPTER VI. The Parts of Speech

1. Aristotle first established two parts of speech: noun and verb. Donatus later defined eight. But all return to those two principal parts, namely noun and verb, which signify a person and an action. The others are appendages and derive their origin from these.

2. For the pronoun arises from the noun, whose function it performs, as in *orator ille* (“that orator”). The adverb arises from the noun, as in *doctus, docte* (“learned, learnedly”). The participle arises from noun and verb, as in *lego, legens* (“I read, reading”). The conjunction, preposition, and interjection [Note: [Col. 0082D] “They fall within the combination of these”: either because they join them, or because they are placed before or inserted among them; hence they also received their names.] fall within the combination of these. For this reason some have defined five parts, since these are superfluous.

## CHAPTER VII. The Noun

1. The noun is so called [Note: [Col. 0082D] *Nomen* (“name”), as though *notamen* (“a mark”). So Boethius and Priscian. Others think it derives from the Greek ὄνομα. We think *nomen* was cut down from *noscimen*, just as *nobilis* comes from *noscibilis*.] as though it were a “mark,” because by its name it makes things known to us. Unless you know the name, knowledge of things is lost. Proper names are so called because they are particular: they signify only one person. There are four kinds of proper names: praenomen, nomen, cognomen, and agnomen. The praenomen is so called because it is placed before the nomen, as *Lucius* and *Quintus*.

2. The nomen is so called because it marks a family or clan, as *Cornelius*: all the Cornelii belong to that group. The cognomen is so called because it is joined to the nomen, as *Scipio*. The agnomen is, as it were, an accidental name, as in *Metellus Creticus*, because he conquered Crete. The agnomen comes from outside, from some circumstance. *Cognomentum* is the popular term, either because it is added to a name for purposes of recognition or because it accompanies the name.

3. Appellative nouns are so called because they are common and apply to many things. [Note: [Col. 0082D] “These are divided into twenty-eight.” Sergius has twenty-seven. Isidore himself lists twenty-seven, so that something seems to be missing.] They are divided into twenty-eight kinds. The first are called corporeal because they are either seen or touched, as *caelum* (“sky”) and *terra* (“earth”).

4. Incorporeal nouns are so called because they lack a body; hence they can neither be seen nor touched, as *veritas* (“truth”) and *justitia* (“justice”).

5. General nouns are so called because they apply to many things, as *animal* (“animal”); for human beings, horses, and birds are all animals.

[Col. 0083A] 6. Specific nouns are so called because they indicate a part, as *homo* (“human being”); for a human being is a species of animal.

7. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Primary,” because they have the first position. They are called both primary and first-position nouns.] Primary nouns are so called because they have a first formation and do not arise from another word, as *mons* (“mountain”) and *fons* (“spring”).

8. Derived nouns are so called because they are led or derived from another noun, as *montanus* (“mountainous”) from *mons* (“mountain”).

9. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Diminutives.” *Scholasticulus*. Donatus and Charisius use the same example.] Diminutives are so called because they lessen the meaning, as *Graeculus* (“little Greek”) and *scholasticulus* (“little student”).

10. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Diminutives in sound.” From Sergius.] Diminutives in sound are so called because they sound like diminutives but are primary in meaning, as *fabula* (“story”) and *tabula* (“tablet”).

11. Entirely Greek nouns are so called because they are declined wholly according to Greek usage, as *Callisto*. A Greek and a Latin speaker both use it in this way.

12. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Entirely Latin.” From Donatus.] Entirely Latin nouns are so called because they are wholly converted into Latin. A Greek says *Odysseus*; a Latin says *Ulysses*.

[Col. 0083B] 13. Half-Greek nouns are so called because they are partly Greek and partly Latin. They are also called *notha* (“bastard”), because they corrupt the final syllables while retaining the initial ones: among the Greeks, *Alexandros* and *Menandros*; among us, *Alexander* and *Menander*. They are called *notha* in the same way that a person born from unequal parentage is called *nothus*.

14. Synonyms, that is, “many-named” words, are so called because one meaning is expressed by several names, as *terra*, *humus*, and *tellus* (“earth”). All mean the same thing.

15. Homonyms, that is, “single-named” words, are so called because one name has several meanings, as *tumulus*, which may mean a small mountain, swollen earth, or a tomb. One name therefore has different meanings.

16. Relative nouns are so called because they refer to another person, as *magister* (“teacher”), *pater* (“father”), and *dominus* (“master”).

[Col. 0083C] 17. Those [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Those which are said to be related in some manner.” This should be read from Sergius, joining the reading of the manuscripts and printed books: the manuscripts have *qualiter* (“in what manner”), while the printed books have *aliter* (“otherwise”).] which are said to be related to something else in a particular way are named from an opposite meaning, as *dexter* (“right”). For one cannot be called right unless there is a left.

18. Words of quality are so called because by them a person’s nature is shown, as *sapiens* (“wise”), *formosus* (“handsome”), and *dives* (“rich”).

19. Words of quantity are so called because they are derived from measurement, as *longus* (“long”) and *brevis* (“short”).

20. Patronymics are so called because they are derived from fathers, as *Tydides*, “son of Tydeus,” and *Aeneades*, “son of Aeneas,” although they may also be derived from mothers and ancestors.

[Col. 0084A] 21. Ctetics, that is, possessives, are named from possession, as *Evandrius ensis* (“Evander’s sword”).

22. Epithets, called in Latin adjectives or “things placed above,” are so called because they are added to nouns to complete their meaning, as *magnus* (“great”) and *doctus* (“learned”). You add them to persons, as *magnus philosophus* (“a great philosopher”) and *doctus homo* (“a learned man”), and the meaning is complete.

23. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Actual nouns.” These are found neither in Donatus nor in Sergius.] Actual nouns derive from an action, as *rex* (“king”), *dux* (“leader”), *cursor* (“runner”), *nutrix* (“nurse”), and *orator* (“speaker”).

Nouns of a people derive from a people, as *Graecus* (“Greek”) and *Romanus* (“Roman”).

24. [Col. 0084A] Nouns of a homeland derive from a homeland, as *Atheniensis* (“Athenian”) and *Thebanus* (“Theban”).

[Note: [Col. 0083D] “Nouns of place,” from a place. The species of number and order have been omitted; thus there will be twenty-eight species.] Nouns of place derive from a place, as *suburbanus* (“suburban”).

25. Verbal nouns are so called because they arise from a verb, as *lector* (“reader”).

[Col. 0084B] Participial nouns are those that sound like participles, as *clemens* (“merciful”) and *prudens* (“prudent”).

26. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Like verbs.” Something may be missing here from Sergius. He says in *Art* 2.2: “There are also words resembling participles, such as *demens* (‘mad’). For *demens* is like *legens* (‘reading’); but *demens* is a noun because it admits comparison, namely *dementior* (‘madder’), whereas *legens* is a participle because it does not similarly admit comparison. There are also words resembling verbs, such as *contemplator* (‘let him contemplate’); but when they take a case ending, they are nouns, as when *contemplator* makes *contemplatoris*. When they have tense, however, they are verbs, as in Virgil’s *Contemplator aquas dulces* (‘Contemplate the sweet waters’).” Accordingly, we have placed “case” here, following Sergius, where all the books had “comparison.” For Sergius had said that participial nouns admit comparison, not words resembling verbs.] Words resembling verbs are so called from their resemblance to verbs, as *contemplator*. It is both a verb in the imperative mood and future tense, and a noun because it takes a case ending. All these species derive from the category of nouns.

27. [Note: [Col. 0084D] “The second part of the noun.” There is no indication what he called the first, unless it was the appellative noun; for he has just said: “All these species derive from the category of nouns.”] The second part is comparison of the noun. Comparison is so called because, by comparing one thing with another, it gives one precedence. It has three degrees: positive, comparative, and superlative. The positive is so called because it is placed first in the scale of comparison, as *doctus* (“learned”). The comparative is so called because, when compared with the positive, it is preferred to it, as *doctior* (“more learned”): for he knows more than the learned man. The superlative is so called because it is placed above the comparative, as *doctissimus* (“most learned”): for he knows more than the more learned man.

28. Genders are so called because they generate, as masculine and feminine. The others are not genders, but human reason and authority have established them as such. The neuter is so called because it is neither this nor that, that is, neither masculine nor feminine. The common gender is so called because one noun is shared by two genders, as *hic canis* and *haec canis* (“this dog,” masculine and feminine).

29. The opposite of this is the epicene, because it expresses both sexes under one gender, as *hic piscis* (“this fish”). Its sex is uncertain, since it cannot be distinguished either by nature or by the eyes, [Note: [Col. 0084D] “But only by the expertise of perception.” Either he used *sensus* to mean the judgment of the intellect, or all the books are defective in reading *sensus tantum peritia*. For if gender cannot be distinguished by nature or by the eyes, how can it be distinguished by perceptive expertise? Chacon therefore regarded these words as suspect. It would not be surprising if Isidore had written *usus tantum peritia* (“only by expertise in usage”). Anyone who has read Servius on this matter will have little doubt. His words are in *Art* 2.5: “The difference between epicene and common is that in the common gender we distinguish sex by the article, as *hic canis* (‘this dog’); but in the epicene one article is used and we understand both sexes, as *haec aquila* (‘this eagle’). We use whichever article authority has established. For since in epicenes we cannot naturally detect sex, we must be confirmed by authority.” *Sexus peritia*, which occurs in one Roman manuscript, seems wholly absurd.] but only by expertise in perception. The term “every gender” is used because it serves all genders: masculine, feminine, neuter, common, and epicene.

[Col. 0085A] 30. Number is so called because by it singular and plural nouns are displayed.

Shape is so called because nouns are either simple or compound.

31. Cases are named from falling; through them inflected nouns change and “fall.” The nominative case is so called because by it we name something, as *hic magister* (“this teacher”). The genitive is so called because by it we seek the class or origin of something, as *hujus magistri filius* (“this teacher’s son”); or because we signify a thing, as *hujus magistri liber* (“this teacher’s book”).

32. The dative is so called because by it we show that we give something to someone, as *da huic magistro* (“give to this teacher”). The accusative is so called because by it we accuse someone, as *accuso hunc magistrum* (“I accuse this teacher”). The vocative is so called because by it we call someone, as *o magister* (“O teacher”). The ablative is so called because by it we signify that we take something away from someone, as *auferam a magistro* (“I shall take it away from the teacher”).

[Col. 0085B] 33. Hexaptote nouns are so called because they have forms in six cases, as *unus* (“one”). Pentaptotes vary in only five cases, as *doctus* (“learned”). Tetraptotes are declined in only four cases, as *latus* (“broad”). Triptotes have only three, as *templum* (“temple”). [Note: [Col. 0085D] Diptotes, as *JUPITER*. Charisius and Sergius likewise say that *Jupiter* is used in two cases. No one would say that it has two variations, for *Jupiter* does not even change its accent in the vocative and nominative. Thus he distinguished variation by case from variation with Sergius.] Diptotes have only two, as *Jupiter*. [Note: [Col. 0085D] Monoptotes. Sergius prefers to call these *aptota* (“indeclinable”).] Monoptotes use only one case, as *frugi*.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Pronoun

1. The pronoun is so called because it is used in place of [Note: [Col. 0085D] “In place of a noun.” So below, chapter 36: “Antonomasia is used in place of a noun.” Donatus, Sergius, and Bede say, “It is used for a noun.” One could read *pro nomine*, that is, “in place of a noun,” as in the same chapter 36: “Antonomasia is *pro nomine*, that is, placed in place of a noun.”] a noun, so that repetition of the noun itself does not become tiresome. For when we say, “Virgil wrote the *Bucolics*,” we add a pronoun: “He also wrote the *Georgics*.” Thus variation of expression both removes tedium and introduces elegance.

2. Pronouns are either definite or indefinite. [Note: [Col. 0086D] “Definite,” because they distinguish a definite person. Servius, commenting on Donatus’ *Art*.] Definite pronouns are so called because they define a particular person, as *ego* (“I”); when you hear *me*, you immediately understand whom it means. Indefinite pronouns are so called because they do not indicate definite persons. They are used of absent and uncertain persons, as *quis*, *quae*, *quod* (“who,” “which,” “what”). Pronouns less than definite are so called because they refer to a known person, as *ipse* (“himself”) and *iste* (“that”); it is certain of whom they are spoken.

3. Possessives are so called because they show that we possess something; for when I say *meus* (“my”) or *tuus* (“your”), I define something as mine or yours. Relatives are so called because they refer back to a question, as “Who is he?”—“He is that one.” Demonstratives are so called because they have the force of pointing something out. By them we point out someone present, as *hic*, *haec*, *hoc* (“this”), which three are also called articles. [Note: [Col. 0086D] These three are also articles. Sergius. Some also call them “articular pronouns,” because, following Greek usage, they are declined with nouns.]

4. They are called articles because they are closely joined to nouns, that is, bound to them, as when we say *hic orator* (“this orator”). The difference between an article and a pronoun is that it is an article when joined to a noun, as *hic sapiens* (“this wise man”). When it is not joined to one, it is a demonstrative pronoun, as *hic*, *haec*, and *hoc* (“this”).

5. All pronouns are either original or derived. Original pronouns are so called because they do not derive their origin from elsewhere. There are twenty-one of them. Three are definite: *ego* (“I”), *tu* (“you”), and *ille* (“that man”). [Note: [Col. 0086D] “Seven indefinite.” Some call these nouns. Charisius, Diomedes, Servius, and Augustine agree with Isidore.] Seven are indefinite: *quis* (“who”), *qualis* (“of what kind”), *talis* (“such”), *quantus* (“how great”), *tantus* (“so great”), *quotus* (“which in number”), and *totus* (“whole”). Six are less than definite: *iste* (“that”), *ipse* (“himself”), *hic* (“this”), *is* (“he”), *idem* (“the same”), and *sui* (“of himself”). Five are possessive: *meus* (“my”), *tuus* (“your”), *suus* (“his/her own”), *noster* (“our”), and *vester* (“your,” plural). The remaining pronouns are called derived because they are drawn and compounded from these, as *quispiam* (“someone”), *aliquis* (“someone”), and so forth.

## CHAPTER IX. The Verb

1. The verb is so called [Note: [Col. 0086D] “The verb, because it strikes.” From Servius’ commentary on Donatus’ *Art*. Quintilian rejects this in book I, chapter 5. The words concerning the perfect form found in the printed editions are rightly absent from certain Lombard manuscripts.] because it sounds when it strikes the air, or because this part of speech occurs frequently in discourse. Verbs are signs of the mind, by which human beings communicate their thoughts to one another in speech. Just as a noun signifies a person, so a verb signifies what that person does or says. In the person of a verb there is an indication of agent and patient. Thus *scribo* (“I write”) indicates an action performed by the agent. Likewise *scribor* (“I am written”) indicates an action done to the person, by one from whom we suffer the action.

2. There are two kinds of verbs: those of grammarians and those of rhetoricians. The verbs of grammarians fall into three tenses: [Col. 0086C] past, present, and future, as *fecit* (“he did”), *facit* (“he does”), and *faciet* (“he will do”). Among rhetoricians, however, all discourse is called “verbs,” as in *verbis bonis nos cepit* (“he captivated us with good words”) and *verba bona habuit* (“he used good words”): here not merely verbs falling into three tenses but the whole discourse is meant. The species of verbs are forms, moods, conjugations, and voices.

3. The forms of verbs are so called because they shape us for each particular action; through them we show what we are doing. The meditative form is named from the intention of one meditating, as [Note: [Col. 0086D] *LECTURIO*, that is, “I want to read.” So the Lombard manuscripts and Servius: “There is one meditative form, which shows not that we are doing something but that we still wish to do it, as *lecturio*; for it means not ‘I read’ but ‘I want to read.’”] *lecturio*, “I want to read.” The inchoative form follows meditation and derives from the indication of one beginning, as *calesco* (“I grow warm”). The frequentative derives from doing something repeatedly, as *lectito* (“I read frequently”) and *clamito* (“I shout repeatedly”). Forms contain meaning; moods contain inflection. For you do not know what inflection is unless you have first learned what meaning is.

4. Moods are so called according to the manner in which they possess their meanings. The indicative mood is so called because it has the force of indicating, as *lego* (“I read”). The imperative is so called because it has the sound of commanding, as *lege* (“read!”). The optative is so called because by it we desire to do something, as *utinam legerem!* (“Would that I were reading!”). [Note: [Col. 0087D] The subjunctive. Servius: “It is called subjunctive because in speech, when it cannot complete an utterance by itself, it joins an indicative to itself.”] The subjunctive is so called because something is joined to it so that the utterance may be complete. For when you say *cum clamem* (“although I shout”), the sense remains suspended; but if I say, *cum clamem, quare putas quod taceam?* (“Although I shout, why do you think that I am silent?”), the sense is complete.

5. The infinitive is so called because, while defining tense, it does not define the person of the verb, as *clamare* (“to shout”) and *clamasse* (“to have shouted”). If you add a person to it—*clamare debeo, debes, debet* (“I, you, he must shout”)—it becomes, as it were, finite. The impersonal is so called because it needs the person of a noun or pronoun, as *legitur* (“it is read”): add a person, *a me*, *a te*, *ab illo* (“by me,” “by you,” “by him”), and the sense becomes complete. The infinitive mood therefore needs only the person of the verb; the impersonal needs the person of either a pronoun or a noun.

6. A conjugation is so called because through it many forms are joined into one sound. It teaches into which syllable the future tense ends, so that through ignorance one does not say *legebo* instead of *legam*. The first and second conjugations form the future in *-bo* and *-bor*; the third in *-am* and *-ar*.

7. The voices of verbs are so called because they generate forms. Add r to the active, and it generates the passive. Conversely, remove r from the passive, and it produces the active. The active verbs are so called because they act, as *verbero* (“I strike”); the passive because they undergo action, as *verberor* (“I am struck”). Neuter verbs are so called because they neither act nor undergo action, as *jaceo* (“I lie”) and *sedeo* (“I sit”). If you add the letter r to these, [Note: [Col. 0087D] “They do not sound Latin.” A manuscript reads “Latin”; shortly afterward, Donatus has “are not Latin.”] they do not sound Latin. Common verbs are so called because they both act and undergo action, as *amplector* (“I embrace”). These likewise, if the letter r is removed, are not Latin. Deponent verbs are so called [Note: [Col. 0087D] Because they set aside the future participle from passive meaning. Charisius says: “*Deponens* (‘setting aside’) is so called by antiphrasis, that is, contrariwise, because a verb ending in r cannot set aside that letter.” Diomedes says the same in exactly the same words. Isidore’s words must therefore be understood in the same way: although a deponent verb has set aside—that is, removed—the other forms from passive meaning, it can never drive away the future form in *-dus* from the meaning of undergoing action. For *sequendus* (“to be followed”), *utendus* (“to be used”), and similar forms retain passive meaning. Alternatively, “they set aside” may mean “they reject” and do not accept the future in *-dus* because of their passive meaning, as *gloriandus* (“to be gloried in”), for *gloriandus* is plainly not in ordinary use. Comminianus, in the same Charisius, says: “Four participles are derived from the common form: present, past, and two futures, *vadans*, *vadatus*, *vadaturus*, *vadandus*. Three are derived from the deponent: present, past, and future, as *luctans*, *luctatus*, *luctaturus*.] because they set aside the future participle from passive meaning; it ends in *-dus*, as *gloriandus* (“to be gloried in”).

## CHAPTER X. The Adverb

1. [Note: [Col. 0088D] The whole chapter is from Sergius.] An adverb is so called because it is attached to verbs, as, for example, *bene legi* (“I read well”). *Bene* is the adverb; *legi* is the verb. It is therefore called an adverb because it is always completed by being joined to a verb. The verb alone completes the sense, as *scribo* (“I write”). An adverb without a verb does not have complete meaning, as *hodie* (“today”); add a verb—*hodie scribo* (“today I write”)—and by joining the verb you have completed the sense.

## CHAPTER XI. The Participle

1. The participle is so called because it shares in the parts of noun and verb, as though *particapium*. From the noun it claims genders and cases; from the verb, tenses and voices; from both, number and shape.

## CHAPTER XII. The Conjunction

1. The conjunction is so called because it joins meanings and sentences. By itself it has no force, but in the joining of speech it supplies a kind of glue. It either joins nouns, as *Augustinus et Hieronymus* (“Augustine and Jerome”), or verbs, as *scribit et legit* (“he writes and reads”). All conjunctions have one function, whether they join or separate.

2. Copulative conjunctions are so called because they join meanings or persons, as *ego et tu eamus ad forum* (“you and I, let us go to the forum”): *et* has joined the meaning itself. Disjunctives are so called because they separate things or persons, as *ego aut tu faciamus* (“either you or I shall do it”). [Note: [Col. 0088D] Subjunctives. Donatus calls them this.] Subjunctives are so called because they are appended, as *-que*. For we say *regique, hominique, Deoque* (“to the king, to the human being, and to God”); we do not say *que regi, que homini* (“and to the king, and to the human being”).

3. [Note: [Col. 0088D] Expletives. Donatus and Diomedes also count them among the expletives, at least among the expletive conjunctions.] Expletives are so called because they fill out the intended expression, as, for example, *si hoc non vis, saltem illud fac* (“if you do not want this, at least do that”). They are called common because they can be placed anywhere and appended, as *igitur hoc faciam* (“therefore I shall do this”) and *hoc igitur faciam* (“this, therefore, I shall do”).

4. [Note: [Col. 0088D] Causals, because they compel one to do something. Chacon rightly corrected the text, since some books had *cogitem* and others *cogitent*. Sergius says: “The difference between causals and rationales is that we use causals when we speak of a cause, and rationales when we speak of a reason. A cause is what compels us—some books read ‘impels us’—to do something; a reason is what we use in doing it.”] Causal conjunctions are named from a cause because they compel one to do something, as *occido illum quia habet aurum* (“I kill him because he has gold”): “because he has gold” is the cause. Rational conjunctions are named from the reason that someone uses in doing something, as *quomodo eum occidam, ne agnoscar: veneno? an ferro?* (“How shall I kill him so that I am not recognized: with poison, or with a sword?”).

## CHAPTER XIII. Prepositions

1. The preposition is so called because it is placed before nouns and verbs. [Note: [Col. 0088D] Accusative and ablative prepositions. So called by Servius and Sergius.] Accusative and ablative prepositions are named from the cases they govern. [Note: [Col. 0088D] “Words of speech.” So called by Probus, Servius, Donatus, Diomedes, Charisius, Festus in *On Amphitruo*, and Bede in *On the Art of Meter*.] They are called words of speech because they are always attached to speech, that is, to verbs, and have no force when placed alone, as *di* and *dis*. Joined to verbs, they form a word-shape, as *diduco* (“I lead apart”) and *distraho* (“I draw apart”).

## CHAPTER XIV. The Interjection

1. [Col. 0089A] The interjection [Note: [Col. 0089C] “Interjection.” Nearly all the wording is from Augustine, *Sermon on the Mount* I.9.] is so called because, being inserted—that is, placed among—words, it expresses the feeling of an agitated mind, as when the joyful person says *vah!*; the sorrowful person, *heu!*; the angry person, *hem!*; and the frightened person, *hei!* [Note: [Col. 0089C] *Vah!* from one exulting. Diomedes: *Evax!* signifies exultation. Donatus and Bede likewise say: *Evax!* expresses joy. Augustine, however, says: “When we are delighted, we say *vah!*”] These words belong specifically to their respective languages and are not easily transferred into another language.

## CHAPTER XV. The Voice

1. Voice is air struck in a manner perceptible to hearing, insofar as it depends on the voice itself. [Note: [Col. 0089D] Everything is from Donatus.] Every voice is either articulate or confused. Articulate voice belongs to human beings; confused voice to animals. Articulate voice is what can be written; confused voice is what cannot be written.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Syllable

1. In Greek, a syllable is called *syllabē*; in Latin, “conception” or “combination.” For the syllable is so called [Note: [Col. 0089D] ἀπὸ τοῦ συλλαμβάνειν τὰ γράμματα. So Sergius, Diomedes, and Charisius.] from *sullambanein ta grammata* (συλλαμβάνειν τὰ γράμματα), that is, “from the conception of letters”: *sullambanein* means “to conceive.” Thus properly that is a syllable which arises from several letters. [Note: [Col. 0089D] “For one vowel used as a syllable is an abusive usage.” Donatus seems to have noted this when he wanted a long vowel to be called properly a syllable. His words are: “A syllable is a gathering of letters, or the utterance of a single vowel capable of temporal measure. For, by abuse, we also call a short vowel a syllable.”] We improperly and not strictly call a single vowel a syllable; it should rather be called a measure of time. Syllables are either short, long, or common.

2. Short syllables are so called because they can never be lengthened. Long syllables are so called because they can never be shortened. Common syllables are so called because, when necessity demands, they may either be lengthened or shortened at the discretion of the writer. Read Donatus. Long and short syllables are so called because, through different durations of sound, they appear to contain either double or single units of time. Diphthong syllables are so called by a Greek name because two vowels are joined in them.

3. We know four genuine diphthongs in our language: *ae*, *oe*, *au*, and *eu*. Among our ancestors, *ei* was also commonly used. Among metricians a syllable is therefore called a half-foot, [Col. 0090A] because it is half a foot. A foot consists of two syllables. When there is only one syllable, therefore, it is as if there were half a foot. [Note: [Col. 0089D] Dionysius Lintius—or rather Lindius, whom Strabo and Suidas mention. He taught grammar at Rome in the time of Pompey.] Dionysius Lintius made single forms most suitable for all syllables, and for this reason was honored with a statue.

## CHAPTER XVII. Metrical Feet

1. [Note: [Col. 0089D] “Feet are those which proceed according to definite times of syllables.” Terentianus most elegantly says:

> A single long syllable cannot produce a foot by itself,

> Because it is formed by two beats, not by a double measure of time.

Sergius likewise says: “Each foot must necessarily contain within itself a fixed number of syllables measured by time.”] Feet are units that proceed according to fixed syllabic durations and never depart from their proper measure. They are called feet because meters walk by means of them. For just as we move with our feet, so meters advance, as it were, on feet. There are 124 feet altogether: four disyllabic, eight trisyllabic, sixteen tetrasyllabic, thirty-two pentasyllabic, and sixty-four hexasyllabic. Feet are so called up to four syllables; the remaining forms are called *syzygiae* (συζυγίαι), “couplings.”

2. The feet themselves have particular reasons for their names. The pyrrhic is so called because it was frequently used either in battle or in children’s games. [Note: [Col. 0089D] “Was practiced.” The Roman manuscript adds: “Or the pyrrhic is so called ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς, that is, ‘from fire’; for this foot moves rapidly, like fire. Hence Virgil’s phrase *ardentes Tyrii*, that is, ‘the Tyrians hurrying.’ The same appears in more recent editions. The earlier etymology is nevertheless correct. Terentianus says:

> The same is called pyrrhic, since it is suited to the Pyrrhiche.”

[Col. 0090C] The spondee is so called because it moves slowly. For *spondein* (σπονδεῖν) means “to move slowly,” whence Horace called spondees steady. Cicero likewise says: “Although it is duller and slower, it nevertheless has a certain steady degree, not lacking in dignity.” Or rather, it may derive from *spondē* (σπονδή), “libation,” whence it was also called *epibomios* (ἐπιβώμιος), “altar-foot,” because priests used it when advancing to the altars, so that the gravity of this foot might ward off ill-omened words and prevent them from reaching their ears. Terentianus says:

> Since, sonorous in the temples from the sound of its voice,

> it blocks and protects the ears of the one making libation from an evil sound, it is *spondeios*.

Those who played long pipes in religious rites were called *spondiales*; Plutarch mentions them.] The spondee is called so because it sounds slowly. For a spondee is said to be a kind of drawing-out, that is, a sound poured forth around the ears of those making sacrifice. Hence those who played pipes in the religious rites of the pagans were called *spondiales*.

3. The trochee is so called because it produces a rapid turning of the song and runs swiftly through meters like a wheel; for *trochos* (τροχός) is the Greek word for “wheel.”

4. The iambus is so called because the Greeks called *iambizein* (ἰαμβίζειν) “to disparage.” Poets commonly filled compositions of this kind with attacks and disparagements. The name was given because it pours out, as it were, a kind of poison in the form of insult or spite.

5. [Note: [Col. 0090D] The tribrach, also called the chorius. It is also called a trochee. Quintilian, book IX, chapter 4: “Three short syllables make the chōreus, which they wish to call the tribrach.” Terentianus, after discussing the iambus, says:

> No less swiftly the trochee runs, with the law of time reversed,

> Long in its first syllable, shorter in its last.

Many teachers call it *chorius* (χόριος). [Col. 0091C] He also says:

> For the trochee is accustomed to dissolve one long syllable into two short ones,

> and hence they call the trochee what we call the *tribrachys* (τρίβραχυς).] The tribrach, also called the chorius, is so called because it is made from three short syllables.

6. The molossus is so called from the dance of the Molossians, which they performed while armed.

[Col. 0091A] 7. [Note: [Col. 0091C] Anapaestus. We have followed the Longobardic manuscripts, which agree on this reading. Another etymology, found in other manuscript and unpublished books, reads as follows: Anapaestus is called “struck back” (for the Greeks call ἀνάπαισις “repercussion”); it is therefore called “struck back” because it is struck back by the dactyl, being its opposite. This was taken from Diomedes. In six books these words are also added: “But this is remarkable in these two feet: the anapaestus receives the quality of a noun; for from the ensuing contrariety it is placed in opposition, because brevity precedes within it. But the one that is placed in opposition does not derive its name from that, but from the quality of its syllables.” This is not entirely absurd—if Diomedes is authoritative enough for anyone—for Terentianus arranges the feet so as to begin with the anapaestus and always to place the shorter feet first. But who does not see that, once this etymology is accepted, so that anapaestus is called “struck back,” it nevertheless takes its name from the quality of its syllables rather than from the fact that it is struck back by the dactyl? The two short syllables are struck back and blunted by the following long syllable.] Anapaestus, because this foot is devoted to relaxation and amusements.

8. Dactylus is so called from a finger, because, beginning with the longer joint, it ends in two short ones. Thus this foot too [Note: [Col. 0092C] One junction. He called a junction an articulation.] has one long junction and two short ones. Hence also the open hand is called the palm, and the hanging fingers are called dactyls.

26 9. Amphibrachus, because it has a short syllable at either end, with a long syllable lying in the middle: βραχύς in Greek means “short.”

10. Amphimacrus is so called because it has two long syllables on either side, enclosing a short one in the middle: μακρός in Greek means “long.”

11. Bacchius is so called because Bacchic rites—that is, the rites of Liber—were celebrated with this foot.

[Col. 0091B] 12. [Note: [Col. 0092C] Antibacchius, or palimbacchius, because it is repeated. The Roman Codex, together with Donatus, reads: “Because it is contrary.” They interpreted this as antibacchium; our manuscripts interpret it as palimbacchium.] Antibacchius, or palimbacchius, is so called because it is contrary to, or repeated from, the bacchius.

13. Proceleumaticus, because it is suited to the celeuma of singers. [Note: [Col. 0092D] To the celeuma of singers. Chacon preferred *calcantium*, from Jeremiah 25: “Celeuma,” as if from *calcantium* (“of those who tread”). Jerome likewise, on Isaiah 16: “The joyful harvester will by no means sing the *celeuma* during the vintage.” See also Jeremiah 48 and 51. Others have published *canendum* (“to be sung”), not incorrectly.]

14. Dispondeus, ditrochaeus, and diambus are so called because they consist respectively of two spondees, trochees, or iambs.

15. Antispastus, because it is composed of contrary syllables: a short and a long, or a long and a short.

16. Choriambus, because a poem composed in this foot is especially suitable for choruses.

17. Ionici are so called because of the unequal sound of their measures; for they contain two long syllables and two shortened ones.

18. Paeones are named after their inventor. They consist of one long syllable and three short ones; the long syllable is placed in varying positions according to their names.

[Col. 0091C] 19. Epitriti are so called because they always have three long syllables and one short.

Cicero, in *The Orator*: “The paeon, since it has more syllables than three, is regarded by some as a measure, not a foot.” But since he called συζυγίαι “declensions,” perhaps “conjugations” should be read.] But these are not feet; they are called pentasyllabic and hexasyllabic because they do not extend beyond five and six syllables. Thus a name in verse ought not to exceed these syllables, as in *Carthaginiensium*, *Hierosolymitanorum*, and *Constantinopolitanorum*.

27 21. [Note: [Col. 0092D] Arsis and thesis belong to each foot. From Sergius. See Terentianus.] Arsis and thesis belong to each foot—that is, the raising and placing of the voice. For feet cannot proceed in measured order unless they are alternately raised and placed, as in *arma*: *ar* is the raising, *ma* the placing. Legitimate feet are gathered by division into these two parts. The division is equal whenever the arsis and thesis are cut off in an equal division of time.

22. The division is double whenever one of these parts exceeds the other twofold. It is sesquialter whenever one exceeds the other by one and a half. For in the simple part one additional unit is found; in the double part one unit is lacking. [Note: [Col. 0092D] *Sescum* means “a half.” Thus the Longobardic manuscripts. Cicero, in *The Orator*: “So it must be that one part of a foot is either equal to the other, or twice as great, or half again as great; thus the dactyl is equal, the iambus double, and the paeon sesquialter.” See Sergius, *Ars*, 1.5, and Quintilian, book 9, chapter 4.] For *sescum* means “a half.” It is triple when the greater part contains the entire lesser part three times—that is, three and one. It is epitrite when the lesser is contained in the greater, together with its third part. The members of feet are divided either equally, or doubly, or sesquialterly, or triply, or epitritically.

23. [Note: [Col. 0092D] “We therefore divide into equal parts.” Everything from Donatus through *Fescenninus*.] We therefore divide these into equal parts:

The spondee, as in *aestas*; the pyrrhichius, as in *fuga*; the dactyl, as in *Maenalus*; the anapaest, as in *Erato*; the dispondee, as in *oratores*; the proceleumaticus, as in *avicula*; the diiambus, as in *propinquitas*; the ditrochaeus, as in *cantilena*; the antispast, as in *Saloninus*; the choriambus, as in *Armipotens*.

24. We divide these feet into double parts:

[Col. 0092C] The trochee, as in *meta*; the iambus, as in *parens*; the molossus, as in *Aeneas*; the tribrach, as in *macula*; the greater ionic, as in *Junonius*; the lesser ionic, as in *Diomedes*.

28 25. There is only one foot that is divided by a triple partition, which is the greatest and therefore occurs least often in meters.

26. Triple: Amphibrachys, as in *carina*.

[Col. 0093A] The sesquialter feet are:

The amphimacrus, as in *insulaees* (thus printed); the bacchius, as in *Achat* (thus printed); the antibacchius, as in *natura*; the first paeon, as in *legitimus*; the second paeon, as in *colonia*; the third paeon, as in *Menedemus*; the fourth paeon, as in *celeritas*.

27. Those remain which we divide by an epitrite partition: [Note: [Col. 0093C] By an epitrite partition. Augustine calls it “sesquitertian”; others call it “supertertiary.” Diomedes, Donatus, and Terentianus call it “epitrite.”]

The first epitrite, as in *sacerdotes*; the second epitrite, as in *conditores*; the third epitrite, as in *Demosthenes*; the fourth epitrite, as in *Fescenninus*.

There are therefore ten equal feet, six double feet, one triple foot, seven sesquialter feet, and four epitrite feet.

[Col. 0093B] 28. The number of syllables in feet extends from two to six; it does not proceed farther, because feet extend only as far as six syllables. The times in feet indicate how many each foot contains. [Note: [Col. 0093C] Synaloepha follows. This occurs when *i* and *u* become consonants; but in *reji cecapellas*, *Eclogue* 3, even the two *i*s must be contracted into one, and that one consonantal, although *i* in the middle cannot be consonantal unless it stands between two vowels.]

29. [Note: [Col. 0093D] “From one long syllable two shorts …, but from two …” Terentianus:

“For it is not so that a long syllable can be dissolved.”

“Because solid magnitude does not forbid being split;

But things divided cannot be joined again into one.”] From one long syllable two short syllables can be made; but from two short syllables one long syllable can never be made. Solid things can be split, but things split apart cannot be made solid. A figure is a sign by which syllables are recognized. When you see the lower half of a circle placed twice, it is a pyrrhichius; when you see two joined horizontal strokes, it is a spondee. For the sign of a short syllable is the lower semicircle, while the sign of a long syllable is a horizontal stroke.

These will be discussed shortly.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Accents

1. *Accentus*, which in Greek is called *prosodia*, takes its name from Greek. For Greek *πρός* means “to,” in Latin *ad*; and Greek *ᾠδή* means “song” in Latin. Thus the name has been rendered word for word. The Latins have other names as well: they call it *accentus*, *tonus*, and *tenor*, because the sound rises and falls there.

2. It is called *accentus* because it is alongside song, just as an adverb is alongside a verb. The acute accent is so called because it sharpens and raises the syllable. The grave is so called because it lowers and depresses it; for it is contrary to the acute. The circumflex is so called because it consists of the acute and the grave: beginning with the acute, it ends in the grave; and thus, while it rises and falls, it becomes circumflex.

3. The acute and circumflex are similar, for each raises the syllable. The grave appears contrary to both, since it always depresses syllables, whereas they raise them, as in: “Whence Titan comes, and where night hides the stars.” Here *Undè* is grave, for it sounds lower than the acute and circumflex.

4. A monosyllabic part of speech, if it is naturally short, as *vir*, or long by position, as *ars*, will have the acute accent. But if it is naturally long, as *rês*, [Col. 0094B] it will have the circumflex. A disyllabic part of speech, if it has a naturally long first syllable and a short final syllable, is circumflexed, as *Musâ*; otherwise it receives the acute. A trisyllabic part of speech, if it has a short middle syllable, as *tibia*, has the first syllable accented. But if it has a naturally long second syllable and a short final syllable, as [Note: [Col. 0094D] “As *Romānus*.” This should be read on the basis of the Tarragon manuscripts, or *Cethegus* from Donatus, so that the example agrees; not *Metellus*, as in the other books. A distinction was made shortly before between a syllable naturally long and one long by position.] *Românus*, we circumflex the middle syllable.

5. Tetrasyllabic and pentasyllabic words follow the rule of trisyllables. [Note: [Col. 0094D] “The grave accent … with neither of the two, never.” There is never more than one acute accent in the same word, as Quintilian says; but the grave can occur in one word not only with the acute but also with the circumflex.] The grave accent can occur with one accent in a single word, but never with both, as in *Catùllus*. In a compound word there is one accent, as in *armipotens* and *omnipotens*.

6. [Note: [Col. 0094D] “Accents were discovered.” Yet Donatus and Sergius, from whom this material is taken, say that accent is altered and dispersed for purposes of reading, distinguishing, or pronunciation, or to remove ambiguity; and no one will deny that both statements are true.] Accents were discovered either for distinction, as in *viridìque in littore conspicitur sus*, so that one does not say *ursus*; or for pronunciation, so that one does not pronounce *méta* short instead of *metâ* with a lengthened vowel; or to distinguish ambiguity, as in *ergò*. When *go* is lengthened, it signifies a cause; when shortened, it is a conjunction.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Forms of Accents

1. [Note: [Col. 0094D] “The forms of accents.” Everything is taken from Donatus.] There are ten forms of accents, which grammarians place to distinguish words. *Ὀξεῖα*, that is, the acute accent, is formed by a line drawn upward from left to right, thus: ´.

2. *Βαρεῖα*, that is, the grave, is a line drawn downward from the upper left toward the right, thus: `.

31 3. *Περισπωμένη*, that is, the circumflex, is formed from the acute and grave and is represented thus: ~.

4. *Μακρά*, that is, the long mark, is a horizontal stroke, thus: —.

[Col. 0095A] 5. *Βραχύς*, that is, the short mark, is the lower part of a circle lying horizontally, thus: ˘.

6. *Ὑφέν*, that is, the conjunction, because it joins two words, is a curved horizontal stroke placed beneath the verse, thus: ‿.

7. *Diastole*, that is, distinction, which separates in the opposite way, is the right-hand part of a circle placed beneath the verse, thus: ).

8. *Apostrophos* is likewise the right-hand part of a circle, placed beside the upper part of a letter, thus: ’. By this sign the omission of a final vowel in speech is shown, as *tribunal’* for *tribunali*.

9. *Δασεῖα*, interpreted as “aspiration,” that is, where the letter H ought to be placed, is marked by this figure: ῾.

10. *Ψιλή*, interpreted as “bareness” or “purity,” that is, where the letter H ought not to be present, is shown by this sign: ᾿.

[Col. 0095B] 11. [Note: [Col. 0095D] “The form of these two accents the Latins …” Thus Donatus and Sergius. Augustine, however, also says that the Greeks first used the letter Η itself for aspiration; for he says that he possessed Greek coins on which Η Η Ρ Α Κ Λ was written. Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 19, and Priscian, in *On Weights*, also testify to this. Nor do the words of Martianus Capella entirely conflict with them: “The Greeks divided the mark of aspiration.” If the word “Latins,” which is absent from the Roman Codex, is removed, the reading is no less satisfactory: “The form of these two accents they made from the letter of aspiration”—namely, the Greeks.] The Latins made the form of these two accents from the letter of aspiration itself. Thus, if you join these signs, you make the same mark of aspiration, H. Again, if you split its middle stroke, you make the *δασεῖα* and the *ψιλή*.

## CHAPTER XX. On Punctuation

1. Punctuation is a figure for distinguishing meanings by cola, commas, and periods. When it is placed in its proper order, it reveals to us the sense of what is read. These marks are called *positurae* either because they are indicated by placed points, or because the voice is lowered there for an interval of distinction.

2. The Greeks call these *θέσεις*, the Latins *positurae*. The first mark is called *subdistinctio*, and is also called *κόμμα*. The middle distinction follows and is itself the *κῶλον*. The final distinction, [Col. 0095C] which closes the whole sentence, is the *περίοδος*. As we have said, its parts are the *κῶλον* and the *κόμμα*, whose difference is shown by points placed in different positions.

3. When, at the beginning of a pronunciation, the sense is not yet complete but it is nevertheless necessary to breathe, a comma is made—that is, a small portion of sense—and a point is placed at the bottom of the letter. It is called *subdistinctio* because it receives a point below, that is, at the bottom of the letter. [Note: [Col. 0095D] “And yet one must breathe.” Donatus and Sergius assign this breathing to the middle distinction.]

4. When, in what follows, the sentence already conveys a meaning but something still remains for the sentence to be complete, a colon is made; we mark the middle of the letter with a point and call it the middle distinction, because we place the point at the middle of the letter.

[Col. 0096A] 5. When, proceeding by stages in pronunciation, we make a complete clause of the sentence, a period is made; we place a point at the top of the letter, and it is called a distinction—that is, a separation—because it has separated the complete sentence.

6. This applies to orators. Among poets, however, when a syllable remains in a verse after two feet, it is a comma, because a cutting-off of the word has occurred there after scansion. But when nothing remains of the part of speech after two feet, it is a colon. The entire verse is a period.

33 ## CHAPTER XXI. On the Marks of Sentences

1. Among the most celebrated authors there were also certain marks of writing, which the ancients placed in poems and histories to distinguish their text. A mark is a distinctive figure set down in the form of a letter to indicate the character of each word, sentence, and verse. Twenty-six marks are placed beside verses, with the names written below.

2. [Note: [Col. 0095D] The asterisk. On the asterisk and obelus, see Augustine, *City of God* 18.42; Jerome in the prefaces to *Chronicles* and *Job*, and in Letter 135 to Sunia and Fretela. Asterisks and obeli are still found in books in figures that differ somewhat: asterisks, ⁕; obeli, —.] The asterisk (*) is placed beside omissions, so that by this mark the things that appear to be missing may be brought to light. For a star is called ἀστήρ in Greek, from which *asteriscus* is derived.

3. [Note: [Col. 0096D] The obelus dotted above. Augustine prefers it to be drawn as it appears in the Florentine Pandects.] The obelus (—), that is, a horizontal stroke, is placed beside words or sentences repeated needlessly, or in places where a reading has been marked as false, so that, like an arrow, it may slaughter what is superfluous and pierce what is false. For an arrow is called ὀβελός in Greek.

[Col. 0096C] 4. The obelus dotted above (—·) is placed beside passages about which it is uncertain whether they ought to be removed.

5. [Note: [Col. 0096D] Limniscus. On the meaning of the word, see Vegetius, *On Veterinary Medicine*. It is remarkable that Isidore omitted the hypolimniscus; for I do not doubt that it was omitted, since he explains all twenty-six marks that he proposed, whereas Origen is known to have used altogether four marks in the Hexapla or Octapla: the asterisk, obelus, limniscus, and hypolimniscus. According to Epiphanius, the hypolimniscus is a horizontal stroke with a point beneath it, indicating that the same sense has been rendered in identical words by only one of the other Septuagint translators. Its figure was: —·.] The limniscus (÷), that is, a horizontal stroke lying between two points, is placed in passages where interpreters of sacred Scripture have translated with the same meaning but in different words.

6. [Note: [Col. 0096D] Antigraphus. It is drawn in two forms. In the Gothic manuscripts only this form occurs: >.] The antigraphus (>) with a point is placed where a different meaning occurs in translations.

7. [Note: [Col. 0096D] Asterisk with an obelus. Augustine wishes this to be drawn as follows: ⁕.] The asterisk with an obelus (⁕—) was used especially by Aristarchus in verses that had not been placed in their proper location.

8. The paragraphus (¶) is placed to separate things from things that occur together in a connection—for example, places from places, regions from regions, prizes from prizes in a contest, and contests from different contests.

9. [Note: [Col. 0097C] *Positura*. Since all the remaining terms are Greek, the word *positura* may appear suspect.] The *positura* (⸿) is a figure contrary to the paragraphus. It is formed this way because, just as the paragraphus marks beginnings, so this mark separates endings from beginnings.

10. The cryphia (⸮), the lower part of a circle with a point, is placed where a difficult and obscure question cannot be opened or resolved.

11. [Note: [Col. 0097C] Antisigma. See Laertius on Plato.] The antisigma (Ͻ) is placed beside verses whose order must be changed; it is found used in this way in ancient authors.

12. [Note: [Col. 0097C] Antisigma with a point. In Augustine’s Laertius this was the figure: ⸮.] The antisigma with a point (Ͻ·) is placed where two verses express the same meaning and it is uncertain which should rather be chosen.

13. [Note: [Col. 0097C] Diple. 27. [Note: [Col. 0098D] Alogus. It is drawn in various ways.] The alogus (※) is used to mark errors.

28. Other small marks are also made in books to identify material displayed at the ends of pages. Thus, when a reader finds such a sign in the margin and returns to the text of the same sentence or verse, he knows that it is an exposition whose corresponding mark he finds above.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Common Marks

[Col. 0098C]

1. [Note: [Col. 0098D] Ennius was the first to devise common marks. I understand this to refer to the later Ennius, who wrote two books on letters and syllables, as Suetonius says in the preface to *On Illustrious Grammarians*.] Ennius was the first to devise 1,100 common marks. 37 The purpose of the marks was that, whenever anything was said before an assembly or in court, several scribes standing together could write it down simultaneously, dividing the work among themselves according to how many words each was to capture and in what order. [Note: [Col. 0098D] The first at Rome was Tullius Tiro. These are Jerome’s words in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. But how could he be the first, if Ennius was also first? Isidore had not yet harmonized these statements.] At Rome, Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman, was the first to devise marks, but only for prepositions.

2. [Note: [Col. 0099C] After him came Vipsanius. Augustine’s conjecture was confirmed by the Codex of the Oviedo college, in which *Vipsanius* is expressly written. But I do not agree with his suspicion that this man was the freedman of Agrippa, who belonged to the Vipsanian family. For I do not think that a patron would have given his freedman a name which he himself rejected. See Seneca’s *Declamations*.] After him Vipsanius Philargyrus [Note: [Col. 0099C] And Aquila, the freedman of Maecenas. Dionysius, book 55, says that the marks were devised by Maecenas himself but published by Aquila.] and Aquila, Maecenas’s freedman, added different marks of their own. Then Seneca, having contracted, arranged, and expanded the whole, produced a work containing 5,000 marks. They are called *notae* because they mark words or syllables with prefixed characters and recall them to the knowledge of readers; those who have learned them are now properly called *notarii*.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Legal Marks

1. Certain letters in law books are marks representing their words, so that writing may be faster and shorter. For example, *bonum factum* (“a good deed”) was written with B and F; *senatusconsultum* (“senate decree”) with S and C; *res publica* (“the republic”) with R and [Col. 0099B] P; *populus Romanus* (“the Roman people”) with P and R; *duntaxat* (“only”) with D and T; [Note: [Col. 0099C] With the inverted letter III. Since nearly all books had the letter M, Augustine most plausibly conjectured that III should be written, representing the third letter. For with C reversed in this way, C, they represented *cujam*, and all women used this as a personal designation. See Plutarch, *Problems*, and Boethius, *Topics*. But when Isidore says “with the inverted letter III,” the Roman Codex has this mark, which also appears in the Gothic manuscript at Oviedo.] *mulier* (“woman”) with an inverted III; *pupillus* (“orphan”) with P in its normal orientation; [Note: [Col. 0099D] With PA, with the head of the P turned around, *pupilla* (“female orphan”). Thus Valerius Probus.] *pupilla* (“female orphan”) with PV, with the head turned around; *kaput* (“head”) with one K; *kalumniae kausa* (“for the sake of a lawsuit”) with two joined Ks; *iudex esto* (“let him be judge”) with I and E; and *dolum malum* (“evil intent”) with D and M.

2. Many similar marks of this kind are also found in ancient books. The new emperors decreed that these legal marks [Note: [Col. 0099D] “The new emperors.” Justinian, in the preface placed before the *Digest* and the *Code*. Justinian died in the year 565 after Christ.] should be abolished from the law books, because clever men deceived many ignorant people through them. They therefore ordered that the letters in the laws be written so as to produce no errors or ambiguities, but openly to show what must be followed and what avoided.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Military Marks

[Col. 0099C] 1. In the small rolls that contained the names of soldiers, too, each name formerly had its own mark, by which one could see how many soldiers remained and how many had fallen [Col. 0100A] in battle. [Note: [Col. 0099D] The mark T, that is, *superstitem* (“survivor”), placed at the beginning of a line. But a Θ was placed beside the name of each deceased person. Hence it has a weapon passing through its middle—that is, the sign of death, of which Persius says:

“And he can set the black theta before the vice.”

2. [Note: [Col. 0100C] “When they wished to signify impurity.” Some manuscripts read *pueritiam* (“childhood”), others *imperitiam* (“inexperience”). There were also special marks for the distribution of military pay.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Letter Marks

1. The ancients also devised marks among letters, so that whatever they wished to signify secretly in writing to one another they could communicate mutually. Brutus is a witness, for he used such letters to mark what he intended to do, while the others did not know what those letters meant to him.

2. Caesar Augustus likewise wrote to his son: “Since innumerable things continually arise that ought to be written between us and kept secret, let us therefore have marks among ourselves, if you wish, of this kind: whenever something must be written in marks, let us write the next letter in place of each letter—in place of A, B; in place of B, C; and so on in the same manner for the remaining letters; [Note: [Col. 0100C] But for Z one must return to the double AA. Suetonius, in *Augustus*, says: “For X, however, to the double AA.” I suppose this is because in Augustus’s time X was the final letter, whereas in Isidore’s time it was Z, as we saw above in chapters 3 and 4.] for Z, however, we must return to the double AA.” Some also wrote with the words reversed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Finger Signs

1. There are certain signs made with the fingers, and also with the eyes, by which people communicate silently with one another from a distance, as is customary in the army. Thus, whenever the army agrees, because it cannot speak aloud, it gives its assent by hand; others, because they cannot speak, give greetings by a movement of their swords. [Note: [Col. 0100C] “By a nod of the swords.” This is how it appears in the Longobardic book of the distinguished G. Loaisa, whereas in all the others it is less elegantly read as “by a movement.”]

2. [Note: [Col. 0100D] Ennius, concerning a certain shameless woman. A learned man, using Festus, advised that *Noevium* should be restored in place of *Ennium*. These are verses from Naevius’s *Tarentilla*, which Gabriel Faernus said consisted of five trochaic lines, though two were corruptly written. He thought the words “in the chorus” should be removed, or rather placed earlier, as though they had been spoken by the poet in the chorus:

“Like a ball at play, she gives herself to each in turn and makes herself common;

She holds one, nods to another … …

She gives another a ring to look at from her lips, calls to another;

She sings with one, yet gives letters by her finger to others.”

The same scholar wished to supplement the second verse from Festus as follows: “She nods to one, winks at another, loves one, holds another.” But it will be worthwhile to hear the same senarii made by another:

“Like a ball in the forum,

At play she gives herself to each in turn and makes herself common,

She holds one, winks at another; elsewhere her hand

Is occupied, but she strikes another’s foot;

Calls to another, and sings with one, yet

Ennius, concerning a certain shameless woman: “Like a ball in the chorus at play, she gives herself to each in turn and makes herself common. She holds one, nods to another, elsewhere her hand is occupied, pinches another’s foot, gives another a ring to look at from her lips, calls to another, sings with one, yet gives letters by her finger to others.” Solomon likewise says: “He winks with his eye, rubs with his foot, speaks with his finger.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Orthography

1. *Orthographia* is interpreted in Latin as “correct writing.” For Greek *ὀρθή* means “correct,” and *γραφή* means “writing.” This discipline teaches how we ought to write. For just as grammar deals with the inflection of parts of speech, so orthography deals with skill in writing.
