Thus *ad*, when it is a preposition, takes the letter d; when it is a conjunction, it takes the letter t.

2. *Haud*, when it is an adverb of negation, ends in the letter d and is aspirated at the beginning; but when it is a conjunction, it is written with the letter t and without aspiration.

43 3. The preposition *apud* is written with d, as in *ad patrem* (“at the father”), because the ancients often used *ad* for *apud*, removing two of the middle letters.

4. Sometimes, however, other letters are properly placed in one another’s stead. There is a certain kinship between B and P; for instead of *birrus* we say *pirrus*. C and G have a certain kinship; for when we say *centum* and *trecentos*, we later say *quadringentos*, using G in place of C. C and Q likewise have a kinship; for we write *hujusce* with C, but *cujusque* with Q. [Note: [Col. 0101C] “But when it is a preposition.” From Velius Longus’s booklet *On Orthography*.] When it is a preposition, it should be written with C; but if it is an adverb, with Q. For we say *quum lego* (“when I read”). *Deus* (“god”) is written with a single E; *daemon* (“demon”) is marked with the diphthong AE.

[Column 0101C] **5.** *Equus*, meaning the animal, must be written with *e*. *Aequus*, meaning just, must be written with the diphthong *ae*. [Note: *Exul* with the added *s*. Since a word ought to preserve its own beginning, says Terentius Scaurus.] *Exul* must be written with the added *s*, because an *exul* is one who is outside his native soil. [Note: *Exultat.* Chacon thought this was added from the margin; for it contains a statement contrary to the preceding one, taken from the glosses of Placidus. We think it does Isidore no harm: his purpose was not so much to judge matters of this kind as to gather disparate material from many places. Velius Longus held the same opinion in his book *On Orthography*. Moreover, in the most ancient tablets of laws engraved in bronze, forms such as *maxsumus*, *proxsumus*, *dixserint*, *faxsit*, *exsigatur*, and many others of this kind are seen.] *Exultat* is better written without the letter *s*. For since *x* itself consists of *c* and *s*, how, when *s* is already contained in it, can another *s* be added to it again?

**6.** *Aequor* must be written with the diphthong, because its name is derived not from *aqua* (“water”) but from *aequalitas* (“equality”).

**7.** *Forsitan* must be written with *n* at the end, because its full form is *si forte tandem* (“if perhaps at last”).

[Column 0102A] **8.** *Fedus*, meaning deformed, must be written with *e* alone; *foedus*, meaning a pact, must be written with the diphthong *oe*.

**9.** [Note: *Formosus* without *n*. Scaurus: “They are quite mistaken who add the letter *n* to *formosus*, which is no more necessary there than in *gloriosus*. Some maintain that many words were contracted from vowel accents placed over long vowels, such as *formosus*, *thesaurum*, *mesam*, *quoties*, and *vicesimum*. Augustine thought this spelling older than the use of accents, since at Genoa there existed a bronze tablet engraved before Cicero’s time on which *vicensumum* appeared. He held the same opinion concerning *thensaurus*, *thensa*, *mensa*, and the remaining examples. Adding accents to long vowels was not so ancient, although it was old, as Quintilian testifies. For earlier writers commonly doubled long vowels, writing *Feelix* for *Felix* and *Vaala* for *Vala*, forms found on coins. As for the fact that *formosus* derives from *formo*, he repeats the same point in books X and XIX, chapter 7, and XX, chapter 13.] *Formosus* is written without *n*, because it derives from *formo*, that is, “warm”; for the warmth of the blood produces beauty.

[Note: *Gnatus* … because it yields *GENERATUS*. He speaks in the same way shortly afterward: *Sat* with *t*, because its full form is *satis*.] *Gnatus*, meaning a son, must be written with *g*, because it yields *generatus* (“begotten”).

**10.** *H*, which is the sign of aspiration, is joined in Latin only to vowels, as in *honor*, *homo*, and *humus*. [Note: It is also aspirated before consonants. Cicero, in *The Orator*: “Although I knew that our ancestors spoke so that they used aspiration nowhere except before vowels, I nevertheless pronounced the words as *pulcros*, *cetegos*, and *Cartaginem*.”] It is also aspirated before consonants, but in Greek and Hebrew names. The interjections *heus* and *heu*, however, must be written with *h*.

**11.** Some thought that the letter *i* placed between two vowels should be written doubled, as in *Troiia* and *Maiia*, [Note: As in *TROJIA*, *MAJIA*. Velius reports that Cicero was accustomed to write in this way. Terentianus seems to have had this in mind: “And the teachers order us to write a doubled *i*.”] but reason does not permit this. For three vowels are never written in one syllable. Rather, the letter *i* placed between two vowels is counted as double.

**12.** *Id*, the neuter pronoun, is written with *d*, from *is, ea, id*, because it yields *idem*.

But if it is a verb of the third person, it will be written with *t*, from *eo, is, it*, because it yields *itur*.

**13.** [Note: “Whenever *a* followed.” Short *a*, as we said from Diomedes, chapter 4.] The ancients prefixed the letter *k* whenever *a* followed, as in *kaput*, *Kanna*, and *Kalamus*. Now, however, only *Kartago* and *Kalendae* are written with it. All Greek names, whatever vowel follows, must be written with *k*.

**14.** *Laetus* is written with the diphthong *ae*, because *laetitia* (“joy”) is said to derive from *latitudo* (“breadth”), whose opposite is *tristitia* (“sadness”), which produces narrowness. Sometimes we use the letter *l* in place of *d*, as in *latum* for *datum*, and *calamitas* for *cadamitas*; for *calamitas* derives its name from *cadere* (“to fall”).

**15.** [Note: *MAXUMUS* or *MAXIMUS*. Velius Longus: “Thus it is now uncertain whether certain words should be pronounced with *i* or with *u*, such as *optumus* and *maxumus*. In these cases it should be noted that the ancient language had a fuller sound and, as Cicero says, was rustic; and the ancients preferred to write and pronounce such words with *u*. Grammarians were mistaken, however, when they thought that superlatives were pronounced with *u*. Even if we grant them *optimo*, *maximo*, *pulcherrimo*, and *justissimo*, what will they do with words in which the same question remains after the superlative force has been removed: *manubiae* or *manibiae*; *lubido* or *libido*? But once the refinement of speech began to please us, we corrected that heaviness entirely toward the letter *i*, though not so as to pronounce the letter *i* fully. I would also maintain that some people write other words with *u*, following the preferences of the ancients, though they do not pronounce them as they write them. See Quintilian, book I, chapter 3, and Gnaeus Cornutus’s book *On Orthography* in Cassiodorus, from which this material has been taken.] The question has been raised how *maxumus*, or *maximus*, and similar forms ought to be written. Varro reported that Caesar habitually pronounced and wrote such words with *i*; hence, because of the authority of so great a man, the practice arose of writing *maximus*, *optimus*, and *pessimus*.

**16.** *Malo* must be written with one *l*, because it means *magis* [Note: [Column 0104D] [[Column 0103] This note appears at the foot of column 104, but its callout letter, *l*, does not occur in the text.] “Its force is that what is doubtful,” etc. These are Quintilian’s words.] *volo* (“I prefer”); *malle* with two *l*s, because it means *magis velle* (“to wish more”). Likewise, *nolo* is written with one *l*, and *nolle* with two. [Note: *NOLO* means *NE VOLO* (“I do not wish”). Festus proves that the ancients used *ne* for *non*. This is frequent in Plautus. Terence too says, “unless you do not wish.”] For *NOLO* is *ne volo* (“I do not wish”), and *NOLLE* is *ne velle* (“not to wish”).

**17.** [Note: *Os* if it signifies the face or a bone. Thus consistently in the oldest codices; nor is it surprising that Isidore used *ossum* here, almost compelled by necessity, since Charisius reports that Gellius had used *osso* much earlier. As for the passage of Terence in the *Eunuchus*, I agree with Faernus that, if *ossum* were read in Terence, neither Varro nor Charisius, who reject it, would have passed it over in silence.] *Os*, if it signifies the face or a bone, must be written with *o* alone; [Note: If it signifies a person. So that it is the accusative of the pronominal article, *hos*.] if it signifies a person, *h* must be prefixed.

**18.** *Ora*, meaning the boundaries, is written with *o*; *hora* (“hour”) must be written with *h*.

*Onus*, if it derives from *onus* (“burden”), must be written with *o* alone; if from *honor* (“honor”), with aspirated *h*.

**19.** The preposition *praepositio* and *praeterea* must be written with the diphthong.

[Note: *Pene*, which is a conjunction, with *e*. Augustine used to say that in the Florentine *Pandects* it was invariably written with *ae*.] *Pene*, which is a conjunction, is written with *e*.

*Poena*, meaning punishment, is written with *oe*.

**20.** The letter *q* is correctly used when it is immediately followed by *u* and one or more other vowels are joined to it, so that one syllable is formed. All other cases are written with *c*.

**21.** The pronoun *quae* is written with *a*; the conjunction *que* without *a*.

*Quid* is written with *d* when it is a pronoun; with *t* when it is a verb whose first principal form is *queo, quis, quit*, and in compounds *nequeo, nequis, nequit*.

**22.** *Quod*, when it is a pronoun, is written with *d*; when it is a numeral, with *t*, because *tot* (“so many”) is likewise written with *t*.

[Note: *Quotidie* with *q*. Quintilian says that this had already disappeared. Velius: “They more often say *quotidie* with *q* than *cotidie* with *c*, since it is both better pronounced and better written; for *quotidie* is not derived from *quotus* (‘how many’), but is drawn from the continuous expression *cotidie* (‘every day’).”] *Quotidie* must be written with *q*, not with *c*, so that it means “on every day.”

**23.** The letter *r* has an affinity with the letter *s*. Thus among the ancients one said *honos*, *labos*, and *arbos*; now one says *honor*, *labor*, and *arbor*.

[Column 0103C] **24.** *Sat* ought to be written with *t*, because its full form is *satis*.

But *sed* ought to be written with *d*. For among the ancients it was said *sedum*; we have cut off the final two letters.

**25.** [Note: *Tamtus* and *quamtus*. See Gnaeus Cornutus and Caesellius in Cassiodorus, *On Orthography*.] *Tamtus*, like *quamtus*, must have *m* in the middle. They derive from *quam* and *tam*; hence also *quamtitas*, *quamtus*, and *tamtus*.

**26.** [Note: The interjection *vae*. Gellius likewise says, book V, chapter 12: “But it is remarkable that in compounds the *a* disappears, since the syllable *ve* in those words is short, as in *vetus* and *vecors*.”] The interjection *vae* is written with *a*; the conjunction *ve* without *a*.

**27.** *Xristus*, because it is Greek, must be written with *x*. [Note: Likewise *XRISMA*. Thus in the oldest codices. If it was preferred to write *Xristus* and *Xrisma* in Latin fashion, I think this was done in order to preserve the shape of the cross; on this matter see above, chapters 3 and 4.] Likewise *Xrisma*.

**28.** The letters *y* and *z* are used only in Greek names. For although *justitia* expresses the sound of the letter *z*, nevertheless, because it is Latin, it must be written with *t*. Thus *militia*, *malitia*, *nequitia*, and other similar words.

**29.** In doubtful words, too, the custom of the ancients was that when the same letter, shortened or lengthened, produced a different meaning, they placed an accent over the long syllable. For example, when *populus* meant either a tree or a multitude of people, it was distinguished by an accent. Likewise, when consonant letters were doubled, they placed a *sicilicus* above them, as in *sel’a*, *ser’a*, and *as’eres*. [Note: “They placed a *sicilicus* above it.” Victorinus says in his book *On Orthography* that this sign was still present in many books in his own day. The sign was of this kind: *ser’a*, *sel’a*. It was called a *sicilicus*—Festus says—because it cuts off a half-ounce. We are surprised that it now appears nowhere in ancient inscriptions or books, since in the inscription of Duilius one sees *clases* and *numei*, and on coins *Pilipus*, without any sign of the *sicilicus*.] The ancients did not double the letters, but placed a *sicilicus* above them. By this sign the reader was warned that the letter had to be doubled.

# CHAPTER XXVIII. On Analogy

**1.** [Note: All this is from Quintilian, book I, chapter 5, and from Sergius’s *Second Art*, the chapter on cases, but it has been arranged in such a way that the parts do not always cohere, nor do they adequately correspond to the authors from whom they were taken.] *Analogia*, in Greek, is called in Latin “comparison of similars,” or proportion. [Note: *Analogia* … “comparison of similars.” This could be accepted, were it not that in Quintilian “comparison of similars” has another sense. For with him it is a part of analogy, whereas here it is the genus itself. Sergius more appropriately said “the relation of similars.”] Its force is that what is doubtful is referred to something similar that is not doubtful, so that uncertain things may be established by certain ones. The comparison of analogy is gathered in eight ways: by quality, comparison, gender, number, form, case, the endings of similar syllables, and similarity of quantities.

**2.** If one of these is lacking, it is no longer analogy—that is, similarity—but anomaly, that is, something outside the rule. Thus *lupus* and *lepus* agree in everything; [Note: “They disagree in case.” Sergius intended them to differ not in case but in gender, because just as *lupus* yields *lupa*, *lepus* does not yield *lepa*.] but they differ in case, for they make *lupi* and *leporis*. When one asks whether *trames* is masculine or feminine, one proceeds regularly, and it will be masculine.

**3.** Likewise, if you think *funis* is of uncertain gender, it resembles *panis* in declension, and it will be masculine. [Note: Likewise from comparison of positive forms. Donatus, in the *Second Art*: “In these rules analogy is recognized either from the comparison of positive nouns or from diminutives.”] It is also determined by comparison of positive forms: if you say *doctus* and *magnus*, they are positives and correspond to one another. It is also determined by diminutives: for example, *funiculus* shows that *funis* is masculine, just as *masculum* indicates that *marmor* is neuter.

**4.** For the gender that a word has in its primary form is usually retained in the diminutive. But this is not always so, as with *pistrinum* and *pistrilla*. Nevertheless, since we must understand [Note: “To derive the declension from the primary form, and the gender from the diminutive.” The oldest codices agree in this wording.] that the declension is inferred from the primary form and the gender from the diminutive—

# CHAPTER XXIX. On Etymology

**1.** Etymology is the origin of words, when the force of a verb or noun is gathered through interpretation. Aristotle called it *symbolon* (σύμβολον), and Cicero called it *notatio*, because it makes nouns and verbs signify the things themselves; for example, *flumen* (“river”) is so called because it has grown by flowing.

**2.** Knowledge of this often has a necessary use in interpretation. For when you see from where a name arose, you understand its force more quickly. Every examination of a thing is clearer once its etymology is known. Not all names, however, were imposed by the ancients according to nature; some were imposed according to convention, just as we too sometimes give names to slaves and possessions according to what pleases our will.

**3.** Hence the etymologies of all names are not found, because some received their names not according to the quality from which they originated but according to human choice. Etymologies of names are derived either from a cause, [Note: For example, *reges* from *recte agendo* (“acting rightly”). Others derive it from *regendo* (“ruling”). Both can be confirmed from the codices and from other passages of Isidore. See book III of *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 48; Burchard, book XV, chapter 38; Ivo, part XVI, chapter 39; and below, book XII, chapter 3.] as *reges* (“kings”) from *regere*, that is, from acting rightly; or from origin, as *homo* (“human being”), because it is from *humus* (“earth”); or from opposites, as *lutum* (“mud”) from *lavando* (“washing”), although mud is not clean, and *lucus* (“grove”), because, being dense with shade, it gives little light.

**4.** Some words have also been formed from the derivation of names, as *prudens* (“prudent”) from *prudentia* (“prudence”). Some arise from sounds, as *graculus* (“jackdaw”) from *garrulitas* (“chattering”). Some have arisen from Greek etymology and have been inflected into Latin, as *silva* (“forest”) and *domus* (“house”).

**5.** Other words have drawn their names from the names of places, cities, and rivers. Many are also called by words from the languages of different peoples. Hence their origin is scarcely discernible. For most are barbarian names, unknown to Latin and Greek speakers.

# CHAPTER XXX. On Glosses

**1.** *Glossa* takes its name from the Greek word meaning “tongue.” [Note: “This the philosophers call *ad verbum*.” Others read *adverbium*. The Greek is πρὸς ἔπος (“toward the word”). Hence arose the expression “οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος” (“nothing to the point”). We know from Aristotle, Galen, Pollux, Suidas, and Quintilian that *glosses* originally meant the words themselves, whether obscure or foreign; later they used the same name for interpretations added to those words. Isidore nevertheless seems to speak too narrowly when he requires the meaning of one word to be explained by one word only, denying that an explanation in several words is a gloss. He repeats this in book XXIV, chapter 30.] Philosophers call it an *adverb*, because it designates the word being sought by one single word. It explains what that word means by means of one word, as *conticescere* means *tacere* (“to be silent”).

**2.** Likewise: “the side drinks in the open wound”; *haurit* means “strikes.” So too when we call *terminus* “end,” or interpret *populatas* as “devastated”; in general, whenever we make the meaning of one word clear by one word.

# CHAPTER XXXI. On Differences

[Column 0106B]

**1.** [Note: “Difference is.” The same material is repeated from Victorinus and Boethius, book I of *On Definitions*, chapter 28, and again in book II, chapter 30.] Difference is a species of definition, which writers on the arts use of one thing in relation to another. For two things, confused through some common feature, are separated when a difference is added; by this it is recognized what each is. Thus, when one asks what difference there is between a king and a tyrant, the addition of a difference defines what each is: the king is moderate and self-controlled, whereas the tyrant is cruel. When a difference has been placed between these two, what each is becomes known. The same applies to other cases.

# CHAPTER XXXII. On Barbarism

**1.** Barbarism is a word uttered with a corrupted letter or sound: with a letter, as *floriet*, when one ought to say *florebit*; with a sound, if the first syllable is lengthened instead of the middle one, as in *latebrae* and *tenebrae*. It is called barbarism from barbarian peoples, who did not know the integrity of Latin speech; [Note: “For every people.” The same point appears below, book IX, chapter 1.] for each people incorporated into the Roman state transmitted to Rome along with its resources the faults both of its words and of its customs.

**2.** [Note: On *barbarism* and *barbarolexis*. Charisius also calls it *barbarolexis*; Donatus and Diomedes call it *barbaralexis*.] The difference between barbarism and barbarolexis is that barbarism occurs in a Latin word when it is corrupted; but when barbarian words are inserted into Latin speech, it is called barbarolexis. Likewise, when the fault occurs in prose, it is called barbarism; when it occurs in verse, it is called metaplasm.

**3.** Barbarism occurs in writing and in pronunciation. In writing it occurs in four ways: if someone adds, changes, transposes, or removes a letter or syllable from a word. In pronunciation it occurs in quantities, accents, aspirations, and the other features that follow.

**4.** Barbarism occurs through quantities if a short syllable is used for a long one, or a long one for a short. It occurs through accents if the accent is shifted to another syllable. It occurs through aspiration if the letter *h* is added where it should not be, or removed where it should be.

**5.** It occurs through hiatus whenever, in pronunciation, a verse is split before it is complete; or whenever one vowel follows another, as in *Musae Aonides*. Barbarism also occurs through metacism, iotacism, and lambdacism.

**6.** Metacism occurs whenever the letter *m* is followed by a vowel, as in *bonum aurum* and *justum amicum*. We avoid this fault either by suspending the pronunciation of the letter *m* or by omitting it.

**7.** Iotacism occurs whenever the sound of the letter *i* is doubled, as in *Troiia* and *Maiia*, where the pronunciation of those letters is so slight that only one *i*, not two, seems to be sounded.

**8.** [Note: Lambdacism. See Martianus Capella.] Lambdacism occurs if two *l*s are pronounced in place of one, as Africans do, for example *colloquium* for *conloquium*; or whenever we pronounce one *l* more heavily and two more lightly. The reverse is the case: [Note: “For one *l* is heavier and two lighter.” The reverse seemed to be indicated: that one should be pronounced more lightly and two more heavily. But all the books forbid this reading. Isidore’s meaning, I think, must therefore be as follows: just as two vowels, when they come together in a diphthong, are not pronounced fully as separate sounds but combine so that each loses something through the mingling of the sound, and neither is heard in full, so a double *ll* in the middle of a word is pronounced more lightly than a single *l*. Nor, if one may argue the point, does this happen without reason. The first *l* is blunted when it strikes against the following one before, receiving the blow, it in turn strikes the following letter; for when it coalesces with it, it removes from it what belonged to a semivowel, so that it may begin from a vowel. Thus both are weakened: the first in its latter part, the latter in its former part. Our own speakers who strive to speak more gently often admit lambdacisms as well. Nor were the Hebrews unfamiliar with such refinements, as when they place a *dagesh* in *et* for elegance.] for one *l* we ought to pronounce more heavily, and two more lightly.

**9.** [Note: “Collision.” Collision had not been mentioned above, but Donatus mentions it.] Collision occurs whenever the ending of the last syllable is contained in the beginning of another word, as in *matertera*.

# CHAPTER XXXIII. On Solecism

**1.** Solecism is an incongruous combination of several words, just as barbarism is the corruption of one word. [Note: “Words joined incorrectly.” From Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 13.] Solecism occurs when words are joined contrary to the proper rule, as when someone says *inter nobis* instead of *inter nos*, or *dare veniam sceleratorum* instead of *dare veniam sceleratis*.

**2.** It is called *solecism* from [Note: From the Cilicians. From Diomedes.] the Cilicians, who came from the city of Soli, now called Pompeiopolis. When they lived among other peoples, they confused their own language with that of the others in a faulty and inconsistent manner, and gave the name to solecism. Hence people who speak in the same way are said to commit solecisms.

**3.** Among poets, solecism is called a *schema* whenever an inversion is found to have been made out of metrical necessity; but when there is no such necessity, the fault of solecism remains.

**4.** Solecism occurs in two ways: either through the parts of speech or through their accidents. It occurs through the parts of speech if we put one part in place of another, for example if [Note: “If we apply prepositions to adverbs.” Thus correctly in the oldest codices: for example, if one says *de longe* (“from afar”). Nonius: “All who follow the art deny that a preposition ought to be added to an adverb, but the authority of the ancients should take precedence. *De subito*, etc.”] we apply prepositions to adverbs. It occurs through accidents—that is, through features belonging to the parts of speech—such as qualities, genders, numbers, forms, and cases. Solecisms are therefore made through all these, as Donatus explained.

**5.** They also occur in many other ways. For Lucilius said that there were a hundred kinds of solecism; anyone who strives to maintain the rule of correct speech ought to avoid all of them rather than imitate them.

# CHAPTER XXXIV. On Faults

**1.** Grammarians call those things faults which we must avoid in speech. These are barbarism, solecism, acyrology, cacemphaton, and the rest.

**2.** Barbarism is the corruption of a single word, as when someone lengthens the third syllable in *ignoscere*.

**3.** Solecism is a faulty combination of words, as when someone says *inter hominibus* instead of *inter homines*.

**4.** Acyrology is an improper expression, as in “may it be permitted for one who fears to hope”; properly, one who fears should *fear*, not *hope*. [Note: “In a grassy field.” Servius notes this in book V of the *Aeneid*.] Likewise, “in a grassy field”: properly, one should say that the field is *graminosus* (“covered with grass”), not *gramineus* (“made of grass”).

**5.** [Note: Cacemphaton. Isidore calls it “sounding discordantly”; Servius calls it *cacemphaton* in speech, and Donatus *cacemphaton* in a compound expression.] Cacemphaton is an obscene expression or one that sounds badly when compounded. Obscene, as in “with their minds aroused by these words.” [Note: “A bad combination.” Servius’s words concerning *Dorica castra* in *Aeneid* II.] Inharmonious, as in “it is pleasing to go to the Doric camp.” For bad composition results when one begins with the syllable with which the preceding word ended.

**6.** Pleonasm is the superfluous addition of one word, as in “Thus far has been the cultivation of the fields and the stars of heaven.” For stars exist nowhere except in heaven.

**7.** Perissology is the superfluous addition of several words, as in “May Reuben live, and not die,” although living is nothing other than not dying.

**8.** Macrology is long-winded speech containing unnecessary matter, as in: “The envoys, having failed to obtain peace, returned back home to the place from which they had come.”

**9.** [Note: *Tautologia*, “same-speech.” Thus shortly before: *Macrologia*, “long-speech,” etc. In chapter 36 he interprets allegory as *alieniloquium*, “other-speech.”] Tautology is repetition of the same meaning, as in: “If the fates preserve the man, if he feeds on the ethereal air, and has not yet fallen beneath the cruel shadows.” Everything repeated there is one and the same thing, but it is announced repeatedly.

**10.** Eclipsis is an omission in an expression, in which necessary words are lacking, as in “to whom a quiver of gold”; for *erat* (“was”) is missing.

**11.** Tapinosis is a lowering of the status of a great matter through one’s words, as in:

> Rare swimmers appear in the vast whirlpool.

**12.** Cacosyntheton is faulty composition, as in “and with our turned spear we weary the backs of the young cattle.”

**13.** [Note: Amphibolia. Thus in the oldest codices, and thus it is called by Charisius, more correctly than by Diomedes and Donatus, who call it *amphibologia*.] Amphibolia is an ambiguous expression, which may arise through the accusative case, as in Apollo’s response to Pyrrhus:

> I say, Aeacides, that you—or the Romans—can conquer.

In this verse it is uncertain whom the speaker has indicated as the victor.

**14.** It also arises through uncertain punctuation, as in “Italy will wage a great war.” The punctuation is uncertain: does it mean “a great war” or “great Italy”?

**15.** It also arises through a verb common to both voices, as in “Cato is entreated, Cicero is accused, Brutus is awaited, Antony is scorned”; and in this ambiguity it is not shown whether they themselves entreated, accused, awaited, or scorned others, or whether others did these things to them.

**16.** It also arises through homonymy, when one name signifies many things, as with *acies*, unless you add whether it means the edge of a sword, the eyes, or troops.

# CHAPTER XXXV. On Metaplasms

**1.** *Metaplasmus* is called in Greek and “transformation” in Latin. It occurs in a single word because of metrical necessity and the license of poets. Its species are as follows.

**2.** Prothesis is addition at the beginning of a word, as *gnato* for *nato*, and *tetulit* for *tulit*. Epenthesis is addition in the middle, as *relliquias* for *reliquias*, and *induperator* for *imperator*.

**3.** [Note: Paragoge, as *MAGIS* for *MAGE*. Donatus uses the same examples; but for Charisius *mage* for *magis* is an example of apocope.] Paragoge is addition at the end, as *magis* for *mage*, and *potestur* for *potest*.

Aphaeresis is cutting away from the beginning, as *temno* for *contemno*.

Syncope is cutting away from the middle, as *forsan* for *forsitan*.

Apocope is cutting away from the end, as *sat* for *satis*.

**4.** Ectasis is lengthening contrary to nature, as in *Italiam fato*, when *Italiam* ought to be pronounced with a short final syllable.

Systole is shortening contrary to nature, as in *aquosus Orion*, when *Orion* ought to be pronounced with a long syllable.

Diaeresis is the division of one syllable into two, as *albai* and *longai* for *albae* and *longae*.

**5.** Episynaloephe is the fusion of two syllables into one, as *Phaeton* for *Phaëton*, *Nerei* for *Nereï*, and *aeripedem* for *aeripedem*.

Synaloephe is the collision of vowels joined to vowels, [Note: “Of vowels joined.” It would have been enough to say “collision of vowels.” But if something had to be added, the reading of the Roman codex, *adjunctarum*, seemed more tolerable than that of our copies, where *juncta* or *adjuncta* is read.] as in “and these things, utterly different, while they are being done in part.”

**6.** Ecthlipsis is the collision of consonants with vowels, as in *multum ille* and *terris*.

[Column 0110A] Antithesis is the substitution of one letter for another, as *olli* for *illi*.

Metathesis is the transposition of a letter, as *Evandre* for *Evander*, and *Timbre* for *Timber*.

**7.** [Note: “Metaplasm occurs in one expression.” The entire passage is from Servius, *Aeneid* V, concerning the words:

> The work of the city, the Dardanian youth, in triple measure.

In both places, however, the text is corrupt; Chacon restored it from an old edition.]

Between barbarism and *lexis*, that is, Latin and perfect expression, metaplasm is a fault in a single word made according to rule. Likewise, between solecism and *phrasis*, that is, perfect connection of expressions, there is a *schema*, or figure, which is a fault in the connection of expressions made according to rule. Thus metaplasms and figures occupy a middle position, and are distinguished by skill and lack of skill. They are made for ornament.

# CHAPTER XXXVI. On Figures

**1.** *Schemata* is translated from Greek into Latin as “figures.” They occur in words or sentences through various forms of arrangement for the ornament of speech. Although there are many of them, [Note: “These are found among the grammarians.” Chacon added *necessaria* from Donatus and Charisius.] the following are found among grammarians.

**2.** Prolepsis is anticipation, where things that ought to follow are placed first, as in: “Meanwhile the kings, with enormous force: Latinus.” It ought to have been said in this way: “Meanwhile the kings, with enormous force,” and immediately what follows should have been added: “Advance from the camp”; then one should say: “Latinus,” and so on. Instead, for ornament, the matter was anticipated, and the kings who ought to have followed were inserted in seven verses; afterward came: “They advance from the camp.” Hence it is called anticipation, because what ought to have followed was placed first.

**3.** Zeugma is a clause in which several meanings are closed by one verb. It occurs in three ways: the verb that joins the sentences is placed either at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle. At the beginning, as:

[Note: “The wine-vessel’s bottom turns.” Cited by Nonius in a passage from Lucilius, book III of the *Satires*.]

> The bottom is turned by the wine-bearers; the judgment is turned by us.

In the middle, as:

> Greece was given to Sulpicius by lot, Gaul to Cotta.

At the end, as:

> For at this time obedience produces friends, truth hatred.

**4.** Hypozeuxis is the opposite figure, in which each meaning has its own proper clause, as:

> He approaches the king and tells the king his name and lineage.

**5.** [Note: “Syllepsis occurs in unlike clauses.” Donatus: “Syllepsis also occurs in unlike clauses, when a singular expression is joined to a plural verb.” Charisius: “Syllepsis occurs when a singular expression is concluded by a plural verb.”] Syllepsis occurs in unlike clauses, either when a plural expression is completed by a singular verb, as in *sociis et rege recepto* (“with the allies and the king received”), or when a singular expression is completed by a plural verb, as in:

> We have tender apples,
>
> Soft chestnuts, and an abundance of pressed milk.

For above he said *sunt* (“there are”); here he ought to have said: “There is an abundance of pressed milk.”

**6.** Syllepsis occurs not only through the parts of speech but also through their accidents. Whenever one is used for many, or many for one, there is syllepsis: one for many, as in “they fill each womb with an armed soldier,” although it is not filled by one soldier but by many. Likewise, many for one, as in the Gospel: “The thieves who were crucified with him reviled him”; there, each of the two is introduced as having blasphemed, although only one did so.

**7.** Anadiplosis occurs when the following verse begins with the same word with which the preceding verse ended, as:

> Let owls contend with swans, let Tityrus be Orpheus;
>
> Orpheus in the woods, Arion among dolphins.

**8.** Anaphora is the repetition of the same word at the beginnings of several verses, as:

> We followed you, when Dardania was burned, and your arms;
>
> We traversed beneath you the swelling sea in our fleets.

**9.** Epanaphora is the repetition of the same word at the beginnings of the clauses within one verse, as:

> You the grove of Angitia, you the glassy waters of Fucinus,
>
> You the clear lakes lamented.

**10.** Epizeuxis is the repetition of a word twice in one clause, as: “thus, thus it pleases me to go beneath the shadows.”

**11.** Epanalepsis is the repetition at the end of a verse of the same expression placed at its beginning, as:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.

**12.** Paronomasia is an expression nearly identical in form but different in meaning, as: “Is it fitting for you to depart or perish?”—that is, “to become an exile or to die?”

**13.** Schesis onomaton is a multitude of nouns joined together in a certain sequence, as “clouds, snow, hail, storms, lightning, winds.” [Note: “Joined in a certain arrangement.” In Donatus it is corruptly read as “joined in the same manner of joining.”]

**14.** Paromoeon is a multitude of words beginning with the same letter, as in Ennius:

> O Titus Tatius, you yourself have brought such great things upon yourself, tyrant.

Virgil uses this figure with restraint: he does not employ it throughout an entire verse as Ennius did, but sometimes only at the beginning of a verse, as:

> Savage, sitting above the arms;

sometimes in the middle, as:

> Both the lakes that spread their clear waters, and the places rough with thorns;

and sometimes at the end, as:

> Cassandra alone foretold such disasters to me.

**15.** Homoeoptoton occurs when many nouns are expressed in the same case, as:

> Yet he recognizes neither himself running nor himself going,
>
> Raising his hands and moving the enormous stone.

**16.** Homoteleuton occurs when many words end in the same way, as *abiit*, *abscessit*, *evasit*, *erupit* (“he went away, withdrew, escaped, burst forth”).

**17.** Polyptoton occurs when a sentence is varied through different cases, as:

> From nothing, nothing; to nothing, nothing can return.

[Note: Marcus Dama. From Persius, *Satire* V.]

> Marcus Dama—oh dear!—with Marcus standing surety, you refuse
>
> To believe the money? With Marcus as judge, you grow pale!
>
> Marcus has spoken. So be it; assign the tablets, Marcus.

**18.** Hirmos is a sentence that preserves its own continuous course of expression all the way to the end, as:

> There is in a long recess a place, an island a harbor, and the rest.

For the sense proceeds at length from there until:

> A black grove, bristling with shadows, hangs over it.

**19.** Polysyntheton is an expression linked by many conjunctions, as “and the roof, and the household shrine, and the arms, and the Amyclaean hound.”

**20.** Dialyton, or asyntheton, is the opposite figure, which is expressed freely and simply without conjunctions, as “we came, we saw, it pleased us.”

**21.** [Note: Antitheton. From here to the end of the chapter these figures belong neither to Donatus nor to Charisius; and several other figures are found in the Roman codex, so these too may appear to be foreign additions.] Antitheton is where opposites are set against opposites and give beauty to the sentence, as:

> Cold things fought with hot, wet with dry;
>
> Soft things with hard; weightless things with those possessing weight.

**22.** Hypallage occurs whenever words are understood in the opposite relation, as “to give south winds to the fleets,” when in fact we give ships to the winds, not winds to the ships.

# CHAPTER XXXVII. On Tropes
# Chapter XXXVII. On Tropes

1. Grammarians call *tropes* by a Greek name; in Latin they are interpreted as modes of expression. They arise from a proper meaning 59 [Col. 0111D] toward an improper likeness. [Note: “Toward a non-proper likeness.” The received reading *similitudinem* can be retained, so that it means what Charisius said, “on account of likeness.” For these expressions seem to derive from that. But since Charisius himself defines metonymy as “a diction transferred from its proper meaning to another related meaning,” either reading may be accepted. Donatus likewise has “toward an improper likeness.”] It is extremely difficult to record the names of all of them, but Donatus compiled thirteen of them as worthy of being handed down for use. [Note: “Thirteen handed down for use.” So Bede. Donatus and Charisius have twelve.]

2. A metaphor is the transferred use of some word, [Col. 0112C] as when we say “the crops ripple” or “the vines put forth gems,” although we find neither waves nor gems in the things to which these words are transferred from elsewhere. Such and other tropical expressions are therefore covered with figurative garments over what is to be understood, so that they may exercise the reader’s mind and not become cheap through being bare and immediately obvious.

3. Metaphors are made in four ways: from animate to animate, as in “he mounted the winged horses.” The metaphorical speaker has mingled a bird’s wings with a four-footed creature, and, in describing how it sought the deserted places, has mingled the movement of a quadruped with that of a flying creature.

From inanimate to inanimate, as in “the pine plows the sea; the tall keel presses a furrow.” He has mingled the use of land with water, since plowing and pressing a furrow belong to land, not to the sea.

[Col. 0112D] 4. From inanimate to animate, as in “flowering youth”: he has mingled inanimate flowers with youth, which possesses a soul.

From animate to inanimate, as in:

> You, father Neptune, whose gray temples,  
> Girt by the crashing sea, resound;  
> From whose ever-enduring chin mighty Ocean flows,  
> And rivers wander through your hair.

[Note: “You, father Neptune.” Cited from Claudian by Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III. Varro attributed it to a certain Albinovanus. Augustine assigns it to an unknown author.] The chin, temples, and hair do not belong to the Ocean but to human beings. [Col. 0113A]

5. In this way, too, other names of things are most suitably transferred from one category to another for the sake of ornament, so that speech may be embellished. A metaphor, however, may belong to one side only, as in “the crops ripple”: one cannot say “the waves crop”; or it may be an *antistrophe*, that is, reciprocal, as in “the oarage of wings.” For both the wings of ships and the oars of wings are so called.

6. *Catachresis* is the application of the name of one thing to another. It differs from metaphor in that metaphor bestows a word upon something that possesses its own name, whereas catachresis uses a foreign word because the thing has no proper one, as in:

> And a face very like a laurel;

and:

> [lacuna] Now both are carried together,  
> With their brows joined, and with their long keel  
> Furrow the salt waters.

[Col. 0113B] A face and a brow belong only to animals and human beings. If the poet had not applied this name to the ship, he would have had no proper term for that part.

60 7. *Metalepsis* is a trope that indicates what follows through what precedes:

[Note: “And into the hands came paper and the knotted reed.” Persius, *Satires* III. What follows—“For through the hand words, etc.”—may be foreign to the passage, as others have thought, or perhaps the reading should be: “For through the hand, the paper, and the reed, letters are signified.”]

> And into the hands came paper and the knotted reed.

For by the hand words are signified, and by the reed letters.

8. *Metonymy* is a renaming transferred from one meaning to another related meaning. It occurs in many ways. Sometimes what contains is used to indicate what is contained, as in “the theaters applaud” and “the meadows bellow,” since people applaud in the former and cattle bellow in the latter; [Col. 0113C] or, conversely, what is contained indicates what contains, as in “now neighboring Ucalegon burns,” although it was not he but his house that was burning.

9. Likewise, the inventor may indicate the invention, as in “without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold,” and “Vulcan [sends] mingled ash to the stars.” By Ceres, the inventor of grain, he wishes bread to be understood; by Liber, the inventor of the vine, wine; by Venus, sexual desire; and by Vulcan, fire.

Conversely, the invention may indicate the inventor, as in:

[Note: “We pray for wine.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “[large] mixing bowls,” etc.: “It is a synecdoche, as when we say *Ceres* for grain.” Likewise Plautus:

> We pray for wine, for this god is present here.]

> We pray for wine,

meaning Liber, who discovered wine among the Greeks.

10. Likewise, the producer may indicate what is produced, as in “sluggish cold,” because it makes people sluggish; and “pale fear,” because it makes people pale.

Conversely, what is produced may indicate the producer, as in:

> The father yokes the horses with gold  
> And places foaming reins upon the wild creatures.

He called the reins “foaming,” although they themselves do not produce foam; rather, the horse that carries them sprinkles them with the foam poured over them. [Col. 0113D]

11. [Note: *Antonomasia*. Donatus: “Antonomasia is a designation placed in place of a name,” and so on, through “Achilles.”]

*Antonomasia* is a designation placed in place of a name, as “the son of Maia” for Mercury. This trope occurs in three ways: from the mind, as “great-hearted descendant of Anchises”; from the body, as “he himself, lofty”; and from something external, as:

[Col. 0114A]

> Unhappy boy, unequal in his encounter with Achilles.

12. 61 *Epithet* means “placed above the name,” for it is placed before a proper name, as “nourishing Ceres,” “obscene dogs,” and “troublesome birds.” [Note: “By these two tropes.” According to Donatus. Charisius likewise says: “An epithet is a word added to a noun, either for the purpose of adorning, disparaging, or indicating.”]

The difference between antonomasia and epithet is that antonomasia is used in place of a name, whereas an epithet never occurs without a name. By these two tropes we either censure, display, or praise someone.

13. *Synecdoche* is a “conceiving,” when the whole is understood from a part or the part from the whole. Through it, too, the genus is shown by the species and the species by the genus, since the species is a part and the genus a whole.

The part is understood from the whole, as in:

> How many birds gather together when the cold year  
> Drives them across the sea.

[Col. 0114B] It is not the entire year that is cold, but one part of the year, namely winter.

Conversely, the whole is understood from a part, as in:

> When the royal stern had raised flames.

Here it is not only the stern but the ship; not only the ship but those in it; and not everyone, but one person, who raised the flames.

14. *Onomatopoeia* is a coined word made to imitate the sound of an indistinct voice, as the creaking of doors, the neighing of horses, the lowing of cattle, and the bleating of sheep.

15. *Periphrasis* is circumlocution, when one thing is signified by many words, as “he gathers the life-giving breezes.” Through the combination of words he signified one thing, namely, “he lives.”

This trope is of two kinds: it either presents a truth splendidly or avoids ugliness by circumlocution.

It presents a truth splendidly, as in:

> And now dawn was scattering her first light over the lands,  
> Leaving the saffron bedchamber of Tithonus.

He means: “it was already becoming light,” or “day had risen.” [Col. 0114C]

It avoids ugliness by circumlocution, as in:

> And, poured through the limbs into the peaceful  
> Lap of her husband, she sought sleep.

By this circumlocution he avoids obscenity and decently indicates sexual intercourse.

16. *Hyperbaton* is “transposition,” when a word or sentence is displaced from its order. Its kinds are five: anastrophe, hysteron proteron, parenthesis, tmesis, and synchysis.

*Anastrophe* is an inverted order of words, as *littora circum* (“shores around”) instead of *circum littora* (“around the shores”).

17. *Hysteron proteron* is a sentence whose order has been reversed, as:

> After he touched the lofty waves and came to the open sea.

[Col. 0114D] He came to the open sea first, and thus touched the waves.

62 18. *Parenthesis* is when we insert a sentence which, if removed from the middle, leaves the rest of the speech complete. [Note: “We insert a sentence.” Donatus: “An inserted formation of a different sentence.”] For example:

> Aeneas—for filial love did not allow him  
> To remain—sends swift Achates ahead to the ships.

The order is: “Aeneas sends swift Achates ahead,” since the words in the middle constitute a parenthesis.

[Col. 0115A] 19. *Tmesis* is the division of a single word by the insertion of other words, as:

> [lacuna] The goddess poured around [him] a great covering of mist,

instead of *circumfudit* (“poured around”).

20. *Synchysis* is when the words are confused in every direction, as in:

> Young men, bravest hearts in vain, if a sure desire  
> Leads you to follow me daring the final dangers,  
> You see what fortune attends our affairs.  
> All the gods have departed, leaving shrines and altars,  
> The gods on whom this empire stood; you hasten to the burning city;  
> Let us die, and rush into the midst of arms.

[Note: “The order is as follows,” etc. Servius on this passage of Virgil.]

The order is: “Young men, bravest hearts, you hasten in vain to aid the burning city, because the gods on whom this empire stood have departed. Therefore, if your resolve is firm to follow me as I dare the final dangers, let us rush into the midst of arms and die.” [Col. 0115D]

21. *Hyperbole* is an elevation exceeding belief, beyond what ought to be believed, as “the wave lashes the stars” and “it opens the earth amid the waves.” In this way something is magnified beyond credibility, yet one does not depart from the path of conveying the truth, although the words expressing it exceed reality, so that the speaker’s intention, not deception, is apparent. [Note: “So that the speaker’s intention does not deceive.” Quintilian, book VIII: “It is enough to observe that hyperbole lies, though not in such a way that it wishes to deceive through a lie.”]

By this trope something is not only increased but also diminished. It is increased in “swifter than the wind”; it is diminished in “softer than a feather” and “harder than stone.” [Col. 0115B]

22. [Note: *Allegory*. Ambrose, *On Abraham*: “Allegory is when one thing is done and another is represented.” Cicero, *On the Orator* III: “One thing is said, and another is to be understood.”]

*Allegory* is “other-speech”: it sounds like one thing, but another is understood. For example:

> He sees three stags wandering along the shore,

where three leaders of the Punic War, or three Punic Wars, are signified.

And in the *Bucolics*:

> I sent ten golden apples,

that is, ten pastoral eclogues to Augustus.

This trope has many kinds, of which seven are prominent: irony, antiphrasis, enigma, charientismos, paroemia, sarcasmos, and astysmos.

[Col. 0115C] 63 23. [Note: *Irony*. Charisius: “Irony is speech that, through the gravity of its delivery, draws the meaning of the words in the opposite direction.”]

*Irony* is a sentence whose meaning is contrary to its delivery. Through this trope something is said cleverly, either by way of accusation or insult, as in:

> [lacuna]  
> Let Aeolus boast of your homes in that palace  
> And rule in the prison of the winds.

How can it be a palace if it is a prison? The matter is resolved by the delivery. “Prison” belongs to the delivery; “let him boast in the palace” is irony; and the whole is uttered through contrary delivery, in the form of irony, which mocks by praising.

24. [Note: *Antiphrasis*. Jerome, *Bonos.* (as cited), Letter 100: “Do you therefore seem handsome to yourself because you are called by a favorable name, as though a grove were not for that reason called a *lucus* because it scarcely gives light, or the Fates (*Parcae*) because they do not spare at all, or the Eumenides and Furies because they are not benevolent, or Ethiopians commonly called ‘silver ones’?”]

*Antiphrasis* is speech to be understood in the opposite sense, as *lucus* (“grove”), because it lacks light through the excessive shade of the trees; and *manes*, that is, “mild” and “gentle,” although they are terrifying and savage; and the Fates and the Eumenides—Furies—because they spare no one or do anyone good. [Col. 0115D]

By this trope dwarfs are called Atlases, the blind are called sighted, and Ethiopians are commonly called “silver ones.” [Col. 0116A]

25. The difference between irony and antiphrasis is that irony indicates what it wishes to be understood solely through delivery, as when we say to someone acting badly, “What you are doing is good.” Antiphrasis, however, does not signify the contrary through the speaker’s voice, but only through its words, whose origin is contrary.

26. An *enigma* is an obscure question that is difficult to understand unless it is explained, as:

> From the eater came forth food,  
> And from the strong came forth sweetness,

meaning that a honeycomb was taken from the mouth of a lion.

The difference between allegory and enigma is that allegory has a double force and figuratively indicates one thing beneath another. An enigma, however, is merely an obscure sense, shaded by means of certain images. [Col. 0116B]

27. [Note: *Charientismos*. From Donatus and Charisius.]

*Charientismos* is a trope by which harsh things to say are expressed more agreeably. Thus, when people ask whether anyone has sought us, one replies, “Good fortune”—from which it is understood that no one has sought us. [Col. 0116D]

28. [Note: *Paroemia*. From Donatus. Charisius: “Paroemia is the use of a common matter with some variation,” as “we shall count the cooked entrails,” when it means “we shall know from the outcome”; and “kicking against the goad,” that is, resisting something contrary. No one is unaware of the meaning of this proverb in the *Acts of the Apostles* and in Terence.]

*Paroemia* is a proverb adapted to circumstances and occasions. 64 To circumstances, as “kicking against the goad,” when it signifies that one must resist adversity. To occasions, as “the wolf is in the story.” [Note: “For country people say.” Servius, commenting on *Eclogue* 9, writes that it was not country people but natural philosophers who affirmed this. See Donatus on *The Brothers*.]

For country people say that a person loses his voice if a wolf sees him first. Hence this proverb, “The wolf is in the story,” is said to someone who suddenly falls silent.

29. [Note: *Sarcasmos*. From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on Pyrrhus’ words “You will therefore report these things,” and *Eclogue* 3, on “Whoever does not hate Bavius.”]

*Sarcasmos* is hostile mockery accompanied by bitterness, as:

> You will therefore report these things, and go as a messenger  
> To the father of the son of Peleus. Tell him to remember  
> My mournful deeds and degenerate Neoptolemus.

[Col. 0116C]

30. Contrary to this is *astysmos*, that is, urbanity without anger, as:

> Whoever does not hate Bavius, let him love your poems, Maevius,  
> And let that same person yoke foxes and milk he-goats;

that is: as a punishment, may whoever does not hate Bavius be made to love Maevius. Maevius and Bavius were very bad poets and enemies of Virgil. Whoever therefore loves them should do things contrary to nature, namely, yoke foxes and milk he-goats.

31. *Homoeosis* is what is interpreted in Latin as “likeness.” Through it, the demonstration of a less familiar thing is disclosed by comparison with one that is better known. It has three kinds: *icon*, *parabola*, and *paradigma*, that is, image, comparison, and example.

[Col. 0116D] 32. An *icon* is an image, when we attempt to express the form of a thing through a similar kind, as:

[Col. 0117A]

> In every way like Mercury—in voice and complexion,  
> In blond hair and the beautiful limbs of youth.

The likeness is appropriate to the kind represented by the person introduced.

33. A *parabola* is a comparison drawn from dissimilar things, as:

> As in the fields,  
> When the lion of summer-bearing Libya sees an enemy nearby,  
> He crouches;

here he compared Caesar to a lion, making a likeness not from Caesar’s own kind but from another.

34. A *paradigma* is an example of some saying or deed, drawn either from a similar or dissimilar kind, and applicable to the matter we propose, as:

[Note: “So bravely Scipio died at Hippo.” He seems to mean Scipio Metellus. Formerly called Publius Cornelius Scipio, he was later, through the adoption of Quintus Metellus Pius, called Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio. As Appian reports, when he encountered Caesar’s fleet and could not escape, he stabbed himself with a sword and threw himself into the sea.]

> Scipio died as bravely at Hippo as Cato at Utica.

65 35. Likeness is made in three ways: from equality, from superiority, and from inferiority.

From equality:

[Col. 0117B]

> Just as, often in a great people,  
> Sedition has arisen.

From greater to lesser:

> As lightning driven through the clouds by the winds;

From lesser to greater:

> If Orpheus could call back the spirit of his wife,  
> Trusting in his Thracian lyre and melodious strings—

as if he were saying: “If he could do it by relying on a small and brief thing, namely a lyre, then I can do it by relying on devotion.”

# Chapter XXXVIII. On Prose

1. Prose is extended speech, released from the law of meter. [Note: *Prosum*: for the ancients called something extended, that is, straight. Glossary: *prosa*, a combed garment (*pektòn himátion* in Greek). See Festus. The learned scholar correctly observes that it makes no difference whether one says *prosum* or *prorsum*, except that the former is older.]

The ancients called *prosum* something extended and straight. Hence Varro, in Plautus, says that *prosis lectis* means “straight beds.” Thus speech which is not bent into a pattern by rhythmic number, but proceeds straight, is called prose, because it extends in a straight line.

Others say that it is called *prosa* because it is poured forth, or because it rushes and flows more spaciously, with no predetermined limit.

2. Moreover, among both Greeks and Romans, concern for verse was much older than concern for prose. Everything was first composed in verse, whereas interest in prose flourished late.

Among the Greeks, the first was [Note: “Pherecydes of Syros.” Apuleius, *Florida* II: “Pherecydes of Syros, who, born on the island of Syros, first dared, rejecting the bond of verse, to write in unrestrained words, in unmetered speech, in free prose.” Pliny mentions him in books V and VII. Strabo, book X, and Eustathius on the *Odyssey*, book 15, on “There is a certain island called Syria, from which,” he says, “Pherecydes [came].” What follows in the same author, *Babylonius*, is corrupt from *Badou huios* (“son of Badus”). See Laertius.]

Pherecydes of Syros, who wrote in prose. Among the Romans, Appius Caecus was the first to practice prose speech against Pyrrhus. From that point onward, the others too competed in prose eloquence.

# Chapter XXXIX. On Meters

1. Meters are so called because they are bounded by definite measures and intervals of feet and do not proceed beyond the established measurement of time. For “measure” is called *metron* (μέτρον) in Greek.

2. 66 Verses are so called because, with their feet arranged in their proper order, they are regulated by a fixed limit through sections called divisions and members. [Note: “So that they would not extend farther,” and so on through “it is called number.” These are Augustine’s words, *On Order* II.14. See also *On Music* III.1.]

So that they would not roll on farther than judgment could sustain, reason established a limit from which they should turn back; and they say that the verse was named from this very fact, because it turns back.

3. Rhythm is attached to this. It is not regulated by a fixed limit, but nevertheless runs through feet arranged rationally; in Latin it means nothing other than “number.” Concerning it there is the line:

> I remember the rhythms, if only I held the words.

4. [Note: “It is called a song.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III.]

Anything contained in feet is called a song. They think it received this name either because it was pronounced in fragments—whence today we say *carminare* of wool that those cleaning it tear apart—or because those who sang such things were thought to be out of their minds. [Col. 0118B] [Note: “Hence *carminare* today.” Pliny uses the verb more than once, for example in book IX, chapter 38.]

5. Meters are named either from their feet, from the subjects written about, from their inventors, from those who frequently use them, or from the number of their syllables.

6. Meters are named from their feet, as dactylic, iambic, and trochaic. The trochaic meter arises from the trochee, the dactylic from the dactyl, and likewise the others from their respective feet.

From their number come hexameter, pentameter, and trimeter. We call certain verses senaries from the number of their feet; the Greeks call them trimeters because they strike in pairs. [Note: “Because they strike in pairs.” Terentianus: “But it is struck three times; hence it is called trimeter.”]

Tradition says that Ennius first made Latin hexameters, [Note: “And calls them long.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II: “In heroic verses, which Ennius calls long.”] and calls them long.

7. Meters are said to be named from their inventors, as Anacreontic, [Col. 0118C] Sapphic, and Archilochian. Anacreon composed Anacreontic meters; the woman Sappho produced Sapphic meters; a certain Archilochus 67 wrote Archilochian meters; a certain native of Colophon practiced Colophonian meters; and the discoverer of Sotadean meters was [Note: “Sotades, a Cretan by origin.” Concerning him, see Suidas and Athenaeus, book XIV.] Sotades, a Cretan by birth. The lyric poet Simonides likewise composed Simonidean meters.

8. They are named from those who frequently use them, as Asclepiadean. Asclepius did not invent them, but they were so called because he used them most frequently and elegantly.

9. They are named from the subjects written about, as heroic, elegiac, and bucolic.

The heroic song is so called because the deeds and actions of brave men are narrated in it. Heroes are called men who are, as it were, aerial and worthy of heaven because of their wisdom and courage. This meter surpasses the others in authority and is suitable for the greatest as well as the smallest works; it is equally capable of sweetness and charm.

10. Because of these qualities [Note: “It obtained only the name.” Although the deeds of heroes were also sung by lyric poets.] it alone acquired the name “heroic,” clearly because it commemorates the deeds of heroes. It is also considered the simplest of all and consists of two feet, the dactyl and the spondee; it is often composed almost entirely of one or the other, except that it is more moderate when the two are mixed than when it is constructed from only one.

11. It is also older than all other meters. Moses is shown to have first sung it in the song of Deuteronomy, [Note: “Long before Pherecydes.” There were two Pherecydeses. Strabo maintains that the Syrian, discussed in chapter 37, was older than the Athenian. Suidas takes the opposite view, unless there is an error here.] long before Pherecydes and Homer. [Note: “Should one read *probatur*?” Editorial note.]

Hence it is also evident that the Hebrews cultivated poetry earlier than the gentiles. [Note: “Insofar as Job [did so].” Jerome, preface to Job.] For Job too, who lived at the same time as Moses, proceeds in hexameter verse, with dactyls and spondees.

[Col. 0119B] 12. Among the Greeks this meter is said to have been first composed by Hecataeus of Miletus; [Note: “Hecataeus of Miletus.” Strabo, book I: “For poetic composition first came forth into public use and gained approval. Then, imitating it, those around Cadmus, Pherecydes, and Hecataeus composed other works, loosening the meter but preserving the other poetic features,” etc.] or, as others think, by Pherecydes of Syros. Before Homer it was called Pythian meter; after Homer it was called heroic.

68 13. They say it was called Pythian because oracles of Apollo were delivered in this kind of meter. For when Apollo pursued the serpent Python with arrows on Mount Parnassus to avenge his mother, the inhabitants of Delphi encouraged him in this meter, as Terentianus says:

> Hail, Paean! Hail, Paean! (ἰὴ Παιάν, ἰὴ Παιάν.)

14. The elegiac meter, however, is said to have received its name because the melody of this song suits the sorrowful. Terentianus writes:

> They called these elegies, because such a cadence  
> Is customarily more suited, they say, to mournful modes.

15. It is scarcely established at all who invented it, except that among us Ennius used it earlier. Among the Greeks the dispute among grammarians remains so unresolved that the matter has been left before the judge. [Note: “The matter has been left unresolved.” So the old Roman manuscript; our manuscripts have “deferred” or “bound.” We consider the two words *res relicta* (“the matter left”) foreign to the text. Horace, *Art of Poetry*: “Who nevertheless first produced the short elegies; grammarians dispute, and the controversy is still before the judge.”]

For some of them consider a certain Colophonian the author and inventor, others Archilochus.

16. Most people think that the bucolic, that is, pastoral song, was first composed at Syracuse by shepherds; some think it was at Lacedaemon.

For when Xerxes, king of the Persians, was passing into Greece, the Spartan maidens, fearing the enemy, dared neither to leave the city nor to perform according to custom the procession [Note: “And rustic chorus of Diana.” F. has *agresti*; the Roman manuscript has *Agrestae*. Pausanias, book VII, mentions Diana the Rustic.] and rustic chorus of Diana. A crowd of shepherds, so that the religious observance would not lapse, celebrated it with unpolished songs. [Col. 0119D]

It is called bucolic from cattle, which constitute the greater part, [Col. 0120A] although the speech and songs of shepherds and goatherds are also inserted in it.

17. It is clear that the prophet David first composed and sang hymns in praise of God. 69 Among the gentiles, the first was Mnemia Timothoe, who composed one for Apollo and the Muses; she lived in the time of Ennius, long after David. [Note: “The first was Mnemia Timothoe.” Most manuscripts have *Memmia*, *Emmia*, or *Inemia*, and *Cymothoe*. This requires further investigation, since no trace of Timothoe has been found. We likewise leave unresolved whether *Mnemia* is part of the name or whether she left *mnemeia* (μνημεῖα), that is, monuments.]

Hymns are translated from Greek into Latin as “praises.”

18. Epithalamia are songs of newlyweds, [Note: “Which is sung by students.” Augustine, on Psalm 44: “Students customarily sing certain songs for those escorting a wife, which are called epithalamia; whatever is sung there is sung in honor of the bridegroom and bride.” As for the term “student,” Jerome, *Catalogue*, on Sarapion: “Sarapion, who earned the name Student because of the elegance of his talent.”] which are sung by students in honor of the bridegroom and bride.

Solomon first produced this kind in praise of the Church and Christ. After that, the gentiles claimed the epithalamium for themselves, and a song of this type was adopted. At first the gentiles celebrated this kind on the stage; afterward it remained only in weddings.

It is called an epithalamium because it is sung in the bridal chambers. [Col. 0120B]

19. The *threnos*, which we call a lament in Latin, was first composed in verse by Jeremiah over the city of Jerusalem when it was destroyed and the people of Israel were led into captivity. After him came the lyric poet Simonides among the Greeks. These songs were used at funerals and in mourning, and are still used in the same way.

20. *Epitaphium* is Greek for “above the tomb” in Latin. It is the inscription of the dead, made at the time of repose for those who have already died. Their life, character, and age are written there.

21. *Poesis* is the Greek term for a work consisting of many books; *poema*, for one book. An *idyllion* consists of a few verses; a distich of two; a monostich of one.

22. An *epigramma* is an inscription, which is translated into Latin as *superscriptio* (“writing above”). 70 For *epi* means “upon” or “above,” and *gramme* means a letter or writing.

23. An *epode* is a short closing section in a poem. It is called an epode because it is sung in accompaniment to the form of an elegiac poem, in which, after one longer line has been set down, a shorter one is composed; thus, in each case, the following shorter lines echo as closings after the longer ones.

24. [Note: “The lyric poets call them closings.” Thus Terentianus shortly before called the pentameter a closing of the heroic line.]

The lyric poets call these “closings,” as though shortened verses were placed beneath complete ones, as in Horace:

> Blessed is he who, far from business—

then follows the shortened line:

> Like the ancient race of mortals.

The same pattern continues with alternating lines, each lacking some portion and resembling the preceding lines but being shorter.

[Col. 0121A] 25. [Note: *Centones*. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*: “[lacuna] since an example of this kind of facility is also available from secular writings. Anyone today can compose an entirely different story from Virgil, arranging the subject according to the verses and the verses according to the subject. Finally, Hosidius Geta expressed the tragedy *Medea* completely from Virgil. A certain relative of mine, among the other leisure exercises of his style, explained the *Pinax* of Cebes. They also customarily call these ‘Homeric centos’: works which, from Homer’s poems, stitch together into one body many pieces composed here and there according to one’s own work, in the manner of a maker of patchwork.”]

Among grammarians, *centones* are usually called works that take passages from the poems of Homer or Virgil and, in the manner of patchwork, stitch many pieces composed here and there into one body for one’s own work, according to the capacity of the subject.

26. Finally, [Note: “Proba, wife of Adelphus.” Proba Falconia, whom Jerome also mentions; a cento is circulated under her name.] Proba, wife of Adelphus, composed from Virgil a complete cento on the creation of the world and the Gospels, arranging the subject according to the verses and the verses according to the subject.

Likewise, [Note: “And a certain Pomponius.” Other manuscripts have *Pomp[in]us*.] a certain Pomponius, among the other leisure exercises of his style, composed a *Tityrus* in honor of Christ from the same poet; similarly, he composed one from the *Aeneid*.

71 # Chapter XL. On Fables

1. Poets named fables from *fari* (“to speak”), because they are not things that happened but are merely fabricated through speech. They were introduced so that, through the invented conversation of speechless animals with one another, some image of human life might be recognized.

Alcmaeon of Croton is said to have invented them first. [Note: “Alcmaeon of Croton, a disciple of Pythagoras.”] They are called Aesopic because he became prominent in this matter among the Phrygians.

2. Fables are either Aesopic or Lybistic. [Note: “Either Aesopic or Lybistic.” Aristotle, *Rhetoric* II, on example: “Of these, one is comparison and the other is fable, such as the Aesopic and Lybistic [fables].” Hesychius: “Lybistic fables.” Chamaeleon says that Lybos discovered these fables. See Theon, *Progymnasmata*.]

Aesopic fables are those in which speechless animals are imagined to converse with one another, or in which things without souls—cities, trees, mountains, rocks, and rivers—are made to speak.

Lybistic fables are those in which intercourse of speech is imagined between human beings and beasts, or between beasts and human beings.

3. Poets fabricated certain fables for the sake of delight; others they interpreted according to the nature of things; and some according to human morals.

Those fabricated for delight are the ones commonly called fables, such as those composed by Plautus and Terence. [Col. 0121C]

4. They invent fables according to the nature of things, as Vulcan is lame, because by nature fire is never straight. So too the three-formed beast—first a lion, last a dragon, and in the middle the Chimaera itself, that is, a she-goat—was invented to distinguish the ages of human beings. Their first age, adolescence, is fierce and horrifying like a lion; the middle period of life is brightest, like a she-goat, because it sees most sharply; then comes old age, bent by declining circumstances, like a dragon. [Note: “Bent by altered circumstances.” Those familiar with Lombardic characters may accept either *cruribus* (“with limbs”) or *cursibus* (“with courses”), because of the similarity of *a* and *u*, and *r* and *s*, especially since the book has *casibus*; the Roman manuscript has *casibus subiacens inflexis*.]

5. The fable of the Hippocentaurs was likewise invented—that is, a human being mixed with a horse—to express the swiftness of human life, since the horse is known to be extremely swift.

[Col. 0122A] 72 6. They invent fables according to morals, as in Horace, where the mouse speaks to the mouse, and the weasel to the fox, so that through a fictitious narrative a truthful meaning may be conveyed concerning the matter at hand.

Hence such fables of Aesop are also directed toward morals. Likewise, in the Book of Judges, the trees seek a king for themselves and speak to the olive, the fig, the vine, and the bramble. All this is invented for the sake of morals, so that one may arrive at the intended matter through a fictitious narrative but truthful meaning.

7. [Note: “So too Demosthenes.” In the *Olynthiacs*.]

The orator Demosthenes likewise used a fable against Philip. When Philip demanded that the Athenians give him ten orators and was departing, Demosthenes invented the following fable to dissuade them:

Wolves once persuaded shepherds, whose diligence they wished to deceive, to enter into friendship with them, on the condition that the dogs, who were the cause of their quarrels, be handed over to them by right. The shepherds agreed and, in the hope of security, handed over the dogs, whom they had kept as the most vigilant guardians of their sheep.

Then the wolves, having removed all fear, tore apart everything in those flocks, not merely to satisfy their hunger but also for pleasure.

So too, Philip was demanding the leaders of the people, so that he might more easily crush a city stripped of its guardians. [Col. 0122B]

# Chapter XLI. On History

1. History is a narration of a deed that was carried out, through which things done in the past are recognized.

It is called *historia* in Greek, [Note: “*Historia*, from *historein*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I.] from *historein* (ἱστορεῖν), that is, “to see” or “to learn.” Among the ancients, no one wrote history unless he had been present and had seen the things that were to be written down. For we apprehend what happens more accurately with our eyes than what we gather by hearing.

73 2. Things that are seen are reported without falsehood. [Note: “This discipline belongs to grammar.” Augustine, *On Order* II.12: “Because grammar, as its very name declares, professes letters, and is therefore called *litteratura* in Latin, it follows that whatever is worthy of remembrance is committed to letters and necessarily belongs to it.”]

This discipline belongs to grammar, because everything worthy of remembrance is committed to writing. The records of history are called *monumenta* (“memorials”) because they preserve the memory of deeds. *Series* (“sequence”) is a transferred expression, derived from garlands of deeds joined together one after another.

# Chapter XLII. On the First Authors of Histories

1. Among our people, Moses was the first to write history, beginning with the creation of the world.

Among the gentiles, Dares of Phrygia was the first to publish a history of the Greeks and Trojans. They say that he wrote it on palm leaves. [Col. 0123A]

2. [Note: “The first historian.” The Roman manuscript has “the first in Roman history,” a reading apparently confirmed by Silius. The Gothic manuscript has *historia*, an error. Likewise Martial: “Crispus, first in Roman history.”]

After Dares, Herodotus was regarded as the first historian in Greece. After him Pherecydes became famous, at the time when Ezra wrote down the Law.

# Chapter XLIII. On the Usefulness of History
1. Histories of nations do not impede readers in the useful things they have related. For many wise men have inserted the deeds of people in former times into histories for the instruction of those living in the present.

[Note: “Histories of nations do not impede readers,” etc. See Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II, chapter 21.]

2. Indeed, history embraces the complete reckoning of past times and years, and through the succession of consuls and kings many necessary matters are investigated. [Col. 0123B]

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the kinds of history [Col. 0123B]

1. There are three kinds of history. A record of the events of a single day is called an *ephemeris* (Greek ἐφημερίς, “daily record”). Among us this is called a *diary*. [Col. 0124A] For what the Latins call a *diary*, the Greeks call an *ephemeris*.

[Note: “The kind of history is threefold.” See Gellius, Book V, chapter 18.]

[Note: “For what the Latins call a *diary*, the Greeks call an *ephemeris*.” Gellius: “This is the term used by those who write a daily record, which the Greeks call an *ephemeris*.”]

2. Those records arranged according to individual months are called calendars.

3. Annals are the affairs of individual years. Whatever worthy of remembrance was accomplished at home or in war, by sea or by land, year by year in the records, they called *annals* after the annual events.

[Note: “Were accomplished in the records.” From the records, first commentaries were compiled; then from the commentaries annals, or history, were composed. Isidore wishes history to be compiled from records into commentaries, from commentaries into annals, and from annals into history; and he says that it is called history when, through an author’s work, a history has been composed from annals, or certainly when several annals have been reduced to a single volume.]

4. History, however, concerns many years or periods of time; through its careful work, annual records have been set down in books. [Col. 0123C] Between history and annals there is this difference: history concerns those times that we have seen, whereas annals concern those years that our own age has not known.

[Note: “Between history and annals.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the words *et vacet annales*: History is so called from those times that we have either seen or could have seen, from ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱστορεῖν, that is, “to see.” Annals, however, concern those years and periods which our own age does not know; hence Livy consists of annals and history.]

Hence Sallustius is composed of history, while Livy, Eusebius, and Jerome are composed of annals and history. [Col. 0124B]

[Note: “Sallustius from history; Livy, Eusebius.” Thus read the Gothic and Ovetan College manuscripts, quite wrongly, since all the remaining manuscripts read *historialibus*. The words “Sallustius from history” seem to be lacking in Servius. Clearly, not only the remaining histories, which Sallust began from the consulship of M. Aemilius Lepidus and Q. Lutatius Catulus, but also the Jugurthine War, which began in the consulship of P. Scipio Nasica, fell within his lifetime. Let this assertion be credited to its author, Servius; this distinction is not approved by the most learned men. See Beroaldus’s critique of Servius’s *Commentaries*.]

5. [Col. 0124B] There is a difference between history, an argument, and a fable. Histories are true events that have happened. Arguments are things that, although they have not happened, nevertheless can happen. Fables are things that have neither happened nor can happen, because they are contrary to nature.
