[Note: “Between history, argument, and fable.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the words “recalled from Teucer’s blood.” That passage can be corrected and supplemented from this source, for it is in very poor condition.]

# BOOK TWO: ON RHETORIC AND DIALECTIC [Col. 0123]

## CHAPTER ONE. On rhetoric and its name [Col. 0123C]

1. Rhetoric is the science of speaking well, with an abundance of eloquence in civil questions for persuading people about what is just and good. [Col. 0123D]

[Note: “Rhetoric is the science of speaking well.” I consider only these words proper to this passage. The additional words found in most books—“necessary for persuading in civil questions, with a just and good abundance of eloquence in matters concerning things and persons”—are not the same in all copies. The earlier words have been brought here from Book I, chapter 2; the final words, “in matters concerning things and persons,” are absent from all the Gothic manuscripts. I have therefore included only what is found in the better books.]

It is called rhetoric by the Greek designation ἀπὸ τοῦ ῥητορίζειν, that is, “from abundance of speech”; for among the Greeks ῥῆσις means “speech,” and ῥήτωρ means “orator.”

[Note: “It is said from ἀπὸ τοῦ ῥητορίζειν.” Thus the ancient manuscripts, nor does the interpretation reject this.]

2. Rhetoric is joined to the art of grammar. In grammar we learn the science of speaking correctly. [Col. 0124C] In rhetoric we learn how to express what we have learned.

## CHAPTER II. On the inventors of the art of rhetoric

1. This discipline was invented by the Greeks—by Gorgias, Aristotle, and Hermagoras—and was translated into Latin by Tullius, namely Cicero, and Quintilian. They treated it so fully and so variously that it is easy for a reader to admire it, but impossible to comprehend it completely. [Col. 0124D]

[Note: “By Gorgias, Aristotle, and Hermagoras.” Since these men especially cultivated this art, although others laid its first foundations, such as Empedocles, Tisias, and Corax.]

[Note: “And Quintilian.” Some books add “and Titianus,” but they are not of better quality. Chacon rightly thought that the name had crept in through a scribal repetition of the final syllables of *Quintilianus*. Jerome says of Titianus in his *Chronicle*: “Titianus, an eloquent man, administers the prefecture of the praetorium in Gaul.” Servius says, *Aeneid* X: “Titianus and Calvus, who extracted themes from Virgil and distorted them for the purposes of speaking.”]

2. For when the sheets have been retained, as though the sequence of the discourse had adhered to the memory, and then put aside, all recollection slips away at once. [Col. 0125A]

[Note: “For when the sheets have been retained, as though…” He appears to have had in mind Cicero’s words in the *Tusculan Disputations*: “But somehow, while I am reading, I assent; when I have put the book down, all assent slips away.”]

A perfect knowledge of this discipline makes an orator. [Col. 0125D]

## CHAPTER III. On the name of the orator and the parts of rhetoric

1. An orator, therefore, is a good man skilled in speaking. The good man consists in nature, character, and accomplishments. The skilled speaker consists in artistic eloquence, which is made up of five parts: invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery; and its final purpose is to persuade someone of something.

2. Skill in speaking itself consists in three things: nature, instruction, and practice—nature in talent, instruction in knowledge, and practice in constant application. These are the qualities observed not only in an orator but in every craftsman, so that he may accomplish something. [Col. 0125B]

[Note: “Are observed in every craftsman.” Another reading is “are expected,” or perhaps “are desired.”]

## CHAPTER IV. On the three kinds of cases

1. There are three kinds of cases: deliberative, demonstrative, and judicial. The deliberative kind is that in which it is discussed, concerning any matters affecting human life, what ought or ought not to be done. The demonstrative kind is that in which a person is shown to be worthy of praise or blame.

2. The judicial kind is that in which judgment is given concerning the person’s deed, whether a penalty or a reward is due. It is called judicial because it judges a person and by its decision shows whether he is worthy of praise and reward, or at least whether he is guilty and should be condemned or released from punishment.

[Note: “And released.” Chacon rejected these words. Isidore frequently alternates conjunctions and disjunctions.]

3. The deliberative kind is so called because in it deliberation takes place concerning each matter. It has two forms: exhortation and dissuasion—that is, discussion of what should be sought and what should be avoided, what should be done and what should not be done.

4. Exhortation is divided according to three considerations: the honorable, the useful, and the possible. It differs somewhat from deliberation, because exhortation requires another person, whereas deliberation sometimes takes place within oneself. In exhortation there are two factors that carry the greatest weight: hope and fear.

5. The demonstrative kind is so called because it displays each matter either by praising or by blaming it. This kind has two forms: praise and blame. The order of praise is distinguished according to three times: before the person, in the person’s own time, and after the person.

6. Before the person, as in:

> What ages brought you forth so joyful.

In the person’s own time, as in:

> O you alone who pitied Troy’s unspeakable sufferings.

After the person, as in: [Col. 0126A]

> As long as rivers run into the sea, as long as shadows  
> Sweep over the mountains, as long as the vaulted sky feeds the stars,  
> Honor, your name, and your praises shall always remain.

7. In the same order, conversely, this form must also be observed in blaming a person: before the person, against the person, and after the person. The common topic belongs to the demonstrative kind of blame, although it differs from it in one respect. For blame, which is the opposite of praise, is applied specifically to a particular person who has acted.

8. A common topic, however, is generally placed before an accusation concerning an act. Hence it is called a common topic, because, in the absence of the person, it is directed not so much against the individual as against the crime itself. For every vice is found not only in one person but commonly in many.

## CHAPTER V. On the twofold status of cases [Col. 0126B]

1. Among rhetoricians, the status of a case is called the matter on which the case rests—that is, its constitution. [Col. 0125D] The Greeks call status, from contention, στάσιν. The Latins, however, derive it not only from a battle by which they attack the opponent’s proposition, but also from the fact that both sides stand upon it. It arises from the claim and the refutation.

[Note: “The Greeks call status from contention.” Herodias and Hermagoras use this explanation. Isidore appears to prefer the Latin word to the Greek στάσις.]

2. There are two statuses of cases: rational and legal. From the rational arise conjecture, definition, quality, and transfer. From definition arise the juridical and the negotiative. From the juridical arise the absolute and the assumptive. From the assumptive arise concession, removal of the charge, attribution of the charge, and comparison. From concession arise exculpation and entreaty.

[Note: “Attribution of the charge, comparison.” Most books read “compensation.” Capella says: “Comparison, which later writers are accustomed to call compensation.” But Cicero has *comparison*, and the present reading derives from him. Below, comparison is likewise defined, with all the books in agreement.]

3. The conjectural status exists when one person denies the fact charged against another. The definitive status exists when it is maintained that the charge is not what it is alleged to be, but what it is is established by means of definitions. [Col. 0126C]

[Note: “Quality is…” These words appear superfluous, having been taken from Cicero, *On Invention* I. The reading should be: “While the question is what kind of matter it is, because the dispute concerns the force and nature of the case…”]

Quality is present when the question is what kind of matter it is; and because the dispute concerns the force and nature of the case, it is called the general constitution.

4. Transfer exists when the case depends upon the fact that the person who ought to act does not appear to be the one acting, or that the action is not being brought before the proper persons, at the proper time, under the proper law, with the proper charge, or with the proper penalty. It is called a translative constitution because the action appears to require transfer and alteration.

5. The juridical status is that in which the nature of equity and right, and the basis of reward or punishment, are examined. The negotiative status is that in which what the law requires according to civil custom and equity is considered. [Col. 0126D]

[Note: “The assumptive.” After *assumptive*, the word *absolute* appears to be missing. He had said that the assumptive and absolute arise from the juridical. Cicero defines the absolute as “that which itself contains the question of right and wrong.”]

The assumptive status is one that, considered in itself, provides no firm basis for rejection, but assumes some ground of defense from outside.

6. Concession exists when the accused does not defend the act that was committed but asks to be forgiven. We have shown this to pertain to penitents.

[Note: “Which we have shown to pertain to penitents.” See distinction 50, chapter “In the Head,” and the following chapters.]

Removal of the charge exists when the accused attempts to shift the charge brought against him, and the blame for it, by force and authority onto another. [Col. 0127A]

7. Attribution of the charge exists when an act is said to have been rightly done because another person first provoked the injury. Comparison exists when it is argued that some other act by another person was honorable or useful, and that the act being charged was committed in order that the other act might be accomplished.

8. Exculpation exists when the act is admitted but the fault is removed. It has three parts: ignorance, accident, and necessity. Entreaty exists when the accused confesses both that he sinned and that he sinned deliberately, yet asks to be forgiven; this kind of case can occur only very rarely.

9. From the legal status arise the following: the written text and the intention, conflicting laws, ambiguity, inference or reasoning, and legal definition. The written text and intention are at issue when the actual words appear to disagree with the writer’s meaning. The status of conflicting laws exists when two or more laws are recognized as inconsistent with one another.

10. Ambiguity exists when what has been written appears to signify two or more things. Inference or reasoning exists when something else, although not written, is discovered from what has been written. Legal definition exists when the force of a word is examined to determine where it lies, as in the definitive constitution. [Col. 0127B]

11. Some authorities have therefore counted both the rational and legal statuses more precisely as eighteen. In Cicero’s rhetorical works, however, nineteen are found, because he assigned transfer principally among the rational statuses. [Col. 0127C]

[Note: “According to Cicero’s rhetoric,” that is, according to Book I of *On Invention*.]

From this, Cicero later also criticized himself and assigned transfer to the legal statuses. [Col. 0127D]

[Note: All this is from the same first book of *On Invention*.]

## CHAPTER VI. On the threefold controversy

1. According to Cicero, a threefold controversy is either simple or compound. If it is compound, one must consider whether it is joined from several questions or arises from some comparison. A simple controversy contains one complete question, as in: “Are we to declare war on the Corinthians, or not?”

2. A compound controversy consists of several questions, in which several matters are asked, as follows: “Is Carthage to be destroyed, or restored to the Carthaginians, or is a colony to be established there?” A controversy arising from comparison is one in which, through contention, it is asked which alternative is preferable or what is most important, as follows: “Is an army to be sent into Macedonia against Philip, to aid our allies; or is it to be kept in Italy, so that the largest possible forces may be available against Hannibal?” [Col. 0127D]

[Note: All this is from the same first book of *On Invention*.]

## CHAPTER VII. On the four parts of a speech [Col. 0128A]

1. In the rhetorical art there are four parts of a speech: exordium, narration, argumentation, and conclusion. The first arouses the listener’s mind; the second explains the events; the third establishes confidence in the assertions; the fourth embraces the end of the entire speech.

2. We must begin in such a way that we make the listener well disposed, teachable, or attentive: well disposed by entreating, teachable by instructing, and attentive by arousing. We must narrate so that we speak briefly and clearly. We must argue so that we first strengthen our own case and then shatter the opposing arguments. We must conclude so that we stir the listener’s mind to carry out what we say.

[Note: “Well disposed.” Isidore himself prescribes this spelling, *benivolum*, in Book X, rather than *benevolum*.]

[Note: From the same passage in Cicero.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the five kinds of cases

1. There are five kinds of cases: honorable, astonishing, humble, doubtful, and obscure. An honorable case is one toward which the listener’s mind is immediately favorable without any speech on our part. An astonishing case is one from which the minds of those who are about to listen are alienated. A humble case is one that the listener disregards. [Col. 0128B]

2. A doubtful case is one in which the judgment is uncertain, or in which the matter partakes both of honor and of disgrace, so that it produces both goodwill and offense. An obscure case is one in which the listeners are slow to understand, or in which the case is seen to be entangled in matters difficult to comprehend.

[Note: From the same passage in Cicero.]

## CHAPTER IX. On syllogisms [Col. 0128C]

1. What is called *syllogism* in Greek is called *argumentation* in Latin. Argumentation is so called as though it were the discourse of an incisive mind, by which we develop something discovered to be probable. A syllogism, therefore, is the final conclusion of a proposition, an assumption, and a confirmation, either from uncertainty that is in doubt or from the confidence of one who proves the point.

[Note: “The final conclusion of the confirmation.” Following Cicero, he has added confirmation to the syllogism, although his example is only of a simple syllogism.]

2. It consists of three parts: proposition, assumption, and conclusion. The proposition is, for example: “What is good cannot have a shameful use.” The listener agrees. The speaker assumes: “Money has a shameful use.” The conclusion follows: “Therefore money is not good.”

3. Syllogisms are used not only by rhetoricians but especially by dialecticians, although the Apostle often proposes, assumes, confirms, and concludes—things that, as we have said, belong properly to the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. [Col. 0128D]

[Note: “Although the Apostle…” These are Jerome’s words to Paulinus of Urbica, letter 155. Chacon thought that Isidore had changed Jerome’s “Apostle” into “philosopher,” and that the original had returned either through scribal error, with both words abbreviated, or through the excessive diligence of someone who took the wording from Jerome.]

4. Among rhetoricians there are two principal kinds of syllogism: induction and reasoning. The parts of induction are three: first, the proposition; second, the inference, which is also called the assumption; third, the conclusion.

5. Induction is that which wins the assent of the person for whom it is undertaken by means of things not in doubt, whether among philosophers, rhetoricians, or speakers in conversation. [Col. 0128D]

[Note: “Or speakers in conversation.” Victorinus says, “in any verbal dispute.”]

The proposition of an induction introduces one or more similarities that must necessarily be granted in the matter under discussion.

6. The inference of an induction, also called the assumption, introduces the matter under dispute, on account of which the similarities have been brought forward. The conclusion of an induction either confirms the concession of the inference or declares what follows from it. [Col. 0129A]

Reasoning is a speech by which the matter under question is proved.

[Note: “Reasoning.” Cassiodorus uses the same explanation. Fortunatianus puts it more briefly: “Reasoning is that by which we approve something.”]

7. *Enthymeme* is therefore translated into Latin as “conception of the mind.” Artigraphers customarily call it an imperfect syllogism. For the form of its argument consists of two parts, when it uses what contributes to establishing belief while passing over the rule of syllogisms, as in: “If a storm is to be avoided, then one must not sail.” For it consists only of the proposition; it has therefore been judged to suit rhetoricians more than dialecticians.

[Note: “Artigraphers.” Donatus and Servius use the same word in their commentary on Donatus’s *Art of Grammar*. Augustine’s letter 59 shows that such Greek-Latin technical terms were used at that time, although Quintilian disliked them. Augustine and Fortunatianus likewise call them technical terms.]

8. There are two modes of reasoning. The first is the enthymeme, which is an imperfect and rhetorical syllogism. The second is the epichereme, which is a fuller syllogism in rhetoric. [Col. 0129B]

9. The parts of an enthymeme are five: first, the demonstratively convincing; second, the ostensive; third, the sentential; fourth, the exemplary; fifth, the collective.

[Note: “The parts of enthymemes.” Isidore treats these more fully than Fortunatianus.]

10. The demonstratively convincing is what convinces by evident reasoning, as Cicero did in his speech for Milo: “You are therefore sitting as avengers of the death of the man whose life, if you thought it could be restored by you, you would not wish restored.”

11. The ostensive is what constrains by a clear demonstration of the matter, as Cicero says against Catiline: “Yet this man lives—lives, indeed, and even comes into the Senate.”

The sentential is what advances a general maxim, as in Terence: “Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred.” [Col. 0129C]

12. The exemplary is what threatens a similar outcome by comparing some example, as Cicero says in the *Philippics*: “I am amazed, Antony, that you do not fear the ends of those whose examples you imitate.”

[Note: Cicero, *Philippics* 2: “Whose examples you imitate, whose ends you do not dread.”]

13. The collective is present when the arguments that have been advanced are gathered into one, as Cicero says in his speech for Milo: “The man whom he would not have with gratitude, he wished to have amid the complaints of certain persons. The man whom he did not dare to kill legally, in the proper place, or at the proper time, he did not hesitate to kill unlawfully, at an improper time, and with danger to his own life!”

[Note: “The arguments that have been advanced.” The Gothic manuscript and the Ovetus read “the arguments,” which is preferable.]

14. According to Victorinus, an enthymeme also has another definition: it consists of the proposition alone, as has already been said, and is formed as follows: “If a storm is to be avoided, sailing must not be undertaken.” [Col. 0129D]

[Note: “From the assumption alone.” We have supplied some words here from the Tarragon manuscripts and Cassiodorus, on the authority of Augustine.]

From the assumption alone, as in: “There are some who say that the world proceeds without divine administration.” [Col. 0130A]

15. From the conclusion alone, as in: “Therefore the divine judgment is true.”

From the proposition and the assumption, as in: “If he is an enemy, he kills; but he is an enemy.” Since the conclusion is missing from it, it is called an enthymeme.

[Note: “The epichereme follows.” From Book I of *On Invention*.]

16. The epichereme follows. It descends from reasoning and is a broader and more fully developed rhetorical syllogism. It differs from dialectical syllogisms in breadth and in the extended form of its discourse; for this reason it is assigned to rhetoricians. [Col. 0130D]

[Note: “A broader and more fully developed rhetorical syllogism.” Earlier he called the epichereme a broader syllogism. Augustine, following Fortunatianus, understood this to mean a broader development.]

It has three forms: the first is tripartite, the second quadripartite, and the third five-part.

17. A tripartite epicherematic syllogism consists of three parts: proposition, assumption, and conclusion. A quadripartite syllogism consists of four parts: first, the proposition; second, the assumption; third, a proof attached either to the proposition or to the assumption; and fourth, the conclusion. [Col. 0130B]

[Note: “And fourth, the conclusion.” The word “fourth” has been restored from the Gothic manuscripts.]

18. A five-part syllogism consists of five parts: first, the proposition; second, its proof; third, the assumption; fourth, its proof; fifth, the conclusion.

Cicero constructs one in this way in the *Art of Rhetoric*: “If deliberation and demonstration are kinds of cases, they cannot properly be considered parts of some kind of case; for the same thing can be a genus in one relation and a part in another. The same thing cannot be both genus and part,” and so forth, until all the parts of this syllogism have been completed.

## CHAPTER X. On law [Col. 0130D]

[Note: “A law is …” See Book V, chapter 10, and distinction 1, chapter 2. The same material is repeated in Book V, chapters 3, 10, 19, and following; see Gratian, distinction I.]

1. A law is an enactment of the people, which the elders sanctioned together with the plebs. [Col. 0130C] What a king or emperor decrees is called an enactment or edict.

[Note: “The institution of equity.” All law consists in statutes and customs. See Book V, chapter 3, and distinction 1, chapter 2.]

The institution of equity is twofold: sometimes it lies in laws, sometimes in customs. The difference between law and custom is that law is written, whereas custom is a practice approved by long usage, or an unwritten law. Law is so called from *reading*, because it is written.

2. Custom is a long-standing usage derived solely from conduct.

[Note: “Derived from conduct, only so.” Thus the Ovetus manuscript; Gratian has “only.”]

Custom is a kind of law established by practice, which is accepted in place of a law when the law is lacking. Nor does it matter whether it consists in writing or in reason, since reason also commends the law.

[Note: “Reason commends the law.” Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “Custom is also accepted in civil matters in place of law when law is lacking. Nor does it matter whether it consists in writing or in reason, since reason also commends the law.”]

3. Moreover, if law is established by reason, everything that has been established by reason will now be law, provided only that it agrees with religion, conforms to discipline, and contributes to welfare. It is called custom because it is in common use. [Col. 0131A]

4. Every law either permits something—for example, that a brave man may seek a reward—or forbids something—for example, that no one may seek marriage with consecrated virgins—or punishes something—for example, that one who has committed murder should be punished by death.

5. Laws were made so that human recklessness might be restrained by fear of them, so that innocence might be safe among the wicked, and so that, among the wicked themselves, the dreaded punishment might restrain the power to do harm. For human life is regulated by the reward or punishment of the law.

[Note: “Human life is regulated.” *Moderatur* is passive, as in Digest XV, title “On Agency”: “According to the status of persons, both the action is framed and the condemnation is regulated.”]

[Note: “Laws were made.” From Augustine, letter 56.]

6. A law must be honorable, just, possible, in accordance with nature, in accordance with the custom of the homeland, suitable to its place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, so that through obscurity it may contain nothing that could entrap anyone. It must be written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of the citizens. [Col. 0131B]

[Note: “So that it may contain nothing as a trap.” Paul, Book V of the *Sentences*, chapter 33: “So that no one may fall into a trap through the wording of a legal provision.”]

## CHAPTER XI. On the maxim

1. A maxim is an impersonal statement, such as: “Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred.” If a person is added to it, it becomes a *chria*, as in: “Achilles offended Agamemnon by speaking the truth”; “Metrophanes earned Mithridates’ favor by showing compliance.”

2. The difference between a *chria* and a maxim is that a maxim is expressed without a person, whereas a *chria* is never stated without a person. Thus, if a person is added to a maxim, it becomes a *chria*; if the person is removed, it becomes a maxim.

## CHAPTER XII. On confirmation and refutation [Col. 0131C]

1. *Catasceve* is confirmation of a proposed matter; *anasceve* is contrary to the preceding. For it refutes the claim that something proposed as having arisen, happened, or been said did in fact exist or occur—for example, if someone denies that the Chimera existed, or confirms that it did.

2. The difference between these and a *thesis* is that although a thesis also involves debate on both sides, it is nevertheless a kind of release or restriction concerning an uncertain matter. *Catasceve* and *anasceve*, however, generally concern matters that are not probable but are proposed as true.

3. The first division of *anasceve* is into inconsistency and falsehood. The forms of inconsistency are what is dishonorable and what is useless. Dishonor, in turn, is treated either in words or in deeds.

In words, as when someone is said to have spoken things unbecoming and inconsistent with his authority—for example, if someone were to defame Cato the Censor by saying that he urged the young toward wickedness and luxury. [Col. 0131D]

4. In deeds, as when someone is said to have done something contrary to his sanctity and character, as in the story of the adultery of Mars and Venus.

Falsehood has three forms. The first is the incredible: something believed not to have happened, as when African fleets departing from the Sicilian shore are said to have seen a young man [the printed syntax is uncertain].

[Note: “African fleets departing.” All the books have the corrupt reading “entering,” from Pliny and Solinus.]

5. The impossible is: “Clodius laid an ambush for Milo, and the same man was killed by Milo.”

The contrary is: “For if he laid the ambush, he killed. He was killed; therefore he did not lay the ambush.”

This arrangement, reformulated as a contrary argument, will serve *catasceve*. Nevertheless, the opening principles must be arranged so that we either say that the authority of the ancients is to be believed or that no credence should be given to fables.

[Note: “Will serve *catasceve*.” In some Gothic manuscripts the following is added: “So that we may establish all the degrees: honorable, useful, probable, possible, consistent; or, conversely, dishonorable, useless, scarcely probable, impossible, contrary.” Since these words neither fit sufficiently with what precedes nor occur in the older books, we have judged that they should not be accepted, although some authorities approved them.]

6. With respect to the final point, let us return to *anasceve*, lest those who invented these stories have intended something else—namely, that Scylla was not a marine monster but a woman living by the sea, and that she was not girded with dogs but was some rapacious and inhospitable woman who preyed upon those who came to her. [Col. 0132B]

## CHAPTER XIII. On prosopopoeia

1. *Prosopopoeia* occurs when both a personality and speech are invented for beings without life. Cicero says against Catiline: “For if my country, which is far dearer to me than my own life, were speaking with me, saying…” and so forth.

[Note: “Prosopopoeia.” These figures, together with ethopoeia, seemed too important to be counted among the other figures; for that reason he placed them among the preliminary rhetorical exercises.]

2. In the same way we introduce mountains, rivers, or trees as speaking, assigning a personality to something that does not possess the nature of speech. This is customary in tragedies and is also found very frequently in speeches.

## CHAPTER XIV. On ethopoeia [Col. 0132C]

1. We call *ethopoeia* the figure in which we invent the character of a person in order to portray feelings, age, pursuit, fortune, joy, sex, grief, and boldness. When the character of a pirate is assumed, the speech will be bold, abrupt, and reckless. When the speech of a woman is imitated, it must suit her sex. Likewise, a different manner must be adopted for a young man, an old man, a soldier, a commander, a parasite, a peasant, and a philosopher.

[Note: “A different manner must be adopted.” From the Gothic and Ovetus manuscripts. Another reading is “a different speech must be delivered.”]

2. One who is affected by joy speaks in one way, and one who has been wounded in another. In this kind of composition, the following must be considered above all: who is speaking, to whom, about what, where, and at what time; what he has done, what he is going to do, or what he may suffer if he neglects this advice. [Col. 0132D]

## CHAPTER XV. On the kinds of questions

1. There are two kinds of questions: one is finite, the other infinite. The finite is called *hypothesis* in Greek and *case* in Latin; it is a controversy involving a definite person.

2. The infinite is called *thesis* in Greek and *proposition* in Latin. It has no definite person, nor does it contain any definite circumstance—that is, neither a place nor a time. [Col. 0133A]

[Note: “Nor does it contain any definite circumstance.” Another reading is: “Nor is there in a thesis any definite circumstance,” with the same meaning.]

In a case everything is definite, and therefore the proposition is, as it were, a part of the case.

[Note: “Hence the proposition is, as it were, a part of the case.” Compare Cicero, *Topics*: “Thus the proposition is a part of the case.”]

## CHAPTER XVI. On style

1. In our styles of expression we must use language as the matter, place, time, and person of the listener demand, so that we do not mix profane things with religious, immodest things with chaste, trivial things with serious, wanton things with solemn, or ridiculous things with sad.

2. We must speak in Latin and with clarity. A person speaks Latin who follows words that are true and natural to the things themselves and does not depart from the speech and refinement of the present time. It is not enough for him to see what he should say unless he also says it clearly and gracefully; nor is even that enough unless he says elegantly what he says. [Col. 0133B]

[Note: “Unless he also says gracefully what he says.” The Roman manuscript reads: “Unless he does and makes what he says.” Another reads: “Unless he does what is fitting.” Another: “Unless he says and claims to do what he says.” We have adopted the present reading with one letter changed.]

## CHAPTER XVII. On the threefold style of speaking

1. Things stated quietly should be expressed lightly, things stated with force gravely, and things stated with modulation moderately. This is the threefold style of speaking: humble, middle, and grandiloquent. When we speak of great matters, they should be expressed grandly; when of small matters, subtly; when of middling matters, moderately.

2. In small cases nothing grand or sublime should be said; one should speak in a gentle and ordinary manner. In greater cases, when we discuss God or the salvation of human beings, greater magnificence and brilliance should be displayed.

3. In moderate cases, in which nothing is done so that the listener may act but only so that the listener may be entertained, we should speak moderately, between the two styles. [Col. 0133C]

[Note: “In which nothing is done so that he may act.” So reads the Ovetus, and such are most cases of the demonstrative kind.]

Even when someone speaks about great matters, he should not always speak grandly. He should speak humbly when teaching, moderately when praising or blaming something, and grandly when calling back minds that have turned away. The words used in the humble style should be adequate, in the moderate style brilliant, and in the grand style forceful.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the colon, comma, and period

1. Every speech is composed and constructed through the comma, colon, and period. [Col. 0133D] The comma is a small part of a sentence; the colon is a member; the period is a circuit or complete turn. A comma is formed from the joining of words, a colon from commas, and a period from cola.

[Note: “Composed and constructed.” The prefixed form is frequent in Gothic writing: *instruitur* is used for *struitur*. The loss of an initial syllable is likewise frequent: *Spania* for *Hispania*, *Spalensis* for *Hispalensis*, and *storia* for *historia*.]

[Col. 0133D] 2. A comma is the end of a clause, as, for example: “And if I fear, judges”—there is one comma. Another comma follows: “that it should be disgraceful for the bravest man to begin by saying that he fears.” Thus a colon, that is, a member, has been formed; it gives sense to the thought, but the sentence still hangs unfinished. Then, from several members, a period is formed, that is, the final closure of the sentence, as in: “They require the ancient custom of the courts.”

[Note: [Col. 0134D] They require the custom. The same words occur in Fabrius. Now, instead of *requirunt*, in the speech *For Milo* we commonly read *minime vident*, although others also affirm that they have read *requirunt* in a manuscript book.]

A period, however, should not be longer than can be uttered in a single breath.

# CHAPTER XIX. On avoiding faults of letters, words, and sentences

1. Moreover, the orator’s pure and dignified eloquence must be free from every fault, whether in letters, words, or sentences.

2. In letters, the joining must be suitable and harmonious. Care must therefore be taken that the final vowel of the preceding word does not run into the same vowel at the beginning of the following word, as in *feminae Aegyptiae* (“Egyptian women”).

[Col. 0134B]

[Note: [Col. 0134D] This construction. Others have *instructura*, arising from the customary prothesis.]

This construction is improved when consonants are attached to vowels. A junction of three consonants, which, colliding with one another, seem to hiss and quarrel, must be avoided—namely *r*, *s*, and *x*—as in *Ars studiorum* (“the art of studies”), *Rex Xerxes* (“King Xerxes”), and 91 *Error Romuli* (“the error of Romulus”). The consonant *m*, too, should be avoided when it is thrust against vowels, as in *verum enim* (“for truly”).

# CHAPTER XX. On the joining of words

1. Faults must also be avoided in words, so that unsuitable words are not employed, which the Greeks call *acyrologia*. Proper usage is therefore to be valued, but in such a way that, sometimes, because of the low or filthy character of a vulgar or offensive word, transferred terms may be used—not terms fetched from far away, but ones that appear close and related to the proper words.

[Col. 0134C]

2. Excessively long hyperbata must also be avoided, since they cannot be formed without confusing the meanings of other words. Ambiguity must likewise be avoided, as must that fault which occurs when certain people, carried away by a display of eloquence, enclose in a long and winding circumlocution what they could have expressed in one or two words by inserting empty phrases. This fault is called *perissologia*.

3. Its opposite fault is to steal even necessary words out of a desire for brevity. Just as in letters and words we avoid the faults recognized in the elementary studies of grammarians, so too we must avoid faults in sentences.

4. These include *cacophaton*, *tautologia*, *eclipsis*, *acyrologia*, *macrologia*, *perissologia*, *pleonasm*, and similar faults. On the other hand, *energia* elevates and adorns speech, as does *emphasis*, which causes something more than what has been said to be understood—for example, if one says, “He will ascend to the glory of Scipio”; and Virgil’s “the one who slipped down by the rope.” For when he says “the one who slipped,” he suggests height.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] It suggests height. Thus the Roman manuscript reads; all our manuscripts have “it suggests the height of the image,” but whether one reads “of the image” or rather “of the imagination,” neither seemed acceptable to us.]

The contrary virtue is to diminish in words things that are great by their nature.

[Col. 0135A]

# CHAPTER XXI. On figures of words and sentences

1. Speech is also enlarged and adorned by figures of words and sentences.

[Col. 0135B]

For since straightforward and continuous speech produces weariness and boredom both for the speaker and the listener, it must be bent and turned into other forms, so that it may refresh the speaker, become more ornamental, and divert the judge by varying his expression and hearing. Many of these figures were noted above by Donatus in the schemes of the *Art of Grammar*.

2. For this reason, only those figures needed to be inserted here which occur either never or only with difficulty in poetry, but freely in prose.

*Anadiplosis* is the doubling of words, as in: “Yet he lives! He lives! Indeed, he even comes into the Senate.”

3. *Climax* is a progression in which the word that ends the preceding thought begins the following one, and the order of speech is maintained, as though by steps. Such is the saying of Africanus: “From innocence arises dignity, from dignity honor, from honor authority, from authority liberty.”

4. Some call this figure a chain, because one thing is linked to another, as it were, by a word, and several matters are thus drawn along through the repetition of words. This scheme occurs not only in individual words but also in the joining of words, as in Gracchus: “Your boyhood was a dishonor to your adolescence, your adolescence a disgrace to your old age, and your old age a scandal to the republic.”

5. Likewise in Scipio:

[Note: [Col. 0135D] “Compelled by force and against my will.” Who could doubt that *coactus* is an interpretation of *ingratiis*? It could therefore be deleted without harm.]

“Compelled by force and against my will, I made a wager with him; after the wager had been made, I brought him before the judge; after he had been brought, I condemned him at the first assembly; after he had been condemned, I released him according to my will.”

6. *Antitheta*, which in Latin are called “contraposed expressions,” are statements placed in opposition to one another, producing beauty of thought and providing a most fitting ornament to speech. Thus Cicero:

“On this side modesty fights, on the other wantonness; here chastity, there sexual violation; here good faith, there fraud; here piety, there crime; here steadfastness, there frenzy; here honor, there disgrace; here restraint, there lust; here, finally, justice, moderation, courage, and prudence—all the virtues—contend with all the vices: luxury with injustice; cowardice with rashness; finally, abundance with poverty, sound reason with what is ruined, and sound sense with madness; finally, good hope struggles with despair concerning all things.”

[Col. 0135D]

7. The Book of Ecclesiasticus used this kind of ornamental expression when it said: “Against evil is good, and against death is life; so the sinner is set against the godly; and so look upon all the works of the Most High: two and two, one opposite one.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Two and two. The Septuagint has δύο, δύο, ἓν κατέναντι τοῦ ἑνός (“two, two, one opposite one”). Some commonly printed books likewise have this. The manuscript has: “two, two, one against one.”]

8. *Synonymia* occurs whenever, in connected speech, we express one thing by several words, as Cicero says: “You accomplish nothing, you devise nothing, you think of nothing.” Likewise: “I will not endure it, I will not suffer it, I will not permit it.”

9. *Epanodos*, which our writers call “returning”: “The dignity of the leaders was almost equal, though perhaps not equal to that of those who followed.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] “The dignity of the leaders,” etc. From the speech *For Ligarius*.]

10. *Antapodosis* occurs whenever the middle elements correspond to the first and last, as in: “Your deed is censured here, Conscript Fathers, not mine—and indeed it was a most honorable deed; but, as I said, it was not mine, but yours.”

[Col. 0136B]

11. *Paradiastole* occurs whenever we distinguish what we say by interpretation, as when you call someone “wise” instead of “cunning,” “brave” instead of “rash,” and “diligent” instead of “ungenerous.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] “Brave instead of thoughtless, diligent instead of ungenerous.” Rutilius said “brave instead of confident, diligent in household affairs instead of ungenerous,” citing the same example from Hyperides. Fabius also uses it, Book IX, chapter 3. Rutilius’ other example of *paradiastole* Fabius adapted as *synoeciosis*, although the figures seem opposed: the former separates things that appear identical, whereas *synoeciosis* joins things that are different.]

12. *Antanaclasis* is a figure that expresses an opposite meaning with the same word.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] *Antanaclasis*. Rutilius calls it *anaclasis*, unless there is an error in his text. Quintilian says it is a species of *paronomasia*.]

“A certain man complained about his son, while awaiting his own death. When the son replied, ‘I do not expect it,’ the father said, ‘Rather, I ask that you expect it.’”

[Note: [Col. 0136D] “A certain man complained.” Fabius and Rutilius call this man Proculeius.]

13. *Antimetabole* is a reversal of words that produces an opposite meaning by changing their order: “I do not live in order to eat; rather, I eat in order to live.” Likewise: “If Antonius is consul, Brutus is an enemy; if Brutus is the preserver of the republic, Antonius is an enemy.”

14. *Exoche*: “Who called them? Appius. Who brought them forth? Appius.”

[Note: [Col. 0136D] *Exoche*. “Who called them forward?” It seems that this passage lacks both the definition of *exoche* with its example and the name of another figure whose example is taken from the speech *For Milo*. Augustine said that this was *symploce*. It will not be difficult to supply both from Servius and the Roman Aquila.]

[Col. 0136C]

15. Let us now proceed to the figures of sentences that are worth knowing.

16. A *sententia* is an impersonal saying, as: “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.” If a person is added to it, it becomes a *chria*, as: “Achilles offended Agamemnon by speaking the truth.” “Metrophanes earned the favor of Mithridates by showing compliance.” The difference between a *chria* and a *sententia* is that a *sententia* is uttered without a person, whereas a *chria* is never spoken without a person. Thus, if a person is added to a *sententia*, it becomes a *chria*; if the person is removed, it becomes a *sententia*.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] A *sententia* is an impersonal saying. Likewise above, chapter 11: “Nevertheless, lest it not be understood.” Servius’ words concerning Virgil’s “Go, follow Italy, driven by the winds” (*Aeneid* IV).]

17. There are many kinds of *sententiae*. Some are indicative, others exclamatory, such as:

“Was there such anger in heavenly hearts?”

[Col. 0136D]

18. Others are comparative, such as:

“If I win and perish, what advantage is there in my winning?”

Others are superlative, uttered with some agitation of spirit and indignation:

“What do you not compel mortal hearts to do,

accursed hunger for gold?”

[Col. 0137A]

19. Others are interrogative, such as:

“Of what race are you, and from what home? Do you bring peace here, or arms?”

“What cause, young men, compelled you

to attempt unknown roads?”

20. Others are responsive, such as “from there, from here.” Others are supplicatory, such as: “Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils.” Others are promissory, such as:

“Dismiss your fear, Cytherea; the destinies

of your people remain unmoved for you.”

Others are concessive, though they prohibit by an urging impulse, such as:

“Go, follow Italy; seek kingdoms across the waves, driven by the winds.”

[Col. 0137B]

Yet, so that the persuasion should not go unrecognized, certain elements that secretly prohibit are mingled into it, such as “driven by the winds across the waves.” Others are demonstrative, such as “behold” and “see.” Others are optative, such as:

“O that Jupiter would bring back for me the years gone by!”

21. Others are derogatory, such as “not at all.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Others are derogatory. Others have “denying.”]

Others are uttered with an exclamation, such as:

“What madness, citizens, turns peace into war?”

And Cicero: “O immortal gods, where in the world are we?”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “What madness?” Petronius, in the *Satyricon*: “What madness,” he exclaims, “has turned peace into war?”]

22. Others are exhortatory, when we urge someone toward a course of action, such as: “Dare, stranger, to despise wealth.”

23. Others are dissuasive, when we lead someone back from an opposite vice or sin. There are also affirmative expressions, such as “why not?” and “indeed.”

24. Preceptive expressions include:

“Plow naked, sow naked;

you will have harvests despite the cold.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “You will have harvests despite the cold.” Rather, “fever,” according to Servius and Virgil. Chacon rightly judged these words to have been inserted from the margin.]

25. Prohibitive expressions include:

“Do not plant the hazel among the vines,

and do not reach for the highest branches.”

26. Negative expressions include “not” and “by no means.” There are also expressions of astonishment, such as:

“Good heavens! One may not live, yet one wishes to commit fornication!”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “Good heavens! One may not live,” etc. These are Jerome’s words in his letter to Rusticus, section 4.]

27. Expressions of grief include:

“Alas for me, that love is curable

by no herbs!”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “Curable.” Ovid has “remediable.”]

Expressions of weeping: . . . . . .

Expressions of comparison:

“As once Crete is said to bear a labyrinth in its depths.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “As once Crete.” From *Aeneid* V.]

Expressions of admonition: . . . . . .

Of mockery: . . . . . . . . .

Of groaning: . . . . . . . . . .

Of exhortation: . . . . . . .

[Col. 0137D]

Of consolation: . . . . . . .

Of compassion: . . . . . . .

[Col. 0138A]

There are as many tones in pronunciation as there are figures of this kind.

28. There are also *amphidoxae*, whose one part is honorable and the other dishonorable, such as:

“Your desire is not secure:

you seek great things, Phaethon.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] There are also *amphidoxae*. See Augustine, *On Rhetoric*, chapter 10.]

29. There are also *procatalepses*, in which we anticipate what could be brought against us in order to refute it, such as: “If any of you, judges, or any of those present, perhaps wonders . . .”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] *Procatalepses*. Fabius calls it *prolepsis* and “anticipation.”]

There are also *aporiae*, a feigned doubt in which one pretends not to know what one does know, or pretends not to know how something should be said.

[Col. 0138A]

30. *Coenonesis* is the sharing of deliberation with judges or opponents, as when one says: “I ask you, judges,” or “you opponents, what ought I to do, or what would you have done?”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] *Coenonesis*. Rufinianus calls this *anacoenosis*; Fabius calls it “communication.”]

[Col. 0138B]

31. *Paradoxon* occurs when we say that something unexpected has happened, as Cicero says in *For Flaccus*: “He who ought to have been the herald of that honor has been made its suppliant in danger.”

32. *Epitrope*, that is, permission, occurs when we leave something to the judges or opponents themselves to assess, as Calvus says against Vatinius: “Rub your forehead and say that you deserved to become praetor more than Cato.”

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Calvus against Vatinius. It is established that Vatinius was accused by Calvus. Catullus writes:

“I laughed at someone—I know not whom—just now in the crowd,

when my Calvus had wonderfully set forth the Vatinian charges.”]

33. *Parrhesia* is speech full of liberty and confidence: “I have killed him, I have killed him—not Spurius Maelius,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] “I have killed him, I have killed him.” From *For Milo*.]

This figure must be used cautiously, as Cicero did; for he first supplied the justification.

34. *Ethopoeia* occurs when we introduce a speech spoken by another person, as Tullius does in *For Caelius*, making the blind Appius speak with Clodia. *Energia* is the bringing of things done or seemingly done before the eyes, about which we have already spoken.

[Col. 0138C]

35. *Metathesis* sends the minds of the judges toward past or future events, as follows: “Recall your minds to the spectacle of the conquered and wretched city, and believe that you see fires, massacres, plunderings, ravages, violations of the bodies of children, the captivity of matrons, and the slaughter of old men.”

[Note: [Col. 0138D] *Metathesis*. Rufinianus and the others call it *hypotyposis*. P. Nunnesius rightly said that Isidore named it *metathesis*, because through it the minds of the judges are transferred from what is present to what is past or what is to come.]

As for the future, it anticipates what the opponent is going to say, as Tullius does in *For Milo* when he directs the minds of the judges toward the condition of the republic that would exist if, after Milo had been killed, Clodius were still alive.

36. *Aposiopesis* occurs when we interrupt in silence what we seemed about to say:

“Whom I—but it is better to calm the troubled waves.”

37. *Epanalepsis* is a digression: “The heat of speaking carried me away, and the importance of the subject led me a little farther than I wished; but I return to the case.”

[Note: [Col. 0138D] *Epanalepsis*. Cicero calls it “returning”; Quintilian calls it ἄφοδος, “a way back.”]

[Col. 0139A] 97

38. *Anamnesis* is a recalling of something that we pretend we had forgotten.

*Apaetesis* occurs when we opportunely reclaim something that we had, as it were, deposited in the minds of the judges.

39. *Aetiologia* occurs when we propose something and provide its cause and explanation.

40. *Characterismus* is an expressed description of someone’s appearance, as:

“Everything resembling Mercury—his voice and his complexion,

his blond hair and his handsome youthful limbs.”

[Note: [Col. 0139C] *Characterismus*. See Rutilius, where the term is corruptly written *chresterismus*.]

41. *Epitrochasmus* occurs when it heaps together several briefly expressed thoughts in one place and runs along with a certain haste, as Cicero says:

“The republic, Quirites, and the life of all of you, your goods, fortunes, wives, and children, and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 0139C] *Epitrochasmus*, when it brings together several thoughts. He seems to confuse two figures, *epitrochasmus* and *synathroesmus*. To heap together several thoughts is common to *epitrochasmus* and *synathroesmus*; to proceed with a certain haste belongs rather to *epitrochasmus*. The example from the Third Speech against Catiline is more properly *synathroesmus*: life, goods, fortunes, wives, and children do not differ greatly from one another, whereas such separation may perhaps be characteristic of *epitrochasmus*. Aquila and Numenius accordingly say that these items are πολυδιεστῶτα (“widely separated”). Thus, although the older editions have *epitrochasmus*, while the manuscripts have *litrismus*, *lintrismus*, and *syntrismus*, we think that Isidore defined both figures in words that were not very different, and that through the ignorance of copyists one definition and one example were left, with only the names of both figures. Augustine noticed a similar error shortly beforehand concerning *exoche* and *symploce*. See Rutilius, Aquila, and Fabius, Book VIII. Vulcanius made *athraesmos*—I believe—from *litrismos*.]

[Col. 0139B]

42. *Ironia* occurs when, by pretending, one wishes a meaning different from what one says to be understood. It happens either when we praise someone whom we wish to blame, or blame someone whom we wish to praise. An example of both would be if you said: “Catiline, a lover of the republic; Scipio, an enemy of the republic.”

43. *Diasyrmos* diminishes great things through words or magnifies very small things.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Diasyrmos*. Several examples occur in Aquila and Rufinianus.]

44. *Epimone* occurs whenever we linger longer over the same meaning:

“Whom, after all, did he spare? Whose friendship did he faithfully preserve? For whose advantage was he not an enemy? When did he not either accuse someone, beat someone, or betray someone?”

45. *Epangelia* is a promise by which we make the judge attentive, promising that we are going to say something either important or insignificant.

46. *Prosopopoeia* occurs when both a person and speech are invented for inanimate things. Cicero says in *Against Catiline*: “For if my country, which is much dearer to me than my life, were speaking with me, saying . . .”

[Col. 0139C] 98

47. *Parathesis* occurs when we seem to set something aside, saying that we will return to it and recall it to the memory of the judges when the opportunity arises.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Parathesis*. *Apaetesis*—discussed shortly before—is its counterpart.]

[Col. 0140A]

48. *Peusis*, that is, soliloquy, occurs when we answer ourselves in response to questions addressed to us.

49. *Synchoresis* occurs when we postpone something, asking that they meanwhile permit us to say something else.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Synchoresis*. We have departed somewhat from the manuscripts: printed editions have *synaeresis*, manuscripts *synerosis*, because we found συγχώρησις, that is, “permission,” listed among the rhetorical figures by Aristides Quintilianus in his work *On Music*.]

# CHAPTER XXII. On dialectic

[Note: [Col. 0140C] This is the beginning of the third book in the Tarraconensian manuscript.]

1. Dialectic is a discipline devised for distinguishing the causes of things.

[Note: [Col. 0140C] “For distinguishing the causes of things.” Others have “for discussing the causes.” But “distinguishing” is shown to be the correct reading by the words that follow: “It teaches how truth and falsehood are judged through disputation.”]

It is a branch of philosophy called logic, that is, rational philosophy, capable of defining, investigating, and discussing. For, in many kinds of questions, it teaches how truth and falsehood are to be distinguished through argument.

2. The earliest philosophers possessed it in their discourses,

[Note: [Col. 0140C] “In their discourses,” that is, in their disputations.]

but they did not reduce it to the systematic practice of an art.

[Note: [Col. 0140C] After these came Aristotle. Cassiodorus writes: “The ancients made very extensive use of it, but they did not bring it under the rule of an art. Aristotle was almost the first among those held in any esteem to bring the arguments of this discipline to certain rules.”]

After them Aristotle brought the arguments of this discipline under certain rules and called it dialectic,

[Note: [Col. 0140D] “And called it dialectic.” He did not mean the whole art, but only that part which reasons probabilistically, as was observed by the ancient Peripatetics, Alexander, Boethius, and others.]

because in it discussion concerns statements; for among the Greeks λεκτόν means “statement.” Thus dialectic follows the discipline of rhetoric because the two have much in common.

[Col. 0140B] 99

# CHAPTER XXIII. On the difference between dialectic and rhetoric

1. Varro defined dialectic and rhetoric in the ninth book of the *Disciplines* by the following comparison: “Dialectic and rhetoric are like the fist clenched in a man’s hand and the palm spread open: the former contracts words, the latter extends them.”

[Note: [Col. 0140D] “The clenched fist in a man’s fighting hand.” Zeno the Stoic had said the same thing long before Varro, as Cicero reports in more than one place.]

[Note: [Col. 0140D] “In the ninth book of the *Disciplines*.” This entire chapter is read in Cassiodorus; but Augustine notes that “ninth” should be read in both places. For Gellius, Acron, and Nonius cite Varro’s third, fifth, and eighth books of the *Disciplines*, although the work can also be transmitted in nine books if “nine” refers not to the disciplines but to the books.]

2. Dialectic is sharper for discussing matters, whereas rhetoric is more eloquent for teaching what it undertakes to teach. The former sometimes enters the schools; the latter constantly proceeds into the forum. The former requires very few students; the latter requires crowds and peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] “Frequently, and crowds.” Cassiodorus has “frequently, and peoples.”]

3. Philosophers customarily set forth a definition of philosophy before proceeding to explain the *isagoge*, so that what belongs to it may be demonstrated more easily.

# CHAPTER XXIV. On the definition of philosophy

[Col. 0141A]

1. Philosophy is the knowledge of human and divine matters, joined with the pursuit of living well. It appears to consist of two things: knowledge and opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] “Knowledge and opinion.” From Lactantius, Book III, chapter 3.]

2. Knowledge exists when something is grasped by a reliable method; opinion exists when a matter still lies uncertain and appears to have no firm basis in reasoning. For example: Is the sun as large as it appears, or is it larger than the whole earth? Is the moon spherical or concave? Do the stars adhere to the heavens, or are they carried freely through the air? Of what size and material is the heaven itself? Is it still and motionless, or does it revolve with incredible speed? How thick is the earth, and by what foundations is it balanced and suspended so that it remains in place?

[Col. 0141B]

3. The very name, interpreted in Latin, professes a love of wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] For the Greeks call φῖλον “love”—perhaps “lover”—and σοφία “wisdom.”]

For the Greeks call φῖλον “love” and σοφία “wisdom.” Philosophy is divided into three branches: one is natural philosophy, called *physica* in Greek, in which the investigation of nature is discussed; another is moral philosophy, called *ethica* in Greek, in which conduct is treated; the third is rational philosophy, called *logica* in Greek, in which it is debated how truth itself is sought in the causes of things or in the conduct of life.

4. Thus in physics lies the cause of investigation; in ethics, the order of living; in logic, the method of understanding. Among the Greeks, Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages, was the first to investigate physics. Before the others, he examined the causes of the heavens and the power of natural things through contemplative reasoning.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] “Having contemplated through reason.” Augustine preferred “having contemplated.”]

Plato later divided this into four disciplines: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.

[Col. 0141C]

5. Socrates was the first to establish ethics for correcting and ordering conduct, and he directed all his study toward the discussion of living well, dividing it into the four virtues of the soul: prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

6. Prudence is the virtue by which good things are distinguished from bad. Courage is the virtue by which adversities are endured with equanimity. Temperance is the virtue by which lust and desire for things are restrained. Justice is the virtue by which, through right judgment, each person is assigned what is his.

7. Plato added logic, which is called rational philosophy. Through it, after examining the causes of things and conduct, he investigated their force rationally, dividing it into dialectic and rhetoric. It is called logic—that is, rational philosophy—because among the Greeks λόγος means both “speech” and “reason.”

[Col. 0141D] 101

8. Divine writings, too, consist in these three branches of philosophy. For they either discuss nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes; or conduct, as in Proverbs and scattered throughout all the books; or logic, which our writers claim for themselves under the name of theory, as in the Song of Songs and the Gospels.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] “In place of which our writers claim theory.” From Jerome’s letter to Paula of Urbica, or from Origen, *Homily 1 on the Song of Songs*.]

[Col. 0142A]

9. Some of the learned have defined philosophy in its name and branches as follows: “Philosophy is the probable knowledge of divine and human matters, insofar as this is possible for human beings.” Alternatively: “Philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines.” Again: “Philosophy is meditation on death.” This definition is more appropriate for Christians, who, having trampled underfoot worldly ambition, live according to disciplined conduct in the likeness of their future homeland.

10. Others have defined the method of philosophy as consisting of two parts, the first contemplative and the second practical. The contemplative is divided into natural, doctrinal, and divine philosophy. Doctrinal philosophy is divided into four parts: arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy.

11. Practical philosophy is divided into moral, administrative, and civic philosophy. It is called contemplative because, rising above visible things, we contemplate something divine and heavenly; we inspect them with the mind alone, because they transcend the power of sight.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] “And these things with the mind alone.” From the same work of Origen, the homily cited above.]

12. Natural philosophy is so called because the nature of each thing is examined, since nothing contrary to nature is generated in life, but each thing is assigned to the uses for which it was established by the Creator—unless perhaps some miracle is shown to occur by the will of God.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] “Because nothing contrary to nature is generated in life.” Origen, the homily on the Song of Songs cited above, reads: “Natural philosophy is so called where the nature of each thing is examined, because nothing contrary to nature is generated in life, but each thing is assigned to the uses for which it was produced by the Creator.” The words “contrary to nature” are absent from the manuscript books; in their place the printed editions and Cassiodorus have a confused reading.]

13. Divine philosophy is so called when we discuss either the ineffable nature of God or spiritual creatures in some portion of their most profound quality.

[Col. 0142A] 102

14. Doctrinal philosophy is the science that considers abstract quantity. Quantity is called abstract when, separating it from matter through the intellect—or from other accidents, such as even and odd, or things of that kind—we treat it in reasoning alone. Its branches are four: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.

15. Arithmetic is the discipline of numerable quantity considered in itself. Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and forms. Music is the discipline that speaks of numbers related to those found in sounds. Astronomy is the discipline that contemplates all the courses and forms of heavenly bodies and stars and investigates, by an examinatory method, the relationships of the stars both to one another and to the earth.

16. Practical philosophy is so called because it explains proposed matters through its operations. Its parts are three: moral, administrative, and civic. Moral philosophy is that by which an honorable manner of life is sought and institutions directed toward virtue are prepared. Administrative philosophy is concerned with wisely arranging the order of household affairs. Civic philosophy is that by which the welfare of the entire state is administered.

# CHAPTER XXV. On Porphyry’s *Isagoge*

1. After the definitions of philosophy, which contain everything in general, let us now explain Porphyry’s *isagoges*. *Isagoge* is Greek for “introduction” in Latin. It contains, for those beginning philosophy, a demonstration of the first principles by which, concerning any matter, what it is may be declared through its certain and substantial definition.

2. For, having posited the genus first, we then add the species and whatever else may be closely related. We separate these by distinguishing their common features and continue inserting differences until we arrive at the proper definition of the thing being sought, marked out by a clear expression of it. For example: “A human being is a rational, mortal, earthly, two-footed animal capable of laughter.”

3. When the genus “animal” has been stated, the substance of the human being has been declared.

[Col. 0143A] 103

For “animal” is the genus of human beings, but because it extended too broadly, the species “earthly” was added, and whatever is either ethereal or aquatic has now been excluded. The difference “two-footed” was added because of animals that rely on many feet. Likewise, “rational” is added because of those that lack reason; “mortal” because the human being is not an angel.

4. After the common features had been distinguished and excluded, the proper characteristic was added at the end: only the human being laughs. Thus the definition, in its several parts, is complete for declaring what a human being is. Aristotle and Tullius considered the full definition of this discipline to consist of genus and differences.

5. Later, some teachers, seeking greater completeness in instruction, divided its perfect substantial definition into five parts, as into its members. The first concerns genus, the second species, the third difference, the fourth the proper characteristic, and the fifth accident.

6. Genus: “animal.” For it is a general and common term for all beings possessing a soul. Species: “human being.” For it is the specific quality by which a human being is separated from other living creatures. Difference: “rational, mortal.” For by these two qualities a human being differs from the rest.

7. When “rational” is said, the human being is distinguished from irrational mute creatures, which have no reason. When “mortal” is said, the human being is distinguished from angels, who do not know death. Proper characteristic: “capable of laughter.” For the human being laughs, and this belongs to no animal other than the human being. Accident: color in the body, learning in the mind.

8. These things both occur and change through the variation of time. From all five parts comes a sentence expressing a complete thought: “A human being is a rational, mortal, laughter-capable creature, capable of good and evil.” Thus, in every substantial definition, we must continue inserting species and differences until, after excluding everything that could also be the same thing, we arrive at the point where the precise property is securely established.

9. Victorinus the orator translated the *isagoges* from Greek into Latin, and Boethius published his commentary on it in five books.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] “Translated.” Boethius, *Dialogue* I: “I ask you to explain to me what Victorinus, the orator and almost the most learned man of his age, is said to have translated from Porphyry by means of the *isagoge*, that is, by an introduction to Aristotle’s Categories.”]

[Col. 0143A] 104

# CHAPTER XXVI. On Aristotle’s Categories

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Most of this is drawn from Aristotle’s *Categories*, in Boethius’ translation.]

1. Aristotle’s categories now follow. In Latin they are called *praedicamenta* (“predicaments”), through which every expression is comprised according to its various meanings.

2. The instruments of the categories are three: first equivocal terms, second univocal terms, and third denominative terms. Terms are equivocal when one name belongs to many things, but the definition is not the same, as with “lion.” For as far as the name is concerned, a real lion, a painted lion, and a celestial lion are all called “lion.” But as far as the definition is concerned, the real lion is defined in one way, the painted lion in another, and the celestial lion in another.

3. Terms are univocal when one name and one definition belong to two or more things, as with “garment.” For both a *birrus* and a tunic can receive the name “garment” and its definition.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] “For a *birrus* and a tunic.” The same is found in Capella. As for what kind of garment a *birrus* is, see Book XIX, chapter 24, and Cassian’s notes.]

Thus this is understood to be univocal in genera, because it gives both its name and its definition to its forms.

4. Denominative terms are those which, differing only in grammatical case from something else, receive their designation according to its name, as *bonus* (“good”) from *bonitas* (“goodness”), and *malus* (“bad”) from *malitia* (“badness”).

5. There are ten species of categories: substance, quantity, quality, relation, position, place, time, possession, acting, and being acted upon.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] “The species of the categories.” Cassiodorus: “Whatever we say or think is found in one or another category.”]

6. Substance, properly and primarily so called, is that which is neither predicated of a subject nor present in a subject, such as an individual human being or an individual horse. Secondary substances are those species in which the things primarily called substances—that is, the substances first mentioned—are contained and enclosed, as Cicero is contained in “human being.”

7. Quantity is the measure by which something is shown to be large or small, such as long or short. Quality concerns what kind of person someone is—for example, an orator or a rustic, black or white. Relation is what is referred to something else. When “son” is said, “father” is also indicated. Relatives begin simultaneously: slave and master take the beginning of their names at the same time. A master is never found prior to a slave, nor a slave prior to a master; for one cannot precede the other.

[Col. 0144C]

8. Position derives its name from placement, as when someone stands, sits, or lies down. Place is where something is, such as in the forum or in the street. Movement in place has six parts: right and left, front and back, upward and downward. These six parts also have two distinctions: far and near. Time includes “today” and “yesterday.”

9. Possession derives its name from having something, as possessing knowledge in the mind or virtue in the body; and, in relation to the body, clothing and other things that belong to the manner of possessing, which teachers have included under a designated category.

[Col. 0144D] 10. Acting and being acted upon derive their meanings from the agent and the patient. For *I write* contains an act of the one doing, since it indicates the action of the doer. *I am written* belongs to the patient, since it shows that the subject undergoes the action. In these nine categories, of which certain examples have been given, and even within the category of substance itself, which is *οὐσία* (*ousia*, substance), innumerable instances are found. For whatever we grasp intellectually, we express in speech under one or another of these ten categories.

[Col. 0145A] 11. The complete statement concerning these matters is as follows: “Augustine, a great orator, the son of that man, standing in the temple, wearing the fillet today, is exhausted by disputing.” It is proper to substance—*ousia*, that is, substance—that it underlies the other things; the remaining nine are accidents. Substance is so called because every thing subsists in itself. A body subsists, and therefore it is a substance.

12. Those accidents, however, which exist in something subsisting and in a subject are not substances, because they do not subsist but undergo change, such as color or form. “Of a subject” and “in a subject” mean, as it were, “of the thing itself” and “in the thing itself.” Whenever something is said to be of a subject, it is substance, as though it were said to be of substance. Whenever something is said to be in a subject, it is an accident—that is, something that occurs in substance—such as quantity, quality, or shape.

[Col. 0145B] 13. Thus genera and species are “of a subject,” while accidents are “in a subject.” [Note: “Of these nine accidents.” From Augustine, *On the Categories*.] Of these nine accidents, three are within substance: quantity, quality, and position. 106 For these cannot exist without substance. Outside substance are place, time, and possession; both within and outside substance are relation, acting, and being acted upon.

14. They are plainly called categories because they cannot be recognized except from subjects. For who could recognize what a human being is unless he placed some human being before his eyes as a subject of “human being”?

15. [Note: “This work … must be read attentively.” Cicero, *Hortensius*, cited by Nonius: “Great concentration of mind must be applied in explaining Aristotle, if you read him.”] This work of Aristotle must be read attentively because, as has been said, whatever a human being says is contained among the ten categories. It will also be useful for understanding books that are employed either by rhetoricians or by dialecticians.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the *Perihermeniae*.

[Note: “On the *Perihermeniae*.” Thus in the old manuscript, and shortly afterward: “Preface to the *Perihermeniae*.”]

[Col. 0145C]

1. Next comes the extremely subtle book *Perihermeniae*, exceedingly careful in its various forms and repetitions. Of it the following is said: “When Aristotle was writing the *Perihermeniae*, he was dipping his pen in his mind.” [Note: “Dipping his pen in his mind.” Suidas, *On all the writings of Aristotle*: “Aristotle was the secretary of nature, dipping his pen into mind.” Greek: Ἀριστοτέλης τῆς φύσεως γραμματεὺς ἦν, τὸν κάλαμον ἀποβρέχων εἰς νοῦν.]

### Preface to the *Perihermeniae*

2. Every thing that is one and is signified by a single expression is signified either by a noun or by a verb. These two parts of speech interpret everything that the mind has conceived for expression. For every utterance is an interpreter of the thing conceived by the mind.

3. Aristotle, a man exceedingly skilled in expressing things and constructing utterances, calls this *hermeneia*, which we call interpretation: namely, that it interprets things conceived in the mind through spoken utterances by *cataphasis* and *apophasis*, that is, by affirmation and negation. By affirmation, as “A human being runs”; by negation, as “A human being does not run.”

4. In this *Perihermeniae*, therefore, the philosopher mentioned above treats seven species: the noun, the verb, the phrase, the enunciation, the affirmation, the negation, and the contradiction.

5. 107 A noun is a significant sound according to convention, without time, no part of which, taken separately, is significant, as “Socrates.” A verb is what signifies time; no part of it signifies anything independently, but it is always a sign of things said of something else, as “he thinks,” “he debates.” A phrase is a significant sound, one of whose parts, taken separately, is significant, as “Socrates debates.” An enunciative phrase is a significant sound concerning whether something is or is not, as “Socrates is,” “Socrates is not.”

6. An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something, as “Socrates is”; a negation is an enunciation of something away from something, as “Socrates is not.” A contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, as “Socrates debates,” “Socrates does not debate.”

[Col. 0146B] 7. [Note: “All these matters … are found.” These additions have been taken from a manuscript; they are also found, somewhat altered, in Cassiodorus.] All these matters are treated in the book *Perihermeniae*, divided and subdivided into the minutest parts. For the present it is enough briefly to have made known their definitions, since a suitable explanation is found in the work itself. The usefulness of the *Perihermeniae* is that syllogisms are constructed from these interpretations. Hence the analytical works are also treated.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Dialectical Syllogisms

1. [Note: See Cassiodorus, Capella, and Apuleius, *On Categorical Syllogisms*, or *Perihermeniae*.] Next come dialectical syllogisms, in which the usefulness and power of the entire art are displayed. Their conclusion greatly assists the reader in investigating the truth, provided that error is absent—namely, the error of deceiving an opponent through sophisms and false conclusions. [Note: “The error of deceiving.” Other copies read “of overcoming” or “of overthrowing.”]

2. The forms of categorical—that is, predicative—syllogisms are three.

The modes of the first form are nine.

3. The first mode is the one that leads directly from universal affirmative premises to a universal affirmative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore everything just is good.” [Note: “The one that leads.” Greek: Συνάγει, “it brings together.” The fact that, in the examples, the second proposition is placed where the assumption ordinarily stands neither diminishes the force of the syllogism nor occurs without precedent in Greek and Arabic examples.]

4. The second mode is the one that leads directly from universal affirmative and negative premises to a universal negative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; nothing honorable is disgraceful; therefore nothing just is disgraceful.”

5. The third mode is the one that leads directly from a particular affirmative and a universal affirmative premise to a particular affirmative conclusion, as follows: “Something just is honorable; everything honorable is useful; therefore something just is useful.”

6. The fourth mode is the one that leads directly from a particular affirmative and a universal negative premise to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Something honorable is just; nothing honorable is disgraceful; therefore something just is not disgraceful.”

7. The fifth mode is the one that leads from universal affirmative premises to a particular affirmative conclusion by conversion, [Col. 0147A] as follows: “Everything just is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore something good is just.” [Note: “By conversion,” *ἀντιστροφὴν*, commonly called *conversio*.]
