8. The sixth mode is the one that leads from a universal affirmative and a universal negative premise to a universal negative conclusion by conversion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; nothing honorable is disgraceful; therefore nothing disgraceful is just.”

9. The seventh mode is the one that leads from particular and universal affirmative premises to a particular affirmative conclusion by conversion, as follows: “Something just is honorable; everything honorable is useful; therefore something useful is just.”

10. The eighth mode is the one that leads from universal negative and affirmative premises to a particular negative conclusion by conversion, as follows: “Nothing disgraceful is honorable; everything honorable is just; therefore something disgraceful is not just.”

11. The ninth mode is the one that leads from a universal negative and a particular affirmative premise to a particular negative conclusion by conversion, as follows: “Nothing disgraceful is honorable; something honorable is just; therefore something just is not disgraceful.”

12. The modes of the second form are four.

The first mode is the one that leads directly from universal affirmative and negative premises to a universal negative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; nothing disgraceful is honorable; therefore nothing just is disgraceful.”

13. The second mode is the one that leads directly from universal negative and affirmative premises to a universal negative conclusion, as follows: “Nothing disgraceful is honorable; everything just is honorable; therefore nothing disgraceful is just.”

14. The third mode is the one that leads directly from a particular affirmative and a universal negative premise to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Something just is honorable; nothing disgraceful is honorable; therefore something just is not disgraceful.”

15. The fourth mode is the one that leads directly from a particular negative and a universal affirmative premise to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Something just is not disgraceful; everything bad is disgraceful; therefore something just is not bad.”

16. The modes of the third form are six.

The first mode is the one that leads from universal affirmative premises to a particular affirmative conclusion, both directly and by conversion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; everything just is good; therefore something honorable is good,” or thus: “Therefore something good is honorable.”

17. The second mode is the one that leads directly from particular and universal affirmative premises to a particular affirmative conclusion, as follows: “Something just is honorable; everything just is good; therefore something honorable is good.”

18. The third mode is the one that leads directly from universal and particular affirmative premises to a particular affirmative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; something just is good; therefore something good is honorable.”

19. The fourth mode is the one that leads directly from universal affirmative and negative premises to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; nothing just is bad; therefore something honorable is not bad.”

20. The fifth mode is the one that leads directly from a particular affirmative and a universal negative premise to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Something just is honorable; nothing just is bad; therefore something honorable is not bad.”

21. The sixth mode is the one that leads directly from a universal affirmative and a particular negative premise to a particular negative conclusion, as follows: “Everything just is honorable; something just is not bad; therefore something honorable is not bad.”

22. Whoever wishes to know these forms of categorical syllogisms fully should read the book entitled *Perihermeniae* by Apuleius and will learn what is treated there more subtly. For, once distinguished and considered, they usefully introduce the reader, by the Lord’s assistance, into the great pathways of understanding. Now let us proceed in due order to hypothetical syllogisms.

23. The modes of hypothetical syllogisms, which are made with a conclusion, are seven.

The first mode is: “If it is day, it is light; now it is day; therefore it is light.”

The second mode is: “If it is day, it is light; now it is not light; therefore it is not day.”

The third mode is: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is not light; but it is day; therefore it is light.”

24. The fourth mode is: “It is either day or night; now it is day; therefore it is not night.”

The fifth mode is: “It is either day or night; now it is not night; therefore it is day.”

[Col. 0148C] The sixth mode is: “It is not the case both that it is day and that it is night; but it is day; therefore it is not night.”

25. The seventh mode is: “It is not both day and night; now it is not night; therefore it is day.” Whoever wishes to know the modes of hypothetical syllogisms more fully should read the book by Marius Victorinus entitled *On Hypothetical Syllogisms*.

26. [Note: “From here to dialectical matters.” Cassiodorus: “From here let us approach the most beautiful species of definitions, which surpass others in such dignity that they may rightly be called ornaments of speech and certain lights. Hence, from the three words of judgments, we did not hesitate rightly to make them parts of discourse, especially since we had found them much more corrupt in the manuscripts of Tarragona. The sense of these words is that he says these definitions serve both to illuminate propositions and to unravel expressions.”] From here let us approach the dialectical species of definitions, which surpass others in such dignity that they may rightly be called clear manifestations of discourse and certain indications of expressions.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Division of Definitions, Abbreviated from the Book of Marius Victorinus

1. The definition of philosophers is one which, in expressing things, explains what the thing itself is, [Col. 0148D] not what it is like, [Note: “Not what it is like.” The negation was absent from all copies. Boethius, *On Definition*, chapter 4: “Therefore the definition, which is proper to philosophers, explains, in expressing things, what it is, not what it is like; we shall explain how it ought to consist of its parts.”] and how it ought to be constituted from its parts. For it is a brief statement that, by its proper signification, encloses the nature of each thing, distinguished from what it shares with others. The division of definitions is made into fifteen parts.

111 2. The first species of definition is *οὐσιώδης* (*ousiōdēs*), that is, substantial. It is properly and truly called a definition, [Col. 0149A] as follows: “A human being is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter and learning.” [Note: “Capable of laughter and learning.” All copies have the faulty reading “capable of the sense and discipline,” although above, chapter 26, the phrase is “capable of laughter.” Likewise in Boethius.] For this definition, descending through species and differences, arrives at the proper characteristic and most fully indicates what a human being is.

3. The second species of definition is called in Greek *ἐννοηματική* (*ennoēmatikē*), and in Latin *notio*, “notion.” We may call it a notion by a common rather than a proper name. It is always formed in this way: “A human being is that which, by rational conception and exercise, presides over all animals.” Here he has not said what a human being is, but by saying what a human being does, he calls it to our knowledge by a kind of sign. In this and in the remaining cases, knowledge of the thing is brought forward, not a substantial explanation; for the substantial definition holds first place among all definitions.

4. The third species of definition is called in Greek *ποιώδης* (*poiōdēs*), and in Latin “qualitative,” because it takes its name from quality, inasmuch as it clearly shows what the thing that is, is like. An example is: “A human being is one who is strong in intellect, powerful in the arts and in knowledge of things, and either chooses what ought to be done or, by careful judgment, rejects what is useless.” By these qualities the human being is expressed and defined.

5. The fourth species of definition is called in Greek *ὑπογραφική* (*hypographikē*), and by Cicero in Latin *descriptio*, “description.” By using a circumstantial account of words and deeds, it declares through description what each thing is. Thus one asks what a miser, a cruel person, or a licentious person is, and the entire nature of the licentious, miserly, or cruel person is described. If we wish to define a licentious person, we say: “A licentious person is one who desires unnecessary but luxurious and burdensome sustenance, who abounds in delights, and is inclined to lust.” [Note: “And costly … inclined to lust.” From Boethius.] These and other statements define the licentious person, but they define by description. This species of definition is more suitable for orators than for dialecticians, because it has breadth and can be applied in the same manner to good things and to bad.

6. The fifth species of definition is called in Greek *κατ’ ἀντίλεξιν* (*kat’ antilexin*), which in Latin we call “word for word.” [Note: “Which the Greeks call *kat’ antilexin*.” From the same author, book 3, *Topics*.] It designates the word whose meaning is being sought by another expression and, in a single and particular word, explains in another single word what that word signifies; for example, “*conticescere* means to be silent.” Likewise, when we say *terminus*, we mean “end,” or when we interpret *populatae* as “devastated.”

7. The sixth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ διαφοράν* (*kata diaphoran*), which we call “by difference.” Writers on the arts speak of it as concerning one thing and another, as when one asks what difference there is between a king and a tyrant. By adding the difference, what each is is defined: “A king is moderate and self-controlled; a tyrant, however, is impious and ruthless.”

8. The seventh species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ μεταφοράν* (*kata metaphoran*), which the Latins call “by transference,” as Cicero says in the *Topics*: “A shore is where the wave plays.” [Col. 0150A] [Note: “Against which the waves break.” *Eludere* is also read in Cicero. A. Augustine approves this reading, and the Gothic manuscripts confirm it. Lambinus and Ursinus prefer *alludere*.]

This can be handled in various ways: sometimes so as to admonish, sometimes to designate, sometimes to praise or blame. To admonish: “Nobility is the burden of ancestors borne by their descendants.” To designate: “The head is the art of the body.” To praise: “Youth is the flower of life.” To blame: “Wealth is a long provision for a short life.”

9. The eighth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, “by removal of the contrary,” which the Latins call “by deprivation of the contrary of the thing being defined”: “Good is what is not bad. Just is what is not unjust,” and similar statements. We should use this kind of definition when the contrary is known, as follows: “If good is what benefits together with honor, that which is not such is bad.”

10. The ninth species of definition is what the Greeks call *καθ’ ὑποτύπωσιν* (*kath’ hypotypōsin*), which the Latins call “by a certain representation,” as follows: “Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises.” This always concerns individuals, which the Greeks call *ἄτομα* (*atoma*), “indivisible things.”

11. The tenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *ὡς τύπος* (*hōs typos*), which the Latins call “an example,” as when, if one asks what an animal is, the answer is: “For example, a human being.” The example given has clarified the thing being sought. It is proper to a definition to declare what the thing being sought is.

12. [Note: “The eleventh … *kat’ elleipes*.” Boethius has *kat’ endeian*. Moreover, all that follows has been restored from Boethius.] The eleventh species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἔλλειψιν πλήρους ὁμοίου γένους* (*kat’ elleipsin plērous homoiou genous*), which the Latins call “through the lack of a complete thing of the same genus.” 113 [Note: “If one asks what a *triens* is, r. c. b. d. u. s. a.” A. Augustine is rightly approved here [the wording is uncertain], although most manuscripts read: “If one asks what a thesis is, let the answer be: ‘That which lacks force in order to be an arsis,’” an example taken from music which could somehow be accepted. But it is not likely that Isidore departed so far from Boethius, whose example, likewise found in Cassiodorus, is: “If one asks what a quarter is, let the answer be: ‘That which lacks a three-quarter measure in order to be an *as*.’” *Assis* is not nominative, a fact that should not trouble anyone in Isidore.] Thus, if one asks what a *triens* is, the answer is: “That which lacks a *bes* in order to be an *as*.”

13. The twelfth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἔπαινον* (*kat’ epainon*), that is, “by praise,” as Cicero says in his speech for Cluentius: “Law is the mind, judgment, will, and considered opinion of the state”; and elsewhere: “Peace is tranquil liberty.” It is also made through blame, which the Greeks call *φόγος* (*phogos*), as follows: “Slavery is the last of all evils and must be repelled not only by war but even by death.”

14. The thirteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἀναλογίαν* (*kat’ analogian*), which the Latins call “according to proportion.” This occurs when an inferior thing is defined by the name of a greater thing, as in the statement: “A human being is a lesser world.” Cicero used this definition as follows: “They call an edict an annual law.”

15. The fourteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ τὸ πρός τι* (*kata to pros ti*), which the Latins call “relative to something,” as in the statements: “A father is one who has a son”; “A master is one who has a slave.” Cicero says in the *Rhetoric*: “A genus is that which embraces several parts.” Likewise: “A part is that which lies beneath a genus.”

16. [Note: “The fifteenth, *kat’ aitiologian*.” Boethius has *αἰτιώδης*, “causal.”] The fifteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ αἰτιολογίαν* (*kat’ aitiologian*), which the Latins call “according to the reason of the thing,” as follows: “Day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth.” We must understand that the species of definitions mentioned above are rightly associated with the topics, since they are included among certain arguments and are mentioned in some passages of the *Topics*. Now let us come to the topics, which are the seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Topics

1. The topics are the discipline of discovering arguments. The division of the topics, or places from which arguments are drawn, is threefold. 114 For some arguments adhere to the very matter under discussion; others are called “related,” because they are recognized as drawn in some way from other things; and others are assumed from outside. Arguments that adhere to the very matter under discussion are divided into three: first, from the whole; second, from the part; third, from a mark.

2. An argument from the whole occurs when a definition is applied to the matter being sought, as Cicero says: [Note: “Glory is praise for right actions.” From the speech *For Marcellus*.] “Glory is praise for right actions and renown for great services to the state.”

3. [Note: “From the parts.” All manuscripts agree. But Cassiodorus has: “From the parts, as, for example: If the eye sees, the whole body does not therefore see.”] An argument from the parts occurs when the person defending himself either denies that an act was committed or defends the act as having been lawfully committed.

4. An argument from a mark occurs when an argument is drawn from the force of a name, as Cicero says: “I was looking for a consul,” he says, “whom I could not find in that castrated boar.” [Note: “Whom in that castrated boar.” This is the reading to be adopted in Cicero’s *Against Piso*, not the usual *animali*, “animal,” as Lambinus also observed. A *majalis* is a castrated pig.]

5. Related arguments are those recognized as drawn in some way from other things. They are fourteen in number. First is the argument from cognates, which occurs when a verb is derived from a noun, as Cicero says that Verres *everrisse*—“swept clean”—the province; or when a noun is derived from a verb, as when a robber is said to *latrocinari*, “to rob.” A noun may also be derived from a noun, as in Terence: [Col. 0151D] “An undertaking is characteristic of madmen, not of lovers,” provided that the ending of one name, formed into another inflection of the word, differs from it. [Note: “For an undertaking is characteristic of madmen, not of lovers.” He allowed himself this play, as is customary in etymologies, by calling *amentium* (“of madmen”) and *amant[ium]* (“of lovers”) cognates. The same example occurs in Cassiodorus. Nor was Augustine displeased with the reading of the Gothic manuscripts: *amentium* or *amantium*.]

6. The second argument is from the genus, when a judgment is made concerning the same genus, as Virgil says: “Woman is always fickle and changeable.”

7. The third argument is from the species, when a species lends credibility to a general question, as follows:

> Yet not so does the Phrygian shepherd penetrate Lacedaemon.

An argument from similarity occurs when things similar to certain things are brought forward:

> Give me weapons; my right hand will not have hurled  
> any spear in vain against the Rutulians—those weapons  
> that stood in a Greek body on the fields of Ilium.

115 8. An argument from difference occurs when things are separated by a difference, as Virgil says:

> Do you not see the horses of Diomedes, nor the chariot of Achilles?

An argument is drawn from contraries when things that differ are set against one another, as Virgil says:

> Should ships made by mortal hands possess immortal rights,  
> and should Aeneas, assured, pass through uncertain dangers?

9. An argument is drawn from consequences when something inevitably follows from a matter that has been established, as Virgil says:

> The vanquished do not possess such strength of spirit,  
> nor so great a pride.

An argument from antecedents occurs when something is proved from things previously done, as Cicero says in his speech for Milo: “Since he did not hesitate to reveal what he had planned, can you hesitate about what he did?”

10. An argument from incompatibles occurs when what is alleged is destroyed by some contradiction, as Cicero says: [Note: “Would he, then, not only … concerning such a matter.” This passage is somewhat different in Cicero’s speech *For Deiotarus*.] “Would he, then, after being freed from such a danger and enriched with the highest honor, have wished to kill you in your own house?”

11. An argument from connected circumstances occurs when it is plausibly shown what will result from each thing, as Virgil says:

> … If they drive us out, they believe that nothing will prevent them  
> from bringing all Hesperia completely beneath their yoke.

12. An argument from causes occurs when each matter is treated according to common custom, as Terence says:

> I was somewhat afraid of you a little while ago, Dave,  
> lest you should do what the common herd of slaves usually does—  
> deceive me by tricks.

An argument from effects occurs when something is approved from what has been done, as Virgil says:

> Fear betrays ignoble spirits.

13. An argument from comparison occurs when, by comparing persons or causes, the force of a judgment is formed by way of imputation, as Virgil says:

> You can draw Aeneas away from Greek hands;  
> is it impious for us to have helped the Rutulians in some way?

14. There are also arguments drawn from outside, which the Greeks call *ἄτεχνα* (*atechna*), that is, “without art,” such as testimony. Every testimony is something taken from an external matter in order to establish credibility.

15. This is divided in five ways: first, from a person; second, from the authority of nature; third, from circumstances; fourth, from the sayings and deeds of ancestors; fifth, from torture. Not every person has the weight of testimony sufficient to establish credibility; rather, that person must be commendable for integrity of character.

16. The authority of nature consists chiefly in virtue. Circumstances provide many things that confer authority: intellect, wealth, age, fortune, skill, experience, necessity, and the concurrence of accidental events. Credibility is sought from the sayings and deeds of ancestors when the sayings and deeds of former generations are recalled. Credibility is supplied by torture, after which no one is believed willing to lie.

17. Matters treated under circumstances, since they are clear by their names, require no definition. It should also be committed to memory that the topics commonly supply arguments to orators, dialecticians, poets, and jurists; but [Note: “But when they prove something specifically.” Boethius, book 6, *Topics*. Cicero, in the section on Causes: “For this is clearly a common topic for orators and philosophers: from causes, philosophers prove the natures of things, which is proper to philosophy, while orators prove facts, which belongs to the rhetorical faculty.”] when they prove something specifically, they belong to rhetoricians, poets, and jurists; when they argue generally, it is clear that they belong to philosophers.

18. It is plainly a remarkable kind of work that everything which the mobility and variety of the human mind could discover in seeking meanings through different causes has been collected into one place: the free and voluntary intellect has been enclosed. For wherever the mind turns, and whatever thoughts it enters, its ingenuity must fall into one of the categories mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Opposites

1. There are four kinds of opposites, which Aristotle calls *ἀντικείμενα* (*antikeimena*), that is, “opposed things,” because they seem to stand against one another as if face to face, like contraries. Yet not everything that is opposed to something else is contrary; rather, everything contrary is opposed. The first kind is that of contraries, [Note: “Which, according to Cicero, is called adverse.” All copies mistakenly read “different.” Nevertheless, it should not be concealed that Boethius ventured to say that Cicero used not the most proper names but the more familiar ones. For what he calls “contraries,” he says, would more properly be called “opposites”; while what are called “adverse” more suitably receive the name “contraries.”] which, according to Cicero, is called “adverse,” because things are opposed to each other in such a contrary way that they do not belong to the things to which they are opposed, as wisdom and folly.

2. This kind is divided into three species. For some of them have an intermediate; some have no intermediate; and some have an intermediate that is without a name, unless it receives its name from both extremes. White and black have an intermediate, because between them the color pale or brown is often found.

3. There is no intermediate whenever one of two alternatives occurs, such as health or illness. There is nothing intermediate between these. Those whose intermediate has no name, such as fortunate and unfortunate, do have an intermediate: “not fortunate.” The second kind is that of relatives, which are opposed to one another in such a way that they are compared with each other, such as double and single.

4. This alone among the kinds of opposites is referred to one another. For “greater” exists only in relation to “less,” and “single” only in relation to “double.” A relative is opposed to a relative in such a way that the very thing that is opposed either belongs to the thing to which it is opposed or is related to it in some manner. A half, for example, is opposed to double and is half of that double; but it is opposed to it in such a way that it belongs to the thing to which it is opposed.

5. In the same way, small is opposed to great, in such a way that the small thing itself is small in relation to the great thing to which it is opposed. The things mentioned above as contraries, however, are opposed to one another in such a way that they neither belong to the things to which they are opposed nor are related to them in any manner. Thus injustice is contrary to justice in such a way that injustice is neither a property of that same justice nor related to it as injustice.

6. The third kind of opposites is possession and deprivation. Cicero calls this kind “privation,” because it shows that someone possessed something of which he has been deprived. Its species are three: the first concerns the thing itself, the second the place, and the third the appropriate time. In the thing itself, as blindness and sight. In place, as: “The place of blindness and sight is in the eyes.” At the appropriate time, as: “One should not say that an infant is toothless when an early age has not yet granted him teeth”; for he has not been deprived of teeth that he has not yet possessed.

7. “The fourth kind is opposed through affirmation and negation, as: ‘Socrates debates’; ‘Socrates does not debate.’ These differ from the preceding kinds because the former can be stated singly, whereas these cannot be stated except in connection. This fourth kind produces much conflict among dialecticians and is called by them strongly opposed, since it does not admit a third term.”

8. For among the preceding kinds some can have a third term, as among contraries, white and black: the third is neither white nor black, but brown or pale. Among relatives also, such as many and few: the third is neither many nor few, but moderate. In possession and deprivation, such as sight and blindness, the third is neither blindness nor sight, but weak or defective vision. Thus “he reads” and “he does not read” have no third term.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE FOUR MATHEMATICAL DISCIPLINES

### Preface

[Col. 0153]

1. Mathematics is called in Latin *doctrinalis scientia*, “instructional science.” It considers quantity abstracted from matter. Abstract quantity is what we separate intellectually from matter, or from other accidents—such as even and odd, or other things of this kind—and treat by reasoning alone. Its species are four: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. Arithmetic is the discipline of numerable quantity considered in itself. Geometry is the discipline of the magnitude of forms. Music is the discipline that speaks of the numbers found in sounds. Astronomy is the discipline that contemplates the courses and forms of the heavenly bodies and all the relations of the stars. We shall next indicate these disciplines at somewhat greater length, so that their causes may suitably be displayed.

119 ## CHAPTER ONE. On the Name of the Discipline of Arithmetic

[Col. 0153D]

1. Arithmetic is the discipline of numbers. For the Greeks call number *ἀριθμός* (*arithmos*). The writers of secular literature therefore wished it to be first among the mathematical disciplines, because it requires no other discipline in order to exist.

2. Music, geometry, and astronomy, which follow, require its assistance in order to exist and endure.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Its Authors

1. [Note: “The discipline of numbers.” The same wording occurs in Boethius.] Among the Greeks, Pythagoras is said to have first written the discipline of numbers; afterward it was arranged more fully by Nicomachus. Among the Latins, Apuleius first translated it, followed by Boethius. [Note: “Arranged more fully.” From the Gothic manuscripts. Other copies read “composed.”]

## CHAPTER THREE. What a Number Is

1. A number is a multitude constituted from units; for one is the seed of number, [Note: “Not a number.” The word *τὸ* (“the”) was added in the printed editions but is absent from the Gothic manuscripts. Such elliptical expressions are frequent throughout this work.] not a number. The coin (*nummus*) gave its name to number (*numerus*) and supplied it with its designation from its frequent use. “One” derives its name from Greek. For the Greeks call one *ἕν* (*hen*); similarly, two and three, which they call *δύο* (*duo*) and *τρία* (*tria*).

[Col. 0155B] 2. [Note: “Four from a square figure.” Rather, the square figure derives from four; four itself comes from the Greek *τέτταρες* (*tettares*). The Greeks often change *k* into *t*, as in *teinos* for *keinos*, and conversely; we too imitate them in this fairly often.] Four took its name from the square figure. Five, however, received its name not according to nature but according to the arbitrary decision of the one who assigned names to numbers. Six and seven come from Greek.

3. [Note: “In many names.” From Servius, on *Eclogue* 2. Another reading has “and *serpillum*, etc.”] For in many words that have an aspiration in Greek, we put *s* in place of the aspiration. Thus, in place of *ἕξ* (*hex*) we have *sex*, and in place of *ἑπτά* (*hepta*) *septem*, just as in place of *herpillum* we have the herb *serpillum*. Eight is formed by transference, as in both Greek and Latin: they have *ἐννέα* (*ennea*), we have *novem*; they have *δέκα* (*deka*), we have *decem*.

4. The tens are so called according to a Greek etymology, because they bind and join the numbers lying beneath them. For among the Greeks δεσμεύειν means “to join” or “to bind.” Twenty is so called because it is twice ten, with *v* substituted for the letter *b*. Thirty is so called because it is generated from three tens; and so on up to ninety.

5. [Note: “But *centum* from *canthus*.” *Canthus* means both the circle of the eyes and the iron band by which the roundness of wooden wheels is tightened and constricted, as Jerome says in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 20. *Canthos* should therefore be read there, not *conthos*, as the Reatine edition has it.] One hundred, however, is called from *canthus*, which means “circle”; two hundred from “two” and “one hundred”; and likewise the remaining numbers up to one thousand. One thousand is derived from “multitude,” whence also *militia*, as if from *multitia*. Hence also *milia*, which the Greeks, with a change of letter, call μυρία. [Note: “*Milia*, which the Greeks [call] with a changed letter.” What is printed in the editions as “i. l. p. r.,” that is, “that is, *l* for *r*,” is not found in the manuscripts; it is therefore permissible to suppose that *milia* is named either from μυρία or from χίλια.]

# CHAPTER IV. What numbers accomplish

1. [Note: “The rationale of number.” These are Augustine’s words, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 30.] The rationale of number must not be despised, for in many passages of the holy Scriptures it is made clear how great a mystery numbers contain. It was not without reason that it was said in praise of God: “You have made all things according to measure, number, and weight.”

2. [Col. 0156A] The number six, which is perfect through its own parts, declares the perfection of the world by a certain significance of its number. Likewise, the forty days during which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted cannot be understood without knowledge of numbers.

3. Thus there are also other numbers in the sacred Scriptures whose figures only those skilled in this discipline can scientifically interpret. [Note: “Those knowledgeable in this art”—that is, experts; so in the older books and in Bede, who transferred this chapter into his book on computation. Likewise Braulio, in the *Life of Isidore*: “Whoever reads this work”—that is, the *Etymologies*—“through repeatedly and attentively will rightly not be unknown in the knowledge of divine and human affairs, since it accords entirely with philosophy.”] It has also been granted to us, for the most part, to exist under the discipline of numbers: through it we learn the hours, calculate the cycles of the months, and recognize the span of the returning year. Through number we are instructed so that we may not fall into confusion. Take number away from all things, and everything perishes. [Note: “Take computation away from the world.” Some editions read “take the computation of calculation away from the world,” but neither Bede nor the older books recognize the word *calculi*.] Take computation away from the world, and everything is enveloped in blind ignorance; [Note: “Nor can he be distinguished.” Thus all manuscripts read, with *differri* meaning “to be distinguished,” except that some, in the plural, have “nor can they be distinguished from the other animals by one who does not know the rationale of calculation.”] nor can one who does not know the rationale of calculation be distinguished from the other animals.

# 122 CHAPTER V. On the first division of even and odd numbers

1. Number is divided into even and odd. Even number is divided into: even-even, even-odd, odd-even, and odd-odd. Odd number is divided into: first and simple; second and composite; and third, intermediate, which in one respect is first and uncompounded, but in another respect second and composite.

[Note: “Odd-odd.” Capella uses the same division, although Boethius omitted this member; nor does it occur here in the Gothic manuscripts, except that Isidore shortly afterward explains what odd-odd means.]

2. An even number is one that can be divided into two equal parts, such as II, IV, and VIII. An odd number is one that cannot be divided into equal parts, because one remains in the middle, or falls short, or exceeds, as III, V, VII, IX, and the rest.

3. An even-even number is one that is divided evenly according to an even number until it reaches the indivisible unit, as, for example, LXIV has as its half XXXII; that in turn has XVI; XVI has VIII; VIII, IV; IV, II; II, I, which is single and indivisible.

4. An even-odd number is one that admits division into equal parts, but whose parts immediately remain indivisible: for example VI, X, XVIII, XXX, and L. As soon as you divide such a number, you encounter a number that cannot be cut further.

5. An odd-even number is one whose parts can also be divided, but which do not reach the unit, as, for example, XXIV. Divided in half, it produces XII; divided again into another half, VI; then III. Beyond this the division does not proceed, but before reaching the unit it encounters a limit that cannot be divided.

6. An odd-odd number is one that is measured oddly by an odd number, such as XXV and XLIX. Although these are odd numbers, they are divided by odd parts as well: XLIX by seven times seven, and XXV by five times five. Among odd numbers, some are simple, some composite, and some intermediate.

7. Simple numbers are those that have no other part except the unit alone, such as the number three, which has only a third; the number five, which has only a fifth; and the number seven, which has only a seventh. Each of these therefore has only one part. Composite numbers are those measured not only by the unit [Note: “But also by another number.” Another number is found in the Roman manuscript and in Boethius.] but also generated by another number, such as IX, XV, XXI, and XXV. For we say three times three is IX, seven times three is XXI, three times five is XV, and five times five is XXV.

8. Intermediate numbers are those that in one respect appear simple and uncompounded, but in another respect are second and composite. For example, when IX is compared with XXV, it is first and indivisible, because it has no common number except the monadic unit. But when it is compared with XV, it is second and composite, because it contains a common number besides the monadic unit—namely, the number three—since nine measures three times three, and fifteen three times five.

9. Likewise, among even numbers some are excessive, [Note: “Others are deficient.” Some read *diminutivi*, “diminutive.”] some deficient, and some perfect. Excessive numbers are those whose parts, added together, exceed their total, such as twelve. It has five parts: a twelfth, which is one; a sixth, which is two; a fourth, which is three; a third, which is four; and a half, which is six. One, two, three, four, and six, added together, make XVI and [Note: “And greatly exceed the number twelve.” That is, they greatly exceed twelve; the same expression is used shortly afterward and elsewhere.] greatly exceed twelve. There are likewise many other similar numbers, such as eighteen and many others of this kind.

10. Deficient numbers are those whose parts, when computed, produce a smaller total, such as ten, whose parts are three: a tenth, which is one; a fifth, which is two; and a half, which is five. One, two, and five, added together, make eight, [Note: “Smaller by far than ten.” Servius, in his commentary on Donatus’ *Ars*: “The comparative degree is joined with three cases: the ablative, the seventh [i.e. ablative], and the nominative, with the particle *quam* inserted before the ablative, as *doctior ab illo*, ‘more learned than he.’ He himself also uses this manner of speaking, as in *Aeneid* I, in the words ‘and the hero had given it to those departing.’ He says: ‘A hero is a brave man, a demigod, having more than a human being,’ and below, chapter 47: ‘While the sun is higher than the moon.’] which is far smaller than ten. Eight is similar to this, as are many other numbers that, when reduced [Note: “Reduced into parts.” Others read “divided into parts.”] into parts, remain below their total.

11. A perfect number is one that is completed by its own parts, such as six. It has three parts: a sixth, a third, and a half. Its sixth is one, its third two, and its half three. These parts, added together—that is, one, two, and three—complete and perfect the same number, six. [Note: “There are, moreover, perfect numbers, and so forth.” Everything is taken from Boethius, *On Arithmetic*, book I, chapter 20.] There are perfect numbers within ten: VI; within one hundred: XXVIII; and within one thousand: CCCCXCVI.

# CHAPTER VI. On the second division of the whole number

[Note: Because of copyists’ ignorance and the similarity of names, much in this chapter had previously been misconstrued. Some definitions had been transposed, others omitted, and the examples corrupted. All these matters have been restored with minimal effort and no danger. It is enough to note one point: the numbers Isidore calls *submultiplex superparticular*, *submultiplex superpartient*, *submultiplex subsuperparticular*, and *submultiplex subsuperpartient* are called by the same names by Boethius in book II of the *Geometry*; but in book I of the *Arithmetic*, chapter 22, Boethius calls them *multiplex subsuperparticular* and *multiplex subsuperpartient*.]

1. Every number is considered either in itself or in relation to something else. The former is divided as follows: some numbers are equal, others unequal. The latter is divided as follows: some are greater, others smaller. The greater are divided into multiples, superparticulars, superpartients, multiple-superparticulars, and multiple-superpartients. The smaller are divided into submultiples, subsuperparticulars, subsuperpartients, submultiple-subs​uperparticulars, and submultiple-subs​uperpartients.

2. A number in itself is one that is produced without any relation, such as III, IV, V, VI, and the other similar numbers. A relative number is one that is compared in relation to others. For example, when four is compared with two, it is called double, or a multiple; six with three, eight with four, ten with five; and again three with one is triple, six with two, nine with three, and so on.

3. Equal numbers are those that are equal in quantity: for example II to II, III to III, X to X, and C to C. Unequal numbers are those that, when compared with one another, display inequality, such as III to II, IV to III, V to IV, X to VI; and universally, when a greater number is compared with a lesser, or a lesser with a greater, it is called unequal.

4. A greater number is one that contains within itself the lesser number with which it is compared, and something more; for example, the number five is greater than the number three because five contains three within itself, together with its other two parts, and similarly in the other cases.

5. A lesser number is one that is contained by the greater number with which it is compared, together with some part of itself, as three in relation to five, for three is contained in five together with its two parts. A multiple number is one that contains the lesser number twice, three times, four times, or repeatedly; for example, when two is compared with one, it is double; three with one, triple; four, quadruple; and so on.

6. Conversely, a submultiple number is one that is contained within the multiple number twice, three times, four times, or repeatedly. For example, one is contained twice in two, three times in three, four times in four, and repeatedly in the other numbers. [Col. 0158D] A superparticular number is one in which the greater number contains within itself the lesser number against which it is compared, together with one of its parts.

7. For example, when III is compared with II, they contain within themselves two and another one, which is half of two; when IV is compared with III, they contain three and another one, which is a third of three. Likewise, when V is compared with IV, they contain the number four and another one, which is a fourth of that four; and similarly in the other cases.

8. A superpartient number is one that wholly contains the lesser number within itself and, in addition, two, three, four, five, or other parts of it. For example, when V is compared with III, five contains three and, in addition, two of its parts; when VII is compared with IV, it contains four and, in addition, three of its parts; when IX is compared with V, it contains five and, in addition, four of its parts.

9. A subsuperparticular number is a lesser number that is contained in the greater number together with one of its parts, whether a half, a third, a fourth, or a fifth; for example II in relation to III, III to IV, IV to V, and other similar cases.

10. A subsuperpartient number is one that is contained in a superpartient number together with two, three, or more of its parts; for example, III is contained in V together with two additional parts of itself; V is contained in IX together with four of its parts.

11. A multiple-superparticular number is one that, when compared with a lesser number, contains the whole lesser number repeatedly together with one of its parts. For example, when V is compared with II, it contains two times two and one of its parts; when IX is compared with IV, it contains two times four and one of its parts.

12. A multiple-superpartient number is one that, when compared with a lesser number, contains it repeatedly together with other parts of it. For example, when VIII is compared with III, it contains two times three together with two other parts of it; when XIV is compared with VI, it contains two times six together with two other parts of it; when XVI is compared with VII, it contains two times seven together with two other parts of it; when XXI is compared with IX, it contains two times nine together with three other parts of it.

13. A submultiple-subs​uperparticular number is one that, when compared with a greater number, is contained in it repeatedly together with one of its parts, as III in relation to VII and IV to IX.

14. A submultiple-subs​uperpartient number is one that, when compared with a greater number, is contained in it repeatedly together with several of its parts; for example, III in relation to VIII is contained twice together with two of its parts, and IV in relation to XI is contained twice together with three of its parts.

# CHAPTER VII. On the third division of the whole number

1. Numbers are either discrete or continuous. The latter is divided as follows: first, linear; second, superficial; third, solid. [Note: “Second, superficial.” So also shortly afterward; others read *superficiosus*.] A discrete number is one that is contained by discrete monadic units. [Note: So in Cassiodorus.] For example, III, IV, V, VI, and the rest.

2. A continuous number is one that is contained by joined monadic units; for example, the number three, when understood in magnitude, whether as a line, an area, or a solid, is called continuous. [Note: “A line, an area, or a solid is called continuous.” Cassiodorus likewise uses *disjunction* for *conjunction*.] The same applies to the numbers four and five.

3. A linear number is one that, beginning from the unit, is written linearly to infinity. Hence alpha is used to designate lines, since this letter signifies one among the Greeks.

4. A superficial number is one that is contained not only by length but also by breadth, such as triangular, square, pentagonal, or circular numbers, and the other figures that are always contained on a plane surface. [Note: “On a plane foot,” that is, on a surface. Vitruvius uses the expression in another sense, book VI, chapter 11, and book VII, chapters 1 and 4.]

5. A circular number, when multiplied by itself, begins from itself and returns to itself. For example, five times five is twenty-five. [Note: “Solid … which has length, breadth, and height.” The word “breadth” is absent from our books, but it occurs below, chapter 11, in the definition of a solid figure, and in the Roman manuscript.] A solid number is one that is contained by length, breadth, and height, such as pyramids, which rise in the form of a flame.

6. Cubes are dice. A sphere has equal roundness in every direction. A spherical number is one that, multiplied by a circular number, begins from itself and returns into itself, such as five times five, twenty-five. When this circle is multiplied by itself, it produces a sphere—that is, five times twenty-five, CXXV.

# CHAPTER VIII. On the difference between arithmetic, geometry, and music

1. The difference between arithmetic, geometry, and music appears as follows when one seeks the mean. In arithmetic one proceeds in this way. You join the extremes, divide, and make the mean. Suppose the extremes are VI and XII: joined together, they make XVIII; divide this in half and you obtain IX, which is the arithmetical proportion, so that the mean exceeds the first by as many units as it is exceeded by the last. For IX exceeds VI by three units, and is exceeded by XII by the same number.

2. [Note: “According to geometry.” These passages are neither complete nor sufficiently connected with what precedes. After proposing the difference between arithmetic, geometry, and music through the discovery of the mean, and giving the method for finding the arithmetical mean from the proposed extremes, he ought to have pursued the same matter with the geometrical mean. He does not do so here, nor below, chapter 13, where the same things are repeated.] According to geometry, one proceeds as follows. The extremes, when multiplied, produce the same result as the means when multiplied; for example, VI and XII, multiplied, produce LXXII, and VIII and IX, the means, produce the same amount.

3. [Note: “According to music.” This passage is no better, except that in chapter 22, in an inappropriate place, the matters proper to this section are explained. Here he does not give the method for finding the musical mean, but rather a definition of musical proportion, and not a complete one. See Boethius, *Arithmetic* II, chapters 34 and following, and 50, and *On Music* II, chapters 12 and 16.] According to music, one proceeds thus: by the same proportion by which the mean exceeds the first, the mean is exceeded by the last; for example, VIII exceeds VI by two units, and these two units are one third; likewise the mean VIII is exceeded by the final number, XII.

# CHAPTER IX. That numbers are infinite

1. It is absolutely certain that numbers are infinite, because, at whatever number you suppose an end should be made, that number can be increased—not merely by adding one, but however great it may be and however immense a multitude it may contain, within the very rationale and science of numbers it can be not only doubled but also multiplied.

2. Yet each number is so bounded by its own properties that none can be equal to any other. Therefore they are unequal and different from one another, each is finite, and all are infinite.

# ON GEOMETRY

# CHAPTER X. On the inventors of geometry and its name

1. The discipline of geometry is said to have been first discovered by the Egyptians. Since the Nile flooded and covered everyone’s possessions with mud, the practice of dividing land by lines and measurements gave the art its name. [Note: “Which was afterward extended further.” From Pliny, book II, chapter 23.] Later, advanced by the acuity of learned men, it measures the spaces of the sea, heaven, and air.

2. For, stimulated by inquiry, scholars began, after measuring the earth, to investigate the spaces of heaven: how far the moon stood from the earth, how far the sun itself stood from the moon, and how great a measure extended to the summit of heaven. Thus, by a credible calculation, they distinguished the intervals themselves and the circumference of heaven and the universe in stadia.

3. But because this discipline began with the measurement of the earth, it preserved its name from its origin; for *geometry* is named from earth and measurement. Earth is called γῆ in Greek, and measurement μέτρον. This discipline contains within itself lines, intervals, magnitudes, and figures, and within figures, dimensions and numbers.

# CHAPTER XI. On the fourfold division of geometry

1. Geometry is divided fourfold into plane figures, enumerable magnitude, rational magnitude, and solid figures.

2. Plane figures are those contained by length and breadth.

[Col. 0162A] Enumerable magnitude is that which can be divided by the numbers of arithmetic.

3. Rational magnitudes are those whose measure we can know; irrational magnitudes are those whose quantity of measure cannot be known.

4. Solid figures are those contained by length, breadth, and height. [Note: “Which are, according to Plato, five in number.” Chacon has properly restored these scattered passages to their appropriate places.]

# CHAPTER XII. On geometrical figures

1. Among plane figures, the first is the circle: a plane figure drawn around, with a point at its center toward which all things converge. Geometers call this point the center; in Latin it is called the point of the circle.

2. A quadrilateral is a plane figure lying beneath four straight lines.

[Note: “Dianatheton grammon.” This is the reading of the better books. Antonius Covarrubias, outstanding for his remarkable knowledge of all disciplines and elegance of expression, wished, with minimal alteration, to read *diacatheton grammon*. Vitruvius and others mention cathetal lines, and it is not inappropriate that, after the square, a rectangle should be introduced as longer in one direction, extended through καθέτους, that is, perpendicular lines. P. Nunes did not accept this at all, since the feature is common to several figures: both a tetragon and a right triangle contain καθέτους lines. He himself substituted διὰ ἀντιθέτων γραμμάτων, “by opposed lines,” since some books contain a figure formed by joining two opposed Γ shapes. A. Aug., retaining the manuscript reading ἀναθέτων, interpreted it as “suspended,” since the lines of such a figure, being longer in one direction, may appear suspended. Covarrubias’ conjecture seemed to us closer to the truth, and it did not displease Chacon. Geometers’ ears do not recognize the word *dianatheton*, while P. Nunes’ opinion is excessively ingenious.] *Dianatheton grammon* is a plane figure, and so forth.

An orthogonal triangle is a plane figure that has a right angle.

An isopleurous figure is a plane figure, and so forth.

3. A sphere is a figure formed into a round shape, equal in all its parts.

[Note: “Cube.” Add: “which is contained by six equal squares.”] A cube is a solid figure contained by length, breadth, and height.

4. [Note: “Cylinder.” The definition of the cylinder requires further consideration.] A cylinder is a square figure having above it a semicircle in solid form.

5. A cone is a solid figure that narrows from broad to narrow, like an orthogonal figure.

6. A pyramid is a solid figure that rises from a broad base to a point in the manner of fire. For fire is called πῦρ among the Greeks.

7. Just as every number is contained within ten, so the entire range of all figures is enclosed within the circle.

# CHAPTER XIII. On the principles of geometry

1. [Note: “The principles of this art.” Cicero, *Academica* IV: “I am not seeking here those beginnings of mathematics: the point, which has no magnitude; the extremity, as it were a balance-point in which there is absolutely no thickness; the line, lacking breadth but possessing length.”] The principle of this art is the point, which has no part. A line is length without breadth. A straight line is one that lies equally among its points. A surface is that which has only length and breadth.

2. The boundaries of a surface are lines; for this reason their forms were not placed among the figures above, [Note: “Because they are found within them.” For a point is found in a circle, a line in plane figures, and a surface and its boundary in solid figures.] because they are found within them.

# CHAPTER XIV. On the numbers of geometry

[Col. 0163A]

1. [Note: “Numbers, moreover.” These matters are repeated from chapter 8 because chapter 11 made enumerable magnitude a part of geometry.] According to geometry, numbers are sought in this way: the extremes, when multiplied, produce the same result as the means when multiplied; for example, VI and XII, multiplied, produce LXXII, and VIII and IX, the means, produce the same amount.

# ON MUSIC

# 132 CHAPTER XV. On music and its name

1. Music is expertise consisting in modulation through sound and song; and *musica* is so called by derivation from the Muses. The Muses, however, are called [Note: “Ἀπὸ τοῦ μῶσθαι.” There is remarkable variation in the manuscripts. We have adopted μῶσθαι from μῶσαι, which was less appropriate; Plato also approved this etymology in the *Cratylus*.] ἀπὸ τοῦ μῶσθαι, that is, “from seeking,” because, as the ancients wished, the power of poetry and the modulation of the voice were sought through them.

2. Since their sound is a perceptible thing, [Note: “Flows away into the past.” Augustine, *On Order* II, chapter 4: “For that which the mind sees is always present; but sound, because it is a perceptible thing, flows away into past time and is impressed upon memory. Since reason, by a reasonable fiction, already favors the poets, it must be asked whether something similar was present in their offspring; hence it was fabricated that the Muses were daughters of Jupiter and Memory.”] it flows away into past time and is impressed upon memory. Hence the poets invented the story that the Muses were daughters of Jupiter and Memory. Unless sounds are retained in memory by human beings, they perish, because they cannot be written down.

# CHAPTER XVI. On its inventors

1. Moses says that Jubal, who belonged to Cain’s line before the Flood, discovered the art of music. [Note: “But the Greeks say Pythagoras.” Macrobius, book II of the *Dream of Scipio*.] The Greeks, however, say that Pythagoras discovered the beginnings of this art from the sound of hammers and the stretched strings that were struck. Others say that Linus of Thebes, [Note: “Linus of Thebes.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] and Zethus and Amphion [Note: “Zethus and Amphion.” From the same source and from Servius, on *Corydon*.] were the first to become distinguished in the art of music.

2. After them this discipline was gradually developed, especially, and enlarged in many ways; and it was considered as shameful to be ignorant of music as of letters. Music was introduced not only into sacred observances, but also into all solemn occasions and every joyful or sorrowful circumstance.

3. [Note: “For just as in divine worship.” Horace: “At the tables of the wealthy, and friendly to temples.”] For just as hymns belong to divine worship, so hymenaei belong to weddings, [Note: “And threnoi at funerals.” Hence the *siticinian* mode in the Twelve Tables; see Aulus Gellius, book II, chapter 2, and Nonius, under *siticines*. Servius, *Aeneid* V: “It should be known that funerals of older persons were customarily conducted to the trumpet, but those of younger persons to the pipes.” See Festus under *funebres tibiae*. The words of Matthew, chapter IX—“and he saw the flute-players and the crowd making a tumult”—also show that the Hebrews used pipes at funerals.] and at funerals threnoi and laments were sung to pipes. [Note: “At banquets, carried around.” From Quintilian, chapter on music.] At banquets, however, a lyre or cithara was carried around, and a convivial type of song was arranged for each of those reclining at table.

# CHAPTER XVII. What music can accomplish

1. [Note: “Therefore without music.” From the same source, Quintilian.] Therefore no discipline can be complete without music, for nothing exists without it. The world itself, it is said, has been composed according to a certain harmony of sounds, and heaven itself revolves under the modulation of harmony. [Col. 0164A] Music moves the emotions and prompts the senses toward different dispositions.

2. In battles also, the concert of trumpets inflames the combatants; and the more vehement the blast, the stronger the spirit becomes for the contest. Song likewise encourages rowers. Music also soothes the mind for enduring toil, and the modulation of the voice consoles the weariness of individual tasks.

3. Music also calms agitated minds, as we read of David, who by the art of modulation freed Saul from an unclean spirit. Music even summons beasts themselves, as well as serpents, birds, and dolphins, to hear its modulation. Whatever we speak, and whatever moves us inwardly through the pulses of our veins, is likewise shown to be joined to the powers of harmony through musical rhythms.

# CHAPTER XVIII. On the three parts of music

1. The parts of music are three: harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. Harmonic music distinguishes high and low in sounds. Rhythmic music [Note: “Which investigates the onset of words.” All the books of Cassiodorus read: “Which judges in the collision of words.” Capella: “That which pertains to melody is called harmonic; that which pertains to numbers, rhythmic; that which pertains to words, metric.”] investigates the coming together of words, determining whether the sound coheres well or badly.

2. Metric music recognizes the measure of different meters by a rational method, such as heroic, iambic, elegiac, and so forth.

# 135 CHAPTER XIX. On the threefold division of music

1. Every sound, which is the material of songs, is evidently threefold by nature. The first is harmonic, consisting of vocal song. The second is organic, consisting of breath. The third is rhythmic, receiving numbers through the striking of the fingers.

2. [Note: “For sound is produced either by the voice.” From Augustine, *Commentary on Psalm 150* and *On Christian Doctrine* II, chapter 17, from which all this is taken. “Which is made musical by striking.” From the same author, *On Order* II, chapter 14.] Sound is produced either by the voice, as through the throat; by breath, as through a trumpet or pipe; by striking, as through a cithara; or by anything else that produces melody through being struck.

# CHAPTER XX. On the first division of music, called harmonic

1. The first division of music, called harmonic—that is, modulation of the voice—belongs to comedians, tragedians, choruses, and all who sing with their own voice. It produces movement from mind and body, and from movement sound; from sound music is gathered, which in a human being is called voice.

2. [Col. 0165A] [Note: “Voice is air struck by breath.” This is the definition of grammarians and philosophers, as Lactantius says, although he himself rejects it entirely, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 15.] Voice is air struck by breath, whence words also receive their name. Properly, however, voice belongs to human beings or irrational animals. In other cases, sound is improperly and not strictly called voice, as in:

> The trumpet’s voice roared, and broken sounds toward the shores.

The proper expression is that shore-side cliffs resound, as in:

> But the trumpet [gives] a dreadful sound from afar through sonorous bronze. Harmony is modulation of the voice and the concord or fitting together of many sounds.

3. Symphonia is the balanced modulation of concordant sounds, high and low, whether in voice, breath, or striking. Through it higher and lower voices agree, so that anyone who departs from it offends the sense of hearing. Its opposite is diaphonia, that is, differing or dissonant voices.

4. Euphonia is sweetness of voice. It is also called *melos*, from sweetness and honey.

5. Diastema is a span of voice formed from two or more suitably arranged sounds.

6. Diesis consists of certain intervals and movements of modulation, and of inclining from one sound toward another.

7. Tone is a high utterance of the voice; it is a difference and quantity of harmony, consisting in the accent or sustained quality of the voice. Musicians divided its kinds into fifteen parts, of which the hyperlydian is the last and highest, while the hypodorian is the lowest of all.

8. Song is an inflection of the voice, for a straight sound precedes song.

9. Arsis is the elevation of the voice, that is, its beginning. Thesis is the placement of the voice, that is, its ending.

10. Sweet voices are delicate and full, clear and high. Distinct voices are those that are extended farther, so that they fill the entire intervening space, as the blast of trumpets.

11. Delicate voices are those in which there is no breath, such as those of infants, women, or the sick, as in strings. For the thinnest strings emit delicate and slender sounds.

12. Voices are full when much breath comes forth at once, as in men. A high voice is thin and elevated, as we see in strings. [Note: “A hard voice … whenever a hammer strikes hard iron.” Others read “a hard hammer strikes iron.”] A hard voice is one that emits sounds violently, like thunder and the sound of an anvil whenever a hammer strikes hard iron.

13. A harsh voice is hoarse and scattered into small and dissimilar pulses. A dull voice is one that falls silent as soon as it has been emitted and, suffocated, cannot be prolonged any farther, as occurs with earthenware vessels. [Note: “*Vinnola*.” Others read *vinnolata*. Festus: *vinnulus*, behaving gently and doing nothing at all in a manly way. Nonius: *vinnolum*, speaking delicately, alluring. Plautus, in the *Asinaria*, uses *vinnula*, “graceful little one.” The Glossary has *vinnulus* as Νωλεχὶς, although *vinnicus* is incorrectly read there.] A *vinnola* voice is soft and flexible. It is called *vinnola* from *vinnus*, that is, from a curl softly bent.

14. A perfect voice is high, sweet, and clear. It is high so that it may reach the elevated region; clear so that it may fill the ears; sweet so that it may charm the minds of those listening. If any one of these qualities is lacking, the voice will not be perfect.

# CHAPTER XXI. On the second division, called organic

1. The second division is organic and consists of those instruments that, when filled by blown breath, are animated into the sound of a voice, such as trumpets, reeds, pipes, organs, the *pandura*, and instruments similar to these.

2. [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Organum” is a general term. From Augustine, On Psalm 150.] The word “organum” is a general designation for all musical instruments. [Note: [Col. 0165D] The instrument to which bellows are attached. Chacon thought that the Greeks called it hydraulon; concerning it, see Vitruvius, Book X, chapter 13, and Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter “On the Mind.” Pliny, Book VII, chapter 37, and Jerome, On Pneumatics. Others, from Pollux, Book IV, chapter 9, think that it was called the Tyrrhenian pipe. Concerning ordinary organs there are very fine verses in Claudian, in his book On the Consulship of Manlius Theodorus.] But the instrument to which bellows are attached the Greeks call by another name. That it should be called “organum,” however, is rather the common usage.

3. [Note: [Col. 0166D] “The trumpet first … devised the pipes.” Clement of Alexandria, Stromata I, says that the Etruscans devised the trumpet and the Phrygians the pipe.] The trumpet was first invented by the Tyrrhenians, concerning whom Virgil says:

> And the Tyrrhenian blast of the trumpet roared through the heavens.

It was used not only in battles, but also on all festival days, for the sake of praise or the splendor of joy. Hence it is also said in the Psalter: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the distinguished day of your solemnity.” For the Jews had been commanded to sound the trumpet at the beginning of the new moon, which they still do to this day.

4. The pipes are said to have been devised in Phrygia; for a long time they were used only at funerals, and afterward also in the sacred rites of the gentiles. They think that they were called *tibiae* because originally they were made from the shins and legs of stags and fawns; afterward, through misuse of the term, even those not made from legs or bones began to be called this, and hence also *tibicen*, as though “singer of the pipes.”

5. [Note: [Col. 0166D] *Calamus* properly means a tree. It is not very surprising if whoever compiled the material from which this was taken called a reed a tree. Why he derived the name from *calendo*, that is, from “pouring forth sounds,” is much more obscure, unless one reads *calando*, that is, “calling.” For we think that *canendo*, “singing,” which appears in most Gothic manuscripts, is erroneous. But learned men of this age have now sufficiently shown that these etymologies, which seemed to many people in Isidore either too far-fetched or even absurd, should not be disregarded.] *Calamus* is the proper name of a tree, called so from *calendo*, that is, from pouring forth sounds.

138 6. Some think that the panpipe was invented by Mercury; [Note: [Col. 0166D] Others say by Faunus. Pliny, Book VII, chapter 56.] others by Faunus, whom the Greeks call Pan. Some say that it was invented by Idi, a shepherd from Acragas in Sicily. [Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167C] For in Greek *phos* is the word for “voice.” It seemed best to follow the simpler reading of the manuscripts, if by chance there is any truth in their discordant testimony. Isidore repeats the same point several times. The form φωνή was not far removed from it.] But the panpipe is so called because it emits a voice. For in Greek *PHOS* means “voice,” while *STOLA* means “sent.”

7. The *sambuca* is a type of symphony among musical instruments. It is made from a fragile kind of wood, and pipes are also made from it.

8. [Note: [Col. 0167D] *Pandura.* Pollux, Book IV, writes that it was invented by the Assyrians. Varro, Book VII: “Why should we not say *citharicen* from *cithara*, *psalterium*, and *pandurus*?”] The *pandura* was named after its inventor, concerning whom Virgil says:

> Pan first devised the joining of several reeds with wax.

Pan cares for sheep and for the shepherds of sheep. For among the gentiles he was a pastoral god who first adapted unequal reeds to song and fitted them together with deliberate skill.

139 **CHAPTER XXII. On the third division, which is called rhythmic.**

1. The third division is rhythmic, relating to strings and percussion. To it belong various kinds of citharas, [Col. 0167B] the drum, cymbal, sistrum, bronze and silver vessels, and other things of this sort which, struck with metallic hardness, produce a ringing sound with sweetness.

2. Jubal is said to have discovered the cithara and the psaltery, as was stated above. According to the opinion of the Greeks, [Note: [Col. 0167D] The use of the cithara is attributed to Apollo. Bion:

> As Pan found the oblique pipe, and Athena the flute,  
> As Hermes found the tortoise-shell, and sweet Apollo the cithara.]

the use of the cithara is believed to have been discovered by Apollo. It is said that at first the shape of the cithara resembled the human chest, since, just as the voice comes from the chest, so song was produced from the instrument itself; and for the same reason it received its name. For in the Doric language the chest is called κιθάρα (*kithara*).

3. Gradually more kinds of it came into existence, [Note: [Col. 0167D] For example, the barbarian psaltery. See Athenaeus, Book IV, and Pollux.] such as psalteries, lyres, barbitons, Phoenician instruments, and pectides, as well as those called Indian instruments, which are struck by two people simultaneously. There are also other kinds, of both square and triangular form.

[Col. 0167C] 4. The number of strings was also increased, and their type was changed. The ancients called the cithara a *fidicula* or *fides*, because its strings harmonize with one another as well as people who are bound by trust agree with one another. The ancient cithara had seven strings; hence Virgil says: “Seven distinctions of voices.”

5. They are called distinctions because no string produces a sound like that of the neighboring string. There are seven strings either because they fill the whole range of the voice or because the heavens sound with seven movements.

140 6. The strings are called *chordae* from *cor*, “heart,” because just as the heart beats in the chest, so the string is struck on the cithara. Mercury first devised them; he was also the first [Note: [Col. 0167D] “He stretched the strings into sound.” All the books corruptly read “he stretched sound into the strings.” Tertullian, On the Crown, chapter 8: “But even if he [Mercury] stretched the strings into sound, I will not deny that he did this invention together with the holy ones.”] to stretch strings into sound.

[Col. 0168A] 7. The psaltery, which is commonly called a song, takes its name from *psallere*, “to pluck,” because a chorus responds to its sound by singing in harmony. It resembles the barbarian cithara [Note: [Col. 0167D] “In the shape of the letter Δ.” Cassiodorus, in the Prologue to the Psalms: “The psaltery is, as Jerome says, a sounding hollow wooden instrument formed in the shape of the letter Δ.”] in the form of the letter Δ. [Note: [Col. 0168C] “But the difference between the psaltery and the cithara.” From Augustine, On Psalm 80.] The difference between the psaltery and the cithara is that the psaltery has the hollow wood from which the sound is produced above, and the strings are struck from below and sound upward. The cithara, by contrast, has the hollow part of the wood below. [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Hebrews used a ten-stringed psaltery. Athenaeus says that among other peoples it had only nine strings.] The Hebrews used a ten-stringed psaltery because of the number of the Ten Commandments of the Law.

8. The lyre is called from Greek *ἀπὸ τοῦ λυρεῖν* (*apo tou lyrein*, “from playing the lyre”), on account of the variety of its sounds. They say that the lyre was first invented by Mercury, as follows. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “When the Nile, returning … had attracted.” From the Commentary of Aratus on the Lyre and from Hyginus, Book II.] When the Nile, withdrawing into its channels, had left various animals behind in the fields, it also left a tortoise. When the tortoise had decayed and its sinews remained stretched within the hide, Mercury struck it and it produced a sound. After this model Mercury made a lyre and gave it to Orpheus, who was especially devoted to this art.

9. Hence he is also thought, by the same art, to have attracted not only wild animals but also rocks and forests by the modulation of his song. Because of their love of study and praise of poetry, musicians imagined that the lyre had even been placed among the stars in the inventions of their myths.

10. A drum is a hide or skin stretched over wood on one side. 141 It is the middle part of a symphony, like a sieve. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “The middle part of a symphony.” So above, chapter 20: the sambuca is a type of symphony.] It is called a *tympanum* because it is in the middle. Hence a central pearl is also called a *tympanum*, [Note: [Col. 0168D] “The middle pearl of the drum.” Pliny, Book IX, chapter 35, calls it *tympanium*.] and it is struck with a rod, like a symphony.

[Col. 0168C] 11. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “Cymbals and vessels.” Augustine, On Psalm 150: “Cymbals touch one another so that they may sound well; for this reason some compare them with our lips.”] Cymbals are certain vessels which, when struck, touch one another and produce a sound. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “They are called cymbals because they are struck together with dances.” The use of dancing was forbidden at the birthdays of the saints. Council of Toledo III, final canon. I think *ballematium* is derived from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ βαλλίζειν. As Suidas says, βαλλίζειν means “to strike the cymbals and to dance to their sound.” Hence our word *bailar*, “to dance.”] They are called cymbals because they are struck together with dances. Thus the Greeks call them dancing cymbals.

12. The sistrum was named after its female inventor. Isis, queen of the Egyptians, is held to have invented this type of instrument. Juvenal says:

> May Isis, and the sistrum wielded in anger, strike my eyes.

Hence women also strike it, because a woman invented this type of instrument. [Note: [Col. 0168D] “Hence among the Amazons.” Capella, Book IX, says that they carried weapons to the reeds; but Isidore seems rather to have had Virgil’s verse in mind:

> The queen summons her troops amid the ancestral sistrum.

Aeneid VIII.] Hence among the Amazons the women’s army was summoned to war by the sistrum.

142 13. The bell takes its name from the sound of the voice, as do the clapping of hands and the creaking of doors.

[Col. 0169A] 14. [Note: [Col. 0169D] “Symphony.” Jerome, To Damasus, Letter 146: “Some Latins wrongly think that *symphonia* is a type of organ, although by this word a harmonious concert in the praises of God is signified. For *symphonia* is expressed in Latin by *consonantia*, ‘harmony.’” This passage of Jerome certainly did not escape Isidore; nevertheless, it appears from his words—“It is commonly called a symphony”—that in his time the custom had prevailed of using the term for a certain type of instrument.] A symphony is commonly called a hollow piece of wood with skin stretched over both ends, which musicians strike on either side with rods. From the harmony produced in it there arises a deep and high, most pleasing song.

**CHAPTER XXIII. On musical numbers.**

1. You calculate numbers according to music as follows. Take the extremes, for example VI and XII. You see by how many units VI is exceeded by XII: it is by VI units. Multiply by the square: six times six makes XXXVI. Add those first extremes, VI and XII; together they make XVIII. Divide XXXVI by XVIII, and the result is a *dipondius* (a unit of two). Add these to the smaller sum, namely VI; the result will be VIII, which is the mean between VI and XII. For VIII exceeds VI by two units, [Note: [Col. 0169D] That is, one third of six. In writing the numbers, we have followed Chacon and rejected certain obsolete adverbs that occur in the printed books and manuscripts. Anyone who prefers them will find more of the same kind in Volusius Maecianus.] that is, one third, and XII exceeds VIII by four units, a third portion. By whatever proportion one exceeds, by the same proportion one is exceeded.

2. But just as this proportion exists in the world through the revolution of the circles, so also in the microcosm it is valid beyond the voice to such an extent that without its perfection even a human being devoid of symphonies cannot exist. Through the perfection of the same music meters also stand firm, in *arsis* and *thesis*, that is, elevation and placing.

**ON ASTRONOMY. CHAPTER XXIV. On the name astronomy.**

1. Astronomy [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Astronomy.” The same above, Book II, chapter 25.] is the law of the stars, which investigates the courses, shapes, and relationships of the heavenly bodies and stars, both in relation to one another and in relation to the earth, by a method capable of inquiry.

**CHAPTER XXV. On its inventors.**

[Col. 0169C]

1. The Egyptians were the first to discover astronomy. The Chaldaeans were the first to teach astrology and the observation of births. Josephus firmly asserts that Abraham taught astrology to the Egyptians. The Greeks, however, say that this art was first devised by Atlas, and that for this reason he was said to have supported the heavens.

2. Whoever he may have been, stirred by the motion of the heavens and the reasoning power of the soul, he observed, through the changing seasons, the fixed and determinate courses of the stars, and the measured intervals of their distances, certain dimensions and numbers; and, defining and distinguishing these and linking them in an ordered system, he discovered astrology.

**CHAPTER XVI. On its teachers.**

[Col. 0169D] 1. In both languages there are volumes written on astronomy by various authors, among whom Ptolemy is considered preeminent among the Greeks. He also established canons by which the courses of the stars may be discovered.

**CHAPTER XXVII. On the difference between astronomy and astrology.**

1. There is some difference between astronomy and astrology. Astronomy contains the revolution of the heavens, the risings, settings, and movements of the stars, and the reasons why they are so called. Astrology, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious.

2. It is natural when it explains the courses of the sun and moon, or of the stars, and the fixed stations of times. It is superstitious when it is the astrology followed by the mathematicians, who make predictions from the stars and arrange the twelve signs among the individual members of the soul or body, attempting through the course of the stars to foretell people’s births and characters.

**CHAPTER XXVIII. On the method of astronomy.**

1. The method of astronomy consists of very many subjects. It defines what the world is, 145 what the heavens are, what the position and courses of the spheres are, what the axis and poles of heaven are, what the climates of heaven are, and what the courses of the sun, moon, and stars are, and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXIX. On the world and its name.**

1. The world [Note: [Col. 0170D] “The world.” Hyginus, from whom Isidore took much, Astronomy, chapter 1: “The world is called that which consists of the sun, moon, earth, and all the stars.”] is that which consists of heaven and earth, the sea, and all the stars. It is therefore called the world [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Because it is always in motion.” That is, as though from *movendus*, “to be moved.” See Book XIII, chapter 1.] because it is always in motion; no rest has been granted to its elements.

**CHAPTER XXX. On the form of the world.**
