1. The formation of the world is demonstrated as follows. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “For just as …” Virgil, Georgics I:

> As the world rises toward Scythia and the lofty Rhipaean peaks,  
> So it sinks down toward Libya and slopes toward the southern winds.]

For just as the world rises toward the northern region, so it declines toward the south. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Its head, however …” Aristotle makes the southern summit the head, following Homer, as some think. See Plutarch for the opinions of philosophers on this matter.] Its head, and as it were its face, is the eastern region; its furthest part is the northern region.

146 **CHAPTER XXXI. On heaven and its name.**

1. Philosophers have said that heaven is round, revolving, and fiery, and that it received this name because, like an engraved vessel, it bears impressed upon it the signs of the stars. [Note: [Col. 0170D] “And it was called.” From Ambrose, Hexameron II, chapter 4.]

2. God distinguished it with brilliant lights, filled it with the shining orb of the sun and moon, and adorned it with the radiant signs of gleaming stars. Heaven is called οὐρανός in Greek, from ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι, that is, “from seeing,” because the air is transparent and purer [Note: [Col. 0171C] “For observing.” From the same author, Book III, chapter 22.] for observation.

**CHAPTER XXXII. On the position of the celestial sphere.**

1. The sphere [Note: [Col. 0171C] “The sphere of heaven is a form.” This chapter has been composed from Hyginus, Astronomy, chapter 1; Ambrose, Hexameron I and II; and the Dream of Scipio.] of heaven is a certain form made round, whose center is the earth, enclosed equally on every side. They say that this sphere has neither beginning nor end, because in a circular form it is not easy to grasp where it begins or where it ends.

2. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “The philosophers, however … believe.” From Ambrose, Hexameron II, chapter 2. Cicero: “All things are joined together for you by nine circles, or rather spheres,” and so forth.] The philosophers introduced seven heavens of the world, that is, the spheres of the planets, moving with harmonious motion. They say that everything is connected with their orbits and believe that these spheres, interwoven with and as though inserted into one another, revolve backward and are carried in opposite directions by fixed motions.

147 **CHAPTER XXXIII. On the motion of the same.**

1. The motion of the sphere revolves upon two axes, [Note: [Col. 0171D] “The motion of the sphere on two axes.” That is, on poles, as others sometimes also say.] one of which is northern; it never sets [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And is called Boreas.” It is also so called by Servius, Georgics I.] and is called Boreas. The other is southern; it is never seen and is called Austronotius. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And Austronotius.” Other copies have *Austronotus*, and Hyginus has *Notius*; but in the commentary on Aratus, *Austronotus* appears, as also below, chapter 36, and Book XIII, chapter 5.]

2. They say that the sphere of heaven moves by these two poles, and that with its motion the stars fixed in it travel around from east to west, while the constellations of the north complete shorter circuits near the pivot. [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And with its motion the stars fixed in it.” Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Book II, chapter 10.]

**CHAPTER XXXIV. On the course of the same sphere.**

1. The sphere of heaven turns from east to west once in a day and night, over a period of twenty-four hours, during which the sun completes its course above the earth and beneath the earth through its revolution.

**CHAPTER XXXV. On the speed of heaven.**

1. The sphere of heaven is said to move with such speed that, unless the stars ran against its precipitous course and slowed it down, they would bring about the ruin of the world.

**CHAPTER XXXVI. On the axis of heaven.**

1. The axis [Note: [Col. 0171D] “The axis is northern.” So again in Book XIII, chapter 5; and Servius, Aeneid II: “The axis is either the northern Wain or part of the north.” Chacon nevertheless deleted the word “northern,” and we do not disagree with him.] is a straight northern line extending through the middle of the sphere, and it is called the axis [Note: [Col. 0172C] “And it is called the axis.” Since in chapter 32 he had mentioned axes, pivots, and poles, he now gives their etymologies.] because the sphere revolves upon it like a wheel, or because the Wain is there.

148 **CHAPTER XXXVII. On the celestial poles.**

[Col. 0172A]

1. The poles [Note: [Col. 0172D] “The poles are circles.” The same below, Book XIII, chapter 5.] are circles that run through the axis. One of them is northern; it never sets and is called Boreas. The other is southern; it is never seen and is called Austronotius.

2. They are called poles because they are the circles of the axes, a term derived from the use of wagons, namely from *polire*, “to polish.” But the Borean pole is always seen, while the Austronotian is never seen, because the right-hand regions of heaven are higher, while the regions of the south are pressed down.

**CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the pivots of heaven.**

1. The pivots of heaven are the extremities of the axis. They are called *cardines* because the heavens turn through them, or because they revolve like a heart.

**CHAPTER XXXIX. On the convex parts of heaven.**

[Col. 0172B]

1. The convex parts of heaven are its extremities, named from their curvature. Hence the verse:

> Whenever humid night encloses the convex heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] “Convex.” From Servius, Eclogues 4; repeated in Book XIII, chapter 5.] For *convexum* means curved or inclined and bent in the form of a circle.

149 **CHAPTER XL. On the doors of heaven.**

1. There are two doors of heaven: the east and the west. Through one gate the sun comes forth; through the other it withdraws. [Note: [Col. 0172D] “Doors.” Book XIII, chapter 1.]

**CHAPTER XLI. On the twofold face of heaven.**

1. The face, or head, of heaven is the eastern region; its furthest part is the northern region. [Note: [Col. 0172D] “The furthest north.” Isidore interprets Lucan’s *ima* as “furthest.” Otherwise how could the lowest part be northern if, as he said in chapter 29, the world rises toward the northern region? Thus he struggles to reconcile Virgil with Lucan. Servius saw the same problem; commenting on Virgil’s words, “As the world rises toward Scythia,” he says: “The definition of our climate, that is, of our inhabited region, now begins in the north and ends in the southern region.” The person who has tried to replace *ima* with *ultima* twice in Isidore, looking only to Lucan, sees less clearly.] Concerning this Lucan says:

[Col. 0172C]

> Thus the lowest part of the world lies hidden, which the snowy zone  
> And perpetual winters press down.

**CHAPTER XLII. On the four parts of heaven.**

1. The climates [Note: [Col. 0172D] “The climates of heaven.” From Jerome, Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter VI.] of heaven, that is, its regions or parts, are four. The first is the eastern part, from which certain stars rise. The second is the western part, where certain stars set for us. The third is the northern part, where the sun reaches during the longer days. The fourth is the southern part, where the sun reaches during the longer nights.

2. The east is named from the rising of the sun. The west is so called because it makes the day set and perish. For it hides the light from the world and brings darkness over it. The north is called *Septentrio* from the seven stars of the axis, which revolve and turn within it. It is also properly called the *vertex*, because it turns.

3. The south is called *midday*, either because the sun makes the middle of the day there, as though *medidies*, or because then the ether shines more purely. For *merum* means “pure.”

4. There are also seven other climates of heaven, like seven lines from east to west, beneath which differing human customs and distinctly different animals are born. They were named after certain famous places. The first is Meroe, the second Syene, [Note: [Col. 0173C] “The third Catachoras.” The manuscripts have *Catagoras*, *cathocoras*, *cathagorius*, and *catacorius*. The words “that is, Africa” are absent from the Roman manuscript and perhaps were brought here from Cassiodorus; he has “the third, Africa.” Capella has “the third, Dialexandrias,” which extends through Cyrene into Africa, toward Carthage, lying to the south; hence some made it “the third, Cyrene in Africa.” Another interpreted *catacaras* or *catamisocaras* as the port of Misocara in Mauretania. Chacon connected the preceding words with “famous places,” reading κατὰ χώρας, “by regions.”] the third Catachoras, that is, Africa; the fourth Rhodes; the fifth the Hellespont; the sixth Mesopontus; and the seventh Borysthenes.

**CHAPTER XLIII. On the hemispheres.**

[Col. 0173B]

1. A hemisphere is half of a sphere. The hemisphere above the earth is that part of heaven which is entirely visible to us. The hemisphere beneath the earth is that which cannot be seen for as long as it remains beneath the earth.

151 **CHAPTER XLIV. On the five circles of heaven.**

1. There are five zones of heaven. Through their divisions, certain regions are inhabited because of their temperate climate, while others are uninhabitable because of the severity of their cold or heat. They are therefore called zones or circles because they exist in the revolution of the sphere.

2. The first circle is called Arctic because [Note: [Col. 0173C] “Because the Bear is within it.” All the Gothic manuscripts have this reading, both here and in Book XIII, chapter 6. Hyginus, Book III, chapter 1, speaks of the Arctic Pole, on which both Bears rest, enclosed within the Arctic circle. Nor is *Arcturus*, which appears in the printed books, objectionable. For the same Hyginus, Book I of Astronomy, from which this seems to have been taken, says: “This circle is called Arctic because within it the figures of the Bears are seen as though enclosed; these constellations, fashioned by us in the form of bears, are called the Septentriones.” The commentator on Aratus likewise says: “There are two Bears, the greater of which they call Helice,” and shortly afterward: “The lesser Bear,” and so forth.] within it the signs of the Bears are seen enclosed.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] “The second circle.” Hyginus, Book I of Astronomy: “It is called ἰσημερινός in Greek, while in Latin it is called *dies aequinox*, ‘the equinoctial day.’ If we translated the word itself, it would rather be called *aequidialis*, ‘equal-day.’ Festus reports that the ancients spoke in this way: ‘Among the ancients *aequidiale* was called what we now call *aequinoctiale*, because the night should more properly be counted with the day than the day with the night.’ The Greeks also agree in this, calling it ἰσημερία, that is, *aequidiale*. But we say *aequinoctium*, not *aequidium*. The Greeks made the name from day, we from night. Nor will we conceal that all the books read: ‘For *hemerinos* in Latin means day and night,’ except two from Tarragona, in which the words ‘and night’ are absent. Chacon reads it this way: ‘For ἡμέρα in Latin means day and night’; Isidore evidently wished the term ἡμέρα to include both day and night, as Vulcanius also printed it. Hyginus, Book I: ‘Then the equinoctial circle is drawn, called *isemerinos* by the Greeks, because when the sun reaches that orbit it produces an equinox. Once this circle has been made, half of the sphere is seen to have been established.’] The second circle is called θερινὸς τροπικός (*therinos tropikos*, “summer-turning”), because at this circle the sun, producing summer at the limits of the north, does not pass beyond that circle but immediately turns back; hence it is called tropical.

3. The third circle is called ἰσημερινός (*isēmerinos*, “equal-day”), which the Latins call equinoctial because when the sun reaches that orbit it produces an equinox. For ἰσημερινός in Latin means “equinoctial day.” By this circle half of the sphere is seen to have been established.

4. The fourth circle is called Antarctic because it is opposite the circle that we call Arctic.

5. The fifth circle is χειμερινὸς τροπικός (*cheimerinos tropikos*, “winter-turning”), which the Latins call wintry or brumal. It is so called because when the sun reaches that circle, it produces winter for those who are in the north, but summer for those who dwell in the southern regions.

**CHAPTER XLV. On the zodiacal circle.**

1. The zodiac [Note: [Col. 0174D] “The zodiac.” All the books have this reading; I cannot say precisely in what sense. There is a different reading in Book XIII, chapter 6. But those words too, since they are foreign to the Gothic manuscripts, are absent.] is a circle consisting of the five angles of lines and one line.

**CHAPTER XLVI. On the white circle.**

1. The Milky Circle is a path seen in the sphere. It is named from its whiteness because it is white. [Col. 0174B] Some say [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Which some say.” Metrodorus, as reported by Plutarch.] that it is the path [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Through which the sun travels.” The reading *currit*, “travels,” appears in R., as in Book XIII, chapter 5.] along which the sun circles and that it shines in this way because of the passage of its radiance.

**CHAPTER XLVII. On the magnitude of the sun.**

1. The magnitude of the sun [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Greater than the earth,” that is, larger, as in the following chapter and above, chapter 6, where he more than once uses *fortior* for “larger.”] is greater than that of the earth. Hence, at the same moment in which it rises, it appears equally both in the east and in the west. But because it seems to us to be only a cubit in size, we must consider how far the sun is from the earth; that distance makes it appear small to us.

153 **CHAPTER XLVIII. On the magnitude of the moon.**

1. The magnitude of the moon is also said to be less than that of the sun. For although the sun is above the moon, [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Although it is above the moon.” We discussed this construction in chapter 5. The passage is from Hyginus, Book IV, the chapter on the moon.] and nevertheless appears larger to us than the moon, if it came nearer to us it would be seen to be much larger than the moon. Just as the sun is greater than the earth, so the earth is greater than the moon by a certain amount.

**CHAPTER XLIX. On the nature of the sun.**

1. Although the sun is fiery, [Note: [Col. 0174D] “Although the sun is fiery.” From the commentary on Aratus near the end.] it grows hotter through the excessive motion of its revolution. [Col. 0175A] [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Whose fire the philosophers say.” Cicero attributes this opinion to Cleanthes, On the Nature of the Gods II. In Book III he says: “Others say that the sun, moon, and remaining stars are nourished by waters, some fresh and some marine; and Cleanthes gives this as the reason why the sun turns back and does not proceed farther at the solstitial circle, and likewise at the brumal circle, lest it move farther away from its food.” Lucretius also says, On the Stars, Book V:

> Whether air flowing from somewhere outside  
> Drives and whirls the fires, or whether they themselves can creep  
> Where each one’s food calls and invites them onward,  
> Feeding their flaming bodies throughout the sky.

Xenophanes said that the sun was compounded from fires gathered from moist vapors and was a kind of burning cloud. See Plutarch, Pliny, and the Commentary on Aratus.] Philosophers say that its fire is nourished by water and, conversely, receives the power of its light and heat from that element. Hence we see it often wet and dewy.

**CHAPTER L. On the course of the sun.**

1. They say that the sun moves by itself and does not revolve with the world. 154 For if it remained fixed in heaven, all days and nights would be equal; but since we see that it will set tomorrow in one place and set yesterday in another, it is evident that it moves by itself and does not revolve with the world. For it completes annual orbits over unequal distances because of the changes of the seasons.

2. When it travels farther toward the south, it produces winter, so that the earth may be enriched by the moisture and frost of winter. [Col. 0175B] When it approaches nearer to the north, it produces summer, so that crops may be hardened by ripeness and whatever is uncooked in moist places may be softened by being heated.

**CHAPTER LI. On the effect of the sun.**

1. The rising sun makes day; the setting sun brings on night. For day is the sun above the earth, and night is the sun beneath the earth. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “From it … the seasons.” Words of Clement, Eighth Recognition.] From it come the hours; from it comes day when it has risen; from it also comes night when it has set; from it the months and years are counted; from it the changes of the seasons take place.

2. When it travels through the south, it is nearer the earth; but when it is near the north, it is raised aloft. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “It is lifted high.” The remainder found in the printed books is absent from the manuscript and was brought here from chapter 17 of the Book on the Nature of Things to Sisebut.] For this reason God established different courses, places, and seasons for it, lest, if it always remained in the same places, its daily heat should consume everything, as Clement says: “It follows different courses, by which the tempering of the air is apportioned according to the seasons, and the order of alternations and changes is preserved. For when it has climbed to the higher regions, it moderates spring; when it has reached the summit of heaven, it kindles the heats of summer; descending again, it restores the mildness of autumn. But when it returns to the lower circle, from the icy structure of heaven it leaves us the severity of winter’s cold.”

**CHAPTER LII. On the journey of the sun.**

1. The rising sun travels through the south. After it has reached the west and bathed itself in the Ocean, [Note: [Col. 0176D] “By unknown paths beneath the earth.” They are now known through the diligence of our people.] it travels by unknown paths beneath the earth and returns again to the east.

**CHAPTER LIII. On the light of the moon.**

[Col. 0176A]

1. Some philosophers say [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Some.” From the Commentary on Aratus.] that the moon possesses its own light, that one part of its sphere is light-bearing and the other dark, and that by gradually turning it produces different shapes. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Others, on the contrary.” The idea is from the same commentaries, but the wording was borrowed from Jerome’s Commentary on Isaiah, chapter LXVI.] Others, on the contrary, say that the moon does not have its own light but is illuminated by the sun’s rays. Hence it suffers an eclipse if the shadow of the earth comes between it and the sun.

**CHAPTER LIV. On the forms of the moon.**

1. The first shape of the moon is horned; the second is cut; the third is half; the fourth is full; the fifth is again half, from the larger part; the sixth is again cut; the seventh is horned. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “The second is cut … the sixth again cut.” Other copies have *sextilis* in both places.]

[Col. 0176B] 2. The seventh-and-a-half and the twenty-second-and-a-half are the middle points in their orbit; the rest are proportional.

156 **CHAPTER LV. On the moon’s interlunium.**

1. The interlunium of the moon is the period between the waning and the waxing moon. It is the thirtieth day, when the moon gives no light. It cannot then be seen because it is darkened by conjunction with the sun; but at that same moment, being reborn, it becomes visible by gradually moving away from it.

**CHAPTER LVI. On the course of the moon.**

1. The moon regulates the monthly periods through the alternation of its lost and recovered light. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “For this reason … encounters.” From Servius, Aeneid I, on the words “Here he sings of the wandering moon.”] For this reason it proceeds on an oblique rather than a straight course, like the sun, so that it may not fall into the center of the earth and suffer frequent eclipses. Its circle is near the earth. When waxing, it faces the east with its horns; when waning, the west—appropriately, because it is about to set and lose its light.

**CHAPTER LVII. On the moon’s nearness to the earth.**

1. The moon is nearer to the earth than the sun. Hence it completes its course more quickly in a shorter orbit. For the journey that the sun completes in 365 days, the moon traverses in thirty days. Hence the ancients reckoned months by the moon and years by the course of the sun.

**CHAPTER LVIII. On the eclipse of the sun.**

1. A solar eclipse [Note: [Col. 0176D] “Eclipse.” From the commentator on Aratus, near the end.] occurs whenever the moon, on the thirtieth day, reaches the same line along which the sun travels and, placing itself before it, darkens the sun. For the sun appears to us to fail when the moon’s sphere is set against it.

**CHAPTER LIX. On the eclipse of the moon.**

1. A lunar eclipse occurs whenever the moon enters the shadow of the earth. For it is thought not to possess its own light but to be illuminated by the sun; hence it suffers an obscuration if the shadow of the earth comes between it and the sun.

2. It undergoes this on the fifteenth day of the moon, for as long as it takes to leave the center and shadow of the intervening earth and to see the sun, or to be seen by the sun.

**CHAPTER LX. On the difference between stars, constellations, and heavenly bodies.**

1. *Stellae*, *sidera*, and *astra* differ from one another. A *stella* is any individual star. *Sidera* are made up of many stars, such as the Hyades and Pleiades.

2. *Astra* are large stellar formations, such as Orion and Boötes. But writers confuse these names, using *astra* for stars and *stellae* for constellations.

**CHAPTER LXI. On the light of the stars.**

1. The stars are said not to possess their own light but to be illuminated by the sun, just like the moon.

158 **CHAPTER LXII. On the position of the stars.**

1. The stars are immovable and, fixed in the heavens, are carried along in perpetual motion; they do not fall during the day but are obscured by the sun’s brightness.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Course of the Stars

[Col. 0177C] 1. The heavenly bodies either are carried along or move. Those are carried along which are fixed in the heavens and revolve with the heavens. Others move, such as the planets—that is, the wandering stars—which complete their wandering courses according to a definite order.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Varying Course of the Stars

1. Because the stars are carried through the various orbits of the heavenly planets [Note: [Col. 0177D] Through the various orbits of the heavenly planets. The Roman manuscript reads “of the heavenly poles,” from which Chacon made “of the parallels.” The remainder comes from the preface of Hyginus.], some, having risen more quickly, set later; others, having risen more slowly, reach the setting point sooner.

2. Others rise together but do not set at the same time; yet all return at their proper time to their own course.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Intervals Between the Stars

[Col. 0177D] 1. The stars are separated from one another and from the earth by different intervals. Therefore they appear to our eyes with unequal brightness, greater or less; for many are larger than those that we see conspicuously, but, being placed farther away, they appear small to us.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the Circular Number of the Stars

[Col. 0178A]

1. The circular number of the stars is the measure by which one is said to learn how much time each star takes to complete its circle, whether in length or in breadth.

2. For the moon is carried along to complete its circle in eight years, Mercury in twenty years, Lucifer in nine years, the sun in nineteen years, [Note: [Col. 0177D] Pyrois. Since all the books read *Vesper*, Chacon rightly advised exchanging the letters. For this is how Mars is called by everyone, including Isidore, chapter 70. Accordingly, Book V, chapter 30, must also be corrected. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, and Censorinus, chapter 13, *On the Birthday*.] Pyrois in fifteen, Phaethon in twelve, and Saturn in thirty. When these periods have been completed, they return to the completion of their circles at the same signs and degrees.

3. Certain heavenly bodies, hindered by the sun’s rays, become anomalous, or retrograde, or stationary, [Note: [Col. 0178D] “According to which,” and the poet likewise. Lucan, Book X, where we read not *aevi* (“of an age”) but *anni* (“of a year”).] as the poet also recalls when he says:

[Col. 0178B]

> The sun divides the periods of the year;  
>   
> By night it changes day, and with its powerful rays  
>   
> Forbids the stars to proceed, and by standing still  
>   
> Delays their wandering courses.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the Planetary Stars

1. Certain stars are called planets—that is, wanderers—because they travel throughout the whole world with varying motion. Hence, because they wander, they are called retrograde, or they become anomalous—that is, when they add and subtract small portions. But when they only subtract, they are called retrograde; they make a station when they stand still.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Precedence and Antegradation of the Stars

1. The precedence, or antegradation, of the stars occurs when a star appears to perform its customary motion and nevertheless advances somewhat beyond its customary position. [Col. 0178C]

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the Recession or Retrogradation of the Stars

1. The recession, or retrogradation, of the stars occurs when a star, while performing its motion, also appears to move backward.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the Stationary Position of the Stars

1. The stationary position of the stars is so called because, although a star is always moving, it nevertheless appears to stand still in certain places.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the Names of the Stars and the Reasons Why They Received Them

1. The sun is so called because it appears alone, all the heavenly bodies being obscured by its brilliance.

[Col. 0178D] 2. [Note: [Col. 0178D] The moon is called as though *Lucina*. Cicero: “The moon is named from shining, and is likewise Lucina.”] The moon is called *Luna*, as though *Lucina*, with the middle syllable removed. Virgil says of it: “Favor me, chaste Lucina.” It took its name by derivation from the light of the sun, [Note: [Col. 0178D] By derivation from the sun’s light. Cicero, in the *Dream*: “Among these, that which was the last in heaven and nearest to the earth shone with light borrowed from another.”] because it receives light from the sun and gives back what it has received.

3. The stars are called *stellae* from *stare*, “to stand,” because they always stand fixed in the heavens and do not fall. [Note: [Col. 0178D] As for what we see falling from heaven: Servius, *Georgics* I. What we see falling from heaven, the stars apparently gliding down, are not stars but little fires fallen from the ether. These arise when the wind, seeking the higher regions, carries ethereal fire with it; by its movement it imitates falling stars.] What we see falling from heaven [Col. 0179A] like stars slipping down are not stars, but little fires fallen from the ether. They arise when the wind, seeking the higher regions, draws ethereal fire along with it; by its movement it imitates falling stars. For stars cannot fall: they are immobile, as was stated above, and are carried fixed with the heavens.

4. [Note: [Col. 0179C] *Sidera*, as though “those that are contemplated.” Varro: “The heavenly bodies that settle upon something and thereby signify something on earth.”] The heavenly bodies are called *sidera* because sailors, by observing them, direct their course and take their bearings, so that deceptive waves or winds may not carry them elsewhere. Certain stars are called signs for this reason: sailors observe them while steering their oars, contemplating their arrangement and brilliance; by these things the future condition of the sky is revealed.

5. All people also observe them in order to foresee the qualities of the air through summer and winter and the temperate season of spring. For by their rising or setting, at fixed stations, they indicate the qualities of the seasons.

6. The first of the signs is the Bear, which is fixed on the pole and revolves with seven stars turning within it. Its name is Greek; in Latin it is called *Ursa*, “the Bear.” Because it turns in the form of a wagon, our people called it the *Septentrion*.

7. For *triones* properly means plow-oxen, so called because they wear down the earth, as though *teriones*. The nearness of the pole causes the Seven Oxen not to set, because they are located there.

8. It is called *Arctophylax* because it follows *Arctos*, that is, Helice the Bear. They also called it *Bootes*, because it clings to the wagon: it is a constellation visible to many observers, among whose stars is Arcturus. [Note: [Col. 0179C] The constellation Arcturus. From Servius, *Aeneid* I.]

9. Arcturus is the constellation situated behind the tail of the Great Bear, in the sign of Bootes. Hence it is called Arcturus, as though **ἄρκτου οὐρά** (*arktou oura*), “the Bear’s tail,” because it is placed at the breast of Bootes. [Col. 0179C] It rises in the autumn season.

162 10. Orion, the constellation, shines before the tracks of Taurus. Orion was so called from urine—that is, from the flooding of waters. For when it rises in winter, it troubles the sea and the lands with waters and storms.

11. [Note: [Col. 0179C] The Latins call this the *Jugula*. From the commentary on Aratus.] The Latins call it the *Jugula*, because it is armed, [Note: [Col. 0179C] With a sword. Aratus: **ξίφεος ἶφι πεποιθώς**, “trusting in the might of his sword.” Cicero: “And holding in his right hand a sword that does not fall from its light.” Varro, however, does not relate the etymology of *jugula* to the sword. He writes as follows: “Orion appears sooner; the head of this constellation is said to consist of three stars, beneath which are two bright stars called the shoulders. Between these what is seen is the throat, whence it is also called *Jugula*.”] like a sword, and is terrifying and exceedingly bright because of the light of its stars. When all its stars shine brightly, fair weather is foretold; when its array is obscured, a storm is perceived to be approaching.

12. [Note: [Col. 0179D] The Hyades. Servius, *Aeneid* I. The Hyades are called so **ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν** (*apo tou huein*), “from raining.” In Latin they are *succulae*, from *sucus*, “juice”; and *Georgics* I: the Hyades **ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑετοῦ** (*apo tou huetou*), “from rain.” It is therefore evident that the readings confused here derive from different sources. The commentator on Aratus likewise says: “The Greeks call them Hyades; our people, thinking that the stars received their name *succulae* from their resemblance to the word for ‘juice,’ called them *succidae* through ignorance. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: ‘The Greeks customarily call these the Hyades, from raining—for **ὕειν** means “to rain”; our people, through ignorance, call them *succulae*, as though they were named from swine, rather than from showers.’”] The Hyades are called **ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν** (*apo tou huein*), that is, “from juice” and from rains. For rain is called **ὑετός** (*huetos*) in Greek. By their rising they bring about rains; hence the Latins also called them *succulae*, because when they rise, signs of rain are displayed. Virgil says of them: “Arcturus and the rainy Hyades.” They are seven in number, on the forehead of Taurus, and rise in springtime.

13. [Note: [Col. 0179D] The Pleiades, from plurality. From the commentary on Aratus. For Servius, *Georgics* I, derives the name **ἀπὸ τοῦ πλέειν** (*apo tou plein*), that is, “from sailing,” because by their rising they show the beginning of the sailing season. [Col. 0180C]] The Pleiades are named from plurality, because the Greeks call plurality **πλειότης** (*pleiotēs*). They are seven stars before the knees of Taurus; six are visible, for one is hidden. The Latins call them the *Vergiliae*, from the indication of the season, which is spring, *ver*, when they rise. For by their setting they indicate winter, by their rising summer, and the beginning of the sailing season.

14. The Dog Star, also called Sirius, is in the middle of the center of heaven during the summer months. When the sun rises toward it and is joined to it, its heat is doubled, bodies are dissolved, and they are vaporized. Hence the days are called the dog days from this star, when purgations are also troublesome.

15. The star is called the Dog because it afflicts bodies with disease. [Note: [Col. 0180C] *Sirius*, on account of the whiteness of its flame. Those who read *Sirius* here—as it stands in nearly all the manuscripts—were misled in their reading by the similarity of sound between *canicula* and *candor*, “whiteness,” and failed to notice that **σειριᾶν** (*seirian*) means “to shine brightly” and “to gleam.” They also failed to observe that Isidore, having earlier said “the Dog Star, which is also Sirius,” now gives the explanation of both names. This is especially clear because the commentary on Aratus, from which this material is taken, reads as follows: “They think that the star Sirius was so called on account of the whiteness of its flame.” Finally, the variation among the manuscripts—for some have *sive*, others *aut* [others *vel*]—sufficiently supports the reading. Properly speaking, Sirius is, as Servius says, *Aeneid* X, “the star in the mouth of the Dog.”] Sirius is so called on account of the whiteness of its flame, which makes it appear to shine more brightly than the others. Therefore, so that it might be more easily recognized, they called it *Sirion*.

16. The comet is called a star because it pours forth from itself a mane of light. When this kind of heavenly body appears, it signifies either pestilence, famine, or wars.

17. [Note: [Col. 0180D] Comets are called *crinitae* in Latin, “long-haired.” Servius, *Aeneid* X: “In Latin comets are called *crinitae*, and the Stoics say that there are more than thirty-two of these stars; Avienus, who wrote the stories of Virgil in iambic verse, records their names and effects. But Isidore perhaps wrote “more than thirty,” overlooking the smaller number.] Comets are called *crinitae* in Latin because they scatter flames in the manner of hair. 18. Lucifer is so called because it brings more light than all the stars; it is one of the planets. It is also properly called *jubar*, “radiance,” because it pours forth manes of light. [Note: [Col. 0180D] Because it produces manes of light. From Servius, *Aeneid* IV. Thus, “at dawn by the gates,” from *jubar*, “radiance.”] The radiance of the sun, moon, and stars is also called *jubar*, because their rays extend in the form of a mane.

19. [Note: [Col. 0180D] Hesperus. Servius, *Aeneid* I and III.] Hesperus is the evening star in the west, which they report to have been named after Hesperus, king of Spain. It too is one of the five planetary stars, ushering in night and following the sun. It is said that when this star rises it makes Lucifer, and when it sets it makes Vesper. Statius speaks of it:

> … and one is lost at its alternate rising.

The words are from Servius, *Georgics* I, on the verse “whom the fire of heaven … Cyllen.”] For at times they are carried toward the south, at times toward the north, usually against the motion of the universe, and sometimes with the universe. [Note: [Col. 0181D] Their names in Greek. Whether this material is taken from Hyginus or Cicero, one thing is certain: for Isidore, Phaethon cannot be Saturn if he is to remain consistent with himself. For in chapter 65 he said that Phaethon completes his course in twelve years, but Saturn in thirty. Thus the learned man labored here in vain. See Plutarch, *On Doctrines* II, and Martianus Capella, *On the Planetary Orbs* VIII.] Their names are Greek: Phaethon, Phaenon, Pyrois, Hesperus, and Stilbon.

21. The Romans consecrated these under the names of their own gods, namely Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. [Note: [Col. 0182D] Deceived, and wishing to deceive. From Augustine, on Psalm 93.] For, deceived themselves and wishing to deceive others, in flattery of those who had granted them something according to the love of the world, they pointed out the stars in heaven, saying that one star belonged to Jupiter and another to Mercury; and an opinion of vanity was formed. The devil confirmed this erroneous opinion; Christ overturned it.

22. As for those things that the pagans themselves call signs, in which the image of animals is formed from the stars—such as the Bear, Aries, Taurus, Libra, and other figures of this kind—those who had observed the stars, counting them, fashioned the appearance of a body under the impulse of superstitious vanity, shaping both images and names from certain stories concerning their gods.

23. Thus they called Aries the first sign, to which, as to Libra, they assign the middle line of the world, because of Ammon; they therefore called it Jupiter, and those who make images of Aries attach horns to its head.

24. The pagans established this sign as the first among the signs because they say that in the month of March, which is the beginning of the year, the sun travels its course through that sign. [Note: [Col. 0182D] But also Taurus. From the commentary on Aratus.] They also place Taurus among the constellations, in honor of Jupiter, because, according to the myth, he was changed into a bull when he carried Europa away.

165 25. [Note: [Col. 0182D] Castor. From Hyginus, *Astronomy* II.] They also placed Castor and Pollux, after their death, among the best-known constellations; this sign they call Gemini.

26. They likewise called it Cancer because, when the sun reaches that sign in the month of June, it moves backward in the manner of a crab and makes the days shorter. For this animal has an uncertain forward direction and directs its steps in either direction, so that what was its front becomes its rear, and what was its rear becomes its front.

27. Hercules killed an enormous lion in Greece and, because of his courage, placed it among the twelve signs. When the sun reaches this sign, it gives the world excessive heat and produces the annual Etesian winds.

28. They also placed the sign of Virgo among the stars because, during the same days in which the sun runs through it, the earth, burned by the sun’s heat, produces nothing; for this is the season of the dog days.

29. They called Libra from the equality of that month, because on the eighth day before the Kalends of October the sun, passing through that sign, produces the equinox. Hence Lucan says:

> To the balance of equal Libra.

30. They also named Scorpio and Sagittarius from the lightning of that month. Sagittarius is a man deformed with the legs of a horse, to whom they attach an arrow and bow, so that the lightning of the month may be indicated by it. Hence it was called Sagittarius.

31. They fashioned the figure of Capricorn among the constellations because of the goat that nourished Jupiter. They formed its hind part in the shape of a fish [Note: [Col. 0182D] “For this reason they formed it.” Another reading: “they fashioned it.”] so as to signify the rains of that season, which that month commonly has toward its end.

[Col. 0182B] 32. Moreover, they called Aquarius and Pisces from the rains of the seasons, because in winter, when the sun turns through these signs, heavier rains are poured down. What astonishing madness among the pagans: they transferred not only fish but also rams, goats, bulls, bears, dogs, crabs, and scorpions into the heavens. They also placed the eagle and the swan among the stars of heaven in memory of Jupiter’s myths.

166 33. They likewise believed that Perseus and his wife Andromeda, after their deaths, were received into heaven, so that their images might be represented by stars; and they were not ashamed to call them by their names.

34. [Note: [Col. 0182D] The Charioteer, also Erichthonius. Hyginus, Book II.] They also placed the Charioteer, Erichthonius, among the stars of heaven because they had seen that he was the first to yoke four-horse chariots. They admired his ingenuity in approaching the example of the sun, and for this reason, after his death, placed his name among the constellations.

35. Thus Callisto, daughter of King Lycaon, after being embraced by Jupiter and, according to the myth, changed by Juno into the form of a bear—for “bear” is called **ἄρκτος** (*arktos*) in Greek—was, after her death, transferred by Jupiter, together with her son, into the northern stars; he called her the Bear and her son the Bear-Warden. [Note: [Col. 0182D] Jupiter together with his son. Jupiter is also used in the nominative case by the commentator on Aratus and by Petronius. The following Ennian verse concerning the gods is also well known:

> Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,  
>   
> Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.]

36. Thus the lyre was placed in heaven for Mercury. Likewise the Centaur, Chiron, was counted among the stars because he had raised Asclepius and Achilles.

37. But however people may name these things according to their various superstitions, they are nevertheless heavenly bodies that God created at the beginning of the world and ordained to distinguish the seasons by their fixed motion.

38. Therefore the observations of these signs, or horoscopes, and the other superstitious practices associated with knowledge of the stars—that is, with knowledge of fates—are without doubt contrary to our faith. [Col. 0183A] Christians should ignore them so completely that they should seem not even to have been written.

39. But some, captivated by the beauty and brilliance of the stars, have fallen, with blinded minds, into the errors of the stars, attempting through harmful calculations—what is called *mathesis*—to foresee the outcomes of events. This has been condemned by teachers not only of the Christian religion but also of the pagans: Plato, Aristotle, and others, moved by the truth of things, have condemned it with one accord, saying that such a belief produces confusion in human affairs rather than knowledge.

[Col. 0184A] 40. For if, as they say, the human race is driven by the necessity of birth toward various actions, why should the good deserve praise, or the wicked receive the punishment of the laws? Although they themselves were not devoted to heavenly wisdom, they nevertheless, by the testimony of truth, rightly endured the consequences of their errors.

41. This order of the seven secular disciplines was therefore carried by philosophers even up to the stars, so that it might draw minds entangled in secular wisdom away from earthly things and place them in contemplation of heavenly realities.

# BOOK FOUR. ON MEDICINE

## CHAPTER ONE. On Medicine

[Col. 0183B]

1. Medicine [Note: [Col. 0183D] Medicine. In this book he followed Caelius Aurelianus very closely.] is that which either preserves or restores the health of the body; its subject matter concerns diseases and wounds.

2. To medicine therefore belong not only the things provided by those who are properly called physicians, [Note: [Col. 0183D] Food, drink, and clothing. Other readings are “food, drink, covering, and clothing,” and “regimen and covering.” We think that *regimen* entered the text from the variation between *tegmen* and *tegumen*.] but also food, drink, and clothing; indeed, every defense and protection by which our body is preserved against external blows and accidents.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Its Name

1. The name of medicine [Note: [Col. 0183D] “The name of medicine from *modus*.” He seems not to have labored so much over the true derivation as to have sought an occasion in the word in order to introduce what follows. This is the sort of philosophical ingenuity that both Plato and Varro often employ.] is thought to have been derived from *modus*, “measure” or “moderation,” that is, from tempering, so that it may be applied not excessively but gradually. For in great quantity it distresses nature, whereas in moderation it delights it. Hence those who drink pigments and antidotes in sufficient quantity or continuously are afflicted. All immoderation brings not health but danger.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Inventors of Medicine

1. Among the Greeks, Apollo is said to have been the author and discoverer of the medical art. His son Asclepius enlarged it through reputation and practice.

2. But after Asclepius perished by a stroke of lightning, care in healing is said to have been forbidden, and the art declined together with its author. It remained hidden for almost five hundred years, until the time of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. Then Hippocrates brought it back to light, [Note: [Col. 0184D] “Brought it back to light.” Pliny, Book IX, chapter 1: “Then Hippocrates, born on the island of Cos, especially famous, strong, and dedicated to Asclepius, brought it back to light.”] born on the island of Cos, with Asclepius as his father. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “With Asclepius as his father.” He was perhaps the last author of the bloodline. For Hippocrates is said to have been the ninth or tenth descendant from Asclepius; he was the son of Heraclides and Phaenarete.]

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the Three Schools of Physicians

[Col. 0183D]

1. These three men accordingly founded three schools. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “These three men.” See Celsus’s preface to *On Medicine*.]

[Col. 0184B] The first, the Methodic school, was founded by Apollo; it pursues remedies and incantations. The second, the Empiric school, that is, the school based most fully on experience, [Note: [Col. 0184D] *Empirical*, that is, “most experienced.” With Pliny he could have said “experimental.”] was founded by Asclepius; it is based not on diagnostic signs but solely on experience. The third, the Logical school, that is, the rational school, was founded by Hippocrates.

2. For Hippocrates, having examined the qualities of ages, regions, and diseases, investigated the practice of the art rationally. The Empiric physicians pursue experience alone; the Logical physicians add reason to experience; the Methodic physicians observe neither the theory of elements, nor seasons, nor ages, nor causes, but only the substances of diseases.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Four Humors of the Body

170 1. Health is the integrity of the body and the balance [Col. 0184C] of nature, consisting of heat and moisture, which is blood. Hence health is so called, as though “the condition of the blood.”

2. Under the general term “diseases” all bodily afflictions are included. The ancients called disease *morbus* for this reason: by the very name they wished to indicate the force of death that arises from it. Between health and disease stands treatment; unless it corresponds to the disease, it does not lead to health.

3. All diseases arise from four humors: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm. As there are four elements, so there are four humors, and each humor imitates its element: blood imitates air, yellow bile fire, black bile earth, and phlegm water. There are therefore four humors, like the four elements, which preserve our bodies.

4. [Note: [Col. 0184D] *Sanguis*, “blood,” from the Greek etymology **ἀπὸ τοῦ ζᾶν** or **ζῆν**, “to live.”] The word *blood* received its name from a Greek etymology because it invigorates, supports, and lives. The Greeks called yellow bile *choler*, because it ends within the space of a single day; hence it was also called *cholera*, that is, “little bile.” [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185C] This means “an outpouring of bile.” Caelius, Book III, *Acute Diseases*, chapter 19: “Some say that the disease *cholera* was named from the flow of bile, as though it were a bile-flowing disease, for the Greeks call bile *cholē* and flow *rheō*.”] That is, an outpouring of bile; for the Greeks call bile **χολή** (*cholē*).

5. Black bile is so called because it consists of an abundance of bile mixed with the sediment of black blood. For the Greeks call black **μέλαν** (*melan*), while they call bile **χολή** (*cholē*).

6. [Note: [Col. 0185C] “Blood” in Latin. All the books have this, but it is likely that an attempt was also made to give a Latin etymology, which he repeats in Book XI, chapter 1.] Blood is called so in Latin because it is sweet; hence people in whom blood predominates are gentle and agreeable.

7. [Note: [Col. 0185D] “Phlegm,” because it is cold. By antiphrasis, **κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν** (*kat’ antíphrasin*). Caelius rightly says, Book III, *Traditions*, chapter 1: “Physicians have adopted many terms with contrary interpretations, such as bile, which the Greeks call *glyce*, ‘sweet,’ although it is extremely bitter. Otherwise, Pollux says that **φλέγμα** (*phlegma*) is called **καῦμα** (*kauma*) by Homer.” In the following chapter, Isidore himself calls *phlegmon* “inflammation.”] They called phlegm so because it is cold. For the Greeks call coldness **φλέγμα** (*phlegma*). From these four humors the healthy are governed, and by them the sick are harmed. For when any of them grows beyond the course of nature, they produce diseases.

[Col. 0185B] 8. From blood and bile arise acute diseases, which the Greeks call **ὀξέα** (*oxea*). From phlegm and black bile arise chronic diseases, which the Greeks call **χρόνια** (*chronia*).

## CHAPTER SIX. On Acute Diseases

1. *Oxea* is an acute disease that either passes quickly or kills more rapidly, such as pleurisy and phrenitis. For **ὀξύ** (*oxy*) means “acute” and “swift” in Greek. *Chronia* is a prolonged bodily disease that lingers for a long time, such as gout and consumption; for **χρόνος** (*chronos*) means “time” in Greek. Certain afflictions have received their names from their particular causes.

2. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Fever, from *fervor*, “heat.” Varro, as quoted by Nonius.] Fever is so called from heat, for it is an excess of warmth.

[Col. 0185C] 3. Phrenitis is so called either from impairment of the mind, because the Greeks call the mind **φρένες** (*phrenes*), or because the patient gnashes his teeth, for *frendere* means “to strike the teeth together.” [Note: [Col. 0185D] “It is a disturbance with agitation.” The Roman manuscript reads “a disturbance of the mind with agitation.”] It is a disturbance with agitation and delirium produced by the force of yellow bile.

4. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Cardiac disease. Caelius, Book II, *Acute Diseases*, chapter 34.] *Cardiace* takes its name from the heart, when someone is afflicted by fear or pain. For the Greeks call the heart **καρδία** (*kardia*). It is an affection of the heart accompanied by fearful dread.

5. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Lethargy. The same author, Book II, *Acute Diseases*, chapter 1: “The Greeks call *lēthē* forgetfulness and *argia* inactivity, which the force of the aforesaid disease imposes upon body and soul.” Chacon believed that these words were omitted not by Isidore, who was fond of such word derivations, but by the scribes.] Lethargy is named from sleep. It is an oppression [Col. 0186A] of the brain, accompanied by forgetfulness and continuous sleep, like that of a snoring person.

6. [Note: [Col. 0186C] Synanche. From the same book, Book III, chapter 1.] Synanche is so called from the holding back of the breath and suffocation. For the Greeks call holding back **συνάγχειν** (*synanchein*); those who suffer from this disease are suffocated by pain in the throat.

7. Phlegmon is heat of the stomach accompanied by swelling and pain. When it begins, restlessness and fever follow. Hence it is called **φλεγμονή** (*phlegmonē*), **ἀπὸ τοῦ φλέγειν** (*apo tou phlegein*), “from inflaming”; this is how it is felt, and from this it received its name.

8. Pleurisy is an acute pain in the side, accompanied by fever and bloody sputum. For the side is called **πλευρόν** (*pleuron*) in Greek, from which the pleuritic disease received its name.

9. Peripneumonia is a disease of the lung, accompanied by severe pain [Col. 0186B] and shortness of breath. For the Greeks call the lung **πνεύμων** (*pneumōn*), from which the disease received its name.

10. [Note: [Col. 0186C] Apoplexy. From chapter 5.] Apoplexy is a sudden outpouring of blood by which the suffocated die. It is called apoplexy because a sudden collapse results from a fatal stroke. For the Greeks call a stroke **ἀπόπληξις** (*apoplēxis*).

11. Spasm is, in Latin, a sudden contraction of parts or nerves, accompanied by severe pain. [Note: [Col. 0186C] They said that this disease was named from the heart, that is, that it arose from the heart, for according to Aristotle the nerves arise from the heart.] They said that this disease was named from the heart because the heart has the chief governing power of vitality in us. It occurs in two ways: either from fullness or from emptiness.

12. Tetanus [Note: [Col. 0186D] “A greater contraction of the nerves.” Caelius, Book III, chapter 6: “A slight tension of the larger nerves, which they call **τένοντες** (*tenontes*).” In our books, however, “a greater contraction” is read erroneously.] is a contraction of the larger nerves from the neck to the back.

13. [Note: [Col. 0186D] *Telum*. Serenus: “There is also a force of disease called *telum*, when sudden, insane fury has been driven in by a blow.”] *Telum* is pain in the side. Physicians gave it this name because the pain pierces the body as though with a sword. [Col. 0186C]

14. Ileus is pain of the intestines, from which the flanks also received their name. For in Greek **εἰλεῖν** (*eilein*) means “to wrap around,” because the intestines twist themselves together from pain. These pains are also called *torminous*, from the torment of the intestines.

15. [Note: [Col. 0186D] Hydrophobia. Caelius, Book III, chapter 9.] Hydrophobia means “fear of water.” For the Greeks call water **ὕδωρ** (*hydōr*) and fear **φόβος** (*phobos*); hence the Latins call this disease *lymphaticus*, “water-mad,” because of its fear of water. It arises either from the bite of a rabid dog, [Note: [Col. 0186D] Or from its foam. Since nearly all the books read “from the foam of the air,” Rodericus Fonteius, a most learned physician, advised reading “from its foam,” based on Aelian, Book IX of *On Animals*. His conjecture was confirmed by the Mejorada manuscript and by the Spanish-written Conches manuscript, which reads: “or from its foam fallen to the ground.” But since all the other books read “from the foam of the air,” and Caelius, whom Isidore clearly follows, says that some people fall into this disease from the odor of the breath alone when it is brought from a rabid dog, when poisonous air is drawn in and enters the vital parts, it seems likely to us that Isidore also mentioned the air. Augustine approved either “of the mouth” or “of the dog itself.”] or from its foam thrown onto the ground. [Col. 0187A] If a human being or animal touches it, the person or animal is either filled with madness or becomes rabid.

16. The carbuncle is so called because at its onset it is red like fire, and afterward black like an extinguished coal.

17. Pestilence is a contagion which, once it has seized one person, quickly spreads to many. It arises from corrupted air and, penetrating inward, takes hold in the viscera. Although it generally occurs through aerial powers, it does not occur at all without the will of Almighty God.

174 18. Pestilence is so called as though *pastulentia*, because it devours like a fire, [Note: [Col. 0187C] “And descends throughout the whole body.” From Virgil, *Aeneid* V.] and “the plague descends throughout the whole body.” It is also called *contagion*, from *contingere*, “to touch,” because whoever it touches, it contaminates.

19. [Note: [Col. 0187C] Also called the inguinal disease. See Paul the Deacon, on the new Italian pestilence before Justinian.] It is also called the inguinal disease, from a blow to the groin. It is likewise called *lues*, from defilement and mourning, [Note: [Col. 0187C] “Which is so acute.” This Gothicizing expression is frequent, perhaps belonging not to Isidore but to the scribes.] and it is so acute [Col. 0187B] that there is no interval of time in which either life may be hoped for or death expected; sudden weakness arrives together with death.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On Chronic Diseases

1. *Chronia* is a prolonged disease that lingers for a long time, such as gout and consumption; for **χρόνος** (*chronos*) means “time” in Greek.

2. [Note: [Col. 0187C] Cephalea. Caelius, Book I, *Chronic Diseases*, chapter 1: “Cephalea received its name from the bodily part that suffers the disease.”] Cephalea takes its name from its cause, for it is an affection of the head. The Greeks call the head **κεφαλή** (*kephalē*).

3. [Note: [Col. 0187C] Scotoma. From the manuscript, chapter 2.] Scotoma received its name from its effect, because it suddenly brings darkness to the eyes, accompanied by dizziness of the head. Vertigo occurs whenever a wind rises and sends the earth spinning around.

4. In the same way, in a person’s head the arteries and veins produce wind from dissolved moisture, and make a circular motion in the eyes; hence it is called vertigo.

5. Epilepsy took its name from the fact that, while seizing the mind, it also takes possession of the body. For the Greeks call seizure **ἐπιληψία** (*epilēpsia*). It arises from a melancholic humor whenever that humor overflows and turns toward the brain. This disease is also called the falling sickness, because when the patient falls, he suffers spasms.

6. The common people also call such sufferers lunatics, because madness accompanies them according to the course of the moon. [Note: [Col. 0187C] “Because madness accompanies them according to the course of the moon.” Another reading: “Because, during the moon’s course, the snares of demons accompany them.” Both readings may be retained, so that the first indicates the phases of the moon, while the second indicates demonic possession.] It is also called possession by spirits. It is likewise the comitial disease, the same as the greater disease, [Note: [Col. 0187C] “And divine.” Rather, “sacred”; Caelius Aurelianus, *Chronic Diseases* I, chapter 4, gives many explanations for this designation. In most books, however, *diutinus*, “long-lasting,” is read instead of *divinus*, “divine.” Unless both words are applied to the disease that follows, namely mania. For that disease is called both “divine” and “long-lasting.” As Caelius says, it is a very slow disease.] and also the divine disease, by which those who suffer the falling sickness are seized. Its force is so great that a healthy person collapses and foams at the mouth.

7. It is called “comitial” because among the Gentiles, if it happened to someone on the day of the assembly, the assembly was dismissed. [Col. 0188B] Now, among the Romans, the solemn day of the assembly was the third day before the Kalends of January. [Note: [Col. 0187D] At Rome the day of the assembly was solemnly observed on the third day before the Kalends of January. All the manuscripts have “on the Kalends of January.” Chacon deleted this as foreign and absurd, since assemblies were not held on the Kalends of January, which was not a day on which assemblies could be held but a fastus day. A. Augustinus interpreted “on the Kalends of January” as meaning the day before those Kalends on which the magistrates began their terms. Anton. Covarruvias observed that the word had arisen from the abbreviation III. He also held that the third day before the Kalends of January was the same as the third day of January, on which day—as Caius says in *If One Has Erred*, Digest, *On the Meaning of Words*—vows were undertaken for the emperor’s safety. It was also the most celebrated gathering of the entire Roman people, maintained from the time of Numa onward. Plutarch likewise said that Cicero was born on the third day of the Kalends, whereas Cicero himself calls it the third day before the Nones. This day was called both the day of the proclamation of vows and the solemn day of the emperors, and simply “the vows and solemnities.” See Suetonius, *Augustus*; Capitolinus, *Pertinax*; Tacitus, *Annals* IV and XV; and Tertullian, *On the Crown*. That “assembly” did not refer only to those gatherings held for the election of magistrates, but could also be understood as a gathering of the people generally, is evident.]

8. Mania is so called from insanity or frenzy. [Note: [Col. 0188C] “For the antiquity of the Greeks.” From the same book of Caelius, chapter 5; but the materials here are confused and disordered.] For the ancient Greeks called frenzy *mantikē* (μαντική), “divination,” [Note: [Col. 0188C] Or from emptiness, which the Greeks call *mania* (μανία). Thus Eustathius interprets *manon* and *mania* in his commentary on the *Iliad*, book ψ, explaining the word *parēoros*. Therefore, in Aurelianus also, “emptiness” might seem preferable to “inequity,” since he adds: “which they call mania, either because it relaxes the spirit or mind beyond measure—for they call *manon* what is loosened or soft.” The Spanish translation likewise has: “Or it is called from emptiness; that is, from emptying, or from an empty thing, which the Greeks call *manie*.” Add also what Isidore says, book V, chapter 28: “Others,” he says, “think that *mane* is so called from the air, because *manus*, that is, thin or rare, is transparent.” But in the earlier statement that the Greek *manein* means “to prophesy,” we followed the Gothic books.] whether from emptiness, which the Greeks called *mania* (μανία), or from divination, since “to divine” is said in Greek as *manein* (μανεῖν).

9. Melancholy is so called from black bile: for the Greeks call black *melan* (μέλαν), while they call bile *cholē* (χολή). Epilepsy occurs in the imagination, melancholy in the reasoning faculty, and mania in the memory.

10. [Note: [Col. 0188D] “Types are cold fevers.” We removed from here the material “which are improperly named from a plant that grows in water,” although it occurred in all the books; for there is no doubt that it was brought here without reason from book XVII. As for the wording “form and condition,” which we printed from the books, Chacon preferred “statute,” since among Justinian’s works a law or pragmatic ordinance is called *typos* (τύπος), *Novels* 165 and 166, and Novel VII is entitled *typos pragmatikos* (τύπος πραγματικός), “pragmatic form.” These same laws are also called *formae* in Latin, book III, *We Decree*, *On Sacred Churches*. Thus, because they arise at fixed times and follow the law that periodic fevers observe, they are called *typoi*.] Types are cold fevers, because *typos* (τύπος) in Latin means “form” and “condition”; for it is the recurrence of attacks or remissions at fixed intervals of time.

11. *Rheuma* is Greek; in Latin it is called “eruption” or “flow.” [Col. 0189A] Catarrh is a continuous flow of *rheuma* from the nostrils; when it reaches the throat it is called *branchos* (βράγχος), and when it reaches the chest or lungs it is called *ptysis* (πτύσις).

12. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Coryza . . . whenever the influx.” From Caelius, book II, chapter 7.] Coryza occurs whenever an influx from the head reaches the bones [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Into the bones of the nose.” The Roman manuscript has “into the mouth of the nose.”] of the nose and causes an irritation [Note: [Col. 0189D] “And an irritation.” Thus all the Gothic manuscripts; all the others have “suffocation.” The error easily arose from the initial digamma.] accompanied by sneezing; hence it also received the name *coryza*.

13. Branchos is suffocation of the throat caused by cold humors. For the Greeks call the throat *branchos* (βράγχος), around which the *fauces* are situated; these we incorrectly call *branchiae*.

14. Hoarseness is the loss of the voice. It is also called *arteriasis*, because injury to the arteries makes the voice hoarse and constricted. *Suspirium* (“shortness of breath”) derives its name from the difficulty of inhalation, which the Greeks call *dyspnoia* (δύσπνοια), that is, suffocation.

15. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Peripneumonia.” He placed this in the preceding chapter among the acute diseases, perhaps following others; here he follows Caelius, who counts it among the chronic diseases.] Peripneumonia takes its name from the lungs. It is a swelling of the lung, with an outpouring of bloody foam.

16. Haemoptysis is the discharge of blood through the mouth, and from this it also takes its name, since *haima* (αἷμα) means “blood.”

17. Phthisis is ulceration and swelling in the lungs, which generally occurs more easily in the young. *Phthisis* (φθίσις), however, is so called among the Greeks because it is a wasting away of the entire body.

18. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Cough,” in Greek. Namely *bēx* (βήξ), as though from *byx*, or *bissos*, or *bythos*.] Cough is called in Greek from height, because it comes from the depths of the chest; its opposite is the cough higher up in the throat, where the uvula drips.

19. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Apostema,” from collection. Recent writers call the condition an accumulation, which Celsus calls an abscess.] *Apostema* takes its name from an accumulation, for the Greeks call accumulations *apostemata*.

20. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Empyema.” Caelius, *Chronic Diseases*, book II, chapter 14: “Likewise, an empyematic disease, because purulent sputum from an internal collection is expelled by a little cough.”] Empyema is an abscess internally, whether in the side or in the stomach, accompanied by pain, fevers, coughing, abundant sputum, and pus.

21. Hepatic disease takes its name from an affection of the liver, for the Greeks call the liver *hēpar* (ἧπαρ).

22. Lienosis takes its name from the spleen. The Greeks call the spleen *splēn* (σπλήν).

23. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Dropsy.” Caelius, book III, chapter 8.] Dropsy takes its name from the watery humor of the skin, for the Greeks called water *hydōr* (ὕδωρ). It is a subcutaneous humor accompanied by swollen inflation and foul-smelling breath.

24. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Nephritis,” which is also *diabetes*.] Nephritis takes its name from weakness of the kidneys, for the Greeks call the kidneys *nephroi* (νεφροί).

25. [Note: [Col. 0189D] “Paralysis, so called from the weight of the body.” Thus all the books; nor is there anyone lacking who defends this reading, since *pensare* means “to weigh” or “to balance.” Paralytic persons therefore struggle under their own weight, since they move their limbs with difficulty, as Seneca says. It occurred to us to suspect that the error arose from scribal abbreviations. The original may have been: “a dissolution of the body impeding action,” that is, “a dissolution of the body hindering movement.”] Paralysis is so called from the body’s burden, [Col. 0190A] caused by severe chilling, either throughout the body or in a part of it.

26. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Cachexia.” Caelius, book III, chapter 6.] Cachexia takes its name from the body’s bad condition; for the Greeks called a bad affliction *kakhexia* (καχεξία). This disease arises from the patient’s lack of moderation, from poor treatment by the physician, or from a slow recovery after illness.

27. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Atrophy.” The same author, book II, chapter 14, and book III, chapter 7.] Atrophy takes its name from the diminution of the body; for the Greeks call the cessation of nourishment *atrophia* (ἀτροφία). It is wasting of the body arising from hidden causes that gradually gain strength.

28. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Sarcia.” Thus all the books. Caelius has *polysarcia*.] Sarcia is an excessive growth of flesh by which bodies are fattened beyond measure; for the Greeks call flesh *sarka* (σάρκα).

29. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Sciatica.” The same author, book V, chapter 1.] Sciatica is so called from the part of the body that it afflicts. [Col. 0190B] For the Greeks call the bones of the vertebrae, whose upper end terminates at the beginning of the hips, *ischia* (ἰσχία). It arises from phlegm whenever it descends into the straight bones, where it produces an adhesion.

30. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Gout.” The same place, chapter 2.] The Greeks say that *podagra* was named from the retention of the feet, or from its savage pain, since anything harsh we improperly call “wild.”

31. Arthritic disease takes its name from an affection of the joints.

32. A calculus is a stone that forms in the bladder, and from this it takes its name. It is produced from phlegmatic matter.

33. Strangury is so called because it constricts through difficulty in urination.

34. Satyriasis is a constant desire for sexual intercourse accompanied by erection of the genitals; the disease is named from the satyrs.

35. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Diarrhea.” Caelius counts diarrhea and satyriasis among the acute diseases.] Diarrhea is a continuous discharge from the bowels without vomiting.

36. Dysentery is a division of continuity, that is, ulceration of the intestine: *dys* (δύς) means “division,” and *entera* (ἔντερα) means “intestines.” [Note: [Col. 0190D] “It occurs when a preceding flow . . .” These words are Caelius’s, book IV, chapter 6.] It occurs after a preceding discharge, which the Greeks call *diarroia* (διάρροια).

37. [Note: [Col. 0190D] “Through smooth intestines.” Another reading: “through soft intestines.”] Lientery is so called because it causes food to slip through as though through smooth intestines, with nothing obstructing it.

38. Colic takes its name from the intestine that the Greeks call *kōlon* (κῶλον).

39. *Ragades* [Al. *Ragadiae*] are so called because they are cracks gathered among the wrinkles around the opening. These are also called hemorrhoids from the flow of blood. For the Greeks call blood *haima* (αἷμα).

## CHAPTER VIII. Diseases That Appear on the Surface of the Body

1. Alopecia is a circumscribed loss of hair, with tawny hairs [Note: [Col. 0191C] “With tawny hairs having the quality of bronze.” Another reading: “of bronze.” Chacon rejected all this as extraneous.] having the quality of bronze. It is called by this name because of its resemblance to the little fox, which the Greeks call *alōpēx* (ἀλώπηξ).

2. Parotid swellings are hardenings or accumulations that arise from fevers or some other cause near the ears; hence they are called *parōtides* (παρωτίδες), for the Greeks call the ears *ōta* (ὦτα).

3. Lentigo consists of small traces of spots formed into a round shape and is named from its resemblance to a lentil.

4. [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Erysipelas.” Some think it is called *erisēpelas* (ἐρισήπελας) from *eri*, meaning “to increase,” and *sypesthai*, “to rot.”] Erysipelas is what the Latins call “sacred fire,” that is, “accursed” by antiphrasis. For the skin reddens on its surface with a fiery redness [Note: [Col. 0191D] “The skin reddens.” Another reading: “the skins redden.”] [Col. 0191B] Then, as the redness moves, it attacks the neighboring areas as if from fire, so that fever is also aroused.

5. Serpedo is redness of the skin accompanied by raised pustules. It takes its name from *serpere*, “to creep,” because it creeps through the limbs.

6. Impetigo is a dry scab, protruding from the body, with roughness and a rounded shape. The common people call it *sarna*.

7. Pruritus is so called from burning and scorching.

8. Nyctalopia is a disease in which sight is denied during the day while the eyes are open, but is restored when the darkness of night arrives—or, as many hold, the reverse occurs: sight is restored by day and denied at night.

9. [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Warts are one thing, satyriasis another.” The old edition has *phthiriasis*; all the manuscripts have *satyriasis*. Both diseases differ greatly from the one consisting of warts. Although the name *satyriasis* also denotes other kinds of disease besides the one discussed in the preceding chapter. If we prefer *phthites* or *phthiriasis*, Eustathius does so in his commentary on the *Iliad*, book β, at the words “those who possess Miletus”: “Phtheiron, the mountain of innumerable leaves. *Phtheir*,” he says, “means the pine and the cones of the pine.” If this is correct, there is a strong resemblance between *phthersi*, or, as Didymus says, *phtheirai*, and warts. If anyone prefers *satyriasis*, let him take the Gothic manuscripts as his authorities.] Warts are one thing and satyriasis another. Warts occur singly, whereas in satyriasis one is larger and several others are found around it.

10. Scabies and leprosy are both diseases consisting of roughness of the skin with itching and scaling; but scabies is slight roughness and scaling. Hence it received its name because it sheds what resembles refuse. For *scabies* is as though from *squammies*, “scales.”

11. [Note: [Col. 0191D] “Resembling a scale,” that is, a flake. Cassius Felix: “A scaly, bark-like form of scabies displaying on itself scales called *lepides* in Greek; hence it received its name from the Greek *lepra*.” Scribonius Largus, chapter 133: “A scale of bronze, which the Greeks call *lepis*.”] Leprosy, however, is a roughness of the skin resembling a scaly flake, and from this it takes its name. Its color sometimes turns black, sometimes white, and sometimes red. Leprosy is recognized on the human body when a different color appears irregularly among healthy areas of skin, or when it spreads everywhere so that it makes all the skin one color, although an unnatural one.

12. Elephantiasis is named from its resemblance to the elephant, whose naturally hard and rough hide gave the disease its name among human beings, because it makes the surface of the body resemble an elephant’s skin; or because it is a huge disease, like the animal itself from which its name is derived.

13. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Icterus . . . from the name of a certain animal.” Galen derives it from *iktis*, a wild weasel; Pliny from *icterus*, a little bird. The Glossary: *aurugo*, *ikteris* (ἰκτερίς). Jerome, on Amos IV: “That is, jaundice”; all translated *icteron*.] Icterus is called in Greek from the name of a certain animal whose color is that of bile. The Latins call this disease “the rainbow disease,” from its resemblance to the heavenly rainbow. Varro says that it is called *aurugo* from the color of gold. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Royal.” Pliny, book XXII, chapter 4: “Varro records that the arched disease was surnamed royal because it is cured with mulsum.”] They think that the royal disease was so called because it is more easily cured by good wine and royal foods.

14. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Cancer.” This passage was taken from Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8; but cancer ought rather to be called an ulcer than a wound, if shortly afterward he truly distinguishes a wound from an ulcer.] Cancer is a wound named from its resemblance to a sea animal which, as physicians say, cannot be healed by any medicines. Therefore, the limb in which it arises is sometimes cut away from the body so that the patient may live somewhat longer, although death will come from it eventually, however slowly.

15. A furuncle is a swelling rising to a point. It is so called because it burns, as though from *fervunculus*, “little fever.” Hence in Greek it is also called *anthrax* (ἄνθραξ), because it is fiery.

16. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Hordeolum . . . from being narrowed on both sides.” The books of A. Augustinus have “narrowed on both sides,” that is, as he himself interpreted it, narrow and almost enclosed or surrounded.] A stye is a very small, purulent collection situated among the hairs of the eyelids, broad in the middle and narrowed at both ends, resembling a grain of barley; hence it takes its name.

17. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Oscedo.” Two diseases seem to have been confused, *oscedo* and what the Greeks call *aphthae* (ἄφθαι). Some therefore distinguished them as follows: *Oscedo* is so called from the weakness of those who yawn; aphthae are the ulcers by which the mouths of infants are affected.] Oscedo is the ulceration of infants’ mouths, so called from the weakness of those who yawn.

18. Frenula are ulcers around the corners of the mouth, resembling those produced in draft animals by the harshness of their bridles.

19. [Col. 0192C] An ulcer is putrefaction itself; a wound is what is made by iron, as though by force. An ulcer is also so called because it smells, as though from *olcus*.

20. A pustule is a swelling on the surface of the body, resembling an accumulation.

21. [Note: [Col. 0192D] “Papula,” perhaps *pupula*. Another reading: “as if a little nipple.” The ancients called woolen dolls *pupulae*.] A papule is a very small elevation of the skin, circumscribed and accompanied by redness; hence it is called *papula*, as though from *pupula*. *Sirimpio* . . . [lacuna].

22. Sanies is so called because it arises from blood: when the heat of a wound is aroused, blood is changed into sanies. For sanies does not form in just any place, but only where blood has arrived, since nothing that putrefies can putrefy unless it is hot and moist, as blood is. [Col. 0193A] [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Sanies and *tabes*.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII, at the words “a kind of torture.”] Sanies and *tabes* differ from each other. To flow as sanies is characteristic of the living; *tabes* of the dead.

23. A scar is the covering over of a wound, preserving the natural color of the parts. It is so called because it covers wounds and obscures them.

## CHAPTER IX. Remedies and Medicines

1. Medical treatment must not be despised. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “For we also remember Isaiah.” These words are Tertullian’s, in *On the Military Crown*.] For we also remember that Isaiah prescribed something medicinal for the sick Hezekiah, and that the apostle Paul said that a little wine was beneficial to Timothy.

2. The treatment of diseases consists of three kinds: pharmacy, which the Latins call *medicamina*, “medicines”; surgery, which the Latins call the work of the hands, [Col. 0193B] for the Greeks call the hand *cheir* (χείρ); and diet, which the Latins call a rule, since it is the observance of law and life.

3. There are three kinds of all treatments: the first is dietary, the second pharmaceutical, and the third surgical. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Diet is the observance of law and life.” Why he says “of law” is not immediately obvious. Earlier writers observed that in Demosthenes *diaitan epitrepsai* (δίαιταν ἐπιτρέψαι) and in Thucydides *diaitōmai* (διαιτῶμαι) mean the same as *politeuomai* (πολιτεύομαι), “to conduct one’s life as a citizen.”] Diet is the observance of law and life. Pharmacy is the treatment with medicines. Surgery is incision with instruments, for with iron those things are cut away that have not responded to the healing power of medicines.

4. The earliest medicine consisted only of herbs and juices. For such was the beginning of the practice of healing; afterward came iron and the other medicines.

5. Every treatment is applied either from contraries or from similars. From contraries, as cold for hot or dry for moist; likewise, pride in a human being cannot be healed unless it is healed by humility.
