6. From similars, as when a round bandage is applied to a round wound or an elongated one to an elongated wound. For the ligature itself is not the same for all limbs and wounds; rather, like is fitted to like. These two methods also signify their own aids by their names.

7. For *antidote* in Greek is said in Latin to mean “given against,” since contraries are cured by contraries according to the method of medicine. Conversely, treatment from a similar is represented by *pikra* (πικρά), which means “bitter,” because its taste is bitter. It received its name from correspondence, since bitterness is usually dispelled by the bitterness of the disease.

8. All medicines derive their names from their particular causes. *Hiera* is so called as if “divine.” *Arteriaca* are so called because they are suitable for the passage of the throat and soothe swellings of the throat and arteries. *Theriaca* is an antidote against serpents, by which poisons are driven out, so that plague may be dissolved by plague. [Col. 0194A] *Cathartica* are called in Greek and in Latin “purgatives.”

9. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Catapotia.” Scribonius Largus, chapter 87: “A *catapotium*, that is, a medicine which is not dissolved but swallowed as it is.”] *Catapotia* are so called because a small quantity is drunk or swallowed. *Diamoron* takes its name from the juice of the mulberry, from which it is prepared; similarly *diacodion*, because it is made *ek tēs kōdeias* (ἐκ τῆς κωδείας), that is, “from the poppy”; and *diaspermaton*, because it is composed from seeds.

10. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Electuary.” Caelius calls it this in *Acute Diseases*, book III, chapter 4; Pliny calls it *ecligma*, books XX, chapters 14 and 22; Celsus calls it this because it melts under the tongue.] An electuary is so called because it is swallowed in a soft form. A troche is so called because it is shaped like a little wheel, for *trochos* (τροχός) means “wheel” in Greek. [Note: [Col. 0193D] “Collyria.” *Apo tou kōlyein ton houn* (ἀπὸ τοῦ κωλύειν τὸν ῥοῦν), that is, “from preventing the flow.”] Collyria, in Latin, are so called because they cleanse disorders of the eyes. An epitheme is so called because it is placed on top after the preceding aids.

11. A cataplasm is so called because it is merely an application. An emplastrum is so called because it is applied. A malagma is so called because it is softened and kneaded without fire. An enema is called in Greek and in Latin a relaxation. [Col. 0194B] [Note: [Col. 0194D] “Pessaries.” Celsus, book V, chapter 21: “The Greeks call the things they place in women *pessoi* (πεσσοί).” Hence *pessarium* is a diminutive form. Isidore, however, seems to have thought that pessaries were so called because they go downward.] Pessaries are so called because they are inserted inside.

12. A certain Greek named Chiron invented the medicine of beasts of burden; hence he is depicted as half man and half horse. He was called Chiron from *cheirizein* (χειρίζειν), “to operate with the hands,” because he was a surgeon.

13. Physicians call certain days critical; I suppose they received this name from the judgment of the illness, because they seem to judge a person and, by their sentence, either punish or release him.

## CHAPTER X. Medical Books

1. An aphorism is a brief statement setting down a complete meaning concerning the matter proposed.

2. Prognostics is the foreseeing of illnesses, so called from “knowing beforehand.” For a physician must recognize the past, know the present, and foresee the future.

3. [Note: [Col. 0194D] “Dynamidia.” Later physicians gave this name to Galen’s books *On Simple Medicines*, and an old translation of those books still preserves the name.] *Dynamidia* is the power of herbs, that is, their force and capacity. For in the treatment of herbs the force itself is called *dynamis* (δύναμις). Hence the work in which their medicinal properties are written is called *Dynamidia*.

4. A botanical work is called an herbarium because herbs are described there.

## CHAPTER XI. Physicians’ Instruments

1. An enchiridion is so called because it is held in the hand while containing many instruments. For the Greeks call the hand *cheir* (χείρ).

2. A phlebotome is named from incision. For incision is called *tomē* (τομή) in Greek.

3. [Note: [Col. 0194D] “Simile . . . Angistrum . . . Spatomele.” Interpretations of these words are lacking. *Smilē* (σμίλη) is used for cleaning wounds. Hence Aristophanes calls what is scraped away *smileuma* in *The Frogs*. From it also comes *smilārion*, a diminutive. Physicians now call the *angistrum* a hook. *Spatomele* is used for examining ulcers; Pollux also mentions *miles* for the same purpose.] Simile . . . Angistrum . . . Spatomele . . .

4. [Note: [Col. 0195C] “Guva.” Thus the better manuscripts. Others, with the old printed edition, have *guviae*. Learned men defend both readings. Those who prefer *guvia* say that it arose from a misreading of the Greek word *guvia*. In Greek, *sykia* or *sikia* means “gourd”; I and U are often exchanged, one taking the place of the other. Chacon, who preferred *guva*, thought that it arose from *cufa*, with G replacing C and V replacing the digamma F. For the Greeks call the light gourds used without scarification *kouphas*, and not only is U frequently substituted for F in Gothic books, but in book XIX, chapter 19, the ancient Oenian manuscript has *gufia*, whereas all the others have *guvia*, the instrument of smiths. Caelius often discusses *cuphae*, as in book IV, chapter 7: “Light gourds are to be applied, which the Greeks call *cuphae*”; and chapter 8: “the application of a light gourd, which the Greeks call a *cupha*.” He also held that Isidore, who thought that all gourds were called *cuphae* by the Greeks, had been misled by Caelius’s reading.] A *guva*, which the Latins call a gourd from its resemblance to one, [Note: [Col. 0195D] “From the breath, a cupping vessel.” The satirist says:

> For a long time this head has been seeking a gourd cupping-vessel.

And Theodorus Priscianus, book II, chapter 6: “These cupping gourds must be applied.” Celsus calls them medicinal gourds.] is called a cupping vessel because of the suction. [Col. 0195A] Finally, when filled with air through a little flame and then placed upon the cut body, it draws to the surface whatever is inflamed beneath the skin or deeper within, whether humor or blood. Clyster . . .

5. A mortar is named from pounding seeds, that is, grinding them. Hence pigments also are so called, because they are worked in a mortar and with a pestle, as though *pilagmenta*. A mortar is a hollow vessel suited to the use of physicians, in which, properly speaking, gruels are made and drugs are crushed.

6. Varro reports that a certain Pilumnus existed in Italy, [Note: [Col. 0195D] “He presided over the pounding of the fields.” Thus all the manuscripts. The Spanish translator, however, read “herbs”: “Varro says that Pilumnus was a man in Italy who ground herbs and kneaded them better than all the others.” But since Servius says, at the beginning of book IX, that he presided over the pounding of grain, we have retained *fields* from the books, with *fields* standing for grain, as in Horace: [Col. 0196C] etc.] who presided over the pounding of the fields; hence the words *pilumni* and *pistores*. From him, therefore, the pestle and mortar were invented, with which grain is pounded, and they were named from him. A pestle is the instrument with which whatever is placed in the mortar is crushed.

7. A mortar is so called because seeds already reduced to powder and, as it were, dead are stored in it.

8. [Note: [Col. 0196C] “Coticula.” Another reading: *citicula*. A. Augustinus has *cotyla*. Pliny, book XXXI, chapter 9, concerning salt: “For this purpose Spanish salt is selected, and against dimness of the eyes it is ground with milk on *cotylae*.”] A *coticula* is a stone on which collyria are rubbed and dissolved; it must be smooth. For a rough one causes the collyrium to be broken rather than dissolved.

## CHAPTER XII. Fragrances and Ointments

1. Odor is so called from the air.

2. *Thymiama* is a Greek word for something fragrant. For *thymus* is the name of a flower that gives off a scent, concerning which Virgil writes:

> And the fragrant honeycombs smell of thyme.

3. Incense is so called because it is consumed by fire while it is offered.

4. *Tetraidos* are elongated forms of incense made from four drugs. For four is *tettares* (τέτταρες) in Greek, while form is called *eidos* (εἶδος).

5. *Stacte* is incense that flows from pressure; it is named by the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0196C] *Apo tou stazein* (ἀπὸ τοῦ στάζειν). An old manuscript has *para to stazein stakēn*, that is, “because it is crushed.” Another has “that is, excellent.”] *apo tou stazein* (ἀπὸ τοῦ στάζειν), meaning “to flow” or “to drip.”

6. Myrobalanum is so called because it is made from a fragrant acorn, concerning which Horace writes:

> And pressed balsam upon your hair.

Oil is pure and mixed with nothing else. An ointment, however, is anything made from ordinary oil and enriched by the admixture of other substances, taking on a pleasant fragrance and retaining its scent for a longer time.

7. Some ointments are named from places, such as *Telinum*, of which Julius Caesar makes mention, saying:

> And we anoint the body with sweet Telinian ointment.

[Note: [Col. 0196C] “Telinum,” concerning which Fulvius Ursinus reports the following from Julius Caesar’s books *On Analogy*. A. Augustinus thought that the words were not those of Julius Caesar the dictator but of Strabo the tragedian, whom Cicero mentions in *Brutus* and Festus under *Prophets*. The fact that the verse itself is almost complete persuades us of this. It may originally have been complete: “And we anoint the body with sweet Telinian ointment.” Tertullian also mentions Telinum in *On the Pallium*, as does Athenaeus, book XV, chapter 15.] This was prepared on the island of Telos, one of the Cyclades.

8. [Col. 0196B] Some are named from their inventors, such as *Amaracinum*. [Note: [Col. 0196D] “For some report that a certain royal boy . . .” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I.] For some report that a certain royal boy named Amaracus, carrying several kinds of ointment, happened to fall, and that a stronger fragrance was produced by their mixture. Hence the finest ointments are now called Amaracine; they are made from flowers.

9. Others are named from the quality of their material, such as rose ointment from the rose and Cyprine ointment from the flower of Cyprus; hence they also reproduce the scent of their particular materials.

10. Some of these are simple ointments, consisting of only one substance, and therefore retaining the fragrance of their own name, such as *Anethinum*, which is made solely from oil and dill. Compound ointments, however, are made from several substances mixed together, and therefore do not retain the fragrance of their name, since the substances added to them predominate and produce an uncertain scent. [Note: [Col. 0196D] “As in *cerotum chalasticum*.” Chacon read these words together from Marcellus, *On Medicines*, chapter 35: “The notable Olympic chalastic wax preparation”; and chapter 25: “The preparation of the chalastic wax.” In Priscianus, book II, when mention is made of a chalastic fomentation, poultice, remedy, water, and clyster, in all these expressions *chalasticus* has the force of “loosening.” *Martiatum*, however, is said to have been named from its inventor, as was *Marcelianum*, concerning which Martial writes:

> Whose greasy hair smells all over of Marcelian ointment,

> And whose arms shine, rubbed smooth after the hair has been plucked.]

11. Cerotum . . . Chalasticum . . . [Col. 0196C] Martiatum . . .

## CHAPTER XIII. The Origin of Medicine

1. Some ask why, among the other liberal disciplines,

> Do not inquire, excellent Quintus, whether my estate  
> Feeds its master with fields or enriches him with olives,

the art of medicine is not included. The reason is that those disciplines contain particular causes, whereas medicine contains the causes of everything. For a physician is also commanded to know grammar, so that he may understand or explain what he reads.

2. Likewise, he must know rhetoric, so that he may define what he treats with truthful arguments. He must also know dialectic, in order to investigate and treat the causes of diseases by applying reason; and arithmetic, because of the number of hours in attacks and the periods of days.

3. He must similarly know geometry, because of the qualities of regions and the situations of places, so that he may teach what one ought to observe. Music, moreover, will not be unknown to him, for many things are recorded as having been accomplished through this discipline in sick persons, as we read concerning David, who rescued Saul from an unclean spirit through the art of melody. The physician Asclepiades likewise restored a certain frenzied man to his former health through symphony.

4. Finally, he will know astronomy, through which he may contemplate the order of the stars and the change of the seasons; for, as a certain physician says, our bodies also change together with the qualities of the stars.

5. Hence medicine is called a second philosophy. Each discipline claims the whole human being for itself. For just as the soul is healed through philosophy, so the body is healed through medicine.

# BOOK FIVE. ON LAWS AND TIMES

## CHAPTER ONE. The Authors of Laws

1. Moses [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Moses to the Hebrew people.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] was the first of all to explain divine laws to the Hebrew people in the sacred Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0197C] “King Phoroneus to the Greeks.” He was the second king of the Argives, as Eusebius relates in the same place.] King Phoroneus was the first to establish laws and judicial ordinances for the Greeks.

2. [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Mercurius Trismegistus.” Lactantius, book I, chapter 16.] Mercurius Trismegistus was the first to transmit laws to the Egyptians. [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Solon was the first.” Draco had written laws before Solon, but the Athenian people were accustomed to credit Solon alone with the beginnings of their constitution.] Solon was the first to give laws to the Athenians. [Note: [Col. 0197C] “Lycurgus.” Augustine, *City of God* II, chapter 16: “Although Lycurgus pretended that he had established laws for the Lacedaemonians on the authority of Apollo, which the Romans wisely did not believe, they therefore did not receive them from that source.”] Lycurgus was the first to devise laws for the Lacedaemonians under the authority of Apollo.

3. [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Numa Pompilius.” Virgil:

> I know the white hair and hoary beard  
> Of the Roman king who first founded the city on laws.

Although Festus, under *Plorare*, and Pomponius, chapter 2, *On the Origin of Law*, say that Romulus and Tatius had established their own laws earlier.] Numa Pompilius, who succeeded Romulus as king, was the first to publish laws for the Romans. Then, [Note: [Col. 0197D] “When the people could not tolerate seditious magistrates.” From *On Illustrious Men*, under Virginius; Chacon read “seditious” from some older books. For at that time there had not yet been seditious magistrates.] when the people could not tolerate seditious magistrates, decemvirs were appointed to write the laws. They translated the laws from Solon’s books into the Latin language and set them forth on the Twelve Tables.

4. [Col. 0197C] These were: Appius Claudius, Titus Genucius, Publius Sextius, Spurius Veturrius, Gaius Julius, Aulus Manlius, Servius Sulpicius, [Note: [Col. 0197D] “Publius Curiatius.” From Livy and Cassiodorus. Another reading: *Curatius*.] Publius Curiatius, Titus Romilius, and Spurius Postumius. [Note: [Col. 0197D] “These ten were decemvirs for the writing of laws, etc.” Yet these were not the authors of the Twelve Tables, but those who replaced them, except for Appius Claudius. “For the purpose of writing laws,” says Gratianus.] These ten were elected as decemvirs for compiling the laws.

### 5.

[Note: [Col. 0198C] “To compile laws.” It is uncertain where he took this from. In one Codex Tarraconensis the word *Pompeius* is absent. Hence A. Augustinus suspected that the original reading was *C. primum scriptum fuisse*, “that C. first wrote,” and that *consul* was then made into a verb, with someone adding *Pompeius* from the margin. But if *C.* referred to Cicero, who is known to have published a work on arranging civil law into an organized system, I do not know whether the statement that he did not persevere through fear of his detractors fits Cicero sufficiently. It fits Pompey very well, however, whose power was envied and regarded with suspicion.]

Pompey, the first consul, wished to undertake the compilation of laws in books, but did not persist through fear of his detractors. [Col. 0198B] [Note: [Col. 0198D] Then Caesar. Suetonius, in the *Life of Julius*.] Caesar then began to do this, but was killed before completing it.

6. Gradually, however, the ancient laws fell out of use through age and neglect; although they now have no practical application, knowledge of them nevertheless seems necessary.

7. [Note: [Col. 0198D] The new laws began with Constantine Caesar. A. Augustinus says: “On account of the Theodosian constitutions, whose collection consists of the constitutions of Christian emperors, and which volume Spain used—not Justinian’s Code—drawn from three Codes containing the laws of pagans and Christians.”]

The new laws began with Constantine Caesar and continued under his successors; 191 they were mixed together and disordered. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Later, under Theodosius the Younger. So also Ivo, *Decretum*, part IV, chapter 170, and *Decretum*, book II, title 12, chapter 17, of Panormitanus. In some books of Gratian and Isidore one also reads “the younger.”]

Later Theodosius the Younger Augustus, following the model of the Gregorian and Hermogenian Codes, arranged a Code of constitutions from the time of Constantine onward, under the separate title of each emperor; he called it Theodosian after his own name.

## CHAPTER II. On divine and human laws

[Col. 0198C]

1. All laws are either divine or human. Divine laws rest upon nature; human laws upon custom. Therefore these differ, since different laws please different peoples.

2. [Note: [Col. 0198D] *Fas* is divine law. From Servius, on *Georgics* I, at the words “*fas* and “the laws permit.”]

*Fas* is divine law; *jus* is human law. [Note: [Col. 0198D] “To cross through another person’s property.” Thus the Gothic Codex; Gratian added “field.”]

It is permitted by divine law to cross through another’s property, but it is not permitted by human law.

## CHAPTER III. How *jus*, laws, and customs differ from one another

[Col. 0199A]

1. [*Jus*] is a general name, whereas a law is a species of *jus*. [Note: [Col. 0199C] “*Jus* is general.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I, at the words “He was giving laws and statutes to men.”]

*Jus* is so called because it is just. [Note: [Col. 0199C] “It is called *jus* because it is just.” Ulpian, chapter 1, *On Justice and Law*: “It is called *jus* from *justitia*, justice”; and Paul, chapter 11: “*Jus* is spoken of in several ways,” and so forth.]

All *jus*, moreover, consists of laws and customs.

2. A law is a written enactment. A custom is a practice approved by long antiquity, or an unwritten law. For *lex* is called so from *legere*, “to read,” because it is written.

3. A custom, however, is a long-established practice derived from conduct. [Note: [Col. 0199C] “Drawn out to the same extent.” Thus most Codices; one Tarraconensis has “drawn out to that extent only.”]

Custom is a kind of law established by practice and accepted in place of a law when a law is lacking. It makes no difference whether it rests upon writing or upon reason, since reason itself also commends the law.

4. [Note: [Col. 0199D] “If a law rests upon reason.” Thus in Tertullian. Another reading has “whether it rests,” as in book I, chapter 10, and in Gratian.]

Moreover, if a law rests upon reason, then everything that has been established by reason will be a law, provided only that it accords with religion, conforms to discipline, and contributes to well-being. It is called a custom because it is in common use.

## CHAPTER IV. What natural law is

1. *Jus* is either natural law, civil law, or the law of nations. Natural law is common to all nations, and is held everywhere by the instinct of nature, not by any enactment—for example, the union of man and woman, [Note: [Col. 0199D] “The bearing of children.” Thus the better Codices, not “succession.” “Succession” would improperly be placed before procreation and upbringing.]

the procreation and upbringing of children, common ownership of all things, a single liberty shared by all, and the acquisition of whatever is taken from the sky, the earth, or the sea.

193 2. Likewise, the restoration of a thing deposited [Note: [Col. 0199D] Or “the restoration of a thing lent.” Another reading has “of entrusted money,” which is less correct.] or lent, and the repulsion of violence by force. [Note: [Col. 0199D] “For this.” Paul, chapter 9, *On Justice*: “*Jus* is spoken of in several ways; in one way, when that which is always equitable and good is called *jus*, as is the case with natural law.”]

For this, and anything similar to it, is never unjust, but is regarded as natural and equitable.

## CHAPTER V. What civil law is

[Col. 0199C]

1. [Note: [Col. 0199D] “Civil law.” From Gaius, chapter 9, *On Justice and Law*.]

Civil law is what each people [Note: [Col. 0199D] Or “each state.” From the chapter beginning “Everyone,” *On Justice and Law*.] or state establishes for itself for human and divine reasons. [Note: [Col. 0199D] “For human and divine reasons.” Gratian has “divine and human.” The conjunction is used in place of a disjunction, a usage not unusual even among jurists.]

## CHAPTER VI. What the law of nations is

1. The law of nations consists of the occupation of settlements, building, fortification, wars, captivities, slavery, the right of return, [Col. 0200A] [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Treaties and peace.” Sallust, in *The Jugurthine War*: “Laws, judgments, treaties, and peace.”] treaties, peace, truces, the religious obligation not to violate ambassadors, and the prohibition of marriages between foreigners. It is called the law of nations because nearly all peoples make use of this law.

## CHAPTER VII. What military law is

1. Military law consists of the solemnity of declaring war, the bond of making a treaty, the advance against the enemy after the signal has been given, and the beginning of battle. It also includes the retreat after the signal; military discipline in the case of deserting one’s post; and [Note: [Col. 0200C] “The scale of pay.” Hence *duplicarii*, soldiers whose pay was doubled as a reward for valor, and those “stripped of their bronze,” from whom pay was deducted as a mark of disgrace. See Festus and Cicero, *Against Verres*.]

the scale of pay, the degrees of rank, and the honor of rewards, such as when a crown or torque is bestowed.

2. 194 It also includes the division of spoils, their equitable distribution according to the status and labors of the persons involved, and the ruler’s share.

## CHAPTER VIII. What public law is

[Col. 0200B]

1. [Note: [Col. 0200C] From Ulpian, chapter 1, *On Justice and Law*.]

Public law concerns sacred matters, priests, and magistrates.

## CHAPTER IX. What the law of the Quirites is

1. The law of the Quirites is properly Roman law, [Note: [Col. 0200C] “To which no one is subject except Roman citizens.” These rules were peculiar to the Romans because of the many legal observances and formalities specific to the Quirites. Otherwise, lawful inheritances, guardianships, and usucaptions also existed among the Greeks under Greek laws. At Rome, however, Greeks were foreigners unless they had become Roman citizens, and they could neither become heirs nor succeed intestate under the law of the Quirites, to which no one was subject except Roman citizens.]

to which no one is subject except Quirites—that is, Romans—as in matters of lawful inheritances, [Note: [Col. 0200D] “Concerning formal acceptances of inheritance.” These are discussed below, chapter 24, and by Ulpian in the *Fragments*.] formal acceptances of inheritance, guardianships, and usucaptions. Such laws are found among no other people, but are peculiar to the Romans and established solely for them.

2. The law of the Quirites consists of laws, plebiscites, decrees of the Senate, enactments of the emperors, and edicts, [Note: [Col. 0200D] “Or the opinions of jurists.” A disjunction is used in place of a conjunction, a frequent occurrence in this work.] or the opinions of jurists.

## CHAPTER X. What a law is

[Col. 0200C]

1. [Note: [Col. 0200D] “A law is.” Above, book II, chapter 10.]

A law is an enactment of the people by which the elders, together with the plebs, have jointly decreed something.

## CHAPTER XI. What plebeian resolutions are

1. [Note: [Col. 0200D] “They are resolutions.” Plebiscites. Gratian, distinction 2, chapter 3.]

Resolutions are what the plebs alone establish. They are called *scita* because the plebs knows them, [Note: [Col. 0200D] Or because it “inquires and decides” (*sciscit*), just as it was asked. Or because it “inquires and asks,” as Salmasius and several very old Codices read, not far from the correct text. Others incorrectly read “because it inquires and asks.” For it was not the plebs that asked, but rather the plebs itself was asked in the formula: “May you wish and order, Quirites,” and at the end: “As I have said this, so I ask you, Quirites.” After the proposal, the plebs was summoned to vote; two tablets were supplied to each person. One bore the letter A, signifying *Antiquo*, “I approve the old measure”; the other bore V. R., that is, *uti rogas*, “as you propose.” According to Festus, *scisco* means “I order,” “I declare an opinion,” or “I cast a vote.” If one reads “it inquires and is asked,” or “it decides and is asked,” as in other books, the latter phrase will interpret the former. The Glossary has: *sciscit*, “it inquires” (Greek: **πυνθάνεται**).]

or because it inquires and decides, just as it was asked.

## CHAPTER XII. What a decree of the Senate is

[Col. 0201A]

1. A decree of the Senate is what the senators decide after giving advice to the peoples. [Note: [Col. 0201C] “To the peoples.” Thus all the books; Chacon read “to the Roman people.” The error arose from the similarity between the Gothic letters for *s* and *r*, of which the former was *s* and the latter *r*.]

## CHAPTER XIII. What an enactment and an edict are

1. An enactment or edict is what a king or emperor establishes or proclaims.

196 ## CHAPTER XIV. What the opinions of jurists are

1. Opinions are what jurists are said to give in response to those who consult them; hence the expression “the opinions of Paul.” [Note: [Col. 0201C] “The opinions of Paul.” He wrote twenty-three books of *Opinions*, from which many passages are found in the books of the *Digest*.]

For there were certain learned men and arbiters of equity who published works composed as introductions to civil law, [Note: [Col. 0201C] “Institutes of civil law.” A. Augustinus said that the tradition had passed from responsa to institutions because of the *Institutes* of Gaius, together with Paul’s *Sentences*, published by Alaric after the Theodosian Code.]

by which they might settle the lawsuits and disputes of litigants who disagreed.

## CHAPTER XV. On consular and tribunician laws

[Col. 0201B]

1. Certain laws are also named after those who enacted them, such as [Note: [Col. 0201D] “Consular and tribunician.” Consular laws were those passed when a consul formally asked the people to approve them. Tribunician laws were those passed through a tribune, although these were properly called plebiscites but were often called laws. Cicero, *On the Laws* III: “They are ancient laws, and not consular laws—if you think there is any difference—but tribunician laws. See Aulus Gellius, book X, chapter 20.”]

consular, tribunician, Julian, and Cornelian laws. Under Caesar Augustus also, [Note: [Col. 0201C] “Suffect consuls.” Suffect consuls were those who entered the consulship during some part of the year rather than on the Kalends of January, as ordinary consuls did. Seneca, *On Anger* III, chapter 31: “He gave me the praetorship, but I had hoped for the consulship; he gave me the twelve fasces, but did not make me an ordinary consul; he wanted me to count the year from my own term, but I am short of the time required for the priesthood,” and so forth. Ausonius, in his *Speech of Thanks*: “But what sort of consulship was that? A suffect consulship substituted for an ordinary one, set apart by an interval of two months, consumed in the sixth part of the year.” See Dionysius, book XLVIII.]

the suffect consuls Papius and Poppaeus enacted a law called the Papia-Poppaea Law after their names, containing rewards for fathers who had children.

2. Under the same emperor, [Note: [Col. 0202C] “Falcidius.” The passage is from Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.]

Falcidius, tribune of the plebs, made a law that no one might bequeath by will more than would leave one quarter for the heirs. From his name the law was called the Falcidian Law. Aquilius also enacted a law that is still called the Aquilian Law.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the *lex satyra*

[Col. 0202A]

1. [Note: [Col. 0202C] “The *lex satyra*.” There was no law specifically called *satyra* by its proper name. Rather, all laws containing many and diverse provisions were called *satyrae*, by analogy either with the platter filled with different kinds of fruit or grain that was carried into the temples of the gods, or with food seasoned with various ingredients. Hence, when they wanted laws to remain permanently in force and be eternal, they added to their sanctions the clause “nor repealed or diminished by a *satyra*,” that is, no one should bring before the people a proposal to repeal one law together with several chapters of another law. For when turbulent or factious magistrates wanted to repeal a law that was not displeasing to the people, they would propose several chapters of laws that were exceedingly fair and very pleasing to the multitude, and among them insert one concerning the repeal of another law. By this device the people, deceived, often repealed useful laws without realizing it. Hence several meanings developed. For anything done confusedly, without regard to the order of time or subject matter, was said to be done “by a *satyra*.” The Glossary has: *satyra*, “a law containing many matters” (Greek: **νόμος πολλὰ περιέχων**). See Festus.]

A *satyra* is a law that speaks at once about several matters, so called from the abundance of its subject matter and, as it were, from satiety. [Note: [Col. 0202D] “And hence to write a *satyra*.” We consider this material extraneous, with Chacon.]

Hence “to write a *satyra*” also means to compose poems of varied content, such as those of Horace, Juvenal, and Persius.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Rhodian laws

1. Rhodian laws concern maritime commerce. They are named after the island of Rhodes, where merchants’ customary practices existed in ancient times.

198 ## CHAPTER XVIII. On privileges

1. Privileges are laws concerning private persons, as it were private laws. For *privilegium* is so called [Note: [Col. 0202D] “Because it is enacted against a private person.” As usual, *in privato* is used for *in privatum*, unless one should rather read *in privatos*. Cicero, *On the Laws* III: “Our ancestors did not wish laws to be enacted against private persons”; that is, this is a privilege.]

because it is enacted against a private person. [Col. 0202B]

## CHAPTER XIX. What a law can do

1. [Note: [Col. 0202D] These chapters are repeated from book II, chapter 10.]

Every law either permits something—for example, that a brave man may seek a reward; or forbids something—for example, that no one may seek marriage with sacred virgins; or punishes something—for example, that whoever commits murder shall be punished capitally. Human life is regulated by its reward or punishment.

## CHAPTER XX. Why a law was made

1. Laws were made so that human boldness might be restrained by fear of them, innocence might be safe among the wicked, and among the wicked themselves the power to do harm might be curbed by fear of punishment.

## CHAPTER XXI. What kind of law ought to be made

[Col. 0203A]

1. A law should be honorable, just, possible, in accordance with nature and the custom of the country, suitable to place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, so that through obscurity it may contain nothing deceptive. It should be written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of the citizens.

## CHAPTER XXII. On causes

1. *Pragma* is a Greek word that is called *causa* in Latin. Hence matters of business are called *pragmata*, and an advocate of causes and business is called a *pragmaticus*.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On witnesses

1. Before the trial, each person binds to himself witnesses whom he has chosen, [Note: [Col. 0203C] “He binds to himself those whom he has chosen ... hence they are called *alligati*, ‘the bound.’ Is this the origin of our words *aliados* and *alianza*, as though from ‘bound persons’ and ‘binding’? Or should we instead accept *sibi placitos*—“those pleasing to him”—from A. Augustinus’ old book, and read *allegat* and *allegati*? We now call the same persons *allegados*, with a meaning not greatly different. For we often see meanings diverge from their ancient senses in countless words; it does not seem plausible to refer this word to testimony.”]

so that afterward it may not be open to anyone either to conceal himself or to withdraw. Hence they are also called “the bound.”

2. Witnesses are likewise so called because they are accustomed to be employed in a will, just as they are called *signatores* because they seal wills.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On legal instruments

1. *Voluntas* is the general name for all legal instruments. Since such an instrument proceeds not by force but by will, it received this name.

2. A will is called a *testamentum* because, unless the testator has died, neither can it be confirmed nor can what has been written in it be known, since it is closed and sealed. It is therefore called a *testamentum* because it has no force until after the testator’s death. Hence the Apostle says: “A testament is confirmed among the dead.” [Col. 0203C]

3. [Note: [Col. 0203D] “A testament, certainly.” These are the words of Augustine on Psalm 82 and of Jerome on Habakkuk II.]

In the Holy Scriptures, however, a *testament* does not mean only something that has no force until the testators are dead; every covenant and agreement was also called a testament. Thus Laban and Jacob made a testament, which certainly had force even between living persons. And in the Psalms we read: “They have established a testament against you,” that is, a covenant; and there are countless examples of this kind.

4. Wills are called “tablets” because, before the use of paper and parchment, not only wills but also letters and communications were written on smoothed tablets. Hence those who carried them were called *tabellarii*, “tablet-bearers.”

5. A will under civil law is one confirmed by the subscriptions of five witnesses. [Note: [Col. 0203D] “Confirmed by the subscriptions of five witnesses.” That many witnesses were employed in a will executed by bronze and scales. Justinian, however, says that under civil law the witnesses’ seals were not necessary, but only under praetorian law.]

6. A will under praetorian law is sealed with the seals of seven witnesses. The former is made among citizens and is therefore called civil; the latter is made before praetors and is therefore called praetorian law. To seal a will is to mark it, so that what has been written may be known.

7. [Note: [Col. 0203D] “A holograph will.” Ambrose, in his Letter to the Galatians, chapter VI: “Where the handwriting is wholly one’s own, it cannot be called false.” The same is called a *hologrammon* or *hologrammaton* will by Justinian. See Novel 107, chapter 1:

“Let us decree that, if someone who knows how to write wishes to make a disposition among his children, he must first write above it the date, then the names of the children in his own hand; and, as for the amounts for which he names them heirs, they must not be indicated by numerical symbols but written out entirely in letters.”

]

A holograph will is written and subscribed entirely in the hand of its author, 201 and hence received its name. For the Greeks call “whole” **ὅλον**, and a written letter **γραφήν**. [Note: [Col. 0204C] “A letter.” *Littera* means writing, as in an unknown poet:

“A letter tells of the deed; the deed itself its marrow.”]

[Col. 0204B]

8. A will is invalid if the person who made it has suffered a reduction in civil status, or if it was not properly executed.

9. An inofficious will is one in which, after children have been disinherited without cause, the estate has been assigned to outsiders without regard for natural affection.

10. A will is called broken because, when a posthumous child is born, it is broken apart if that child was neither expressly disinherited nor instituted as heir.

11. A suppressed will is one that has not been publicly produced through fraud against heirs, legatees, or freedpersons. Even if it is not concealed, it is nevertheless considered suppressed if it is not produced to the persons mentioned above.

12. [Note: [Col. 0204C] “*Nuncupatio* ... ‘these things, as in these tablets.’” Ulpian, *Fragments*, title XX: “A will is declared in this manner: while holding the tablets of the will, the testator says: ‘As these things are written in these tablets or wax tablets, so I give, so I bequeath, so I testify; therefore, Quirites, bear witness.’” That Ulpian adds “so I testify,” which Isidore omits, is not surprising. Pomponius says, chapter 120, *On the Meaning of Words*, that in the Twelve Tables the word “to bequeath” also includes the institution of an heir.]

*Nuncupatio* occurs when the testator reads aloud from tablets and wax tablets, saying: “As these things are written in these tablets and wax tablets, so I give, so I bequeath; therefore, Roman citizens, bear witness for me.” This is called *nuncupatio*, for *nuncupare* means to name publicly and to confirm.

13. [Note: [Col. 0204D] “The right of children.” Spouses who had no children could not institute one another as universal heirs unless they had obtained from the emperor the *ius liberorum*. Ulpian, title XVI. This is also confirmed by the words of the old interpreter of the Novel of Theodosius and Valentinian on Wills, which is placed at the end of the Theodosian Code.]

The right of children is the reciprocal institution of spouses without children as heirs in place of children.

14. [Note: [Col. 0204D] “A codicil.” Seneca, *On the Brevity of Life*: “Let us also grant this to those who ask the question: who first persuaded the Romans to board a ship? It was Claudius, who was called Caudex for this very reason, because among the ancients a structure made by joining several tablets was called a *caudex*. Hence public tablets are called *codices*, and even today ships that, following the ancient custom, transport cargo along the Tiber are called *caudicariae*. Hence *codicils*, which were made from wax-coated tablets so that they could easily be carried in one’s bosom. The word also denotes writing by which someone records his wishes without any formal ceremony.”]

A *codicil*, as the ancients say, was undoubtedly named from its author, who established this kind of writing. It is a form of writing requiring no solemnity of words, but expressed solely by the testator’s will through any written indication whatsoever. By this means the wishes of the dead were often supported because of the difficulty of the legal words, or at least because of the need to employ solemn forms. Thus whoever writes the title of such a document calls it a codicil. Just as a codicil serves in place of a will, so a letter serves in place of codicils.

15. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “*Cretio*.” See Ulpian, title XXII.]

*Cretio* is a fixed number of days during which an instituted heir either accepts the inheritance or is excluded when the period of *cretio* has expired. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “Nor is he free to do so.” Understand “right” or “discretion.”]

He has no freedom to claim the inheritance after that time.

16. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “*Cretio* was so called.” Varro, book VI: “*Crevi* means ‘I have determined’; thus, when an heir determines that he is an heir, he is said to *cernere*, and when he has done this, to have *crevisse*.”]

*Cretio* was so called as if from *decretio*, that is, “to decide” or “to determine,” as in: “Let that man be my heir,” followed by: “Let him decide within so many days.” [Col. 0205B] For accepting inheritances, the hundredth day was fixed when no *cretio* had been added.

17. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “*Fideicommissum*.” Ulpian, title XXV: “A *fideicommissum* is something left not in civil-law words but in words of entreaty.”]

A *fideicommissum* is so called because what is entrusted by the deceased is to be carried out. 203 For *fides*, “trust,” is so called from the fact that it is fulfilled; yet the request is made not in direct words but in words of entreaty.

18. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “A pact is so called.” Bernard of Pavia, chapter 11, *On the Meaning of Words*, in the first collection of the Decretals, and Gregory IX, chapter 11 under the same title, report these words. In the old books *pactum* is correctly derived from *pagus*, “district,” not from *pango*, “I fasten.”]

A pact is a written agreement between parties arising from peace and approved by laws and customs. It is called a *pact* as though made from peace, from the word *pango*, “I fasten,” whence also *pepigit*, “he agreed.”

19. An agreement (*placitum*) is similarly named from *placere*, “to please.” Others say that a *pact* is what someone does willingly, whereas one may be compelled even unwillingly to an agreement—for example, when someone is ready to answer in court. No one can call that a pact, but rather an agreement.

[Col. 0205C] 20. A mandate is so called because formerly, when a task was entrusted, one person gave his hand to another.

21. *Ratum* means, as it were, rational and right. Hence someone who makes a promise says: “I declare it ratified,” that is, firm and perpetual.

22. [Note: [Col. 0205D] “To be properly.” Not “to be right.” This does not disagree with Servius, who interprets *rite* as meaning not only “rightly” but “rightly according to ritual.”]

To be *rite* [Probably *est*, “is”] means not “rightly,” but “according to custom.”

[Note: [Col. 0205D] “*Chirographum* ... *cautio*.” These words are read separately in the better books without interpretation; in the printed editions they explain themselves sufficiently. The Neapolitan Codex has: “*Chirographum*, *cautio*, that is, a written document in one’s own hand.”]

*Chirographum* ... *cautio* ...

23. Buying and selling is the exchange of things and a contract arising from agreement.

24. [Note: [Col. 0206C] “Buying is so called.” Or rather, because “what is mine becomes yours,” unless this etymology concerns a loan in Justinian.]

Buying is so called because something passes from me to you; selling is as though *venundinatio*, that is, something derived from the market.

[Col. 0206A] 25. A donation is the transfer of any thing whatsoever. They say that *donatio* is called so as if from *doni actio*, “the action of a gift,” and a dowry (*dos*) as if from *do item*, “I also give.” For a donation precedes the wedding, and the dowry follows.

204 26. [Note: [Col. 0206D] “For the ancient wedding ... as we find in the law.” These are Servius’ words at the beginning of book I of the *Georgics*, where perhaps the words “lest the wife appear to be a slave” are missing.]

The ancient wedding ceremony was such that husband and wife bought one another, so that the wife would not appear to be a slave, as we find in the law. Hence, when the husband’s donation precedes, the wife’s dowry follows.

27. A usufructuary donation is so called because the donor still retains the usufruct from it, while preserving the right of the person to whom it was donated.

28. A direct donation is so called because by law and in practice it immediately passes to another, and nothing from it afterward reverts to the donor’s right.

29. [Note: [Col. 0206D] “The conditions of witnesses, properly.” Thus written in the Gothic text, and the etymological explanation proceeds accordingly.]

The statements of witnesses are properly called *conditions*, and are so named from *condicere*, “to declare together,” as though *condictions*, because one witness does not swear there alone, but either two or more do so. For the entire force of the testimony rests not in the mouth of one person but in that of two or three witnesses. They are also called *conditions* because the witnesses’ statements agree with one another, as though they had been jointly declared.

30. A stipulation is a promise or undertaking; hence those who make promises are called stipulators. The word *stipulatio* is derived from *stipula*, “straw.” [Note: [Col. 0206D] “The ancients ... acknowledged.” Chacon deleted this passage.]

For when the ancients promised something to one another, they held a stalk of straw and broke it; then, joining it together again, they acknowledged their undertakings. Or else because, according to Paul the jurist, they called something firm *stipulum*. [Note: [Col. 0206D] In accordance with Paul the jurist, book V of the *Sentences*, title 8. See below, book X, “Stipulation.”]

205 31. An oath is the pledge of an undertaking. It is called an oath because violating what one has promised is an act of bad faith.

## CHAPTER XXV. On things

[Col. 0206C]

1. An inheritance is a thing that passes to someone upon another person’s death, neither having been bequeathed by will nor retained through possession. [Note: [Col. 0206D] “And neither bequeathed by will nor retained in possession.” These are Cicero’s words in the *Topics*, preserved in full in only one book of the Ovetensis College.]

An inheritance is called *haereditas* from things added, or from *aes*, “bronze” or “money,” because the person who possesses a field and pays the census thereby becomes an heir.

[Note: [Col. 0206D] “Hence also *heres*, ‘heir.’” Another reading has “hence also *res*, ‘thing.’”]

2. Things are whatever fall within our right. [Note: [Col. 0206D] “Rights, moreover, are ...” From Augustine, Letter 54, quoted by Gregory, chapter 12, *On the Meaning of Words*, and by the canon beginning “What shall I say?” in question 4, as well as by Bernard of Pavia in the first collection.]

Rights are what we possess justly and what does not belong to another.

3. A thing is so called from “having rightly,” and a right from “possessing justly.” For that is possessed by right which is possessed justly, and that is possessed justly which is possessed well. What is possessed wrongly belongs to another. A person possesses wrongly if he either misuses what is his own or presumes upon what belongs to another. He possesses justly if he is not ensnared by greed. Whoever is held by greed is possessed, not a possessor.

4. Goods are the possessions of honorable or noble persons. They are therefore called goods because they do not have a shameful use, but are used by people for good purposes.

206 5. *Peculium* properly belongs to persons of inferior status or to slaves. For a *peculium* is what a father or master permits his son or slave to manage as his own. *Peculium* is so called from *pecus*, “cattle,” in which the entire substance of the ancients consisted.

6. Possession of goods is a right of possession acquired in a definite order and under a definite title.

[Col. 0207B] 7. An intestate inheritance is one that has not been set down in a will, or, if it has been set down, has nevertheless not been lawfully added.

8. It is called *caduca*, “lapsed,” because its heirs have fallen away.

9. *Familia herciscunda* is the division of an inheritance among heirs. Among the ancients, the division itself was called *herciscunda*.

10. An action for division of common property lies between those who own a thing in common. This action orders that an arbitration be granted to the petitioners, according to whose decision the property is to be divided.

11. The action for fixing boundaries is so called because by it the boundaries of both parties are regulated, so that they are not dispersed, [Note: [Col. 0207D] “Provided that the dispute is not over a place narrower than five feet.” A. Augustinus removes the negation, following the Twelve Tables, chapter 20.]

provided that the dispute does not concern a place narrower than five feet.

[Col. 0207C] 12. A lease is a thing given for use with the rent specified.

13. A hiring is a thing received for use with the rent agreed upon.

14. A thing credited is one brought into an obligation in such a way that, from the time the contract was made, it is certain that it is owed.

15. Interest is an increase on a loan, so called from the use of the borrowed money.

16. [Note: [Col. 0207D] “*Commodatum*.” All the books incorrectly have *commodum*.]

A loan for use is something belonging to our right that has been temporarily transferred to another [Note: [Col. 0207D] “With a limitation of time,” that is, with a specified period. Another reading has “through temporary benefit.”] with a limitation of time, for as long as it remains with that person. Hence it is called *commodatum*.

17. A precarious tenure exists when a creditor, asked by entreaty, permits a debtor to remain in possession of land pledged to the creditor and to take its fruits. [Col. 0207D] It is called *precarium* because it is granted by entreaty, as though *prece adium*, with *r* changed into *d*. [Note: [Col. 0207D] “Called *precarium* because it is granted by entreaty.” The derivation of the word is *arium*, as in *armarium*. But who would deny that this meaning is explained conveniently in this way?]

18. A loan (*mutuum*) is so called because what is given from me to you becomes yours from mine.

19. A deposit is a pledge entrusted for a time, as though “placed for a long period.” A person is considered to make a deposit when, through fear of theft, fire, or shipwreck, he deposits something with another for safekeeping.

20. In common usage there is a difference between a pledge and earnest money. A pledge is something given on account of a debt; when the debt is repaid, the pledge is immediately taken away. Earnest money, however, is given initially as part of the price in a good-faith contract of sale and is completed afterward.

21. Earnest money is to be completed, not taken away. Therefore whoever holds earnest money does not return it as he would a pledge, but expects the completion of the transaction. [Note: [Col. 0208D] “Earnest money is called from the thing.” Rather, the word is shortened from *arrhabo*, “earnest.”]

It is called earnest money from the thing for which it is delivered. There is likewise a difference between a pledge, a fiduciary transfer, and a hypothecation:

22. A pledge is something obligated on account of a debt, and the creditor obtains only possession of the thing for a time. [Col. 0208B] Ownership, however, remains with the debtor.

23. A fiduciary transfer occurs when a thing is either formally conveyed [Note: [Col. 0208D] Or “transferred through legal cession.” Ulpian explains how legal cession is carried out in the *Fragments*, and Gaius is cited by Boethius in the *Topics*.] or ceded in court for the purpose of obtaining a mutual loan.

24. A hypothecation occurs when a thing is lent without the delivery of a pledge, with only an agreement or security intervening.

25. [Note: [Col. 0208D] “A moment ... as quickly, immediately.” Thus the better books.]

A moment is so called from the brevity of time, so that what is claimed may be restored as quickly and immediately as possible, without disrupting the transaction, and may not be prolonged into any delay. There is no duration belonging to a moment, since its point of time is so brief that it cannot in any way be prolonged into a delay.

208 26. An instrument is something by which we construct something, such as a knife, pen, or axe.

[Col. 0208C] 27. An implement is what is produced through an instrument, such as a staff, book, or tablet.

28. Use is the activity by which we employ an implement, as leaning on a staff, reading in a book, or playing on a tablet. Even the produce of fields is called use, because we use it. These are the three things ...

29. Usufruct is so called because the produce of a thing is enjoyed through use alone, while the right remains with another.

30. Usucaption is the acquisition of ownership through the continuation of just possession, [Note: [Col. 0208D] Or “two years.” “A year, or two years.” Ulpian gives a fuller account.] for two years or for some other period.

31. *Mancipatio* is so called because a thing is taken by hand. Hence the person who receives something by *mancipatio* must grasp the very thing that is conveyed to him by *mancipatio*.

32. Cession is the granting of one’s own property, as in the expression: “I yield by right of kinship.” For we say *cedere*, “to yield,” as though “to grant,” in the case of things that are one’s own; things belonging to another we restore, not yield. Properly, someone yields when he agrees with another against the truth, as Cicero says: [Note: [Col. 0208D] “As Cicero says.” In the speech *For Ligarius*.]

“He yielded,” he says, “to the authority of the most distinguished man”—or rather, he obeyed.

[Col. 0209A] 33. An interdict is what a judge pronounces not permanently but temporarily, to restore a situation for the moment, while leaving the bringing of the action intact.

34. A price is so called because we give it first, so that in exchange for it we may possess the thing we desire.

35. Commerce is named from merchandise, the term by which we call things offered for sale. Hence a market is also called a gathering of many people who customarily sell or buy things.

36. Restitution in integrum is the repair of a case or thing.

209 37. A case is restored when it has not been completed through the force of authority. A thing is restored when it has been taken away and wrested from someone through the force of authority.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On crimes set down in the law

[Col. 0209B]

1. *Crimen* is named from *carere*, “to lack,” as in theft and falsehood, which do not kill but bring disgrace.

2. *Facinus* is named from doing evil, because it harms another.

3. [Note: [Col. 0209D] “*Flagitium*.” Nonius says: “The ancients wished *flagitium* to mean a vice inflicted upon a virgin.”]

*Flagitium* is named from demanding sexual corruption, by which a person harms himself. These are the two categories of all sins.

4. Force is the power of authority by which a case or thing is either taken away or wrested from someone.

5. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Private force … Public force.** From Paul, *Sententiae*, book V, title 26; from this it seemed that Chacon’s earlier reading—“before the people”—should be read “before a judge,” or “before a king,” which also seems right to us, unless you prefer to regard “before the people” as a Gothicism.] Private force exists if anyone, before judgment, has driven someone from his property or overpowered him with armed men.

6. Public force exists if anyone has killed, tortured, beaten, or bound a citizen who was appealing before the people, a judge, or a king.

7. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Deceit is the cleverness of the mind.** Labeo and Aquilius discuss *dolus malus*, “malicious deceit”; for there is also *dolus bonus*, “benevolent deceit,” so that the word *malus* seems to be missing.] Deceit is the cleverness of the mind, named from deceiving; for one thing is done, while another is pretended. Petronius thinks otherwise, saying: “What is deceit, judges? Surely, when something has been done which causes the law pain, you have deceit; now accept malicious deceit.”

8. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Calumny**, from *calvendo*, that is, “deceiving.” Hence in the Twelve Tables: “If he deceives or lays a snare.”] Calumny is a quarrel concerning another person’s lawsuit, named from *calvendo*, that is, from deceiving.

210

9. Falsehood is so called from *fari*, “to speak,” when one says something other than the truth.

10. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Injury** is injustice. These are Servius’s words on *Aeneid* IX, at “with Turnus’s injury.”] Injury is injustice; hence among the comic poets one who dares anything contrary to the order of the law is called *injurious*.

[Col. 0210A] 11. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Sedition.** These words are cited by Nonius from Cicero, book VI of *The Republic*, under *Seditio*.] Sedition is called the dissension of citizens, because some go off separately from others. For such people especially delight in the disturbance of affairs and in turmoil.

12. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Sacrilege.** Servius, *Aeneid* IX: *legere*, “to steal”; hence *sacrilegi*, those who steal sacred things.] Sacrilege properly means the theft of sacred things; later this name also adhered to the worship of idols. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **It adhered to the worship of idols.** Some interpret in this way Paul’s statement in Romans II: “You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?”]

13. [Note: [Col. 0209D] **Adultery is deception. — Abuse**, Oventius and Festus of Naples: “An adulterer and an adulteress are so called because he goes to another woman and she to another man.”] Adultery is the violation of another person’s marriage; because one person has defiled the other’s bed, it received the name *adultery*.

14. [Note: [Col. 0210D] **Sexual violation …** There is a lacuna in the better books; in others, the material concerning rape is supplied as an interpretation.] Sexual violation [lacuna].

15. [Note: [Col. 0210D] **Rape.** From Servius, *Aeneid* IV.] Rape properly means illicit intercourse, so called from corrupting; hence Virgil: “He possesses the raped woman,” that is, “he enjoys sexual violation.”

16. The word *homicide* is composed of *homo*, “human being,” and *caedes*, “slaughter.” For the ancients called one who was discovered to have committed slaughter against a human being a *homicide*.

[Col. 0210B] 17. An action for parricide was brought not only against one who had killed a parent, that is, a father or mother, but also against one who had killed a brother. It was called *parricide*, as though “the slaughter of a parent.”

18. [Note: [Col. 0210D] **Internecive.** Thus in all the most ancient books. Festus: “An internecive testament, on account of which its owner was killed.” Nor do we reject the readings of other books, in which *interniciei*, *internicii*, and *internicidii* are found. We also accept *internicidi* with Jacobus Cujacius. Agellius likewise used *internicium morbum*, “an internecive disease.”] An *internecive* action was brought against one who had made a false testament and on that account had killed a person. The possession of his property followed his accuser. The meaning of *internecive* is, as it were, a kind of killing of a person; for the ancients used the preposition *inter* in place of *e*. Naevius: “To drink up the sea” (*interbibere*). And Plautus: “To drain the sea” (*interluere*), that is, “to drink it up and empty it.”

19. Theft is the secret handling of another person’s property, named from *furvus*, that is, “dark,” because it is committed in darkness. [Note: [Col. 0210D] **Capital theft.** According to the laws of the Twelve Tables, as Theophilus says, *Institutes* IV, title XII. Draco’s laws, however, condemned even the thief of the smallest object to death. Plutarch and Agellius.] Among our ancestors theft was a capital crime [Col. 0210C] before the penalty of fourfold restitution. [Note: [Col. 0210D] **Before the penalty of fourfold restitution.** But Cato says in the preface to *On Agriculture*: “Our ancestors held this view and established it in their laws: that a thief should be condemned to double restitution, and a usurer to fourfold restitution.” See Agellius, book XI, chapter 18, who reconciles this dispute.]

20. *Pervasio* is the manifest appropriation of another person’s property. Theft is committed with respect to things that can be moved from place to place; *pervasio*, however, applies both to things that are moved and to things that are immovable.

21. *Inficiatio* is the denial of a debt when it is demanded by a creditor. The same is *abjuratio*, that is, denial of something entrusted or lent.

22. An action for canvassing is brought against one who obtains office by bribery and solicits votes, forfeiting the dignity which he seizes by payment.

23. An action for embezzlement is brought against those who defraud the treasury and divert public money; for *peculatus* is named from *pecunia*, “money.” The theft of public property, however, is not judged in the same way as theft of private property; the former is judged like sacrilege, because the thief is a thief of sacred things.

24. A charge of extortion is brought against one who has taken money from allies. In this action, if the defendant dies beforehand, the action is transferred against his property.

25. An action for incest was established against consecrated virgins or blood-relatives; for those who have intercourse with such persons are regarded as *incestuous*, that is, unchaste.

26. Those who have injured or violated royal majesty, or who have betrayed the commonwealth or reached an agreement with enemies, are held liable for treason.

27. *Piaculum* is so called because it can be expiated; for acts were called *commissa* when they had to be expiated in some manner.

# CHAPTER XXVII. On the penalties established in the laws

1. Evil is understood in two ways: one is what a person does, the other what he suffers. What he does is sin; what he suffers is punishment. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **But evil is then complete … and threatens.** — *Planum* … and *impedit* is the reading of the Spanish interpreter, who rendered it: “Evil is then plain when it is past and hinders the person who is to suffer pain and fear.”] Evil is complete when it is both past and threatening, so that there are both pain and fear.

2. Punishment is called *poena* because it punishes. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **It is a necessary epithet.** In most books *nomen*, “name,” appears in place of *necessarium*, “necessary,” an error arising from the manuscript abbreviation *nomen*, which is found in the book of Salamanca.] It is a necessary epithet, and without an addition it does not have a complete meaning: add “the punishment of imprisonment,” “the punishment of exile,” or “the punishment of death,” and you complete the sense.

3. *Supplicium* properly means not any kind of punishment, but condemnation of such a kind that the person’s property is consecrated and transferred to the public treasury; for *supplicia* meant supplications. *Supplicium* is also used when something is taken from the condemned person for God, whence also *supplicare*, “to offer supplication.”

4. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **Eight kinds of punishment.** From Augustine, *City of God* XXI, chapter 11. Cicero, *On the Orator* I: “The vices and frauds of human beings are punished by fines, bonds, disgrace, beatings, exile, and death.” As far as I know, Cicero does not mention retaliation; Augustine does.] Tullius writes that the laws contain eight kinds of punishment: financial loss, bonds, beatings, retaliation, disgrace, exile, slavery, and death; for every crime committed is avenged by these penalties.

5. *Damnum* is named from the diminution of property.

6. *Vincula*, “bonds,” is named from *vinciere*, that is, “to tighten,” because bonds constrict and restrain, or because they bind by force.

7. *Compedes*, “fetters,” is so called because they contain the feet.

[Col. 0212A] 8. *Pedicae* are nooses by which the feet are caught; they are named from catching the feet.

9. *Catenae*, “chains,” are so called because, by grasping, they hold both feet so that a person cannot advance. They are also called *catenae* because, by catching one another, they hold together through many knots.

10. *Manicae* are bonds by which the hands are seized, although *manicae* also means the sleeves of tunics.

11. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **The nerve …** There is a lacuna in the old manuscript. The interpretation in other books may seem to have been taken from the epitome of Festus, but Festus himself is somewhat more reliable.] The nerve [lacuna].

12. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **Boia.** Festus: “*Boiae* are a kind of bond; they are said to be both wooden and iron.”] A *boia* is a collar of condemned persons, like a yoke on an ox; it belongs to the category of bonds.

13. A prison is a place in which criminals are guarded. It is called *carcer* because people are restrained and enclosed in it, as though from *arcer*, “to ward off,” namely, from restraining. We use *carcer* in the singular only for the place where criminals are kept; but the places from which chariots are sent out we call *carceres* [Col. 0212B] only in the plural. [Note: [Col. 0211D] **Only in the plural.** Yet Virgil used the singular: “And the chariots rush forth from the starting gate.”]

14. *Verbera*, “blows,” is so called because, when they are wielded, they strike the air. Hence *flagra*, “whips,” *plagae*, “strikes,” and *flagella*, “whips,” because they sound against the body with breath and noise. For *plagae* is as though *flagae*; but *plagae* and *flagra* are primary forms, whereas *flagella* is formed by diminution.

15. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **The eel.** Pliny, book IX, chapter 23: “The skin of the moray is very thin, whereas that of eels is thicker”; Verrius reports that youths wearing the toga praetexta were accustomed to be beaten with it, and for this reason says that no fine was imposed upon them.] An eel is the instrument with which boys are disciplined in schools; it is commonly called a *scutica*, “scourge.”

16. *Fustes* are sticks with which young men are beaten for crimes. They are so called because they stand fixed in ditches, which country people call poles.

17. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **Levers … and stones are pulled away.** A. preferred *vehuntur*, “are carried”; yet everywhere we see stones pulled and moved by levers.] *Vectes*, “levers,” are so called because they are carried by hand; with them doors and stones are pulled away. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **But these do not belong to the punishments of the laws.** Why, then, are they mentioned here? Perhaps because we often read that martyrs were tortured with levers?]

18. *Virgae*, “rods,” are the tips of branches and trees, so called because they are green, or because they have the power to chastise. If one is smooth, it is a *virga*; if it is truly knotted or thorny, it is most properly called a *scorpio*, “scorpion,” because it is driven into the body with a curved wound. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **Because of the curved wound.** These are Jerome’s words, or rather perhaps Tertullian’s. See below, book XII, chapter 5.] [Note: [Col. 0212D] **If smooth.** Others read, “if light.”]

19. *Ictus*, “blows,” properly means blows from whips, so called from wielding them.

20. *Ungulae*, “claws,” are so called because they dig out flesh. They are also called *fidiculae*, “little strings,” because the accused are tortured with them on the *equuleus*, “little horse,” so that the truth may be discovered. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **And the *fidiculae* … so that the truth may be discovered.** Or rather, from their resemblance to strings.]

215

21. [Note: [Col. 0212D] **The little horse … because it stretches.** Others read, “because it is stretched.”] The *equuleus* is so called because it stretches.

22. *Tormenta*, “tortures,” are so called because, by twisting, they discover the mind.

23. There is also the *latomia*, a kind of punishment [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0213D] **Suitable for beating.** We consider these words foreign to the passage.] invented by Tarquinius Superbus for punishing criminals. He was the first to devise stone quarries, instruments of torture, clubs, mines, and exiles; and he was also the first of the kings to deserve exile. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **The *latomia*.** Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*: “Tarquinius Superbus devised bonds, bull-hide whips, clubs, stone quarries, prisons, fetters, chains, exiles, and mines.” Yet they should not be called *lautumiae*, as some think, because Seneca says in book V of the *Controversiae*: “Let none of you be deceived by the name itself, *latumiae*; it is by no means a luxurious thing.” See Festus and Asconius.]

24. Retaliation is a likeness of vengeance, so that a person suffers in the same manner as he acted. Nature and law alike have established this, so that a similar vengeance follows the one who inflicts injury. Hence the statement of the law: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” Retaliation is used not only for returning an injury but also for repaying a benefit. It is a common expression for both injury and beneficence.

25. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **Disgrace.** This is the reading of the better books, followed immediately by *infamium*, “of infamy,” a word frequently found in the Councils of Toledo.] *Ignominium*, “disgrace,” is so called because the person detected in some crime ceases to possess the name of honor. It is called *ignominium* as though “without a name,” just as *ignarus* means “without knowledge,” and *ignobilis* “without nobility.”

[Col. 0213B] 26. This too is called *infamium*, as though “without good reputation.” *Fama*, “reputation,” is so called because, through speech—that is, through speaking—it spreads, creeping along the channels of tongues and ears. It is a name both for good things and for bad things. For there is sometimes a reputation for happiness, [Note: [Col. 0213D] **As in the phrase “illustrious reputation.”** From the speech *For Marcellus*.] as in “illustrious reputation,” which means praise; and a reputation for bad things, as in Virgil:

> Reputation, an evil than which nothing is swifter.

[Note: [Col. 0213D] **Than which nothing else.** This is the reading in all the Gothic manuscripts, not *quo*; in my judgment, not without justification.]

27. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **The name of reputation.** The entire passage is from Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 8.] The name of reputation has no fixed place, because it is for the most part deceitful, adding much to the truth or altering it. It lives only so long as it is not tested. But once you have tested it, it ceases to exist, and from then on the thing itself, not the reputation, is named.

28. Exile is called as though “outside one’s soil.” For an exile is one who is outside his soil. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **Hence the restoration of civic rights … of the fatherland.** We have marked these words with an obelus, following the judgment of A. Augustinus and Chacon.] [lacuna] Hence the restoration of civic rights for those returning, that is, for those being recalled from exile, who had been unjustly expelled beyond the boundary of their fatherland. Exile is divided into relegation and deportation.

29. A relegated person is one whose property follows him; a deported person is one whose property does not follow him.

30. Proscription is condemnation to distant exile, as though “writing away”; and a proscribed person is so called because he has been publicly written down.

31. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **The mine … are assigned.** The Neapolitan manuscript reads “are deported.”] A mine is a place where exiles are assigned to extract ore and cut marble into slabs.

217

32. [Note: [Col. 0213D] **Slavery.** From Augustine, *City of God* XIX, chapter 15.] Slavery is named from preserving, for among the ancients those who were preserved from death in war were called *slaves*. [Note: [Col. 0214D] **This is the last of all evils.** Cicero, *Philippic* II: “Slavery is the last of all evils, to be rejected not only by war but even by death.”] This is the last of all evils, and for free people it is heavier than every punishment; for when liberty perishes, everything perishes with it.

[Col. 0213D] 33. There are various forms of death, among them the cross [Col. 0214A] or the *patibulum*, on which people are hung and tortured or made to suffer; hence they have their names.

34. The *patibulum* is commonly called a fork, as though “bearing the head.” For it kills by leaving the person suspended and strangled; but the punishment of the *patibulum* is less severe than that of the cross. The *patibulum* kills those hung upon it immediately, whereas the cross tortures those fastened to it for a long time. Hence in the Gospel the thieves’ legs were broken so that they would die and be taken down from the wood before the Sabbath, because those suspended on the wood could not die quickly.

33. The very manner of death also differs. [Note: [Col. 0214D] **In the very kind of death as well.** From Tertullian’s *Apology*.] It is more cruel to be extinguished in water that torments the breath, to be burned by fire, killed by cold or hunger, or exposed to dogs and wild beasts. To die by the sword, however, was even desired by the aged. For the sword knows how to end life by a shortened death without prolonged torture.

36. The *culleus* is a small vessel for parricides, named from *occulere*, that is, “to enclose.” It is a leather bag in which parricides are enclosed with a monkey, a rooster, and a serpent and thrown into the sea. This class of all these deaths is called *animadversio*, “punishment.” [Note: [Col. 0214D] **And with a serpent.** Juvenal, *Satire* 8:

> For whose punishment there should not have been prepared  
> One monkey, one serpent, and one bag.

What is read in some books about the serpent, rooster, and monkey is absent from the better books, except for one very old manuscript at Salamanca; even there it is relegated to the end of the entire chapter, so that it is plainly evident that it is extraneous. These books have been badly corrupted by such additions.]

37. Execution occurs when a judge punishes the accused. The judge is said *to take notice*, that is, to turn his mind toward the matter, concentrating on punishing the accused because he is a judge.

38. The Romans therefore prohibited certain condemned persons from using water and fire, because air and water are open to everyone and have been given to all, so that those persons might not enjoy what nature has granted to everyone.

# ON TIMES. CHAPTER XXVIII. On the term “chronicle”

[Col. 0214C]

1. [Note: [Col. 0214D] What is contained in these twelve chapters concerning times has been brought here from Isidore’s book *On the Stars*, addressed to King Sisebut, and from his *Chronicle*.] *Chronicle* is called in Greek what in Latin is called a sequence of times, such as the work published among the Greeks by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and translated into Latin by the presbyter Jerome. For Greek *chronos* means *time* in Latin.

# CHAPTER XXIX. On moments and hours

1. Times are divided into moments, hours, days, months, years, lustrums, centuries, and ages. A moment is the smallest and narrowest measure of time, named from the movement of the stars.

2. It is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when one thing yields to and succeeds another. *Hora* is a Greek word, yet it sounds Latin. For an hour is the end of a period of time, just as the edges of the sea, rivers, and garments are also called *horae*.

219

# CHAPTER XXX. On days

1. Day is the presence of the sun, that is, the sun above the earth, just as night is the sun beneath the earth. For the cause of day or night is either the sun above the earth or beneath the earth. A complete day consists of twenty-four hours, until the revolving movement of the heavens completes the periods of day and night in their course from the eastern point back to another eastern point. In ordinary usage, however, one day is the span from the sun’s rising in the east to its setting in the west.

2. The periods of a day are two: the daytime and the nighttime. The day itself consists of twenty-four hours, while each of these periods consists of twelve hours. [Note: [Col. 0215C] **Daytime.** This is the reading of all the books.]

[Col. 0215B] 3. [Note: [Col. 0215C] **Day named from the better part.** From Servius, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “The damp night drives through the middle.”] Day is named from the better part. Hence it is customary to speak of a number of days without mentioning the night, just as it is written in divine law: “There was evening and morning, one day.”

4. According to the Egyptians, the day begins at sunset; according to the Persians, at sunrise; [Note: [Col. 0215C] **According to the Athenians, at the sixth hour of the day.** From the same passage of Servius, who cites Agellius; Agellius, however, in book III, chapter 2, says from Varro that among the Athenians the day begins at sunset. Macrobius, book I, and Censorinus, chapter 19, also affirm this. Therefore either Servius or Agellius must be emended. Bede followed Isidore in chapter 2 of *On the Reckoning of Time*. What if readers wrote *sexta*, “sixth,” from the preceding abbreviation, when Isidore understood *suprema*, “the final hour,” or rather read *sexta hora* in place of *suprema*? For I do not know how else we can honestly make sense of this passage.] according to the Athenians, at the sixth hour of the day; according to the Romans, at midnight. Hence there is then the cockcrow, [Note: [Col. 0215D] **That is, the crowing of the cocks.** These words were added from the Neapolitan manuscript, so that what follows—“whose voice,” and so on—would have a grammatical connection.] that is, the crowing of the cocks, [Note: [Col. 0215D] **Whose voice is the herald of day.** Ambrose: “Awakened by this, Lucifer releases the sky from darkness.”] whose voice proclaims the approach of day, [Note: [Col. 0215D] **When the mesonyctial breath also blows.** Since the better part of the night has passed and the sun is already turning toward us, this is said to be breathed upon by its rays. *To be breathed upon* is a term of the magi, who believed that, as the sun approached, nocturnal apparitions fled. Hence Philostratus, book III of *Life of Apollonius*, denies that Achilles’ apparition waited for cockcrow. To this also belongs Anchises’ statement:

> And now farewell; the damp night drives through its middle course,  
> and the fierce East has breathed upon me with panting horses.

Servius interprets the following passage of *Aeneid* VI in the same way:

[Col. 0216C]

> Behold, at the first light of the sun and its rising …

so that “the first light of the sun” means the middle of the night.] when the mesonyctial breath also arises.

5. Days are named from the gods, whose names the Romans consecrated to certain heavenly bodies. They first named the day after the Sun, which is chief among all the stars, just as that day is the head of all days.

6. The second was named after the Moon, which is nearest to the Sun both in brightness and in size and borrows its light from it. The third was named after the star of Mars, called Pyrois.
