[Note: [Col. 0216C] **The star of Mars, which is Pyrois.** We have agreed here with Chacon, as also above, book III, chapter 70, although in all the books *vesper*, “evening star,” is read in both places instead of *Pyrois*.] The fourth was named after the star of Mercury, which some call Stilbon. [Note: [Col. 0216C] **Which some call Stilbon.** The same Chacon also made an excellent conjecture here. The books read: “which some call the bright circle,” but *bright* appears to have been a gloss for Greek *to stilbon*, “the shining one.” An inexperienced reader removed the gloss and added *Stilbon*; *circle* was then lost, although Isidore calls the Milky Way the bright circle in book III, chapter 45. Strong evidence for this is that the word *circle* is still absent from some books.]

7. The fifth was named after the star of Jupiter, which they call Phaethon; the sixth after the star of Venus, which they assert is Lucifer, since it has more light than all the other stars; the seventh after the star of Saturn, which is placed in the seventh heaven and is said to complete its course in thirty years.

8. The pagans therefore gave the days their names from these seven stars, believing that through them something was brought about for them. [Note: [Col. 0216D] **Saying that they receive spirit from the Sun.** Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “owing nothing now to any heavenly power”: “We owe everything to the powers above as long as we live, because, as the physicists say, when we begin to be born we receive spirit from the Sun, body from the Moon, blood from Mars, understanding from Mercury, desire from Jupiter, passions from Venus, and moisture from Saturn.” In what concerns Jupiter, Servius appears to require correction from Isidore. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “Among them the star of Jupiter shines and tempers all things.” For this reason he calls it a health-giving radiance in the *Dream of Scipio*. Bede, chapter 4, assigns slowness to Saturn.] They said that they received spirit from the Sun, body from the Moon, understanding and speech from Mercury, pleasure from Venus, blood from Mars, temperance from Jupiter, and moisture from Saturn. Such was the folly of the pagans, who invented for themselves such ridiculous fictions.

9. Among the Hebrews, the first day is called “one of the Sabbath,” which among us is the Lord’s Day, dedicated by the pagans to the Sun; the second is “second of the Sabbath,” the second feria, which secular people call the day of the Moon; the third is “third of the Sabbath,” the third feria, which they call the day of Mars; the fourth is “fourth of the Sabbath,” the fourth feria, which the pagans call the day of Mercury.

[Col. 0216B] 10. The fifth is “fifth of the Sabbath,” the fifth feria, that is, the fifth day from the Lord’s Day, which the pagans call the day of Jupiter; the sixth is “sixth of the Sabbath,” the sixth feria, which those same pagans call the day of Venus. The Sabbath itself is the seventh day from the Lord’s Day, which the pagans dedicated to Saturn [Note: [Col. 0216D] **And called Saturn’s day.** Augustine, *Against Faustus* XVIII, chapter 5: “You try to introduce Saturn because the pagans called that day Saturn’s day.”] and called Saturn’s day. *Sabbath* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “rest,” because on that day God rested from all his works.

11. [Note: [Col. 0216D] **Better in the vocabulary of the days.** From Augustine on Psalm 93.] In the names of the days, it is better for the ecclesiastical manner of speaking to proceed from the Christian mouth. Nevertheless, if habit should perhaps lead someone to utter what he rejects in his heart, let him understand that all those after whom these days were named were human beings. Because they had achieved and excelled greatly in this world through certain mortal benefits, their admirers transferred divine honors to them, both in the days and in the stars. First the stars were named after human beings, and then the days were named after the stars.

12. The *feriae* are named from *fari*, “to speak,” because on them we have time for speech—that is, for speaking in divine or human service. But among these, festival days were instituted for the sake of human beings, as days of rest for divine rites.

13. [Note: [Col. 0217C] **Parts of the day.** From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] There are three parts of the day: morning, midday, and the final period.

14. Morning is mature and full light, when twilight has already passed. [Note: [Col. 0217C] **And morning is named from *mano*.** From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “he holds the enormous rocks.” Varro, book V: “*Mane*, because then the day flows from the east,” unless rather because the ancients called what is good *manum*. See also Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “the altars stand in the presence of the spirits.”] Morning is called *mane* from *manus*: the ancients called a good thing *manum*. What is better than light? Others think morning is called from the *manes*, whose dwelling is from the Moon to the earth. Others think it comes from the air, because *manus* means thin and transparent.

222

15. Midday is called as though *medidies*, that is, “middle of the day,” or because the day is then purer. For *merum* means “pure.” In the whole day nothing is clearer than midday, when the Sun gleams from the middle of the sky and illuminates the entire sphere with equal brightness.

[Col. 0217B] 16. [Note: [Col. 0217D] **The final period is the last.** Varro: “*Suprema*, the highest part of the day, from *superrima*. The Twelve Tables call this time sunset.”] The final period is the last part of the day, when the Sun turns its course toward setting. It is so called because what remains of the day belongs to its final part.

17. [Note: [Col. 0217D] **Late.** Others read *sero*, “late.”] Late is so called from closed bolts, when night has already arrived, so that everyone may be safer in sleep.

18. *Hodie*, “today,” is as though *hoc die*, “on this day”; and *quotidie*, not *cotidie*, so that it means “on each day.”

19. [Note: [Col. 0217D] **Tomorrow, which means afterward.** Something seems to be missing, and perhaps *postera*, “the following day,” should be read.] Tomorrow means afterward.

20. Yesterday is the day before, and it is called *hesternum* because that day has already become foreign and alien to us by passing away.

21. *Pridie* means, as it were, “on the preceding day.”

22. *Perendie*, “the day after tomorrow,” means “through the preceding day,” or “in advance,” that is, beforehand. [Note: [Col. 0217D] **In advance**, that is, beforehand. A gloss reads *in antecessum*, Greek *prochreia*; and Seneca says *in antecessum solvere*, “to pay in advance,” that is, before the due date arrives.]

# CHAPTER XXXI. On night

[Col. 0217C]

1. Night is named from harming, because it harms the eyes. [Note: [Col. 0217D] **Night is so called.** From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “black night lies upon the sea.” Rabanus, book X, chapter 6: “Night is so called because it harms the eyes or human activities, or because in it thieves and robbers find an opportunity to harm others. Unless it is rather from Greek *nyx*, as Varro says.”] It has the light of the Moon and stars for this reason: so that it would not be unbecoming, so that it might console everyone working at night, and so that it might provide sufficient illumination for certain living creatures unable to bear the Sun’s light. [Note: [Col. 0218C] **So that it might console human beings.** Others read “everyone.”]

2. The alternation of night and day was established both for the alternation of sleeping and waking and so that the rest of night might temper the labor of daytime work.

3. [Note: [Col. 0218C] **Night occurs … light.** Lucretius, book V:

> But night overwhelms the earth with immense darkness;  
> either when the Sun, wearied by its long journey,  
> has driven to the outermost part of heaven  
> and, weakened by its course, breathed out its fires,  
> shaken by its journey and enfeebled by much air;  
> or because the same force above compels it  
> to turn its course beneath the earth,  
> the force that carried its sphere above the earth.] Night occurs either because the Sun is wearied by its long journey and, when it reaches the farthest region of heaven, grows weak and breathes out its exhausted fires; or because it is forced beneath the earth by the same force with which it carried its light above the earth, and thus the shadow of the earth creates night. Hence Virgil also says:

> Night rushes up from Ocean,  
> enveloping earth and heaven in great shadow.

4. [Note: [Col. 0218D] **The parts of night.** Servius, *Aeneid* II: “According to Varro, the solid divisions of night are evening, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, and the morning light.”] The parts of night are seven: evening, twilight, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

5. Evening is named from the western star, which follows the setting Sun and precedes the darkness that follows. Virgil speaks of it:

> Before day, Vesper will put all things to rest with Olympus closed.

6. Darkness is so called because it holds shadows.

7. Twilight is uncertain light. For we call something *creperum*, “doubtful,” that is, between light and darkness. [Note: [Col. 0218D] **Uncertain.** Ambrose elegantly says: “May this joyful day pass; let modesty be like dawn, faith like midday; let the mind know no twilight.” *Creperum* is a Sabine word, as Varro says.]

[Col. 0218B] 8. The time of silence is when everything is quiet. For *conticescere* means “to be silent.”

9. [Note: [Col. 0218D] **The dead of night … that is, without activity.** All this is from Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “the untimely night held sway.”] The dead of night is the middle and inactive period of night, when nothing can be done and everything is quiet in sleep. For time in itself is not understood except through human activities; the middle of the night is without activity.

224

10. Therefore *intempesta* means inactive, as though “without time,” that is, without activity, by which time is distinguished. Hence the phrase, “You came at an inopportune time.” Thus *intempesta* is so called because it lacks time, that is, activity.

11. Cockcrow is so called because the cocks announce the light.

12. Morning is the interval between the departure of darkness and the arrival of dawn. It is called *matutinum* because at this time morning begins.

[Col. 0218C] 13. Dawn is as though the small light of day already beginning. It is also called *aurora*, because it precedes the Sun.

14. [Note: [Col. 0218D] **Dawn.** From the same passage, *Aeneid* XI. Varro, however, book VI: “*Aurora* is called the time before sunrise because then the air grows golden (*aurescit*) from the Sun’s fire.”] Dawn is the beginning of the day’s brightening and the first radiance of the air. In Greek it is called *eōs* (ἠώς); by derivation we call it *aurora*, as though *eorora*. Hence the line:

> The joyful East Wind with Eastern horses,

and:

> The Eastern battle lines.

# CHAPTER XXXII. On the week

1. The week is named from the number seven, because through the repetition of its days months, years, and centuries are completed; for the Greeks call seven *hepta* (ἑπτά). We call it *septimana*, as though “seven lights,” for *mane* means “light.” The eighth day is also the first day, to which the cycle returns and from which the sequence of weeks begins again.

# CHAPTER XXXIII. On months

1. *Month* is a Greek word derived from the name of the Moon. For the Moon is called *mēnē* (μήνη) in Greek. Hence among the Hebrews the official months are counted not from the Sun’s cycle but from the Moon’s course, which runs from new moon to new moon.

225

2. The Egyptians, however, being concerned with the Moon’s faster course and wishing to prevent an error in calculation caused by its speed, devised the length of a month from the Sun’s course, since the Sun’s slower movement could more easily be measured.

3. [Note: [Col. 0219D] **January … or because it is the boundary and gate.** Jerome, *Commentary on Ezekiel* XXVIII: “January is so called because among the Romans it is the gate of the year.” It is surprising that all the books read *limes*, “boundary,” rather than *limen*, “threshold.”] January is named from Janus, to whom it was consecrated by the pagans, or because it is the threshold and gate of the year. Hence Janus is also depicted with two faces, to show the entrance and exit of the year.

4. February is named from *Februus*, that is, Pluto, to whom sacrifices were offered in that month. For the Romans consecrated January to the heavenly gods and February to the spirits of the dead. Therefore February is named from *Februus*, that is, from Pluto, not from fever, that is, illness. [Note: [Col. 0219D] **February from *Februus*.** Varro derives it from *februatus*, “purified”; Macrobius from Februus, the god of purification; Censorinus from *februum*, that is, “purification.” Isidore followed Servius, *Georgics* I, and Augustine, *Against Faustus* XVIII, chapter 5.]

5. March is named from Mars, the founder of the Roman people, or because at that time all living creatures are driven toward the male and toward the pleasure of intercourse.

[Col. 0219C] 6. It is also called the month of new things, because March is the beginning of the year. It is likewise called the new spring, from the signs—namely, the shoots—because in it, when new fruits become green, the end of what has passed is demonstrated. [Note: [Col. 0219D] **The same, “new spring,” from the signs.** Servius, *Georgics* I, on “in the new spring.” Others read “from the beginnings.”] [Note: [Col. 0219D] **The same, “new spring,” from the signs.**]

7. [Note: [Col. 0219D] **April … as though Aphrodis.** Macrobius, book I, chapter 12: “He named the second month April, as though *Aphril*, from the foam, which the Greeks call *aphros* (ἀφρός), from which Venus is believed to have arisen.”] April is named for Venus, as though *Aphrodis*. For Venus is called *Aphrodite* (Ἀφροδίτη) in Greek. [Note: [Col. 0219D] **Or because in this month everything opens into flower.** This opinion pleased Varro.] Or it is so called because in this month everything opens into flower, as though *aperilis*, “opening.”

8. May is named from Maia, the mother of Mercury, or from the elders, who were the leading men of the commonwealth. For the Romans consecrated this month to the elders and the following month to the younger men.

9. Hence June is also so called. Formerly the people had been divided into centuries of elders and juniors.

226

10. [Note: [Col. 0220D] **Julius and Augustus.** Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II, chapter 21.] July and August were named from the honors paid to the men Julius and Augustus Caesar. [Col. 0220A] Previously they were called Quintilis and Sextilis: Quintilis because it was the fifth month from March, which the Romans testify was the first month of the year; Sextilis similarly because it was the sixth.

11. September takes its name from number and rain, because it is the seventh month from March and brings rain. Thus October, November, and December likewise received their names from number and rain; December brings the sequence of numbers to an end, because the number ten closes the preceding numbers.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] From number and rain. Varro, Augustine, and Servius derive it from number alone; Isidore undoubtedly took this from Servius. But all these explanations are full of additions. Although I know that Cassiodorus also derived the name from rain.]

12. The Romans instituted the Kalends, Nones, and Ides either because of the festival days or because of the official duties of magistrates. On those days people gathered in the cities.

13. Some, however, think that the Kalends are so called from *colere*, “to cultivate” or “to worship.” Among the ancients, the beginnings of all the months were celebrated, as also among the Hebrews. Most Latins, however, think that the Ides were named from *edere*, “to eat,” because among the ancients those days were occasions for banquets.

14. The Nones were called from the *nundinae*, for the *nundinae* are public gatherings or markets.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR. On the Solstices and Equinoxes

1. “Solstice” is so called as if it meant “the sun’s standing,” because at that time, when the sun stands still, the days or nights grow longer.

“Equinox” is so called because at that time day and night remain equal in duration of hours.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] They remain equal in duration. Thus all our Roman manuscripts consistently read.]

2. There are two solstices: one in summer, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, at which time the sun begins to return toward the lower circles; the other in winter, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, at which time the sun begins to seek the higher circles. Hence the day of the winter solstice is found to be the shortest, just as that of the summer solstice is the longest.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] There are two. From Servius, *Georgics* I, on “Moist solstices.” But the better Latin authors recognize only the summer solstice; they call the other not a solstice but the winter season, *bruma*.]

3. There are likewise two equinoxes: one in spring and the other in autumn, which the Greeks call *ἰσημερίαι* (“equinoxes”). These equinoxes occur on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and the eighth day before the Kalends of October, because formerly the year was divided into only two parts, namely, the summer and winter solstices, and into two hemispheres.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] And into two hemispheres. All the books read this way. A. Augustine wanted it to read “into two *equinoxes*,” *ἰσημερίας*.]

## CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE. On the Seasons of the Year

1. There are four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They are called seasons from the tempering of things in common, because they temper one another through moisture, dryness, heat, and cold.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] From the tempering of what they share. One Roman manuscript reads “from the common tempering.”]

They are also called courses, because they do not stand still but run.

[Col. 0221A]

2. It is agreed that, after the creation of the world, the seasons were divided according to the character and course of the sun into three-month periods. The ancients distinguish these seasons in the following way: in the first month spring is called “new,” in the second “mature,” and in the third “declining.”

[Note: [Col. 0221C] It is agreed that after the creation. From two passages of Servius, *Georgics* I, on “New spring,” and *Georgics* II, on “Not otherwise at first.”]

3. Summer likewise is called new, mature, and declining in its three months; so also autumn is new, mature, and declining; likewise winter is new, mature, and declining, or “extreme.” Hence the line: “At the fall of extreme winter.”

Spring is so called because it becomes green. For then, after winter, the earth is clothed with grasses, and everything bursts into flower.

[Note: [Col. 0221C] Everything bursts open. Other manuscripts read “breaks forth” or “pushes forth.”]

4. Summer is called from *aestus*, “heat,” that is, from warmth; and *aestas* is as if from *usta*, “burned,” that is, scorched and dry. For heat is dry.

[Note: [Col. 0221C] Summer from heat. Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “And the burning heat draws nearer”: “Heat,” he says, “is warmth; hence summer is so called.” See Varro, book V.]

5. Autumn is called from the season, when the leaves of the trees also fall and everything ripens.

[Note: [Col. 0221C] Autumn from the season. Does he understand *tempestas* as “seasonableness”? Thus *autumnus* would be *auctus annus*, “the increased year,” with the *c* removed, as in *sartor*, *fartor*, *auctor*. Festus: “Some think autumn was so called because at that time human resources are especially increased.”]

6. Winter was named according to the nature of the hemisphere, because at that time the sun moves through a shorter circle. Hence this season is also called *bruma*, as if from Greek *βραχὺς ἡμέρα*, “a short day,” or from food, because the appetite for eating is then greater. Gluttony is called *βρῶμα* in Greek; hence those who have an aversion to food are also said to be *imbrumari*.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] *Bruma*, as if from *βραχύς* (“short”). Varro, Festus, Servius, and Macrobius.]

[Note: [Col. 0221D] Hence also *imbrumari*. Other manuscripts read *imbrumati*, likewise *brumati* and *brumatici*, a word still in use among us.]

[Note: [Col. 0221D] Those who have an aversion to food. One Tarrac manuscript reads, “those who have an interest in food.”]

7. *Hibernus* (“wintry”) lies between winter and spring, as if *hiemevernus* (“winter-spring”); it generally signifies the whole winter by reference to one part of it. These seasons are also assigned to the several regions of the sky.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] As if *hiemevernus*. From the Neapolitan and Oviedo manuscripts; others read *hibernus*, so that it means “declining winter.”]

8. Spring is assigned to the East, because then everything rises from the earth; summer to the South, because that region is more fiercely ablaze with heat; winter to the North, because it is numb with cold and perpetual frost; and autumn to the West, because it brings serious illnesses. Hence the leaves of the trees fall at that time.

Autumn’s abundance of illnesses is caused by this boundary between cold and heat, and by the conflict between opposing kinds of air.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] From the conflict of contrary airs. Servius, *Georgics* I, on “What weather the autumn has”: “From the conflict of contrary things.”]

## CHAPTER THIRTY-SIX. On Years

1. A year is the sun’s circuit, when, after 365 days have been completed, it returns to the same regions of the stars. The year is so called because it turns through months that return within it. Hence also *annulus* (“ring”), as if *annuus* (“annual”), that is, a circle, because it returns into itself. Virgil:

> And the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] “A year is.” The whole chapter up to *aera* is compiled from various passages of Servius, *Aeneid* I, III, and V.]

2. Thus among the Egyptians too, before letters were invented, the year was represented by a painted dragon biting its own tail, because it returns into itself. Others say that “year” comes from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνανεοῦσθαι*, “from renewal,” for it is always renewed.

3. There are three kinds of years. One is the lunar year of thirty days; another is the solar year, which contains twelve months; and another is the great year, when all the planets return to the same place, which occurs after very many solar years.

[Col. 0222B]

4. The era of individual years was established by Caesar Augustus, when he first levied the census and registered the Roman world. It was called an *aera* because the whole world professed that it would pay bronze or money to the republic.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] The era of individual years. This is found in most manuscripts of Eusebius, but Chacon denied that it existed in the oldest ones. Concerning the *aera*, many people in our age have written much. We trust Nonius, who writes as follows: “*Aera*, a mark of reckoning.” Lucilius, book XXIX: “This is a reckoning: a distorted *aera*, a total, and a sum dishonestly subtracted.” Marcus Tullius, in *Hortensius*, quoted by the same Nonius: “What do you usually do, I ask, when you receive an account from the steward? If you have approved the individual amounts, do you not approve the total formed from them?” See below, book VI, chapter 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0222C] When he levied the census. Thus book III. The Tarrac manuscript of Naples reads, “when the census was driven out”; and the expression is frequent in Eusebius: “When the census was conducted at Rome, so many thousands of people were found,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN. On Olympiads, Lustrums, and Jubilees

1. The Olympiad was established among the Greeks at Elis, a city of Greece. The Eleans conducted a contest, a five-year competition, with four intervening years left vacant; and for this reason they called the period of the contest at Elis an Olympiad, reckoning four years within one Olympiad.

[Note: [Col. 0222C] And a five-year contest. Eusebius, *Chronicle*: “The Eleans conduct a five-year contest; after four intervening years have been completed, Iphitus, son of Praxonides or Haemodius, first established what is called an Olympiad.”]

2. A lustrum is a *πεντετηρίς* (“period of five years”), which is said by the Romans to be completed in the fifth year because of the Olympiads; for at that time there were not yet consuls or eras. It is therefore a five-year period. It is so called because, after the census had been completed every five years in the republic, the city of Rome was purified.

[Note: [Col. 0222D] “A lustrum.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Age conquers through five-year periods”: “He reckons time in five-year periods and properly in Olympiads, because there were not yet eras or consuls.” The words “for there were not yet consuls or eras” serve only Servius’ interpretation of Virgil and do not detract from Isidore. Isidore, while reading Servius, does not seem to have considered Virgil’s words. You may interpret *propter Olympiadas* as “for the Olympiads” or “in place of Olympiads.”]

3. “Jubilee” is interpreted as “the year of remission.” It is a Hebrew word and number, formed from seven weeks of years, that is, forty-nine years. In it trumpets were sounded, the ancient property returned to everyone, debts were released, and liberties were confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0222D] And a number that is composed of seven years … of the Holy Spirit. From Jerome, on Amos, chapter 5; and Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 8.]

4. We also celebrate this number in the days of Pentecost after the Lord’s Resurrection, with guilt remitted and the written record of every debt canceled, receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit that comes upon us as people freed from every bond.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT. On Ages and Periods

1. Ages consist of generations, and are called *saecula* because they follow one another. As some depart, others succeed them.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Ages consist of generations. One Neapolitan manuscript reads, “Six ages consist of generations,” but, I think, without any intelligible sense.]

Some say that this is the fiftieth year, which the Hebrews call the Jubilee.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Some say this. From Jerome, *Commentary on Galatians* II.]

2. For this reason, the Hebrew slave who, because he loves his wife and children, loves his master and is subjected to slavery with his ear pierced is ordered to serve “forever,” that is, until the fiftieth year.

3. “Age” is commonly used for one year, as in annals; for seven years, as in the case of a human being; for one hundred years; and for any period of time. Hence an age is also a period formed from many centuries.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] “Age,” as if *aevitas*. For formerly *aevitas* had the same meaning.]

It is called *aetas* as if *aevitas*, that is, a likeness of eternity.

4. For *aevum* is perpetual age, whose beginning and end are unknown; the Greeks call this *αἰῶνες*. Among them the word is sometimes used for an age and sometimes for eternity. Hence it has also been derived into Latin.

5. “Age” properly has two meanings: it may refer to a human being, as infancy, youth, and old age; or to the world. The first age of the world extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation of Judah to Babylon; the fifth thereafter until the coming of the Savior in the flesh; and the sixth, which is now in progress, until this world comes to an end.

6. The course of these periods through generations and kingdoms was first drawn out by one of our writers, Julius Africanus, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, in the style of a simple history. Afterwards Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and Jerome, the presbyter of holy memory, published a multifaceted history in chronological canons, arranged simultaneously by kingdoms and periods.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] “The course of which … may be known as the age of the world.” These words are not found in the older manuscripts, but were nevertheless taken from Isidore’s *Chronicle*.]

7. Afterwards various others followed. Among them, Victor of Tunnuna, especially, bishop of the Church, having reviewed the histories of his predecessors, completed the deeds of the succeeding ages up to the consulship of the emperor Justin the Younger.

[Note: [Col. 0224D] Victor of Tunnuna. This should be read in this form from the book *On Illustrious Men*, not, as formerly, “of Tours.”]

8. We have noted a summary of these periods, from the beginning of the world to the emperor Heraclius Augustus and the Gothic king Suinthila, with as much brevity as we could manage. Alongside it runs a descending line of chronology, by whose indication the summary of the past ages of the world may be known.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE. On the Division of Time

[Col. 0224A]

1. The first age contains, at its beginning, the creation of the world. On the first day God created the angels under the name of light; on the second, the heavens under the name of firmament; on the third, the form of the waters and the earth under the name of separation; on the fourth, the lights of heaven; on the fifth, living creatures from the waters; and on the sixth, living creatures from the earth and the human being, whom he called Adam.

2. In the year 230 Adam begot Seth, from whom came the sons of God: 230. In the year 205 Seth begot Enos, who began to invoke the name of the Lord: 435. In the year 190 Enos begot Cainan: 625. In the year 170 Cainan begot Mahalaleel: 715.

[Col. 0224B]

3. In the year 165 Mahalaleel begot Jared: 960. In the year 172 Jared begot Enoch, who was taken up: 1,122. In the year 165 Enoch begot Methuselah: 1,287.

4. In the year 167 Methuselah begot Lamech: 1,454. In the year 188 Lamech begot Noah. The ark was built: 1,643. In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood occurred: 2,242.

### The Second Age

5. In the second year after the Flood, Shem begot Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldeans: 2,244. In the year 135 Arphaxad begot Shelah, from whom came the Samaritans and Indians: 2,379. In the year 130 Shelah begot Eber, from whom came the Hebrews: 2,509.

6. In the year 134 Eber begot Peleg. The tower was built: 2,643. In the year 130 Peleg begot Reu. The gods were first worshiped: 2,773. In the year 132 Reu begot Serug. The kingdom of the Scythians began: 2,905.

7. In the year 130 Serug begot Nahor. The kingdom of the Egyptians arose: 3,035. In the year 79 Nahor begot Terah. The kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose: 3,114. In the year 70 Terah begot Abraham. Zoroaster discovered magic: 3,184.

[Col. 0224D]

### The Third Age

8. In Abraham’s hundredth year he begot Isaac; for Ishmael had been born earlier, from whom also came the Ishmaelites: 3,284. In his sixtieth year Isaac begot Jacob. The kingdom of the Argives began: 3,344. In his ninety-first year Jacob begot Joseph. Phoroneus gave laws to Greece: 3,435.

9. Joseph lived 110 years. Greece began to have crops: 3,545. The Hebrews’ enslavement in Egypt lasted 144 years. Atlas discovered astrology: 3,689. Moses ruled the people in the wilderness for 40 years. The Hebrews began to have the law and letters: 3,729.

10. Joshua, for 27 years. Erichthonius was the first in Greece to yoke a four-horse chariot: 3,756. Othniel, for 40 years. Cadmus gave letters to the Greeks: 3,796. Ehud, for 80 years. Fables were invented: 3,876. Deborah, for 60 years. Apollo discovered the art of medicine and invented the lyre: 3,916.

11. Gideon, for 40 years. Mercury constructed the lyre: 3,956. Abimelech, for 3 years. The chorus was invented in Greece: 3,959. Tola, for 23 years. Priam reigned in Troy: 3,982. Jair, for 22 years. Carmentis discovered the Latin letters: 4,004. Jephthah, for 6 years. Hercules threw himself into the flames: 4,010. Ibzan, for 7 years. Alexander abducted Helen: 4,017.

12. Abdon, for 8 years. Troy was captured: 4,025. Samson, for 20 years. Ascanius founded Alba: 4,045. Eli the priest, for 40 years. The Ark of the Covenant was captured: 4,085. Samuel, for 40 years. Homer is thought to have existed: 4,125.

### The Fourth Age

13. David, for 40 years. Carthage was founded by Dido. Gad, Nathan, and Asaph prophesied: 4,165. Solomon, for 40 years. The Temple was built in Jerusalem: 4,205.

14. Rehoboam, for 17 years. The kingdom of Israel and Judah was divided: 4,222. Abijah, for 3 years, under whom Abimelech was high priest: 4,225. Asa, for 41 years. Ahijah, Amos, Jehu, Joel, and Azariah prophesied: 4,266.

15. Jehoshaphat, for 25 years. Elijah, Obadiah, and Micah prophesied: 4,291. Jehoram, for 8 years. Elijah and Elisha prophesied: 4,299. Ahaziah, for 1 year. Elijah was taken up: 4,300. Athaliah, for 7 years. The priest Jehonadab became renowned: 4,307.

16. Joash, for 40 years. Elisha died: 4,347. Amaziah, for 29 years. Carthage was founded: 4,376. Uzziah, for 52 years. The Olympiad was established by the Greeks: 4,428. Jotham, for 16 years. Romulus was born: 4,444.

17. Ahaz, for 16 years. Rome was founded: 4,460. Hezekiah, for 29 years. The Senate was established at Rome: 4,489. Manasseh, for 55 years. The Samian Sibyl became renowned: 4,544. Amon, for 12 years. The census was first conducted: 4,556.

18. Josiah, for 32 years. The philosopher Thales became known: 4,588. Jehoiakim, for 11 years. Nebuchadnezzar captured Judea: 4,599. Zedekiah, for 11 years. The Temple at Jerusalem was burned. The woman Sappho became renowned for poetry of a different kind: 4,610.

### The Fifth Age

19. The captivity of the Hebrews lasted 70 years. The history of Judith was written: 4,680. Darius, for 34 years. The captivity of the Jews was ended: 4,714. Xerxes, for 20 years. Sophocles and Euripides were celebrated as tragedians: 4,734.

20. Artaxerxes, for 40 years. Ezra renewed the law that had been burned: 4,774. Darius, also called Nothus, for 19 years. This age had Plato and Gorgias, the first of the rhetoricians: 4,793. Artaxerxes, for 40 years. The history of Esther was completed: 4,833.

21. Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, for 26 years. Demosthenes and Aristotle were celebrated: 4,859. Xerxes, for 4 years. Xenocrates was held in high esteem: 4,863. Darius, for 6 years. Alexander seized Jerusalem: 4,869.

22. Alexander of Macedon, for 5 years. He gained possession of Asia: 4,874. Ptolemy, for 40 years. The first book of the Maccabees began: 4,914. Philadelphus, for 38 years. The seventy interpreters became known: 4,952. Euergetes, for 26 years. Jesus composed the Book of Wisdom: 4,978.

23. Philopator, for 17 years. The history of the second book of the Maccabees was composed: 4,995. Epiphanes, for 24 years. The Romans gained possession of the Greeks: 5,019. Philometor, for 35 years. Scipio conquered Africa: 5,054.

24. Euergetes, for 29 years. Brutus subdued Spain: 5,083. Soter, for 17 years. The Thracians were subjected to the Romans: 5,100. Alexander, for 10 years. Syria was subjected to the Romans: 5,110.

25. Ptolemy, for 8 years. The art of rhetoric began at Rome: 5,118. Dionysius, for 30 years. Pompey captured Judea: 5,148. Cleopatra, for 2 years. Egypt was subjected to the Romans: 5,150. Julius Caesar, for 5 years. He was the first to hold sole rule: 5,155.

### The Sixth Age

26. Octavianus, for 56 years. Christ was born: 5,211. Tiberius, for 23 years. Christ was crucified: 5,234. Gaius Caligula, for 4 years. Matthew wrote the Gospel: 5,233.

27. Claudius, for 14 years. Mark published the Gospel: 5,252. Nero, for 14 years. Peter and Paul were killed: 5,266. Vespasian, for 10 years. Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus: 5,276.

28. Titus, for 2 years. He was eloquent and devout: 5,278. Domitian, for 16 years. John was exiled to Patmos: 5,294. Nerva, for 1 year. John returned to Ephesus: 5,295. Trajan, for 19 years. The Apostle John died: 5,314.

29. Hadrian, for 21 years. Aquila was regarded as an interpreter: 5,335. Antoninus Pius, for 22 years. Valentinus and Marcion became known: 5,357. Antoninus, for 19 years. The heresy of the Cataphrygians arose: 5,376.

30. Commodus, for 13 years. Theodotion was regarded as an interpreter: 5,389. Aelius Pertinax, for 1 year. His history contains nothing: 5,390. Severus, for 18 years. Symmachus was regarded as an interpreter: 5,407.

31. Antoninus Caracalla, for 7 years. The Fifth Edition was found at Jerusalem: 5,415. Macrinus, for 1 year. The brevity of his life has no deeds worth recording: 5,416. Aurelius Antoninus, for 4 years. The heresy of Sabellius arose: 5,420.

32. Alexander, for 13 years. Origen was held in high esteem: 5,433. Maximinus, for 3 years. He defeated the Germans: 5,436. Gordian, for 7 years. He celebrated a triumph over the Parthians and Persians: 5,443.

33. Philip, for 7 years. He was the first Christian emperor: 5,450. Decius, for 1 year. Antony the monk became renowned: 5,451. Gallus, for 2 years. Novatus founded a heresy: 5,453. Valerian, for 15 years. Cyprian was crowned with martyrdom: 5,468.

34. Claudius, for 2 years. He expelled the Goths from Illyricum: 5,470. Aurelian, for 5 years. He persecuted the Christians: 5,475. Tacitus, for 1 year. Because of the brevity of his life, no notation is supplied: 5,476.

35. Probus, for 6 years. The heresy of the Manichaeans arose: 5,482. Carus, for 2 years. He celebrated a triumph over the Persians: 5,484. Diocletian, for 20 years. By burning the divine books, he produced martyrs: 5,504. Galerius, for 2 years. The brevity of his life contributed nothing worthy to history: 5,506.

36. Constantine, for 30 years. The Council of Nicaea was convened: 5,536. Constantius, for 24 years. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites arose: 5,560. Julian, for 2 years. He was changed from a Christian into a pagan: 5,562.

37. Jovian, for 1 year. He became a Christian again: 5,563. Valens, for 14 years. The Goths became heretics: 5,577. Gratian, for 6 years. Priscillian became known: 5,583. Valentinian, for 7 years. Jerome was preaching at Bethlehem: 5,590. Theodosius, for 3 years. John the anchorite became renowned: 5,593.

38. Arcadius, for 13 years. John Chrysostom flourished: 5,606. Honorius, for 15 years. Augustine became renowned as a bishop: 5,621. Theodosius, for 27 years. Nestorius became a heresiarch: 5,648.

39. Marcian, for 6 years. The Council of Chalcedon was held: 5,654. Leo the Great, for 16 years. Egypt rages in the error of Dioscorus: 5,670. Zeno, for 17 years. The heresy of the Acephali arose: 5,687.

40. Anastasius, for 27 years. Bishop Fulgentius was acclaimed: 5,714. Justin, for 8 years. The heresy of the Acephali was repudiated: 5,722. Justinian, for 39 years. The Vandals were destroyed in Africa: 5,761. Justin, for 11 years. The Armenians accepted the faith of Christ: 5,722.

41. Tiberius, for 7 years. The Lombards seized Italy: 5,779. Maurice, for 21 years. The Goths became Catholics: 5,800. Phocas, for 8 years. The Romans were slaughtered by the Persians: 5,808.

42. Heraclius is now in the seventeenth year of his reign; the Jews of Spain are becoming Christians. The remainder of the sixth age is known to God alone.

# BOOK SIX. ON ECCLESIASTICAL BOOKS AND OFFICES

[Col. 0229]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Old and New Testament

[Col. 0229A]

1. The Old Testament is so called because, when the New came, it ceased; the Apostle mentions this, saying: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.”

2. The New Testament is so called because it makes things new. For no one learns it except people renewed from their former state through grace and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven.

3. According to the tradition of the Hebrews, Ezra is said to have established the books of the Old Testament at twenty-two, corresponding to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] “The Hebrews, however.” From Jerome’s *Prologue to the Galeate*, his preface to the Books of Kings, and Epiphanius, *On Weights*.]

4. The first order, the Law, consists of five books. The first is *Beresith*, which is Genesis; the second *Veelle Semoth*, which is Exodus; the third *Vaicra*, which is Leviticus; the fourth *Vajedabber*, which is Numbers; and the fifth *Elleaddebarim*, which is Deuteronomy.

5. These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Thora* and the Latins call the Law. Properly speaking, however, “Law” is the name of what was given through Moses.

6. The second order is that of the Prophets, containing eight books. The first is Joshua son of Nun, who is called in Latin *Jesus Nave*; the second is *Sophtin*, which is Judges; the third is Samuel, which is First Kings; the fourth is *Melachim*, which is Second Kings; the fifth is Isaiah; the sixth Jeremiah; the seventh Ezekiel; and the eighth *Thereazar*, which is called the Twelve Prophets. Since these books are joined together because of their brevity, they are counted as one.

7. The third order is that of the Hagiographa, that is, “the writings of holy writers.” It contains nine books. The first is Job; the second the Psalter; the third *Misse*, which is the Proverbs of Solomon; the fourth *Coheleth*, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth *Sir hassirim*, which is the Song of Songs; the sixth Daniel; the seventh *Dibrehajamim*, which is “Words of Days,” that is, Paralipomenon; the eighth Ezra; and the ninth Esther. Together these, namely the fifth, eighth, and ninth books, make twenty-two, as stated above.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] This is Paralipomenon. The words added after this in the printed editions are absent from the manuscript and ought not to be present. For that book was not called the Chronicle, although the name suits it very well, as Jerome says.]

8. Some add Ruth and *Cinoth*, which in Latin is called the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, making twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, corresponding to the twenty-four elders who stand before the presence of the Lord.

9. Among us there is a fourth order of the Old Testament, consisting of those books that are not in the Hebrew canon. The first is the Book of Wisdom; the second Ecclesiasticus; the third Tobit; the fourth Judith; and the fifth and sixth the books of the Maccabees. Although the Jews separate these among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ nevertheless both honors and proclaims them among the divine books.

10. In the New Testament there are two orders. The first is the Evangelical order, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the second is the Apostolic order, containing Paul in fourteen Epistles, Peter in two, John in three, and James and Jude in one each. It also contains the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse of John.

11. The whole of both Testaments is divided in three ways: into history, morals, and allegory. These three are again divided in many ways: what was done and said by God, by angels, or by human beings; what was foretold by the prophets concerning Christ and his body; what concerns the devil and his members; what concerns the old and new people; and what concerns the present age, the future kingdom, and judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Most of this is from Jerome, letter to Paulinus.]

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Writers and Titles of the Holy Books

1. According to the tradition of the Hebrews, the following are regarded as the authors of the Old Testament. Moses was the first to publish the cosmography of divine history in five volumes, which is called the Pentateuch.

2. The Pentateuch is so called from its five volumes: *πέντε* means “five” in Greek, and *τεῦχος* means “volume.”

3. The Book of Genesis is so called because it contains the beginning of the world and the origin of the age.

4. Exodus recounts the departure from Egypt, or the going out, of the people of Israel, and received its name for this reason.

5. Leviticus is so called because it treats the ministries of the Levites and the varieties of sacrifices, and because the whole Levitical order is recorded in it.

6. The Book of Numbers is so called because in it the tribes that went out from Egypt are numbered, and because it contains a description of the forty-two encampments in the wilderness.

7. Deuteronomy is called by a Greek term that is translated into Latin as “second law,” that is, repetition, and a prefiguration of the evangelical law. It contains the earlier things in such a way that everything repeated in it is nevertheless new.

8. The Book of Joshua received its name from Jesus son of Nun, whose history it contains. The Hebrews assert that Joshua himself was its author. In its text, after the crossing of the Jordan, the kingdoms of the enemies are overthrown, the land is divided among the people, and through its individual cities, villages, mountains, and boundaries, spiritual kingdoms are prefigured: the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem.

9. Judges is named from the leaders of the people who ruled Israel after Moses and Joshua, before David and the other kings existed. Samuel is believed to have published this book and Ruth. The Book of Samuel describes Samuel’s birth, priesthood, and deeds, and therefore received its name from him.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] “This book and Ruth.” The words “and Ruth” were absent from many copies, but they should not be rejected, since the same author says so in book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12.]

10. Although this book contains the history of Saul and David, both are nevertheless referred to Samuel because he anointed Saul for kingship and David as the future king. Samuel himself wrote the first part of the book, while David wrote the remainder of it down to the end.

11. *Melachim* is therefore so called because it sets out in chronological order the deeds of the kings of Judah and of the Israelite people. *Melachim* means “of kings” in Hebrew and is translated into Latin as “of Kings.” Jeremiah was the first to bring this book together into a single volume, for previously it had been scattered among the histories of the individual kings.

12. *Paralipomenon* is a Greek word that we may render as “things omitted” or “things left over,” because matters omitted from, or not fully related in, the Law or the Books of Kings are explained here in summary and briefly.

13. Some think that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others, that one of the prophets did; and still others think that Job himself wrote it after the ordeal of his suffering. They reason that the one who endured the struggles of a particular combat should himself recount the victories he achieved.

14. Among the Hebrews, the beginning and end of the Book of Job are composed in prose; but its middle, from the passage where he says, “Let the day perish in which I was born,” to the passage, “Therefore I condemn myself and repent,” proceeds entirely in heroic meter.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “The beginnings and the end.” From Jerome’s preface to the Book of Job.]

15. The Book of Psalms is called *Psalterium* in Greek, *nebel* in Hebrew, and *organum* in Latin. It was called the Book of Psalms because, when one prophet sang to the psaltery, a choir responded in harmony.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “The title includes.” From the letter to Sophronius.]

Its Hebrew title in the Psalms is *Thehilim*, which is translated as “Book of Hymns.”

16. The authors of the psalms are those whose names are placed in the titles: namely Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Jeduthun, and the sons of Korah—Heman the Ezrahite—and the others, whom Ezra gathered into one volume.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “The authors.” From the same letter.]

17. It is agreed that among the Hebrews all the psalms were composed in metrical verse. For, in the manner of the Roman Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, some now proceed in iambics, now resound in Alcaics; now they shine in Sapphics, proceeding in trimeter or tetrameter feet.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “In the manner of the Roman Flaccus.” From the preface to Eusebius’ *Chronicle* and the preface to Job.]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “Now they shine in Sapphics.” Jerome’s text has *tument* (“swell”); the Seguntine manuscript has *tinent*. From this some read *tinniunt* (“ring”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “In trimeter or tetrameter.” Jerome says nothing about trimeter or tetrameter: “Now it proceeds by half-feet.” Chacon wanted this reading, regarding the other as a gloss.]

18. Solomon, son of David and king of Israel, published three volumes according to the number of his names. The first is called *Misle* in Hebrew, *Parables* by the Greeks, and *Proverbs* by the Latins, because in it he displayed figures of speech and images of truth through comparative likenesses.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “Solomon.” From Jerome, on chapter 1 of Ecclesiastes.]

19. He reserved the truth itself for readers to understand. He called the second book *Coheleth*, which is called *Ecclesiastes* in Greek and *Concionator* (“Preacher”) in Latin, because its discourse is directed not specifically to one person, as in Proverbs, but generally to everyone. It teaches that all the things we see in the world are fleeting and brief, and therefore should by no means be desired.

20. He entitled the third book *Sir hassirim*, which is translated into Latin as the Song of Songs. In the form of an epithalamial poem it mystically sings of the union of Christ and the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] “Where, through an epithalamium.” See Origen, *Homily 1 on the Song of Songs*, translated by Jerome.]

It is called the Song of Songs because it is preferred above all the songs found in the sacred Scriptures, just as certain things in the Law are called holy, while the Holy of Holies is greater than them.

21. Josephus and Jerome write that the poems of these three books were composed among the Hebrews in hexameter and pentameter verses.

22. Isaiah, more an evangelist than a prophet, published his book, whose entire text proceeds in eloquent prose.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] “Prose eloquence.” As above, “in prose discourse.” Other manuscripts read “the prose of eloquence.”]

But its song proceeds in hexameter and pentameter verse.

23. Jeremiah likewise published his book together with its Lamentations, which we call *Lamenta* because they are used on sadder occasions and at funerals. In them he composed an alphabet in four different meters. The first two are written, as it were, in Sapphic meter, because three verses joined together and beginning with one and the same letter conclude with a heroic colon.

[Note: “Which we call *Lamenta*”: see the note above, because they were perhaps sung, as Job’s words now are, in connection with funerals in Isidore’s time, in the Office for the Dead.]

24. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and the same three verses begin with each letter in turn. The fourth alphabet is considered similar to the first and second.

25. [Note: “Ezekiel and Daniel”: the same author reports in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, drawing on the opinion of the Hebrews, that these prophecies were imagined not to have been written by the prophets themselves but recorded by others from dreams. Yet in Jerome’s time there seems to have been no doubt concerning Ezekiel. Regarding Daniel’s book, the same author reports that Porphyry claimed it had been written later, a claim refuted by Eusebius, Apollinarius, and Methodius.]

Ezekiel and Daniel are said to have been written by certain wise men. Ezekiel’s beginnings and endings are wrapped in many obscurities. Daniel, however, proclaims the kingdoms of the world in clear language and marks the time of Christ’s coming with the clearest possible prophecy.

26. These are the four prophets who are called Major because they composed lengthy books. The Book of the Twelve Prophets is designated by the names of its authors. They are therefore called Minor because their discourses are brief.

27. Hence they are joined together and contained in a single volume. Their names are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

28. The book of Ezra is designated by the title of its author; in its text the discourses of Ezra himself and of Nehemiah are likewise contained. Let no one be troubled by the fact that it is called one book of Ezra, since the second, third, and fourth are not found among the Hebrews but are classified among the apocrypha.

[Note: “Because the second, third, and fourth are not found among the Hebrews”: because, as Jerome says, the discourses of Ezra and Nehemiah were compressed into one volume, they likewise do not recognize a second book; among us, however, Nehemiah is entitled the Second Book of Ezra.]

29. Ezra is believed to have written the book of Esther. In it the same queen is said, under the figure of the Church, to have rescued God’s people from slavery and death; and, after Haman—whose name means “iniquity”—was killed, the celebration of that day was transmitted to later generations.

30. [Note: “The Book of Wisdom”: from Jerome’s preface, where, in the *Prologue*, he attributes it to Jesus son of Sirach, following Augustine in Book XVII of *The City of God.]

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews, and consequently its style has more the flavor of Greek eloquence. The Jews assert that it belongs to Philo; it is accordingly called *Wisdom* because in it the coming of Christ, who is the Father’s Wisdom, and his Passion are clearly expressed.

31. [Note: “The Book of Ecclesiasticus … which book among the Latins”: it is not surprising that in Isidore’s time it bore the title of Solomon, since Jerome says of it: “I found it designated in Hebrew not as Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but as *Parables*. Joined to it were Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that it might equal Solomon not only in the number of books but also in the kind of subject matter.”]

The book of Ecclesiasticus was certainly composed by Jesus son of Sirach, a Jerusalemite and grandson of Jesus the high priest, whom Zechariah mentions. Among the Latins, this book is designated by the title of Solomon because of the similarity of its eloquence.

32. It is called Ecclesiasticus because it was published with great care and method concerning the discipline of the whole Church and religious conduct. It is also found among the Hebrews, but is considered apocryphal.

33. As for Judith, Tobit, and the books of the Maccabees, it is by no means established by whom they were written. They bear the names of those whose deeds they recount.

34. The four books of the Gospels were written individually by the four evangelists.

35. Matthew was the first to write the Gospel in Hebrew letters and language in Judea. He began his evangelizing with Christ’s human birth, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” He thereby signified that Christ descended bodily from the seed of the patriarchs, as had been promised through the Holy Spirit in the prophets.

36. Mark, second, wrote Christ’s Gospel in Greek eloquence, full of the Holy Spirit, having followed Peter in Italy as his disciple. He began with the prophetic spirit, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord,” to show that, after assuming flesh, Christ preached the Gospel in the world. For Christ himself was also called a prophet, as it is written: “And I have appointed you as a prophet among the nations.”

[Note: “And I have appointed you as a prophet among the nations”: from the Septuagint, τέθεικά σε (“I have appointed you”); the Vulgate has “I have given you.”]

37. Luke, third among all the evangelists and especially learned in the Greek language—indeed, a physician in Greece—wrote the Gospel for the bishop Theophilus. He began with the priestly spirit, saying: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah,” to show that, after his bodily birth and the preaching of the Gospel, Christ became a sacrifice for the salvation of the world.

[Note: “Of the Greek language”: from Jerome’s Letter to Damasus 145; there, however, Luke is said to have written the Gospel in Greek, not in Greece.]

38. For he is the Priest of whom it is said in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” When Christ came, the Jewish priesthood fell silent; the Law and prophecy came to an end.

39. John, fourth, wrote the Gospel last, in Asia. He began with the Word, to show that the same Savior who graciously deigned to be born and suffer for us was himself the Word of God before the ages; that he himself came from heaven and, after his death, returned again to heaven.

40. These are the four evangelists whom the Holy Spirit signified through Ezekiel by means of the four living creatures. They are four living creatures because through the preaching of these men the faith of the Christian religion was disseminated throughout the four regions of the world.

41. They are called living creatures because the Gospel of Christ is preached for the sake of the human soul. They were also full of eyes within and without, because they perceive clearly both what was spoken by the prophets and what had been promised to be fulfilled.

[Note: “And what had been promised to be fulfilled”: from the Neapolitan manuscript; another reading has this in the preceding passage.]

42. Their legs were straight, because there is nothing crooked in the Gospels. Their six wings covered their legs and faces; for the things that had been concealed were revealed at Christ’s coming.

[Note: “Their legs were straight”: from the Septuagint; the Vulgate has “Their feet were straight.”]

43. The word *Gospel* means “good announcement.” In Greek, εὖ means “good,” and ἀγγελία means “announcement.” Hence *angel* is interpreted as “messenger.”

44. The apostle Paul wrote fourteen Epistles. Of these, he wrote nine to seven churches and the remaining ones to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon.

[Note: “Paul the apostle”: likewise in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12, and in Rabanus, Book II of *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 54.]

45. Most Latins consider the Epistle to the Hebrews of uncertain authorship because of the difference in its language. Some suspect that Barnabas wrote it; others that it was written by Clement.

[Note: “To the Hebrews”: from Jerome’s *Catalogue*.]

46. Peter wrote two Epistles bearing his name. They are called Catholic because they were written not merely to one people or city but generally to all nations.

47. James, John, and Jude also wrote Epistles bearing their names.

48. The Acts of the Apostles sets out the beginnings of the Christian faith among the nations and the history of the nascent Church. It is established that Luke the evangelist was the author of the Acts of the Apostles. In this work the infancy of the newborn Church is woven together and the history of the apostles is preserved. Hence it is called the Acts of the Apostles.

49. John the evangelist wrote the book of the Apocalypse at the time when he was exiled to the island of Patmos because of his preaching of the Gospel. *Apocalypse* is translated from Greek into Latin as “revelation.” Revelation means the manifestation of things that had been hidden, as John himself says: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known openly to his servants.”

50. These are the writers of the sacred books. Speaking through the Holy Spirit for our instruction, they composed both commands for living and the rule of faith.

51. Besides these, other books are called apocryphal. They are called *apocrypha*, that is, “secret,” because they are subject to doubt. Their origin is hidden, and they are not attested by the Fathers, through whom the authority of the true Scriptures has come down to us by an absolutely certain and well-known succession. Although some truth is found in these apocryphal books, their many falsehoods deprive them of canonical authority. Sensible people rightly judge that what they contain should not be believed to belong to the persons to whom the books are attributed.

52. For many works are produced by heretics both under the names of prophets and, more recently, under the names of apostles. All of these have been removed from canonical authority through careful examination under the designation “apocrypha.”

## CHAPTER III. On Libraries

1. *Bibliotheca* takes its name from Greek, because books are stored there. For βιβλίων means “of books,” and θήκη means “a repository.”

2. [Note: “The library of the Old Testament”: sacred books are often called a library. Jerome writes in his *Catalogue*: “Eusebius, most devoted to the divine Scriptures, and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, the most diligent investigator of the divine library.” And in his Letter to Marcella 141: “The blessed martyr Pamphilus, wishing to equal Demetrius of Phalerum and Pisistratus in devotion to the sacred library.” Gratian also cites Jerome’s *Prologue to the Library* more than once.]

After the Chaldeans had burned the Law, when the Jews had returned to Jerusalem, Ezra the scribe, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored the library of the Old Testament. He corrected all the books of the Law and the prophets that had been corrupted by foreign peoples and arranged the entire Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

3. [Note: “Among the Greeks”: the whole passage is taken from Aulus Gellius, Book VI, final chapter. See also Athenaeus and Cicero, *On Oratory* III. Eustathius says that Pisistratus used Aristarchus and Zenodotus for this purpose. Plato, in the *Hipparchus*, says that Hipparchus, the son of Pisistratus, brought Homer’s books to Athens and ordered them to be recited at the Panathenaic games.]

Among the Greeks, Pisistratus, tyrant of the Athenians, is believed to have been the first to establish a library. Xerxes later carried it off to Persia, after it had been enlarged by the Athenians and after he had burned Athens. Much later Seleucus Nicator brought it back to Greece.

4. From this arose among kings and other cities the desire to acquire books from various peoples and to translate them into the Greek language through interpreters.

5. Afterward, Alexander the Great and his successors devoted themselves to furnishing libraries with books of every kind, especially Ptolemy surnamed Philadelphus, who was exceptionally skilled in every branch of learning. In his zeal for libraries he emulated Pisistratus and brought into his own library not only the writings of the nations but also the divine Scriptures.

[Note: “Ptolemy … exceptionally skilled in every branch of learning”: the words are from Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 18.]

For in his time seventy thousand books were found at Alexandria.

[Note: “Seventy thousand”: all the books have this number—seventy thousand—in Aulus Gellius and Marcellinus, Book XXII.]

## CHAPTER IV. On Interpreters

1. He also requested the Scriptures of the Old Testament from Eleazar the high priest and arranged for them to be translated from Hebrew into Greek by seventy interpreters, keeping them in the Alexandrian library.

[Note: “And from Eleazar”: from Jerome, *Chronicle*.]

2. For, separated individually in separate cells, they interpreted everything through the Holy Spirit in such a way that nothing was found in one of their copies that differed from the others, not even in the order of the words.

[Note: “Each individually”: Augustine reports the same in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine* and Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 42; Epiphanius also reports it in his book *On Weights and Measures*. Much has been said about this matter by our contemporaries.]

3. There were also other interpreters who translated the sacred utterances from Hebrew into Greek, such as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, as well as that common translation whose author is not apparent and which therefore lacks the interpreter’s name. It is called the Fifth Edition.

[Note: “And the common translation”: these words are not found in Augustine.]

4. Origen also discovered the Sixth and Seventh Editions through extraordinary labor and compared them with the other editions.

[Note: “He found them through extraordinary labor”: from Jerome’s *Catalogue*, under Origen. According to Epiphanius, he found these editions in jars, while Jerome says in his preface to Origen’s homilies translated by him that he found the Fifth Edition on the Actian shore.]

5. The presbyter Jerome, who was skilled in three languages, likewise translated these Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin eloquence and rendered them over with elegance. His translation is deservedly preferred to the others, for it is both more faithful to the words and clearer in the transparency of its meaning, and, being by a Christian interpreter, truer.

[Note: “Whose translation”: from the same work, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*. Augustine, however, applies these words not to Jerome’s translation but to the Itala.]

[Note: “And, as being by a Christian interpreter”: some books omit these words, and they are not found in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; nevertheless, they occur in the older manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER V. On the Person Who First Brought Books to Rome

1. Aemilius Paulus first brought a large supply of books to Rome after defeating Perseus, king of the Macedonians; afterward, Lucullus brought books from the Pontic spoils. After these men, Caesar commissioned Marcus Varro to construct as large a library as possible.

[Note: “Aemilius Paulus”: it must be considered whether Plutarch’s account is sufficient for this claim. In praising Aemilius’ moderation, Plutarch says that he allowed only the king’s books to be given to his sons, who were studying literature, while he did not even wish to look at the piles of gold and silver or the rest of the booty.]

[Note: “Then Lucullus”: Cicero, in *Lucullus* and *On the Ends* III. Isidore attributes this to Lucullus, whereas Pliny, Book VII, chapter 30, attributes it to Pompey, who succeeded Lucullus and completed the war.]

2. Pollio was the first to make libraries public at Rome, both Greek and Latin, adding portraits of the authors in the atrium that he had magnificently built from the spoils of war.

[Note: “The first at Rome”: Pliny, Book VII, chapter 30, says that in the library first made public in the world by Asinius Pollio at Rome from public spoils there stood the image of Marcus Varro, the only image of a living person. Although those kings had established libraries long before Pollio, they perhaps had not made them public—that is, had not made them public institutions.]

## CHAPTER VI. Those Who Established Libraries among Us

1. Among us also, the martyr Pamphilus, whose life Eusebius of Caesarea wrote, first strove to equal Pisistratus in his devotion to the sacred library.

[Note: “Among us”: from Letter 141 to Marcella.]

For he possessed nearly thirty thousand volumes in his own library.

2. Jerome and Gennadius likewise searched throughout the world for ecclesiastical writers and followed them in orderly succession, gathering their studies into a single little index-volume.

## CHAPTER VII. Those Who Wrote Many Works

1. Marcus Terentius Varro wrote innumerable books among the Latins. Among the Greeks, too, Chalcenterus is extolled with extraordinary praise because he published so many books that scarcely anyone among us could copy them all by hand, even if they were works of others.

[Note: “M. T. Varro”: the passage comes from a lost work of Jerome, although Rufinus quotes the relevant section in his *Invective* as follows: “Antiquity admires Marcus Terentius Varro because among the Latins he wrote an innumerable number of books. The Greeks praise Chalcenterus with extraordinary encomia because he composed so many books that none of us could copy the works of others by his own hand.” This was the surname of Didymus of Alexandria, the grammarian, according to Hesychius in his book on those distinguished in the disciplines. See Suidas.]

2. Among our own writers, Origen surpassed both Greeks and Latins in the number of his works and in his labor on the Scriptures. Jerome even admits that he selected six thousand of his books.

[Note: “Six thousand books”: so Rufinus says in his *Apology*, but Jerome accuses him of lying and claims that scarcely a third of that number is reported by Eusebius. Nevertheless, Epiphanius transmitted the same figure as Rufinus.]

3. Yet Augustine surpassed the industry of all these men by his genius and learning. For he wrote so much that no one, even if he worked day and night, could manage not only to write his books but even to read them.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Kinds of Short Works

1. There are three kinds of short works. The first consists of excerpts, called in Greek *scholia*. In them, matters that appear obscure or difficult are touched upon briefly and in summary fashion.

[Note: “Short works”: from Jerome’s preface to his homilies on Ezekiel by Origen, which Rufinus also repeats in his *Invective*.]

2. The second kind consists of homilies, which the Latins call *verba*, “words,” because they are delivered before the people. The third consists of *tomi*, which we call books or volumes. Homilies address the common people, whereas *tomi*, that is, books, contain more extensive discussion. A dialogue is an exchange between two or more persons, which the Latins call a *sermo*. For what the Greeks call *dialogues*, we call *sermones*.

3. A *sermo* is so called because it is “sown” (*seritur*) between the parties. Hence Virgil says:

> They were sowing many things among themselves in varied conversation.

A *tractatus* is a many-sided exposition of one matter, because it draws the meaning into many things, by handling the thought within oneself.

[Note: “Handling the judgment within oneself”: so Augustine’s manuscript A reads, whereas in all books *sentiendi* is found without meaning; or perhaps the phrase derives from *contrectando secum*, “handling it within oneself,” as Chacon suggests.]

4. A *sermo*, a *tractatus*, and a *verbum* differ. A *sermo* requires another person; a *tractatus* is addressed specifically to oneself; a *verbum* is addressed to everyone. Hence one says: “He delivered a word to the people.”

5. *Commentaria* are so called as if they were “with the mind.” They are interpretations, such as legal commentaries and commentaries on the Gospel.

[Note: “Legal commentaries, Gospel commentaries”: A. Augustinus thought that *commenta* had been written precisely instead of *commentaria*. But the same word, now shortened, remains in common speech, so we may suspect that it was used in the same way in Isidore’s time.]

6. An *Apologeticus* is an excuse or defense, in which certain people customarily reply to their accusers. It consists solely in defense or denial, and the name is Greek.

[Note: “Apologeticus”: from Lactantius, Book V, chapter 4.]

7. A *Panegyricus* is a free-flowing and elaborate kind of speech in praise of kings, in whose composition people flatter them with many falsehoods. This evil arose among the Greeks, whose frivolity, equipped with eloquence and an incredible abundance of expression, raised up many clouds of falsehood.

[Note: “Panegyric”: from the same author, Book I, chapter 15.]

8. The books of *Fasti* are those in which kings or consuls are recorded. They are called *Fasti* from the *fasces*, that is, from offices of authority. Hence books are called *Fasti* because they are published concerning kings and consuls.

[Note: “Books of the Fasti … from the fasces”: the author adapted the etymology to the meaning, as he customarily does, although he knew that the word was derived from *fari*, “to speak.”]

[Note: “Hence, and for that reason”: from the Neapolitan manuscript. The remaining manuscripts corrupt the name Ovid.]

9. A *prooemium* is the beginning of a discourse. Prooemia are the beginnings of books, composed before the narration of the case to prepare the ears of the listeners. Many experts in Latin have retained the word without translation; among us, however, this term is translated as *praefatio*, “preface,” as though it meant a preliminary speech.

10. Precepts are teachings that instruct what should or should not be done. An example of what should be done is: “Love your God, and honor your father and your mother.” An example of what should not be done is: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal.”

11. Likewise, the precepts of the pagans either command or forbid. They command what should be done, as in:

> Plow naked; sow naked.

They forbid, as in:

> Do not plant the hazel among the vines, nor seek the topmost branches.

12. Moses was the first to write precepts among the Hebrews. Among the Latins, the seer Martius was the first to compose precepts. Among them is the saying:

> Speak last; be silent first.

[Note: “The poet of Mars”: see Lilius Gyraldus, *Dialogue* 4, on Latin poets.]

13. *Parables* and *problems* indicate by their names that they ought to be examined more deeply. A *parable* itself conveys the likeness of something. Although the word is Greek, it is now used in place of a Latin word. It is well known that in parables—called likenesses of things—the matters under discussion are compared with other things.

14. Problems, which in Latin are called *propositiones*, are questions containing something that must be resolved by discussion.

15. A question is an inquiry, when one asks whether something exists, what it is, or what sort of thing it is.

16. An argument is so called as though it were “clever” or “cleverly discovered,” for proving matters.

17. The Greeks properly call an *epistle* what is translated in Latin as *missa*, “a thing sent.”

18. Before the use of paper and parchment, messages in letters were written on tablets smoothed from wood. Hence those who carried them were called *tabellarii*, “tablet-bearers.”

[Note: “On smoothed tablets”: from Jerome’s Letter 32 to Nicaea.]

## CHAPTER IX. On Wax Tablets

1. Wax tablets are the material of writing, the nurses of little children; they themselves [lacuna] give children intelligence, the beginnings of understanding.

Its use is said to have been first handed down by the Greeks. The Greeks and Etruscans first wrote on wax with iron; afterward the Romans ordered that no one should possess an iron stylus.

[Note: “They themselves give intelligence”: this is a poem of Dracontius, Book II of *On the Creation of the World*.]

Hence it was said among scribes: “Do not cut the wax with iron.” Later it was established that people should write on wax with bones, as Atta indicates in a satire:

> Let us turn the plowshare into wax and plow with an  
> osseous point …

A *stylus* is called in Greek *graphium* and in Latin *scriptorium*. For γραφή means “writing.”

[Note: “As Atta indicates”: concerning why Atta bore this surname, see Festus under *Atta*.]

## CHAPTER X. On Paper

1. Egypt first supplied the use of paper, which began near the Memphitic city. Memphis is a city of the Egyptians, where the use of paper was first discovered, as Lucan says:

> Memphian paper is made from thirsty papyrus.

He called papyrus “thirsty” because it drinks up moisture.

[Note: “The use of paper”: Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 12.]

2. Paper is so called because the covering of the papyrus is torn away piece by piece and glued together. There are many kinds of it. The first and finest is the Augustan, or royal, kind, larger in format and named in honor of Octavian Augustus.

[Note: “Augustan, royal”: Chacon thought “royal” was a gloss.]

3. The second is Livian, named in honor of Livia. The third is called hieratic because it was selected for sacred books; it resembles the Augustan kind but is somewhat darkened.

4. The fourth is Taeniotic, named after a place near Alexandria so called, where it was made. The fifth is Saïtic, named after the town of Sai.

5. The sixth is Cornelian, first made by Cornelius Gallus, prefect of Egypt. The seventh is emporetic, because goods are wrapped in it, since it is less suitable for writing.

[Note: “The sixth, Cornelian”: Pliny says nothing about the Cornelian kind. It is established from Dio and others that Cornelius Gallus was prefect of Egypt under Augustus.]

## CHAPTER XI. On Parchments

1. When the kings of Pergamum needed paper, they first devised parchment. Hence the name *parchment* has been preserved down to the present through succeeding generations.

[Note: “The kings of Pergamum”: Eumenes, king of Pergamum, first devised parchment.]

These are called *membranae* because they are stripped from the limbs of animals.

[Note: “These are also called *membrana*”: the word occurs in both feminine and neuter gender. The glossary has *membranum*, Greek ὑμήν.]

2. At first they were made yellow, that is, saffron-colored; later, white parchment was discovered at Rome. This proved unsuitable because it is easily soiled and harms the readers’ eyesight. More experienced architects, moreover, think that neither gilded ceilings should be installed in libraries nor floors made of anything other than Carystian marble, because the gleam of gold dulls the eyes, while the green of Carystus refreshes them.

3. Those who learn the money-changing trade place myrtle-colored cloth beneath specimens of coins; sculptors of gems repeatedly look at the backs of scarabs, than which nothing is greener; and painters do the same, so that the exertion of their sight may be restored by the color green.

4. Parchments are either white, yellow, or purple. White ones are naturally so. Yellow parchment is two-colored, because one side is dyed by the maker—made saffron-colored. Persius refers to it:

> Now the book is free, and the two-colored parchment, its hairs removed …

5. Purple parchments are dyed purple, so that melted gold and silver may shine forth in the letters.

[Note: “Purple”: Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium on virginity, says: “Parchments are dyed purple, and gold is melted into the letters.” Chacon proposed restoring *liquescit* here.]

## CHAPTER XII. On the Preparation of Books

1. Among the pagans, certain kinds of books were produced in prescribed formats. Poems and letters were made in a shorter form. Histories, however, were written in a larger format, not only on paper or parchment but also on elephant stomach-skins and on woven leaves of mallow and palm.

[Note: “On elephant hides”: hence the expression “elephant books,” unless one prefers to understand ivory codices or ivory tablets, mentioned by Ulpian, *On the Laws* II, chapter 52, and Pomponius, chapter 2 of *On the Origin of Law*.]

2. Cinna refers to this kind of material:

> These poems for you, composed with much wakefulness by the lamps of Aratus,  
> by which we know the aerial fires,  
> written in a light little book of dry mallow,  
> I carried in a little boat as gifts from Prusa.

[Note: “Airy fires”: all the Gothic manuscripts and Basil read *aerios*. Zanchus read *aetherios*, following those who believed that the stars were not fixed in spheres but were carried through the air.]

3. Trimming books first became common in Sicily. At the beginning, they were polished with pumice. Hence Catullus says:

> To whom shall I give this charming new little book,  
> polished just now with dry pumice?

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Names of Books
