1. A *codex* is composed of many books, whereas a *liber* is a single volume. *Codex* is a metaphorical term taken from the trunks of trees—or vines—as though it were a tree-trunk, because it contains within itself a multitude of books like branches.

2. A *volume* is a book named from rolling, as among the Hebrews there are the volume of the Law and the volumes of the prophets.

3. A *liber* is the inner layer of bark that adheres to the wood. Virgil refers to it: “The bark dries on the tall elm.” Hence the book in which we write is also called a *liber*, because before the use of paper or parchment, volumes were made—that is, assembled—from the bark of trees. Hence writers were called *librarii*, after the books of trees.

[Note: “Before the use of paper”: from Jerome’s letter to Nicaea.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On Scribes and Their Instruments

1. It is established that booksellers were formerly called *librarii*. The Greeks call a book βίβλος. *Librarii* are also called *antiquarii*, but *librarii* are those who write both new and old works, whereas *antiquarii* write only old ones; hence they took their name.

2. The word *scriba* derives from writing and expresses the office through the quality of the term.

3. The scribe’s instruments are the reed pen and the quill. By these words are impressed upon pages. The reed is from a tree or plant; the quill is from a bird. Its point is divided in two while unity is preserved throughout the body, I believe, on account of the mystery: so that in its two tips the Old and New Testaments might be signified, through which the sacrament of the Word is expressed, poured out in the blood of the Passion.

4. The reed is called *calamus* because it deposits liquid. Hence among sailors *calare* means “to put down.”

[Note: “Hence among sailors *calare*”: our Spaniards likewise use this word when they say *calar el sombrero*, “to lower the hat,” or *calar la visera*, “to lower the visor,” and in similar expressions. He also wants the intercalary days to have been called so as though they were inserted; see below, chapter 17.]

5. The quill is called *penna* from *pendere*, “to hang,” that is, “to fly.” For, as we have said, it belongs to birds.

6. The pages of books are called *folia*, either from their resemblance to the leaves of trees or because they are made from *follis*, that is, hides customarily stripped from slaughtered animals. Their parts are called *paginae*, because they are joined together with one another.

7. Verses are commonly so called because the ancients wrote in the same way that land is plowed. They first drew the stylus from left to right; then they turned downward and again toward the right. Even today farmers call such a return a *versus*.

[Note: “Because the ancients wrote as the earth is plowed”: the Greeks called this writing βουστροφήδον γράφειν, “to write in the manner of an ox’s turning,” according to Pausanias, Book I of the *Solar Treatises*. Farmers called it a *versus* when, after bringing a furrow to its end, they returned along it to the place where plowing had begun; this is *versum peragere*, according to Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 19.]

8. A *scheda* is something still being corrected and not yet incorporated into books. It is a Greek word, as is *tomus*.

[Note: “*Scheda*”: Charisius, Book I, says: “*Scida*, without aspiration, is a sheet of paper, named from *scindere*, ‘to cut apart’; but others, with aspiration, think *scheda* derives from the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ σχίζειν, ‘from splitting.’”]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Canons of the Gospels

1. Ammonius, bishop of Alexandria, first devised the Canons of the Gospels; Eusebius of Caesarea later followed him and composed them more fully. They were made so that through them we might discover and know which things the other evangelists said in common and which things each said individually.

[Note: “Ammonius”: from Jerome’s *Catalogue* and his preface to the Gospels, and from Eusebius’ preface to the Canons of Ammonius.]

2. There are ten in number. The first contains the numbers in which all four said the same things: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second contains those in which three did so: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The third contains those in which three did so: Matthew, Luke, and John. The fourth contains those in which three did so: Matthew, Mark, and John.

3. The fifth contains those in which two did so: Matthew and Luke. The sixth, those in which two did so: Matthew and Mark. The seventh, those in which two did so: Matthew and John. The eighth, those in which two did so: Mark and Luke. The ninth, those in which two did so: Luke and John.

4. The tenth contains those passages in which each of them said certain things individually. Their arrangement is as follows. A certain number is assigned beside the chapters of each evangelist. Beneath these numbers there is a figure marked in red ochre, which indicates in which canon the number to which the figure is attached is found.

[Note: “Beneath it is placed a certain figure”: from this passage it appears that *aera* means nothing other than a numerical mark. What Isidore calls *aera*, Jerome calls a number; Victor of Capua likewise says in his preface to Tatian’s *Harmony of the Gospels*: “If the attentive reader wishes first to inspect the numbers mentioned, he can easily verify the reading by means of the number-mark once it has been found.” See above, Book V, chapter 34.]

5. For example, if the figure is the first, the passage belongs to the first canon; if the second, to the second; if the third, to the third; and so on in order until the tenth.

6. Therefore, if, after opening any Gospel, you wish to know which of the other evangelists said similar things, take the adjacent chapter number and look for that number in the canon it indicates. There you will find how many evangelists said it and which ones. Then, by searching the text of the individual Gospels for the places indicated by those numbers, you will find the passages in which they said the same things.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Canons of Councils

1. *Canon* in Greek is called *regula* in Latin. It is called a *regula* because it leads straight and never draws anything in another direction. Others have said that it is called a *regula* either because it governs, because it provides a standard for living rightly, or because it corrects whatever is distorted and wrong.

[Note: “A canon”: this chapter appears to have been taken from another volume of Isidore by Braulio, who interpolated and arranged the work into books. For below it is said that the Acts of the councils are contained in this work, and many words from this passage are found in the preface entitled “The Origin of Councils.”]

## Chapter XVI. On the Canons of Councils

2. [Note: “The canons of general councils.” Gratian cites these in *Decretum*, Distinction 15, chapter 1; and Ivo, Book II, Title XI, chapter 16; Panormitanus from chapter 18 of Book VI of the *Etymologies*. The same material is found in the margin of Rabanus from chapter 17.] The canons of general councils began in the time of Constantine. In the preceding years, while persecution was raging, no opportunity was given for teaching the people.

3. Hence Christianity was divided into various heresies, because bishops were not permitted to assemble together except in the time of the emperor mentioned above. For he granted Christians the freedom to gather openly.

[Col. 0243B] 4. Under this emperor also, the holy Fathers, assembling at the Council of Nicaea from every part of the world, handed down, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, the creed that came after the apostles.

5. Among the other councils, we know of four venerable synods that principally embrace the whole faith, like the four Gospels or the equal number of rivers of paradise.

6. The first of these, the Council of Nicaea, was held under the rule of Constantine Augustus by three hundred and eighteen bishops. At it, the blasphemy of Arian perfidy was condemned—the blasphemy that Arius himself asserted concerning the inequality of the Holy Trinity. By means of a creed, the same holy synod defined the Son of God to be consubstantial with God the Father. [Note: “God the Son.”—Some copies read “the Son of God”; so Gratian.]

[Col. 0243C] 7. The second synod was assembled at Constantinople under Theodosius the Elder by one hundred and fifty Fathers. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving the form of the creed that the entire confession of Greeks and Latins proclaims in the churches. [Note: “At Constantinople.” Others read *Constantinopolim*, “to Constantinople.”]

8. [Note: “The third synod.” Before these words Ivo, chapter 20, has: “This synod was held during the time of Damasus, Roman pope; Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem; and Nectarius of Constantinople.” Thus it should be read, not “Nestorius.”] The third synod, the First of Ephesus, was held under Theodosius Augustus the Younger by two hundred bishops. It condemned Nestorius with a just anathema for asserting two persons in Christ, [Note: “Showing that there remains.” Gennadius: “Sixtus, bishop of the city of Rome, describing in a volume the decree of the synod held by him against Nestorius, sent it to the churches of the East and West, confirming that, while two natures remain perfectly in Christ, one person of the Son of God must be believed”; and nearly the same statement occurs again in Leporius.] showing that one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

9. [Note: “The fourth synod.” Before these words Ivo, chapter 21, has: “This synod was held during the time of Celestine, Roman pope, and Juvenal, bishop of Constantinople.” A. Augustinus warned that “bishop of Constantinople” should be read “bishop of Jerusalem.”] The fourth synod, that of Chalcedon, was held under the emperor Marcian by six hundred and thirty priests. In it, with the unanimous judgment of the Fathers, it condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh have one nature; Dioscorus, a certain bishop of Alexandria, his defender; and Nestorius himself, again, together with the other heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and the human nature. [Note: “Christ the Lord.”—Other books, Gratian, Ivo, and Rabanus read “Christ God.”] [Note: “That we confess the nature.” Ivo alone adds after these words: “This synod was held during the time of Leo, Roman pope; Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem; and Anatolius of Constantinople.” Thus it should be read, not “Athanasius.”]

10. These are the four principal synods, proclaiming the doctrine of the faith with the fullest authority. But if there are any councils that the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have decreed, they remain established with complete force after the authority of these four, [Note: “Whose acts are contained in this work.” This phrase ought to have been omitted.] whose acts are contained in this volume.

11. *Synod* is translated from Greek as “a company” or “an assembly.”

12. [Note: “The name *concilium*, that is, in Roman usage.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, at “Nor indeed …”; the words “what a council might be” are shown by the statement of Laelius Felix in Aulus Gellius, Book V, chapter 27: “He who orders not the whole people, but only some part, to be present ought to announce not a *comitia* but a *concilium*.” A. Augustinus taught that this is the correct reading from Cicero and Livy.] The name *council* (*concilium*) is derived from Roman custom. For when legal cases were being heard, everyone assembled in one place and deliberated with a common purpose. Hence *concilium* was named from *common purpose* (*communis intentio*), [Note: “As though *communicilium*.” Thus Rabanus; older books read “as though *consilium*.” One copy from Salmantica, written more than 860 years ago, has “as though *conscilium*,” which, with respect to this passage, is erroneous; yet if the whole matter is examined more carefully, it is not entirely unreasonable. For I have no doubt that *conscilium* was commonly written in Isidore’s time; shortly afterward the same codex has, “or *conscilium* from fellowship,” and so forth. From this spelling I myself constructed two etymologies: either *conscilium* is *concilium*, with the *s* neglected, and this is as though *communicilium*; or it is *consilium*, with the *c* neglected, and this is as though *considium*, with *d* passing into *l*. On this point Festus says: “*Consilium*, either from *consulendo* [consulting], or because the minds of several *consider* one matter.” That this spelling *conscilium* was in use is attested by Pierius Valerianus, Book IX, on *Aeneid* “Counsel of the highest …” Gratian’s correctors did not notice this, although nothing else supports their interpretation so well. We have reproduced the spelling of the ancient codices; once this is recognized, it can easily be corrected or supplemented, so that nothing further remains to be desired.] as though *communicilium*. For the eyelashes are called *cilia*. Hence also *considium*, meaning *consilium*, with the *d* passing into the letter *l*.

267 13. An assembly (*coetus*) is a gathering or congregation, from *coire*, that is, “to come together in one place.” Hence it is also called a *conventus*, just as a *conventus* is an assembly or council formed by the association of many into one.

## Chapter XVII. On the Paschal Cycle

1. [Note: “The Paschal cycle: Hippolytus, bishop.” After the word “bishop” there is a lacuna in the Naples codex. Jerome, in his catalogue, says that he was unable to discover of what city Hippolytus had been bishop. Pope Gelasius makes him bishop of the metropolis of the Arabs (perhaps Bostra), for the subscription of that city is sometimes read in councils. Zonaras and Nicephorus report that he was bishop of the Port of Rome. A marble statue of him seated was discovered at Rome twenty years ago; this Paschal cycle, together with a catalogue of his works—though not complete, because the stone is broken at that point—is inscribed on the sides of the seat.] Bishop Hippolytus was the first to write out the Paschal cycle during the reign of the emperor Alexander. After him, the most approved authors—Eusebius of Caesarea, [Note: “Theophilus.” From the catalogue of Gennadius.] Theophilus of Alexandria, Prosper, also by nationality an Aquitanian, and [Note: “Victorius.” This must unquestionably be read, on the authority of Bede, Book VI, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 48, and of Gennadius, whose words are: “Victorius, an Aquitanian, invited by Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome, composed the Paschal cycle—or, in some copies, *recurrence*—with very careful investigation, after the four earlier writers who had composed one, namely Hippolytus, Eusebius, Theophilus, and Prosper.” Victorius is also found in the oldest books of Salamanca and Alcalá.] Victorius—expanded the calculations for the same feast and published multiple cycles.

2. The most blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, calculated its reckoning over ninety-five years and briefly noted on which day before the Kalends, or under which moon, the Paschal solemnity ought to be celebrated. [Note: “Through five times nineteen.” The Neapolitan copy reads, “through five times ten and nine.”] [Note: “On which day before the Kalends, or under which moon.” Council of Braga II, chapter 9: “On which calendar day, or under which moon.”]

[Col. 0245B] 3. It is called a *cycle* because it is arranged in a circle and embraces the ordered succession of years as though placed in a circle, without variation and without any artifice.

4. Hence it came about that poems of any subject, composed in simple form, were called cyclical. [Note: “Cyclical poems made in simple form.” Others, with Rabanus, read *cyclia*, whether this kind of poem was produced by a certain art, as the interpreter of Aristophanes says in *The Birds*. Indeed, some wished Homer to have been the author of the poem of the Cycle (*Κίκλου ποίημα*), as Philoponus says on Book I of the *Analytics* (*Ἀναλυτικά*). Or whether it was produced rather through ignorance, as Acron thinks concerning Horace’s poem: “Nor will you begin in the manner of an old cyclical poet.” Hence among many Greeks *cyclia* refers to commonplace and marketplace poets.] Hence also the term *laterculum* was used, because it possesses an ordered arrangement of years. [Note: “A layer of years.” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “The order of times is laid out.”] [Note: “From this comes *laterculum*. Thus the better books, and correctly. The Fourth Council of Toledo, at which Isidore was present, chapter 4: “In Spain there is often variation in the proclamation of the Paschal solemnity, for different observance of the *laterculi* sometimes produces the error of the Paschal feast.” And Cedrenus: “The fired brick among the Greeks is called *laterculum* among the Romans,” and so forth. And Jerome, on Ezekiel, chapter 4: “For *brick*, which in Greek is feminine, *ἡ πλίνθος*, Symmachus more clearly translated *πλινθεῖον*, which we may call *laterculum* and *abacus*.”]

10. [Note: “After its completion.” In the printed editions, the years from the creation of the world up to this final year of the cycle are reckoned as 5,912. This is absent from the older manuscripts, and the same number is not found in the others; they read either 5,900, 5,911, or 5,921.] After its completion, one must return to the beginning. In ancient times the Church celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day it happened to fall on. The holy Fathers prohibited this practice at the Council of Nicaea, determining that it was necessary not only to seek the Paschal moon and month, but also to observe the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. For this reason they extended Easter from the fourteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first, so that the Lord’s Day would not be omitted.

[Col. 0248A] 11. [Note: “The word *Pascha*.” From Augustine, Letter 119 to Januarius. See Jerome, on Matthew 26.] The word *Pascha* is not Greek but Hebrew. It is not derived from the Passion, because in Greek *πάσχειν* (*paschein*) means “to suffer,” but it is called *Pascha* from the Hebrew word for “passing over,” because at that time the people of God passed over from Egypt. Hence also the Gospel says: “When Jesus saw that the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father.” [Note: “Because the people passed from Egypt.” Rather, because the angel who struck the houses, seeing the doorposts smeared with the blood of the lamb, passed over them without killing them. So Jerome at the cited passage, and Philo; but these words belong to Augustine.]

12. [Note: “Whose night is therefore called all-vigil.” From Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 19.] Its night is therefore kept as a vigil because of the coming of our King and God, so that the time of his Resurrection may find us not sleeping but keeping watch. There are two explanations for this night: either because on it he received life again when he suffered, or because he will come to judge at the same hour at which he later rose.

13. We celebrate Easter in such a way that we recall to mind not only Christ’s death and Resurrection, but also examine the other events attested concerning him [Note: “Which are attested concerning him.” These words are absent from the best Toledo manuscript.] for their sacramental significance.

14. Because of the beginning of the new life and of the new human being whom we are commanded to put on and to remove the old, cleansing out the old leaven so that we may be a new dough, since “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” the first month was therefore mystically assigned among the months of the year to the celebration of Easter. [Note: “The first month.” We have removed the word *novorum* (“of new things”), since it is absent from Augustine and ought not to be present. See Exodus 12.]

15. The fact that Easter is celebrated on the day of the third week—that is, on whichever day falls between the fourteenth and the twenty-first—signifies that, in the entire period of the world, which is ordered by the number seven of the days, the third age has now disclosed this sacrament.

16. The first age was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In the third, the sacrament formerly concealed in prophetic mystery has been revealed. For this reason also, on account of these three ages of the world, the Lord’s Resurrection lasts three days.

17. The fact that the Paschal day is sought over seven days, from the fourteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first, is due to the number seven itself, by which the meaning of totality is often represented. This number is also attributed to the Church because of its likeness to totality; hence the apostle John writes in the Apocalypse to seven churches.

18. The Church, while still established in this mortal flesh, is signified in Scripture by the name of the moon, because of its very mutability.

19. Diverse observance of opinions concerning the Paschal feast sometimes gives rise to error. The Latins seek the moon of the first month from the third day before the Nones of March through the third day before the Nones of April; and if the fourteenth day of the moon falls on the Lord’s Day, they postpone Easter to another Lord’s Day.

20. The Greeks observe the moon of the first month from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day before the Nones of April; and if the fifteenth day of the moon falls on the Lord’s Day, they celebrate holy Easter. Such disagreement therefore disturbs the Paschal rule between the two groups.

21. A common year is one that has only twelve moons, that is, 354 days. It is called “common” because two such years often proceed in conjunction, so that they follow one another in the Paschal solemnity; for an embolismic year is always solitary. [Note: “Which has only twelve moons.” Others read “twelve lunations.”]

22. An embolismic year is one that is shown to have thirteen lunar months, that is, 384 days. It is the year divinely revealed to holy Moses, in which those who lived farther away were commanded to celebrate the Passover in the second month.

23. *Embolismic* is a Greek word translated into Latin as “super-increase,” because it completes the number of the common years, which are found to lack eleven lunar days.

24. Embolismic and common years are discovered in the following manner. If there are 384 days from the fourteenth moon of the preceding Easter to the fourteenth moon of the following Easter, it is an embolismic year; if 354, it is a common year.

25. A leap day is one day added after four years. For each year, a quarter of the unit increases. When it has completed the unit in the fourth year, it makes one leap day.

26. It is called *bissextus* because, when six is multiplied twice, it makes a unit, which is one day, just as a quarter is named from being multiplied four times; this is the leap day, which the sun produces in the course of the days of the year. [Note: “The sun produces.” We did not think the words that follow should be admitted, although they are read in certain manuscripts, including Gothic ones, such as the copies from Oña and Zaragoza: “Because three days passed without the sun as their author at the beginning of the creation of days. From this, a quarter of the unit increases each year, and in the fourth year it restores a complete day. Hence the Egyptians, inventors of this art, because of the exaltations of the stars, with the sun as author of the day, which was created on the fourth day, added one day to every fourth year in honor of the sun and moon.”] Or it is called so because the year cannot be inserted unless you count the leap day at the Kalends of March—that is, both the first day before the sixth day before the Kalends of March and, after adding the leap day, you repeat another sixth day before the Kalends of March. [Note: “Because the year cannot be inserted.” Others read “because it cannot insert the year.”]

27. From the sixth day before the Kalends of March through the day before the Kalends of January, the leap day is added in the course of the moon, and from that point it is subtracted.

28. The days are called intercalary because they are inserted so that the reckoning of the moon and sun may agree. *Calare* means “to place”; *intercalare*, “to insert.”

29. The Greeks call them *epacts*; the Latins call them annual lunar additions, which revolve within themselves through the number eleven up to thirty. The Egyptians add them for this reason: so that the lunar reckoning may be brought into equality with the solar reckoning.

30. The moon is known to shine, according to its course, for twenty-nine and a half days, and the lunar year contains 354 days. Eleven days remain in relation to the course of the solar year, and the Egyptians add them. [Note: “The moon.”]

31. Hence they are also called “additions.” Without them, you will not discover what day of the moon it is in any year, month, or day. These epacts are always found on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the same lunar phase that occurs on that day.

32. They are contained within a nineteen-year cycle. But when the epacts have reached twenty-nine, which is the nineteen-year cycle, in the following year you no longer add eleven to twenty-nine so as to announce ten after subtracting thirty; instead, you return from that point so as to announce eleven.

## Chapter XVIII. On the Remaining Festivals

1. *Festivity* is named from festive days, as though *festiditas*, because on them only a divine act is performed. The *fasti*, on which legal business is spoken—that is, announced—are opposed to them. *Solemnity* is named from sacred things, being adopted in such a way that it ought not to be changed for the sake of religion. [Note: Others read *solio*, that is, “I make firm.” See Festus.] It is named from *solum*, “firm” and “solid.”

2. *Celebration* is so called because in it nothing earthly, but only heavenly matters, are performed.

3. [Note: “Easter, the first of the feasts.” On these three festivals see Jerome, on Zechariah, chapter 1.] Easter is the first of all the festivals; its name has already been discussed above.

4. Pentecost, like Easter, was a celebrated day among the Hebrews. It is celebrated after five decades from Easter, and from this it received its name. For *πέντε* (*pente*) means “five” in Greek. On that day, according to the Law, loaves of the presentation were offered from the new harvest.

5. The jubilee year in the Old Testament represented its figure; now, again through the figure of a promise, it prefigures eternal rest.

6. [Note: “Epiphany.” This day was dedicated by the Greeks to Christ’s baptism; but, says Saint Maximus, let the one who made it know what especially took place on this day.] *Epiphany* is called in Greek, and in Latin “appearance” or “manifestation.” On that day Christ appeared more manifestly, indicated by a star, as one to be worshiped. This was a figure of the firstfruits of the believing nations.

[Col. 0250C] 7. On that day both the sacrament of the Lord’s baptism and the beginning of the signs performed by the Lord—the changing of water into wine—took place.

8. There are two Epiphanies. The first is the occasion on which Christ, having been born, appeared to the shepherds of the Hebrews when an angel announced it. The second is the occasion on which, among the peoples of the Gentiles, he displayed the cradle of the manger, with a star as guide, to those who were to worship him more manifestly.

277 9. *Scenopegia* is translated from Greek into Latin as “the dedication of the tabernacles.” It was celebrated by the Jews in memory of the expedition when, after setting out from Egypt, they lived in tabernacles; hence the name *Scenopegia*. For *σκηνή* (*skēnē*) means “tabernacle” in Greek. Among the Hebrews this solemnity was celebrated in the month of September.

10. [Note: “Neomenia.” From Jerome, Letter to Sunnia.] *Neomenia* is, among us, the Kalends; among the Hebrews, since the months are reckoned according to the lunar course—and in Greek *μήνη* (*mēnē*) means “moon”—it means “new moon.”

11. Among the Hebrews the days of the Kalends themselves were solemn by legal institution. Concerning them it is said in the psalm: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the distinguished day of your solemnity.”

12. [Note: “Encaenia.” From Augustine, *Tractate 18 on John*.] *Encaenia* is a new dedication of a temple. For in Greek *καινόν* (*kainon*) means “new.” Whenever something new is dedicated, it is called *encaenia*. The Jews celebrate this solemnity of the temple’s dedication in the month of October.

13. The Day of Palms is so called because on it the Lord and our Savior, as the prophet sang, is said to have sat upon a donkey while proceeding toward Jerusalem. Then, as the crowd advanced with palm branches to meet him, the multitude cried out: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

14. The common people call that day *Capitilavium* [“washing of the head”] because it is then customary to wash the heads of the infants who are to be anointed, so that, having been soiled by observing Lent, they would not approach the anointing in an unclean state. [Note: “Capitilavium.” See Book I, *On Offices*, chapter 27, and Rabanus, Book II, chapter 35.]

278 15. [Note: “On this day the creed is handed over.” On those called “the competentes,” below, Book VII, final chapter.] On this day the creed is handed over to the candidates for baptism because of the approaching solemnity of the Lord’s Easter, so that those who are already hastening to receive God’s grace may recognize the faith they are to confess.

16. It is called the Lord’s Supper because on that day the Savior celebrated the Passover with his disciples. Today it is celebrated as it has been handed down, and on it the holy chrism is prepared; [Note: “And the beginning of the new and the cessation of the old Testament is declared.” These words have been added from ancient books; they were absent from the printed editions, while in manuscripts where they were lacking there was a lacuna of the same extent.] the beginning of the New Testament and the cessation of the Old Testament are declared.

17. The Sabbath is called “rest” by the Hebrews according to the interpretation of its name, because God rested on it after completing the world.

[Col. 0251C] 18. On that day also the Lord rested in the tomb, to confirm the mystery of that rest, which the Jews were commanded to observe as a shadow of what was to come. But after Christ fulfilled its figure in his burial, its observance came to rest.

19. The Lord’s Day is therefore so called because on it the joy of the Resurrection of our Lord is celebrated. [Note: “The day not belonging to the Jews.” The words are Augustine’s, Letter 119, chapter 13.] This day was declared not for the Jews but for Christians, in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection, and from that time it began to have its own festivity.

20. For the Jews alone were commanded to celebrate the Sabbath, because before then there was only rest for the dead; [Note: “But the Resurrection.” The same source.] but there was no resurrection of anyone who, rising from the dead, would not die.

[Col. 0252A] 21. After such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body that what the body of the Church hoped for at the end might go before it in the Head, the Lord’s Day—that is, the eighth day, which is also the first—began to be celebrated.

279 ## Chapter XIX. On Offices

1. There are very many kinds of offices, but the chief is the one found in sacred and divine matters. [Note: “The word *officium* from *efficere*.” From Ambrose, Book I, *On Offices*, chapter 8.] *Officium* is named from *efficere* (“to accomplish”), as though *efficium*, with one letter changed for elegance of speech; or certainly because each person should do those things that harm no one but benefit everyone.

2. The evening office is so called because it takes place at the beginning of the night, from the star Vesper, which rises as night begins. [Note: “From the star Vesper.” Virgil: “Finally, what the late evening brings,” and often elsewhere.]

3. The morning office takes place at the beginning of the light and is named from the star Lucifer, which rises as morning begins. [Col. 0252B] The meaning of these two times shows that God must always be praised by day and by night.

4. [Note: “The Mass.” He follows Ambrose, Leo, and other Fathers. Claudius Sanctus discusses the etymology of *missa* at length in the preface to the Liturgy.] The Mass, at the time of the sacrifice, is the occasion when the catechumens are sent outside, while the deacon cries: “If any catechumen remains, let him go outside.” Hence it is called *missa*, because those who are not yet known to be regenerated cannot take part in the sacraments of the altar.

280 5. A choir is a multitude gathered for sacred purposes. It is called a choir because at the beginning they stood around the altars in the form of a crown and thus sang psalms. [Note: Others derived *chorus* from *concordia* (“harmony”). From Augustine, on Psalm 87.] Others have said that *chorus* comes from harmony, which consists in charity, because if it does not have charity, it cannot respond appropriately.

6. When one person sings, it is called *monody* in Greek and *sincinnium* in Latin. [Note: “In Latin, *sincinnium*.” Festus: “*Sincinnium*, a solitary song.” Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 2: “Those who spoke more correctly called them *sincinnistae*, with a doubled *n*. For *sincinnium* was a kind of ancient song.” Shortly afterward: “The poet Accius says that they were called *sincinnistae* by an obscure name, because it was unclear to him why it was called *sincinnium*.” But since Asconius and Nonius interpret the word alone as *assicinium*, as in *assipondium*, Chacon conjectured that it was derived from *assa*. Rabanus has *sicinnium*.] When two sing, it is called *bicinium*; when many sing, a choir. For a *chorea* is a musical performance, [Note: “Or dances of classes.” Thus the older books; others read “dances of clapping.” The Neapolitan copy has: “A musical performance or dances of clapping without voice.”] or dances in groups.

7. *Antiphon* is translated from Greek as “reciprocal voice,” namely, when two choirs sing psalms alternately in an exchanged order; or from one to one. The Greeks are said to have invented this kind of psalmody.

8. [Note: “Responsories.” Or *responsoria*, for both forms occur in the Book *On Offices* and in the *Rule of Monks*, in the chapter on the Office.] The Italians handed down the responsories; hence they call the songs responsories because, when one singer finishes, another responds. The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person recites the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses.

9. A reading is so called because it is not sung, like a psalm or hymn, but is read only. In the former there is musical modulation; here, only pronunciation is required.

10. [Note: “A canticle is a voice.” From Hilary, in the prologue to the Psalms.] A canticle is the voice of one singing in joy.

[Col. 0253A] 11. [Note: “A psalm.” From Augustine, on Psalm 4.] A psalm is so called when it is sung to the psaltery, which history reveals the prophet David used with great mystery. These two terms are placed alternately beside one another in certain psalm titles, according to musical art.

12. [Note: “For a canticle of a psalm.” From the same Hilary, or from Rufinus.] A canticle of a psalm occurs when the voice of the singer later expresses what the instrument has modulated. A psalm of a canticle occurs when the art of the modulating instrument imitates what the human voice has first spoken. A psalm is named from the psaltery; hence it is not customary to compose it from another work.

13. There are three degrees in singing: [Note: “The first is that of the *succentor*.” Chacon wished these to be rearranged so that the first place would belong to the *incentor*, on the basis of Varro, Book I, *On Agriculture*, chapter 2: “Just as the right flute differs from the left, yet is in a certain way joined to it, so one is the initiating instrument of the modes of the same song and the other the supporting instrument. Indeed, you may add that the life of shepherds is initiating, while that of farmers is supporting.” But since Isidore followed the custom of the churches, in which the person who begins the song is called the *succentor*, this is more probable. The lowest Neapolitan copy reads *succentoris* first.] the first is that of the *succentor*, the second of the *incentor*, and the third of the *accentor*.

14. [Note: “Some wish *diapsalma* to be Hebrew.” I think no one before Isidore—and certainly not Isidore himself—said this, since he had so often read in Jerome that the Hebrew word is *sela*, which the Septuagint, Theodotion, and Aquila rendered *διάψαλμα* (*diapsalma*), while the Fifth Edition consistently rendered it otherwise. See Letter 138 to Marcella.] Some wish *diapsalma* to be a Hebrew word signifying “always,” that is, affirming that the things between which it is inserted are everlasting.

[Col. 0253B] 15. [Note: “Others, however.” From Augustine, on Psalm 4.] Others think it is a Greek word signifying an interval in singing: a *psalma* is what is sung, whereas a *diapsalma* is the silence inserted during singing. Just as *sympsalma* means the joining of voices in singing, so *diapsalma* means their separation, where a certain rest in the interrupted continuation is indicated.

16. It is therefore probable that the sentences should not be joined in singing wherever a *diapsalma* has been inserted, because it is inserted to show that there is a change of meanings or of persons.

17. A hymn is a song of those who praise; [Note: “A song of praise.” Augustine, on Psalm 39.] the word is translated from Greek into Latin as “praise,” because it is a song of joy and praise. [Note: “Properly, however, hymns.” From the same author, on Psalm 72.] Properly speaking, hymns are songs containing the praise of God. If there is praise but it is not praise of God, it is not a hymn. If it is both praise and praise of God, but is not sung, it is not a hymn. If, therefore, it is for praise, is praise of God, and is sung, then it is a hymn.

18. Opposed to it is the *threnos*, which is a song of lament and mourning.

19. [Note: “Alleluia … praise of God.” From Ambrose, on Psalm 118. Jerome interprets it as “praise God,” as the logic of the expression requires, Letter 137.] *Alleluia* is the interpretation of two words, namely “praise of God,” and it is Hebrew. *Ia* is one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

20. *Amen* means “truly” or “faithfully,” and it too is Hebrew. These two words, *amen* and *alleluia*, may not be transferred wholly into the language of the Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, or pronounced in another language. Although they can be interpreted, their antiquity in their own language has nevertheless been preserved by the apostles because of their more sacred authority.

[Col. 0253D] 21. For these names are so sacred that John also reports in the Apocalypse that, through revelation by the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly host, like the voice of many waters and of mighty thunder, saying “amen” and “alleluia.” Therefore both words ought to be spoken on earth just as they resound in heaven.

22. [Note: [Col. 0254D] *Osianna*. From Jerome, *Letter to Damasus* 145.] *Osianna* cannot be completely transferred into the interpretation of another language. For *osi* is interpreted as “save,” while *anna* is an interjection expressing a movement of the soul in a supplicatory mood.

23. Properly, however, it is said *osianna*, which we pronounce *osanna*, corrupting and eliding the middle letter of the word, just as happens in verses when we scan them. For the first letter of the following word, coming upon the final letter of the preceding word, excludes it. In Hebrew it is therefore said *osianna*, which is interpreted as “save,” with either “your people” or “the whole world” understood. [Col. 0254B]

24. *Offertory* took its name for the following reason. [Note: [Col. 0254D] *Fertum*. Festus: “*Ferc­tum* [or *fertum*], a kind of cake, so called because it was frequently *carried* to sacred rites.” Certain Latin glosses of the Vatican Library: “*Fertores*, those who make libations with a *fertum*.”] For *fertum* means an offering that is presented to the altar and sacrificed by priests; from this it is called *offertory*, as if on account of the *fertum*.

25. It is called an *oblation* because it is offered.

26. [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Gifts” properly divine. Thus the Gothic version; others have “of God.”] Divine presents are properly called *dona*; human presents, *munera*.

27. For *munera* means services that the poor render to the rich in place of gifts. Thus a *munus* is given to a human being, but a *donum* to God; hence in temples we also speak of *donaria*—dedicatory offerings. *Munera* are so called because they are either received or given by hand.

28. There are two things that are offered: a gift and a sacrifice.

29. A *gift* is whatever is fashioned from gold, silver, or any other material.

30. A *sacrifice*, however, is a victim, and anything that is burned or placed upon the altar. Everything that is given to God is either dedicated or consecrated. What is dedicated is given by pronouncing the dedication, and hence receives its name. Therefore those who think that *dedication* signifies *consecration* are mistaken.

31. [Note: [Col. 0254D] “Immolatio … because in the *mola*.” Augustine, *On the Psalms*, on the word *mola*.] *Immolatio* was so called by the ancients because the victim was slaughtered after being placed upon the altar-mound (*mola*); hence *mactatio*—slaughter—follows *immolatio*. Nowadays, however, *immolatio* applies to the bread and the cup, whereas *libatio* is the offering of the cup alone.

32. Hence the expression: [Note: [Col. 0254D] “And he poured a libation from the blood of the grape,” from Ecclesiasticus, chapter 50.] “And he poured a libation from the blood of the grape.” So also one of the secular poets: [Note: [Col. 0254D] “As also a certain poet,” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.] “Now pour libations from the bowls to Jupiter …” For *libare* properly means “to pour,” and the word is derived from a certain Liber who introduced the cultivation of the vine into Greece.

33. [Col. 0255A] [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Hostiae* among the ancients. From Servius, *Aeneid* I.] Among the ancients, *hostiae* were sacrifices performed before they went forth against the enemy.

34. *Victimae*, on the other hand, were sacrifices that, after victory and the defeat of the enemy, were offered in sacrifice; and *victimae* were greater sacrifices than *hostiae*. Others thought that *victima* was so called because it fell when struck by a blow, or because it was led bound to the altars.

35. [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Holocaustum*. From Jerome, on Ezekiel, chapter 45.] A *holocaust* is an offering in which everything offered is consumed by fire. For when the ancients performed very great sacrifices, they were accustomed to consume the entire victims in the sacred flame, and these were called *holocausta*. [Note: [Col. 0255D] Greek *ὅλον*. From Augustine, on Psalm 64.] For *ὅλον* in Greek means “whole,” *καῦσις* means “burning,” and a *holocaust* is therefore “wholly burned.”

36. [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Caeremoniae*. Servius, *Aeneid* IV: “It should certainly be known that among the Greeks *orgia* is the name for all sacred rites, just as among the Latins they are called *caeremoniae*.” On the etymology, see Festus.] Among the Latins, *ceremonies* are all the sacred rites that among the Greeks are called *orgia*. Properly, however, the teachers have thought that *ceremoniae* is derived from *carere*—“to lack”—as though *carimoniae*, because in the divine rites people were deprived of the ordinary use of the things offered in them. This name is also used in the sacred writings.

37. Others believe that *ceremoniae* properly refers to the observances of the Jews: namely, abstinence from certain foods according to the ancient law, because those who observe them lack the things from which they have abstained.

38. *Sacrifice* is so called as if from *sacrum factum*, “a sacred act,” because it is consecrated by a mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s passion endured for us. Hence, at his command, we call this the body and blood of Christ: although it comes from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament through the visible action of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of the bread and cup *Eucharist*, which is interpreted in Latin as “good grace.” And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

39. [Note: [Col. 0255D] “A sacrament is present in some celebration.” From Augustine, *Letter* 119, at the beginning.] A *sacrament* occurs in some celebration when an event is performed in such a way that it is understood to signify something, and this must be received as sacred. The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood.

40. They are called sacraments for this reason: beneath the covering of bodily things, divine power secretly works the saving effect of those same sacraments. Thus they are called *sacraments* either from their hidden powers or from sacred things.

41. They are therefore fruitfully performed within the Church because the Holy Spirit, who dwells in it, secretly brings about the same effect of the sacraments.

42. Consequently, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by wicked ministers, because the Holy Spirit mystically gives them life—he who once appeared through visible works in the apostolic age—these gifts are neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by those of wicked ones, since “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.” Hence in Greek it is also called *mystērion*, because it contains a secret and hidden arrangement.

43. [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Baptismus* in Greek. See Tertullian, *On Baptism*.] *Baptism* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “washing.” It is called *tinctio* because there a person is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and becomes something far different from what he was.

44. Previously we were foul with the ugliness of sins; in the washing itself we are made beautiful by the whitening of virtues. Hence it is written in the *Song of Songs*: [Note: [Col. 0255D] “Who is this who ascends whitened?” Thus the Septuagint has *λελευκανθισμένη*, “whitened”; and Ambrose, Sermon 19 on Psalm 118. The Vulgate has “who is this who ascends from the wilderness, flowing with delights?”] “Who is this who ascends whitened?”

45. Its mystery is fulfilled in no other way than under the designation of the Trinity, that is, by the joint naming (*cognominatio*) of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

46. For just as every statement rests upon three witnesses, so this sacrament is confirmed by the threefold number of the divine names.

47. [Col. 0256B] The reason baptism is given through water is as follows. The Lord willed that the invisible reality should be bestowed through a suitable, yet entirely tangible and visible, element—the element over which the Holy Spirit was also borne in the beginning.

48. For just as water cleanses the body outwardly, so through the mystery of water the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit. Its sanctification occurs in this way.

49. [Note: [Col. 0256D] “When God has been invoked.” From Tertullian.] When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, healing the waters, sanctifies them from himself. They receive the power of purification, so that in them the flesh and the soul, defiled by sins, may be cleansed.

50. [Note: [Col. 0256D] *Chrisma*. From the same source.] *Chrism* is called in Greek and *unctio*, “anointing,” in Latin. From its name Christ is also named, and after the washing the human being is sanctified.

51. For just as the remission of sins is given in baptism, so through anointing the sanctification of the spirit is applied. This derives from the ancient practice by which people were accustomed to be anointed for the priesthood and kingship; hence Aaron too was anointed by Moses.

52. Although this is performed bodily, it produces a spiritual effect. Thus in baptism itself the visible act is that we are immersed in water, while the spiritual effect is that we are cleansed from sins.

53. This is signified by the ointment which the sinful woman is recorded to have poured over Jesus’ feet, and by that which the woman who is said not to have been sinful is recorded to have poured over his head. [Note: [Col. 0256D] “And the one who is not said to have been sinful.” All the books read this. But Rabanus does not appear to have read it.]

54. The laying on of hands is performed so that, through blessing, the Holy Spirit may be summoned. [Col. 0256D] [Note: [Col. 0256D] “Then that Paraclete.” The words are Tertullian’s.] Then that Paraclete willingly descends from the Father upon the bodies after they have been cleansed and blessed, and, recognizing as though upon the water of baptism his former seat, rests upon it. For we read that in the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters.

55. [Col. 0257A] *Exorcism* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *conjuratio*, “adjuration,” or as a speech of rebuke directed against the devil, so that he may depart. Thus it is written in Zechariah: “And he showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘The Lord rebuke you, who has chosen Jerusalem.’”

56. This is exorcism: to rebuke and adjure the devil. It should therefore be understood that it is not God’s creature in infants that is exorcized or expelled by breath, but the one under whose power are all who are born with sin. For he is the prince of sinners.

57. [Note: [Col. 0257D] *Symbolum*. From Rufinus, *On the Creed*.] *Symbolum* is interpreted from Greek as “sign” or “contribution.” When the apostles were about to depart to preach among the nations, they established this as the sign or indication of their preaching.

58. It contains the confession of the Trinity, the unity of the Church, and the entire sacramental teaching of Christianity. This creed of our faith and hope is not written on parchment with ink, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart.

59. Prayer is called a petition. For *orare* means “to ask,” just as *exorare* means “to obtain by entreaty.” Prayer, however, is constituted by place and time. By place, because it is not everywhere—for Christ forbids us to pray in public—but wherever opportunity is given or necessity requires. For what the apostles did cannot be counted as contrary to the command: they prayed and sang to God in prison while the guards listened.

60. As for time, it is said: “Pray without ceasing.” But this concerns individuals. There is also an observance of certain common hours that mark the intervals of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and likewise certain hours of the night.

61. These hours were therefore divided for prayer so that, if we should happen to be detained by some task, the appointed time itself might remind us of our duty. These times are found in the Scriptures.

62. First, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the disciples when they had assembled at the third hour. On the day when Peter experienced the vision of inclusion in that vessel, he had gone up at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer. Likewise, at the ninth hour he went with John to the temple, when he restored the paralytic to health.

63. We also read that Daniel observed these times in prayer, and certainly according to the discipline of Israel, so that we might worship no fewer than three times a day. For we are debtors to the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—apart, of course, from the other lawful prayers owed without any prompting at the beginning of light and of night, or at the watches; and also from not taking food before prayer has been offered. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “With prayer interposed”; the Codex of Chacon has “with prayer placed first.”]

64. [Col. 0258A] The refreshment of the spirit must be given priority, because heavenly things come before earthly things. Whoever wishes his prayer to fly to the Lord should give it two wings: fasting and almsgiving; then it will ascend swiftly and be heard. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “It will ascend swiftly.” A passage from Augustine on the Psalms.]

65. Fasting is frugality of food and abstinence from nourishment. Its name is derived from a certain part of the viscera, which is always thin and empty and is commonly called the *jejunum*. Hence the name *jejunium* is believed to have arisen, because through hunger its viscera remain empty and exhausted.

66. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Fasting is also called a station.” Thus Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobia* V, chapter 24: “Throughout the monasteries of Egypt we were received with such cheerfulness of heart that, apart from the regular fasts of the fourth and sixth days, wherever we went the daily station was relaxed.”] Fasting is also called a *station*. [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Station,” from military usage. Tertullian, *On Prayer*, at the end: “If *station* took its name from military usage—for we too are God’s army—then surely no joy or sorrow that befalls the camp breaks up the stations of the soldiers. For joy will perform the discipline more willingly, sorrow more anxiously.”] *Station* took its name from military usage, because no joy or sorrow that comes upon the camp breaks up the station of the soldiers. For joy administers discipline more willingly, sorrow more anxiously; [Note: [Col. 0258D] “Hence also soldiers.” From the same source, *On Fasting*.] therefore soldiers, never forgetful of their oath, are especially obedient to their stations.

67. Some distinguish between fasting and a station. For fasting is abstinence on any day indiscriminately, not according to a law but according to one’s own will, whereas a station is observance of appointed days or times.

68. Of days—for example, the fast of the fourth and sixth days, commanded by the ancient law. Concerning this station, that man said in the Gospel: “I fast twice on the Sabbath,” that is, on the fourth and sixth days of the week.

69. Of times, however, are those established at fixed periods by legal and prophetic institutions: the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months; or, as in the Gospel, those days on which the bridegroom was taken away; or the observance of Lent, which throughout the world is maintained by apostolic institution near the time of the Lord’s passion. [Note: [Col. 0258D] “The fast of the fourth.” The words of Zechariah, chapter 8. See Jerome there, and Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* I, chapter 37.]

70. Some add a third kind to these, which they call *xerophagy*, namely, abstinence from moist foods. Hence this name was given because some people use dry foods. [Note: [Col. 0258D] “Which they call *xerophagy*.” Tertullian, Jerome, and Cassian often use this word.]

71. *Penance* is so called as if from *punitentia*, “punishment,” because a person punishes himself through repentance for what he has done wrongly. For those who truly repent do nothing other than refuse to let what they have done wrongly go unpunished. By not sparing themselves in this way, they are spared by the one whose profound and just judgment no contemptuous person escapes. [Note: [Col. 0258D] “As if *punitentia*.” Others have “as if *punientia*.” The same, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* II, chapter 16: “The word *poenitentia* took its name from *poena*, punishment.”]

72. Penance is perfect when one mourns past deeds and does not admit future ones. This is a second purification, in the likeness of a spring, so that if, when the devil attacks, some sin should creep in, it may be cleansed through satisfaction.

73. Satisfaction is to exclude the causes of sins and their suggestions, and not to repeat the sin thereafter.

74. Reconciliation is what is applied after penance has been completed. For just as we are reconciled to God when we are first converted from paganism, so we are reconciled when, after sin, we return through repentance.

75. *Exomologesis* is a Greek word interpreted in Latin as *confessio*, “confession”; the word has a double meaning. For confession is understood either as praise, as in: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” or as when someone confesses his sins to the one whose mercy is unfailing, so that they may be forgiven.

76. [Note: [Col. 0259B] “Therefore from this Greek word.” Tertullian, *On Penance*: “That act which is more fully expressed and commonly used by the Greek word is *exomologesis*, by which we confess our offense to our Lord—not indeed as though he were ignorant, but because God is appeased by the penitence of confession, insofar as satisfaction is arranged through confession.”] Thus *exomologesis* is expressed and regularly used from this Greek word: through it we confess our offense to the Lord—not as though he were ignorant, since nothing is hidden from his knowledge, but confession is the avowal of a matter, namely, the professed acknowledgment of what was unknown.

77. A person had thought it useful and pleasurable for himself to rob, commit adultery, and steal. But when he learned that these things were subject to eternal condemnation, once he has learned this, he confesses his error.

78. Confession of error is an avowal that one will cease. One must therefore cease from sins while making confession. Confession comes first, forgiveness follows; otherwise, the person who recognizes his sin but does not confess the sin he has recognized remains outside forgiveness.

79. [Col. 0260A] [Note: [Col. 0259B] “Therefore *exomologesis* is the discipline of prostrating and humbling a person.” Words of Tertullian, in the same work.] Thus *exomologesis* is a discipline by which a person prostrates and humbles himself—in dress and food, by lying in sackcloth and ashes, by covering the body with filth, by casting down the spirit in grief, and by changing through sorrowful treatment those things in which he sinned.

80. *Litanies* are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are called *rogationes*, “supplications.” The difference between a litany and *exomologesis* is that *exomologeses* are performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are appointed for asking the Lord and obtaining his mercy in some matter.

81. [Note: [Col. 0260B] “But now both terms …” The origin of this usage is taken from the Council of Agde. So also in the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, chapter 6: although the heading concerns the celebration of litany-days throughout all twelve months, the canon itself says that *exomologesis* should be celebrated with growing vows.] But now both terms are held under one designation, and in common usage it makes no difference whether they are called litanies or *exomologeses*. The name *supplication* is now retained, in a certain sense, from paganism.

82. [Col. 0260B] [Note: [Col. 0260B] “For the festivals, or the appointed days.” These are the words of Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “He proclaims honor to the temples.”] For among them the festivals were either regular or proclaimed. They were proclaimed because the ancient poverty of the Romans offered sacrifices through contributions, or at any rate from the property of condemned persons. Hence punishments are called *supplications*, which were made from the property of those who had suffered punishments. Sacred things were made from the possessions of accursed persons.

# BOOK SEVEN. ON GOD, ANGELS, AND THE ORDERS OF THE FAITHFUL

[Col. 0259]

## CHAPTER ONE. On God

[Col. 0259C]

1. The most blessed Jerome, a man highly learned and skilled in many languages, was the first to translate the interpretations of Hebrew names into Latin. Of these, omitting many for the sake of brevity, I have undertaken to insert certain ones into this work, together with their interpretations.

2. The explanation of names sufficiently indicates what they are intended to mean. Some names derive their rationale from the particular causes of their names. At the beginning, therefore, we set down ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

3. [Note: [Col. 0259D] “The first among the Hebrews.” From Jerome, *Letter* 136.] The first name of God among the Hebrews is *El*. Some have interpreted it as “God,” while others, expressing its etymology, have rendered it *ἰσχυρόν*, that is, “strong,” because he is oppressed by no weakness but is strong and sufficient for accomplishing all things. [Note: [Col. 0259D] “Is oppressed.” Others have “is pressed down.”]

4. The second name is *Eloim*.

5. The third is *Eloe*; both are translated into Latin as “God.” The name itself, however, has been transferred into Latin from a Greek designation. For God is called *Θεός* in Greek, [Note: [Col. 0259D] “As if *δέος*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on the verse “Goddess to the goddess.”] as if from *δέος*, that is, “fear.” Hence the name *God* was derived, because he is an object of fear to those who worship him.

6. [Note: [Col. 0260D] “God properly is the name of the Trinity.” From Jerome, *Letter to Amandus* 147.] God is properly the name belonging to the Trinity, that is, to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The other names placed below that are said of God also refer to this Trinity.

7. The fourth name of God is called *Sabaoth*, which is translated into Latin as “of hosts” or “of powers.” Concerning him the angels say in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers.”

8. There are many powers in this ordering, such as angels, archangels, principalities, and powers, and all the orders of the heavenly army; yet he is their Lord. For they are all beneath him and subject to his dominion.

9. [Col. 0260D] [Note: [Col. 0260D] “The fifth, *Helion*.” Hence some think that the Greeks formed *ἥλιον*, “sun.”] The fifth is *Elion*, which is translated into Latin as “most high,” because he is above the heavens, as it is written of him: “The Lord is most high; his glory is above the heavens.” He is called *excelsus*, “exalted,” because he is exceedingly high. For *ex* is used in the sense of “very,” as in *eximius*, “outstanding,” as if “very eminent.”

10. [Col. 0261A] The sixth name is *Eie*, that is, “the one who is.” Since God alone is eternal—that is, since he has no beginning—he truly possesses the name of being. [Note: [Col. 0261D] “This name … does not have mortality.” This passage is falsely cited by the *Magister Sententiarum*, Book I, distinction 8, chapter 1, as from Jerome’s letter to Damasus; rather, it is compiled from various passages of Augustine and Gregory. The first part, up to “let them not be,” is from Augustine, *City of God* VIII, chapter 11.] This name was conveyed to holy Moses through an angel.

11. When Moses asked what the name was of the one who commanded him to go to the people and deliver them from Egypt, he replied: “I am who I am,” and: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” In comparison with the one who truly is, because he is unchangeable, things that have been made and are changeable are as though they did not exist.

12. [Note: [Col. 0261D] “For what is said ‘was’ …” From the same source, *On the Creed*, chapter 4, and on Psalm 101. The Greek word *τὸ* could twice be deleted here without affecting the sense.] For what is said “was” is not; and what is said “will be” does not yet exist. [Note: [Col. 0261D] “But God knows only being.” From Gregory, *Moralia* IV, chapter 27, or chapter 32.] But God knows only being; he does not know “having been” or “being destined to be.”

13. [Note: [Col. 0261D] “For the Father alone.” From the same work, *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 27, or chapter 32.] For the Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, truly is; compared with his essence, our being is non-being. Hence in ordinary speech we also say: [Note: [Col. 0261D] “God lives because essence lives.” From the same work, chapter 3, or chapter 1.] “God lives,” because life lives as essence, which death does not possess.

14. The seventh is *Adonai*, which is generally interpreted as “Lord,” either because he rules the whole creation or because every creature serves his dominion. Thus “Lord” and “God” mean either that he rules over all or that he is feared by all.

15. [Col. 0262D] [Note: [Col. 0262D] “The eighth.” From Jerome, *Letter* 136.] The eighth is *Ia*, which is applied only to God and which also sounds in the final syllable of *alleluia*.

16. [Note: [Col. 0262D] “The ninth.” From the same letter, and Letter 142. Also in the *Questions* on Genesis 17: “Nor is it surprising,” he says, “that although among the Greeks and among us a letter appears to have been added, we say that a letter has been added; for it is the idiom of that language to write *i* but read *a* [the transmitted text is corrupt], just as conversely they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*.”] The ninth is *Tetragrammaton*, that is, “of four letters,” a name applied properly to God among the Hebrews. It consists of two *ia*s, *ia*, which, doubled, form that ineffable and glorious name of God. It is called “ineffable” not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot in any way be bounded by human sense and understanding; and therefore, because nothing worthy can be said about it, it is ineffable.

17. The tenth is *Saddai*, that is, “Almighty.” He is called Almighty because he can do all things—not because he suffers what he does not wish, but because he does what he wishes. If that happened to him, he would by no means be Almighty. For he does whatever he wishes, and hence he is Almighty.

18. He is also called Almighty because everything that exists everywhere belongs to him. For he alone possesses dominion over the whole world. Certain other names are also applied substantially to God, such as Immortal, Incorruptible, Unchangeable, and Eternal. Hence he is rightly placed before the whole of creation.

19. [Col. 0261D] He is Immortal, as it is written of him: “Who alone possesses immortality,” because there is no change in his nature. [Note: [Col. 0262D] “For every mutability.” From Gregory, *Moralia* XII, chapter 17, from which most of the remainder of this chapter is taken.] For every change may appropriately be called mortality. In this sense the soul too is said to die—not because it is changed and transformed into a body or into some other substance, but because, within its own substance, whatever it now is or was in another condition is found to be mortal insofar as it has ceased to be what it was. Thus God alone is called Immortal, because he alone is unchangeable.

20. He is called Incorruptible because he cannot be corrupted, dissolved, or divided. Whatever admits division also admits destruction. He can neither be divided nor perish; therefore he is incorruptible.

21. He is Unchangeable because he always remains and does not know how to change. He does not increase, because he is perfect; nor does he diminish, because he is eternal.

22. He is Eternal because he is without time. For he has neither beginning nor end. Hence he is also called Everlasting, because he is always eternal. Some believe that *eternal* derives from *aether*, since heaven is regarded as his dwelling. Hence the verse: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord.” These four names all signify one thing, for the same reality is designated whether one says eternal God, immortal, incorruptible, or unchangeable.

23. He is Invisible because the Trinity has never appeared to mortal eyes in its own substance, except through the appearance of a subordinate created, bodily thing. For no one can see the very manifestation of God’s essence and live, as was also said to Moses. Hence John says in his Epistle: “No one has ever seen God.” He is invisible, and therefore must be sought not with the eye but with the heart.

24. He is Impassible because he is affected by none of the disturbances to which human frailty succumbs. No passions touch him—lust, anger, desire, fear, grief, envy, and the other states by which the human mind is troubled.

25. When God is said to become angry, or to be jealous, or to grieve, this is said according to our customary usage. There is no disturbance in God, with whom there is perfect tranquility.

26. He is called Simple either because he does not lose what he has or because he himself is not one thing and what is in him another, [Note: [Col. 0262D] “As in a human being, whose being is one thing …” From *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 27, or chapter 34.] as in a human being, whose being is one thing and whose wisdom is another.

27. For a person can exist without being wise; but God possesses essence and wisdom. Yet what he possesses, that he is, and all things are one in him. Therefore he is simple, because there is nothing accidental in him; both what he is and what is in him are essential, [Note: [Col. 0262D] “Except what is relative.” From Augustine, *City of God* XI, chapter 10.] except what is relative to any person.

28. He is supremely good because he is unchangeable. A creature is good, but not supremely good, because it is changeable. Although it is indeed good, it cannot also be supreme.

29. God is called incorporeal, or without a body, so that he may be believed or understood to be spirit rather than body. For when he is called spirit, his substance is signified.

30. He is Immeasurable because he contains all things, while he himself is contained by none; rather, all things are confined within his omnipotence.

31. He is called Perfect because nothing can be added to him. Yet perfection is spoken of in relation to the completion of some deed. God, however, was not made; how then is he perfect? This word, like the other terms, has been taken from our usage because of human inadequacy, so that what is ineffable may in some manner be expressed. For human speech says nothing worthy of God, as is also true of the other names.

32. He is called Creator because all the things of the world were created by him; there is nothing that did not derive its origin from God. He is also One, either because he cannot be divided or because there can be nothing else that possesses an equal measure of power.

33. These names, then, which have been said of God, belong to the whole Trinity because of its one and coeternal substance—whether in the Father, in his Only-begotten Son in the form of God, or in the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of God the Father and of his Only-begotten Son.

34. Certain names are also applied to God from our customary usage, drawn from our bodily members or from lower things. Because he is invisible and incorporeal in his proper nature, the forms of things are nevertheless attributed to him because of the effects he produces, so that he may make himself more readily understood according to our manner of speaking. Thus, because he sees all things, he is called an eye; because he hears all things, an ear; because he turns away, he walks; because he observes, he stands.

36. The likeness of such other things is likewise drawn from human minds and applied to God, [Note: [Col. 0263D] “From human minds.” From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, chapter 5, or 6.] as when he is said to forget and to remember. Hence the prophet also says: “The Lord of hosts has sworn by his soul”—not because God has a soul, but because the prophet speaks according to our manner of feeling.

37. [Note: [Col. 0263D] “For the face of God also.” From the same source, *On the First Book of Kings* X.] In the sacred Scriptures, the face of God does not mean flesh but divine knowledge, for the same reason that a person is known by seeing his face. Thus in prayer one says to God: “Show us your face,” as if saying: “Give us knowledge of yourself.”

38. God’s footprints are likewise spoken of because now God is known through a mirror. In perfection, however, the Almighty will be found when, in the future, he is presented face to face to each of the elect, so that they may contemplate the very form whose footprints they now strive to grasp—that is, the one whom they are said to see through a mirror.

39. Position, appearance, place, and time are likewise spoken of God not properly but metaphorically. He is said to sit upon the cherubim, which concerns position; “the abyss, like a garment, is his covering,” which concerns appearance; “your years shall not fail,” which concerns time; and “if I ascend into heaven, you are there,” which concerns place.

40. [Note: [Col. 0263D] “Also in the prophet Amos,” chapter 2.] In the prophet too, the appearance of a cart carrying hay is applied to God. All these expressions are figurative, because none of them belongs properly to the nature of his substance.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Son of God

1. Christ is found to be called by many names in the divine Scriptures. For he himself, the Only-begotten Son of God the Father, although equal to the Father, assumed the form of a servant for our salvation. Accordingly, some names are applied to him from the substance of his divinity, and others are assumed from the dispensation of the humanity he took upon himself.

2. Christ was so called from *chrism*, that is, “anointed.” [Note: [Col. 0263D] “For it had been commanded to the Jews.” From Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 7. Histories also report that the Gothic kings were accustomed to be anointed by the bishops of Toledo.] For the Jews had been commanded to prepare a sacred ointment with which those summoned to the priesthood or kingship could be anointed. [Note: [Col. 0263D] “And just as now purple clothing …” Hence purple signifies a king in Virgil, and “purple tyrants” in Horace.] Just as now a purple garment is the insignia of royal dignity, so for them anointing with sacred ointment conferred the name and authority of kingship. Hence they were called *christs*, from *chrism*, which means “anointing.”

3. For *chrism* is called *unctio*, “anointing,” in Latin. It also bestowed a name upon the Lord when it became spiritual, because he was anointed by God the Father with the Spirit, as it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “For they gathered together in this city against your holy Son, whom you anointed.” This was not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace signified by the visible ointment.

4. [Note: [Col. 0264D] “Christ is not the Savior’s proper name.” Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 12: “For *Christ* is not a proper name but a designation of authority and kingship.”] *Christ* is not the Savior’s proper name but a common designation of authority. [Note: [Col. 0264D] “For when he is called Christ.” From Jerome, on Matthew 16.] When he is called *Christ*, it is a common name of dignity; when he is called *Jesus Christ*, it is the proper name of the Savior.

5. The name *Christ* had never existed anywhere else at all, nor among any people, except in that kingdom where Christ was prophesied and from which he was to come.

6. *Messiah* is called *Christ* in Greek and *anointed* in Latin usage.

7. [Col. 0264D] *Jesus*, a Hebrew name, is interpreted as *Σωτήρ* in Greek, [Note: [Col. 0264D] “But in Latin, *Salvator*.” From Lactantius, IV, chapter 12.] and *Salutaris*, “Salutary,” or *Salvator*, “Savior,” in Latin, because he came as the bringer of salvation to all nations.

8. [Note: [Col. 0264D] “The etymology.” From Jerome, on Matthew 1.] The evangelist himself also indicates the etymology of this name when he says: “You shall call his name Jesus, because he will save his people.” For just as *Christ* signifies “King,” so *Jesus* signifies “Savior.”

9. Therefore it is not just any king who saves us, but the King who is Savior. [Col. 0265A] 301

[Note: [Col. 0265D] This word was previously absent from the Latin language. Those who think they have adequately expressed Σωτήρ by the word *servator* are greatly mistaken. Cicero, *Against Verres* 2.11: “And so at Syracuse I saw him inscribed not only as patron of that island, but also as SOTER. How significant is this? So significant that it cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word. He is certainly the SOTER who gave salvation.”]

This word the Latin language did not previously possess, though it could have possessed it, just as it was able to do so whenever it wished.

10. Emmanuel, translated from Hebrew into Latin, means “God with us,” namely because God, born through the Virgin, appeared to human beings in mortal flesh, so that he might open for earthly beings the way of salvation to heaven. The following names pertain to the substance of divinity: God, Lord.

11. He is called God because of his one substance with the Father.

“Lord,” because of the created nature that serves.

12. He is God and human because he is Word and flesh. Hence he is also called “twice-born,” either because the Father begot him without a mother in eternity, or because the Mother bore him without a father in time.

[Col. 0265B] 13. He is called “Only-begotten” in accordance with the excellence of his divinity, because he has no brothers; “Firstborn” in accordance with his assumption of humanity, in which he deigned, through the adoption of grace, to have brothers, so that he might be their firstborn.

14. He is called *homoousios* with the Father from the unity of substance. For “substance,” or “essence,” is called οὐσία in Greek, and ὅμος means “one.” Joined together, therefore, the two words signify “one substance.” This is called *homoousion*, which means: “I and the Father are one”—that is, he is of the same substance as the Father.

15. Although this name is not found written in the sacred Scriptures, it is nevertheless defended in the affirmation of the whole Trinity, because a reason is available by which it can properly be shown to be said; just as “Unbegotten” is nowhere read of the Father in those books, 302 yet no one doubts that he must be called and believed to be so.

[Col. 0265C] 16. *Omoeousios*: “of similar substance,” because as God is, so also is his image. God is invisible, and his image is invisible.

17. “Beginning,” because all things are from him, and because there was nothing before him.

18. “End,” either because at the end of time he deigned humbly to be born in the flesh, to die, and himself to undertake the final judgment; or because we refer everything we do to him, and when we have reached him, we have nothing further to seek.

19. He is the “mouth of God” because he is his Word. For just as, instead of the words produced by the tongue, we often say “that tongue” or “that other tongue,” so “mouth” is used for the Word of God, because it is customary for words to be formed by the mouth.
