20. [Note: [Col. 0266D] “But the Word”: see the book *On the Unity of the Father and the Son* among Hilary’s works; some material here was taken from its conclusion.]

He is therefore called “Word” because through him the Father created, or commanded, all things.

21. “Truth,” because he does not deceive, but grants what he promised.

“Life,” because he created.

He is called “Image” because of his equal likeness to the Father.

22. He is “Figure,” because, having assumed the form of a servant, he represented in himself the image and immeasurable greatness of the Father through the likeness of his works and virtues.

23. He is the “Hand of God,” because all things were made through him. Hence he is also called the “right hand,” because of the effect of the whole creation, which was formed through him.

[Col. 0266A] He is the “Arm,” because all things are held together by him.

24. “Power,” because he possesses in himself all the power of the Father and governs, sustains, and rules every creature of heaven and earth.

25. “Wisdom,” because he himself reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. Yet although the Father and the Holy Spirit are also wisdom, power, and light, the Son is properly called by these names.

26. He is called “Radiance” because he makes things manifest. “Light,” because he illuminates. “Brightness,” because he opens the eyes of the heart to contemplate the truth. “Sun,” because he is the illuminator.

27. “Dawn,” because he is the source of light and the illuminator of created things, [Col. 0266B] and because he causes us to rise to eternal life.

303 28. “Fountain,” because he is the origin of things, or because he satisfies the thirsty. He is also Α and Ω: no letter precedes alpha, for it is the first of the letters, just as the Son of God is first; for, when questioned by the Jews, he answered that he was the beginning. Hence John, in the Apocalypse, expressly placing this very letter, says: “I am Α and Ω, the first and the last” (Rev. 22:13). “First,” because nothing exists before him; “last,” because he himself will undertake the final judgment.

29. [Note: [Col. 0266D] “Mediator”: from Lactantius, cited above.]

“Mediator,” because he was placed between God and humanity in order to lead humanity to God; hence the Greeks also call him μεσίτης.

30. “Paraclete,” that is, “advocate,” because he intercedes for us with the Father; as John also says of him: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” [Col. 0266C] (1 John 2:1).

31. *Paraclete* is a Greek word, which in Latin is *advocatus*, “advocate.” This name is attributed both to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16).

32. He is likewise called “Intercessor,” because he takes care to remove our guilt and devotes himself to cleansing away our crimes.

33. “Bridegroom,” because, descending from heaven, he joined himself to the Church, so that the two might be one flesh in the peace of the New Testament.

34. [Note: [Col. 0266D] “Angel”: from Tertullian, *On the Trinity*.]

He is called “Angel” because he announces the will of the Father and his own will. Hence he is read of in the prophet as the “Angel of great counsel,” although he is God and Lord of the angels.

35. He is called “Sent” because the Word appeared in this world having become flesh; hence he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:26).

36. He is called “Human” because he was born.

“Prophet,” because he revealed future things.

“Priest,” because he offered himself as a sacrifice for us.

“Shepherd,” because he is the guardian.

304 “Teacher,” because he is the one who shows.

[Col. 0267A] “Nazaraeus,” from the place.

“Nazaraeus,” by merit—that is, “holy” or “pure”—because he committed no sin.

37. Indeed, Christ also takes to himself forms of names drawn from other, lower things, so that he may be understood more easily.

38. For he is called “Bread,” because he is flesh.

“Vine,” because we have been redeemed by his blood.

“Flower,” because he is chosen.

“Way,” because through him we go to God.

“Door,” because through him we enter to God.

“Mountain,” because he is strong.

“Rock,” because he is the firmness of believers.

39. “Cornerstone,” either because he joins two walls coming from opposite directions—that is, from circumcision and uncircumcision—into the one structure of the Church; or because in himself he establishes peace between angels and human beings.

[Col. 0267B] 40. “Stone of stumbling,” [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Because, coming humbly.” An absolute nominative construction, which—if it is relevant to our present matter—Budaeus also noted occurs in Cicero, in his commentary on the Greek language.]

because, coming humbly, unbelieving people stumbled over him; and he became a rock of offense, as the Apostle says: “To the Jews, indeed, a stumbling-block.”

41. He is called “Foundation” because faith in him is most firm, or because the catholic Church has been built upon him.

42. For Christ is also “Lamb,” on account of innocence.

“Sheep,” on account of patience.

“Ram,” on account of leadership.

“Kid,” on account of the likeness of sinful flesh.

43. “Calf,” because he was sacrificed for us.

“Lion,” on account of kingship and strength.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] “Serpent”: see Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Moses*.]

“Serpent,” on account of death and wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] “The same is also ‘worm.’” On account of the worm that arises from the ashes of the phoenix; concerning it, see Clement of Rome, *Constitutions*, book 5, chapter 6; also the poem circulated with Lactantius’s works under the title *The Phoenix*, and Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*. Although he may have understood this as the silkworm—through which a more familiar and perhaps more convincing image of resurrection is established—it nevertheless does not seem likely.]

“The same is also ‘worm,’” because he rose again.

44. “Eagle,” because after the resurrection he returned to [Col. 0267C] the stars. Nor is it surprising that he is represented by lowly symbols, since he is known to have descended as far as our sufferings and the humiliations of the flesh.

45. Although he is the Son of God, coeternal with God the Father before the ages, when the fullness of time came, he assumed the form of a servant for our salvation and became the Son of Man.

46. Accordingly, some things are said of him in Scripture according to the form of God, and others according to the form of a servant. By way of example, two statements are recalled, so that each may be referred to its proper category. According to the form of God, he said of himself: “I and the Father are one”; according to the form of a servant: “For the Father is greater than I.”

47. People who understand less clearly what is said in one sense and [Col. 0267D] what in another wish to transfer to the form of God those things that were said according to the form of a servant; and again, they wish the things said so that the persons might be related to one another to be names of nature and substance, thereby creating error in the faith.

48. Human nature was so joined to the Son of God that from the two substances there came to be one person. Therefore, only the human being endured the cross, but because of the unity of the person, God too is said to have endured it.

49. Hence it is written: [Col. 0268A] “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). We therefore confess that the Son of God was crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of humanity; not through the permanence of his own nature, but through his assumption of ours.

## CHAPTER III. On the Holy Spirit

1. The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, 306 and possesses their substance. For nothing other than what the Father himself is could proceed from the Father.

2. He is called “Spirit” according to what is referred to something else; and one who breathes is indeed one who breathes into by a spirit, and from this is called Spirit. In a particular sense he is called the Holy Spirit according to his relation to the Father and the Son, because he is their Spirit.

[Col. 0268B] 3. For the name “Spirit” is not always used according to what is related to something else, but also according to what signifies a certain nature.

4. Every incorporeal nature is called “spirit” in the sacred Scriptures. Thus this name applies not only to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but also to every rational creature and to the soul.

5. He is therefore called the Holy Spirit of God because he is the holiness of the Father and the Son. For although the Father is Spirit, the Son is Spirit, the Father is holy, and the Son is holy, he alone is properly called the Holy Spirit, as the coessential and consubstantial holiness of both.

6. The Holy Spirit is not called “begotten,” lest two Sons be supposed to exist in the Trinity. He is not proclaimed “unbegotten,” lest two Fathers be believed to exist in the Trinity itself.

[Col. 0268C] 7. He is called “proceeding,” according to the testimony of the Lord, who says: “I have many things still to say to you, but you cannot hear them now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father and will receive from what is mine, he will declare all things to you” (John 16:12–13). He proceeds not only according to nature, but continually proceeds in order to accomplish the works of the Trinity without ceasing.

8. The difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds is that the Son is born from one, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore the Apostle says: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

9. The Holy Spirit is also understood as an angel from his work; for it was said of him: “He will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16:13). In Greek, *angelos*, and in Latin, *nuntius*, means “messenger.” Hence two angels appeared to Lot, in whom the Lord is singularly named; we understand them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, for the Father is never read of as having been sent.

10. The Holy Spirit is called “Paraclete” from consolation; παράκλησις in Greek is called *consolatio* in Latin. Christ sent him to the mourning apostles after he himself had ascended into heaven from their sight.

[Col. 0269A] 11. A consoler is sent to the sorrowful, according to that saying of the same Lord: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). He also said: “Then the children of the bridegroom will mourn when the bridegroom has been taken away from them” (Matt. 9:15).

12. Likewise, he is called “Paraclete” because he provides consolation to souls that lose temporal joy. Others translate *Paraclete* into Latin as “speaker” or “advocate.” The Holy Spirit himself speaks; he himself teaches; through him the word of wisdom is given; by him the sacred Scripture was inspired.

13. The Holy Spirit is therefore called “sevenfold” because of the gifts that, from his unified fullness, each person is deemed worthy to receive in portions according to his merit. For he is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, 308 [Col. 0269B] the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] “From his unified fullness.” Others: “of unity.”]

14. The “principal Spirit” is read of in the fiftieth psalm. Because “Spirit” is repeated there three times, some have understood the Trinity, particularly because it is written: “God is Spirit.” For what is not a body, yet exists, seems to remain as spirit. Some therefore understand the Trinity to be signified there: in the principal Spirit, the Father; in the upright Spirit, the Son; in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit.

15. The Holy Spirit is called “gift” because he is given. The name “gift” derives from giving. It is very well known that the Lord Jesus Christ, after he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, gave the Holy Spirit, and that believers, filled with him, spoke in the languages of all nations.

16. He is the gift of God to the extent that he is given to those who love God through him. In himself he is God, but among us he is a gift; and the Holy Spirit is an eternal gift, distributing the gifts of grace to each person as he wills.

17. He grants prophecies to whomever he wishes, and forgives sins to whomever he wishes. For sins are not forgiven without the Holy Spirit.

18. The Holy Spirit is therefore properly called “love,” either because he naturally joins those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he brings it about in us that we remain in God and he in us.

19. Hence among the gifts of God nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0269D] 20. He is also “grace,” which is so called because it is given freely, not on account of our merits but by the divine will. Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name “Wisdom,” although the Holy Spirit and the Father himself are also universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name “Love,” although the Father and the Son are also universally love.

21. The Holy Spirit is most clearly declared to be the “Finger of God” in the books of the Gospels. [Col. 0270A] [Note: [Col. 0269D] “When one evangelist…” Luke 11.]

When one evangelist had said: “By the finger of God I cast out demons,” [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Another.” Matthew 12.] another said the same thing in this way: “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons.” Hence the law was also written by the finger of God, given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb; and on the fiftieth day after the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit came.

22. He is called the Finger of God so that his operative power with the Father and the Son may be signified. Hence Paul says: “All these things are effected by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). Just as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so we are marked by the Spirit, who is the Finger of God and the spiritual seal.

It is therefore written that the Holy Spirit came in the form of a dove, [Note: [Col. 0269D] “So that its nature … lacks bile.” These are Tertullian’s words in *On Baptism*, and the same is said, with many others, by the divine Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* III, question 39, article 6—not that it entirely lacks bile, but because it has very little bile, as Aristotle says in book 3 of *On the Parts of Animals*.] so that his nature might be indicated through the bird by simplicity [Col. 0270B] and innocence. Hence the Lord also says: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). For this bird bodily lacks bile, possessing only innocence and love.

23. The Holy Spirit is therefore called “Fire,” because in the Acts of the Apostles he appeared like fire through the division of tongues and settled upon each of them.

24. For this reason he gave the apostles the grace of different languages, so that they might be made capable of instructing believing peoples.

25. The fact that he is remembered as having sat above each individual serves to make it understood that he was not divided among the many, but remained wholly in each, as is generally the nature of fire.

310 26. For kindled fire has this nature, [Col. 0270C] that, as many as look upon it, [Note: [Col. 0270D] “As many as look upon it, as many as [look] upon a lock of purple splendor.” Virgil and Tibullus spoke of purple hair and purple locks, and Solomon says in the *Song of Songs* 7: “The locks of your head are like royal purple joined in channels.” But why mention a lock of hair here? Let others explain.] as many as [look] upon a lock of purple radiance, to so many it imparts the sight of its light and grants the service of its function, while nevertheless remaining whole in itself.

27. The Holy Spirit is called “Water” in the Gospel, when the Lord cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The evangelist explained what he meant. For he continued: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).

28. But the water of the sacrament is one thing, and the water that signifies the Spirit of God is another. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place in the soul; through the Holy Spirit, however, the soul itself is cleansed and nourished.

[Col. 0270D] 29. The Holy Spirit is therefore called “Anointing,” as the apostle John testifies, because just as oil, by its natural weight, rises above every liquid, so at the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne above the waters. Hence the Lord is also read to have been anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit.

30. The apostle John likewise calls the Holy Spirit “anointing,” saying: “And as for you, let the anointing that you received from him remain in you; and you have no need for anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27). For the Holy Spirit himself is the invisible anointing.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Same Trinity

1. It is called “Trinity” because a whole one is made from certain three things, as though it were “Tri-unity”—for example, memory, understanding, and will, in which the mind possesses within itself a certain image of the divine Trinity. Although there are three, they are one, because each remains in itself and all are in all.

2. The Father, therefore, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are Trinity and unity. The same is one, and the same is three. They are one in nature and three in persons. They are one because of the communion of majesty, and three because of the distinctness of the persons.

3. For the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; [Col. 0271B] [Note: [Col. 0271D] “But another, not another thing.” From Augustine, *City of God* XI, chapter 10.] yet “another,” not “another thing,” because they are equally simple, equally immutable in goodness, and coeternal.

4. The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called “unbegotten.” The Son alone is born from the Father; therefore he alone is called “begotten.” The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son; therefore he alone is called the Spirit of both.

5. In this Trinity, some names are appellative and others proper. The proper names are essential, such as God, Lord, Almighty, Immutable, and Immortal. They are proper because they signify the substance itself, by which they are one.

6. The appellative names are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Unbegotten, Begotten, and Proceeding. These are also relational, because they refer to one another. When “God” is said, it is an essential term, because it is said with reference to himself. But when Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said, they are said relationally [Col. 0271C] because they refer to one another.

7. For “Father” is said not with reference to himself but relationally to the Son, because he has a Son; likewise “Son” is said relationally because he has a Father; and likewise the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

8. These appellations signify that they refer to one another, not the substance itself by which they are one. Accordingly, the Trinity exists in the relational names of the persons; the deity is not tripled but remains singular, because if it were tripled, we would introduce a plurality of gods.

9. The name “gods” is therefore applied in the plural to angels and holy human beings because they are not equal.

10. Concerning them the psalm says: “I said, You are gods.” But concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, it is shown that the name is not “Gods” but “God,” as the Apostle says: “Yet for us there is one God”; or as the divine voice says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God”—namely, so that there may be both a Trinity and one Lord God.

11. Among the Greeks, faith concerning the Trinity is expressed in this way: one οὐσία, as though one were to say “one nature” or “one essence”; three hypostases, which translates into Latin as either three persons or three substances.

[Col. 0272A] 12. For Latin usage properly speaks of God only in terms of essence; it does not properly use “substance” but uses it improperly, because among the Greeks “substance” truly means person, not nature.

## CHAPTER V. On Angels

1. In Greek they are called *angeloi*, in Hebrew *melachim*; 313 in Latin they are translated as “messengers,” because they announce the Lord’s will to peoples.

2. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “The name of angels”: from Gregory, *Homily 34 on the Gospels.]

The name “angels” is the name of an office, not of a nature; they are always spirits, but when they are sent, they are called angels.

3. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “To whom the license of painters…” From Jerome, on Isaiah 6.]

Painters therefore give them wings in order to signify their swift movement in every direction, just as, according to the stories of the poets, winds are also said to have wings, [Col. 0272B] namely because of their speed. Hence sacred Scripture says: “Who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103:3).

4. [Note: [Col. 0271D] “There are nine orders”: from Gregory, the same homily.]

Sacred Scripture testifies that there are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim. We shall explain by interpretation why the names of these offices were given in this way.

5. They are called “angels” because they are sent from heaven to announce things to human beings; for *angelos* in Greek means “messenger” in Latin.

6. In Greek, *archangels* is translated into Latin as “chief messengers.” Those who announce small or minor matters are called angels; those who announce great matters are called archangels. They are called archangels because they hold primacy among the angels; for ἀρχὸς in Greek is translated as “prince” in Latin. They are leaders and princes, under whose order the duties of the individual angels have been assigned.

7. [Note: [Col. 0272D] “For since archangels … had known”: from *Moral Expositions* IV, chapter 27; elsewhere chapter 31.]

Since archangels preside over angels, the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: “And behold, the angel who was speaking with me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: Run and speak to that boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” (Zech. 2:3).

8. For if higher powers among the angels did not in some way direct the lower powers in their offices, the angel would in no way have learned from another angel what he should say to the human being.

9. [Note: [Col. 0272D] “Some of the archangels”: from the same homily.]

Some archangels are called by personal names, 314 so that their power in their work may be indicated by the names themselves.

10. [Col. 0272D] [Note: [Col. 0272D] “Gabriel … Michael”: from Gregory and Jerome, on Daniel 8.]

Gabriel is translated from Hebrew into our language as “strength of God.” Wherever divine power or strength is manifested, Gabriel is sent.

11. Hence, at the time when the Lord was to be born and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Mary to announce him who deigned to come humbly in order to defeat the aerial powers.

12. Michael is translated as “Who is like God?” Whenever something of wondrous power occurs in the world, this archangel is sent. His name derives from his work, because no one is able to do what God is able to do.

13. Raphael is translated as “healing” or “medicine of God.” Wherever the work of curing and healing is necessary, this archangel is sent by God, and therefore he is called the medicine of God.

14. Hence this same archangel was sent to Tobias, applied healing to his eyes, and, when his blindness had been removed, restored his sight. Through the interpretation of the name, the angel’s office is also indicated.

15. Uriel is translated as “Fire of God,” just as we read that fire appeared in the bush. We also read that fire was sent from above and fulfilled what had been commanded.

16. Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and virtues—the orders and dignities of the angels—are understood as comprising the whole heavenly society, which the Apostle encompasses. According to this very distribution of offices, some are called thrones, others dominions, others principalities, others powers, according to the particular dignities by which they are distinguished from one another.

17. The virtues are said to be certain angelic ministries through which signs and miracles occur in the world; for this reason they are called virtues.

18. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Powers”: from Gregory, cited above.]

The powers are those to whom hostile powers are subject; hence they are called “powers,” because evil spirits are restrained by their authority, so that they cannot harm the world as much as they desire.

19. The principalities are those who preside over the ranks of angels. Because they arrange subordinate angels to fulfill the divine ministry, they have received the name “principalities.” For some administer, while others attend, as Daniel says: “A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand attended him” (Dan. 7:10).

20. The dominions are those who surpass even the virtues and principalities. Because they exercise dominion over the other ranks of angels, they are called dominions.

21. The thrones are ranks of angels who, in Latin speech, are called seats. They are called thrones because the Creator presides over them and arranges his judgments through them.

22. The cherubim are likewise described as exalted powers of heaven and angelic ministries. Translated from Hebrew into our language, they mean “abundance of knowledge.” They are exalted ranks of angels who, because they are placed nearer [to God] and are more fully filled with divine knowledge than the others, are called cherubim—that is, “fullness of knowledge.”

23. They are those two creatures fashioned from metal above the mercy seat of the ark, to signify the presence of angels, in whose midst God is shown.

24. The seraphim likewise constitute a multitude of angels who, translated from Hebrew [Note: [Col. 0273D] Into Latin, “burning.” So Gregory; Jerome has “those who burn.”] into Latin, mean “burning” or “setting aflame.” They are called burning because no angels stand between them and God; and therefore, the nearer they stand before him, the more they are inflamed by the radiance of the divine light.

25. Hence they cover the face and feet of him who sits on God’s throne. For this reason the rest of the angelic host cannot fully behold the essence of God, because the seraphim veil it.

26. These names of the ranks of angels are so specific to the individual orders that they are nevertheless partly common to all. For although “thrones” specifically designates the seats of God in one order of angels, the Psalmist nevertheless says: “You who sit upon the cherubim” (Ps. 79:2).

27. These orders are therefore called by private names because they have received this same office more fully within their own order. Although these names are common to all, they are nevertheless assigned specifically to their respective orders.

28. As stated above, each has been entrusted with particular offices, which they are known to have merited at the beginning of the world. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “For since angels preside both over places …”: from Gregory, *Moral Expositions* IV, chapter 27.]

Since angels preside both over places and over human beings, the angel testifies through the prophet, saying: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me” (Dan. 10:13).

29. Hence it is evident that there is no place over which angels do not preside. [Note: [Col. 0273D] “For they also preside over the beginnings of all works.” Others: “of human beings.” The Neapolitan manuscript reads: “For they preside in order to observe the works of human beings.”] For they also preside over the beginnings of all works.

30. This is the order or distinction of the angels who, after the fall of the wicked, remained steadfast in heavenly strength. For after the apostate angels fell, these were established in the perseverance of eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven, the statement is repeated at the beginning: “Let there be a firmament,” and “the firmament was called heaven” (Gen. 1:6, 8).

31. Clearly this shows that, after the ruin of the evil angels, those who remained attained the steadfastness of eternal perseverance: no longer turned aside by any fall, falling through no pride, but remaining firmly in the love and contemplation of God, finding nothing else sweet except him by whom they were created.

32. The fact that two seraphim are read of in Isaiah figuratively shows the significance of the Old and New Testaments. But the fact that they cover the face and feet of God means that we cannot know what was before the world or what will be after the world, but contemplate only the intermediate things through their testimony. [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Through their testimony.” Chacon rejected these words because they are absent from Jerome.]

33. Each has six wings, [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Because from the making…” Jerome, cited above.] because in the present age we know only about the making of the world, which was accomplished in six days. By crying “Holy” three times, one to another, they demonstrate the mystery of the Trinity in one divinity.

## CHAPTER VI. On Human Beings Who Received Their Names through a Certain Foreshadowing

1. Most [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Most.” Almost everything is from Jerome.] of the first human beings have the origins of their names from particular causes. Their names were prophetically assigned in such a way that they correspond either to causes that would follow or to causes that had preceded them.

2. While the spiritual sacrament remains in these names, we shall now pursue only the historical meaning according to the letter. Where we have not touched upon the interpretation of the etymologies, we have given only the etymology itself in Latin.

3. When one Hebrew name is interpreted in different ways, this results from differences in accents and letters, so that the names change according to their various meanings.

4. Adam, as the blessed Jerome has handed down, is translated as “human being,” or “earthly,” or “red earth.” For flesh was made from earth, and soil was the material from which the human being was fashioned.

5. Heva (Eve) is translated as “life,” or “calamity,” or “woe”: [Col. 0275B] “Life,” because she was the origin of birth; “calamity” and “woe,” because through transgression she became the cause of dying. [Note: [Col. 0275D] “For *calamity* took its name from *falling*.” Victorinus, *On Orthography*, and Terentius Scaurus. *Calamitas* was formerly said as *cadamitas*.] For *calamity* took its name from falling.

6. Others say that Eve was also called “life” and “calamity” for this reason: a woman is often the cause of salvation for her husband, often the cause of calamity and death, which is “woe.”

7. Cain is translated as “possession”; [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Hence the etymology”: from Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 4.] therefore, expressing its etymology, his father said: “Cain,” that is, “I have possessed a man through God.” [Note: [Col. 0275D] “The same also means ‘lamentation.’ Jerome: ‘Cain’ means possession or acquisition; ‘Cainam,’ lamentation or their possession. It should therefore not seem surprising if, just as *Cainam* means possession, conversely *Cain* should mean lamentation for Isidore.”] It also means “lamentation,” because he was killed on account of the slain Abel and paid the penalty for his crime.

318 8. Abel is translated as “mourning,” by which name he was prefigured as one who would be killed. It also means “vanity,” because he was soon released and taken away.

9. Seth is translated as “resurrection,” because he was born after the killing of his brother, as though he raised up his brother’s resurrection from the dead. It also means “placing,” because God placed him in place of Abel.

10. Enos, according to the variation of his own language, is called “human being” or “man.” The name was appropriately given to him. For it is written of him: “Then the invocation of the name of the Lord began.” Although many of the Hebrews think that it was then that idols were first fashioned in the name of the Lord and in his likeness.

11. Enoch means “dedication.” Later Cain built a city in his name.

12. Cainam means “lamentation” or “their possession.” Just as Cain means “possession,” so the derivative name *Cainam* means “their possession.”

13. Mathusalem is interpreted as “he has died.” The etymology of the name is evident. [Note: [Col. 0276D] For some thought that he was taken away with his father and passed through the Flood. From the *Questions*, on chapter 5.] Some indeed thought that he was translated with his father and survived the Flood. For this reason the name is expressly translated “he has died,” so that it might be shown that he did not live after the Flood but died in that same cataclysm. For only eight people escaped the Flood in the Ark.

14. LAMECH, “striking.” For he struck and killed Cain; this he himself later confessed to his wives that he had done.

15. NOE is interpreted as “rest,” because under him all former works ceased through the Flood. Hence his father, when naming him Noe, said: “This one will make us rest from all our labors” (Gen. V, 29).

16. Sem is called “named,” having received this name as a prophecy of his posterity. For from him came patriarchs and prophets and apostles and the people of God; from his stock also came Christ, whose name is great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting.

17. CHAM means “hot,” and he too was surnamed by foreknowledge of what would come. For his posterity possessed that part of the earth which, being nearer to the sun, is hotter. Hence even to this day Egypt is called Cham in the language of the Egyptians. [Note: [Col. 0276D] In the language of the Egyptians, CHAM. Or Ham, from the *Questions* on chapter 9.]

18. JAPHETH means “breadth.” For from him the people of the nations was born, and because the multitude of believers from the nations is broad, he was called Japheth from that breadth.

19. Chanaan, son of Cham, is interpreted as “their movement.” What else is this but their deed? For he was cursed because of his father’s movement—that is, because of his deed.

20. ARFAXAT, “healing desolation.”

21. Chus is interpreted in Hebrew as “Ethiopian,” receiving from the posterity of his race the name that he bore. For the Ethiopians were descended from him.

22. Nembrod is interpreted as “tyrant.” For he was the first to seize an unfamiliar tyranny over peoples, and he himself undertook to build a tower of impiety against God.

23. HEBER, “crossing over.” His etymology is mystical: God would pass over from his stock and the grace transferred to the nations would not remain among them. For the Hebrews arose from him.

24. PHALEG, “division.” His father therefore gave him this name because he was born when the earth was divided through the languages.

[Note: [Col. 0276D] THARA, “exploration of ascent.” In the *Names* from Genesis: THARA, “exploration of fragrance,” or “EXPLORATION OF ASCENT,” or “PASTURING.”]

THARA, “exploration of ascent.”

25. MELCHISEDECH, “righteous king.” He was a king because he afterward ruled Salem; righteous because, discerning the mysteries of the Law and the Gospel, he offered in sacrifice not the victims of animals but an offering of bread and the cup.

26. LOTH, “turning aside.” For he did not consent to the deeds of the Sodomites but turned aside from their illicit fires of the flesh.

27. MOAB, “from the father”; the entire name has an etymology. For the firstborn daughter conceived him from her father.

28. Ammon, for which the meaning of the name is given as “son of my people,” is derived so that part of the expression conveys the sense of the name and part is itself the word. For Ammi, from whom the Ammonites were named, means “my people.”

29. Sarai is interpreted as “my princess,” because she was the mistress of only one household. Later, when the reason for the name had changed and the letter *i* was removed from the end, she was called Sara, that is, “princess.” For she was destined to be the princess of all nations, just as the Lord had promised Abraham: “I will give you a son from Sara, and I will bless him, and he will become nations; moreover, kings of peoples will come from her” (Gen. XVII, 16).

30. AGAR, “stranger,” or “converted.” For she was an Egyptian woman, given as a stranger to Abraham’s embrace for the purpose of begetting children; after she had shown contempt, she was converted to Sara when the angel rebuked her.

31. [Note: [Col. 0277D] CETURA, “incense.” Jerome: CETURA, “offering incense,” or “joined,” or “united.”]

CETURA, “incense.”

32. Ismael is interpreted as “hearing of God,” for it is written: “And he called his name Ismael, because God heard him” (Gen. XVI, 11).

33. Esau is three-named and is called by different names for different reasons. He is called Esau, that is, “red,” because of the cooking of the red lentil stew, by eating which he lost his birthright. He was called Edom because of the redness of his body, which in Latin is called “blood-colored.” He was called Seir because he was rough and hairy; for when he was born, he was entirely hairy, like a pelt. [Note: [Col. 0277D] Esau, three-named. Likewise in *On Obadiah*.]

34. Therefore he is called by three names: ESAU, that is, “red”; EDOM, that is, “blood-colored”; and SEIR, that is, “hairy,” because he lacked smoothness.

35. REBECCA, “patience,” or “she who has received much.”

36. LIA, “laborious,” especially in childbearing. For she experienced more pains than Rachel through the fruitfulness of giving birth.

37. Rachel is interpreted as “sheep,” for Jacob tended Laban’s sheep because of her.

38. [Note: [Col. 0277D] ZELPHA, “gaping mouth.” Jerome: “flowing mouth.”]

ZELPHA, “gaping mouth.”

BALA, “grown old.” Dina is translated as “cause”; for she became the cause of the quarrel at Shechem.

39. THAMAR, “bitterness,” because of the dead men. She is also called “changing,” for she changed herself into the appearance of a prostitute when she slept with her father-in-law.

40. PHARES, “division,” because he divided the membrane of the afterbirth; from this division he received the name Phares. Hence the Pharisees, who separated themselves from the people as though they were righteous, were called “divided.”

41. Zara, his brother, in whose hand was the scarlet thread, is interpreted as “rising,” either because he appeared first or because many righteous people were born from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles. Zara, that is, “rising,” was his name.

42. Job is rendered in Latin as “suffering,” appropriately because of the striking of his flesh and his painful afflictions. For the etymology of his name prefigured his calamities.

43. [Note: [Col. 0277D] PHARAO is the name not of a man but of a title. From the same source, on Isaiah XXX.]

Pharao is the name not of a man but of a title; thus among us too kings are called Augusti even though they are registered under their own names. PHARAO is rendered into Latin as “stripping him bare,” namely, God, or “his destroyer,” for he was the persecutor of God’s people. [Note: [Col. 0277D] PHARAO, “stripping him bare.” In the *Names* from Acts: PHARAO, “stripping him bare,” or “HIS DESTROYER.” Likewise in the *Names* on the Epistle to the Hebrews.]

44. JANNES, “maritime,” or “where there is a sign.” His sign yielded and failed before the signs of Moses; hence the magicians said: “This is the finger of God.”

45. [Note: [Col. 0277D] MAMBRES, “leathery sea.” Thus all books read it, and Jerome also. But since Jerome himself interprets MAMBRE as “clear,” JAMBRES, “lucid sea,” may perhaps be the correct reading, so that there may be some basis both for “sea” and for “clear.” For in Paul, too, Ἰαμβρῆς is read at II Tim. III; and he is so called by Palladius in the *Life of Macarius of Alexandria* and by Eusebius, book IX of the *Preparation*, chapter 3.]

MAMBRES, “concubine’s sea,” or “sea at the head.”

46. Moyses is interpreted as “taken from the water.” For Pharaoh’s daughter found him exposed on the bank of the river; taking him up, she adopted him and called his name Moyses because she had taken him from the water.

47. AARON is interpreted as “mountain of strength,” because, taking a censer, he stood in the midst of the survivors and the slain to confront them, and, like a strong mountain, shut out the spread of death.

48. ELEAZAR, “the help of God.”

BALAC, “bringing down,” or “devouring.”

BALAAM, “empty people.”

49. PHINEES, “sparing the mouth.” For he pierced Zambri with a dagger together with the Midianite prostitute and appeased the Lord’s fury, so that He might spare.

50. ZAMBRI, “this one provoking,” or “making bitter.” The name is properly prefigured by bitterness, because through sin he made the people bitter.

51. RAAB, “breadth,” or “hunger,” or “impetus.”

Josue is interpreted as “savior.” For, as a figure of Christ, he saved the people from the desert and led them into the land of promise.

52. CALEB, “as a heart,” or “dog.”

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Othoniel. In the *Names* from Joshua: OTHONIEL, “answer of God,” or “revelation of God,” or “my time is God,” or “sign of God.”]

OTHONIEL, “his time is God,” or “answer of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Aoth. In the *Names* from the same source.]

AOTH, “glorious.”

BARACH, “flashing.”

53. DEBBORA, “bee,” or “talkative.” “Bee,” because she was extremely ready for battle, fighting against Sisara; after he was killed, she sang a song, and hence she was “talkative.”

JAHEL, “ascension.”

54. GEDEON, “the testing of their iniquity.” For through frequent proofs he was instructed by what omen he might secure future victory against the enemies; from this future test he derived the etymology of his name.

55. ABIMELECH, “my father is king.”

THOLAH, “worm,” or “scarlet.”

JAIR, “illuminating.”

JEPHTE, “opening,” or “opened.”

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Hesebon. In the *Names* from Numbers: “thought,” or “bond of grief.”]

HESEBON, “thought,” or “bond of grief.”

ABDO, “his servant.”

56. SAMSON, “their sun,” or “strength of the sun.” For he was renowned for his power and delivered Israel from its enemies.

DALILA, “little poor woman,” or “bucket.”

BOOZ, “in strength,” or “in whom there is strength.”

57. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Noemi. From the letter to Furia, near the end.]

Noemi, which we may interpret as “comforted,” because, after her husband and children had died abroad, she kept her Moabite daughter-in-law as her consolation.

58. Ruth is interpreted as “hastening.” For she was a foreign woman from a gentile people who, leaving her homeland, hastened to cross into the land of Israel, saying to her mother-in-law: “Wherever you go, I will go.”

59. ANNA is interpreted as “his grace,” because although she had previously been barren by nature, she was at last made fruitful by God’s grace.

HELI, “my God.”

60. OPHNI, “barefoot.” For he was the son of Heli, chosen for priestly service; he expressed its loss in his name. For the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace.”

61. And the prophet says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace.” He is therefore interpreted as “barefoot,” so that by his name it might be signified that the priesthood of the Old Testament had been taken away from the old people.

62. Phinees, the brother of Ophni, is interpreted as “mute mouth,” signifying the silence of the old priesthood and its teaching.

SAMUEL, “his name is God.”

JESSAI, “sacrifice of the islands,” or “incense.”

63. SAUL is interpreted as “request.” For it is known how the people of the Hebrews requested him as their king and received him not according to God but according to their own will.

64. DAVID, “strong of hand,” because he was exceedingly strong in battle. He is also “desirable,” namely, in his lineage, concerning which the prophet had foretold: “The Desired One of all nations will come.”

65. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Three names. From the commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter I.]

Solomon is said to have had three names. His first name is said to be Salomon, that is, “peaceful,” because there was peace in his kingdom. His second name was Idida, because he was beloved and pleasing to the Lord. His third name was Coheleth, which in Greek is called *ecclesiastes*, and in Latin “preacher,” because he spoke to the people.

66. JONATHAS, “gift of the dove.”

67. [Note: [Col. 0279D] ABSALON, “peace of the father.” Not from Jerome, who interprets it as “father of peace,” but from Gregory in the prologue to Psalm VII on penitence—if indeed that work is Gregory’s—for he says: ABSALON is interpreted as “peace of the father,” not because he had any peace with his father, but because, in the face of Absalon’s perversity, his father showed how great his peace and patience were.]

ABSALOM, “peace of the father” by antiphrasis, because he waged war against his father; or because, in that very war, David is recorded to have remained reconciled to his son, to such an extent that he even mourned his death with great grief.

68. ROBOAM, “breadth of the people,” also by antiphrasis, because after ten tribes had separated from him, only two were left to him.

69. ABIA, “the father is Lord,” or “the father was.”

ASA, “taking away,” or “lifting up.”

JOSAPHAT, “judgment of the Lord.”

JORAM, “he who is exalted.”

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Ochozias. In the *Names* from Matthew.]

ACHAZIAS, “grasping the Lord.”

70. ATHALIA, “time of the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0279D] JOAS, “breathing.” Thus all manuscripts. But since Jerome reads in the *Names* from the Book of Judges: JOAS, “hoping,” or “temporal,” or “strength of the Lord,” we think “breathing” should be restored here. There is one etymology, “breathing” or “temporal,” derived from a verb meaning “he despaired,” which fits “breathing” or “temporal” very well. The addition “strength of the Lord” has another basis, namely, “Lord” and “strong,” or “strength.” Jerome frequently confuses Hebrew names, whether because they were once written differently or because they become identical in Latin writing and pronunciation; nevertheless, he sometimes gives the reason for their divergent interpretations, and often neglects to do so, as he himself admits in the preface to the book *On Hebrew Names*, and Isidore notes at the beginning of this chapter.]

JOAS, “breathing,” or “strength of the Lord.”

AMASIAS, “lifting up the people.”

OZIAS, “strength of the Lord.”

AZARIAS, “help of the Lord.”

71. [Note: [Col. 0280D] “Ozias is the same as he who…” Jerome’s words in Isaiah I.]

Ozias is the same as Azarias, under two names.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] “He is the one who…” Likewise in Amos I, where he is called a priest unlawfully claiming what was not his.]

He is the one who, attempting to claim for himself an unlawful priesthood, was struck with leprosy on the forehead.

72. Joathan means “perfect.” His name has a beautiful etymology: he did what was right in the sight of the Lord and built the high gate of the temple.

73. ACHAZ, “grasping.”

EZECHIAS, “the Lord is strong.”

MANASSES, “forgetful.” For through many crimes and sacrileges he had abandoned and forgotten God; or because God forgot his sins.

74. [Note: [Col. 0280D] Amon. In the *Names* from Matthew: AMON, “faithful” or “nourished,” if it begins with the letter *a*; but if it is written *ex*, it is interpreted as “laden.”]

AMON, “faithful” or “laden.”

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Josias. In the *Names* from Matthew.]

JOSIAS, “where the incense of the Lord is”; this is the proper etymology of the name. For he was the one who burned the idols.

75. JOACHAZ, “strong.”

JOACHIM, “where there is preparation.”

ELIACHIM, “resurrection of God.”

JECHONIAS, “preparation of the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Sedechias. In the *Names* from III Kings and in Ezekiel II.]

SEDECHIAS, “righteous of the Lord.”

76. [Note: [Col. 0280D] Jeroboam. In Amos I: JEROBOAM, “judgment,” or “cause of the people,” δικασμὸς λαοῦ, although some, reading the Greek letter χ, suppose it to mean “division of the people.”]

JEROBOAM, “judgment,” or “cause of the people,” or, as some say, “division,” because in his reign the people of Israel was divided and cut off from the kingdom of David’s stock. For he became the cause of the people’s division.

77. ZAMBRI, “psalm,” or “my song.”

OMRI, “my curling.”

ACHAB, “brother of the father.”

78. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Jezabel. In the *Names* from the Apocalypse.]

JEZABEL, “flow of blood,” or “she who flows blood,” but better, “where there is a dungheap.” For, having been thrown down, the dogs ate her flesh, as Elijah had foretold: “The flesh of Jezabel,” he said, “will be like dung upon the face of the earth.”

79. OCHOZIAS, “grasping God.”

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Jehu. In the *Names* from III Kings.]

JEHU, “he himself,” or “he is.”

[Note: [Col. 0281D] JOATHA, “strong.” Roman manuscript: JATHAR, “burned.” Jerome: ETHAM, “strong.” Joatham and Joachaz, which are read in some manuscripts, have the interpretations given shortly before, so that the whole matter seems to require further investigation.]

JOATHA, “strong.”

SELLA, “his shadow,” or “request.”

MANAHEM, “comforting.”

PHACEAS, “opening.”

80. NABUCHODONOSOR, “prophecy of a narrow flask,” or “prophesying such a sign,” namely, of future events through a dream, which he is said to have seen and Daniel interpreted; or “sitting in the knowledge of distress,” on behalf of those whom he led into captivity.

81. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Zorobabel. In Haggai I.]

Zorobabel is reported among the Hebrews to be composed of three complete names. *Zo*, “this one”; *ro*, “master”; *Babel* properly means “Babylonian.” Thus the name ZOROBABEL is formed: “this master from Babylon.” For he was born in Babylon, where he also became leader of the Jewish people.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Patriarchs

1. The etymologies of certain patriarchs should be noted, so that we may know what their names signify. For most of them received their names from particular circumstances. *Patriarch* is interpreted as “chief of fathers.” For ἄρχος in Greek means “chief.”

2. [Note: [Col. 0281D] ABRAM, “father seeing.” From the *Names* in Matthew.]

Abram was first called “father seeing the people,” with reference, namely, only to Israel. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Later he was called ABRAHAM. From the *Questions* on chapter 17.] Later he was called Abraham, which is translated “father of many nations,” something that was still future through faith. “Of nations” is not contained in the name but is understood, according to the saying: “Your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations.”

3. Isaac received his name from laughter. For his father had laughed when Isaac was promised to him, marveling with joy. His mother also laughed when he was promised through the three men, doubting with joy. For this reason, then, he received the name Isaac; for it is interpreted as “laughter.”

4. [Note: [Col. 0282D] “It should be known.” On chapter 17. Some wrongly substitute Samuel for SOLOMON. See I Chronicles XXII.]

It should be known that four persons in the Old Testament were called by their names, without any concealment, before they were born: Ismael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josias. Read the Scriptures.

5. JACOB is interpreted as “supplanter,” either because at birth he grasped the heel of his brother as he was being born, or because he later deceived his brother by cunning. Hence Esau also said: “Justly has he been called Jacob, for behold, he has supplanted me a second time.”

6. [Note: [Col. 0282D] ISRAEL, “man seeing God.” Thus in the *Names* and in Isaiah I. But he rejects this interpretation in the *Questions*, chapter 32, where it is interpreted as “prince with God.” Again, in the commentary on Joel, εὐθύτατον θεοῦ, that is, “most upright of God.”]

ISRAEL, “man seeing God.” He received this name when he wrestled throughout the night and prevailed in the struggle with the angel, and was blessed at the rising of the morning star. Hence he was called Israel because of the vision of God, just as he himself said: “I saw the Lord, and my soul was saved.”

7. [Note: [Col. 0282D] Ruben. On chapter 29.]

Ruben is interpreted as “son of vision.” For when Lia gave birth to him, she called his name Ruben, saying: “Because God has seen my humiliation.”

8. [Note: [Col. 0282D] Simeon. The same place.]

Simeon is interpreted as “hearing.” Thus Lia said when she gave birth to him: “Because God has heard me.”

9. LEVI, “added.” For when Lia gave birth to him, she said, no longer doubting her husband’s love: “Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons.”

10. JUDAS is called “confession.” For when Lia gave birth to him, she returned praise to the Lord, saying: “Now for this I will confess to the Lord”; and for this reason he was called Judas. His name was therefore derived from confession, which is thanksgiving.

11. [Note: [Col. 0282D] Issachar. On chapter 30.]

Issachar is interpreted as “there is a reward.” For *ie* means “there is,” and *sachar*, “reward.” This was because Lia had purchased for herself the intercourse with her husband that was owed to Rachel, in exchange for Reuben’s mandrakes. Hence, when he was born, Lia said: “God has given me my reward.”

12. ZABULON is interpreted as “dwelling.” For Lia had given birth to this sixth son; therefore, now secure, she said: “My husband will dwell with me.” Hence her son was called “dwelling.”

13. [Note: [Col. 0282D] Nephthalim. The same place.]

The name Nephthalim derives from “conversion” or “comparison.” Hence Rachel said when her maid Bala had given birth to him: “God has made me dwell with my sister.”

14. Dan is interpreted as “judgment.” For when Bala had given birth to him, her mistress Rachel said: “The Lord has judged me, and hearing me has given me a son.” She expressed the reason for the name, giving the son of her maid the name of judgment because the Lord had judged her.

15. Gad was named from “fortune” or “battle array.” For when Zelpha gave birth to him, his mistress Lia said: “By fortune”—that is, “in battle array,” or “by event.”

16. ASER is called “blessed.” For when Zelpha had given birth to him, Lia said: “I am blessed, and women will call me blessed”; and because she was called blessed, she named him “Blessed,” according to the etymology of the name.

17. Joseph was called “increase,” because his mother had desired that another child be added to her. [Note: [Col. 0282D] “Pharaoh named him.” On chapter 41.] Pharaoh called him Zaphanath Phaaneca, which in Hebrew means “finder of hidden things,” because he revealed obscure dreams and foretold the coming famine.

18. Nevertheless, since this name is Egyptian, its meaning must be sought in that language. Thus Zaphanath Phaaneca in Egyptian is interpreted as “savior of the world,” because he freed the world from the impending destruction of famine.

19. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Benjamin. On chapter 35.]

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” which signifies strength. For the right hand is called *Jamin*. His mother, dying, had called his name Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” His father changed this, naming him “son of the right hand.”

20. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Manasses … Ephraim. On chapter 41.]

Manasses was named because his father had forgotten his labors. For in Hebrew this means “forgetfulness.”

21. Ephraim, because God had increased him; from this name it is translated into our language as “increase.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Prophets

1. Those whom paganism calls seers, our people call prophets, as though they were “fore-speakers,” because they speak forth and proclaim the truth about future things. Those whom we call prophets were called “seers” in the Old Testament, because they saw what others did not see and perceived beforehand what had been hidden in mystery. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Prophets in the Old Testament. From the prologue to the *Library*.]

2. Hence it is written in Samuel: “Let us go to the seer.” Hence Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne.” And Ezekiel: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.”

3. The etymologies of certain prophets’ names should also be noted. For their names clearly show what they foretold in the future by their deeds and words.

4. Elias is interpreted as “the Lord God.” He is therefore so called by anticipation of what was to come. For when he disputed over the sacrifice with the four hundred priests of Baal, after invoking the name of the Lord, fire descended from heaven upon the burnt offering. When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said: “The Lord himself is God” (III Kings XVIII, 30).

5. For this reason he first received such a name, because through him the people would later come to know the Lord God. [Note: [Col. 0283D] He is also “strong of the Lord.” From Letter 61 to Pammachius.] He is also interpreted as “strong of the Lord,” either because he killed those same priests or because he endured the hostility of Achab.

6. ELISAEUS is interpreted as “salvation of the Lord,” and he received this name by anticipation of what was to come. Indeed, he performed many miracles and, driving away famine, saved the people from death.

7. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Nathan. In the *Names* from Luke.]

NATHAN, “he gave,” or “of the giver.”

[Note: [Col. 0283D] ISAIAS. “Salvation of the Lord” in the *Names* from Acts; “saving act of the Lord” in the *Names* from the Epistle to the Romans; “Savior of the Lord” in chapter I of Isaiah, according to his own interpretation.]

Isaias is interpreted as “Savior of the Lord.” And rightly so: for more than the others he proclaims the Savior of all nations and his mysteries. [Note: [Col. 0283D] “For he is a savior.” From the preface to the same Isaiah.]

8. JEREMIAS, “exalted of the Lord,” because it was said to him: “I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms” (Jer. I, 10).

9. EZECHIEL, “strength of God.”

DANIEL, “judgment of God,” either because, in the judgment of the elders, he delivered the sentence of divine examination, rescuing Susanna from death after discovering their falsehood; or because, discerning with an attentive mind the visions and dreams in which future things were displayed through signs [perhaps sigla] and riddles, he revealed them. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Here also “man of desires.” From the letter to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity.] He was also called “man of desires,” because he did not eat the bread of desire and did not drink the wine of lust.

10. OSEE, “savior,” or “saving.” For although he prophesied God’s anger against the people of Israel because of the crime of idolatry, he foretold salvation for the house of Judah. For this reason King Ezechias of Judah is shown to have cleansed and purified the Lord’s temple after removing the idols that earlier kings had consecrated.

11. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Joel. In the preface to Malachi: JOEL, who is interpreted as “THE LORD GOD.” In the *Names*: JOEL, “BEGINNING,” or “HE IS GOD,” or “OF GOD.” In the preface to Joel: Joel, ἀρχόμενος, that is, “BEGINNING.”]

JOEL, “the Lord God,” or “beginning for God,” or “was of God.” For this is what the uncertain etymology of his name signifies.

12. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Amos … because he had already been torn away. From the commentary on chapter I.]

AMOS, “people torn away.” For his prophecy concerned the people of Israel, because they had already been torn away from the Lord and served golden calves, or because they had been torn away from the kingdom of David’s stock.

13. [Note: [Col. 0284D] NAHUM, “mourning.” This should be read in Jerome’s *Names* from the Epistle of Barnabas, not “sprout,” from the Toledo manuscript; the others have “sprout” corruptly.]

NAHUM, “mourning,” or “consoler.” For he rebukes the city of bloodshed, and after its overthrow he consoles Zion, saying: “Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the evangelizer and announcer of peace” (Isa. XLII, 7).

14. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Habacuc. From the prologue to the commentaries.]

HABACUC, “embracing,” either because, as one beloved of the Lord, he is called “embrace,” or because he entered into a contest with God and received the name “embracing,” that is, “wrestling.” For no one else dared with such bold speech to challenge God to a dispute over justice, asking why in human affairs and in the *politeia*—πολιτεία, “constitution” or “ordering”—of this world there is such an abundance of injustice.

15. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Micheas … concerning which it is said of Elihu. Job XXXVIII.]

MICHEAS, “who is this?” or “who is he?” For he threatens Samaria because of the idols in the manner in which it is said of Elihu: “Who is this who wraps up words?” (Job, XXXVIII, 2).

16. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Sophonias. On chapter I.]

SOPHONIAS is interpreted as “watchtower,” or “secret of the Lord”; both meanings suit the prophet. For they know the mysteries of God. Hence it is said to Ezechiel: “He has appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III, 17). And elsewhere: “The Lord will do nothing unless he has revealed it to his servants the prophets” (Amos, III, 7).

17. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Abdias. On chapter I.]

ABDIAS, “servant of the Lord.” For just as Moses was the servant of the Lord and the Apostle the servant of Christ, so this man, sent as an ambassador to the nations, sees and proclaims things worthy of prophetic ministry and service; hence he is called “servant of the Lord.”

18. [Note: [Col. 0285D] JONAS … he is the same as AMATHI, etc. From the preface to Jonah.]

Jonas is interpreted as “dove,” or “suffering.” “Dove,” because of his groaning when he was in the belly of the whale for three days. “Suffering,” either because of the sorrow he felt over the salvation of the Ninevites or because of the ivy that suddenly withered, whose shade had sheltered him from the sun’s heat.

19. He is also Amathi, the son of the widow of Sarepta, as the Jews assert—the boy whom Elias raised from the dead, after whose mother said to him: “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of God in your mouth is true” (III Kings XVII, 24). For this reason the boy himself was called Amathi. For *Amathi* in Hebrew is rendered in Latin as “truth,” and because Elias spoke truth, the one who was raised was called the son of truth.

20. ZACHARIAS, “memory of the Lord.” For when the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation had been completed, the Lord remembered his people while Zacharias was preaching; and at the command of Darius the people of God returned, and both the city and the temple were rebuilt.

21. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Aggaeus. From the prologue to the *Library*.]

Aggeus in Latin sounds as “festive” and “joyful.” For he prophesies that the destroyed temple will be rebuilt and proclaims the joy of return after the mourning of captivity.

22. Malachias is interpreted as “angel of the Lord,” that is, “messenger.” For whatever he said was believed to have been commanded by the Lord, and therefore the Seventy translated his name in this way, saying: “The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel by the hand of his angel” (Mal. I, 1).

23. ESDRAS, “helper.”

NEHEMIAS, “comforter from the Lord.” These names were received by a certain anticipation of future events. For they became a help and consolation to all that people returning to their homeland. They also rebuilt the Lord’s temple and restored the work of the walls and towers.

24. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Ananias. From the *Names* from Jeremiah and Daniel.]

ANANIAS, “grace of God.” He is also called Sidrac in the Chaldean language, which is interpreted as “my adornment.”

25. AZARIAS, “help of the Lord.” He is also called Abdenago, which is rendered in Latin as “serving—I am silent.”

26. [Note: [Col. 0285D] MISAEL, “who is the pool of the Lord.” From the *Names* from Daniel. Therefore all manuscripts are corrupt when they read “people of the Lord …” In the *Names* from Exodus: MISAEL, “touched by God,” or “who has asked?”]

MISAEL, “what is the marsh of the Lord?” He is also called Misach, which is interpreted as “laughter,” or “joy.” [Note: [Col. 0286D] Misach, in the same place.]

27. AHIA, “his brother.”

SEMEIA, “hearing the Lord.”

ASAPH, “gathering.”

[Note: [Col. 0286D] ETHAN, “strong,” or “ascent.” Jerome too has “kindled”; Augustine preferred that reading.]

ETHAN, “strong,” or “kindled.”

28. IDHITUM, “leaping over them,” or “springing over them.”

For while some people cling to the earth, bent toward the ground, thinking about the things below and placing their hope in passing matters, this man, called “leaping over,” passed over them in song.

29. EMAN, “receiving,” or “their dread.”

BARACHIA, “the Lord is blessed,” or “blessed of the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Olda. From the *Names* from III Kings.]

OLDA, “destruction,” or “a byway.”

JUDITH, “praising,” or “confessing.”

ESTHER, “hidden.”

30. ZACHARIAS, “memory of the Lord,” because he sings: “To remember his holy covenant …” (Luke I, 72).

31. JOANNES BAPTISTA, “grace of the Lord,” because he is the boundary of prophecy, the herald of grace, or the beginning of baptism, through which grace is administered.

32. These are the prophets of the Old and New Testaments, whose end is Christ, to whom the Father says: “I have appointed you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. I, 5).

33. There are seven kinds of prophecy. The first kind is ecstasy, which is an excess or departure of the mind, as when Peter saw the vessel lowered from heaven in a state of mental amazement, containing various animals.

34. The second kind is vision, as when Isaiah said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne” (Isa. VI, 1). The third kind is a dream, as when Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder resting upon heaven. The fourth kind is through a cloud, as when God speaks to Moses and to Job after the plague.

35. The fifth kind is a voice from heaven, as when it sounded to Abraham, saying: “Do not lay your hand upon the boy” (Gen. XXII, 12). And to Saul on the road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4).

36. The sixth kind is a received parable, as in Solomon’s Proverbs and in the case of Balaam, when he was summoned by Balac. The seventh kind is the filling of the Holy Spirit, as occurs in nearly all the prophets.

37. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Others have said that there are three kinds of vision … governs. All from Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, final chapter.]

Others have said that there are three kinds of vision. One is according to the eyes of the body, as when Abraham saw three men beneath the oak of Mambre, Moses saw fire in the bush, and the disciples saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain between Moses and Elias, and other things of this kind.

38. The second is according to the spirit, by which we imagine the things we perceive through the body, as when Peter saw that disk lowered from heaven with various animals, and as when Isaiah saw the Lord on the highest throne—not bodily but spiritually.

39. For God is not bounded by bodily form; but just as many things are said figuratively rather than literally, so many things are also shown figuratively.

40. The third kind of vision is that which occurs neither through bodily senses nor through that part of the soul by which images of bodily things are received, but through the mind’s gaze, by which truth is perceived through understanding. Thus Daniel, endowed with this kind of mind, saw what Balthasar had seen bodily. Without this kind, the other two are either fruitless or even lead into error. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit governs all these kinds.

41. Not only a good person but also an evil person can possess prophecy; for we find that King Saul prophesied. He was persecuting holy David, and, filled with the Spirit, he began to prophesy.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Apostles

1. Apostles is interpreted as “those who are sent”; for their name indicates this. For just as in Greek ἄγγελοι are called *nuntii*—“messengers”—in Latin, so in Greek *apostoli* are called *missi*—“those who are sent”—in Latin. Christ sent them to evangelize throughout the whole world, so that some of them reached the Persians and Indians, teaching the nations and performing great and incredible miracles in the name of Christ, so that, with signs and wonders bearing witness, people might believe them in what they said and had seen. Moreover, most of them have explanations for their names.

2. Peter received his name from *petra*, that is, from Christ upon whom the Church is founded. For it was not *petra* that received its name from Peter, but Peter who received his name from *petra*, just as Christ is not called from Christian, but Christian from Christ. Therefore the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock, etc.,” because Peter had said: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” Then the Lord said to him: “Upon this rock,” he said, “which you have confessed, I will build my Church.” For Christ was the rock, upon whose foundation Peter himself also was built.

3. He was called Cephas because he was appointed head of the apostles; for *kephalē* (κεφαλή) is Greek for “head,” and the name itself is Syriac in Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] “Cephas … because he is in the head.” He supplied the Greek etymology following the example of Anacletus III, Dionysius the Areopagite, and Optatus of Milevis, although it is clear that the word is Syriac, and he himself immediately confirms this. Other examples and a not inelegant explanation of the matter may be found in Turrianus, Book II against the Magdeburgians, chapter 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0287D] “And the name itself in Peter is Syriac.” See Jerome, on Matthew VI, and in *Names*, from the same source.]

4. Simon Barjona, in our language, means “son of a dove,” and is equally a Syriac and Hebrew name. For *bar* means “son” in Syriac, while *Jona* means “dove” in both languages.

5. Others take it simply to mean that Simon, that is, Peter, was the son of John, according to the question: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” They hold that it was corrupted through a scribal error, so that *Barjona* was written instead of *Barjoanna*, that is, “son of John,” with one syllable omitted. *Joanna*, however, is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord.”

6. It is also established that Peter had three names: Peter, Cephas, and Simon Barjona. Simon, however, is interpreted in Hebrew as “obedient.”

[Note: [Col. 0287D] “Simon … obedient.” Jerome: “For *Simon* is said to mean ‘obedient.’”]

7. Saul is called “temptation” in the Hebrew language, because he had previously been engaged in the persecution of the Church. For he was a persecutor, and received that name when he was persecuting Christians.

8. Later, his name being changed, he became Paul instead of Saul; this is interpreted as “wonderful” or “chosen.” “Wonderful,” either because he performed many signs, or because he preached the Gospel of Christ among all the nations from East to West.

[Col. 0288A] 9. “Chosen,” as the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts XIII, 12). In Latin, however, Paul is named from *modicus*, “small” or “humble”; hence he himself says: “I am the least of all the apostles” (I Cor. XV, 9). When he was Saul, he was proud and exalted; when he was Paul, humble and small.

10. This is why we say: “I will see you shortly” (*Paulo post*), that is, “after a little while.” For because he became small, he himself says: “For I am the last of the apostles,” and: “To me, the least of all the saints” (Eph. III, 8). Cephas and Saul likewise received changed names so that they might be new even in name, just as Abraham and Sarah were.

11. Andrew, Peter’s brother according to the flesh and fellow-heir of grace, according to the Hebrew etymology is interpreted as “beautiful” or “answering”; in Greek, however, he is called *manly* from *anēr*, “man.”

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “In Greek, however.” In *Names*, from Acts.]

12. John received his name by a kind of prophecy corresponding to his merit; for it is interpreted as “in whom there is grace,” or “the grace of the Lord.” Jesus loved him more than the other apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “James.” In the chapter on Matthew X.]

13. James, son of Zebedee, is surnamed from his father. Leaving him, he and John followed the true Father. These are the sons of thunder, who were also called *Boanerges* because of the firmness and greatness of their faith. This is James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, who, after the Lord’s Ascension, is reported to have been killed by Herod.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “Boanerges.” In the same place. But in Daniel I, “sons of Zebedee” are called “sons of thunder,” and the more correct reading is not, as most think, *Boanerges*, but *Beneraham*; likewise in Isaiah LXII and in *Names*, from John.]

14. James, son of Alphaeus, is surnamed for distinction from the former, who is called the son of Zebedee, just as this one is the son of Alphaeus. Thus both received their surnames from their fathers.

[Col. 0288C] 15. This is James the younger, who in the Gospel is called the brother of the Lord, because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of the Lord’s mother. The evangelist John calls her Mary of Cleophas, assigning her that name from her father, or from the family’s ethnic origin, or for some other reason. *Alphaeus*, in Hebrew rendered into Latin, means “thousandth” or “learned.”

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “Because Mary was the wife of Alphaeus.” From the same source, *Against Helvidius*.]

16. Philip: “mouth of lamps” or “mouth of hands.”

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “Philip: mouth of lamps.” In *Names*, from Acts: “mouth of lamps”; in *Names*, from Luke: “mouth of the lamp,” or “mouth of hands.”]

Thomas: “abyss,” or “twin,” whence he is called *Didymus* (Δίδυμος) in Greek.

Bartholomew: “son of the one who suspends waters,” or “son of the one who suspends me.” This is Syriac, not Hebrew.

17. Matthew, in Hebrew, is rendered “given.” He is also called Levi, from the tribe from which he originated. In Latin he received the name from his occupation as a publican, because he was chosen from among the publicans and transferred into the apostolate.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] “Simon Cananaeus … Judas.” On Matthew X.]

18. Simon Cananaeus, to distinguish him from Simon Peter, was from the Galilean village of Cana, where the Lord changed water into wine. He is the one who in another Gospel is written as “the Zealot”; for *Cana* is interpreted as “zeal.”

19. Judas of James, elsewhere called Lebbaeus, has a figurative name derived from “heart,” which we may render diminutively as “little heart.” In another Gospel he is written as Thaddaeus. Ecclesiastical history records that he was sent to Edessa to King Abgar.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “Whom ecclesiastical history records.” The history of Eusebius, Book I, final chapter.]

20. Judas Iscariot received his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, as a forewarning of what would happen, namely, his condemnation. For *Issachar* is interpreted as “payment,” signifying the price of the betrayer for which he sold the Lord, as it is written: “And they took my payment, thirty pieces of silver, the price at which I was valued by them” (Matt. XXVII, 9).

21. Matthias, who alone among the apostles is found without a surname, is interpreted as “given,” with “in place of Judas” understood. He was chosen by the apostles in his place, when the lot was cast for the two.

[Col. 0289B] 22. Mark: “exalted by command,” certainly on account of the Gospel of the Most High which he preached.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “Mark: exalted by command.” Jerome repeats this frequently. But in *Names*, in the letter to the Colossians: “Mark, exalted by command,” or “bitter,” or certainly “worn down and polished.”]

23. Luke: “he himself rising” or “he himself raising,” because he raised up the preaching of the Gospel after the others.

24. Barnabas: “son of the Prophet,” or “son of consolation.”

## CHAPTER X. On the Remaining Names in the Gospel

1. Mary: “illuminatrix,” or “star of the sea”; for she bore the Light of the world. In Syriac, however, *Mary* is called “Lady,” appropriately, because she bore the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “Mary, illuminatrix.” In *Names*, from Matthew: most judge *Mariam* to mean “these illuminate me,” or “illuminatrix,” or “myrrh of the sea.” But this does not seem at all satisfactory to me. It is better to say that it signifies “star of the sea,” or “bitter sea.” It should also be known that *Mary* in Syriac is called “Lady.”]

2. Elizabeth: “fullness of my God,” or “the oath of my God.”

3. Magdalene: “tower.” Martha: “irritating” or “provoking”; in Syriac, however, it is interpreted as “ruling.”

4. Nathanael: “gift of God,” because deceit, that is, hypocrisy, was not in him through the gift of God.

5. Zebedee: “given,” or “this one flowing.”

Zacchaeus: “just,” or “justified,” or “to be justified.” The name is Syriac, not Hebrew.

6. Lazarus: “helped,” because he was raised from the dead.

Herod: “leathern,” “glorious”—a clear etymology.

7. Caiaphas: “investigator,” or “shrewd,” or “vomiting with the mouth”; for with his wicked mouth he condemned the righteous man, although by a prophetic mystery he had announced this beforehand.

8. Pontius: “turning aside counsel,” namely, the counsel of the Jews. For after receiving water he washed his hands, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. XVII, 24).

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “Pontius: turning aside counsel.” So the Gothic manuscript reads, and so too in Jerome; the printed editions have “council.” The remainder of this chapter is taken from the same Jerome.]

[Col. 0289D] 9. Pilate: “mouth of a hammerer,” because, while with his mouth he both justifies and condemns Christ, he strikes in both directions like a hammerer.

[Col. 0290A] 10. *Barraba*: “son of the master,” unquestionably the master of the Jews, who is the devil, the author of murders, who reigns among them even to this day.

## CHAPTER XI. On Martyrs

1. In Greek, martyrs are called “witnesses” in Latin; hence testimonies are also called *martyria* in Greek. They are called witnesses because they endured sufferings for the testimony of Christ and contended for the truth even unto death.

2. The reason we call them not “witnesses,” which we could certainly say in Latin, but *martyrs* in Greek, is that this Greek word sounds more familiar to the ears of the Church, as do many Greek names which we use in place of Latin ones.

3. The first martyr in the New Testament was Stephen. In Hebrew his name is interpreted as “standard,” because he was first in martyrdom for the imitation of the faithful. In Greek, however, it is translated into Latin as “crowned,” prophetically, so that what would follow in reality might first resound in the name as a kind of prophecy of the future.
