For he suffered and received what he was called. *Stephen* means “crown”: he was humbly stoned but sublimely crowned.

4. There are two kinds of martyrdom: one in open suffering, the other in the hidden virtue of the soul. For many, enduring the enemy’s snares and resisting every carnal desire, became martyrs even in a time of peace because they sacrificed themselves in their hearts to Almighty God; and if they had lived in a time of persecution, they too could have been martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “There are two kinds of martyrdom.” From Gregory, *Dialogues* III, chapter 26.]

## CHAPTER XII. On Clerics

1. We believe that *cleros* and *clerics* received their names from the fact that Matthias was chosen by lot; he was the first whom we read was ordained by the apostles. For *klēros* (κλῆρος) in Greek means “lot” or “inheritance.”

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “Cleros and clerics.” From Augustine, on Psalm LXVII.]

2. They are therefore called clerics either because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because they have the Lord as their portion. In general, all who serve in the Church of Christ are called clerics; their ranks and names are as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “Or because they have the Lord as their portion.” Another reading has “the Lord’s portion.” Both are reported in the *Book of Offices*.]

3. Doorkeeper, psalmist, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “Psalmist, reader.” “Psalmist or reader,” Rabanus, Book I, chapter 4. “Psalmist” is not a proper name of an order or rank. Yet St Thomas admits in the *Supplement*, question 37, article 2, that it is sometimes counted under the name of an order.]

[Col. 0290D] 4. The order of bishops is fourfold, namely, patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “The order of bishops is fourfold.” So Rabanus, Gratian, and the older books; but the same Rabanus, Book I, chapter 5, says: “It is threefold, namely, patriarchs, archbishops, who are also metropolitans, and bishops.”]

5. *Patriarch* in Greek is interpreted as “highest of the fathers,” because he holds the first, that is, the apostolic, place; and because he exercises the highest honor, he is designated by this name, as in the case of the Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian patriarchs.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “Because he holds the first, that is, the apostolic, place.” So Rabanus and the old book of Gratian, along with the Gothic books.]

6. *Archbishop* is a Greek term meaning “highest of bishops”; he holds the apostolic office and presides over both metropolitans and the other bishops. “Metropolitans, however, are so called from the measure of cities.”

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “Metropolitans, however.” We have enclosed this in parentheses either because it may be extraneous, as Chacon thought, since Rabanus preserves the more accurate interpretation, or because the following material—“They preside over individual provinces,” etc.—may, according to the opinion of Antonius Augustinus, be connected with archbishops. Two old books support him; in them, after all this material, the following etymology of *metropolitans*, however inadequate, is placed. Thus the order of bishops will also be threefold.]

7. For they preside over individual provinces, and the other priests are subject to their authority and teaching. Without them the other bishops may do nothing, for responsibility for the entire province has been entrusted to them.

8. All the orders designated above are called bishops by one and the same term; but some use a private title for the sake of distinguishing the authority which they have individually received.

9. *Patriarch*: prince of fathers; for *archos* (ἄρχος) means “prince.”

10. *Archbishop*: prince of bishops, just as *metropolitan* derives from the measure of cities.

11. The term *episcopate* is derived from the fact that the one placed over others watches over them, caring for those subject to him; for *skopein* (σκοπεῖν) in Greek means “to look attentively” in Latin.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “The term episcopate.” From Augustine, *City of God* XIX, chapter 19.]

12. *Bishops* in Greek are interpreted in Latin as “watchers.” For a watcher is a superior in the Church, so called because he watches over and looks after the conduct and life of the peoples placed beneath him.

13. *Pontiff* is “prince of priests,” as though he were the way of those who follow; he is also called the high priest and the chief pontiff. For he creates priests and Levites, arranges all the ecclesiastical orders, and shows what each person ought to do.

14. Formerly, pontiffs were also kings; for it was the custom of the ancestors that the king should also be priest and pontiff. Hence Roman emperors too were called pontiffs.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “For it was the custom of the ancestors.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on the verse “King Anius.”]

15. *Vates* is named from “power of the mind,” and its meaning is multiple: sometimes it signifies a priest, sometimes a prophet, and sometimes a poet.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Vates, from power of the mind.” “From fashioning verses,” Varro, Book VI.]

16. *Antistes* means “priest,” from the fact that he stands before others. For he is first in the order of the Church and has no one above him.

17. The name *priest* is composed from Greek and Latin, as though meaning “one who gives what is sacred.” Just as *king* is named from ruling, so *priest* is named from sanctifying; for he consecrates and sanctifies.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “From sanctifying.” Likewise, Book IX, chapter 3.]

18. The priests of the pagans were called *flamines*. They wore on their heads a cap on which there was a short rod above, with some wool attached. Since they could not bear this during the heat, they began merely to bind their heads with a thread.

19. For it was forbidden for them to walk with their heads completely bare. Thus, from the thread they used, they were called *flamines*, as though *filamines*. On feast days, however, after setting aside the thread, they put on the cap as a sign of the eminence of the priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Flamines.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII. See Festus and Varro.]

20. *Presbyter* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as “elder,” not merely on account of age or decrepit old age, but because of the honor and dignity they have received. They are called presbyters; hence among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, because the former is a name of dignity, the latter of age.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Hence among the ancients they were also bishops.” From Jerome, Letter 83, to Oceanus.]

21. Presbyters are also called priests because they give what is sacred, as bishops do. Although they are priests, they do not possess the summit of the pontificate, since they neither sign the forehead with chrism nor give the Spirit, the Paraclete; the reading of the Acts of the Apostles shows that these duties belong to bishops alone.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Although they are priests.” From Innocent I, Letter 1, chapter 3.]

22. Levites were named from their ancestor. For the Levites arose from Levi, and through them the ministries of the mystical sacrament were carried out in the temple of God. In Greek they are called *deacons*, and in Latin “ministers,” because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of the mystery belongs to the deacon.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Just as consecration belongs to the priest.” From the letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, concerning the seven degrees of the Church, circulated with Jerome’s works.]

23. *Hypodeacons* in Greek are what we call subdeacons. They are so called because they are subject to the commands and duties of the Levites. For they themselves receive the offerings of the faithful in the temple of God and carry them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars. Among the Hebrews these men are called *Nathinaei*.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Among the Hebrews, Nathinaei.” Another reading has *Nathanaei*. See *Book II of Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 10, and Rabanus.]

24. Readers are so called from reading; *psalmists* are called from singing psalms. The former proclaim to the peoples what they ought to follow; the latter sing in order to stir the hearts of their hearers to contrition. Some readers, however, also pronounce the words so mournfully that they compel certain people to weeping and lamentation.

25. These same men are also called “proclaimers,” because they announce things farther abroad. Their voice will be so great and so clear that it will fill the ears even of those standing far away.

26. A cantor is so called because he modulates his voice in song. Two types of cantor are mentioned in the art of music, as learned men have been able to express them in Latin: the precentor and the succentor.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Two types … responded.” From Augustine, on Psalm LXXXVII.]

27. A precentor is one who sends forth the voice first in singing.

[Col. 0293A] A succentor is one who responds by singing afterward.

28. A *concentor* is so called because he sings in harmony. But one who does not harmonize and does not sing together will not be a *concentor*.

29. *Acolytes* in Greek are called in Latin “candle-bearers,” from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “When the Gospel is read.” From Jerome, Letter against Vigilantius.]

30. At that time they light and carry the lamps—not to dispel darkness, while the sun is shining brightly at the same time, but to display a sign of joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be shown of which it is written in the Gospel: “That was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.”

31. Exorcists are called in Greek-derived Latin “those who adjure” or “those who rebuke.” For they invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over the possessed, or over those who have an unclean spirit, adjuring them through him to depart from them.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “Over the possessed.” See *Book II of Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 13, and distinction 23, chapter 27.]

32. Doorkeepers, also called gatekeepers, are those who in the Old Testament were chosen to guard the temple, so that no unclean person might enter it in any matter. They are called doorkeepers because they preside over the doors of the temple. Holding the key, they guard everything inside and outside; exercising judgment between the good and the wicked, they receive the faithful and reject unbelievers.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “For they themselves hold the key.” From the same letter to Rusticus of Narbonne.]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Monks

1. *Monk* is named from a Greek etymology because he is solitary; for *monas* (μονάς) in Greek means “singularity.” Therefore, if the name of the monk means “solitary,” what is someone who is alone doing in a crowd? There are, however, several kinds of monks.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “There are several kinds of monks.” From Jerome, Letter 22, to Eustochium.]

2. *Coenobites* are those whom we may call “living in common.” For a *coenobium* is a community of many.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] “For a coenobium.” From Cassian, *Conferences* XVIII, chapter 10, and chapter 4 and following.]

3. *Anchorites* are those who, after a communal life, seek the deserts and live alone in the wilderness. They are called by this name because they have withdrawn far from human beings. Anchorites imitate Elijah and John, while coenobites imitate the apostles.

4. *Hermits* are those who are also anchorites, removed from the sight of human beings and seeking the desert and deserted solitudes. For *eremus* is said as though it meant “removed.”

5. *Abba* is a Syriac name meaning “father” in Latin, as Paul explained when writing to the Romans, saying: “In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father,’” using two languages in one expression. For *abba* is the Syriac name for “father,” and then he names “father” again in Latin.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Other Faithful

1. *Christian*, as the interpretation shows, is derived from anointing, or from the name of the Author and Creator. Christians are named from Christ, just as Jews are named from Judah. For a surname was given to followers from the name of their Master.

2. In former times Christians were called by the Jews, as an insult, *Nazarenes*, because our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene from a certain village of Galilee.

3. Let no one who possesses the name but not the deeds boast that he is a Christian. When the work follows the name, he is certainly a Christian, because he shows himself to be a Christian by his deeds, walking as the one walked from whom he also took his name.

4. *Catholic* is interpreted as “universal” or “general”; for the Greeks call “universal” *katholikon* (καθολικόν).

5. *Orthodox* is one who believes rightly and lives as he believes. For *orthōs* (ὀρθῶς) in Greek means “rightly,” while *doxa* (δόξα) means “glory”; that is, “a man of right glory.” One who lives otherwise than he believes cannot be called by this name.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] “Doxa: glory.” “Opinion” would be more suitable, so that the rest may correspond.]

6. *Neophyte* in Greek may be interpreted in Latin as “new,” “inexperienced,” “faithful,” or “recently reborn.”

7. A *catechumen* is so called because he is still hearing the teaching of the faith, though he has not yet received baptism. For *katēchoumenos* (κατηχούμενος) in Greek means “hearer.”

8. A *competent* is one who, after instruction in the faith, seeks the grace of Christ; hence they are called *competentes*, from seeking.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] “He is called a competent.” From Augustine, sermon to the competentes. Jerome, to Pammachius, Letter 61: “Are you not rather the one who tears the Church apart, having instructed the presbyters of Bethlehem not to give baptism at Easter to our competentes?”]

9. *Laic* means “of the people”; for *laos* (λαός) in Greek means “people.”

10. *Proselyte*, that is, “newcomer” and “circumcised person,” one who was joined to the people of God, is a Greek term.

## BOOK EIGHT. ON THE CHURCH AND VARIOUS SECTS

[Col. 0293]

## CHAPTER I. On the Church and the Synagogue

[Col. 0293D]

1. *Church* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “convocation,” because it calls everyone to itself. *Catholic* means “universal,” from *apo tou kath’ holon* (ἀπὸ τοῦ καθ’ ὅλον), that is, “according to the whole.” For it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain parts of the regions, but, spread throughout the entire world, extends everywhere.

2. The Apostle also approves this when he says to the Romans: “I give thanks to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Epistle to the Romans I, 8). Hence it is called “universality” from “one,” because it is gathered into unity. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI, 23).

3. Why, although the Church is one, does John write of seven churches, unless so that the one Catholic Church might be designated as filled with the sevenfold Spirit? We likewise know that Solomon said of the Lord: “Wisdom built herself a house and hewed out seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1); yet these seven are undoubtedly one, since the Apostle says: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15).

4. The Church began at the place where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled those who were sitting together in one place.

5. With reference to the present pilgrimage, the Church is called *Zion*, because from the length of this pilgrimage it contemplates the promise of heavenly things. For this reason it received the name Zion, that is, “contemplation.”

6. With reference to the future peace of the homeland, however, it is called *Jerusalem*, for *Jerusalem* is interpreted as “vision of peace.” There, after every adversity has been swallowed up, it will possess peace, which is Christ, in present sight.

7. *Synagogue* in Greek means “congregation,” and this became the proper name of the Jewish people. Their gathering is properly accustomed to be called a synagogue, although it too has been called a church.

[Note: [Col. 0295C] “Synagogue.” From Augustine, on Psalm LXXXI.]

8. The apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a church—either for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between a congregation, from which *synagogue* derives its name, and a convocation, from which *church* derives its name. Animals are accustomed to be gathered together, and we properly call their gatherings flocks; human beings, however, are more properly called together because they use reason.

## CHAPTER II. On Religion and Faith

1. Philosophers named *dogma* from “thinking,” that is: “I think this is good; I think this is true.”

[Note: [Col. 0295C] “Dogma, from thinking.” Namely, from *apo tou dokein* (ἀπὸ τοῦ δοκεῖν).]

2. Religion is so called because through it we bind our souls to the one God for divine worship by the bond of service. The word is composed from *religendo*, that is, “choosing,” so that the Latin *religo* appears analogous to *eligo*, “I choose.”

[Note: [Col. 0295C–D] “Religion.” Augustine, *Retractations* I, chapter 13: “As we strive toward the one God and bind our souls to him alone, religion is believed to have received its name from this.” I prefer the explanation given in these words as to the origin of *religion*. I am not unaware that Latin authors have explained another origin of this name: that *religion* is so called because it is *religata*, “bound,” a compound from *legere*, that is, *eligere*, “to choose,” so that the Latin form is *religo* just as *eligo*. But we think Augustine’s final words should be rejected as ill-fitting and added by someone copying the complete passage without noticing that Isidore followed the etymology most approved by Augustine and Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 28. Augustine himself also uses the other explanation in *City of God* X, chapter 4: “For he himself is the source of our blessedness and the end of every desire. Choosing, or rather re-choosing, him—for we had lost him by neglecting him—let us, therefore, re-choose him; hence religion is said to have received its name, and let us move toward him in love.” A third explanation remains, from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “Those who carefully considered everything pertaining to the worship of the gods, and as though re-read it, were called religious, from *relegere*, just as *elegantes* comes from *eligere*.” Thus *religion* may derive from binding, re-choosing, or re-reading.]

3. There are three things sought in human beings for the practice of religion and the worship of God: faith, hope, and charity. Faith concerns what must be believed; hope, what must be hoped for; charity, what must be loved.

4. Faith is that by which we truly believe what we are wholly unable to see. For we can no longer believe what we see. Properly, the name *faith* is derived from the fact that what has been said or promised is entirely carried out. Hence *faith* is so called because it is what has been agreed between two parties, as between God and human beings; hence also the word *foedus*, “covenant.”

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “If what is said is entirely carried out.” From Cicero, *On Duties* I.]

5. Hope is so called because it is a foot for advancing, as it were, a foot. Hence, conversely, *despair* means that the foot is absent, and there is no ability to advance; for when someone loves sin, he does not hope for future glory.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “Because it is a foot.” This is correctly said of hope as a virtue. Those who look upon a deceptive hope interpret *hope* as though it meant “without a foot”; hence on ancient coins it is represented not with a fixed foot but with its feet raised upward. For others, hope is *elpis* (ἐλπίς).]

6. *Charity* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as “love,” because it binds two within itself. For love begins from two things: love of God and love of neighbor. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII, 10).

7. It is greater than all these, because whoever loves also believes and hopes. But whoever does not love, even if he does many good things, labors in vain. Carnal love, however, is usually called not *dilectio*, “charity,” but rather *amor*, “love.” The name *dilectio* is ordinarily reserved for better things.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “All love.” Augustine, *City of God* XIV, chapter 7.]

## CHAPTER III. On Heresy and Schism

1. *Heresy* is called in Greek from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him, as with the Peripatetics, Academics, Epicureans, and Stoics, or with others who, devising a perverse doctrine, withdrew from the Church according to their own judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “Heresy, Greek.” From Jerome, on Galatians V and Titus III.]

2. Hence *heresy* is named from the Greek word, according to the interpretation “choice,” by which each person, according to his own judgment, chooses for himself whatever he wishes either to establish or to accept. We, however, may introduce nothing according to our own judgment, nor may we choose something that another has introduced according to his own judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “Hence heresy … will be called.” From Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*. In that passage, instead of *indulgere*, “to grant,” it is permissible to restore *inducere*, “to introduce,” from this text. He uses that word shortly afterward and frequently elsewhere.]

3. We have the apostles of God as our authorities. They themselves did not choose anything from their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully handed on to the nations the teaching they had received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should preach another gospel, he will be called accursed.

4. *Sect* is named from “following” and “holding.” For we call sects the dispositions of minds and institutions concerning discipline, or the purpose which they follow by holding to it, thinking very differently from others about religious worship.

5. *Schism* is named from a division of minds. A schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as others, but delights only in the division of the assembly. Schism occurs when people say: “We are righteous; we sanctify the unclean,” and other similar things.

6. *Superstition* is so called because it is an excessive or superimposed observance. Others say that it derives from old people, because those who survive for many years become senile with age and wander in a kind of superstition, not knowing what ancient practices they worship or what things, ignorant of the ancients, they adopt.

[Note: [Col. 0297C–D] “Superstition.” The words of Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “Vain superstition,” etc.; the passage of Lucretius to which he alludes is in Book I:

“While human life lay foully before their eyes,  
Oppressed upon the earth beneath heavy religion,  
Which showed its head from the regions of heaven,  
Hanging over mortals with a terrible aspect.”

See also Balbus in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.]

7. Lucretius, however, says that superstition concerns things that stand above us, that is, heavenly and divine things which stand over us—but he speaks wrongly. The doctrines of heretics ought to be displayed by giving their causes or names, so that they may easily be recognized.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Heresies of the Jews

1. *Jews* is interpreted as “confessors.” For confession follows many of those whom unbelief formerly possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] “Jews.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, chapter 21, reports from Hegesippus that there were seven sects among the Hebrews, whose names are these: Essenes, Galileans, Hemerobaptists, Masbothaeans, Samaritans, Sadducees, and Pharisees. Justin, *Against Trypho*: “Just as no one who correctly examines the Jews would acknowledge that the Sadducees, or the similar sects of the Genistae, Meristae, Galileans, Hellenists, Pharisees, Baptists, etc., are Jews.”]

2. *Hebrews* is interpreted as “those who cross over.” By this name they are admonished to pass from worse things to better and to abandon their former errors.

3. The Pharisees and Sadducees are opposed to one another. For *Pharisees* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “divided,” because they put forward the righteousness of the traditions and observances which they call *deuterōseis* (δευτερώσεις). Hence they are called “divided” from the people, as though on account of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] “Pharisees … Sadducees.” From Jerome, on Matthew XXII, and Isidore, Book XIX.]

4. *Sadducees* is interpreted as “righteous.” For they claim for themselves what they are not, deny the resurrection of the body, and proclaim that the soul perishes with the body. They accept only the five books of the Law and reject the prophecies of the prophets.

5. The Essenes say that the one who taught them complete abstinence is himself the Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0297D–0298C] “Essenes.” Or *Essaens*, from Eusebius. It agrees with Jerome, *Against Jovinian* II, who reports from Josephus concerning them that they abstained from wives, wine, and meat, and turned daily fasting into a natural condition.]

6. The Masbothaeans say that the one who taught them to keep the Sabbath in every matter is himself the Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] “Masbothaeans.” That this was their proper name, apart from the words of Eusebius cited above, is sufficiently shown by the heresy itself of observing Sabbaths, especially to those acquainted with Hebrew letters.]

7. The Genistae are so called because they boast that they are of the lineage of Abraham. For when the people of God came into Babylon, most of them abandoned their wives and joined themselves to Babylonian women. Some, however, content with Israelite marriages, or born from such marriages, separated themselves from the whole people when they returned from Babylon and assumed this name of boastfulness.

8. The Meristaeans are so called because they divide the Scriptures, not believing all the prophets and saying that the prophets spoke under different spirits; for *meros* (μέρος) in Greek means “part.”

[Note: [Col. 0298D] “Meristaeans.” *Meristae* in the Roman manuscript. Concerning the Essenes, Epiphanius says in the prologue: “They used other Scriptures after the Law, but rejected most of the later prophets.”]

9. The Samaritans are so called because they observe the Law alone; for they do not accept the prophets.

10. [Note: [Col. 0298D] *Hemerobaptists*. Epiphanius, book . . . chapter 17. The Fessani Moors retain this custom of repeatedly washing their undergarments.] The Hemerobaptists are so called because they wash their clothes and bodies every day.

# CHAPTER V. On the Heresies of Christians

[Col. 0298B] 1. Some heretics also withdrew from the Church and are named after their founders; others, however, are named from the causes which they chose and established.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] *Some*. Taken largely from Augustine, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, and from Gennadius’s catalogue. See 24, q. 3.]

352 2. The Simonians are named after Simon, skilled in magical arts, whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he had wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit from the apostles with money. They say that creation was made not by God but by some power above.

3. The Menandrians are named after Menander, a magician and disciple of Simon, who asserted that the world was made not by God but by angels.

4. The Basilidians are named after Basilides, who, among his other blasphemies, denied that Jesus had suffered.

5. [Note: [Col. 0298D] *Nicolaitans*. Augustine. When he was blamed because of his zeal for his very beautiful wife, he is said, as though to clear himself, to have permitted anyone who wished to use her; this act was turned into a most shameful sect, which approves the indiscriminate use of women.]

The Nicolaitans are named after Nicolas, a deacon of the Church of Jerusalem, who was appointed by Peter together with Stephen and the others. Because of his wife’s beauty, he abandoned her so that anyone who wished might use her; this custom was turned into such a practice of fornication that they exchanged wives with one another. John condemns them in the Apocalypse, saying: “But you have this, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans.”

6. The Gnostics wished to call themselves by this name because of the excellence of their knowledge. They say that the soul is of the nature of God, and in their doctrines invent a good God and an evil God.

7. The Carpocratians are named after a certain Carpocrates, who said that Christ was merely a human being and had been born from both sexes.

[Col. 0299A] 8. The Cerinthians are named after a certain Cerinthus. Among other practices, they observe circumcision and preach that they will live for a thousand years after the resurrection in bodily pleasure. Hence in Greek they are called *Chiliasts*, and in Latin *Millenarians*.

9. The Nazaraeans are so called because, although they confess Christ—the one called Nazaraean from the village of Nazareth—to be the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all the prescriptions of the old Law.

353 10. [Note: [Col. 0299C] *Ophites*. From Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, with which Isidore differs somewhat. Tertullian says that the serpent was the power that bestowed on the human race knowledge of good and evil; for this reason Chacon rejected the word “power.” See Epiphanius, Philaster, and Augustine.]

The Ophites are named from the serpent. For “serpent” is called *ὄφις* (*ophis*) in Greek. They worship the serpent, saying that it introduced the knowledge of virtue into paradise.

11. [Note: [Col. 0299D] *Valentinians*. . . . “A follower of Platonic philosophy.” Thus the Neapolitan manuscript, correctly. Tertullian: “Where now is Marcion, devoted to Stoicism? Where Valentinus, a follower of Platonism?”]

The Valentinians are named after a certain Valentinus, a follower of Platonic philosophy, who introduced certain *αἰῶνες* (*aiōnes*), that is, ages or aeons, into the origin of God the Creator. He also asserted that Christ assumed no bodily substance from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a conduit.

12. [Note: [Col. 0299D] *Apellites*. From the same source. See Epiphanius and Irenaeus.]

The Apellites took their name from Apelles, who was their leader. He made the creator—the God of the Law and of Israel—a certain glorious angel of the higher God; asserting that this god was fiery, he said that Christ was not truly God, [Note: [Col. 0299D] *But appeared as a human being in an apparition*. Tertullian says of Apelles: “He says that Christ was neither in an apparition, as Marcion held, nor in the substance of a true body, as the Gospel teaches.” In both *On the Flesh of Christ* and *On the Resurrection* he separately declares that he is arguing against Marcion, who removed the reality of Christ’s flesh and introduced the unreality of an apparition, and against Apelles, who accepted a solid body and flesh, though not born, but drawn from the stars and higher substances. Chacon therefore denied that this passage was intact, and we agree with him.] but appeared as a human being in an apparition.

13. [Note: [Col. 0300C] *Archontians*. . . . “The work of archangels.” Chacon read *Archontes*, for Augustine also interprets the term as “rulers.”]

The Archontians are named from the rulers. They maintain that the universe which God created is the work of archangels.

14. The Adamites are so called because they imitate Adam’s nakedness. Hence they pray naked, and naked men and women meet together among themselves.

15. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Cainites*. See the note in Gratian.]

The Cainites are so called because they worship Cain.

[Col. 0299C] 16. The Sethians took their name from Adam’s son, who was called Seth, saying that he was the same as Christ.

17. The Melchisedecians are so called because they consider Melchisedec the priest of God to have been not a human being but the power of God.

18. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Angelicists*. See Epiphanius, Augustine, and Theodoret on Colossians 2, and the Council of Laodicea, canon 35.]

The Angelicists are so called because they worship angels.

354 19. The Apostolics assumed this name for themselves because, possessing nothing of their own, they utterly refuse to receive those who use or possess anything in this world.

20. The Cerdonians are named after a certain Cerdon, who asserted two contrary principles.

[Col. 0300A] 21. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Marcionists*. . . . “From whom [came] the two principles.” Augustine follows this account, for Epiphanius reports that they introduced three principles.]

The Marcionists are named after Marcion, a Stoic philosopher, who followed Cerdon’s doctrine and asserted one good God and another just God, as though they were two principles of creation and goodness.

22. The Artotyrites are named from their offering. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that the first human beings made an offering from the fruits of the earth and from the produce of sheep.

23. The Aquarians are so called because they offer only water in the sacramental cup.

24. The Severians arose from Severus. They do not drink wine, and they reject the Old Testament and the resurrection.

25. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Tatians*. . . . “Who are also called Encratites.” Thus it should be read, on the authority of Augustine, Epiphanius, and the older books—not *Encreatites*. For although Isidore mentions only their abstinence from meat, it is established that they abstained from wine, meat, and marriage.]

The Tatians are named after a certain Tatian, who are also called Encratites because they abominate meat.

[Col. 0300B] 26. The Alogians are so called as though they were “without the Word”; for *λόγος* (*logos*) means “Word” in Greek. They do not believe that God is the Word, rejecting the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse.

27. The province of Phrygia gave the Cataphrygians their name, because their founders, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, arose there. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit was transmitted not through the apostles but through themselves.

28. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Cathari*. . . . “They condemn widows if they marry.” The words are Augustine’s, in *On the Contest of the Christian*, chapter 31.]

The Cathari called themselves by this name because of their purity. Boasting of their own merits, they deny forgiveness of sins to penitents; if widows marry, they condemn them as adulteresses; and they proclaim themselves purer than the rest. If they wished to understand their own name, they would call themselves worldly rather than pure.

29. The Paulinians arose from Paul of Samosata, who [Col. 0300C] said that Christ had not always existed but took his beginning from Mary.

355 30. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Hermogenians*. . . . “Whom the Apostle condemns.” From Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*.]

The Hermogenians are named after a certain Hermogenes, who, introducing uncreated matter, compared it with the uncreated God and asserted that it was the mother of the elements and a goddess. The Apostle condemns them as servants of the elements.

31. [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Manichaeans*. . . . “Who was called MANES.” Other copies have *Manis*; Augustine has *Manin*.]

The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian who was called Manes. He introduced two natures and substances, namely, a good one and an evil one, and asserted that souls flowed from God as if from some spring. They reject the Old Testament and accept the New Testament only in part.

[Col. 0301A] 32. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Anthropomorphites*. From Jerome, *Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*.]

The Anthropomorphites are so called because, with rustic simplicity, they believe that God has the human limbs described in the divine books. For *ἄνθρωπος* (*anthrōpos*) means “human being” in Greek. They fail to understand the Lord’s saying: “God is spirit”; for he is incorporeal, is not distinguished by limbs, and is not measured by bodily mass.

33. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Hieracites*. Hilary also calls Hieracas their founder, in book VI of *On the Trinity*.]

The Hieracites arose from Hieracas, their founder. They admit only monks, reject marriage, and do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven.

34. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *NOVATIANS, from NOVATIAN*. Thus it should be read from Jerome’s catalogue, not *Novatians from Novatus*, although Novatus was the sect’s first founder. It is not necessary to identify them with the Cathari, mentioned shortly before, though they had something in common.]

The Novatians arose from Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, who attempted to seize the priestly see against Cornelius and established a heresy, refusing to receive apostates and rebaptizing those who had already been baptized.

35. The Montanist heretics are so called because, during a persecution, they hid in the mountains; on this occasion they separated themselves from the body of the Catholic Church.

36. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Ebionites*. Eusebius, book III of the *History*, chapter 27, in Rufinus’s translation: “The Ebionites think him to be merely a human being, made a righteous man through progress in life and virtue.” A little later: “Hence they are appropriately called EBIONITES, on account of their poverty of understanding.” Jerome often mentions them, as does Tertullian in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*.]

The Ebionites are named after Ebion, or from poverty; for they believe that Christ became a righteous man solely through progress. Hence they are appropriately called Ebionites, on account of their poverty of understanding. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *These are half-Jews*. Jerome calls Ebion this in his commentary on Galatians 3.]

These are half-Jews, [Note: [Col. 0301D] *And in this way they hold the Gospel*. From the same source, on Isaiah 1.] and they hold the Gospel in such a way that they observe the Law carnally. [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Against whom, in Galatians*. From Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, where a very few words are brought together from various passages.] Against them the Apostle inveighs in his letter to the Galatians.

37. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Photinians*. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, and Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 31. In Damascenus it is erroneously printed *Smyrnensis* instead of *Sirmiensis*.]

The Photinians are named after Photinus, bishop of Sirmium in Gallograecia. Reviving the heresy of the Ebionites, he asserted that Christ was conceived by Mary through marital intercourse with Joseph.

38. The Aerianists are named after a certain Aerius. They disdain offering sacrifice for the dead.

[Col. 0301C] 39. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Aetians*. . . . “They say that no sin is imputed to those who remain in the faith.” Luther revived their error.]

The Aetians are named after Aetius; they are also called Eunomians, after Eunomius, a certain dialectician and disciple of Aetius, from whose name they became better known. They assert that the Son is unlike the Father and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son. They also say that no sin is imputed to those who remain in the faith.

40. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Origenists*. . . . “As far as the Son.” From Jerome’s *Apology*. The remainder is from Augustine, book XI of *The City of God*, chapter 23.]

The Origenists arose from Origen, their founder. They say that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son. They also say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world and, according to the diversity of their sins, earned different bodies, as bonds, from heaven down to earth; and that the world was made for this reason.

41. The Noetians are named after a certain Noetus, who said that Christ was the same as the Father and the Holy Spirit. They understand the Trinity as referring to the names of offices, not to persons. Hence they are also called Patripassians, because they say that the Father suffered.

42. The Sabellians are said to have sprung from this same Noetus. They report that Sabellius was his disciple, and they became especially known by his name; hence they are called Sabellians. They assert one person of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

43. The Arians arose from Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who, not acknowledging the Son to be coeternal with the Father, asserted different substances in the Trinity, contrary to what the Lord says: “I and the Father are one.”

44. The Macedonians are named after Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople; they deny that the Holy Spirit is God.

45. The Apollinarists are named after Apollinaris. They say that Christ assumed a body only, without a soul.

46. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Antidicomarites*. Epiphanius and Augustine also call them *Antidicomarianites*.]

The Antidicomarites are so called because they contradict Mary’s virginity, asserting that after Christ was born she had intercourse with her husband.

47. The Metangismonites received this name because *ἄγγος* (*angos*) means “vessel” in Greek. For they assert that the Son is in the Father as a smaller vessel inside a larger vessel.

48. The Patricians are named after a certain Patricius, who says that the substance of human flesh was created by the devil.

49. The Coluthians are named after a certain Coluthus, who say that God does not make evil, contrary to what is written: “I am the Lord, creating evil.”

[Col. 0302C] 50. The Florinians are named after Florinus, who, on the contrary, say that God created evil, contrary to what is written: “God made all things good.”

51. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Donatists*. . . . “Deceived.” Jerome’s words in his catalogue.]

The Donatists are named after a certain Donatus, an African, who, coming from Numidia, deceived almost the whole of Africa by his persuasion. He asserted that the Son was lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son, and he rebaptized Catholics.

52. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Bonosians*. They do not occur in Augustine and may have been inserted here by someone. Strong evidence for this is that they are read before the Circumcellions and are separated from them by the Donatists, contrary to Isidore’s words and intention. It is clear that the Circumcellions were Donatists, not Bonosians. Innocent I counts the Bonosians among the Photinians, in his letter to Laurentius of Siena.]

The Bonosians are said to have arisen from a certain bishop Bonosus, who asserted that Christ was the adopted, not the natural, Son of God.

53. [Note: [Col. 0302D] *Circumcellions*. Augustine says in his commentary on Psalm 82 that they called themselves *Agonistici*, because they fought for Christ against the devil. They were truly called Circumcellions because they wandered around cells, settling nowhere and changing their dwelling every day. In the Oviedo, Gothic, Tarragona, and Roman manuscripts they are called *Circiliones*. Augustine also calls them *Montenses*, and Philaster calls them *Circuitores*. Instead of *Cotopitae*, *Coropitae*, *Catropitae*, *Catotopisci*—for this name is read in these or still more forms in the old books—Augustine’s *Catoptae* is supported by manuscript A. Their practice was not only to kill themselves by various forms of death but also to lie in wait for others in deserted places, so that they might incite those whom they could to the same madness and persuade them to bring about their own deaths. If they failed in this, they themselves attacked those people, worshipping the slain as martyrs. Philaster calls them *Biothanati*.]

The Circumcellions are so called because they are rustic people, whom they call Cotopites, possessing the doctrine of the heresy mentioned above. Out of love for martyrdom they kill themselves, so that, departing violently from this life, they may be called martyrs.

54. The Priscillianists are named after Priscillian, who in Spain composed a mixed doctrine from the errors of the Gnostics and Manichaeans.

55. [Note: [Col. 0303D] *Luciferians*. The opening words are Augustine’s, from *On Heresies*; the remainder is from *On the Contest of the Christian*, chapter 30. But the words “by their founder,” which are not Augustine’s, could be rejected. Lucifer was bishop of Caralis; Caralis is a famous city of Sardinia. His book still survives. See Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, and Nicephorus, book X, chapter 17.]

The Luciferians arose from Lucifer, bishop of Sardinia. He condemned the Catholic bishops who, during the persecution of Constantius, had consented to the treachery of the Arians and afterwards, having corrected themselves, chose to return to the Catholic Church—condemning either what they had believed or what they pretended to have believed. The Catholic Church received them into her maternal embrace, like Peter after the weeping of his denial. Proudly accepting this maternal charity and refusing to receive them, the Luciferians withdrew from communion with the Church and, together with Lucifer himself, their founder—he who rose in the morning—deserved to fall.

56. The Jovinianists are named after a certain monk, Jovinian, who asserted that there was no difference between marriage and virginity, and no distinction between those who abstain and those who simply feast.

57. The Helvidians are named after Helvidius, who says that after Christ was born Mary bore other sons by the man Joseph.

58. The Paterniani arose from a certain Paternus. They believe that the lower parts of the body were made by the devil.

59. The Arabians are so called because they arose in Arabia. They say that the soul dies with the body and that both will rise again at the last.

60. The Tertullianists are named after Tertullian, a presbyter of the African province and of the city of Carthage. They preach that the soul is immortal but corporeal, and believe that the souls of sinful human beings are transformed into demons after death.

61. The Tessarescaedecatites are so called because they contend that Easter should be observed with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon. For *τέσσαρες* (*tessares*) means “four,” and *δέκα* (*deka*) means “ten.”

62. [Note: [Col. 0303D] *Nyctages*. Or *Nystages* or *Nystazontes*, from sleeping. See the book *On Offices*, in the chapter on nocturnal vigils.]

The Nyctages are named from sleep because they reject the night watches, saying that it is superstition to violate the divine laws, since God assigned the night for rest.

63. The Pelagians arose from Pelagius, a monk. They place free will before divine grace, saying that the will is sufficient to fulfill the divine commands.

64. The Nestorians are named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. He asserted that the blessed Virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being, making one person of the flesh and another of the divinity. Nor did he believe in one Christ, in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and distinctly proclaimed one Son of God and another son of a human being.

65. The Eutychians are named after Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who denied that Christ, after assuming humanity, existed from two natures, and asserted that there was in him only the divine nature.

360 66. [Note: [Col. 0303D] *Acephali*. . . . “These opponents of the three chapters of Chalcedon.” Why these three chapters are called Chalcedonian, although they were treated at the Fifth Council, and why Isidore should or should not be considered their defender, may be seen in the annotations of the bishop of Segovia on chapter 4 of the book *On Illustrious Men*.]

The Acephali are so called, that is, “headless”; for none of them is found to have a founder from whom they arose. They are opponents of the three Chalcedonian chapters; they deny the distinct property of the two substances in Christ and proclaim one nature in his person.

67. [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Theodosians and Gaianites*. The former are called “corrupticolae,” the latter “phantasiastae,” in Liberatus’s *Breviary*. Thomas explains the reasons for these names in *Quodlibet* 4. See the notes in Gratian, Evagrius, and Anastasius the Librarian, whose statements are taken from the book of Peter of Theophanes preserved in the Vatican.]

The Theodosians and Gaianites are named after Theodosius and Gaianus, who, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, were ordained bishops on the same day in Alexandria by the election of a rebellious people. Following the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus, they reject the Council of Chalcedon and assert one nature in Christ from two. The Theodosians maintain that this nature is corruptible, while the Gaianites contend that it is incorruptible.

68. [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Agnoites and Tritheites*. Gregory, *Register*, book VIII, letters 35 and 42, and Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 49, report that Themistius, leader of the Agnoites under Valens, and John Philoponus, leader of the Tritheites under Phocas, were distinguished Peripatetic philosophers.]

The Agnoites and Tritheites arose from the Theodosians. The Agnoites are named from ignorance because they add this to the perversity from which they arose: that Christ’s divinity does not know the future things written concerning the final day and hour. They do not remember Christ’s person speaking in Isaiah: “The day of judgment is in my heart.”

The Tritheites are so called because, just as they assert three persons in the Trinity, so they also assert three gods, contrary to what is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

69. There are also other heresies without a founder and without names. Some of them believe that God is threefold; [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Others say that Christ’s divinity is passible*. The Greeks call these people *θεοπασχῖται* (*theopaschites*).] others say that Christ’s divinity is passible; others assign a beginning in time to the Son’s birth from the Father; 361 others [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Others [believe in] the liberation of all*. This must certainly be the reading, on the authority of three manuscripts—Toletan, Salamanca, and Roman—and of Augustine’s index prefixed to *On Heresies* and of the work itself. The index reads: “Believing that the liberation of all in the underworld was accomplished by Christ’s descent.” In the work itself: “Another [group] believed that, when Christ descended to the underworld, the unbelievers were liberated and considered that all were freed from there.”] believe that the liberation of all was accomplished in the underworld through Christ’s descent; others deny that the soul is the image [Col. 0305A] of God; others believe that souls are transformed into demons and into animals of every kind; others disagree about the state of the world; others suppose that there are innumerable worlds; others make water coeternal with God; others [Note: [Col. 0305D] *Others walk barefoot*. Not because this is intrinsically unlawful, but because they themselves think it unlawful to walk otherwise.] walk barefoot; others do not eat with human beings.

70. These are the heresies that arose against the Catholic faith and were condemned in advance by the apostles and holy Fathers, or by councils. Although they are divided among themselves by many errors and disagree with one another, they nevertheless conspire under a common name against the Church of God. Moreover, anyone who understands Holy Scripture in a manner different from what the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, demands may be called a heretic, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church.

# CHAPTER VI. On the Philosophers of the Nations

[Col. 0305B]

1. The philosophers are so called by a Greek designation which is translated into Latin as “lovers of wisdom.” For a philosopher is one who possesses knowledge of divine and human matters and follows the entire path of living well.

2. [Note: [Col. 0305D] *The name “philosopher”*. From Augustine, book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 2, and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* V.]

The name “philosophers” is said to have first arisen from Pythagoras. For previously the ancient Greeks arrogantly called themselves sophists—that is, wise men or teachers of wisdom. When he was asked what profession he claimed, he modestly replied that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom, since to profess oneself wise seemed exceedingly arrogant.

3. Thereafter it pleased later generations that, however much learning anyone seemed to possess concerning matters pertaining to wisdom, whether for himself or for others, he should be called only a philosopher. [Note: [Col. 0305D] *The philosophers themselves are divided threefold*. Augustine, in the same place.]

The philosophers themselves are divided into three kinds: they are either physicists, ethicists, or logicians.

4. The physicists are so called because they discuss natures. For nature is called *φύσις* (*physis*) in Greek.

362 5. The ethicists are so called because they discuss morals. For custom or character is called *ἦθος* (*ēthos*) among the Greeks.

6. The logicians are so called because they add reasoning to the discussion of natures and morals. For reason is called *λόγος* (*logos*) in Greek. These too were divided according to their own schools, [Note: [Col. 0305D] *Some having names . . . ACADEMICS*. The words are Tertullian’s, from the *Apology*.] some taking their names from their founders, such as the Platonists, Epicureans, and Pythagoreans; others from the places of their gatherings and stations, such as the Peripatetics, Stoics, and Academics.

[Col. 0306A] 7. The Platonists are named after Plato the philosopher. They assert that God is the creator of souls and angels the creators of bodies, and say that after many cycles of years souls return to different bodies.

8. The Stoics are named from a place. For there was a portico in Athens [Note: [Col. 0305D] *Which they called the Pisianactian and the Painted Stoa*. Thus the older books; the printed editions have *Pisianaction*. In fact, both forms are attested as names of the portico. Diogenes Laertius, in his account of Zeno: “Returning to the Painted Stoa, which was also called the Pisianactian, and which was painted from the work of Polygnotus,” etc. Unless you prefer *Pleasianactian*, from Plutarch, in *Cimon*, whose words are: “And for this reason they say that at that time it was called the Pleasianactian; it was a painted stoa,” etc.] which they called the Pisianactian and the Painted Stoa. In it were painted histories of the deeds of wise men and brave men. The wise men philosophized in this portico, from which the Stoics also took their name. For a portico is called *στοά* (*stoa*) in Greek. Zeno was the first to establish this school.

9. They deny that anyone can be made blessed without virtue. They assert that every sin is equal, saying: the one who steals straw is as guilty as the one who steals gold; the one who kills a diver as the one who kills a horse. For it is not the animal but the intention that makes the crime.

[Col. 0306B] 10. They also say that the soul perishes with the body. They love the virtue of continence and pursue eternal glory, although they admit that they themselves are not eternal.

11. The Academics are named after Plato’s villa, the Academy at Athens, where Plato taught. They believe that everything is uncertain. Yet just as it must be admitted that many things are uncertain and hidden, which God has willed to place beyond human understanding, so there are nevertheless very many things that can be grasped by the senses and comprehended by reason.

12. This school was founded by the philosopher Arcesilaus of Cyrene; [Note: [Col. 0305D] *Arcesilaus of Cyrene*. Either because he was devoted to pleasure or because he sailed to Cyrene and there became passionately enamored of the young Demetrius. For it is established that he was from Pitane. See Diogenes Laertius.] 363 [Note: [Col. 0306D] *Whose follower was Democritus*. Not a follower of Arcesilaus—for Democritus was certainly much earlier than Arcesilaus—but a follower of the school or opinion. Therefore translate *fuit* as “had been.”] Democritus was its follower, and he said that truth lay hidden as though in a deep well whose bottom did not exist.

13. The Peripatetics are named from walking about, because Aristotle, their founder, was accustomed to debate while walking. They say that a certain part of the soul is eternal, but that for the rest it is mortal to a great extent.

14. [Note: [Col. 0306D] *Cynics, from the filth of shamelessness*. “Shameless,” according to Antonius Augustine.]

The Cynics are named from the filth of shamelessness. For, contrary to human modesty, they were accustomed to have intercourse with their wives in public, judging it lawful and honorable to sleep with one’s wife openly because marriage is legitimate. They publicly preached that this should be done, like dogs in the streets or squares. Hence they derived both their designation and their name from dogs, whose life they imitated.

15. The Epicureans are named after Epicurus, a certain philosopher who loved vanity rather than wisdom. The philosophers themselves even called him a pig, [Note: [Col. 0306D] *Because he wallowed*. Augustine, on Psalm 73. In the Venice edition of 1493: “And perhaps the man who says, ‘When I am dead, I shall be nothing,’ both learned his letters and learned this from Epicurus, that mad philosopher—or rather lover of vanity, not wisdom—whom the philosophers themselves also called a pig, because he declared bodily pleasure to be the highest good. Horace:

‘When he wishes to laugh, a pig from Epicurus’s herd.’”] because he wallowed in carnal filth and asserted that bodily pleasure was the highest good. He also said that the world was neither equipped nor governed by any divine providence.

16. He assigned the origin of things to atoms, that is, indivisible and solid bodies, from whose chance collisions all things arise and have arisen. He asserted that God does nothing, that everything consists of bodies, and that the soul is nothing other than a body. Hence he also said: “I shall not exist after I have died.”

17. The Gymnosophists are said to philosophize naked in the shadowy solitudes of India, wearing coverings only over their genitals. [Note: [Col. 0307D] *Gymnasium*. The same author below, book XVIII, chapter 17.] A gymnasium is so called because young men exercise naked in the field, covering only their private parts. These philosophers also abstain from procreation.

18. The theologians are the same as the physicists. They are called theologians because in their writings they spoke about God. Their opinions about what God was are known to have been various, as they investigated the question. Some, understanding him corporeally, said that this visible world, composed of the four elements, was God, like Dionysius the Stoic. Others understood him spiritually as mind, like Thales of Miletus.

19. Some said that God was a soul moving through all things and luminous, like Pythagoras. [Note: [Col. 0307D] *Moving through all things and luminous*. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I: “For Pythagoras held that God is a soul extended and moving through the whole nature of things.” Minucius in the *Octavius*: “For Pythagoras, God is a soul moving through and extended throughout the whole nature of things.” He perhaps called it “luminous” because he had read *shining* instead of *extended* in Cicero.] Others said that God was unchanging and without time, like Plato. Others said that he was a mind set free, like Cicero. Others said that he was both spirit and mind, like Maro. [Note: [Col. 0307D] *For they merely discovered God*. Tertullian, in the *Apology*: “For they merely discovered God; they did not discuss him as they had discovered him.” Isidore has “explained”; the Vulgate has “glorified,” since *δόξα* means both “glory” and “opinion.”]

For they merely discovered God, but did not explain him as they had discovered him; for they became futile in their thoughts. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools.

20. The Platonists assert that God is a guardian, arbiter, [Col. 0307C] and judge. The Epicureans say that he is idle and [Note: [Col. 0307D] *And inactive*. Tertullian has “unexercised.”] inactive. Concerning the world, the Platonists affirm that it is incorporeal, the Stoics that it is corporeal, Epicurus that it is made from atoms, Pythagoras from numbers, and Heraclitus from fire.

21. Hence Varro says that fire is the soul of the world, because fire governs everything in the world just as the soul governs everything in us. How absurdly! “When it is present in us,” he says, “we ourselves exist; when it departs, we die.” Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0307D] *When fire departs from the world*. That is, from heaven, as above, book III, chapter 63.] when fire departs from the world through lightning, the world dies.

22. [Note: [Col. 0307D] *These errors of the philosophers*. Everything through the end is from Tertullian’s *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, from which we have corrected some passages, with no disagreement from the manuscripts.]

These errors of the philosophers also introduced heresies into the Church. From them came the *αἰῶνες* (*aiōnes*), and certain forms—I do not know what they were; from them came, in Arius, the Trinity of the name, and in Valentinus [Note: [Col. 0308D] *Platonic madness*. We have not departed from the older books, whose agreement is considerable at this point. Chacon, following Tertullian, reads: “From them came the aeons and certain forms, and the trinity of man in Valentinus; it was Platonic.” We have retained “of the name.” For although both expressions could apply to Valentinus, since he introduced three kinds of human beings—*πνευματικόν, ψυχικόν, καὶ σαρκικόν* (*pneumatikon, psychikon, kai sarkikon*: spiritual, psychic, and fleshly), as found in the book *Against the Valentinians*—nevertheless, if Isidore connected Arius with Valentinus, we may suspect that the first aeon was three-named. For in the same book, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, it says: “But when he names indeterminate genealogies, Valentinus is recognized, in whom that certain aeon, new and not of one name, generates from his love understanding and truth,” etc.] Platonic madness.

365 23. Hence Marcion’s better god came from tranquility—for this had come from the Stoics; and when it is said that the soul perishes, Epicurus is being followed; and when the restoration of the flesh is denied, this is taken from the single school of all the philosophers; and wherever matter is made equal to God, it is the teaching of Zeno; and wherever something is read about a fiery god, Heraclitus is involved. The same material is tossed about among heretics and philosophers, and the same arguments are entangled together.

# CHAPTER VII. On Poets

1. Concerning the origin of the name “poets,” Suetonius says: “When human beings, having shed their wildness, first began to regulate their lives by reason and to know themselves and their gods, they devised a modest ritual and necessary speech; and for the religion of their gods they conceived the magnificence of both.

2. “Accordingly, just as they made temples more beautiful than houses and statues larger than bodies, so they thought that the gods should be honored with speech that was, as it were, more august; and they exalted their praises both with more splendid words and with more pleasing rhythms.” This kind of composition, because it is produced by a certain form called poetry, was called a *poem*, and its makers were called *poets*.

366 3. Varro says that *vates* (“seers” or “poets”) were so called from the force of the mind, or from “weaving” songs—that is, bending or modulating them. Accordingly, poets were formerly called *vates* in Latin, and their writings were called prophecies, because they were moved in writing by a certain force and a kind of frenzy, or because they joined words together according to rhythmic patterns. For the ancients used *viere* in the sense of “to bind.” Those who prophesied through frenzy likewise bore the same name, because they too expressed many things in verse.

[Col. 0308C] 4. Lyric poets are so called *ἀπὸ τοῦ λυρεῖν* (*apo tou lyrein*), that is, “from varying songs.” Hence the lyre also received its name.

5. Tragic poets are so called because at the beginning a goat was the prize for singers; the Greeks call a goat *τράγος* (*tragos*). Hence Horace:

“With song, he who contended in tragedy for a worthless goat.”

From that time onward, later tragedians attained great honor, excelling in plots of plays fashioned in the likeness of truth.

6. They are called comedians either from the place, because they went around the villages, which the Greeks call κῶμαι (*kōmai*), or from feasting. For people were accustomed to come to hear them after eating. But comedians proclaim the deeds of private persons, whereas tragedians present public affairs and the histories of kings. Likewise, the subjects of tragedies are drawn from sorrowful events, while those of comedies are drawn from joyful events.

[Col. 0309A] 7. [Note: There are two kinds of comedians. It is known from Horace that satirical poets succeeded the old comedy, whose license was restrained by law. But who would believe that these were called the new comedians, or that Plautus and Terence were called the old, or that Attius—or Actius—was a comic poet? I have no doubt that either this material is extraneous or that it is badly corrupted.] There are two kinds of comedians, namely, the old and the new. 367 The old, who also became ridiculous through their jokes, include Plautus, Actius, and Terence. The new, who are also satirical, generally attack vices, include Flaccus, Persius, Juvenal, and others. For they correct the faults of everyone; nor were they forbidden to describe the worst sort of person or to criticize anyone’s sins and morals. Hence they are also depicted naked, because through them individual vices are laid bare.

8. [Note: They are also called satirical poets. See above, Book V, “On Satire.”] Satirical poets are so called either because they are full of every kind of eloquence, or from *saturitas*, “fullness” and “abundance,” since they speak about several matters at once; or from that platter which, filled with various kinds of grain or fruit, used to be carried to the temples of the pagans; or their name was derived from the Satyrs, who leave unpunished the things said under the influence of wine.

[Col. 0309B] 9. [Note: Certain poets are called theologians. Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 14.] Certain poets were called theologians because they composed songs about the gods.

10. [Note: The poet’s function. The words are Lactantius, Book I, chapter 11.] The poet’s function is to transform and convey into other forms, through indirect figurative expressions and with some ornament, things that truly happened. [Note: Hence Lucan. From Servius, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “The goddess-mother shows the way.”] Hence Lucan is not counted among the poets, because he seems to have composed history rather than poetry.

11. [Note: Among the poets. From the same source, *Eclogue* III.] Among poets there are three styles of speech. One is that in which only the poet speaks, as in the books of Virgil’s *Georgics*. Another is dramatic, in which the poet nowhere speaks, as in comedies and tragedies. The third is mixed, as in the *Aeneid*. For there both the poet and the introduced characters speak.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Sibyls

[Col. 0309C]

1. In general, all female prophets are called Sibyls in the Greek language. For Σιός (*Sios*) means “God” in the Aeolic language, while the Greeks call the mind βουλήν (*boulēn*), so that the name means, as it were, “the mind of God.” Therefore, because they were accustomed to interpret the divine will to human beings, they were called Sibyls.

2. Just as every prophesying man is called either a seer or a prophet, so every prophesying woman is called a Sibyl. This name derives from her office, not from the proper meaning of the word.

[Col. 0310A] 3. The most learned authorities report that there were ten Sibyls. The first was from Persia. The second was the Libyan. The third was the Delphic, born in the temple of Delphic Apollo, [Note: She prophesied before the Trojan wars. From Solinus, chapter 8.] who prophesied before the Trojan wars and whose many verses Homer inserted into his own work.

4. The fourth was the Cimmerian, in Italy. The fifth was the Erythraean, named [Note: Herophyla; or Heriphile. But there is great confusion generally in the names of the Sibyls. For Lactantius, following Varro, identifies Demophile, Amalthea, and the Cumaean with Herophila. See Suidas and Vives on the book *On the City of God*.] Herophyla, born in Babylon. When the Greeks were setting out for Ilium, she prophesied that Troy would perish and that Homer would write falsehoods. She was called Erythraean because her songs were discovered on that island.

[Note: The Samian, who was Phemonoe. Suidas, following Eratosthenes, calls the Samian Phyto. Phemonoe, however, seems to have been Delphic. Pausanias, in the Phocian section, concerning the Delphic oracle: “The prevailing opinion among most people is that Phemonoe became the god’s first prophetess and was the first to sing in hexameters.” Strabo likewise says in Book IX: “They say that Phemonoe was the first Pythian prophetess.” Lucan too places Phemonoe at Delphi giving responses to Appius.] The sixth was the Samian, who was called Phemonoe from the island of Samos, from which she came and received her name.

5. The seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea. She brought nine books to Tarquinius Priscus, [Note: In them were written the decrees. From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “For here I shall disclose your lots.” But Servius has “remedies,” not “decrees.” Chacon preferred “secrets.”] in which the Roman decrees were written. She is also the Cumaean of whom Virgil wrote:

> The final age of the Cumaean song has now come.

369 She was called Cumaean from the city of Cumae, which is in Campania; her tomb still remains in Sicily.

6. The eighth was the Hellespontine, born in the Trojan territory; she is said to have lived in the time of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea.

7. The songs of all these women are circulated, and it is most clearly established that they wrote much about God, Christ, and the nations. But the Erythraean is said to have been the most celebrated and distinguished among them all.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Magi

1. [Note: The first of the magi. Augustine, Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 14.] The first of the magi was Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, [Col. 0310C] whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, killed in battle. Aristotle writes about him that the titles of his books indicate that he himself composed two million verses. [Note: Concerning him, Aristotle. From Pliny, Book XXX, chapter 1. But Pliny seems to cite Hermippus, not Aristotle. Isidore erred by attaching Pliny’s words to the preceding rather than the following material, as he should have done.]

2. Many centuries later Democritus enlarged this art, at the time when the discipline of medicine also flourished through Hippocrates. Among the Assyrians, however, magical arts are abundant, as Lucan testifies:

> Who can know the fates by examining the entrails, who can reveal the birds, who can observe the lightning of heaven and search the stars with Assyrian care?

3. Thus this vanity of magical arts, [Note: From the tradition of evil angels. From Lactantius, Book II, chapter 16; and Tertullian, *Apology*: “They perform the same services, those who consult astrologers, auspices, augurs, and magi about the Caesars’ destiny. Christians do not employ these arts even for their own purposes, since they were handed down by rebellious angels and forbidden by God.”] which arose from the tradition of evil angels, prevailed throughout the whole world for many centuries through a certain knowledge of future things and evocations of infernal beings. From it came the practices of examining entrails, augury, and what are called oracles, as well as necromancy.

4. Nor is it surprising that the magi possessed such illusions, since their magical arts advanced to the point that they even resisted Moses with signs very similar to his, turning rods into dragons and water into blood.

370 5. [Note: It is also reported that a certain famous witch … transformed. From Augustine, Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 17.] A certain very famous witch, Circe, is also said to have changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. We also read about a sacrifice that the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus: whoever partook of it was transformed into the shape of a beast.

6. From this it appears that what that famous poet wrote about a certain woman who excelled in magical arts is not altogether doubtful:

> She promises by her songs to release the minds  
> Of whomever she wishes, but to inflict harsh cares upon others;  
> To halt water in the rivers and turn the stars backward;  
> And to summon the nocturnal shades. You will see the earth bellow  
> Beneath her feet and the ash trees descend from the mountains.

7. What more need be said, if it is permissible to believe that the Pythoness summoned the soul of the prophet Samuel from the hidden places of the underworld and presented it to the sight of the living—provided, that is, that we believe it was the prophet’s soul, and not some phantasmal illusion produced by Satan’s deception? [Note: “If it is permissible to believe.” A problem much debated by our theologians. See Jerome, on Isaiah VII; Cyril, Book VI of *Worship*; Augustine, *To Simplicianus*; and Thomas Aquinas in several places.]

8. [Note: Prudentius also. The book *Against Symmachus*.] Prudentius likewise says this about Mercury:

> He is said, by the power of his lifted wand,  
> To have brought extinguished souls back into the light …  
> But to have condemned others to death …

And a little later he adds:

[Col. 0311C]

> For magical murmuring knows how to summon slender shapes  
> And skillfully enchant the sepulchral ashes.  
> Likewise, the wicked art knows how to deprive others of life.

9. [Note: “Magi are those whom the common people call sorcerers.” The words are Jerome’s, on Daniel II. The same appears in Augustine, Book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 9, and Lactantius, Book II, chapter 17.] Magi are those whom the common people call sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes. They shake the elements, disturb human minds, and kill through nothing but the force of a spell, without anyone drinking poison.

10. Hence Lucan writes:

> A mind polluted by no poison’s filthy gore  
> Perishes when enchanted.

[Note: “Perishes when enchanted.” Lucan has “when disenchanted.” Horace likewise: “What stars, enchanted by a Thessalian voice, and the moon, she snatches from the sky.”] For, having summoned demons, [Note: “They dare to toss about.” Quintilian also calls sorcerers *ventilatores*, “tossers” or “whirlers.”] they dare to toss things about so that each person may destroy his enemies by evil arts. They also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead. [Note: “They also use the blood … of the dead.” From Jerome, on Daniel II.]

371 11. Necromancers are those whose incantations make the dead appear to be revived so that they may foretell things and answer questions. Νεκρός (*nekros*) in Greek means “dead,” while μαντεία (*manteia*) means “divination.” [Note: “To question those who are raised.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “Moreover, there lies the lifeless one.”] To question them, blood is added to the corpse; for demons are said to love blood. Therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water so that they may more readily be summoned by the color of blood.

12. Hydromancers are named from water. [Note: Such is hydromancy. From Augustine, Book VII of *The City of God*, at the end.] Hydromancy consists in summoning the shadows of demons by looking into water, seeing their images or deceptions, and hearing certain things from them there. When blood is added, they are also said to question the inhabitants of the underworld. [Note: “They are also said to question the underworld.” From the same source.]

13. This kind of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians. [Note: “Brought from the Persians.” Varro says, “There are four kinds of divination,” and so forth. We have followed Augustine, not the older books, whose text is: “It is said to have been brought from the Persians. Varro says …” The first statement is established from Augustine; we do not dare affirm that the second comes from Varro. The infinitive form in an indefinite expression is frequent in Isidore, as we noted earlier.] Varro says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. From these come geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy.

14. Diviners are so called as though they were full of God; for they represent themselves as full of divinity and, through a certain deceitful cunning, conjecture future events for human beings.

There are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy.

15. [Note: Enchanters. From Jerome, on Daniel II.] Enchanters are so called because they perform their art through words.

16. Soothsayers (*arioli*) are so called because around the altars of idols they utter abominable prayers, offer deadly sacrifices, and at such celebrations receive responses from demons.

17. [Note: Haruspices. Donatus on *Phormio*: “Haruspices are inspectors of entrails,” that is, of sacrificial victims. Therefore we believe that the words “For they attend to days and hours” were added from the margin. Isidore had written: “Haruspices are inspectors of entrails” (or *haruigae*, from Festus). “They inspect the internal organs,” and so forth.] Haruspices are named as though they were inspectors of hours—for they observe days and hours in conducting business and carrying out tasks, and they consider what a person ought to observe at each particular time. They also inspect the entrails of animals and foretell the future from them.

18. Augurs are those who attend to the flight and voices of birds, as well as other signs or unexpected observations of events that confront human beings; they are also called auspices. [Note: For auspices are the signs observed by travelers. Horace:

> If a perverse desire should make an omen for him,  
> Tomorrow you will carry iron to Teanum, craftsmen …

But the examples are everywhere abundant.] For auspices are the signs that travelers observe.

19. Auspices are so called as though from *avium aspicia*, “observations of birds”; auguries as though from *avium garria*, that is, the cries and language of birds. Likewise, *augurium* is as though *avigerium*, because birds carry or bear the sign.

20. There are two kinds of auspices: one belonging to the eyes and the other to the ears. To the eyes belongs the flight; to the ears, the voice of birds.

21. [Note: Pythons. Some copies have *Pythonesses*.] Pythons are so called from the Pythian Apollo, because he was the originator of divination.

22. Astrologers are so called because they practice augury from the stars.

23. [Note: Genethliacs. Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21, and Jerome, on Daniel II.] Genethliacs are so called because they consider the days of birth.
