For they describe human births through the twelve signs of heaven and attempt to foretell, from the course of the stars under which people are born, their morals, actions, and fortunes—that is, under what sign each person was born or what effect the sign has on the life of the one who is born.

24. These are the people commonly called mathematicians. The Latins call this kind of superstition *constellations*, that is, observations of the stars and of their positions when each person is born.

[Col. 0313B] 25. At first these same interpreters of the stars were called magi, as we read concerning those who announced in the Gospel that Christ had been born; afterward, only mathematicians were called by this name. [Note: They were also interpreters of the stars. From Tertullian, *On Idolatry*.]

26. Knowledge of this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that after Christ had been born no one would thereafter interpret anyone’s birth from heaven. [Note: The knowledge of this art. From the same source.]

27. Horoscopes are so called because they observe the hours of people’s births, which are subject to unequal and differing fates.

28. Sortilegers are those who, under the name of a fabricated religion, profess a knowledge of divination through certain objects they call “the lots of the saints,” or who promise the future by inspecting any writings whatsoever.

29. [Note: Salisators. Some copies have *salitores*. Glossary: *salisatio*, παλμός (*palmos*), “pulsation.” A small book by Melampus of Egypt, *On Pulsations*, is extant. See Justin Martyr, *Reply to the Orthodox*, question 19. Coelius and Vives incorrectly call them *saliatores*.] Salisators are so called because whenever any part of their limbs has twitched, they predict that this signifies something favorable or sad for them.

[Col. 0313C] 30. [Note: To all these things belong. From Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 20.] To all these things also belong the bindings of accursed remedies, which the medical art condemns, whether in incantations, characters, or any objects that are hung up or tied. [Note: Whether in incantations or in characters. See Thomas Aquinas, *Against the Gentiles* III, chapter 105.]

374 31. In all these practices there is the art of demons, arising from a harmful association between human beings and evil angels. Therefore a Christian must avoid all of them and reject and condemn them utterly with every execration.

32. The Phrygians were the first to invent the augury of birds.

33. Mercury is said to have been the first to invent prestidigitation. It is called *praestigium* because it dazzles or obstructs the sharpness of the eyes.

34. A certain Tages is said to have first taught the Etruscans the art of haruspicy. [Note: A certain Tages. From Cicero, *On Divination* II. Columella:

> Hence Tages, the Tyrrhenian, is said to have fixed  
> The bare head of the Arcadian ass at the boundary of the field.]

He dictated haruspicy from the [OCR: “mouths”; perhaps “while plowing” or “from the fields”] and afterward disappeared.

35. For, as the fable goes, while a certain peasant was plowing, Tages suddenly sprang from the clods and dictated haruspicy; on that same day he also died. The Romans translated his books from the Etruscan language into their own.

## CHAPTER X. On the Pagans

1. [Note: They are called pagans. They show that Athens was divided into *pagi* by listing the names of the districts themselves, Areopagus, Cronapagus, and others. But Festus gives the better explanation: “Pagans” are named from *pagi*; *pagi* are named from springs, because they used the same water. For in the Doric language παγαί (*pagai*) means “springs.”] Pagans are named from the districts of the Athenians, where they originated. For there, in rural places and districts, the pagans established sacred groves and idols, and from such a beginning they acquired the name “pagans.”

2. Gentiles are those who are without the Law and have not yet believed. They are called gentiles because they are as they were born—that is, as they descended in the flesh under sin, serving idols and not yet regenerated.

3. Accordingly, they are first called gentiles; in Greek they are called *ethnici*. For *ethnici* is translated from Greek into Latin as “gentiles,” since ἔθνος (*ethnos*) means “nation” in Greek.

4. After faith, however, those who believe from among the nations ought no longer to be called nations or gentiles. In the same way, after faith one can no longer be called a Jew, as the apostle Paul testifies when he says to Christians: “For when you were gentiles,” that is, unbelievers.

5. Apostates are those who, after receiving Christ’s baptism, return to the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices. The name is Greek.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Gods of the Pagans

1. Those whom the pagans assert to be gods are reported to have once been human beings. On account of the life or merits of each one, they began after death to be worshiped among their own peoples: [Note: Among the Egyptians, Isis. From Lactantius, Book I, chapter 15.] in Egypt, Isis; in Crete, Jupiter; [Note: Among the Moors, Juba. In captivity he became highly educated from being a barbarian and wrote a history. Minucius Felix, *Octavius*; Appian; and Plutarch.] among the Moors, Juba; [Col. 0314C] among the Latins, Faunus; among the Romans, Quirinus.

2. In the same way, at Athens there was Minerva; at Samos, Juno; at Paphos, Venus; at Lemnos, Vulcan; at Naxos, Liber; and at Delphi, Apollo. Poets also contributed to their praises and, composing songs, raised them to heaven.

3. For certain inventions of the arts are said to have produced worship, such as medicine in the case of Aesculapius and craftsmanship in the case of Vulcan. [Note: From their activities. Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on the verse “Sacred rites to Jupiter Stygian.”] They are also named from their activities, such as Mercury because he presides over merchandise, and Liber from liberty.

4. There were also certain brave men or founders of cities. After their deaths, the people who had loved them fashioned images of them [Note: They fashioned images. From Lactantius.] so that they might have some consolation from contemplating their likenesses. But gradually, through the persuasion of demons, this error clearly crept into later generations, so that those whom their predecessors had honored merely in memory of their names were believed and worshiped by their successors as gods.

[Col. 0315A] 5. The use of images arose when likenesses or effigies were established out of longing for the dead, who were regarded as having been received into heaven. In their place, demons put themselves forward to be worshiped on earth and persuaded the deceived and ruined to sacrifice to them.

6. Images (*simulacra*) are so called from resemblance, because the hand of the craftsman imitates in stone or another material the faces of those in whose honor the images are fashioned. Thus *simulacra* means either “things that are similar” or “things fabricated and feigned”; hence they are also false.

7. 377 It should also be noted that the Latin word occurs among the Hebrews. For among them an idol or image is called *selem*. [Note: The Latin word in Hebrew. It is *zelem*, “image” or “idol.”] The Jews say that Ishmael was the first to make an image from clay.

8. The pagans, however, report that Prometheus first fashioned images of human beings from clay, and that from him arose the art of fashioning images and statues. Hence poets also figuratively invent that human beings were first made by him, referring to effigies.

9. Among the Greeks, Cecrops, under whom an olive tree first grew on the citadel and the city of the Athenians [Note: From the name of Minerva. For Minerva is called Ἀθήνη (*Athēnē*).] received its name from the title of Minerva—

[Note: Cecrops, under whom. The complete passage is from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*.]

10. He was the first of all to invoke Jupiter by name, to devise images, to establish altars, and to sacrifice victims, although such practices had never before been seen in Greece.

11. *Idololatria* is interpreted as “the service or worship of idols.” For λατρεία (*latreia*) is translated into Latin as *servitus*, “service.” [Note: Insofar as it concerns true religion. Otherwise, *latreia* and *latreuein* have a broader sense of serving.] In relation to true religion, this service is owed only to the one and only God.

12. Just as impious pride—whether of human beings or demons—either commands or desires that this service be offered to itself, so pious humility—whether of human beings or holy angels—refuses what is offered to itself and shows to whom it is owed.

13. An idol is an image made and consecrated in human form, according to the interpretation of the word. [Note: For εἶδος (*eidos*) in Greek. From Tertullian, *On Idolatry*.] For εἶδος means “form” in Greek; *idolum* is derived from it by diminishment, just as among us it gives *formula*, “a little form.”

14. Therefore every form or little image demands to be called an idol. From this comes *idololatria*, every service and servitude directed toward an idol. Some Latins, ignorant of Greek, ineptly say that *idolum* takes its name from *dolus*, “deceit,” because the devil introduced the worship of the creature under the name of divine worship.

15. [Note: Demons. From Lactantius, Book II, chapter 14, and Servius, *Aeneid* III.] They say that demons are so called by the Greeks as though they were δαήμονες (*daēmones*), that is, “skilled” and “knowing about things.” For they foresee many future events, and therefore are accustomed to give certain responses.

16. [Note: For knowledge of things is present in them. From Augustine, Book II of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 17.] They possess a knowledge of things greater than human weakness, partly through the keenness of a subtler sense, partly through the experience of a very long life, and partly through angelic revelation by God’s command. They are powerful by the nature of their aerial bodies.

17. [Note: Before the transgression. From the same work, Book III, chapter 10.] Before the transgression they possessed heavenly bodies. After their fall, however, they were changed into an aerial substance and were permitted to occupy not the purer regions of that air but these murky places, which are for them like a prison until the time of judgment. These are the transgressing angels, whose prince is the devil.

18. [Note: “Devil” in Hebrew. Καταρρέων (*katarrheōn*), “flowing downward.” From Jerome, on Ephesians VI.] In Hebrew, *diabolus* means “flowing downward,” because he scorned to remain at rest on the summit of heaven but, falling downward under the weight of pride, collapsed. In Greek, however, *diabolus* means “accuser,” either because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices people, or because he accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated charges. Hence in the Apocalypse he is called in the angelic voice “the accuser of our brothers, who accused them before our God day and night.”

19. *Satan* means “adversary” or “transgressor” in Latin. 379 For he is the adversary who is the enemy of truth and always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints. He is also the transgressor because, having become a prevaricator, he did not remain in the truth in which he was created. He is likewise the tempter, because he requests that the innocence of the righteous be tested, as is written in Job.

20. He is called Antichrist because he will come against Christ. It is not as certain simple people understand it—that Antichrist is so called because he will come before Christ, that is, that Christ will come after him. Rather, *Antichrist* in Greek means “contrary to Christ” in Latin; for ἀντί (*anti*) means “against” in Latin.

[Col. 0316C] 21. When he comes, he will falsely claim to be Christ, fight against him, and oppose Christ’s sacraments, so as to overthrow the Gospel of his truth.

22. For he will also attempt to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem and restore all the ceremonies of the old Law. [Note: That one too is Antichrist. From Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*.] But that person too is Antichrist who denies that Christ is God, for he is opposed to Christ. Indeed, all who go out from the Church and are cut off from the unity of faith are themselves antichrists.

23. Bel is a Babylonian idol, and its name is interpreted as “old.” Belus was the father of Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians. Some call him Saturn, [Note: This name among the Assyrians. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “Where Belus was,” and on all passages concerning Belus.] and this name was later worshiped both among the Assyrians and among the Africans. [Note: Hence also in the Punic language. From Jerome, on Ezekiel XXIII: “The idol Baal, or Bel, or, to say it more clearly, Belis. The religion of the Assyrians was consecrated by Ninus, son of Belis, in honor of his father, whom he identifies with Saturn.” Isaiah XLVI.] Hence in the Punic language *Bal* means “god.” [Col. 0316D] 380 Among the Assyrians, however, Bel is called, according to a certain principle of their sacred rites, both Saturn and the Sun.

24. Beelphegor is interpreted as “image of disgrace.” [Note: It was an idol of the Moabites. From the same author, *On Hebrew Place-Names*, under “Fogor,” and Hosea IX; also Servius, *Georgics* IV, on the verse “the Hellespontian servant.”] It was an idol of Moab, surnamed Baal, on Mount Phegor. The Latins call him Priapus, the god of gardens.

25. He came from the city of Lampsacus in the Hellespont, from which he was expelled. Because of the size of his male member, the Greeks transferred him into the number of their gods and consecrated him as the divinity of gardens. Hence he is also said to preside over gardens because of their fertility.

26. [Note: Beelzebub. Jerome, on Ecclesiastes X, and Matthew X. The Greeks likewise call him ἀπόμυιος (*apomuios*), “the repeller of flies,” because he drove flies away from Olympus across the Alpheus, whether he was Jupiter, as Pausanias seems to hold, or Hercules.] Beelzebub was an idol of Ekron, whose name is interpreted as “man of flies.” For *zebub* means “fly.” Thus this most filthy idol is called “man of flies” either because of the filth of idolatry or because of its uncleanness.

Belial [lacuna].

27. [Note: Behemoth. The words are Gregory’s, *Moralia* XXXII, chapter 10.] *Behemoth*, from a Hebrew word rendered into Latin, means “animal,” because he fell from lofty places to earthly ones [Col. 0317B] and, according to his desert, became like a dumb animal. He is also Leviathan, that is, “the serpent of the waters,” because he moves about with cunning in the shifting sea of this world.

28. [Note: Leviathan. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 13.] Leviathan, however, is interpreted as “their addition,” namely, the addition of those who are none other than human beings. For in paradise he once introduced the guilt of transgression to them, and every day he adds to or extends it by persuasion, leading them to eternal death.

29. [Note: Certain names of their gods. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*.] The pagans attempt through their vain tales to transfer certain names of their gods to physical explanations, interpreting them as composed from the causes of the elements. But all this was fabricated by the poets so that they might adorn their gods with various figures—gods whom histories acknowledge to have been depraved and full of disgraceful infamy. For there is no room at all for invention where truth is absent.

[Col. 0317C] 30. Saturn is designated by the pagans as the origin of the gods and of all posterity. [Note: The Latins say that he was named from *satus*, “sowing.” From Augustine, Book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 19.] The Latins say that he was named from *satus*, as though the sowing of all things belonged to him, or from the length of time, because he is filled with years.

31. [Note: Hence the Greeks also call him so. From Servius, *Aeneid* III.] Hence the Greeks say that he bears the name Κρόνος (*Kronos*), as though Χρόνος (*Chronos*), that is, “time,” because he is said to have devoured his children. This means that he rolls back into himself the years that time has produced, [Note: Or because seeds return. From Augustine, Book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 19.] or because seeds return again to the place from which they arise.

32. They say that he cut off the genitals of his father Caelus because nothing is born from seeds in heaven. They say that he holds a sickle to signify agriculture, or years and seasons, because they return into themselves, or wisdom, because it is sharp within.

33. In certain cities the pagans sacrificed their children to Saturn, because the poets handed down the story that Saturn was accustomed to devour his children.

[Col. 0318A] 382 34. Jupiter is said to have been named from *juvare*, “to help,” and *Jupiter* as though “helping father,” that is, one who provides for all. They also called him Jupiter the Best by a private title, although he was incestuous with his own relations and immodest with outsiders.

35. Sometimes they represent him as a bull because of the abduction of Europa—for he was in a ship whose emblem was a bull; [Note: Sometimes as Danaë’s lover through a shower. From the same source, Book XVIII, chapter 13.] sometimes as having sought intercourse with Danaë through a shower of gold, where it is understood that the woman’s chastity was corrupted by gold; sometimes in the likeness of an eagle, because he carried off a boy for sexual violation; sometimes as a serpent, because he crawled; and as a swan, because he sang.

36. Therefore these are not merely figures but plainly crimes drawn from reality. It was thus shameful to believe in gods of the sort that human beings ought not to be.

37. [Note: They speak of Janus. From Book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 8.] They call Janus as though he were the door of the world, or of heaven, or of the months. They give Janus two faces because of the East and the West. When they make him four-faced and call him double Janus, they refer this to the four regions of the world, or to the four elements or seasons. But in inventing this they make him a monster, not a god.

38. [Note: Neptune. From chapter 16.] They proclaim Neptune to be the waters of the world, and say that he was called Neptune as though “thundering from the cloud.”

39. They take Vulcan to be fire and say that Vulcan was named as though from “flying brightness,” or as though *volicanus*, because he flies through the air; for fire is born from the clouds. [Note: And the name Vulcan. From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “No less powerful in fire.”]

40. [Note: Hence Homer also. *Iliad* I, and Eustathius there.] Hence Homer also says that he was hurled from the air onto the earth, 383 because every bolt of lightning falls from the air. [Note: Why this is so. From the same passage of Servius.] Vulcan is therefore represented as born from the thigh of Juno, because lightning bolts arise from the lower air.

[Col. 0318C] 41. Vulcan is said to be lame because by nature fire is never straight, [Note: But it has the appearance of a lame thing. Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX.] but has a movement and appearance resembling that of a lame person. They therefore also call Vulcan the originator of the smiths’ furnace, because without fire no kind of metal can be melted and extended.

42. [Note: *Pluto* in Latin, *Diespiter*. From Lactantius, Book I, chapter 14.] Pluto in Greek is *Diespiter* in Latin, [Note: Or “Father Dis.” Others have also used *Ditis* in the nominative. Petronius: “Among these seats Father Dis raised his face.”] or “Father Dis,” whom others call Orcus, as though “the receiver of the dead.” [Note: Others call him Orcus, as though “the receiver of the dead.” Augustine, Book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 3: “What of truth? What of happiness? Although they had these as goddesses, they did not wish to give them a place among the select gods, where they gave one to Mars and one to Orcus, one the producer of deaths, the other the receiver of the dead.”] Hence *orca* is also the name of a vessel that receives water. He is also called Charon in Greek.

43. [Note: They wish Liber to have been named from *liberamentum*, “liberation.” Same source, chapter 2.] They wish Liber to have been named from *liberamentum*, because males are, as it were, released through his benefit when they emit seed in intercourse. This same Liber is depicted with a womanly and delicate body; for they say that women were assigned to him, as was wine, to arouse lust.

44. Hence his forehead is encircled with a vine leaf. But he has a wreath of vine leaves and a horn because, when wine is drunk gratefully and moderately, it provides joy; when drunk beyond measure, it arouses quarrels—that is, it gives, as it were, horns. He is also called Lyaeus, ἀπὸ τοῦ λύειν (*apo tou lyein*), “from loosening,” because the limbs are relaxed by much wine. He is also called Διόνυσος (*Dionysus*) in Greek [Note: From Mount Nysa in India. From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “Liber, driving from lofty Nysa.”] from Mount Nysa in India, where he is said to have been raised. There is also a city called Nysa, where this same Liber is worshiped; hence he is called Nysaeus.

384 45. They interpret Mercury as speech. [Note: Hence Mercury. From the same book of Augustine, chapter 14.] For he is called Mercury as though *medius currens*, “running in the middle,” because speech runs as an intermediary among human beings. Therefore he is also called Ἑρμῆς (*Hermes*) in Greek, because speech—or interpretation, which certainly pertains to speech—is called ἑρμηνεία (*hermēneia*).

46. Therefore he is also said to preside over commerce, because speech serves as an intermediary between sellers and buyers. For this reason he is depicted with wings, because words travel swiftly. [Note: [Col. 0319D] Hence also “swift.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, and Augustine.] Hence he is also represented as swift and wandering; for the wings on his head and feet signify that speech becomes winged as it passes through the air.

[Col. 0319B] 47. He is called a messenger because through speech all thoughts are proclaimed. They say that he is the master of theft because speech deceives the minds of those who hear it. He holds a wand with which he separates serpents—that is, poisons.

48. For the speeches of interpreters calm those who are warring and at variance; hence, according to Livy, ambassadors of peace are called *caduceatores*. Just as wars were declared through the *fetiales*, so peace was established through the *caduceatores*.

49. Hermes, however, is called in Greek “from interpretation” (ἀπὸ τῆς ἑρμηνείας), in Latin “interpreter”; on account of his excellence and knowledge of many arts, he was called [385] *Trismegistus*, that is, “thrice greatest.” [Note: [Col. 0319D] *Trismegistus*. From Lactantius, *On Anger*, book 11, and book I, chapter 6.] When they depict him with a dog’s head, the reason given is that among all animals the dog is considered the most shrewd and perceptive species.

50. They say that Mars is the god of war, and that he was called *Mars* because fighting is done by men, [Note: [Col. 0319D] So that *MARS* would mean *maris ars*, “the art of the male.” All manuscripts have *Mars mas*, “Mars the male,” but the conjecture was not difficult.] so that *MARS* would be *maris ars*, “the art of the male,” although there are also three customary forms of warfare: that of the Scythians, in which both women and men go into battle; that of the Amazons, in which only women fight; and that of the Romans and other nations, in which only males fight.

51. Likewise, they say that Mars means, as it were, “the maker of deaths.” For death is named from Mars. [Note: [Col. 0319D] “They also call him an adulterer,” etc. Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX, chapter 9: Venus is the wife of Vulcan and the adulteress of Mars, because she is inappropriate for those engaged in warfare.] They also call him an adulterer because he is uncertain amid those engaged in war.

52. The reason he stands with his chest bare is that each person may expose himself to war without fear in his heart. [Note: [Col. 0319D] Mars among the Thracians is called *Gradivus*. This does not mean that *Gradivus* was the Thracian name; rather, among them he is the same as θούριος Ἄρης, “impetuous Ares,” among the Romans, *Gradivus*. For, as Servius says, *Aeneid* I and III, there were two temples of Mars at Rome: one within the city, belonging to Quirinus, as guardian and peaceful god; the other outside the city on the Appian Way near the gate, as warrior and *Gradivus*.] Mars among the Thracians is called *Gradivus*, either because those who fight advance their step in battle, or because they march energetically.

53. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Although they wished Apollo…” Augustine, chapter 16.] Although they wished Apollo to be both a diviner and a physician, they nevertheless also called him the Sun, as though *solum*, “the sole one”; they called him Titan as well, as though he were one of the Titans [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Who did not act against Jupiter.” A Hispanic usage: *hacer por alguno* or *contra alguno*, “to act for or against someone.” There was no reason to add “war,” which appears in the printed books but not in the manuscript.] who did not act against Jupiter.

54. They called him Phoebus, as though *Ephaebus*, that is, “young man”; hence the Sun is depicted as a boy, because each day he rises and is born with new light. They also say that the same Apollo is called Pythius, after Python, a serpent of immense size, whose venom terrified no less than its magnitude.

55. Apollo struck him down with arrows and carried away the spoils of his name as well, so that he was called Pythius; hence, in honor of the victory, he established the Pythian rites to be celebrated.

56. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Diana also.” From Augustine, chapter 16.] They likewise say that Diana, his sister, is the Moon and the guardian of roads. Hence they wish her to be a virgin, because a road produces nothing. For this reason both are represented as carrying arrows, because those two heavenly bodies send rays from heaven down to the earth. They say that Diana was called as though *Duana*, because the moon appears by day and by night.

57. They also assert that she is Lucina, because she gives light. They call her likewise Trivia, because she is imagined in three forms. Concerning her Virgil says:

> . . . the three faces of virgin Diana,

because she is called the Moon, Diana, and Proserpina alike.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] Because she is the same as the Moon. From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on the verse “She honors the sacred rites by the sea.” In Servius, *Juno* is erroneously read for *Moon*.]

58. But when she is represented as the Moon:

[Note: [Col. 0320D] “She shines in a subtly gleaming garment.” A poem of Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.]

> . . . she shines in a subtly gleaming garment.
>
> When, girded, she casts her shafts, she is the virgin daughter of Latona;
>
> When she sits supported upon a throne, she is the wife of Pluto.

She is called Latonian Diana because she was the daughter of Latona.

387 59. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Ceres.” From Augustine, chapter 24.] They assert that Ceres, that is, the earth, was so called from the creation of crops, giving her many names. They also call her *Ops*, because through cultivation the earth becomes better.

60. They call her Proserpina because crops *proserpunt*, “sprout forth,” from her.

61. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Vesta,” because of herbs. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “Ancient faith and Vesta.”] They say that Vesta was so called because she is clothed with herbs or with various things, or from her power of standing. They also represent her as Tellus and the Great Mother, wearing a towered crown, with a tympanum, eunuch priests, and the clamor of cymbals. They call her Mother because she produces very many things; Great because she generates food; nourishing because she feeds all living creatures with her fruits. For the earth is the nurse of foods.

62. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Because her image is depicted with a key.” From the same source, *Aeneid* X, on the verse “Nourishing mother Idaea.”] Her image is depicted with a key because the earth is closed in winter and opened in spring, so that crops may be born. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Because she has tympana.” From Augustine.] They wish the tympanum to signify the globe of the earth.

63. [Note: [Col. 0320D] “Because she is carried in a chariot.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on the verse “And the yoked chariot of the lady…”] She is said to ride in a chariot because she herself is the earth, [Col. 0321A] which hangs in the air. She is supported by wheels because the universe revolves and is in motion. They place tame lions beneath her to show that there is no species on earth so wild that it cannot be subdued or overcome by her.

64. The towered crown that she wears on her head shows the cities placed upon the earth, which are known to be marked by towers. Seats are imagined around her because, although all things move, she herself does not move.

65. The reason the Corybantes, her attendants, are depicted with drawn swords is to signify that everyone ought to fight for his land. The reason they made eunuchs serve this goddess is to signify that those who need seed ought to follow the earth, since everything is found in it.

66. Since, they say, they throw themselves about before her, it is commanded that those who cultivate the earth should not sit idle, for there is always something for them to do. The sound of bronze cymbals signifies the clatter of tools in cultivating the fields; [Note: [Col. 0321D] “And therefore of bronze, because the ancients cultivated the earth with bronze.” Lucretius, book V:

> And the use of bronze was known before that of iron,
>
> For its nature is more tractable and its supply greater.
>
> With bronze they worked the soil of the earth,
>
> And with bronze they stirred the waves of war and sowed vast wounds.]

and therefore it is bronze, because the ancients cultivated the earth with bronze before iron had been discovered.

67. [Note: [Col. 0321D] “They also say that Vesta is fire.” Augustine, *City of God* IV, and Servius, *Aeneid* I.] They maintain that Vesta is also fire, because it is beyond doubt that the earth contains fire, as can be understood from Aetna and Vulcan. [Note: [Col. 0321D] “From Aetna and Vulcan.” So it stands in Servius; otherwise I would read *Vulcanian*, since below, in book XIV on the Aeolian islands, they are also called Vulcanian because, like Aetna, they burn.] They therefore consider her a virgin, [Note: [Col. 0321D] “And therefore a virgin.” Lactantius I, chapter 12.] because fire is an inviolable element and nothing can be born from it, since it consumes everything it seizes.

68. Ovid says in the *Fasti*:

> Nor should you understand Vesta as anything other than a living flame;
>
> You see that no bodies are born from flame;

and therefore they say that virgins serve her, because just as nothing comes from a virgin, so nothing is born from fire.

69. They say that Juno means, as though *janonem*, that is, “door,” for the purification of women, and because she opens, as it were, the doors of mothers to their offspring and the bodies of brides to their husbands. [Note: [Col. 0321D] “For the purifications of women.” From *City of God* VII, chapters 2 and 3.] But this is the philosophers’ account. The poets, however, assert that Juno is the sister and wife of Jupiter; [Note: [Col. 0321D] “For fire and air are generated.” The words are Servius’s, *Georgics* II.] for they interpret Jupiter as fire and air, and Juno as water and earth, from the mingling of which all things are generated.

70. They call her Jupiter’s sister because she is a part of the universe; his wife because, when mingled, she agrees with him. Hence Virgil says:

> Then the almighty Father descends in fruitful showers
>
> into the joyful lap of his consort . . .

389 71. [Note: [Col. 0321D] “Minerva … that is, female.” Or rather, “without a female.” For she arose from Jupiter’s brain, and hence is called ἀμήτωρ, “motherless.” Thus *Athena* may mean ἄνευ θηλύας, “without a female,” or perhaps ἄθήλη, “without a nipple.”] Among the Greeks Minerva is called ἀθήνη, that is, “female.” Among the Latins, however, they say that she was called Minerva as if “goddess” and “gift of the arts.” For they describe her as the inventor of many skills, [Note: [Col. 0321D] “Inventor of many talents.” Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 8: “Minerva, truly the inventor of many works.”] and therefore interpret her as art and reason, because nothing can be contained without reason.

72. Since reason arises from the mind alone, and they believe that the mind is located in the head and brain, they therefore say that she was born from the head of Jupiter, because the perception of the wise person, who discovers everything, is in the head.

73. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “On whose breast.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “And the entwined serpents.”] The head of the Gorgon is therefore represented on her breast because all wisdom is there—wisdom that confounds others and proves the ignorant to be stone-like. We also see this on ancient statues of commanders, in the middle of the breastplate, to suggest wisdom and courage.

74. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “This Minerva … became known.” Augustine’s words, in the same place.] This Minerva is also called Tritonia. For Triton is a marsh in Africa, near which she is said to have appeared in maidenhood; for this reason she was called Tritonia. Hence she was believed to be a goddess all the more readily because her origin was less known.

75. She was called Pallas either from the island of Pallene in Thrace, where she was raised; [Note: [Col. 0322D] Or ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν τὸ δόρυ … “because she killed him.” Servius’s words, *Aeneid* I.] or ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν τὸ δόρυ, that is, “from brandishing the spear”; or because she killed the giant Pallas.

390 76. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “They say that Venus was therefore called…” From Augustine, *City of God* VI, chapter 9.] They say that Venus was so called because, without force, a woman does not cease to be a virgin. The Greeks call her ἀφροδίτη because of the foam that generates blood; for ἄφρος means “foam” in Greek.

77. As for their story that Saturn cut off the genitals of his father Heaven, that blood flowed into the sea, and that Venus was born from the sea-foam that congealed, they say that it signifies that through intercourse there is a substance of salty moisture. Hence Venus is called ἀφροδίτη, [Note: [Col. 0322D] “Aphrodite.” Servius, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “Hence the race of the leader.”] because in intercourse there is a foam of blood, which consists of the liquid and salty fluid of the entrails.

78. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “They therefore call Venus…” From the same source, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “He received the accustomed flame.”] They therefore call Venus the wife of Vulcan, because the function of Venus depends entirely upon heat. Hence the saying: “The old man is cold for Venus.”

79. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “For the reason that Saturn … is created.” His words, *Georgics* II, on the verses “The rustic,” and “with curved Saturn.”] Since Saturn is said to have cut off the virility of his father Heaven, and since these parts, falling into the sea, created Venus, the story is invented because, unless moisture descends from heaven to the earth, nothing is created.

80. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “Cupid.” From the same source, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “Therefore winged…” See Propertius, *Elegies*:

> Whoever that man was who painted Love as a boy.]

They say that Cupid was named from love; for he is the demon of fornication. He is depicted with wings because nothing is found lighter or more changeable than those in love. He is depicted as a boy because love is foolish and irrational. [Note: [Col. 0322D] “A bow.” From Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX, chapter 9.] He is represented holding an arrow and a torch: the arrow because love wounds the heart; the torch because it inflames.

[Col. 0323A] 81. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “They call him Pan.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 2.] The Greeks call him Pan, the Latins Silvanus: the god of country people, whom they fashioned in the likeness of nature. Hence he was called Pan, that is, “everything.” For they imagine him in the universal form of the elements.

82. He has horns in the likeness of the rays of the Sun and Moon. His skin is marked with spots, on account of the stars of heaven. His face is red in the likeness of the ether. He carries a pipe of seven reeds, on account of the harmony of heaven, in which there are seven sounds and seven distinctions of pitch.

83. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “He is hairy because the earth is clothed and stirred by the winds.” Nothing of this appears in Servius, from whom the rest is taken, and the manuscripts read it in various ways; Chacon therefore regarded it as suspect.] He is hairy because the earth is clothed and stirred by the winds. 391 His lower part is foul on account of the trees, wild beasts, and livestock. He has goat’s hooves to show the solidity of the earth. They wish him to be the god of things and of all nature; hence, they say, Pan means “everything.”

[Col. 0323B] 84. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Isis,” in the Egyptian language. From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “The queen in the midst of the peoples…”] In the language of the Egyptians, the earth is called Isis, and they wish Isis to be the earth. Isis was the queen of the Egyptians, the daughter of King Inachus. Coming from Greece, she taught the Egyptians letters and instructed them to cultivate the land; for this reason they also called the earth by her name.

85. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Serapis.” Augustine’s words, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 5.] Serapis is the greatest of all the Egyptian gods. He is the same as Apis, king of the Argives, who was carried by ship to Egypt and, after dying there, was called Serapis. The reason is that the chest in which the dead man is placed, which they call a sarcophagus, is called σορός in Greek; and they began to worship him as buried there before his temple had been built. Thus, as it were, σορὸς Apis—first *Sorapis*, and then, with a change of letters, *Serapis*.

86. Apis was an Egyptian bull consecrated to Serapis, [Col. 0323C] and was named after him. Egypt worshiped it as a divine power because it gave certain clear signs concerning the future; for it appeared at Memphis. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Whom a hundred priests accompanied.” From Solinus, chapter 35.] A hundred priests accompanied it, and suddenly, as though possessed, they sang before it. The Jews made an image of its head [Note: [Col. 0323D] “For themselves in the desert of Judea.” Lactantius, book IV, chapter 10.] for themselves in the desert.

87. Fauns are said to be named from *fari*, “to speak,” or ἀπὸ τῆς φωνῆς, “from the voice,” [Note: [Col. 0323D] Or “from the voice.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VII.] because they seemed to reveal the future by voice rather than by signs. For pagans consulted them in sacred groves, and they gave them responses not by signs but by voices.

88. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Genius.” From Augustine, *City of God* VII, chapter 13.] They call him Genius because he is thought to possess, as it were, the power of generating all things, or because of the begetting of children. Hence the marriage beds prepared for a new husband by the nations were called *genial beds*.

89. These and other things are the fabulous inventions of the pagans, [Col. 0323D] which, when interpreted in this way, are nevertheless worshiped damnably by those who do not understand them.

90. They say that Fate is whatever the gods speak—whatever Jupiter speaks. 392 [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Therefore they call it fate from *fari*.” From the same Augustine, *City of God* V, chapter 9, and Servius, *Eclogue* 4.] Thus they call it *fatum* from *fari*, that is, from “speaking.” [Note: [Col. 0324D] “If this name were not already…” From the same Augustine.] If this name were not already customarily understood in another sense, toward which we do not wish to incline human hearts, we could reasonably call it *fatum* from *fari*.

91. For we cannot deny that it is written in the sacred Scriptures: “Once God has spoken, I have heard two things,” and so forth. The statement “Once he has spoken” is understood to mean that he has spoken immutably—that is, unchangeably—just as he knows unchangeably all the things that will happen and all the things he himself will do.

92. [Note: [Col. 0324D] “The three Fates.” From *Against Faustus* XX, chapter 9.] They imagine the three Fates with a distaff and spindle, twisting threads from wool with their fingers, on account of the three times: the past, which has already been spun and wound onto the spindle; the present, which is passed between the fingers of the spinner; [Col. 0324B] [Note: [Col. 0324D] *Neentis*. Thus consistently in the Gothic books here; and shortly afterward, preserving the analogy, *non neentis*, whether it belongs to the second or third conjugation, as in Tibullus:

> The threads which they draw out and spin for what is to come.]

and the future, which is in the wool entangled on the distaff and which is still to be transferred by the fingers of the spinner to the spindle, just as the present is transferred into the past.

93. [Note: [Col. 0324D] “The Parcae.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 4.] They say that the Parcae were called κατ᾽ ἀντίφρασιν, “by way of contrary meaning,” because they spare not at all. They wished them to be three: one who begins a person’s life; another who weaves it; and a third who breaks it. We begin when we are born; we exist while we live; we cease when we die.

94. They say that Fortune derives her name from fortuitous events, [Note: [Col. 0324D] “As a certain goddess.” From Lactantius, book III, chapter 27.] as though she were a goddess who mocks human affairs with various accidents and chance occurrences; [Note: [Col. 0324D] “Hence also blind.” From *City of God* IV, chapter 18.] hence they also call her blind, because she falls indiscriminately upon anyone without examining merit and comes to both the good and the wicked. They separate Fate from Fortune, saying that Fortune is concerned with things that come by chance, with no evident cause, whereas Fate is assigned and determined for each individual.

95. They also say that there are three female Furies, their hair formed of serpents, on account of the three passions that generate many disturbances in human minds and sometimes compel people to sin in such a way that they do not permit them to have regard either for reputation or for their own danger: anger, which desires vengeance; greed, which desires wealth; and lust, which seeks pleasures. They are therefore called Furies because they strike the mind with their goads and do not allow it to be at peace.

96. They think that the Nymphs, goddesses of waters, were named from clouds; for waters come from clouds, from which the word is derived: nymphs of waters, as though they were the divinities of streams. [Note: [Col. 0324D] “They also call them.” *Muses*. From Servius, *Eclogue* 8.] They also call them Muses, as well as Nymphs, and not without reason, for the movement of water produces music.

[Col. 0325A] 97. Among the pagans the Nymphs have various names. [Note: [Col. 0325B] “They call the Nymphs of mountains…” From the same source, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “Here and there the Oreads gather,” and *Eclogue* 10.] They call the Nymphs of mountains Oreads, those of forests Dryads, [Note: [Col. 0325B] *Bampor*. *Hamadryads*. Servius: “Those who are born together with the forests are Hamadryads.”] those of fields Hamadryads, those of springs Naiads, and those of the sea Nereids.

98. [Note: [Col. 0325B] “Heroes, the dead.” From Augustine, *City of God* X, chapter 21.] They say that Heroes drew their name from Juno, for Juno is called ἥρη in Greek; and therefore, according to the Greek story, some son of hers was called ἥρως, “hero”? “Hero” is thus derived from ἥρη, “Hera/Juno.” This evidently signifies through a kind of mystical meaning in the story that the air is assigned to Juno, and they wish the Heroes to dwell there. By this name they call the souls of the dead who possessed some merit, as though ἀηρῶας, that is, “airy men,” worthy of heaven on account of their wisdom and courage.

99. [Note: [Col. 0325B] “The Penates … they worshiped.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] The pagans called all the gods whom they worshiped at home Penates. [Note: [Col. 0325B] “Called Penates.” Arnobius, book III: Varro considers the gods who are within and in the innermost shrines to be the Penates.] They were called Penates because they were in the *penetralia*, that is, in secret places. Which gods these were, or what names they had, is unknown.

100. [Note: [Col. 0325C] “The Manes.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on the verse “Altars stand for the Manes.”] They say that the Manes are the gods of the dead, whose power they place between the moon and the earth. They think that *morning* (*mane*) was also named from them, and that the Manes were named from the air, which is *manus*, that is, “thin,” or because they flow broadly through the breezes; or because they are gentle in contrast with the savage, and are called by this contrary name. [Col. 0326A] [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Apuleius, however, says…” The passage is not intact. Although the rest comes from Apuleius, who is also cited by Augustine, *City of God* IX, chapter 9, in *On the God of Socrates*, this part is more likely from Servius, who writes that the Manes are called κατ᾽ ἀντίφρασιν, “by contrary meaning.”] Apuleius, however, says that they are called Manes κατ᾽ ἀντίφρασιν—that is, “gentle and mild,” although they are terrifying and savage—as are the Parcae and Eumenides.

101. They say that Larvae are demons made from human beings who have deserved evil. [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Their nature.” From Jerome, preface to the *Hebrew Questions*.] Their nature is said to be to frighten little children and to chatter in dark corners.

102. Lamiae, whom the stories relate to have been accustomed to seize and tear infants, are specifically named from *laniando*, “tearing.”

103. [Note: [Col. 0326B] “The Hairy Ones,” who are called in Greek *Panitae*. Gregory, *Moralia* VII, chapter 15: “Who else are represented by the name Hairy Ones except those whom the Greeks call Pans and the Latins Incubi?” This is how the more correct books of Gregory read, not “Fauns,” although both are true, since they were called both Pans and Fauns. But here we think *Panisci* should be read, not *Pauitae*.] The Hairy Ones, who are called *Panitae* in Greek and Incubi in Latin, are also called [Note: [Col. 0326B] “Invi,” from *ineundo*, ‘entering or having intercourse.’ From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “The fortress and castle of Inuus.”] Invi, from *ineundo*, because they have intercourse promiscuously with animals. Hence they are also called Incubi, from *incumbendo*, that is, “violating.” 395 [Note: [Col. 0326B] “For they are often depraved.” Augustine’s words, *City of God* XV, chapter 23.] For they are often depraved even toward women, and engage in intercourse with them. [Col. 0326B] The Gauls call these demons *Dusii*, because they constantly practice this impurity.

104. The one whom the common people call an Incubus, [Note: [Col. 0326C] “The Romans call this a Fig Faun.” Jerome, *Isaiah* XIII: “The Hairy Ones, or Incubi, or Satyrs, woodland beings whom some call Fig Fauns.” Likewise Eutropius, book XII: “Woodland beings whom some call Fig Fauns.” The same being seems to be *Fatuus Fatuelis* as well as the Fig Faun, insofar as one may infer from the passage of Servius cited above.] the Romans call a Fig Faun. To him Horace says:

> Faun, lover of the fleeing Nymphs,
>
> Through my lands and sunny fields
>
> Walk gently.

## BOOK NINE. ON LANGUAGES, PEOPLES, KINGDOMS, MILITARY AFFAIRS, CITIZENS, AND RELATIONSHIPS

[Col. 0325]

### CHAPTER ONE. On the Languages of Peoples

1. The diversity of languages arose during the construction of the tower after the Flood. 396 For before the pride of that tower divided human society into different sounds of speech, [Note: [Col. 0325D] “There was one language of all nations … in the sacred writings.” From Augustine, *City of God* XVI, chapter 11.] there was one language of all nations, which is called Hebrew and which the patriarchs and prophets used not only in their speech but also in the sacred writings. At the beginning, there were as many languages as peoples; afterward there were more peoples than languages, because many peoples arose from one language.

2. In this passage, “languages” means the words produced by the tongue, according to that figure of speech in which the agent is named by what is produced: just as *mouth* is commonly used for words, and *hand* for writing.

[Col. 0326C] 3. There are three sacred languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which are preeminent throughout the whole world. For in these three languages Pilate wrote the charge against the Lord above the cross. Hence, because of the obscurity of the Holy Scriptures, knowledge of these three languages is necessary, so that one may turn to another if the speech of one language introduces any uncertainty concerning a word or its interpretation.

4. Greek is considered more distinguished than the other languages of the nations. It is more sonorous than Latin and all other languages. Its variety is divided into five forms, the first of which is called κοινὴ, that is, “mixed” or “common,” which everyone uses.

5. The second is Attic, namely Athenian, [Note: [Col. 0326D] “Which all the writers of Greece used.” Or rather, the more elegant writers; or he takes “Greece” for Hellas. On its boundaries, see Eustathius, *Iliad* π, on the verse Χάλκωνος φίλον υἱὸν ὃς Ἑλλάδι οἰκία ναίων, “the dear son of Chalkon, who dwelt in Hellas.” Jerome also, in the *Hebrew Questions*, calls the Ionians, who are related to the Attic people and were once the same, simply “Greeks”: “From the Ionians,” he says, “that is, from the Greeks, arose the Eliseans, who are called Aeolians.”] which, so to speak, all the writers of Greece used. 397 The third is Doric, [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Doric, which the Egyptians have.” Alexandrians.] which the Egyptians and [Note: [Col. 0327D] “And the Sicilians.” “Syrians” is an error in all the books.] Sicilians use. The fourth is Ionic. The fifth is Aeolic, in which the Aeolians spoke. Such distinctions are observed in the Greek language, for their speech is divided in this way.

6. [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Some have said that there are four Latin languages.” If there is any error here, Isidore ought not to bear responsibility for it; the author should be sought instead.] Some have said that there are four Latin languages: namely, the ancient, Latin, Roman, and mixed. The ancient was used by the earliest inhabitants of Italy under Janus and Saturn, in an uncultivated form, as the songs of the Salii show. Latin was spoken under Latinus and the kings of Tuscany by the other inhabitants of Latium, [Note: [Col. 0327D] “From which the Twelve Tables came.” Not because they were written under the kings, but because their language may perhaps have been used in them so that their ancient wording would carry greater authority; Cicero also admits that he did the same, *On the Laws* II: “There are certain words of the laws, Quintus, and they are not so ancient as in those old and sacred laws,” etc.] and in this language the Twelve Tables were written.

7. Roman began after the kings had been expelled by the Roman people. [Note: [Col. 0328D] “In which … Ennius … poured forth.” From manuscript N; since *scripta sua* is absent from all our copies, the reading indicated by Vulcanus from an old manuscript, *effulserunt*, “shone forth,” is not implausible.] In it the poets Naevius, Plautus, Ennius, and Virgil, and among the orators Gracchus, Cato, Cicero, and the others, poured forth their writings. Mixed is the language that, after the empire had been extended more widely, invaded Roman citizenship together with foreign customs and peoples, corrupting the purity of speech through solecisms and barbarisms.

8. All the peoples of the East strike their language and words in the throat, as do the Hebrews and Syrians. All the peoples of the central regions strike their speech against the palate, as do the Greeks and Asians. All the peoples of the West break their words against the teeth, as do the Italians and Spaniards.

9. [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Syrian and Chaldean are neighboring.” From Ambrose, *Hexameron* I, chapter 8, and Basil, homily 1.] Syrian and Chaldean are close to Hebrew in speech, agreeing with it in most respects and in the sound of their letters. [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Some, however, think…” Jerome’s words on Daniel I.] Some, however, think that Hebrew itself is Chaldean because Abraham was from the Chaldeans. But if this is accepted, how are the Hebrew boys in Daniel ordered to be taught the language that they already knew? [Col. 0327C]

10. Every person can acquire any language, whether Greek, Latin, or that of another nation, either by hearing it or by learning it from a teacher through reading. Although knowledge of all languages is difficult for anyone, no one is so lazy that, while living among his own people, he does not know the language of his own people. For what else should he be considered except [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Worse than brute animals.” From two manuscripts of Tarragona and Rab.] worse than brute animals? For they express the cry of their own proper voice, whereas he is worse because he lacks knowledge of his own language.

11. What language God spoke at the beginning of the world when he said, “Let there be light,” is difficult to discover, since languages did not yet exist. Likewise, in what language he later sounded into the external ears of human beings—especially when speaking to the first man, or to the prophets, or when the voice of God speaking sounded bodily, “You are my beloved Son”—is uncertain. Some believe that it was that one and only language which existed before the diversity of languages; others believe that among the various nations God speaks to them in the same language that those people themselves use, so that they may understand him.

12. God speaks to human beings not through his invisible substance but through a bodily creature, through which he also wished to appear to human beings when he spoke. The Apostle also says: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels.” Here the question arises: In what language do angels speak? This does not mean that angels have particular languages, but is said by way of exaggeration.

13. It is likewise asked in what language human beings will speak in the future, but this is nowhere found. For the Apostle says: “Whether there will be an end of tongues.”

14. We have therefore placed languages before peoples because peoples arose from languages, not languages from peoples.

### CHAPTER TWO. On the Names of Peoples

1. A people (*gens*) is a multitude arising from one origin, or distinguished from another nation by its own gathering, as in the case of Greece and Asia; hence the term *gentility* is also used. A people is called *gens* because of the generations of families, that is, from *gignere*, “to beget,” just as *nation* comes from *nasci*, “to be born.”

2. [Note: [Col. 0328D] “The peoples by whom…” Augustine, *City of God* XVI, chapter 6: “From those three men, therefore, the sons of Noah, there were seventy-three, or rather, as the reckoning makes clear,” etc. He had explained this in chapter 3.] The peoples by whom the earth was divided numbered seventy-three: fifteen from Japheth, 400 thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem, making seventy-three—or rather, as the calculation shows, seventy-two. An equal number of languages began to exist throughout the lands, and as they multiplied they filled provinces and islands.

3. The five sons of Shem each individually became the ancestor of a people. The first was Elam, from whom came the Elamites, the leading people of Persia; the second was Asshur, from whom the empire of the Assyrians arose; the third was Arphaxad, from whom the people of the Chaldeans originated; the fourth was Lud, from whom came the Lydians; and the fifth was Aram, from whom came the Syrians, whose capital was Damascus.

4. The sons of Aram, grandchildren of Shem, were four: Uz, Ul, Gether, and Mash. [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Uz, the founder of Trachonitis.” From Jerome, in the *Hebrew Questions*, from which much of this chapter is taken.] Uz, founder of Trachonitis, held dominion between Palestine and Coelesyria; Job was from there, according to what is written: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job.” The second was Ul, from whom came the Armenians; the third was Gether, from whom came the [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Acarnanians, or Curetes.” Jerome mistakenly has *Cariae* for *Curiae*. Stephanus: Ἀκαρνάνια χώρα κεχωρισμένη τῶν Κουρήτων πρὸς Ἀχελώῳ, “Acarnania is a land separated from the Curetes by the Achelous.” Hence some are called Curetes, from *keiresthai*, “to cut the hair,” while those who do not cut their hair are called Acarnanians. Strabo relates that Jerome and Isidore, in confusing the Curetes with the Acarnanians, were not alone in doing so.] Acarnanians, or Curetes; and the fourth was Mash, from whom came those who are called Maeonians.

5. The descendants of Arphaxad, son of Shem, included Eber, the grandson of Arphaxad, from whom came the Hebrews. JECTAN, the son of Eber, was the ancestor of the people of India. Saleh, the son of Jectan, was the ancestor of the Bactrians, although some suspect that they were exiles of the Scythians.

6. Ishmael, son of Abraham, was the ancestor of the Ishmaelites, who are now called Saracens by a corrupted name, as if from Sarah, and Hagarenes, from Hagar.

7. Nebaioth, son of Ishmael, was the ancestor of the Nabataeans, [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Who live from the Euphrates.” The same author below, book XIV, chapter 13. See Jerome, *Questions on Genesis* XXV.] who live from the Euphrates to the Red Sea.

8. Moab and Ammon were the sons of Lot, from whom came the Moabites and Ammonites.

[Col. 0329B] 401 9. [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Edom, son of Esau.” What is read in Genesis XXXVI, “These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom,” is to be understood of the Idumaeans. Esau himself is Edom, as the passage says; he had no son bearing that name except the Idumaeans, who were always called Edom, and never Idumaeans except in the Greek translation, according to Jerome on Ezekiel XXV. In fact, Chacon stated that in the most ancient Bibles of the Vatican one can still read: Αὗται δὲ γενέσεις Ἐσαὺ πατρὸς τῶν Ἐδουμαίων, “These are the generations of Esau, father of the Idumaeans.” Eusebius likewise says in the *Chronicle*—from which this seems to have been taken—“The first was Esau, who is also Edom, from whom came the nation of the Idumaeans.” Thus the passage may be read without corruption as: “Edom, who is also Esau,” or rather, “Edom, that is, Esau.”] Edom, son of Esau, was the ancestor of the Idumaeans. These are the peoples who descended from the line of Shem and occupied the southern land, from the rising of the sun to Phoenicia.

10. The four sons of Ham, from whom the following peoples arose, were:

Cush, from whom the Ethiopians descended.

Mizraim, from whom the Egyptians are said to have originated.

11. Put, from whom came the Libyans. Hence a river of Mauretania is still called Put, as is the whole region around it, the land of Put.

12. [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Canaan, from whom the Africans.” Jerome, *Genesis* X: “The firstborn of Canaan was Sidon, from whom the city of Sidon in Phoenicia is named. Then came the Arcaean, who founded Arca, a town opposite Tripoli,” etc. No mention of the Africans occurs there. Isidore may nevertheless have had the migration of Dido in mind.] Canaan, from whom came the Africans, the Phoenicians, and the ten nations of the Canaanites.

13. Likewise, among the grandchildren of Ham, there were six sons of Cush, the grandchildren of Ham.

[Col. 0329C] [Note: [Col. 0330D] “The sons of Cush.” From Jerome, in the same place.] The sons of Cush were Saba, Hevila, Sabatha, Rhegma, and Sabathaca.

14. Saba, from whom the Sabaeans were descended and named, concerning whom Virgil says: “The Sabaeans possess a branch of incense.”

15. Hevila, from whom came the Gaetuli, dwelling in the more remote region of Africa, adjoining the desert.

16. Sabatha, from whom came the Sabatheni, who are now called Astabari.

17. Rhegma and Sabathaca, however, gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones.

18. The sons of Rhegma were Saba and Dadan. This Saba is written with a letter in Hebrew; but the earlier Saba [Col. 0330A] is written with [a missing or illegible character], from whom the Sabaeans are named; SABA is now interpreted as Arabia.

19. Dadan, from whom comes a people of Ethiopia in the western region.

402 [Note: [Col. 0330D] “The sons of Mesraim.” The names found in Jerome seem to be missing: “Mesraim fathered Ludim, Aramim, Labaim, Nephthuim, Phetrosim, and Chasloim,” etc.] The sons of Mesraim were Labaim, from whom came the Libyans, who were formerly called Phuthaei.

20. Casloim, from whom came the Philistines, whom the ancients called Ἀλλόφυλοι (“foreigners”), while we now corruptly call them Palestinians.

21. The remaining six peoples are unknown, because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war and their former names passed into complete oblivion.

22. The sons of Chanaam were eleven, from whom came the ten nations of the Canaanites, whose land the Jews possessed after expelling them. Their firstborn was Sidon, from whom came the Sidonians; hence their city in Phoenicia is also called Sidon.

[Col. 0330B] 23. The second was Cheth, from whom came the Chethaeans. The third was Jebus, from whom came the Jebusites, whose city was Jerusalem. The fourth was the Amorite, from whom came the Amorites. The fifth was Gergesaeus, from whom came the Gergesites. The sixth was Hevaeus, from whom came the Hevites; these are the Gibeonites, named from their city Gibeon, who came as suppliants to Jesus.

24. The seventh was Aracaeus, who founded Arcas, a town situated opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. The eighth was Sinaeus, from whom came the Sineans. The ninth was Aradius, from whom came the Aradians, who possessed the island of Aradus, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait.

25. The tenth was Samaraeus, [Note: [Col. 0330D] “From whom Edessa of Syria [came] … Coeles.” Jerome’s words; from him we have supplied the word “Edessa.”] from whom came Edessa, a distinguished city of Syria, which is called Coeles. The eleventh was Amathaeus. These are the nations descended from the line of Ham, occupying the whole southern region from Sidon to the Strait of Cádiz.

26. Seven sons of Japhet are named: Gomer, from whom came the Galatians, that is, the Gauls.

27. [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Magog, from whom some [think them to have come].” These are Jerome’s words; he seems to be referring to Ambrose, who in Book II of *On the Faith* said that Gog meant the Goths.] Magog, from whom some believe that the Scythians and Goths derived their origin.

403 28. Madai, from whom they think the Meaoi came.

Javan, from whom came the Ionians, who are also the Greeks; hence the Ionian Sea.

29. Thubal, from whom came the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Although some …” Jerome, on Genesis. The same author, on Ezekiel 38. The Hebrews suspect that the Italians came from him. In Isaiah 66, Thubal, or Tobel, is interpreted either as Italy or Iberia.] although some also suppose that the Italians came from him.

30. Mosoch, from whom came the Cappadocians; hence a city among them is still called Mazaca.

[Col. 0331A] 31. Thiras, from whom came the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered, being almost “Tiraces.”

32. The sons of Gomer, descendants of Japhet. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Aschanaz, from whom came the Sarmatians.” The words found in Jerome seem to require supplementation: “from whom came the Sarmatians”; and, following Josephus, it should be read: “From Chanaxas came Aschanaz, whom the Greeks call Rhegini.”] Aschanaz, from whom came the Sarmatians, whom the Greeks call Regini.

33. Riphath, from whom came the Paphlagonians.

Thogorma, from whom came the Phrygians.

34. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “The sons of Javan.” Jerome, *Questions on* chapter 10: “From the Ionians, that is, from the Greeks, are descended the Elisaeans, who are called Aeolids.”] The sons of Javan were Elisa, from whom came the Greek Elisaeans, who are called Aeolids; hence the fifth language of Greece is also called Aeolic.

35. Tharsis, from whom came the Cilicians, as Josephus believes; hence their chief city is called Tarsus.

36. Cethim, from whom came the Citians, that is, the Cypriots; from them the city Citium still takes its name.

Dodanim, from whom came the Rhodians.

37. These are the nations descended from Japhet, occupying from Mount Taurus northward the central part of Asia and all of Europe, [Col. 0331D] [Note: “As far as the British Ocean.” Jerome said “as far as Cádiz.”] as far as the British Ocean, leaving their names both to places and to peoples. Many of these names were later changed; the rest remain as they were.

38 [Note: [Col. 0331D] “For the names of many nations … may appear.” Augustine’s words, *City of God* XVI, chapter 11.] For the names of many nations have partly remained, so that even today it is apparent from where they were derived, as the Assyrians from Assur and the Hebrews from Heber; 404 but others have been so altered by the antiquity of time that even the most learned men, searching through the most ancient histories, have scarcely been able to discover the origins of all—or even of more than some—of these nations.

39. For although the Egyptians arose from the son of Ham called Mesraim, no trace of this origin appears in their name, just as no trace appears in the name of the Ethiopians, who are said to belong to that son of Ham called Chus. And if everything is considered, more names of peoples appear to have been changed than preserved; different causes later assigned them different names. Thus the Indians were named from the river Indus, which encloses them on the western side.

40. The Seres took their name from their own city. They are a people situated in the East, among whom wool is woven from trees. Of them is the verse:

“Unknown in face, though not in fleece, are the Seres.”

41. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “The Gangaridae … the Hyrcanians.” From Servius, on *Georgics* III and *Aeneid* VII.] The Gangaridae are a people dwelling between the Assyrians and the Indians, around the river Ganges; hence they are also called Gangaridae.

42. The Hyrcanians were named from the Hyrcanian Forest, where there are very many tigers.

43. The Bactrians were Scythians who, driven from their homes by a faction among their own people, settled beside the eastern river Bactron, from whose name they also took their own. The king of this people was Zoroaster, inventor of the magical art.

44. The Parthians likewise derive their origin from the Scythians. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “For they were exiles of theirs … they obtained [the territory].” Justin’s words, Book XLI.] They were indeed their exiles, as is made clear even by their name: in the Scythian language, Parthians means “exiles.” Like the Bactrians, they were driven from Scythia by internal rebellions; first they secretly occupied the deserted regions near Hyrcania, and afterward by their valor they acquired most of the surrounding territory.

45. [Note: [Col. 0331D] “The Assyrians from Assur.” From Jerome, on Isaiah 19.] The Assyrians were called after Assur, son of Sem. They were a most powerful people, holding all the intervening region from the Euphrates to the borders of India.

405 46. The Medes are thought to have been named after their king. For [Note: [Col. 0331D] “For Jason.” From Justin, Book XLII.] Jason, brother of King Pelias, was driven from Thessaly by the sons of Pelias, together with his wife Medea, [Note: [Col. 0331D] “Whose stepson he was.” From the same source.] whose stepson was Medus, king of the Athenians. After Jason’s death, Medus subdued the eastern region, [Note: [Col. 0332D] “And there [he founded] Media.” Justin, *Medea*, Book XLII; his wording is: “Afterward Medus, Jason’s rival in valor, founded the city of Media in honor of his mother Medea.”] and there founded the city of Media, naming the people of the Medes after himself. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “But we find in Genesis.” Not indeed in Genesis itself, but in Jerome, on Genesis; thus, with Chacon, we believe that “Jerome” should be read instead of “we find.”] But Jerome states in his commentary on Genesis that Madai was the founder of the Median people, from whom they were also named, as was said above.

47. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “But the Persians.” From Jerome, on Isaiah 21.] The Persians were named after King Perseus, who crossed from Greece into Asia and there subdued barbarian peoples in a long and arduous war; at last, as victor, he gave his name to the subjected people. Before Cyrus, however, the Persians were obscure and were counted as having no standing among the nations. The Medes had always been most powerful.

48. Chasdim, who are now called Chaldaeans, were named after Chased, son of Nachor, Abraham’s brother.

[Col. 0332C] 49. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “The Sabaeans are so called.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I, concerning the words “a hundred Sabaean incense-offerings.” Above, however, he derived the Sabaeans from Saba, son of Chus.] The Sabaeans are called ἀπὸ τοῦ σέβεσθαι, that is, “from worshiping,” because we venerate the divinity through their incense. They are also the Arabs who live in the mountains of Arabia called Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, where incense is gathered.

50. The Syrians are said to have been named from the Assurim, who was Abraham’s grandson through Keturah; what the ancients called Assyrians, we now call Syrians, naming the whole from a part.

51. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “The Hebrews were named from Heber.” Thus Jerome, on Genesis 10. Ambrose vehemently insists, in chapter 3 of his Epistle to the Philippians, that they were derived from Abraham.] The Hebrews were named from Heber, who was a great-grandson of Sem.

406 52. The Israelites, however, were named from Israel, son of Isaac. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “For the patriarch of the Hebrews.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] Israel is acknowledged to have been the patriarch of the Hebrews, from whom the twelve tribes of the Jews took the name Israel. [Note: [Col. 0332D] “But the division gave the Jews [their name].” Jerome, on Jonah 1, and elsewhere.] The division of the ten tribes, however, gave the Jews their name. For previously they were called Hebrews or Israelites.

53. When God’s people were divided into two kingdoms, the two tribes that had kings from the line of Judah took the name “Jews.” The remaining part, the ten tribes that established a king for themselves in Samaria, retained the ancient name Israel because of the greatness of the people.

54. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “The people of the Samaritans … Also Phoenix, son of Cadmus.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] The people of the Samaritans originated from the Assyrians who, after being transferred, settled in Samaria. In Latin their name means “watchers,” because, after Israel had been taken captive, they were stationed in the land of that region to guard it.

55. Phoenix, brother of Cadmus, departed from Thebes in Egypt for Syria and reigned at Sidon. He named those people Phoenicians after himself and called that province Phoenicia.

56. The Sidonians, however, are said to have derived their name from the city called Sidon.

57. The Saracens are so called either because they proclaim themselves descended from Sarah, or—as the pagans claim—because they are of Syrian origin, as though “Syrian-born.” They [Note: [Col. 0333D] “They inhabit a very extensive desert.” Jerome, on Isaiah 21.] inhabit a very extensive desert. They are also the Ishmaelites, as the Book of Genesis teaches, since they are descended from Ishmael. They are also the Qedarites, from Ishmael’s son Qedar. They are also the Hagarenes, from Hagar; as we have said, they are called Saracens by a perverse name because they boast that they were born from Sarah.

58. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “The Philistines are these same people.” From Jerome, on Ezekiel 25; there he says “from their people,” whereas here it says “from their city.”] The Philistines are the Palestinians, because the Hebrew language does not have the letter *p*, but uses the Greek φ in its place. Thus the Philistines are called Palestinians, plainly from their city. They are also called Allophyli, that is, “foreigners,” because they were always enemies of Israel and were separated far from their lineage and fellowship.

407 59. The Canaanites were named from Chanaam, son of Ham; the Jews possessed their land. Emor, father of Shechem, was descended from him, and from Emor the Amorites were named.

60. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “The Egyptians from Aegyptus.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] The Egyptians were named after a certain king of their own called Aegyptus. Previously they were called Aerii. In the Hebrew language, however, “Egyptians” is interpreted as “afflicting,” because they afflicted God’s people before they were freed by divine aid.

61. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Armenius from Thessaly.” Justin, Book XLII.] Armenius was one of Jason’s commanders who departed for Colchis from Thessaly. After gathering together the multitude that had wandered about after the loss of King Jason, he founded Armenia and gave the people a name from his own.

[Col. 0333D] 62. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “The Persian frontier.” Pliny and Solinus, chapter 52.] There is a Persian frontier that separates the Scythians from them; it is called Scythian, and from this frontier some say that the Scythians were named. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “A most ancient people.” From Justin, Book II, at the beginning.] They have always been regarded as a most ancient people. They founded the kingdoms of the Parthians and Bactrians, while their women founded the kingdoms of the Amazons.

63. The Massagetae are of Scythian origin. They are called Massagetae, as if “mighty Getae,” that is, “strong Getae.” [Note: [Col. 0333D] “For Livy says this.” Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, concerning the verse “a young man outstanding in appearance”: “For which he was rewarded with heavy bronze,” that is, with ingots. Thus Livy also calls silver “heavy,” that is, ingots.] For Livy uses “heavy silver” to mean ingots. These are the people who inhabit the northern mountain ranges between the Scythians and the Albanians.

64. The Amazons were so called either because they lived together without men, as though ἅμα ζῶσαι, “living together,” or because their right breasts were burned away so that the shooting of arrows would not be impeded, as though ἄνευ μαζοῦ, “without a breast.” For they exposed the breast that they had burned. [Note: [Col. 0333D] “Titianus calls them one-breasted … they have been destroyed.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I, concerning “he leads the ranks of Amazons,” and *Aeneid* XI, concerning “in the midst of them.”] Titianus calls them “one-breasted women.” For this is what Amazon means, as though ἀνευ μαζοῦ, that is, “without a breast.” It is now established that they no longer exist, since some were destroyed to the last man by Hercules, some by Achilles, and some by Alexander.

65. [Note: [Col. 0334D] “In the Asiatic region.” Chacon considered the words “from constant snows,” and also “that is, painted,” to be foreign to the passage; indeed they are not found in Solinus, from whom the rest is taken.] In the Asiatic part of Scythia there are peoples who believe themselves descended from Jason. They are born with white hair because of the continual snows, and the color of their hair gave the people its name; hence they are called Albanians. Their pupils are gray, that is, mottled, so that they see better at night than by day. The Albanians, moreover, were neighbors of the Amazons.

408 66. The Ugnos, formerly called Huns, were eventually called Avars after their king, it is said. They had previously lived at the edge of Lake Maeotis, between the icy Tanais and the savage peoples of the Massagetae. [Note: [Col. 0334D] “Then, on swift horses.” Jerome’s words, Letter 30.] Then, on swift horses, they burst through the crags of the Caucasus, where Alexander’s barriers hold back savage peoples; they held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians.

67. The Trojan people were formerly Dardanian, named from Dardanus. For Dardanus and Jasius were brothers who set out from Greece: Jasius reached Thrace, [Note: [Col. 0334D] “Dardanus and Jasius.” Servius, on *Aeneid* V, concerning “Dardanus of Ida”; and Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] while Dardanus reached Phrygia and was the first to reign there. After him came his son Ericthonius, and then his grandson Tros, from whom the Trojans were named.

68. The GALATIANS are known to have been Gauls. Summoned by the king of Bithynia to provide assistance, they divided the kingdom with him after achieving victory; [Note: [Col. 0334D] “After victory had been won.” Another reading: *peracta* (“after it had been completed”). From Justin, Book XXV, and Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*; repeated in Book XIV, chapter 3.] afterward they mingled with the Greeks and were first called Gallograeci. Now, from the ancient name of the Gauls, they are called Galatians.

69. The Greeks were first called Thessalians, from Thessalus, and afterward Greeks, from King Graecus. [Note: [Col. 0334D] “For properly speaking, the Greeks are Thessalians.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* II, concerning “the Danaans will have rescued”; and Pliny, Book VII, chapter 4. “Hellas is the same as Thessaly, and Dryopis, always named after its kings. There King Graecus was born, from whom came Greece; there Hellen, from whom came the Hellenes; there perhaps Thessalus, from whom came Thessaly, lest we detract from Isidore’s reliability.”] For properly speaking, the Greeks are Thessalians.

[Col. 0335A] 70. The Lapiths are said to have been a people of Thessaly, formerly dwelling around the river Peneus, and named from Lapitha, daughter of Apollo.

71. The Sicyonians are Greeks, named after King Sicyon. They were first called Aegialaeans, after King Aegialeus, [Note: [Col. 0335D] “After King Aegialeus.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] who first ruled the Sicyonians; from him Aegialaea was also named, which is now called the Peloponnese after its king Pelops. They are also called Arcadians, from King Arcades, son of Jupiter and Calisto.

409 72. The Danaans were named after King Danaus. They were also called Argives, after their founder Argus. After Apis, king of the Greeks, died, his son Argus succeeded him in the kingdom; from him they were called Argives. After his death they also began to regard him as a god, honoring him with a temple and sacrifice.
