[Col. 0335B] 73. The Achaeans, also called Achivi, were named after Achaeus, son of Jupiter.

74. The Pelasgi were so called because they were seen to have arrived in Italy in spring with their sails spread, like birds. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “They appeared like birds. Thus Pelasgi, as though *pelagroi*, that is, ‘storks.’”] [Note: [Col. 0335D] “For Varro records that they were the first.” Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “They are said to have been the first to possess Italy.”] Varro records that they were the first to land in Italy. The Greeks, however, say that the Pelasgi were named after Pelasgus, son of Jupiter and Larissa.

75. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “The Myrmidons were …” From Servius, on *Aeneid* II, concerning “of the Myrmidons or Dolopians.”] The Myrmidons were the companions of Achilles; the Dolopians were those of Pyrrhus. The Myrmidons were so called because of their cunning, as though μύρμηκες, “ants.” Eratosthenes, however, says that the Myrmidons were named after their leader Myrmidon, son of Jupiter and Eurymedusa.

76. Cranaus succeeded Cecrops, king of the Athenians. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “Cranaus succeeded him.” From Eusebius, *Chronicle*.] Cranaus’s daughter Atthis gave her name both to the region and to the people. From her they were called Attici, who are the Athenians.

[Col. 0335C] 77. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “Ion, a brave man.” From the same source.] Ion, a brave man, called those same Athenians Ionians after his own name.

78. The Macedonians were formerly called Emathians, after the name of King Emathion; afterward they were called Macedonians, after King Macedon, the maternal grandson of Deucalion.

79. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “The Epirotes from Pyrrhus.” Justin, Books XVII and XVIII.] The Epirotes, formerly called Pyrrhidae after Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, later ventured to cross into Italy under King Pyrrhus.

80. Dorus was the son of Neptune and [Note: [Col. 0335D] “And son of Ellepis.” Servius, on *Aeneid* II, concerning “the Dorian camp”: “Dorus was indeed the son of Neptune, from whom the Dorians derived their origin”; he makes no mention of Ellipes or Ellopis.] Ellepis; from him the Dorians derive both their origin and their name. They are a part of the Greek people, from whom the third language of the Greeks, called Doric, also takes its name.

410 81. The Lacedaemonians were named after Lacedaemon, son of Semele. [Note: [Col. 0335D] “These, persevering for a long time in the war.” Strabo reports this from Ephorus, Book VI; Lactantius also mentions it, Book I, chapter 20: “Thus the young men, having previously been sent away, lay with the maidens, from whom the Parthenii were born.” Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, has Parthenitae; Ephorus, Partheniae; Servius, on *Aeneid* III and *Georgics* IV, calls them Partheniatae. Thus “Sparthini” in most manuscripts is erroneous. The Gothic and Ovetus manuscripts, which read “Sparthenii,” are closer to the correct form.] These, persevering for a long time in the war against the Messenians and fearing that the prolonged conflict would deprive them of the hope of offspring, ordered their maidens to sleep with the young men who had been left at home. Thus, from the promiscuous intercourse of maidens and husbands, young men were born of uncertain parentage, and, because of the recognized chastity of their mothers, were called Parthenii. For they are the same people as the Spartans, who are also the Lacedaemonians. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “But the Spartans.” Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*: “Those things that are related about Sparta, which Palephatus writes, say that they, being from neighboring regions, stood against Cadmus and, because they suddenly gathered as if drawn from the earth, converging from every side, were called Sparthoi.” See also Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 3, and Isidore below, concerning Phalantus, leader of the Parthenii.] They were called Spartans because they suddenly gathered against Cadmus, as if drawn from the earth, and fought from every side.

82. The Thracians are said to have originated from and been named after the son of Japhet called Thiras, as was said above, although the pagans think that they received this name from their character, because they are savage (*traces*). For they were the fiercest of all peoples. Hence many fabulous stories are told about them: that they sacrificed captives to their gods and were accustomed to drink human blood from skulls. Of them Virgil says:

“Alas, flee the cruel lands, flee the greedy shore,”

that is, “of the cruel and greedy.”

83. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “The people of the Istri … who were sent.” By King Arethas. Justin, Book XXXII.] The people of the Istri derive their origin from the Colchians, who were sent to pursue the Argonauts. When they entered the river Ister from the Pontus, they were named from the river, through which they had withdrawn from the sea.

411 84. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “The Romans … Quirites … the Tuscans.” From Servius, in various places.] The Romans were named after Romulus, who founded the city of Rome and gave his name to the people and the state. Earlier they were called Saturnii, after Saturn, and Latini, after Latinus. Latinus was king of Italy, who named the Latins after himself; afterward they were called Romans. They were also called Quirites, because Romulus was called Quirinus, since he always used a spear, which in the language of the Sabines is called *quiris*.

85. Italus, Sabinus, and Sicanus were also brothers, and their names were imposed upon peoples and regions. From Italus came the Italians, from Sabinus the Sabines, and from Sicanus the Sicani, who are also called Siculi; they are likewise the Sicilians.

86. The Tuscans are a people of Italy, named from the frequency of their sacrifices and incense, that is, ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν, “from sacrificing.”

87. [Note: [Col. 0336D] “The Umbri … at the time of the watery disaster.” Solinus, chapter 8; Pliny, Book III, chapter 14.] The Umbri are a people of Italy, but descendants of the ancient Gauls who inhabit the Apennine mountain. Histories relate that they survived a time of watery disaster and rains; for this reason they were called ὀμβρίους in Greek.

88. The Marsi, a people of Italy, were named [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Named after the companion of Liber, Marsyas.” Silius, Book VIII:

“But the people gave the name, the more fearful stranger,

when Marsyas Crenos fled across the Phrygian seas.”

Pliny, however, Book VII, chapter 2, derives the name from Marsa, daughter of Circe.] after Marsyas, companion of Liber, who showed them the use of vines; for this reason they made a statue of him, which the Romans later took away after conquering the Marsi. [Col. 0337A] [Note: [Col. 0337D] “The Greeks call the Marsi …” Servius, on *Aeneid* VII, concerning “the hands of the Oscans,” writes: “He means the Capuans, who were formerly called Osci because many serpents abounded there.” But why Isidore later says that these lived with the Umbri, when they are very far from the Capuans, must be investigated.] The Greeks call the Marsi Osci, as though ὀφιούχους, “snake-handlers,” because they possess many snakes, and because ὄφις means “snake.” They are unharmed by the powers of spells; they inhabit the region of the Apennine mountain together with the Umbri.

412 89. The Goths are thought to have been named after Magog, son of Japhet, because of the similarity of the final syllable. The ancients called them Getae rather than Goths. They were a brave and most powerful people, formidable for the massive stature of their bodies and terrifying in their manner of warfare. Lucan speaks of them:

“From here may the Dacian press on; from there may the Getae meet the Iberians.”

90. [Note: [Col. 0337D] “The Daci, however, are Goths.” These are Justin’s words, Book XXXIII. The verse is from Saint Paulinus.] The Daci were descendants of the Getae, and they are thought to have been called Daci, as though *Dagi*, because they were born from the stock of the Goths. Of them the poet says: “You will go far toward the North, as far as the Daci.”

91. The Bessi were barbarians, believed to have been so called because of their multitude of cattle. Of them someone says: [Note: [Col. 0337D] “Of whom someone [writes].” The same Paulinus.]

“He who inhabits the middle of the earth, or that dweller of the rich bank, crowned with many cattle.”

92. The Gipedes used infantry battle more than cavalry battle, and for this reason they were so called.

93. The Sarmatians rode armed across open plains until Lentulus barred them from the Danube; from their devotion to arms they are therefore thought to have received the name Sarmatians.

94. The river Lanus is said to lie beyond the Danube; from it the Alans were named, [Note: [Col. 0337D] “As also the peoples living here.” The same lemma. Servius, on *Georgics* IV, concerning “near the streams of the Mella.”] just as the peoples dwelling beside the river Lemannus are called Alemanni. Of them Lucan says:

“They abandoned the tents fixed beside the hollow Lemannus.”

95. The Longobards are commonly said to have been named from their long beards, which were never shaved.

96. The river Vindilicus bursts forth from the farthest parts of Gaul. The Vandals are said to have lived beside this river and to have derived their name from it.

413 97. The peoples of Germany were so called because they have enormous bodies and immense nations, hardened by the fiercest cold. They derived these customs from the very harshness of the climate: they are fierce in spirit, always untamed, and live by plunder and hunting. Most of their peoples differ in arms, vary in dress, speak different languages, and have uncertain origins for their names; [Note: [Col. 0337D] “Such as the Tolosates.” There is remarkable variation in the books, since individual names are written in many forms: Tolerates, Tolorates, Dolerates, Olarates, Coloniates. Likewise Amsivari, Samsi, Vari, Amisi, Vari Anismani. Likewise Quadi, Quadivi. Likewise Tungrii, Turingii, Ungari, Mungrii. Likewise Bruteri, Bruteni, Brutei, Bructeri. Likewise Camasi, Clamassi, [Col. 0338D] Chasuasi, Chamavi. Likewise Blangiani, Blanciani. Likewise Tubantes, Abantes. We prefer Tolosates, with Rhenanus, Book I of *Germanic Matters*. Likewise, from Tacitus, Angrivari, Quadi, Tungrii, Marcomani, Bructeri, Chamavi, Wangiones, Tubantes. Although *Clamosi* is read for *Chamavi* in Nazarius’s panegyric to Constantine Augustus, doubtless incorrectly, as I believe. Antonius Augustus approved the same reading, except that he substituted Tencteri for Tolosates, departing still farther from the manuscript reading, on the authority of Tacitus.] such as the Tolosates, Angrivari, Quadi, Tungrii, [Col. 0338A] Marcomani, Bructeri, Chamavi, Wangiones, and Tubantes. Their barbaric savagery itself seems to signify a certain horror even in their names.

98. The Suebi were a branch of the Germans in the far North. Of them Lucan says:

“He sends forth the blond Suebi from the utmost North.”

Many have related that they consisted of a hundred districts and peoples. They are thought to have been called Suebi from Mount Suevo, which begins Germany at its eastern extremity and whose regions they inhabited.

99. The Burgundians, after the Romans had subdued inner Germany, were once stationed by Emperor Tiberius along the boundaries of the military camps. They grew into a great people and thus took their name from those places, because the numerous settlements established along the frontiers are commonly called *burgi*. Later, having rebelled against the Romans, they occupied the bank of the Rhine with more than eighty thousand armed men and retained the name of the people.

414 100. The Saxon people were situated on the shores of the Ocean and amid impassable marshes; they were skilled in valor and agility. Hence they were so called because they are a hard and exceedingly strong race of men, surpassing the others in piracy.

101. The Franks are thought to have been named after a certain leader of their own. Others believe that they were named from the savagery of their customs. Their ways are indeed uncultivated and their spirits naturally fierce.

102. Some suspect that the Britons were named in Latin because they are brutish, a people placed between the Ocean and the intervening sea, as though outside the world. Of them Virgil says: “The Britons, separated from the whole world.”

103. The Scots have a name in their own language derived from their painted bodies, because they mark themselves with iron needles and ink in the form of designs.

104. [Note: [Col. 0338D] “The Gauls from their whiteness.” Jerome, in the preface to Book II of his Epistle to the Galatians, from Lactantius; from whose wording “the Sibyl” entered some of our manuscripts in place of “Virgil.”] The Gauls were named from the whiteness of their bodies, for γάλα means “milk” in Greek. Hence Virgil also describes them in this way when he says of them: “Then their milk-white necks are encircled with gold.”

105. For according to the diversity of the climate there arise differences in the faces, colors, and bodily sizes of human beings, as well as differences in their spirits. 415 Thus we observe that the Romans are grave, the Greeks light-minded, and the Africans changeable; [Note: [Col. 0338D] “The Gauls are naturally fierce and keener.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, concerning “At first, the sky and lands”—although there the reading is “not keener but duller in intellect.” Also Julius Firmicus, Book I, chapter 1, and Hilary, as Jerome reports in the cited passage, call the Gauls foolish.] the Gauls are naturally fierce and keener in intellect, as the nature of the climates produces.

106. The Gauls called the Senones were formerly called Xenones, because they had received Liber as a guest; afterward the *x* was changed into the letter *s*.

[Col. 0339A] 107. [Note: [Col. 0339D] “Vacca was a town near the Pyrenees.” Augustine thought that *Jacca* should be read. Strabo too, Book III, discussing the peoples between the Pyrenees and the Idubeda Mountains, praises Jaccetania as most distinguished; there is now the city of Jacca. Accordingly, Augustine deleted the words that follow as foreign, for they are absent from two manuscripts. The verse is from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book IV, “and the Vaccaei wandering far and wide,” a corrupt reading, though it is found in the same form in Jerome’s letter to Dardanus.] Vacca was a town near the Pyrenees, from which the Vaccaei were named. Of them the poet is thought to have said: “And the Vaccaei wandering far and wide.” They inhabit the extensive mountain wilderness of the Pyrenean heights. They are also the Vascones, as though *Vaccones*, with *c* changed into *s*.

108. [Note: [Col. 0339D] “Whom Gnaeus Pompey … received their name.” From Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*; it is still called Comenge.] After conquering Spain and hastening to return for his triumph, Gnaeus Pompey brought them down from the Pyrenean heights and gathered them into one town. Hence the city received the name of Convenae.

109. The Spaniards were first called Iberians, from the river Iberus, and afterward [Note: [Col. 0339D] “From Hispalo, Spaniards.” “Spaniards from Hispanus,” Justin, Book XLIV, and the *Chronicle of Naples.*] were called HISPANI from Hispalo.

110. [Note: [Col. 0339D] “The Gallaeci.” From the same Justin; but the words “hence they are naturally skilled” are not found in him.] The Gallaeci were named from their whiteness, as were the Gauls. For they are fairer than the other peoples of Spain. 416 They claim a Greek origin for themselves. Hence they are also naturally clever.

[Col. 0339B] 111. It is said that after the end of the Trojan War, Teucer, hated by his father Telamon because of the death of his brother Ajax, went to Cyprus when he was not received back into the kingdom, and there founded a city named Salamis after his ancient homeland. [Note: [Col. 0339D] “From there he departed for Gallaecia.” Much has been omitted, not by Isidore, as Chacon judged, but by a copyist; seek it in Justin.] From there he departed for Gallaecia, settled there, and gave the people their name from the place.

112. The Austures, a people of Spain, were so called because they live enclosed by mountains and dense forests around the river Astura.

113. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “The Cantabri … from the name of the city.” Our annals often mention this city, and its ruins are still visible.] The Cantabri, a people of Spain, were named from the name of the city and from the river Iberus beside which they dwell. Their spirit is obstinate, and they are always more ready for banditry and warfare or to endure blows.

114. The Celtiberians were descended from the Celtic Gauls, from whose name the region Celtiberia was called. They were named Celtiberians from a combination of the two names: from the Spanish river Iberus, where they settled, and from the Gauls, who were called Celts.

115. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “The Africans were named.” All of this is from Jerome, *Questions on* Genesis 25.] The Africans were named after one of Abraham’s descendants, who was called Afer. He is said to have led an army against Libya, settled there after defeating the enemy, and named his descendants Atavi, the Africans, and Africa after himself.

116. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “The Poeni … from the Phoenicians.” Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “Poeni is a transposition of letters, as though Phoeni.”] The Poeni were the Carthaginians, named after the Phoenicians who departed with Dido.

117. The Tyrians, however, were named after the Phoenician city of Tyre, from which they set out and came to the coast of Africa.

118. THE GAETULI are said to have been Getae who, embarking on ships in a great multitude from their own regions, occupied the territory of the Syrtes [Col. 0339D] in Libya. Because they had come from the Getae, they were called Gaetuli by a derivative name. Hence there is also a belief among the Goths that, because of their ancient kinship, they call the Moors their relatives by blood.

119. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “Africa … was held by the Libyans.” From Sallust, *Jugurtha*.] In the beginning, Libya was held by the Libyans; afterward by the Africans, then by the Gaetuli, and finally by the Moors and Numidians.

120. The Moors and Numidians, as the Africans believe, derived both their origin and their name in the following way. After Hercules died in Spain, his army, composed of various peoples, sought settlements for themselves in different places after losing its leader. From among them, the Medes, Persians, and Armenians were transported by ship to Africa and occupied the regions nearest the sea.

121. But when the Persians could not find timber in the fields for building dwellings, and their unfamiliar language prevented communication, they wandered through open country and various deserts. From their wandering for pasture they called themselves Numidians in their own language, that is, “wanderers and strayers without a town.”

122. The Medes, however, mingled with the Libyans who inhabited the region nearest Spain. The Libyans gradually corrupted their name, calling the Medes “Moors” in their barbarian language, although the Greeks call them Moors because of their color. For the Greeks call black μαυρόν, “dark”; scorched by the heat of summer, they take on the appearance of a dark color.

123. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “Massylia.” See Servius, in the same place.] Massylia is a city of Africa, not far from Atlas and the Gardens of the Hesperides. From this city the Massylii were named, whom we corruptly call Massuli. Of them Virgil says:

“Here a priestess of the Massylian people was shown to me.”

[Col. 0340C] 418

**124.** The Gaulali are peoples ranging from the south as far as the Western Ocean. [Note: [Col. 0340D] Their name is *Gauloe*. From Solinus. But why “nearest to Ethiopia”? Perhaps because Solinus immediately proceeds to discuss Ethiopia.] They took their name from the island of Gauloe, which lies near Ethiopia, where no serpent is born or lives.

**125.** The Garamantes are peoples inhabiting Africa near Cyrene. They were named after King Garamantes, the son of Apollo, who founded there the town of Garama, after his own name. They are neighbors of the Ethiopian peoples, of whom Virgil says: “the outermost Garamantes.” [Note: [Col. 0340D] “Outermost,” because savage. From Servius, on Eclogue 8, approximately “savage.”] They are called “outermost” because they are savage and removed from human society.

**126.** The Hesperians are those who dwell around Spain. For Spain is HESPERIA.

**127.** The Ethiopians were named after the son of Ham, who was called Cush; from him they derive their origin. [Note: [Col. 0340D] *Cush* in the Hebrew language. From Jerome, in *On Hebrew Names*.] For *Cush* is interpreted in Hebrew as “Ethiopian.”

[Col. 0340D] **128.** These peoples, once rising from the river Indus, settled near Egypt, between the Nile and the Ocean, in the south, beneath the very proximity of the sun. [Note: [Col. 0340D] “These once,” etc. Jerome’s words, in *On Hebrew Places*.] There are three peoples among them: the Hesperians, the Garamantes, and the Indians. The Hesperians belong to the West, the Garamantes to Tripoli, and the Indians to the East.

**129.** [Note: [Col. 0341C–D] The people of the Troglodytes. Greek: Ἀπὸ τῆς τρώγλης, that is, “from a cave,” because they live in caves. Solinus, chapter 34. But Isidore’s derivation better suits *Trogodites*, that is, “devourers of the road.” Pliny likewise says in Book VI, chapter 29: “Juba reports that the peoples of the Troglodytes are called *Therothoae* from hunting, because of their marvelous speed.” Nevertheless, I would not therefore suppose that Isidore called them *Trogodites*, especially since *Troglodytes* is read in all the manuscripts; rather, he played somewhat freely upon the word, as he is accustomed to do.] The Troglodytes are a people of the Ethiopians. They were so named because they possess such speed that they overtake wild animals by the running of their feet.

**130.** [Note: [Col. 0341D] *Pamphagi*. Solinus’s words, chapter 33.] The Pamphagi are also in Ethiopia. For them, anything that can be chewed is food, as is everything that grows spontaneously; hence they were so named.

**131.** [Note: [Col. 0341D] *Ichthyophagi*. From the same work, chapter 57.] The Ichthyophagi are so called because they are effective at hunting in the sea and are nourished solely by fish. 419 They occupy the mountainous regions beyond the Indians. After Alexander the Great had subdued them, he forbade them to eat fish.

**132.** [Note: [Col. 0341D] *Anthropophagi*. From the same work, chapter 53.] The Anthropophagi are an exceedingly savage people situated below the region of the Seres. Because they eat human flesh, they are therefore called Anthropophagi, “man-eaters.” Thus, among these peoples and among all the others, names have been altered over the centuries—after kings, places, customs, or any number of other causes—so that the original origin of their names is no longer apparent because of the antiquity of the ages.

**133.** [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Antipodes. From Augustine, *City of God* XVI, chapter 9, who followed Lactantius and also incorporated certain words from Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, at “Nights and days …” Our own age, penetrating even to the Antipodes themselves, has refuted all these claims. But Servius is speaking not of the Antipodes but of the underworld and the center of the earth.] Now, as for those who are called the Antipodes, because they are thought to have footprints opposite to ours—as though placed beneath the earth, they trample the ground with feet opposed to ours—this must not be believed in any way, since neither the solidity of the earth nor its center permits it. Nor is it supported by any knowledge of history; rather, poets have conjectured it as though reasoning it out.

**134.** [Note: [Col. 0341D] The Titans. From Lactantius, Book V, chapter 6.] They say that there were in Greece certain Titans, a powerful people distinguished by their strength, [Note: [Col. 0341D] “Whom the fables say.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI: “Here is the ancient race of Troy.”] whom the fables say were created by the earth, angered against the gods, for the purpose of avenging her.

**135.** Hence they were also called Titans, ἀπὸ τῆς τίσεως, that is, “from vengeance,” because they supposedly arose armed against the gods in order to avenge their mother, the earth. The fables invent that they were defeated and destroyed by Jupiter in war, and that they perished because thunderbolts were hurled from heaven against them.

## CHAPTER III. On the names of kingdoms and military terms

**1.** *Kingdom* is named from *kings*: for just as kings are called from ruling, so *kingdom* is named from kings.

[Col. 0342A] **2.** All nations have possessed kingdoms at their respective times—the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Egyptians, and Greeks—whose succession the lot of the ages has rolled onward, so that one was displaced by another. Among all the kingdoms of the earth, however, two are handed down as more glorious than the rest: first that of the Assyrians, 420 and afterward that of the Romans, arranged and distinguished from one another according to their times and places.

**3.** For just as the former came first and the latter afterward, so the former arose in the East and the latter in the West; [Note: [Col. 0342C–D] “Finally, at the end of that one, the beginning of this one occurred.” For at the time when Sardanapalus, the last king of the Assyrians, was defeated by Arbaces the Mede and committed himself to the flames, Romulus and Remus were born, as can be gathered from Eusebius.] ultimately, at the end of the former, the beginning of the latter immediately occurred. The remaining kingdoms and kings are regarded as appendages of these.

**4.** [Note: [Col. 0342D] Kings, from ruling. From Augustine, on Psalm 44.] Kings are called from ruling, [Note: [Col. 0342D] “For just as a priest is named from sanctifying.” From the same source, as also above, Book VII, chapter 12.] just as a priest is named from sanctifying and a king from ruling. But he does not rule who does not correct. Therefore the name *king* is rightly retained by doing what is right and lost by sinning. Hence among the ancients there was this proverb: [Note: [Col. 0342D] “You will be king if you act rightly.” Horace.] “You will be king if you act rightly; if you do not, you will not be.”

**5.** The chief royal virtues are two: justice and piety. Piety, however, is more highly praised in kings, for justice is severe in itself.

**6.** Consuls were named from *consulting*, just as kings from ruling and laws from reading; [Note: [Col. 0342D] “For when the Romans could not endure the arrogant domination of kings.” From Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 12. He took this from Sallust, *Catiline*, where Chacon said that he had also read *superbam dominationem*—“arrogant domination”—in an ancient manuscript, not, as is commonly printed, *in superbiam dominationemque*.] for when the Romans could not endure the arrogant domination of kings, they established annual authority and two consuls for themselves. Royal arrogance did not consist in the goodwill of one who gives counsel but in the pride of one who dominates. Thus they were called consuls either from consulting for the citizens or from governing all things by deliberation.

**7.** Nevertheless, they arranged for these men to be changed every year, so that no one might remain insolent for long and a more moderate person might quickly take his place. They were two and equal because [Col. 0342C] one administered civil affairs and the other military affairs. [Note: [Col. 0342D] “They ruled for 464 years.” Jerome, in the preface to Haggai, and Eusebius in his *Chronicle* count the same number. Our books mistakenly read 467, probably through the easy slip of copyists.] They ruled for 464 years.

421 **8.** Proconsuls were subject to the consuls and were called proconsuls because they performed the office of a consul, [Note: [Col. 0342D] “Just as a procurator is the agent of a curator.” See the following chapter.] just as a procurator is the agent, that is, the administrator, of a curator.

**9.** Ex-consuls were so called because they had already gone out from, or withdrawn from, the consulship after completing the year of their term.

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0342D–0343C] “Dictators in the ninth year.” Eusebius—or rather Jerome—in the *Chronicle* says: “In the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings, a new dignity was created,” namely, the dictatorship. In this he seems to have followed Livy. Cassiodorus says it was in the eighth year after the expulsion of the kings; the disagreement requires consultation of the *Fasti*. Antoninus Augustinus gives the twelfth year. All our books, with great agreement, retain the fifth year; the error may perhaps have arisen from the abbreviation IIX or XII.] The Romans created dictators for themselves in the ninth year after the kings had been expelled, when the son-in-law of Tarquinius had assembled a huge army against Rome in order to avenge the wrong done to his father-in-law.

[Col. 0343A] **11.** [Note: [Col. 0343C] “These held authority for a five-year period.” This seems to belong to the censors, about whom the next chapter speaks, for the dictatorship lasted six months.] They exercised authority for a period of five years; for they were greater in honor than the consuls, because they held annual powers. [Note: [Col. 0343C–D] “And they were called dictators.” Varro, Book V: “Hence in military maniples commanders were called *dicti*. Hence *dictata* in school. Hence the dictator was the master of the people.” Cicero, *On the Laws* III: “But whenever a more serious war or civil discord demands it, let there be a dictatorship, not exceeding six months if the Senate so decrees; and let him possess the same authority as the two consuls. He who is appointed by the left side of the augur shall be called master of the people.” He was called a dictator because he was appointed by a consul.] They were also called dictators, as though they were leaders and instructors; hence they were called masters of the people. Hence the term *dicta* is also used.

**12.** [Note: [Col. 0343D] “Of the Caesars.” That is, of the emperors. Before Julius Caesar the dictator, *Caesar* was a family name of the Julians. Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*: “Gaius Julius Caesar was the first among the Romans to obtain sole power; from him Roman rulers were called Caesars.”] The name *Caesar* began with Julius, who, after civil war had broken out, was the first of the Romans to obtain sole sovereignty. Caesar was so called, [Note: [Col. 0343D] “Because he was brought forth from the cut-open womb of his dead mother.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, at the verse “Caesar shall be born …” How true this is—since Caesar’s mother Aurelia lived for a long time while Caesar himself was alive—Servius himself may judge.] because he was brought forth and extracted from the womb of his dead mother after it had been cut open; or because he was born with a full head of hair. From this the succeeding emperors were also called Caesars 422 (because they were long-haired). [Note: [Col. 0343D–0344C] “Those who were extracted from a cut womb.” Pliny, Book VII: “Those born after the mother has been cut open are considered more auspicious, as was the elder Scipio Africanus, and the first of the Caesars, who was so called from the cutting open of his mother’s womb; for this reason they were called *Caesones*. See Festus. We regard the words “because they were long-haired” as foreign to the passage, along with Chacon.] For those who were extracted from a cut womb were called *Caesones* and *Caesars*.

**13.** Julius was so called because he derived his origin from Iulus, the son of Aeneas, as Virgil confirms:

> Julius, a name descended from great Iulus.

[Col. 0343B]

**14.** Among the Romans, the name *emperor* originally belonged only to those in whose hands supreme command of military affairs rested. Thus they were called *imperatores* from commanding the army. But when commanders had long borne imperial titles, the Senate decreed that this name should belong exclusively to Augustus Caesar, because he was distinguished from the other kings of the nations. The succeeding Caesars likewise used the title thereafter.

**15.** [Note: [Col. 0344C] “It commonly happens.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on the verse concerning Murranus and his ancestors.] It commonly happens that the name of the first king is also possessed by his successors. Thus among the Albans, from the name of Silvius, all the kings of the Albans were called Silvii; likewise among the Persians, Arsacids; among the Egyptians, Ptolemies; and among the Athenians, Cecropids.

**16.** [Note: [Col. 0344C] “Augustus … because they increased.” Suetonius derives the name from increase, or from the movement or taste of birds. Ovidius indicated both in *Fasti* III:

> From this man’s augury the word derives its origin;
>
> And whatever Jupiter increases by his own power.

] *Augustus* became a name of imperial power among the Romans because in former times they increased the state by enlarging it. The Senate first bestowed this name upon Octavian Caesar, so that, because he had enlarged the territories, he might be consecrated by the name and title itself.

**17.** Although Octavian was already called Caesar and emperor, or Augustus, [Note: [Col. 0344C] “Afterward, while he was watching the games.” Suetonius, chapter 53.] afterward, while he was watching the games and the people had proclaimed that he should be called *Lord*, he immediately restrained the indecorous flattery by turning away his hand and face. He rejected the title *Lord* as an omen, [Note: [Col. 0344C–D] “He rejected it as an omen.” A. Covarruvias most correctly restored this passage, where the manuscripts read *ut homo*—“as a man.” Nor do I place as much confidence in the Isidorian manuscript, from which these words are absent, as I do in this emendation. Suetonius says: “He always detested the title ‘Lord’ as a curse and an insult.” What follows—“who was born of the sister of Julius Caesar”—is Servius’s wording, at the beginning of the *Aeneid*.] and on the following day he rebuked the entire people in a very severe edict. Thereafter he did not permit himself to be called *Lord*, not even by his own children. For he was the son of Attia, who was born of the sister of Julius Caesar.

423 **18.** Kings are called *Basileis* among the Greeks, Βασιλεῖς, for the reason that they support the people as though they were bases; hence bases also bear crowns. For the more highly someone is placed above others, the more heavily he is burdened with the weight of responsibilities.

**19.** *Tyrants* are called by this name in Greek, but in Latin they are also called kings; [Note: [Col. 0344D] “For among the ancients.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IV and VII, and Augustine, *City of God* V, chapter 19: “But no one should suppose that tyrants were not the worst and most wicked kings, but were called ‘strong’ according to an ancient usage.” Hence Virgil says:

> It will be part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.

] for among the ancients there was no distinction between a king and a tyrant, as in the verse:

> It will be part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.

For strong kings were called tyrants. *Tiro* means “strong”; concerning such rulers the Lord says: “Through me kings reign, and through me tyrants hold the earth.”

**20.** Later, however, the usage arose of calling the worst and most wicked kings tyrants—those who exercised over peoples a desire for luxurious domination and the most cruel form of rule.

**21.** [Note: [Col. 0344D] *Princeps* signifies both a degree of dignity and a position of rank. Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “Gyas in the middle, and …”] *Princeps* signifies both a degree of dignity and a position of rank, as in Virgil’s line:

> Turnus, first, hurled the blazing torch,

where *first* is meant.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] “The word *princeps*.” From Augustine, *On Grammar*.] The word *princeps* is derived from the meaning “to take first,” because he takes the first place, just as a *municip* is so called because he receives public duties.

[Col. 0344C] **22.** [Note: [Col. 0344D] “The word *dux*.” From *City of God* XVIII, chapter 45.] *Dux* is so called because he is the leader of the army. But not everyone who is a prince or leader can immediately also be called a king. In war, however, it is better to call someone a *dux* than a king, for this name expresses the person who leads in battle. Hence Virgil says, “of Evander the leader,” and Sallust: “With what greater eagerness each man showed himself good in the presence of the leader.” He did not say “in the presence of the consul.”

[Col. 0345A] **23.** Monarchs are those who possess sole authority, such as Alexander among the Greeks and Julius among the Romans. Hence the term *monarchy* is also used: Μονὰς means “singularity” in Greek, while ἀρχὴ means “authority” or “rule.”

**24.** Tetrarchs are those who hold a fourth part of a kingdom. For τέτταρα means “four”; such was Philip in Judaea.

424 **25.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] “From this they were called patricians.” On the new class of patricians that existed in Justinian’s time, A. Augustinus.] Patricians were so called because, just as fathers provide for their children, so they provide for the state.

**26.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] Prefects. On the prefects of the praetorium.] Prefects were so called because they preside with praetorian authority.

**27.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] “Praetors, who are also prefects.” Understand the ancient praetors, that is, magistrates; in this sense consuls were called praetors, and there were a praetorium and a praetorian gate. As for the derivation “as though they were those placed in front,” it is better, with Varro, to say “as though they went in front.”] Praetors are the same as prefects, as though they were those placed in front.

**28.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] Presidents. In the *Glossary*, *praeses*, ἡγεμῶν, “leader” or “governor.”] Presidents were so called because they hold the protection of some place in the capacity of guardians.

**29.** Tribunes were so called because they assign rights to soldiers or plebeians.

**30.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] Chiliarchs. From Jerome, on Isaiah II.] Chiliarchs are those who command a thousand; we call them *millenarians*. The name is Greek.

**31.** Centurions were so called because they command a hundred soldiers, just as *quinquagenarians* are those who command fifty soldiers, and *decurions* are named from being placed over ten soldiers.

**32.** [Note: [Col. 0345D] “Soldier … because previously there were a thousand in one unit.” Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* III, Book I, chapter 7, reports that the Romans customarily called cohorts by numerical names. Varro, however, in Book IV, says: “Soldiers, because the legion was originally made up of three thousand, and each of the three tribes—Tities, Ramnes, and Luceres—supplied one thousand.”] A soldier was so called because formerly there were a thousand in one unit, or because he is one selected from a thousand. Romulus, however, [Note: [Col. 0346D] “From the people.” That is, from the plebs.] was the first to take soldiers from the people and give them their name. Liber was the first to teach the order of military service.

**33.** A soldier is called either ordinary or extraordinary. An ordinary soldier is one who serves in the regular order and has not yet attained any rank of honor; he is a common soldier, that is, of humble military status. An extraordinary soldier, however, is one who is promoted out of the ranks because of his valor.

425 **34.** Veterans who have been discharged from military service are called *emeriti*. They are no longer engaged in active warfare, because *mereri* means “to serve as a soldier,” namely, for the pay that they earn. They are likewise called veterans because they are no longer engaged in warfare but, after many labors of military service, obtain the benefit of repose.

**35.** Cavalry soldiers were so called because they sit on horses. One may likewise say that someone serves in the equestrian order.

**36.** Recruits are called strong young men who are selected for military service and are found capable of bearing arms. They are judged not merely by their profession or birth but by the appearance and physical vigor of their bodies. Hence they are called recruits: before they have been called to take the military oath, [Col. 0345D] they are not soldiers.

[Col. 0346A] **37.** [Note: [Col. 0346D] “But the custom of Roman military service.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “Before the City, the youths …”] It was the custom of Roman military service for young men first to be trained in arms after reaching puberty. For recruits served at the age of sixteen; at that age alone they also lived under guard. Of them Virgil says: “and youth in its first flower.”

**38.** [Note: [Col. 0346D] “It is certain that slaves never served in the army.” From the same source, *Aeneid* IX, on “and he had sent them to Troy with forbidden arms.”] It is certain that slaves never served in the army unless they had laid aside slavery, except in the time of Hannibal, when after the battle of Cannae the Romans were in such dire necessity that they were not even given the opportunity to liberate the slaves.

**39.** [Note: [Col. 0346D] Deserters. See the title *On Deserters*, section 3, in the *Digest* on military affairs, and Quintilian, Book VII, chapter 7.] Deserters were so called because, having abandoned their military duties, they wander about. They are forbidden to enlist under other military numbers; but if they have not incurred guilt for a long period, they are beaten and restored to their own units. Those who abandon the army and go over to the enemy are also called deserters.

[Col. 0346B] 426 **40.** Enrolled soldiers are so called because they are entered on the registers by the person who is going to lead them. They are called transferred soldiers when they pass from one legion to another; they are called *transcripti* because they give their names so that they may be transferred.

**41.** [Note: [Col. 0346D] “Options … for *optare* means ‘to choose.’” From Servius and Festus. “The man now called an *optio* was formerly called an *accensus*. He was assigned as an assistant to the military tribune for the centurion, so that the centurion might choose whomever he wished; hence he received his name.”] Options were so called because they were chosen. For *optare* means “to choose,” as in the line: “And he chose a place for his kingdom,” that is, “he selected.”

**42.** Guards are called *excubitores* because they are always on watch. They are drawn from the number of soldiers and keep watch in the colonnades for the protection of the ruler. [Note: [Col. 0346D] “Watches, moreover, are daytime …” From the same source, *Aeneid* IX.] Watches, however, are daytime duties, while vigils are nocturnal; hence the term *watchmen*.

**43.** Among the Romans, the *velites* were a class of soldiers, named from *volitare*, “to fly about.” Young men selected for their agility sat behind the cavalry with their weapons, and as soon as they approached the enemy they leapt down from the horses. Then, fighting on foot while the cavalry who had carried them engaged the enemy from another side, they threw the enemy into confusion. It was by these *velites* that Hannibal’s elephants were once driven back. When they could no longer be controlled by their own men, the elephants were killed by driving a carpenter’s chisel between their ears.

**44.** A camp is where a soldier has stood. [Note: [Col. 0346D] “The word *castra*.” From the same source, *Aeneid* III, on “We move the camp.”] The camp was called *castra*, as though *casta*, “chaste,” because lust was castrated there. For a woman was never present among them.

**45.** *Militia* is derived either from *milia*, “thousands,” or from *multa*, “many,” as though *multitia*, “the business of many,” or from *moles*, “a mass,” as though *moletia*. [Note: [Col. 0346D–0347C] “As though *moletia*.” Some have *molestia*, “trouble,” supported by the vernacular *la mollitia* and by Rabanus. Festus likewise says: “Aelius thinks that *miles*, soldier, was named from *mollitia*, ‘softness,’ by antiphrasis, because it produces nothing soft but something harsh.”]

**46.** A legion consists of six thousand armed men and is named from selection, as though from *lecti*, “chosen,” that is, chosen for arms. Properly speaking, the Macedonian phalanx, [Note: [Col. 0347C] The Macedonian phalanx. From Servius, *Aeneid* II, and “Now the Argive phalanx.”] the Gallic host, [Note: [Col. 0347C] The Gallic troop. Vegetius, Book II, chapter 2.] and our formation called a legion are corresponding terms.

**47.** [Note: [Col. 0347C–D] “A legion has sixty.” Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “Order the standards by maniples.” “The standard-bearers,” he says, “because according to the ancient custom there were thirty in a legion. A legion had seven cohorts and sixty centuries.” We think that Servius mistakenly wrote VII instead of XII. For in Isidore everything is consistent: shortly afterward he says that a cohort consists of five hundred soldiers. Although, as Servius says in the same passage, the diversity of commanders has always changed military discipline over the passage of time. Gellius, Book XVI, chapter 4: “In a legion there are sixty centuries, thirty maniples, and ten cohorts.” Vegetius likewise, Book II, chapter 6: “It must be understood that there ought to be ten cohorts in one legion. But the first cohort surpasses the others both in the number of soldiers and in dignity.”] A legion has sixty centuries, thirty maniples, twelve cohorts, and two hundred troops of cavalry.

**48.** A century is a division of the army consisting of one hundred soldiers. Hence those who command them are called centurions.

**49.** The *sub-centuries* are not those in the first century but those in the second, as though beneath the first century. Nevertheless, they too are drawn up in close order and stationed on watch in war, so that if the first century should fail, these men, whom we have said are beneath it, may come to the aid of the first when it is in difficulty. Hence a sub-century is also placed for ambush, as though equipped with deceptive arms.

429 **50.** A maniple consists of two hundred soldiers. Maniples were so called either because at first soldiers began battle hand-to-hand, or because, before there were standards, they made for themselves maniples—that is, bundles of straw or some kind of grass—as standards. From this sign the soldiers were called *manipulares*. Lucan refers to them:

> Immediately he summons the armed maniples to the standards.

[Col. 0347B]

**51.** [Note: [Col. 0347D–0348D] “A troop … and a troop was formed.” It seems that this passage—which everyone can see is not now complete—was pieced together from Servius and Varro, so that something of each remains. Therefore, leaving aside the reading found in all the books, we shall present the words of both authors. Servius, *Aeneid* IX: “All three hundred were shield-bearing.” The Roman cavalry, he says, originally numbered three hundred; ten were supplied from each of the curiae, which we have said numbered thirty. Varro, Book IV: “*Turma*, from *terma*, changed *e* into *u*, because thirty cavalrymen were formed from each of the three tribes—the Tities, Ramnes, and Luceres; hence the first men of each group of ten were called decurions.” Chacon, rejecting the rest, wanted only the following from Servius to be retained: “The Roman cavalry originally numbered three hundred, for ten were supplied from each curia. A cohort,” and so forth.] A troop consists of thirty cavalrymen. For the Roman cavalry in one tribe numbered three hundred. Ten were supplied from each century, and a troop was formed.

A cohort contains five hundred soldiers.

428 **52.** There are three kinds of military service: the oath, the summons, and the conspiracy.

**53.** The oath is the form in which, after selection, each soldier swears that he will not withdraw from military service until he has completed his terms of service—that is, the periods of military duty. These are the men who complete full military service, for they are bound for twenty-five years.

[Col. 0347C] **54.** The summons occurs when, for a sudden war, not only soldiers but also others are called out. Hence a consul was accustomed to say: “Let whoever wishes the state to be safe follow me.”

**55.** The conspiracy is formed in an emergency, when the danger threatening the city is so close that it does not allow each individual to swear an oath; instead, a multitude is suddenly gathered and brought together in tumultuous anger. This is also called a *tumultuation*.

**56.** In battle there are generally these formations: an army, a division, a knot, a wedge, wings, horns, and a column. [Col. 0348A] They borrow their forms and names from the very things from which the terms have been transferred.

**57.** *Battle line* is so called because it is armed with iron and with the sharpness of swords.

**58.** An army is a multitude of one kind, named from the exercise of war.

**59.** Divisions (*classes*) were so called because of the division of the army; they were later called maniples. Hence Virgil says:

> Here divisions, here battle lines, were accustomed to contend.

Later *classis* was also applied to a fleet of ships.

**60.** [Note: [Col. 0348D] “A knot is properly a dense mass.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on:

> … Abantem,
>
> Standing in his way, he kills the knot and delay of battle.

What follows—“A knot is named from difficulty”—is another meaning of the word in Servius, not the explanation of the earlier one, as Isidore seems to have thought, perhaps because he consulted Servius’s commentaries without Virgil’s verses.] A knot is properly a dense multitude of infantry, just as a troop is a multitude of cavalry. A knot is also named from difficulty, because it can scarcely be undone.

**61.** A wedge is a multitude of soldiers gathered into one. Hence, because it comes together into one, that very gathering is called a wedge, as though *couneus*, since all are driven together into one.

429 **62.** It is said that the wings in an army consist of thirty cavalrymen. [Note: [Col. 0348D] “The wings are cavalry.” Vegetius, Book II, chapter 1, and Gellius XVI, chapter 4.] The cavalry are called wings because they cover the infantry in the manner of wings.

**63.** The horns are called the extremities of the army because they are bent inward.

**64.** A column is so called when the army is on the march; it is named from *agere*, “to drive” or “to go.” Plautus says: “Where are you driving yourself?” It is an army in motion. For a column is what is arranged lengthwise, as happens when an army proceeds through the gates; anything else is called a column only by abuse of the term.

## CHAPTER IV. On citizens

[Col. 0348C] **1.** We have spoken in part about the terms for command and military service; next we briefly append the names of citizens.

**2.** Citizens were so called because they live by coming together into one, so that communal life may become both more orderly and safer.

**3.** A household is the dwelling of one family, just as a city is the dwelling of one people and the world is the dwelling of the entire human race. A household is a lineage, a family, or the union of husband and wife. It begins with two and is a Greek word. For the Greeks call roofs δώματα, “houses.” [Col. 0349A] A family consists of children received under free laws; the name is derived from *femur*, “thigh.”

**4.** *Lineage* is named from begetting and generating offspring, or from the definition of particular ancestors, as with nations which, bounded by their own relationships of kinship, are called peoples.

**5.** [Note: [Col. 0349C] “A people is an assembly.” The word *coetus*, “assembly,” was absent from the books; we restored it from Augustine, *City of God* XIX, chapters 21 and 24, who quotes these words from Cicero’s *Republic*.] A people is an assembly of a human multitude united by agreement in law and harmonious fellowship. A people differs from the plebs in this respect: the people consists of all citizens, including the elders of the state; the plebs is the remaining common crowd without the elders of the state.

430 **6.** The people, therefore, is the whole citizen body; the common crowd is the plebs. The plebs was so called from its plurality, for the number of the lesser people is greater than that of the elders. [Note: [Col. 0349C–D] “But the people …” How many monstrosities there are here in the Greek characters! The reading we have printed comes closest to that of the Oviedo and Gothic manuscripts. See whether Jerome’s phrase τὸ «πολὺς συμμικτὸς», “a great mixed multitude,” in Nahum III, on “The locust has spread itself,” may bear on this.] The people, however, is called συχνὸς δῆμος, “a numerous people,” that is, Κοιτὸς πολὺς, “a large assembly.” Hence the people received its name. [Note: [Col. 0349D] “In Greek, however, the people.” From Servius, *Georgics* I, on “From where human beings, a hard race, were born.”] In Greek, however, the people is called λαὸς, “laos,” from stones. The common crowd is a multitude dwelling everywhere, as though each person goes wherever he wishes.

**7.** Tribes are like distinct curiae and congregations of peoples. They were called tribes because at the beginning the Romans were divided by Romulus into three groups: [Note: [Col. 0349D] “Into senators, soldiers, and plebeians.” We regard these words as foreign to the passage.] senators, soldiers, and plebeians. [Note: [Col. 0349D] “Although these tribes are now multiplied.” Varro, Book IV. A century was first named from one hundred *jugera*; after being doubled, it retained its name, just as the tribes, though multiplied, retain the same name. Columella, Book V, chapter 1, reports the same account from the same Varro; perhaps Isidore took it from him, for Chacon thought that Isidore had not read Varro’s books *On the Latin Language*.] Nevertheless, although the tribes have now multiplied, they retain their original name.

**8.** The Senate received its name from age, because its members were older. [Note: [Col. 0349D] Others derive the name from *sinere*, “to permit.” These are Servius’s words, *Aeneid* V, on “and gives laws to the fathers who have been summoned.” But who, I ask, has not laughed at these words in Isidore? Yet in Servius the same people admire them.] Others understand senators to have been named from *sinere*, “to permit,” because they granted the ability to act.

**9.** The *senate decree* was named from consulting and deliberating, because it is made in such a way that it gives counsel and cannot cause harm.

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0349D] “The fathers.” Servius, in the same passage.] The Fathers, as Sallust says, were called from their similarity to those who care for others. For just as fathers cared for their children, so they [Col. 0350C] cared for the state.

[Col. 0349C] **11.** [Note: [Col. 0350C–D] “Conscript Fathers.” The origin of this account must be investigated. Dionysius says: Οἴ δὲ μετέχοντες πατέρες ἔγγραφοι προσηγορεύθησαν, καὶ μέχρις ἐμοῦ ταύτης ἐτύγχανον τῆς προσηγορίας, ἐλληνικὸν δὲ τοῦτο ἔθος ἦν—“Those who participated were called enrolled fathers, and down to my time they obtained this designation; but this was a Greek custom.” Yet even this cannot give sufficient satisfaction, and even if one were to turn bronze tablets into golden ones, we would not be persuaded that these words are not spurious.] They were called Conscript Fathers because, when Romulus had selected ten senatorial curiae, he entered their names on golden tablets in the presence of the people; hence they were called Conscript Fathers.

431 **12.** [Note: [Col. 0350D] “Of the first rank.” From the glosses of Placidius; Chacon deleted the word “senators” from it.] Senators of the first rank are called *illustrious*, those of the second *spectabiles*, and those of the third *clarissimi*. There is no fourth class below these. Although each person might be of senatorial origin, until he reached the lawful age he was a Roman knight; afterward he received the dignity of the senatorial rank.

[Col. 0350A] **13.** Among the ancient Romans there were censors. The name *censor* denotes a judicial dignity, for *censere* means “to judge.” Censors are likewise judges of estates, named from the assessment of wealth.

**14.** [Note: [Col. 0350D] “Judges were so called.” Below, Book XVIII, chapter 15; Gratian, 23, question 2, chapter 1; and Gregory, chapter 10, *On the Meaning of Words*.] Judges were so called as though they were those who declare the law to the people, or because they decide legal cases. To decide legally is to judge justly. But a person is not a judge if justice is not in him.

**15.** Presidents are governors of a province, so called because they preside over it.

**16.** Praetors are as though they were instructors and leaders of the state. They are also called quaestors, as though “inquirers,” because they preside over inquiries; deliberation and litigation are entrusted to them.

**17.** [Note: [Col. 0350D] “The leading men … hence also the projecting ends of beams.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “afterward other leading men.”] The leading men are the rulers of the state, as though they were those who advance ahead, because they precede everyone else in honor. Hence the projecting ends of beams, which extend beyond walls, are also called *proceres*, because they project first. From this the term was transferred to the foremost men, because they rise above the remaining multitude.

[Col. 0350B] **18.** [Note: [Col. 0350D] “Tribunes … in the sixteenth year.” All the books mistakenly read “sixth.” Asconius, on the *Cornelian Oration*: “Such was their courage that in the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings, because of the excessive domination of the powerful, they seceded, restored the sacred laws to themselves, and created two tribunes.” Pomponius, chapter 2, *On the Origin of the Law*: “Approximately in the seventeenth year after the expulsion of the kings, the Roman people created tribunes for themselves on the Sacred Mount.”] Tribunes were so called because they grant rights or aid to the plebs. They were established in the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings. For when the plebs was oppressed by the Senate and the consuls, it then created tribunes for itself as its own judges and defenders, to protect its liberty and defend it against the injuries of the nobility. Hence they were also called defenders, because they defended the plebs entrusted to them against the arrogance of wicked men. [Note: [Col. 0350D] “But now some are instead …” These words must have belonged to some ancient writer, for tribunes did not exist in Isidore’s time.] But now some exist as subverters rather than defenders.

**19.** [Note: [Col. 0350D] *Numerarii*. An edict of King Egica survives in the sixteenth Council of Toledo, where the office of the *numerarii* is mentioned.] *Numerarii* are those who pay public money into the treasury.

**20.** Officials are so called from the fact that they perform some honor or office. Hence we also call the dead *defuncti*, those who have completed the duties of life, for they now do nothing.

**21.** Municipals are those born in the same municipality; they are named from the performance of public duties, because they undertake public services. Public services are called *munia*; hence those who perform no office are called *immune*.

**22.** Original municipal citizens, and those who perform an office in place of another.

[Col. 0351A] **23.** Decurions are so called because they belong to the order of the *curia*. For they administer the office of the *curia*. Hence a man is not a decurion [Note: [Col. 0351D] “Who has not paid in the required sum, or has not taken part in the *curia*.” Concerning this Chacon writes as follows: “The man who became a decurion paid in the sum prescribed for entry, and before he paid it he was not a member of the *curia*. When, according to custom, nothing was paid, he was not called a member of the *curia* until he entered it with the others and deliberated on public affairs.” See Pliny, Book X, Letter 33. Antonius Augustinus said: “Two kinds of decurions are shown: one, that of the honorary members, who obtain the honor by giving money but abstain from the service; the other, that of the ordinary members, who perform the office of decurions—for this is what it means to take part in the *curia*.”], who has not paid in the required sum or has not taken part in the *curia*.

**24.** Curiales are likewise called decurions. They are called curiales because they manage and carry out civil duties.

[433] **25.** The principal magistrates and the *duumvirales* belong to the order of curial offices. They are called principal because they are first among the magistrates.

**26.** Magistrates, on the other hand, are so called because they are greater than the remaining offices.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] *Duumvirales.* Augustine, in his *Book on Grammar*: “*Duumvirales*, as though ‘the man of two men.’” Some books, however, wrongly fill the lacuna found in all the Gothic manuscripts.]

*Duumvirales* [lacuna].

**27.** A *tabellio* is so called because he is a carrier of tablets. He is also called an *exceptor*, and likewise a public scribe, because he writes only those matters that are made public in the official records.

**28.** *Burgarii* are named from *burgi*, because the frequent settlements established along the frontiers are commonly called *burgi*. Hence the name also adhered to the people of the Burgundians, whom the Romans, after subduing Germany, distributed among military camps; thus they took their name from the places.

**29.** [Note: [Col. 0351D] *Collegiati.* Some matters concerning the colleges are discussed in the title “On the Law of Immunity,” Book L of the *Digest*, but they do not sufficiently illuminate this passage.]

*Collegiati* are so called because those who have committed some crime are assigned to their college and prisons [434]. For it is the most degraded class of people, born of an uncertain father.

**30.** Private persons are outsiders with respect to public offices. The name is opposed to that of one who holds a magistracy; and they are called private persons because they are released from the duties of the *curia*.

**31.** Mercenaries are those who serve for wages. They are also called *barones*, a Greek term, because they are strong in labor. For **βαρύς** (*barýs*) means “heavy,” and hence one who is strong [Col. 0351C]. Their opposite is the light person, that is, the weak.

**32.** Publicans are called the contractors of the revenues of the treasury or of public properties, or those who collect public taxes, or those who pursue profits through worldly business. Hence they received this designation.

**33.** [Note: [Col. 0351D] “*Villicus* . . . signifies.” These are Jerome’s words in Question 6 to Algasia. Hence Cicero appears to have translated *οἰκονόμος* as *villicus* and *dispensator* in his *Oeconomicus* of Xenophon. In the *Hortensius* too, as Nonnius reports, he used the word *dispensator*: “What, I ask, do you usually do when you receive an account from the steward? If you have approved each individual sum, do you not approve the total that has been made up from them?”]

A *villicus* is properly the governor of an estate. Hence the name *villicus* is derived from *villa*. Sometimes, however, *villicus* signifies not the administration of an estate but, in Cicero’s interpretation, the management of the entire household—that is, the steward of all possessions and estates.

**34.** [Note: [Col. 0352D] “*Actores* . . . *procuratores*.” The jurists say that an *actor* represents someone present, while a *procurator* represents someone absent; a guardian cannot appoint a *procurator*, but can appoint an *actor*.]

Actors are also called curators, from *agere* (“to act”) and *curare* (“to care for”).

[Col. 0352A] **35.** Procurators, on the other hand, are so called because they perform the function of a curator [Note: [Col. 0352D] “As though on behalf of curators.” We consider this extraneous.], just as *proconsul* means “in place of a consul.”

[435] **36.** Coloni are called immigrant cultivators, from the cultivation of the soil. They are people who come from elsewhere, cultivate rented land belonging to another, and, because of their agriculture, owe a status to the native soil under the control of the possessor, in return for the farm that has been rented to them. Coloni, however, are of four kinds: Roman coloni, Latin coloni, auxiliary coloni, and coloni of private rural land.

**37.** Inquilines are so called as though they were “inhabitants of another’s property.” They do not possess a dwelling of their own but live on another’s land.

**38.** There is a difference between an inquilinus and an immigrant. Inquilini are those who move in from elsewhere and do not remain permanently [Col. 0352B]. Immigrants, or newly arrived inhabitants, are likewise people who come from elsewhere but remain; hence they are called *incolae*, because they are already inhabitants, from *incolere* (“to inhabit”).

**39.** Indigenous people are those born there and born in the same place in which they live.

**40.** *Incola*, however, indicates not an indigenous person but an immigrant.

**41.** Peregrines are so called because their parents, from whom they were born, are unknown; they come from a distant region.

**42.** Those who lived at Rome were called urbanites; those who lived in other places were called townspeople. [Note: [Col. 0352D] For Rome alone is called a city, while all the others are towns. When Roman historians mention a “town” without adding anything further, they understand the Palatine town, where Rome was first founded, which Ennius called square:

“And those among whom it had arisen to rule square Rome.”]

For Rome alone is called a city; all the others are towns.

**43.** Famuli are those born from a particular household of slaves. [Note: [Col. 0352D] “*Servi* . . . because those who.” The words are Augustine’s, *City of God* XIX, chapter 15.]

Slaves derived their designation from the fact that those whom the victors could have killed by the law of war were preserved and made slaves; they were therefore called *servi*, from *servare* (“to preserve”).

[Col. 0352C] **44.** Female slaves are called *ancillae* from “support,” for **ἀγκών** (*ankōn*) in Greek means “elbow”; hence we also say *ancon*.

**45.** A *mancipium* is anything that can be seized by hand and subjected to ownership, such as a human being, a horse, or a sheep. These animals are considered *mancipia* as soon as they are born; even animals belonging to the class of wild beasts are regarded as *mancipia* when they begin to be captured or tamed.

**46.** *Ingenui* are so called because they possess freedom by birth, not by an act, as freedmen do. Hence the Greeks call them **εὐγενεῖς** (*eugeneis*), because they are of good birth.

**47.** A freedman is so called as one who has been liberated. Previously he had been subjected to the yoke of slavery. [Note: [Col. 0352D] “The sons of freedmen among the ancients.” Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 24: “He showed that Appius Caecus, the censor and promoter of his family, had enrolled the sons of freedmen in the Senate,” unaware that in the time of Appius, and for some time afterward, *libertini* meant not those who were manumitted themselves but those born from them.]

Among the ancients the sons of freedmen were called *libertini*, as though born from freedmen; now, however, *libertinus* means either one made a freedman or one possessed by a freedman.

**48.** A manumitted person is called one who has been “sent forth by hand.” Among the ancients, whenever they manumitted slaves [437], they led them around after striking them with a slap [Note: [Col. 0353C] “They led them around after striking them with a slap.” It was customary to strike the slave’s head with the *vindicta*, and to beat his face with the palm or his back with a rod. They were also turned and led around by their masters. Hence Persius:

“. . . Alas, barren of truth, for whom one turning makes a Roman citizen.”], and confirmed them as free. Hence they were called *manumissi*, because they were sent forth by hand.

**49.** *Dedititii* were first named from surrender. For surrender occurs when enemies who have been captured or are about to be captured hand themselves over in bonds to the victors; this was the origin of the name. Once, when slaves had taken up arms and fought against the Roman people, they surrendered in bonds, and after being captured were subjected to various forms of disgrace.

**50.** [Note: [Col. 0353C] “Some of these were afterward manumitted by their masters.” Augustine, in his *Letter to the Galatians*: “Stigmata are certain marks of servile punishments. Thus, if someone, for example, had been placed in chains as a slave because of an offense—that is, because of a fault—or had suffered something of this kind, he was said to bear stigmata; and for that reason, in the law of manumission, he belonged to an inferior order.”]

Some of these, although later manumitted by their masters, did not attain the rank of Roman citizens because of the marks of punishment that they had visibly endured.

[Col. 0353B] **51.** [Note: [Col. 0353D] “Latin freedmen—before Rome was founded.” Concerning Latin freedmen, the matter is sufficiently clear from the Julian Norban law, and from the *Tituli* of Ulpian, and the Institutes of Gaius and Justinian; these statements agree with them in no way. A. Augustinus therefore disregarded and rejected them. For what does “before Rome was founded, they were made among the Latins” mean? And what of the final statement, “They were first granted access to remain in the city of Rome”? And so forth. But because something true is interwoven—namely, that they were made free by letter and did not possess the right of making a will—Chacon conjectured that Isidore meant by “Latin freedmen” those who had the legal status once possessed by persons manumitted among the Latin peoples before Rome was founded. No one will deny that this contributes something to the etymology of Latin freedmen. But how did Isidore look so far back? The matter therefore requires further inquiry.]

Latin freedmen—among the Latins before Rome was founded—obtained freedom not by will but by letter. [438] Since they were not made free by will, they could neither receive anything under a will nor make their own heirs; later, under the consuls, they became Roman citizens by wills in the city of Rome.

**52.** They were called Roman citizens because, having been made free by will, they were enrolled among the number of Roman citizens. They were the first to be granted access to remain in the city of Rome; [Note: [Col. 0354C] “But this was forbidden to other freedmen.” “No one,” says A. Augustinus, “has ever said this.” Nevertheless, Latin citizens were sometimes expelled from the city if they obstructed the elections.] other freedmen, however, were prohibited from remaining either in the city of Rome or within seven miles of the city.

# CHAPTER V. On Affinities and Degrees

[Col. 0353C]

**1.** The name *heir* was imposed by the assessment of money [Note: [Col. 0354C] “For he pays the tax of the author,” that is, of the person who instituted him as heir.]; for in this word lies the first succession of inheritance and descent, as in sons and grandsons.

**2.** A *proheir* is one who performs the function of an heir, as though “in place of an heir”; he is either instituted or substituted.

[Col. 0354A] **3.** A father is the one from whom the beginning of a lineage arises; hence he is called the head of a household. A father is so called because, after the act has been completed, he begets a son. [Note: [Col. 0354C] “For *patratio* is the completion of the sexual act.” That *patrare* was an obscene word is shown by Quintilian, Book VIII, chapter 3: “To lead an army and to accomplish a war, expressions used by Sallust in a solemn and ancient manner, are ridiculous to us.” And in the glossary: *patrat*—“he is sexually gratified,” expressed indecently in Greek as **μασσᾶται κακεμφάτως, ὡς ἐπ’ αἰσχρῶς** (“he is sexually gratified, in an obscene manner”); this usage is common in the ancient writers Catullus, Persius, and others.]

For *patratio* is the completion of the sexual act. [Note: [Col. 0354D] Lucretius: “And they accomplish what has been well acquired.” Antonius Covarruvias most successfully restored to Lucretius, and at the same time to Isidore, their original wording from the slightly corrupted reading of our manuscripts.]

Lucretius: “And they accomplish what has been well acquired.”

**4.** *Genitores* (“begetters”) comes from *gignere* (“to beget”), and *parentes* (“parents”) is as though from *parientes* (“those giving birth”).

**5.** They are also called creators. [Note: [Col. 0354D] “The generative substance.” He repeats the same point in Book XI, chapter 1. Placidus’ glossary: “Excrement, which we spit out or discharge, is so called. Also, male semen, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived.” Hence parents are called creators.]

For the generative substance is the male seed, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived. Hence parents are called creators.

**6.** A mother is so called because something is made from her; [Note: [Col. 0354D] “*Mater* is as though *materia* (‘matter’).” This is not an etymology of the word—which he knew to be Greek—but of its meaning.] for *mater* is as though *materia* (“matter”), whereas the father is the cause.

**7.** The head of a household is so called because he cares for all the slaves placed in his household with the affection of a father toward sons, and does not distinguish the condition of slaves from the affection due to sons, but embraces them as though they were one member of the household. Hence the name *paterfamilias* arose. Those who rule their slaves unjustly should in no way suppose that they are called by this name.

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0354D] “*Materfamilias* is so called from this.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on the verse “through Tyrrhenian towns, the mothers.” See also Boethius on Cicero’s *Topics*.]

A woman is called the head of a household because, through a certain formality of law, she passes into her husband’s family. The marriage tablets are instruments of her purchase. [440] Just as [Note: [Col. 0354D] “*Matrona* . . . mother of a child,” or of one who is to be born, also according to Gellius and Isidore himself, who below, in chapter 7, says: “As though mother of a child, or because she can now become a mother.”] a *matrona* is the mother of the first child, that is, “as though the mother of one born,” so the female head of a household is one who has given birth to several children. For a household begins from two persons.

**9.** A grandfather is the father of one’s father, called from *aevum* (“age”), that is, from antiquity. A great-grandfather is the father of a grandfather, as though “near the grandfather.” A great-great-grandfather is the father of a great-grandfather, already far removed from the grandfather. A great-great-great-grandfather is the father of a great-great-grandfather.

**10.** A *tritavus* is the father of an *atavus*, as though *tetravus*, that is, “fourth above the grandfather.” But *tritavus* is the final name in the degrees of kinship. For a family begins with the father and ends with the *tritavus*.

**11.** [Note: [Col. 0354D] “*Filius* and *filia*.” As though from *familius*; this explanation too should not be rejected.]

A son and a daughter are named from the family; they are the first in the order of those born. Hence the Cornelian family is the entire stock that arose from Cornelius.

[Col. 0355A] **12.** A family, however, is named from the thigh. [Note: [Col. 0355C] “For lineage is shown by the thigh.” In the Gothic text: *femor enim*; undoubtedly the *e* was omitted by the scribe before another *e*. It should therefore be read *femure* or *femore*, since the ancients are known to have used both forms.]

For lineage and stock are shown by the thigh. The word *familia*, however, is improperly, not properly, used for slaves.

**13.** *Stirps* (“stock”) is so called from the extended meaning of lineage. *Gnatus* (“born”) is so called because he has been generated; hence it is written with a *g*. [Note: [Col. 0355D] “*Suboles*, because it is a substitution.” From this explanation too it appears that *suboles*, not *soboles*, should be written.]

*Suboles* is so called because it is a succession of the lineage.

**14.** The order of sons is divided into four kinds: only-begotten, firstborn, middle, and last. The only-begotten is one after whom no one follows. The firstborn is one before whom no one exists. The middle is among all the others. The last is after all the others. [Note: [Col. 0355D] “Also the youngest, from *monas* (‘unit’).” See the following book, letter M.]

The last is also called the youngest, from *monas*. *Novissimus* (“last”) is so called because he is new, since the others, by preceding him, are older.

**15.** [Note: [Col. 0355D] “In four ways.” From Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chapter 5, and *Retractions* I, chapter 22.]

Sons are also called by four designations: by nature, by imitation, by adoption, and by instruction [441]. By nature, as when the Jews are called sons of Abraham. By imitation, as when Gentiles imitate the faith of Abraham, the Gospel saying: “God is able from these stones to raise up sons for Abraham”; or as when the Lord calls those same Jews sons of the devil, not because they were born from him, but because they had imitated him.

**16.** They are also called sons by adoption, since no one can be unaware of this human custom; likewise we call ourselves God’s children not by nature but by adoption: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” They are called sons by instruction, as the Apostle calls those to whom he preached the Gospel his sons.

**17.** Sons are called *liberi* (“free persons”) in the laws so that by this term they may be distinguished from slaves. For just as a slave is in the power of his master, so a son is in the power of his father. Hence emancipation is also granted to a son, so that he may be free from his father, just as manumission is granted to a slave, so that he may be liberated from his master.

**18.** They are also called *liberi* because they are born from a free marriage [Col. 0355C]. For children born from a free person and a female slave possess servile status. The person who is born always takes the inferior status of the parent.

**19.** Natural children are the sons of freeborn concubines, whom nature alone has generated, not the respectability of marriage. They are also called *pueri* (“boys”), from *pubes* (“puberty”).

**20.** An adopted son is one who has been transferred by emancipation into another’s power by his lawful father, grandfather, or great-grandfather, under whose power he is; he bears the name of both, [Note: [Col. 0355D] Such as Fabius Aemilius or Scipio Paulus; or Fabius Aemilianus, Scipio Paulinus.]
