**21.** Twins are not only two born at the same time, but also more than two. If, in the case of twins, one is miscarried, the other, who has been born legitimately, is called a *vopiscus*.

**22.** [Note: [Col. 0355D] “*Posthumus*, because he is born after burial.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “your posthumous offspring.” A. Augustinus and Jacques Cujas, however, prefer *postumus*, with only the first syllable of *post* lengthened, as in *postremus*; ancient coins support their view.]

A posthumous child is so called because he is born after the burial of his father, that is, after his death. He also receives the name of the deceased; for the law ordained that one born from a deceased person should be called by the deceased person’s name.

[442] **23.** [Note: [Col. 0355D] *Nothus.* Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on the verse “bastards born of a mother.” “*Nothos*,” he says, “are ignoble on the mother’s side.” The word is Greek, for there is no Latin term for it.]

A *nothus* is one born of a noble father and an ignoble mother, as from a concubine. This is a Greek word, and has no equivalent in Latin.

**24.** The opposite of this is a *spurius*, one born of a noble mother and an ignoble father. A *spurius* is also one born of an uncertain father and a widowed mother, as though merely the son of a *spurius*, [Note: [Col. 0355D] “Because the ancients called the female nature **σπόριον**.” Plutarch, *Problems*: “One must also mention the other account, which is rather strange: for they say that the Sabines call the female sexual organ *sporion*.”]

because the ancients called the female nature **σπόριον** (*sporion*), as though from **ἀπὸ τοῦ σπόρου** (“from the seed”), not from the name of the father.

**25.** [Note: [Col. 0356C] “The same people were also called *favonii*.” Varro, *On Agriculture* II: “In breeding, there is an incredible but true phenomenon in Spain. In Lusitania, near the Ocean, in the region where the town of Olisipo is located, on Mount Tagus, certain mares conceive from the wind at a particular season, just as hens sometimes do here, and their eggs are called **ὑπηνέμια** (‘wind-conceived’). Thus, just as the eggs are *hypenemian*, so the horses are *favonian*, for the mares conceived when the Favonius wind blew, as Pliny says, Book IV, chapter 22.”]

They also called them *favonii*, because certain animals are thought to conceive after drawing in the breath of the Favonius wind. Hence those who are not born from a legitimate marriage follow the mother rather than the father. In Latin they are called *spurii*, as though “outside purity,” that is, as though unclean.

**26.** A grandson is one born from a son. He is called *nepos*, as though “born afterward.” First a son is born, then a grandson. For this is a degree of succession. Hence *posterity* is likewise as though “a later generation.” [Note: [Col. 0356D] “A grandson is of either sex . . . admitted.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on the verse “and a poor household.”]

A *nepos* may be of either sex. For the term *neptis* (“granddaughter”) has been admitted in legal usage for the sake of distinguishing succession.

**27.** A great-grandchild is one conceived and born from a grandson. He is called *pronepos*, as though “born farther afterward.” From this degree the term *progeny* also begins to be used, as though “those born farther afterward.” For sons and grandsons [443] are not called progeny, because they do not yet contain an extended posterity.

[Col. 0356C] **28.** Just as those born far below are called progeny, so those above—*proavi* and *atavi*—are called progenitors, as though “generating farther onward.” *Pronepos* is also said to mean “near the grandson.”

**29.** An *abnepos* is so called because he is separated from the grandson. A great-grandchild stands between him and the grandson. An *adnepos* is the son of an *abnepos*.

**30.** A *trinepos* is the son of an *adnepos*, because he is fourth in order after the grandson, as though *tetranepos*.

**31.** [Note: [Col. 0356D] “We do not use *minores* except whenever the name of the degrees runs out,” from the same source, *Aeneid* VIII. In some books a complete title, “On the Degrees of Kinship,” from Justinian’s *Institutes*, had been inserted here. Since it was absent from the older books, and since other material under Isidore’s name on the same subject is transmitted by Burchard, Book VII, chapter 28; by Ivo, Book VII, title 12 of the *Panormia*; in Part IX, chapter 64 of the *Decretum*; and by Gratian, 35, question 5, chapter 6—and since these passages are also read in the Gothic Laws and in Julius Paulus, *Sentences* IV, title 11, “On Degrees”—we have not admitted the Justinianic material. We have thought it sufficient to indicate the sources from which this material, if indeed it belongs to Isidore, may be obtained.]

We do not use *minores* (“younger descendants”) except when the names of the degrees fail—for example, son, grandson (*nepos*), great-grandson (*pronepos*), *abnepos*, *adnepos*, and *trinepos*. When these degrees have run out, we rightly call them *minores*, just as we call people *majores* (“senior ancestors”) after the names father, grandfather, *proavus*, *abavus*, *atavus*, and *tritavus* have run out.

# CHAPTER VI. On Agnates and Cognates

**1.** Agnates are so called because they take the place of sons when there are no sons. They are recognized first within the lineage because they come through male persons—for example, a brother born of the same father, or the son of a brother, or a grandson through him, and likewise a paternal uncle.

**2.** Cognates are so called because they too are joined by the relationship of kinship. They are placed after agnates because they come through female persons; they are not agnates but are cognates by natural law in another sense.

**3.** A near relative is called *proximus* because of closeness of blood.

[Col. 0357B] [444] **4.** Blood relatives are so called because they are born from one blood, that is, from the seed of one father. For a man’s seed is foam from blood, like water dashed against rocks, which produces white foam, or like dark wine which, when stirred in a cup, produces whitish foam.

**5.** [Note: [Col. 0357C] “*Fratres* (‘brothers’).” Festus: “*Frater* is said from the Greek **φρήτωρ**, or because he is almost another self.”]

Brothers are so called because they are born from the same fruit, that is, from the same seed.

**6.** [Note: [Col. 0357C] “*Germani* are so called from the same mother, not from the same seed, from the same origin.” You see that the meaning diverges from the word’s apparent etymology; it is therefore necessary to devise another etymology of the underlying sense, **τοῦ σημαινομένου ἔτυμον**, “the etymology of what is signified.” At least this makes the matter clearer and distinguishes a brother from a *germanus*. These are Servius’ words, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “This Eryx, your brother.” “According to Varro, in his books *On Degrees*, a *germanus* is one who descends from the same mother, not—as many say—from the same stock; those others he calls merely brothers. In accordance with this, Aeneas rightly says here that Eryx, the son of Butes and Venus, was his *germanus*. Cornelius Fronto, however, says: ‘A brother may be from another mother or another father; a *germanus* must necessarily be from the same parents.’ Justinian, *Institutes* III, chapter 2, says: ‘Thus brothers born from the same father are agnates to one another and are also called blood relatives; it is not required that they have also had the same mother.’ Cujas observes that these too are called *germani*.]

*Germani* are those who descend from the same mother—not, as many say, from the same stock; those latter are merely called brothers. Thus brothers are from the same seed, while *germani* descend from the same mother.

**7.** Uterine siblings are so called because they are born from different fathers and from one womb; [Note: [Col. 0357D] “For the womb belongs only to a woman.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on the verse “and the womb . . .”] for the womb belongs only to a woman.

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0358C] “Brothers are called so in four ways.” From Jerome, *Against Helvidius*.]

In the divine Scriptures, brothers are called so in four ways: by nature, by race, by kinship, and by affection [Col. 0357C]. By nature, as Esau and Jacob, or Andrew and Peter, or James and John. By race, as all Jews are called brothers among themselves, as in Deuteronomy: “But if you buy a brother who is a Hebrew” (Deut. 15:12). And the Apostle says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9:3).

**9.** Brothers are also called so by kinship when they belong to one family, that is, one paternal lineage, which the Latins interpret as *paternitates*, when a multitude of descendants spreads from one root. Thus in Genesis Abraham said to Lot: “Let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between your shepherds and my shepherds, for we are all brothers” (Gen. 13:8). Yet Lot was not Abraham’s brother, but the son of his brother Aram.

**10.** In the fourth manner, people are called brothers by affection, and this is divided into two kinds: spiritual and common. Spiritual brotherhood is that by which all Christians are called brothers, as in: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together” (Ps. 132:1). Common brotherhood is that by which, since all human beings are born from one father, we are joined to one another by equal kinship, as Scripture says: “Say to those who hate you: You are our brothers.”

**11.** *Germana* is understood in the same way as *germanus*: one who descends from the same mother.

**12.** [Note: [Col. 0358C] “*Soror* (‘sister’), because she is alone with her brother.” Antistius Labeo, quoted by Gellius: “*Soror*, because she is born, as it were, separately, and is separated from the household in which she was born and passes into another family.”]

A sister is defined like a brother; for a sister is said to be from the same seed because she alone, together with her brothers, is included in the allotment of agnation [Col. 0358B].

**13.** Paternal cousins are so called because their fathers were brothers by the same parent.

**14.** [Note: [Col. 0358D] *Consubrini.* In the most ancient books, both *subrini* and *consubrini* are consistently written with *u*.]

*Consubrini* are those born either from a sister and a brother or from two sisters, as though *consororini*.

**15.** Maternal cousins are the sons of a maternal aunt. *Subrini* are the sons of *consubrini*. [Note: [Col. 0358D] *Thius.* Glossary: **θεῖος πρὸς πατρός** (“paternal uncle”), **θεῖος πρὸς μητρός** (“maternal uncle”). Simplicius gives a not inelegant account of this name in his commentary on Epictetus: since parents are, as it were, **θεοί** (“gods”) to their children, and we are afraid to call them gods out of reverence for the divine power, some trace of that honor and piety has nevertheless remained in the word *thius*. See Stobaeus, chapters 42 and 77.]

*Thius* is a Greek name.

[446] **16.** A paternal uncle is the father’s brother, as though another father. Hence, when the father dies, the paternal uncle first takes charge of an orphan and legally protects him as though he were his son.

**17.** A maternal uncle is the mother’s brother. His name appears to have the form of a diminutive, because it is shown to derive from *avus* (“grandfather”).

**18.** A paternal aunt is the father’s sister, as though another mother. A maternal aunt is the mother’s sister, as though a second mother. A father-in-law is one who has given his daughter in marriage.

**19.** [Note: [Col. 0358D] “*Gener* . . . for increasing the lineage.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on the verse “and he had admitted sons-in-law into the city.”]

A son-in-law is one who has married a daughter. He is called *gener* because he is admitted in order to increase the lineage. A father-in-law and mother-in-law are so called because they have joined a son-in-law or daughter-in-law to themselves.

**20.** A stepfather is one who marries a woman who has a son or daughter by another man. He is called *vitricus*, as though *novitricus* (“newly introduced”), because a new man is brought in by the mother.

**21.** [Note: [Col. 0358D] *Privignus.* Two explanations are offered: either from *privo*, “one’s own,” meaning one’s own father; or because he was born earlier, before the later father. Paulus, quoted by Festus, says: “*Privignus* is so called because he was born before his mother married a second time”; the ancients used *pro* for *prae*. In common usage: *antenado* (“stepson”).]

A stepson is one born from another father. He is thought to be called *privignus*, as though *privigenus*, or as though “born earlier”; hence the common term *antenatus*.

**22.** The following terms appear to be derived from *gens* (“stock” or “clan”): *genitor*, *genitrix*; *agnati*, *agnatae*; *cognati*, *cognatae*; *progenitores*, *progenitrices*; *germani*, *germanae*.

## Likewise concerning the affinities mentioned above

**23.** My father is the author of my lineage; I am his son or daughter. My father’s father is my grandfather; I am his grandson or granddaughter. My father’s grandfather is my great-grandfather; I am his great-grandson or great-granddaughter. My father’s great-grandfather is my great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-grandson or great-great-granddaughter. My father’s great-great-grandfather is my great-great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-great-grandson or great-great-great-granddaughter. My father’s great-great-great-grandfather is my *tritavus*; I am his *trinepos* or *trineptis*.

[447] ## Concerning paternal uncles

**24.** My father’s brother is my paternal uncle; I am his brother’s son or daughter. My paternal uncle’s father is my *pater magnus*; I am his brother’s son’s or daughter’s son. My paternal uncle’s grandfather is my *propatruus*; I am his son’s or daughter’s grandson or granddaughter [Col. 0359B]. My paternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my *adpatruus*; I am his grandson’s or granddaughter’s son or daughter.

## Concerning paternal aunts

**25.** My father’s sister is my paternal aunt; I am her brother’s son or daughter. My paternal aunt’s mother is my *amita magna*; I am her brother’s daughter’s son or daughter. My paternal aunt’s grandmother is my *proamita*; I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter. My paternal aunt’s great-grandmother is my *abamita*; I am her grandson’s or granddaughter’s son or daughter.

## Concerning maternal uncles

**26.** My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; I am his sister’s son or daughter. My maternal uncle’s father is my *avunculus magnus*; I am his sister’s son’s or daughter’s son or daughter. My maternal uncle’s grandfather is my *proavunculus*; I am his son’s grandson or granddaughter. My maternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my *abavunculus*; I am his granddaughter’s son or daughter.

## Concerning maternal aunts

**27.** My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt; I am her sister’s son or daughter. [448] My maternal aunt’s sister is my *matertera magna*; I am her sister’s grandson or granddaughter. My grandmother’s sister is my *abmatertera*; I am her sister’s great-grandchild [Col. 0360B]. My great-grandmother’s sister is my *promatertera*; I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter.

[449] **28.** [Note: [Col. 0359B] “Genealogical trees are called *stemmata*.” L. *Stemmata*, *Digest* “On Degrees.” In all the most ancient books, only these two genealogical trees are described.]

[Col. 0359] **THE TREE OF LAW.**

[Col. 0361] **THE DEGREES OF HUMAN LINEAGE.**

Genealogical trees are called the little branches that advocates make in matters of lineage when they divide the degrees of kinship—for example: this one is a son, that one a father, that one a grandfather, this one an agnate and a cognate, and so forth. Their diagrams are as follows.

**GENEALOGICAL TREES OF THE HUMAN STOCK**

[Col. 0363]

[451] **29.** When this blood relationship, gradually separating itself through the successive branches of descent, has withdrawn to the final degree and ceased to be a close relationship, this law of marriage again takes it up by the bond of marriage and, in a certain sense, calls back what was fleeing (from *City of God* XV, chapter 16). Blood relationship was therefore established up to the sixth degree so that, just as the generation and condition of humanity end with the six ages of the world, so the closeness of lineage might be terminated by the same number of degrees.

[452] # CHAPTER VII. On Marriages

[Col. 0363D]

**1.** *Vir* (“man”) signifies sex, not marriage, unless one adds *vir ejus* (“her husband”).

**2.** *Maritus* (“husband”), however, denotes a spouse even without any addition; it is derived from *mare* (“male”), as though *mas* (“male”). It is a primary noun that forms *masculus* as a diminutive and *maritus* as a derivative.

**3.** A bridegroom is called *sponsus* from *spondere* (“to pledge”). Before the use of marriage tablets, men and women exchanged guarantees in which they promised one another consent to the rights of marriage and gave sureties.

**4.** Hence it became customary to call the man *sponsus*, from *spondere*, and likewise the woman *sponsa*. [Note: [Col. 0364D] Properly speaking, *spondere* means “to be willing.” Hence *sponte* (“of one’s own accord”). See Varro, Book V, and Gellius, Book IV, chapter 4.] Properly, however, *spondere* means “to be willing.” Thus the bridegroom is not so called because he is promised, but because he makes a pledge and gives sureties.

**5.** *Arrabo* (“pledge”) is said to mean “a good pledge.” Whatever is given for marriage is well given, because marriage is good. What is given for the sake of fornication or adultery is evil; therefore it is not an *arrabo*.

**6.** A pledge is called *arrha* from the thing for which it is handed over. A pledge is not only a marriage promise but also anything given in advance for any promised matter so that the promise may be fulfilled.

[Col. 0365A] **7.** [Note: [Col. 0365C] *Proci* from *procari*. From Servius.]

Suitors, applicants for marriage, are called *proci* from *procari*, that is, “to seek.”

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0365C] *Pronuba* is so called because she presides over those marrying. From Servius, on the verse “bridal Juno,” *Aeneid* IV. Festus: “*Pronubae* are brought to married women; having married once, they invoke the perpetuity of the marriage.”]

A *pronuba* is so called because she presides over those marrying and joins the bride to the bridegroom. She is also called a *paranympha*. For *nympha* means a bride at a wedding, and *nympha* also refers to the service of bathing, a word that alludes to the name of the bride.

**9.** [Note: [Col. 0365C] “*Conjuges*, and so forth.” Everything is from Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* I, chapter 11.]

Spouses are called *conjuges* because a yoke is imposed upon those joined in marriage [453]. Those marrying are accustomed to be placed under a yoke for the sake of future harmony, so that they may not separate. More properly, however, they are called *conjuges* from the first pledge of betrothal, even though sexual intercourse between them may not yet be known, as Mary is called Joseph’s wife, although there had been, and was to be, no bodily union between them.

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0365C] *Nuptae.* From the same author, *On Duties* II, chapter 19.]

Married women are called *nuptae* because they cover their faces. The term is transferred from clouds, by which the sky is covered [Col. 0365B]. Hence weddings are also called *nuptiae*, because there the heads of the marrying couple are first veiled. For *obnubere* means “to cover.”

**11.** The opposite is *innuba*, that is, an unmarried woman, who has not yet veiled her face.

**12.** [Note: [Col. 0365D] *Uxores*, as though *unxores* (“anointers”). For this was the custom. From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on the verse “of the spouse,” according to the ancient custom preserved here.]

Wives are called *uxores*, as though *unxores*. For in ancient times it was customary for girls who were marrying to come together to the threshold of the husband, adorn the doorposts with woolen ribbons before entering, and anoint them with oil. Hence they were called *uxores*, as though *unxores*. [Note: [Col. 0365D] “For this reason they were forbidden to tread on the thresholds.” An elegant explanation. Servius, however, following Varro, says that married women did not touch the threshold so that they would not begin with sacrilege, if, about to surrender their virginity, they trod upon something consecrated to Vesta; on *Eclogue* 8.]

For this reason they were forbidden to tread on thresholds, because there the doors both come together and are separated.

13. **Matron.** [Note: *Matrona*. Above, ch. 5.] A matron is a woman who has already married. She is called *matrona*, as though “mother of one born” (*mater nati*), 454 or because she can already become a mother; hence *matrimonium* is also so called. A distinction is made between a matron, a mother, and a mother of a household. [Col. 0365C] Matrons are so called because they have already entered into marriage; mothers because they have given birth; mothers of households because, through a certain solemnity of law, they have already passed into the family of their husband.

14. **Monogamous** is so called because she has married only one man. For among the Greeks, *μόνον* (*monon*) means “one alone,” while *γάμος* (*gamos*) means “marriage.”

15. **Bigamous** and **trigamous** are named from the number of wives, as though “a husband of two” or “of three.”

[Col. 0366A] 16. **Widow.** [Note: *Vidua*, “widow,” so called because she had been two with her husband—as though to say that now she is one; in this way the reading of the older books can apparently be retained. Some, following Rabanus, read it thus: “because, having been separated from her husband, she did not attach herself to the companionship of another husband.”] A widow is so called because she had been two with her husband and, after the death of her first husband, did not attach herself to the companionship of another. For women who marry another after the death of their former husband are not called widows. [Note: A widow is also so called because she is alone. As though *vidua* meant “without being two”; for, as Labeo says, *vidua* is formed like *vecors* and *vesanus*, “one without heart or sanity.” Or perhaps, more truly, as though it meant “very much divided”: for *ve-* usually intensifies, as in *vehemens* and *vescus*; and *iduare* means “to divide” or “to cleave.” Horace seems to have had this in mind:

> The Ides must be observed for you—  
> that day which cleaves April,  
> the month of sea-born Venus.

] A widow is also so called because she is alone and does not preserve the marital rights of a husband’s companionship.

17. [Note: *A brother’s wife*, *fratrissa*. Festus: “A brother’s wife is *fratria*.” Nonius: “The wives of brothers in relation to one another are called *fratriae*.”] A brother’s wife is called a *fratrissa*. A husband’s brother [Note: *Levir* … gloss … *janitrices*. Modestinus, in *Digest* “On Degrees”: “A husband’s brother is *levir*.” Among the Greeks he is called *δαήρ* (*daēr*). “A husband’s sister” is called *glos*; among the Greeks, *γάλως* (*galōs*). The wives of two brothers are called *janitrices*; among the Greeks, *εἰνατέρες* (*einateres*). Gloss: *Janitrices*, “the wives of two brothers.”] is called *levir*. The wives of two brothers in relation to one another are called *janitrices*, as though they wore down the same doorway or traveled through the same doorway. A husband’s sister is called *glos*.

18. A sister’s husband has no special name, nor does a wife’s brother.

19. [Note: *Marriage is for nobles.* Augustine. Why “for nobles”? Was it because it belonged only to Roman citizens? Or because it was performed with auspices, whereas the plebeians had no ancient auspices, as in Livy?] Marriage is the lawful agreement and condition of noble persons.

[Col. 0366B] 20. **Conjugal union** is the marriage of legitimate persons for joining and coupling with one another. It is called *conjugium* because they are joined together, or from the yoke by which they are coupled in marriage and cannot be released or separated.

21. **Connubium**, however, is formed not from *nupta* (“married woman”) but from *nubendo* (“marrying”). *Connubium* is said to exist when equals enter into marriage, for example Roman citizens of equal dignity. There is no *connubium* when a Roman citizen is joined to a Latin woman. Whenever there is no *connubium*, the children do not follow the father.

22. **Hymenaeus** is named after a certain Hymenaeus, who was the first to use marriage successfully; [Note: Or from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑμένος* (*apo tou hymenos*), “from the membrane,” which is the enclosure of virginity. Donatus, on Terence’s *Adelphoe*, at “Away with this torch, Hymenaeus,” etc. Others derive it from *ὕμην* (*hymēn*), which they say is a certain membrane by which virginity is protected.] or from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑμένος* (*apo tou hymenos*), “from the membrane” that is the enclosure of virginity.

23. **Cohabitation** is an agreement to have intercourse for a time; hence also *tabernaculum* (“tent”), because it is fixed now here, now there.

24. **Repudiation** is what is sent under the testimony of witnesses, whether in the presence or absence of the other party.

25. **Divorce** occurs whenever, after the marriage has been dissolved, one of the two pursues another marriage.

[Note: *Divortium* … from the turning of roads. Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on: “The horsemen cast themselves toward the familiar diverging roads.” “*Divortia*,” he says, “are branches of a military road.”] *Divortium* is so called from the branching of roads, that is, from roads extending in different directions.

26. [Note: *Frivolum est.* Ulpian, in the *Digest*, “On Gifts between Husband and Wife”: “If,” he says, “no divorce has intervened but only a little separation, the gift will certainly be valid if the little separation comes to an end.”] A *frivolum* is when people separate with the intention of returning to one another again. For a *frivolum* is like a shaken and dissipated mind, not a stable one. [Note: Properly, *frivola* are earthen vessels that have been broken. Hence *frivola* are words that are not supported by much credibility.] Properly, however, useless earthen vessels are called *frivola*.

27. A wife is taken for three reasons. The first is for offspring, concerning which we read in Genesis: “And he blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply’” (Gen. 1:28). The second is for assistance, concerning which it is said there in Genesis: “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2:18). The third is for the sake of incontinence; hence the Apostle says that the one who cannot contain himself should marry.

28. [Note: *In choosing a husband.* The same, Book II, *On Duties*, ch. 6. Except that there he put “eloquence” in place of “wisdom,” so that the same may perhaps be intended here in the enumeration.] In choosing a husband, four things are usually considered: virtue, lineage, beauty, and wisdom. Of these, wisdom is more powerful in producing affection of love. Virgil relates these four things concerning Aeneas, saying that they moved Dido to love him: beauty—

> Showing what a face he bore;

virtue—

> How strong in heart and arms;

eloquence—

> Alas! by what fates  
> was he tossed, and what wars  
> did he recount as endured;

lineage—

> I indeed believe—and my belief is not vain—  
> that he is of the race of the gods.

29. [Note: Likewise, four things are considered in choosing a wife. In the *Duties*, however: “Among women three things were considered: whether she was noble, whether she was well-mannered, and whether she was beautiful.” And Donatus, on Terence’s *Phormio*, Act I, scene 2: “There are four things sought in brides: beauty, uprightness, dowry, and nobility.” What he followed in the *Duties*, when he omitted the dowry or wealth—if indeed he omitted it—is not unclear.] Likewise, in choosing a wife, four things impel a man to love: beauty, lineage, wealth, and character. It is better, however, that character be sought in her rather than beauty. But nowadays those women are sought whom wealth or beauty commends, not those whom uprightness of character commends.

457 30. Women remain under the authority of a man because they are generally deceived by fickleness of mind. Therefore it was also right that they should be restrained by a man’s authority. Accordingly, the ancients wished unmarried women, even when they had reached full adulthood, to remain under guardianship because of this very fickleness of mind.

# BOOK TEN: AN ALPHABET OF CERTAIN WORDS

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367B] 1. [Note: *The origin of certain names.* Before these words, all printed books read: “The origin of certain names—that is, whence they come—is not clear to almost everyone; therefore we have inserted some things into the work for the sake of knowledge.” These words are absent from certain manuscripts; in others (as in the Salmasian and the Silian Gothic), they are separated from this beginning both by a different typeface and by the inserted title, “On Certain Human Terms.”] Although the origin of names—whence they derive—is maintained by the philosophers according to the principle that *HOMO* (“human being”) is named from *humanitas* (“humanity”), and *SAPIENS* (“wise”) from *sapientia* (“wisdom”), because wisdom comes first and the wise person afterward, nevertheless another specific explanation of the origin of certain names is clearly available, as when *homo* is derived from *humus* (“earth”), from which the human being was properly named. We have inserted some examples of these in this work.

## A

2. **Aeros**, a strong and wise man.

**Auctor** (“author”) is named from *augere* (“to increase”).

[Note: They think that *auctor* cannot be used in the feminine gender. Charisius: “He is called *auctor* because he increases and produces; and we shall say *auctrix* of a woman, because she too can increase, but when the word refers to authority it should be understood as common to both genders.” Servius says the same on *Aeneid* IX, at “I am the author of daring.” But this passage is not complete. For *cursor*, however, there is another explanation.] They think that *auctor* cannot be used in the feminine gender. For there are certain words that cannot be inflected in the feminine, such as *cursor* (“runner”).

**Actor** (“actor”) is named from *agere* (“to act”).

3. [Note: *Alumnus* … but better, “the one who nourishes.” So the older books read it. This may perhaps have seemed right to Nonius, despite ordinary usage; for he says: “Usage wishes those whom you nourish or rear, or those who are nourished, to be called *alumni*, as though reason demanded something else.”] **Alumnus** (“nursling”) is named from *alere* (“to nourish”). Yet both the one who nourishes and the one who is nourished can be called *alumnus*, that is, both the one who nurtures and the one who is nurtured; nevertheless, it is better used of the one who nourishes.

4. **Amicus** (“friend”) is, by derivation, as though “guardian of the mind” (*animi custos*). Properly, however, *amicus* is named from *hamus* (“hook”), that is, the chain of affection; hence also *hami*, because hooks hold fast.

[Col. 0367D] 5. **Lover of shameful conduct**, because such people are tormented by love of lust. **Amiable**, however, because one is worthy of love.

[Note: *Amasius*, because he is inclined toward love. Julianus the Rhetorician, quoted by Aulus Gellius, Book IX, ch. 9: “Hear and learn that even our earlier poets, whom you mentioned, were lovers and devoted to Venus.”] **Amasius** (“lover”) is so called because he is inclined toward love.

6. **Astutus** (“cunning”) is named from *astus*, which belongs to a crafty and cautious person who can do something boldly without danger.

**Argutus** (“clever”) is so called because he quickly finds an argument in speaking.

[Col. 0368C] **Acer** (“vigorous”), active and excessive in every form.

**Alacer** (“lively”), from speed and running, as though one said *aliger* (“winged”).

**Armiger** (“arms-bearer”), because he carries arms.

**Alacris** (“lively”), joyful, exulting energetically, and not disturbed by the novelty of anything.

**Agilis** (“agile”), from acting quickly at something, like *docilis* (“teachable”).

7. [Note: *Aemulus*. From Servius, *Aeneid* V, 6. As for Isidore’s addition of “amiable,” Hesiod had said the same:

> It is not only one race of Strife,  
> but upon the earth there are two:  
> the one, if understood, one would praise …

] **Aemulus** (“rival”) is devoted to the same pursuit, as an imitator and lovable; elsewhere it is found in the sense of “enemy.”

**Aequus** (“just”) is said to be just according to nature, from *aequalitas* (“equality”), that is, from being equal. Hence **aequitas** (“equity”) is also named from a certain equality. [Note: *Equity from equality.* From Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, ch. 9.]

**Aequaeuus** (“of equal age”), from being equal to another in age, that is, a contemporary.

**Arrogant**, because he is asked much and is disdainful.

**Bold** is properly used for an arrogant person.

**Courageous**, because he is full of spirit and strength.

**Animated**, as though strengthened and fortified by spirit.

[Col. 0369A] 8. **Elated**, because he raises himself above his own measure, imagining himself great because of what he does.

**Exalting**, because he raises and erects himself.

**Ambitious**, because he seeks honors.

9. **Avid** is named from *avere*, for *avere* means “to desire.” Hence also **avaricious**. For what is it to be avaricious? To proceed beyond what is sufficient. [Note: *Avaricious.* Jerome’s words, *Ecclesiastes* 5.] **Avaricious** is so called because he is greedy for gold, is never filled with riches, and the more he has, the more he desires. Horace agrees on this point when he says, “The avaricious man is always in need,” and Sallust: “Avarice is diminished neither by abundance nor by want.”

10. **Bitter** has its name transferred from taste. For it is unpleasant and knows how to invite no one into its company by any sweetness.

[Col. 0369B] **Adulterer**, a violator of marital modesty, because he pollutes another man’s marriage bed.

11. [Note: *Anceps.* Augustine, *On Grammar*.] **Uncertain**, wavering this way and that, and doubtful whether to choose this or that, anxiously inclining to one side or the other.

**Atrocious**, because he has grim character.

**Abstemious**, from *temetum*, that is, wine, as though abstaining from wine.

**Weaned**, because he has been taken away from milk.

12. **Sick**, because he is driven for a time by illness or sadness.

**Ill**, because he is sick more frequently, just as *iratus* (“angry”) and *iracundus* (“irascible”) differ.

**Miserable**, named from *rumen* (“throat” or “stomach”), because, made wretched by poverty, he hungers and thirsts.

13. **Auspice**, because he attends to the omens of birds, just as **bird-catcher** is so called because he catches birds.

[Note: *Astrosus.* The common language retains the same word.] **Astrosus**, named from *astrum* (“star”), as though born under an evil star.

14. **Enormous**, because it exceeds rule and measure.

[Col. 0369C] **Cattle-raider**, a thief of beasts of burden and livestock, whom common usage calls an *abigeus*, from driving them away.

15. [Note: *Atratus.* — *Atamus*, in an old codex.] **Clad in black**, and **clad in white**: the former from a black garment, the latter from a white one.

[Note: *Advena.* Ambrose, on Psalm 38: “An *advena* is one who comes from elsewhere; an *accola* is one who inhabits a place for a time.”] **Stranger**, because he comes from elsewhere.

**Foreigner**, one born from another people and not from the one among whom he is. Likewise, a foreigner is one who belongs to another region and not to the one where he is.

16. **Resident**, because, having arrived, he cultivates the land.

**Farmer**, from cultivating a field, like *silvicola* (“forest-dweller” or “forest-cultivator”).

**Follower**, because he follows someone for the sake of profit.

17. [Note: *Assiduus.* Charisius: “Some write *adsiduus*, as though it were formed from sitting, but they are mistaken. When Servius Tullius divided the people into five classes, so that each contributed by tribes according to his property, the wealthier, who paid *asses*, were called *assidui*. And because only they were regularly present at public business, those who frequently attend were called *assidui*, from *asses*. Hence Gellius says that *assiduus* in the Twelve Tables, meaning wealthy and easily able to perform a service, was derived from *asses*. Caper derives it from *adsidere*. We read “for the expense of the treasury” from the Roman codex. The remaining reading, “to the treasury expense,” makes no sense unless one prefers “treasury expense.”] Among the ancients, **assiduous** was said of one who contributed *asses* toward the expense of the treasury and was also frequent in public business. Hence it should be written with *s*, not with *d*.

[Col. 0370A] 18. **Apparitor** (“attendant”) is named because he appears, is seen, and is ready for service.

**Attentive**, as one who retains what he hears.

19. [Note: *Attonitus.* Servius, *Aeneid* III: “*Attonitus*, astonished. Properly, one is called *attonitus* when the circumstance and sound of a nearby thunderbolt produce stupor.”] **Thunderstruck**, as though stirred by a kind of frenzy and rendered stupefied. He is called *attonitus* from the crash of thunder, as though stunned by thunder and by nearby lightning or by being struck close at hand.

20. **Chosen**, because openly chosen.

[Note: *Abactus*, “removed,” because he has been taken away from office. Festus: “Magistrates were called *abacti* when, compelled, they laid down their authority.”] **Removed**, because he has been removed from action.

**Aborted**, because it does not arise but miscarries and falls away.

**Adopted**, because he has been openly desired as a son.

21. **Both** derives from the Greek *ἄμφω* (*amphō*), a Greek name made Latin by changing the third letter.

[Note: *Alius* in relation to many. From Servius, *Aeneid* XI.] **One other** is used of several, whereas **the other** is used of two.

**Ambidextrous**, so called because he uses a sword without hesitation with either hand.

[Col. 0370B] ## B

22. **Blessed** [Note: *Beatus*, as though “well increased.” Cassiodorus, on Psalm 1: “*Beatus*, according to the authority handed down to us by our ancestors, is said as though *bene aptus*, ‘well fitted,’ one to whom all desired things succeed.] is so called as though “well increased,” namely, from possessing what he wishes and suffering nothing he does not wish. Truly blessed, however, is the one who both possesses all good things he wishes [Note: “And wishes nothing evil.” Thus the Gothic books and Augustine, *On the Trinity* XIII, not “badly.”] and wishes nothing evil. From these two things the human being becomes blessed.

23. **Good** is thought to have been named from bodily beauty; afterward the name was transferred to the spirit. We call one good whom evil does not prevail over; [Note: And “best” is the one who sins least. Horace:

> No one is born without faults; the best person is he  
> who is burdened by the fewest.

] and we call best the one who sins least.

24. **Kind** is a person spontaneously ready to do good and sweet in speech. Yet “kind” does not differ greatly from “good,” since the kind person also appears ready to do good. The difference is that a good person may be somewhat gloomy and may do good and provide what is requested, yet may not know how to be pleasant company. A kind person, however, knows how to invite everyone by his sweetness.

25. **Beneficent** is named from doing good to another; hence also **beneficence**, which benefits one’s neighbor.

462 26. **Well-disposed** is so called because he wishes well. Yet we do not say *benevolus*, just as we do not say *malevolus*. Often a compound word corrupts either the first or the second letter of its two parts; [Note: For *benevolentia* sounds absurd. The parts cohere less well if one remains intact, and *volentia* by itself is an absurd word to Latin ears; moreover, as the Halicarnassian says, *i* is a lighter sound than *e*, and in composing words we strive for a less burdensome conjunction of several words. Nevertheless, this later age adopted *benevolentia*.] hence *benevolentia* sounds absurd.

27. **Affectionate**, sweet and inviting others to intimacy with him.

28. **Brutus**, as though *obrutus* (“buried”), because he lacks understanding. For he is without reason and prudence. Thus that Junius Brutus, born of the sister of Tarquinius Superbus, fearing the fate that had befallen his brother—who had been killed by his uncle because of his wealth and intelligence—pretended a useful stupidity for the time. Hence he was also surnamed Brutus, although he was called Junius.

29. **Stammerer**, named from bleating rather than speaking, because he cannot articulate words. Hence also **lisping**, because he breaks his words.

30. [Note: *Bucco.* Gloss: *Buccones*, *παράσιτοι* (*parasitoi*, “parasites”), *βουκκιώνες* (*boukkiōnes*). Apuleius, *Apology* 2: “They will appear utterly gaunt, like *buccones*.”] **Babbler**, a chatterer, because he surpasses others in loquacity of mouth, not in understanding.

**Bilious**, because he is always sad, from the black humor called bile.

31. [Note: *Baburrus.* Gloss: *Baburra*, *ἄφρων* (*aphrōn*), *ἀνόητος* (*anoētos*), *μάταιος* (*mataios*), “senseless, foolish, vain.”] **Baburrus**, foolish and inept.

[Note: *Biothanatus.* Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on “I shall be present as a shade in every place”: Physicists say that the souls of those who die by violence are not received back into their origin. The word is frequent in Julius Firmicus, Cassian, and Tertullian.] **Biothanatus**, one who has died by violence; for *θάνατος* (*thanatos*) means “death” in Greek.

## C

[Col. 0371B] 32. **Bright** is named from heaven, because it shines; hence also “a bright day,” from the brightness of the sky.

**Lofty** is named from heaven, because it is elevated and high, as though “heavenly.”

463 33. **Chaste** was first named from castration; afterward the ancients also chose to call those chaste who promised perpetual abstinence from lust.

34. [Note: *Caeles.* Augustine, *On Grammar*: “*Praeses*, *dives*, *haeres*, *coeles*, *coelites*—those who make their way to heaven.” Ovid also uses *coelite* in the singular, *Letters from Pontus* V:

> What I could, Brutus, from a recent inhabitant of heaven,  
> I have sent as a poem to your shores, though placed far away.

] **Heaven-bound** is so called because he makes his way to heaven.

[Note: *Caelebs.* Quintilian, Book I, ch. 5: “Gaius seems ingeniously to have said *coelibes*, as though *coelites*, because they lack a very heavy burden.” And Jerome, *Against Jovinian* II: “*Caelebs*, because they are worthy of heaven, is the name given to them.”] **Celibate**, without marriage, [Note: Such are the divine beings in heaven. Augustine’s words at the cited passage.] like the divine beings in heaven who are without spouses. And *caelebs* is said [Note: As though “blessed by heaven.” Another reading: “fitted to heaven.”] as though “blessed by heaven.”

**Heaven-dweller**, because he inhabits heaven; he is an angel.

35. **Self-controlled** is said not only of chastity but also of food and drink, and likewise of anger, mental distress, and the desire to slander. He is self-controlled because he abstains from many evils.

[Col. 0371C] 36. **Merciful**, because he *cluat*, that is, protects and defends, as a patron customarily protects his client.

37. **Harmonious** is named from the joining of the heart; for just as one is called a partner who joins his lot to another’s, so one is called harmonious who is joined in heart.

38. **Orator**, one who addresses a multitude.

**Comforter**, one who addresses a single person. He is called a comforter because he applies himself to the one whom he addresses and lightens his solitude by his speech; hence also *solacium* (“comfort”).

39. [Note: *Consultus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “They depart without counsel.”] **Advised** is one who is consulted; opposed to him is the **unadvised** person, who does not accept counsel.

40. **Steadfast** is so called because he stands firm on every side and cannot be made to incline in any direction.

[Col. 0372A] **Confident**, because he is full of trust in everything. Hence Caecilius: “If you have confidence, trust everything.”

41. **Cautious** is named from *cavere* (“to beware”).

**Crafty**, fraudulent, because he knows how to conceal and is skilled in wrongdoing.

[Note: *Callidus* … used for “cleverly learned.” Horace:

> I was setting down a hundred thousand for this sign, cleverly.

] The ancients used **crafty** not only for “cunning” but also for “cleverly learned.” Such a person is also **versatile**, because he quickly turns his mind.

42. **Greedy** is named from *capere* (“to take”) in the sense of taking much, that is, receiving.

**Loud**, as though *calamosus* (“reed-like”), from *calamus* (“reed”), because it makes a sound.

[Note: *Calumniator* … from *calvere*. Gaius, ch. 233, *On the Meaning of Words*: “If he deceives, delays, and frustrates.” Hence accusers were called *calumniatores*, because by fraud and harassment they troubled others with lawsuits. Hence also *cavillatio* (“quibbling”) is so called.] **Calumniator**, an accuser of a false crime, is named from *calvere*, that is, from frustrating and deceiving.

43. **Calculator** is named from *calculi*, that is, small stones, which the ancients held in their hands while arranging numbers.

44. [Note: *Compilator.* Festus: “To compile is to collect into one and store up” [or “crush together”]. He likewise says: “*Pilare* and *compilare* are words of Greek origin … for the Greeks call thieves *πειραταί* (*peiratai*).”] **Compiler**, one who mixes the words of others with his own, as apothecaries customarily crush different ingredients together in a mortar.

[Col. 0372B] This crime was once charged against that Mantuan poet, when, transferring certain verses of Homer, he mixed them with his own; and when his rivals called him a compiler of the ancients, he replied: “It requires great strength to wrest Hercules’ club from his hand.”

45. **Obstinate**, from despising.

**Chromatic**, because he does not become confused or change color; for in Greek *χρῶμα* (*chrōma*) means “color.”

46. **Insulting**, because he is swift and swells up in words of abuse.

**Contentious**, named from contention, one who asserts something not by reason but by sheer stubbornness.

47. **Contemptible**, either because he is suited to contempt or because he has been despised and is worthless, that is, without honor.

48. **Cruel**, that is, raw; the Greeks call such a person *ὠμός* (*ōmos*), by metaphor, as though uncooked and unfit for eating. For he is harsh and hard.

49. [Note: *Carnifex.* Donatus, on *Hecyra*: “Flesh properly refers to the dead; hence executioners are called *carnifices*, because they make flesh out of a human being.”] **Executioner**, because he makes flesh.

[Note: *Cruciarius.* Petronius: “And so, when the parents of that crucified man saw that the guard had been relaxed, they took him down at night while he was hanging.”] **One worthy of crucifixion**, because he is deserving of the cross.

**Colleague** is named from the binding together of partnership and the embrace of friendship.

**Contemporary**, as though an equal in age.

465 50. **Accomplice**, one who has been attached to another in evil through one sin or crime. We never use *complice* of a person attached to another for good.

51. **Partner**, because a share of the goods belongs to him; for the ancients used *sors* (“lot”) for “share.” Thus *consors* means “sharing the same lot,” just as *dissors* means “of a different lot.”

[Note: As in *dissors*. Augustine, *On Grammar*: *Dissors* means “of a dissimilar lot.”]

[Col. 0373A] 52. **Swift** is named from swiftness, because he does quickly what necessity requires.

**Neighboring**, from being related by origin or place.

**Colonist**, from a colony or from cultivating a field.

53. **Guardian**, because he assumes care of children who are still of an age at which they cannot adequately manage their own affairs.

**Legal representative**, named from recognizing or hearing a case.

[Note: *Clientes.* From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “whether a parent has been struck, or an injured client.”] **Clients** were first called *colentes* (“cultivators” or “worshipers”), from cultivating or honoring their patrons.

54. **Captus** … [lacuna]

**Captive** is said as though “diminished in head,” for the fortune of free birth has fallen away from him; hence jurists also call him *capite diminutus* (“diminished in status”).

55. [Note: *Colomis.* Hence *incolumis*, from *columna* (“column”) or *columen* (“summit”). Donatus, on *Phormio*: “*Columen*, *culmen*—or is *columen* a column? Vitruvius, Book IV, ch. 20: ‘*Columen* is at the highest point of the roof’s ridge; hence columns are also so called.’”] **Colomis** is named from *columna* (“column”), because he is upright and extremely firm.

56. **Well-groomed** is named from *coma* (“hair”), because he is handsome in his hair, or because he tends his hair.

57. **Curled**, from *calamistrum*, that is, an iron instrument made in the shape of a reed, in which the hair is twisted so that it becomes curly. Those who curl their hair customarily heat it in ashes, so that it may be *calamistratus* (“curled”).

58. **Corpulent**, because he is strong in body and has soft flesh.

**Fat**, from the body’s fatness, from producing flesh.

**Glutton**, from eating excessively. 466 For he is immoderately devoted to his throat and belly.

[Note: *The worst tavern-keeper.* Jerome, on Isaiah I: “Heretics also corrupt evangelical truth through perverse interpretation, and they are the worst tavern-keepers, making water out of wine.”] **The worst tavern-keeper**, one who makes water out of wine.

59. **White**: *canus* (“hoary”) is named from whiteness, and *candidus* (“bright white”) as though “whiteness bestowed.” Whiteness is acquired through cultivation or care, whereas being white is a matter of nature.

[Col. 0373C] 60. [Note: *Clodus … Curvus … Crispus.* Some more recent books fill these gaps, but in such a way that it is not worth reporting.] **Clodus** … **Curved** … **Curly** …

**Blind** is so called because he lacks sight. For he has lost the light of his eyes. A blind person is one who cannot see with either eye.

61. **Fallen** is named from falling; it also means **lunatic**, because he suffers at a fixed time of the moon.

**Confused** is named from the confusion of crime; hence also *confusion*.

62. **Wrenched away** is said of one from whom his possessions are taken by some force. Hence also a ship is said to be wrenched apart when its projecting parts are torn away by the force of a storm. Thus Virgil says: “Scarcely seven, torn by the waves,” as though “mutilated.”

63. **Consumed**, entirely used up and devoured.

**Procuress**, named from the association of shameful collusion, because she intervenes and traffics in another person’s body. She is also called a *laena*.

[Col. 0373D] 64. **Forum-rover**, one who wanders around forums and assemblies for the sake of legal advocacy.

[Note: *Collegiatus.* There is a title “On Collegiate Associations” in Book XI of the Code.] **Member of a corporation** … **Carpenter** …

[Col. 0374A] 65. **Lord** is named by derivation from presiding over a household.

**Eloquent**, learned, from *disserere* (“to discuss”), for he discusses matters in an orderly way.

66. **Learned** is named from teaching; hence also *teacher*.

**Teachable** does not mean one who is learned, but one who can be taught; for he is intelligent and suited to learning.

**Student** is named from *disciplina* (“discipline”), and *disciplina* is named from learning.

67. **Steward** is called one to whom the administration of money is entrusted. 467 He is called *dispensator* because formerly those who gave money did not count it but weighed it.

68. [Note: *Dives* (“rich”) from *aes* (“bronze, money”). Some Gothic books derive it from *habere* (“to have”).] **Rich** is named from money.

[Note: *Decorus* … from *decem* (“ten”). Seguinus: from *decere* (“to be fitting”).] **Becoming**, perfect, from ten.

[Col. 0374B] **Sweet** … **Decent**, orderly, is named from the number ten. Hence also *decorus* (“becoming”) and *decibilis* (“suitable”).

69. **Straight** is so called because it goes in a straight line.

**Beloved** is named from diligence. For these are the signs of loving.

70. [Note: *Delibutus.* From Donatus on *Phormio*, at “If I return you drenched in joy.”] **Anointed**, smeared with oil, as athletes are, or as boys are in the wrestling school. Hence *delibutus gaudio* (“drenched in joy”), that is, “filled” or “covered over.”

**Delicate**, because he has been nourished on luxuries, living at banquets and in bodily refinement.

71. **Exhausted**, always weak, as though long wearied.

**Weak**, because he has been made fragile through bile. For bile is a humor that affects the body.

**Discolored**, because color is lacking in him.

72. **Desperate** is commonly used of a bad and ruined person, with no remaining hope of anything prosperous. It is said by analogy with the sick, who, afflicted and without hope, are laid down. It was customary among the ancients for the desperate to be placed before their doors, either to give back their final breath to the earth or so that passersby who had once suffered from a similar illness might perhaps treat them.

[Note: *Desperati … it was customary.* These are Servius’s words, not an interpretation of *desperati* but of *depositi*. *Aeneid* XII, on “he, like one laid aside by a serious illness.” If these words do not fit sufficiently, this is less surprising because Isidore used Servius’s commentaries without Virgil’s verses, as Chacon correctly inferred and as is clear from other passages of this work.]

73. **Degenerate**, either ignoble, or one of unequal birth, or one who, although born of the best lineage, nevertheless lives dishonorably.

74. **Decrepit**, because he is nearer to death and as though turning toward the darkness of death, like twilight, the time of night. Others say that *decrepit* refers not to one removed by old age but to one who has already ceased to make a sound, that is, ceased to speak.

[Col. 0374D] 75. [Note: *Depretiatus.* This word is used by the ancient translator of the Bible, Tertullian, and other ecclesiastical writers.] **Worthless**, because he is vile and worthy of no price.

[Note: *Dirus*, “very sparing” and “grim.” This is not unreasonable, for *dirus* is opposed to *comis* (“courteous”). Cicero, in *Cato Maior*: “How much courtesy in one, how much grimness in the other?” The remainder is from Servius, *Aeneid* II and VI.] **Dire**, extremely sparing and grim, as though driven to this by divine anger. For something is called *dirum* when it is inflicted by divine wrath. Elsewhere **dire** means “great.”

76. [Note: *Dehiscens.* From the same source, *Aeneid* I, on “the water opening wide.”] **Gaping open**, very widely opening. Here *de-* is an intensifier, as in *deamare* (“to love intensely”) and *desidere* (“to sit very much”).

**Looking down**, because he looks downward or holds something in contempt.

**Deceitful**, treacherous or malicious, from deceiving. To deceive, he adorns hidden malice with flattering speech.

77. **Doubtful**, uncertain, as though standing at two roads.

**Informer**, so called because he reveals what was hidden.

**Delayer**, because he postpones bringing something forward.

**Lazy**, slow and idle, named from *desidere*, that is, “to sit very much”; likewise *reses* (“sluggish”), from *residere* (“to sit back”). Here *de-* is an intensifier.

78. [Note: *Delirus* … “they direct furrows into which the whole crop runs.” He used *sulcos* (“furrows”) for *porcos* or *liras*; for the crop does not run into furrows, but water does from the *lirae*. See Varro and Columella.] **Deranged**, mentally impaired through age, from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ληρεῖν* (*apo tou lērein*, “to rave”), or because he strays from the straight course and, as it were, from a *lira*. A *lira* is a type of plowing in which, after sowing, farmers make straight furrows into which the whole crop runs.

79. **Mad**, the same as *amens*, that is, “without mind,” or because he has a diminished mind.

**Unwise**, because he begins to have less wisdom than he was accustomed to have.

80. **Condemned** and **condemnable**: the former has already been sentenced, while the latter can be sentenced.

[Note: *Degulator.* Apuleius, *Apology* 2: “All these things, nevertheless, this glutton diligently stored in his belly within a few years.” Augustine also uses *degulo* in his *On Grammar*.] **Glutton**, because he is devoted to his throat.

469 ## E

81. **Elated**, because he raises himself above his own measure, imagining himself great because of what he does.

[Note: *Enormis.* Some had preferred *anormis*, since the Gothic book has *aenormis* and another also has *anormis*; but the interpretation does not agree. For *anormis* means “without rule.” Horace:

> A rustic, wise without rule, and with a thick Minerva.

*Enormis* means “outside the rule.” It is still more absurd that above, under A, we find *Enormis*, *Helatus*, and *Heros*, because in the books there are *Aeros*, *Aenormis*, and *Aelatus*.] **Enormous**, because it exceeds rule and measure.

82. **Eloquent**, lavish in speech.

[Col. 0375C] **Ready-spoken**, fluent in speaking. For *exerere* means “to bring forth” or “to make ready.”

[Note: *Eruditus.* See Cassiodorus, on Psalm 2.] **Learned**, because he is not uncultivated but already educated.

83. **Experienced**, very skilled; here *ex-* means “very.”

**Unskilled**, one who is outside skill and understanding.

**Highly adorned**, very richly adorned; here *ex-* means “very,” as in *excelsus*, “very high.”

84. **Distinguished**, as though “very eminent.”

**Effective** is so called because he encounters no difficulty in carrying out any matter; hence also **effecting**, named from doing.

**Hopeless**, because he is without hope.

**Without a share**, because he is outside a portion and has lacked a share.

**Without a lot**, because he is outside the lot.

[Col. 0376A] 85. [Note: *Exsul.* From Servius, *Aeneid* III.] **Exile**, because he is outside his own soil, as though sent across the soil or wandering outside it.

[Note: For they are said to *exsulare*. From the same source, *Aeneid* XI.] For those who go outside their own soil are said to be in exile.

86. [Note: *Extorris.* From the same source, *Aeneid* IV, on “an exile from his borders.”] **Banished**, because he is outside his own land, as though “out of the lands.” Properly, however, one is *extorris* when expelled by force and driven from his native soil with terror; an *extorris* is one driven from his own land.

87. **Extorris**, outside one’s land—or outside one’s own boundaries, because one is terrified away.

88. [Note: *Exterminator.* The Greek characters are not uniform here. Manuscripts have nothing for *ἐξορίστου* (*exoristou*), while all have something for *ἀφανίστου* (*aphanistou*). Therefore we wrote what the books seemed to prefer, *ἀφανὴς εἶναι* (*aphanēs einai*, “to be invisible”); nor do we reject *ἀφανιστής* (*aphanistēs*, “destroyer”), which Augustine preferred.] **Exterminator**, not the one commonly called *ἀφανὴς εἶναι* (*aphanēs einai*, “to be invisible”), but the one who casts down and expels from the boundaries of the city.

**Exterminated**, from being driven outside one’s own boundaries; likewise **foreign**, because it belongs to another land.

89. Egens and egenus, “without a people” and “without lineage,” that is, needy.

Exiguus, greatly needy. For *ex* is used to mean “very.”

[Note: *Exilis* ... or “without them.” See Festus, or rather Servius.] Exilis, thin, because it can pass out through a narrow opening (or “without them”).

90. Exesus, as though “eaten through.” For it is dry, thin, and slender.

Exhaustus, because it has been consumed and rendered empty.

Exsanguis, because it is “outside the blood,” that is, bloodless.

91. [Note: *Exanimis*. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “and lifeless with gold.”] Exanimis means dead. We also say *exanimis* and *exanimus*, just as *unanimus* and *unanimis*, *inermus* and *inermis*; this is subject to our discretion.

92. Exustus is said of something of which nothing remains, as though “thoroughly burned.” For *ex* is used to mean “very.”

Exosus is derived from *odium*, hatred; [Note: For the ancients said both *odi* (“I hate”) and *osus sum* (“I am hateful”). From the same source, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “if you have not yet hated utterly.”] for the ancients said both *odi* and *osus sum. Hence comes *exosus*, which we use, [Col. 0376C] although we no longer say *osus*.

93. Effractor, because he is a conqueror of barriers.

Exitiosus, because he is ruinous to many.

Exsecutor, from *exsequi*, “to carry out”; the same as *exactor*.

Efferatus, made savage in mind and exceeding the human manner.

Effrenatus, from being headlong and inclined forward, and without the bridle of reason.

94. Eunuchus is a Greek word, meaning *spado*, a castrated man. Some of these engage in intercourse, but there is nevertheless no generative power in their seed. For they have fluid and emit it, but it is empty and incapable of generation.

95. [Note: *Effeta*. From the same source, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “and the strength in her body grows cold, exhausted.”] Effeta is derived from having been exhausted by frequent childbirth; for continual birth has made her weak.

[Col. 0377A] 471 F.

96. Facundus is so called because he can speak easily.

Facetus is one who commends jokes and amusements by gestures and actions; it is derived from *facere*, “to do.”

Frugalis is named from *frux*, “produce,” that is, from fruitfulness or thrift—or, as others wish, from modesty and self-restraint.

97. [Note: *Fenerator* is Latin. From Augustine, on Psalm XXXVI.] Fenerator is one who places money with a debtor, as though an agent of interest; for *fenus* means money. In Latin, however, *fenerator* means both the one who lends and the one who borrows.

Flamines, priests of idols.

98. [Note: *Felix*. Servius, *Aeneid* I: *felix* is said both of one who possesses happiness and of one who makes another happy.] Felix is said of one who gives happiness; *felix* of one who receives it; and *felix* of that through which happiness is given, as “a fortunate time” or “a fortunate place.”

[Col. 0377B] 99. Fidelis, because what he says or what he promises is made true by him.

Facilis, from *facere*, “to do,” because he is not slow.

Firmus, from which also comes *formosus*.

Fortis, because he bears adversities or whatever may occur; or from *ferrum*, iron, because he is hard and does not soften.

100. [Note: *Formosus* ... The ancients called *formum* “hot.” Thus it should be read below, book XIX, chapter 7, under *Forcipes*, and in Servius—whose words these are, *Aeneid* VIII—not *forvum*; and in Nonius under *Faunus*. See Festus under *Forcipes* ... *Forma* ... and *Formucalis*, and Donatus, on *Phormio*, act I, scene 2, at the words “These would extinguish the beauty.”] Formosus is derived from *formus*. For the ancients called *formum* “hot” and “boiling.” Heat stirs the blood, and blood produces beauty.

101. [Note: *Foedus*. Festus: the ancients said *foedum* for *hoedum*, “kid”; *folus* for *holere*, “to smell”; *fostem* for *hostem*, “enemy”; and *fostiam* for *hostiam*, “victim.”] Foedus takes its name from the he-goat and the kid, with the letter *f* added. [Note: The ancients used this word in a serious sense. Servius, *Aeneid* II: in Virgil as well as in Sallust, *foedus* does not mean shameful but cruel.] The ancients used it in a serious sense, as in:

> Staining with blood the fires that he himself had consecrated.

472 Fragilis is so called because it can easily be broken.

102. Fessus, as though *fissus*, “split”; for it is no longer whole in health. It is a general term. We speak of being weary in spirit, as in “three times weary, he sat down in the valley”; of being weary in body, which is the more proper sense; and of being weary from circumstances that come through misfortune.

Fatigatus, as though “driven by the Fates.”

103. Formidolosus is derived from *formus*, that is, blood, when the blood, fleeing from the skin toward the heart, contracts; for fear chills the blood, and the blood, being constricted, produces dread. Hence the line:

> And the blood, chilled by fear, congeals.

[Note: *Formidolosus*, since it means “timid.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IV.] *Formidolosus*, however, means both “timid” and “to be feared.”

104. [Note: *Fatuus*. From the same source, *Aeneid* VII, on the verse “to Faunus and the nymphs.” But Justin, book XLIII: Faunus had a wife named Fatua, who, filled continually with divine inspiration, foretold future events as if in a frenzy. Hence those who are accustomed to be inspired are still called *fatui*. Faunus himself, as we reported above from Servius, was also called *Fatuus Fatuelis*.] Fatuus is thought to have been so called because he understands neither what he himself says nor what others say. Some think that *fatuus* derives from those who gazed in wonder at Fatua, the prophetic wife of Faunus, and that they were first called *fatui* because they were excessively stupefied by her prophecies, even to the point of madness.

105. Fautor, from favoring and agreeing.

[Note: *Fictor* ... “softens.” Others read “anoints.”] Fictor is named from *fingere*, “to fashion” or “compose” something, as one who softens and handles women’s hair, oils it, and makes it glossy.

Fallax, because he deceives by *fari*, that is, by speaking.

473 106. Fervidus, irascible, for anger inflames.

Frendens, because, by threatening, he breaks and clenches his teeth.

Fremens ...

Ferox, because he exercises savagery, like a beast.

107. [Note: *Fur*. See Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 8.] Fur is derived from *furvus*, that is, dark, because he operates at night.

[Note: *Factiosus* ... when it means “influential” and powerful. Glossary: *factio*, τάγμα, “a formation.” Suetonius, *Nero*: “He selected five thousand young men who, divided into factions, learned the various kinds of applause.” And Plautus, *Aulularia*: “I care nothing for those great factions, those lavish dowries.” Hence *factiosi* means powerful and influential within factions.] Factiosus, as an insult, when we intend “seditious”; but when we mean “influential and powerful,” it is as though one belonged to a great faction.

108. Facinorosus is named from a deed committed; for he does what harms another.

[Note: *Femellarius*. This word was absent from most Gothic manuscripts; it was present in Ovetus.] Femellarius, devoted to women, whom the ancients called *mulierarius*.

Flagitiosus, because he frequently demands and desires lust.

109. [Note: *Furcifer*. From Donatus. See the Glossary under *furcifer*, σταυροκόμιστος, “cross-bearer,” and so forth.] Furcifer was formerly said of one who, for a minor offense, was compelled by his masters to carry a forked stake along the road—not so much as punishment as for disgrace—proclaiming his offense and warning others not to commit anything similar.

110. Futilis, empty, vain, superfluous, and talkative; it is a metaphor from earthen vessels, which, when cracked and fissured, do not retain what one pours into them.

111. Fornicarius ...

Fornicatrix is one whose body is public and common. Such women stood for sale beneath arched structures, which are called *fornices*; hence *fornicariae*. Virgil:

> And beneath the facing arch.

112. Fecunda is derived from *fetus*, “offspring,” as though “abundant in offspring”; for she is prolific in childbirth.

Feta ...

Flens, as though “flowing with tears.”

No one is properly called *fugitivus* except one who flees from his master. If a little boy leaves his nurse or his school, he is not a fugitive.

G

113. Gloriosus is named from an abundance of brightness, with the letter *g* substituted for *c*. Gloriosus is also derived from the laurel awarded to victors.

Gnarus, knowing; its opposite is *ignarus*, unknowing.

Gravis, venerable; hence we also call contemptible people *leves*, “light.” *Gravis* is named from deliberation and steadfastness, because one does not leap away with a light movement but remains fixed through the gravity of constancy.

114. Grandis ...

Gracilis ...

Grandaevus, because he is great in age.

Gratus, preserving gratitude; but *gratus* is said only of the mind, whereas *gratissimus* is said of both mind and body.

Gratificus, because he does good freely.

[Note: *Gratiosus*. Aulus Gellius, book IX, chapter 12: *gratiosus* means both one who shows favor and one who receives it.] Gratiosus, one who grants each person more than he deserves.

115. Garrulus is properly said of one commonly called *verbosus*, “wordy,” who, with joy added, is unable or unwilling to be silent. The word is taken from the birds called *graculi*, which constantly make an intrusive racket and never rest.

[Note: *Ganeo* ... “as if in hidden and underground places.” Festus: the ancients called a hidden place, as if beneath the earth, a *ganeum*. Donatus, on *Adelphoe*: the ancients called a brothel a *ganeum*, ἀπὸ τῆς γᾶς, τοῦτό ἐστι τῆς γῆς, “from the earth,” because it itself is in the earth, unlike upper chambers; hence *taberna*, as though *trabena*, from the stronger beams by which upper stories are suspended.] Ganeo, a pleasure-seeker, and as though located in hidden and underground places, which the Greeks call *ganea*.

[Note: *Glutto*. Augustine, in *On Grammar*: *heluo*, also *glutto*. Festus: *ingluvies* is derived from *gula*, “throat”; hence *ingluviosus*, *glutto*, and *gulo*.] Glutto, from *gula*, that is, a glutton.

H

116. Heros [Note: *Heros*. The same author above, book I, chapter 39: heroes are called men, as though “aerial” and worthy of heaven, on account of wisdom and courage. See Servius, *Aeneid* I, and Augustine, *City of God* X, chapter 21; Socrates in the *Cratylus* differs greatly from them. In old books *aeros* is written with an *A*.] is a wise and courageous man.

Humilis, [Note: *Humilis* ... “inclining toward the ground.” Thus all the Gothic manuscripts.] as though inclined toward the ground.

Honorabilis, as though “suited to honor,” that is, worthy of it.

117. [Note: *Honestus* ... “a state of honor.” Others read “honor standing.”] Honestus, because it contains nothing shameful; for what is *honestas* except perpetual honor, that is, as though a state of honor?

Humanus, because he possesses love and a disposition of compassion toward human beings; hence *humanitas*, by which we protect one another.

[Col. 0379C] 475 118. Habilis, because it is convenient and suitable for possessing.

Honorosus is more than *honoratus*, just as *scelerosus* is more than *sceleratus*.

Hirsutus, because it is *hirtus*, “rough,” and bristling with hair.

119. [Note: *Hypocrita*. From Augustine, sermon 1 on the Friday after Pentecost.] Hypocrita, translated from the Greek into Latin, means “pretender.” Although inwardly evil, he publicly presents himself as good. For ὑπό means “false,” and κρίσις means “judgment.”

120. The name *hypocrita* is taken from the appearance of those who walk about in spectacles with their faces covered, distinguishing their features with blue, red, and other pigments. They wore likenesses of mouths made of linen, coated with plaster and marked in various colors; sometimes they also smeared their necks and hands with chalk, so as to achieve the color of the character and deceive the people while acting in the games—now in the appearance of a man, now of a woman; now shaven, now long-haired; now old, now maidenly; and in every other appearance, age, and sex, so as to deceive the people while they performed in the games.

121. This kind of theatrical device has been transferred to those who walk about with a false appearance and pretend to be what they are not. For they cannot be called hypocrites from the moment they have gone outside.

122. Humatus, because it is covered with earth, that is, buried.

Hilaris is a Greek word.

I

123. Ingeniosus, because inwardly he possesses the power to generate any art.

Inventor is so called because he comes upon what he seeks. Hence *inventio* itself, if we retrace the origin of the word, suggests nothing other than that *invenire* means “to come upon that which is sought.”

124. [Note: *Interpres*. Servius, *Aeneid* X, on the verse “that third interpreter of the gods” ... *Interpres* is a mediator: both the interpreter of the gods and the interpreter of human beings, who makes the divine intentions known, is called an *interpres*.] Interpres, because he stands between the parties of two languages [Col. 0380B] while translating. The one who stands between God, whom he interprets, and human beings, to whom he reveals divine mysteries, is also called an *interpres*.

125. Juridicus, because he speaks the laws and legal rights.

Indoles is properly a certain image of future virtue.

Justus is so called because he preserves legal rights and lives according to the law.

126. [Note: *Innox*. Glossary: *innox*, ἀβλαβής, “harmless.”] Innox, because it causes no harm.

Innocuus, one who has not been harmed; but among the ancients the two words are interchangeable.

Jocundus, because he is always suited to jokes and cheerfulness; it is derived from abundance, as is *iracundus*.

Jocosus, one who uses jokes.

127. Inclytus is a Greek word. For the Greeks call κλυτόν “glorious.”

[Col. 0380C] Illustris is a name of renown, because one shines before many through the splendor of lineage, wisdom, or virtue. Its opposite is *obscure natus*, “of obscure birth.”

Idoneus ...

128. Incolumis takes its name from *columna*, “column,” as though upright, strong, and stable.

Immarcescibilis, incorruptible and everlasting, because it is without decay or languor.

Intemeratus, incorruptible and violated by no rashness.

129. Infirmus, because it is without *formus*, that is, without heat.

Imbecillis, as though “without a staff,” fragile and unstable.

Inanis, light.

130. Inconstans, because it is not stable: what pleases it displeases it again.

Jactans, or arrogant, is one who does not submit to the institutions of his predecessors but seeks some private path of justice and holiness.

[Note: *Iracundus* ... “for just as a flame.” This is often repeated. In Hebrew, “light.”] Iracundus is so called because one whose blood has been kindled is driven into fury; for just as a flame is said to burn, so anger inflames.

131. Incentor, from kindling and inflaming.

[Note: *Incentor*, because he incites to evil. *Succentor*, because he incites to evil, and so forth. The Neapolitan manuscript has a reading better suited to the interpretation of suggesting and succeeding.] Incentor, because by an evil suggestion he sets the hearts of others ablaze with vices and inflames them by persuasion.

132. Inexpiabilis, because it can never be expiated or cleansed.

477 [Note: *Inlaudabilis*. From Servius, *Georgics* III. This interpretation concerns not one who has not been praised, but one who has not deserved praise. We explained earlier why this arises so often.] Inlaudabilis, not because it has not been praised, but because it has not deserved to be praised.

Iratus, driven by anger.

133. Impius, because he is without the piety of religion.

Iniquus is properly so called because he is not *aequus*, “equal,” but unequal. [Note: On the distinction between *impius* and *iniquus*. Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*: “Every impious person is unjust and a sinner, but the converse does not hold,” and so forth.] Sometimes this is the difference between *impius* and *iniquus*: every impious person is unjust, but not every unjust person is impious. *Impius* is used for an unbeliever and is so called because he is alienated from the piety of religion. *Iniquus*, however, is said of one who is not equal but is stained by wicked deeds, even if he bears the name of Christianity.

134. Inimicus, because he is not a friend but an adversary. Two things make enemies: deceit and terror. Terror, because they fear; deceit, because of the evil they have suffered.

135. Invidus is named from looking upon another’s happiness.

[Note: *Invidiosus* means “one who suffers envy from another.” Aulus Gellius, book IX, chapter 12.] Invidiosus is one who suffers envy from another.

Invisus, hateful, derived from envy and jealousy.

136. Intestabilis, one whose testimony has no validity and whose statement is rejected as invalid and disapproved.

Infamis, of no good reputation.

Improbus is so called because he persists even when forbidden.

137. Importunus, restless, because he has no *portus*, that is, no rest. Hence the *importuni*, because they are quickly carried into shipwreck.

Infrenis is one who is not controlled by reins, as the unbridled Numidians.

138. Infrendens properly means “clenching the teeth against one another.” [Note: For *frendere* also means “to break with the teeth.” Festus.] For *frendere* also means to break with the teeth; hence *nefrendes*, infants who do not yet have teeth.

Ingluviosus, derived from *gula* and greediness.

139. [Note: *Inglorius*. Servius, *Aeneid* X: *inglorius*, without triumphs, forgetful of glory.] Inglorius, because he is without glory, that is, without triumphs. Likewise, *inglorius* means forgetful of glory.

Informis, immense—not because it lacks form, but because it possesses a size beyond form.

478 140. [Note: *Inveterator*. Thus all the old manuscripts. In Daniel XIII, however: “You ancient one of evil days.”] Inveterator, because he has long and longstanding experience in wickedness.

[Note: *Immanis*. Festus: *immanis*, savage or great. Glossary: *immanis*, μέγιστος, “greatest,” ἄγριος, “savage.” See Servius and Nonius.] Immanis, because he is not good but cruel and terrible. For *manus* is said to mean “good.” Hence, by antiphrasis, the *dii manes*, “the spirits of the dead,” are called so although they are by no means good.

[Col. 0382A] 141. [Note: *Immunis*. Glossary: *immunes*, ἀτέλεῖς, “exempt from dues,” ἀνέπαφοι, “untouched,” ἀλειτούργητοι, “not performing public service.”] Immunis, not at all generous, as in the old proverb: “Their fellow citizens hate the ungenerous.” Likewise, *immunis* is one who does not perform duties, that is, does not discharge an office; for he is empty of every privilege.

142. Indemnis, because he lives without damage, guilt, or danger.

Iners, without skill and therefore suited to no work.

Inermis, either without weapons or without strength. For *arma*, “weapons,” always stands for strength.

143. Ignavus, “ignorant of the way,” that is, of reason and life.
