Ignarus, not *gnarus*, that is, ignorant, or “without nostrils.” [Note: The ancients used *olfacere*, “to smell,” in the sense of “to know.” The same author below, book XI, chapter 1. Terence: “Would I not have smelled it out six whole months before he began anything?”] For the ancients said *olfacere*, “to smell,” meaning “to know.”

[Note: *Ignarus* has two meanings. From Servius, *Aeneid* I and VI.] *Ignarus* has two meanings: one who does not know, or one who is not known.

[Col. 0382B] 144. Immemor, one who has forgotten, for he has lost his memory.

Inscius, because he is without knowledge.

Idiota, inexperienced. It is Greek.

Imperitus, without experience.

145. [Note: *Inconsultus*. See above, under *consultus*.] Inconsultus, because he does not accept advice. Likewise, *inconsultus* means one who is without counsel, ignorant of affairs, and unknowing.

Ineptus is the opposite of *aptus*, as though *inaptus*.

146. [Note: *Inops*. From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “the needy and unburied crowd.”] Inops, one who is without earth; for we understand *ops*, “help,” as earth, because it gives help by producing fruit. Others understand *inops* to mean one who is unburied, without burial, for whom no empty mound has arisen in his absence.

147. Ignobilis, because he is unknown, lowly, and of obscure lineage, whose very name is not known.

[Col. 0382C] Ircosus, because he stinks from the foul sweat of his body.

Ignotus, unknown, or coming unexpectedly.

148. Improvisus is so called because it happens suddenly and was not seen beforehand.

Index, informer, from *indicare*, “to point out.”

[Note: *Indigena*. From the same source, *Aeneid* VIII.] Indigena is so called because he was born there, that is, born in the same place.

149. Impudens, because shame and modesty are far from him.

Impudicus, named from *paedor*, “filth”; for they call stench *paedor*.

Incestus, so called because of unlawful intercourse, as though *incastus*, “unchaste,” such as one who has violated a consecrated virgin or a woman closely related to him by marriage.

[Col. 0382D] 150. [Note: *Internicida*. Festus under *internicivum testamentum* and *internectio*. See Cujas, *Observations*.] Internicida is one who forged a will and for that reason killed a person.

[Col. 0383A] Inficiator, a denier, because he does not confess but relies on falsehood against the truth.

Impostor ...

151. Interceptus is properly said of one who is removed from the midst between two people.

152. Insidiosus, because he lies in wait; for properly *insidere* means to await someone deceitfully. Hence *insidiae*, “ambush,” is also named.

[Note: *Incincta*. Our people use the same word.] Incincta, that is, without a girdle, because pregnancy does not permit the womb to be tightly girded.

153. [Note: *Investis*, that is, “without clothing.” Thus far correctly: “without pubic hair,” according to Servius, Macrobius, and Nonius. What follows does not fit very well, for she does not yet have the *stola*, which is a sign of marital dignity. Therefore this addition belongs to someone who did not understand “without clothing” and expanded the interpretation to its detriment, borrowing these words from book XIX, chapter 29.] Investis, that is, without clothing; for she does not yet have the *stola*, which is a sign of marital dignity.

Iscurra is so called because, for the sake of food, he follows everyone around.

480 K

154. Katholicus, universal. It is Greek.

[Col. 0383B] Karus is a Greek word, as is *karitas*, “charity”; hence also *karistia*, “gifts of grace.”

L

155. Luculentus, because he is clear in speech and splendid in discourse.

Lector is said from *legere*, “to read,” that is, “to pass through.” Hence a ship is also said to *legere* whatever it passes. For *legit* means “passes,” “goes by,” as in: ...

> We traverse the seas stirred by frequent lands.

Likewise, *lector* comes from gathering in the mind what one reads, as though *collector*, as in:

> You who read the flowers.

156. Loquax is not eloquent.

[Note: *Laetus*, from breadth. Varro, book V: *laetari* comes from joy spread more broadly because of the expectation of a great good.] Laetus, from breadth.

[Note: *Locuples*. See Nonius under *pecuniosus*.] Locuples, as though “full of places,” and the possessor of many estates, as Tully teaches in book II of *The Republic*: “With extensive dominion over sheep and cattle—for at that time wealth consisted in livestock—and in possessions of land; from this they were called wealthy and rich.”

157. Liberalis is so called because he gives willingly and does not grumble.

Largus ...

Longus is derived from a line, because it is extended.

Longaevus, as though “of long life” and “of long duration.”

158. Longanimis, or magnanimous, because he is disturbed by no passions but is patient in enduring all things. Its opposite is [Note: *Pusillonimis*, exceedingly foolish. From the Septuagint edition; the Vulgate has: “But the impatient person exalts his foolishness.” Proverbs XIV.] pusillanimis, narrow-minded and unable to endure any tribulation. Of him it is written: “The pusillanimous person is exceedingly foolish.”

159. Levis is named from the instability of wandering, because with a light movement of mind he desires now this thing, now that.

Lubricus, because it slips.

[Col. 0384A] [Note: *Labens*, sometimes “swift.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on the verse “so many years now slipping away.”] Labens, sometimes “swift,” as in:

> Glide, nymph, through the sky, and glide on wings.

For a sliding movement is swifter than running.

160. [Note: *Latro*. See Varro, book VI.] Latro, one who occupies the roads, is derived from *latere*, “to hide.” Aelius, however, says: “*Latro* is from *latero*, from *latus*, ‘side,’ one who lies in wait on the road.”

Lanista, a gladiator, that is, a butcher, is called by a Tuscan word, from *laniare*, “to tear apart,” namely, bodies.

161. Lacessitor is used metaphorically of dogs or wild beasts, which customarily provoke by tearing.

Leno, a procurer of sexual vice, because he flatters the minds of wretched people and seduces them by soothing them.

Libidinosus, because he does whatever he pleases.

Libidinosus, from Liber, who is depicted with a youthful body.

Luxuriosus, as though released into pleasures; hence limbs displaced from their proper position are called *luxa*.

[Col. 0384B] Lascivus, because he is *laxus*, that is, unrestrained and frivolous.

162. Lymphaticus, because he fears water, whom the Greeks call ὑδροφόβος, “water-fearing.” Properly, *lymphaticus* is one who acquires an illness from water, an illness characterized by running here and there, a defect derived from the flow of water. But poets now use this kind of word for madmen.

163. Languidus ...

[Note: *Luridus*, from *lorum*, “leather strap.” Varro is correct: *lorica*, “breastplate,” comes from *lora*, because they made breast armor from raw leather straps. People of this sort of complexion are *luridi*. Festus: *luridi* are excessively pale.] Luridus, because he is pale, is derived from *lorum*, because he has skin of this kind.

Leprosus, named from the excessive itching of the leprous scab; hence it should be written with *p*.

164. Luscus, because he perceives light only partially; likewise [Note: *Luscitiosus*, one who sees nothing in the evening. But Festus says the opposite: *luscitio* is an eye defect whereby one sees more clearly in the evening than in the morning. See Fulgentius and Placidus.] *luscitiosus*, one who sees nothing in the evening.

[Note: *Luscos coclites*. From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII.] The ancients called the one-eyed *lusci coclites*; hence we read that the Cyclopes were also called *coclites*, because they were said to have had one eye.

[Col. 0384C] Lotus, washed, that is, clean.

Lupa, a prostitute, named from rapacity, because she snatches wretched men to herself and seizes them.

M

165. Misericors [Note: *Misericors*. From Gregory, *Moralia* XX, chapter 23, or 24.] has received its name from compassion for another’s misery. Hence *misericordia*, “mercy,” is so called because it makes the heart of one who grieves for another’s misery itself miserable. This etymology, however, does not apply everywhere; for there is mercy in God without any misery of heart.

166. [Note: *Mactus*, more fully “increased.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX.] Mactus, “increased in glory,” is a term taken from sacred rites. Whenever incense or wine was poured over a sacrificial victim, they said: “The bull is *mactus* with wine” or “with incense,” that is, “the victim has been enriched and increased.”

167. Munificus is so called either because he gives many gifts to someone or because he fulfills his gift, that is, the duty he owes. Likewise, *munifex*, because he bears gifts.

[Col. 0385A] 168. Magnus ...

Magnanimus, because he is great in spirit and great in virtue. Its opposite is *pusillanimis*.

Magnificus derives its name from doing great things.

169. [Note: *Mansuetus*. See Cassiodorus on Psalm XXIV.] Mansuetus, gentle or tamed, as though accustomed to the hand.

[Note: *Modestus*. From Ambrose, *On Duties* I, chapter 18.] Modestus is derived from *modus*, “measure,” and moderation, doing neither more nor less than is proper.

Mitis, gentle, mild, and tame; yielding to wickedness and silent in bearing injury, as though *mutus*, “mute.”

170. [Note: *Mutus* ... for he emits a vocal breath through his nostrils as though bellowing. From Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 11.] Mutus, because his voice is not speech but only a bellow; for he emits vocal breath through his nostrils as though bellowing.

Memor, either one who retains memory or one who is retained in memory.

171. [Note: *Magister* ... *στερρόν* in Greek means “station.” Glossary: *στερρός*, strong, weighty, stable; *στάσις*, “a station,” “a standing.” See Festus under *magisterare* and *magisteria*.] Magister, “greater in station,” for *στερρόν* in Greek means “station.”

Minister, “lesser in station,” or because he performs the duty owed with his hands.

172. Major ...

Minor ...

Minimus, from the number one, because after him there is no other.

Maximus, more distinguished either in merit, age, honor, eloquence, virtue, or in all of these.

173. Modicus, small—but improperly so; properly, reasonable.

Moderatus, from *modus*, “measure,” that is, restraint.

[Col. 0385C] Mediocris, because a small amount suffices for him.

174. [Note: *Miser* ... according to Cicero. From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on the verse “the wretched after the death of Sichaeus.”] Miser properly means one who has lost all happiness. According to Cicero, however, it properly means “dead”; in the *Tusculan Disputations* he calls the dead *miseri*, because they have already lost life.

Miserabilis, because it is suited to misery.

175. [Note: *Maestus*, naturally sad. From Servius, on the verse “he sends the grieving Onites,” *Aeneid* XII: *maestus*, naturally sad and severe, whom the Greeks call ἀγέλαστος, “unlaughing.”] Maestus, naturally sad, not sad by accident. For it arises from the nature of the mind and spirit; [Note: Hence also *maestus*, perhaps from *metus*, “fear.” See Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and the mournful fear.”] hence also *maestus*.

176. Mendicus is so called because he has too little by which to live, or because among the ancients it was customary for a poor man to close his mouth and extend his hand, as though speaking with his hand.

Mendax, because he deceives another’s mind.

177. Malignus, because he carries out the intention or deed of malice.

[Col. 0385D] Malus is named from black bile, which the Greeks call μέλαν, “black”; hence melancholy people are also so called. They shun human company [Note: “They distrust dear friends.” This is a Gothicism.] and distrust their close friends.

Malitiosus, worse than *malus*, because he is frequently evil. [Note: From *malus* comes *pejor*, “worse”; from *bonus*, *deterior*, “inferior.” From Servius, *Georgics* IV, on the verse “worse in appearance.”] From *malus* comes *pejor*, “worse,” whereas from *bonus* comes *deterior*, “inferior.”

178. Melior is so called because it is softer, not hard or ironlike; for *melius* is as though “softer.”

Minax, from the expression of the eyes, [Note: When they blaze furiously. Others read “in fury.”] when they burn furiously, so that the one who sees them more closely becomes afraid.

Minator is a warner, but *monitor* is used when he announces good things, while *minator* is used when he announces adverse things.

179. [Note: *Mulcator*. Donatus, on *Hecyra*, scene 1: *Mulciber* is properly so called because he softens everything; and in *Adelphoe*, scene 2: “He softened the master himself and the entire household.” Gabriel Faernus noted that this is how it is read in the old manuscripts. What concerns *mulsum*, however, seems to come from Pliny, book II, chapter 94.] Mulcator, because he soothes with pleasant words in order to bend the mind; this is a metaphor from *mulsum*, “honeyed wine,” which, when taken, ordinarily soothes the sore throat or the stomach clogged with impurities.

180. Metatores are called those who lay out a camp, from *metiri*, “to measure,” as Lucan says:

> Let the bold surveyor come into the Hesperian fields.

Mollis, because he dishonors the vigor of the male sex through an enervated body, and is softened as though a woman.

181. Macer, from *macies*, “leanness”; and *macies* from *moechia*, “adultery,” because immoderate lust makes people thin, or from *maceratio*, “wasting.”

[Note: *Mancus* ... “with a hand bent inward.” Festus: *ancus* is one who has a crooked arm, so that it cannot be extended. Glossary: *ancus*, *mancus*, κυλλός, “crippled,” πηρός, “maimed.”] Mancus, “with a bent or disabled hand.”

182. [Note: *Moribundus* ... “like one who is dying.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X.] Moribundus, like one who is dying, just as *vitabundus* is like one who is fleeing. When we say “he is about to die,” he truly is about to die; *moribundus*, however, does not mean truly dying but resembling one who is dying.

[Col. 0386C] 183. Meretrix is so called because she earns the price of lust. Hence also *meritoriae tabernae*, “brothels”; for soldiers are also said to *mereri*, “earn,” when they receive their pay.

184. Morio, named from *mors*, “death,” because he does not possess an active intellect.

Mulio, named from *muli*, “mules,” because he presides over the vehicles drawn by them.

Manifestum is said of what is ready at hand, as though “in the hand.”

485 N.

185. Nobilis, “not base,” one whose name and lineage are known.

Nubilis, suitable for marriage.

[Note: *Nemo*, that is, *ne homo*, “not a person,” or *nec homo*, “not even a person.” Servius and Festus.] Nemo is derived from *homo*, “person,” that is, *ne homo*, “not a person,” used for “no one.”

[Col. 0386D] Nullus, as though *ne ullus*, “not any.”

[Col. 0387A] 186. [Note: *Nihili*. Festus: they think *hilum* is what adheres to a bean, from which come *nihil* and *nihilum*.] Nihili is composed of *ne* and *hilo*. Varro says that *hilum* means the pith of the plant that the Greeks call *asphodelos*; thus among us it is said to mean “nothing,” just as among the Greeks οὐδὲ γρῦ, “not even a trifle.”

187. [Note: *Nequam* ... Others read *nequitiam*. See Varro at the end of book IX, and Aulus Gellius, book VII, chapter 11.] Most people distinguish *nequam* from *malus*, considering one person harmful and the other a trifler, [Note: As Monatius says. Perhaps Munatius, or rather Matius, whose *Mimiambi* are praised by Terentianus. The Tarragon manuscript has *Numatius*.] as in: “This young man is *nequam*, not bad”—that is, a trifler, not harmful. Others confuse the words, as though they signified one and the same thing.

188. Nequaquam, because it is “not anything,” that is, the ancients wished it to be derived from its being nothing.

Neuter, neither this one nor that one, as though saying “not either.”

189. [Note: *Nefarius*, not worthy of *far*, “spelt.” Nonius: Varro revealed the proper meaning of *nefarius* in book I of *The Life of the Roman People*: it derives from *far*, a kind of grain, from which *ador*, the sacrificial grain, is made and which criminals ought not to use. Asconius: *nefarium* is what pollutes rites customarily celebrated with sacred grain; therefore *nefarii* are sacrilegious.] Nefarius, not worthy of *far*, the first kind of food by which human life was sustained. Otherwise, *nefarius* means impious.

[Col. 0387B] Nefandus, that is, not even to be named.

Nutritor, as though “educated by a nod.”

190. [Note: *Nuntius*. Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “so the true messenger for me”: properly, the one who announces is masculine; what is announced, although expressed in the neuter, is also sometimes found in the masculine.] Nuntius is both the one who announces and what is announced, that is, ἄγγελος καὶ ἀγγελία, “messenger and message.” [486] The messenger himself, however, is masculine in gender; what he announces is neuter, as *hoc nuntium*, “this message,” and feminine in the form *haec nuntia*.

191. Nazaraeus, that is, holy to God. In former times *Nazaraeus* was said of one who grew holy hair and accepted nothing defiled, abstaining from wine and every kind of strong drink, which distorts the mind from complete soundness.

192. [Note: *Nugas* is Hebrew. From Jerome, on Zephaniah III. It is a Hebrew word. Charisius, book I: although *nugas* is indeclinable, it is common to all three genders—*hic*, *haec*, and *hoc nugas*—and shortly afterward: indeclinable neuters include *nugas*, which is common to all three genders.] *Nugas* is a Hebrew name. Thus it is explained in the prophets, where Zephaniah says: “Nugas are those who have departed from the law,” so that we may know that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages.

[Col. 0387C] 193. Nugigerulus, named from being a disgraceful messenger.

Negligens, as though *nec legens*, “not reading.”

194. [Note: [Col. 0387D] “Nepos” from a certain kind of scorpion. Gloss: *Nepa*, “scorpion.” Nonius: “For *nepa* truly means ‘scorpion.’ Festus gives another account of the etymology of *nepos*, as does Isidore himself, Book IX.] *Nepos* (“grandson”) is so called from a kind of scorpion that devours its offspring, except the one that climbs onto its back; for afterward the one that has been spared itself devours its parent. Hence people who consume their parents’ property through extravagance are called *nepotes*. From this too comes *nepotatio*, used for extravagance, by which certainly every possession is consumed.

195. *Niger* (“black”), as though *nubiger* (“cloud-bearing”), because it is not clear but covered with a dusky hue. Hence we also call a cloudy day gloomy.

O.

196. *Orthodoxus*, “of right glory.”

*Orator* (“speaker”) is called from *os* (“mouth”), and is named from *perorare* (“to speak at length”), that is, “to speak”; for *orare* means “to speak.”

[Note: [Col. 0388C] *Orator.* But Festus says: “*Oratores* are named from the Greek, as though from ἀρατῆρες, because those sent to kings and nations used to *ἀρᾶσθαι*—*ἀρατῆρες*, that is, “to bear witness.”]

197. *Obaudiens* (“obedient”), from *auris* (“ear”), because he listens to one giving orders.

[Note: [Col. 0388C] *Ospes. Hospes.* This word is rightly absent from four Tarrentine manuscripts.]

*Ospes* (“guest”), because he brings his foot to the doorway.

*Ospes* also means easy, open, and accessible at the doorway; hence a welcoming person is called *ospitalis*.

198. *Osor* (“hater”), “enemy,” is derived from *odium* (“hatred”), just as *amator* (“lover”) is derived from *amor* (“love”); and it is common to both genders.

*Odibilis* (“hateful”), suitable for hatred.

*Obsitus* (“beset”), “surrounded,” that is, enclosed on every side by ambushes.

199. [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Obscenus.* Varro, Book VI: “*Obscenum*, shameful, something that ought not to be spoken openly except on the stage.”] *Obscenus* (“obscene”), pertaining to impure lust, is derived from an obscure vice.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] *Obtunsus.* L.: “*Obtusus* … more closed.” Another reading: “more hardened.” The Gothic letter-forms permit either reading.] *Obtunsus* (“blunted”), more dull and more closed, as though struck on every side.

*Obnixus* (“striving against”), having exerted oneself against something and making every effort.

*Obnoxius* (“liable”), because one is bound by the chains of guilt.

200. [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Oblectator.* Festus, under the word *Lacit*.] *Oblectator* (“entertainer”), as though “with milk” and by deceit, as in Terence: “Unless you had beguiled me, your lover.” Hence *oblectare* (“to entertain”) is also derived.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] *Obtrectator* … “by obstructing.” Or rather, “by scraping against,” as in Varro, *On Agriculture*, chapter 20.] *Obtrectator* (“detractor”) is malicious, and by obstructing and impeding does not allow someone to advance and grow.

201. *Orbus* (“bereaved”), because he has no children, as though he had lost his eyes.

*Opifex* (“craftsman”), because he makes some work.

*Opilio* (“shepherd”), a keeper of sheep; *ovilio*.

P.

202. *Prudens* (“prudent”), as though *porro videns* (“seeing ahead”); for he is perceptive and foresees the contingencies of uncertain things.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] *Patiens* (“patient”), derived from *paviendo*. Festus: “*Obpuviat*, he strikes, from *paviendo*, that is, from striking. Hence boys, because they are restrained by punishment; hence also *pavimenta* (“pavements”).” This clearly refers to the Greek *παίειν*, “to strike and beat.” The most learned scholar says that *paimenta* is also read for *pavimenta* in an ancient inscription.] *Patiens* (“patient”) is derived from *paviendo*, for *pavire* means “to strike”; one is struck and endures.

203. [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Perfectus.* Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “O fame great, greater than great”: “There are other names concerning which there is doubt whether they admit comparison, as *perfectus*; for if you wish to compare it, what is perfect begins not to be perfect.”] *Perfectus* (“perfect”) is that to which nothing can now be added. Grammarians do not attach comparison to this word, because if you say, “That man is more perfect,” he will not be perfect.

204. *Pulcher* (“beautiful”) is derived from the appearance of the skin, which is (red) [Col. 0389A] skin; afterward this word passed into a general category. For a person’s beauty may be in the face, as in:

> His face and shoulders like a god;

or in the hair, as in:

> For she herself had beautiful hair;

or in the eyes, as in:

> He breathed bright honors upon her eyes;

or in whiteness, as in:

> Such beauty as hands impart to ivory;

or in features, as in:

> The guest’s figure and features pleased you much more;

or in height, as in the case of Turnus:

> He turns amid the ranks and rises above them by the whole height of his head.

205. *Pellax* (“seductive”), from *pelliciendo* (“enticing”).

*Perspicax* (“keen-sighted”), brilliant, because it shines through.

*Perpetuus* (“perpetual”) …

*Perennis* (“everlasting”), from being perpetual through the years.

206. [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Praesul* … because he presides with solicitude. Paul, Romans XII: “The one who presides, with diligence.” But according to Phocas, *praesul* is derived from *praesilire* (“to leap before”); thus the first among the Salii was called *praesul*, because he initiated the ritual dance. Hence Lucilius:

> The leader, so that he may leap, and from there the crowd leaps back after him.

This is the *praesultor*, which the old Glossary interprets as “the one who leads the dance in sacred rites.”] *Praesul* (“presiding officer”) is so called because he presides with solicitude.

*Praepositus* (“prefect,” “superior”) is so called because he organizes or governs those subject to him [Col. 0389B] and serving him.

*Patroni* (“patrons”) are named from *patres* (“fathers”), because they show their clients such affection that they govern them as fathers would.

207. [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Paedagogus*, one assigned to children. From Jerome, on Galatians III.] A *paedagogus* (“pedagogue”) is one assigned to children. The word is Greek and is formed from the idea of leading children—that is, guiding them—and restraining an unruly age.

208. *Praesens* (“present”) is so called because it is *prae sensibus* (“before the senses”), that is, before the eyes, which are bodily senses.

*Prior* (“earlier”), because it is first in order; and *primus* (“first”), as though “standing foremost.”

*Primus* …

*Postremus* (“last”) …

209. *Potens* (“powerful”), broadly extending over affairs; hence also *potestas* (“power”), because everything is open to him wherever he wishes to go, and no one can shut him out or resist him.

[Col. 0389C] *Praeopimus* (“very rich”), abundant in resources above others.

210. [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Pecuniosos.* From the same source, Ecclesiastes V.] Cicero reports that *pecuniosi* (“wealthy”) originally meant those who possessed the greatest amount of *pecunia*, that is, cattle. For the ancients called them by this name. Gradually, however, through misuse, the word shifted to another meaning.

211. [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Pervicax.* Donatus, in the *Hecyra*: “*Pervicax*, persevering with a certain force,” and shortly afterward: “*Pervicax*, acting by force.”] *Pervicax* (“stubborn”) properly denotes one who perseveres in his purpose until victory. 489 [Note: [Col. 0389D] “For the ancients said *viciam*.” Ovetus has *vicam*. I think the latter is erroneous.] For the ancients called victory *viciam*; I believe that the plant *vicia* (“vetch”) is named from this, that is, “victorious.”

212. [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Pernix*, from *pernitendo*. From Servius, *Georgics* III.] *Pernix* (“nimble”) is derived from *pernitendo*, that is, persevering in one’s efforts.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Others understand *pernicem* as “swift.” From the same source, *Aeneid* XI.] Others understand *pernicem* to mean swift in the feet.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] “For *pernicitas* is swiftness of the feet.” From the same source, *Aeneid* IV.] For *pernicitas* (“swiftness”) belongs to the feet, as in:

> With fiery feet;

just as the speed of wings is expressed in:

> And gliding beneath the stars in swift flight.

213. [Col. 0389D] *Piger* (“sluggish”), as though *pedibus aeger* (“sick in the feet”). For he is slow to walk, and through usage the word also passed to the mind.

*Pernox* (“all-night”), keeping watch throughout the night.

*Perseverans* (“persevering”) …

[Note: [Col. 0390D] *Pertinax*, as though *pertinens* (“holding fast”). As though *pertendens* (“straining toward”), Varro, Book IV.] *Pertinax* (“obstinate”), holding on shamelessly, as though “holding fast.”

214. *Petulans* (“insolent”) is now used for a bold and wicked person; formerly, however, harsh extortionists—and specifically the boys employed by moneylenders—were called *petulantes*, because they demanded the prices of things too frequently and too harshly. They were so named from *petere* (“to seek,” “demand”).

215. [Note: [Col. 0390D] *Procax.* From Servius, *Aeneid* I.] *Procax* (“forward,” “bold”) properly means the same as *petax* (“demanding”). For *procare* means “to ask”; hence suitors for marriage are called *proci*.

216. *Prodigus* (“prodigal”), lavish and wasteful, one who does everything “forward,” as though throwing it away.

*Profugus* (“fugitive”) properly denotes one who wanders far from his dwelling, as though driven far away.

*Peregrinus* (“foreigner”), situated far from his homeland, like an alien.

217. *Projectus* (“thrown forward”), as though cast a long way and far off; likewise *produxit* (“led forward”), as though he led him onward, and *provocavit* (“challenged”), as though he called him forward.

*Projectus* also means as though “thrown far out” and cast away; hence:

> And the rocks thrown out from Pachynus,

that is, “cast far forward.”

218. *Proscriptus* (“proscribed”), one whose property is publicly and openly listed.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] *Praescriptus* signifies order. Jurists call *praescriptiones* (“prescriptions”) exceptions, especially those that exclude actions by pleading the lapse of a long period. The origin of the term may perhaps be that their formula was written beforehand, either in the praetors’ edicts or in the formulas of actions. So too, an action *praescriptis verbis* (“with words prescribed beforehand”).] *Praescriptus* signifies order, as do *praescriptiones* among jurists.

219. [Note: [Col. 0390D] *Procinctus.* See Festus.] *Procinctus* (“in readiness for battle”) means equipped and armed; hence:

> And in battle array,

that is, when they took up arms for war.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] *Praecinctus.* From Augustine, on Psalm XCII.] *Praecinctus* (“girded”) is so called because he places something before himself by which he is girded. Hence it is said of the Lord:

[Col. 0390C]

> Girded with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of his disciples.

220. [Note: [Col. 0390D] *Praedo.* From Servius, *Aeneid* X.] A *praedo* (“plunderer”) is one who invades another’s province while ravaging it. *Praedo* is derived from taking away *praedae* (“booty”); and a *praedo* is one who possesses booty.

A *praedator* (“predator”) is one to whom something is owed from the booty.

221. *Plagiator* (“kidnapper”) is from the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ πλαγίου, that is, “from what is oblique,” because he does not proceed by a straight path but by enticing through deceit.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] *Piratae*, from burning. But in Greek the word is πειρατής, not πυρατής. Hesychius: πειρατής, “evildoer.”] *Piratae* (“pirates”) are maritime plunderers, so called from burning the ships of those traveling by sea, whom they captured. For πῦρ (*pyr*) means “fire.”

222. *Pugillator* (“pickpocket”), one who secretly removes something of the money from hand to hand.

*Peculator* (“embezzler”), because he is a defrauder of public money.

*Proditor* (“betrayer”), because he exposes or discloses. *Proditor* also means “destroyer,” as in:

> Because of the anger of one man, we are betrayed.

223. [Col. 0391A] *Perfidus* (“faithless”), because he is fraudulent and without faith, as though “destroying faith.”

[Note: [Col. 0391D] *Perjurus* under the letter R is not found. Rather, even the noun itself is written *pejurus*, twice without R, in the oldest Salzburg manuscript. These are Servius’ words, *Aeneid* II.] *Perjurus* (“perjured”), because he swears wrongly—that is, swears falsely. But *perjurus* does not have the letter R in the verb. For we say *pejero* and *dejero*.

224. [Note: [Col. 0391D] *Praevaricator.* Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 19: “Unless a plowman bends over, he *praevaricatur*.” From there this offense was transferred to the law court. It should therefore be sought where it was first found. Cicero, however, seems to derive it from *varius* (“varied”) in the *Partitions*, when he says: “The name *praevaricatio* signifies one who, in opposing cases, seems to be placed as though in different positions”; this is not entirely a different derivation, for *varius* perhaps also descends from *varus*. Although it is unfair to demand this, especially since in some books one reads *Quid enim tam praevarium* …] A *praevaricator* (“collusive advocate”) is a lawyer acting in bad faith, one who, whether in accusing, passes over what would be damaging, or in defending, what would be useful, or sets it forth ineffectively and ambiguously, evidently because he has been bribed. Cicero says: “For what is so *praevarum*?” that is, “so very *varum*,” or “crooked.”

225. *Pellax* (“deceitful”), crafty and deceptive, from *pellis* (“skin”), that is, from the face. Outwardly he smiles in order to deceive, but inwardly he harbors wickedness.

*Profanus* (“profane”), as though “far from the sanctuary.” For such a person is not permitted to take part in sacred rites.

226. [Note: [Col. 0391D] *Parracida.* Thus the Gothic books read it, not *parricida*.] *Parracida* (“parricide”) properly means the killer of a parent, [Col. 0391B] although some of the ancients called such a person *parenticida*, since *parricidium* and *homicidium* can be understood of anyone, because human beings are equal to one another.

227. *Persecutor* (“persecutor”) is not always understood in a bad sense; hence *persecutus* means “one who has followed completely.”

[Note: [Col. 0391D] *Publicanus.* Gaius, chapter 16, *On the Meaning of Words*: “We call a *publicanus* one who has contracted for the collection of the taxes of the Roman people.”] A *publicanus* (“tax collector”) is one who collects public taxes, or one who pursues profits through the public business of the world; hence he received this designation.

228. *Peccator* (“sinner”) is named from *pellice* (“mistress”), that is, “prostitute,” as though *pellicator* (“one who consorts with a mistress”). Among the ancients this word signified only a disgraceful person; later it passed into a designation for all the wicked.

229. Prostitutes are called *meretrices* (“harlots”) from *prosedendo* (“sitting out in public”) in places of prostitution or in arches.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] *Pellex* among the Greeks. See Festus, Gellius, and Paulus, chapter 144, *On the Meaning of Words.*] Among the Greeks, *pellex* is properly what the Latins call a *concuba* (“concubine”). It is derived from *fallacia* (“deceit”), that is, cunning, under cover of fraud or falsehood.

230. *Procurvus* (“bent forward”), as though curved lengthwise.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] *Pavidus* … “for it has the beating of the heart.” He appears to have had in mind Virgil’s words: “Fear beating upon the heart.”] A *pavidus* (“fearful person”) is one whom trembling of mind disturbs (for he has beating of the heart, movement of the heart); for *pavire* means “to strike,” hence also *pavimentum* (“pavement”).

231. Rocks and cliffs (*petrae* and *rupes*) are named from the hardness of stones.

492 *Pusillanimis* (“faint-hearted”), small in spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] *Petulcus.* From Servius, *Georgics* IV, on “the frolicking kids.”] *Petulcus* (“wanton”) is derived from *appetendo* (“seeking eagerly”); hence we also call prostitutes *petulcae* (“wanton”).

*Pisinus* (“small”) from *pusio* (“little boy”).

*Productus* (“led forward”), as though led onward.

Q

232. *Quaestor* (“quaestor”) is derived from *quaerendo* (“seeking”), as though *quaesitor* (“inquirer”).

[Col. 0392A] *Quaestuosus* (“profitable”), given to complaints.

233. *Querulus* (“complaining”), because he brings a complaint.

*Quietus* (“quiet”), because he is inwardly secure, troubling no one.

R

234. [Note: [Col. 0392D] Cicero says this of *religiosus*, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*.] Cicero says that *religiosus* (“religious”) is called from *relegendo* (“rereading”), because the religious person revisits and, as it were, rereads matters pertaining to divine worship. Such people are called *religiosi* from *relegendo*, just as from *eligendo* (“choosing”) come *eligentes* (“those who choose”), from *diligendo* (“loving carefully”) *diligentes* (“diligent”), and from *intelligendo* (“understanding”) *intelligentes* (“intelligent”).

235. [Note: [Col. 0392D] *Rationator.* Thus in all the Gothic manuscripts, and Chacon preferred this spelling. For *ratiocinator* is something else.] *Rationator* (“reasoner”) is called a great man, [Note: [Col. 0392D] *Vir magnus.* Augustine wanted *magus* (“magician”).] because he can give an account of all matters known to be remarkable.

*Retractator* (“reviser”), one who repeats, [Note: [Col. 0392D] For *retractare* (“to repeat”). From Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “It was the custom in Hesperian Latium.”] for *retractare* means to repeat what one had omitted.

236. *Resipiscens* (“recovering one’s senses”) is so called because he recovers his mind as though after madness, or because one who had ceased to be wise becomes wise again. For he chastises himself for his folly and strengthens his spirit for living more rightly, taking care not to fall again.

237. *Repentinus* (“sudden”), from *repente* (“suddenly”).

[Note: [Col. 0392D] *Repens* (“sudden”). From the same source, *Aeneid* XII.] *Repens* can be both an adverb and a noun.

*Robustus* (“robust”), strong and powerful, is named from the strength of the oak tree.

*Rapidus* (“swift”), fast in the feet.

*Raptor* (“abductor”), because he is a corruptor. Hence a woman abducted is called *rapta*, because she has been violated.

238. [Note: [Col. 0392D] *Reus*, from the matter for which he is liable. Cicero, Book II of *On Oratory*: “I call *rei* not only those who are accused, but all whose case is under dispute.”] *Reus* (“defendant”) is named from the matter for which he is liable, and *reatus* (“liability”) is named from *reus*.

493 A *reus maiestatis* (“defendant for treason”) originally meant one who had done something against the state or had agreed with its enemies. He was called a *reus maiestatis* because harming the fatherland is a greater offense than harming a single citizen. Later, those who appeared to have acted against the majesty of the emperor were also called *rei maiestatis*, as were those who introduced laws harmful to the state or repealed useful ones.

239. *Rixosus* (“quarrelsome”) is named from the canine *rictus* (“snarl”). He is always ready to contradict, delights in wrangling, and provokes the person arguing with him.

*Rusticus* (“rustic”) is so called because he works the countryside, that is, the land.

S

240. *Sapiens* (“wise”) is named from *sapor* (“taste”), because just as taste is suited to distinguishing the flavors of foods, so the wise person is suited to recognizing things and causes: he distinguishes each thing and discerns truth through perception.

[Col. 0393A] The opposite is *insipiens* (“unwise”), because he is “without taste,” possessing neither discernment nor understanding.

241. *Studiosus* (“devoted”), as though curious about learning.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] *Sanctus.* See Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on “Who ratifies treaties with a thunderbolt,” or rather he may have been referring to Paul’s words: “Almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.”] *Sanctus* (“holy”) was named according to ancient custom because those who wished to be purified were touched with the blood of a sacrificial victim, and from this they received the name *sancti*.

242. [Note: [Col. 0393D] *Sincerus.* From Servius, *Georgics* IV.] *Sincerus* (“sincere”), as though “without corruption.” Its opposite is *insincerus* (“insincere”), spoiled and corrupted.

*Supremus* (“supreme”), highest, from being elevated above others. Hence we also say *Supreme Father*.

*Sublimis* (“lofty”) is named from height of honor; properly, something high is called *sublime*, as in:

> And you will carry him lofty to the stars of heaven.

243. [Note: [Col. 0393D] *Speciosus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* I. Elsewhere, although, Isidore derives *formosus* not from *forma* (“form”) but from *formus* (“warm”).] *Speciosus* (“beautiful”) is derived from *species* (“appearance”) or *aspectus* (“appearance”), just as *formosus* (“handsome”) is derived from *forma* (“form”).

[Col. 0393B] [Note: [Col. 0393D] *Solers.* Donatus, in the *Eunuchus*.] *Solers* (“skilled”) is one who is attentive in an art and useful. Among the ancients, *solers* denoted one equipped with every good skill. Terence says: “I shall produce a skillful young man.”

244. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Cicero discusses *superstitiosi*, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*.] Cicero says that *superstitiosi* (“superstitious people”) were called those who prayed and sacrificed all day long so that their children might survive them.

*Sollicitus* (“anxious”), because he is skilled, active, and restless.

*Sedulus* (“assiduous”) is a familiar word of Terence; it means “without deceit,” and elsewhere “persistent.”

245. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Festus indicates three etymologies for *sodales*: they may be so called either because they eat from their own resources, because they sit together—as though *sedales*—or because they give counsel. Isidore gives the first two.] *Sodales* (“companions”) are those accustomed to meet for a shared contribution, as though “eating their own,” or alternatively as though *sedales*, because they sit together.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] *Socii.* As though standing in the same shoe.] *Socii* (“associates”) are so called because they share danger and work, as though remaining in one shoe and following one footprint.

246. *Stultus* (“foolish”), dull of heart, as someone says: “I consider myself foolish, but I do not think myself senseless,” that is, possessing blunted senses, but not no senses at all.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] *Stultus* is one who is unmoved through torpor. From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “What fear?”] A *stultus* is one who, through apathy, is not moved by an injury: he endures cruelty, neither avenges himself nor is moved by any pain of disgrace.

247. [Note: [Col. 0393D] *Segnis*, that is, “without fire.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I. We restored this passage by punctuation alone.] *Segnis* (“sluggish”) means “without fire,” lacking intelligence (*se* signifies “without,” as in *sedulus*, “without deceit,” and *securus*, “without care”); that is, cold, by which we understand useless people.

248. *Stupidus* (“stupid”), repeatedly dazed.

*Superbus* (“proud”) is so called because he wishes to appear above what he is. For whoever wishes to overstep what he is is proud.

249. *Susurro* (“whisperer”) is named from the sound of speech, because he does not speak about another to that person’s face but in the ear of someone else, slandering him.

250. *Seditiosus* (“seditious”), one who creates dissension among minds and gives rise to discord; the Greeks call this διάστασις (*diastasis*), “separation” or “dissension.”

*Severus* (“severe”), as though *saevus verus* (“truly savage”); for he maintains justice without compassion.

251. *Simulator* (“pretender”) is named from *simulacrum* (“image”). For he bears the likeness of something that he himself is not.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] *Suasor*: “drawing someone into his own lot.” Another reading: “*Suasor*, from persuading one whom he wishes to deceive.” Both spellings occur in the Gothic books.] *Suasor* (“persuader”), one who deceives, that is, draws someone into his own lot.

*Studiosus* …

252. [Note: [Col. 0394D] *Scrupulosus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* VI.] *Scrupulosus* (“scrupulous”), petty-minded and harsh. A *scrupus* is a rougher grain of sand.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] *Sacrilegus.* From the same source, *Eclogue* 8.] *Sacrilegus* (“sacrilegious”) is named from taking sacred things, that is, stealing them.

A *sicarius* (“assassin”) is one who is armed with weapons for committing a crime. A *sica* (“dagger”) is named from *secare* (“to cut”).

253. [Note: [Col. 0394D] *Scaevus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “And I embrace the thresholds of the left-hand gate.” Glossary: σκαιός, “left,” *scaevus*; and *Scaeva*, “the left hand.” See also Nonius under *Obscaecavit*.] *Scaevus* (“left,” “perverse”), sinister and crooked, ἀπὸ τοῦ σκαιοῦ, “from the left.” For he is of a very bad and cruel disposition.

*Scenicus* (“theatrical”), one who acts in a theater. For a theater is a *scena* (“stage”).

[Note: [Col. 0394D] *Scorta.* See Festus and the Epitome.] *Scorta* (“prostitutes”), which were also called σκύτεα by the Greeks, are named from the skins that are rubbed and from which corruption is produced.

254. *Spurcus* (“filthy”), because he is impure.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] *Scelerosus* … But *scelerosus* is the stronger term. Donatus, in the *Eunuchus*: “*Scelerosus* is properly the author of crimes; *sceleratus*, one in whom a crime has been established or committed.”] *Scelerosus* (“criminal”), full of crimes, as a place may be full of stones or sand. *Scelerosus* is a stronger term than *sceleratus* (“criminally tainted”).

255. *Sator* (“sower”), a planter or father, from *semen* (“seed”).

[Col. 0394C] [Note: [Col. 0394D] *Scurra.* See Festus and Scaliger.] A *scurra* (“parasite,” “buffoon”) is one who habitually follows someone for the sake of food. He is therefore called *scurra* from *sequendo* (“following”). The same person is an *assecla* (“attendant”), from *sequendo*.

*Satelles* (“attendant”), because he clings to another, or from guarding the side.

256. *Suffectus* (“substituted”), placed in another’s position, as though *suffactus*. Hence we call a consul *suffectus* when he is substituted for another.

257. *Secundus* (“second,” “favorable”), because it is *secus pedes* (“beside the feet”); the expression is derived from following servants who walk at one’s feet. Hence *secunda fortuna* (“good fortune”) is so called because it is *secundum nos* (“beside us”), that is, near us. Hence also *res secundae* (“prosperous circumstances”), that is, favorable circumstances. *Secundae* are named from *sequendo* (“following”).

258. [Note: [Col. 0394D] *Stipulator* … for *stipulari* means “to promise.” Correctly, all the Gothic glossaries have ἐπερωτῶμαι, “I promise, give assurance, stipulate.” Likewise, ἐπερωτῶ means “I consult, ask, stipulate,” or, if you prefer, “I make a stipulation.” For *stipulor* is common in gender, as Priscian says in Book V, citing Suetonius, Book VIII, *On the Praetors*. Festus, under *Stips*: “That *stips* is coined money is shown by the fact that what is given to a soldier is called *stipendium*; and when money is promised, this is called *stipulari*; or, as Fulvius Ursinus edited it: ‘They called coined money *stips*, because it was stipulated; therefore the person who, when asked, promises is called *stipulari*.’ Since *stipulari* is therefore common in gender and contains both a question and a promise, the same glossaries are also correct in giving ἐπερώτησις, “question, stipulation,” and *stipulatio*, ἱκανοδοσία; likewise, ἱκανοδοσία means *satisdatio* (“giving security”). But *satisdatio* and ἱκανοδοσία belong to the person promising, not to the person asking. This is explained at greater length because Augustine wanted *stipulari* to mean “to ask,” not “to promise,” and wanted *stipulator* to mean one who asks, in no way one who promises.] *Stipulator* (“stipulator”) means “promisor.” For *stipulari* means “to promise,” according to the language of jurists, who also called something firm *stipulum*.

259. *Sanus* (“healthy”), from *sanguis* (“blood”), because he is without pallor.

*Sospes* (“safe”) …

[Note: [Col. 0395D] *Salus*, from *sal* (“salt”), because salt prevents corruption.] *Salus* (“health,” “safety”) is thought to have received its name from *sal* (“salt”).

*Subtilis* (“subtle”), named from being made thin.

260. [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Sequester.* Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “with peace as intermediary”: “The intermediary, for a *sequester* is one who stands between two disputants, with something temporarily deposited with him.” Glossary: *sequester*, μεσίτης (“mediator”), ἔντριτος, συνθηκοφύλαξ (“keeper of agreements”). See Gellius, Book XX, chapter 10, and the books of the jurists.] A *sequester* (“intermediary”) is one who intervenes between disputants; among the Greeks he is called ὁ μέσος (“the middle one”), with whom pledges are customarily deposited. The word is formed from *sequendo* (“following”), because both parties follow the trustworthiness of the person they have chosen.

261. *Sessilis* (“seated”), because it does not appear to stand but to sit.

*Surdus* (“deaf”), from foul moisture gathered in the ear; and although this condition arises in many ways, the affected person nevertheless retains the name from the defect mentioned.

262. [Col. 0395B] *Siccus* (“dry”), because it has been drained of moisture, or, by antiphrasis, because it is without moisture.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] *Sepultus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “buried with a guardian.”] *Sepultus* (“buried”) is so called because it is without touch or without a pulse, that is, without movement.

263. [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Sajo.* A Gothic word, which we also retain; it is often read in Gothic laws and parchments and in Cassiodorus. In the Council of Mérida, chapter 8, some manuscripts mistakenly have *Salomonem* instead of *Sajonem*. It should be noted that the Goths pronounced the consonantal *i* in the manner in which we pronounce *gi* and *ge*. This is demonstrated not only by the spelling *sagio*, found in some books, and by German *sager* with the same meaning, but also sufficiently by Isidore’s etymology.] *Sajo* (“bailiff,” “official”) is named from *exigendo* (“exacting”).

*Sutor* (“shoemaker”), named from sewing skins.

*Subulcus* (“swineherd”), a keeper of pigs, just as *bubulcus* (“herdsman”) comes from caring for cattle.

T. 497

264. *Tutor* (“guardian”), one who protects a ward, that is, watches over him. In ordinary speech one says: “Why do you admonish me?” “In former times I overwhelmed both guardian and pedagogue.”

265. [Note: [Col. 0396C] *Testes.* Above, Book V, chapter 21.] *Testes* (“witnesses”) are so called because they are customarily brought in for a will, just as *signatores* (“signatories”) are so called because they sign a will.

266. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Tetricus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “the dreadful crags of Tetrica.”] *Tetricus* (“gloomy”) is a very rugged mountain in the Sabine country. Hence we also call sad people *tetri* (“gloomy”).

*Taciturnus* (“taciturn”), enduring in silence.

267. *Trutinator* (“weigher,” “examiner”), an examiner who weighs things on the scales of judgment; this is a direct metaphor from a *trutina*, which is a balance with two pans.

268. *Tristis* (“sad”) …

*Tenax* (“grasping”), especially desirous of money, because he holds on to it.

[Note: [Col. 0396D] Sometimes also “stubborn.” Plautus elegantly joined both meanings: “What do you say—is his father grasping?” “By heaven, yes, stubborn.”] Sometimes also “stubborn.”

*Truculentus* (“savage”) …

269. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Torvus*, “terrible.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “the terrible Abas.” We use the same term *rostrituerti* (“with twisted snouts”).] *Torvus* (“grim”), terrible, because he has a twisted face and turbulent expression, as in:

> The grim lioness;

and:

> We see them standing there, though in vain, with grim eyes.

270. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Turbidus.* From Servius, *Aeneid* IV.] *Turbidus* (“turbid”) …

*Terribilis* (“terrible”) …

*Teter* (“dreadful”), from a dark and gloomy life. *Teterrimus* (“most dreadful”) means excessively savage. For the ancients used *tetrum* for “savage,” as Ennius says:

> And savage elephants.

*Terribilis* is so called because it possesses fear and is feared.

271. *Tergiversator* (“shuffler”), because he turns his mind, as though his back, here and there, and is not easily understood for what he is.

*Temulentus* (“drunken”), named from *temetum*, that is, wine.

272. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Timidus* … that is, from blood. This means: it occurs because of the blood; “for fear … blood,” and so forth. These are Servius’ words, *Aeneid* III.] *Timidus* (“fearful”), because he fears for a long time, that is, from the blood; for fear freezes the blood, and blood congealed produces fear.

273. [Col. 0396B] *Turpis* (“ugly”), because he is deformed and sluggish.

V. 498

274. *Vir* (“man”), [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Vir* from *virtus* (“virtue”). This is a physical, not a grammatical, derivation—that is, not the origin of the word’s sound but of the thing itself; see the preface to this book. For rather, *virtus* comes from *vir*, and *vir* from *vis* (“force”), because a man has greater strength in him than a woman, as Lactantius says in *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 12. He follows the same reasoning shortly afterward in *verus* and *veritas*.] from *virtus* (“virtue”).

*Utilis* (“useful”), from using one’s own resources well, or because he can use something well, just as *docilis* (“teachable”) means one who can be taught.

275. *Verus* (“true”), from *veritas* (“truth”); hence also *verax* (“truthful”). *Veritas* is greater than *verus*, because *veritas* does not descend from *verus*, but *verus* from *veritas*.

*Veridicus* (“truth-speaking”), because he speaks the truth and is an advocate of truth.

*Verecundus* (“modest”), because he blushes at a true deed.

276. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Viridis*, full of strength and sap, as though “raw with strength.” Varro: “*Viridis* comes from a certain force of moisture; when it dries up, the thing dies.”] *Viridis* (“green”), full of strength and sap, as though “raw with strength.”

*Venustus* (“beautiful”), from *venae* (“veins”), that is, blood.

*Vivens* (“living”) …

[Col. 0396C] *Vivus* (“alive”) …

277. *Varius* (“varied”), as though not of one path but of an uncertain and mixed judgment.

*Versutus* (“cunning”), because his mind easily turns toward any deception in any action; hence *versutia* (“cunning”) is called a twisted judgment. Plautus says:

> More cunning than a potter’s wheel.

278. [Note: [Col. 0397A] *Villis* from *villa*, and so forth. These words are not found in the older books.] *Villis* (“boorish”), from *villa* (“country estate”), for it possesses no urban refinement.

*Versipellis* (“changeable”), because he turns his face and mind in different directions. Hence also *versutus* (“cunning”) and *callidus* (“crafty”).

*Violentus* (“violent”), because he inflicts force.

279. [Note: [Col. 0397A] *Vecors.* Festus: “*Vecors*, of disturbed and evil heart.” But Labeo: “*Vecors*, without heart; *vesanus*, without health.”] *Vecors* (“mad,” literally “heartless”), of an evil heart and bad conscience.

*Vagus* (“wandering”), because he is without a road.

*Vanus* (“empty,” “vain”) derives its etymology from Venus. *Vanus* also means empty and false, because it fades away without memory.

280. *Vesanus* (“insane”), not properly healthy.

*Vinolentus* (“wine-loving”), one who drinks enough and is difficult to intoxicate.

[Col. 0398A] [Note: [Col. 0397A] *Vexatus.* From Servius, *Eclogue* 6.] *Vexatus* (“carried,” “tormented”), that is, borne along, from *veho* (“carry”), *vexo*, *vecto*; thus *vexasse* means “to have carried.”

281. *Veneficus* (“poisoner”), because he prepared, supplied, or sold poison for the purpose of causing death.

[Note: [Col. 0397A] *Vector.* From the same source, *Aeneid* IV, on “unaware of that flight,” and so forth.] *Vector* (“carrier”), as though *vehitor* (“one who carries”). A *vector* is both one who transports and one who is transported.

282. *Venator* (“hunter”), as though *venabulator*, from *venabulum* (“hunting spear”), with which he presses hard upon wild beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0397B] There are four tasks of hunters. The duty of trackers is sufficiently shown by the word itself. Virgil expressed the other two in one verse:

[Col. 0398A]

> While the wings tremble and surround the woodland with a tracking net.

The function of pursuers will be clear from the elegant meaning of the verb *premere* (“press”). It sometimes means to pursue someone fleeing and press him so closely that you almost seize him; we say *ir al alcance* (“to go in pursuit”):

> The Greeks would flee from him, while the Trojan youth would press upon them.

*Aeneid* I. And again:

> … him, blazing with a hostile wound, Pyrrhus  
> Pursues, and now, now, holds him in his hand and presses him with his spear.

] There are therefore four tasks of hunters: trackers, searchers, beaters, and pursuers.

Here begins Volume IV of the Arevalian Edition. BOOK ELEVEN. ON MAN AND PORTENTS.

[Col. 0397]

CHAPTER ONE. On man and his parts.

[Col. 0397B]

1. [Note: [Col. 0397D] *Natura* (“nature”) is so called. These are Servius’ words, *Georgics* II, on “For nature lies beneath the soil.”] *Natura* (“nature”) is so called from making something be born. For it has the power of generating and making.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] “This indeed.” From Lactantius, Book II, chapter 1.] Some have said that nature is God, from whom all things were created and exist.

2. *Genus* (“kind,” “race”) is derived from *gignendo* (“begetting”); its name is derived from the earth, from which all things are generated, for γῆ (*gē*) means “earth” in Greek.

3. *Vita* (“life”) is so called because of vigor, or because it possesses the force of being born and growing. Hence trees are also said to have life, because they are generated and grow.

4. *Homo* (“human being”) is so called because he was made from *humus* (“earth”), as it is said in Genesis:

> And God created [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Man from the dust of the earth.” Thus all the oldest books read, and the author followed the Seventy translators, as he usually does.] man from the dust of the earth.

By an extended use of language, the whole human being is spoken of from both substances, that is, from the union of soul and body.

5. [Note: [Col. 0397D] For properly *homo* comes from *humus*. Jerome, Joel II.] Properly, then, *homo* comes from *humus*.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] But the Greeks call a human being ἄνθρωπος. From the same place in Lactantius.] But the Greeks called a human being ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*) because he looks upward, lifted from the earth to contemplate his maker. The poet Ovid indicates this when he says:

> While all the other animals look downward toward the earth,  
> He gave the human being an elevated face, and ordered him  
> To look upon heaven and raise his upright countenance to the stars.

He is therefore upright and looks toward heaven so that he may seek God, not focus upon the earth like cattle, [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Like cattle.” From Sallust, *Catiline*.] which nature fashioned bent forward and obedient to the belly.

6. [Note: [Col. 0397D] “Human being is twofold.” From Jerome, *Ezekiel* XIV.] The human being is twofold: inward and outward. The inward human being is the soul; the outward human being is the body.

7. [Note: [Col. 0397D] “But *anima* among the pagans.” Thus in the Gothic manuscript. See Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 17.] The soul (*anima*) received its name among the pagans because it is wind. Hence wind is called ἄνεμος (*anemos*) in Greek, because we seem to live by drawing air through the mouth. But this is plainly false, because the soul is generated much earlier than air can be drawn through the mouth, since it already lives in the mother’s womb.

8. Therefore air is not the soul, as some thought, who were unable to conceive of its incorporeal nature.

9. [Note: [Col. 0397D] “The evangelist declares.” John X.] The evangelist declares that spirit is the same as soul, saying:

> I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.

Regarding this same soul of the Lord at the time of his Passion, the evangelist likewise says:

> And bowing his head, [Note: [Col. 0398D] “He gave up the spirit.” John XIX has “gave up the spirit”; Matthew has “sent forth.” But the author of *On Spirit and Soul* uses the same form.] he gave up the spirit.

10. For what is it to give up the spirit if not to lay down the soul? But the soul is called *anima* because it lives; *spiritus* (“spirit”), either because of its spiritual nature [Note: [Col. 0398D] Or because it breathes in the body. The same wording occurs in the book *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 34. That this work is not by Hugh of Saint Victor is sufficiently shown by the fact that these and other passages occur in our manuscripts, which are older than Hugh.] or because it breathes into the body.

11. Likewise, [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Animus* is the same as *anima*. From Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 18.] *animus* (“mind,” “spirit”) is the same as *anima* (“soul”).

[Note: [Col. 0398D] But *anima* belongs to life, *animus* to deliberation. From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “blood and spirit follow.” The same expressions occur in the book *On Spirit and Soul*.] But the soul is concerned with life, the mind with deliberation. Hence philosophers say that life can remain even without a mind, and a soul can endure without intellect; hence also *amentes* (“mindless persons”). For the mind is called *mens* so that it may know, and *animus* so that it may will.

12. [Note: [Col. 0399A] *Mens* (“mind”) is so called because it stands out in the soul, or because it remembers; hence also *immemores* (“forgetful persons”) are called *amentes* (“mindless”).] *Mens* (“mind”) is so called because it stands out in the soul, or because it remembers; hence also the forgetful are called *amentes* (“mindless”). Therefore it is not the soul itself but what excels in the soul that is called the mind, as its head or eye. Hence the human being himself, according to the mind, is called the image of God. All these faculties are so joined to the soul that they are one thing. For the soul has received different names according to the effects of its operations.

13. For memory too is mind; hence the forgetful are called mad. [Note: [Col. 0399D] “While therefore it gives life . . . receives.” In the same book, *On the Spirit*, chapter 34.] While it gives life to the body, it is soul; while it wills, it is mind (*animus*); while it knows, it is mind; while it recalls, it is memory; while it judges what is right, it is reason; [Col. 0399B] while it breathes, it is spirit; while it perceives something, it is sense. For this reason the mind (*animus*) is called sense with reference to what it perceives; hence the word *sententia* (“judgment,” “opinion”) is derived.

14. The body (*corpus*) is so called because, once corrupted, it perishes. For it is dissoluble and mortal, and is destined one day to be dissolved.

Flesh (*caro*) is named from *creare* (“to create”).

15. [Note: [Col. 0399D] *Crementum* (“creation,” “seed”). From the glosses of Placidus, as above, Book IX, chapter 5.] For *crementum* is the male seed, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived. Hence parents are called creators.

16. [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Flesh, however, is composed of the four elements.” Thus all the codices read. Chacon wrote “body,” on the authority of Lactantius and Jerome; this is incorrect unless one writes “our bodies,” following Lactantius, or “human bodies,” following Jerome, since he is immediately going to say that life is contained under the name “flesh,” but not under “body.” Nor is there any objection in the fact that he appears to make “flesh” both the whole and a part, when he adds, “for earth is in flesh”; for this is said as though he were presenting something obvious and evident, before proceeding to assign somewhat less conspicuous locations to the remaining elements.] Flesh, however, is composed of the four elements. [Note: [Col. 0399D] “For earth is in flesh.” Lactantius, Book II, chapter 12.] For earth is in flesh, air in the breath, moisture in the blood, and fire in vital heat. Each of the elements has its own allotted part in us; when the structure is dissolved, each returns to what is owed to it.

[Col. 0399C] 17. [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Flesh and body.” From Jerome, Letter to Pammachius against the error of John of Jerusalem.] Flesh and body signify different things. There is always body in flesh, but not always flesh in body; for flesh is what lives, and that same thing is body. Body that does not live is not flesh. 4 For “body” is said either of what is dead after life, or of what was formed without life. Sometimes, even with life, there is body but not flesh, as in grass and wood.

18. There are five senses of the body: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Of these, two are opened and closed, while two are always open.

19. [Note: [Col. 0399D] “The senses are so called.” From the same book, *On the Spirit*.] They are called senses because through them the soul moves the whole body with the utmost subtlety by the power of perception.

[Col. 0400A] [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Hence they are also called presences.” Above, Book X, under the letter P.] Hence they are also called “presences,” because they are before the senses, just as things that are present to the eyes are before the eyes.

20. Sight is what philosophers call the “vitreous humor.” [Note: [Col. 0399D] “How sight is produced.” Aristotle is the authority for the earlier opinion; Empedocles and Plato for the other, and Galen followed them. [Col. 0400D]] Some assert that sight is produced either by external ethereal light, or by an inner luminous spirit [Note: [Col. 0400D] “Through narrow passages.” Others read “veins.”] coming through narrow passages from the brain, emerging into the air after penetrating the membranes, and then, through the mixture of similar matter, producing vision.

21. [Note: [Col. 0400D] “Sight is so called because it is more vivid.” Thus, when the Greeks assign the genitive case to the words for the other senses, they give the accusative to the word for seeing, because it possesses greater efficacy; this is thought to support Plato’s opinion.] Sight is so called because it is more vivid than the other senses, superior, or swifter, and has greater power, just as memory does among the other functions of the mind. For it is nearer to the brain, from which everything flows; consequently, we say that we “see” what belongs to the other senses also, as when we say, “See how it sounds,” or “See how it tastes,” and similarly in other cases.

[Col. 0400B] 22. Hearing is so called [Note: [Col. 0400D] “Because it draws in voices.” From Lactantius, chapter 8 of *On the Workmanship of God*.] because it draws in voices—that is, receives sounds from struck air.

Smell (*odoratus*) is as though one were touched by the odor of air. For it is perceived when the air is touched; similarly, *olfactus* (“smelling”) is so called because it is affected by odors.

Taste (*gustus*) is named from the throat (*guttur*).

5 23. Touch is so called because it handles and touches, and spreads the power of sensation through all the limbs. [Note: [Col. 0400D] “For by touch we test.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* VI, chapter 9: “For commonly we test by touch what we cannot test with our eyes.”] For by touch we test whatever we cannot judge through the other senses. There are two kinds of touch: either it comes from outside, striking us, or it arises within the body itself.

24. Each sense has been given its own nature. What must be seen is grasped by the eyes, what must be heard [Col. 0400C] by the ears; soft and hard things are assessed by touch, flavor by taste, and odor is drawn in through the nostrils.

25. [Note: [Col. 0400D] “The first part of the body is the head, and this name was given to it.” Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 5: “At the top he placed the head, and gave it this name, as Varro writes to Cicero, because the senses and nerves take their beginning from it.”] The first part of the body is the head, and this name was given to it because all the senses and nerves take their beginning from it, [Note: [Col. 0400D] “And from it every cause of being alive arises.” Ambrose, in the same passage: “The eyes are nearer to the brain, from which all the use of being alive flows.”] and from it every cause of being alive arises. For all the senses appear there. Hence it somehow represents the person of the soul itself, which governs the body.

26. The crown of the head (*vertex*) is the part where the hair of the head is gathered and in which the locks turn; hence it receives its name.

[Col. 0401A] 27. The skull (*calvaria*) is named from the bare bones, [Note: [Col. 0401D] “By loss.” That is, from *calvendo*, as with *calumnia* and *cavillatio*, according to Gaius, chapter 233, *On the Meaning of Words*. Gloss: *Calvor*, “I deceive,” Greek ἐξαπατῶ.] through a process of loss, [Note: [Col. 0401D] “And it is pronounced as a neuter.” That is, not only in the feminine gender. Gloss: *Calvarium*, “skull,” Greek κράνιον. Likewise *calvaria*, κράνιον.] and it is also pronounced as a neuter.

The back of the head (*occipitium*) is the rear part of the head, as though it were opposite the front of the head, or because it is toward the rear of the head.

28. [Note: [Col. 0401D] “Hair, as though hairs of the head.” Augustine, *Dialectic*, chapter 6.] The hair of the head (*capilli*) is so called, as though “hairs of the head,” because it provides adornment, protects the brain against cold, and shields it from the sun.

The hairs (*pili*) are named from the skin from which they emerge, [Note: [Col. 0401D] “Just as *pilum* is named from *pila*.” Varro derives it from *pinsere* (“to pound”), Servius from *Pilumnus*.] just as *pilum* (“pestle”) is named from *pila*, where pigment is pounded.

29. [Note: [Col. 0401D] “The *caesaries* … belongs to men.” Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on the verse “For the beautiful locks themselves.”] The *caesaries* (“head of hair”) is named from cutting, and therefore belongs only to men. [Note: [Col. 0401D] “For a shorn man.” Ambrose, *On the Hair*: “One sex is suited by long hair, another by cropped hair.”] A shorn man is becoming; a woman is not.

6 30. [Note: [Col. 0401D] “Locks of hair.” The words are Servius’, *Aeneid* V, on the verse “The cropped hair pressed by a crown.”] *Comae* are properly uncut hair, and the word is Greek. [Note: [Col. 0401D] “For the Greeks call locks *caimos*.” Thus nearly all the Gothic books read. *Culmos* in the Salamanca manuscript may also be referred here because of the similarity of the letters. It is not worthwhile to report the monstrosities of other books, such as occur nearly every time something is taken from the Greek language.] For the Greeks call locks *caimos*, from cutting, [Col. 0401B] and hence they call cutting hair κείρειν (“to cut, shear”). Hence curls are also called *cirri*, because the same Greeks call them μαλλὸν (“a lock of hair; wool”). [Note: [Col. 0402D] “The Greeks, μαλλὸν.” Gloss: Μαλλός, “curl, wool.”]

31. *Crines* (“locks”) properly belong to women. They are called *crines* because they are divided by ribbons. Hence the ribbons with which they are divided and tied are called *discriminalia*.

32. The temples (*tempora*) are the parts lying beneath the right and left sides of the skull. They are so called because they move, and by that movement change at certain intervals, like times (*tempora*).

33. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “The face, etc.” Ambrose, in the same passage: “What is a human being without a head? Since the whole person is in the head, when you see the head, you recognize the human being.”] The face (*facies*) is named from *effigies* (“likeness,” “image”). For the whole figure of a human being and the recognition of each individual person are there.

34. The countenance (*vultus*) is so called because through it the will of the mind is displayed; according to the will, it changes into various movements. Thus the two terms differ: *facies* is used simply of each person’s natural [Col. 0401C] appearance, while *vultus* signifies the qualities of the mind.

35. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “The brow.” From Lactantius, chapter 8, and Ambrose, in the passage cited.] The brow (*frons*) is named from the openings of the eyes. It is a kind of image of the mind, expressing by its appearance the movement of the mind when it is joyful or sad.

36. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “The eyes are so called.” From the same passage of Lactantius.] The eyes (*oculi*) are so called either because the coverings of the eyelashes conceal them, so that they are not injured by the impact of some harmful object, or because they contain a hidden light—that is, a secret or inwardly placed light. Among all the senses, they are closest to the soul; for every indication of the mind is in the eyes, and disturbance or cheerfulness of spirit appears in the eyes. 7 The eyes are also called lights (*lumina*). [Col. 0402A] They are called lights because light flows from them, or because at their origin they hold light shut, or reflect back light received from outside so that it may be presented to sight.

37. The pupil (*pupilla*) is the central point of the eye, in which the power of seeing resides. Because small images appear to us there, they are called *pupillae* (“little dolls”); for little boys are called *pupilli*. Many call this a *pupula*. It is called *pupilla* because it is pure and undefiled, like young girls. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Physicians say.” The words are Servius’, *Aeneid* IV, on the verse “It gives sleep and takes it away,” etc.] Physicians say that those about to die lack, three days beforehand, the same pupils that we see in eyes; when these are not seen, despair is certain.

38. The circle by which the white parts of the eye are separated from the pupil by a distinct blackness is called the *corona* (“crown”), because by its roundness it adorns the circumference of the pupil.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] “Some call them *volvi*.” Book XVII, chapter 10: “They are called *volvi* because they are rolling and round”; others call them βολβοί, and *bulbi*. Isidore has *volvi* throughout, with all the books agreeing. Others read “from the likeness of *valvae*.” The Tarragona manuscript adds: “Little valves, bean pods.”] Some call the very globes of the eyes *volvi*, because of their resemblance to bulbs.

39. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “Eyelids.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on the verse “Filling her lap with welling tears,” and Lactantius, chapter 10 of *On the Workmanship of God*.] The eyelids (*palpebrae*) are the folds of the eyes, named from fluttering because they are always moving. For they come together in turn, so that by their constant movement they refresh the sight. [Note: [Col. 0402D] “They are fortified.” From Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, or from Ambrose, in the passage cited.] They are fortified by a rampart of hairs, so that if something falls into the open eyes it may be repelled, and so that, when they close in sleep, the eyes may rest hidden as though wrapped up.

40. At the upper edge of the eyelids, where the two closed lids meet, hairs grow in an orderly row. They provide protection for the eyes, so that the eyes may not readily receive and be harmed by invading irritants; they prevent contact with dust or any denser substance, and by breaking up the air itself they soften it, making the vision fine and clear.

41. Some think that tears are called *lacrymae* from the laceration of the mind; others think they are so called because the Greeks call them δάκρυα (“tears”).

42. The eyelashes (*cilia*) are coverings by which the eyes are covered. They are called *cilia* 8 because they conceal and cover the eyes with secure protection.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] “The eyebrows.” Ambrose: “Twin ridges of the eyebrows follow the brow, extending defenses before the eyes.”] The eyebrows (*supercilia*) are so called because they are placed above the eyelashes. They are covered with hairs for this reason: to provide protection before the eyes, [Note: [Col. 0402D] “And drive away sweat flowing down from the head.” These are Cicero’s words.] and to drive away sweat flowing down from the head.

The space between the eyebrows (*intercilium*) is the middle area between them, which is without hair.

43. The cheeks (*genae*) are the lower parts of the eyes, from which the beard begins; for in Greek γένειον means “beard.” Hence *genae* also, because beards begin to grow from there.

44. The cheekbones (*malae*) are the projecting parts beneath the eyes, placed there for their protection. They are called *malae* either because they project beneath the eyes in a rounded form—the Greeks call such things μῆλα (“cheeks”)—or because they are above the jaws.

45. The jaws (*maxillae*) are named by diminution from *malae*, just as *paxillus* (“little stake”) comes from *palus* (“stake”), and *taxillus* (“small ankle bone”) from *talus* (“ankle”).

The mandibles (*mandibulae*) are parts of the jaws, and their name is derived from this.

The ancients called the beard (*barba*) so because it belongs to men, not women.

46. The ears (*aures*) received their name from drawing in voices, hence Virgil: “And I drank in the voice with these ears.” Or because the Greeks call the voice itself αὐδή, from hearing. By changing a letter, the ears were called *aures*, as though *audes*. [Note: [Col. 0403C] “For the voice, striking back.” Ambrose, in the same passage.] For the voice, reflected through the winding passages of the ears, produces a sound by which they receive the sense of hearing. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “The *pinnula* is the uppermost part.” Gloss: “The upper part of the ear,” πτερίγιον.] The *pinnula*, the uppermost part of the ear, is named from its pointed shape. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “For the ancients called *pinnum* …” Thus in Book XVII, chapter 7, and Book XIX, chapter 19.] For the ancients called a pointed thing *pinnum*; hence *bipennis* (“double-edged axe”) and *pinna* (“fin,” “wing”).

47. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “The nostrils … does not cease to breathe.” Thus the Roman codex and Lactantius, chapter 11. Our copies erroneously read *manare* (“to flow”).] The nostrils (*nares*) are so called because through them either odor or breath does not cease to flow (*nare*); or [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Because they warn us by odor.” From Donatus, on *Adelphoe*.] because they warn us by odor, so that we may recognize and know something, 9 and hence, by contrast, those who are uninformed, inexperienced, and ignorant are called *inscii* and *rudes*. For the ancients used *olfacere* (“to smell”) to mean “to know.” Terence: “And I would have smelled it out a full six months before he began anything.”

48. The straight part of the nostrils, because it extends evenly in length and roundness, is called the column (*columna*); its extremity is the little pear-shaped part (*pirula*), from the shape of a pear. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “*Pirula*. The Greeks call this σφαίριον, the little wings πτερύγια, and the middle partition ἰσθμόν. Arnobius likewise calls this middle partition an *interfinium*. Lactantius seems to have intended *septum* when he said: ‘As though by a wall drawn through the middle, he divided and separated it.’ Theophilus, Book [lacuna], *On Construction* [title abbreviated in the source]. *Among physicians it is called διάφραγμα (“partition”), but among poets κίων (“column”) and στύλη (“pillar”)*.”] The parts to the right and left are the little wings (*pinnulae*), from their resemblance to wings; the middle part is the partition (*interfinium*).

49. The mouth (*os*) is so called because through it, as through a doorway, we send food inside and spit outside; [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Or because things enter through it.” So in the Gospel: “because he was going to pass through there.” But *illuc* or *illac* may also be read from the Tarragona books.] or because food enters through it and speech goes out through it.

50. The lips (*labia*) are named from licking. The upper one is called *labium*; the lower, because it is thicker, is called *labrum*. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Others say *labra* of men.” Servius criticizes those who say this in his commentary on *Corydon*.] Others say that men have *labra* and women *labia*.

[Col. 0404A] 51. Varro thinks that the tongue (*lingua*) received its name from binding food. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “From binding food, he thinks.” Varro. Lactantius: “Thus Varro thinks that the name *lingua* was given from binding food.” [Col. 0404C]] Others think it is so called because through articulated sounds it binds words together. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “For just as a plectrum.” From Jerome, in the epitaph of Paula.] For just as a plectrum strikes the strings, so the tongue is struck against the teeth and produces a vocal sound.

52. The Greeks call teeth ὀδόντες, and the Latin name appears to be derived from that. The first teeth are called incisors (*praecisores*) because they are the first to cut whatever is taken in.
