The next are called canine teeth; there are two on the right jaw and two on the left. They are called canine because they resemble those of dogs, and a dog breaks bones with them, as does a human being; whatever the incisors cannot cut through, they hand over to the canines to break. The common people call these, because of their length and roundness, [Note: [Col. 0404D] “Little columns.” Varro, *On Agriculture*, also says they are called *columnares*.] *colomelli* (“little columns”). The last are the molars, which knead, grind, and mash what has been cut and broken by the earlier teeth; hence they are called molars.

53. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “The number of teeth.” Solinus’ words, chapter 4.] The number of teeth differs according to sex. For men have more, women fewer.

54. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “The gums.” Lactantius, chapter 10.] The gums (*gingivae*) are named from producing the teeth. They were also made for the beauty of the teeth, so that the teeth would not appear bare and more frightening than ornamental.

55. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “Our palate is like the sky.” Cicero, on Epicurus: “But while he judges by the palate what is best, he did not look up at the palace of the sky, as Ennius says.”] Our palate is positioned like the sky, and hence *palatum* is derived from *polus* (“pole,” “sky”). The Greeks likewise call the palate οὐρανός (“sky”), because by its concavity it resembles the sky.

56. The throat (*fauces*) is named from pouring forth voices, or because through it we utter sounds.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] “The arteries.” He confuses the windpipe with the other arteries distributed throughout the body, which contain the vital spirit, and rightly adapts a Latin explanation to the Greek word.] The arteries (*arteriae*) are so called either because through them air, that is, spirit, is carried from the lung, or because they retain the vital spirit in tight and narrow passages, from which they emit the sounds of the voice. These sounds would all sound alike if the movements of the tongue did not produce variations in the voice.

57. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “*Tolles* in the Gallic language.” Festus writes the same. Gloss: *tolae*, *tolia*, παρίοθμια (“tonsils”), and *tusillae*, παρίσθμια (“tonsils”). Chacon said that *tosillas*, not *tonsillas*, should be read in the manuscripts of Cornelius Celsus, Book VI, chapter 10; *tonsilla* in Festus means a hewn stake.] In the Gallic language they are called *tolles*; in common speech, by diminutive form, they are called *tusillae*. They commonly swell in the throat.

The chin (*mentum*) is so called because the mandibles begin there, or because they are joined there.

58. [Note: [Col. 0404D] “*Gurgulio* from *guttur*.” See Lactantius and Servius, *Georgics* I.] The *gurgulio* takes its name from the throat. Its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils, and it has a channel through which the voice is transmitted to the tongue, 11 so that it can strike words together; hence we also say *garrire* (“to chatter”).

[Col. 0405A] 59. [Note: [Col. 0405C] “The *rumen*.” Also Festus.] The *rumen*, next to the *gurgulio*, is the place through which food and drink are swallowed. Hence animals that bring food back up and chew it again are said to ruminate.

[Note: [Col. 0405C] “The *sublinguium*.” Gloss: “Under the tongue,” ὑπόγλωσσον.] The *sublinguium* is the covering of the *gurgulio*, as though a little tongue, which closes or covers the opening of the tongue.

60. The neck (*collum*) is so called because it is stiff and rounded, like a column carrying the head and supporting it, [Note: [Col. 0405C] “As though a capital.” Perhaps *capitulum*, or, as Isidore says, *capitellum*. For the head is to the neck what the capital is to a column.] like a capital. Its front part is called the throat (*gula*), its rear part the nape (*cervix*).

61. The nape (*cervix*) is so called because through that part the brain is directed toward the marrow of the spine, as though it were the brain’s pathway. The ancients, however, used *cervices* only in the plural; [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Hortensius was the first.” From Quintilian, Book VIII, chapter 3. Varro also reports the same, Books VII and IX. Cicero alluded to this in the fifth action against Verres: “Do we nevertheless suppose that your patron [Col. 0405D] will toss his little neck about in this accusation?”] Hortensius was the first to use *cervix* in the singular. In the singular, *cervix* signifies the body part itself; [Note: [Col. 0405D] “For in the plural it often indicates stubbornness.” This has been produced merely by punctuation, so that Isidore would not contradict himself in this passage.] in the plural, it often indicates stubbornness. Cicero, in *Against Verres*: “You accuse the praetor—break his neck.”

62. The shoulders (*humeri*) are so called as though they were *armi*, the name having been changed to distinguish them from dumb animals, so that humans are said to have *humeri* and animals *armi*; for properly speaking, *armi* belong to quadrupeds.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] *Ola*. Others read *aula*.] *Ola* is the rear part of the upper shoulder.

63. The arms (*brachia*) are named from strength, for in Greek βαρύ means “heavy” and “strong.” [Note: [Col. 0405D] “For in the arms are the bulges of the muscles.” From Lactantius. Ambrose likewise says: “The arms follow, and the strong bulges of the muscles.”] In the arms are the bulges of the muscles, and there is a conspicuous strength of musculature. These bulges are called *tori*, that is, muscles, [Note: [Col. 0405D] “And called *tori*.” Because Servius writes that *torus* is named from twisted grasses. Isidore wished the bulges of the arms to be named from twisted viscera.] and they are called *tori* because the twisted viscera appear there.

64. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “The elbow.” Horace: “Let the languid banqueter recline upon his elbow.”] The elbow (*cubitus*) is so called because on it we recline when taking food.

[Col. 0405C] 12 [Note: [Col. 0405D] “The forearm.” From Servius, *Georgics* III.] According to some, the *ulna* is the extension of either hand; according to others, it is the elbow, which is more correct, because in Greek ὠλένη means “elbow.”

65. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “The armpits, beneath the arms.” We too say *sobaci*.] The armpits (*alae*) are called the parts beneath the arms because from them the movement of the arms begins in the manner of wings. Some call them *ascillae*, because through them the arms are *cilluntur*, that is, moved; hence masks (*ora*) are also called *oscilla* from the fact that they are *cillantur*, that is, moved. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “*Oscilla* … to move.” From Servius, *Georgics* II. See Festus, Macrobius, Hyginus, the interpreters of Aratus, and Ovid in the *Fasti*.] For *cillere* means “to move.” Some call these parts *subhirci* (“under-goats”), because in most people they produce the odor of goats.

66. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “The hand.” From Ambrose, in the passage cited.] The hand (*manus*) is so called because it is the function of the whole body. It supplies food to the mouth, performs and manages everything; through it we receive and give. By an extended usage, *manus* also means a craft or craftsman, and hence we say *manupretium* (“the price of workmanship”). [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Hence *manupretium*.” Others read *manuspretium*. As in Ulpian, chapter 13, *On the Meaning of Words*.]

67. The right hand (*dextra*) is so called from giving, for it is given as a pledge of peace, and it is employed as a witness of faith and safety. [Note: [Col. 0406C] “A witness of faith.” Servius, *Aeneid* III, on the verse “He had spoken and embraced his knees.” Physicians say that individual body parts are consecrated to particular divinities: the ear to Memory, the brow to Genius, the right hand to Faith.] This is what Cicero means: “I gave the public pledge by order of the Senate”—that is, I gave the right hand. Hence the Apostle says: “They gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas.”

68. The left hand (*laeva*) is so called because it is more suitable for lifting. The left (*sinistra*) is also called as though “without the right,” [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Or because it permits something to be done.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II. See Festus, under *Sinistrae aves* and *Sinistrum*.] or because it permits a thing to be done. [Col. 0406B] It is named *sinistra* from *sinere* (“to permit”).

69. The palm (*palma*) is the hand with the fingers spread; with the fingers contracted, it is a fist (*pugnus*).

The fist is named from *pugillus* (“little fist”), just as the palm is named from the spread branches of the palm.

70. [Note: [Col. 0406C] “The fingers.” From Lactantius.] The fingers (*digiti*) are so called either because there are ten of them, or because they are joined together gracefully. For they contain both a complete number and the most orderly arrangement. The first is called the thumb (*pollex*) because it excels the others in strength and power. [Note: [Col. 0406D] “The second is the saluting finger.” It is called this by Suetonius in *Augustus*, and even today at Rome, when married women greet one another, they bring the index finger to the mouth. Men do the same in public prayers when they greet Christ.] The second is the saluting or pointing finger, because with it we generally salute and point things out.

71. The third is the indecent finger, because an insulting gesture is commonly expressed through it. The fourth is the ring finger, because a ring is worn on it; [Note: [Col. 0406D] “It is also medicinal.” Macrobius and Aulus Gellius say that a very delicate nerve extends from the finger of the left hand to the heart; therefore this finger would more properly be called medicinal than the right.] it is also called medicinal because physicians use it to collect eye salves that have been rubbed together. The fifth is the little or ear finger, because with it we scratch the ear.

72. We call the nail (*ungula*) by a Greek-derived name; for the Greeks call nails ὄνυχες.

The trunk (*truncus*) is the middle part of the body, from the neck to the groin. [Note: [Col. 0406D] Concerning this Nigidius says: “The head is carried by the neck,” etc. Nonius, under *Coxendices*, gives *coxendicae* for hips. Lucilius: “The head is supported by the neck, the trunk is supported by the hips.” We therefore suspect that this entire passage—“by the hips, knees, and legs”—arose from failure to understand the word *coxendices*. The seven-syllable line, whether by Lucilius or Nigidius, could be supported as follows: “The head is supported by the neck, the trunk by the hips,” if the penultimate syllable of *coxendice* is lengthened. Or, to make a six-syllable line from Isidore: “The head is carried by the neck, the trunk by the hip, or by the hips.”] Concerning this Nigidius says: “The head is carried by the neck; the trunk is supported by the hips, knees, and legs.”

73. The thorax (*thorax*) is called by the Greeks the front part of the trunk, from the neck to the stomach. [Col. 0407A] We call it the chest (*arca*), because a secret is there—that is, a hidden thing from which others are kept away. Hence *arca* and *ara* are also said, as though they referred to hidden things. Its projecting fleshy parts are the breasts. Between them, the bony part is called the chest (*pectus*); to the right and left are the ribs.

74. The chest (*pectus*) is so called because it is combed (*pexum*) between the projecting parts of the breasts; hence we also call a comb *pecten*, because it makes the hair smooth.

The breasts (*mamillae*) are so called because they are round like apples, the term being a diminutive.

75. The nipples (*papillae*) are the tips of the breasts, which nursing infants grasp. They are called *papillae* because infants, while sucking milk, treat them as though they were eating (*pappant*). [Note: [Col. 0407C] “Therefore the breast is …” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, and Festus, [Col. 0407D] under the word *Papillae*.] Thus the breast (*mamilla*) is every prominence of the udder, while the nipple (*papilla*) is the small part [Col. 0407B] from which milk is drawn.

76. The breasts (*ubera*) are so called either [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Because they are filled with milk.” Agellius uses the same expression, Book VIII, chapter 14.] because they are filled with milk, or because they are moist, being full of the moisture of milk in the manner of grapes.

77. [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Milk derives the force of its name from color.” He repeats this in Book XX, chapter 2.] Milk (*lac*) derives the force of its name from color, because it is a white liquid; for in Greek λευκός means “white.” Its substance is transformed from blood. For after childbirth, if any blood has not yet been consumed as nourishment for the womb, it flows by its natural passage into the breasts and, becoming white through their power, takes on the quality of milk.

78. The skin (*cutis*) is so called because it is the first covering of the body; when placed over the body, it is the first to suffer an incision, [Note: [Col. 0407D] “For κοπτή in Greek means ‘incision.’” Thus Augustine’s copy reads, whereas in all the books *cutis enim Graece* makes no sense. Festus, however, has *cutis* from ἀπὸ τοῦ σκύτους; we would gladly read that here, if Isidore were not interpreting it as “incision.”] for κοπτή in Greek means “incision.” It is also called *pellis* (“hide”), because by covering the body it repels external injuries and withstands rain, winds, and the heat of the sun.

[Col. 0407C] 79. Hide (*pellis*), once removed and already treated, is called leather (*corium*).

Leather (*corium*) is named by derivation from flesh (*caro*), because flesh is covered by it; but this is proper to brute animals.

80. The pores of the body are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are properly called openings or vents (*spiramenta*), because through them the life-giving spirit is supplied outwardly.

81. [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Arvina*. Servius, *Aeneid* VII: “According to Suetonius, *arvina* is hard fat located between the skin and the viscera.”] *Arvina* is fat adhering to the skin.

Flesh without fat is called *pulpa* (“flesh”), because it throbs; for it often springs back. Many also call it *viscum* (“flesh, tissue”), because it is sticky.

[Col. 0408A] 82. Limbs (*membra*) are the parts of the body.

Joints (*artus*), by which the limbs are joined, are named from tightening (*arctare*).

83. The sinews (*nervi*) are named by derivation from Greek; the Greeks call them νεῦρα. Others think they are called *nervi* in Latin because the joints adhere to one another through them—that is, from *inhaerere* (“to adhere”). It is certain that the sinews constitute the greatest substance of strength: the denser they are, the more strongly firmness increases.

84. The joints (*artus*) are so called because, joined together by sinews, they are tightened—that is, bound. Their diminutives are *articuli* (“small joints”). We call the larger limbs *artus*, such as the arms; smaller limbs, such as the fingers, we call *articuli*.

15 85. [Note: [Col. 0407D] *Compago*. Thus most Gothic books read; others have *compagia*.] *Compago* (“joint,” “framework”) refers to the heads of the bones. They are so called because, compacted together by sinews, they adhere as though by a kind of glue.

86. Bones (*ossa*) are the solid supports of the body. For all its position and strength rests upon them. Bones are called *ossa* from burning (*urere*), because the ancients burned them, or, as others think, from the mouth (*os*), because there they are open; elsewhere they are hidden beneath the skin and viscera.

87. The marrow (*medullae*) is so called because it moistens the bones; for it irrigates and strengthens them.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] “Vertebrae … cartilages.” Lactantius, chapter 5, *On Bones*: “He gathered their upper parts into thicker knots, so that they might more easily be bound by sinews and turned; hence they were called vertebrae. He covered those firmly solidified knots with a certain smooth covering called cartilage, so that they might bend without friction or any sensation of pain.”] Vertebrae (*vertibula*) are the upper parts of the bones, gathered into thicker knots; they are so called because the limbs turn upon them in bending.

88. Cartilages (*cartilagines*) are soft bones without marrow, such as are found in the ear, the partition of the nostrils, and the ends of the ribs; or they are coverings of bones that move. [Col. 0408C] They are called cartilages because, when they bend, their gentle friction is without pain.

89. Some think the ribs (*costae*) are so called because the interior parts are guarded by them, so that all the softness of the belly, enclosed as though by a rampart, may remain safe.

90. The side (*latus*) is so called because, when we lie down, it is hidden. [Note: [Col. 0408C] “For it is the left part of the body.” Hence Servius calls the inner side the left side. In his commentary on *Aeneid* V, on “When he raises the prow toward the rocks,” he interprets *interior* as “more left.” Likewise, in *Aeneid* V, on “Marks out the city with the plow”: “Cato says in the *Origins* that this was the custom. When founding cities, they yoked a bull on the right and a cow on the inside.” Asconius interprets the joke in Cicero about Aspendius the cithara player, who sang everything *inside*, in the same way. This also illuminates the passage of Catullus:

> Marrucine Asinius, you do not use  
> Your left hand well in jest and wine;  
> You lift the napkins of careless men.

Thus “to cover the left side” means to go, and it belongs to one who could stab the left side—what Horace said of the nomenclator. We know what a very learned man thinks about the whole matter; concerning him I will say this: why Servius raged so fiercely about this issue is unclear, since he could equally have been angry with Cato and Asconius.] For it is the left part of the body, [Note: [Col. 0408D] “Movement is more serviceable … to the right side.” The words of Solinus at the end of chapter 5.] while movement is more serviceable to the right side, but the left is stronger and better suited to carrying a burden. Hence it too is called *laeva*, because it is more suitable for lifting and carrying something. For it bears the shield, sword, quiver, [Col. 0408D] and other burdens, so that the right hand may be free for action.

[Col. 0409A] 91. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “The back.” Properly, as though “hard upward.” But Festus says: “The back is so called because that part of the body slopes downward.”] The back (*dorsum*) extends from the nape to the kidneys. It is called *dorsum* because it is the harder surface of the body, like a stone, strong both for carrying and for enduring.

92. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “The back.” From Lactantius, chapter 10.] The *terga* (“backs”) are so called because we lie supine upon them in the earth. For only a human being can do this; dumb animals lie either on the belly or on the side. Hence *terga* is used improperly of animals.

93. The shoulder blade (*scapula*) [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0409D] “The space between the shoulder blades.” Others read *interscapulum* or *interscapilium*. *Interscaplium* occurs in Caelius, Book III, chapter 2, and should accordingly be restored in the gloss, where *interscapulum*, Greek μετάφρενον, is read.] The space between the shoulder blades (*interscaplium*) is the area between the shoulder blades, and hence receives its name.

94. The shoulder blades (*palae*) are the projecting limbs on the right and left of the back. They are so called because we press them in wrestling; the Greeks call wrestling παλαίειν.

95. The spine (*spina*) is the jointed structure of the back. It is so called because it has sharp little projections; the joints of this structure are called vertebrae (*spondilia*), because a part of the brain is carried through them along a long course to the other parts of the body.

96. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “The sacral spine.” Jerome, on Ecclesiastes XII: “The blossom of the almond tree, which we interpreted as gray hair, some interpret as the sacral spine, because as the flesh of the buttocks diminishes, the spine increases and flourishes.” Caelius, *On Acute and Chronic Diseases* IV, chapter 3: “The sacral spine is called the sacred bone, which the Greeks also call ἱερὸν ὀστέον.”] The sacral spine (*sacra spina*) is the lowest part of the continuous spine, which the Greeks call ἱερὸν ὀστοῦν (“sacred bone”), because it is formed first when the fetus is conceived. [Note: [Col. 0409D] “And therefore from the sacrificial victim.” Menander: “But those who sacrificed the tip of the loin.” [Col. 0410D]] Therefore, among the gentiles, that part was first offered from the sacrificial victim to their gods; hence it is called the sacral spine.

97. [Note: [Col. 0410D] “The kidneys.” From Lactantius, chapter 14.] Varro says that the kidneys (*renes*) are so called because streams of obscene moisture arise from them. For the veins and marrow sweat out a thin liquid in the kidneys, and this liquid, again dissolved by the kidneys’ venereal heat, flows downward.

98. [Note: [Col. 0410D] “The loins.” From Gregory’s words, Homily 13, he fashioned whatever explanation of the name he could.] The loins (*lumbi*) are named from the wantonness of sexual desire, because in men the cause of bodily pleasure lies there, just as in women it lies in the navel. Hence at the beginning of the discourse on Job 17 it is said: “Gird your loins like a man,” so that preparation for resistance might be in those parts in which the customary opportunity for lust to exercise dominion resides.

99. The navel is the central place of the body, so called because it is the *umbo*—the protuberance—of the hips; hence *umbo* is also called the place in the middle of a shield from which it hangs. [Note: [Col. 0410D] For from it the infant hangs. From Lactantius, chapter 10.] For from it the infant hangs in the womb, and from it also receives nourishment.

100. The hip is called *ilium* in Greek usage because we wrap ourselves there; for in Greek εἱλύειν means “to wrap.”

101. The buttocks are called *clunes* because they are beside the colon, [Note: [Col. 0410D] Which is *longao*. Gloss: *longao*, κωλέντερον. In Caelius both *longao* and *longano* occur; in the manuscripts of Arnobius and Varro, *longano*; in Vegetius, *Veterinary Medicine* I.42, the intestine is *longanon*.] which is *longao*.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The buttocks. From Lactantius, chapter 13.] The buttocks are so called because we rest upon them when sitting; hence the flesh is gathered into a mass there, so that the bones would not hurt beneath the weight of the pressing body.

[Col. 0409D] 102. The parts of the body called the genitals—as the name itself indicates—received their name from the begetting of offspring, because offspring are conceived and generated by them. They are also called the shameful parts, on account of modesty, or from the pubic region, and therefore they are covered by clothing. They are also called the indecent parts because they do not possess the same kind of beauty as the limbs that are placed in view.

103. The same organ is also called the *veretrum*, either because it belongs only to a man, or because *virus* is emitted from it; for *virus* properly means the fluid that flows from a man’s nature.

104. The testicles are called *testiculi*, a diminutive of *testes*, “witnesses,” whose number begins with two. They supply semen through a channel, receiving it from the marrow of the spine, the kidneys, and the loins for the purpose of procreation.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] *Viscus* is skin. Gothic: *fiscus*, with the digamma.] The *viscus* is the skin in which the testicles are contained.

105. The posterior parts are so called because they are behind and turned away from the face, lest, while we cleanse the bowels, we soil our sight.

The passage is called *meatus* because things pass through it—that is, feces are expelled.

106. The thighs are called *femora* because by this part the male sex differs from the female; they extend from the groins to the knees.

The *feminae*, derived from *femora*, are the parts by which, when riding, we cling to the backs of horses; hence warriors were formerly said to have driven their horses beneath their thighs.

107. The hips are called *coxae*, as though “joined axles”; for the thighs move in them, and their cavities are called sockets, because the heads of the thighs turn within them.

The hocks are called *suffragines* because they bend beneath—that is, they are flexed below, not above, as in the arms.

[Col. 0410C] 108. The knees are the joints of the thighs and legs. They are called *genua* because in the womb they lie opposite the cheeks. For there they are joined to one another and related to the eyes, the indicators of tears and compassion: [Note: [Col. 0410D] For *genua* is derived from *genae*, “cheeks.” The same explanation is repeated in the book *Differences* and in the exposition of the *Song of Songs*.] thus the knees are named from the cheeks.

109. Finally, they say that the human being is conceived and formed folded together, with the knees raised upward, so that the eyes may be formed hollow and recessed. Ennius: “And the *artagena* presses its knees together.” Hence, when people prostrate themselves at the knees, they immediately weep. Nature intended them thereby to remember their mother’s womb, where they sat, as it were, in darkness before coming into the light.

110. The legs are called *crura* because with them we run and take steps. They extend below the knees as far as the calves.

[Col. 0410D] The shins are called *tibiae*, as though “trumpets,” for they resemble trumpets both in length and appearance.

[Col. 0411A] 111. The ankle is called *talus* from *tolus*, for a *tolus* is a prominent rounded form; hence the rounded summit of a temple is also called a *tolus*. The ankle is beneath the leg, and beneath the ankle is the heel.

112. The feet received their name from a Greek etymology; for the Greeks call them πόδας, “feet,” [Note: [Col. 0411C] Which move by alternating motions. Lactantius’ words have been somewhat altered.] because they advance with alternating movements, fixed upon the ground.

113. [Note: [Col. 0411C] The soles. Lactantius, in the same passage.] The soles are named from their flatness, because they are not rounded, as in quadrupeds—for otherwise a two-footed human being could not stand—but are formed flat and elongated so as to make the body stable. The soles are the forward parts of the feet, which also consist of many bones.

19 114. [Note: [Col. 0411D] The heel, the first part of the sole. *Calcis* is correct, as in *lancis*, book XX, chapter 4; but we think both forms are scribal errors.] The heel is the first part of the sole. Its name is derived from the callus with which we tread the earth; hence also *calcaneus*, “heel.”

115. [Note: [Col. 0411D] The sole. Servius’ words, on *Aeneid* VII, at the verse “And the Certalian sole.”] The sole is the lower part of the foot, so called because with it we imprint traces upon the earth; but everything that supports something is also called a sole, as though “solid.” Thus the earth is called the sole because it supports all things, and the sole of the foot because it bears the entire weight of the body.

116. [Note: [Col. 0411D] The viscera. From the same source, *Aeneid* I.] We call not only the intestines *viscera*, but everything beneath the hide, [Note: [Col. 0411D] From *viscum*, which is between the skin and the flesh. Servius, *Aeneid* VI, where it is said to be between the bones and the flesh.] from *viscum*, which is between the skin and the flesh. Likewise, *viscera* means the vital organs, that is, the areas surrounding the heart, as though *viscora*, because life—that is, the soul—is contained there.

117. Likewise, the viscera are the heads of the nerves joined together from blood and nerves. They are also called muscles, or mice, because in the individual limbs they occupy the place of the heart, just as the heart is in the middle of the whole body; and they are named after similar animals that hide beneath the earth. Hence *musculi* derives from their resemblance to mice. [Col. 0411C] They are also called *tori*, because the viscera there appear twisted.

118. The heart derives its name from the Greek designation, for the Greeks call it καρδία, or from *cura*, “care.” For every anxiety and the source of knowledge reside in it.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] For this reason it is near the lungs. From Ambrose VI.9.] For this reason it is near the lungs, so that when anger is kindled it may be tempered by the moisture of the lungs. It has two arteries, of which [Note: [Col. 0411D] The left has more blood. Thus the best manuscripts, correctly, I think, although the construction may seem somewhat unusual.] the left contains more blood and the right more breath; hence we examine the pulse in the right arm.

119. [Note: [Col. 0411D] The parts before the heart. From Servius, *Aeneid* VII, at the verse “To him the blue goddess.”] The *praecordia* are the regions near the heart, [Note: [Col. 0411D] By which perception is received. This follows Aristotle’s view, for physicians attribute perception to the brain.] by which perception is received. They are called *praecordia* because the origin of the heart and of thought is there.

[Col. 0412A] 20 120. The pulse is so called because it throbs; by its indication we understand either illness or health. Its movement is of two kinds. Simple is that which consists of a single leap. Compound is that which arises from several movements and is irregular and unequal. These movements have definite intervals: a dactylic beat, so long as they are without defect; but if they become quicker, like δορκαδάζοντες, “moving like gazelles,” or slower, like μυρμίζοντες, “moving like ants,” they are signs of death.

121. The veins are so called because they are the paths of the swimming blood, [Note: [Col. 0411D] And streams. From Lactantius, chapter 7.] and streams divided throughout the whole body, by which all the limbs are irrigated.

122. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Blood. Above, book IV, chapter 3.] *Sanguis*, “blood,” derives its name from a Greek etymology, because it grows, is sustained, and lives. Blood is called *sanguis* while it is in the body; when poured out, it is called *cruor*. For *cruor* is so called because, once poured out, it runs down, or because it falls while running. Others interpret *cruor* as corrupted blood that is discharged. Others say that blood is called *sanguis* because it is sweet.

123. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Blood is not whole. From Servius, *Aeneid* II, at the verse “You whose blood is whole with age.”] Blood is not whole except in the young. For physicians say that blood diminishes with age, and therefore old people tremble. Properly, however, blood is the possession of the soul; [Note: [Col. 0412C] Hence the tearing of the cheeks. These matters are treated more fully by Servius, *Aeneid* XII, at the verse “Having torn her rosy cheeks,” and *Aeneid* VI, at “Upon her purple robe,” and “I shall scatter purple flowers.” Yet the Twelve Tables imposed the restriction: “Let a woman not claw her face.”] hence women customarily tear their cheeks in mourning; hence purple garments and purple flowers are offered to the dead.

124. The lung derives its name from Greek. [Note: [Col. 0412D] For the Greeks call the lung πλεύμων. Among the Attic writers it is πλεύμων; among others πνεύμων. Alcaeus, in Plutarch: “Moisten the lungs with wine.”] For the Greeks call the lung πλεύμων, because [Note: [Col. 0412D] The fan of the heart. The author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 33, calls it the ventilator of the heart.] it is the heart’s fan, in which πνεῦμα—that is, breath—is present. Through it the lungs are agitated and moved, and hence they are called lungs. For in Greek πνεῦμα means “breath,” which, by blowing and stirring the air, admits and expels it; from this the lungs move and palpitate, opening themselves to receive the breath and contracting to expel it. It is an organ of the body.

125. [Note: [Col. 0412D] The liver: because fire is there. The form is as though *jacens ur*, “where fire lies,” since for Isidore *ur* means fire, not in only one place.] The liver is so named because fire has its seat there, which flies about beneath the brain. From there it is distributed to the eyes, the other senses, and the limbs; by its heat it converts into blood the juice drawn from food and supplies it to the individual limbs for nourishment and sustenance. According to those who discuss physical matters, pleasure and desire reside in the liver.

126. [Note: [Col. 0412D] The fibers are those of the liver. From Servius, *Aeneid* X, at the verse “The fibers of the victims.”] The fibers are the extremities of the liver, [Note: [Col. 0412D] Like the end portions of leaves in endives. Servius, *Georgics* I, at “Endives with bitter fibers”: “The word *fibers* is used loosely because the roots of endives run here and there like fibers through the liver—that is, certain veins and nerves. Hence these are badly affected. Chacon read *filorum*, ‘of threads,’ but what similarity is there to protruding tongues?”] like the end portions of leaves in endives, or like projecting tongues. They are called *fibrae* because among the gentiles they were carried in sacred rites to the altars of Phoebus by diviners, who received answers after offering and burning them.

127. The spleen is named as a supplement on the opposite side of the liver, so that there would not be an empty space; some even think it was made for the sake of laughter. [Note: [Col. 0413D] For we laugh with the spleen. From the same source, *Aeneid* VIII, at “Pain had flared up with dark gall.”] For we laugh with the spleen, grow angry with the gall, reason with the heart, and love with the liver. When these four elements are in balance, the animal is whole.

128. The gall is called *fel* because it is a little sac (*folliculus*) bearing a fluid called bile.

The stomach is called “mouth” in Greek because it is the entrance of the belly: it receives food and passes it into the intestines.

129. The intestines are so called because they are confined in the inner part of the body. For this reason they are arranged in long coils in the form of circles, so that they may gradually discharge the food they have received and not be obstructed by additional food.

130. [Note: [Col. 0413D] *Omentum*, a membrane. Gloss: *omentum*, ἐπίπλους; *membranum*, ὑμήν.] The *omentum* is a membrane that contains the greater part of the intestines, which the Greeks call ἐπίπλουν.

The intestinal partition is what separates the belly and the other intestines from the lungs and the heart.

131. The blind intestine is so called because it has neither an opening nor an outlet; the Greeks call it τυφλὸν ἔντερον, “blind intestine.” [Note: [Col. 0413D] “Blind intestine.” Varro calls it *fundulum*, and *jejunum* “hilum.”]

The jejunum is the thin intestine, and is called *jejunum* for that reason.

22 132. [Note: [Col. 0413D] The belly. From Servius, *Aeneid* II, at “And the womb of the mother.”] The belly, the abdomen, and the womb differ from one another. The belly is what digests the food received; it is visible externally and extends from the chest to the groins. The belly is so called because it transmits the nourishment of life throughout the body.

133. The abdomen is what receives food and is accustomed to be cleansed. Sallustius: “Pretending that his abdomen was being cleansed.” It is called *alvus* because it is washed—that is, cleansed. For from it the filth of feces flows out.

134. Only women have a womb, in which they conceive, shaped like a little cup. Nevertheless, authors commonly use *uterus* for the belly of either sex, not only poets but also others.

135. The womb is called *uterus* because it is double and [Note: [Col. 0413D] From both sides into two. From Lactantius 12.] divides itself from either side into two parts. These parts, spreading in opposite directions and folded back, coil around like the horns of a ram—or because it is filled internally with a fetus. Hence also *uter*, because it contains something inside, such as limbs and viscera.

[Col. 0413D] 136. [Note: [Col. 0413D] The *aqualiculus* properly belongs to a pig; hence the transfer of the word to the belly. The same words are cited by an ancient commentator on Persius.] The *aqualiculus* properly belongs to a pig; hence the word is transferred to the belly.

The womb is called *matrix* because the fetus is generated in it. [Note: [Col. 0414D] “It receives the semen, and so on.” These are Jerome’s words in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem.] For it receives the semen, nurtures what it has received, gives bodily form to what it has nurtured, and divides what has been formed into limbs.

[Col. 0414A] 137. The vulva is called *vulva*, as though *valva*, “door,” that is, the door of the belly, either because it receives the semen or because the fetus proceeds from it.

The bladder is so called because, just as a vessel is filled with water, so it is filled with urine collected from the kidneys and is distended with fluid. Birds do not possess this function.

138. Urine is called *urina* either because it burns or because it is discharged from the kidneys. By its indications both future health and illness are revealed. This fluid is commonly called *lotium*, because by it washed—that is, cleansed—garments are made.

23 139. Semen is what, once cast forth, is received either by the earth or by the womb for the generation of fruit or a fetus. It is a fluid produced from the digestion of food and the body and diffused through the veins and marrow. From there, exuded in the manner of a sediment, it thickens in the kidneys; expelled through intercourse and received in the woman’s womb, it is formed into a body by the heat of the viscera and by irrigation with menstrual blood.

140. The menses are the superfluous blood of women. They are called *menstrua* from the cycle of the moon’s light, with which this flow usually coincides. For the moon is called μήνη in Greek; these are also called the “womanly fluids,” since woman is the only menstruating animal.

141. At contact with this blood, crops do not sprout, must becomes sour, plants die, trees lose their fruits, [Note: [Col. 0414D] Rust attacks iron. From Solinus, chapter 4; Pliny VII.15.] rust attacks iron, and bronze turns black. If dogs eat any of it, they become violently rabid. Asphalt glue, which is dissolved neither by iron nor by water, is itself polluted by this blood and spontaneously falls apart.

142. After many days following menstruation, suitable semen is not capable of germination, [Note: [Col. 0414D] Capable of germination. Gothic and all manuscripts, as well as Rabanus, read *generabile*, “capable of generation.”] because there is no longer menstrual blood by which it may be soaked and nourished. Thin semen does not adhere to the female organs, but slips away and lacks the power of adhesion. Likewise, thick semen lacks the power of generation, because it cannot mix with the woman’s blood on account of its excessive density. Hence, they say, males and females become sterile either through excessive thickness of semen or blood, or through excessive thinness.

143. [Note: [Col. 0414D] They say that the heart is formed first. From Lactantius, chapter 12.] They say that the human heart is formed first, because in it are both human life and wisdom; then, on the fortieth day, the entire work is completed, as has reportedly been gathered from abortions. [Note: [Col. 0414D] Others say that the fetus begins from the head. From the same source, chapter 11.] Others say that the fetus begins from the head; hence we see that in the eggs of birds the eyes are formed first.

[Col. 0414D] 144. The fetus is called *fetus* because it is still being warmed in the womb. The afterbirth is called *secundinae*; it is born together with the infant and contains it, and is so called because it follows it when it is delivered.

145. [Note: [Col. 0414D] On being born. Chapter 12.] They say that children resemble their fathers if the paternal semen is stronger, [Col. 0415A] and their mothers if the maternal semen is stronger; in this way similar faces are produced. Those who reproduce the appearance of both parents are conceived from paternal and maternal semen mixed equally. People come to resemble grandparents and great-grandparents because, just as many seeds lie hidden in the earth, so seeds are hidden within us that will reproduce the forms of our parents. Girls are born from paternal semen and boys from maternal semen, because every birth consists of two kinds of semen; when one part becomes stronger, it determines the resemblance of the sex.

146. In our body some things were made solely for utility, such as the viscera; others for both utility and beauty, such as the senses in the face and the hands and feet in the body. The utility of these limbs is great, and their appearance is especially fitting.

[Col. 0415B] 147. [Note: [Col. 0415D] Some things are for beauty. Chapter 10.] Some things are solely for beauty, such as the nipples in men and the navel in both sexes. Some are for distinction: in men, the genitals, a full beard, and a broad chest; in women, smooth cheeks and a narrow chest, while for conceiving and carrying fetuses the kidneys and flanks are expanded. What has been said concerns the human being and the parts of the body; I shall now add his ages.

# CHAPTER II. On the Ages of Human Beings

1. [Note: [Col. 0415D] The stages of life. See Servius, *Aeneid* V; Ambrose, letter 49; Philo, *On the Creation of the World*.] There are six stages of life: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age.

2. The first age, infancy, is that of a child being born into the light; it extends over seven years.

3. The second age, childhood—that is, purity, and not yet suitability for generation—extends to the fourteenth year.

4. The third, adolescence, [Note: [Col. 0415D] “Mature for generation.” These words are absent from some manuscripts.] is mature for generation and extends to the twenty-eighth year.

25 5. The fourth, youth, the strongest of all the ages, ends in the fiftieth year.

6. [Note: [Col. 0415D] The fifth age, that of the older person, not yet old age. Servius, *Aeneid* V, at “Then, being older, such as he was”: “According to Varro, *junior* and *senior* are comparatives formed by diminution,” and likewise *Aeneid* VI, at “Now older”: “Either he used it for the positive, or *senior* means a vigorous old man, just as *junior* lies within *juvenis*; Varro treats this matter, and Pliny also confirms it.” Varro distinguishes *seniores* from *senes* in Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, saying that *seniores* are those from forty-five to sixty, because the body then first begins to age, whereas after sixty it already suffers from old age.] The fifth age, that of the older person, that is, maturity, is the decline from youth into old age. It is not yet old age, but it is no longer youth, since it is the age called *senior* [Note: [Col. 0415D] Which the Greeks call πρεσβύτης. From Augustine, *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans* I.23.] by the Greeks. For among the Greeks an old man is called not *presbyter* but γέρων. This age begins at fifty and ends at seventy.

[Col. 0416A] 7. The sixth age is old age. It has no fixed limit in years; after those five ages, however much life remains is assigned to old age.

8. *Senium*, “extreme old age,” is the final part of old age, so called because it is the limit of the sixth age. In these six spans, therefore, philosophers have described human life, in which a person changes, runs its course, and reaches the limit of death. Let us therefore proceed briefly through the aforesaid stages, demonstrating their etymologies in human beings.

9. *Infans* is the human being of the first age. He is called *infans* because he does not yet know how to speak—that is, he cannot talk; for before the teeth have been properly arranged, the expression of speech is less developed.

10. [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Puer* from purity. Varro, in Censorinus: “They are called *pueri* because they are pure, that is, prepubescent.”] A boy is called *puer* from purity, because he is pure and does not yet have down or the bloom of the cheeks. [Note: [Col. 0416D] These are ephebes, that is, named from Phoebus. Rather, from Hebe.] These are ephebes, that is, they are said to be named from Phoebus; they are not yet men, [Note: [Col. 0416D] Lightly built adolescents. Another reading: *lenes*, “gentle.”] but slight young adolescents.

11. The word *puer* is used in three ways: of birth, as in Isaiah, “A child is born to us”; of age, as in an eight-year-old or ten-year-old. Hence the line:

> Already he bore the childish yoke upon his tender neck.

It is also used of obedience and purity of faith, as when the Lord says to the prophet, “You are my child; do not fear,” although Jeremiah had already far exceeded the years of childhood.

12. [Note: [Col. 0416D] A girl is a little one, as though *pulla*. Festus: “A favorite of Jupiter was called *pullus*; Quintus Fabius, surnamed Eburnus, was so called because of his whiteness, since his buttocks had been struck by lightning. In ancient times, a boy whom someone loved was called his *pullus*.”] A girl is a little one, as though *pulla*. Hence we also call children *pupilli*, not because of their legal condition but because of their childish age. *Pupilli* are so called as though “without eyes,” that is, deprived of their parents. [Note: [Col. 0416D] These are truly called *pupilli* … so that they might receive their name from them. Understand “first name,” which was not received before puberty. The clan or family name was received on the day of purification, according to Festus, Macrobius, and Plutarch, *Problems*. Julius Paris—or Probus—in his epitome of book X of Valerius Maximus says: “Quintus Scaevola states that boys were not given first names until they assumed the manly toga, nor girls until they married.” He adds: “The Publii who had earlier become *pupilli* before they possessed first names.” Others derive the name from puberty. See A. Augustinus, note 1 to the *Collection of Decretals*, chapter 7, *On the Betrothal of the Impubescent*, and chapter 3 under that title, Gregory IX.] Those whose fathers died before they received a name from them are properly called *pupilli*. The rest are called *orbi*, “orphans,” likewise *pupilli*; the former name is Greek, the latter Latin. For in the psalm where it reads, “You will be a helper to the orphan,” the Greek has ὀρφάνῳ.

13. Pubescent persons are named from the pubic region, that is, from the shameful parts of the body, because these places then first begin to grow down. Some determine puberty by years, saying that a person is pubescent after completing fourteen years, although puberty may occur very late. The most certain indication, however, is that someone is pubescent who both displays puberty in bodily appearance and is already capable of procreation.

14. *Puerperae* are women who give birth during their years of childhood. Hence Horace:

> Women who bear offspring like their own are praised.

[Col. 0417A] [Note: [Col. 0417D] They are also called *puerperae*. Jerome, on Jeremiah IV: *Puerpera* means one who gives birth to her first children. But Donatus, on *Andria*: Every woman who has given birth is a *puerpera*; one giving birth for the first time is πρωτότοκος, “bearing for the first time.” Paulus, chapter 163, *On the Meaning of Words*: *Puerperae* are women recently delivered.] They are called *puerperae* either because they are burdened by their first childbirth or because they give birth to children for the first time.

15. An adolescent is so called because he is mature for generation, or from growing and increasing.

16. A young man is called *juvenis* because he begins to be able to help, as with young oxen, *juvenci*, when they have left the stage of calves. A young man is positioned at the very increase of age and prepared for assistance. For to help is the work of one who contributes something. Just as thirty is the year of full maturity in human beings, so in cattle and beasts of burden the third year is the strongest.

17. [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Vir*, “man.” From Lactantius, chapter 12.] A man is called *vir* because there is greater strength in him than in a woman. Hence *virtus*, “strength” or “virtue,” received its name; or because he acts upon a woman by force.

18. A woman is called *mulier* from softness, as though *mollior*, “softer,” with a letter removed or changed.

19. The two sexes are separated by the strength and weakness of their bodies. But the man’s strength is greater and the woman’s less so that she might be submissive to the man—namely, lest, if women resisted, desire should compel men to seek something else or rush toward another sex.

20. A person is therefore called *mulier* according to the female sex, not according to the corruption of virgin integrity; this usage comes from the language of Holy Scripture. For Eve, immediately made from the side of her husband and not yet touched by a man, was called *mulier*, when Scripture says: “And he formed her into a woman.”

21. [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Virgo* from the greener age. From Servius, *Eclogue* 3, at “Twice she comes to the milking pail.”] A virgin is called *virgo* from a greener age, as are *virga*, “rod,” and *vitula*, “heifer.” Alternatively, she is so called from incorruption, as though *virago*, because she is ignorant of the female condition.

22. [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Virago*. From the same source, *Aeneid* XII, at “Juturna, a virago.”] A *virago* is so called because she performs a man’s role—that is, she performs manly deeds and possesses masculine strength. In ancient times they called brave women by this name. A virgin is not properly called a *virago* unless she performs a man’s duty. A woman, however, if she performs manly deeds, is rightly called a *virago*, like an Amazon.

23. What is now called *femina*, “woman,” was formerly called *vira*, just as *serva* comes from *servus*, “female slave,” and *famula* from *famulus*, “female servant”; so *vira* comes from *vir*, “man.” Hence some derive the name *virgo*.

24. A woman is called *femina* from the parts of the thighs, where the form of the sex is distinguished from the man. 28 Others [Note: [Col. 0417D] Others derive it from a Greek etymology. Perhaps from ἐφιεμένη, “one who desires”?] think that *femina* is derived from an “fiery force,” because she desires intensely. Women are more lustful than men, both among human beings and among animals. Hence excessive love was formerly called feminine.

25. An older man is still more vigorous. *Ovidius*, in book VI:

> The older man … between the young man and the old man.

Terence: “By what right I have acted as the younger man.”

26. *Adolescentior* does not necessarily mean “more adolescent,” but “less adolescent,” just as *senior* means “less old”; here the comparative degree [Note: [Col. 0417D] It signifies “less” than the positive. These are Donatus’ words in the prologue to *Hecyra*.] signifies “less” than the positive. Therefore *senior* means “not sufficiently old,” just as *junior* lies within *juvenis*, and *pauperior* within *pauper*.

27. Some think that old men are called *senes* from a diminution of the senses, because through the burden of age they have already become foolish. [Note: [Col. 0417D] For physicians say so. From Servius, *Georgics* II, at “The cold will have stood around the breast.”] For physicians say that foolish people have colder blood, while prudent people have warm blood. Hence old men, in whom it has already grown cold, and children, in whom it is not yet warm, have less understanding; thus the ages of infants and old men correspond.

28. Old men become delirious through excessive age, while children, through playfulness and childishness, do not know what they are doing. *Senex* is masculine only, just as *anus* is feminine; for *anus* refers only to a woman. *Anus* is called so from many years, as though “aged.” [Note: [Col. 0417D] For if it were a common noun, why would Terence say “an old woman”? I agree with Chacon, who thought these words extraneous, and with the person to whom Isidore’s view was displeasing and who therefore objected: “If it were a common noun, why …?” But Donatus, whom Isidore follows, labors in vain to deny that *senex* is a common noun. Papinius, or Pomponius, in Varro, book VI:

> It is ridiculous when your mistress calls you “old woman,”  
> Son of Potonus, a half-old boy.  
> Call her “little girl,” and thus the change will be mutual:  
> For truly you are a little boy, and your mistress an old woman.  

And Tibullus:

> Young men and old men alike see her with joyful hearts.  
> Rightly they say that an old man bears so many evils.]

For if it were a common noun, why would Terence say “an old woman”? Hence also *vetula*, “old woman,” because she is aged. Just as *senectus*, “old age,” comes from *senex*, so *anilitas*, “old age in a woman,” is named from *anus*.

29. Gray hair is called *canities* from its whiteness, as though *ties*. Hence the line:

> Flowering youth, milky gray hair,

as though it said “white.”

30. [Note: [Col. 0418D] Old age. From Jerome, preface to book II on Amos.] Old age brings with it many good things and many bad. Its good effects are that it frees us from the most uncontrolled masters, imposes a limit on pleasures, breaks the assaults of lust, increases wisdom, and provides more mature counsel. [Col. 0418C] Its bad effects are that old age is most wretched because of weakness and hatred. Illnesses come upon us, and old age is sad. [Note: [Col. 0418D] For there are two things. From Servius, *Georgics* II, at “Illnesses come upon us, and sad old age.”] For there are two things by which the strength of the body is diminished: old age and illness.

31. Death is called *mors* because it is bitter, or from Mars, who is the author of deaths.

32. There are three kinds of death: bitter, untimely, and natural. 30 The death of infants is bitter; that of young people, untimely; and that of old people, mature—that is, natural.

33. It is uncertain from which part of speech *mortuus*, “dead,” is declined. For, as Caesar says, from *morior*, “I die,” the past participle should have ended in *-tus* with one *u*, not two. For where the letter is doubled, the word is a noun, not a participle, as in *fatuus*, “foolish,” and *arduus*, “steep.” It was therefore appropriately arranged that, just as what it signifies cannot act, so the noun itself cannot be declined through speech. Every dead person is either a funeral or a corpse.

34. [Note: [Col. 0419D] The funeral. From the same source, *Aeneid* I, at “Night with torches of flame.” See also book XX, chapter 10.] It is a funeral if the body is buried. The funeral is called *funus* from the burning cords that were carried before the bier, wrapped in papyrus and wax.

35. [Note: [Col. 0419D] The corpse. From the same source, *Aeneid* VI, at “And fallen in war.”] It is a corpse if it lies unburied. For *cadaver* is named from falling, because it can no longer stand. [Note: [Col. 0419D] When it is carried. From the same source, *Aeneid* II, at “You have defiled the ancestral …”] When it is carried, we call it a funeral procession; when cremated, remains; when already laid away, buried. *Corpus*, “body,” is used by ordinary custom, as in: “Then the bodies of those deprived of light …”

36. A dead person is called *defunctus* because he has completed the duty of life. For we say *defunctus officio*, “one who has discharged an office,” of those who have completed their obligations; hence also those who have held offices. From this comes *defunctus*, because he has been relieved of life’s duty, or because he has completed his day.

37. [Note: [Col. 0419D] Buried. From the same source, *Aeneid* III, at “Spare the buried man.”] A buried person is so called because he is now without pulse and palpitation—that is, without movement. To bury is to put away a body. We call *humare* “to cover over,” that is, to cast earth upon it.

31 # CHAPTER III. On Portents

1. [Note: [Col. 0419D] Portents. From Augustine, *City of God* XXI.8.] Varro says that portents are things that appear to be born contrary to nature; but they are not contrary to nature, because they occur by divine will, since the will of the Creator of each thing is the nature of every created thing. Hence even the gentiles call God sometimes Nature and sometimes God.

2. A portent therefore occurs not contrary to nature, but contrary to nature as it is known. Portents, omens, monsters, and prodigies are so named because they appear to foretell, show, indicate, and predict something future.

3. [Note: [Col. 0419D] For *portenta*. Cicero, *On Divination* II: “Because they show, foretell, indicate, and predict, they are called omens, monsters, and prodigies.”] Portents are said to be called *portenta* from *portendere*, “to foretell,” that is, “to show beforehand.” Omens are called *ostenta* because they appear to show something future. Prodigies are called *prodigia* because they speak of what is ahead, that is, they predict the future. Monsters are called *monstra* from admonition, because they demonstrate that something is to be signified, or because they immediately show what appears; this is the proper meaning of the word, although through the misuse of writers it is often corrupted.

4. Certain creations of portents appear to be established as signs of future events. For sometimes God wishes to signify what is to come through harmful abnormalities among those being born, just as through dreams and oracles by which he warns and signifies to certain nations or individuals a future disaster; this has also been confirmed by many experiences.

5. [Note: [Col. 0419D] A hare for Xerxes. We have printed *hare* from Herodotus, *Polyhymnia*, and Valerius Maximus, *On Prodigies*, although all the manuscripts read *fox* with the letters reversed.] For a hare born from a mare foretold to Xerxes the dissolution of his kingdom. A monster born to Alexander from a woman had the upper parts of a human being, but dead, and the lower parts of various beasts, but alive; it signified the sudden death of the king, for the worse parts had outlived the better. But these monsters, 32 which are given as signs, do not live long; as soon as they are born, they die.

6. There is a difference between a portent and something portentous. Portents are things that are transformed, as a woman in Umbria is said to have given birth to a serpent. Hence Lucan:

> And her own infant terrified its mother.

Portentous things, however, undergo only a slight alteration.

7. For example, when people are born from fingers … Portents or portentous beings therefore occur in various ways: some in the size of the entire body, beyond the ordinary human measure, [Col. 0420B] as large as Tityos, who lay extended over nine acres. [Note: [Col. 0420D] Such was Tityos. “Over nine whole acres his body stretches.” *Aeneid* VI.] So Homer bears witness. [Note: [Col. 0420D] Homer, *Odyssey*.] Others occur in the smallness of the entire body, such as dwarfs, or those whom the Greeks call pygmies, because they are a cubit in stature. Others occur in the size of particular parts, such as an ill-formed head or superfluous limbs, for example, two-headed or three-handed people, [Note: [Col. 0420D] Or *cynodonts*. From Solinus IV.] or *cynodonts*, who have twin teeth.

8. Some are so because of a defect in their parts, in which one part is greatly deficient in comparison with the other, as one hand compared with the other, or one foot with the other. Others are so because of amputation, being born without a hand or head; the Greeks call such persons *steresioi*. [Note: Others are *privimeria*. Thus Rabanus; nor should the composition of the Latin word be considered suspect, since Quintilian likewise does not reject *epitogium*. Agellius, Book IX, chapter 4, calls these persons *monomereis* (“having a single part”).] Others are *privimeria*, when only a head or a leg is born. Others are transformed in one part, such as those who have the face of a lion or a dog, or the head or body of a bull; for example, they say that the Minotaur was born from Pasiphae. The Greeks call this *heteromorphia*.

9. Others are transformed in every part into a portent of an alien creation, as history says that a calf was born from a woman. Others undergo a change in the position of their organs without transformation, such as eyes in the chest or forehead, ears above the temples, or, as Aristotle reported, a certain person who had the liver on the left side and the spleen on the right.

10. Others are so according to conjoined growth: on one hand more fingers are found grown together and joined, on the other fewer, or the same occurs with the feet. Others are so according to an immature and disordered formation, such as those born with teeth, or bearded, or gray-haired. Others combine many differences, like the many-formed portent concerning Alexander that we mentioned earlier.

11. Others arise from a mixture of sex, such as the *androgynoi*, who are also called *hermaphrodites*. [Note: *Hermaphroditae*. It is strange that *hermaphroditae*, not *hermaphroditi*, is read in all the books, since Augustine says, *The City of God*, XVI, chapter 8: “Custom has prevailed in speech that they should be named after the better sex, that is, the masculine.” For, he says, “No one has ever called them either androgynes or hermaphrodites.” Pliny, however, XI, chapter 49, called mares *hermaphroditae*.] They are called *hermaphrodites* because both sexes appear in them. For *Hermes* among the Greeks is Mercury, while *Aphrodite* is called Venus. [Note: They have a masculine right breast. From Pliny, VIII, chapter 2.] They have a masculine right breast and a feminine left breast, and by intercourse with one another they both beget and give birth.

12. Just as there are certain monstrous human beings among individual peoples, so among the human race as a whole there are certain monstrous peoples, such as Giants, Cynocephali, Cyclopes, and others.

13. [Note: *Giants*—those who consider them earth-born. Thus Callimachus, in *The Bath of Pallas*, and the Glossary: *Terrigenae*, “earth-born,” *gēgeneis*.] Giants are so called according to the etymology of the Greek term, since the Greeks consider them *gēgeneis*, that is, “earth-born,” because, in the fables, their parent Earth bore them, immense in size and resembling herself. For *gē* means “earth” and *genos* means “race,” although common usage also calls them sons of the earth, whose origin is uncertain.

14. [Note: “But some wrongly suppose this.” These words are taken from *The City of God*, III, chapter 4. The opinion rejected here was held by very weighty authorities: Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Cyprian, Ambrose, and Lactantius. Augustine raised the question but did not pronounce what he himself thought.] But certain ignorant people wrongly suppose from the Holy Scriptures that the transgressing angels had intercourse with the daughters of men before the Flood, and that Giants were born from them—that is, men of extraordinary size and strength, by whom the earth was filled.

15. [Note: *Cynocephali*. These are Augustine’s words, *The City of God*, XVI, chapter 8. See Aelian and Pliny.] Cynocephali are so called because they have dogs’ heads; their barking itself, more than anything else, declares them to be beasts rather than human beings. They are born in India.

16. India also produces Cyclopes, who are called Cyclopes because they are said to have one eye in the middle of the forehead. [Note: They are also called *agriophagitae*. Pliny, VI, chapter 36. Solinus calls them *agriophagi*.] They are also called *agriophagitae*, because they eat only the flesh of wild animals.

17. [Note: *Blemmyes*. Pliny, V, chapter 8; Solinus, chapter 34.] In Libya they believe that Blemmyes are born without heads, with their mouths and eyes in their chests. [Note: Others are born without necks. From Pliny, VII, chapter 2. See Augustine, *The City of God*, XVI, chapter 8, and Aulus Gellius, IX, chapter 4.] Others are born without necks, with their eyes in their shoulders.

18. [Note: “In the farthest East.” From Solinus, chapter 32.] In the farthest East, monstrous forms of peoples are reported. Some have no noses, their entire faces being equally flat and shapeless. Others have so prominent a lower lip that, in the heat of the sun, they cover their entire faces with it while sleeping. Others are said to have mouths sealed together, drawing nourishment through only a small opening with reeds. Some are said to be without tongues, using nods or gestures in place of speech.

19. They say that the Panotii live in Scythia, with ears so broad that they cover their entire bodies with them. For *pan* in Greek means “all,” and *ōta* means “ears.”

20. [Note: *Artabalitae*. Thus in the more accurate manuscripts of Pliny; in Solinus, *Arthabathitae*.] The Artabalitae in Ethiopia are said to walk bent forward, like cattle. None lives beyond the fortieth year.

21. [Note: *Satyrs*. From Jerome, *Life of Paul the Hermit*.] Satyrs are little men with hooked noses, horns on their foreheads, and feet resembling those of goats, like the one Saint Antony saw in the wilderness. When questioned, he is said to have replied to the servant of God: “I am a mortal, one of the inhabitants of the desert, whom the pagan nations, deceived by various errors, worship as Fauns and Satyrs.”

22. [Note: “Some are also said to be wild men.” See Book VIII, final chapter.] Some are also said to be wild men, whom certain people call *fig-fauns*. [Note: *Fig-fauns*. The Codex of Cardinal Sirleto and many Gothic manuscripts read *fatuos ficarios*; so does Jerome in *Jeremiah* L, “with foolish fig-fauns.”]

23. A race called Sciopods is said to exist in Ethiopia, with only one leg and astonishing speed. [Note: “Whom the Greeks therefore call Sciopods.” Pliny, Book VII, chapter 2; Augustine, *The City of God*, XVI, chapter 8; Aulus Gellius, IX, chapter 4.] Hence the Greeks call them *skiopodes*, because during the heat, when they lie on their backs on the ground, they shade themselves with the great size of their feet.

24. [Note: In one manuscript: “Antipodes in Libya …”; Chacon read “Androphagi in Scythia,” from Pliny, VII, chapter 2.] The Antipodes in Libya have the soles of their feet turned backward behind their legs, and eight toes on each foot.

25. Hippopodes live in Scythia, possessing human form and horses’ feet.

26. They say that in India there is a people called *Macrobioi* (“Long-lived”), having a height of eight feet. [Note: “Who are called Macrobioi, eight feet tall.” Chacon restored this passage very well. All the books read “twelve,” but he detected a scribal error: the copyists had written XII instead of IIX. Pliny, following Onesicritus, makes their bodies five cubits and two palms. Five cubits, each consisting of a foot and a half, together with two palms, which make half a foot, amount to eight feet, not twelve.] There is also a people there of cubit height, whom the Greeks call Pygmies from the cubit; we spoke of them above. They occupy the mountainous regions of India, near which lies the Ocean.

27. They also report that in the same India there is a race of women who conceive at the age of five and do not live beyond their eighth year.

28. Other fabulous portents of human beings are also described, which do not exist but are inventions; they are interpreted as explanations of things. Thus Geryon, king of Spain, is said to have been of triple form. [Note: “Reported as having a triple form.” Some read “endowed with” instead. We have retained “reported,” following Justin, Book XLIV: “Geryon himself was not, as the fables relate, of a triple nature.”] In fact, there were three brothers of such harmony that, in three bodies, they seemed to possess a single soul.

29. [Note: “The Gorgons too.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI.] The Gorgons, too, are said to have been harlots with hair of serpents, who turned those looking at them into stones, and to have had one eye, which they used in common. In fact, they were three sisters of equal beauty, as though possessing a single eye; they made their spectators so stupefied that they were thought to turn them into stones.

30. [Note: *Sirens*. From the same source, *Aeneid* V.] They invent three Sirens, partly virgins and partly birds, having wings and talons. One sang with her voice, another with pipes, and the third with a lyre. By their song they drew enchanted sailors into shipwreck.

31. In truth, they were harlots who, because they reduced passersby to poverty, were fictitiously said to cause them shipwreck. They were said to have wings and talons because love both flies and wounds. They are said to have dwelt among the waves because the waves created Venus.

32. [Note: “Scylla also.” The passage is adapted from Justin, Book IV.] Scylla, too, is said to have been a woman girded with canine heads, accompanied by great barking. Near the strait of the Sicilian sea, sailors terrified by the whirlpools formed by converging waves imagine that the waves bark; the waves are dashed together by the chasm of the consuming current.

33. They also invent certain monsters among irrational animals, such as Cerberus, the dog of the underworld with three heads. Through him they signify the three ages by which death devours a human being: infancy, youth, and old age. [Note: Some think that Cerberus was so called for this reason. From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on the verse “guardian.”] Some think that he was called Cerberus as though he were *kreoboros*, that is, “flesh-devouring.”

34. They also describe the serpent Hydra with nine heads, [Note: “Which in Latin is *Excetra*.” From the same passage of Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “the monster of Lerna.”] which in Latin is called *Excetra*, because when one head was cut off, three heads grew in its place. But it is established that the Hydra was a place vomiting forth waters and devastating a neighboring city; when one channel was blocked, many others burst forth. Hercules, seeing this, burned the places themselves and thus closed the channels of the waters.

35. For *hydra* is named from water. [Note: Ambrose mentions it, *On the Faith*, Book I, chapter 4.] Ambrose refers to it as an image of heresies, saying: “For heresy, like a certain fabled Hydra, grew through its wounds; and while it is repeatedly cut down, it sprouts again, destined for fire and doomed to perish in the flames.”

36. [Note: “They also invent the Chimaera.” From the same passage of Servius.] They also invent the Chimaera, a three-formed beast: a lion in its face, a dragon in its hind parts, and a she-goat in its middle. Certain natural philosophers say that it was not an animal but a mountain in Lycia, nourishing lions and goats in some places, burning in others, and full of serpents in still others. Bellerophon made it habitable, and hence he is said to have killed the Chimaera.

37. The Centaurs—that is, men mixed with horses—received their name from their appearance. Some say that they were horsemen of Thessaly; but because, racing about in battle, they appeared to be a single body of horses and men, they assert that the Centaurs were invented from this appearance.

38. Further, the Minotaur is said to have taken its name from bull and man, such a beast as the fables say was shut up in the Labyrinth. Of it Ovid writes:

> Half bull and half man, and half man and half bull.

39. [Note: *Onocentaur*. Jerome, on Isaiah XIV: “The name Centaurs”—the marginal reading is *onocentaurs*—is composed of asses and Centaurs. Isidore seems to have written “man” in place of “Centaur.”] The Onocentaur is so called because it is said to be half human in form and half ass, just as the Hippocentaurs are so called because the natures of horses and men are thought to have been joined in them.

## CHAPTER IV. On Transformations

1. Certain monstrous transformations and changes of human beings into beasts are also recorded, such as that of the famous enchantress Circe, who is said to have changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts, and that of the Arcadians who, having drawn lots, swam across a certain lake and there were transformed into wolves.

2. They also affirm, not through fabulous falsehood but through historical testimony, that the companions of Diomedes were changed into birds. Some likewise assert that witches are made from human beings. For the forms of criminals are changed for many acts of brigandage, and whether by magical songs or through the power of herbs, they pass with their entire bodies into wild beasts. [Note: “And whether by magical arts.” Almost all of this is taken from Augustine, *The City of God*, XVIII, chapter 16 and following.]

3. Indeed, many things undergo transformation by nature and, when corrupted, are changed into different species: thus bees arise from the rotting flesh of calves, beetles from horses, locusts from mules, and scorpions from crabs. Ovid writes:

> If you remove the hollow claws of the sea-crab,  
> a scorpion will emerge and threaten with its hooked tail.

# BOOK TWELVE. ON ANIMALS

## CHAPTER I. On Cattle and Beasts of Burden

1. [Note: Adam gave names to all living creatures. From Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*.] Adam first gave names to all living creatures, assigning each one a name from its present designation, according to the condition of the nature it was to serve.

2. [Note: But in the language that existed before the Flood. Above, Book IX, chapter 1.] Peoples, however, gave names to each kind of animal in their own languages. Adam did not impose those names according to the Latin or Greek language, or according to the names of any barbarian peoples, but according to the language that before the Flood was one language shared by all and is now called Hebrew.

3. In Latin they are called *animalia*, or living creatures, because they are animated by life and moved by spirit.

4. [Note: Called quadrupeds. From Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, III, chapter 11.] They are called quadrupeds because they walk on four feet. Although they resemble cattle, they are not under human care, as deer, does, and wild asses are. Yet they are not wild beasts, such as lions, nor beasts of burden, such as can be useful to human beings.

5. [Note: *Pecus*. From Servius, on the verse “the sluggish herd,” *Aeneid* I.] We call every creature *pecus* that lacks human speech and form. [Note: Properly, however, the name *pecus*, and so forth. From Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, III.] Properly, the name *pecus* is usually applied to those animals that are either suitable for eating, such as sheep and birds, or useful for human purposes, such as horses and oxen.

6. There is, however, a difference between *pecora* and *pecudes*. The ancients commonly used *pecora* for all animals, but *pecudes* only for those animals that are eaten, as though from *pecuedes*. In general, every animal is called *pecus* from grazing.

7. Beasts of burden (*jumenta*) took their name from the fact that they assist our labor, carrying our loads with their help or plowing. [Note: For the ox draws wagons. From Jerome, on Isaiah I.] The ox draws wagons and turns over the hardest clods of earth with the plowshare. The horse and ass carry burdens and lessen human labor in walking. Hence they are also called *jumenta*, from assisting human beings; for they are animals of great strength.

8. These are also called *armenta*, either [Note: Because they are suited to arms. From Servius, on the verse “these arms for war,” *Aeneid* III; and likewise *Georgics* III.] because they are suited to arms, that is, to war, or because we use them in arms. [Note: Others understand *armenta* only in reference to oxen. From the passage of Servius cited immediately above.] Others understand *armenta* to mean only oxen, from plowing, as though *aramenta*, or because they are armed with horns. There is a distinction between *armenta* and flocks: *armenta* are herds of horses and oxen, whereas flocks are of goats and sheep.

9. [Note: *Ovis* from offering. Why not from Greek *ois*? He often prefers to consider things or their functions rather than words, as we have noted more than once.] The sheep (*ovis*) is a soft-fleeced animal, defenseless in body and peaceful in spirit. It is said to be named from offering, because among the ancients, at the beginning, not bulls but sheep were slaughtered in sacrifice. [Note: Some of these are called *bidentes*. See Servius on the verse “they slaughter the chosen two-year-olds according to custom,” *Aeneid* IV; and Aulus Gellius, Book XVI, and Festus, under *bidental*.] Some of them are called *bidentes*, because among their eight teeth they have two that are higher; the pagans especially offered such sheep in sacrifice.

10. [Note: *Vervex*, either from strength. Varro, *On the Nature of Words*.] A ram (*vervex*) is so called either from strength, because it is stronger than the other sheep, or because it is a male—that is, a masculine animal—or because it has a worm in its head. Stimulated by the irritation caused by this, they strike one another and, fighting, hit with great force.

11. [Note: *Aries*, either from *apo tou areos*, that is, “from Mars.” Varro: “*Aries*, because the ancients called it *ares*; our people call it *arviga*.”] The ram (*aries*) is called either *apo tou Areos*, that is, “from Mars,” whence among us the males in flocks are called *mares*; or because this animal was first sacrificed by the pagans upon altars. It is called *aries* because it was placed upon altars. Hence the saying: “A ram is slaughtered at the altar.”

12. [Note: *Agnus*, “lamb,” from *agnos*, as though “pious.” Perhaps *purum*, from Festus. The Glossary has: “*Agnus*, *arneion* or *arneios,” and “*agnos*, pure and chaste.” Varro, however, wishes *agnus* to have been so called from Latin origin, because it is related to the sheep.] Although the Greeks too call the lamb from *hagnos* (ἄγνου), “pure” or “pious,” the Latins nevertheless think it bears this name because, more than other creatures, it recognizes its mother; [Note: So that, even if it wanders in a large flock. From Ambrose, *Hexameron* VI, chapter 4.] thus, even if it wanders in a large flock, it immediately recognizes the voice of its parent by its bleating.

13. [Note: *Hoedi*, kids, from eating. Festus reports that the ancients said *foedum* for *haedum*, “kid”; moreover, it is sufficiently clear from Isidore’s manuscripts that they customarily wrote the Greek digamma for *v*, and conversely. A little later, all our manuscripts read *Cynyvi* for *Cynyphii*, and *Tragelavi* for *Tragelaphi*. The form therefore should be *haedus* or *faedus*, as though *vedus* or *vescus*—although in such matters we may sometimes dispute even with very weighty authorities. The reasoning that Isidore supplies seems sufficiently to show that he followed this form: “For the young are very fat and of pleasant taste.” We also willingly retain the words “hence *edere*,” which some had judged should be removed, since they occur in all the books, and therefore write *hederae* as well.
