Festus thinks that *hedera* was so called either because it clings, because it eats, or because it seeks what has been set forth.] Kids (*hoedi*) are so called from eating, for when young they are very fat and of pleasant taste; hence they are called *edible* (*edulium*) from *eating* (*edere*).

14. The goat is a lascivious, wanton animal, always ardent for intercourse. Because of lust its eyes look sideways, and from this it derives its name. [Note: For *hirqui* are the corners of the eyes. From Servius, on Eclogue 3. Whether one writes *hirqui* or *hirci* for the same thing makes no difference, as Pierius Valerianus correctly observes.] For according to Suetonius, *hirqui* are the corners of the eyes. Its nature is so extraordinarily hot that its blood alone is said to dissolve the diamond, a stone that neither fire nor the substance of iron can subdue. [Note: The larger ones are from the river Cinyphus in Libya. Hence Theocritus, *Idyll* 3: “Beware the Libyan wrinkled goat, lest he butt you with his horn.”] The larger goats are called Cinyphian, from the river Cinyphus in Libya, where large ones are born.

15. Some have said that male and female goats (*capri* and *caprae*) take their names from cropping shrubs. Others say it is because they seize rough things. Some derive the name from the creaking of their legs, from which the ancients also called them *crepae*. [Note: Hence they call them *crepae*. Festus: “Goats were so called either because they crop every shrub, or from the creaking of their legs; hence the ancients also called them *crepae*.”] These are wild goats, which the Greeks, because they see extremely sharply, called *dorkades*, from *oxy derkesthai*, “to see sharply.”

16. [Note: Which the Greeks call this because they see extremely well. Origen, *Homily* 2 on the *Song of Songs*, in Jerome’s translation: “The doe,” he says, “that is, *dorcas*, sees extremely sharply.] They live in high mountains and, although from far away, nevertheless see all who approach. They are also called *capreae*, and likewise *ibices*, as though *avices*, because, like birds, they occupy steep and lofty places and dwell on high, so that from their elevation they are scarcely visible to human eyes.

17. [Note: Hence the southern region also calls them birds. From Gregory, *Morals* XXX, chapter 9, elsewhere chapter 16.] For this reason the southern region also calls ibexes birds, since they inhabit the waters of the Nile. These animals, as we have said, dwell among the highest rocks; and whenever they sense danger from wild beasts or human beings, they hurl themselves from the highest rocky peaks and receive themselves unharmed upon their own horns.

18. [Note: Deer are so called. From Servius, on the verse “three deer on the shore,” *Aeneid* I.] Deer (*cervi*) are called *apo ton keraton*, that is, “from horns.” For *kerata* in Greek means “horns.” [Note: They are enemies of snakes. From Origen, *Homily* 2 on the *Song of Songs*, and Servius, on Eclogue 8, and Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 32.] They are enemies of snakes. When they feel themselves weighed down by illness, they draw the snakes from their caves by the breath of their nostrils; having overcome the danger of the venom, they restore themselves by eating them. [Note: *Dictamnus*, or *dictamum*—both spellings have their own authorities. From Solinus, chapter 22.] They themselves have transmitted the knowledge of the herb dittany. For after feeding on it they shake out arrows that have struck them.

19. They marvel at the whistling of pipes. With their ears erect they hear keenly; with them lowered, they hear nothing. [Note: Whenever they cross immense rivers. From Gregory, *Morals* XXX, elsewhere chapter 9.] Whenever they swim across immense rivers or seas, they place their heads upon the hindquarters of those ahead of them, and, taking turns with one another, feel none of the burden’s weight.

20. [Note: *Tragelaphi*. Solinus, chapter 22, and Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 33.] *Tragelaphi* is the Greek name for animals that have the same form as deer but shaggy shoulders like goats and long, bristling chins with beards. They are found nowhere except around the Phasis.

21. [Note: *Innuli*. This is written thus in the Gothic manuscripts and in the Horatian manuscripts, Book I, Ode 23: “You flee me like a fawn, Chloe.” Canterus, Lambinus, and Hartung followed them. Perhaps *innulus*, Greek *nebros* (“fawn”), should therefore be written differently from *hinnulus*, “the offspring of a horse and an ass.”] Fawns are the offspring of deer, called *innuli* from *innuere*, “to nod,” because they hide at their mother’s nod.

22. A doe (*damula*) is so called because it escapes from the hand. It is a timid and defenseless animal. Martial writes:

> The boar is feared for its tooth, the stag is defended by its horns.  
> We defenseless does—what are we but prey?

23. [Note: *Lepus*, “hare,” as though *levipes*, “swift-footed.” Varro, *On Agriculture* III, chapter 12: “Lucius Aelius thought that *lepus* was named from its speed, because it was *levipes*; I think it comes from an ancient Greek word, by which the Aeolians of Boeotia called it *lepōris*.” See Aulus Gellius and Quintilian, Book I, chapter 6.] The hare (*lepus*) is so called as though *levipes*, “swift-footed,” because it runs quickly. [Note: Hence the Greeks call it *lagōs* from running. Thus, *la* is a particle of intensification in *agein*, “to drive.” Others derive it from *lan*, “to see,” because it sleeps with its eyes open.] Hence in Greek it is called *lagōs* from running; for it is a swift and very timid animal.

24. [Note: *Cuniculi*, “rabbits,” as though *caniculi*, “little dogs.” It was easier for the Greeks to derive the word from dogs, *apo ton kynon tous kyniklous* (“the *kynikloi* from dogs”); thus Polybius and Aelian, *On the History of Animals*, Book XIII, chapter 15, call them, except that each says the word is Spanish. Varro, *On Agriculture* III, chapter 12, says: “There is a third kind, which is born in Spain, similar to our hare but low-growing, which they call *cuniculus*.” *Cuniculi* are said to be so called because they themselves make underground passages beneath the earth, where they hide in the fields. Pliny follows Varro, Book VIII, chapter 55. One may see on Hadrian’s coinage an image of Spain holding an oak branch in her hand, with a rabbit at her feet.] Rabbits, a species of wild animal, are called *cuniculi*, as though *caniculi*, because they are caught by the tracking of dogs or driven out of their caves.

25. [Note: The pig, because it works the pasture. This is not inelegant if one considers the thing itself, but with Varro one may prefer to regard it as a Greek word, *hys*.] The pig (*sus*) is so called because it works the pasture—that is, after turning over the earth, it searches for food.

The boar (*verres*) is so called because it has great strength.

[Note: *Porcus*, as though *spurcus*, “filthy.” Unless with Varro one prefers to regard it as Greek.] A piglet (*porcus*) is so called as though *spurcus*, “filthy.” For it stuffs itself into dung, immerses itself in mud, and smears itself with mire. Horace writes: “The sow friendly to the mud.” Hence *filth* and *filthy* also derive their names from it.

26. We call the hairs of pigs *setae*, and say that *setae* comes from *sus*, “sow”; from these also come *sutores*, “shoemakers,” because they sew, that is, stitch, hides with bristles.

27. [Note: *Aper*, “boar,” from wildness. Varro: *apri* comes from rough places, unless from the Greek, in which it is *kapros*.] The boar (*aper*) is named from its wildness, with the letter *f* removed and *p* substituted. Hence among the Greeks it is called *syagros*, that is, “wild.” For everything wild and untamed we loosely call *agrestis*, “of the fields.”

28. [Note: *Juvencus*, “young bull.” From Varro, Book IV.] A young bull (*juvencus*) is so called because it begins to assist human use in cultivating the earth, [Note: Or because among the pagans. From Servius, on the verse “I was sacrificing to the ruler of heaven’s dwellers,” *Aeneid* III, and *Aeneid* IX, on “I will set it before the altars.” See Macrobius, on Virgil’s verse “a bull to Neptune.”] or because among the pagans a young bull was always sacrificed to Jupiter everywhere, never a mature bull. For even in sacrificial victims age was taken into account.

29. *Taurus*, “bull,” is a Greek word, as is also *bos*. [Note: Indian bulls. Pliny, VIII, chapter 21, and Solinus.] Indian bulls are tawny in color, swift as birds, with their hairs turned backward. They can turn their heads in whatever direction they wish; by the hardness of their backs they repel every weapon, with savage ferocity.

30. The Greeks call an ox *bous*. [Note: The Latins call it *trio*. Varro, Book VI, and Aulus Gellius, Book II, chapter 21.] The Latins call it *trio*, because it wears down the earth, as though *terio*. Naevius writes: “Here is the rustic driver of the oxen.” The broad fold of skin from the chin to the legs is called the dewlap, from the skin itself, as though *pellearia*; it is a sign of nobility in an ox. [Note: The extraordinary devotion of oxen toward their companions. These are Ambrose’s words in his *Oration on the Death of His Brother Satyrus*: “An ox seeks its fellow ox and does not think itself complete; with frequent lowing it bears witness to its faithful affection if the one with whom it was accustomed to draw the plow by its neck should happen to die.” Basil, in his *Oration on the Martyr Julian*: “And once I saw an ox at the manger weeping for its companion and yokemate who had died.” Virgil writes:

> … the sad plowman goes,  
> unhitching the young ox mourning its brother’s death.]

Oxen show extraordinary devotion toward their companions. For one seeks out the other with which it has been accustomed to draw the plow by its neck, and with frequent lowing gives evidence of its faithful affection if the other should have died.

31. [Note: *Vacca*, “cow,” from the quality of changeable nouns. Donatus, *On the Secondary Art*: “There are fixed kinds of nouns, and there are changeable kinds. Fixed nouns cannot be inflected into another gender, such as *pater*, *mater*, *soror*. Changeable nouns are either proper names, which form two genders from themselves, such as *Caius*, *Caia*, *Marcus*, *Marcia*; or common nouns, which form three genders, such as *bonus*, *bona*, *bonum*, and so forth.] A cow (*vacca*) is called as though *boacca*. It belongs to the class of changeable nouns, like *leo*, *leaena*, and *draco*, *dracaena*.

32. [Note: *Vitulus*, calf. From Servius, on Eclogue 3.] *Vitulus* and *vitula*, “calf,” are named from greenness, that is, from the freshness of youth, like *virgo*, “maiden.” A female calf is therefore small and has not yet given birth. Once she has given birth, she is a young cow or a cow.

33. [Note: Buffaloes are so untamable. From Jerome, on Amos VI, and Solinus, chapter 23.] Buffaloes (*bubali*) are so called by derivation because they resemble oxen. They are so untamable that, because of their wildness, they do not accept a yoke upon their necks. Africa produces them.

34. Aurochs are wild oxen in Germany, with horns so greatly extended that they make from them drinking vessels of remarkable capacity for royal tables. [Note: Drinking vessels are made from them. From Solinus, chapter 23. See Caesar, *Gallic War* VI; Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 15; and Servius, on the verse “the persistent wild aurochs,” *Georgics* II.] They are called *uri* from *oron*, “mountains.”

35. Camels received their name either from their nature, because when they are loaded they lie down, becoming shorter and lower, since [Note: The Greeks say *chamai*, “on the ground.” A Greek etymological work says: “The camel is the animal that, sitting upon the ground, lifts its load, as though *chamelos*. It is etymologized from bending its thighs when sitting, being *kameros*.” Varro gives the better account, Book IV: “The camel came into Latium with its Syrian name.” For among the Syrians it is *gemal*, among the Hebrews *gamal*.] the Greeks say *chamai*, “low” and “short”; or because its back is curved. [Note: For *camur* means “curved.” From Servius, *Georgics* III, *camuris*, “curved”; but Festus says that *camera* and *camuri*, “curved oxen,” come from the Greek *kampē*.] For the Greek word *camur* means “curved.” Although other regions also send camels, Arabia produces the greatest number. They differ from one another. [Note: Arabian camels. From Solinus, chapter 52. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 18, attributes this to Bactrian camels.] Arabian camels have two humps on their backs; those of other regions have one.

36. [Note: *Dromeda*, or *dromedary*. For *dromeda* seems to have been written precisely in the Gothic manuscripts in place of *dromedarii*.] The dromedary is a kind of camel, smaller in stature but faster. Hence it also takes its name. For in Greek *dromos* means “running” or “speed.” [Note: For it usually travels one hundred thousand or more units in a single day. From Jerome, on Isaiah, chapter 21.] It usually travels one hundred thousand miles or more in a single day. Like the ox, sheep, and camel, this animal ruminates.

37. [Note: Rumination is named from *ruma*. From Servius, on Eclogue 6; or from *rumen*, as the printed editions read: “The rumen is the part of the neck through which food is swallowed.” For Varro, Nonius, and the Glossary, *ruma* means “udder.”] Rumination is so called from *ruma*, the protruding part of the throat through which food, once swallowed by certain animals, is brought back up.

38. The ass and little ass (*asinus* and *asellus*) are named from sitting, as though *assedus*. This name, however, was more suitable to horses; the animal took it because, before human beings captured horses, they began to ride this animal. It is a slow creature, resisting in no way, and as soon as a human being wished it, he placed it beneath himself.

39. *Onager* means “wild ass”: the Greeks call an ass *onos*, and *agrion* means “wild.” Africa has large and untamable ones wandering in the desert. [Note: Wandering in the desert. Solinus and Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 3.] Each male presides over herds of females. [Note: They are jealous when males are born. Orosius speaks in the same way, in the preface to his *History*: “They do not hate those whom they pursue, but are jealous of those whom they love.”] When male offspring are born, they become jealous and bite off their testicles. The mothers, however, guard against this by hiding them in secluded places.

40. Arcadian asses are so called because large and tall ones were first brought from Arcadia. [Note: But the smaller ass is more useful for the farm. Some printed editions have the worst reading, “wild ass.” These are Palladius’ words, Book IV, chapter 14; see also Columella, Book VIII, chapter 1.] The smaller ass is more useful for farm work, because it endures labor and almost never refuses neglect.

41. Horses (*equi*) are so called because, when they were yoked to four-horse chariots, they were made equal, being joined as equals in form and alike in running.

42. [Note: *Caballus*. He had Virgil in mind:

> And the double spine is driven through the loins, hollowing  
> the earth, while the hoof rings heavily with its solid horn.]

The horse (*caballus*) is called from digging, because as it walks its hoof presses into and hollows the earth, which other animals do not do. Hence also *sonipes*, “sounding-foot,” because it makes a sound with its feet.

43. Horses possess great vitality. They leap about in the fields, scent battle, are roused by the sound of trumpets to combat, [Note: They are stirred by a voice and challenged to run. This is the more accurate reading than that found in Solinus: “Some are also challenged to run by lighted torches.”] are aroused by a voice and challenged to run, grieve when they have been defeated, and rejoice when they have conquered. Some recognize enemies in battle, to such a degree that they attack their opponents with their teeth. [Note: Some even recognize their own masters. Solinus: “Some have been found that recognized only their first masters, forgetting their gentleness whenever they changed their accustomed service.”] Some also recognize their own masters, forgetting their gentleness if they are transferred to different masters; some admit no one but their master onto their backs. [Note: When their masters have been killed or are dying. The verses of Homer and Virgil concerning the horses of Achilles and Pallas are well known.] When their masters have been killed or are dying, many shed tears. The horse alone is said to weep for a human being and to feel the force of grief. Hence in the Centaurs the nature of horses and human beings is mingled.

44. [Note: [Col. 0430D] They also customarily infer future events. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 42.] They also customarily infer the outcome of a future battle from the horses’ sadness or liveliness. The Persians, Huns, Epirotes, and Sicilians are reputed to have long-lived horses, exceeding fifty years; the Spanish, Numidian, and Gallic horses are shorter-lived.

45. [Note: [Col. 0430D] In a thoroughbred horse, four qualities. Palladius, Book IV, chapter 13: “In a stallion four things are considered: form, color, merit, and beauty.”] In thoroughbred horses, as the ancients say, four qualities are considered: form, beauty, merit, and color. Form requires a strong, solid body; height proportionate to its strength; breadth; a long flank; [Col. 0431A] [Note: [Col. 0431C] “The belly drawn in.” The word *venter* (“belly”) did not occur in the books; but since all the Gothic copies consistently read *substrictus*, not *substrictum*, we did not doubt that this was the true reading, as Chacon indicated from Columella, Book VI, chapter 29. We likewise believe, with the same Chacon, that the passage in Palladius is corrupt and should be supplemented from Isidore.] a belly drawn in; very large, rounded haunches; a broad, open chest; the whole body knotted with dense muscle; a dry foot; and a hoof made solid by its hollow horn.

46. Beauty requires a small, dry head, with the skin close to the bones; short, pointed ears; large eyes; [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Open nostrils.” If these are narrow, they are commonly slit open so that, becoming overheated during a long run, the horses may not suffocate, as Theophilus says, Book IV, *On the Structure of the Human Body*.] open nostrils; an erect neck; a thick mane and tail; [Note: [Col. 0431C] “The solid, fixed roundness of the hoofs.” Palladius: “The solid and fixed roundness of the hoofs.”] and hooves round in shape, firm and securely set.

47. Merit requires that the horse be bold in spirit, lively in its feet, with trembling limbs—an indication of strength—and that it can easily be roused from complete stillness, yet can readily be restrained from rapid haste. [Note: [Col. 0431C] “The horse’s movement is understood from its ears.” Solinus, chapter 30: “The horse’s movement is understood from its ears; the brow and tail reveal the courage of lions.”] The horse’s movement is understood from its ears, and its strength from its trembling limbs.

48. [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Color is especially considered here.” From Palladius, Book IV. Varro, quoted by Nonius: “Horses are born differing in color: this one bay, that one dun, the other mouse-colored.” See Gellius, Book II, chapter 26, and Book III, chapter 9, and Alciatus, Book II of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 1.] Color is especially to be considered here: bay, golden, rose-colored, myrtle-colored, deer-colored, dun, bluish-gray, dappled, gray, bright white, white, spotted, and black. Next in order comes the varied color distinguished by black and bay; every other mixed color, or ash-gray, is the worst.

49. The ancients called the bay horse *vadius*, because among the other animals it advances more vigorously. [Note: [Col. 0431D] “It is also the spadix.” From Servius, *Georgics* III. These are what the Spaniards call *bayos* and *datilados.*] It is also the *spadix*, which they call *phoenicatus*; *spadix* derives from the color of the palm tree, which the Sicilians call *spadica*.

50. [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Glaucus is as though it had painted eyes.” Servius: “Glaucus, with catlike eyes—that is, eyes suffused with brilliance.”] *Glaucus* is as though it had painted eyes, suffused with a certain brilliance; [Note: [Col. 0431D] “For the ancients called *glaucum* white.” For *glaucum* is a pale blue diluted with white. Hence Virgil: “The poplar and the willow groves, whitening with bluish foliage.” But he treats *glaucus* somewhat differently in Book XIX, chapter 28. There is nevertheless a lacuna in three Gothic copies: “For *glaucum* . . . the ancients say.”] for the ancients called *glaucus* white.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] “*Gilvus*, honey-colored.” From Servius.] *Gilvus* is a somewhat whitish, honey-colored hue.

*Guttatus* is white with black spots interspersed.

51. *Candidus* and *albus* differ from each other. [Col. 0432A] *Albus* has a certain pallor, whereas *candidus* is snow-white and suffused with pure radiance.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] “*Canus* is called so because it is made from white and black.” Tilesius, *On Colors*: “A horse is sometimes born gray and also whitish, not the same as bright white or white, though not without some of these qualities; our people call such horses *tordilli*.”] *Canus* is so called because it is composed of white and black.

*Scutulatus* is named from the disks it has, white among purple-colored markings.

52. *Varius* is so called because it has paths of unequal colors. Horses that have only white feet are called *petili*; [Note: [Col. 0431D] “They are called *petili*.” Festus says that Scaevola calls a horse’s white lower leg and hoof *petila*. In the glossary, where *perfilis*, μακροσκελής (“long-legged”), is read, I think *petilis*, μικροσκελής (“short-legged”), should be read instead. Nonius quotes this verse from Plautus under *petilis* and *frons*: “For the *petilis* has a colored forehead.” He interprets it, as usual, according to his own preference as “thin and slender.”] those with a white forehead are *callidi* (“clever” or “marked-fronted”). [Note: [Col. 0432C] “Those with a white forehead are *callidi*.” Glossary: *callidus*, λευκομέτωπος (“white-fronted”). Most books nevertheless read *calidi*. But A. August preferred *callidi*.]

53. *Cervinus* is what people commonly call [Note: [Col. 0432C] “They call it *gauranus*.” The Italians retain the same word with one letter changed, for they say *sauro*.] *gauranus*.

The common people also call it *aeranus*, because its color resembles bronze.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] “*Myrteus* is a dense purple.” Palladius also counts *pressus* among the colors of horses; but what *pressus* means in him, while Servius calls the same color *professus murteus*, and what *pressus in purpura* means here, has not yet been sufficiently determined. I nevertheless think that *pressus* signifies a denser color, so to speak, by comparison with grapes: the more they are pressed by feet or a winepress, the less watery the resulting wines become, whether reddish from white grapes or darkish from red ones.] *Myrteus* is a dense purple.

54. [Note: [Col. 0432C] “*Dossinus*.” Is this because Varro calls *dossuarii* the asses suitable for carrying loads? The glossary has *dorsuaria*, νωτοφόρα (“back-bearing”). Palladius and Columella call this color mouse-colored.] *Dossinus* is so called because its color is that of an ass; it is also ash-gray. These animals are descended from the wild breed, which we call *equiferi* (“wild horses”), and therefore [Col. 0432B] cannot pass into the rank of domesticated horses.

55. *Maurus* is black. For the Greeks call black μαῦρον (*mauron*).

A *mannus* is a shorter horse, [Note: [Col. 0432D] “The animal commonly called a *buricus*.” Jerome, on Ecclesiastes 10: “Those elevated in rank traverse the public roads on *manni*, commonly called *burici*”; and in his letter to Pammachius: “The hot *burici*, the *manni*.” Paulinus, to Seneca: “Seated on a thin and inferior little ass, a *buricus*.” And the glossary: *mannis*, βουρίχοις. But Porphyry says: “*Manni* are small horses, commonly called *burdi*”; and Acron: “*Mannus*, *burdo*.” They call smaller horses *manni*; we today call small asses *burrici*.] commonly called a *buricus*.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] “*Veredi*.” These are Festus’s words; from Isidore the form *veredi* should be restored. Procopius, Book II, *Persian War*: “He who travels on the public horses, which they customarily call *beredi*.” Julian the Antecessor, in the epitome of Justinian’s *Novels*, Novel 130, translated the Greek τῶν δημοσίων ἵππων δρόμον (“the course of the public horses”) as “the course of the *veredi*.”] The ancients called them *veredi*, because they carried *rhedae*—that is, because they drew them—or because they ran along the public roads, on which *rhedae* were also accustomed to travel.

56. There are three kinds of horses: one noble, suitable for battles and burdens; [Note: [Col. 0432D] Some books read “for honors” instead of “for burdens.”] another common and ordinary, suitable for transport but not for riding; and a third born from the mingling of different kinds, also called *bigener*, because it is born from different parents, like a mule.

57. [Note: [Col. 0432D] “*Mulus*, μύλον, a mill; and μύλη, a millstone. We have therefore retained the reading of the editors, for all the Gothic copies corruptly read: “*Mulus* … Greek … or because of the yoke …” Unless Isidore thought *mulus* was a Greek word and *mola* alone Latin. One should seek the author of this not inelegant senarius, which no one has noticed: “Let him lead the slow millstones around in grinding.”] The mule has a name derived from Greek, because, placed beneath the miller’s yoke, it slowly turns the millstones in a circle by grinding.

[Note: [Col. 0433C] “The Jews assert that Ana, Esau’s great-grandson …” From Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 36. Homer attributes this to the Paphlagonians, *Iliad* II.] The Jews assert that Ana, Esau’s great-grandson, was the first to make herds of mares mount asses in the wilderness, so that new animals contrary to nature, mules, might be born from them. They also say that female asses were bred with wild asses for this purpose, and that he himself discovered such a mating, so that the fastest asses might be born from it.

58. Human ingenuity forced different animals to mate, and thus adulterine mixing produced another species; in the same way Jacob brought about, contrary to nature, likenesses of colors. [Note: [Col. 0433D] “For such offspring.” From the same book, on Genesis 30.] For his sheep conceived offspring of the appearance of the rams’ shadows that they saw reflected in the surface of the water as the rams mounted above them.

59. Finally, the same thing is said to occur among herds of mares: noble stallions are displayed before the eyes of mares that are conceiving, so that they may conceive and produce offspring resembling them. Lovers of pigeons likewise place beautifully painted pigeons in the same places where the real birds live, so that, their sight being carried away by the images, they may produce similar offspring.

60. Hence some people order pregnant women not to look upon the most hideous faces of animals, such as cynocephali and apes, lest, encountering them with their eyes, they give birth to similar offspring. [Note: [Col. 0433D] “For they say that this is the nature of women.” Jerome’s words in the same place.] For they say that this is the nature of women: that whatever they have looked upon or conceived in their minds at the final heat of pleasure, while conception is taking place, such offspring they also produce. Indeed, during sexual intercourse the soul conveys external forms inward; once filled with their impressions, it seizes their shapes and gives them its own quality.

61. Among living creatures, those born from different species are called *bigenera*, such as the mule from a mare and an ass; [Note: [Col. 0433D] “The *burdo* from a horse and a female ass.” Varro, Book II, *On Agriculture*, chapter 8: “From a mare and an ass comes a mule; conversely, from a horse and a female ass comes a *hinnus*.” Glossary: ἡμίονος ἐξ ἵππου θηλείας καὶ ὄνου (“a mule from a female horse and an ass”). *Burdo*: ἡμίονος ἐξ ἵππου καὶ ὄνου θηλείας (“a mule from a horse and a female ass”).] the *burdo* from a horse and a female ass; [Note: [Col. 0433D] “Hybrids from boars and pigs.” Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 53. Acron, however, commenting on Satire 7 of Book I, says: “The term is taken from the eagle, which is born from an eagle and a vulture, or from dogs, which are born from a hunting dog and a shepherd’s dog.”] hybrids from boars and pigs; [Note: [Col. 0433D] “*Tityrus*.” Servius, *Eclogue* 1: “In the language of the Laconians, *tityrus* means a larger ram accustomed to lead the flock.”] the *tityrus* from a ewe and a he-goat; [Note: [Col. 0433D] “*Musmo*.” From the Gothic copies; and *musmones* are also mentioned by Strabo, Book V. *Musomones*, from Servius, *Georgics* III, on “the ram wet in the deep water.” Nonius: *musimones*, short asses, mules, or horses.] the *musmo* from a she-goat and a ram. The latter is the leader of the flock.

# CHAPTER II. On Beasts

1. The term *beasts* properly applies to lions, leopards, tigers, wolves, foxes, dogs, apes, and the rest that attack with their mouths [Col. 0434A] or claws, except snakes. [Note: [Col. 0434C] “The term *beasts* … snakes.” From Augustine, Book III, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 11.] They are called *beasts* from the force with which they rage.

2. [Note: [Col. 0434C] “They are called *wild animals*.” From Servius, on “and the fat flesh of wild animals,” *Aeneid* I.] They are called *wild animals* because they exercise natural freedom and move according to their desire. Their wills are free: they wander here and there and are carried wherever their spirit leads them.

3. The word *lion* has been adapted from Greek into Latin. In Greek it is called λέων (*leōn*), and it is a hybrid name because it is partly corrupted. [Note: [Col. 0434C] “The lioness.” From the same source, on “the lioness that has forgotten her cubs,” *Georgics* III.] *Leaena*, however, is wholly Greek, as is *dracaena*. [Note: [Col. 0434C] “That *leaena* should be called *lea*.” From the same source, *Aeneid* XII. Lucretius:

“Enraged, the lionesses hurled their bodies in a leap.”] That *leaena* should be called *lea* is a usage introduced by poets. [Note: [Col. 0434D] “*Leo* means ‘king’ in Greek and Latin.” Antonius Augustinus says of this passage: “In an old Greek book, after the etymology of Orion, there is: Λέων, διὰ τὸ λεαίνειν, ἤγουν νικᾷν (‘lion, from *leaínein*, that is, conquering’).”] *Leo* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “king,” because it is chief among all beasts.

4. Its species are said to be threefold. The short ones with curly manes are weak; the long ones with smooth hair are fierce. [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Their courage is shown by their brow and tail.” Solinus, chapter 50.] Their courage is shown by their brow and tail. Their strength is in their chest, and their firmness in their head. When surrounded by hunters, they look at the ground so that the sight of the spears may not frighten them. They fear the noise of wheels, but fire even more.

5. When they sleep, their eyes remain watchful; when they walk, they cover their tracks with their tails so that the hunter may not find them. [Note: [Col. 0434D] “When they have given birth.” These are the words of Origen, Homily 17 on Genesis.] When they have given birth to a cub, the cub is said to sleep for three days and three nights; afterward, when the place of its bed has been shaken as if by the father’s growling or roar, the father is said to awaken the sleeping cub.

6. [Note: [Col. 0434D] “The nature of lions toward human beings.” Servius, on “Then at last the lion moves his weapons,” *Aeneid* XII: “For this is the nature of lions: they cannot become angry unless provoked.”] The nature of lions toward human beings is kindly, so that they cannot become angry unless they have been harmed. Their mercy is evident in repeated examples. They spare those who have been thrown down; [Col. 0434C] [Note: [Col. 0434D] “They allow encountered captives to return home.” Solinus: “When many captives have encountered lions, they have returned home unharmed.”] they permit captives whom they encounter to return home; they kill a human being only when extremely hungry. Of them Lucretius says: “And the whelps of lions …”

7. [Note: [Col. 0434D] “The tiger.” From Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 18, and Solinus. Varro also says that among the Armenians *tigris* signifies an arrow.] The tiger is so called because of its swift flight. For the Persians and Medes call an arrow by that name. It is a beast marked with varied spots, remarkable for strength and speed, and from its name the river Tigris is called so, because it is the swiftest of all rivers. [The source reads “Has cretius,” evidently an uncertain or corrupt reading.] Hyrcania produces more of them.

8. [Col. 0435A] The panther is so called [Note: [Col. 0435C] “Either because it is the friend of all animals.” This etymology is supported by what Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 17, and Aelian, Book VI, *On the History of Animals*, report. It is commonly thought to be called *panthera* because it is wholly a wild animal.] either because it is the friend of all animals except the dragon, or because it delights in the companionship of its own kind and returns whatever it receives in a similar form. [Note: [Col. 0435C] “For πᾶν means ‘all.’” Either something is missing—as A. Augustinus thought—or this is rather a superfluous gloss by some foolish interpreter who knew only that one fact.] Πᾶν (*pan*) means “all” in Greek. It is a beast painted over with small circles, so that black or white variation is distinguished by tawny circles marked like eyes. [Note: [Col. 0435C] “With small circles.” Solinus, chapter 21: “Covered with small circles, so that the surface of the back is marked with eye-like circles, either tawny with blue or white.”]

9. This animal gives birth only once, for the reason is clear. When the cubs have grown together in the mother’s womb and possess mature strength sufficient for birth, they cannot tolerate delays. Thus they tear with their claws the womb burdened with offspring, as though it were obstructing birth; the mother expels—or rather releases—the young, compelled by pain. Thereafter, because the reproductive passages have been damaged and scarred, semen poured into them does not remain and take hold but springs back fruitlessly. [Note: [Col. 0435C] “For Pliny says.” From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “the savage seed of lions.” The passage in Pliny is Book VIII, chapter 16.] For Pliny says that animals with sharp claws cannot give birth frequently. Their insides are injured by the young moving within them.

10. [Note: [Col. 0435D] “The leopard is second after the panther.” From Solinus, in the same place.] The leopard is second after the panther: it is a variegated and extremely swift species, precipitately eager for blood. For it rushes by a leap toward death.

11. The leopard is born from the adulterous mating of a lioness and a panther and forms a third origin. Pliny likewise says in his *Natural History* that a lion mates with a female leopard, or a panther with a lioness, and that degenerate offspring are produced from either mating, [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Like a mule and a *burdo*.” From three manuscripts, according to A. Augustinus.] like a mule and a *burdo*.

12. The rhinoceros is called by the Greeks; in Latin the name is interpreted as “horn in the nose.” [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Also called the monoceros.” From Gregory, Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 10, elsewhere chapter 13. Pliny considers the rhinoceros different from the monoceros, Book VIII, chapters 20–21. He says that the former was often seen at Rome, but denies that the latter can be captured alive. Solinus reports the same: “Alive, it does not come under human control”; and in the Balearic manuscript this is added here: “It is said to possess such fierceness that, once captured, it immediately dies.”] It is also called the *monoceros*, that is, the unicorn, because it has a single horn in the middle of its forehead, [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Four feet.” Solinus says the same; but Pliny says two cubits, Ctesias, in the *Indian* material preserved by Photius, one cubit, and Aelian, Book IV, chapter 52, *On Indian Asses*, one and a half cubits. The same authors give greatly varying accounts of the color of its horn. Pliny seems to have identified the monoceros with the Indian ass, for in Book XI, chapter 46, he denies that there is any other one-horned animal besides the Indian ass and the oryx. He took this from Aristotle, Book II, chapter 1, *History of Animals*. On the rhinoceros’s battle with the elephant, see Pliny, Solinus, Aelian, Diodorus, Strabo, and Agatharchides, in his *On the Red Sea*.] four feet high, and so sharp and powerful that whatever it attacks it either tosses into the air or pierces. It often also fights with an elephant and, wounding it in the belly, brings it down.

13. It is of such strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. But, as those who have written about the natures of animals assert, a virgin girl is placed before it; she opens her lap to the approaching animal, and it, laying aside all its ferocity, rests its head there. Thus, lulled to sleep and defenseless, it is captured.

14. The Greeks think that the elephant was named from the size of its body, [Note: [Col. 0436C] “For in Greek *lophos* means ‘mountain.’” The Gothic copies have *elepho*, which yields no sense, as often happens with Greek words. We have followed A. Augustinus’s not unreasonable conjecture. There is no point in offering other origins or explanations of *elephant*.] because it resembles a mountain. In Greek, *lophos* (λόφος) means “mountain.” Among the Indians it is called *barrus*, from which its voice is called a *barritus*, and its teeth *ivory*. [Note: [Col. 0436C] “Its trunk is called *promuscis*.” From Ambrose, Book IX of the *Hexameron*, chapter 5.] Its trunk is called a *promuscis*, with which it brings food to its mouth, and it is [Note: [Col. 0436D] “And it resembles a snake.” Lucretius:

“India, with its snake-handed elephants, whose ivory rampart is fortified by many thousands …”] like a snake, protected by an ivory rampart.

15. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “These were called Lucanian oxen.” Varro, Book VI, and Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 6. Lucretius, Book V:

“Then the dreadful Lucanian oxen, with tower-like bodies …

The Carthaginians taught the snake-handed beasts of war

To endure wounds …”] The ancient Romans called these “Lucanian oxen”: “oxen,” because they saw no animal larger; “Lucanian,” because Pyrrhus first brought them against the Romans in battle in Lucania. This species of animal is suited to warfare. Among the Persians and Indians, men fight from wooden towers placed upon them, as if from a wall, hurling javelins. They possess great intelligence and memory.

16. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “They proceed in herds.” From Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 5. Solinus: “They wander in groups.”] They proceed in herds; [Note: [Col. 0436D] “They greet with whatever movement they can.” Solinus: “At sunrise they greet it with whatever movements they are capable of.”] with whatever movement they can, they greet the sun. They flee from a mouse. They mate facing away from each other. When they give birth, they leave their young in water or on islands because of dragons, which are their enemies and kill them by entwining them. They carry their young for two years, give birth no more than once, and produce not several young but only one.

[Col. 0436D] They live for three hundred years. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “They live for three hundred years.” The Greek contains a half-line of verse concerning this etymology.] Elephants once were born only in Africa and India; now only India produces them.

17. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “They are called *gryphons* because they are …” This does not provide an etymology, nor does Servius, from whom this passage comes, in *Eclogue* 3.] Gryphons are called so because they are winged animals and quadrupeds. This species of beast is born in the Hyperborean mountains. In every part of their bodies they are like lions; [Col. 0436C] in their wings and face they resemble eagles, and they are intensely hostile to horses. They also tear apart human beings whom they see.

18. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “The chameleon … is called.” After these words there is a lacuna in the Gothic copies.] The chameleon does not have a single color but is sprinkled with varied hues, like a panther. It is called this because it resembles both a camel and a lion. [Col. 0437A] The body of this chameleon changes with the greatest ease to match the colors it sees, whereas the bodies of other animals do not adapt to change so readily.

19. [Note: [Col. 0437C] “*Camelopardus* …” Pliny and Solinus call it *camelopardalis*. See Varro, Book IV.] The *camelopard* is so called because, although it is like a panther, sprinkled with white spots, its neck resembles a horse’s, its feet are like those of an ox, and its head resembles a camel’s. Ethiopia produces it.

20. [Note: [Col. 0437C] “The lynx is so called.” The Gothic copy has *lyncis*, as above in Book XI, with *calcis* for *calx*.] The lynx is so called because it is counted among the kind of wolves: it is a beast whose back is marked with spots like a panther’s, but which resembles a wolf. Thus one is called λύκος (*lykos*), the other *lynx*. They say that its urine turns into a hard precious stone called *lyngurium*; [Note: [Col. 0437C] “*Lyngurium*.” Dioscorides, Pliny, Solinus, and Aelian.] this also proves that the lynxes themselves know this, for they cover the liquid they have excreted with sand as far as they can, through a kind of natural jealousy, lest such an excretion pass into human use. [Note: [Col. 0437C] “Pliny says that lynxes …” From Servius, on “to live in the manner of a wild beast,” *Aeneid* IV.] Pliny says that lynxes admit no more than one [mate].

21. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “*Castores*, from castrating.” From Servius, on “the poisonous castoreum of Pontus,” *Georgics* I.] Beavers are called *castores* from castration. Their testicles are suitable for medicines; consequently, when they sense a hunter, they castrate themselves and bite off their own organs of strength. Cicero speaks of them in the *Scaurian Speech*: “They ransom themselves with that part of the body for which they are especially sought.” Juvenal writes:

“... who himself makes himself  
A eunuch, wishing to escape the loss  
Of his testicles.”

They are also called *fibres*, and are likewise called Pontic dogs.

22. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “*Ursus*, as though from *orsus*.” Varro: “The bear has a Lucanian origin.”] The bear is said to be called *ursus* because it shapes its young with its mouth, as though from *orsus* (“begun” or “formed”). For they say that bears give birth to shapeless offspring, and that a mass of flesh is born which the mother forms into limbs by licking it. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Hence the following line: ‘Thus the tongue forms …’” A poem by Dracontius, discussed shortly afterward.] Hence the following:

[Col. 0437C] “Thus the tongue forms the young when the she-bear has brought it forth.”

But premature birth causes this; in fact, the bear gives birth on the thirtieth day. Thus hurried fecundity produces shapeless offspring. Bears have weak heads; their greatest strength is in their forelegs and loins, and therefore they sometimes stand upright.

23. *Lupus* (“wolf”) is transferred into our language from a Greek derivation. The Greeks call wolves λύκοι (*lykoi*), [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Λύκος in Greek.” There are also λύσσα, “madness,” and λυσσᾷν, “to rage madly.” The old book of Orion says: Λύκος διὰ τὸ κακῶς λιὰν λύειν τὴν ποίμνην (“wolf, because it cruelly destroys the flock”).] and λύκος is said in Greek to derive its name from biting, because in the madness of its rapacity it slaughters whatever it finds. Others say that wolves are called *lupi* as though *leopi*, because, just as the lion has strength in its paws, so the wolf has strength in its feet; hence whatever it presses with its foot does not live.

24. It is a predatory beast, eager for blood. Concerning it country people say [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Concerning which country people say.” The same author above, Book I, chapter 36. See Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 28; Solinus, in the chapter on Italy; Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexameron*, chapter 4.] that a person loses his voice if the wolf sees him first. Hence, when someone suddenly falls silent, it is said: “There is a wolf in the story.” Certainly, if the wolf realizes that it has been seen first, it lays aside its bold ferocity. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Wolves mate … for twelve days.” From Solinus, chapter 8, or Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 22. Aristotle reports not that they mate, but that they give birth throughout twelve days of the year, which he himself considers a fable, Book VI, chapter 35, *History of Animals*. Aelian says that they are pregnant for twelve days, Book IV, chapter 4, *On Animals*, in these words: Οὐ ῥαδίως οἱ λύκοι τὴν ὠδίνα ἀπολύουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐν ἡμέραις δώδεκα, καὶ νυξὶ τοσαύταις (“Wolves do not readily complete their labor, but do so in twelve days and as many nights”). Ἐπεὶ τοσούτῳ τὴν Λητῶ εἰς Δῆλον ἐξ Ὑπερβορέων ἐλθεῖν Δήλιοι φασιν (“for the people of Delos say that Leto came from the Hyperboreans to Delos in that same period”). The translation of Theodore Gaza is confirmed by the words of Antigonus, *Collection of Remarkable Tales*, chapter 61: Φησὶν γὰρ αὐτοὺς ἅπαντας ἐν ιβʹ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τίκτειν (“for he says that all of them give birth in twelve [days] of the year”). Yet some think that they carry the young in the womb for only twelve days; this opinion was prompted by an old, word-for-word translation of Aristotle. Read Pierius Valerianus, Book XI of the *Hieroglyphics*, under “The Wolf” and “Haste.”] Wolves mate for no more than twelve days in the entire year; they endure hunger for a long time and, after prolonged fasting, devour much. [Note: [Col. 0437D] “Ethiopian wolves.” Solinus, in the chapter on Ethiopia: “Ethiopia produces the *lycaon*, a wolf with a maned neck and so varied in appearance that they say no color is absent from it.”] Ethiopia produces wolves with maned necks, so varied that they are said to lack no color.

25. The name *canis* (“dog”) appears to have a Greek etymology. In Greek it is called κύων (*kyōn*), although some believe it is named from the sound of barking, because it resounds, whence also *canere* (“to sing” or “sound”). [Note: [Col. 0438D] “Some derive it from the sound of barking.” Varro, Book IV: “A puppy is named from its keen and acute perception. Hence *canis*, unless because when the trumpet and horn give the signal, it is called *canere*, since this animal also gives the signal by its voice, both at night in guarding and in hunting.” Some read *neictaculus* instead of *nocticulus*.] Nothing is more perceptive than dogs, for they possess more senses than the other animals.

26. For they alone recognize their own names; [Note: [Col. 0438D] “They alone recognize their names.” From Pliny and Solinus.] they love their masters; they defend their masters’ homes; they expose themselves to death for their masters; they willingly run with their master to the hunt; and even when their master is dead, they do not leave his body. Finally, their nature is such that they cannot exist outside human society. In dogs two qualities are to be considered: either strength or speed.

27. [Note: [Col. 0438D] “*Catuli*, by extension.” From Servius, *Georgics* III.] *Catuli* (“cubs” or “puppies”) is used by extension for the offspring of any beasts; properly, *catuli* are the young of dogs, the word being a diminutive.

28. [Note: [Col. 0438D] “*Lycisci*.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 3.] *Lycisci*, as Pliny says, are dogs born from wolves and dogs when they happen to mate with one another. [Note: [Col. 0438D] “Indian women also customarily …” From Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 4, and Solinus.] Indian women also customarily tie female dogs in the forests at night and expose them to tiger beasts. The dogs are attacked by the tigers, and from the same litter are born dogs so fierce [Col. 0438C] and strong that, when they grapple with lions, they bring them down.

29. [Col. 0438D] The fox is called *vulpes*, as though *volupes*. [Note: [Col. 0438D] “The fox is so called.” Varro: “*Volpes*, as Aelius said, because it flies with its feet.”] It is nimble-footed and [Note: [Col. 0438D] “And never on straight paths.” From Gregory, Book XIX of the *Moralia*, chapter 1.] never runs along straight paths but through winding turns and bends; it is a deceitful animal, misleading its prey by ambushes. When it has no food, it pretends to be dead, and so, when birds descend as though to a carcass, it seizes and devours them.

30. [Col. 0439A] [Note: [Col. 0439C] “Apes.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 10.] *Simia* is a Greek word, meaning “with flattened noses.” Hence we call them *simiae*, because they have flattened noses and ugly faces, [Note: [Col. 0439C] “Wrinkles folding into ugly folds.” Apuleius uses the same word, Book IX: “Like those old mules or weakened geldings around the manger, with heads lowered, they gnawed at heaps of chaff with their withered necks, their languid nostrils folding into folds from the putrefaction of wounds.” Jerome also uses it in his letter to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*: “If the foot does not fold into loose skin,” and shortly afterward, “loose sleeves” and “boots folding into folds.”] though goats too have flattened noses. Others think that *simiae* is a Latin name, [Note: [Col. 0439C] “Because in them there is much resemblance.” Ennius:

“The ape, that most hideous beast, how like us!”] because much resemblance to human reason is perceived in them; but this is false.

31. These animals are clever in the elements; [Note: [Col. 0439C] “The new moon.” From Solinus; see Aristotle and Pliny.] they rejoice at the new moon and are sad at the half and waning moon. They carry the young they love before them; those they neglect cling around the mother. There are five kinds of them, among which the *cercopitheci* have tails. For an ape with a tail is [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Which some call οὐράν.” Chacon’s conjecture, so that the word refers to the tail rather than to the ape. To Vulcanius’s readings one may add other, no less foolish forms from our copies: *cluram*, *cram*, *diuram*, and *cuuram*.] what some call οὐράν (*ouran*, “tail”).

32. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Sphinxes … callitriches … leontophoni.” From Solinus.] Sphinxes are hairy in their manes, have prominent breasts, and are docile, forgetting their wildness.

Cynocephali are also like apes, but have faces in the form of a dog, from which they are named.

33. Satyrs have a very attractive face and are restless in their gesticulating movements.

Callitriches differ almost entirely in appearance from the others: they have a long beard on the face and a broad tail.

34. [Col. 0439D] The *leontophonos* is a small beast, so called because it is burned when captured. Meat sprinkled with its ashes and placed at crossroads kills lions if they consume even the smallest amount of it.

35. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “The porcupine is an African animal.” So Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 35; but Solinus places it in Ethiopia, chapter 33.] The porcupine is an African animal resembling a hedgehog. It is named from the shrill sound of its spines, which it releases from its loosened back so as to wound pursuing dogs.

36. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “The *enhydros*.” Solinus; Pliny; Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXII of his *History*; Diodorus Siculus; and Plutarch, in *Whether Land or Aquatic Animals Are More Intelligent*.] The *enhydros* is a little animal so called because it lives in water, especially in the Nile. If it finds a crocodile sleeping, it first rolls itself in mud, then enters through its mouth into its belly, devours all its internal organs, [Col. 0439C] [Note: [Col. 0439D] “It emerges alive from the crocodile’s entrails after the crocodile itself has died.” In old books, only these words are found instead: “and thus it dies.” See Pliny and Solinus.] and emerges alive from the crocodile’s entrails after the crocodile itself has died.

37. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “*Ichneumon*, because by its scent …” Herodotus, Nicander, and Hesychius interpret ἰχνευτήν as “tracker” or “investigator.”] The ichneumon is called in Greek because by its scent it reveals both wholesome and poisonous foods. [Col. 0440A] [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Of it Dracontius says …” The reading is also *praecidit* (“cuts off”). Dracontius composed a poem on the six days of creation during the reign of Athanagild. Eugenius III, bishop of Toledo, corrected this poem under Chindaswinth and Reccesuinth and enlarged it with verses concerning the seventh day. This book, written in Gothic letters, is now preserved in the library of Martín Rodríguez de Azagra.] Of it Dracontius says: “The swine-like creature foretells the force of every poison.” It is called *suillus* (“swine-like”) from its bristles. It also pursues snakes; when it fights an asp, it raises its tail, which the asp immediately begins to watch, as though it were threatening. When the asp directs its force toward the tail, it is deceived and seized.

38. The *musio* is so called because it is hostile to mice. The common people call it a *cat* from catching. [Note: [Col. 0440C] “Others say because it *catat*, that is, sees sharply.” Varro, Book VI: “*Cata*, sharp; for the Sabines use this word. Therefore *Catus Aelius Sextus* does not mean ‘wise,’ as they say, but ‘sharp’; likewise *cata dicta* is to be understood as ‘spoken sharply.’”] Others say that it is called *catus* because it *catat*, that is, sees. For it sees so sharply that by the brilliance of its vision it surpasses the darkness of night. [Note: [Col. 0440C] “Hence *catus* also comes from Greek.” From Servius, on “the burning Tyrians press on,” *Aeneid* I.] Hence *catus*, meaning “clever,” also comes from Greek, ἀπὸ τοῦ καίεσθαι (“from burning”).

39. [Note: [Col. 0440C] “*Furo*, from *furvus*.” Today we call it *huron*; I think it is the same as Pliny’s *viverra*.] The *furo* is named from *furvus* (“dark”), whence also *fur* (“thief”). For it digs out dark, hidden tunnels and drives out whatever prey it finds.

40. [Col. 0440B] [Note: [Col. 0440D] “*Melo*.” Georgius Agricola calls it this in *On Subterranean Animals*, and—unless I am mistaken—Pliny does too, Book VIII, chapter 38. Or, as it is written in Varro published by P. Victorius, *moelem*. Georgius Alexandrinus, in his explanation of words found in the ancient books on agriculture, says: “The *meles* is an animal hostile to birds; I think it is what the common people call *fovinus* and *maturelus*, while others call it the badger.”] The *melo* is so called either because it has a very round body or because it seeks honeycombs and continually captures honey.

# CHAPTER III. On Small Living Creatures
1. **Mouse** (*mus*) is a small animal; its name is Greek. Whatever is derived from it, however, becomes Latin. [Note: Whatever is derived from it. Words derived from *mus* (mouse).] Some say that mice are so called because they are born from the moisture of the earth. [Note: For *mus* means earth. He repeats this in Book XX, chapter 3.] For *mus* means “earth,” whence also *humus* (“soil”). [Note: Their liver at the full moon. Cicero, in *On Divination*: “The livers of mice are said to grow larger in winter.” Likewise Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37: “The fibers in the livers of mice are said to correspond in number to the moon’s phases during the month.”] At the full moon their liver grows, just as certain sea creatures increase, which again diminish when the moon wanes.

2. **Shrew** (*sorex*) is Latin, because it gnaws and cuts through things in the manner of a saw. [Note: The ancients used *soricen*. From Servius, *Georgics* II, 3.] The ancients, however, called it *soricen* or *sauricen*, just as they called *clodum* “lame” (*claudum*).

3. [Note: Why it is called *mustella*. From Servius, on “But this is not the weapon,” *Aeneid* IX. See Festus, under *Arma* and *Tela*, and Gaius, chapter 233, *On the Meaning of Words*.] **Weasel** (*mustella*) is so called as though from *mus longus*, “long mouse”; for a weapon (*telum*) is named from its length. This creature is cunning by nature: in houses, where it raises its young, it moves and changes its dwelling. It also pursues snakes and mice. There are two kinds of weasels. One is wild and larger in size, which the Greeks call **ἰκτίδες** (*iktides*, martens or polecats); [Note: The other wanders about in houses. The Greeks call the domestic one simply **γαλή** (*galē*, “weasel”), and the wild one **ἀγρία γαλή** (*agria galē*, “wild weasel”).] the other wanders about in houses. Those who say that the weasel conceives through its mouth and gives birth through its ear are mistaken. [Note: It conceives through the mouth. It gives birth through the ear. On the contrary, two manuscripts from Tarragona read: “To conceive through the ear and give birth through the mouth,” which Augustine prefers.]

4. [Note: *Musaraneus*. Here there are two lacunae in the Gothic manuscripts, except for one manuscript from Oviedo, which reads: “The *musaraneus*, whose …”; in the others it is either “is killed” or “dies,” so that the interpretation seems wholly doubtful to me. Dioscorides calls it **μυογαλή** (*myogalē*). Glossary: **Μυογαλή, musaraneus**. The manuscript of Salmantica: *Musaraneus* or *musaranea*.] **Shrew-mouse** (*musaraneus*) [lacuna].

**Spider** [lacuna].

[Note: It exists in Sardinia. From Solinus, chapter 10.] In Sardinia there is a very small animal, shaped like a spider, called the *solifuga* (“sun-fleeing creature”) because it flees the daylight. It is extremely numerous in silver mines, creeping about unseen, and through people’s carelessness it brings death upon those who sit down upon it.

5. [Note: *Mole* … which the Greeks call. From Jerome, on Isaiah II. Glossary: *Talpa*, **ἀσφάλαξ** (*asphalax*). The Gothic manuscripts have **ἀσφάλακα** (*asphalaka*), not **ἀσπάλακα**, as Jerome does.] **Mole** (*talpa*) is so called because it is condemned to perpetual blindness and darkness. It is indeed without eyes, constantly digs the earth, throws up soil, and eats the roots beneath crops. The Greeks call it **ἀσφάλακα** (*asphalaka*).

6. **Dormice** (*glires*) are so called because sleep makes them fat. [Note: *Glires* grow. The words are from Servius, *Aeneid* XII, at the beginning.] For we say *gliscere* for “to grow.” They sleep throughout the entire winter and lie motionless, as though dead; in summer they revive. [Note: They revive. After these words a manuscript from the Balearic Islands adds:

> “All winter long I sleep, and I am fatter  
> At that season when nothing but sleep nourishes me.”]

7. [Note: Hedgehog. From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* VI.] **Hedgehog** (*ericius*) is an animal covered with spines. It is so named because it raises itself when it closes itself within its spines, by which it is protected on every side against ambushes. As soon as it senses anything, it first raises itself and, turning into a ball, draws itself back within its armor. It possesses a certain cleverness. For when it has bitten off a grape from the vine, it rolls over it on its back and thus carries it to its young.

8. **Cricket** (*grillus*) takes its name from the sound of its voice. [Note: It walks backward. Pliny, *Natural History* XIX, at the end.] It walks backward, burrows into the earth, and chirps at night. It is hunted by an ant tied by a hair and thrown into its hole, after dust has first been blown in so that it cannot hide. It is then dragged out by the ant’s grip.

9. [Note: Why it is called *formica*. From Servius, *Aeneid* IV: “Indeed,” he says, “it is called *formica* because it carries crumbs in its mouth.” The word *farris* has nothing to do with the etymology, but Isidore was misled because he possessed Servius’ commentary without the poet’s verses. See Servius.] **Ant** (*formica*) is so called because it carries crumbs of grain; it is remarkably industrious. It looks ahead to the future and prepares in summer what it will eat in winter. At harvest it chooses wheat and does not touch barley. [Note: When it rains upon it. Other manuscripts read: “When it rains upon its grain … it throws it all out,” that is, exposes it to the sun.] When it rains upon its grain, it throws it all out. [Note: Ants are said to be found in Ethiopia. From Solinus, chapter 43.] Ants are said to exist in Ethiopia in the form of dogs; they dig out gold-bearing sands with their feet, guard them so that no one may carry them away, and pursue to the death those who try to take them.

10. [Note: *Formicoleon*. From Gregory, *Morals* V, chapter 16, except that he has *myrmicoleon*.] **Ant-lion** (*formicoleon*) is so called because it is either the lion of ants or simultaneously an ant and a lion. It is a small animal, highly hostile to ants, which hides itself in the dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is therefore called both lion and ant: toward other animals it is like an ant, but toward ants it is like a lion.

## CHAPTER IV. On Serpents

1. **Snake** (*anguis*) is the name for every kind of serpent that can bend and twist. Hence *anguis*, because it is angular and never straight. [Note: In place of the guardian spirits of locations. From Servius, *Aeneid* V.] Among the pagans snakes were always regarded as the guardian spirits of places. Hence Persius:

> “Paint two snakes, boys; the place is sacred …”

2. **Coluber** is so called because it inhabits shady places, [Note: Or because it glides in slippery tracks with winding bends. From Lactantius, chapter 8, *On the Workmanship of God*.] or because it slips along slippery paths in sinuous coils. Anything that slips while being held is called slippery, such as a fish or a snake.

3. **Serpent** (*serpens*) received its name because it creeps forward by hidden approaches. It does not move with open strides, but crawls through the tiniest exertions of its scales. Those creatures that move with four feet, such as lizards and geckos, are called not serpents but reptiles. Serpents are reptiles because they crawl on their belly and breast. They have as many poisons as kinds, as many dangers as species, and as many pains as colors.

4. **Dragon** (*draco*) is the greatest of all serpents, or of all living creatures on earth. The Greeks call it **δράκων** (*drakōn*). From this the Latin word *draco* was derived. [Note: It is often dragged from caves. From Augustine, on Psalm 148.] It is often said to be drawn from caves into the air, and the air is stirred because of it. It is crested, with a small mouth and narrow tubes through which it draws breath, [Note: With a small mouth … and protruding its tongue. See Solinus, chapter 33, on Ethiopia. The dragon is called *draco* from **δέρκειν** (*derkein*), that is, “to see,” because it sees extremely sharply. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I; and Festus, under *Dracones*.] and it protrudes its tongue. Its power, however, lies not in its teeth but in its tail; it harms more by striking than by biting.

5. It is harmless with respect to poison, but it does not need poison to kill, because if it coils around someone, it kills him. [Note: Not even the elephant is safe. Lucan, Book IX: “Nor is the elephant safe because of its size.” For dragons themselves are enormous. Diodorus, Book IV: “Some report that in deserts and wild regions there are serpents which fight elephants for water and are astonishing in size and number,” and so forth. Also Pliny, VIII, chapter 11.] Not even the elephant is safe from it because of the elephant’s bodily size. For the dragon lurks beside the paths along which elephants customarily walk, ties their legs together in knots, and kills them by suffocation. It is born in Ethiopia and India, amid the very blaze of unremitting heat.

6. [Note: Basilisk. From Jerome, on Isaiah XIV, and Letter 83 to Oceanus. Some material is also from Pliny VIII and Solinus.] **Basilisk**, in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as *regulus* (“little king”), because it is the king of serpents, to such an extent that those who see it flee. It kills them by its odor, and it also kills a human being if it merely looks at him. Indeed, at its gaze no flying bird passes unharmed; even if it is far away, the bird is burned by its mouth and devoured.

7. Nevertheless, it is defeated by weasels, which people introduce into the caves where it lies hidden. When it sees one, it flees; the weasel pursues and kills it. That parent of all things established nothing without a remedy. It is half a foot in length and marked with white spots.

8. [Note: Basilisks … make people hydrophobic. These are Jerome’s words in the cited letter to Oceanus.] Basilisks, like scorpions, seek dry places; and after they have come to water, they make people **ὑδροφόβους** (*hydrophobous*, hydrophobic) and delirious.

9. [Note: The *sibilus* is the same as the *regulus*. I suspect that the *sibilus*, *regulus*, and basilisk are the same animal. This is clear regarding *regulus* in the Glossary: **Βασιλικὸς ὁ ὄφις**, “the *regulus* is a serpent,” and afterward: **Βασίλισκος, regulus**. On the basilisk’s hissing, see Pliny, Solinus, and Lucan.] **Sibilus** is the same as the *regulus*. For it kills by hissing before it bites or burns.

10. [Note: Viper. From Servius … “or the viper, harmful to the touch, lay hidden,” *Georgics* III. Likewise Gregory, *Morals* XV, chapter 9. But Isidore did not examine how appropriately Servius cites Lucan’s poem. It is nevertheless called *vipera*, as though *vivipara* (“live-bearing”), because it gives birth not to eggs but to a living creature. See Aristotle, Book I, *History of Animals*.] **Viper** (*vipera*) is so called because it gives birth by force. When its belly groans in labor, [Note: “Groans.” The Gothic manuscripts have this, not “swells.”] the young, without waiting for nature’s appointed release, gnaw through its sides and burst out, bringing about the mother’s death. Lucan:

> “The viper’s knotted coils unite in a body torn apart.”

11. [Note: It is said that the male … Herodotus, Nicander, Pliny.] It is said that the male inserts himself into the viper’s mouth and pours out his seed. She, overcome by the pleasure of lust and driven into fury, bites off the male’s head, which she has taken into her mouth. Thus both parents perish: the male while mating, the female while giving birth. From the viper are made medicinal pastilles called **θηριακοί** (*thēriakoi*, antidotes) by the Greeks.

12. **Asp** (*aspis*) is so called because it injects and spreads poison by its bite. The Greeks call poison **ἰός** (*ios*), and hence *aspis*, because it kills with a poisonous bite. There are various kinds and appearances of this creature, with differing effects for causing harm. [Note: It is said that the asp … From Augustine, on Psalm 57.] It is said that when an asp begins to suffer under an enchanter—someone who summons it with certain special incantations in order to draw it out of its cave—if it does not wish to come out, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks and covers the other with its tail. Thus, not hearing the magical words, it does not come out to the enchanter.

13. [Note: *Dipsas*, which in Latin is *situla*. I would prefer *siticula*. Glossary: *siticula*, **δίψας** (*dipsas*). On the *dipsas*, see Solinus, chapter 30, and Aelian, Book VI, chapter 50.] **Dipsas**, a kind of asp, is called *situla* in Latin, because whoever it bites dies of thirst.

14. [Note: *Hypnalis*. See Solinus.] **Hypnalis** is called a kind of asp because it kills by sleep. Cleopatra applied one to herself and thus was released from life by death as though by sleep.

15. [Note: *Haemorrhois*. Lucan, Book IX:

> “The harsh *haemorrhois* sank its teeth into Tullus,  
> The high-spirited young man and admirer of Cato.

> And as the pressure of Corycian saffron  
> Commonly spreads at once through all its threads,  
> So all his limbs simultaneously emitted  
> Bright venom instead of blood.”

See Solinus and Dioscorides.] **Haemorrhois** is an asp so called because one bitten by it sweats blood, so that, when the veins are dissolved, it draws out through the blood whatever life remains. The Greeks call blood **αἷμα** (*haima*).

16. **Praester** is an asp that always runs with its mouth open and steaming. A poet remembers it thus:

> “And the eager *praester*, stretching wide its steaming jaws.”

Anyone it strikes swells up and dies from monstrous bloating; [Note: “Swollen.” From Solinus, chapter 30. Since that passage itself is corrupt, we make no alteration here.] putrefaction follows the swelling.

17. [Note: The deadly *seps*. He had Lucan’s verse in mind, Book IX:

> “The deadly *seps*, dissolving bones together with the body.”

See Nicander’s scholia and Dioscorides, Book II, chapter 70.] **Seps**, the deadly asp, consumes a person immediately after biting him, so that his entire body melts within the serpent’s mouth.

18. [Note: *Cerastes*. From Solinus, chapter 30. From this passage you must understand “birds” as the animals that are enticed.] **Cerastes** is a serpent so called because it has horns on its head resembling those of rams; the Greeks call horns **κέρατα** (*kerata*). It has four little horns, by displaying which it kills animals lured as though by bait. It covers its entire body with sand and gives no indication of itself except in the place where it catches the birds or animals it has enticed. It is more winding than other serpents, so that it seems not to possess a spine.

19. [Note: *Scytale*. From the same chapter. Isidore seems to derive the word from **στάζειν** (*stazein*, “to drip”), whereas others derive it from **σκυτάλη** (*skytalē*), that is, “a smooth rod.” The Spartan *scytale* was well known: the state of Sparta used it so that intercepted letters could not be understood. Dioscorides calls the amphisbaena a *scytale*; his translator calls it *caecilia*.] **Scytale** is a serpent so called because the variety of markings on its back shines so brightly that it delays those who look at it for the sake of examining the markings. Since it is slower in crawling and cannot overtake those fleeing from it, it captures them by the marvel of its appearance, leaving them stupefied. It possesses such heat that even in winter it casts off the skin of its burning body. Lucan writes of it:

> “And the *scytale*, even now amid scattered frost,  
> Alone will lay aside its cast-off skin.”

20. **Amphisbaena** is so called because it has two heads, one in its proper place and the other at its tail; it moves from either head, its body following a circular course. It alone of serpents exposes itself to the cold, coming forth first of all. Lucan writes of it: [Note: Viper. From Servius … “or the viper, harmful to the touch, lay hidden,” *Georgics* III. Likewise Gregory, *Morals* XV, chapter 9. But Isidore did not examine how appropriately Servius cites Lucan’s poem. It is nevertheless called *vipera*, as though *vivipara* (“live-bearing”), because it gives birth not to eggs but to a living creature. See Aristotle, Book I, *History of Animals*.] [Note: “And heavy, turning toward a double …” Lucan also reads *surgens* (“rising”), which Solinus appears to have read, since he says *consurgere in geminum caput*, “to rise up into a double head.” See Nicander, *Theriaca*.]

> “And the heavy *amphisbaena*, turning toward a double head.”

Its eyes shine like lamps.

21. [Note: *Enhydris*. From Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 7.] **Enhydris** is a coluber that lives in water. The Greeks call water **ὕδωρ** (*hydōr*).

22. [Note: Aquatic *hydros*. Festus’ words, from *Boa*.] **Hydros** is an aquatic serpent. Those struck by it swell up; some call the disease it causes *boa*, [Note: Because of ox dung. Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 18. Ox dung cures *boas*, from which the creatures also took their name.] because it is cured by ox dung.

23. **Hydra** is a many-headed dragon, such as existed in the marsh of Lerna in the province of Arcadia. [Note: In the marsh of Lerna. From Servius, on “the monster of Lerna.” *Aeneid* VI.] In Latin it is called *excetra*, because when one head was cut off, three grew in its place—but this is a fable. In fact, it is agreed that the hydra was a place that spewed forth waters devastating the neighboring city; when one channel was blocked, many others burst forth. Hercules, seeing this, burned the places themselves and thereby closed the channels of the waters. The hydra was named from water.

24. [Note: *Chelydros*. These are Servius’ words, on “to stir with the galbanum,” *Georgics* III. The words of Lucan that followed in all the manuscripts after this—“For it is always straight …”—were supplied by A. August so that *cenchris* might be fitted to the passage. I believe no one will doubt that this is correct.] **Chelydros** is a serpent also called *chersydros*, because it lives both in water and on land. The Greeks call land **χέρσος** (*chersos*) and water **ὕδωρ** (*hydōr*). Wherever it glides, it makes the ground smoke. Macer describes it thus:

> “Whether its back breathes foaming venom,  
> Or the earth smokes wherever the foul serpent glides.”

And Lucan:

> “And the *chelydri*, dragged along a smoking path.”

25. [Note: *Natrix*. All the manuscripts incorrectly have *rinatrix*, including in Lucan’s verse. They say that this creature, because it resembles an eel, was often fatal to those who ate it.] **Natrix** is a serpent that infects water with poison. Whatever spring it is in, it mingles poison with it. Lucan writes:

> “And the *natrix*, violator of the water.”

26. [Note: *Cenchris*. It is so called because its spots resemble millet, which the Greeks call **κέγχρος** (*kengchros*).] **Cenchris** is an unbending serpent that always travels in a straight path. Lucan writes:

> “And the *cenchris*, always about to glide along a straight track.”

It always walks straight. For if it twists while running, it immediately bursts.

27. [Note: *Parias*. From the Greek etymologist: **παρὰ τὸ πεφυσιωμένας ἔχειν τὰς παρειάς**, that is, “from having swollen cheeks.” Aelian wishes this to be the serpent of Asclepius, Book III, chapter 11.] **Parias** is a serpent that always walks on its tail and seems to make a furrow. Lucan writes of it:

> “And the *parias*, content to furrow its path with its tail.”

28. [Note: *Boas*. From Solinus, chapter 8.] **Boas** is an Italian snake of enormous bulk. It pursues herds of cattle and cowherds, coils itself around their udders flowing with abundant milk, and kills them by sucking. It therefore received the name *boas* from the destruction of oxen.

29. [Note: *Jaculus*. From the same work, chapter 30.] **Jaculus** is a flying serpent, of which Lucan writes:

> “And the winged *jaculi*.”

They spring out from trees, and whenever an animal passes by, they throw themselves upon it and kill it; hence they are called *jaculi*. In Arabia there are also winged serpents called [Note: *Sirenae*. Pliny, Book X, chapter 49.] **sirens**. They run faster than horses and are also said to fly. Their poison is so powerful that death overtakes the victim before pain.

30. [Note: *Ammodytes*. This is unquestionably the correct reading, and *ammodytes* is so called from **τὸ δύειν τὸν ἄμμον**, “to sink into the sand.” The poem of Lucan caused *ophites* to replace *ammodytes*, because both words had been corrupted in the text, though *ammodytes* more seriously: when it was changed into *admotus*, it completely lost the appearance of a serpent. Glossary: *harenarius*, *ammodytes*.] **Ammodytes** is so called because it has the color of sand. The poet writes of it:

> “The Theban *ophites*, painted with tiny spots,  
> Of one color with the scorched and indistinguishable sands—  
> The *ammodytes*.”

31. [Note: A small *seps*. I do not see why this had to be repeated.] **Seps** is a small serpent that consumes not only the body but also the bones with its poison. The poet remembers it thus:

> “The deadly *seps*, dissolving bones together with the body.”

32. **Dipsas** is said to be a serpent so small that it cannot be seen when stepped on. Its poison extinguishes life before it is felt, so that the face, overtaken by death, does not even assume the sadness of one who is dying. The poet writes:

> “The *dipsas*, crushed beneath him, bit Aulus,  
> The standard-bearer, a young man of Tyrrhenian blood,  
> Twisting his head backward.
>
> There was scarcely any pain or sensation from the tooth.”

33. [Note: *Solpunga*. This word shows remarkable variation both in Isidore’s manuscripts and in other authors: *salpiga, salpuga, solipuga, salpinga, scalpiga,* and *scalpia*; Solinus has *solifuga*, and the Glossary has *solipaga*, **ἠλιοκεντρίς μυίας εἶδος**, “a kind of fly, the ‘sun-stinger.’” Pliny, Book XXIX: “There is also a poisonous kind of ant, not generally found in Italy; Cicero calls them *solipugae*, the Baeticians *salpugae*.” It is therefore unsurprising that most Gothic manuscripts retain the name *salpyga*. Festus: “*Solipunga* is a kind of harmful little creature that becomes more intense and active through the heat of the sun, from which it also derives its name.” Lucan, however, writes:

> “Who would fear to tread upon your darkness, *salpuga*?”

Other manuscripts read *solpuga*, “your hiding places.”] **Solpunga** is a serpent that cannot be seen.

[Note: *Caecula*. Glossary: *Caeca*. Columella, Book VI, chapter 17: *Caecilia*.] **Caecula** is so called because it is small and has no eyes.

**Centipede** (*centupeda*) is named from its multitude of feet.

34. **Lizard** (*lacertus*) is a kind of reptile, so called because it has arms. There are several kinds of lizards, such as the *botrax*, salamander, *saura*, and *stellio*.

35. [Note: *Botrax* is so called because it has the appearance of a frog; the Greeks call a frog **βότραχον** (*botrachon*).] **Botrax** is so called because it has the appearance of a frog; the Greeks call a frog **βότραχον** (*botrachon*).

36. [Note: Why it is called *salamandra*, “because it withstands fires.” Pliny says: “If that were true, Rome would already have tested it.” But I will never believe that Isidore was thinking about etymology in these words.] **Salamander** (*salamandra*) is so called because it is effective against fires. Of all poisons, it has the greatest power. Other poisonous creatures strike individuals; this one kills many people at once. For if it crawls into a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison and kills those who eat it. Indeed, even if it falls into a well, the force of its poison kills those who drink from it. This creature, resisting fires, alone among animals extinguishes flames. It lives in the midst of fires without pain or being consumed; not only is it not burned, it extinguishes the fire.

37. **Saura** is a lizard whose eyes become blind when it grows old. It then enters a hole in a wall facing east, fixes its gaze when the sun rises, and is restored to sight.
