38. **Stellio** takes its name from its color. Its back is marked with shining spots in the form of stars. Ovidius writes of it:

> “[lacuna] and it has received a name suited to its color,  
> Its body starred with varied spots.”

[Note: It is hostile to scorpions. From Pliny XXIX, chapter 4.] It is said to be so hostile to scorpions that when they see it, they are overcome by fear and torpor.

39. [Note: There are other kinds. From Solinus. But *ammodytes* could have been omitted, since he had already discussed it. These things, however, may be found in his notebooks.] There are also other kinds of serpents, such as *ammodytes*, *elephantiae*, and *chamaedracontes*. In short, there are as many deaths as there are names. All serpents by nature are cold, and they do not strike unless they become warm; when they are cold, they touch no one.

40. Hence their poisons do more harm by day than by night. They are numb from the cold of night, and rightly so, because they are cold from the nighttime dew. Their naturally cold bodies draw icy vapor into themselves, bringing destruction. Thus in winter they lie stiffened in coils, while in summer they become loose.

41. This is why, when anyone is struck by the poison of a serpent, he first becomes numb; afterward, when the poison has been heated within him and flares up, it immediately destroys the person. [Note: *Poison*. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and deceive with poison.”] Poison (*venenum*) is so called because it travels through the veins. Once infused, its destructive substance spreads through the veins as the body’s vitality increases, and [Note: It takes away the soul. Manuscripts 4 and 5 from Tarragona, and Rabanus.] it takes away the soul.

42. Therefore poison cannot harm unless it has touched a person’s blood. Lucan writes:

> “The serpent’s deadly power lies in mingled blood.”

Every poison is cold, and therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees cold poison. Among the natural gifts that we see to be shared by us and irrational animals, the serpent surpasses them in a certain vividness of sensation.

43. Hence it is also written in Genesis: “Now the serpent was wiser than all the beasts of the earth.” [Note: Pliny says this. From the same source, on “Then he hid his swollen head deep,” *Georgics* III.] Pliny says—if he is to be believed—that even if a serpent’s head escapes with only two fingers’ breadth attached to it, it nevertheless lives. [Note: Hence it exposes its whole body. From Augustine, on Psalm 57.] For this reason it presents its whole body to those striking at its head.

44. [Note: The sight of all snakes. From Solinus, chapter 30.] All snakes have dull vision. They rarely look straight ahead, and not without reason, since their eyes are not in the forehead but at the temples; consequently they hear more quickly than they see. [Note: No animal … From Servius, on “with quivering tongues,” *Aeneid* II.] No animal moves its tongue with such speed as a serpent, so that it seems to have three tongues, although it has only one.

45. [Note: The wetness of snakes. From Servius, on “with dripping poison,” *Aeneid* VII.] Snakes’ bodies are moist, so that wherever they go, they mark their path with moisture. The tracks of snakes are such that, although they appear to lack feet, they crawl by means of their ribs and the exertions of their scales. They have scales arranged in an even pattern from the top of the throat to the bottom of the belly. They rely on their scales as though on claws, and on their ribs as though on legs.

46. Therefore, if anywhere on the body—from the belly to the head—it is struck by some blow, the snake is weakened and cannot continue its course, because wherever the blow falls, it dislocates the spine by which the rib-legs and movements of the body were driven. Snakes are said to live a long time, to such an extent that, after shedding their old skin, they are said to shed their old age and return to youth.

47. The cast-off skins of snakes are called *exuviae*, because when they grow old they strip themselves of them; once stripped, they return to youth. They are also called *exuviae* and *induviae*, because they are removed and put on.

48. [Note: Pythagoras says this. From the same source, *Aeneid* V, on “the spirit of the place or its attendant.” See Pliny X, chapter 66; Plutarch, *On Clemency*; Aelian, Book I, chapter 53; and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.] Pythagoras says that a serpent is created from the marrow of a dead human being, which is in the spine. Ovidius also records this in the books of the *Metamorphoses*, saying:

> “There are those who believe that, when the spine has rotted  
> Within the closed tomb,  
> Human marrow is changed into a snake.”

If this is believed, it rightly follows that just as death came to humanity through the serpent, so the serpent comes through the death of a human being. [Note: It is said that a serpent does not dare touch a naked human being. From the letter to Praesidius, on the Paschal Candle, in Jerome, volume IX.] It is also said that a serpent does not dare touch a naked human being.

## CHAPTER V. On Worms

1. [Note: A worm is an animal. Augustine, on Psalm 21: “A worm is born from flesh without sexual intercourse.”] A **worm** (*vermis*) is an animal that generally comes into being without any sexual intercourse from flesh, wood, or any earthly substance, although some are occasionally born from eggs, such as the scorpion. Worms are of the earth, water, air, flesh, leaves, wood, or clothing.

2. **Spider** (*aranea*) is a worm of the air, named from its nourishment from the air. It draws out long threads from its tiny body and, always intent upon its web, never ceases working, enduring perpetual suspension [Note: “In its craft.” The Gothic manuscripts have this; others read “in its labor.”] in its art.

3. **Leech** (*sanguisuga*) is an aquatic worm, so called because it sucks blood. It lies in wait for drinkers, and when it slips into the throat or attaches itself somewhere there, it draws blood. When it has become saturated with an excess of blood, it vomits up what it has taken in so that it may suck fresh blood again.

4. [Note: The scorpion is counted among worms, not serpents. From Solinus, chapter 30.] **Scorpion** (*scorpio*) is a worm of the earth, assigned rather to worms than to serpents. It is an animal armed with a sting, and it received its Greek name from the fact that it pierces with its tail and spreads poison [Note: With a curved wound. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*: “Tertullian rightly called it *scorpiacum*, because through a curved wound he poured poisons into the body of the Church.” Also in the prologue to *Joshua*.] through a curved wound. [Note: Its distinctive characteristic. Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 4.] The scorpion’s distinctive characteristic is that it does not strike the palm of a hand.

5. **Cantharis** is an earthworm that, as soon as it is applied to a human body, produces blisters filled with fluid through its burning action.

6. [Note: *Multipes*. The Greeks call it **ὀνίσκος** (*oniskos*). See Galen, Book XI, *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*.] **Multipes** (“many-footed”) is an earthworm named from its many feet. When touched, it curls itself into a little ball. It is born beneath stones from moisture and earth.

7. **Slug** (*limax*) is named from mud (*limus*), because it is born in mud or from mud. Hence it is always considered filthy and unclean.

8. **Silkworm** (*bombyx*) is a worm of leaves, from whose weaving silk is made. It is called by this name because it is emptied when it produces its threads, and only air remains within it.

9. **Caterpillar** (*eruca*) is a worm of leaves, wrapped among vegetables or vine leaves. It is named from “eating away.” Plautus mentions it:

> “It imitates a worthless and destructive beast, wrapped up in the vine.”

It wraps itself up in the same way, [Note: And it does not fly away like a locust. From Jerome, on Amos IV.] and it does not fly away like a locust, darting here and there and leaving the crop only half-eaten. Instead, it remains among the doomed crops and consumes everything by its slow crawling and sluggish bites.

10. [Note: The Greeks call woodworms *teredones*, because they eat by boring.] The Greeks call woodworms **teredones**, because they eat by boring. We call them **termites**. In Latin, this is what woodworms are called; they are produced by trees cut down at an unsuitable time.

11. **Clothes moth** (*tinea*) is a worm of clothing, so called because it holds on and remains there until it eats through the material. Hence the word *pertinax* (“persistent”), because it presses repeatedly toward the same object.

12. Worms of flesh include: *hemicraneus*, *lumbricus*, *ascaridae*, *costi*, lice, fleas, nits, *tarmus*, *ricinus*, *usia*, and bedbugs.

13. [Note: *Hemicranius*. Chacón says: “Since Marcellus writes in Book II of *On Medicine*: ‘Earthworms immediately cure hemicrania, in equal number on the left side of the bed,’ I fear that Isidore derived *hemicranius* the worm from this passage, although there is nothing to prevent the disease and the medicine from being called by the same name.”] **Hemicranius** is called a worm of the head.

**Intestinal worm** (*lumbricus*) is so called as though from *lubricus* (“slippery”), because it slips, or because it is in the loins.

[Note: *Ascaridae*. Gaza renders this as *tipulae* instead of *ascarides*. Hesychius: **Ἀσκαρίδες εἶδος σκωλήκων**, “*ascarides*, a kind of worms.” The medical books concerning them should be consulted.] **Ascarides** [lacuna].

[Note: *Costi*. See Festus and Pliny, on *cossi*.] **Costi** [lacuna].

14. **Lice** (*pediculi*) are worms of the skin, named from feet. Hence those in whose bodies lice swarm are called lice-infested (*pediculosi*).

15. [Col. 0450A] **Fleas** (*pulices*) are so called because they are nourished more by dust.

**Nits** (*lendes*) [lacuna].

[Note: *Tarmus*. Festus: “*Tarmes* is a kind of worm that eats flesh.” But examples cited by Scaliger at this passage of Festus show that it may also be understood as *termite*.] **Tarmus** is a worm of bacon.

[Note: *Ricinus*. Glossary: *riginus*, **κρότων** (*krotōn*), and afterward **Κρότων φθείρ**, “the *ricinus* louse.” Columella uses this word in *On the Diseases of Dogs*, Book VII, chapter 13.] **Ricinus** is a worm of dogs, so called because it clings to dogs’ ears; **κύων** (*kyōn*) is the Greek word for dog.

16. [Note: *Usia*. Since *s* and *r* are scarcely distinguishable in the Gothic characters, A. August preferred *uria* to *usia*.] **Usia** is a worm of pigs, so called because it burns. When it bites, the place burns so intensely that blisters immediately form there.

17. [Note: *Cimex*, from its resemblance to a certain herb. Or to *hypericum*, since the name **κόρις** (*koris*) is common to both?] **Cimex** (“bedbug”) is named from its resemblance to a certain herb, whose odor it possesses.

18. Properly speaking, a *vermis* is born in rotting flesh, a *tinea* in clothing, an *eruca* in vegetables, a *teredo* in wood, and a *tarmus* in bacon.

19. A worm does not crawl, like a serpent, by open strides or by the exertions of scales, because it does not possess a rigid spine like a coluber. Rather, by alternately extending and contracting the sections of its little body—contracting those it has extended and extending those it has contracted—it unfolds its movement and thus glides along when set in motion.

## CHAPTER VI. On Fish

1. **Fish** (*pisces*) are named from *pasci* (“to feed”), and so is *pecus* (“cattle”), evidently.

2. [Note: Reptiles. From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 1.] These swimming creatures are called **reptiles** because they have the appearance and nature of crawling. Although they plunge into the depths, they crawl as they swim. Hence David says: “This sea is great and [Note: And spacious. This word is found in the printed editions but is absent from the Gothic manuscripts and also from the Septuagint, which Isidore follows. We express the Hebrew word when we say *brazos de mar* (“arms of the sea”). The Septuagint was content to say **εὐρύχωρον** (*eurychōron*), “spacious.”] spacious; there are reptiles there without number.”

3. **Amphibians** are certain kinds of fish, so called because they possess the ability to walk on land and the function of swimming in water. **Ἀμφί** (*amphi*) in Greek also means “both,” that is, because they live both in water and on land, such as seals, crocodiles, and hippopotamuses—that is, river horses.

4. They gave names to cattle, wild beasts, and birds before they did so to fishes, because these were seen and known earlier. [Note: “But to fishes afterward.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 2.] The names of fishes, however, were gradually established later, once their kinds had become known—either from their resemblance to terrestrial animals, or from their own appearance, habits, color, shape, or sex.

5. From resemblance to terrestrial animals: frogs, lions, [Col. 0451A] calves, [Note: “Black *merulae*. Varro denies that *merulum* is said, but it occurs three times in the Glossary.”] black merulae [blackbirds], peacocks marked with varied colors on neck and back, and [Note: “White-speckled thrushes.” *Albovarii* is also read in certain books of Isidore and Ambrose. On the colors of thrushes, see Aristotle, Athenaeus, and Massarius in their discussions of fishes appended to Pliny.] white-speckled thrushes, and the rest that have claimed names for themselves according to the forms of terrestrial animals. From the habits of terrestrial animals: sea-dogs, named after land dogs because they bite; and wolves, because they pursue others with shameless voracity.

6. [Note: “From color, such as the umbrae.” Varro mentions this fish in Book IV; the Greeks call it σκίαινα [*skiaína*]. Pliny, XXXII, chapter 11, and Ovid in the *Halieutica*. Glossary: σκιὸς ἰχθύς, “shadow-fish.”] From color, such as the umbrae, because they are the color of a shadow; and [Note: “And the gilt-heads.” *Chrysophrys*, in Ovid.] gilt-heads, because they have the color of gold on their heads; and the variegated fish, from their variety, which the common people call trout. [Note: “From shape, such as the orb.” *Orchis*, in Pliny, XXXII, chapter 2; let others judge which account is more accurate.] From shape, such as the orb, because it is round and consists entirely in the head; and the sole, because it is shaped like the sole of a shoe. From sex, such as the musculus, because it is the male of the whale; for the whale is said to conceive through intercourse with it. [Note: “Hence also the musculi of oysters.” Pliny, IX, chapter 35.] Hence also the musculi of oysters, from whose milk oysters conceive.

[Col. 0451B] 7. Whales are enormous beasts, named from emitting and pouring out water. For they cast up waves higher than the other beasts of the sea: βάλλειν [*bállein*] in Greek means “to emit.”

8. [Note: “They are called *cete*.” Τὸ κῆτος, καὶ τὰ κήτη [“the sea monster, and sea monsters”]. From Servius, *Aeneid* V; but this passage, like others, shows Isidore using Servius’s commentary without Virgil’s words. What follows—“that is, because of their monstrous size”—he seems to have thought he was transcribing from Servius, as though Servius had interpreted *cete* as “monstrous,” whereas “monstrous whales” are Virgil’s words. I do not think this etymology of *cetus* needs defending, although I know that other things too, such as ships, are called *cete* because of their size. The remainder is from Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 9.] They are called *cete*, τὸ κῆτος, καὶ τὰ κήτη, that is, because of their monstrous size. They are enormous kinds of sea beasts, with bodies as large as mountains, such as the whale that swallowed Jonah, whose belly was so vast that it resembled hell, as the prophet says: “He heard me from the belly of hell.”

9. Sea-horses are so called because in their front part they are horses, while behind they dissolve into a fish.

[Note: “Seals.” Some manuscripts have *bocas*, derived from the digamma.] Seals are said to be sea oxen, as it were *boacas*.

10. The *caerulei* are named from their color; for *caeruleum* is green mixed with black, as the sea is.

11. [Note: “Dolphins.” Not *delphin*, but *simon*, or, in other books, *sinomon*, from Solinus, chapter 18.] Dolphins have received their name because they follow human voices, or because they gather together in herds to musical harmony. Nothing in the sea is faster than they, for they often leap over ships in flight. When they sport in the waves and strike themselves against the masses of water in precipitous leaps, they seem to signal storms; these are properly called *Simones*. [Note: “There is also a kind of dolphin.” In the Nile. Solinus, chapter 35, on Egypt: “These dolphins entice crocodiles to swim by artfully, and, diving beneath them by a crafty stratagem, cut and kill them by swimming under the tender parts of their bellies.”] There is also a kind of dolphin in the Nile with a serrated back; it kills crocodiles by cutting their tender bellies.

12. [Note: “Sea pigs, commonly called *suilli*.” We too commonly call them *solli*, and we gladly agree with those who think they are the same as catfish.] Sea pigs, commonly called *suilli*, dig up the earth beneath the water like pigs while searching for food. For they have the function of a mouth around the throat, and unless they plunge their snout into the sand, they cannot gather food.

13. Crows are named from the sound of their hearts, because they grunt from the breast and are caught when betrayed by their own voice.

78 14. [Note: “Tunnies … they enter.” Understand the open sea, from Solinus, chapter 18; in his manuscripts *ingrediuntur* (“they enter”) is read, not *illabuntur* (“they glide in”). See Aristotle, *History of Animals* VIII, chapter 13, and Pliny, IX, chapter 15.] Tunnies have a Greek name. They enter in spring: they go in on the right side and leave on the left. They are believed to do this because they see more sharply with their right eyes than with their left.

15. [Note: “Swordfish.” From Pliny, XXXII, chapter 2.] The swordfish is so called because it has a pointed snout, and for this reason it pierces ships and sinks them.

16. The sawfish is so called because it has a saw-shaped crest and, swimming beneath a ship, cuts it.

17. The scorpion-fish is so called because it injures anyone who lifts it by hand. [Note: “They report [this] concerning ten crabs.” From the same chapter, chapter 5.] They report that when ten crabs are tied together with a bundle of basil, all the scorpion-fish in the vicinity gather at that spot.

18. [Note: “The *aranea*.” Pliny, IX, chapter 48: “The araneus is a poisonous water animal, dangerous because of a spine-like barb on its back.” The etymology is fitted to the word as best it can be; for we do not believe Isidore even considered striking as relevant to the word.] The *aranea* is a kind of fish, so called because it strikes with its ear; for it has spines with which it attacks.

19. [Note: “The crocodile, from its saffron color.” Correct, if what Peter Martyr relates in Book III of his *Embassy to the Sultan* is true: he says he learned from sailors that crocodiles are yellow. But Eustathius gives a Greek etymology, namely that it flees saffron, which is why saffron is scattered in apiaries; but this concerns the land crocodile. For the sea crocodile, the explanation is that it fears τὰς κρόκας, that is, the shores.] The crocodile is named from its saffron color. It is born in the Nile, [Note: “A four-footed animal.” From Solinus, chapter 35.] is a four-footed animal on land and powerful in water, [Note: “Usually twenty cubits in length.” Eighteen according to Pliny and Herodotus.] usually twenty cubits long, [Col. 0452C] armed with enormous teeth and claws, and has such hardness of hide [Note: “So that, however strong the blows of stones may be.” Solinus: “So that it rebounds from its hide blows driven by any engine.” See Aristotle, Herodotus, and Pliny.] that it does not feel even the blows of powerful stones rebounding from its back.

[Col. 0453A] 20. It rests in the water at night and on land by day; it lays its eggs on land; the male and female take turns. Certain fish having a serrated crest kill it by cutting through the tender parts of its belly. It alone among animals is said to move its upper jaw.

21. [Note: “The hippopotamus.” From Solinus, in the same place.] The hippopotamus is so called because it resembles a horse in its back, mane, and neighing, with an upturned snout, boar-like teeth, and a twisted tail (and cleft hooves). It spends the day in the water; at night it grazes on crops, and the Nile produces it.

22. [Note: “The *pagrus*.” Strabo, Book XVII: Φαγρόριος ὃν καὶ φάγρον καλοῦσι [“Phagrorius, which they also call phagrus”]. Glossary: Φάγρος, ἰχθὺς dentatus, “a toothed fish.”] The *pagrus*, which the Greeks call φάγρος [*phágros*], is so named because it has hard teeth, so that it feeds on oysters in the sea.

23. [Note: “The *dentix*, or *dentex*.” *Dentices*, fishes. Columella, VIII, chapter 18.] The *dentix* is named from the multitude and size of its teeth.

[Col. 0453B] [Note: “The hare, from resemblance of head.” Aelian, XVI, chapter 19, says that the hare of the open sea resembles the land hare in every respect except its hair. But Pliny, IX, chapter 48, says: “The hare in our sea is an amorphous mass, resembling the hare only in color.” Hence Chacon read “from resemblance of color.”] The hare is named from the resemblance of its head.

24. As has been said, the wolf was named for its greed—a fish skillful at escaping capture. [Note: “Finally, when surrounded by a net.” From Pliny.] For when surrounded by a net, it is said to plow the sand with its tail and, having buried itself, pass beneath the net.

25. [Note: “The mullet, because it is soft.” Or because Pliny says that a mullet becomes tender if it feeds on a hare, and becomes less agreeable and less valuable? I do not defend this, since these are Isidore’s words. On the etymology, see Pliny, IX, chapter 17, and below, Book XIX, final chapter.] The mullet is so called because it is soft and extremely tender. They say that eating it [Note: “Checks lust.” Pliny attributes this to the echeneis, Book XXXII, chapter 10.] checks lust, [Note: “But dulls the sharpness of the eyes.” So Pliny, in the same book, chapter 7.] while people on whom it has often fed [Note: “Smell of fish.” The Gothic compilation has *horrent*, “shudder”; if examined closely, this is attributed by Pliny to the hare, not the mullet, Book XXXII, chapter 1, though in a different form: “People,” he says, “upon whom it has been thrown smell of fish.”] smell of fish. [Note: “A mullet killed in wine … causes.” From the same book, chapter 10.] A mullet killed in wine causes those who drink it to loathe wine.

26. The mullet (*mugilis*) has its name because it is very agile. For when it senses the fishermen’s traps laid out, it immediately turns back and leaps over the net so that you would think you saw a fish flying.

27. The *melanurus* is so called because it has a black tail, black fins, and black lines on its body; μέλαν [*mélan*] is the Greek word for “black.”

28. The *glaucus* is named from its color, because it is white. [Note: “For the Greeks call white λευκόν.” We follow Vulcan and Antonius Augustinus, although we do not reject γλεύκὸν in place of γλαυκὸν, which occurs in the Gothic manuscripts. Virgil:

> … the poplar, and the willows gray-green with pale foliage.”] For the Greeks call white λευκὸν [*leukón*]. It rarely appears in summer, except when the weather is cloudy.

[Col. 0454A] 29. [Note: “The *thymallus*.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 2, in a very elegant passage.] The *thymallus* received its name from a flower. For *thymus* is the name of a flower; and although it is pleasing in appearance and agreeable in taste, it nevertheless gives off fragrance like a flower and breathes odors from its body.

30. [Note: “The *scarus*.” From the same source. Nor is it necessary to suppose that Isidore wrote *escarum* merely to make the etymology fit; it is much more difficult that Pliny says it was so unknown on the shores of Italy that it had no Latin name. Horace certainly indicates that it was sufficiently rare:

> The Lucrine shellfish would not please me,  
> nor the sea-bream, or scarus,  
> if winter, roaring from the eastern waves,  
> should drive them to this sea.

] The *scarus* is so called because it alone is said to chew the cud; other fish, in fact, do not ruminate. They say that it is clever. When enclosed in a fish-trap, it does not burst out headfirst or thrust its head into the hostile wickerwork, [Note: “But, turning backward, by blows of its tail.” Pliny, XXXII, chapter 2.] but loosens the entrance by repeated blows of its tail and thus retreats backward. If another scarus happens to see its struggle from outside, it seizes its tail in its teeth and tries to help the escaping fish.

31. The *sparus* took its name from a missile spear, because it has the same shape. Terrestrial things were discovered before marine things; [Note: “For *sparus* is a weapon.” From Servius on the verse “The rustic arms himself with the *sparus*,” *Aeneid* XI.] for the *sparus* is a rustic missile weapon, named from scattering.

32. [Note: “The southern fish.” We have often remarked that Isidore did not compare Servius’s commentaries with Virgil’s text and therefore sometimes departed from Servius’s meaning. Thus here, while he was catching marine fish, he unwittingly enclosed celestial bodies in the same net. Chacon therefore ordered these words deleted. Servius’s passage is on the verse “or fleeing the same constellation,” *Georgics* IV.] The southern fish is so called either because it receives the wave of water into its mouth, or because this fish appears at the time when the Pleiades begin to move toward the setting sun.

81 33. [Note: “*Hamia*.” This is the spelling required by Plutarch, in *Which Animals Are More Prudent?*; he derives it from ἅμα [*háma*], “together,” because these fish move in schools.] The *hamio*, a rock-dwelling fish, is marked on its right and left sides by continuous purple stripes and by other differently colored markings. It is called *hamio* because it can be caught only with a hook.

34. [Note: “The *echeneis*.” Pliny, XXXII, chapter 1.] The *echeneis*, a small fish half a foot long, took its name because it holds back a ship by clinging to it. Though winds may rush and storms rage, the ship nevertheless seems to stand in the sea as though rooted and does not move—not because the fish restrains it, but merely because it clings to it. [Col. 0454C] The Latins called it *remora*, because it compels ships to stop.

35. [Note: “The *uranoscopus*.” Some think it is the same as the *anthias* and *callionymus*. Pliny, XXXII, chapter 7.] The *uranoscopus* is named from the eye it has in its head, with which it always looks upward.

36. [Note: “The *milvago* … storms change.” Pliny, in the same place, says “storms change,” chapter 7. Trebius Niger is the authority. The old books, however, have *milago*, not *milvago*.] The *milvago* is so called because it flies up above the water; whenever it is seen fluttering outside the water, it indicates that storms are changing.

37. [Note: “The *squatus*.” Pliny, XXXII, chapter 11, and the final chapter: “The *rhina*, which we call *squatus*,” although in Book IX he calls the same fish *squatina*. Glossary: *squatus*, ῥίνα εἰδὸς ἰχθύος, “a kind of fish.” The English too now call it *skate*.] The *squatus* is so called because it has sharp scales; hence its skin is also used to polish wood.

38. [Note: “A city of Syria, now called Tyre.” From Servius on the verse “May Tyrian purple cover him,” *Georgics* II. Festus: “Sarra, the island of Tyre, which is now Epiros, that is, the mainland.”] The Syrian city now called Tyre was formerly called Sarra, after a certain fish that abounds there and that they call *sar* in their own language. From this, little fish resembling it came to be called *sardae* and *sardinae*. [Note: “*Sardas*, *sardinas*.” The ancient codices have *sarras*, perhaps not incorrectly; for one of two adjacent *r*s is often changed into *d*. Yet the name *sarda* is still retained in the vernacular.]

39. The *halec* is a little fish suitable for making fish sauce, and from this it was named.

40. [Note: “*Aphorus*.” Isidore’s etymology indicates that he wrote *aphorus*, but *aphros* is correct, from Aristotle, Book IV of the *History of Animals*, chapter 15. Athenaeus likewise says in Book VII: τὸν θαλάττιον γόνον, ὃν ἡμεῖς μὲν ἀφύην, ἀλλοὶ δὲ ἄφρύην ὀνομάζουσιν, οἱ δὲ ἄφρον, “the offspring of the sea, which we call *aphyē*, others *aphrȳē*, and others *aphron*.”] The *aphorus* is a little fish that cannot be caught with a hook because of its smallness.

82 41. The eel received its name from its resemblance to a snake; it originates in mud. Hence, when caught, it is so slippery that the harder one presses it, the more quickly it slips away. [Note: “They report, moreover.” From Pliny, IX, chapter 3.] They report that the eastern river Ganges produces eels thirty feet long. [Note: “An eel killed in wine.” From the same source, Book XXXII, chapter 10.] An eel killed in wine causes those who drink it to loathe wine.

42. [Note: “The sea dragon.” He seems to make this the same as the scorpion-fish. See Pliny, Book II, final chapter.] The sea dragon has spines on its gills pointing toward its tail. When it strikes, it pours out poison wherever it wounds; hence its name.

43. [Note: “The *muraena*, because it coils itself into circles.” Did he have in mind the golden *muraenulae* in Solomon’s Song, which earlier writers wanted to be derived from the fish *muraena*, just as he had previously said that the weapon *sparus* preceded the fish *sparus*? Moreover, μύραινα, or σύραινα—for it is pronounced both ways—is derived, as Eustathius thinks, from μύρω, “I flow.”] The Greeks call the moray μύραινα [*múraina*], because it coils itself into circles. [Note: “This fish is of the feminine sex.” From Pliny, XXXII, chapter 2.] They say that it is exclusively female and conceives from a serpent; for this reason fishermen call it out and catch it with a hiss, as though it were a serpent. It is difficult to kill with a blow from a stick, but a reed kills it immediately. It is certain that it has its life in its tail: when struck on the head it is scarcely killed, but when struck on the tail it dies at once.

[Col. 0455C] 44. Conger [lacuna]

The octopus, that is, the many-footed creature, has very many joints. When seeking a hook, it embraces it with its arms, not with a bite; nor does it release it until it has gnawed the bait all around.

45. The torpedo is so called because it makes the body numb if anyone touches it while it is alive. [Note: “Pliny relates this from the Indian Sea.” Book XXXII, chapter 1. But I think *Antico*, or *Antiaco*, should be read instead of *Indico*, for Pliny is speaking there of that sea. Unless one prefers to delete this note, following the opinion of Antonius Augustinus.] Pliny the Elder relates: “From the Indian Sea the torpedo, even at a distance and from afar, or if touched with a spear or rod, makes even very powerful limbs numb and fetters feet that are exceedingly swift for running.” For its power is so great that even the air from its body affects the limbs.

83 46. The cuttlefish is so called because, when enclosed by hedges, [Note: “Enclosed by barriers … conceives.” The words are Pliny’s, Book IX, chapter 51.] it is more easily caught. In mating it is an obscene creature, for it conceives through its mouth, like a viper. Its ink has such power that, when added to a lamp, some say that Ethiopians become visible once the former light has been removed. [Note: “Ethiopians become visible.” From Pliny, XXXIII, chapter 10.]

47. [Note: “The *lulligo* … flying out of the water.” Varro: *loligo*, because it leaps upward; with the letter changed, at first *voligo*.] They report that in the Ocean of Mauretania, not far from the river Lixus, such a multitude of squids (*lulligines*) flies out of the water that they can even sink ships.

48. [Note: “*Conchae* and *concleae*.” Elsewhere *cochleae*.] Shellfish and snails are called by these names because, when the moon wanes, they become hollow, that is, emptied. [Note: “Of all enclosed marine animals.” The words are Palladius’s, Book XIV, chapter 6.] For the bodies of all enclosed marine animals and shellfish swell with the waxing of the moon and are emptied with its waning. When the moon is waxing, it increases moisture; but when it declines, moisture decreases. So the natural philosophers say. *Conchae* is the original form of the name, while *cochleae* is a diminutive, as though *conchulae*.

49. There are many kinds of shellfish, [Note: “Among them are pearl-bearing shells.” Pliny, XXXII, final chapter.] including pearl-bearing shells, [Note: “Which are called *celoe* … and below, hence also *celoe*.” They are also read as *eceloe*, *occeloe*, *ocoele*, and *cocleae*. Antonius Augustinus preferred *ocelli* or *ocellati*, although the etymology from *coelum* does not fit. Varro in *Marcipor*, quoted by Nonius: “One begs her father for a pound of spotted pearls, another her husband for half a measure of pearls.” Suetonius, *Augustus*: “He plays with spotted nuts.” The etymology of *ocellati* comes from their resemblance to eyes. Athenaeus, Book LXXXIII, chapter 8, also compares pearls twice to the large eyes of fishes.] which are called *celoe*, [Note: “In whose flesh a precious stone is formed.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 11: “Thus nature fixed the most precious pearl in oysters and solidified it with seawater in such soft flesh.”] in whose flesh a precious stone is formed. Those who have written about the nature of animals report that at night they seek the shore and conceive a pearl from heavenly dew; hence they are called *celoe*.

50. [Note: “The *murex*.” From Servius on the verse “The shaken rocks,” *Aeneid* V.] The murex is a sea snail, named from its sharpness and roughness. By another name it is called *conchylium*, [Note: “*Conchyl*.” From Vitruvius, Book VII, chapter 13. The same is repeated in Book XIX, chapter 28.] because, when cut with iron, it emits tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made. It is therefore called *ostrum*, because this dye is extracted from the moisture of its shell.

51. Crabs are so called because they are shellfish possessing legs, [Note: “Hostile to oysters.” Plutarch, in the book already cited, and Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 8. Pliny, IX, chapter 30, attributes the same behavior to the octopus.] animals hostile to oysters; for they live on their flesh with remarkable ingenuity. Since the oyster’s strong shell cannot be opened, the crab watches for the moment when the oyster opens the valves of its shell. Then the crab secretly inserts a pebble, preventing the oyster from closing, and eats away its flesh. Some report that when ten crabs are tied together with a bundle of basil, all the scorpion-fish in the vicinity gather at that spot. There are two kinds of crabs: river crabs and sea crabs.

52. The oyster is named from its shell, by which the softness of its inner flesh is protected. For the Greeks call a shell ὄστρακα [*óstraka*]. [Note: “*Ostrea* is neuter.” See Servius on the verse “The oyster-bearing shores of Abydos are tested,” *Georgics* I, and Nonius. Yet from the passages they cite, one might rather conclude that the Latins used both genders indiscriminately.] *Ostrea* is neuter, while its flesh is spoken of in the feminine gender.

53. As we said earlier, *musculi* are shellfish, from whose milk oysters conceive, [Note: “From whose milk oysters conceive.” All Gothic manuscripts read this. Yet if Isidore wished to be consistent with himself, or to follow Servius, he ought to have said otherwise. Pliny, IX, chapter 51: “Recently it has been discovered that in oyster-beds a generative fluid flows from them like milk.”] and they are called *musculi*, as though *masculi*, “males.”

54. The *pelorides* are named after Cape Pelorus in Sicily, where they are abundant. (Hence Virgil says:)

> Behold, the North Wind from the narrow seat of Pelorus.

55. [Note: “Claws.” From Pliny.] The *ungues* are named from their resemblance to human fingernails.

56. [Note: “The turtle … [lacuna]. There are four kinds.” Also from Pliny.] The turtle is so called because it is covered with a shell as with a roof, in the manner of a vaulted chamber. There are four kinds: land turtles, sea turtles, mud turtles—that is, those living in mud and marshes—and, fourth, river turtles, which live in fresh water. Some report, incredibly, that ships carrying the right foot of a turtle move more slowly.

57. [Note: “The sea urchin.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* VI, chapter 4: “This terrestrial echinus, which the common people call a hedgehog.” Glossary: *ericius*, ἐχῖνος, *erinacius*.] The echinus took its name from the terrestrial echinus, which the common people call a hedgehog. Its double shell is covered with spines, like chestnuts when they are still enclosed and fall from trees. Its flesh is soft and resembles vermilion. It is also called in three ways: *testudo*, *peloris*, and *conclea*; for both the thing we eat and the place where the flesh is contained are called *peloris*.

58. Frogs are named from their chattering, because they croak around marshes near the genitals, [Note: “Around the genitals.” From Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 10.] and produce the sounds of their voices in disruptive cries. [Note: “And make their voices heard in unwelcome sounds.” From Origen, Homily 4 on Exodus.] Some of them are called water frogs, some marsh frogs, [Note: “Some are *rubetae*.” Pliny, XXXII, chapter 5.] and some *rubetae*, because they live in thorn bushes and are larger than all the others. [Note: “Others are *calamitae*.” The same author, chapter 10.] Others are called *calamitae*, because they live among reeds and shrubs; they are the smallest of all and the greenest, [Note: “Mute and voiceless.” Pliny, XXXII, chapter 6.] being mute and without a voice.

59. [Note: “*Agredulae*.” From the Gothic manuscripts; others have *agridulae*.] *Agredulae* are small frogs that remain on dry ground or in fields, from which they received their name. Some deny that dogs bark when they have been given a live frog in a morsel of food.

60. [Note: “*Sfungia*, from *fingere*.” Some writers indicate that they wrote *sphingia* for *spongia*. Charisius says: “*Spongia* must be said without *h*, for in Greek it is pronounced without aspiration, σπόγγος.” The Greeks derive it either from ἀπὸ τοῦ σπᾷν τὰ ὑγρὰ, “from drawing out liquids,” or from ἀπὸ τοῦ σφίγγειν κατὰ τὰς ἐκθλίψεις, “from pressing them out”—that is, either from absorbing or expressing moisture. Suetonius’s well-known remark in *Vespasian* says that he used his procurators as sponges, because he made the dry wet and squeezed out those who were wet. Servius enabled Isidore to derive it from *effingere*, interpreting *fingere* as “to wipe,” citing a passage of Cicero from Sextius. What is said about the kinds of sponges seems to have been taken from Aristotle, *History of Animals* V, chapter 16, and Pliny, IX, chapter 45.] The sponge (*sfungia*) is named from *fingere*, that is, “to polish and wipe away.” Afranius says:

> I come to you to wipe your neck with linen,

that is, to wipe it clean. Cicero says: “The blood was wiped away with sponges,” that is, it was removed. [Note: “It is shown to be an animal.” Pliny, XXXI, final chapter.] That it is an animal is shown by the blood adhering to rocks. Hence, when it is cut off, it releases blood.

61 For some things living in water are alive and move about, such as fish, [Note: “Others stand fixed.” Aristotle, *History of Animals* IV, chapter 6.] while others stand fixed, such as oysters, sea urchins, and sponges. Of these, some are called males because they have a slender tube and are denser; others females, because they have larger and continuous tubes; and others are harder, which the Greeks call τράγους [*trágous*], and which we may call “goat-like” on account of their roughness.

62. [Note: “Their softest kind is called *pennicilli*.” These are Pliny’s words. But in the very old Pliny manuscript of the Church of Toledo, not *pennicelli* but *pennicillis* is read: “Their softest kind, with little brushes, relieves swellings of the eyes.” Perhaps Pliny did not call any kind of sponge *pennicellus*; nevertheless Festus writes: “*Penniculi* are long sponges, named from their resemblance to tails.”] Their softest kind is called *pennicilli*, because they are suitable for eye swellings and useful for wiping away inflammation of the eyes. White sponges are made by treatment; for during the summer they are spread out in the sun and, [Col. 0458C] like Punic wax, absorb whiteness.

63. [Note: “The names of all animals living in water: 144.” The same number occurs in the Pliny manuscript of the Church of Toledo; printed editions have 176. Jerome, in his commentary on Ezekiel XLVII, citing Oppian and others who wrote *Halieutica*, reports 153 kinds of fish and wants all of them to have been caught by the apostles in John XXI.] Pliny says that there are 144 names of all animals living in water, divided among kinds of sea beasts, snakes common to land and water, crabs, shellfish, lobsters, *pelorides*, octopuses, soles, lizards, cuttlefish, and similar creatures. Many of these, through a certain natural intelligence, recognize the order of their seasons, while others wander about in their own places without changing.

64. Among female fish, some conceive through intercourse with a male and give birth to young; others lay eggs without [Note: “Received without the intercourse of a male.” Others read “conceived without reception.”] having received the contribution of a male, [Note: “Which he then follows.” Aristotle, *History of Animals* VI, chapter 13, on fish eggs, in Gaza’s translation: “Nor are all these eggs fertile, but only those upon which the male has sprinkled his generative seed after they have been laid. For during spawning the male follows and sprinkles the eggs with seed, and from those touched by it little fish are born.”] and the male, following them, covers them with a discharge of his own seed. Those touched by this substance become fertile; those not covered by it remain sterile or rot.

## CHAPTER VII. On Birds

1. There is one name, but different kinds, among birds. [Note: “One name for birds … parrot.” All this is from Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 14, apart from the examples that Chacon thought Isidore had also omitted.] For just as they differ in appearance, so too they differ in nature. Some are simple, such as doves; others crafty, such as the partridge; some submit themselves to the hand, such as the hawk; others are fearful, [Note: “Such as the Garamantes.” Concerning them, see Nicephorus, Book IX.] such as the Garamantes; some delight in human society, such as the swallow; others love a secluded life in deserts, such as the turtle dove. Some feed only on seed when they find it, such as the goose; others eat flesh and devote themselves to plunder, such as the kite. [Note: “Others are *enchoriae*.” The copyists derived this from *encuriae* or *encoriae*, “native,” not entirely implausibly. Basil, from whom Ambrose took the passage, has ἐγχείρια.] Others are *enchoriae*, which always remain in their native places, such as the ostrich; others are visitors, which return at their appointed seasons, such as storks and swallows; others are gregarious, that is, flying in flocks, such as starlings and quails; others are solitary, that is, alone because of the ambushes involved in hunting, such as the eagle, the hawk, and anything else of this kind; some make a din with their voices, such as the swallow; others produce very sweet songs, such as the swan and the blackbird; and others imitate human words and voices, such as the parrot and the magpie.

88 2. But there are also countless other differences, both in kind and in habits. [Col. 0459C] For no one can discover how many kinds of birds there are. [Note: “For no one has penetrated all of India.” From Pliny, XXXIII, chapter 11.] No one has been able to penetrate all the deserts of India, Ethiopia, or Scythia and learn their kinds or distinctions.

3. Birds (*aves*) are so called because they do not have fixed paths, but move through every trackless place.

Winged creatures (*alites*) are so called because they direct themselves high with their wings and climb to lofty places by rowing with their wings.

4. Flying creatures (*volucres*) are named from flying; [Note: “For from where we say ‘to fly,’ we also say ‘to walk.’” From Servius on the verse “Only those feeding,” *Aeneid* VI.] for from the same root as “to fly” we also derive “to walk.” The sole (*vola*) is the middle part of the foot or hand; in birds, the *vola* is the middle part of the wings, by whose movement the feathers are stirred. Hence they are called *volucres*.

5. The offspring of all birds are called chicks; but the young of four-footed animals are also called chicks, and a small human being is called a chick. [Note: “And a small person, a chick.” As we showed above from Festus.] Newborn young are therefore called chicks because they are soiled; hence a black garment is also called *pulla*.

6. Wings are the parts in which feathers are fixed in orderly rows and provide the means of flying. They are called wings because birds nourish and warm their young by enfolding them in them.

7. The feather (*penna*) is named from *pendere*, “to hang,” that is, from flying, and hence also *pendere*, “to hang.” For birds move with the help of their feathers when they commit themselves to the air.

8. *Pluma* is as though *piluma*, “hair-like”; for just as quadrupeds have hair on their bodies, so birds have feathers.

9. It is clear that many names of birds are composed from the sound of their voices: the crane, crow, swan, peacock, kite, owl, cuckoo, jackdaw, and so forth. For the variety of their voices taught people what they should be called.

10. The eagle (*aquila*) is named from the sharpness of its eyes. [Note: “For it is said to have such great vision.” From Jerome on Obadiah I.] For it is said to have such powerful sight that, while it is carried motionless above the sea on its wings and is beyond human vision, from so great a height it can see little fish swimming below; then, descending like a thunderbolt, it drags its captured prey to the shore with its wings.

11. [Note: “For it also does not turn away from the rays.” From Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 18, and his commentary on Psalm CXVIII.] It is also said not to turn its gaze away from the sun’s ray. Therefore it holds its young suspended in its talons before the sun’s rays, and those whose gaze it sees remaining fixed it preserves as worthy of their kind; but those who turn their gaze away it casts aside as degenerate.

12. The vulture is thought to be named from its slow flight. Because of the size of its body, it does not have a swift flight. [Note: “Some of these, they say.” Ambrose, chapter 20.] They say that some of them do not mate, but conceive and give birth without intercourse, and that their offspring live for almost a hundred years. [Note: “Vultures, moreover.” The same author, in his sermon on the death of Theodosius.] Vultures, like eagles, can sense corpses even beyond the sea; flying higher, they see from above many things hidden by the obscurity of mountains.

13. [Note: “*Bradypus* among the Greeks.” It was easy for this word to slip into *gradipes*, which is read in most manuscripts. Pliny, X, chapter 22: “Next are those which Spain calls *avutardae* and Greece *otides*.”] Among the Greeks it is called *bradypus*, but among us it is the slow bird, because, held back by its heavy flight, it cannot rise with the speed of its feathers as other flying creatures do.

14. Cranes took their name from their characteristic voice, for they murmur with such a sound. When they travel, one follows another in a written-letter formation. [Note: “In alphabetical order.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “They enclosed the heavens in a company.” The remainder is from Solinus’s manuscript concerning Thrace.] Lucan writes of them:

> And the letter, scattered among the feathers, is lost in confusion.

They seek lofty places so that they may more easily see what lands they should seek.

15. It disciplines them by a voice that gathers the flock. But when it grows hoarse, another takes its place; at night they divide the watches and take turns keeping guard, holding pebbles in their suspended claws, so that when these fall they expose their sleep; a cry indicates what must be guarded against. Their age is revealed by their color, for they grow black in old age.

16. Storks (*ciconiae*) are so called from the sound with which they make their rattling, as though *cicaniae*—a sound that, as is established, comes rather from the mouth than from the voice, because they produce it by shaking their beak. These are heralds of spring, companions of fellowship, enemies of snakes; they fly across the seas and proceed in assembled formation toward Asia. Crows go before them as guides, and the storks themselves follow as though an army.

17. They show extraordinary devotion toward their offspring. For they tend their nests so assiduously that, through constant brooding, they lose their feathers. And for as long as they have devoted themselves to raising their young, they themselves are likewise nourished by their offspring in turn.

18. The *olor* is a bird that the Greeks call κύκνος (*kyknos*, “swan”). [Note: “*Olor* is so called.” The Latin word *olor* is immediately suggested, but there is nothing to prevent deriving it from the Greek, unless you prefer, with Chacon, to regard this as unrelated.] *Olor* is so called because it is wholly white in its feathers; for no one remembers a black swan. In Greek, ὅλον (*holon*) means “whole.”

[Note: “*Cygnus*.” A somewhat more forced etymology.] *Cygnus* (“swan”), however, is named from singing, because it pours forth the sweetness of song in measured tones. They say that it sings sweetly because it has a long, curved neck, and its voice, struggling through a long and winding passage, necessarily produces various melodies.

19. They say that in the regions of the Hyperboreans, when harpists begin to play, very many swans fly there and sing together with remarkable harmony. [Note: “*Olor* in Latin.” From Servius, on “and the Strymonian crane,” *Aeneid* XI.] *Olor* is a Latin name; in Greek they are called κύκνοι (*kyknoi*, “swans”). [Note: “Sailors regard it as a favorable omen.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “You will see six joyful...”] Sailors say that it gives them a favorable omen, as Aemilius says:

[Note: “As Aemilius says.” Aemilius Macer, in the *Ornithogonia*; Chacon considered this the correct reading in Nonius under *Prosecta*, rather than “Licinius.” For although Pliny mentions both authors, when discussing birds he cites Aemilius, who is also cited by Nonius under *Luculentus*. So too Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “the idle herd of drones.”]

> The swan, in auspices, is always the happiest bird.

Sailors desire this bird, because it does not plunge itself into the waves.

[Col. 0461C] 20. [Note: “*Struthio*.” From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXI, on Job XXXIX.] *Struthio* is called by a Greek name because the animal appears to have feathers in the likeness of a bird; nevertheless, it does not rise high from the ground. It neglects to brood its eggs; when they have merely been laid out, they are brought to life by the warmth of the dust.

21. The heron (*ardea*) is so called as though from *ardua*, “high,” because of its lofty flights. Lucan writes: [Note: “And the heron that dared to fly.” From Lucan; the passage itself is from Servius, *Georgics* I and *Aeneid* VII.]

> And the heron that dared to fly.

[Note: “It fears.” From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 13.] For it fears rainstorms and flies above the clouds so that it may not experience the storms within the clouds; but when it has flown higher, it signifies that a storm is coming. Many call it the *tantalus*. [Note: “They call it the *tantalus*.” It should be considered whether *taurus* is preferable; Aristotle calls the stellar heron by this name because it imitates the bellowing of an ox with its voice, as Pliny also mentions, book X, chapter 42.]

22. [Note: “The bird called the phoenix.” Pliny, book XIII, chapter 4: from *phoenix*, that is, “palm.”] The phoenix, a bird of Arabia, is so called either because it has a Phoenician color or because it is singular and unique throughout the whole world. For the Arabs call a singular and unique thing a *phoenix*. Living for five hundred years or more, when it sees that it has grown old, it gathers twigs of aromatic plants and builds itself a funeral pyre. Then, turning toward the sun’s rays, it kindles its voluntary fire by beating its wings, and thus rises again from its own ashes.

23. [Note: “*Cinnamulgus*.” Pliny X, chapter 33, and Solinus, chapter 46. “It is the same as *cinnamomum*. But the Greeks write *cinnamomum* with a single *n*, and the ancient grammarian Nestor prescribes that it be written so in Latin.”] The *cinnamolgus* is also a bird of Arabia. It is so called because, in lofty groves, it builds its nests from cinnamon branches. Since people cannot climb there because of the height and fragility of the branches, they attack the nests with lead-weighted arrows and so bring down the cinnamon, selling it at a higher price because merchants value that cinnamon more than other kinds.

24. [Note: “The parrot.” From Solinus, chapter 55.] The parrot is produced on the shores of India. It is green in color, has a crimson collar, a large tongue broader than those of other birds, and consequently articulates words so distinctly that, if you did not see it, you would think a human being was speaking. By nature it greets people by saying *ave* (“hail”) or χαῖρε (*chaire*, “rejoice”); it learns other names by instruction. Hence the following lines:

> From you I shall learn the names of others, parrot;
>
> This I learned for myself to say: “Hail, Caesar.”

25. [Note: “*Halcyon* ... as though an oceanic bird.” Gothic manuscripts: *cyanea*.] The halcyon is called a bird of the sea, as though a blue-colored bird, because in winter it builds its nest and raises its young on the waters of the Ocean. While it keeps watch, the sea, it is said, grows calm across the extended waters, with winds silent, in an uninterrupted tranquility lasting seven days; and nature herself offers her service for raising its offspring.

26. [Note: “The pelican ... of the river.” Augustine’s words on Psalm 101.] The pelican is an Egyptian bird living in the solitude of the Nile River, from which it also took its name. [Note: “For Canopus is called Egypt.” The editor prefers “Pellaean Canopus,” since that better suits the etymology. Virgil, *Georgics* IV: “For where the fortunate race of Pellaean Canopus...” Yet, in book XIX, chapter 5: “For Canopian Egypt...”] For Canopus is called Egypt. It is said—if the story is true—that it kills its young and mourns them for three days; then it wounds itself and brings its children back to life by sprinkling them with its own blood.

27. [Note: “The Stymphalian birds, from the Stymphalian islands.” The Gothic manuscript reads: “The Stromphalian birds, from the Strophades islands.” Both readings are defective. For, as I think, no islands called the Stymphalides are known, nor are there any birds called *stromphalidae*. There is, however, the Stymphalian marsh in Arcadia, and likewise the Strophades islands in Epirus; birds are associated with both places. Hercules is said to have pierced the former with arrows, while Zethus and Calais, sons of Boreas, drove away the latter. Of the former Lucretius writes, book V:

> ... and feared for their hooked claws,
>
> the birds of Arcadia inhabiting Stymphalus.

Of the latter Virgil writes, *Aeneid* III:

> ... the Strophades, so called by their Greek name,
>
> islands in the great Ionian Sea, where dread Celaeno
>
> and the Harpies ...

] The Stymphalian birds are so called from the Stymphalian islands, where they abound in great numbers. Hercules used arrows against them; for they are sea birds living on islands.

28. [Note: “The Diomedean birds.” This passage is compiled from several authors: Servius, on “Now also by their terrible appearance,” *Aeneid* XI; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 16; Solinus, chapter 9; Pliny; and Ovid.] The Diomedean birds are named after the companions of Diomedes, whom the myths say were changed into these same birds. They resemble coots in form, swans in size, and are white in color, with hard and large beaks. They fly around among the cliffs and rocks along the shores near Apulia, on the island of Diomedes, and distinguish between their own people and strangers.

29. For if a Greek approaches, they come near and flatter him; if a foreigner approaches, they attack and wound him with bites, lamenting in voices like tears, as though grieving either their own transformation or the death of their king. For Diomedes was killed by the Illyrians. These birds are called Diomedean birds; the Greeks call them ἡρωδίους (*herodious*, “herons”).

30. [Note: “The Memnonides.” Pliny X, chapter 26; Solinus, chapter 43; Albert the Great, *On Animals* XXIII. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII:

> Three times they circle the pyre, and a harmonious wail
>
> three times rises into the air.]

The Memnonides are Egyptian birds, named from the place where Memnon died. They are said to fly in flocks from Egypt to Ilium, near the tomb of Memnon; therefore the people of Ilium call them Memnonian birds. Every fifth year they come to Ilium, and after flying around it for two days, on the third day they enter battle and tear one another apart in turn with claws and beaks.

31. [Note: “The Hercynian birds.” From Solinus XXXII.] The Hercynian birds are named from the Hercynian Forest of Germany, where they are born. Their feathers shine so brightly through the darkness that, even when night is covered with dense shadows, those feathers, cast before travelers as a guide, glimmer and reveal the course of the road by the indication of their shining plumage. [Note: “Although night is covered with dense darkness.” Virgil, *Georgics* I: “And shadows are always thickened by enveloping night.”]

32. [Note: “The *onocrotalus* ... of which there are two kinds.” From Jerome, on Zephaniah II. This is an extremely voracious bird; hence Martial: “The shameful throat of the Ravenna *onocrotalus*.” See Nebrissensis, *On the Book of Sacred Places*.] The Greeks call the *onocrotalus* a bird with a long beak. There are two kinds: one aquatic, the other belonging to the wilderness.

33. [Note: “The ibis, a bird of the Nile.” Pliny VIII, chapter 27; Aelian II, chapter 35.] The ibis is a bird of the Nile River that cleanses itself by pouring water into its anus with its beak. [Note: “It eats the eggs of snakes.” From Solinus, chapter 45.] It feeds on the eggs of snakes, carrying from them to its nests food it especially enjoys.

34. [Note: “*Meropes* ... them and the *gauli*. This is what the Italians call them; we call them *jaruci*.”] The *meropes*, also called *gauli*, are said to conceal and nourish their parents.

The *coredulus* is a flying creature, as though “heart-eating.”

35. The *monedula* is so called as though *monetula* (“little coin”), because when it finds gold it carries it away and hides it. Cicero, *Against Valerius Flaccus*: “No more gold should be entrusted to you than to jackdaws.” [Note: “Than should be entrusted to jackdaws.” *Committebant* is read in Cicero. See Pliny, book X, chapter 29.]

36. [Note: “The bat.” From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 24.] The bat (*vespertilio*) received its name from the time of day, because, fleeing the light, it flies about at evening twilight, driven by rapid movement and suspended by the very thin membranes of its arms. [Note: “An animal resembling mice.” Jerome’s words, on Isaiah II.] It is an animal resembling mice, making itself heard not so much by its voice as by a screech; in form it is both winged and four-footed, something not ordinarily found among other birds.

37. [Note: “The nightingale.” From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 11. Varro nevertheless preferred a different origin: “*Lusciola*, or *luscinia*,” he says, “because it is thought to sing mournfully, and to have been made a bird from the Athenian Procne in mourning.”] The nightingale (*luscinia*) took its name from the fact that by its song it usually announces the rising of the approaching day, as though *lucinia*. It is also called *acredula*, of which Cicero writes in the *Prognostics*:

[Note: “And in the morning ...”]

> And the *acredula* applies itself to morning songs;
>
> it applies itself to songs and pours forth continual laments from its mouth.

*On Divination*, from the same *Prognostics*, by Quintus, his brother.

38. [Note: “The owl.” From Servius, *Eclogues* 8.] The owl (*ulula*) is named ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀλολύζειν (*apo tou ololuzein*), that is, from wailing and mourning. [Note: “For when it cries out.” Servius says this of the horned owl, not of the *ulula*. *Aeneid* IV.] For when it cries out, it either imitates weeping or resembles a groan. Hence among augurs, if it laments, it is said to show sadness; if it is silent, prosperity.

39. The horned owl (*bubo*) has a name formed from the sound of its voice. It is a bird of ill omen, heavily burdened with feathers and always weighed down by sluggish idleness. It moves about among tombs by day and night and continually dwells in caves. Of it Ovid writes:

> And the foul bird becomes a herald of coming grief,
>
> the sluggish horned owl, a dreadful omen to mortals.

Finally, among augurs it is said to portend evil; for when it has been seen in a city, they say that solitude is signified.

40. The *noctua* is so called because it flies about at night and cannot see during the day. [Note: “For when the brightness has arisen.” Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 24.] For when the sun’s brightness has arisen, its sight is dulled. [Note: “But the island of Crete.” From Solinus, chapter 16.] The island of Crete does not have this bird, and if one comes from elsewhere, it immediately dies. [Note: “The *noctua* is not the *bubo*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XII.] The *noctua* is not the *bubo*, for the *bubo* is larger.

41. [Note: “The *nycticorax* is itself the *noctua*.” Jerome, letter 135, to Sunnia.] The *nycticorax* is itself the *noctua*, because it loves the night. [Note: “For it is a light-fleeing bird.” From Servius, *Georgics* I, on “In vain he prolongs the late night.”] For it is a bird that flees the light. [Note: “And cannot bear to see the sun.” Jerome said this of the bat, on Isaiah II.] It cannot bear to see the sun.

42. [Note: “The *strix*. See Festus. But since he reports that it is commonly called *amma*, some think that our people therefore call nurses *ammae*. Others, however, think that the word is not Latin but was brought from Germany by the Goths. Yet whoever says it is Hebrew, I think, will be less mistaken.] The *strix* is a nocturnal bird whose name comes from the sound of its voice: when it cries out, it screeches. Lucan writes:

> What the trembling horned owl, what the nocturnal *strix* lament.

This bird is commonly called *amma*, from *amare* (“to love”) children; hence it is also said to offer milk to newborns.

43. [Note: “The raven ... this bird is said to...” From Gregory, *Moralia* XXX, chapter 9, elsewhere chapter 15.] The raven, or *corax*, takes its name from the sound of its throat, because it croaks (*coracinet*). This bird is said not to provide its fledglings with food in full until, from the blackness of their feathers, it recognizes in them a likeness to its own color. But once it sees them dark with feathers, recognizing them completely, it feeds them more abundantly. It is the first to attack the eye in corpses. [Note: “It attacks the eye.” Catullus, *On Cominius*:

> I do not doubt that first the tongue, hostile to the good,
>
> cut out, was given to the greedy vulture;
>
> the raven devours the dug-out eyes with its black throat,
>
> the dogs, the intestines; the wolves, the remaining limbs.]

44. The crow (*cornix*) is a long-lived bird and is called among the Latins by a Greek name. Augurs claim that it increases human anxieties by its signs [Note: “To increase by signs.” Only Vulcanius has this reading; the others read *agere* (“to act” or “do”).], shows the paths of ambushes, and foretells the future. It is a great impiety to believe such things, as though God entrusted his counsels to crows. Among many other auspices, they also attribute to it the power of predicting rain by its cries. Hence the line:

> Then the wicked crow calls for rain in a full voice.

45. The jackdaw (*graculus*) is named from its chattering, not, as someone wished, because it flies in flocks, since it is clear that its name comes from its voice. For it is an extremely talkative kind of bird and troublesome in its cries.

46. [Note: “*Picae*, as though *poetricae*. Perhaps he had Persius in mind ... ‘poet ravens and poet magpies’ ... or the story of the Pierides changed into magpies.”] Magpies (*picae*) are so called as though *poetricae* (“poetic”), because they reproduce words with distinctions of sound like a human being. Hanging from the branches of trees, they make an incessant and irritating noise. Although they cannot unfold their tongues in speech, they nevertheless imitate the sound of the human voice. Of this someone aptly said:

[Note: “The talkative magpie.” A poem of Martial.]

> Talkative magpie, in a distinct voice I greet you as my master.
>
> If you do not see me, you will deny that I am a bird.

47. The woodpecker (*picus*) took its name from Picus, son of Saturn, because Picus used it in auspices. They say that this bird possesses something divine, as is shown by the fact that, in whatever tree it nests [Note: “In whatever tree it nests.” From Pliny X, chapter 18.], a nail or anything else fixed into it cannot remain there long: as soon as the bird has settled upon it, the object falls out. [Note: “This is the *picus Martius*.” From Servius, on “the golden wand struck,” *Aeneid* VII.] This is the *picus Martius*, for the magpie is a different bird.

48. [Note: “The peacock ... so that it scarcely senses decay.” From Augustine, *City of God* XXI, chapter 4.] The peacock (*pavo*) takes its name from the sound of its voice. Its flesh is so hard that it scarcely undergoes decay and is not easily cooked. [Note: “Of it someone said.” Martial.] Someone wrote of it as follows:

> You marvel whenever it spreads its jeweled wings,
>
> and yet, hard-hearted man, you can hand it over to a savage cook.

49. The pheasant (*phasianus*) is named from Phasis, [Note: “From the island of Phasis in Greece.” More likely from the river, or the city.] from which it was first brought. An old distich bears witness to this:

> I was first transported in an Argive keel.
>
> Before that, nothing was known to me except Phasis.

50. The rooster (*gallus*) is so called from castration. For among all birds, only this one has its testicles removed. The ancients called castrated males *galli*. Just as *leaena* (“lioness”) comes from *leo* (“lion”), and *dracaena* (“female dragon”) from *draco* (“dragon”), so *gallina* (“hen”) comes from *gallus* (“rooster”). Some say that if its parts are mixed with molten gold, they consume it. [Note: “They are consumed”—namely, the gold. Pliny XXIX, chapter 4: “If the parts of a hen are mixed with molten gold, they consume it within themselves; thus this is poison to gold.”]

51. The duck (*anas*) received an appropriate name from its constant swimming. Among this kind, some are called *germanae* (“native” or “true”), because they nourish their young more than the others.

52. The goose (*anser*) received the name *anas* by derivation, either from resemblance or because it too frequently swims. [Note: “This one bears witness to the night watches.” From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 13.] It bears witness to the night watches by its continual honking. [Note: “No animal.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII.] No animal detects the scent of a human being as keenly as a goose; hence by its honking the ascent of the Gauls to the Capitol was detected.

53. [Note: “The *fulica* is so called because its flesh tastes like hare. I believe it tastes of soot or dampness; but what is the point of that? For *lagos* means ‘hare.’ It is surprising if this is not a gloss.”] The *fulica* is so called because its flesh tastes like hare. For *lagos* means “hare,” and therefore among the Greeks it is called *lagois*. [Note: “For it is a bird that inhabits ponds.” From Augustine, on Psalm 103.] It is a bird that inhabits ponds, building its nest in the middle of the water or on rocks surrounded by water, and it always delights in the depths of the sea. When it senses a storm approaching, it flees and plays in the shallows. [Note: “And in the depths of the sea.” From Ambrose, chapter 13.]

54. [Note: “The *mergus*, from its constant plunging.” This is how it appears in the Gothic manuscript and in Ambrose. The remainder is from Virgil, *Georgics* I.] The *mergus* received this name from its constant plunging. Often, with its head lowered into the depths, it gathers signs of the winds beneath the waves; foreseeing a storm at sea, it heads toward the shore with a cry. For it is established that the storm at sea is already extremely severe when the *mergus* has fled to the shores for refuge.

55. The hawk (*accipiter*) is a bird more heavily armed in spirit than in claws, carrying greater strength in a smaller body. It took its name from *accipere*, “to seize,” that is, from capturing. For it is a bird eager to snatch other birds; therefore it is called *accipiter*, that is, “seizer” or “raptor.” Hence the Apostle Paul says: “For you tolerate it if someone seizes you.” [Note: “If someone seizes you.” From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 11, elsewhere chapter 16.] In order to say “if someone robs you,” he said “if someone seizes you.”

56. [Note: “The hawk, however, is said...” From Ambrose, chapter 8.] Hawks are said to be cruel toward their young. For when they see that the young are able to attempt flight, they provide them with no food; instead, they beat them with their wings, hurl them from the nest, and force them from an early age to seek prey, lest, when grown, they become sluggish.

57. [Note: “*Capys*.” Servius, on “and from this comes the name *Capys*.” He says: “Capua was founded by the Etruscans after they saw an omen involving a falcon, which in the Etruscan language is called *capys*.” Also Festus, under *Capua*.] *Capys* in the Italian language is derived from *capere*, “to seize.” Our people call this bird the falcon because it has curved talons.

58. The kite (*milvus*) is weak in strength and flight, as though a soft bird, from which it also receives its name; nevertheless, it is extremely rapacious and always lies in wait for domestic birds. [Note: “Extremely rapacious, etc.” Jerome’s words, on Zechariah V.]

59. The bird commonly called the bone-breaker (*ossifragus*) is so named because it drops bones from above and breaks them. Hence it received its name from breaking bones.

60. [Note: “The turtledove, a chaste bird.” Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I: “The most chaste turtledove.” Origen, *Homily* 2 on the Song of Songs, translated by Jerome: “The turtledove always dwells on mountain ridges and the tops of trees.”] The turtledove (*turtur*) is named from its voice. It is a chaste bird, always dwelling on mountain peaks and in deserted wildernesses. It flees human roofs and society and lives in the woods. It is also said to live through winter, stripped of feathers, in hollow tree trunks. The dove, by contrast, loves human dwellings and is always a gentle inhabitant of houses.

61. Doves (*columbae*) are so called because the colors of their necks change with each turn. They are tame birds, living among crowds of human beings and without gall. [Note: “And without gall.” They have very little gall, as we said above. See Aristotle, *History of Animals* II, chapter 15.] The ancients called them *veneriae* (“love birds”), because they frequently build nests and conceive love through kissing.

62. The *palumbes* is so called because they are stuffed with food, [Note: “Which the common people call *titi*.” Servius, *Eclogue* 1: “Doves, which the common people call *tetae*.”] and is called a chaste bird by its habits, because it is a companion of chastity. For it is said that, once its bodily companion has been lost, it goes about alone and seeks no further carnal union.

63. [Note: “The partridge derives its name from its voice. For πέρδεσθαι (*perdesthai*) is to commit the offense— as Plautus says—of making a noise by farting, in an honorable manner. Statius: ‘And the partridge that repeats joined words.’ Jerome, however—rhetorically, I believe, in order to serve his argument—said that the partridge was named from *perdere*, ‘to destroy.’ Letter 48.”] The partridge (*perdix*) derives its name from its voice. It is a deceitful and unclean bird. For the male mounts the male, and uncontrolled lust forgets its sex. [Note: “So deceitful, indeed.” From Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* VI, chapter 3, and Jerome, on Jeremiah XVII and Letter 48.] It is so deceitful that it steals another bird’s eggs and broods them, but the deceit bears no fruit. For when the chicks hear the voice of their own mother, by a kind of natural instinct they leave the bird that brooded them and return to the one that gave them birth.

64. Quails (*coturnices*) are so called from the sound of their voice. The Greeks call them ὄρτυγες (*ortyges*), because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They have fixed times for arriving; for, once summer has passed, they cross the seas.

65. [Note: “*Ortygometra*.” From Solinus.] The *ortygometra* is the bird that leads the flock. When a hawk sees it approaching the ground, it seizes it; for this reason the whole flock is concerned to urge on a leader of foreign stock, by whose means they may avoid the first dangers. Their most favored food is the seed of poisonous plants, which is why the ancients forbade people to eat them. For this is the only animal, like the human being, that suffers the falling sickness.

66. [Note: “The hoopoe.” From Jerome, on Zechariah XXV, through “dwelling.”] The Greeks call the hoopoe *upupa*, because it dwells among human excrement and feeds on stinking dung. It is an extremely filthy bird, helmeted with projecting crests, always dwelling among tombs and human excrement. Whoever anoints himself with its blood, when going to sleep, will see demons strangling him.

67. [Note: “*Tucos*, which the Spaniards call *cuculi*. In all books I have read the order reversed, with Chacon: ‘*Cuculi*, which the Spaniards call *cuci*.”] The *tucos*, which the Spaniards call *cuculi*, are plainly named from their own cry. They have a season for arriving, carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and weak flights, so that they do not grow exhausted and fail while traversing long stretches of air. Cicadas are born from their saliva. It eats the eggs found in a sparrow’s nest and lays its own eggs there; the sparrow receives them, broods them, and raises them.

68. Sparrows are small flying creatures, named from their smallness; hence they are called little and small.

69. [Note: “The blackbird ... as though ‘flying alone.’” Varro and Festus say this, but Quintilian rejects it, book I, chapter 5.] In ancient times the blackbird (*merula*) was called *medula*, because it produces melodies. Others say it was called *merula* because it flies alone, as though *mera volans* (“flying alone”). [Note: “Although this bird is black everywhere.” From Solinus.] Although it is black in every region, in Achaea it is white.

70. The swallow (*hirundo*) is so called because it does not take food while sitting, but catches and eats its food in the air. It is a chattering bird, flying through twisting circles and winding circuits, and extremely skillful at building nests and raising its young. It also possesses a kind of foreknowledge: it abandons and does not seek peaks that are about to collapse. [Note: “It is not attacked even by evil birds.” This is correctly read in the Gothic manuscripts. Solinus: “They are certainly not attacked by evil birds, nor are they ever prey, since they are sacred.”] It is not attacked even by evil birds and is never their prey. It flies across the seas and spends the winter there.

71. Thrushes (*turdi*) are named from slowness, [Note: “For they return at the approach of winter.” Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 14.] since they return at the approach of winter.

The *turdela* is, as it were, a larger thrush. Mistletoe is thought to be generated from its dung. Hence the ancients had the proverb: “A bird shits evil for itself.”

72. [Note: “*Furfurio*, or *farfario*; both readings are permitted by the Gothic letters and by Varro’s own etymology, *On Agriculture* III: ‘Twenty days before someone wishes to catch thrushes, he gives them more food, because he puts more in; he begins to feed them with finer meal.’”] The *furfurio* is so called because it was formerly fed on grain reduced to flour.

73. Fig-eating birds (*ficedulae*) are so called because they eat figs more than other things. This is illustrated by the old verse:

> Since the fig feeds me, since I dine on sweet grapes,
>
> why did the grape not give me my name instead?

74. [Note: “The *carduelis*.” From Servius, *Georgics* III, on “and the shores resound with the halcyon.”] The *carduelis* is so called because it feeds on thorns and thistles. Hence among the Greeks it is also called ἀκανθίς (*akanthis*), from ἀκάνθαις (*akanthais*), “thorns,” on which it feeds.

75. Augurs say that signs are established in the posture, movement, flight, and voice of birds.

76. [Note: “*Oscines*.” From Festus.] They call *oscines* those birds that furnish an omen by their mouth and song, such as the raven, crow, and woodpecker.

77. *Alites* are those that appear to reveal the future by their flight. [Note: “If they are adverse, they are called *inebrae*.” Festus: “*Inebrae* are birds which, in augury, forbid something to be done; and in general all things that delay or hinder one acting are called *inebrae*.” Glossaries: *enibra*, ἐναντία (“opposed”); *inebra*, ὄρνεον μαντευτικόν (“a divinatory bird”); *ember picus*, ὄρνις πονηρά (“an evil bird”); *enibrum*, πράγματος ἐπιβλαβές (“harmful to an undertaking”).] If their flight is unfavorable, they are called *inebrae*, because they inhibit—that is, forbid something; if favorable, they are called *praepetes*. [Note: “*Praepetes*.” See Servius, on “the winged omens,” *Aeneid* III; Aulus Gellius VI, chapter 6; and Festus.] They are called *praepetes* because all birds, when flying, seek what lies ahead.

78. They make a third category of bird omens, which they call common, mixed from both kinds: that is, when augury is taken from birds both by their mouths and by their flight.
