[Note: “They practice augury.” Thus Varro, chapter 1: “They make auguries.”] But it has no credibility. [Note: “But it has no credibility.” That is, such omens are not certain or valid. All the books have the corrupt reading *fides hoc*, or *haec non habet*; Rabanus reads, “but the faith of Christ does not accept this,” as though the faith of Christ condemned what was said above less strongly.]

79. [Note: “All kinds of birds.” From Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 3.] All kinds of birds are born twice. First eggs are produced; then, through the warmth of the mother’s body, they are formed and brought to life.

80. Eggs (*ova*) are so called because they are moist (*uvida*). [Note: “Hence also *uva*, ‘grape.’” From Servius, *Eclogue* 10.] Hence also the grape is called *uva*, because it is full of moisture within. For that which has moisture on the outside is *humidum* (“damp”), while that which has it within is *uvidum* (“moist”). Some think, however, that *ovum* has a Greek origin. They say that it is ὦα (*ōa*), with the letter *v* removed.

81. Some eggs are conceived by empty wind, but only those conceived through male intercourse and penetrated by seminal breath can produce offspring. [Note: “The power of eggs.” From Pliny XXIX, chapter 3.] They say that eggs have such power that wood soaked with egg does not burn, and even cloth touched with it is not scorched. Mixed with lime, it is also said to glue together fragments of glass.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On Small Flying Creatures

1. [Note: “Bees are so called.” From Servius, *Georgics* IV, on “or those whose feet are joined together.”] Bees (*apes*) are so called either because they fasten themselves to one another with their feet, or because they are born without feet. [Note: “For afterward they also receive feet.” From the same source, on “first mutilated in their feet.”] For afterward they acquire both feet and wings. They are skilled in the work of producing honey; they inhabit assigned dwellings, construct their homes with indescribable artistry, make honeycombs from various flowers, fill their fortress of woven wax with countless offspring, and have an army and kings. They wage battles, flee smoke, and are provoked by disturbances.

2. Many people with experience have claimed that bees are born from the corpses of cattle. [Note: “For producing them.” Servius, on “and the slaughtered bullocks.”] To produce them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten so that worms may be created from the rotting blood; these later become bees. [Note: “Bees properly so called.” From the same source, on “the idle herd of drones,” *Aeneid* I.] Properly speaking, however, bees are those born from cattle, just as hornets are born from horses, drones from mules, and wasps from donkeys.

3. [Note: “The Greeks call them *costros*.” The printed books have *castros*; Chacon read *aestros*, although *costros* appears in all the books. He thought these words belonged elsewhere because they are said to lead armies. Why would one fit a Latin etymology to a Greek word? Servius and Charisius call this exceedingly perverse. The account is taken from Palladius, book VI, chapter 10: “This month the swarms begin to increase, and larger little bees are created at the outer parts of the honeycombs. Some think these are kings, but the Greeks call them οἴστρους (*oistrous*) and order them to be killed.” Nearly the same appears in Columella, book VI, chapter 10. But since the subject of gadflies occurs again shortly afterward, it seemed unsafe to alter *costros* here.] The Greeks call *costros* those larger creatures that are produced at the outer parts of the honeycombs, which some think are kings, said to be so called because they lead armies.

The drone (*fucus*) is larger than a bee and smaller than a hornet. It is called *fucus* because it consumes the labor of others, as though *fagus* (“eater”). For it devours what it did not labor to produce. Virgil writes of it:

> They drive the idle herd of drones away from the mangers.

4. Wasps [lacuna].

Hornets (*crabrones*) are so called from *caballus*, that is, “horse,” because they are created from horses. Just as hornets are born from the rotting flesh of horses, so scarabs often arise from them in turn; hence they too received their name.

5. [Note: “The scarabs called ‘bulls.’” From Pliny XXX, chapter 5.] The scarabs called “bulls” are terrestrial beetles resembling ticks.

[Note: “The *buprestis*.” From the same book, chapter 4.] The *buprestis* is a small animal found in Italy, very similar to a long-legged scarab. It deceives cattle especially among the grasses, and hence receives its name; once swallowed, it inflames the animal through contact with the gall so violently that it bursts.

6. The *cicendela* is a kind of scarab, so called because it shines while walking or flying.

7. Cockroaches (*blattae*) are named from their color. When caught, they stain the hand, and hence they call the color *blatteus* (“purple-red”). This animal cannot bear to see the light and is the opposite of the fly: the fly seeks the light, while the cockroach flees it, walking only at night.

8. Butterflies (*papiliones*) are little flying creatures that abound especially among flowering mallows and cause little worms to be born from their excrement.

9. The locust (*locusta*) is so called because it has long legs, like spears. Hence the Greeks call both the sea locust and the land locust *astacon*.

10. Cicadas (*gicadae*) are born from the spittle of cuckoos. [Note: “They are numerous in Italy near Rhegium.” From Solinus, chapter 8.] In Italy they are numerous near Rhegium and nowhere else.

11. *Musca* (“fly”) comes from the Greek, as does *mus* (“mouse”). Like bees, flies killed in water sometimes come back to life after the space of an hour.

12. In Greek it is called *cynomyia*, that is, “dog-fly.” For κύων (*kyōn*) is the Greek word for “dog.”

13. [Note: “The mosquito from *aculeus*, ‘sting.’” I have no doubt this comes from Augustine, on Psalm 148: “Who gave the mosquito its sting, so that it might suck blood? How slender is the tube through which it drinks!”] The mosquito (*culex*) is named from its sting because it sucks blood. For it has in its mouth a tube shaped like a spike, with which it pierces the flesh in order to drink blood.

14. [Note: “*Cyniphes*.” Augustine, *On the Trinity* III, chapter 7: “*Cyniphes* are exceedingly small flies, by which the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague.” The Greeks call them σκνίφες (*sknifes*), κνίπες (*knipes*), and κνίφες (*knifes*), according to Aetius.] *Cyniphes* are very small flies, but they are extremely troublesome because of their stings. By them the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague.

15. [Note: [Col. 0472B] *Oestrum* is Greek. Servius’s words, *Georgics* III, on the verse “The Greeks translated *oestrum*, calling it …”] The *oestrus* is an animal exceedingly troublesome to herds with its stings. *Oestrum* is a Greek word; in Latin it is *asilus*, commonly called *tabanus* [gadfly].

16. [Note: [Col. 0472B] *Bibiones*. Others read *bibones*. Nothing is more elegant than Afranius’s senarii.] *Bibiones* are creatures born in wine, commonly called *mustiones* from *mustum* [must], whence Afranius also says:

> When you look at me and begin to speak,  
> *bibiones* fly from your mouth into your eyes.

17. [Note: [Col. 0472B] *Gurgul*. From Servius, *Georgics* I.] It is called *gurgulio* because it is almost nothing other than a throat.

# BOOK THIRTEEN. ON THE WORLD AND ITS PARTS

106 ## Preface

[Col. 0471]

In this little book, as on a brief tablet, we have noted certain causes relating to the heavens, the situations of the lands, and the expanses of the sea, so that the reader may run through them in a small compass and, in compact brevity, learn their etymologies and causes.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the World

[Col. 0471C]

1. The world [Note: [Col. 0471D] The world is heaven and earth. From Augustine, *Tractate II on John*.] is heaven, earth, sea, and the works of God that are in them; concerning it Scripture says: “And the world was made through him.” In Latin, philosophers call it *mundus* [world] [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Because it is in everlasting motion.” Festus appears to have followed the same etymology when he said: “*Mundus* is called heaven, earth, sea, and air. *Mundus* is also the name for a woman’s adornment, because it is nothing other than what can be set in motion.” Varro and Pliny, however, derive *mundus* from its complete and perfect elegance, following the Greek usage; and Cicero, *On the Universe*: “So that the Greeks, distinguishing this by variety, might call it *kosmos*, while we call it the shining *mundus*.”] because it is in perpetual motion: heaven, the sun, the moon, the air, and the seas. For none of its elements has been granted rest, and therefore it is always in motion.

2. Hence Varro also thinks that the elements are living beings, since, he says, they move of themselves. The Greeks, however, applied to the world a name deriving from adornment, on account of the diversity of the elements and the beauty of the stars. Among them it is called **κόσμος** (*kosmos*), which means “ornament.” [Note: [Col. 0471D] “For we see nothing more beautiful than the world with the eyes of the flesh.” These are Jerome’s words, *On Jonah* I.] For we see nothing more beautiful than the world with the eyes of the flesh.

[Col. 0471D] 107 3. [Note: [Col. 0472D] “Now it is established that there are four climates.” Jerome speaks in the same way in *Hebrew Names*, from Exodus, and in *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 13: “He placed,” he says, “four climates of the world: east, west, north, and south.” See Servius, *Georgics* I, on the verse “The world,” in connection with Scythia.] It is established that there are four climates of the world, that is, regions: east, west, north, and south.

[Col. 0472C] 4. The East (*Oriens*) is so called from the rising of the sun. The West (*Occidens*) is so called because it makes the day set and perish. For it hides the light from the world and brings darkness upon it.

5. The North (*Septentrio*) is called after the seven stars of the axis, which revolve in that region. Properly, this is also called the *vertex* [summit], because it turns, as the poet says: “Meanwhile heaven turns.”

6. [Note: [Col. 0472D] *Meridies*. In the same way above, Book III, chapter 41, and Book V, chapter 31.] The South (*Meridies*) is so called either because the sun makes midday there—almost *medidies*—or because the ether then shines more purely. For *merum* means “pure.”

7. There are two gates of heaven, East and West: through one gate the sun emerges, through the other it withdraws.

8. [Note: [Col. 0472D] “The pivots of the world.” Above, Book III, chapter 37.] There are two pivots of the world, North and South, for heaven revolves upon them.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Atoms

[Col. 0472D]

1. Philosophers call certain parts of bodies in the world *atoms* [Note: [Col. 0472D] “Philosophical atoms.” See Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapter 3; Stobaeus, *Eclogues* I, *Physics*, chapter 17; and Servius, on Silenus.] so extremely minute that they are not visible to the eye [Col. 0473A] and do not admit of **τομή** (*tomē*), that is, division; hence they are called **ἄτομοι** (*atomoi*), “indivisibles.” They are said to fly through the void of the entire world in restless motion and to be carried here and there, like the finest dust, which is visible when rays of sunlight enter through windows. Certain pagan philosophers have thought that trees, plants, and all crops arise from them, and that fire, water, and everything else are generated from them and composed of them.

2. Atoms exist either in body, time, number, or a letter. In body, for example, take a stone. You divide it into parts, and divide those parts into grains, such as grains of sand; then divide those grains of sand into the finest dust, until, if possible, you reach some minute particle that no longer can be divided or cut. This is the atom in bodies.

[Col. 0473B] 3. The atom in time is understood as follows: suppose you divide a year into months, months into days, and days into hours. The parts of hours still admit division, until you reach such a point of time and such a drop of a moment that it cannot be extended by any delay and therefore can no longer be divided. This is the atom of time.

4. In numbers, for example, eight is divided into four, four again into two, and two into one. But one is an atom, because it cannot be divided. [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Likewise in a letter.” From Sergius, *On Donatus’s Art*.] The same applies to a letter: you divide speech into words, words into syllables, and a syllable into letters. A letter is the smallest part, an atom, and cannot be divided. An atom, therefore, is what cannot be divided, like a point in geometry. For **τομή** in Greek means “division,” while **ἄτομος** means “undivided.”

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Elements

[Col. 0473C]

1. The Greeks call *hyle* [Note: [Col. 0473D] *Hyle*. From Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX, chapter 14.] a certain first matter of things, wholly without form but capable of receiving all bodily forms; from it these visible elements were formed. Hence they also received their name [Note: [Col. 0473D] “From its derivation it received its name.” That is, the elements are almost *hyle-elements* (*hylementa*).]. [Note: [Col. 0473D] “This *hyle* the Greeks …” Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “For fields and flocks to the god.”] The Latins called this *hyle* *materia* [matter], because everything unformed from which something is to be made is always called *materia*. Therefore poets also called it *silva* [forest or woodland]. Not inappropriately, since forests provide the materials.

109 2. [Note: [Col. 0473D] “The Greeks call the elements *stoicheia*.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 4: “Hence in Greek they are also called **στοιχεῖα**, because they agree and harmonize with one another.”] The Greeks call the elements **στοιχεῖα** (*stoicheia*), because they come together through a concord and a kind of communion with one another—for they are said to be joined among themselves by a certain natural relationship. Sometimes they trace their origin from fire down to earth, sometimes from earth up to fire: fire ends in air, air is condensed into water, water thickens into earth; then earth is dissolved into water, water becomes rarified into air, and air is thinned into fire.

3. Thus all the elements are present in all, but each receives its name from the element it contains in greater measure. By divine Providence they have been assigned to their proper living creatures: the Creator himself has filled heaven with angels, air with birds, sea with fish, and earth with human beings and the other living creatures.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On Heaven

1. Heaven (*coelum*) [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Why heaven is so called.” From Ambrose, *Hexameron* II, chapter 4. Others have *coelum*, as if from **κοῖλον**, that is, “hollow.”] is so called because, like an embossed vessel, it bears the imprinted lights of the stars like figures. For a vessel is called *caelatum* [embossed] when it gleams with raised figures. God distinguished heaven with bright lights [Col. 0474B] and filled it—namely, with the shining orb of the sun and moon—and adorned it with the gleaming signs of the sparkling stars. [Note: [Col. 0473D] “Or, from concealing the things above.” These words are absent from the Roman manuscript.] Alternatively, it is so called from concealing the things above.

2. [Note: [Col. 0474D] “This is **οὐρεινός** in Greek.” From Ambrose, *Hexameron* V, chapter 22. The author of *On the World* addressed to Alexander derives it from being above **τὰ οὔρεα**, that is, “the mountains.”] In Greek it is **οὐρανός** (*ouranos*), from **τοῦ ὀρᾶσθαι**, that is, “from seeing,” because the air is transparent and purer for observation. In the sacred Scriptures heaven is called the firmament because it is secured by the course of the stars, by fixed laws, and by established principles.

110 3. Sometimes “heaven” is also understood as air, where winds and clouds, storms and whirlwinds arise. [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Lucretius.” Book IV: “There are also things that arise spontaneously and are themselves formed in this heaven, which is called air.”] Lucretius says: “The heaven that is called air.” The Psalm also calls birds “birds of heaven,” although it is evident that birds fly in the air; [Note: [Col. 0474D] “And we use this customary expression.” From Augustine, *On Christian Combat*, chapter 3.] and in ordinary speech we too call this air “heaven.” For when we ask about clear or cloudy conditions, we sometimes say, “What is the air like?” and sometimes: [Col. 0474C] “What is the heaven like?”

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Parts of Heaven

1. The ether [Note: [Col. 0474D] *Ether*. This chapter is repeated from Book III, chapters 32, 36, 38, and 45.] is the region in which the stars are, and it signifies that fire which has been separated upward from the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0474D] “Properly, ether is …” Servius’s words on the verse “Bright ether,” *Aeneid* II.] Properly speaking, *aether* is the element itself, while *aethra* is the radiance of the ether; the word is Greek.

2. The sphere of heaven is so called because its form is shaped into a circle. Anything of this kind is also called a sphere by the Greeks, from its revolving motion, as are the balls with which children play. Philosophers say that heaven is everywhere convex in the form of a sphere, equal in all its parts, enclosing the earth, balanced at the center of the mass of the world. They say that it moves and that, during its motion, the stars fixed in it [Col. 0474D] circle from East to West, while those near the North perform shorter circuits beside the pivot.

[Col. 0475A] 3. The axis is the straight line of the North that extends through the middle of the sphere like a ball. It is called the axis because the sphere turns upon it like a wheel, or because the wagon is there.

4. The pivots are the extremities of the axis, and are called pivots because heaven turns through them.

111 5. The poles are circles that run through the axis. [Note: [Col. 0475C] “One of these is northern.” From commentaries on Aratus, at the end.] One of them is northern; it never sets and is called Boreas. The other is southern; it is never seen and is called Austronotius. [Col. 0475B] They are called poles because they are the circles of the axes, named from the use of wagons, specifically from *polire* [to polish]; but the Boreal pole is always visible, while the Austronotian is never visible, because the right-hand parts of heaven are higher, the South having been pressed down.

6. The convex regions are the outermost parts of heaven, named from their curvature. For *convex* means curved, inclined, and bent in the form of a circle.

7. The Milky Way is the path visible in the sphere. It is named from its whiteness, because it is white. Some say that it is the path along which the sun circles and that it shines in this way from the passage of the sun’s radiance itself.

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Circles of Heaven

1. This habitation of heaven, divided into zones by circles, has allowed some regions to be inhabited because of their temperate climate and has denied others because of the extremity of cold or heat. There are five zones themselves. They are called zones, or circles, because they exist in the sphere’s circular revolution.

2. The first circle is therefore called Arctic [Note: [Col. 0475D] “Because the constellations of the Bears are within it.” This too is from Book III, chapter 43. *Arcturi*, which appears in the printed editions, is not objectionable, although *Arctorum* occurs in the Gothic manuscripts. These are Hyginus’s words, *Astronomy* I, as we noted there.], because within it the constellations of the Bears are visible. Our people, representing them in the form of bears [Col. 0475C], call them the Septentriones.

3. The second circle is called **τροπικὸς θερινὸς** (*tropikos therinos*), “summer tropic,” because in this circle the sun, producing summer in the regions of the North, does not pass beyond that circle but immediately turns back; hence it is called the Tropic.

4. The third circle is **ἰσημερινὸς** (*isēmerinos*), which the Latins therefore call Equinoctial, because when the sun reaches that orbit it produces the equinox. 112 **ἰσημερινὸς** in Latin means “equal day,” the equinox, when half of the sphere is seen to be established along that circle.

5. The fourth circle is called Antarctic because it is opposite the circle that we call Arctic.

[Col. 0476A] 6. The fifth circle is **χειμερινὸς τροπικὸς** (*cheimerinos tropikos*), which the Latins call Hiemal or Brumalian, because when the sun reaches that circle it produces winter for those who are in the North, but summer for those dwelling in the regions of the South.

7. [Note: [Col. 0475D] “The zodiacal circle is …” There is a lacuna in some Gothic manuscripts after these words, here and in Book III. I do not wish to fill it, since the manuscripts that supply it disagree with one another in both places.] The zodiacal circle is the circle that contains twelve signs; it is called this **ἀπὸ τῶν ζώων**, that is, “from the animals.”

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On Air and Cloud

1. Air is a voidness containing a very large admixture of rarity [Note: [Col. 0475D] “Than the other elements.” I agree with Chacon, to whom these words appear spurious.] in comparison with the other elements. Concerning it Virgil says: [Note: [Col. 0475D] “Having followed through the long void.” These words are not found in Maro. One may therefore read either “driven through the great void” from *Silenus*, or “rolling through the empty void” from *Aeneid* XII.] “Having followed through the long void.” Air is called *aer* from **ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵρειν**, because it carries the earth, or because it is carried. It belongs partly to heavenly matter and partly to earthly [Col. 0476B] matter. The subtle air, in which windy and stormy movements cannot arise, belongs to the heavenly region; the more turbulent air, which becomes bodily through moist exhalations, is assigned to the earth. From itself it produces many forms: [Note: [Col. 0475D] “For when it is stirred, it makes winds, and so forth.” These are Augustine’s words, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* III, chapter 10.] when stirred, it makes winds; when driven more violently, fire and thunder; when contracted, clouds; when thickened, rain; when clouds freeze, snow; when denser clouds freeze more turbulently, hail; when spread out, it produces clear weather. 113 For dense air is understood to be cloud, and cloud that has become rarified and dispersed is air.

2. [Note: [Col. 0475D] “Clouds are so called.” From Servius, on the verse “And covers the burning locks with a mantle.”] Clouds are called *nubes* from *obnubere*, “to cover,” that is, to cover heaven. Hence brides are also called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces; [Note: [Col. 0476C] “Hence also Neptune.” Arnobius, *Against the Pagans* III: “Because water marries the earth.” Chacon thought that Isidore had written: “Hence also Neptune, because he marries the earth”; that “let Neptune be read as the sea” should be read; and that *nubat* [“marries”] was an alien gloss.] hence also Neptune, because he “marries,” that is, because the sea covers the earth. [Note: [Col. 0476D] “Cloud, however, is the density of air.” From the same source, *Aeneid* V: “And the air is gathered into a cloud.”] The density of air makes clouds. Winds gather air together and make a cloud, as in the line: “And the air is gathered into a cloud.”

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On Thunder

1. Thunder (*tonitruum*) is so called because its sound terrifies, [Note: [Col. 0476D] “For *tonus* means sound.” Seneca, *Natural Questions* II, reports that Caecina derived *tonitruum* from *tonus*. In earlier times *tonitruum* was used; in his own age it was used only in the plural, *tonitrua*.] for *tonus* means “sound.” It sometimes shakes everything so violently [Note: [Col. 0476D] “So that heaven seems to have split apart.” One also finds *discessisse* and *decidisse*. Just as I entirely reject none of these readings, I prefer *discidisse*, understanding it as “to have split itself apart,” as elsewhere. The Roman manuscript also reads *discindi*, while others corruptly have *discis­se*; and the following verb, *praescindit* or rather *perscindit*, is used three times by Lucretius in the same context, whom Isidore is imitating here. The example of a burst bladder also seems more to require *discidisse*. As for *discessisse*, one does not find “the departure of heaven” in the books *On Divination*.] that heaven seems to have split apart. When a violent storm-wind has suddenly driven itself into the clouds, and the whirlwind grows stronger while seeking an exit, it tears apart with great force the cloud it has hollowed out, and thus the sound is carried to the ears with dreadful crashing.

[Col. 0477A] 2. [Note: [Col. 0477C] “No one should be surprised at this, since a small bladder …” Lucretius, Book VI:

> Nor is it surprising, when a small bladder filled with air  
> Often, burst suddenly, gives forth such a sound.]

No one should be surprised at this, since even a small bladder, when burst, emits a great sound. With thunder, lightning is also produced at the same time, but lightning appears more quickly because it is bright, whereas thunder reaches the ears more slowly. The light that appears before thunder is called *fulgetra*. [Note: [Col. 0477D] “It is called *fulgetra*.” Others read *fulgetrum*. But *fulgetra* must certainly be read, from Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “now terrifying flashes.” Vulcanius printed *fulgor* [radiance].] As we have said, it is seen first 114 because the light is bright, whereas thunder reaches the ears more slowly.

## CHAPTER NINE. On Lightning

1. *Fulgur* and *fulmen* are blows from a heavenly javelin, named from striking. [Note: [Col. 0477D] “For *fulgere* means to strike.” Festus: “The ancients used *fulgere* for *ferire*, ‘to strike’; hence *fulgur* was named.”] For *fulgere* means to strike and hit. [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Lightning, however …” From Servius, on the verse “Having hurled fire from the clouds,” *Aeneid* I.] Lightning is produced by the collision of clouds; [Note: [Col. 0477D] “For the collision of all things … trees.” Servius’s words, *Aeneid* I, on “From which rain and fires arise.”] for the collision of all things creates fire, as we see with stones, by the rubbing of wheels, and in the trees of forests. [Col. 0477B] In the same way fire is produced in clouds. Hence they are first clouds, and then fires.

2. It is certain that lightning is formed in clouds from wind and fire and is sent forth by the force of winds. The fire of lightning has greater power to penetrate [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Because it is made from subtler elements.” He was looking to Lucretius’s verses, Book II:

> Therefore the fire of lightning penetrates much more deeply  
> Than ours, arising from earthly torches, flows.  
> You may say that the fire of heavenly lightning  
> Is subtler, composed of smaller shapes.]

because it is made from subtler elements than ordinary fire—that is, the fire used by us. It has three names: *fulgur*, *fulgor*, and *fulmen*. It is *fulgur* because it touches; *fulgor* because it sets fire to and burns; *fulmen* because it splits; for this reason it is also represented with three rays.

## CHAPTER TEN. On the Rainbow and the Effects of Clouds

1. The heavenly bow is called from its likeness to a curved bow. [Col. 0477C] *Iris* is its proper name. It is called *Iris* [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Iris is named as if from *aeris*.” The Greeks derive it from **εἴρειν**, “to speak,” because it is the messenger of the gods. Servius interprets *Irin* as if from **ἔριν**, “discord,” because just as Mercury is often sent to produce concord, Iris is sent to produce discord.] as if from *aeris*, because it descends through the air to the earth. 115 It shines by the sun when hollow clouds [Note: [Col. 0478C] “Receive the sun’s ray from the opposite side.” From Servius, on “drawing a thousand …,” *Aeneid* IV.] receive the sun’s ray from the opposite side and form the appearance of a bow. That phenomenon gives it various colors: thin water, shining air, and a dark cloud struck by light produce these different colors.

2. Rains are called *pluviae* because they flow, almost *fluviae* [rivers]. [Note: [Col. 0478D] “For they arise from the breath of earth and sea.” Servius’s words, *Aeneid* I, on “From which rain and fires arise.” The passage of Lucretius cited by Servius is from Book VI: “In like manner, from all rivers, moisture …”] They arise from the breath of earth and sea. When these vapors have been lifted higher, whether dissolved by the sun’s heat or compressed by the force of winds, they drip down upon the earth.

[Col. 0478A] 3. A *nimbus* is a cloud’s untimely, dark density; hence *nimbus* is derived from *nubes*, “cloud.” [Note: [Col. 0478D] “These are nimbi.” From Servius, on “the storm-cloud into its homeland,” *Aeneid* I.] Nim­bi are sudden and precipitous rains. We call rains *pluviae* when they are slow and continuous, almost rivers, or as if flowing.

4. *Imbres* [showers] refer both to clouds and to rains. [Note: [Col. 0478D] “Derived from the Greek word **ὄμβρος**.”] They are named from the Greek word **ὄμβρος**, because they make the earth drunk for germination. From them everything is created. [Note: [Col. 0478D] “Hence also Lucretius.” Lucretius’s verse is transmitted in the same way by Servius, from whom this material comes, though somewhat differently in the Lucretian manuscripts:

> And those who think that everything can arise from four things,  
> From fire, earth, breath, and rain.]

Hence Lucretius says:

> Earth and breath are born from fire and rain.

The name is Greek.

5. Hail is called *grando* because its form resembles grains. It is hardened in a cloud by the force of winds and solidified into snow; when the air breaks open, it is released.

[Col. 0478B] 6. Snow (*nix*) is named from the cloud from which it comes.

Ice (*glacies*) is named from frost (*gelu*) and water, almost *gelaquies*, that is, “frozen water.”

7. Frost (*gelu*) is so called because the earth is constricted by it; for **γῆ** (*gē*) means “earth.” The earth is constricted by the most severe frost when the night is clear.

8. Hoarfrost (*pruina*) is the cold of the morning; it received this name 116 because it burns like fire. For **πῦρ** (*pyr*) means “fire.” [Note: [Col. 0478D] “To burn also applies to cold.” See Servius, on “let the penetrating cold burn,” *Georgics* I. Chacon rightly observed that Servius was read by Isidore here without Virgil’s verses, as often elsewhere, which led to the confusion. “In one expression,” says Servius, “the poet combined two different things, because the verb *adur­at* [burns] refers both to the sun’s power and to cold.”] To burn applies both to the sun and to cold. For one expression signifies two different things because they have one effect. The force of heat and cold is similar, and therefore both split rocks. Heat burns, as in: “Unhappy Dido burns.” Cold likewise burns, as in: “Or let the penetrating cold of Boreas burn.”

[Col. 0478C] 9. *Ros* [dew] is Greek; the Greeks call it **δρόσος** (*drosos*). Others think *ros* is so called because it is thin, not dense like rain.

10. *Nebula* [mist] is named from the same source as *nubila* [clouds], namely from *obnubere*, “to cover,” because it covers the earth, or because a flying cloud produces it. Moist valleys exhale mists, and clouds are formed; hence come cloudy weather and then snow. When the weather is clear, mists seek the low places; when it is cloudy, they rise to the heights.

11. *Caligo* [haze or gloom] is a shadow produced by the thickness of the air. It is called *caligo* because it is generated especially by the air’s heat.

[Col. 0479A] 12. Darkness (*tenebrae*) is so called because it “holds” shadows. [Note: [Col. 0479C] “Darkness is nothing … is called.” Augustine’s words, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, chapter 4.] Darkness is nothing in itself, but the absence of light is called darkness. Just as silence is not a thing but is called silence where there is no sound, so darkness is not something in itself; wherever there is no light, that is called darkness.

13. A shadow is air deprived of the sun. It is called *umbra* because it occurs when we place ourselves in the sun’s rays. It is mobile, uncertain, and results from the sun’s circuit and [Note: [Col. 0479D] “And from the movement of the winds.” Servius, *Eclogues* V, on “or beneath uncertain …”] from the movement of the winds. Whenever it moves in the sunlight, it appears to move with us, because [Note: [Col. 0479D] “Wherever we stand.” Thus in the very ancient Salmasian manuscript; the Complutensian has “everywhere where …”] wherever we stand in the way of the sun’s rays, we remove the light from that place. Thus the shadow seems to enter with us and imitate our movements.

14. Light (*lux*) is the substance itself; illumination (*lumen*) is what flows from light, that is, the brightness of light. But authors confuse these terms.

117 ## CHAPTER ELEVEN. On Winds

1. Wind is air stirred and driven into motion, and it receives different names according to the various regions of heaven. It is called *ventus* because it is forceful and violent. Its power is so great that it not only uproots rocks and trees but also disturbs heaven and earth and moves the seas.

2. There are four principal winds or spirits. The first, from the East, is Subsolanus; from the South comes Auster; from the West, Favonius; and from the North, the wind of that same name. Each has two neighboring winds on either side.

3. Subsolanus has Vulturnus on its right and Eurus on its left; Auster has Euroauster on the right and Austroafricus on the left; Favonius has Africus on the right and Corus on the left. North has Circius on the right and Aquilo on the left. These twelve winds turn the globe of the world with their blasts.

4. Their names have been assigned for particular reasons. Subsolanus is so called because it arises beneath the rising sun. Eurus is so called because it blows from *Eous*, that is, from the East. It is joined to Subsolanus.

5. Vulturnus is so called because it thunders aloft. Lucretius says of it:

> High-thundering Vulturnus, and Auster powerful with lightning.

6. Auster is called from *haurire* [to draw up], because it draws up waters; hence it makes the air thick 118 and nourishes clouds. [Note: [Col. 0479D] “Notus, because it sometimes corrupts.” *Notheuein* means “to corrupt,” whence Horace, on illegitimate sons:

> Ages fertile in guilt first  
> Defiled marriages, lineage, and households.]

In Greek it is called **νότος** (*notos*), because it sometimes corrupts [Col. 0480A] the air. For Auster, blowing into other regions, carries the pestilence that arises from corrupted air; but just as Auster produces pestilence, Aquilo drives it away. Euroauster is so called because on one side it has Eurus and on the other Auster.

7. Austroafricus is so called because it is joined on either side to Auster and Africus. It is also [Note: [Col. 0479D] “It is Libonotus.” Seneca: “From the southern axis comes Euronotus, then Notus, in Latin Auster, then Libonotus, which among us has no name.”] called Libonotus, because it has Libs on one side and Notus on the other.

8. Zephyrus is called by a Greek name because its breath brings flowers and shoots to life. In Latin it is called Favonius, because it fosters what is born. Flowers are loosened by Auster and produced by Zephyrus.

9. Africus is named from its own region. It begins to blow in Africa.

10. Corus is the wind that blows from the summer West. It is called Corus because it closes the circle of the winds and forms, as it were, a chorus. Formerly [Col. 0480B] it was called Caurus; most people call it Argestes, not *Agrestis*, as the ignorant common people do. [Note: [Col. 0479D] “Caurus, which most people call Argestes.” Seneca, *Natural Questions* III: “Corus comes from the solstitial West; among some it is called Argestes.” I do not think so, because Corus has a violent force and carries things off in one direction. Argestes, however, is gentle and equally favorable both to those going and to those returning.]

11. Septentrio is so called because it rises from the circle of seven stars, which, as the world turns, appear to be carried with their heads thrown back.

12. [Note: [Col. 0480C] “Circius … the Spaniards call this Gallecus.” Others have *Gallicus*, “from the region of Gaul,” but this is corrupt; we retain the name *Gallecus* today.] Circius is so called because it is joined to Corus. The Spaniards call it Gallecus because it blows upon them from the region of Gallaecia.

119 13. Aquilo is so called because it contracts waters and disperses clouds. It is a cold and dry wind. It is also called Boreas because it blows from the Hyperborean mountains. Its origin is there, and therefore it is cold. For the nature of all northern winds is cold and dry, while that of the southern winds is moist and warm.

[Col. 0480C] 14. Of all the winds, two are cardinal: Septentrio and Auster.

15. [Note: [Col. 0480D] “The Etesian blasts of Aquilo.” Lucretius, Book VI: “The Etesian blasts of the Aquilones … drive together the clouds.”] The Etesian winds are blasts of Aquilo. They received this name because they begin to blow at a fixed season of the year. [Note: [Col. 0480D] **Ἐνιαυτός**. **ἔτος** and **ἐτήσιος** would be closer, but he followed Hyginus, whose old manuscripts read **ἐνιαυτός**, as appears from Giovanni Battista Pio’s note on Lucretius, Book V: “Then comes the dry heat of the region”; now **ἔτος** is preferable.] For **ἐνιαυτός** (*eniautos*) means “year” in Greek. They travel in a straight course from Boreas to Egypt, and Auster is contrary to them.

16. There are also two spirits outside these, more properly breezes than winds: Aura and Altanus.

17. Aura is named from *aer* [air], almost *aerea* [airy], because it is a gentle movement of air. Stirred air makes a breeze; hence Lucretius also says: [Note: [Col. 0480D] “Hence also Lucretius: airy breezes.” Book I: “And airy breezes and the dew of liquids,” and Book IV: “Since it is touched by neighboring airs.”] “Airy breezes.”

18. [Note: [Col. 0480D] *Altanus*. Servius, on “When the winds have subsided”: “Every breeze,” he says, “both that of the shore and that of the sea, is called Altanus.” Pliny, Book II, chapter 43: “For we see them arise from rivers, snow, and the sea, even when it is calm, and others, which they call Altani, arise from the earth. When they return from the sea, they are called Tropaei; if they continue, Apogaei.”] Altanus is the wind at sea, named by derivation from [Col. 0481A] *altum*, that is, “the sea.” For there is another breeze along the shores, which we have called Aura. Aura belongs to the land.

19. A whirlwind (*turbo*) is the revolving motion of winds. It is called *turbo* when a wind rises from the earth and sends the earth whirling around.

20. *Tempestas* [weather or storm] is used for *tempus* [time], as historians commonly do when they say “at that time.” Alternatively, it derives from the state of the sky, [Note: [Col. 0481C] “Because it arises for many days owing to its magnitude.” How these words, taken from Servius on “stormy Orion,” *Aeneid* I, fit this passage requires further investigation.] because it arises for many days on account of its magnitude. [Note: [Col. 0481C] “In spring and autumn.” From the same source, on *Georgics* I: “What autumn storms …”] Storms are greatest in spring and autumn, 120 when summer is neither complete nor winter complete. Thus the intermediate and bordering season of the two periods produces storms through the conjunction of opposing kinds of air.

21. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “*Fragor* from *fracta*.” From the same source, on “dry crashing.”] *Fragor* [crashing] is named from the sound of broken things, which dry and brittle objects make when they are broken.

[Col. 0481B] 22. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “*Procella*.” From the same source, *Aeneid* I, on “frequent with storms.”] *Procella* [storm] is so called because it strikes and tears up. It is the force of winds together with rain. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “Storms, or from rivers.” From the same source, *Aeneid* V, on “the three Erician calves.”] Storms arise either from lightning or from winds. Nothing is swifter than winds; hence, because of their speed, poets represent both winds and lightning as winged, as in: “the winged South.”

## CHAPTER TWELVE. On Waters

1. Water is so called because its surface is level. Hence it is also called *aequor* [level expanse], because it rises evenly.

2. There are two especially powerful elements of human life, fire and water; hence those to whom fire and water are forbidden are severely condemned.

3. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “The element of waters.” From Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 1. From this it seems that one should read: “And as if it were not enough, they snatch them up and carry them away.”] The element of waters governs all the others. [Col. 0481C] Waters regulate heaven, fertilize the earth, incorporate air through their exhalations, rise into the heights, and claim heaven for themselves. For what is more marvelous than waters standing in heaven?

4. As if it were too little for them to have reached so great a height, they carry shoals of fish up there with them. When poured out, they become the cause of everything that grows on earth. They produce crops, trees, [Col. 0482A] shrubs, and grasses; they wash away filth, [Note: [Col. 0481D] “They wash away sins.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 5. The remainder is from Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 22.] wash away sins, and provide drink for all living creatures.

121 ## CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On the Variety of Waters

1. The nature of waters is greatly varied. Some contain salt, some nitre, some alum, some sulfur, some bitumen, and some provide remedies for diseases. Near Rome, [Note: [Col. 0481D] “The waters of Albula.” Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 2.] the waters of Albula heal wounds.

2. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “A spring of Cicero in Italy.” The same source.] In Italy, the spring of Cicero cures wounds of the eyes. In Ethiopia there is a lake in which bodies, when washed, [Note: [Col. 0481D] “Shine as if with oil.” From Solinus, chapter 43.] shine as though covered with oil. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “Zama.” See Vitruvius, Book VIII, chapter 3. Likewise concerning Clitorius, from which *Italy* should perhaps be read instead of *Arcadia*.] The spring of Zama in Africa makes voices melodious. Those who drink from the Clitorius lake in Italy develop a loathing for wine.

3. [Note: [Col. 0481D] “On the island of Chios.” From Pliny, the same book.] On the island of Chios, they say, there is a spring that makes people dull-witted. In Boeotia there are two springs: one brings memory, [Col. 0482B] the other forgetfulness. A spring at Cyzicus removes the love of Venus.

4. In Boeotia there is a fury-inducing lake; whoever drinks from it is inflamed with the ardor of lust. In Campania there are waters said to remove female sterility and male insanity. Whoever drinks from the red spring in Ethiopia becomes delirious.

### 5

[Note: [Col. 0482C] Linus, a spring of Arcadia.—We have written *Linus* on the authority of Pliny. The manuscripts, however, have various forms: *lechnus*, *lecinus*, *lethinus*, and *lethnus*. Pliny’s old Toledo manuscript also has *Levius*.]

Linus, a spring of Arcadia, does not allow miscarriages to occur.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] Two springs in Sicily. From Solinus, chapter 11.]

In Sicily there are two springs: one makes a barren woman fertile, the other makes a fertile woman barren.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] In Thessaly.—In Boeotia, Solinus, chapter 12. From Varro. Pliny places them in Hestiaeotis, which is a part of Thessaly.]

In Thessaly there are two rivers. They say that sheep drinking from one become black, from the other white, and from both together variegated.

### 6

[Note: [Col. 0482C] Clitumnus … which produces the largest cattle. Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> Hence elsewhere the herds of Clitumnus, and the bull,  
> the greatest victim …

Silius, book VIII:

> And Clitumnus bathes the enormous bull,  
> pouring water over it in the sacred stream.

Thus Clitumnus produces both white and very large bulls.]

Clitumnus, a lake in Umbria, produces the largest cattle.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] In the Reatine marshes. The words are Pliny’s, book XXXI, chapter 2.]

They say that in the Reatine marshes the hooves of beasts of burden are hardened.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] In the Asphalt Lake. Josephus, *Jewish War* V, chapter 5; Hegesippus, book 4, chapter 18; Pliny, V, chapter 16; Solinus, chapter 48. Nothing can sink in it, as Pliny also said, book II, chapter 103.]

In the Asphalt Lake of Judaea nothing that has life can sink.

### 7

[Note: [Col. 0482D] In India, Siden.—The Toledo manuscript has *Siderin*. Silia reported this. Strabo, book XV: “In the mountainous country there is a river called Silia, in which nothing floats.” Nunnensis read *Solan* from the *History of Antigonus* and from the epitome of Strabo; we have adopted *Siden* from the Gothic manuscripts and Pliny, XXXI, chapter 2.]

In India a pond is called Siden, in which nothing floats, but everything sinks. By contrast, in the lake of Apuscidamum in Africa everything floats and nothing sinks.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Apuscidamum … The spring of Marsyas in Achaea. From the same passage of Pliny.]

The spring of Marsyas in Phrygia casts out rocks. In Achaea water flows from rocks, called the Styx, because whoever drinks it dies immediately.

### 8

[Col. 0483A]

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Lake Gelonium. From Solinus, chapter 11.]

Lake Gelonium in Sicily drives away those who approach it with its foul odor.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] There is a spring in Africa. From Solinus, chapter 40.]

There is a spring in Africa near the temple of Ammon, which binds the ground with its networks of moisture. It even hardens ashes into a clod.

The spring of Job in Idumaea is said to change its color four times a year—that is, becoming dusty, blood-red, green, and clear—and to retain one of these colors for three months at a time.

### 9

[Note: [Col. 0483D] In the land of the Troglodytes. From Pliny.]

Among the Troglodytes there is a lake that becomes bitter three times a day and then just as often becomes sweet.

The spring of Siloa, at the foot of Mount Zion, does not bubble continuously, but at fixed hours and on fixed days.

In Judaea there was once a stream that dried up every Sabbath.

### 10

In Sardinia hot springs heal the eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] They heal the eyes. From Solinus, chapter 10.]

They expose thieves, for their crime is revealed through blindness.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] In Epirus. Pliny, II, chapter 103, and Solinus, chapter 12.]

They say that in Epirus there is a spring in which lighted torches are extinguished and extinguished torches are lit.

[Col. 0483B]

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Among the Garamantes. Pliny, in the same passage, and Solinus, chapter 42.]

They say that among the Garamantes there is a spring so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, and so hot by night that it cannot be touched.

### 11

Now in many places waters flow perpetually hot, with such force that they heat baths. For there are certain regions of earth that contain much sulfur and alum. Thus, when cold water comes through hot veins, it is touched by the neighboring heat of the sulfur and grows hot; it does not flow out in that condition from its origin, but is altered as it comes.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] When it comes through hot veins. See Vitruvius, book VIII, chapter 3.]

For waters carry sulfur and alum with them, each substance being full of fire and growing hot at the slightest movement.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Sea

[Col. 0483C]

### 1

The sea is the general collection of waters.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] For every gathering. From Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, chapter 12.]

For every gathering of waters—whether they are salt or fresh—is, by an extended use of the term, called “seas,” in accordance with the words: “And he called the gatherings of waters seas.”

Strictly speaking, however, it is called *mare* because its waters are bitter.

### 2

It is called *aequor* because it is level above. Although its surging waters rise like mountains, when the storms have subsided they become level again. For the depth of the sea varies, but the evenness of its surface remains undivided.

### 3

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Why the sea does not increase in volume. The entire passage is taken from Lucretius, book VI:

> Now the reason must be explained why the sea does not know increase.]

The reason why the sea does not increase, although it receives all rivers and all springs, is this: partly, because its own great size does not perceive the waters flowing into it; then because salt water consumes the fresh water that flows into it; or because the clouds themselves draw much water up to themselves; or because winds carry part of it away and the sun dries up part; and finally because it is filtered through certain hidden openings in the earth, returns to the sources of rivers, and flows back again.

### 4

[Note: [Col. 0484D] That the color of the sea is not constant. From Servius on the verse “And he cleft the dark waves with the North Wind,” *Aeneid* V. The reading *luculentum* is clear from Servius and one Roman manuscript; we preferred it to the reading in our Gothic manuscripts, so that *luculentum* may derive from *lux*, “light.” See Aulus Gellius, book II, final chapter.]

The sea does not have a fixed color, but changes according to the character of the winds.

[Col. 0484A]

For at one time it is yellow, at another bright, and at another dark.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Ocean

### 1

Both Greeks and Latins call it *Oceanus* because it surrounds the world in the manner of a circle;

[Note: [Col. 0484D] Or from its swiftness. From Solinus, chapter 26, concerning Spain.]

or from its swiftness, because it runs more rapidly; also because, like the sky, it shines with a purple color.

*Oceanus* is virtually *κυάνεος*—“dark blue.” It is the body of water that embraces the shores of the lands, advancing and retreating with alternating tides. For when winds breathe into the depths, the ocean either draws the seas away or sucks them back.

### 2

It has received different names from the regions nearest to it: Gallic, Germanic, Scythian, Caspian, Hyrcanian, Atlantic, and Gaditanian.

The Strait of Gadiz was named from Gadiz, where the entrance to the Great Sea first opens from the Ocean. Hence, when Hercules reached Gadiz, he placed columns there, hoping that the end of the terrestrial world was located there.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Mediterranean Sea

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0484D] The Great Sea. Not the Ocean, but the Mediterranean Sea, as often in the sacred books—for example, in Numbers beginning with chapter XXXIV and in the book of Joshua.]

The Great Sea is that which flows from the Ocean in the west, turns toward the south, and then extends toward the north.

It is called “Great” because the other seas are smaller in comparison with it. It is also the Mediterranean, because it extends through the middle of the land as far as the east, separating Europe, Africa, and Asia.

### 2

[Col. 0484C]

[Note: [Col. 0484D] Which spreads over Spain.—“It spreads over Spain.” Solinus.]

The gulf of its first section, which spreads over Spain, is called the Iberian and the Balearic. Next comes the Gallic Gulf, which washes the province of Narbonensis. Then the Ligurian Gulf, which lies near the city of Genoa. After this comes the Tyrrhenian Gulf, which touches Italy; the Greeks call it the Ionian, while the Italians call it the Lower Sea.

Then comes the Sicilian Gulf, which extends from Sicily to Crete. Next is the Cretan Gulf, which reaches toward Pamphylia and Egypt.

### 3

From there comes the Hellespont, which turns northward and, with great winding channels beside Greece and Illyricum, narrows to a width of seven stadia. Xerxes crossed there into Greece after constructing a bridge of ships; Abydos is located there.

From there it spreads out over an open expanse of sea, then narrows again and forms the Propontis. Soon afterward it contracts to five hundred paces and becomes the Thracian Bosphorus, across which Darius transported his armies.

### 4

From there comes the enormous Pontic Gulf, behind the Maeotian marsh.

[Note: [Col. 0485C] That this sea is sweeter because of the number of rivers flowing into it. This is reported from Sallustius by Servius, *Aeneid* XI. Anyone who reads Pliny will readily believe it: he says that the Danube, after receiving seventy rivers—half of them navigable—washes Illyricum and then flows into the Pontus, joined by six other huge rivers. Yet Pliny, book VI, chapter 17, attributes this to the Caspian Sea.]

Because of the multitude of rivers flowing into it, this sea is sweeter than the others, misty, and shallower.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Misty and shallower. From Mela, book I, chapter 19.]

Hence it is also called the Pontic Sea: it is shallower and, apart from seals, tunny fish, and dolphins, does not admit other large beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] It does not admit other larger animals. From Solinus.]

### 5

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Just as the earth, although it is one. From Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 3.]

Just as the one earth is called by different names according to different places, so this Great Sea is called by different names according to its regions.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] For the Iberian and Asiatic. Solinus: “The diversity of names has different causes: for the Iberian and Asiatic,” and so forth.]

The Iberian and Asiatic seas are named from provinces. From islands come the Balearic, Sicilian, Cretan, Cyprian, Aegean, and Carpathian seas.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Namely, between Tenedos and Chios. From Solinus, chapters 4 and 17; or, according to the more accurate manuscripts of Pliny, it should be read *Tenem* and *Cium*, book IV, chapter 11, since Pliny and Strabo number these among the Cyclades.]

For between Tenedos and Chios there is a rock in the sea rather than an island, which those who see it from a distance believe resembles a goat. They call it *αἶγα* (“goat”), and from this the Aegean Sea was named.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Likewise the Carpathian Sea … located there. From Servius on the verse “The Carpathian and Libyan seas,” *Aeneid* V.]

Similarly, the Carpathian Sea lies between Egypt and Rhodes and takes its name from the island of Carpathus located there.

### 6

From peoples come the Gallic, Ausonian, Dalmatian, and Ligurian seas.

From towns come the Argolic, Corinthian, Tyrian, and Adriatic seas. Adria was a certain city near the Illyrian sea, and it gave its name to the Adriatic Sea.

### 7

From the position of the heavens come names such as Upper and Lower, because the east is higher and the west lower. The sea is also called Tuscan and Adriatic.

From the memory of a king comes the name Ionian.

[Note: [Col. 0486C] Ion was a leader. Eusebius, *Chronicle*: “Ion, a brave man, called the Athenians Ionians after his own name.”]

For Ion was a king of Greece, and from him came the name of the Athenian Ionians.

This sea was also called Tyrrhenian, either because it washes Tuscia—that is, Tyrrhenia—or from the Tyrrhenian sailors who threw themselves into this sea.

[Note: [Col. 0486C] It should also be understood that the Ionian Gulf… From Servius on “the Ionian islands in the Great Sea,” *Aeneid* III.]

It should also be understood that the Ionian Gulf is immense, extending from Ionia to Sicily, and that the Adriatic, Achaean, and Epirote seas are its parts.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] From the customs of its inhabitants. From Solinus.]

From the customs of its inhabitants comes the name Euxine, previously called *AXENOS* (“inhospitable”).

### 8

[Col. 0485C]

From people who fell into the sea come such names as Hellespontic, Icarian, and Myrtoan.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] For the Myrtoan Sea. From Servius, *Georgics* III, at the beginning.]

The Myrtoan Sea was so called from the fall of Myrtilus, who was thrown there by Oenomaus.

Icarus, however, a Cretan, as the story goes, sought higher regions; when his wings melted in the heat of the sun, he fell into the sea, and gave his name to the sea in which he fell.

Phrixus, too, fleeing with his sister Helle from the plots of his stepmother, boarded a ship bearing the sign of a ram, by which he was saved. His sister Helle, however, suffered shipwreck, fell into the sea, and died; she gave the Hellespont its name.

### 9

[Col. 0486A]

From the order of its flow comes the name Propontis, for it was called Propontis because it precedes the Pontus.

From passage, or from the narrow paths of oxen, comes the name Bosphorus.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The Egyptian sea is assigned to Asia. Solinus and Mela say this; Ptolemy, however, says concerning Asia: “Everyone agrees that the part of Egypt beyond the Nile belongs to Asia.”]

The Egyptian Sea is assigned to Asia, the Gallic Sea to Europe, and the African Sea to Libya. These have entered into the divisions of their respective regions according to the lands nearest to them.

### 10

[Col. 0486D]

A *pelagus* is a breadth of water—a sea without shore or harbor. It is named from the Greek *ἀπὸ τοῦ πλαγίου*, that is, “from breadth.”

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Hence also *plagia*, because it lacks a harbor. Servius, commenting on Statius, incorrectly says: “A place without a harbor is called *plagia*, and we call it *playa*.”]

Hence also the term *plagia*, because such a sea has no harbor.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Gulfs of the Sea

### 1

Gulfs are the larger recesses of the sea: in the Great Sea, the Gulf of Junius; in the Ocean, the Caspian, Indian, Persian, and Arabian gulfs—the last also called the Red Sea.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Which belongs to the Ocean.—Which is counted as a gulf, not as a sea.]

The Arabian Gulf is assigned to the Ocean.

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Why the Red Sea is called so. See Solinus.]

The Red Sea was so called because it is tinged with rosy waves. Yet it does not naturally possess the character that it appears to display. Rather, the water is corrupted and stained by the neighboring shores, because all the land surrounding the sea is red and close to the color of blood.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The sharpest vermilion. Perhaps “the most valued.”]

For this reason the sharpest vermilion is extracted from there, along with other colors used to vary painting.

### 3

Since the earth has this character, it is repeatedly washed by the waves, and whatever has been gnawed away falls into the color.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Has been eaten away. This is the reading of the Gothic manuscripts; others have “has been attached.”]

For this reason red gems are also found on these shores. A stone of this kind, enclosed in the earth, when it has been rubbed among the sands, possesses both the color of the earth and that of the sea.

### 4

This sea is divided into two gulfs. Of these, the one to the east is called the Persian Gulf, because the Persians inhabit its shore. The other is called the Arabian Gulf, because it lies around Arabia.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Tides and Straits

### 1

The term *tide* belongs to the Ocean, while *strait* belongs to both seas.

For a tide is the advance or retreat of the sea—that is, its agitation. Hence also the term *estuaries*, through which the sea alternately advances and retreats.

### 2

A strait is so called because the sea there is always boiling. For a strait is a narrow and almost boiling sea, named from the boiling motion of its waves.

Varro says that *freta* (“straits”) is virtually *fervida*, that is, “boiling,” possessing the motion of boiling.

### 3

[Note: [Col. 0487C] The Strait of Sicily. From Servius, *Aeneid* III: “These regions were once devastated by force,” and so forth.]

Sallustius writes that the Strait of Sicily, called Rhegium, received its name for the following reason. He says that Sicily was once joined to Italy, and that, while the land was one, the intervening space was either broken apart by the waters because it was low-lying, or split because of its narrowness.

From this it was called *ῥήγιον*, because in Greek this word means “broken off” or “torn apart.”

It is extremely narrow, separating Sicily from Italy by a distance of three thousand paces. It is notorious for the fabulous monsters displayed on either side, Scylla and Charybdis.

### 4

[Note: [Col. 0487C] The inhabitants call it Scylla. Servius cites this from Sallustius in his commentary on “Scylla on the right-hand side,” *Aeneid* III.]

The inhabitants call Scylla a rock projecting over the sea, which from a distance appears to resemble the famous form.

[Col. 0487B]

Hence the stories also gave it a monstrous appearance, as though it had the shape of a human being girdled with dogs’ heads, because the waves breaking there seem to produce the sound of barking.

### 5

Charybdis was so called because it swallows ships with hidden whirlpools. It is a sea full of whirlpools, and there the wreckage torn apart by shipwrecks rises up from the depths.

[Note: [Col. 0487C] Where the wreckage of shipwrecks is torn apart. The ancient grammarian Fronto cites these same words, proving that Sallustius said that the wreckage “emerges.”]

Three times a day it raises the waves, and three times it swallows them.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] It raises the waves. He had in mind Virgil’s words, *Aeneid* III: “It sucks the waves into the abyss.”]

For it receives the waters in order to vomit them out, and vomits them in order to receive them again.

### 6

[Note: [Col. 0487D] The Syrtes are sandy places. From Servius on “and drive them into the savage shallows of the Syrtes,” *Aeneid* X.]

The Syrtes are sandy places in the sea.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] “The Syrtes,” according to Sallustius. In the *Jugurthine War*.]

Sallustius says that the Syrtes were named from their dragging action, because they draw everything toward themselves and make all things stick fast as the shallow sea approaches.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] And cling to everything approaching in the shallow sea.—That is, to everything. We have followed the Gothic manuscripts, for the printed editions have *appropinquantes* (“those approaching”) and *appropinquantia* (“things approaching”). The latter may have been the correct form.]

They lie near the Egyptian Sea and are joined to it.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Shallows. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “shallows and Syrtes.”]

Shallows are places through which people or animals walk on foot in the sea or in rivers. Virgil calls them *brevia*, while the Greeks call them *βραχεῖα*.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Lakes and Ponds

[Col. 0487C]

### 1

There are also certain seas that do not mingle with the waves of the Ocean or with the Great Sea; they are called lakes and ponds.

### 2

A lake is a receptacle in which water is retained and does not mingle with waves, such as the Asphalt Lake, Lake Benacus, Lake Larius, and the others that the Greeks call *λιμένες*, that is, ponds.

For springs flow into rivers, and rivers run into straits. A lake remains in one place and does not flow onward. It is called *lacus*, virtually “a place of water.”

### 3

[Note: [Col. 0487D] The Asphalt Lake. Hegesippus, book IV, chapter 18, and Josephus, *Jewish War* IV.]

The Asphalt Lake is also called the Dead Sea because it produces nothing living and receives nothing belonging to the class of living things.

For it has neither fish nor birds accustomed to the water and delighted by diving. Whatever living creatures one attempts to submerge in it, by whatever method they are sunk, immediately spring back up; however violently they are thrown into it, they are instantly cast out again.

Nor is it moved by winds, since the bitumen with which the whole water is made stagnant resists the whirlwinds. Nor does it permit navigation, because everything lacking life sinks into the depths and it supports no material except what is brightened with bitumen.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Except what is brightened with bitumen. Justin, book XXXVI: “Nor does it support any material except what is smeared with alum.” Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, has “coated with bitumen.” Since all the Gothic manuscripts have *illustratur* (“is brightened”), I suspect that Isidore wrote *incrustatur* (“is encrusted”).]

### 4

[Note: [Col. 0488C] A lighted lamp. The words are Jerome’s, in his letter to Dardanus.]

They say that a lighted lamp floats on its surface, but when its flame is extinguished it sinks.

[Col. 0488B]

This is also called the Salt Sea, or the Asphalt Lake—that is, the lake of bitumen—and it is in Judaea between Jericho and Zoara.

[Note: [Col. 0488C] Its length … five hundred and eighty stadia. We followed Hegesippus, from whom this passage derives, and Josephus, whom Hegesippus used, rather than the Isidorian manuscripts, which consistently read “seven hundred and eighty.”]

Its length extends to Zoara of Arabia for five hundred and eighty stadia; its width is one hundred and fifty stadia, reaching to the vicinity of Sodom …

### 5

Lake Tiberias was named from the town of Tiberias, which Herod once founded in honor of Tiberius Caesar.

It is the most healthful of all the lakes in Judaea and is in some way especially effective for the health of bodies.

Its circumference is … stadia.

### 6

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Genasar. From Hegesippus, book III, chapter 26. But Solinus read the passage as establishing three lakes in Judaea. The remaining authorities make Genasar, or Genesareth, identical with Tiberias. Jerome, in his letter to Dardanus: “The lake of Genesareth, which is now called Tiberias.” Bede, on the lake, chapter 5: “They say that the lake of Genesareth is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias.” Josephus, however, mentions only two lakes.]

Genasar, the largest lake in Judaea, extends for one hundred and forty stadia in length and spreads for forty stadia in width. Its waters ripple, generating a breeze not from the winds but from itself.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Generating a breeze, not wind—that is, producing it from itself. I did not think *excreans* (“producing”) should be rejected, although Hegesippus and Bede read *excitans* (“rousing”).]

Hence it is also called Genasar, a Greek expression meaning virtually “generating a breeze for itself.” Indeed, across the lake’s wider spaces it is stirred by frequent breezes that arise within it.

[Col. 0488C]

Hence its water is purer when drunk and is sweet and suitable for drinking.

### 7

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Benacus … imitates sea storms. Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> … and you, Benacus, rising  
> with waves and a roar like the sea.

See Servius on this passage.]

Benacus is a lake of Italy, in Venetia, from which the river Mincius rises. By its size, the lake imitates storms at sea.

### 8

The Lucrine and Avernian lakes are in Campania.

Lucrine was so called because formerly, on account of its abundance of fish, it provided a large revenue.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] The Avernian Lake. From Servius on “the divine lakes,” *Aeneid* III.]

The Avernian Lake was so called because birds could not fly over it. Formerly it was so surrounded by dense forests that the extremely foul odor of the sulfurous waters exhaling through narrow passages killed birds flying overhead with its breath.

When Augustus Caesar understood this, he felled the forests and transformed the pestilential region into a pleasant place.

### 9

A lake is also called a pond when an immense quantity of water gathers there. It is called *stagnum* because the water stands there and does not run away.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Abyss

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0489C] Abyss, depth. From Augustine, on Psalm XII.]

The abyss is an impenetrable depth of waters; or it is a cavern of hidden waters from which springs and rivers proceed; or it consists of waters lying secretly beneath.

[Col. 0489B]

Hence it is called the abyss.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] For all waters … to the mother abyss. From Jerome, on Ecclesiastes I. Plato calls this mother abyss Tartarus in the *Phaedo*.]

For all waters, whether torrents or otherwise, return through hidden channels to the mother abyss.

### 2

Waves are so called because they are made by blasts. For waters are agitated into waves by the force of the winds.

[Col. 0489D]

Water is stationary and level when it is without motion.

### 3

A wave, however, is a raised body of water that is always in motion.

Lucretius:

[Note: [Col. 0489D] “Aerial waves,” that is, motions. There should not be the slightest doubt about this reading; Isidore explains the nature of waves with great elegance. Virgil: “Where the thickest smoke drives the wave,” *Aeneid* VIII. Elsewhere:

> And it is pleasant to await Cythorus  
> undulating with boxwood.]

“Aerial waves”—that is, motions—and the body that surges back and forth.

For a wave is not water in itself, but water in a certain motion and agitation. It is called *unda*, as though from *eundo* and *redeundo*, “going” and “returning.”

### 4

[Note: [Col. 0489D] *Latex* properly means liquid. From Servius on “and the liquid of Lyaeus,” *Aeneid* I. In Servius the word does not mean a spring.]

*Latex* properly means the liquid of a spring. It is called *latex* because it lies hidden in the veins of the earth.

### 5

[Note: [Col. 0489D] A drop is what remains still. Jerome, in the *Chronicle*, under the year A.D. 50: “Palaemon,” he says, “a distinguished grammarian, was once asked what difference there was between a *gutta* and a *stilla*. ‘A *gutta* remains still,’ he replied, ‘while a *stilla* falls.’”]

A *gutta* is what remains still; a *stilla* is what falls.

[Note: [Col. 0489D] Hence also *stillicidium*. From Servius on “and frozen drops hang thickly,” with a difficult reading. Servius does not say that *stiria* is a Greek word. For this reason Chacon ordered that the Greek term be deleted. Glossary: *stiria*, “the hanging crystal of water.”]

Hence also *stillicidium*, virtually “a falling drop.” *Stiria* is Greek, meaning “a drop”; from it the diminutive is formed, so that we say *stilla*. When it remains still or hangs from roofs or trees, as though sticky, it is a *gutta*; when it has fallen, it is a *stilla*.

### 6

Foam is so called because it is spat out; for it is the dirt of waves. Hence must and cooked foods are cleansed of foam. From this also comes *sputum*, “spittle.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On Rivers

### 1

A river is a continuous flow of waters, perpetually named from flowing.

Properly speaking, *flumen* is the water itself, while *fluvius* is the course of the water. The *flumen* therefore comes before the *fluvius*: the water precedes the flowing.

There are two kinds of rivers: one is a torrent, the other a living river, of which Virgil says:

> Until I have washed myself in the living stream.

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0489D] A torrent. From Servius on “a torrent in the mountain stream,” *Aeneid* II.]

A torrent is water coming with force. It is called *torrens* because it grows through rain and, in drought, becomes dry—that is, it is parched.

[Note: [Col. 0490C] Concerning this, Pacuvius. Chacon correctly deletes the words “concerning this”; Pacuvius is not speaking about a torrent but about the sun. His verse is quoted to show that *torrere* means the same as “to become dry.” Pacuvius’ complete verse is found in Festus under *Torrens*: “The parching heat will burn up the produce of the earth,” which plainly refers to the sun according to Varro, *On Agriculture* I. Whether Varro intended to quote Pacuvius’ words or merely his meaning, we agree with Chacon, who thinks the words “or by night, or by cold” were added in Varro.]

Pacuvius:

> The parching heat will burn up the produce of the earth.

The Greeks gave it a name from winter; we derive ours from summer. They named it from the season in which it increases, we from the season in which it dries up.

### 3

An *amnis* is a river surrounded by woodland and foliage, and it is called *amnis* from this very pleasantness.

### 4

A *decursus* is properly the end of a course, whether the course is that of waters or of any other things.

[Col. 0490B]

Rivulets are so called because they are diverted for irrigation—that is, for introducing water into fields. For *irrigare* means “to introduce.”

A *gurges* is properly a deep place in a river.

### 5

A well is a place dug out, from which water is drawn. It is named from drinking.

A spring is the source of newly arising water, virtually “pouring out waters.”

### 6

Some rivers, however, received their names for particular reasons. Among them are several that should be noted because they are famous in histories.

### 7

Geon is the river flowing out of Paradise and encircling all Ethiopia. It received this name because, through the increase of its flooding, it irrigates the land of Egypt. For *γῆ* in Greek means “earth” in Latin.

[Col. 0490C]

Among the Egyptians it is called the Nile because of the mud that it carries, which produces fertility.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Hence it was also called the Nile. From Servius on “the Nile with its fertile stream,” *Aeneid* IX.]

Hence it was also called the Nile, virtually “carrying new matter,” *νέαν ὕλην*.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] For previously the Nile was called Melo. From the same source, *Aeneid* IV, on “cloudy, and now already flying upward.”]

Previously the Nile was called *Melo* in Latin.

It appears in Lake Nilides, from which, flowing southward, it is received by Egypt. There, beaten back by the northern winds, it swells with waters struggling backward and produces the flooding of Egypt.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] From which it turns southward. From Solinus, chapter on Egypt. In Isidore, “into the Egyptian Sea” may perhaps have to be restored instead of “into Egypt,” and “struggling in a narrow passage” instead of “struggling backward.”]

### 8

The river Ganges, which sacred Scripture calls Phison, flows out of Paradise and proceeds toward the regions of India.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Phison, that is, “multitude.” From Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*.]

It was called Phison, that is, “multitude,” because it is filled by fifteen great rivers joining it and becomes one river.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Because of fifteen rivers. The same number is counted by Arrian, book V, *On Alexander*, but Pliny, book VI, chapter 18, counts nineteen. All the manuscripts read “because of ten,” but the similarity of repeated syllables plainly deceived the copyists.]

The Ganges was named from Ganges, a king of India.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] From King Ganges. Suidas and Plutarch, in their book on rivers, also call Ganges a king. All the manuscripts incorrectly read “from King Gangarus.”]

It is said to rise like the Nile and to burst forth over the lands of the East.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] To rise. The Solinus manuscript also has *exaltari* (“to rise”), not *exundare* (“to overflow”), as the printed edition reads.]

### 9

The Tigris is a river of Mesopotamia, rising from Paradise, proceeding toward the Assyrians, and, after many windings, flowing into the Dead Sea.

It received this name because of its swiftness, running with the extraordinary speed of a wild beast.

### 10

The Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia, rising from Paradise and extremely rich in gems. It flows through the middle of Babylonia.

It received its name from crops or from fertility.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] For in Hebrew *Ephrata* means fertility. I write this on the authority of Jerome, not *Euphrata*, a word that does not exist among the Hebrews. Rather, it is *perath*, that is, Euphrates; *peri* means “fruit.”]

For in Hebrew *EPHRATA* is interpreted as “fertility.” In some places it irrigates Mesopotamia just as the Nile irrigates Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 0491D] But Sallustius … most authoritative. Jerome, in *On Hebrew Places*: “Moreover, Sallustius, a most reliable authority, asserts that the sources of both the Tigris and the Euphrates are shown in Armenia.” Isidore therefore read Jerome’s passage differently. See the book of Vibius Sequester on rivers; Strabo indeed reports different sources for the two rivers.]

Sallustius, however, a most reliable authority, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one source in Armenia; then, proceeding in different directions, they diverge farther apart, leaving an interval of many thousands between them. Nevertheless, the land enclosed by them is called Mesopotamia.

From this Jerome observed that the rivers of Paradise must be understood differently.

### 11

The Indus is a river of the East, which empties into the Red Sea.

### 12

Hydaspes was a very ancient king of the Medes, from whom the eastern river received its name. It is now called Hydaspes, concerning which Lucan writes:

> The Indus, with its vast waters, does not feel the mingled Hydaspes.

And:

> Where the Median Hydaspes approaches the sea  
> from the fire of the rising Phoebus.

[Col. 0491C]

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Although it is a river of the Persians, it is said to flow toward the East. Lucan wrote this not of the Hydaspes but of the Ganges, book III:

> The fame of war stirs the retreats of the East,  
> where the Ganges is worshiped, alone in all the world,  
> daring to open its mouths opposite the rising Phoebus  
> and driving its waves against the East.

These verses, which are read in the printed books of Lucan, are absent from the Gothic manuscripts.]

Although it is a river of the Persians, it is nevertheless said to flow toward the East.

### 13

[Note: [Col. 0491D] The Arar, a river of Germany. From Servius, *Eclogue* 1. The words found in the printed editions and in some manuscripts—“For it runs through Parthia and Assyria”—we preferred to delete, since they were absent from most manuscripts, rather than attach them to the Tigris, as Vulcanius did.]

The Arar is a river of Germany. Virgil says of it:

> Either the Parthian will drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris.

### 14

The Bactrus is a river of the East, said to have been named from King Bactrus. From it came the Bactrians and their city.

[Note: [Col. 0492C] From King Bactrus. Josephus makes not Bactrus but Cetrus, son of Aram, the first founder of the Bactrians.]

### 15

Choaspes is a river of the Persians. It was called by that name in their language because its water has extraordinary sweetness, so much so that the Persian kings, as long as it flows between the banks of Persia, appropriated its water for their own drinking.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] So much so that the kings. From Solinus, chapter on Cilicia.]

Some believe that the Cilician river Cydnus is derived from this river.

### 16

The Araxes is a river of Armenia, rising from the same mountain as the Euphrates but with a different appearance. It was so called because by its violence it throws everything down.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Hence also when Alexander … Curtius mentions the bridge, book V, but not the flooding. Servius likewise reports an attempt by Xerxes, commenting on “Araxes, indignant at the bridge,” *Aeneid* VIII.]

Hence, when Alexander wished to cross it, he built a bridge, but the river swelled with such force that it destroyed the bridge.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] It raises its head at short intervals … into the sea. From Solinus, chapter 25.]
