It raises its head at short intervals from the source of the Euphrates and is then said to carry its waters into the Caspian Sea.

### 17

The Syrian river called the Orontes runs beside the walls of Antioch. Rising in the east, it is buried in the sea not far from the city.

The ancients called it Orontes in Latin from the course of its source. Because its waters are made cooler by their own rushing force and because the west winds continually blow there, almost the entire city is cooled at nearly every moment.

### 18

[Note: [Col. 0492D] The Jordan, a river of Judaea. Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*.]

The Jordan is a river of Judaea, named from two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan. When these, although far apart, are joined together in one channel, the river is thereafter called the Jordan.

It rises beneath Mount Lebanon and divides Judaea from Arabia. After many windings, it flows near Jericho into the Dead Sea.

### 19

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Phasis. These are the words of Ambrose, *Hexameron* II, chapter 3. All the manuscripts had *Eusis* until Chacon restored the text by identifying Ambrose’s passage.]

The Phasis, issuing from the Caucasian mountains, plunges with several other rivers into the Euxine Sea.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Hence it is also called so. We delete this sentence with Chacon.]

### 20

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Cydnus. From Solinus.]

The Cydnus is a river of Cilicia, flowing down from Mount Taurus. Its waters have remarkable sweetness, and in the language of the Syrians everything white is called *cydnus*.

[Col. 0492C]

Hence the river received this name, because it swells in summer when the snows melt; during the rest of the year it is small and quiet.

### 21

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Hylas, a river of Asia. See Solinus, chapter on Bithynia, and Pliny, book V, chapter 32.]

Hylas is a river of Asia.

The Pactolus is a river of Asia, carrying golden sands. Virgil says of it:

> And the Pactolus waters with gold.

Because of its golden flow, others call it Chrysorrhoas, “Gold-flowing.”

22. [Note: [Col. 0492D] Hermus. Pliny, book V, chapter 29: “From Smyrna the river Hermus makes plains and adopts them into its own name.” But this is rather from Solinus.] Hermus, a river of Asia, which cuts through the plains of Smyrna [Col. 0493A] and is itself full of golden waves and sands, [Note: [Col. 0493D] From which Smyrna was named. Is this because of Pliny’s statement: “and adopts them into its own name”? Yet the same Pliny, following Herodotus, says that the city of Smyrna was named after Smyrna the Amazon.] from which Smyrna was named.

23. The Maeander, a winding river of Asia, which, with its banks turning back upon themselves, flows between Caria and Ionia and plunges into the gulf that divides Miletus and Priene. It was called Maeander because it is winding and never runs straight. Concerning it Ovid says:

> And the Maeander, bending back, plays among the waves.

24. Tanus was the first king of the Scythians, from whom the river Tanais is said to have received its name. Coming from the Rhipaean forests, it separates Europe from Asia, running midway between the two parts of the world and flowing into the Pontus.

25. [Note: [Col. 0493D] Inachus … gave. These are the words of Solinus, in the chapter on Greece.] Inachus, a river of Achaia, watering the Argolic plains, which King Inachus named after himself and who first gave an origin [Col. 0493B] to the Argive people. There too is the Erimanthus, descending from Mount Erimanthus.

26. The Po, a river of Italy, poured forth from the ridges of the Alps, rises from three springs, one of which is called the Po. Spread out in the form of a pond, [Note: [Col. 0493D] “Directs the river into a hollow.” *Digerit* in the old manuscript. One Roman manuscript has *arinem sinum*.] it directs the river into a bay, from which the Po also received its name. By the Greeks it is called the Eridanus, after Eridanus, the son of the Sun, whom they call Phaethon; struck by lightning, he was cast into this same river and perished. [Note: [Col. 0493D] “It is increased … is carried.” From Solinus, in the chapter on Italy.] It is increased at the rising of the Dog Star, when the snows melt, and, with the addition of thirty rivers around Ravenna, is carried into the Adriatic Sea.

27. The Tiber, a river of Italy, is said to have been named after Tiberinus, king of the Albans, who fell into this river and gave it his name upon his death. Formerly it had the ancient name Albula from its color, [Col. 0493C] [Note: [Col. 0493D] “Because it is white with snows.” These words appear to be Chacon’s interpolation.] because it is white with snows. [Note: [Col. 0493D] “It is itself the Tibris.” From Servius, on the verse “And you, O Tiber,” *Aeneid* VIII.] It is in fact Tibris, also called Tiberis; but Tiberis is used in ordinary speech, while Tibris is used in verse.

28. [Note: [Col. 0493D] Danube, from the abundance of clouds. On the etymology of the Danube, see Stephanus, who reports that it was first called *matóan*, that is, *aísion*, “fortunate,” and then *danoubin* or *danousin*, named by the Scythians from adverse fortune.] The Danube, a river of Germany, is said to be called so because of the abundance of snows, by which it is especially increased. This is the river that enjoys greater renown than all others in Europe. It is also called the Ister, because as it travels through innumerable peoples it changes its name, and by winding around itself gathers greater strength. It rises in the German mountains and [Note: [Col. 0493D] “And from the western regions of the barbarians.” Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* II, chapter 3, has it somewhat differently: “The Danube from the western regions of the barbarians, cutting across the Roman peoples, until it is itself swallowed by the Pontus.”] from the western regions of the barbarians, proceeds toward the East, receives sixty rivers into itself, and flows through seven mouths into the Pontus.

29. The Rhône, a river of Gaul, was named after the town of Rhoda, which settlers from Rhodes established. [Col. 0494A] [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Which, driven on by a swift current.” From Ambrose, except that in his text it is said that it brings no small danger to sailors.] Driven on by a swift current, it cuts through the waters of the Tyrrhenian sea and often creates no small danger for sailors, while the waves of the sea and the stream of the river contend with one another.

30. The Rhine is said to have been named from its association with the Rhône, since it rises with it in one province. It is a river of Germany, counted among the three greatest rivers of Europe, [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Which from the ridge of the Alps.” From the same source.] directing its course from the ridge of the Alps into the depths of the Ocean.

31. The Iberus, a river that once gave its name to all Spain.

32. The river Minius in Galicia took its name from the color of the pigment, which is found in it in great abundance.

33. [Note: [Col. 0494D] *Durius.* Some books have *Dorius*.] Durius, as though from the Greek, “Doric.”

[Note: [Col. 0494D] “Called Tagus … Carthage of Spain.” I consider the claim that it was named after King Tagus from the fictitious Berossus no more certain.] Carthage of Spain named the river Tagus, [Col. 0494B] from which it arose and proceeded. It is a river rich in gold-bearing sands and for this reason preferred above the other rivers of Spain.

34. The Baetis, a river that also gave its name to the province of Baetica, concerning which Martial writes: 140

> Baetis, wreathed in your hair with an olive-bearing golden crown,  
> you who dye fleeces in your shining waters.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] “Because wool is there …” Pliny, book VIII, chapter 48.] because wool is dyed there in a beautiful color. The Baetis was so called because it runs through low-lying ground. The Greeks call *bathý* [βαθύ] “low” or “submerged.” [Note: [Col. 0494D] The Greeks indeed use *bathý*. Or *bythón* [βυθόν], Gothic *bytin*.]

35. Some rivers, having been released in the Flood, were blocked by masses of earth; others, which had not existed before, burst forth when the channels of the abyss were broken open.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Floods

[Col. 0494C]

1. A flood is so called because, through the destruction caused by water, it destroys everything over which it has spread.

2. The first flood occurred in the time of Noah, when the Almighty, offended by the crimes of humanity, covered the whole world, destroyed everything, and left only one expanse of sky and sea. To this day we see evidence of it in stones that we commonly observe in remote mountains, concreted with shells and oysters, and often hollowed out by the waters. [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Often rough and hollowed out.” Orosius has: “Often rough and excavated.”]

3. [Note: [Col. 0494D] The second flood. Orosius, chapter 7.] The second flood occurred in Achaia, in the time of the patriarch Jacob and of Ogyges, who was the founder and king of Eleusis and gave his name to the place and the period.

4. [Note: [Col. 0494D] The third. The same source, chapter 9, which drew from Justin, book II.] The third flood occurred in Thessaly, in the time of Moses—or of Amphictyon, who reigned third [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Who reigned after Cecrops.” Orosius adds: “at Athens.”] after Cecrops. [Col. 0495A] In his time the inundation of the waters consumed most of the peoples of Thessaly; a few were saved by fleeing to the mountains, especially Mount Parnassus, in whose region Deucalion then held royal power. He received, cherished, and fed those who fled to him on rafts, through the twin ridges of Parnassus. Hence, according to Greek mythology, the human race was afterward restored from stones, on account of the innate hardness of the human heart.

5. Rivers too, when swollen beyond their customary amount, duration, or size by unusual rains, overflow, overthrow many things, and are themselves called floods. It should be understood, however, that when rivers rise beyond measure they not only bring immediate damage but also signify certain future events.

# BOOK FOURTEEN, ON THE EARTH AND ITS PARTS

[Col. 0495]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Earth

[Col. 0495B]

1. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “The earth is in the middle.” Hyginus, book I, *On Astronomy*, final chapter: “The earth, placed in the middle region of the universe and separated from all its parts by an equal interval, occupies the center of the sphere.”] The earth is placed in the central region of the universe, standing at an equal distance from all parts of the sky in the manner of a center. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Which in the singular number signifies the whole world.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “And I returned through the midst of the enemy”; likewise on “I have entered so many seas.”] In the singular number it signifies the whole world; in the plural, its individual parts. Its names vary according to the reason for which they are given. For it is called *terra* from the upper part, where it is trodden; *humus* from the lower part, as though “moist,” beneath the sea; and *tellus* because we take up its fruits. It is also called *ops*, because it brings aid to crops. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “The same is also *arva*.” Varro, book 4: “*Arvum* and *arationes* come from *arare*, ‘to plow.’”] It is also called *arva*, from plowing and cultivating.

2. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Properly, however, the earth.” From Ambrose, book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 4; in his text the word “water” does not occur.] Properly speaking, the earth, to distinguish it from water, is called dry land, just as Scripture says that God called the earth dry. For dryness is the natural property of the earth; that it is moist, it derives from its association with water. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Some say that its movement … until ‘they shake.’” From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “By what force the deep seas swell.” But since Sallustius is also cited here by Servius, it does not seem plausible to me that Sallustius wrote a half-line together with a complete hexameter. Another author must therefore be sought for those words. In place of *genitalem*, all the books of Isidore’s tradition had *generalem*.] Some say that its movement is wind in its hollows, and that this movement shakes it. Sallustius says: “Winds driven headlong through the cavities of the earth burst apart certain mountains, and the hillocks settle.”

3. Others say that generative water moves within the earth and [Note: [Col. 0496D] “And shakes them like a vessel,” as Lucretius says in book VI:

> So that a vessel cannot stand upon the earth  
> Unless the moisture within has ceased  
> To be tossed about in uncertain fluctuation.

] shakes them at the same time, like a vessel, as Lucretius says. Others believe the earth to be *spongo-eidēs* [σπογγοειδῆ], “sponge-like,” whose usually hidden collapses shake everything placed above them. [Note: [Col. 0496D] “The fissures of the earth,” through the end. From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “Just as if the earth were deeply shaken by some force.”] The fissures of the earth likewise arise either from the movement of the water below, from frequent thunder, or from winds bursting forth from the hollows of the earth.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the World

1. The world is called *orbis* from the roundness of a circle, because it is like a wheel; hence a small wheel is also called an *orbiculus*. [Col. 0495D] For the Ocean, flowing around it on every side, surrounds its boundaries in a circle. It is divided into three parts: one is called Asia, another Europe, and the third Africa.

2. The ancients did not divide these three parts of the world equally. Asia extends from the South through the East as far as the North. Europe extends from the North to the West, and from there Africa extends from the West to the South. [Col. 0496B]

3. Thus it is clear that Europe and Africa together possess one half of the world, 143 while Asia alone possesses the other half. But these two parts were made [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Because between the two, from the Ocean, the Great Sea enters.” Here the Great Sea is plainly called the Mediterranean Sea.] because the Great Sea enters between them from the Ocean and cuts them apart. Therefore, if you divide the world into the two parts of East and West, Asia will be in one, and Europe and Africa in the other.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Asia

1. Asia was named after a certain woman who held dominion over the East among the ancients. Situated in the third part of the world, it is bounded on the East by the rising of the sun, on the South by the Ocean, on the West by our sea, and on the North by Lake Maeotis and the river Tanais. It has many provinces and regions, whose names and locations I shall briefly explain, beginning with Paradise.

2. Paradise is a place established in the eastern regions, whose name is translated from Greek into Latin as “garden”; in Hebrew it is called *Eden*, which in our language is interpreted as “delight.” Joined together, these two terms produce “garden of delight.” For it is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree, and also contains the tree of life. There is neither cold nor heat there, but a perpetual temperateness of spring.

3. From its midst a spring bursts forth, watering the entire grove, and is divided into four rivers that arise from it. Access to this place was closed to humanity after the sin. For it is enclosed on every side by a flaming sword, that is, girded with a wall of fire, so that its blaze is almost joined with the sky. [Col. 0496D] [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Almost joins it.” The Gothic manuscripts have *jungat*, “joins.”]

144 4. The Cherubim also—that is, a guard of angels—were stationed above the blazing sword to drive away evil spirits, so that the angels might repel human beings from the flame, and good angels might repel the evil ones, lest access to Paradise be open to any flesh or spirit of transgression. [Col. 0497A]

5. India was named from the river Indus, by which it is enclosed on its western side. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “This extends from the southern sea.” From Solinus, chapter 55.] It extends from the southern sea to the rising of the sun, and from the North reaches as far as Mount Caucasus. It contains many peoples and towns, as well as the island of Taprobane, filled with elephants; Chryse and Argyre, rich in gold and silver; [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Tylen as well.” On this below, chapter 6. See Theophrastus, Pliny, and Solinus.] and Tylen, whose trees never lose their leaves.

6. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “It also has rivers.” From the same Solinus, from whom we have substituted *Indus* for *Nidus* and *Hypasis* for *Hypanis*.] It also has the rivers Ganges, Indus, and Hypasis, which make the Indians famous. The land of India is made very healthy by the breath of the west wind and harvests its crops twice a year; instead of winter [Note: [Col. 0497D] “It enjoys the Etesian winds.” These are Solinus’s words.] it has the Etesian winds. It produces people of a dark complexion, enormous elephants, the one-horned beast, the parrot, ebony, cinnamon, pepper, [Col. 0497B] and aromatic reed.

7. It also sends forth ivory and precious stones—beryls, chrysoprases, diamonds, carbuncles, lychnites, pearls, and large pearls—which kindle the ambition of noble women. There are also mountains of gold there, which it is impossible to approach because of dragons, griffins, and monsters of enormous human size.

8. Parthia is generally named from the borders of India as far as Mesopotamia. 145 Because of the unconquered valor of the Parthians, Assyria and the other neighboring regions also passed into its name. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “In it are Arachosia … Arbela.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] For it contains Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Media, and Persia. These regions, joined together along their borders, begin at the river Indus and are closed by the Tigris. They are situated in mountainous and rugged places and have the rivers Hydaspes and Arbelus. [Col. 0497C] They are separated from one another by their boundaries and derive their names from their respective founders.

9. Arachosia was named after its town.

The Parthians, coming from Scythia, occupied Parthia and called it by their own name. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “To the north, the Hyrcanian forest.” From Solinus, chapter 59, on Parthia. Camertes read it this way, and so it appears in the manuscripts of the Church of Toledo, unless one prefers *Hyrcanian forests*, which Solinus mentions more than once. Isidore mentions the Hyrcanian forests above, book IX, chapter 2.] To the south it has the Red Sea, to the north the Hyrcanian Sea, and to the west Media. It contains eighteen kingdoms, extending from the Caspian shore as far as the lands of the Scythians.

10. Assyria was named after Assur, son of Shem, who first inhabited that region after the Flood. On the East it touches India, on the South Media, on the West the Tigris, and on the North Mount Caucasus, where the Caspian Gates are. In this region the use of purple was first discovered; from there also first came ointments for hair and body, and fragrances through which the luxury of the Romans and Greeks overflowed.

[Col. 0498A] 11. Media and Persia were named after the kings Medus and Perses, who attacked these provinces in war. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Of these, Media.” From Solinus, in the same place.] Of these, Media embraces the Parthian kingdoms transversely from the West; it is surrounded on the North by Armenia, looks toward the Caspian Sea on the East, and borders Persia on the South. Its land produces the medicinal tree, which no other region produces. There are two Medias, Greater and Lesser.

146 12. Persia extends from the East as far as the Indians. On the West it has the Red Sea; on the North it touches Media; and on the South Carmania, which is joined to Persia. Susa is its most celebrated town. In Persia the magical art first arose. After the confusion of languages, the giant Nimrod went to it, and there taught the Persians to worship fire. For all the peoples of those regions worship the sun, [Col. 0498B] which in their language is called *El*. [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Which in their language is called El.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Drawn through so many men,” etc.]

13. Mesopotamia has a Greek etymology, because it is surrounded by two rivers. For on the East it has the Tigris, and on the West the Euphrates. [Note: [Col. 0498D] “It begins in the North.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] It begins in the North between Mount Taurus and Mount Caucasus. To its South lies Babylonia, then Chaldea, and finally Arabia *Eudaimon* [εὐδαίμων], “fortunate.”

14. The chief city of the region of Babylonia is Babylon, from which the region was named. It was so famous that Chaldea, Assyria, and Mesopotamia sometimes passed into its name.

15. Arabia was so called, that is, “sacred.” [Note: [Col. 0498D] “This is what the interpretation signifies.” From Solinus, chapter 36.] This is what the name is interpreted to mean, because it is a region bearing incense and producing fragrances. Hence the Greeks called it *Eudaimon* [εὐδαίμων], and our people called it “blessed.” Myrrh and cinnamon grow in its forests; the phoenix is born there; and sardonyx, iris, malachite, and *paederotes* are found there. [Col. 0498C] [Note: [Col. 0498D] “It is also called Sheba.” Josephus, book I, *Antiquities*.] It is also called Sheba, after the son of Cush, who was named Sheba. [Note: [Col. 0498D] “This, by a narrow strip of land … the Arabian Gulf.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] It extends eastward by a narrow strip of land toward the Persian Gulf; Chaldea closes it on the North, and the Arabian Gulf on the West.

147 16. A certain Syrian is said to have named Syria, an indigenous inhabitant, after himself. [Note: [Col. 0498D] “On the East, the Nabataeans.” From the same chapter.] It is bounded on the East by the river Euphrates, and on the West by our sea and Egypt; it touches Armenia and Cappadocia on the North, and the Arabian Gulf on the South. Its position stretches to immense length but is narrower in breadth.

17. It contains the provinces of Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, of which Judaea is a part, apart from the Saracens and Nabataeans. Commagene, the first province of Syria, [Col. 0498D] [Note: [Col. 0498D] “From the name of the city Commagene.” The old Roman manuscript has: “from the name by which the city was called, which once …” Thus the city was called Gommagene, not Commage, or Commagene.] was named after the city of Commagene, which was once regarded as the metropolis there. [Col. 0499A] It has Armenia on the North, [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Armenia on the North.” So the old books read, not Cappadocia; Ptolemy also confirms this in table 6 of his *Geography of Asia*, as does Juvenal in satire 6, where he joins the Armenian and Commagenian soothsayers.] Mesopotamia on the East, Syria on the South, and the Great Sea on the West.

18. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Phoenix, brother of Cadmus. Above, book IX, chapter 2, from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius.] Phoenix, the brother of Cadmus, went from Egyptian Thebes to Syria and reigned at Sidon. He called that province Phoenicia after his own name. It is the region where Tyre is situated, the city to which Isaiah speaks. It has Arabia on the East and the Red Sea on the South.

19. Palestine had the city of Philistin as its metropolis; it is now called Ascalon. From that city the whole surrounding region was named Palestine. On the East it meets the Red Sea; on the southern side it is bordered by Judaea; on the North it is closed by the territory of the Tyrians; and on the West it ends at the Egyptian frontier.

[Col. 0499B] 20. Judaea, a region of Palestine, was named after Judah, from whose tribe it had its kings. It was formerly called Chanaan, after the son of Ham, or after the ten nations of the Canaanites; after these had been expelled, the Jews possessed the same land. [Note: [Col. 0499D] “The beginning of its length … the regions of the whole.” From Hegesippus, book III, chapter 6. “Rich in waters.” From Solinus, chapter 33.] Its length begins at the village of Arfa and extends as far as the village of Juliadis, where Jews and Tyrians share a common settlement. Its breadth extends from Mount Lebanon as far as the Lake of Tiberias.

21. In the middle of Judaea lies the city of Jerusalem, as though the navel of the whole region. The land is rich in various resources, fertile in crops, renowned for its waters, and abundant in balsam. [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Hence, according to the excellence of the elements … promised.” This is from Hegesippus, in the same chapter, concerning Samaria.] Therefore the Jews, considering the excellence of its natural elements, believed it to be the land promised to their ancestors, a land flowing with milk and honey, since God was thereby promising them the privilege of resurrection.

22. [Note: [Col. 0499D] Samaria. From Jerome, on Hosea, chapter XIV.] Samaria, a region of Palestine, took its name from a certain town called Samaria, once the royal city in Israel, which is now called Sebastia after the name of Augustus. This region lies between Judaea and Galilee, beginning [Note: [Col. 0499D] “At a village called Eleas.” Hegesippus, in the same place.] at a village called Eleas and ending in the land of Agrabat. Its situation is naturally similar and differs in no respect from Judaea.

23. [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Galilee … because they produce whiter people.” A Greek etymology, although the word is Hebrew.] Galilee, a region of Palestine, was so called because it produces people whiter than those of Palestine. [Note: [Col. 0499D] “It is twofold … fertile.” In the same place, Hegesippus.] It is twofold, Upper and Lower, though the two are connected and adjoin Syria and Phoenicia. Their land is rich and productive, and sufficiently fertile in fruits.

24. The Pentapolis is a region situated on the border of Arabia and Palestine. It was named from the five cities of the wicked, [Col. 0499D] which were consumed by heavenly fire. The land, once exceedingly fertile beyond Jerusalem, [Col. 0500A] [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Now completely deserted.” From Hegesippus, book IV, chapter 18; Solinus, chapter 35; and Augustine, book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 5.] is now deserted and burned out. 149 For on account of the crime of its inhabitants, fire descended from heaven and dissolved that region into eternal ashes.

25. A kind of shadow and appearance of it can still be seen in the ashes and even in the trees themselves. Fruits grow there, green beneath such an appearance of ripeness that they arouse the desire to eat them. If you pluck them, they split open and dissolve into ash, exhaling smoke as though they were still burning.

26. [Note: [Col. 0500D] Nabataea. Above, book IX, chapter 2, and Jerome, *Hebrew Questions* on Genesis, chapter 25.] Nabataea was named after Nabath, the son of Ishmael. It lies between Judaea and Arabia, rising from the Euphrates and extending to the Red Sea; it is a part of Arabia.

27. [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Egypt … received its name.” Above, book IX, chapter 2, and Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*.] Egypt, formerly called Aeria, received its name from Aegyptus, the brother of Danaus, who later reigned there. [Col. 0500B] [Note: [Col. 0500D] “It has Syria on the East.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] On the East it is joined to Syria and the Red Sea; on the West it has Libya; on the North the Great Sea; [Note: [Col. 0500D] “On the South.” Solinus, chapter 33.] on the South it recedes inland and extends as far as the Ethiopians. It is a region unaccustomed to the rains of heaven and ignorant of rainfall.

28. The Nile alone, flowing around it, irrigates it and makes it fertile by its inundation. [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Hence fertile … in lands.” From Hegesippus, book IV, chapter 27.] Hence it is fertile in crops and supplies a large part of the lands with grain. It is also so abundant in other commodities that it fills the whole world with necessary merchandise. Egypt’s boundary is the Canopic island, named after Canopus, Menelaus’ pilot, who was buried on that island; it forms the beginning of Libya and the mouth of the Nile.

150 29. Seres is a town of the East, from which both the Seric people and the region received their names. [Col. 0500C] [Note: [Col. 0500D] “This extends from the Scythian Ocean.” The entire passage is from Solinus, chapter 33. We supplied two words that exclude the meaning of “trade,” since in the old manuscript the reading is *caeterarum gentium commercia abnuentes*, not *caeteris gentibus*, as some have published.] It bends from the Scythian Ocean and the Caspian Sea toward the Eastern Ocean. It is fertile in noble foliage, from which fleeces are plucked; the Seres, who reject commercial dealings with other nations, sell these for use as clothing.

30. The river Bactrus, native to the region of Bactria, gave it its name. [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Its parts that lie behind.” Others read “sloping” or “level.” See Solinus and Pliny, book VI, chapter 16.] Its rearward parts are surrounded by the ridges of the Paropamisus; its forward parts are bounded by the sources of the river Indus. The remaining side is enclosed by the river Ochus. Bactria sends forth exceedingly strong camels whose feet are never worn down.

31. Scythia, like Gothia, is said to have been named after Magog, son of Japheth. Its land was once immense, extending from India in the East, and from the northern Maeotian marshes between the Danube and the Ocean as far as the borders of Germany. Later, when it had become smaller, [Col. 0501A] [Note: [Col. 0501C] “From the right-hand side of the East … wandering.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] it extended on the eastern side, where the Seric Ocean stretches, as far as the Caspian Sea, which lies to the West. From there it was drawn southward as far as the ridge of the Caucasus. Hyrcania lies beneath it; on the West it likewise has many peoples wandering widely because of the barrenness of the land.

32. Some of these peoples inhabit fields; others, monstrous and savage, live on human flesh and the blood of human beings. [Note: [Col. 0501C] “Many lands of Scythia … rare.” From Solinus, chapter 20.] Many lands of Scythia are rich, but still more are uninhabitable. For although in most places they abound in gold and gems, because of the ferocity of the griffins human access is rare. This land is especially rich in excellent emeralds. The blue stone and the purest crystal also belong to Scythia. It has great rivers as well: the Moschorus, [Note: [Col. 0501C] “Moschorus, Phasis, Araxes …” Solinus has: “The mountains of the Heniochi pour forth the Araxes, the Moschorus, and the Phasis.” All Isidore’s books have *Oscorum*.] the Phasis, [Col. 0501B] and the Araxes.

33. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Hyrcania, named from the Hyrcanian forest. The same source above, book IX, chapter 2, from Servius, *Aeneid* VII.] Hyrcania was named from the Hyrcanian forest, which lies beneath Scythia. It has the Caspian Sea on the East, Armenia on the South, Albania on the North, and Iberia on the West. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “It is a forest rough …” Solinus, chapter 21.] It is harsh with forests and abounds in huge wild beasts—tigers, panthers, and leopards. Of it Virgil says:

> And the Hyrcanian tigresses pressed forward their udders.

34. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Albania, named from the color of its people. Perhaps from their hair.] Albania was named from the color of its people, because they are born with white hair. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “This rises in the East.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] Rising in the East beneath the Caspian Sea, it extends along the shore of the northern Ocean [Note: [Col. 0501D] “As far as the Maeotian marshes.” Orosius has: “as far as the river Tanais and the Maeotian marshes.”] through deserts and uncultivated lands as far as the Maeotian marshes. This land has enormous dogs of such ferocity [Note: [Col. 0501D] “That they overpower bulls and kill lions.” Solinus: “Among the Albanians, dogs born there are preferred to all wild beasts; they break bulls and kill lions.” From this, Chacon preferred *frangant*, “that they break.”] that they overpower bulls and kill lions.

35. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Armenia was named. Above, book IX, chapter 2, and Justin, book XLII.] Armenia was named after Armenus, a companion of Jason of Thessaly. After losing King Jason, Armenus gathered his scattered multitude, founded Armenia, and named it after himself. It lies between Taurus and Caucasus and extends from Cappadocia to the Caspian Sea. To the North it has the Ceraunian Mountains, from whose hills the river Tigris rises; and in whose mountains the ark is said to have come to rest after the Flood. Armenia is twofold, Upper and Lower, just as there are two Pannonias.

36. Hiberia is a region of Asia, joined to Armenia near the Pontus. Useful plants for dyeing grow there.

[Col. 0502A] 37. Cappadocia was named after its own city. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “This is situated at the head of Syria … Cyprus.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2. Orosius drew from Sallustius, whom Servius cites in *Aeneid* XI, on “Such as the Thracian …”] It is situated at the head of Syria. On the East it touches Armenia; on the West, Asia Minor; on the North, the Cimmerian Sea and the Themiscyran plains, which the Amazons possessed; and on the South, Mount Taurus, beneath which lie Cilicia and Isauria as far as the Gulf of Cilicia, which faces the island of Cyprus. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Its land, before all others, is a nurse of horses.” From Solinus, chapter 57.] Its land, before all others, is a nurse of horses. The river Halys flows through it; it once separated the kingdoms of Lydia from the Persians.

38. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Asia Minor … the sea.” From Orosius, book I, chapter 2. In his text Cappadocia is said to be “touched,” not “surrounded,” as in Isidore’s books.] Asia Minor is touched by Cappadocia on the East and is surrounded on every other side by the sea. For on the North it has the Euxine Pontus, on the West the Propontis, and on the South the Egyptian Sea. It has the provinces of Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycia, and [Col. 0502B] Cilicia.

39. Bithynia is the first province of Asia Minor, lying at the beginning of the Pontus toward the rising of the sun and opposite Thrace. It was formerly called by many names. [Note: [Col. 0502C] “For it was first Bebrycia.” Solinus, chapter 44.] First it was called Bebrycia, then Mygdonia, and afterward Bithynia, after King Bithynus. It is also Greater Phrygia. [Note: [Col. 0502C] “It is also Greater Phrygia.” From Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “Bebrycia came,” where Sallustius says: “Thus, within, the first province of Asia is Bithynia, formerly called by many names; it is also Greater Phrygia.”] The city of Nicomedia is in it, 153 where [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Hannibal … breathed out his life.” *Expulit* in Solinus, chapter 44; *exhalavit* in the manuscript of Margarinus.] Hannibal, fleeing, breathed out his life by drinking poison.

40. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Galatia. From Solinus, chapter 43, or from Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*, based on Acts.] Galatia was named after the ancient peoples of the Gauls, by whom it was occupied. [Note: [Col. 0502D] “For the Gauls.” From Justin, book XXV, and the book *On Hebrew Places*, based on the Acts of the Apostles, among Jerome’s works.] For the Gauls, summoned by the king of Bithynia as auxiliaries, divided the kingdom with him after victory had been agreed upon. Thus, having afterward been mingled with the Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks; now, from the ancient name of the Gauls, they are called Galatians, and their region is called Galatia.

41. [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Phrygia … daughter of Aesop.” So the old books read, as does Messalla Corvinus in his book *On the Lineage of Augustus*.] Phrygia was named after Phrygia, the daughter of Aesop. [Note: [Col. 0502D] “This is also Dardania.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] It was also called Dardania after Dardanus, the son of Jupiter. Concerning him Homer says:

> Whom Jupiter first begot in the heavenly citadel.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] “For he came forth from the city of Corythus.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III, on verse 170: “Corythus and the lands …”; and Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, concerning Dardanus: “From here he came forth from Corythus.”] For he first came to Phrygia after departing from the city of Corythus. It is a region [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Placed above the Troad.” From Solinus, chapter 43, on Asia Minor.] lying above the Troad. On the northern side it borders Galatia; on the southern side it is adjacent to Lycaonia; on the East it adjoins Lydia; and on the West it is bounded by the Hellespont. [Note: [Col. 0502D] “This region is Troy.” From Servius, *Georgics* III, on “And Tros, the father.”] Troy is in this region, named after Tros, king of the Trojans and father of Ganymede. There are two Phrygias, Greater and Lesser. Greater Phrygia contains Smyrna; [Col. 0503A] [Note: [Col. 0503C] “But Lesser contains Ilium.” From the cited book *On Hebrew Places*, based on Acts.] Lesser contains Ilium.

42. Lycaonia [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0503C] Caria. From Solinus, chapter 43.] The river Hermus separates Caria from Phrygia.

43. Lydia, the ancient seat of kings, was raised to riches by the waters of the Pactolus, with its streams of gold. It was formerly called Maeonia. Since it could not, because of its small size, support two brothers as kings, Lydus and Tyrrhenus, Tyrrhenus, chosen by lot, departed with a great multitude and occupied lands [Note: [Col. 0503C] “Occupied the lands of Italy.” So Servius and all the older printed books; some have “of Gaul.”] in Italy, calling them Tyrrhenia. Lydia, however, was named after Lydus, [Note: [Col. 0503C] “After Lydus, the king’s brother.” Chacon deleted the word “king’s.” These statements appear to have been taken from Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “The site of the city Agylla.”] the king’s brother, who had remained in the province. On the West it joins Lesser Phrygia; on the East it has the city of Smyrna, which [Note: [Col. 0503D] “The river Meles.” So the old books. Concerning it, see above, book [V], and Pliny, book V, chapter 29.] the river Meles encircles. Its plains are surrounded by the Pactolus and Hermus, exceedingly rich in golden sands.

[Col. 0503B] 44. Pamphylia [lacuna]

Isauria is said to have received its name from the situation of the place, because it lies open on every side to the blasts of the winds. Its metropolis is the city of Seleucia.

45. [Note: [Col. 0503D] Cilicia, from Cilix. From Solinus, in the chapter on Cilicia.] Cilicia derived its name from a certain Cilix, whom they say was Phoenician by birth and assert to have lived before Jupiter. It lies for the most part in plains; on the West it receives Lycia, on the South the Issic Sea, and behind it the ridges of Mount Taurus. The river Cydnus cuts through it. [Note: [Col. 0503D] “It has Tarsus as the mother of cities, and the Cydnus …” From Solinus. These statements occur in reverse order in Isidore’s manuscripts and in the cited book *On Hebrew Places*, based on the Acts of the Apostles.] It has Tarsus as the mother of cities. The town of Corycus is also in it, from which a great quantity of excellent saffron comes, more fragrant in scent and more golden than gold.

46. Lycia was so named because it is joined to Cilicia on the eastern side. For it has Cilicia to the east, the sea to the west and south, and Caria to the north. [Note: [Col. 0503D] There is Mount Chimaera. From Solinus, chapter 42, “On Lycia.” From this it should have been read here *Vesuvius*, not *Vesulus*, as it appears in the manuscripts. See Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “Many a Vesulus,” and *Georgics* II, on the verse: “Thus rich Capua plows, and neighboring Vesuvius.”] There is Mount [Col. 0503C] Chimaera, which exhales fire in nocturnal eruptions, as Aetna does in Sicily and Vesuvius in Campania.

# CHAPTER IV. On Europe

## 1

After Asia, we turn our pen toward Europe. Europe was the daughter of Agenor, king of Libya, [Note: [Col. 0503D] Jupiter’s. Thus all the Gothic manuscripts, as we have also noted earlier.] whom Jupiter carried off from Africa and brought to Crete, and named the third part of the world after her. [Note: [Col. 0503D] This, then, is Agenor, son of Libya. Apollodorus, concerning Agenor: “From Libya and Poseidon were born twin sons, Agenor and Belus.” The Greek reads: Λιβύης δὲ καὶ Ποσειδῶνος γίγνονται παῖδες δίδυμοι Ἄγενωρ καὶ Βῆλος.] This, then, is Agenor, son of Libya, and from him Libya—that is, Africa—is said to have received its name. Hence it appears that Libya received its name first, and Europe afterward.

## 2

Europe, divided into a third part of the world, begins at the river Tanais and descends westward along the northern ocean as far as the boundaries of Spain. Its eastern and southern portion, rising from the Black Sea, is joined entirely [Note: [Col. 0503D] It is joined to the Great Sea. — It is bordered. Chacon.] to the Great Sea, and ends at the island of Gades.

## 3

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The first region of Europe. From Orosius, Book I, chapter 2.] The first region of Europe is Lower Scythia, which begins at the Maeotian marshes and extends between the Danube and the northern ocean as far as Germany. Because of the barbarian peoples who inhabit it, this land is generally called Barbaria. Its first part is Alania, which reaches the Maeotian marshes. After this comes Dacia, where Gothia also lies; then Germany, [Col. 0504B] where the Suebi inhabited the greater part.

## 4

Germany, which follows Lower Scythia and is enclosed from the Danube between the river Rhine and the Ocean, is bounded on the north and west by the Ocean; on the east it is separated by the Danube, and on the south by the river Rhine. [Note: [Col. 0503D] A land rich in virility. Others read, “rich in men.” Solinus, [Col. 0504C] chapter 23.] It is a land rich in men and crowded with numerous peoples, [Note: [Col. 0504C] “And filled with monstrous creatures.” — We restored *frequens* from Solinus.] and filled with monstrous creatures. 156 Hence, because of its fecundity in producing peoples, Germany was so called; [Note: [Col. 0504C] It produces birds. From Solinus, same passage.] the Hercynian Forest produces birds whose feathers shine through at night. [Note: [Col. 0504C] Also wild bison, aurochs, and elks. Solinus, same passage; Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 15; Caesar, Book VI, *On the Gallic War*; Servius, *Georgics* II.] It also produces wild bison, aurochs, and elks. It sends forth gems, crystal, and amber. [Note: [Col. 0504C] Also green callaic stone. — *Callaim*, Pliny, Book XXXVII, [Col. 0504D] chapter 8.] It also produces green callaic stone and white ceraunian stone. There are two Germanies: Upper Germany beside the northern Ocean, and Lower Germany around the Rhine.

## 5

[Col. 0504C] [Note: [Col. 0504D] “As for the provinces.” From Orosius, same passage.] Of the provinces that the Danube separates from Barbaria to the Mediterranean Sea, [Note: [Col. 0504D] “The first is Moesia.” — Whether *Moesia* or *Mysia* is the more correct spelling has not yet been sufficiently determined. The manuscripts of Isidore and Solinus, whose text this is, vary; in Orosius the form is consistently *Moesia*. Servius, *Georgics* I, on “Moesia submits to no cultivation,” says: “Moesia is a city of Phrygia. Mysia is a province.” Yet if one considers the matter itself, it would be safer to write *Mysia*. Geographers plainly place Mysia both in Asia and in Europe. Indeed, in Virgil—if we trust the Pierian edition—the authority of Servius caused *Moesia* to be read against the manuscripts. But the derivation from harvests suggests that Isidore called it *Moesia*, or rather *Mesia*, a form that Chacon also preferred. As for what *μῦσος* or *μύσην* means among the Lydians, according to Eustathius on Dionysius the African and Hesychius, it has no bearing on Isidore.] the first is Maesia, so called from the yield of crops. Hence the ancients called it Ceres’ granary. [Note: [Col. 0504D] This is joined on the east to the mouths of the Danube. From Orosius, Book I, chapter 2.] It is joined on the east to the mouths of the Danube; on the southeast to Thrace; on the south to Macedonia; and on the west to Histria. After Moesia comes Pannonia. Then comes Noricum, a cold land and less productive. After these is Raetia, fertile in grain, which borders Belgic Gaul.

## 6

Thrace is said to have received its name from Thiras, son of Japheth, who came there. Others have said that Thrace was named from the savagery of its inhabitants. [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Propontis lies to its east. From Orosius, same passage.] To its east lie the Propontis and, opposite it, the city of Constantinople; to the north the Ister extends; to the south it adjoins the Aegean Sea; and Macedonia lies beneath it to the west. Its region was formerly inhabited by the Bessi, 157 Massagetae, Sarmatians, Scythians, and many other nations. For it is extensive and therefore contained very many peoples. Thrace produces the river Hebrus, which also touches many barbarian peoples.

## 7

Greece was named after a Greek king who ruled the whole region. The provinces of Greece are seven: the first from the west is Dalmatia, then Epirus, then Hellas, then Thessaly, then Macedonia, then Achaea; and two lie in the sea, Crete and the Cyclades. Illyricum, however, is the general name for all Greece.

## 8

Dalmatia is thought to have taken its name from Delmi, the greatest city of that province. It borders [Note: [Col. 0505D] “It borders on the east … and is enclosed.” From the same source. After these words, some Gothic manuscripts contain the following: “The Illyrian region lies beside the Adriatic Sea, where the Dardani have their dwelling. It is also Dardania, named after King Dardanus; its people, descended from the Trojan stock, have been made savage in their customs.” These words perhaps should not be rejected. See Pliny, Book IV, chapter 1, and Solinus, chapter 8.] Macedonia on the east, Moesia on the north, and is bounded by Istria on the west; on the south it is enclosed by the Adriatic Gulf.

## 9

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Epirus from Pyrrhus … destroyed. From Servius, in many places in *Aeneid* III, on “Andromache’s ancestral land”; in the books printed by Robert Stephanus, the reading is “placed by his brother Chaon.” Others may judge this reading.] Epirus was named after Pyrrhus, son of Achilles. One part of it is Chaonia, formerly called Molossia after Molossus, son of Pyrrhus, whom he had by Andromache. But after Pyrrhus was killed through the plotting of Orestes, Helenus took Andromache and held the kingdom [Col. 0505C] of his stepson, 158 who had succeeded his father. From him the part of Epirus was called Molossia; afterward Helenus named it Chaonia after his brother Chaon, whom he is said to have killed unknowingly while hunting, as a kind of consolation for his dead brother.

## 10

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Hellas named after a king. From Eusebius’ *Chronicle* and Servius, *Eclogue* II, on “Actaean Aracynthus.”] Hellas was named after King Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha; from him the Greeks were also first called Hellenes. It is also the land of Attica, formerly called Acte. [Note: [Col. 0505D] “For a certain Cranaus, a native, etc.” These are the words of Eusebius.] For a certain Cranaus was a native of Greece, and from his daughter, named Attis, the land of Attica received its name. It lies between Macedonia and Achaea and is joined to Arcadia on the north. [Note: [Col. 0505D] “It is also true Greece.” All this is excerpted from Solinus, chapter “On Greece.”] It is also true Greece, where stood the city of Athens, [Note: [Col. 0505D] “Mother of liberal studies … more noble.” From Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, [Col. 0506D] chapter 9.] mother of the liberal arts and nurse of philosophers, than which Greece possessed nothing more illustrious or noble. In it is also the plain of Marathon, once reputed the bloodiest because of a battle.

## 11

Hellas has two provinces: Boeotia and the Peloponnese.

Boeotia received its name for the following reason. When Cadmus, son of Agenor, was searching by his father’s command for his sister 159 Europa, who had been carried off by Jupiter, and could not find her, he feared his father’s anger and, having strengthened his resolve, chose exile. For, following the tracks of a bull that he happened to see, he embraced the place where it had lain down, and thus named the place BOEOTIA after the bull. There he also built the city of Thebes, where civil wars once raged, and [Note: [Col. 0506D] Where Apollo and Hercules were born. But Solinus, chapter 13, on Thebes, says: “That city boasts of gods born among its people, as those who celebrate Hercules and Liber in sacred songs relate.” For Apollo, Chacon substituted Liber, against all the manuscripts.] where Apollo and Hercules—the latter, that greater Theban—were born. It is also called [Note: [Col. 0506D] It is also Aonia. From Servius, *Eclogue* 10, on “Aonian Aganippe.”] Aonia, after a certain spring [Col. 0506B] consecrated to Apollo and the Muses, which is in Boeotia itself.

The Peloponnese is the second part of Hellas, ruled and named after Pelops.

## 12

Thessaly was named after King Thessalus. It is joined on the southern side to Macedonia, [Note: [Col. 0506D] Pieria lies behind it. Thus Solinus, chapter “On Thessaly,” though Pliny, Book IV, chapter 8, differs somewhat.] with Pieria behind it. Thessaly has many rivers and towns, among which Thessalonica and Thebes are especially notable. Mount Parnassus is there, once consecrated to Apollo. 160 Thessaly was the homeland of Achilles and the origin of the Lapiths, of whom [Note: [Col. 0506D] “Of whom it is said that they first …” Virgil, *Georgics* II: “The Lapiths of Pelethron”; and Servius.] it is said that they first subdued horses with bridles; hence they were also called Centaurs. In Thessaly solid gold coins were first made, and the practice of breaking horses was first discovered there.

## 13

At first Macedonia was called Emathia, after King Emathius, but [Note: [Col. 0506D] Macedon, grandson of Deucalion. From Solinus, chapter “On Macedonia.”] Macedon, Deucalion’s maternal grandson, after receiving the rule there, changed the name and called it Macedonia after himself. [Note: [Col. 0506D] It borders Mysia. From Orosius, Book I, chapter 2.] It borders on the east the Aegean Sea, on the south Achaea, on the west Dalmatia, and on the north Moesia. It was the homeland of Alexander the Great and [Note: [Col. 0506D] “And the region.” From Solinus.] a region rich in veins of gold and silver. It produces the stone called *paeanitis*. Mount Olympus is there, [Note: [Col. 0506D] “Which rises to such height with its lofty summit.” From the same source, chapter “On Thessaly.”] and rises so high with its lofty summit that on its peak neither clouds nor winds are felt.

## 14

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Achaea from Achaeus. From Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.] Achaea was named after King Achaeus, both the city and the province. It is almost an island. For, except on the northern side, where it joins Macedonia, it is surrounded by sea on every side. To the east it has the Myrtoan [Col. 0507A] Sea, to the southeast the Cretan Sea, and to the south the Ionian Sea; to the southwest and west [Note: [Col. 0507D] Cephalonian and Cassiopian islands. Orosius, same passage, chapter 2: “To the southwest and west, the islands of Cephalonia and Cassiope; to the north, the Corinthian Gulf; to the northeast, the narrow strip of land by which it joins Macedonia—or rather Attica—which place is called the Isthmus, where Corinth is situated.”] it has the islands of Cephalonia and Cassiope; only on the northern side is it joined to Macedonia or the land of Attica. Its chief city is Corinth, the glory of Greece. The river Inachus is in Achaea.

## 15

161 [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Arcadia, a gulf … like a plane-tree leaf.” These statements are confused. Arcadia lies in the gulf of the Peloponnese, that is, in its middle. The Peloponnese, however, extends like a plane-tree leaf.] Arcadia is a gulf of Achaea, spread out like a plane-tree leaf between the Ionian and Aegean Seas. [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Which Arcas, son of Jupiter …” From Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.] Arcas, son of Jupiter and Callisto, brought the Pelasgians under his power and named it Arcadia after himself. It is also Sicyonia, after King Sicyon, from whom the kingdom of the Sicyonians was likewise named. Arcadia has the great river Erimanthus and also the asbestos stone, which, once kindled, is never extinguished. The blackbirds born there are exceptionally white.

## 16

Lacedaemonia . . . .

[Col. 0507B] [Note: [Col. 0507D] Pannonia. From Orosius, same passage.] Pannonia was named after the Poenine Alps, by which it is separated from Italy. It is a region [Note: [Col. 0507D] Strong in men. Thus the old books and Solinus, chapter “On Gaul.”] strong in men and fertile in soil, enclosed by two sufficiently swift rivers, the Dravus and the Savus. It is joined to Noricum and Raetia; to the east it has Moesia, [Note: [Col. 0507D] To the southeast, Istria. — We would prefer “to the south.”] to the southeast Istria; to the southwest the Apennine Alps; to the west Belgic Gaul; and to the north the source or boundary of the Danube, which separates Germany and Gaul.

## 17

Istria was named after the river Ister, which flows through its land; this is the Danube. Istria has Pannonia to the north.

## 18

Italy, once occupied by Greek peoples, was called Greater Greece; [Note: [Col. 0507D] Italy … Greater Greece. Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Whether you are great Hesperia,” etc. It was called Μεγάλη Ἕλλας, “Greater Hellas,” because the Greeks founded all the cities from Tarentum to Cumae. See Justin, Book XX.] afterward it was called Saturnia after a king’s name, and then Latium, because Saturn, driven by Jupiter from his own seat, had hidden there; finally, when ruled there by Italus, 162 king of the Siculi, it was named Italy after him. [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Its extent is greater in length.” From Solinus, chapter “On Italy”: “Greater in length than in breadth.”] Its shape extends farther in length than in breadth [Note: [Col. 0508D] From the northwest to the southeast … terminates. From Orosius.] from the northwest to the southeast; it is bounded on the south by the Tyrrhenian Sea, on the north by the Adriatic, and on the west by the ridges of the Alps. It is a land most beautiful in every respect, especially pleasing for the fertility of its soil and the abundance of its pastures.

## 19

It has Lake Benacus, Lake Avernus, and Lake Lucrinus; the rivers Eridanus and Tiber; and Baiae, warm from its springs. It produces the gems called *syrtites*, *lyncurium*, and coral; also the boa serpent, the wild lynx, and the birds of Diomedes. Italy and Spain are called Hesperiae because the Greeks sail by the star Hesperus both to Italy and to Spain. [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Which are distinguished in this way,” etc. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “There is a place, Hesperia,” and Book III: “From Hesperus,” he says, “king of Spain, or from the star which those seeking Italy observe.”] They are distinguished in this way: if one says simply “Hesperia,” Italy is meant; but if one adds “the farther,” Spain is meant, because it lies at the end of the west.

## 20

Tuscia is a part of Italy, [Note: [Col. 0508D] Umbria, in turn, is part of Tuscia. From the same source, *Aeneid* XII. Umbria is also mentioned in the history. Solinus, chapter 8.] while Umbria is a part of Tuscia. Tuscia was so called from the frequency of sacred rites and incense, ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν, “from sacrificing.”

## 21

Histories relate that Umbria was so called because, at the time of the watery catastrophe, it survived the rains; for this reason it was given the Greek name Umbria. It lies on the ridges of the Apennine mountain, in the southern part of Italy.

## 22

[Note: [Col. 0508D] Etruria, a part of Italy. From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, “And the Etruscan leaders,” and II, “You will come to the land of Hesperia.”] Etruria, a part of Italy, was so called because its boundaries extended as far as the bank of the Tiber, as though from ἕτερος ὅρος. For ἕτερος means “other,” and ὅρος means “boundary.” 163 Formerly, the boundaries of Rome occupied only one bank of the Tiber. Others think that Etruria was named after the Etruscan leader.

It is also called Tyrrhenia, after Tyrrhenus, brother of the Lydian, who came from Maeonia to Italy by lot with part of the people. This is also Tuscia, but we should not say *Tuscia* in this sense, because we nowhere read it. Tuscia was called from the frequency of sacrifices and incense, ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν, “from sacrificing”; divination by inspection of entrails (*aruspicina*) is also said to have been discovered there.

## 23

[Note: [Col. 0508D] Apulia, where Brundisium is … which the Aeolians … These are the words of Justin, Book XII.] Apulia, where Brundisium is situated, was founded by the Aetolians, who followed Diomedes as their leader.

## 24

Campania has lands that bloom in winter and summer. The sun there is mild, the climate pleasant, and the air pure and gentle.

## 25

Gaul was named from the whiteness of its people, for γάλα means “milk” in Greek. The mountains and the severity of the climate on that side exclude the sun’s heat, with the result that the whiteness of their bodies is not darkened. The ridges of the Alps guard it on the east; the Ocean encloses it on the west; the steep Pyrenees lie to the south; and the streams of the Rhine, together with Germany, lie to the north. Its beginning is Belgica and its end Aquitania. It is a region with rich, pasture-producing soil, suitable for the use of living creatures, and watered and flooded by rivers and springs—especially by the two great rivers, the Rhine and the Rhône.

## 26

[Note: [Col. 0508D] The Belgians. “Belgium” is the term used by Caesar.] Belgis is a city of Gaul, from which the province of Belgica was named.

Cisalpine means “on this side of the Alps.”

Transalpine means “across the Alps,” toward the north.

Raetia, in turn, is so called because it lies near the Rhine.

## 27

[Note: [Col. 0508D] Aquitania. From Orosius.] Aquitania was named from the oblique waters of the river Loire, [Col. 0509A] because for the greater part the river forms its boundary and almost encircles it.

## 28

[Note: [Col. 0509C] Spain. From Justin, Book XLIV.] Spain was first called Iberia after the river Iberus. Later it was called HISPANIA after Hispalo. [Note: [Col. 0509C] It is also true Hesperia. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “There is a place, Hesperia.”] It is also truly Hesperia, named after Hesperus, the western star. 164 It lies between Africa and Gaul; it is closed off on the north by the Pyrenees, and surrounded on every other side by the sea. Its climate is temperate, its soil fertile in every kind of crop, and it is extremely rich in gems and metals.

## 29

Great rivers flow through it: the Baetis, Minius, and Iberus, and the Tagus, which carries gold like the Pactolus. It has six provinces: Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Baetica, and, across the strait in the region of Africa, Tingitania.

## 30

[Col. 0509B] [Note: [Col. 0509C] There are two Spains. From Orosius.] There are two Spains: Citerior, which extends in the northern region from the Pyrenees to Carthage; and Ulterior, which stretches southward from Celtiberia to the Strait of Gades. Citerior and Ulterior mean, as it were, “nearer” and “farther”; but *citra* means “around these lands,” while *ultra* means either “the last” or “that beyond which there is no other”—that is, no other land.

# CHAPTER V. On Libya

## 1

Libya was so called [Note: [Col. 0509D] Libya, because the Libs wind blows from there. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “The coming blast of Libya.”] because the Libs wind blows from there—that is, the southwest wind. [Note: [Col. 0509D] Others say Epaphus. Hyginus, *Fabulae*, chapter 149, and Placidus on *Thebaid* IV.] Others say that Epaphus, son of Jupiter, who founded Memphis in Egypt, fathered by his wife Cassiope a daughter named Libya. She later possessed a kingdom in Africa, and from her name the land was called Libya.

## 2

Some think that Africa was named from this circumstance, [Col. 0509C] as though *aprica*, because it is open to the sky and the sun and free from the terror of cold. 165 [Note: [Col. 0509D] Others say “Africa.” Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*, on chapter 25.] Others say that Africa was named after one of the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, who was called Afer, [Note: [Col. 0509D] Of whom above. Book IX, chapter 2.] whom we mentioned above.

## 3

It begins at the borders of Egypt and proceeds southward through Ethiopia as far as Mount Atlas. On the northern side it is joined to and enclosed by the Mediterranean Sea, ending at the Strait of Gades. It contains the provinces of Cyrenaican Libya, Pentapolis, Tripolitania, [Col. 0510A] [Note: [Col. 0509D] Byzacium. — *Byzancium* is read in the most ancient books and inscriptions, and in Stephanus. Chacon nevertheless thought *Byzatium* the correct spelling, on the basis of ancient manuscripts of Varro, Book I, *On Agriculture*, chapter 44; Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, Book XVII, chapter 5, and Book XVIII, chapter 10; and Augustine on Psalm XXXVI, sermon 2. The printed books of Isidore and many of the Gothic manuscripts also preserve this form.] Byzacium, Carthage, Numidia, [Note: [Col. 0509D] Mauritania Sitifensis and Mauritania Tingitana. As some books add Caesariensis and thus seem, from Orosius, to make three Mauritanias, there is no need to dwell on it, since from the same Orosius and from Isidore it is shortly afterward clear that Caesariensis and Sitifensis—or even Sitifensis and Tingitana [Col. 0510C] from the Council of Carthage VII—are joined together, with one of the Caesarienses serving almost as an appendix to the other; nevertheless in the councils one of the two is often designated by the name Tingitana.] Mauritania Sitifensis, Mauritania Tingitana, and, beneath the sun’s heat, Ethiopia.

## 4

[Note: [Col. 0510D] Cyrenaican Libya … extending. From Orosius, Book I, chapter 2.] Cyrenaican Libya is the first region of Africa. It was named after the metropolitan city of Cyrene, which lies within its boundaries. To the east it has Egypt; to the west the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes; to the north the Libyan Sea; and to the south Ethiopia, various barbarian nations, and inaccessible deserts that also breed basilisk serpents.

## 5

Pentapolis received its name in Greek from its five cities: Cyrene, Berenice, [Note: [Col. 0510D] Theuchira. It was formerly read incorrectly as Ceutria. See Ptolemy’s fourth map.] Theuchira, Apollonia, and Ptolemais. Of these, Ptolemais and Berenice were named after kings. Pentapolis is joined to Cyrenaican Libya and counted within its boundaries.

## 6

[Col. 0510B] [Note: [Col. 0510D] Oea, Sabrata, and Leptis Magna. Solinus, chapter 30. “The Achaeans call Tripolis in their language by the number of three cities: Taphra, Abrotan, and Leptis Magna.” Our manuscripts variously read *Oetabrate*, *Oea Tabrace*, and *Oea Sabrete*. Silius, Book III:

“Sabrata, then the Tyrian people, and Leptis of the Sarans,  
And Oea, with African settlers mingled among the Trinacrians.”

Here I would more readily read *Oeaque* from Isidore.] The Greeks designate the province of Tripolitania in their language by the number of its three great cities: Oea, Sabrata, and Leptis Magna. It has the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes to the east; 166 the Adriatic Sea to the north; Byzacium to the west; and to the south the Getuli and Garamantes, extending as far as the Ethiopian Ocean.

## 7

Byzacena received its name from two very famous towns, one of which is called Hadrumetum, the other Byzacium. It lies below Tripolitania and extends for two hundred thousand—or more—paces. [Note: [Col. 0510D] Extending two hundred thousand paces. From Solinus, chapter 30.] It is fertile in olives, and its soil is so extraordinarily rich that seeds cast there grow again as crops with almost a hundredfold increase.

## 8

[Note: [Col. 0510D] Zeugis, where great Carthage is situated. These are the words of Orosius.] Zeugis, where great Carthage is situated, is also true Africa. It lies between Byzacium and Numidia, joined to the Sicilian Sea on the north and extending southward as far as the region of the Getuli. Its nearer parts are fertile in crops; the farther parts are full of wild beasts and serpents, and of large wild asses wandering in the desert.

Getulia, however, is the inland part of Africa.

## 9

[Note: [Col. 0510D] Numidia from inhabitants wandering here and there. Sallust, *Jugurthine War*: “And because, often trying one region after another, they had sought one place and then another, they called themselves Numidians.” The same in Pliny, Book V, chapter 3, though Festus differs somewhat.] Numidia was so named after its inhabitants, who wandered about everywhere because they had no fixed dwelling. For in their language “uncertain and wandering settlements” are called *Numidia*. It begins at the river Ampsaga and ends at the boundary of Zeugis. [Note: [Col. 0511D] Having the Lesser Syrtes to the east. Orosius, same passage.] It has the Lesser Syrtes to the east; to the north, the sea that faces Sardinia; to the west, Mauritania Sitifensis; and to the south, the peoples of Ethiopia. It is a region exceedingly rich in plains. Where it is wooded, it raises wild beasts; where it is steep with mountain ridges, it breeds horses and wild asses. 167 It is also renowned for its excellent marble, which is called Numidian marble. Its principal cities are [Note: [Col. 0511D] Hippo, Rhegium, and Rusicada. The same source, and Orosius.] Hippo, Rhegium, and Rusicada.

## 10

Mauritania was named from the complexion of its peoples. For the Greeks call black μαῦρον (*mauron*). Just as Gaul received its name from the whiteness of its people, so Mauritania received its name from their blackness. Its first province is Mauritania Sitifensis, which contains the town of Sitifis, from which the region is said to have taken its name.

## 11

Mauritania Caesariensis was a colony; its city was Caesarea, and the province received its name from it. [Col. 0511B] [Note: [Col. 0511D] Thus both provinces. Orosius.] Both provinces, therefore, joined to one another, have Numidia to the east, the Great Sea to the north, the river Malva to the west, and Mount Astrix to the south, [Note: [Col. 0511D] Which separates fertile land. Orosius: “Which divides living land from recumbent sands as far as the Ocean.”] which separates fertile land from stretches of sand extending to the Ocean.

## 12

Mauritania Tingitana was named after Tingis, the metropolitan city of that province. [Note: [Col. 0511D] This last region of Africa … wandering throughout. From Orosius, though he has: “It rises from seven mountains.” The rest is from Solinus, chapter “On Mauritania.”] This last region of Africa rises from seven mountains. It has the river Malva to the east; [Note: [Col. 0511D] The Strait of Gades to the north. Orosius: “To the north, our sea and the Strait of Gades.”] the Strait of Gades to the north; the Atlantic Ocean to the west; and [Note: [Col. 0511D] To the south, the peoples of the Gaulali. Orosius: “To the south, the peoples of the Autololes, whom they now call Gaulales.”] to the south the peoples of the Gaulali, who wander as far as the western Ocean. It is a region that produces wild beasts, apes, dragons, and ostriches; formerly it was also full of elephants, which now only India produces.

## 13

[Col. 0511C] 168 [Note: [Col. 0511D] Garamantis. “The chief city.” From Solinus.] The chief city of the Garamantes’ region was the town of Garama. It lies between Cyrenaica and Ethiopia, where there is a spring [Note: [Col. 0512D] Which is cold in the heat. Thus the Gothic manuscripts; Solinus reads “is hot in the cold.”] that is cold in the heat of day and hot in the cold of night.

## 14

Ethiopia was named from the complexion of its peoples, whom proximity to the sun scorches. [Note: [Col. 0512D] “Finally, the color of the people reveals the force of the heavenly body.” These are the words of Solinus, chapter “On India.”] Indeed, the color of its people reveals the force of the heavenly body, for there is continual heat there. [Note: [Col. 0512D] “For whatever portion of it there is lies beneath the southern axis.” From Solinus, chapter “On Ethiopia.”] For whatever part of it there is lies beneath the southern axis. Around the west it is mountainous; in the middle it is sandy; toward the east it is desert. Its extent stretches from the west, at Mount Atlas, eastward as far as the boundaries of Egypt. It is bounded on the south by the Ocean and on the north by the river Nile, and contains very many peoples, terrifying in their varied faces and monstrous appearance.

## 15

It is also filled with a multitude of wild beasts and serpents. [Col. 0511D] For there are found there the rhinoceros, the camelopard, the basilisk, enormous dragons, from whose brains gems are extracted, as well as hyacinth and chrysoprase. [Col. 0512A] Cinnamon is gathered there.

## 16

There are two Ethiopias: one around the rising of the sun, the other around its setting, in Mauritania.

## 17

Beyond the three parts of the world, there is a fourth part across the inner Ocean, in the south. It is unknown to us because of the sun’s heat, and at its boundaries [Note: [Col. 0512D] The fable of the Antipodes. What follows is based on Lactantius and Augustine.] the Antipodes are said, fabulously, to dwell. Next to Spain lies Mauritania, then Numidia, then the region of Carthage; after these we have Getulia, afterward Ethiopia, and then places scorched by the sun’s heat.

## 18

It should certainly be understood that some provinces were first named after the name of their founder, and afterward the name of the people was derived from that of the province. Thus from Italus came ITALIA, and again from Italia came ITALUS; and so we use the name of the people itself in the same way as the name of the founder from whom the province received its name. [Col. 0512B] Hence it happens that one man gives his name to a city, a region, and a people. 169

## 19

Provinces, however, received their names from their circumstances. For when the chief territories of peoples, which had belonged to other kings, were brought under their own jurisdiction by the Romans through conquest, they called the distant regions provinces. A homeland (*patria*) was so called because it is common to all who were born in it.

## 20

[Note: [Col. 0512D] We stated above that “land” signifies the element. Above, chapter 1, from Servius, *Aeneid* VI.] We stated above that “land” signifies the element; but individual lands signify particular parts, such as Africa and Italy; the same term also signifies places. For places and expanses of land in the world contain many provinces within themselves, just as, in a body, one place contains many limbs; and just as a house contains many rooms. Thus “lands” and “places” signify expanses of land, whose parts are provinces: for example, in Asia, Phrygia; in Gaul, Raetia; in Spain, Baetica.

## 21

Asia, then, is a place; Phrygia is a province of Asia; Troy is a region of Phrygia; and Ilium is a city of Troy. Regions, in turn, are parts of provinces, which the common people call districts: for example, Troy in Phrygia, and Cantabria and Asturia in Gallaecia. A region is so called from its rulers; its parts are territories.

## 22

[Note: [Col. 0512D] “Territory,” so called. Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “He marks out the city with a plow”: “Hence territory is also called *terribovium*, as if ‘trampled by oxen and the plow.’ But we have retained *tauritorium* from a Gothic manuscript, unless one prefers *territerium* from the edition of Vulcanius, or *territaurium*.”] A territory was so called, as if *tauritorium*, “trampled by oxen and the plow.” For the ancients marked out the boundaries of possessions and territories by drawing a furrow.

170

# CHAPTER VI. On the Islands

## 1

[Col. 0512D] Islands were so called because they are in the salt water—that is, in the sea. Among them, the best known and largest, which many of the ancients investigated with diligent study, should be noted.

## 2

[Col. 0513A] [Note: [Col. 0513C] Britain, an island of the Ocean, etc. Hegesippus, Book V, chapter 15: “What need is there to add Britain, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea?” And Orosius, Book I, chapter 2: “Britain, an island of the Ocean.”] Britain, an island of the Ocean, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea, was named after its own people. [Note: [Col. 0513C] It lies opposite Gaul. Orosius, same passage: “Since the Ocean contains islands called Britain and Ireland, which lie opposite Gaul, facing Spain.”] It lies opposite Gaul, facing Spain. [Note: [Col. 0513D] “Its circumference … very great.” From Solinus, chapter “On Britain.”] Its circumference is 4,875,000 paces. It has many large rivers, hot springs, and an abundant and varied supply of metals. Gagates stone is found there in great quantity, as are pearls.

## 3

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Thanatos. Solinus, *Athanatis*.] Thanatos is an island of the Ocean, separated from Britain by a narrow Gallic channel, [Note: [Col. 0513D] “Separated from Britain by a narrow tidal inlet.” From Solinus, same passage; this passage, corrupt in all the books, has been restored from him.] with grain-producing fields and fertile soil. It was called Thanatos because it causes the death of serpents: although the island itself does not know them, whenever soil carried from it is transported to any country, it immediately kills snakes.

## 4

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Thyle, the last island of the Ocean. The passage is taken from Servius, *Georgics* I, on “Let farthest Thule serve you,” and from Solinus, chapter “On Britain.” We shall append their words, so that anyone who wishes may use them to remedy the passage. “Thule,” says Servius, “is an island of the Ocean between the northern and western regions, beyond Britain, Ireland, and the Orkneys. It is the last island in the Ocean; there, when the sun is in Cancer, there are said to be unbroken days without nights.” Solinus says: “There are many other islands around Britain, among them Thule, the last. At the summer solstice, when the sun passes through the constellation of Cancer, there is almost no night; at the winter solstice, likewise there is no day, so that sunrise is joined to sunset. Beyond Thule we are told that the sea is sluggish and congealed.” Chacon read it as follows: “Between the northern and western region, where, when the sun makes the winter solstice, there is no day; hence beyond it the sea is sluggish and congealed.” But he says that the name Thule comes from the sun, not, I think, so that it is called Thule as a name, but so that it is called “the last” because of the reason reported by Servius and Solinus.] Thyle, the last island of the Ocean, lies between the northern and western regions, beyond Britain. It takes its name from the sun, because the sun makes its summer 171 solstice there and there is no day beyond it; hence its sea is sluggish and congealed.

## 5

The Orkneys are islands of the Ocean beyond Britain, thirty-three in number. [Note: [Col. 0514C] Of which twenty are deserted. From Orosius, same passage.] Twenty of them are deserted, and thirteen are inhabited.

## 6

[Note: [Col. 0514C] Scotland, the same as Ireland. From the same source, although not entirely the same.] Scotland, also called Ireland, is an island near Britain. It is narrower in extent of land but more fertile in situation. It stretches from the southwest toward the north; its foremost parts face Iberia and the Cantabrian Ocean. Hence it was also called Ireland. It was called Scotland because it is inhabited by Scotoi peoples. [Note: [Col. 0514C] No snake there. From Solinus. See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. [Col. 0514D]] There is no snake there, birds are rare, and there are no bees, so much so that if someone carries soil or stones from there and scatters them elsewhere among beehives, the swarms abandon their honeycombs.

[Col. 0513C] **7. Gades**, an island situated at the end of the province of Baetica, which separates Europe from Africa, [Note: [Col. 0514D] In which the columns of Hercules [lacuna] the tide is admitted. From Orosius.] on which the columns of Hercules are seen, and from which the tide of the Ocean is admitted through the mouths of the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is separated from the mainland by one hundred and twenty paces. [Note: [Col. 0514D] “From the continental land, 120.” Chacon emended this to 140, on the basis of Solinus’s manuscripts, where seven hundred feet are read, not paces, as in the common editions. But the manuscripts, and the fact itself—Isidore being sufficiently well informed about Gades, which was near him, as was proper—forbid this.] The Tyrians, coming from the Red Sea and occupying it, called it in their language *Gadir*, that is, “fence,” [Note: [Col. 0514D] In their language, *Gadit*. The Hebrew word *ghadar* also means “to enclose,” “to fence.” From Solinus, chapter on Spain.] because it is enclosed by the sea. [Col. 0514A] A tree resembling a palm grows there; its gum, when used to color glass, produces a *Ceraunian* gem.

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Fortunate … to be the same as Paradise.” Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “and I inhabit Elysium.” According to the philosophers, Elysium is the Fortunate Islands.] The Fortunate Islands, by their name, signify that they bear every good thing, as though they were happy and blessed through the abundance of their fruits. By their own nature they produce the fruits of precious forests. The ridges of their hills are clothed with vines that grow without cultivation; grain and vegetables are commonly found there in place of grass. Hence the error of the pagans and the poems of secular poets led them, because of the fertility of the soil, to suppose that these islands were Paradise. [Note: [Col. 0514D] “They are situated.” From Solinus, final chapter.] They are situated in the Ocean opposite the left side of Mauretania, near the West, and are separated from one another by intervening sea.

**9.** [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Gorgades.” Thus the old books, and the manuscripts of Pliny and Solinus.] The Gorgades are islands of the Ocean lying opposite a promontory called Hesperuceras. They were inhabited by female Gorgons, winged with extraordinary speed, with shaggy and rough bodies; [Col. 0514B] from them the islands received their name. They are two days’ sail from the mainland.

**10.** The Hesperides Islands were named from the city Hesperis, which existed at the end of Mauretania. They lie beyond the Gorgades, beneath the coast of Atlas, in the innermost recesses of the sea. In their gardens, according to the myths, a sleepless dragon guards golden apples. It is said that there is there an inlet of the sea so twisted by winding shores that, to those who view it from afar, it imitates the track of a serpent.

**11.** [Note: [Col. 0514D] Chryse and Argyre. Solinus, Pliny, and Mela.] The islands Chryse and Argyre are situated in the Indian Ocean, so rich in an abundance of metals that many writers have reported that they possess a golden surface and a silver one; hence they received their names.
