**12.** Taprobana is an island lying beneath India toward the southeast wind, from which the Indian Ocean begins. It extends 875,000 paces in length and [Col. 0514C] 625,000 paces in breadth. [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Six hundred and twenty-five thousand.” We have removed the word “stadia,” on the authority of Solinus, Pliny, and Chacon.] It is divided by a river flowing between its parts, and is everywhere filled with pearls and gems. One part is filled with wild beasts and elephants; human beings occupy the other. On this island, they say, there are two summers and two winters in a single year, and that during these seasons the land blooms with flowers.

[Col. 0515A] **13.** [Note: [Col. 0515C] “Tylos … bearing leaves at all times.” Some copies read “green at all times.”] Tylos is an island of India, bearing leaves throughout the year. Thus far concerning the islands of the Ocean.

**14.** There are also islands situated in the great sea from the Hellespont as far as Gades.

The island of Cyprus received its name from the city Cyprus, which is on it. That city is also Paphos, [Note: [Col. 0515C] “It is also Paphos.” This does not refer to the island of Cyprus but to a city on it, which was once called Cypros; Chacon said that it was Paphos.] consecrated to Venus in the Carpathian Sea, near the south wind. It was once famous for its wealth, especially for copper; [Note: [Col. 0515C] “For there the first discovery of this metal.” Pliny, book VIII, chapter 56, and book XXXIV, chapter 2.] for there the first discovery and use of this metal took place.

**15.** Crete is a great part of Greece opposite the Peloponnese. [Note: [Col. 0515C] “First named from the mildness of its climate.” From Solinus, chapter 17.] It was first called Macaronesos from the temperateness of its climate, and afterward Crete, from a certain native named Crete, whom they say was one of the Curetes, by whom Jupiter was hidden and nourished there. It is an island of Greece, extending in a very long tract between east and west; on the north it is washed by the waters of Greece, and on the south by Egyptian waters. It was once famous for its hundred cities, whence it was also called Hecatompylos, “the Hundred-Citied.”

**16.** [Note: [Col. 0515C] “It was also the first …” From the same source.] It was also the first to become famous for oars and arrows; it was the first to establish laws; [Note: [Col. 0515D] “It established laws.” Solinus reads “joined laws.” See Plato, *Minos*.] it was the first to teach cavalry squadrons. The study of music began there with the Idaean Dactyls. It is rich in goats but lacks deer; [Note: [Col. 0515D] “But it lacks deer.” From Solinus and Pliny, book VIII, chapter 58: “More remarkably, on that same island [Crete], deer are not found except in the region of the Cydonians.”] it produces nowhere wolves, foxes, or other harmful wild animals; there are no snakes there, nor any owl, and if one is brought in, it dies immediately. It is rich in vines and trees. The herb dittany grows in Crete, as does *alimos*, which, when chewed, prevents hunger for a day. [Note: [Col. 0515D] “But it produces phalangia.” Solinus reads as follows: “The phalangium is a kind of spider. If you seek its strength, it has none; if its power, its bite kills a person with poison.”] It also produces poisonous phalangia and the stone called the Idaean dactyl.

**17.** [Note: [Col. 0515D] “The island of Abydos.” Abydos is neither an island nor in Europe; rather, as Solinus says while discussing the Hellespont: “Abydos belongs to Asia, and Sestos to Europe.” Servius, on “the straits of Abydos are tested,” *Georgics* I. Sestos and Abydos are cities of the Hellespont, separated by a narrow and dangerous sea. We leave the task of reconciling these statements to others.] Abydos is an island situated in Europe above the Hellespont, separated by a narrow and dangerous sea. It is called *Abydos* in Greek (ἄβυδος) because it is the entrance to the sea of the Hellespont, at which Xerxes made a bridge from ships and crossed into Greece.

**18.** [Note: [Col. 0515D] “Coos.” Solinus: “Many islands lie alongside the mainland of Attica, but those that are almost suburbs are Salamis, Sunium, Cos, Ceos, and so forth. As Varro testifies, Ceos was the first to provide women’s ornamental clothing through the art of woolworking and the skill of weaving.” In the manuscript of Solinus belonging to the Church of Toledo, *Ceos, Cos* is read. Hermolaus Barbarus long ago complained that copyists frequently confused these words in good authors because of their similarity, so that what perhaps properly belonged to Ceos has nearly been appropriated by Cos. Yet, according to Pliny, the art of woolworking was common to both. Hippocrates, however, could not have been common to both, since he is known to have been a native of Cos. But Hippocrates’ Cos does not lie alongside Attica in the Aegean Sea, but near Rhodes in the Icarius Sea.] The island of Cos lies beside the province of Attica. The physician Hippocrates was born there; and, as Varro testifies, it was the first to become famous for the art of woolworking as an ornament for women.

[Col. 0516A] **175 19.** [Note: [Col. 0516D] “The Cyclades … which they therefore suppose were called Cyclades.” From Solinus.] The Cyclades were formerly islands of Greece. They are thought to have been called Cyclades because, although they project from Delos at considerable distances, they are nevertheless situated in a circle around Delos. For the Greeks call a circle *kyklos* (κύκλος). [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Some, however, think they were not so called because they were arranged in a circle.” See Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “the Cyclades,” and frequently elsewhere.] Others think that they were not named because they are arranged in a circle, but because of the reefs that lie around Delos itself.

**20.** These islands are situated in the Hellespont, between the Aegean and Malean Seas, and are also surrounded by the Myrtoan Sea. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “They are all, however, …” From Orosius.] They number fifty-three in all, [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Extending.” All the Gothic manuscripts read “occupying.” “Extending” is not implausible, according to Vulcanius.] occupying 500 miles from north to south and 200 miles from east to west. Their metropolis is Rhodes.

**21.** The island of Delos lies in the middle of the Cyclades. It is said to have been called Delos because, after the flood recorded as having occurred in the time of Ogyges, when continuous night had covered the world for many months, it was illuminated by the rays of the sun before all other lands. It received its name from this, because it was the first to become manifest to human sight. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “For the Greeks call something manifest *delon*.” These are Servius’s words, *Aeneid* III.] For the Greeks call a manifest thing *delon* (δῆλον). [Note: [Col. 0516D] “It is also Ortygia.” From Solinus, chapter 17.] It is also Ortygia, because quail were first seen there; the Greeks call these birds *ortyges* (ὄρτυγες). [Col. 0516D] On this island Latona gave birth to Apollo and Diana. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “On this island Latona …” Words of Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “sacred, worshiped in the sea.”] Delos is both the name of a city and of an island.

**22.** [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Rhodes, first of the Cyclades.” From Orosius.] Rhodes is the first of the Cyclades toward the east. There, it is said, the bud of the rose was discovered while the city was being founded; from this both the city and the island were called Rhodes. In this city stood a bronze colossus of the sun seventy cubits high. There were also one hundred smaller colossi on the same island. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “The bud of the rose.” Other copies read *capitolium*, *capulum*, or *capulum*, perhaps *cohivum* or *coivum*. A glossary has *coivum*: “the calyx of the closed rose” (κάλυξ ῥοδοῦ μεμυκότος).]

**23.** [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Tenedos.” From Orosius.] Tenedos is one of the Cyclades, situated to the north. A city was once founded there by a certain Tene; hence the name of that city, or rather of the island, arose. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “For this Tennes … the island was called.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “Tenedos, famous in every report.”] This Tene, having been disgraced because he had intercourse with his stepmother, fled and obtained this island, which was without inhabitants. Hence the island was called Tenedos. [Col. 0517A] [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Thus Cicero.” Varro III.] Thus Cicero writes: “Tene himself, from whose name Tenedos is named.”

**24.** [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Carpathos.” From Orosius.] Carpathos is one of the Cyclades, situated to the south [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Opposite Egypt, from which the Carpathian Sea takes its name.” Acro on Horace.] opposite Egypt. It was named from the rapid ripening of its fruits. [Col. 0517D] [Note: [Col. 0517D] “For it lies between Egypt and Rhodes.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III.] It lies between Egypt and Rhodes. Ships that are large and spacious are also called Carpasian ships from this island.

**25.** [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Cythera.” From Orosius and Solinus; it may also be called *Cytherea*. Stephanus: “Both the island and the birth are called Cytherean.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Cytherea, devising new arts.” “Cytherea,” he says, “takes its name from the island, which is used only in the plural, as in *alta Cythera*.” *Aeneid* X.] Cythera is one of the Cyclades, situated toward the west. Its former name was Porphyris. It was called Cythera because Venus was born there.

**26.** [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Icaria, one of the Cyclades.” Solinus: “Icaros belongs to the Sporades.” But Virgil appears to have made the Sporades into Cyclades as well when he said, “and the Cyclades scattered across the sea.”] Icaria is one of the Cyclades and gave its name to the Icarium Sea. It is inhospitable, with projecting rocks between Samos and Myconos, and has no bays suitable for harbors. It is said that the Cretan Icarus perished there in a shipwreck, and that the place received its name from the man’s fate.

**27.** [Note: [Col. 0517D] “The island of Naxos was formerly called Dionysias.” Solinus: “It was first called Dionysias, before it was called Naxos, either because it was hospitable to Liber Pater or because it surpasses the other islands in the fertility of its vines.” Why it was called Naxos is discussed by Diodorus Siculus, book VI. I consider the expression “as though *Dionaxon*” corrupt.] The island of Naxos was formerly called Dionysias, as though *Dionaxos*, because it surpasses the other islands in the fertility of its vines. It is eighteen thousand paces from Delos. From it Jupiter is said once to have set out against the Titans.

**28.** [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Melos.” From Solinus.] Melos is one of the Cyclades and the most perfectly round of all the islands; hence it received its name.

**178 29.** History says that Philomelus and Plutus were born from Jason; from Philomelus came Pareantus, who named the island and town Paron after himself. It was formerly called Minoia, and afterward Paros. [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Of which Virgil says, ‘and snowy Paros.’ *Aeneid* III.] Virgil speaks of it: “and snowy Paros.” For it produces the whitest marble, which is called Parian. It also yields *sardanus* stone, superior indeed to marble, but the least valuable among gems.

**30.** The island of Chios is called *Chios* in the Syrian language because mastic grows there. [Note: [Col. 0517D] “For the Syrians call mastic *chios*.” The same statements are found in the little book *On Hebrew Places*, from the Acts of the Apostles, among Jerome’s works.] For the Syrians call mastic *chios*.

**31.** Samos is an island in the Aegean Sea, where Juno was born. From it came the Samian Sibyl and Pythagoras of Samos, from whom the name of philosophy was devised. It is said that earthen vessels were first discovered on this island; hence such vessels were called Samian.

**32.** Sicily was called Sicania after King Sicanus, and afterward Sicily after Siculus, the brother of Italus. It was formerly called Trinacria because of its three *akra* (ἄκρα), that is, promontories: Pelorum, Pachynum, and Lilybaeum. [Note: [Col. 0518C] “Trinacria … which in Latin is *Triquetra*.” Pliny and Solinus have *triquetra*, “three-cornered”; but it is likely that Isidore wrote *triquadra*, both from the etymology and from Quintilian, book I, chapter 5: “Etymology sometimes attempts to distinguish barbarous forms from correct ones, as when the question is whether Sicily should be called *Triquetra* or *Triquadra*,” and so forth.] *Trinacria* is Greek and in Latin is called *triquetra*, as though divided into three quarters. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “This is separated from Italy by a narrow strait.” From Justin, book IV, at the beginning.] It is separated from Italy by a narrow strait. Facing the African Sea, it is fruitful in crops and rich in gold, yet penetrable by caves and passages, and full of winds and sulfur. Hence the fires of Mount Etna rise there. In its strait are Scylla and Charybdis, by which ships are either swallowed up or dashed to pieces.

**179 33.** It was once the homeland of the Cyclopes and afterward the nurse of tyrants. It is fertile in grain and was the first land anywhere to be plowed after seed had been entrusted to the earth. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “It was once the homeland.” From Orosius, book II, chapter 4.] Its chief city is Syracuse. It produces the fountain Arethusa and the river Alpheus, a great breeder of horses. [Col. 0518B] [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Comedy was first discovered there.” From Solinus.] Comedy was first invented on this island.

**34.** It first yielded the agate stone from the river Achates. Its sea also produces coral; [Note: [Col. 0518D] “It also produces the salts of Agrigentum.” From the same source. The same author below, book XVI, chapter 2.] it produces the salts of Agrigentum, which dissolve in fire and crackle in water. Its entire circumference is three thousand stadia. Sallustius says that Sicily was once joined to Italy, but that the intervening space was divided by the force of the sea and split by a narrow channel. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “And split by a narrow passage.” The same author above, book XIII, chapter 18.]

**35.** The island of Tapsus lies ten stadia from Sicily and is flatter; hence it received its name. Of it Virgil writes: [Note: [Col. 0518D] Virgil: “and lying Tapsus.” Servius says there: “An island not far from Syracuse, nearly level with the waves.”] “and lying Tapsus.”

**36.** The Aeolian Islands of Sicily were named after Aeolus, son of Hippotas, whom the poets imagined to have been king of the winds. But, as Varro says, he was ruler of these islands; and because he foretold future winds from their mists and smoke, ignorant people thought that he restrained the winds by his own power. These islands are also called Vulcanian, because, like Etna, they too burn.

**37.** There are nine of them, with proper names. The first, Lyparus, was called Lyparen by a certain Lyparus, who ruled it before Aeolus. The second is called Hiera because it has exceptionally high hills. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Hiera, because it rises above the hills; or because they use *hieros* (ἱερὸς), that is, ‘sacred,’ as a term for something great, just as we do the Greek word; or, as Solinus says, because it is especially sacred to Vulcan.] The remaining ones are Strongyle, Didyme, Ericusa, [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Hephaestias.” This island is absent from Margarini’s edition, and the number is complete without it. Solinus and Pliny say that there are only seven.] Hephaestias, Phaenicusa, Evonimos, Ericodes, and Phaenicodes. Since they burn at night, they are called Aeolian or Vulcanian; some of them did not exist at the beginning but later rose from the sea and have remained to this day.

**38.** The Stoechades Islands lie sixty thousand paces from the mainland, opposite the province of Narbonensis, at the point where the river Rhône flows into the sea. [Note: [Col. 0519C] “Opposite the province of Narbonensis.” Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] They are called *Stoechades* in Greek, as though they had been arranged in a row.

**39.** Sardus, son of Hercules, set out from Libya with a large multitude, occupied Sardinia, and gave the island its name. In the African Sea, it projects in the shape of a human footprint. [Note: [Col. 0519C] “Wider toward the east than toward the west.” This passage is from book II of Sallustius’s *Histories*, cited by Aulus Gellius, book XII, chapter 28. The following may be added from Isidore: “Its sides are almost equal, and face south and north.” The same passage should be corrected in Nonius under *facies*. Chacon had already suspected the words before “commerce.”] It is broader toward the east than toward the west, with sides that face approximately south and north. For this reason, before commercial contact, Greek navigators called it *ichnos* (ἴχνος), “a footprint.”

**40.** The land extends 140 miles in length and 40 in breadth. No snake or wolf is born there, but only the *solifuga*, a small animal harmful to human beings. [Note: [Col. 0519D] “But only the solifuga.” Above, book XII, chapter 3.] Nor does poison grow there, [Note: [Col. 0519D] “Except for an herb.” Servius’s passage, *Eclogue* 8, should be emended from Isidore; hence the following.] except for an herb mentioned by many writers and poets, resembling *apiastrum*, which contracts the mouths of human beings and kills them as though they were laughing. Sardinia has hot springs that provide healing to the weak but blindness to thieves, if, after taking an oath, they touch their eyes with the waters. [Note: [Col. 0519D] “It has springs.” From Solinus.]

**41.** The inhabitants of Corsica gave the island its beginning, calling it from the name of their leader. [Col. 0519D] For a Ligurian woman named Corsa, when she saw a bull that she tended near the shore habitually swim across and return after intervals with its body increased in size, wished to discover the pastures unknown to her. She followed the bull as it departed from the others, sailing all the way to the island. When the Ligurians learned from her return about the island’s fertility, they went there on rafts and named it after the woman who had been its discoverer and leader. [Note: [Col. 0519D] “A Ligurian woman.” Priscian cites this in book VI from Sallustius’s book II of the *Histories*: “But they themselves say that a bull from the herd, which a Ligurian woman named Corsa tended near the shore …” From this it is clear that the entire passage belongs to Sallustius.]

**42.** This island is called *Cyrne* (κύρνη) in Greek, having been inhabited by Cyrnus, the son of Hercules. Of it Virgil writes: “Cyrnean yews.” [Note: [Col. 0519D] “It is divided from Sardinia.” Orosius, in the same place.] It is separated from Sardinia by a strait twenty thousand paces wide and surrounded by a bay of the Ligurian Sea, facing Italy. It is angular, with many promontories, produces very rich pastures, and yields a stone that the Greeks call *cathochites*.

**43.** [Note: [Col. 0519D] “Ebusus.” Orosius, in the same place. As for the etymology—“because it is not far from Zanio”—this requires further investigation, whether one reads *Zanio* or *Dianio*.] Ebusus is an island of Spain, so called because it is not far from Zanio, as though *Ebozos*. It lies seventy stadia from it, and snakes flee from its soil. Opposite it is Colubraria, which is filled with snakes.

**44.** [Note: [Col. 0519D] “The Balearic Islands are two.” Aphrosiades and Gymnasiades. Perhaps *Aphrodisiades*, so called because, as Aristotle says in *On Marvelous Things Heard*, among these people women are held in greater honor than men. Concerning the Gymnasiades, Pliny, book III, chapter 5, says: “The Greeks called the Balearic Islands, warlike with the sling, Gymnasiae.” Diodorus Siculus, book VI, chapter 1, says they were called Gymnasiae because in summer the inhabitants went naked, like athletes in a wrestling school.] The Balearic Islands of Spain are two: Aphrosiade and Gymnasie, the larger and the smaller. Hence ordinary people call them Majorca and Minorca. [Col. 0520A] **182** The sling, by which stones are hurled, was first invented on these islands; hence they were called Balearic. [Note: [Col. 0520C] For in Greek *ballein* (βάλλειν) means “to throw.” The same explanation occurs below, book XVIII, chapter 10.] From the same word come *ballista*, “a thing thrown,” and *fundibalum*. [Note: [Col. 0520C] “Hence *ballista*, as though ‘something thrown,’ and *fundibalum*.” Thus the ancient books read here and in book XVIII, chapter 10, and in Augustine, on Psalm 54. Vegetius, book I, chapter 16, says: “Rounded stones from a sling or from a *fustibalus*”; and book II, chapter 15: “Slingers who use slings or *fustibali*”; and book III, chapter 4: “The *fustibalus* is a long staff.” Therefore *fundibalum* must certainly be read, not *fundibulum*.] Virgil writes: “the Balearic sling’s lash.”

# **CHAPTER VII. On Promontories**

[Col. 0520B]

**1.** It is common to islands that they project outward; hence their projecting places are also called promontories. Thus Sallustius writes of Sardinia: “It projects more broadly toward the east than toward the west.” [Note: [Col. 0520D] “Thus Sallustius concerning Sardinia.” He is cited, as we said in the preceding chapter, by Aulus Gellius and Nonius from book II of the *Histories*.]

**2.** [Note: [Col. 0520D] “The promontory of Sigaeum … *sige*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “the Sigaean straits gleam broadly with fire.” The Vatican manuscript of Servius reads: “that is, *sige* (σιγή).”] Sigaeum is a promontory of Asia, where the Hellespont expands more openly. It was called Sigaeum because of Hercules’ silence: when refused hospitality by Laomedon, king of the Trojans, he pretended to withdraw, and then came against Troy in silence. This is expressed by the Greek word *sige* (σιγή), “silence.”

**3.** Maleum is a promontory of Greece that projects into the sea and extends for fifty miles. There the wave is so violent [Note: [Col. 0520D] “So that it seems to pursue sailors.” Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “Malea’s pursuing waves”: “pursuing,” he says, means “following after.”] that it seems to pursue sailors. [Col. 0520C] This promontory received its name from Maleus, king of the Argives.

**183 4.** [Note: [Col. 0520D] “The promontory of Pelorum.” From the same source, *Aeneid* III, on “the barriers of Pelorus will grow thin.” The phrase “looking toward the north,” however, comes from Orosius, book I, chapter 2.] Pelorum is a promontory of Sicily facing north. According to Sallustius, it was named after Hannibal’s helmsman, who was buried there.

**5.** [Note: [Col. 0520D] “Pachynum.” Also from Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “the rocks of Pachynus projected”; Chacon rightly regarded the words “fat” and “foreign” as suspect.] Pachynum is a promontory of Sicily facing the south wind, named from the thickness of the air. For *pachys* (παχύς) means “fat” and “thick”; it is blown through by the south wind.

[Col. 0521A] **6.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “Lilybaeum.” From Orosius, in the same place.] Lilybaeum is a promontory of Sicily facing the setting of the sun. It was named after the city of the same name situated there.

**7.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “The promontory of Borion.” Solinus, chapter 30: “The promontory of Borion, which is struck by the north wind, was so called by Greek settlers.” What follows concerning Hippo, later called Rhegium, is indeed from the same Solinus, but did not belong in this place, much less should it have been attached to what precedes.] Borion is a promontory of Numidia, so called because it faces the north wind. It was afterward called Hippo Rhegium because it is interrupted by the sea.

**8.** Calpe is a promontory of Spain.

# **CHAPTER VIII. On Mountains and Other Terms for the Earth**

**1.** Mountains are called the highest swellings of the earth because they rise above it. Some, however, received their names for particular reasons; among these are those celebrated as the greatest according to common opinion.

**2.** Mount Caucasus extends from India to Taurus. According to the variety of peoples and languages, it is called by different names wherever it runs. When it rises toward the east to a loftier height, it is called Caucasus because of the whiteness of its snow. For in the eastern language *Caucasus* means “white,” that is, gleaming with very dense snows. Hence the Scythians who are joined to the same mountain called it *Croacasin*. [Note: [Col. 0521D] “Croacasin.” Other copies read *Graucasum*. See Pliny, book VI, chapter 18, and Solinus, chapter 52.] Among them *casim* means whiteness or snow.

**3.** Mount Taurus is called by most people the same mountain as Caucasus.

**4.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “Libanus … named from incense.” In Hebrew, *lebona* means incense.] Mount Lebanon is the highest mountain of Phoenicia, and the prophets mention it. It was named from incense because incense is gathered there. The part of it that lies above and faces the eastern region is called Antilibanus, that is, “opposite Lebanon.”

[Col. 0521C] **5.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “Ararat.” From Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*, Genesis, chapter 8.] Mount Ararat is in Armenia. History testifies that the ark came to rest there after the flood. Hence, even to this day, traces of its timbers are said to be visible there.

**185 6.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “The Acroceraunian Mountains.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “nearby Ceraunian peaks,” and *Georgics* I, on “the lofty Ceraunian mountain hurls it down.”] The Acroceraunian Mountains were named from their height and their striking by lightning. For in Greek lightning is called *keraunos* (κέραυνος). They lie between Armenia and Iberia, beginning at the Caspian Gates and extending to the source of the river Tigris.

**7.** The Hyperborean Mountains of Scythia were so called because Boreas blows above them, that is, beyond them.

**8.** [Note: [Col. 0521D] “The Riphaean Mountains.” From Servius, *Georgics* III, on “the unrestrained race of men of Riphaeus.”] The Riphaean Mountains are at the head of Germany and were named from the perpetual blowing of the winds. For in Greek *rhipē* (ῥιπή) means “impulse” and *hormē* (ὁρμή) means “force,” from *rhiptein* (ῥίπτειν), “to cast.”

**9.** Olympus is an exceedingly lofty mountain of Macedonia, so high that clouds are said to be beneath it. [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Of it Virgil writes: ‘Olympus surpassed the clouds.’” These words are nowhere found in Virgil.] Of it Virgil writes: “Olympus surpassed the clouds.” [Col. 0522A] It is called Olympus as though *Ololampus*, that is, “sky.” [Note: [Col. 0522D] “As though ‘sky.’ This is certainly not Isidore’s own statement.] This mountain divides Macedonia from Thrace.

**10.** [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Athos … from which it is seventy-six thousand [paces].” Thus Solinus, chapter 21.] Athos is a mountain of Macedonia, also higher than the clouds, and so lofty that its shadow reaches Lemnos, which is seventy-six thousand paces away.

**11.** [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Parnassus.” Servius, *Aeneid* X. “Parnassus is a mountain of Thessaly near Boeotia. It divides into two ridges: Cithaeron, belonging to Liber, and Helicon, belonging to Apollo and the Muses.” Likewise book VII: “Cyrrha and Nysa are cities situated beneath the same ridges.”] Parnassus is a mountain of Thessaly near Boeotia, rising toward the sky with a double peak. It divides into two ridges, Cyrrha and Nissa, and received its name because Apollo and Liber were worshiped on the individual ridges. These ridges are called after two brothers, Cithaeron and Helicon. For Helicon was named after Helicon, the brother of Cithaeron.

**12.** The Ceraunian Mountains are also mountains of Epirus, named from their frequent lightning strikes. For lightning is called *keraunos* (κέραυνος) in Greek.

[Col. 0522B] **13.** The Apennine Mountains were called as though “the Paenine Alps,” because Hannibal, coming into Italy, opened those same Alps. Hence Virgil writes: “He will let in the Alps, opened.” Hannibal broke through them with vinegar after the wars in Spain. [Note: [Col. 0522D] “After the wars in Spain.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “the great ruin.”] Juvenal writes: “And he broke through the mountain with vinegar.” Hence the very places he broke through are called the Paenine Alps.

**14.** Mount Etna was named from fire and sulfur; [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Hence also Gehenna.” I do not know what force this statement has.] hence also Gehenna. On the side from which the east and southwest winds blow, it has caves full of sulfur, extending all the way to the sea. These caves receive the waves into themselves and create wind; when the wind is stirred, it produces fire from the sulfur. Thus the appearance of a conflagration is produced.

**15.** The Pyrenees were likewise named from the frequent fires of lightning. For in Greek fire is called *pyr* (πῦρ). This is the mountain that lies between Gaul and Spain as though deliberately placed there as a fortification.

**16.** [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Solorius.” See Pliny, book III, chapter 1.] Solorius received its name from its singularity, because it alone appears higher than all the mountains of Spain, or because, when the sun rises, its ray is seen there before the sun itself.

**17.** Calpe is a mountain at the farthest boundaries of the Ocean, separating Europe from Africa. They say that it is the end of Atlas. [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Of which Lucan speaks.” Book I.] Lucan writes of it:

> “He filled Hesperian Calpe and the highest Atlas.”

Atlas was the brother of Prometheus and king of Africa. They say that he first devised the art of astrology, and for this reason he was said to support the heavens. Because of his learning in that discipline and his knowledge of the sky, his name was transferred to the mountain of Africa now called Atlas. [Col. 0523A] Because of its height, it appears to support, as it were, the machinery of the sky and the stars.

**18.** The Alps properly belong to the mountains of Gaul. Of them Virgil writes: “the airy Alps.” By saying “airy,” he expressed the word from the word itself. For [Note: [Col. 0523C] “For in the language of the Gauls *Alpes* means high mountains.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on “the Alpine north wind.” But Festus says: “… *album*, which we call ‘white,’ was named from the Greek word *alphos* (ἀλφός) … Nevertheless, the Sabines said *alpum*.” Hence it may be believed that the name of the Alps derives from the whiteness of their snows.] in the language of the Gauls *Alpes* means “high mountains.” These mountains serve as a kind of wall for Italy.

**19.** Hills are the more prominent ridges of mountains, as though they were their necks.

**20.** Mountain ridges (*juga*) received their name because, by their proximity, they are joined together.

**21.** A mound (*tumulus*) is a short mountain, as though “swollen earth.” Likewise, a *tumulus* is a heap of earth where no memorial exists. [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Likewise, a mound is heaped-up earth.” Something seems to be missing. Servius, *Aeneid* III, on “perhaps there was a mound nearby,” says: “By this expression he signifies both a hill and a tomb.”]

**22.** Valleys are low places, as though “stripped away.” Hence *convalleys* are depressed tracts of land between mountains.

[Col. 0523B] **188 23.** A plain is a level expanse of land. It was called *campus* because it is low underfoot, not upright like mountains, but open, extended in its own breadth, and lying flat. Hence in Greek it is called *pedion* (πεδίον). It took its name from a Greek etymology: for the Greeks call something short *chamai* (χαμαὶ). [Note: [Col. 0523C] “For *chamai* …” See above, book XII, under *camel*, and below, book XX, chapter 11, under *cama*.]

**24.** [Note: [Col. 0523D] “The ground is everything that supports.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “the grain-bearing ground.” The passage cited by Isidore is in *Aeneid* V.] The ground is everything that supports; it was named from its solidity. Thus Virgil also speaks of the sea: “And the ground is withdrawn.”

**25.** Forest tracts are vast and wooded places where trees spring upward.

**26.** [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Gorges are …” From Servius, on “that I may block the two-way passage with armed men,” *Aeneid* XI.] Gorges are entrances to narrow places between two mountains, narrow passages through which one can travel. They were named from their resemblance to throats, as though *foces*.

**27.** [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Confrages.” Festus: “*Conflages* are places into which winds flow from every direction.” Nonius: “*Confluges* are places into which different streams flow.”] *Confrages* are places toward which winds run from every direction and where they break themselves, as Naevius says: “Into the mountains, where the winds were breaking the place.”

**28.** [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Rough places are …” From Servius on “rough with rust,” *Georgics* I. The word “places” is not found in Servius.] Rough places are harsh through their condition; hence *scabies*, “scab,” is named from the roughness of the body.

**29.** [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Lairs.” The same author, *Aeneid* I, on “they will cleanse the vaulted places.” We use *lustra* by contrast both for wild animals’ lairs and for brothels, because they are poorly illuminated.] *Lustra* are dark hiding places and lairs of wild animals and wolves. Hence brothels are also called *lustra*, by contrast, because they are scarcely illuminated.

[Col. 0524A] **189 30.** A *lucus* is a place enclosed by dense trees, which deprive the ground of light. It may also have been named from *collucere*, “to shine together,” because frequent lights were placed there for pagan religious worship. [Note: [Col. 0523D] “A sacred grove.” The same author, on “There was a sacred grove in the city,” *Aeneid* I: A *lucus* is so called because it does not shine, not because lights are present there for religious purposes.]

**31.** Deserts are so called because they are not sown and therefore are, as it were, abandoned. Such are the places of forests and mountains, opposed to the richest lands, which consist of very fertile soil.

**32.** Byways are secluded and hidden places, as though outside the road; they are also called impassable places. Hence there are *aviaria*, secret places remote from the road, or places accessible only to birds. Thus comes the line: “The uncultivated bee-yards redden with berries.” [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Bird-haunts.” The same author, *Georgics* II: “Secret groves frequented by birds.”]

33. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Pleasant places, Varro. Here Verrius and the other Varro had occupied one another’s position, as is clear from Festus and Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “Pleasant green places,” and *Aeneid* V, where they have *Tartara*.] Verrius Flaccus says that *amoena loca* (“pleasant places”) are so called because they bestow love alone and attract to themselves things that are to be loved. Varro says they are so called because they are without a gift or service, as though *amunia*, that is, “without benefit,” from which no produce is paid out. Hence also those who provide nothing are called *immunes* (“without obligation”).

34. [Note: [Col. 0524C] Sunny places. From Servius, *Aeneid* VI: “He drives them across the sea.”] *Aprica loca* (“sunny places”) are those that enjoy the sun, as though from Greek ἄνευ φρίκης (*aneu phríkēs*), that is, “without cold,” or because they are beneath an open sky.

35. Shaded places, on the other hand, are as though covered over by the sky, the opposite of sunny places.

36. [Note: [Col. 0524C] And *lubricum* is said not because it slips. This applies to a place; otherwise *lubricum* is also said of what slips and of that on which one slips. Servius, *Aeneid* II: “*Lubricum* is said of what slips while it is being held, such as a fish, and of that on which one slips, as in:

[Col. 0524D] ‘. . . rising, he placed himself in Salius’s way over the slippery ground.’

And Isidore himself, Book X: ‘*Lubricus*, from that which slips.’ Therefore no correction is needed here, especially since all the books agree; one need only have attended to what is being discussed.] It is established that a place is called *lubricum* from the fact that someone slips there; and *lubricum* is said not of what slips, but of that on which one slips.

37. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Summer quarters. From Servius, *Georgics* III.] Summer quarters are shady places in which herds avoid the heat of the sun during summer. Statius:

[Col. 0524C] “And the shady summer quarters of Lycaeus lay open.”

38. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Shipyards. From the same source, *Aeneid* XI.] Shipyards are places where ships are built. This is also called a [Note: [Col. 0524D] “Shipbuilding workshop.” Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “They build, and weave together the cut timber”: “The metaphor,” he says, “is taken from ships, as Cicero says: ‘That a ship was built for you at Messana.’ Likewise, ‘they weave together,’ as in:

‘Let us weave twice ten ships from Italian oak.’

Cicero seems to have had this meaning of *textrinum* (“weaving workshop”) in mind in Book IV, Second Action, *Against Verres*, when he says: ‘Melita, gentlemen, is an island separated from Sicily by a sufficiently broad and dangerous sea; on it is a town of the same name, to which this man never went, yet it served him for three years as a *textrinum* for making women’s clothing.’ He was, of course, playing on the ambiguous word.”] weaving workshop.

190 39. [Note: [Col. 0524D] A station. From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] A station is a place where ships remain for a time.

[Col. 0525A] A harbor is where they spend the winter; [Note: [Col. 0525C] “*Importunum* is a place without a harbor,” Servius, *Aeneid* XI: “A place is *importunus* when it lacks a harbor, that is, shelter or rest, where there is no harbor.”] a place is *importunus* (“harborless”) when it has no refuge, as though it had no harbor.

40. [Note: [Col. 0525C] “A harbor is a place from access . . .” I believe this has been taken from the margin. The words are Virgil’s, *Aeneid* III:

“An unmoving harbor, protected from the approach of winds . . .”

Nor are the following words any less relevant; they are from *Georgics* III:

“And to set stables facing away from the winds and the winter sun.”] A harbor is a place removed from the approach of winds, where people customarily set up winter quarters. A harbor was also called *baiae* from the carrying away of merchandise; the ancients called it *baias*, with the declension *baia, baias*, just as *familia, familias*.

[Note: [Col. 0525C] “From carrying merchandise, *baias*.” The Baiae near Cumae have a different explanation: they were named after Baius, the companion of Ulysses, who was buried there, as Servius says, *Aeneid* III, on “Here, when he had been brought to Cumae.” Silius:

“. . . he shows that from there the warm

Baiae derive their name, and that the companion

Of the Dulichian ship gave his name to the pool.”]

41. [Note: [Col. 0525D] “A shore is land near water . . .” Servius indeed defines *littus* sometimes as land near water, sometimes as land near the sea; Isidore has included both.] A shore is land near water and the sea. It is called *littus* (“shore”) because it is struck by the wave, [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Because it is struck by the wave.” Other copies: “because it eludes the wave.”] or because it is washed by the water. [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Or because it is washed by the water.” Other copies: “because it is struck by the water.”] Cicero, in the *Topica*: “A shore is where the wave strikes.”

[Note: [Col. 0525D] “Cicero . . . where the wave strikes.” Other copies: “where the wave strikes against it”; see Book II, chapter 30. This is not Cicero’s definition, however, but Aquilius’s.]

42. *Circumluvium* is a place around which water flows. *Alluvium* is the wearing away of banks by water.

A margin is a part of any place—for example, of the sea—and from this it takes its name.

[Col. 0525B] Seaside places are, as it were, the innermost parts of the sea.

43. Estuaries are so called from the entry and exit of a river into the sea.

The mainland is continuous land, separated by no sea; the Greeks call it ἤπειρος (*ḗpeiros*), “mainland.”

191 **CHAPTER IX. On the Lower Parts of the Earth**

1. A cave is a hollow beneath the earth that can be seen into; [Note: [Col. 0525D] “A cave . . . that can be seen into.” It is evidently named from looking into it. On the gender and declension of this noun, see Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “Here is a dreadful cave,” and Priscian, Book VI.] in Greek, σπήλαιον (*spḗlaion*), in Latin, *spelunca* (“cave”).

[Note: [Col. 0526C] Greek σπήλαιον, Latin *spelunca*. From Servius, *Eclogue* X.]

2. *Spiracula* (“air vents”) is the name given to all places with poisonous vapors, [Note: [Col. 0526C] “Which the Greeks call *charoneia*.” Galen: “Often harm comes merely from the breath during inhalation, as in those places called *charoneia*.”] which the Greeks call χαρώνεια (*charṓneia*), or Acherontea. Varro also uses *spiraculum* for such a place, and *spiracula* is derived from it for places where the earth emits breath.

[Col. 0525C] 3. A *hiatus* is a deep rupture in the earth, as though from *itus* (“going”); properly, however, *hiatus* is every opening of the mouth, transferred from wild beasts, whose greed is shown by the opening of their mouths.

4. [Note: [Col. 0526C] “Properly, *profundum*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] Properly, *profundum* (“deep”) is as though “that which has its bottom far below”; improperly, however, *profundum* is said of what is either above or below, as in:

[Note: [Col. 0526C] “The seas and lands, and the deep sky.” Virgil’s words, *Aeneid* I.] “. . . the seas and lands, and the deep sky.”

[Col. 0526A] 5. [Note: [Col. 0526C] “*Barathrum*, a name of excessive depth.” From Servius, *Aeneid* III: “It blocks the way, and at the bottom of Tartarus,” etc.] *Barathrum* is a name for excessive depth. It is called *barathrum* as though “a black abyss,” evidently because of its depth.

6. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Erebus.” From the same source, *Aeneid* IV.] Erebus is the depth and recess of the underworld.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] “Styx, from *stugeros*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI.] Styx is called [Note: [Col. 0526D] “from the sorrowful,”] ἀπὸ τοῦ στυγεροῦ (*apò tou stugerou*), that is, “from sadness,” because it makes people sad or because it produces sadness.

7. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Cocytus.” Servius, *Aeneid* VI: “Cocytus, a river of the underworld, is called ἀπὸ τοῦ κωκύειν (*apò tou kōkúein*), that is, ‘to mourn.’”] Cocytus is a place of the underworld. The name Cocytus, according to its Greek interpretation, derives from lamentation and groaning.

8. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Tartarus.” From the same source, *Aeneid* VI, on “Then Tartarus itself—twice extends,” etc.] Tartarus is so called either because everything there is in confusion, ἀπὸ τῆς ταραχῆς (*apò tēs tarachēs*), “from disorder,” or—which is more correct—from ἀπὸ τοῦ ταρταρίζειν (*apò tou tartarízein*), that is, “from the trembling of cold,” meaning to be chilled and stiffened, evidently because it lacks light and sun. For there are neither vapors there, which are generated by the sun’s light, nor winds, which are stirred by the sun’s movements, but [Col. 0526B] perpetual numbness. For among the Greeks *tartarizein* is recorded as meaning “to shudder” and “to tremble.” Here there are weeping and the gnashing of teeth.

9. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Gehenna.” From Jerome on Matthew, chapter 10.] Gehenna is a place of fire and sulfur. It is thought to have been named from a valley consecrated to idols beside the wall of Jerusalem, once filled with the corpses of the dead. For there the Hebrews sacrificed their children to demons, and the place itself was called *Gehennon*. Thus the place of future punishment, where sinners are to be tormented, is designated by the name of this place. We read in Job, moreover, that Gehenna is twofold: of fire and of cold.

10. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “The underworld . . . is said.” From Augustine, Book XII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 34.] The underworld is called *inferus* because it is below. Just as, bodily, if all things retain the order of their weight, everything lower is heavier, so, spiritually, everything lower is sadder. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Hence also in the Greek language . . . the origin . . . which has nothing pleasant.” Evidently ἅδης (*hádēs*), as though ἀηδής (*aēdḗs*), “unpleasant.”] Hence, it is said that in the Greek language the origin of the name by which the underworld is called echoes the idea that it contains nothing pleasant.

11. [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Just as the heart of an animal.” From Jerome on Jonah, chapter 2. This passage should be restored from the present text.] Just as the heart of an animal is in the middle, [Note: [Col. 0526D] “So the underworld is in the middle of the earth.” Servius on the verse “to penetrate beneath the rocks of the earth,” *Aeneid* VI.] so the underworld is said to be in the middle of the earth. Hence also we read in the Gospel: “In the heart of the earth.” Philosophers, however, say that the underworld is so called because souls are carried from here to there.

**BOOK FIFTEEN. ON BUILDINGS AND LANDS**

[Col. 0527]

193 **CHAPTER ONE. On Cities**

[Col. 0527A]

1. [Note: [Col. 0527C] “Concerning the founders . . . disagreement.” From Servius, [Col. 0527D] *Aeneid* VII, on: “Nor was the founder of the city of Praeneste lacking.”] Concerning the founders of cities, disagreement is generally found, so much so that even the origin of the city of Rome cannot be carefully ascertained. For Sallust says: “The city of Rome, as I have received it, was founded and at first held by the Trojans and the Aborigines with them.” Others say that it was founded by Evander, according to Virgil:

“Then King Evander, founder of the Roman citadel.”

Others say that it was founded by Romulus, as in:

“Behold, my son, under whose auspices that famous Rome . . .”

2. If, then, the certain account of so great a city is not evident, it is not surprising that there is uncertainty about the origins of others. Therefore we should not condemn historians or commentators who offer differing accounts as ignorant, because antiquity itself created the confusion. Certainly, concerning certain cities whose definite origin is reported either by Holy Scripture or by the histories of nations, we should give a brief account.

3. Before the Flood, Cain was the first to found the city of Enoch, named after his son, in [Note: [Col. 0527D] “In Naid he founded it.” In all the books, with the letters transposed, *Naid* had become *India*. The Septuagint reads: “And Cain went out from the presence of God and dwelt in the land of Naid, opposite Eden.” Josephus, Book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4: “After traveling through a great extent of land, Cain settled with his wife in a place called Naida.” As for Jerome’s interpretation of that place, it has no bearing on Isidore, who, as usual, followed the Septuagint. Add that Jerome himself says in his book *On Hebrew Place-Names*: “Naid, the land in which Cain dwelt.” Unless, with Chacon, you prefer to read *India* for *Eden*.”] Naid; he filled that city with the great multitude of his descendants alone.

4. [Note: [Col. 0527D] “The first after the Flood.” From Orosius, Book II, chapter 6.] After the Flood, the giant Nimrod was the first to found the city of Babylon in Mesopotamia. 194 Queen Semiramis of the Assyrians enlarged it and built the city wall with bitumen and baked brick. It took its name from the confusion because there the languages of those building the tower were confused and mixed.

5. [Note: [Col. 0527D] “The Jews assert this.” From Jerome, *On Hebrew Place-Names*.] The Jews assert that Shem, Noah’s son, whom they identify with Melchizedek, was the first after the Flood to found the city of Salem in Syria, where the kingdom of that same Melchizedek was situated. The Jebusites later held it; from them it also received the name Jebus. Thus, by joining the two names Jebus and Salem, it was called Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Later called Hierosolyma by Solomon.” Eusebius says the same in Book IX of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.] which was later called Hierosolyma by Solomon, as though *Hierosolomonia*. Poets also corruptly called it Solyma, and later Aelius Hadrian called it Aelia. It is Sion, [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Which in Hebrew means ‘watchtower.’” Thus all books read it. Jerome has “watchtower.”] which in Hebrew is interpreted as “watchtower,” because it was built on a height and looks out upon those coming from afar. In our language Jerusalem is translated as “peaceful.”

**Who founded the notable towns and cities**

6. [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Dionysius . . . founded it.” From the *Chronicle* of Eusebius.] Dionysius, who is also called Father Liber, after traversing India as a conqueror, founded the city of Nysa beside the Indus River in his own name and filled it with fifty thousand people.

7. [Note: [Col. 0528C] “Medus, son of Aegeus.” And of Medea, as Diodorus says, Book V.] Medus, son of Aegeus, built Media; hence the region also took the name Media.

8. The very famous and exceedingly wealthy city of Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom, was founded by Perseus, son of Danaë, [Note: [Col. 0528D] “Perseus, son of Danaë.” Since the corrupt books read *Athei*, *Athe*, *Audiae*, and *Andiae*, why did Isidore not help himself, when shortly afterward he says that Tarsus in Cilicia was built by Perseus, descendant of Danaë? See Hyginus, *Fables* 275.] and from him Persia also received its name.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] “From him, Persia.” Rufinus, in his translation of Josephus, calls Susa the metropolis of Persia.]

9. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “Ctesiphon.” Pliny, Book VI, chapter 26.] The Parthians also founded Ctesiphon in Parthia, in rivalry with the city of Babylon.

[Col. 0528B] 10. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “The town of Susa.” Jerome calls this city *Susis*, *Susa*, and *Susae* in Daniel, chapters VIII and IX; see Pliny, Book VI, chapter 27. “They have the father of Memnon.” The Gothic manuscripts we have seen read “father,” not “brother,” as the printed copies do.] They say that Memnon’s father founded the town of Susa in Persia. It was called Susa because it overlooks the Susa River. There is the palace of Cyrus, decorated with white and variegated stone, golden columns, coffered ceilings, and gems; it also contains an image of the heavens marked out with shining stars, as well as other things incredible to human minds.

11. The Bactrians founded the town of Bactra, giving it its name from their own river, which is called the Bactrus.

12. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “Carrhae.” From Jerome, *On Hebrew Place-Names*.] Carrhae is a city of Mesopotamia, founded by the Parthians beyond Edessa. There the Roman army was once defeated and its commander Crassus captured.

13. Nimrod, son of Cush, founded the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia 196 after migrating from Babylon; [Col. 0528C] he also ruled there. It was formerly called Arach. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “He also built Chalanne.” Jerome says in his *Questions on Genesis* and on Amos, chapter 6, that this is the same city as Ctesiphon. The same author should be consulted in *Hebrew Place-Names*.] He also built Chalanne, which later, with its name changed, was called Seleucia after King Seleucus.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] “Philadelphia.” From the same book.] Raphaim, a most ancient people whom the sons of Lot destroyed, founded the city of Philadelphia in Arabia.

14. Seleucus, one of Alexander’s attendants, after Alexander’s death seized the kingdom of the East, founded a city in Syria, named it Antioch after his father Antiochus, and made it the capital of Syria. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “He also founded Laodicea.” Eusebius, *Chronicle*: “Seleucus founded the cities of Antioch, Seleucia, Laodicea, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pella.”] He also built the cities of Laodicea and Seleucia, as well as Apamea and Edessa.

15. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Damascus.” From Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*.] Damascus in Syria was founded and named after Damascus, the son of Abraham’s steward. It formerly held primacy throughout all Syria. For Antioch, Laodicea, and Apamea had not yet flourished there; we know that these cities were built after Alexander. This is the Damascus whom Abraham had said would be his future heir before Isaac was promised to him.

16. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Gaza.” From the same author, *On Hebrew Place-Names* and on Ezekiel, chapter 40.] The Hivites founded Gaza, a town of Palestine; the Cappadocians lived there after killing its former inhabitants. It was called Gaza because King Cambyses of Persia placed his treasures there when he made war upon the Egyptians. In the language of the Persians, a treasure is called *gaza*.

[Col. 0529B] 197 17. The Allophyli founded the city of Philistim. It is Ascalon, which we mentioned above, named after Cesloim, who was a grandson of Ham and son of Mesraim.

18. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Dor.” From Jerome, *Epitaph of Paula*. But Jerome’s passage, left incomplete in the palimpsest, was not polished by Isidore or Braulio.] Dor was once a very powerful city and, by a reversal of fortune, became the Tower of Strato. Later King Herod of Judaea called it Caesarea in honor of Caesar Augustus. There the Church saw the house of Cornelius, the small buildings of Philip, and the chamber of the four prophetic virgins.

19. Joppa, a maritime town of Palestine, was built by those same Palestinians, [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Where a rock is shown.” From Solinus, chapter 47. This passage has been restored from that source.] where a rock is shown that still bears traces of Andromeda’s chains; the monster to which she was exposed was larger in appearance than elephants.

[Col. 0529C] 20. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Jericho.” From Jerome, *On Hebrew Place-Names*.] Jericho is said to have been founded by the Jebusites, from whom it is also thought to have taken its name; Jesus overthrew it. In its place Oza of Bethel, from the tribe of Ephraim, built another city. But this too, at the time when Jerusalem was being attacked by the Romans, was captured and destroyed because of the treachery of its inhabitants. A third city was built in its place, which still exists today.

21. Emor built Shechem, a city of Samaria, which in Latin and Greek is called Sichima, and named it after his son Shechem. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Shechem, which is now Neapolis.” Jerome, in the same work and in the *Epitaph of Paula*.] It is now Neapolis, the city of the Samaritans.

22. The Jebusites founded Bethel, a city of Samaria, which was previously called Luz. But after Jacob, sleeping there, saw a ladder leaning against heaven and said, “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven,” the place received the name [Col. 0529D] Bethel, [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Beth.” From the book *On Hebrew Place-Names*.] that is, “house of God.” When golden calves were made there by Jeroboam, [Col. 0530A] it was called Bethaven, that is, “house of the idol,” although formerly it had been called “house of God.”

23. [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Bethlehem, etc.” Jerome, *Commentary on Amos*: “It is six miles from holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world.” And in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “Hail, Bethlehem, [Col. 0530D] house of bread, in which was born that bread which descended from heaven.”] Bethlehem of Judah, the city of David, which gave birth to the Savior of the world, is said to have been founded by the Jebusites and first called Ephrata. When Jacob pastured his flocks there, he gave the same place the name Bethlehem, by a kind of prophecy of what was to come; it is interpreted as “house of bread,” because there the bread that descended from heaven was born.

24. [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Chebron.” Jerome writes it this way as well. Other copies have *Hebron*.] Chebron, a city of Judaea formerly called Arbe, was founded by giants seven years before the Egyptian city of Tanis was founded by them. It is called Arbe from a number, because three patriarchs and the fourth, Adam, were buried there. It is also called [Note: [Col. 0530D] “It is also Mamre.” From *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 35.] Mamre, after one of Abraham’s friends.

25. [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Samaria, etc.” See Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 36.] Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, built Samaria, from which the entire surrounding region took its name, and called it Samaria, that is, “watch-post,” because, when he transported Israel, he settled Medes there as guards. After it was captured by siege, Antiochus leveled it to the ground. Later Herod rebuilt it from its foundations and, in honor of Augustus, called it Augusta—that is, Sebastia in Greek. The prophets Elisha and Obadiah lie buried there, as does John the Baptist, greater than any born of women.

26. Herod the other, in Judaea, founded Tiberias in the name of Tiberius Caesar.

27. [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Tyre.” The same author, on chapter 33.] Tyre was a city founded by the Phoenicians. It is the city from which gold was brought to King Solomon and where the finest purple is dyed. Hence the noble purple is also called Tyrian.

[Col. 0530C] 28. [Note: [Col. 0530D] “The Phoenicians.” From Justin, Book XVIII.] The Phoenicians, departing from the Red Sea, founded the wealthy city of Sidon; [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Which they named from the abundance of fish.” I myself saw coins found at Gades, which was a Phoenician colony; on one side was Hercules, the god of the Sidonians, and on the other two fish.] because of the abundance of fish they called it Sidon. For the Phoenicians call a fish *sidon*. They also founded Tyre in Syria, Utica in Africa, Hippo, Leptis, and other cities along the coast.

29. They founded Thebes in Boeotia under the leadership of Cadmus; finally, advancing to the farthest limits of the world, they built a city in the Ocean and called it Gades in their own language. For it was an ancient custom of the Phoenician people for many men to set out together from home for the sake of trade; after winning the goodwill of the inhabitants through commerce in things previously unknown to them, they occupied places that seemed suitable for founding cities.

30. From these people Dido also set out and founded a city on the shore of Africa, [Col. 0530D] naming it [Note: [Col. 0530D] “She named it Carthada.” From Solinus, chapter 40. Servius also says, *Aeneid* IV, on “Carthage, or ancient Tyre,” that Carthage was named from *Cartha*.] Carthada, which in the Phoenician language means “new city”; 200 later, after the language had changed, it was called Carthage. [Col. 0531A] Scipio destroyed it. The city that now exists was later founded by the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0531C] “Carthage was formerly Byrsa.” From Servius, in the same passage. Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “And they bought the ground.”] Carthage was formerly called Byrsa, afterward Tyre, and then Carthage.

31. [Note: [Col. 0531C] “Memphis . . . was reigning.” These are the words of Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.] Epaphus, son of Jupiter, built the city of Memphis in Egypt while he was ruling Lower Egypt. This is the city where papyrus grows and where the best mathematicians also lived.

[Note: [Col. 0531C] “For this city.” From Jerome on Isaiah XIX.] For this city, devoted to magical arts, still displays to the present day the former traces of its error.

32. [Note: [Col. 0531C] “Tanis.” From the same author, on Isaiah III.] Tanis is the capital of Egypt, where Pharaoh was situated and where Moses performed all the signs recorded in Exodus. The Titans, that is, the Giants, are said to have built it and named it after themselves.

33. [Note: [Col. 0531C] “Heliopolis.” From the same author, in the book *On Hebrew Place-Names*, under *On*.] Heliopolis is a city of Egypt, which in Latin is translated “city of the sun,” [Col. 0531B] as the interpreters of the Septuagint understand it. For thus they read in Exodus I: [Col. 0531C] “And they built fortified cities for Pharaoh, Pithom, Rameses, and On, which is Heliopolis.” [Note: [Col. 0531D] “As the translators of the Septuagint.” The words “and On, which is Heliopolis” occur in the Septuagint text of Exodus I, but are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Latin books.] It was built by the children of Israel; there [Note: [Col. 0531D] “Petephres.” Jerome also has this form. The Vulgate has *Puthiphares*. Hebrew writing, often lacking vowels, frequently produces such variation in names.] Petephres the priest lived, whom Ezekiel mentions.

34. [Note: [Col. 0531D] “The city of Alexandria.” From Hegesippus, Book IV, chapter 27. See Strabo, Book XVII.] Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria, which retains his name. He established it at the boundary of Africa and Egypt and ordered it to be the capital of the region of Egypt. It lies 201 between Egypt and the sea, like a barrier, and has no harbor.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] “This is the Egyptian city . . .” Jerome, *Epitaph of Paula*: “And the city of No, which was afterward changed into Alexandria.”] This is the Egyptian city of No, afterward transformed into Alexandria.

35. Thebes of Egypt was founded by Cadmus, [Note: [Col. 0531D] “Which among the Egyptian cities is distinguished by the number of its gates.” From Solinus, chapter on Egypt, 45.] and is considered among the Egyptian cities the most distinguished for the number of its gates; to it the Arabs bring merchandise from everywhere. Hence the region of Egypt was called Thebaid. There are Thebes in both Boeotia and Egypt, though they were founded by the same founder.

[Col. 0531C] 36. Ptolemais and Berenice were named after Egyptian kings, by whom they were also built.

37. [Note: [Col. 0531D] “Caesarea of Cappadocia.” After these words there is a lacuna in the better books, most foolishly filled out by later writers.] Caesarea of Cappadocia [lacuna].

Perseus, descendant of Danaë, built Tarsus in Cilicia. The apostle Paul was from this city: “Born,” he says, “in Tarsus of Cilicia.”

[Note: [Col. 0531D] “A certain place in India is called Tharsis.” This should doubtless be read, not *Tarsus*. Jerome, Isaiah LXVI: “In the Hebrew language *Tharsis* means ‘sea,’ and, as they say, it is a region of India, although Josephus, changing a letter, thinks it is called *Tarsus*, after the city of Cilicia to which Jonah wished to flee from Joppa. Again, in Letter 133, he criticizes Josephus for thinking Tarsus and Tharsis to be the same.”] A certain place in India is also called Tharsis.

[Col. 0532A] 38. Seleucus, who also founded Antioch, founded Seleucia in Isauria.

Ilus, son of Apollo, founded Ilium in Phrygia.

[Note: [Col. 0532C] “The Amazons founded Ephesus.” From Solinus.] The Amazons built Ephesus in Asia.

39. Theseus built Smyrna, which became the homeland of the poet Homer, and [Note: [Col. 0532C] “Called Smyrna.” The same author above, Book XIII, chapter 21.] it was called Smyrna because the Hermus River cuts through its fields.

40. [Note: [Col. 0532C] “Amphytus and Tilchius.” Pliny, Book VI, chapter 5; Ammianus, Book XXII; and Solinus. *Circius*, which appears in many books, arose from *Tilcius*, as is also found in the Toledo Church manuscript of Pliny.] Amphytus and Tilchius, charioteers of Castor and Pollux, built Dioscurias, the city of the Colchians, naming it after them. For Castor and Pollux are called διόσκουροι (*dióskouroi*), “sons of Zeus,” in Greek.

41. [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Nicomedia, from Nicomedes.” Eusebius, *Chronicle*: “Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, enlarged the city of Astacus and called it Nicomedia.”] Nicomedia was built by Nicomedes, king of Bithynia.

202 [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Bithynia founded.” The same Eusebius: “Bithynia was founded by Phoenice; it was previously called Mariandyna.”] Bithynia was founded by Phoenice; it was first called [Col. 0532B] Mariandyna.

42. [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Constantinople.” From Orosius, Book VII, chapter 28, in almost the same words.] Constantine established the city of Constantinople in Thrace, naming it after himself. In merit and power it alone equaled Rome. [Note: [Col. 0532D] “First founded by Pausanias.” From Justin, Book IX.] It was first founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans, and called Byzantium, [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Or because it extends so far.” See Pliny, Book IV, chapter 11; Solinus and Capella. The etymology nevertheless remains uncertain.] either because it stretches so far between the Adriatic Sea and the Propontis, or [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Or because it is a receptacle, etc.” From Justin, Book IX.] because it is a receptacle for the resources of land and sea. Hence Constantine judged it especially suitable to establish as a city, so that it might become a receptacle for him by land and sea. Hence it is now the seat of the Roman Empire and the capital of the entire East, just as Rome is the capital of the West.

43. Epirus in Thrace was founded by Pyrrhus and named after him.

44. Cecrops founded Athens in Hellas and called it Cecropia after himself. [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Amphictyon . . . gave it.” From the same author, Book II.] Amphictyon, who ruled in Greece third after Cecrops, dedicated it to Minerva and gave the city the name Athens. For Minerva is called Ἀθήνη (*Athḗnē*) in Greek. Hence the Greeks also assert that Minerva was the inventor of many arts, [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Because letters . . . also had their home there.” From the same source.] because letters, the arts of various disciplines, and philosophy itself had Athens as their temple, so to speak.

45. Corinth in Achaea [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Corinth, son of Orestes, founded it.” Strabo says it was founded by Sisyphus and first called Corcyra, then Ephyra, after Ephyra, daughter of Oceanus; afterward it was destroyed and rebuilt by Corinth, son of Orestes.] was founded by Corinth, son of Orestes. The Greeks call it *Corinthea*, that is, “administration of the state.”

46. Cadmus, coming from the Phoenicians, founded Thebes of Boeotia, after he had previously built Thebes of Egypt.

203 47. Mycenae [lacuna].

Lacedaemon was founded by Lacedaemon, son of Semele.

Sparta was named after Sparto, son of Phoroneus, who was the son of Inachus.

[Note: [Col. 0533C] “That this is Sparta itself, etc.” From Orosius, Book I, final chapter.] Sparta itself is the city also called Lacedaemon; hence the Lacedaemonians are called Spartans.

48. [Note: [Col. 0533C] “Achaea, from Achaeus.” From the *Chronicle* of Eusebius.] Achaea was founded by Achaeus.

[Note: [Col. 0533C] “Pelops, who . . . the Peloponnese.” Eusebius: “Pelops ruled at Argos for fifty-three years, from whom the Peloponnese was named.”] Pelops, who ruled at Argos, founded the city of the Peloponnese.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] “Cecrops.” Thus all books read. But I would prefer *Cercapus*, whose sons founded Lindus, Talyson, and Camirus. “Lindus,” says Stephanus, “is a city on Rhodes, belonging to Cercaphus, son of Helios, and Cydippe, daughter of Ochimus.” See Strabo, Book XIV, and Diodorus, Book XI.] Cecrops built Rhodes on the island of Rhodes.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] “Carpathus, Cos.” These passages are incomplete, but they could be supplied from Diodorus and Stephanus as follows: “Joclus founded Carpathus; Merops founded Cos.”] Carpathus, Cos.

Aeos, son of Typhon, founded Paphos.

Angaeus, son of Lycurgus, founded Samos.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] “Dardanus . . . Dardania.” From the *Chronicle* of Eusebius.] Dardanus founded Dardania.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] “Thessalonica, Thessalus.” I would prefer “Thessaly,” since Stephanus says that Thessalonica was founded by Cassander.] Thessalus, son of Graecus, built Thessalonica and also ruled there.

49. [Note: [Col. 0533D] “Brundisium.” The author Hesychius says that βρένδον (*bréndon*) means “deer.” According to Stephanus, βρεήδιον (*breḗdion*), or according to Strabo, βρεντέσιον (*brentésion*), was called “the head of a deer” by the Messapians.] The Greeks built Brundisium. Brundisium was called so in Greek because *brunda* means “the head of a deer.” Its shape is such that the horns, head, and tongue all seem to be represented in the arrangement of the city itself.

50. [Note: [Col. 0533D] “In Italy, Janiculum by Janus.” From Solinus, chapter on Italy.] In Italy, Janiculum was founded by Janus, Saturnia by Saturn, and Latium was also founded and named because Saturn, fleeing there, had hidden himself.

204 51. [Note: [Col. 0533D] “Pompeii in Campania by Hercules.” Pompeii in Solinus, in the same passage; *Pompeia* in Strabo, Book V.] In Campania, Pompeii was founded by Hercules, who, victorious after returning from Spain, had driven along a procession of cattle.

[Col. 0533C] 52. Aeneas, coming to the same Italy after the destruction of Troy, founded Lavinium, naming it after his wife.

53. Ascanius, having abandoned the kingdom of his stepmother Lavinia, built Alba Longa. It was called Alba because of the color of its pigs; Longa, because it is a long town beside the length of the hill on which it lies. From this city the Alban kings also began to be named.

54. [Note: [Col. 0534C] “Capua, Capys.” Servius, *Aeneid* X, on: “And Capys; from him the name of the Campanian city is derived.” He says that Campania was named from Capys, but Livy wants it named from the flat lands on which it lies.] Capua was built by Capus Silvius, king of the Albans, and called by the name of its founder. Some, however, say that Capua was named from its capacity, because its soil receives every fruit necessary for life; others derive the name from the flat lands on which it lies. It is the chief city of Campania and is counted among the three greatest cities, Rome and Carthage; from it the Italian province was also called Campania.

55. After Romulus had killed Amulius at Alba and restored his grandfather Numitor to the kingdom, he came to the place where Rome now stands. There he established a settlement, built walls, and called the city Rome after himself. It is said, however, that Evander had founded it earlier, hence the line:

“Then Father Evander, founder of the Roman citadel.”

56. Ancus Martius, born from the daughter of Numa Pompilius, founded a city at the mouth of the Tiber. It was intended both to receive foreign merchandise and to delay the enemy; from its location he called it Ostia.

57. [Note: [Col. 0534D] “Certain Gauls, because of internal discord.” From Livy, Book V.] Certain Gauls, moved by internal discord and the continual dissensions of their people, set out for Italy in search of new settlements. After expelling the Tuscans from their ancestral homes, they founded Mediolanum and other cities.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] “It was called Mediolanum . . . because a woolly sow was said to have been found there.” Claudian, *On the Marriage of Honorius*:

“Now the triton, with foaming breast, had reached

The lands of the Ligurians,

And had stretched his weary limbs upon the waves.

Immediately, flying high, he came to the walls

Founded by the Gauls, displaying the fleece-bearing sow.”

A marble sow can still be seen in the Milanese curia. Other copies: “a sow with wool in the middle.”] It was called Mediolanum because a sow with wool in the middle was said to have been found there.

58. Histories favor the view that Messapia received its origin from the Greek Messapus, later changing its name to Calabria. At the beginning, Peucetius, brother of Oenotrus, had called it Peucetia.

59. [Note: [Col. 0534D] “Manto, daughter of Tiresias.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “Manto, the prophetess.”] After the destruction of the Thebans, Manto, daughter of Tiresias, is said to have been carried to Italy and founded Mantua.

[Col. 0534C] It is in Venetia, which is called Cisalpine Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] “And it was called Mantua because it watches over the empty.” Thus the older books read, and perhaps correctly. For in Book IV he says that *mania*, a disease, is named from emptiness, which the Greeks call μανία (*manía*), and *mane* as though from μανόν (*manón*), “thin” or “empty.” This fits beautifully with the story of the prophetic Manto fleeing there. If anyone prefers *Manes*, we shall not object.] It was also called Mantua because it watches over the empty.

60. Parthenopia was named Parthenopea after a certain maiden named Parthenope, who was buried there; later Augustus preferred that town to be called Neapolis.

61. At the promontory of Leucas, where there was a temple of the Actian Apollo, Augustus waged war against Antony. After defeating him, he founded a city in the Actian Gulf, which he called Nicopolis (“City of Victory”) after his victory.

[Col. 0535A] 62. [Note: Phalantus … Taras. See Servius, *Aeneid* III:

> Here, if the report is true, is the race of Herculean Tarentum.]

Phalantus, leader of the Parthenii, established the Parthenii.

Taras was the son of Neptune; from him the city of Tarentum was both founded and named.

206 63. [Note: When Cyrus … The same account is found in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XV.]

When Cyrus was occupying the coastal cities of Greece, and the Phocaeans, having been defeated by him, were being pressed by every extremity, they swore that they would flee as far as possible from Persian rule, to a place where not even their name would be heard. [Note: And thus they founded themselves in the remotest … From Justin, Book XLIII.]

And so they departed by ship for the remotest shores of Gaul and, defending themselves with weapons against Gallic savagery, founded Massilia and named it after their leader. [Note: These Varro says were trilingual, etc. From Jerome, Prologue to Book II of the *Epistle to the Galatians*.]

Varro says that these people were trilingual, because they spoke Greek, Latin, and Gaulish.

64. Narbo, Arelate, and Pictavium were founded by their own colonists.

[Col. 0535B] They say that Burdigala was named because it first had Burgi Gauls as colonists, by whom it had previously been filled with inhabitants.

65. The Scipios built Tarraco in Spain; therefore it is the capital of the province of Tarraconensis.

66. [Note: Caesaraugusta … sepulchres. This entire passage is absent from Cardinal Sirlet’s book and from one of the Toledo manuscripts.]

Caesaraugusta, a town of Tarraconensian Spain, was both established and named by Caesar Augustus. Because of the pleasantness of its location and its attractions, it surpassed all the cities of Spain in distinction and renown, flourishing in the burial places of holy martyrs.

67. The Africans, occupying the coast of Spain under Hannibal, built Carthago Spartaria, which, soon captured by the Romans and made a colony, also gave its name to the province. But now it has been overthrown by the Goths and reduced to desolation.

[Col. 0535C] 68. [Note: Saguntum. From Jerome, Book II of the *Epistle to the Galatians*.]

The Greeks who came from the island of Zacynthus founded Saguntum in Spain; the Africans later attacked and destroyed it in war.

69. [Note: Emerita was built by Caesar Augustus. Dio, Book LIII.]

Caesar Augustus built Emerita after he had conquered Lusitania and certain islands of the Ocean, giving it its name because he had settled veteran soldiers there. For *emeriti* means veterans discharged from military service.

70. Olyssipona was founded and named by Ulysses, at the place where, as the historians say, the sky and the seas are distinguished from the lands. [Note: At this point, as the historians say. Pliny, Book IV, chapter 21: “Then a promontory projects far out into the open sea in a vast horn, which some have called Artabrum, others Magnum, and many Olyssiponense, separating lands, seas, and sky from the town.” Solinus and Capella say nearly the same; Isidore has compressed the passage too much.]

71. Julius Caesar founded Hispalis, which he named Julia Romula after himself and after the name of the city of Rome. [Note: Hispalis … because it was situated on marshy ground. Others offer no more certain explanations.]

Hispalis, however, received its additional name from its location, because it was situated on marshy soil, supported by piles driven deep into the ground so that it would not give way upon a slippery and unstable foundation.

72. The town of Gades was founded by the Carthaginians, who also founded Carthago Spartaria.

73. [Note: Septa, a town … The Seven Brother Mountains are mentioned by Pliny, Book V, chapter 2, and by Capella. Ptolemy likewise calls them *heptadelphoi* (ἑπταδέλφους), “seven brothers.”]

Septa is a town overlooked by seven mountains which, because of their resemblance to one another, are called the Brothers and rise above the Strait of Gades.

208 74. [Note: And Lixus. Solinus also calls it *Lix*, Pliny *Lixos*, and others *Lixa*.]

Antheus is said to have founded the cities of Tingis and Lixus; Hercules is reported to have defeated and killed him in a wrestling match. Lixus was named from the Lixus River of Mauretania, where the royal palace of Antheus stood; Sala was so called because it overlooks the Sala River.

75. The city of Caesarea in Mauretania was founded by Juba, king of the Moors, in honor of Caesar Augustus, and he named it Caesarea after him, just as Herod founded another Caesarea in Palestine, which is now a very famous city.

76. [Note: Icosium. From Solinus, chapter on Mauretania.]

Icosium was a town of Caesarean Mauretania. When Hercules passed through that region, twenty men from his retinue separated from him and built it. So that no one might boast individually of having given the city its name, it was named Icosium from the number of its founders.

77. [Note: Cyrene was a queen. Servius, *Aeneid* IV: “Cyrene and Barce were queens, and each gave her name to a city.”]

Cyrene was a queen of Libya. She founded the city of Cyrene after her own name, and from it she also called Libya Cyrenaica.

## CHAPTER II. On Public Buildings

1. [Note: A city is … Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 8: “A city is nothing other than a multitude of people bound together by some bond of fellowship.”]

A *civitas* (“city-state”) is a multitude of people united by a bond of fellowship. It is named from *cives*, that is, from the inhabitants themselves, because it gathers and contains the lives of many. For the city itself consists of walls, whereas the *civitas* is called not stones but inhabitants.

2. There are three kinds of communities: of families, of cities, and of peoples.

3. *Urbs* (“city”) is said to derive from *orbis* (“circle”), because in ancient times cities were laid out in a circle; [Note: Or from *urbum*. Varro, Book IV.] or from *urbum*, the part of the plough with which walls were marked out. Hence the line:

[Note: “And he chose a place.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “A place for a dwelling.” The same, Book III: “And he chose a place for his kingdom.” Isidore joined these passages.]

> And he chose a place for his kingdom, and to enclose it with a furrow.

The site of the future city was marked out by a furrow—that is, by a plough. [Note: Cato on founding a city. Servius, apparently referring to this passage, *Aeneid* V, on “He marks out the city with a plough.” See Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*.]

Cato says: “Whoever founds a new city shall plough with a bull and a cow; where he has ploughed, let him make a wall; where he wishes the gate to be, let him lift up the plough, carry it across, and call it a gate.”

4. A city was therefore surrounded by a plough drawn by young animals of different sexes, because of the mingling of families and as an image of the sower who produces and returns fruit. [Note: A city is founded by the plough and overturned by the plough.
