Acron on Horace’s passage: “When cities are founded and overturned, this custom was followed, that it be done with a plough.” Gaius, title “On Usufruct,” says that a plough was driven over destroyed Carthage.]

A city is founded by the plough and overturned by the plough. Hence Horace:

> And the hostile plough might be driven into the walls.

5. Some have said that *oppidum* (“town”) derives from the opposition of walls; others, from storing resources, because it is fortified; others, because a gathering of inhabitants there gives mutual aid against the enemy. For at first human beings were, as it were, naked and unarmed: they had neither defenses against wild beasts nor shelters from cold and heat, nor were people themselves sufficiently safe from one another.

6. At length, through natural ingenuity, they wove huts and cottages for themselves from branches and reeds, using caves and woodland coverings, so that life might be safer and access might be denied to those who could cause harm. This is the origin of towns, which, because they gave aid, were said to have been called *oppida*. A town differs in size and walls from a village, a fort, and a rural settlement.

7. Settlements are called either cities, colonies, municipalities, villages, forts, or rural districts.

8. Strictly speaking, a *civitas* is one founded not by newcomers but by people born in the same soil. Therefore cities founded by their own citizens are called *civitates*, not colonies.

9. A colony, by contrast, is a place filled with new inhabitants because of a shortage of native residents. Hence *colonia* is also said to derive from the cultivation of the land.

[Col. 0537C] 210 10. A *municipium* is a place which, while retaining the status of a city, obtains from the ruler some right involving lesser or greater official responsibility. It is called a *municipium* from *munia*, that is, from official duties, because its inhabitants render only the duties—that is, the taxes owed—or services. For matters involving liberal and highly distinguished causes, and those proceeding from the ruler, are not handled there. These belong to the dignity of cities.

11. Villages, forts, and rural districts are places adorned with no civic dignity, but inhabited by an ordinary gathering of people; because of their smallness, they are assigned to larger cities.

12. [Note: *Vicus* from neighboring inhabitants. So the imperial manuscripts. The reference is only to the dwellings themselves. The Gothic manuscripts favor the editors’ reading, since shortly afterward he affirms that the dwellings themselves are called villages.]

A *vicus* (“village”) is so called from inhabitants who are merely neighbors, or because it has only streets and no walls. It is without the protection of walls, although the dwellings themselves within a city are also called *vici*. It is called a *vicus* because it serves in place of a city, or because it has only streets and no walls.

13. The ancients called a *castrum* a town situated in a very high place, as though it were a “high hut”; its plural is *castra*, and its diminutive is *castellum* (“fortlet”). Alternatively, it may be so called because permission was restricted there for its inhabitants, lest the place lie exposed to the enemy through indiscriminate wandering.

14. *Pagi* (“rural districts”) are places suitable for buildings, where people live among the fields. They are also called *conciliabula* (“meeting places”), from the gathering and fellowship of many people in one place.

15. *Compita* (“crossroads”) are places where country people customarily gather. They are called *compita* because many places in the fields converge there and because country people come together there.

16. *Suburbana* are buildings situated around a city, as though “under the city.”

17. *Moenia* (“city walls”) are the walls of a city. They are so called because they protect the city, as if they were the city’s defenses, that is, its safeguards.

18. *Munium* is said to derive from “made by hand”; walls likewise are named from fortification, as though “fortified,” because they protect and guard the interior of the city. *Moenia* has two meanings. For sometimes, by an abuse of language, all the public buildings of a city are called *moenia*, as in:

> We divide the walls and open up the city’s buildings.

Strictly speaking, however, *moenia* means only walls.

19. A wall is adorned with towers and defensive works.

Towers are so called because they are rounded and tall.

For something is *teres* (“rounded”) when it is circular together with height, like a column. [Note: *Teres* means something round. Servius, *Aeneid* VI: “Teres” is something rounded with height. And *Eclogue* VIII: “Teres” means oblong and round, like a column.]

Although towers may be built square or broad, they nevertheless appear round to those viewing them from a distance. This is because the image of each angle gradually vanishes and is consumed over the long expanse of air, so that the object appears round. [Note: Although they are square. The passage is from Lucretius, Book IV:

> And when from afar we see the city’s square towers,  
> It consequently happens that they often appear round,  
> Because the obtuse angle …]

20. *Propugnacula* (“defensive works”) are the battlements of walls, so called because defense is conducted from them.

21. A *promurale* is so called because it serves as a defense in front of a wall. It is close to the wall, that is, before the wall.

22. [Note: A gate is called that through which something can … Servius, *Aeneid* I: “Every exit is called a gate, as if it were the means by which something can be brought in or carried out.”]

A gate is that through which something can be brought in or carried out. Strictly speaking, the term is applied to a city gate or a camp gate, as stated above. A *vicus*, as previously explained, consists of the dwellings themselves within a city, and hence its inhabitants are called neighbors. Roads are the narrow spaces themselves that lie between the *vici*.

23. [Note: Streets. Augustine, Sermon 10 on Psalm 118.]

*Plateae* (“streets”) are the continuous and broader roads of cities, named according to the proper usage of the Greek language from their breadth; for the Greeks call something broad *platos* (πλάτος).

24. A *quintana* is a fifth section of a street through which a wagon can pass.

25. *Cloacae* (“sewers”) are so called because waters are filtered through them. They say that Tarquinius Priscus first constructed them at Rome so that whenever a flood of rain occurred, the waters might be discharged through them outside the city, lest, during the greatest and continued storms, the force of the waters overturn the level ground or the foundations of the cities.

212 26. [Note: *Imboli*. Thus the old manuscripts; I think *emboli* should be read, from *subvolaminia* … and that it signifies what Asconius, in *On the Divination*, called projecting upper stories. It is well known what an *embolon* (ἔμβολον) is among the Greeks.]

*Imboli* are so called either because they are projecting upper structures or because people walk beneath them; for they are porticoes on either side of streets.

27. [Note: A *forus* is a place for conducting lawsuits. Those who have boldly criticized Isidore’s account of the origin of this word have made themselves objects of ridicule. Charisius, Book I: *forum*, in the neuter gender, means a place designated for conducting affairs, or signifies commerce: Lucilius, “when they go about those marketplaces.” In the masculine gender, however, it means the decks of ships and is always plural, although Gellius used *fora* of ships in the neuter and Lucilius used *forum* of business in the masculine, Book III. *Forus* was formerly decorated with lamps. Victorinus, in his book *On Orthography*: “*Forus* means a standing-place, whether in a marketplace, ship, or winepress.” As for the etymology, since we have already discussed this entire class of words once, I will merely point out that these explanations too should not be despised: why should *forum* not derive from *fari* (“to speak”), or from Greek *phō* (φῶ), just as *agora* derives from *agoreuein* (ἀγορεύειν), “to speak publicly”? In the mention of King Phoroneus there is a certain careful negligence shared by Isidore with other very authoritative writers.]

A *forus* is a place for conducting lawsuits, named from *fari* (“to speak”), or from King Phoroneus, who first gave laws to the Greeks. These places are also called *pro-rostra* (“before the Rostra”), because after the Punic War, when the Carthaginian ships had been captured, their beaks were removed and fixed in the Roman Forum, so that they might serve as the emblem of this victory. [Note: They are called the Rostra. The same is found in Book XVIII, chapter 15.]

28. The *curia* is so called because there the senate administers all matters with care.

29. The *praetorium* is so called because the praetor sits there to deliberate. [Note: “Sits there to examine matters.” Another reading: “to discuss”; perhaps “to adjudicate.” Compare Book IX, chapter 4, and Book XVIII, chapter 15: “A judge is so called because he adjudicates according to law.”]

30. A *gymnasium* is generally a place for exercises. At Athens, however, it was a place where philosophy was learned and the study of wisdom practiced. For in Greek it is called *gymnasion* (γυμνάσιον), which in Latin means “exercise,” that is, training. Baths, running grounds, and athletes’ training places are also called gymnasia, because everyone there trains in the study of his own art.

31. The Capitol at Rome was so called because it was the supreme head of the Roman city and religion. Others say that when Tarquinius Priscus was opening the foundations of the Capitol at Rome, he found a human head marked with Etruscan letters at the place of the foundation, and therefore called it the Capitol.

32. Citadels are the elevated and fortified parts of a city. [Note: Whatever is safest. Varro, Book IV: “A citadel is named from *arcere* (‘to ward off’), because it is the most strongly fortified place in a city, from which the enemy can most easily be kept away.”]

For all the safest parts of cities are called *arces* (“citadels”) because they ward off the enemy; hence also *arcus* (“arch”) and *arca* (“chest, strongbox”).

33. [Note: The Roman Circus. These words are repeated in Book XVIII, chapter 28.]

The Romans are thought to have called it the *circus* from the circling of the horses, because there the horses run around the turning-posts.

34. [Note: *Theatrum*, from *theōria* (ἀπὸ τῆς θεωρίας). From Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “the theater in the middle of the valley.”]

The theater was named from the spectacle, *apo tēs theōrias* (ἀπὸ τῆς θεωρίας), because in it the people stood above and watched as they contemplated stage games.

35. An amphitheater is so called because it is composed of two theaters. For an amphitheater is round, whereas a theater forms a semicircle from the middle of the amphitheater.

36. [Note: Labyrinth. From Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “as once the labyrinth in lofty Crete is said to have been.” See Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 13.]

A labyrinth is a building with walls arranged in intricate confusion, such as the one made by Daedalus in Crete, where the Minotaur was confined. Whoever entered it without a ball of thread could not find the way out. The building was constructed so that, when its doors were opened, a terrifying thunderous sound could be heard within. One descended more than a hundred steps; inside were images and monstrous figures, countless passages leading in different directions through the darkness, and other features designed to confuse those entering, so that it seemed impossible to come from its darkness into the light. There are four labyrinths: the first Egyptian, the second Cretan, the third on Lemnos, and the fourth in Italy. All were constructed in such a way that not even the passage of ages could destroy them.

37. [Note: Lighthouse. From Hegesippus, Book IV, chapter 27; Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 12; and Solinus, chapter 45.]

A *pharus* (“lighthouse”) is a very large tower. Greeks and Latins alike have called it *pharus* from the use of the thing itself, because it is seen from far away by sailors as a signal of flames. Such a tower is said to have been built by Ptolemy near Alexandria at a cost of eight hundred talents. Its purpose is to display fires for ships sailing at night, announcing shoals and the entrances to harbors, so that sailors deceived by the darkness may not strike the rocks. [Note: For Alexandria has deceptive and treacherous approaches. From Solinus, chapter 35; in another source, chapter 35.]

For Alexandria has dangerous approaches with deceptive shoals. Hence in harbors structures built to provide a guiding light are called *phari*. For *phōs* (φῶς) means “light” and *horasis* (ὅρασις) means “sight”; hence Lucifer is called in Greek *phōsphoros* (φωσφόρος), “light-bearer.”

38. Spiral towers are tall and round, and are called *cochleae* (“snails”), as though *cycleae* (“circular”), because in them one ascends as if by a circular path and circuit. Such a tower existed at Rome and was 175 feet high. [Note: At Rome, 175 feet. This appears to have been the Column of Antoninus, which Philander, commenting on Vitruvius, Book IX, chapter 2, says was 176 feet high.]

39. *Thermae* (“hot baths”) are so called because they are hot; for the Greeks call heat *thermon* (θερμόν).

40. [Note: Baths … remove sorrow. From Augustine, Book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 12.]

The name *balneae* (“baths”) was given from the lifting of sorrow. For the Greeks called them *balaneion* (βαλανεῖον), because the place removes anxiety of mind. These are also called gymnasia, because athletes exercise there with their bodies oiled and their limbs rubbed by their hands; for *gymnasion* (γυμνάσιον) in Greek means “exercise” in Latin, and *gymnos* (γυμνός) means “naked.”

41. The *apodyterium* is the place where the clothing of bathers is put; it is named from undressing, for *apodyein* (ἀποδύειν) in Greek means “to undress.”

215 42. *Popina* is a Greek word, which among us is corruptly pronounced *propina*. It is a place beside public baths where people recover from hunger and thirst after bathing. Hence also *propina* and *propinare* (“to drink, to offer a drink”) are used. For *peina* (πεῖνα) in Greek means “hunger,” because this place removes hunger.

43. Taverns were formerly the small, plain dwellings of common people in the villages, enclosed with poles and boards. [Note: With poles and boards. Another reading: “with planks.”]

Hence they were also called *tabernariae*, because people customarily sat there. They are called *tabernae* because they were constructed from boards and wood; although they no longer retain their former appearance, they retain their ancient name.

44. The *macellum* (“meat market”) is so called because animals sold to merchants are slaughtered there.

45. A market is named from commerce; for there it is customary to sell and buy goods. The *telonium* is similarly named, [Note: Where the goods of ships … This appears to refer to Ambrose’s words on Luke V, which mention the profits of sailors.] because there the goods of ships and the earnings of sailors are rendered. There the collector of customs sits, setting a price upon goods and demanding it aloud from the merchants.

46. [Note: A prison is a place from which we are forbidden to leave. Servius, *Aeneid* I: “A prison is a place from which we are forbidden to leave in any direction, called as if *arcer*, from *arcere*, ‘to ward off.’” But in Book III of the *Georgics*, on “and the chariots rush forth from the prison,” where the Vulgate manuscripts read “which are called from *arcere*,” the Vatican manuscript has “which are called from *coercere*.” Servius therefore appears to require correction on the basis of Isidore. Varro, Book IV, likewise says: “A prison is named from *coercere* (‘to restrain’), because those inside are forbidden to leave.”]

A prison is a place from which we are forbidden to leave, and *carcer* is said to derive from *coercere* (“to restrain”). Hence Fronto says:

> So that they might appear to enjoy themselves in pleasant places rather than be confined in prison.

216 ## CHAPTER III. On Dwelling Places

[Col. 0541B]

1. *Habitatio* (“dwelling”) is named from *habere* (“to have”), as in “to inhabit houses.”

The word *domus* (“house”) derives from a Greek designation, [Note: For the Greeks call roofs or dwellings *domata* (δώματα). These are Jerome’s words in Daniel VI. See also the letter to Sunia and Fretela.] for the Greeks call dwellings *domata* (δώματα). A house is the dwelling of one family, just as a city is the dwelling of one people, and the world is the dwelling place of the whole human race.

2. The ancients called every building an *aedes*. Some think that *aedes* received its name from *edere* (“to eat”), giving Plautus as an example:

> If I had invited you to the house for dinner—

Hence also *aedificium* (“building”), because it was first made for eating.

3. [Note: An *aula* is a royal house. Augustine, in Questions on Exodus, near the end: “What the Greeks call *aulē* (αὐλή), we call *aula*. But in Latin this word now signifies not an atrium but a royal house; and likewise in Greek, as Athenaeus says, citing Menander and Diphilus, Book V.]

An *aula* is a royal house, or a spacious dwelling enclosed by four porticoes.

4. [Note: An *atrium* is a large or more spacious building. Augustine, on Psalm 133: “By atria are understood the larger spaces of a house.”]

An *atrium* is a large building, or a broader and more spacious house. It is called an *atrium* because three porticoes are added to it on the outside. [Note: *Atrium* … because three porticoes are added to it. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*: “There was, as it were, a three-porticoed structure which enclosed the space of the atrium.” And on Psalm 133: “It had an atrium with ten columns, not arranged in a straight order, but, as we have shown, as though it were three-porticoed.”]

[Note: Others said *atrium* was derived from *atrum* (“black”), as if from fire and a lamp. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and they roll the voice through the broad atria.” We have written *lichno* from the Roman manuscript. Other manuscripts read *ligno* or *lignis*.]

Others said that *atrium* was derived from fire and a lamp, as if from *atrum* (“black”), for something becomes black from smoke.

[Col. 0542A] 217 5. The *palatium* (“palace”) was named after Pallas, a prince of the Arcadians. In his honor the Arcadians built the town of Pallanteum and called the royal residence founded in his name the Palatium.

6. They say that the *thalamus* (“bridal chamber”) was called so for the following reason. [Note: When the Sabine women had been abducted by the Romans. See Livy, Book I, and Festus, under *Talassio*. Since our manuscripts read *Talamoni*, we have restored *Talassioni* from Servius, for he calls that figure both *Talassius* and *Talassio*.]

When the Sabine women had been abducted by the Romans, one of them, distinguished above the others in beauty, was carried off amid the great admiration of everyone. An oracle replied that she should be given to the leader Talassius. Since this marriage turned out successfully, it was established that the name “Talassius” should be repeated at every wedding. The Egyptians too, in their own language, call the places into which newlyweds enter and lie the *thalamus*.

7. The *coenaculum* (“dining room”) was named from the sharing of food; hence also *coenobium* (“common dwelling”), a community. For the ancients ate publicly and communally, and no one had a private banquet, lest hidden pleasures give rise to extravagance.

8. [Note: A *triclinium* is a dining room. Isidore is correct. Servius, however, is incorrect in *Aeneid* I, on “He arranged a golden couch”; he says that those who call the basilica or dining room itself a *triclinium* are mistaken. Cicero, *On the Orator* II, Servius: “When Galba had brought his friends before the tribune of the plebs, Lucius Scribonius Libo, and Libo had said, ‘When will you finally leave your dining room, Galba?’ ‘When you leave another man’s bedroom,’ he replied. And *Letters to Atticus* XIII, letter 50: “When he had come to Philip in the evening on the second day of the Saturnalia, the villa was so full of soldiers that scarcely was the dining room vacant where Caesar himself was to dine.” Vitruvius, Book VI, chapter 5: “The length of dining rooms should be twice their width.” And Suetonius, in *Tiberius*: “At Misenum, ashes from embers and charcoal were brought in to heat the dining room.”]

A *triclinium* is a dining room named from the three couches on which diners reclined. Among the ancients, in the place where the banquet’s arrangements were displayed, three couches were spread, on which the reclining guests feasted. For *klinē* (κλίνη) in Greek means “bed” or “reclining place”; from this the term *triclinium* was formed.

9. [Note: A *cella* is so called because it hides us. Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “They fill the chambers with nectar”: “Or from *celare* (‘to hide’), whence they called them *cellae*.”]

A *cella* (“chamber”) is so called because it conceals and hides us.

A *cubiculum* (“bedroom”) is so called because we lie down there and rest while sleeping.

A *cubile* (“sleeping place”) is a place for lying down.

[Col. 0542C] A *secessus* (“retreat”) is so called because it is a secluded place, that is, without access.

10. A *diversorium* (“lodging place”) is so called because people arrive there from different roads.

[Note: *Hospitium* is a Greek word. Perhaps because they use *spithi* (σπίθι) for “house”? Hence the saying: “A fine day in the house of a fine companion.” (So the text.)]

*Hospitium* is a Greek term for a place where someone resides temporarily under the law of hospitality and then, passing onward, departs from it. Hence also *metatum* (“billeted place”), because it is changed. Thus we read, “and they measured out a camp,” meaning “they changed their location.” For an army does not remain there but passes through.

[Note: Hence also *metatum*. Vegetius, Book II, chapter 7, says that *metatores* are so called because they designate the sites of lodging places and guesthouses.]

11. [Note: Maenius, the colleague of Crassus. Festus: “Buildings with upper stories were named *Maeniana* after Maenius, who first extended beams beyond the columns so that the upper portions might be enlarged.” Asconius, in *On the Divination*, on the Maenian Column: “When Maenius sold his house to the censors Cato and Flaccus so that a basilica might be built there, he reserved for himself the right to project the roof of a single column by means of projecting upper stories.” Chacon therefore thought that the word *tabulata* (“upper stories”) should here be connected with what precedes.]

Maenius, the colleague of Crassus, projected beams over the Forum so that there would be places where spectators could stand. These were called *Maeniana* after him. They are also called *solaria* (“sun terraces”) because they are open to the sun. Later some built the *Maeniana* of stone and others of timber, and added them to porticoes, doors, and houses.

219 12. Formerly houses were built of wood and were called *tabulata* (“board structures”); hence the name *Tabulatorum* remains.

An *hypogaeum* is a building constructed beneath the earth, which we call a cave or cavern.

A *solarium* (“sun terrace”) is so called because it is open to the sun and breezes. Such was the place from which David saw Bathsheba bathing and fell in love with her.

[Note: When Antiochus besieged Jerusalem … for the reception of pilgrims. From Hegesippus, Book I, chapter 6. See Josephus, *Jewish War* I, chapter 2, and *Antiquities* XIII, chapter 15.]

13. When Antiochus was besieging Jerusalem, Hyrcanus, ruler of the Jews, opened David’s tomb and removed three thousand talents of gold from it. Of this he gave three hundred talents to Antiochus so that he would abandon the siege. In order to dispel the unpopularity of his act, he is said to have been the first to establish xenodochia, where he might receive poor pilgrims. Hence they took their name. For *xenodocheion* (ξενοδοχεῖον) is translated from Greek into Latin as “reception of pilgrims.”

[Note: Where the sick are gathered, etc. Jerome, in his letter to Oceanus, concerning Fabiola. “She was the first of all to establish a *nosokomeion* (νοσοκομεῖον), in which she gathered the sick from the streets and cared for the limbs of the poor, exhausted by illness and hunger.”]

Where the sick are gathered from the streets is called in Greek a *nosokomeion* (νοσοκομεῖον), in which the limbs of the wretched, exhausted by illness and hunger, are tended.

## CHAPTER IV. On Sacred Buildings

[Col. 0543C]

1. Sacred places are those established for divine worship, such as those in which altars are consecrated according to custom by priests offering sacrifices.

According to the ancients, the *sancta* (“holy places”) are the exterior parts of the temple.

2. The *Sancta sanctorum* (“Holy of Holies”) is the more secluded place of the temple, to which no one had access except the priest. It is called the Holy of Holies because it is holier than the outer sanctuary, or [Note: Because they surpass holy things by comparison. From Jerome, *Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 1.] because it is holier in comparison with holy things, just as the *Song of Songs* surpasses all songs.

*Sanctum* (“holy”) is named from the blood of a sacrificial victim. Among the ancients nothing was called holy unless it had been consecrated or sprinkled with the blood of a victim. It is also called *sanctum* because it exists as something sanctioned. To sanction is to confirm and to defend against injury by imposing a penalty. [Note: Thus laws and walls are called holy. So the Gothic manuscripts, correctly. Digest 1.8.6: “Holy things include walls and gates”; and in the same title, “Sanctum.” Cassius correctly reports that Sabinus answered that in municipalities walls too are holy. Zonaras, volume II: “For among the Romans walls are *sankta* (σάγκτα).”] Thus laws are called holy, and walls are called holy.

3. A *propitiatorium* (“propitiatory”) is, as it were, an oratory of propitiation; for propitiation means appeasement.

*Oracula* (“oracles”) are so called because responses are given from them, and *oraculum* derives from *os* (“mouth”).

4. [Note: *Penetralia*. Servius, *Aeneid* VI: “The hidden chambers of temples.”]

*Penetralia* (“inner chambers”) are the secret places of oracles. They are called *penetralia* from *penitus* (“deep within”), that is, “almost inside.”

[Note: An oratory … received its name. From Augustine, Letter 109 to a monk.]

An *oratorium* (“oratory”) is consecrated solely to prayer. No one ought to do anything there except what it was made for; hence it received its name.

5. A *monasterium* is the dwelling of a single monk. For *monos* (μόνος) means “alone” in Greek, and *sterium* means “station,” that is, the dwelling of one living alone.

6. *Coenobium* appears to be composed of a Greek and a Latin element. It is a dwelling of many people living together; for *koinon* (κοινόν) in Greek means “common.”

7. *Templum* (“temple”) is a general name, for the ancients called any large place a temple. Temples are also so called as if they were “broad covered structures.” [Note: Also a place marked out toward the east. So all the manuscripts. Chacon read “marked out by an augury” or “for an augury.” Festus: “Places marked out by augury.” Varro, Book VI: “On earth, a temple is a place bounded by certain words for the purpose of augury or auspices,” etc. See Servius, *Eclogue* VIII, and Livy I, on the inauguration of Numa.]

A place marked out toward the east was also called a temple, from contemplation. It had four parts: the front facing east, the rear facing west, the left facing north, and the right facing south. [Note: Hence also the orientation observed when they built a temple. From Vitruvius, Book IV, chapter 5.]

Therefore, when they built a temple, they faced the equinoctial east, so that lines drawn from east to west would make the right and left parts of the sky equal, and so that whoever consulted and prayed might look directly toward the east.

8. *Fana* (“shrines”) are named after the Fauns, for whom the delusion of the pagans built temples, so that those consulting them might hear the responses of demons.

9. [Note: The ancients called them *delubra*. Servius, *Aeneid* II: “Some say that a *delubrum* is the place before a temple where water flows,” from *diluere* (“to wash away”); and in Book IV: “A *delubrum* is so called because of the pool in which hands are washed.”]

The ancients called temples having springs *delubra*, because people washed themselves in them before entering; they are called *delubra* from *diluere* (“to wash”). Today these are buildings with sacred fonts in which the faithful, reborn, are purified. The name *delubra* is an apt omen, for they serve for the washing away of sins.

10. [Note: The fountain in the shrine … bodily. The entire passage is repeated in *On the Offices* II, chapter 24.]

The font in a *delubrum* is the place of the reborn, in which seven steps are formed as a mystery of the Holy Spirit: three in the descent and three in the ascent. The seventh is the one who is also the fourth, like the Son of Man, extinguishing the furnace of fire, the support for the feet, and the foundation of the water, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

222 11. Basilicas were formerly called the dwellings of kings, from which they derive their name. For *basileus* (βασιλεύς) means “king,” and basilicas are royal dwellings. Now, however, temples of God are called basilicas because worship and sacrifices are offered there to God, the King of all.

[Col. 0545B] 12. A *martyrium* is a place of martyrs, named by Greek derivation because it was built in memory of a martyr, or because the tombs of holy martyrs are located there.

13. Some have said that **ara** (“altar”) was so called because burned victims blaze there. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Others derive *arae* from *precatio* (“prayer”). Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “In vain around the altars.”] Others derive *arae* from prayers, that is, from what the Greeks call **ἀραί** (*araí*); hence a curse is called **κατάρα** (*katára*). Others think that *arae* comes from height, but wrongly.

14. **Altare** is evidently named from *altitudo* (“height”), as though *alta ara*, “a high altar.”

15. A **pulpit** (*pulpitum*) is so called because a reader or psalmist standing upon it can be seen publicly by the people and therefore heard more freely.

16. A **tribunal** is so called because from it the priest assigns rules for living. It is a place established on high, from which all can hear. [Col. 0545C] Alternatively, *tribunal* is derived from *tribus* (“tribe”), because the tribes are summoned to it.

### 17. The analogium

[Note: [Col. 0545D] In the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 9: “Let three readings be read from the analogium.”]

The **analogium** is so called because a discourse is proclaimed from it; for **λόγος** (*logos*) means “speech” in Greek. It too is situated higher up.

## CHAPTER V. On Repositories

1. A **sacrarium** properly means the part of a temple in which sacred objects are stored, just as a *donarium* is the place where offerings are deposited, and *lectisternia* are places where people customarily sit or recline; thus *sacrarium* is named from bringing in and carrying away sacred things.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] “*Sacrarium* … customarily.” The words are Servius’s, *Aeneid* XII, on “And the shrines of dreadful Dis.”]

2. A **donarium** is so called because gifts, which are customarily offered in temples, are stored there.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] *Donaria*. From the same source, *Georgics* III, on “To the high shrines … the chariots.”]

[Col. 0546A] 3. An **aerarium** (“treasury”) was so called because originally stamped bronze (*aes signatum*) was stored there. In ancient times bronze was the material in use, before gold and silver had been stamped; although money was later made from those metals, the name *aerarium* remained from the metal from which money first took its beginning.

4. An **armarium** is a place where instruments of every kind of craft are kept. An **armamentarium**, however, is a place for weapons alone. Hence Juvenal:

> Whatever weapons the armories of heaven contain.

Both words are derived from *arma*, that is, “arms,” the limbs by which things are exercised.

5. A **library** (*bibliotheca*) is a place where books are stored; for **βίβλος** (*biblos*) means “book” in Greek, and **θήκη** (*thēkē*) means “repository.”

6. A **storehouse** (*promptuarium*) is so called because from it the things necessary for food are brought forth—that is, produced or taken out.

7. A **cellar** (*cellarium*) is so called because table equipment is collected there, or because the provisions remaining for food are stored there.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] “Between the storeroom … a long time.” From the same source, *Aeneid* I, on “The care to build up the storeroom.”]

The difference between a *promptuarium* and a *cellarium* is that a *cellarium* contains provisions for a few days, whereas a *promptuarium* contains supplies for a long period.

8. An **apotheca**, or **granary**, may be translated from the Greek word-for-word as a repository or storage place, because people store processed crops in them.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] “Hence *entheca*.” Ecclesiastical writers often use this word. Cassian, *On the Institutions of the Monks*, book 4: “And although he believes that the whole *entheca* of the monastery is his own property.” Gelasius, *Book XII, Question 2*, chapter [uncertain]: “For if anyone among you should perhaps remain with an annual expenditure, let it be entrusted to a suitable guardian chosen by both parties, for the *enthecae*.”]

Hence, in Greek usage, we also call a well-stocked store of goods an **entheca**.

## CHAPTER VI. On Workplaces

1. An **ergasterium** is a place where some work is done. In Greek, *erga* means “works” and *sterion* means “station”; that is, it is a working station.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] “*Ergastula* … where offenders are assigned.” See Lipsius, *Selectae*, chapter 15.]

2. **Ergastula** too are so called by a Greek word: places where offenders are assigned to perform some work, as gladiators and exiles commonly are—those who cut marble and yet are bound under the custody of chains.

3. A **gynaeceum** is so called in Greek because an assembly of women gathers there to practice wool-working. For a woman is called **γυνή** (*gynē*) in Greek.

4. A **mill** (*pistrinum*) is as though *pilistrinum*, because grain was formerly pounded with a pestle.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] “Hence among the ancients … with a stone.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “And to roast.”]

Thus among the ancients people were called not *molitores* (“millers”) but *pistores*, as though *pinsores*, from pounding (*pinsere*) wheat grains.

[Note: [Col. 0546D] “From pounding wheat grains.” “From splitting wheat grains.” All *Gotth.* witnesses read *a findendis granis*; and shortly afterward, *findebant* for *pinsebant*. But we have followed Servius and the old edition.]

For the use of the mill had not yet begun; rather, they pounded grain with a pestle. Hence Virgil:

> Now roast the crops in the fire; now break them with a stone.

[Col. 0547A] 5. A **clivanus** is named from *clivus* (“slope”), because it is gathered together in an ascent.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] “For we call a *clivus* an ascent.” Festus: “They called *clivia* omens that prohibited something from being done; for they called all difficult things *clivia*, whence also *clivi*, steep places.”]

For we call a *clivus* an ascent, or a winding slope.

6. A **furnus** (“oven”) is said by derivation to come from *far* (“spelt”), because bread made from it is baked there.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] “*Furnus* from *far*.” Porphyry derives it from *furvus* (“dark”).]

7. A **winepress** (*torcular*) is so called because grapes are trodden there and, having been pressed, are expressed.

8. A **press-floor** (*forus*) is a place where grapes are trodden. It is so called because grapes are carried there, or because they are struck there by the feet. Hence it is also called a *calcatorium*, although that word has many meanings.

[Note: [Col. 0547C] “*Forus* is a place where grapes …” Victorinus, at the end of his book *On Orthography*: “*Forus* means a standing-place, whether in a forum, on a ship, or in a winepress.” Columella, book XII, chapter 18: “Then the wine vats, winepresses, and press-floors, and all the vessels, if the sea is nearby, are to be washed with seawater; otherwise with fresh water.” On the other meanings of *forus*, see Festus.]

The first kind of *forus* is a place in a city left for conducting markets; the second is where a magistrate customarily gives judgment; the third is the place described above, which we call a *calcatorium*; the fourth consists of the flat spaces on ships. Concerning these Virgil says:

> And he loosens the ship’s decks.

[Col. 0547B] A **vat** (*lacus*) is so called because the liquid of the crops flows down there.

## CHAPTER VII. On Entrances

1. An **entrance** (*aditus*) is named from *adeundum* (“approaching”), because through it we enter and are admitted.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] “*Aditus* from *adeundum*.” Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “What they call broad entrances.” —When we are prevented from entering by someone, the place is called an *ostium*, from *obstare* (“to stand against”); when we enter, it is an *aditus*, from *adire* (“to approach”).]

2. A **vestibule** is either the entrance of a private house or the space adjoining public buildings. It is called a *vestibulum* because the doors are clothed or covered, or because it covers the entrance with a roof, or from *stare* (“to stand”).

[Note: [Col. 0547D] “*Vestibulum*.” Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “The vestibule before it.” “A vestibule,” he says, “as Varro states, has no proper etymology, but is explained according to the capacity of one’s ingenuity. For *vestibulum*, as we said above, is so called because it clothes or covers the door. Others derive it from Vesta by diminution, since the threshold is consecrated to Vesta. Others derive it from the fact that no one stands there. For on the threshold there is only passage; just as *vesanus* means ‘not sane,’ so *vestibulum* is as though *non-stabulum*, ‘not a standing-place.’”]

3. A **portico** is so called because it is more a passageway than a place for standing, as though *porta* (“gate”); and because it is open.

4. A **door** (*janua*) is named from a certain Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance and exit.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] “To Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance.” He himself says in Ovid, *Fasti* I:

> I preside over the gates of heaven with the kindly Hours,
>
> and Jupiter himself returns to his office through mine.]

Hence Lucan:

[Col. 0547C]

> May the iron threshold of warlike Janus restrain.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] “Hence Lucan.” Book I.]

A *janua* is the first entrance of a house.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] “The rest within the door.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “The hinge creaked on its bronze doors”: “A *janua*,” he says, “is the first entrance of a house, so called because every beginning was consecrated to Janus. All the rest within the *janua* are generally called *ostia*, whether they are *valvae* or *fores*, although usage has corrupted these distinctions.”]

The rest within the *janua* are generally called *ostia*.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] “*Ostium* … from *obstare*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “Where broad paths lead.”]

An **ostium** is an opening through which we are prevented from entering by someone; it is named from *obstare* (“to stand against”), or because an *ostium* displays something inside. Others say that it is called *ostium* because it delays an enemy. For there we expose ourselves to adversaries; hence the Tiberine **Ostia**, because they are set against enemies.

[Col. 0548A] **Fores** and **valvae** are closures.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] “But *fores* are called …” Servius, *Aeneid* I, at the passage cited: “*Fores*,” he says, “properly means doors that open outward, as was the ancient practice. *Valvae*, however, are, as Varro says, doors that turn inward and fold or close upon themselves.”]

But *fores* are doors that turn outward, whereas *valvae* turn inward and are double and foldable. In general, however, usage has corrupted these terms.

5. **Claustra** (“barriers”) are so called because they are closed.

6. **Windows** (*fenestrae*) are openings whose outer part is narrow and whose interior part is wider, such as we see in granaries. They are called *fenestrae* because they provide light.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] “Windows.” From Servius, *Georgics* IV, on:

> Four windows, with slanting light, from the winds.

But Servius interpreted not merely *fenestrae* (“windows”) but “windows with slanting light”; Isidore failed to notice this because, as we have often said, he read Servius’s commentaries without Virgil’s verses.]

For light is called **φῶς** (*phōs*) in Greek; or they are so called because a person inside sees outside through them. Others think *fenestra* is named because it supplies light to the house—a compound word from Greek and Latin, since **φῶς** in Greek means “light.”

7. A **hinge** (*cardo*) is the place on which a door turns and continually moves. It is called *cardo* **ἀπὸ τῆς καρδίας** (*apo tēs kardias*, “from the heart”), because just as the heart governs the whole human body, so that wedge governs and moves the door.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] “*Cardo*.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, at the passage cited: “*Cardo* is named as though the heart of the door, by which it is moved.” And in the same book, on “It will not cease at so great a hinge”: “This,” he says, “is taken from a proverb: ‘The matter is on the hinge.’”]

Hence the proverbial expression: “The matter is on the hinge.”

8. **Thresholds** (*limina*) are so called because they are transverse, like a boundary (*limes*); through them one enters or exits just as through a boundary in a field.

9. **Doorposts** (*postes*) and **jambs** (*antae*) are named as though from *post* (“behind”) and *ante* (“before”). *Antae* are so called because they stand in front, or because we approach them before entering the house. *Postes* are so called because they stand behind the door.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] “Posts and jambs.” Festus: “*Antae* are the outermost rows of vineyards, from which the name *antae* is also derived for the sides of doors.” See Servius, *Georgics* II, on:

> Now the vine-dresser sings of the outermost exhausted rows.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Parts of Buildings

1. A **foundation** (*fundamentum*) is so called because it is the ground or base (*fundus*) of a house. A **cement or masonry** (*caementum*) is likewise named from *caedere* (“to cut”), because it rises from rough stone.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] “*Caementum* … because of rough stone.” Thus all the books read. “Because of cut stone” would be preferable.]

[Col. 0548C] 2. A **wall** (*paries*) is so called because there are always two equal sides, whether viewed from the front or from the side. Whether a structure is four-sided or six-sided, the surfaces that face one another are equal; otherwise the construction is misshapen.

3. We call ruins **parietinae**, as though “ruins of walls.” They are standing walls without a roof and without inhabitants.

[Col. 0549A] 4. An **angle** (*angulus*) is so called because it joins two walls into one.

[Note: [Col. 0549C] “Roof-peaks.” From Servius, *Eclogues* I.]

**Roof-peaks** (*culmina*) are so called because among the ancients roofs were covered with straw (*culmus*), as rustic roofs still are. Hence the top of a roof is called its *culmen*.

5. **Vaults** (*camerae*) are curved surfaces facing inward. They are named from their curvature; for **κάμπυλον** (*kampylon*) means “curved” in Greek.

6. **Ceilings** (*laquearia*) are what cover and adorn a vault; they are also called *lacuniaria*.

[Note: [Col. 0549C] “Ceilings.” This entire passage is repeated below, book XIX, chapter 12, where it is somewhat fuller; it is found in the best manuscripts.]

Primarily, however, *lacus* (“recess” or “panel”) is the term, as Lucilius says:

> The buildings and the recessed panels resound.

Its diminutive produces *lacunar*, as in Horace:

> Nor does a golden
>
> ceiling gleam in my house.

From this comes the further diminutive *lacunarium*, and by **ἀντιστίχον** (*antistichon*, a transposition of letters), *laquearium*.

7. **Apse** (*absida*) is translated from Greek into Latin as “bright,” because, having received light, it shines back through its arch. But whether we ought to say *absidam* or *absidem*, some learned men consider this form of the word ambiguous.

8. A **vaulted ceiling** (*testudo*) is an oblique vault of a temple. For the ancients made the roofs of temples in the form of a tortoise shell; they were constructed in this way so as to reproduce the appearance of the sky, which is convex.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] “A *testudo* is a vault … convex.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “And in the middle of the vaulted temple.”]

Others hold that a *testudo* is a place in the part of an atrium facing those who enter.

9. **Arches** (*arcus*) are so called because they are bent in a tightly enclosed curve; they are also called **vaults** (*fornices*).

[Note: [Col. 0549D] “They themselves are also *fornices*.” The same source, *Aeneid* VI, on “And gates with an opposing vault.” “A *fornix*,” he says, “is an arch.” Cicero: “He saw [it] at the Fabian arch itself.”]

10. **Pavements** (*pavimenta*) originated among the Greeks, produced by an elaborate art of painting (*lithostrota*, made with small crusts or tesserae stained in various colors).

[Note: [Col. 0549D] “Pavements originated … colors.” Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 25: “Pavements originated among the Greeks through the elaborate art of painting, until stone pavements drove it out. The most famous in this genre was Sosus, who paved at Pergamum the pavement they call *asarotos oecos*, because he represented, as though left behind, the scraps of a meal and whatever is customarily swept up from the pavement, using small tesserae stained in various colors.”]

They are called *pavimenta* because they are *paviantur*, that is, “beaten” or “struck.” Hence also *pavor* (“fear”), because fear strikes the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] “They are called *pavimenta* … because they are beaten.” The passage seems to refer to Virgil’s words “fear beating the heart,” *Aeneid* V. See above, book X, under *Patiens*. The whole passage is repeated below, book XIX, chapter 10.]

11. **Ostracus** is a brick pavement, so called because it is beaten with broken pottery mixed with lime. For the Greeks call pottery **ὄστρακον** (*ostrakon*).

12. A **compluvium** is so called because the portions of water that are all around converge there.

**Tesserae** are the pieces with which dwellings are paved. They are named from *tesserae*, that is, square stones, in the diminutive form.

13. **Bases** are the supports of columns, rising from the foundation and bearing the weight of the superimposed structure.

[Note: [Col. 0550C] “*Bases* is the name of a stone.” Perhaps *basaltes* or *basanites*. For Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 7, says: “Egypt also discovered in Ethiopia the stone they call basalt, the color and hardness of iron.” Drawing on this passage, Isidore writes *basanites*, not *basaltes*, in book XVI, chapter 5. Pliny also says in the same book, chapter 22: “Physicians preferred *basanites* for mortars; for this stone gives off nothing from itself.”]

The name *bases* belongs, in the Syriac language, to a very hard stone.

14. **Columns** are so called from their length and roundness; the weight of the entire structure is raised upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “Columns.” The same passage is found below, book XIX, chapter 10.]

The ancient proportion of columns was that their height was one-third of the width of the temple or shrine.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “One-third of the height.” Add “of the temple or shrine,” from Vitruvius, book IV, chapter 7, and Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 23.]

There are four kinds of round columns: Doric, Ionic, Tuscan, and Corinthian. They differ from one another in the measurements of their thickness and height. A fifth kind consists of those called **Attic**, with four angles, or more, and equal intervals between their sides.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “Or more.” This is not supported by Pliny. For that reason Chacon wished these words deleted.]

15. **Capitals** (*capitella*) are so called because they are the heads of columns, just as the head is above the neck.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “Capitals.” Saint Augustine and others use this word.]

**Epistyles** (*epistylia*) are the elements placed above the capitals of columns. The word is Greek and means “placed above.”

**Tiles** (*tegulae*) are so called because they cover buildings, and **roof tiles** (*imbrices*) because they receive rain.

16. **Bricks** (*lateres*) and **bricklets** (*laterculi*) are so called because they are formed broad, with four boards turned around them on every side.

A **channel** (*canalis*) is so called because it is hollow in the manner of a reed.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “It is better to pronounce *canalem* in the feminine gender than in the masculine.” These are Servius’s words, *Georgics* III; the passage is also repeated below, book XIX, chapter 10. See Nonius Marcellus.]

17. **Water pipes** (*fistulae*) are so called because they pour out and convey water. For **στέλλειν** (*stellein*) means “to send” in Greek. Their forms are made according to the size of the water and the measure of their capacity.

## CHAPTER IX. On Fortifications

[Col. 0550C] 1. **Munitum**, or **munimentum**, is so called because it is made by hand.

An **enclosure** (*cohors*) is so called either because it constrains everything within—that is, encloses it—or because by its obstruction it restrains outsiders and prevents them from approaching.

2. A **rampart** (*vallum*) is something raised from a mass of earth so that a defensive barrier may be extended. *Vallum* is derived from *vallus* (“stake”).

[Note: [Col. 0550D] “For *valli* are …” These are Servius’s words on “Who could cut the rampart with iron?” *Aeneid* IX.]

For *valli* are stakes by which a rampart is fortified. They are called *valli* because they are driven in and pulled out. **Intervals** (*intervalla*) are the spaces between the tops of the stakes—that is, between the posts from which the rampart is made. Hence other spaces too are called *intervalla*, from the stakes.

3. An **agger** is a heap or accumulation of any material, by which ditches or valleys can be filled through heaping.

[Note: [Col. 0551C] “An *agger* is …” From the same source, on “They fill the ditches with an embankment,” *Aeneid* IX.]

Properly, an *agger* is earth heaped up and placed close to a completed rampart.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “An *agger* properly … we call it.” From the same source, *Aeneid* X, on “The embankments of the walls.”]

But by an abuse of language we also call walls and all fortifications *aggeres*.

4. **Maceriae** are long walls enclosing vineyards and other things.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “By which certain vineyards are enclosed.” The same source, *Georgics* II, on “Now the vine-dresser sings of the outermost exhausted rows.” “Some,” he says, “understand *antes* as the outermost rows of vineyards; others understand walls by which vineyards are enclosed.”]

For the Greeks call “long” **μακρόν** (*makron*).

5. **Formatum**, or **formatium**, is the African or Spanish name for walls made of earth, because the earth is packed between two boards enclosing it on either side, and is thus rather stuffed into a mold than built. They endure through the ages without decay and are stronger than winds, fires, and every kind of mortar.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “*Formatum*, or *formatium*.” From Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 14. Pliny should be emended from this passage of Isidore. We still retain the same name today, for in Spanish we call concrete *hormigón*.]

[Col. 0551B] 6. **Hedges** (*saepes*) are defenses for planted crops; hence their name.

**Folds** (*caulae*) are defenses for sheep, or enclosures for sheepfolds. The word is Greek, with the initial sound removed; for the Greeks call animal enclosures **αὐλαί** (*aulai*).

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “*Caulae*, etc.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “When he roars toward the sheepfolds.”]

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “By which certain vineyards are enclosed.” The same source, *Georgics* II, on “Now the vine-dresser sings of the outermost exhausted rows.” “Some,” he says, “understand *antes* as the outermost rows of vineyards; others understand walls by which vineyards are enclosed.”]

## CHAPTER X. On Tents

1. **Tabernacles** (*tabernacula*) are soldiers’ tents, by which on campaign they avoid the heat of the sun, storms of rain, and the hardships of cold. They are called *tabernacula* because curtains stretched by ropes were hung from intervening boards, which supported the tents.

2. A **tent** (*tentorium*) is so called because it is stretched by ropes and stakes. Hence the word *praetendere* (“to stretch out before,” or “to extend”) is still used today.

3. **Butterfly tents** (*papiliones*) are named from their resemblance to a small flying creature that is especially abundant among flowering mallows. These are little birds that gather around a light when it is lit and, flying about it, are compelled to perish from the nearby fire.

## CHAPTER XI. On Tombs

1. A **tomb** (*sepulcrum*) is named from *sepelire* (“to bury”).

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “Formerly each person in his own house …” These are Servius’s words on “He returns him to his ancestral dwelling,” *Aeneid* VI.]

Formerly each person was buried in his own house.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “Later this was forbidden by law.” The same source, *Aeneid* XI, on “They restore him to the city.” “Formerly,” he says, “people were buried in the city; later, under the consulship of Duillius, the senate prohibited this and enacted by law that no one should be buried within the city.”]

Later this was forbidden by law, so that the bodies of the living would not be contaminated by contact with the stench itself.

A **monument** (*monumentum*) is so called because it reminds the mind of the dead person.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “Monument.” From the same source, at the end of book XII.]

When you do not see a monument, what is written has occurred: “He has vanished as one dead from the heart.” But when you see one, it admonishes the mind and brings you back to remembrance, so that you recall the dead person.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] “Monument.” From the same source, at the end of book XII.]

Thus *monumenta* and *memoriae* are named from admonishing the mind.

2. A **mound** (*tumulus*) is so called as though “swelling earth.”

A **sarcophagus** is a Greek word, so called because bodies are consumed there; for **σάρξ** (*sarx*) means “flesh” in Greek, and **φαγεῖν** (*phagein*) means “to eat.”

3. **Mausolea** are tombs or monuments of kings, named from Mausolus, king of Caria. When he died, his wife built a tomb of extraordinary size and beauty for him.

[Note: [Col. 0552C] “His wife, etc.” The passage is taken directly from Jerome, book I against Jovinian.]

It was so magnificent that even today all costly monuments are called *mausolea* from his name.

[Col. 0552B] 4. A **pyramid** is a type of tomb, square and rising to a peak beyond every height that can be constructed by human hands. Hence, because they exceed the measure of shadows, they are said to cast no shadow.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “Pyramid.” From Solinus, chapter 35 in some editions, chapter 45 in others. What is said there about shadows should therefore not be held against Isidore.]

They rise in such a form that they begin broad and end narrow, like fire. For **πῦρ** (*pyr*) means “fire.” Egypt possesses these structures.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “Such a building.” See Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII.]

Among the ancients, powerful people were buried either beneath mountains or in houses.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “Among the ancestors, the powerful …” Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “There was a great one beneath a high mountain.” “Among the ancestors,” he says, “nobles were buried either beneath mountains or in houses.”]

From this arose the practice of constructing pyramids or setting up huge columns over corpses.

## CHAPTER XII. On Rustic Buildings

1. A **cottage** (*casa*) is a rural dwelling woven from stakes, brushwood, and reeds, by which people can be protected from the force of cold or the harmful effects of heat.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “By which people may protect themselves.” *Tueri* is used here in the passive sense, as by Vitruvius and others.]

2. A **hut** (*tugurium*) is a little shelter made by vineyard keepers for their own protection, as though *tegurium* (“covering”), whether for avoiding the heat and rays of the sun or for driving away from that place people or small animals that commonly lie in wait for newly growing crops.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “This the country people call a *capanna*.” Thus today the Italians say *cabana*, and so do we.]

Country people call it a *capanna*, because it accommodates only one person.

3. Some think **tesqua** means huts.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “Some think *tesqua* means huts.” Thus all the books. Acron says it is a Sabine word.]

Others think it means precipitous and rugged places.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “Others, precipitous places, etc.” Glossary: *tesqua*, or *tesca*, **κατάκρημνοι καὶ ῥαχίαι καὶ ἔρημοι τόποι**—“precipitous places, crags, and deserted places.”]

4. **Magalia** are the elongated buildings of the Numidian country people, roofed with curved sides as though they were the keels of ships, or round like ovens.

[Note: [Col. 0552D] “*Magalia*, buildings of the Numidians, etc.” The words are Sallust’s, in the *Jugurthine War*, concerning *mapalia*, which, as Servius says, mean the same as *magalia*.]

They are also called *magalia*, as though *magaria*, because the Punic people call a new farmstead *magar*, with one letter changed—*l* for *r*—from *magaria*, “huts.”

[Note: [Col. 0553C] “And *magalia* is so called as though *magaria*, etc.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “He marvels at the former *magalia*.” Isidore added the new material, perhaps because he knew the Punic language better.]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Fields

1. In Latin, a **field** (*ager*) is said to be so called because something is done (*agitur*) in it. Others more plausibly believe that *ager* is named from Greek. Hence a farmstead is called *choragros* in Greek.

[Note: [Col. 0553C] “*Ager* in Latin, etc.” Thus Varro, book VI, though Quintilian criticizes him.]

2. A **farmstead** (*villa*) is named from a rampart, that is, an embankment of earth, because such a structure is commonly established as a boundary.

3. **Possessions** (*possessiones*) are broad tracts of public and private land that at first were not acquired by formal conveyance, but which each person occupied and possessed as he was able; hence their name.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “Possessions, etc.” All from Festus, under *Possessiones*.]

4. An **estate** (*fundus*) is so called because a patrimony is founded or stabilized upon it. *Fundus* must be understood to mean both an urban building and a rural property.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “*Fundus* is so called.” Servius, *Georgics* II: “*Fundus* is so called because it is the foundation of all things.”]

5. A **property** (*praedium*) is so called because, more than anything else, it is foreseen by the head of a household—that is, it is apparent—as though *praevidium* (“something foreseen”); or because the ancients regarded lands captured in war as booty.

6. Every field, as Varro teaches, is divided in four ways. It is either **arable** (*arvus*), that is, suitable for sowing; **planted** (*consitus*), that is, suitable for trees; **pastureland** (*pascuus*), which is given over only to grasses and animals; or **flowering land** (*floreus*), containing gardens suited to bees and flowers. Virgil followed this classification in book IV of the *Georgics*.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “Every field.” Servius, at the beginning of the *Georgics*, from Varro.]

7. The ancients called uncultivated fields **rura**, that is, woods and pastures, whereas they called a cultivated field an *ager*. For a *rus* is a place where honey, milk, and livestock can be found. Hence the term *rusticus* (“rural”): this is the first and effortless happiness of country people.

8. A **sown field** (*seges*) is a field in which seed is sown. Hence Virgil:

> That crop at last answers the hopes of the greedy
>
> farmer.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “A *seges* is …” Servius, in the same place.]

9. A **common pasture** (*compascuus ager*) is a field left by the surveyors of lands for common grazing by neighboring inhabitants.

10. An **alluvial field** (*alluvius ager*) is land that a river gradually adds to a field.

11. An **arcifinius field** is so called because it is not enclosed by fixed measurements of lines; rather, its boundaries are restricted by the obstruction of rivers, mountains, and trees. Hence no surplus strips intervene in such fields.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “*Arcifinius ager*, etc.” Frontinus, *On the Classification of Lands*: “An *arcifinius ager* is one contained by no measurement; according to ancient practice, it is bounded by rivers, ditches, mountains, roads, trees, pre-existing divisions of waters, and so forth. Therefore, instead of *unde* (‘from where’), *viarum* (‘of roads’) may perhaps have to be read here.”]

12. A **newly ploughed field** (*novalis ager*) is one ploughed for the first time, or one that lies fallow every other year in order to renew its strength. *Novalia* therefore bore fruit one year and lay empty the next.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “A *novalis ager*.” These are Servius’s words, *Georgics* I.]

13. A **waste field** (*squalidus ager*) is as though *excolidus*, so called because it has already withdrawn from cultivation, just as an *exconsul* has withdrawn from the consulship.

14. A **marshy field** (*uliginosus ager*) is always wet. For land that dries out at times is called *humidum* (“damp”), whereas *uligo* is the natural moisture of the soil, never departing from it.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “*Uliginosus*.” From the same source, on “Rich with sweet moisture,” *Georgics* I.]

15. **Subseciva** are properly the pieces that a tailor cuts away from material and throws aside as superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “Hence *subsecivi* … and likewise *subseciva*.” See Siculus Flaccus and Frontinus, chapter “On the Classification of Lands.” As for the term *centuria*, Varro is altogether preferable: he says it was named from one hundred *jugera*, rather than Flaccus, who derives it from one hundred men. We shall give both authors’ words, but Varro’s in the form emended by Chacon:

[Col. 0554C]

> “When the Romans divided land captured from the enemy among the victorious people, allotting two *jugera* apiece, they gave two hundred *jugera* to one hundred men; from this act it was rightly called a *centuria*.”

Varro, *On Agriculture* I, chapter 10:

> “The smallest part of a *jugerum* is called a *scrupulum*, that is, a square ten feet in length and width. From this starting point surveyors sometimes say that an ounce, a sixth, or something else has been left as *subsecivum* when they have reached a *jugerum*. A *jugerum* contains 288 *scrupula*, corresponding to the weight of the ancient *as* before the Punic War. The two *jugera* said to have first been distributed individually by Romulus, because they passed to the heir, were called a *haeredium*; later this was called a *centuria* from *centum* (‘one hundred’).”

Varro, book V, *On the Latin Language*:

> “*Centuria* was first named from one hundred *jugera*; later, when doubled, it retained the name, just as tribes retain their name after being multiplied.”

Festus likewise says:

> “In land measurement, *centuria* signifies two hundred *jugera*.”

See the notes on Varro published by Fulvius Ursinus.]

Thus *subsecivi agri* are fields that, when divided by the surveyor’s measuring rod, are rejected as barren or marshy. Likewise, *subseciva* are pieces that, in the division of land, do not make up a *centuria*, that is, two hundred *jugera*.

16. An **area** is an expanse of level boards. It is called *area* from its flatness and equality, whence also *ara* (“altar”). Others say that it is called *area* because it is scraped bare for threshing crops, or because only dry crops are threshed there.

17. A **meadow** (*pratum*) is a place whose abundance of hay sustains herds. The ancient Romans gave it this name because it is immediately ready and does not require much labor of cultivation. Meadows are places that can be mown.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] “A *pratum* … because it is immediately ready.” Thus Varro: “Meadows are so called because they are ready without labor.”]

18. **Marshes** (*paludes*) are named from **Pales**, the pastoral goddess, because she nourishes *palea*, that is, fodder for draft animals.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] “Marshes named from Pales.” Varro: “A *palus* is a little water in depth but widely spread in the open.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Boundaries of Fields

1. **Boundaries** (*fines*) are so called because fields are divided by cords. For lines of measurement are stretched out in the partitioning of lands, so that equality of dimension may be maintained.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] “*Fines* are so called because … by cords.” We have often discussed this kind of etymological explanation.]

[Col. 0555A] 2. **Survey lines** (*limites*) are called by an ancient word meaning “transverse.”

[Note: [Col. 0555C] “*Limites* are called … transverse.” Hyginus, *On Establishing Survey Lines*: “*Limites* are called from *limum*, an ancient word meaning ‘transverse.’ For the ancients also called everything transverse *limum*. From this come the thresholds of doors, through which one goes out and in, and *limites*, because through them one goes out into the fields. *Limus* also gave its name to the garment with which public slaves were girded by a diagonal purple band. Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on “Their temples bound with *limus* and sacred branches” (Servius reads *limus* there as well): “*Limus* is a garment by which the private parts of the *popae* are covered from the navel to the feet. At its lower edge this garment has a purple *lima*, that is, a winding band, and from this it received its name. For we call *limum* something oblique.”]

For the ancients called everything transverse *lima*. Hence also the thresholds of doors, through which one goes outside and inside; and the *limites*, because through them one goes out into the fields. From this the word *limus* also received its name: a sash with which public slaves were girded by a diagonal purple band.

3. **Boundary markers** (*termini*) are so called because they distinguish and indicate measurements of land. Through them the evidence of boundaries is understood, and the extension of fields and disputes are removed.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “And the *agrorum intentio*.” Thus the variant manuscripts read. *Intentio* means extension or stretching.]

4. The two greatest survey lines in fields are the **cardo** and the **decumanus**.

The *cardo* is so called because the north is aligned with the celestial axis, since without doubt the heavens revolve around the northern region.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “Because the North Star …” Thus the oldest manuscript of Salamanca reads.]

The *decumanus* is the line directed transversely from east to west. It is called *decumanus* because it makes the shape of an X. For a field divided twice produces the figure of the number ten.

[Col. 0555B] 5. An **arca** is so called from *arcere* (“to restrain”). For it guards the boundaries of a field and prevents access to them.

A **trifinium** is so called because it binds together the boundaries of three properties. Hence a **quadrifinium** is one involving four. The remaining survey lines are narrower and separated from one another by unequal intervals, and are designated by their respective names.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “*Arca* … *trifinium*.” See Hyginus, *On the Boundaries of Fields*, and Siculus Flaccus, *On the Formation of Fields*. Glossary: *arcae*, **ἄκρα κτημάτων**—“the extremities or boundaries of properties.”]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Measurement of Fields

1. **Measurement** (*mensura*) is whatever is bounded by weight, capacity, length, height, or the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “Measurement … is bounded.” These are the words of Boethius, *Geometry*, chapter 1.]

Accordingly, the ancients divided the world into parts, parts into provinces, provinces into regions, regions into places, places into territories, territories into fields, fields into *centuriae*, *centuriae* into *jugera*, *jugera* into **climata**, and then *climata* into *actus*, *perticae*, *passus*, *gradus*, cubits, feet, palms, ounces, and fingers. Such was their ingenuity.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “The world into parts.” The Gothic manuscripts read “into parts,” as in Boethius.]

2. **[Note: [Col. 0555D]** *Digitus* is the smallest part of agricultural measurement. From Frontinus.] A *digitus* is the smallest unit of agricultural measurements. Hence an *uncia* contains one digit and one-third. **[Note: [Col. 0555D]** *Hence an uncia containing one digit and one-third.* Chacon emended this most aptly, since all the books read “an uncia containing three digits.” Frontinus, Book I, *On Aqueducts*: “A digit, as is agreed, is one-sixteenth of a foot; an uncia is one-twelfth,” and shortly afterward: “Therefore the modulus of an uncia has a diameter of one digit and one-third of a digit.”] **[Note: [Col. 0555D]** “A *palmus*, however, [has] four digits.” This passage does not appear complete [Col. 0556C], for he proposed to discuss all the measures found in the human body—palms, feet, cubits, steps, paces—yet does not explain them all. It could be completed as follows: “A *palmus* has four digits, a foot sixteen, a cubit a foot and a half, a step two feet and a half, and a *passus* five feet.”] A *palmus*, however, contains four digits; a foot, sixteen; a *passus*, [Col. 0556A] five feet; a *pertica*, two *passus*, that is, ten feet.

3. A *pertica* is so called from *portare*, “to carry,” as though *portica*. For all the preceding measurements are found in the human body—the palm, foot, *passus*, and the rest—whereas the *pertica* alone is carried. It is ten feet long, like the reed in Ezekiel that measures the Temple.

4. **[Note: [Col. 0556C]** “The smallest *actus*, etc.” Everything that follows, to the end of the chapter, is from Columella, Book V, chapter 1.] The smallest *actus* is four feet in width and one hundred twenty in length.

The *clima* also measures sixty feet in every direction.

A square *actus* is bounded on every side by one hundred twenty feet. **[Note: [Col. 0556D]** The Baeticans call this an *arapennis*. Isidorus perhaps read it thus, deriving the name from *arare*, “to plow”; but in Columella, even in the manuscript books, it is *arepennis*; in the Gothic laws, Book VIII, chapter 4, line 25, and Book III, line [—]: “If within an *aripennis*.” The Glossary, however, has *arpendia*, πλέθρα, “plethra”; *arvipendium*, σχοῖνος γεωμετρικός, “a geometric rope.”] The Baeticans call this an *arapennis*, evidently from plowing.

[241] 5. A double *actus* makes a *jugerum*, which received its name from being joined together. [Col. 0556B]

A *jugerum* consists of two hundred forty feet in length and one hundred twenty in width.

[Col. 0556C] The farmers of the province of Baetica call an *actus* an *agna*. **[Note: [Col. 0556D]** “They call it an *agna*.” Victorius, in his notes on Varro, Book I, *On Agriculture*, chapter 10, and on Columella, Book V, chapter 1, testifies that he found *acnua* in the old books of Columella and Varro. Chacon likewise read *acnam* in both places in an old codex. Since *g* was changed to *c* in an archaic manner, it seemed preferable to retain *agna* from the Gothic codex.]

6. These same Baeticans define a *porca* as thirty feet in width and one hundred eighty in length. But a *porca* is what remains raised during plowing. What is dug out is a *lira*. The Gauls call a space of one hundred feet in urban areas a *candetum*, as though *centetum*. **[Note: [Col. 0556D]** “In rural areas they call one hundred fifty square feet a *candetum*.” Columella: “In rural areas, however, the plowmen call one hundred fifty feet a *cadetum*.” But all Isidorean codices have *candetum*.] In rural areas they call one hundred fifty square feet a *candetum*. Furthermore, a *stadialis* field has one hundred twenty-five *passus*, that is, six hundred twenty-five feet; when this measure is reckoned eight times, it makes a mile, which consists of five thousand feet.

7. A *centuria* is a field of two hundred *jugera*, although among the ancients it was named from one hundred *jugera*; afterward it was doubled but retained its former name. For although the number of *centuriae* was multiplied, they could not change the name.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Roads and Journeys

1. We call the measurements of roads *milliaria*, the Greeks *stadia*, the Gauls *leugae*, [Col. 0557A] the Egyptians *schoeni*, and the Persians *parasangae*. [242] Each has its own proper extent. **[Note: [Col. 0556D]** “We call them miles, the Gauls leagues, etc.” Jerome, on Joel 3: “It is not surprising if each nation calls fixed distances along roads by its own names, since the Latins call them a thousand *passus*, the Gauls leagues, the Persians parasangs, and all Germany *restae*, with a different measure attached to each name.” Shortly afterward: “The Egyptians call them *schoeni*.”]

2. A *milliarium* is measured by one thousand *passus*, and is called *milliarium*, as though *mille adium*, because it contains five thousand feet.

3. A *leuca* is measured by one thousand five hundred *passus*.

A *stadium* is one-eighth of a mile and consists of one hundred twenty-five *passus*. They say that Hercules first established it and marked off that distance because he could cover it in a single breath; hence he called it a *stadium*, because at its end he drew breath and stopped at the same time.

4. A road is a way along which a vehicle can travel, and *via* is so called from the movement of vehicles. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “From the movement of vehicles”—*from the driving force*, according to the Complutensian and Gothic codices.] For it contains two *actus*, because vehicles going and coming meet one another there. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “For it contains two *actus*.” The two are to be referred to vehicles. Servius, on *Aeneid* 4, at “They carry along the narrow road”: “A road is half an *actus*, along which a vehicle can travel. For an *actus* accommodates two wagons, because vehicles going and coming meet one another.”]

5. **[Col. 0557B]** Every road is either public or private. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “Every road is either public…” From Ulpian, title “The Praetor,” section “Road,” in *Digest* 43.8.] A public road is one situated on public land, on which passage and the right of driving are open to the people. It leads either to the sea or to towns. A private road is one granted to a neighboring municipality.

6. *Strata* is so called as though “trodden by the feet of the common people.” Lucretius:

> And now the roads, worn down by the feet of the common people.

It is also called *delapidata*, that is, “paved with stones.” The Carthaginians are said to have been the first to pave roads with stones; afterward the Romans laid them throughout almost the whole world, both for the straightness of travel and so that the common people would not be idle. [243]

7. **[Col. 0557C]** An *agger* is the raised middle of a paved road, surfaced with stones piled together. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “The middle of the road.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* 5, at “As often a snake is caught on the raised road.”] It is called an *agger* from *agger*, that is, from “heaping up”; **[Col. 0557C]** historians call it a military road. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “Which historians call a military road.” From the same author, on *Aeneid* 12, at “He saw them coming from the opposite side.”] Thus:

> As often a snake, caught upon the raised middle of the road.

8. **[Col. 0557C]** An *iter*, or *itus*, is a road along which a person can go in any direction. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “An *iter* is a road.” See chapter 1 of the title “On Rural Servitudes of Estates.”]

*Iter* and *itiner* have different meanings. An *iter* is a place easy to pass through, from which we also use the word *itus*, “a going.” An *itiner* is the going of a long journey, and also the labor of walking, so that one may reach wherever one wishes.

9. **[Note: [Col. 0557C]** “A path is half a journey.” Servius, on *Aeneid* 4, at “They carry along the narrow path”: “A *semita* is half a road, whence it is called *semita*; and Varro, Book IV: ‘The way along which they went they called an *iter* from *itus*; where it was narrow, a *semita*, as though *semi-iter*.”] A *semita* is half an *iter*, so called from *semi-itus*, “half-going.” A *semita* belongs to human beings; a *callis* to wild animals and livestock.

10. **[Note: [Col. 0557D]** *Callis*. Servius, in the same place: “A *callis* is a path made narrower by the hardened callus of livestock.”] A *callis* is a narrow and trodden route of livestock among mountains, called from the callus of the feet, or hardened by the callus of animals.

*Tramites* are crosswise routes in fields, or a straight road, called so because they cross through.

11. **[Col. 0558B]** *Divortia* are bends in roads, that is, roads extending in different directions. **[Note: [Col. 0558C]** “The same are *diverticula* … at the side of the road.” Servius, on *Aeneid* 9, at “Others place themselves at the crossroads”: “*Diverticula* are transverse paths situated at the side of a military road.” Therefore the reading found in all the books, “other roads,” is incorrect.] The same are *diverticula*, that is, different and divided roads, [244] or transverse paths situated at the side of a road.

12. A *bivium* is so called because it is a twofold road.

**[Note: [Col. 0558C]** *Compita*. The same author, on *Georgics* 2, at “Around the villages and crossroads”: “That is, through the crossroads, which are called *compita* because many roads converge into one.”] *Compita* are so called because several roads converge there, as it were *trivia* and *quadrivia*—three-way and four-way roads.

**[Note: [Col. 0558C]** “*Ambitus*, that is, a circuit around; the words are Festus’s.” Varro, Book IV: “*Ambitus* means a circuit, and therefore the interpreters of the Twelve Tables describe *ambitus* as a circuit around a wall. I think the law was framed in these words: ‘The circuit of a wall shall be a *sestertius* foot.’” Volusius Maecianus, *On Weights*: “The law of the Twelve Tables is also evidence, in which two feet and a half are called a *sestertius* foot.”] An *ambitus* is a space of two feet and a half left between neighboring buildings to permit passage around them, and is called from walking around.
