13. An *orbita* is the track of a cart, named from the circle of its wheel.

Moreover, an *actus* is the route along which livestock is usually driven.

A *clivosum* is a winding route.

**[Note: [Col. 0558C]** *Vestigia*. Servius, on *Aeneid* 11, at “He had set his tracks upon the soles”: “He had marked the signs of his feet with the front parts of the soles; for these are *vestigia*, images of feet.” **[Col. 0558D]** In the word “front,” however, Isidorus did not notice that the term belongs to Virgil, not Servius. He should have removed it entirely, for it contributes nothing to the interpretation of the word.] *Vestigia* are signs of feet impressed by the front parts of the soles, called so because by them the paths of those who went ahead are investigated, that is, recognized.

# BOOK SIXTEEN. ON STONES AND METALS

[Col. 0559]

[245]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Powders and Clods of Earth

[Col. 0559A]

1. **[Note: [Col. 0559C]** “*Pulvis* … because it is driven by force.” Another reading has “because it is struck.” But one must consider what Pliny intended when, in Book 35, chapter 13, he said: “For who sufficiently values the worst part of the earth, and therefore calls it *pulvis*?”] *Pulvis* is so called because it is driven by the force of the wind. For it is lifted by the wind’s breath and neither resists nor knows how to remain still, as the Prophet says:

> Like dust that the wind casts from the face of the earth.

2. **[Note: [Col. 0559C]** “*Limus* is so called because it is smooth.” It is remarkable that Isidorus overlooked Tertullian’s words in *On the Soul*: “What else is mud than rich fluid?” It is even more remarkable that, although many such passages are found in the most authoritative writers, certain men who think themselves clever rage against Isidorus alone.] *Limus* is so called because it is smooth.

*Mud* (*coenum*) is a chasm of filth.

*Ash* (*cinis*) is named from burning, for it is produced by it.

*Ember* (*favilla*) is so called because it is produced through fire. For φῶς (*phōs*) means “fire.”

3. A *gleba* is so called because it is clotted together. For it is compacted by the gathering of dust and united into a single lump. Earth that is bound together is a *gleba*; earth that is loosened is dust.

4. A *labina* is so called because it causes those walking to slip, its name being derived from *labi*, “to slip.” [Col. 0559B]

Some think that *lutum*, “mud,” is called so by antiphrasis, because it is not clean—for everything washed (*lotum*) is clean.

5. *Volutabra* is so called because wild boars roll about there.

**[Note: [Col. 0559D]** *Uligo*. See the preceding book, chapter 13.] *Uligo* is the filth of mud or water. [246]

*Sand* (*sabulum*) is the lightest kind of earth.

6. **[Note: [Col. 0559D]** *Argilla* from Argos. Hesychius and Suidas interpret ἄργιλλον as “white and pure earth.”] *Argilla* is called from Argos, where vessels were first made from it.

*Creta*, “chalk,” is named from the island of Crete, where it is better.

**[Note: [Col. 0559D]** Cimolian chalk. From Pliny, Book 35, chapter 17. See Strabo, Book 10.] Cimolian chalk is white, named from the Italian island of Cimaea. One kind softens the precious colors of garments and brightens those darkened by a certain sulfurous sheen; the other gives brilliance to gems.

Silver chalk, also called white, is so named because it restores brilliance to silver.

[Col. 0559C] 7. **[Note: [Col. 0559D]** Samian earth. From the same book, chapters 16 and 22.] Samian earth is named from the island of Samos. It is white, smooth, and adhesive to the tongue, and is necessary for medicines and vessels.

8. **[Note: [Col. 0559D]** Puteolan powder. From the same author, chapter 13.] Puteolan powder is collected in the hills of Puteoli in Italy and is set against the sea to support it and break the waves. For when submerged in water it immediately becomes stone, and, growing stronger every day through the waves, is transformed into rock, [Col. 0560A] just as clay is transformed into stone by fire. **[Note: [Col. 0559D]** “Just as clay is changed into stone by fire.” The reference is to Pliny’s story of Dibutades of Sicyon.]

9. Sulfur is so called because it is kindled by fire. **[Note: [Col. 0559D]** “For *ur* means fire.” Thus Jerome, in *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 11: “Ur of the Chaldeans,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.”] For *ur* means “fire.” Its power is felt in boiling waters, and nothing else is more easily kindled. It is produced in the Aeolian Islands between Sicily and Italy, which are said to burn. It is also found dug out in other places. **[Note: [Col. 0560C]** “There are four kinds.” From Pliny, Book 35, chapter 15. We have restored some portions from this source.] [247] There are four kinds of it. The first is “living” sulfur, which is dug up and is translucent and green; of all the kinds, physicians use this one alone. The second is what they call a “clod,” used only by fullers. The third is a liquid, used for fumigating wool, since it gives it whiteness and softness. The fourth is especially suitable for making lamp wicks. Sulfur has such power that, placed upon fires, its odor detects epileptic illnesses. Anaxilaus, carrying around a cup of wine with glowing coals beneath it, cast a terrible pallor over the banqueters, like that of the dead, by the reflection of the flames as they blazed up.

## CHAPTER II. On Clods Produced from Water

1. **[Note: [Col. 0560C]** Bitumen in Judea. The passage is from Hegesippus, Book 4, chapter 18.] Bitumen rises in the Asphaltite Lake of Judea. Sailors approach its floating clods in small boats and collect them. **[Note: [Col. 0560C]** “But in Syria it is mud.” Pliny: “Its nature is close to that of bitumen: in one place it is mud, in another earth; mud rises, as we have said, from the lake of Judea, and earth in Syria around the maritime town of Sidon. Both are thickened and coalesce into a dense substance.”] In Syria, however, it is mud that rises everywhere from the earth through heat. Both substances are thickened, become dense, and both are called by the Greeks πισσάσφαλτον (*pissasphaltos*), “pitch-bitumen.” **[Note: [Col. 0560D]** The Greeks call it *pissasphaltos*, or *asphaltopissa*, as it is indeed read in the Vatican manuscript of the Septuagint at Exodus 2: Καὶ κατὲχρισεν αὐτὸν ἀσφαλτοπίσσῃ, “And she coated it with asphalt-pitch.”] Its nature is fiery and related to fire, and **[Note: [Col. 0560D]** “And it cannot be broken by iron.” Hegesippus: “Bitumen is said to adhere to itself, so that it cannot be cut by iron or by any sharpened form of metal,” and so forth.] it cannot be broken by iron, except by the pollutants of women alone. It is useful for joining the timbers of ships.

2. Alum is so called from *lumen*, “light,” because it gives light to colors being dyed. But it is **[Note: [Col. 0560D]** “It is a saltiness of the earth.” Pliny, Book 35, chapter 15.] a saltiness of the earth, produced in winter from water and mud [248] and ripened by the summer sun. There are two kinds of it: liquid and [Col. 0560C] thick.

3. Some think that salt is so called because it leaps in fire. **[Note: [Col. 0560D]** “For it flees fire.” From the same author, Book 31, chapter 9.] For although it is fiery, it flees fire; yet it follows nature, because fire and water are always hostile to one another. Others think that salt is named from *salum*, “the sea,” and from the sun, **[Note: [Col. 0560D]** “For it is produced from seawater.” From chapter 7.] since it arises spontaneously from seawater: foam left at the edges of shores or on rocks and boiled down by the sun. There are also lakes, rivers, and wells from which it is drawn. [Col. 0561A] Then, when placed in saltworks, it is dried by the sun; rivers too become thickened into salt, while the remaining stream continues to flow beneath the ice. Elsewhere it is gathered after the sands have been removed, growing with the moon during the nights; for in Cyrenaica ammoniac salt is found beneath the sands. **[Note: [Col. 0561C]** “There are also natural mountains.” From the same chapter. We removed the word *majus*, “greater,” which alone had either remained from Pliny’s complete sentence about revenues or crept into the text.] There are also natural mountains of salt, in which it is cut with iron like stone that grows again. In some places it is so hard that they build walls and houses from blocks of salt, as in Arabia.

4. There are also differences in the nature of salt. In one place it is mild, in another extremely salty. Ordinary salt crackles in fire. Tragasian (*Tragasaeum*) salt neither crackles in fire nor leaps out. Agrigentine salt of Sicily, though it withstands flame, leaps in water and, contrary to nature, flows in fire.

5. There are also differences of color. Memphite salt is red; in a certain part of Sicily it is purple, **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “Purple.” Solinus, in the chapter on Sicily: “Etna sends forth purple salt.”] where Mount Etna is. Likewise, in the same Sicily at Pachynus it is so brilliant and clear that it reflects images. In Cappadocia it is dug up saffron-colored.

6. The nature of salt is necessary for every kind of food.

For it gives flavor to dishes, stimulates appetite, and creates desire for all foods. From it come the delight of every meal and the highest cheerfulness. Hence it is also thought to have received the name *salus*, “health.” **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “Nothing is more useful, etc.” From chapter 9.] Nothing is more useful than salt and sun. Finally, we see the bodies of sailors hardened like horn. Even sheep, cattle, and beasts of burden are especially stimulated by salt to feed, **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “With much more abundant milk and much more agreeable cheese.” From chapter 7; Virgil, *Georgics* 3:

> Hence they love the streams, and stretch their udders more and more,  
> and reproduce the hidden flavor of salt in their milk.]

giving much more abundant milk and cheese made much more agreeable by its presence. Salt also contracts, dries, and binds bodies. It even protects the dead from the corruption of decay, so that they endure. [249]

7. **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** Nitrum. From chapter 10; Sozomen, Book 6 of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 30, concerning the Scythian region of Egypt: “They call this place Nitriā, because it is a neighboring village where they gather nitrum.” Cassian also mentions Nitrea, *Conferences* 6, chapter 1, and Jerome, on Proverbs 25.] *Nitrum* took its name from the place. For it is produced in the town or region of Nitria in Egypt, from which medicines are made and the dirt of bodies and garments is washed away. Its nature is not greatly different from salt. For it has the power of salt and similarly arises when shores whiten through dryness.

8. *Aphronitrum* in Greek, in Latin “the foam of nitrum,” **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “Concerning which someone says.” Martial, who has the line: “I am also called *aphro*.”] concerning which someone says:

> You are rustic; you do not know what I am called by my Greek name.  
> I am called the foam of nitrum; in Greek, *aphronitrum*.

It is collected in Asia, dripping in caves, and then [Col. 0562A] dried by the sun. It is considered best if it is as light as possible, extremely friable, and almost purple in color.

9. *Chalcantum* is so called because it is the flower of *chalcitis*—that is, its blossom—and hence it is also called by the Latins “the flower of bronze.” It is now produced in many regions; **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “Formerly in the wells of Spain.” From Pliny, Book 34, chapter 12.] formerly in Spanish wells or pools containing water of this kind, which they boiled and poured into wooden basins. Ropes stretched over them by means of small stones were suspended above the basins, and mud adhered to them in the likeness of a [Col. 0561D] glass bead. **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “In the likeness of a glass bead.” From the same author.] It was then removed and dried for thirty days.

[250] 10. Now it is produced elsewhere in caves: collected in liquid form and then spread out, it hardens into certain clusters. It is also produced in excavated pits, where drops falling from the sides coalesce; and it is produced like salt from the most intense sunlight. Its power is so constricting [Col. 0562B] that, when scattered into the mouths of lions and bears, **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “It has such power.” These are Pliny’s words in the same place.] it has such a binding force that they are unable to bite.

## CHAPTER III. On Ordinary Stones

1. A stone is commonly recognized as something denser than earth. A stone is called *lapis* because it injures the foot. **[Note: [Col. 0561D]** “A stone is movable.” This must unquestionably be the correct reading, despite all the books, which have *mollis*, “soft”; what follows is “rocks adhere.”] A stone is movable and scattered.

Rocks adhere and break away from mountains.

*Petra* is a Greek word.

*Flint* (*silex*) is a hard stone, so called because fire leaps from it.

2. **[Note: [Col. 0562C]** “*Scopulus* from an elevated rock, etc.” These are Servius’s words, on *Aeneid* 1, at “And fixed him upon a sharp crag.”] A *scopulus* is named from a projecting rock, as though from “observing,” or from the protection of ships, ἀπὸ τοῦ σκέπειν, “from protecting.”

*Spelaea* in Greek, **[Note: [Col. 0562D]** “A cave in Latin; it is a hollowed rock.” The same author, at “Beneath the hollowed rock”: “It is a circumlocution for a cave.”] *spelunca* in Latin, is a hollowed rock. [Col. 0562C]

3. **[Note: [Col. 0562D]** “A *crepido* … because it is the height of a sheer rock.” These are Servius’s words, on *Aeneid* 10, at “A vessel joined to the lofty ledge.” The additional material that follows in the printed editions is not Isidorus’s, but belongs to someone who copied more from Servius than was appropriate.] A *crepido* is the edge of a sheer rock, and is therefore called *crepido*, because it is the height of a sheer rock.

*Cautes* are rough rocks in the sea, called from *cavere*, “to beware,” as though “things to beware of.”

*Murices* are rocks on the shore, [Col. 0562D] as sharp as living sea-snails and dangerous to ships. **[Note: [Col. 0562D]** “Like living *murices*.” Servius, on *Aeneid* 5, at “With a sharp *murex* the oars”: “A *murex* is the projecting sharpness of a rock during calm weather.” See also Nonius.] [251]

4. **[Note: [Col. 0562D]** “Echo is a rock.” Echo does indeed occur more often in rocks, but I would not want the rock itself to be called “echo.”] Echo is a rock that catches the sound of a human voice and also imitates the words of speakers. Echo **[Note: [Col. 0562D]** “Echo in Greek, *imago* in Latin.” Not because the Greek word ἠχώ literally means *imago* in Latin, but because the Latins call the image of a voice what the Greeks call ἠχώ. Virgil, *Georgics* 3:

> Or where the hollow rocks, struck by the blow,  
> resound, and the image of the voice rebounds.

Horace:

> May the image of Vatican Hill return your praises.

And elsewhere:

> … whose name the playful image echoes again.

Therefore some people have not edited the text correctly when they printed εἰκών, “image.”] is called *imago* in Latin because, responding to a voice, it becomes an image of another’s speech. This occurs through the nature of places, especially valleys.

5. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** *Calculus*. Servius, on “The pebble-strewn fields,” *Georgics* 2: “A *calculus* is a small stone mixed with earth.” It is called *calculus* because, being small, it can be trodden without discomfort.] A *calculus* is a small stone mixed with earth, round and extremely hard, and perfectly smooth in every respect. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** “And perfectly smooth in every respect.” Some manuscripts have “perfectly smooth on every side.” The same author below, Book 18, chapter 62: “They are called *calculi* because they are smooth and round.”] It is called *calculus* because, owing to its smallness, it can be trodden without discomfort. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** “Its opposite is a *scrupulus*.” See Servius, on “The rough rocks of the lake,” *Aeneid* 6.] Its opposite is a *scrupus*, a tiny, rough stone which, if it gets into a shoe, causes pain and disturbs the mind. Hence we also call mental distress a *scrupulus*, and therefore *scrupea saxa* means “rough rocks.”

6. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** *Cos*. See above.] A *cos* received its name because it sharpens iron for cutting; for in Greek *kotis* means “cutting.” Of these stones, some are water stones and others require oil for sharpening. Oil makes the edge gentle, while water makes it extremely sharp. **[Col. 0563B]**

7. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** Pumice. From the same author, chapter 21.] Pumice is so called because it is formed by the congealing density of foam. It is dry, somewhat white, and has such a cooling nature that, when placed in a vessel, it causes fermenting must to cease boiling.

8. **[Note: [Col. 0563C]** *Rudos*. The same author, Book 19, chapter 10. See Vitruvius, Book 7, chapter 1, and Palladius, Book 1, chapter 6.] Artisans call *rudos* stones that have been crushed and mixed with lime, which they pour over floors when making pavements; hence they are also called *rudera*. [252]

9. Gypsum is related to lime and its name is Greek; it has several varieties. **[Note: [Col. 0563D]** “The best of all is the stone used for windows.” From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 24.] The best of all is the window-stone. It is highly valued for the figures of buildings and for moldings.

10. **[Note: [Col. 0563D]** “Quicklime.” This and everything that follows are repeated in Book 9, chapter 10.] Quicklime is so called because, although cold to the touch, it contains hidden fire within. Hence, when water is poured over it, the concealed fire immediately bursts out. Its nature does something remarkable. For after it has burned, water sets it on fire, although water usually extinguishes fire; oil extinguishes it, although oil usually kindles fire. Its use is necessary for building structures. **[Note: [Col. 0563D]** “For stone cannot adhere firmly to stone unless joined with lime.” From Augustine, *City of God*, Book 5, chapter 27.] For one stone cannot adhere firmly to another unless joined with lime. **[Note: [Col. 0563D]** “Lime from white stone.” Pliny, Book 36, chapter 23; Palladius, Book 1, chapter 10; Vitruvius, Book 2, chapter 5.] Lime made from white stone, and from hard stone, is better for masonry; that made from soft stone is useful for plasterwork.

11. **[Note: [Col. 0563D]** *Arena* from dryness. Servius, on *Aeneid* 1, at “The Trojans possess the sand”: “The question is whether this word has an aspiration, and Varro defines it thus: If it is derived from dryness, it has none; if from adhering, as we see in building, it has one. The former etymology, however, is better.” Charisius takes the opposite view: “*Harena* is so called because it adheres, and *arena* because it is dry; nevertheless it sounds more agreeably with the aspiration.”] *Arena*, “sand,” is so called from dryness, not from adhering in building, as some maintain. **[Note: [Col. 0564C]** “The proof of this, if it grates when compressed in the hand.” From Palladius, Book 1, chapter 10.] Its quality is tested if it grates when pressed in the hand, or if scattered on a white garment leaves no dirt.

[253]

## CHAPTER IV. On More Distinguished Stones

1. **[Note: [Col. 0564C]** Indian magnetic stone. Pliny, Book 36, chapter 16: “It was called *magnes* after its discoverer, according to Nicander; it was found on Mount Ida,” and so forth. If this reading is correct, the word “Indian” must be removed, and *Ida*, not *India*, must be written. But since Nicander’s verses about the magnet do not survive, and there is also variation in Pliny’s codices, as Hermolaus observed, we have decided to change nothing—not because we do not prefer *Ida* (for Ida is also more suitable to a pastoral tale), but because we believe Isidorus read *India* in Pliny. The fact that the Arab Serapion and the Gallic poet Marbod call the magnet an Indian stone is of little importance. Lucretius, moreover, whom I follow in the etymology more than Nicander, writes:

> The Greeks call them magnets from their native name,  
> because the magnet was born in its native lands.]

The *magnes*, or magnet, is an Indian stone named after its discoverer. It was first found in India in the following way: when the same Magnes was pasturing his herds, it adhered to the nails of his sandals and to the tip of his staff; afterward it was found in many places. It is rust-colored, but its quality is proved when, placed against iron, it causes it to be drawn away. **[Note: [Col. 0564D]** “For it grips iron so strongly that it forms a chain.” From Augustine, *City of God* 21.4, and Pliny, Book 34, chapter 14.] For it grips iron so strongly that it forms a chain of rings. Hence ordinary people call it “living iron.”

2. It is also believed to draw glass liquid, just as it draws iron. Its power is so great **[Note: [Col. 0564D]** “As the blessed Augustine reports.” In the same place.] that, as the most blessed Augustine reports, someone held the same magnet beneath a silver vessel and placed iron upon the silver; then, when the hand moved the stone underneath, the iron moved rapidly above it. **[Note: [Col. 0564D]** “Hence it happened that in a certain temple…” The same author, chapter 6; Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* 11; Pliny, in the same place; and Suidas, under Μάγνης.] Hence it happened that in a certain temple an image made of iron appeared to hang in the air. [254] **[Note: [Col. 0564D]** “There is another kind in Ethiopia.” From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 16.] There is another magnet in Ethiopia that drives away and rejects every kind of iron.

**[Note: [Col. 0564D]** “Every magnet…” From Dioscorides, Book 5, chapter 148.] Every magnet is better in proportion as it is more blue. [Col. 0564C]

3. **[Note: [Col. 0564D]** *Gagates* … in Cilicia. Dioscorides, Book 5, chapter 146: Γεννᾶται δὲ ἐν Κιλικίᾳ κατά τινα ποταμοῦ εἰσρυσιν εἰς θάλασσαν ἐκχεομένου. Ἐστὶ δὲ πλησίον τῆς λεγομένης πλαγίου πόλεος. Καλεῖται δὲ ὁ τόπος, ἢ ὁ ποταμὸς Γάγας, “It is produced in Cilicia, at a certain inflow of a river pouring into the sea. It is near the city called Plagios. The place, or the river, is called Gagas.” Pliny, however, Book 36, chapter 19: “The *gagates* stone takes its name from the place and river Gagis of Lycia.”] The *gagates* stone was first found in Cilicia, cast up by the current of the river Gagas. Hence it was named so, although it is very abundant in Britain. It is black, flat, smooth, and burns when brought near fire. **[Note: [Col. 0565C]** “Black and flat.” Dioscorides seems to have read πλακώδης, “plated,” in Pliny; the current reading is πλατώδης, “crust-like.”] **[Note: [Col. 0565C]** “Written objects, etc.” From Pliny, in the same place.] Writing made with it on earthenware is not erased; when burned, it drives away snakes, exposes demoniacs, and detects virginity. It is remarkable that it is kindled by water and extinguished by oil.

4. **[Note: [Col. 0565C]** Asbestos. From Augustine, Book 21, chapters 5 and 6.] Asbestos is a stone of Arcadia, iron-colored, taking its name from fire because, once kindled, it is never extinguished. Human ingenuity devised something mechanical from this stone, which the pagans, captivated by their sacrilege, marveled at. Indeed, they say that in a certain temple there was a shrine of Venus, and in it a candelabrum with a lamp burning under the open sky so steadily that no storm and no rain could extinguish it.

5. **[Note: [Col. 0565C]** Pyrites. From the same author, chapter 5.] Pyrites is a Persian stone, tawny and resembling the quality of bronze, with an abundance of fire; for it easily emits sparks. [255] If the hand holding it is pressed too hard, it burns the hand, and therefore it received its name from fire. [Col. 0565B] **[Note: [Col. 0565C]** “There is also another common pyrites.” From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 16.] There is another common pyrites, called “living stone,” which emits sparks when struck with iron or stone. These sparks are caught by sulfur, dry fungi, or leaves, and it provides fire more quickly than one can say. Ordinary people call it “hearth-stone.”

6. **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** Selenites. From Augustine, in the same place.] *Selenites* is interpreted in Latin as “lunar,” because they say that its inner whiteness increases and diminishes with the moon. It is produced in Persia.

7. **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** Dionysias. The same below, chapter 11; from Solinus, chapter 50; and Pliny, Book 37, chapter 9.] *Dionysias* is a dark stone sprinkled with reddish markings. It is so called because, if it is ground after being mixed with water, it smells strongly of wine, and—what is remarkable in that operation—it resists drunkenness.

8. **[Col. 0565C]** **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** “Thracian … in Equitia.” Thus all the books read, but I believe *Scythia* should be read; Dioscorides says of it in Book 5: Γεννᾶται μὲν ἐν Σκυθίᾳ ἐν ποταμῷ λεγομένῳ Πόντῳ, “It is produced in Scythia, in a river called Pontus.” The reading *Equitia*, ἱππόβοτος, “rich in pasturage for horses,” which Strabo discusses in Book 11, is not very convincing.] Thracian stone is black and resonant. It is produced in a river whose name is Pontus, in Equitia.

9. **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** Phrygian stone. From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 19.] Phrygian stone took its name from the place. For it is produced in Phrygia, is pale in color, and moderately heavy. It is a pumiceous clod. First it is burned after being soaked in wine, and air is blown upon it with bellows until it becomes red; then it is again extinguished with sweet wine, three times in succession. It is useful only for dyeing garments.

[256] 10. **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** Syrian stone. From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 17. But whereas it is commonly read in Pliny as coming from the island of Scyros, it should be noted that *Syrian* is also found in the manuscripts of Pliny.] Syrian stone is named from Syria, where it is found. It is said to float when whole but to sink when broken apart.

11. **[Note: [Col. 0565D]** Arabic stone is like ivory and without any blemish. From Dioscorides, Book 5, chapter 149. But the words are taken from Pliny, who in Book 36, chapter 21 says: “The Arabian stone is like ivory.” And in chapter 20, concerning hematite: “He makes a third kind Arabian, of similar hardness, scarcely yielding juice to a water whetstone, sometimes like saffron.” Chacon seemed to have added this latter part from the margin, both here [Col. 0566C] and in the following chapter.] Arabic stone is like ivory, without any blemish. When rubbed against a whetstone, it gives off a juice resembling saffron.

12. **[Note: [Col. 0566C]** Judaean stone. Dioscorides, Book 5, chapter 155: Ὁ δὲ ἰουδαϊκὸς λίθος γεννᾶται μὲν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ τῷ σχήματι βαλανοειδής, λευκός, εὔρυθμος ἰκανῶς, ἔχων καὶ γραμμὰς παραλλήλους ὡς ἀπὸ τόρνου, “The Judaean stone is produced in Judaea, acorn-shaped, white, fairly well formed, and having parallel lines as if made by a lathe.” Isidorus’s words come from an old translator of Dioscorides. Chacon read *scriptulis*, “little writings,” instead of *scripturis*, “writings”; for the ancients interpreted γράμματα in this way. But where Isidorus translated it as “modulated,” he seems to have read ὡς ἀπὸ τόνου, “as if from a tone.”] Judaean stone is white and, in the shape of an acorn, marked with lines arranged one beneath another, which the Greeks call γραμμαί, “lines.”

13. **[Note: [Col. 0566D]** Samian stone. From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 21, and Dioscorides, Book 5, chapter 173.] Samian stone is named from the island of Samos, where it is found. It is heavy and white, and useful for polishing.

14. **[Note: [Col. 0566D]** Memphite stone. From Pliny, Book 36, chapter 7, and Dioscorides, chapter 158.] Memphite stone is named from a place in Egypt and has a gem-like nature. When ground and applied with vinegar to things that are to be burned or cut, it so numbs the body that it does not feel the pain.

15. **[Note: [Col. 0566D]** Sarcophagus. Pliny, Book 36, chapter 17.] The sarcophagus stone is so called because the bodies of the dead placed in it are consumed within forty days. For σάρξ (*sarx*) means “flesh” in Greek, and φάγειν (*phagein*) means “to eat.” **[Note: [Col. 0566D]** “It is produced in the Troad.” From Pliny, in the same place. The words that follow “bodies” in nearly all the books—“but gentler toward preserving bodies, not consuming them”—were rightly removed by Vulcanius, for they are Pliny’s words, spoken no longer of the sarcophagus but of *chernites*.] It is produced in the Troad and is split along a fissile vein. There are also rocks of the same kind in the East which, when fastened even to living people, corrode their bodies.

16. **[Note: [Col. 0566D] Haematites. From the same, chapter 20, and Dioscorides. See also Georg Agricola, Book V, *On the Nature of Fossils*.]** Haematites is so called because, when rubbed on a whetstone, it comes to resemble the color of blood. It is very livid in appearance. There is also a rusty variety. It is found in the remotest parts of Egypt, in Babylonia, and in Spain.

17. **[Note: [Col. 0566D] Androdamas. From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 20.]** Androdamas is black, remarkable for its weight and hardness; hence its name. It is found especially in Africa. It is said to draw silver or copper to itself, and, when rubbed, to be reduced to the color of blood, like haematites. **[Col. 0566C]**

18. **[Note: [Col. 0566D] Schistos. From Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 145.]** Schistos is found in the remotest parts of Spain; it resembles saffron, has a slight sheen, and crumbles easily.

19. **[Note: [Col. 0566D] Amiantos. From the same, chapter 156.]** Amiantos was so called by the ancients because, **[Note: [Col. 0566D] If a garment has been woven from it. Another reading is *contacta*, “touched”; but *contexta*, “woven,” must be read, following Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 93.]** if a garment was woven from it, it resisted fire; when placed upon fire, it did not burn but, having taken on its brightness, shone. It resembles split alum and resists all magical preparations, especially those of magicians. **[Col. 0567A]**

20. **[Note: [Col. 0567C] Ostracites, that is, “resembling a shell, layered, and easily split.” The words are Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 156: Ὀστρακίτης ὅμοιός ἐστιν ὀστράκῳ, πλακώδης, καὶ εὔσχιστος, “Ostracites resembles a shell, is layered, and easily split.” Since what follows shortly afterward concerning ostracites is taken from Pliny, it would be unsurprising if, using a corrupt copy of Dioscorides, Isidore read *Batrachites* at this point. Those who wish *Bostrychites* to be read here are merely trifling.]** Ostracites resembles a shell, is layered, and easily split.

**[Note: [Col. 0567C] Gallactites. From Dioscorides, chapter 50.]** Gallactites is ash-colored and sweet to the taste; it is so called because, when rubbed, it releases from itself something milky.

21. **[Note: [Col. 0567C] Obsidius. From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 26.]** Obsidius is a black, translucent stone resembling glass. It is placed in wall mirrors to reflect the shadows of images. Many make gems from it. It is found in India and in Samnium in Italy.

**[Note: [Col. 0567D] Mitridax. From Solinus, chapter 50. Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, calls the same stone *mitrax*. Isidore places it below, in chapter 10, among the gems.]** Mitridax is a stone of the Euphrates; struck by the sun, it sparkles with various colors.

22. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Aetliites. From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 21.]** Aethitae stones are found in eagles’ nests. They say that two are found, a male and a female, and that eagles cannot give birth without them. The male is hard, like a gallnut, and reddish; the female is small and soft.

**[Note: [Col. 0567D] Bound on, they hasten childbirth. We shall quote Pliny’s words, in case anyone should attempt to mend this passage from him: “Aethitae, bound to pregnant women, or to four-footed animals in the skins of sacrificial animals, delay childbirth; they must be removed only when the creatures are in labor, otherwise the wombs fall out. But unless they are removed from those in labor, they do not give birth at all.” We have reproduced the reading of the Gothic manuscripts.]** When bound on, they cause childbirth to occur rapidly; even something of the wombs falls out unless they are quickly removed from those in labor.

23. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Phengites. From the same, chapter 22.]** Phengites is a stone of Cappadocia, white and translucent with the hardness of marble. A certain king once built a temple from it, with golden doors; when the doors were closed, daylight brightness remained inside.

24. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Chernites. From the same, chapter 17. See Theophrastus, *On Stones*.]** Chernites resembles ivory. They say that Darius was buried in it. It resembles Parian marble in whiteness and hardness, but is less heavy; it is called *porus*.

25. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Ostracites. From the same, chapter 19.]** Ostracites is so called because it resembles a shell; it is used in place of pumice.

26. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Melitites. From the same, chapter 19, and Dioscorides, chapter 151.]** Melitites is so called because it emits a honey-colored and sweet juice.

27. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Smyris … gems are rubbed with it. The Gothic manuscripts read “are pounded.”]** Smyris is a rough and unconquerable stone that wears everything down; gems are polished with it.

28. **[Note: [Col. 0567D] Chrysites is similar in color to ochre. It must likewise be read this way in Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10. Dioscorides also mentions Attic ochre in Book V, chapter 62.]** Chrysites, similar in color to ochre, is found in Egypt. **259**

29. **[Note: [Col. 0568C] Hammites. From the same, Pliny, Book XXVII, chapter 10.]** Hammites resembles nitre but is harder; it is produced in Egypt and Arabia.

**[Col. 0568A] 30. [Note: [Col. 0568C] “Thyites is produced in Ethiopia.” Chacon admirably restored this passage from Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 154; it will suffice to append his words: Λίθος ὁ καλούμενος θυίτης γεννᾶται μὲν ἐν τῇ Αἰθιοπίᾳ· ἔστι δὲ ἀπόχλωρος, ἰασπίζων, ἐν δὲ τῷ ἀνίεσθαι γαλακτώδης φαινόμενος, ἀναδάκνων σφοδρῶς, “The stone called thyites is produced in Ethiopia; it is somewhat greenish and resembles jasper, but when dissolved it appears milky and bites sharply.” The reading of the Gothic manuscripts is: “It is produced in Ethiopia.”]** Thyites is produced in Ethiopia; it is greenish in appearance but milky and very biting when dissolved.

31. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] Coranus is white and harder than Parian marble. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 18: “Conversely, white Corani are harder than Parian marble.” Thus the passage in Pliny must be read, as both the better manuscripts show and these words of Isidore sufficiently confirm.]** Coranus is white and harder than Parian marble.

32. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] Molotius. Thus the old manuscript reads. But I think *Morochthius* should be written, following Dioscorides.]** Molotius, somewhat green and large, is found in Egypt.

33. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] Tusculanus. From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 18.]** Tusculanus is named from a place in Italy; it is said to split apart in fire.

34. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] Sabinus. From Pliny, the same passage. There is no reason for any corrector to substitute *Gabineus* for *Sabinus* here from Tacitus because of the following words, which are also taken from Pliny and are spoken neither of a Gabine nor even of a Sabine stone.]** Sabinus is dark-colored and is said to shine when oil is added.

**[Note: [Col. 0568D] There is also a certain green stone. From the same, chapter 22.]** There is also a certain green stone that strongly resists fire.

35. Siphinius is soft and white; when heated with oil, it turns black and becomes hard.

36. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] Stones suitable for medicinal mortars. Ephesian. Chalazian … Theban … Basanites … Specular. All these are excerpted piecemeal from the same chapter.]** There are also stones suitable for medicinal mortars and for preparing pigments. The Ephesian is the finest, and next comes the Chalazian.

**[Col. 0568B]** The Theban and basanite stones likewise give off nothing from themselves.

37. Specular stone is so called because it shines through like glass. It was first found in Nearer Spain, around the city of Segobriga. It is found underground; once dug out, it is cut and split into crusts of any desired thinness.

## CHAPTER V. On Marbles

1. **[Note: [Col. 0568D] “After the kinds of stones.” From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapters 5–8.]** After the kinds of stones, let us come to marbles. For there is a distinction between stones and marbles. Marbles are called exceptional stones, distinguished by spots and colors. *Marmor* is a Greek word, named from greenness; although other colors are later found in them, they retained their original name from greenness.

**[Col. 0568C] 2. [Note: [Col. 0568D] The colors and kinds of marbles. From chapter 7.]** The colors and kinds of marbles are innumerable. Yet not all are quarried from cliffs; many are scattered underground and are of the most precious kind, such as Lacedaemonian green marble, brighter than all others, first found among the Lacedaemonians, from whom it also took its name.

**[Col. 0569A]** 3. Ophites resembles the markings of snakes, from which it also took its name. It has two kinds: soft white and hard black.

4. Augustaeum and Tiberium were first found in Egypt during the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius. Their difference from ophites is that the latter, as we said above, resembles the markings of snakes. These collect their spots differently: Augustaeum is rippled and curled into whorls, while Tiberium has scattered, uncoiled grayish markings.

**261** 5. Porphyrites comes from Egypt; it is red with intervening white specks. The reason for its name is that it is red like purple.

6. **[Note: [Col. 0569C] Basaltes. All manuscripts have *Basantes*, but *Basaltes* occurs in Pliny, whose words these are. He discussed the superior basanite in the preceding chapter.]** Basaltes is the color—or the hardness—of iron. Hence its name was given to it. It is found in Egypt and Ethiopia.

7. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Alabastrites. From chapter 8.]** Alabastrites is a white stone streaked with various colors, from which the vessel of that famous Gospel ointment was made. They hollow it out for perfume vessels because it is said to preserve their contents unspoiled exceptionally well. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, and is whiter there than elsewhere; the finest is found in India.

8. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Parian, also called Lychnites. From chapter 5.]** Parian marble is of extraordinary whiteness and is surnamed Lychnites. It is produced on the island of Paros, from which it is called Parian.

**[Note: [Col. 0569D] Lygdinus. From chapter 8. We do not think this passage was badly restored by us. The similarity of the words *lychnit* and *lygdin* had made both readings suspect. Thus only one of them remained in the Isidorian manuscripts, although both are necessary.]** Lygdinus is no larger than plates and mixing bowls; it too is suitable for perfume vessels.

9. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Coraliticus. From the same chapter.]** Coraliticus is found in Asia. It is no more than two cubits in size and, in whiteness, closely resembles ivory. By contrast, black Alabandicus is named from its native land and resembles purple in appearance. In the East it is melted by fire and cast for use as glass.

10. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Theban. From the same source. We add the word “Africa,” which is entirely necessary.]** Theban marble, streaked with golden drops, is found in the part of Africa assigned to Egypt. It is naturally suitable for small stones used to grind eye ointments. **[Col. 0569C] 262**

11. Syenites is produced near Syene or Thebes; kings made beams from it.

12. Marbles used in workshops are produced in cliffs, **[Note: [Col. 0569D] “Among them is Thasian.” The old manuscripts also confirm this reading; most have *Itasius*, while others plainly read *Thasius*. See Pliny, chapter 6; that passage too requires correction.]** among them Thasian, distinguished by spots of different colors. The Cyclades first introduced its use.

13. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Lesbian, somewhat livid. Philostratus, in *Lives of the Sophists*, says of Lesbian stone: Κατηφὴς ὁ λίθος, καὶ μέλας, “The stone is gloomy and black.”]** Lesbian marble is somewhat more livid than this, but it too has spots of different colors.

14. Corinthian marble resembles a drop of Ammonian stone, with a variety of different colors. It was first found at Corinth. Great columns, thresholds, and beams are made from it.

15. Carystian marble is green. Its excellent name comes from its appearance, because it is pleasing to those who carve gems; its greenness refreshes the eyes.

16. **[Note: [Col. 0569D] Numidian … releases a saffron-like juice onto the whetstone. Chacon deleted this, as he did in the preceding chapter.]** Numidian marble is supplied by Numidia. On the whetstone it releases a juice like saffron, from which it also took its name; **[Note: [Col. 0570C] Not only into slabs, but into a mass, and suitable for thresholds. The word *tantum*, which was missing from Pliny, made the sentence absurd; I prefer *aptatum*, “adapted,” to *aptum*, “suitable.”]** it is suitable not only for slabs but also as a mass for use in thresholds.

17. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] Lucullean … is produced on the island of Chios. Pliny has “on an island of the Nile.”]** Lucullean marble is produced on the island of Chios. The consul Lucullus gave it its name: delighted with it, he first brought it to Rome, and this alone among marbles received its name from an admirer.

18. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] There is also Lunensian … There is a lacuna in the better manuscripts; afterward comes Tephria, a different kind of marble.]** There is also Lunensian marble … **[Col. 0570B]** Tephria is named from the color of ash; binding this stone on is praised as a protection against snakes.

19. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] Ivory from *barro*. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “What splendor hands add to ivory.”]** Ivory is named from *barro*, that is, an elephant. Horace:

> What do you want, woman, most worthy of black elephants?

## CHAPTER VI. On Gems

1. After the kinds of marbles come gems, which greatly enhance gold by the beauty of their colors. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] Their origin from the Caucasian rock. From Pliny’s preface to Book XXXVII.]** Their beginnings are traced to the rock of Caucasus. Fables say that Prometheus first enclosed a fragment of its stone in iron, put it around his finger, and thus began the use of rings and gems.

2. The kinds of gems are said to be innumerable; of these **264** we shall record only those that are principal or best known.

3. They are called gems because they shine through like gum.

4. Precious stones are so called because they are highly valued, or so that they may be distinguished from cheap stones, or because they are rare. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] For everything rare, etc. From Jerome on Isaiah 13.]** Everything rare is called great and precious, as is also written in the Book of Samuel: “The word of the Lord was precious in Israel,” that is, rare.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Greener Gems

1. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] Of all green gems. Most of this is from Pliny, Book XXXVII.]** Among all green gems, emerald holds first place. **[Note: [Col. 0570D] The ancients assign it third rank. No one who has examined Pliny’s fourth and fifth chapters will doubt that the words found in all manuscripts after “pearls and unions” are extraneous. These words come from Pliny, but the cause of the error is not obscure. The writer had evidently read in Pliny, Book IX, chapter 35: “Pearls hold the first place and highest rank among all valuable things.” He did not consider the passage from which Isidore drew this material, where unions are mentioned. Pliny actually says in chapter 4: “Among human possessions, the diamond has the greatest value, not only among gems”; and at the end: “Among us, Indian and Arabian pearls rank next in value”; and at the beginning of chapter 5: “Third rank is attributed to emeralds.”]** The ancients assign it third rank after pearls and unions. Emerald is so called from its excessive greenness. **[Note: [Col. 0571D] “Everything sufficiently green is called bitter.” Thus the Gothic manuscripts; others read “the emerald.”]** Everything sufficiently green is called bitter.

**[Note: [Col. 0571D] “No gems or herbs have greater austerity than this.” The words “gems or herbs” are absent from all Roman manuscripts. It is well established that colors and flavors borrow names from one another; Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 6, divides colors into “florid” and “austere.” We too derive our word *amarillo*, “yellow,” from *amaro*, “bitter,” on the same basis.]** No gems or herbs have greater austerity than this. For it surpasses green herbs and foliage, dyeing the air around it with reflected greenness. For those who carve gems, no restoration of the eyes is more pleasing. If its body is extended, like a mirror it returns images. Indeed, Nero Caesar watched gladiatorial combats in an emerald. There are twelve kinds, but the noblest are the Scythian, found among the Scythian people. The Bactrian occupy second place.

**[Note: [Col. 0571D] “They are collected in the joints of rocks.” One should read “in the joints,” if one wishes to defend Pliny, who translated this from Theophrastus’ *On Stones*: Διὸ καὶ εἰς τὰ λιθοκόλλητα χρῶνται, “Therefore they also use them in stone joints.” What *lithokollēta* are is not obscure. Solinus plainly read “in joints”: “Others, less noble, appear in the joints of rocks or in copper mines.”]** They are collected in the joints of rocks when the north wind blows; then, once the earth has been uncovered, they glimmer, because those winds move the sand most strongly. The Egyptians possess the third kind. The rest are found in copper mines, but they are defective, bearing marks like copper, lead, hair, or salt.

2. Emeralds improve through pure wine and oil, **[Note: [Col. 0571D] Although they are imbued by nature. These are Solinus’ words, chapter 25. Pliny says the same more clearly: “Those that are not born entirely green are improved by wine and oil.” Thus *imbui*, “to be imbued,” should be understood as “to be colored.” Horace writes: “The jar, once imbued, will long retain the scent”; and Virgil: “The tender lamb from our folds will often imbue his altar.”]** although they are naturally imbued.

3. Chalcosmaragdus is so called because it is green and clouded by veins of copper. It is produced in Egypt or on the island of Cyprus.

4. Prasius is named from its green color but is of little value. One kind **[Note: [Col. 0572D] “Bristles with blood-red spots.” From Pliny, chapter 8.]** bristles with blood-red spots. A third is marked with three white streaks.

5. Beryl is produced in India and has a name in the language of its people. It resembles emerald in greenness but is paler. The Indians polish it into six-sided forms so that the dullness of its color may be enlivened by the reflection from its angles. If polished otherwise, it has no brilliance. There are nine kinds.

6. Chrysoberyl is so called because its pale greenness shines into a golden color; India supplies it.

7. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Chrysoprasius. From the same source, chapter 8.]** Chrysoprasius is Indian. Its color resembles the juice of a leek, with intervening golden drops, from which it also took its name. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Which some assign to the class of beryls. From chapter 5.]** Some have assigned it to the class of beryls.

8. Jasper is translated from Greek into Latin as “green gem.” **[Col. 0572A] [Note: [Col. 0572D] *Ias* means “green,” while *pina* means “gem.” Vulcanius did not have this material; it is enough that we have retained it. I know that πῖνα means “gem” in Greek; *ias* remains uncertain.]** *Ias* means “green,” while *pina* means “gem.” It resembles emerald but has a thicker, denser color. There are seventeen varieties.

**[Note: [Col. 0572D] Some maintain this. See Pliny, chapter 9.]** Some maintain that the jasper gem brings grace and protection to those who wear it; believing this belongs not to faith but to superstition.

9. Topaz belongs to the green kind and shines with every color. It was first found on an island of Arabia, where the Troglodyte raiders, exhausted by hunger and storms, dug up the roots of plants and discovered it. The island was later sought and, covered by mists, eventually found by sailors. Thus both the place and the gem received their name from this event. For τοπάζειν, *topazein*, means “to seek” in the language of the Troglodytes. It is the largest of gems and the only one among the noble stones that feels the file. There are two kinds.

10. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Callaica. *Callais* in Pliny and Solinus.]** Callaica is green in color but pale and excessively dense; **[Note: [Col. 0572D] “Nothing is more pleasing for adorning gold.” From Solinus, chapter 33.]** nothing is more pleasing for adorning gold, **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Hence its name, because *kalon* means “beautiful.”]** and hence its name. It is produced in India or **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Germany. Solinus has “Carmania”; Pliny has “Carmania.”]** Germany, in icy rocks, projecting like an eye.

11. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Molochites. From Pliny, chapter 8, and Solinus, chapter 35.]** Molochites is a deeper and denser green than emerald; it takes its name from the color of mallow and is praised for producing engraved figures. It is found in Arabia.

12. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Heliotrope. From chapter 10.]** Heliotrope is green and cloudy, sprinkled with crimson stars and streaked with blood-red veins. The reason for its name comes from the stone’s effect. For when it is thrown into bronze basins, it changes the sun’s rays by a bloody reflection. Outside water, it receives the sun like a mirror and reveals its eclipses, showing the moon passing before it. It is also the clearest example of the impudence of magicians: they claim that, when the herb heliotrope is mixed with the stone and certain added incantations are spoken, it makes its wearer invisible. It is produced in Cyprus and Africa, but the best comes from Ethiopia.

13. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Sagda. From the same chapter and Solinus, chapter 50.]** Sagda is a gem of leek-green color among the Chaldaeans. Its power is so great that it seeks out ships passing in the depths and clings so firmly to their keels that it can scarcely be separated except by scraping away part of the wood.

14. **[Note: [Col. 0572D] Myrrhites. From Solinus, chapter 40, and Pliny, the same passage.]** Myrrhites is so called because it has the color of myrrh. When pressed until warm, it gives off the fragrance of nard. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Aromatites is found. From the same chapter of Pliny.]** Aromatites is found in Arabia or Egypt; it has the color and scent of myrrh, from which it also takes its name.

15. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Melichloros. From chapter 11.]** Melichloros is two-colored: green on one side and like honey on the other.

16. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Choaspites. From chapter 10.]** Choaspites is named from the river Choaspes of the Persians; it is green with a golden sheen.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Red Gems

1. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Coral … is called. Pliny consistently has *curalium*, as does Theophrastus. These words are from Book XXXII, chapter 2.]** Coral is produced in the sea. It is branch-shaped, green in color, and especially red. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Its veins are white. Thus the old manuscripts; others read “berries,” as does Pliny.]** Its veins are white and soft under water; once removed, they immediately harden and redden, and at once turn to stone when touched. It is therefore usually seized and torn out with nets, or cut with a sharp tool; for this reason it is called coral. **[Col. 0573B]** Among us Indian pearls are as precious as coral is among the Indians.

**[Note: [Col. 0573D] “The magicians claim that this withstands lightning.” This is repeated in chapter 14; Pliny, Book XXXVIII, chapter 10. Gorgonia is nothing other than coral; its name refers to the claim that it turns into the hardness of stone, softens the seas through lightning, and resists Typhon.]** The magicians claim that it resists lightning, if one believes them.

2. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Sardius. From Book XXXVII, chapter 7.]** Sardius is so called because it was first found by the Sardians. It is red, surpassing marbles in this respect, but the least valuable among gems. It has five kinds.

3. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Onyx. From chapter 6.]** Onyx is so called because it contains a mixture of white resembling a human fingernail. For the Greeks call a fingernail ὄνυξ, *onyx*. India or Arabia produces it. The two kinds differ: the Indian has sparks encircled by white bands, while the Arabian is black with white bands. It has five kinds.

4. Sardonyx takes its name from the combination of two names. It has the whiteness of onyx and the red of sard. It consists of three colors: black underneath, white in the middle, and red above. It alone, when used for engraving, removes none of the wax. It is found among the Indians and Arabs, exposed by torrents. It has five kinds.

5. **[Note: [Col. 0573D] Haematites. From chapter 10.]** Haematites is blood-red and is therefore called haematites, since αἷμα, *haima*, means “blood.” The principal kind is produced in Ethiopia, but it is also found in Arabia and Africa. Of it the magicians promise some means of exposing the plots of barbarians.

6. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Succinum. From chapter 2.]** Succinum, which the Greeks call *electron*, is tawny and wax-colored. It is said to be the sap of a tree and for that reason is called *succinum*. It was given the name *electron* by a fabulous account. After Phaethon was killed by a thunderbolt, his sisters, changed by grief into poplar trees, are said to shed amber as tears each year beside the river Eridanus; hence it was called *electron*. **[Col. 0573D] [Col. 0574A] [Note: [Col. 0574D] Because the sun was called *Elector*. Homer, *Iliad* VI:

> Thus Priam’s son Paris, from the summit of Pergamum,  
> Shining in his armor like the sun, advanced.

]** This was because the sun was called *Elector*, as many poets have said. In fact, it is not the sap of the poplar but of the pine. For when it is burned, it gives off the fragrance of a torch.

**7.** It is produced on the islands of the northern Ocean, and, like gum, is hardened **[Note: [Col. 0574D] By cold or warmth. Pliny has “by autumnal warmth.” Hermolaus Barbarus argues that Solinus should likewise be read “by warmth,” not “at the autumnal season.”]** by cold or warmth. Necklaces are made from it for the adornment of country women. Some call it *harpaga*, because, once warmed by the friction of the fingers, it seizes leaves, straw, and the fringes of garments, like a magnet seizing iron.

**[Note: [Col. 0574D] “It is dyed in whatever manner one wishes,” etc. From chapter 3.]** It can be dyed in whatever manner one wishes, for it is colored with the root of alkanet and with purple dye.

8. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Lyncurius. From chapter 2 and Solinus, chapter 8.]** Lyncurius is so called because it is formed from the urine of the lynx, hardened in time. Like succinum, it is tawny and attracts nearby leaves by its emanation.

## CHAPTER IX. On Purple Gems

1. Among purple gems, Indian amethyst holds first place. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Amethyst. From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 4.]** Amethyst is purple mixed with violet, with something like the brilliance of a rose, and gently emitting certain little flames. One of its kinds shades into hyacinths. They give this reason for its name: in its purple there is something not wholly fiery but possessing the color of wine. It is easy to engrave. It has five kinds.

2. Sapphire is blue with purple, sprinkled with golden dust. The best is found among the Medes, but it is never fully transparent.

3. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Hyacinth. Solinus, chapter 53.]** Hyacinth is named from the flower of the same name. It is found in Ethiopia and has a blue color. The best is neither too sparse nor clouded by excessive density, but shines with light and purple through a balance of both. It does not gleam evenly: in clear weather it is transparent and pleasing, but in cloudy weather it vanishes and withers before the eyes. Put into the mouth, it is cold; in engraving it is extremely hard, though not unconquerable, for it is inscribed and engraved with a diamond.

4. Hyacinthizon is Indian and closely resembles hyacinth. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Some of them. From chapter 53.]** Some of these, like crystals, are darkened by hairs running through them; it is from this defect that they also receive their name.

5. Amethystizon is so called because its final little flame passes into the violet of amethyst.

6. **[Note: [Col. 0574D] Chelidonia. From Pliny, chapter 10.]** Chelidonia is named from the color of swallows and has two kinds, one of which is pure purple on one side **[Col. 0574D] [Col. 0575A]** and purple on the other with black spots intervening.

7. **[Note: [Col. 0575D] Cyanea. From Solinus, chapter 20, and Pliny, chapter 9.]** Cyanea is a gem of Scythia, flashing with a blue sheen; sometimes it is pure, and sometimes varied with tiny points and glittering golden dust.

8. Rhodites is rose-colored and took its name from this.

## CHAPTER X. On White Gems

1. **[Note: [Col. 0575D] Pearl. From Pliny, Book IX, chapter 35, and Book XXXVII, chapters 9–11, and Solinus, chapter 50.]** Pearl is the first of the white gems. It is said to be called *margarita* because this kind of stone is found in the little shells of the sea. A pebble is born within the flesh of the shellfish, just as a stone is found in the brain of a fish. It is produced from heavenly dew, which shellfish absorb at a certain season of the year. Some of these pearls are called *unions*, an apt name because only one, never two or more together, is found. White pearls are better than those that turn yellow. Youth or the absorption of morning dew makes the former white; old age or evening air makes the latter dark.

2. Paederos is second among white gems after pearl. The question arises into which color it should be counted, since its name is repeatedly thrown among other beauties, to such a degree that the word itself has become a distinction of beauty.

3. Asterites is white and contains an enclosed light, as though a star were moving inside it; it reflects the whitening rays of the sun, from which it also received its name.

4. Galactites is milky. When rubbed, it produces a white juice with the taste of milk; when tied to nursing women, it is said to make their breasts fertile. Suspended around infants’ necks, it is also said to produce saliva; placed in the mouth, it melts and takes away memory. The rivers Nile and Achelous supply it. Some call an emerald encircled by white veins galactites.

5. Chalazias displays both the whiteness and shape of hail. It is unconquerable in hardness, like diamond, and even when placed in fire retains its coldness.

6. Solis is a white gem. It took its name because it scatters shining rays in a circle like the sun.

7. Selenites shines through with a white and honey-colored gleam and contains the image of the moon, which they say decreases and increases day by day according to the course of the heavenly body itself. **[Note: [Col. 0575D] It is produced in Persia. Pliny, however, chapter 10, says it is thought to be produced in Arabia.]** It is produced in Persia.

8. Cynaedia is found in the brain of a fish of the same name. It is white and oblong. Magicians claim that it foretells to those who possess it signs of calm or storm.

**[Col. 0576A]** 9. Belioculus is whitish and surrounds a black pupil shining with a golden gleam in the middle. Because of its appearance, it was dedicated to the Assyrian king Bel and was named from him.

10. Epimelas is so called when a black color appears above on a white gem; hence it has its name.

11. Exhebenus is beautiful and white; goldsmiths polish gold with it.

1. **[Note: [Col. 0575D] Achates. Hugutio says that it makes people gracious.]** in many lands. It is black, with joined and varied black and white circles in the middle, resembling haematites. Magicians claim that, if one believes them, fumigation with it averts storms and stops rivers.

2. Apsyctos is black and heavy, marked with reddish veins. When heated by fire, it retains its warmth for seven days.

3. **[Note: [Col. 0576D] Aegyptilla is black, with a blue face on a root. Pliny: “Iachus understands Aegyptilla as a white sard with a black vein passing through it; ordinary people make a blue face on a black root.” One must consider which reading should be restored from the other.]** Aegyptilla is black at the root and blue in appearance; it is named from Egypt, where it is found.

4. Medea is black and was discovered by that mythical Medea. **[Note: [Col. 0576D] It has veins the color of copper. All the Gothic manuscripts have “the color of copper”; Pliny reads “the color of gold.”]** It has veins the color of copper, releases saffron-colored moisture, and tastes of wine.

5. Veientana is an Italian gem discovered at Veii. It is black in appearance, with white markings shining through.

Baroptis is black with red and white markings.

6. Mesomelas is black, with a vein cutting through the middle in any color.

Venus’s hair is of the deepest black brilliance and contains within it the appearance of reddish hair.

**[Col. 0576C]** 7. Trichrus is black and comes from Africa, but it releases three juices: black at the root, blood-red in the middle, **[Note: [Col. 0576D] “At the top, ochre.” Others read “wax-colored at the top”; others, “saffron at the top.”]** and ochre at the top.

8. **[Note: [Col. 0576D] Dionysias. From Solinus, chapter 50.]** Dionysias is black with mixed reddish markings. When ground with water, it exhales wine, and it is thought that its odor resists drunkenness.

Pyrites is indeed black, but when rubbed it burns the fingers.

## CHAPTER XII. On Variegated Gems

1. Panchrus is composed of nearly every color, and is named accordingly.

**[Note: [Col. 0576D] Orca. The Gothic manuscripts have *Orca* or *Olca*.]** Orca, a name of barbarian origin, is tawny, black, green, and white. **[Col. 0577A]**

2. Mitrydax, struck by the sun, sparkles with various colors. It is produced in Persia.

**275** Droselytus is variegated. Its name comes from the fact that, when placed near fire, it gives off something like sweat.

3. Opal is marked with the colors of different gems. In it there is the delicate fire of carbuncle, the shining purple of amethyst, the gleaming greenness of emerald, and all these lights shining together in a kind of variegation. **[Note: [Col. 0577D] It takes its name from its homeland. We think this has been added.]** It takes its name from its homeland. For India alone gives birth to it.

4. Pontic stones are named from Pontus. They are of different kinds: **[Note: [Col. 0577D] “Now flashing with golden drops.” Pliny has “black.”]** some now flash with golden drops, others have stars, and others are marked with long lines of color.

5. Hexecontalithus is multicolored despite its small size, from which it adopted its name. It is so scattered with different markings that sixty gem-colors can be detected in its small circular body. It is produced in Libya among the Troglodytes.

6. Murrina is produced among the Parthians but is finest in **[Note: [Col. 0577D] Germany. Pliny has “Carmania.”]** Germany. They think it is moisture beneath the earth condensed by heat, **[Note: [Col. 0577D] “Hence it took its name.” Chacon thought this, too, was extraneous.]** and hence it took its name. Its variety consists of purple, white, and fiery colors, with a kind of reflection of colors such as is seen in the rainbow. The contrary process produces crystal, when frost has been condensed more intensely.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Crystals
1. Crystal is reported to be gleaming and watery in color, [Note: [Col. 0577D] That it is snow hardened into ice. So Pliny, chapter 2, and Augustine, on Psalm 147. Solinus, however, chapter 25: “They think,” he says, “that ice congeals and becomes crystal, but mistakenly; for if that were so, neither Alabanda in Asia nor the island of Cyprus would produce this material, though those regions have extremely intense heat. But it is not our task to settle these disputes.] because it is snow hardened into ice over many years. Hence the Greeks gave it its name. It is produced in Asia and Cyprus, especially in the Alps of the north, where even in summer the sun is not found to be intensely hot. Therefore the snow itself is stripped bare, and its age-long hardness produces this substance called crystal. When exposed to the sun’s rays, it seizes the flame so powerfully that it can supply fire to dry fungi or leaves. It is also used for drinking cups. It can endure nothing except cold.

2. The Indian diamond is a small and unattractive stone, having a rusty color and the brilliance of crystal. It has never been found larger than a hazelnut kernel. It yields to no material—not even iron or fire—and never becomes hot; hence, according to the Greek interpretation, it received its name from its unconquerable nature. Yet although it is invincible against iron and scorns fire, it is broken when soaked in the fresh, warm blood of a he-goat, and thus, by many blows of iron, is shattered. Engravers use its fragments for setting and perforating gems.

[Col. 0578A] 3. [Note: [Col. 0577D] Here he disagrees with the fuller account of Solinus, in the chapter on India.] It is so opposed to the magnetic stone that, when placed beside it, it does not allow iron to be drawn away; but if it is brought near a magnet, it snatches away and carries off the iron that the magnet has grasped. It is also said, like electrum, to detect poisons, drive away groundless fears, and resist magical arts. There are six kinds of it.

4. Chalazias has the color, whiteness, and form of hail, with diamond-like hardness. Even when placed in fire, it retains its coldness.

5. There are two kinds of ceraunium. [Note: [Col. 0577D] One kind is sent from Germany. Others read Carmania. See Pliny, book 36, chapter 9, and Solinus, chapter 33, concerning Scandinavia. [Col. 0578D] It is unclear which of these Isidore followed.] One kind, which Germany sends, resembles crystal but shines blue; and if it is placed beneath the open sky, it seizes the radiance of the stars. [Note: [Col. 0578D] The other ceraunium is Spanish. Solinus, in the chapter on Spain: “The Lusitanian coast is especially rich in the ceraunium gem, which they even prefer to the Indian varieties. Its color is that of a red pyrope, and its quality is tested by fire: if it endures fire without damage to itself, it is believed to aid against the force of lightning.” From this passage some read “its quality seems to be fire,” so that *vidēri* (“to seem”) replaces what Solinus wrote, *probāri* (“to be tested”).] Spain produces the other ceraunium on the Lusitanian shores. It has the color of a red pyrope and the quality of fire. It is said to aid against the force of lightning, if we believe it. They are called ceraunia because they are found nowhere except in a place near the point struck by lightning. For in Greek “lightning” is called κέραυνος (*keraunos*).

6. [Note: [Col. 0578D] Iris. This account is partly from Solinus and partly from Pliny. Its occurrence in Arabia and its hexagonal form are from Solinus; the rest is from Pliny.] Iris is produced near Arabia in the Red Sea. It is crystal-colored and hexagonal, and is called iris because of its resemblance to the rainbow. For when struck by sunlight beneath a roof, it casts the appearance and colors of the heavenly rainbow [Note: [Col. 0578D] onto the nearby walls. All the books mistakenly read *immittatur* (“may be sent”); Pliny has *ejaculatur* (“projects”).] onto the nearby walls.

7. Astrios comes from India and is close to crystal. In its center a star shines with the radiance of the full moon. It received its name because, when set opposite the stars, it seizes and reflects their brilliance.

8. [Note: [Col. 0578D] Alectria. From Pliny, book 37, chapter 10.] Alectria, as though *alectoria*, is found in the stomachs of roosters. It has a crystalline appearance and the size of a bean. Magicians claim that whoever possesses it will become invincible in contests, if we believe them.

9. Enhydros is named from water. For it exudes water, so that one might think a spring were enclosed within it.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Fiery Stones

1. [Note: [Col. 0578D] “Of all.” From Pliny, book 37, and Solinus.] Of all fiery gems, the carbuncle holds first place. It is called carbuncle because it is fiery like a coal, whose brilliance is not overcome even by night. It shines in darkness so strongly that it shoots flames into the eyes. There are twelve kinds, but the finest are those that seem to glow and, as it were, pour forth fire. In Greek the carbuncle is called ἄνθραξ (*anthrax*). It is produced in Libya among the Troglodytes.

2. Anthracites is so called because it too is fiery in color, like the carbuncle, but is encircled by a white vein. Its distinctive property is that, when thrown into fire, it is extinguished as though it had died out; but, when sprinkled with water, it blazes up again.

5. Sandasirus is produced in India, in a place of the same name. Its appearance is such that golden drops shine within it as though in transparent fire. Everyone agrees [Note: [Col. 0579D] As regards the number of drops. Pliny reads “stars.”] that the more it approaches them in the number of its drops, the more it also increases in price.

4. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Lychnites. From Solinus, chapter 65.] Lychnites belongs to the same class of fiery stones and is named from the flame of lamps. It is produced in many places, but the most highly valued specimens come from India. Some have said that it is a milder carbuncle. It has a double appearance: one kind radiates purple; the other has the redness of scarlet. When warmed by the sun or rubbed by the fingers, it is said to attract toward itself bits of straw and threads of paper. It resists engraving; and if it is engraved, while making an impression it seems, like some animal’s bite, to retain part of the wax. There are four kinds.

5. Carchedonius is said to do what lychnites does, although it is much less valuable than the stones mentioned above. It is produced among the Nasamones by what is said to be a divine rain. It is found by the reflected light of the full moon. All its varieties resist engraving.

6. Alabandina is named from Alabanda, a region of Asia. Its color tends toward that of carchedonius, but it is rare.

7. Dracontites is extracted from the brain of a dragon; unless it is cut from a living dragon, it does not become a gem. [Note: [Col. 0579D] “Does not become gemlike.” Thus the old manuscript. Pliny reads *gemmescit* (“becomes gemlike”).] Hence magicians cut it from dragons while they sleep. Bold men investigate the dragons’ caves and scatter there medicated grasses to induce the dragons’ sleep; then, when the dragons have been lulled to sleep, they cut off their heads [Col. 0579C] and remove the gems. They are translucent in whiteness. The kings of the East especially pride themselves on using them.

8. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Chrysoprase. In Solinus’s manuscript copy, in the chapter on Ethiopia, it reads as follows: “Where hyacinth appears, chrysoprase also appears; light conceals this stone, while darkness reveals it. For it has this peculiarity: by night it is fiery, by day pale.” Pliny, Isidore in the following chapter, and the printed copies of Solinus attribute all these properties to chrysolampis. Therefore these words could safely have been deleted.] Ethiopian chrysoprase is a stone that light conceals and darkness reveals. For by night it is fiery, and by day golden.

9. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Phlogites. Solinus uses this form; Pliny has *phlegontis*.] Phlogites comes from Persia and displays within itself what seem to be burning flames that do not emerge.

10. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Syrtites. From Pliny, chapter 10, or rather from Solinus, chapter 8.] Syrtites is so called because it was first found on the shore of the Syrtes, in a part of Lucania. Its color is saffron-yellow, and it contains within it dim stars that gleam beneath a cloudy sky.

11. Hormesion is regarded as one of the most pleasing stones. It radiates with a fiery color and bears gold within it, while at its extremities it carries a white light.

[Col. 0580A]

1. Certain kinds of gems are named from the appearance of metals or stones.

2. [Note: [Col. 0579D] Chrysopis. Others also use this form. Pliny has *chrysophis*.] Chrysopis appears to be nothing but gold.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Glass

1. [Note: [Col. 0582D] Glass. See Pliny, book 36, chapter 26.] Glass is so called because it shines through with transparency to the eye. In other metals, whatever is contained inside is concealed; but in glass every liquid or object displays externally what it is like within, and, in a certain sense, what is enclosed is visible. Its origin was as follows. In that part of Syria called Phoenice, bordering on Judaea, near the foot of Mount Carmel, there is a marsh from which the river Belus arises. It flows for five thousand paces into the sea near Ptolemais. [Note: [Col. 0582D] “Whose sands are washed clean of impurities by the rushing current.” The meaning is plain: the rushing current washes the sands clean of impurities. There is no need to display ingenuity here, although Pliny expressed the same point somewhat differently.] Its sands are washed clean of impurities by the rushing current.

2. It is said that, when a ship carrying merchants’ soda put in there, the merchants prepared a meal scattered along the shore. Since there were no stones on which to set up their vessels, they placed lumps of soda from the ship underneath them. When these were ignited, the shore’s sand mixed with them, and streams of a transparent [Note: [Col. 0582D] “New liquid.” Others read “noble liquid.”] new liquid flowed forth. This was the origin of glass.

3. Soon, with human ingenuity and skill, the art was not content with soda alone [Note: [Col. 0582D] “But also worked at this art with other mixtures.” I agree with Chacon, who thought these additions adulterations.], but experimented with other mixtures as well. It is cooked with light, dry wood, with the addition of copper ore and soda, in continuous furnaces, as bronze is melted, and masses are formed. Later the material is melted again from these masses in workshops: some of it is shaped by blowing, some is worn down on a lathe, and some is engraved like silver. It is also colored in many ways, so that it imitates hyacinths, sapphires, green stones, and onyxes, or the colors of other gems. There is no other material [Col. 0583A] [Note: [Col. 0583D] “More suitable for mirrors.” Pliny has “more compliant.”] better suited to mirrors or more suitable for painting.

4. The greatest esteem, however, belongs to clear glass and to that which most closely resembles crystal. Hence glass displaced vessels of silver and gold for drinking. Formerly it was also made in Italy; throughout Gaul and Spain, very soft white sand was ground with a ball and millstone. Then it was mixed, by weight or measure, with three parts of soda and, after being melted, was poured into other furnaces. This was called ammonitrum; when reheated, it became pure, clear glass.

5. Obsidian stone is also counted among the varieties of glass. It is sometimes burning, sometimes black, and translucent when viewed through its thick surface, reflecting shadows like an image in wall mirrors. Many people make gems from it. They say that this stone is produced in India, in Italy, and by the Ocean in Spain.

6. [Note: [Col. 0583D] They report that this happened under Tiberius. See Pliny and Dio, book 57.] They report that, under Tiberius Caesar, a certain craftsman devised a method of tempering glass so that it would be flexible and ductile. When he had been admitted to Caesar, he handed Caesar a small glass vessel, which Caesar, enraged, threw onto the pavement. The craftsman then picked up the vessel from the pavement; it had folded in on itself like a bronze vessel. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Then he brought out a small hammer. Others read “hammer.”] He then brought a small hammer from his bosom and straightened the vessel. After this, Caesar said to the craftsman: “Does anyone else know this method of preparing glass?” When the man swore that no one else knew it, Caesar ordered him to be beheaded, lest, once this became known, gold should be considered mere clay and the value of all metals should be destroyed. And in truth, if glass vessels did not break, they would be better than gold [Col. 0583C] and silver.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Metals

1. The Greek word for metal is derived from ἀπὸ τοῦ μεταλλᾶν (*apo tou metallan*, “from mining”), because its nature is such that, wherever one vein appears, there is hope of searching for another. There are seven kinds of metal: gold, silver, bronze, electrum, tin, lead, and iron, which subdues them all.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Gold

1. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Gold from *aura*, “breeze” or “radiance.” From Servius, *Aeneid* 6, on the phrase “the varied radiance of gold.” Nevertheless, the Gothic manuscripts consistently have this wording in Virgil’s verse.] Gold is named from *aura*, that is, from radiance, [Col. 0584A] because it shines more brightly in reflected air. Hence Virgil also wrote:

> From there the varied radiance of gold flashed back through the branches,

that is, the splendor of gold. For it is natural that the brilliance of metals should shine more brightly when reflected by another light. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Hence also *aurarii* are so called, that is, “those who make the splendor shine forth.” These are Servius’s words in the same passage, except that he reads “the gilded and the favor”; but the same Servius, in the same book, on “Rejoicing in popular breezes,” says: “Breezes means favors, and hence *aurarii* are also called supporters.”] Hence *aurarii* are also so called, whose brilliance makes things splendid.

2. [Note: [Col. 0583D] Obryzum gold, so called because it shines brilliantly. It was enough to have noted this kind of etymology once. Perhaps Isidore took the opportunity from Jerome’s words on Jeremiah 10: “Among the Hebrews,” he says, “gold is called by seven names. One of them is *ophaz*, which we may render *obryzum*, so that it shines on the surface of idols.” And in his letter to Principia: “Ophir is a kind of gold named either from a place in India or from its color.”] Obryzum is called gold because it shines brilliantly. It is of the finest color; the Hebrews call it *ophax*, [Note: [Col. 0583D] The Greeks call it κιρρόν (*kirrhon*). This makes the spelling less doubtful. In the Gothic manuscripts of the Ovetus Collegium and in the Silian manuscript it is written in Latin letters as *ciaron*. The form is κιρρόν, meaning tawny or yellowish.] and the Greeks call it κιρρόν (*kirrhon*).

3.
