[Note: [Col. 0584D] *Bractea* … from ἀπὸ τοῦ βρέμεσθαι, which is an *onomatopoeia*—a word formed by imitation of a sound—“or from ἀπὸ τοῦ βράσσειν, which means ἠχεῖν, ‘to resound.’ Even though the manuscripts have distorted this reading, there is no reason to doubt it.”] A bractea is a very thin sheet, named ἀπὸ τοῦ βράχειν (*apo tou brachein*), which means ἠχεῖν (*echein*), “to resound,” that is, from rattling.

4. Money originally had both its property and its name from cattle. [Note: [Col. 0584D] Coins were cut and stamped from cattle hide. Cassiodorus, book 7 of the *Variae*: “Money was named from the hide of cattle.” In Gallic authorities the term was transferred to metals without any mark yet being attached to it. See Suidas, under Ἀσσάρια (*assaria*, “small coins”).] For coins were cut and stamped from cattle hide. Later Saturn invented the bronze coin; he himself established that coins should be stamped and inscribed. Therefore the treasury was also consecrated to Saturn by the pagans. Others, as stated above, derived *pecunia* from cattle, just as *jumenta* (“beasts of burden”) is derived from *juvare* (“to help”). [Note: [Col. 0584D] “All property among the ancients.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 1, on “Nor concern for the small estate.”] Among the ancients all property was called *peculium*, from cattle, in which their entire wealth consisted. Hence a wealthy person was called *pecuarius*, [Note: [Col. 0584D] “Now *pecuniosus*.” Jerome, on Ecclesiastes: “Cicero reports that those who possessed larger *peculia*, that is, herds, were originally called *pecuniosi*; for antiquity called them so. Gradually, however, through misuse, the name passed to something else.] whereas today he is called *pecuniosus*.

5. The most ancient peoples, before gold and silver had been discovered, used bronze. Bronze money was first in use, silver followed, and gold came afterward; but money retained the name from the material with which it began. Hence the treasury was called *aerarium*, because originally only bronze was in use, and only bronze was stored away, before gold and silver had been stamped. Although money was later made from those metals, the name *aerarium* remained from the metal with which it began.

6. *Thesaurus*, according to the Greek derivation, comes ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως (*apo tes theseos*), “from placing,” that is, from something stored away. For θέσις (*thesis*) means “placing,” and the word is compounded from Greek and Latin speech. The Greeks call something stored away θές (*thes*), while the Latins call it gold; joined together, the expression sounds like “stored gold.”

*Auraria* is named from gold.

7. [Note: [Col. 0584D] *Tributa*. Thus Varro, book 4.] *Tributa* are so called because formerly they were collected from each of the tribes, just as now they are collected from individual territories. [Note: [Col. 0584D] “Thus the Roman people were divided.” These are Servius’s words, *Aeneid* 5, on “Three squadrons in number,” and so forth.] It is established that the Roman people were divided into three parts, so that those who presided over each part were called tribunes. Hence the expenses that the people paid were called *tributa*.

8. *Vectigalia* are taxes, named from carrying.

*Stipendium* is named from a stake or contribution being weighed out. For the ancients were accustomed to weigh money rather than count it.

*Moneta* was so called because it warns that no fraud should occur in the metal or its weight.

9. [Note: [Col. 0585D] These statements are repeated below, chapter 24, because coins bear the names of rulers.] *Nomisma* is a solid gold, silver, or bronze coin. It is called *nomisma* because it was stamped with the names and likenesses of rulers. The first coin was called ἄργυρος (*argyros*), “silver,” because it was struck chiefly from silver.

10. [Note: [Col. 0585D] Coins named from Numa. From Epiphanius, *On Weights*; Suidas also reports the same under Ἀσσάρια (*assaria*, “small coins”), from Suetonius.] Coins were called *nummi* after Numa, king of the Romans, who first marked them among the Latins with images and inscribed them with the title of his own name.

11. *Folles* are named from the pouch in which they are stored, the container being named for what it contains.

12. Three things are sought in a coin: metal, design, and weight. If any one of these is lacking, it will not be a coin.

13. There are three kinds of silver, gold, and bronze: stamped, worked, and unworked. Stamped is what is found in coins; worked is what is found in vessels and statues; unworked is what is found in masses, [Note: [Col. 0585D] Which is also called *grave*, that is, “mass.” *Aeneid* 6, on “A youth remarkable in form,” and so forth.] which is also called *grave*, that is, a mass.

Metals came to be known in the following way. [Note: [Col. 0585D] From “For whenever forests burn for whatever reason” through the end of the chapter, the whole passage is modeled on Lucretius, book 5: “Whatever it is, that is, from whatever cause the flame’s heat with dreadful sound,” and so forth.] Whenever, for whatever reason, burning forests melted the earth, the heated veins poured out streams [Note: [Col. 0585D] “Of whatever kind of mass.” So Virgil, *Aeneid* 7, uses *stricturas chalybum* (“masses of steel”). As Servius says there, a *strictura* is earth or ore of iron compressed into a mass.] of whatever kind of material.

14. Whether, therefore, that material had been bronze or gold, when it flowed down into the lower places of the earth, it took the shape formed for it either by the flowing stream or by the hollow that received it. Captivated by the brilliance of these things, people lifted the masses after binding them together. They saw in them impressions of the earth’s forms, and from this they conceived that melted substances could be brought into every shape.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Silver

1. *Argentum* is not far removed from the Greek name. For the Greeks call it ἄργυρον (*argyron*). [Note: [Col. 0585D] It possesses this remarkable property. Pliny and Augustine, *City of God*, book 21, chapter 7, mention it.] Although it is white, when pressed against the body it leaves black lines.

2. Quicksilver is so called because it slips out of the materials into which it is poured; it is also called liquid because it runs. [Col. 0586A] It is found especially in mines, clinging in drops that have congealed over the roofs of silver-working furnaces; often also in very old sewage, or in the mud of wells. It is also made from cinnabar placed in a small iron dish, with an earthen vessel set over it. After the vessel has been sealed around, coals are placed around it, and thus quicksilver distills from the cinnabar. [Note: [Col. 0585D] “Without this neither silver nor …” Vitruvius, book 7, chapter 8.] Without it neither silver nor bronze can be gilded.

3. It has such power that, if a hundred-pound stone is placed upon a sextarius of quicksilver, it immediately resists the weight. But if a scruple of gold is placed upon it, it quickly receives the lightness of the gold into its hollow, from which it is understood that it yields not to weight but to nature. It is best preserved in glass vessels, for it perforates other materials. [Note: [Col. 0586D] “When given as a drink, it kills because of its weight.” From Dioscorides.] When given as a drink, it kills because of its weight.

4. The refuse of silver is called λιθάργυρος (*lithargyros*), which we call silver foam. It is made from silver and lead.

## CHAPTER XX. On Bronze

1. Bronze is named from the brilliance of bronze, just as gold and silver are. [Note: [Col. 0586D] “Among the ancients the use of bronze came first.” Lucretius, book 5:

> The use of bronze was known before that of iron.

From this point through “and what had been valued is held in no honor,” the passage is from Lucretius. The remainder of this chapter is from Pliny, book 3.] Among the ancients the use of bronze was known before that of iron. With bronze they first plowed the earth; with bronze they fought the battles of war, and bronze was more highly valued. Gold and silver, on the other hand, were rejected because they were useless. Now the reverse has happened: bronze lies neglected, while gold has risen to the highest honor. Thus rolling time changes the seasons of things, and what was once valued is finally held in no honor. [Note: [Col. 0586D] “The use of bronze.” From Pliny, chapter 3 and following, through chapter 9; most of the wording here comes from that source.] Later the use of bronze passed to statues, vessels, and the structures of buildings; above all, for the preservation of monuments, even public decrees were written on bronze tablets.

2. [Note: [Col. 0586D] Cyprian bronze. From chapters 2, 4, and 10.] Cyprian bronze was first discovered on the island of Cyprus, from which it received its name. It is made from a corroded stone, which they call *cadmia*, and it is ductile. If lead is added to it, it becomes purple in color.

3. [Note: [Col. 0586D] Orichalcum, which possesses both the brilliance of gold and the hardness of bronze. These are Servius’s words, *Aeneid* 12, on “He himself thereafter in gold.” For its etymology, see Festus.] Orichalcum is so called because it possesses both the brilliance of gold and the hardness of bronze. Its name is compounded from Latin and Greek. For bronze is called χαλκός (*chalkos*) in Greek. [Note: [Col. 0586D] “It is made from bronze, and so forth.” The source of this medicinal preparation should be investigated; these words are not from Pliny.] It is made from bronze and much fire, and by chemical treatments it is brought to a golden color.

4. Corinthian bronze is a mixture of all metals, which chance first mixed at Corinth when the city was captured and burned. [Note: [Col. 0586D] “For when Hannibal … captured this city.” A mnemonic error. Hannibal did not capture Corinth; the consul Gaius Mummius did, in the year 608 from the founding of the City.] For when Hannibal had captured this city, [Col. 0587A] he piled all the bronze, gold, and silver statues into a single pyre and burned them. From this mixture craftsmen took the material and made serving dishes. Thus Corinthian bronze arose from all metals combined into one, being neither this nor that. Hence, to this day, whether made from the original material or in imitation of it, it is called Corinthian bronze, or Corinthian vessels. There are three kinds: one is white and approaches the brilliance of silver; another has the tawny nature of gold; and the third has an equal balance of all the metals.

5. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Coronarium, regulare … pyropum … Campanian. From chapter 8.] Coronarium bronze is thinned from ductile bronze into sheets and, when dyed with bull’s gall, provides the appearance of gold on the crowns of actors; hence its name.

6. Pyropum is named from its fiery color. For when six scruples of gold are added to each ounce of bronze, the very thin sheet glows and imitates flames; hence it is called *pyropum*.

7. Regular bronze is what others call ductile bronze, such as all Cyprian bronze is.

8. Ductile bronze is so called because it is extended by a hammer, whereas cast bronze is only melted. The latter is also called *caldarium*, because it is only melted. It is fragile under hammers. Indeed, all bronze becomes regular bronze when its impurities have been carefully purified and burned out by fire.

9. Campanian bronze is also called by the name of the province of Campania, which is in Italy. It is highly valued for all tools and vessels.

10. [Note: [Col. 0587D] All bronze is better cast in severe cold. From chapter 9.] All bronze is better cast in very cold weather. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Bronze draws rust more quickly. Pliny says: “Cleaned bronzes draw rust more quickly than neglected ones unless they are smeared with oil,” and so forth. Something therefore seems to be missing here.] Bronze draws rust more quickly unless it is smeared with oil; they say that it is best preserved in liquid pitch.

[Col. 0587C] 11. Among all metals, bronze is the most resonant and the most powerful. Hence bronze thresholds, and Virgil’s line:

> The hinge groaned on bronze doors.

The impurities of bronze are *cadmia* and *chalcitis*. Cadmia is bronze rust; chalcitis is the flower or bloom of bronze.

12. Cadmia is produced in the furnaces of bronze and silver mines, settling upon them as a fume. Just as the stone from which bronze is made is called *cadmia*, so the substance arises again in the furnaces and receives the origin of its name.

13. The bloom of bronze is made or produced in the smelting process when the bronze has been melted and separated, with cold water poured over it. For through sudden thickening the bloom is restored, as though from spittle.

14. [Note: [Col. 0587D] It also produces verdigris. For bronze plates … This concerns white lead in Pliny, chapter 18.] Bronze also produces verdigris. Bronze plates are placed over a vessel of the sharpest vinegar on sprigs, [Note: [Col. 0587D] “And thus dripping.” Others read “while dripping.”] and whatever falls from them [Col. 0587D] into the vinegar itself is ground and sifted.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Iron

[Col. 0588A]

1. Iron is so called because it conceals *farra*, that is, the seeds of grain, in the earth. It is also called steel from the river Chalybes, where iron is tempered to produce the finest edge. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Hence, by an abusive extension, and so forth. From Servius, *Georgics* 1, on “But the naked Chalybes iron.”] Hence the material itself is also improperly called steel, as in “the wound-dealing steel.”

2. [Note: [Col. 0587D] The use of iron was discovered after the other metals. Lucretius:

> Then, little by little, the iron sword advanced,

> and the bronze sickle’s form was turned to shame.

] The use of iron was discovered after the other metals. Its appearance was later turned to shame. For from the material with which the earth was once worked, blood is now poured. No body has elements so densely joined, clinging, and intertwined as iron; hence it possesses hardness together with coldness. [Note: [Col. 0588D] “The metal of iron is found almost everywhere.” From Pliny, book 34, chapter 14, from which most of what follows is taken.] Iron ore is found almost everywhere, but among all its varieties the highest place is given to Seric iron. For the Seres send it along with their garments and hides. Parthian iron is second; no other kinds of iron are tempered to a pure edge. [Note: [Col. 0588D] For in the other kinds a softer mixture is added. The passage of Pliny should likewise be punctuated in this way.] For in the other kinds a softer mixture is added.

3. The varieties of iron are very numerous according to the nature of the soil. For one kind is soft and nearly like lead, suitable for making wheels and nails; another is brittle and bronzy, suitable for working the soil; another is valued only for its shortness and for shoemaker’s nails; another contracts rust more quickly. [Note: [Col. 0588D] Suitable for working the soil. Whether Isidore added this from Pliny, or someone else added it to Isidore, I would not say.] All these are called *stricturae*, a fitting name derived from *stringere* (“to draw tight”), a term not used of other metals. [Note: [Col. 0588D] The name is aptly imposed from *astringere* (“to bind tight”). Thus all the books. Pliny has “from the sharpening of the edge.” Let others decide which should be restored from the other. The reading of the Isidorian manuscripts does not displease me. Servius, *Aeneid* 8: “A *strictura* is iron-earth compressed into a mass.” Nothing about an edge.] The greatest difference, however, lies in the waters into which red-hot iron is plunged, so that it may become more useful—such as those at Bilbilis and Tirasone in Spain, and at Como in Italy. [Note: [Col. 0588D] “As at Bilbilis.” Something appears to be lacking. See Pliny.]

4. In sharpening iron, oil gives a more pleasing edge; hence it is customary to quench thinner iron tools in oil, lest water harden them into brittleness. [Note: [Col. 0588D] “More delicate in oil.” Thus all the books; Pliny has “more delicate.”] Iron takes vengeance upon human blood: for, upon contact, it draws rust more quickly. [Note: [Col. 0588D] “Iron takes vengeance upon human blood.” These are Pliny’s words.] The lodestone has an affinity with iron. For this substance alone receives power from that stone and retains it for a long time. From the same stone a certain architect vaulted a temple at Alexandria, so that within it a statue appeared to hang in the air by means of iron. [Note: [Col. 0588D] Iron heated red-hot. From chapter 15.]

Iron heated by fire is ruined unless it is hardened by repeated blows. When red, it is not suitable for hammering, nor is it so before it begins to turn white. Iron smeared with vinegar or alum becomes like bronze.

5. [294] The impurities of iron are rust and slag.

Rust is a defect that eats away iron itself—or crops, as though *rodigo* (“gnawing”) had been altered by one letter. This is also called *aerugo*, from *erodere* (“to eat away”). For *aerugo* is a defect of iron, named from *erodere*, not from *aes* (“bronze”).

[Col. 0589A] 6. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Slag. From Jerome, on Ezekiel 22.] Slag is the waste and dross that are smelted out by fire. It is called *scoria* because it is beaten out of iron.

7. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Iron is free from rust, etc. From Pliny, in the same place.] Iron is free from rust if it is coated with white lead, gypsum, and liquid pitch. Likewise, rust does not damage iron tools if they are coated with deer marrow, or with white lead mixed with rose oil.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Lead

1. Lead (*plumbum*) is so called because the depth of the sea was first tested with it after balls had first been made from it. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Its kinds are black, etc. From Pliny, 34.16.]

There are two kinds of it, black and white; the white is the better, and was first discovered in the islands of the Atlantic Ocean. It is also produced in Lusitania and Galicia, at the surface of the earth, in sandy soil, black in color and heavy in weight. Small stones are mixed with it, especially when the streams have dried up. The sands are washed, and what settles is smelted in furnaces. Black, heavy stones are also found in gold mines when water is introduced; while the gold is collected, they remain with it, and afterward, once separated, they are melted and transformed into white lead. Hence lead has the same heaviness as gold.

2. Black lead is abundant around Cantabria, and has a twofold origin. For it either emerges alone from its own vein, or is produced together with silver and is smelted from mixed veins. Its first liquid in the furnaces is tin; the second is silver; what remains, after an additional vein has been placed upon it and it has been melted again, becomes black lead.

3. [Note: [Col. 0589D] India has neither lead, etc. From chapter 17.] India possesses neither lead nor bronze; it exchanges only gems and pearls. We use black lead for pipes and sheets. Lead is extracted with greater difficulty in Spain and Gaul; in Britain it lies just beneath the surface of the earth.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Tin

1. The etymology of *stannum* (“tin”) is ἀποχωρίζων (*apochōrizōn*), that is, “separating” and “distinguishing.” For when metals are mixed and adulterated with one another, it separates them through fire and distinguishes bronze and lead from gold and silver. It also protects other metals from the fire; and although bronze and iron are by nature extremely hard, without tin they are burned and consumed.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] The etymology of *stannum* … is derived from Jerome, on Zechariah 4. The entire passage has been composed from Jerome’s words; for the etymology, it is enough to report the following: “The stone”—that is, the mass—which among the Hebrews is written as meaning “tin,” is etymologically interpreted as ἀποχωρίζων, that is, “separating” and “distinguishing,” so that, just as tin separates mixed and adulterated [metals], and so forth.]

2. Tin spread over bronze vessels makes their flavor more agreeable and restrains the poisonous effect of verdigris. Mirrors are also prepared from it. White lead is made from it as well as from lead.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Electrum

1. It is called *electrum* because, in the sun’s rays, it shines more brightly than gold and silver. [Note: [Col. 0589D] The sun is called *elector* by the poets. From Pliny, 37.2.] For the sun is called *elector* by the poets. [Note: [Col. 0589D] This metal is more purified than the others. From Servius, *Georgics* 3, on “Purer than electrum.”] For this metal is more purified than all other metals.

2. [Note: [Col. 0589D] There are three kinds of it. From the same source, *Aeneid* 7, on the passage “which is made.” We leave the examination of Servius’s words to others.]

There are three kinds. One flows from pine trees and is called amber; another is a metal found naturally and held in esteem; the third is made from three parts of gold and one part of silver. Even if you dissolve the natural kind, you will find these same proportions. Hence it makes no difference whether it is naturally formed or manufactured, for both are of the same nature.

3. [Note: [Col. 0590D] Natural electrum, etc. From Pliny, 33.4.] Natural electrum is of such a nature that at a banquet and by lamplight it shines more brightly than all other metals and reveals poison. For if poison is poured into it, it gives off a hissing sound and emits various colors like a rainbow.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Weights

1. [Note: [Col. 0590D] It is useful to know weights and measures. Rhemnius Palaemon:

“It is useful to know the weights recalled in the ancient books of Paeonia.”]

It is useful to know the system of weights and measures. For all corporeal things, as it is written, from the highest to the lowest, have been ordered and formed by measure, number, and weight. [Note: [Col. 0590D] Weight has been given to all corporeal things. Palaemon:

“Nature has assigned weight to corporeal things; weight governs all the elements.”]

For nature has given weight to all corporeal things. Weight also governs everything according to its proper measure.

2. Moses was the first—preceding all the pagan philosophers in time—to describe measures, numbers, and weight for us in various passages of his Scripture. [Note: [Col. 0590D] Phidon was the first. From Eusebius, *Chronicle*. Strabo likewise reports from Ephorus that the stamping of silver began with Phidon.]

Phidon of Argos was the first to establish a system of weights in Greece. Although others may have existed earlier, he was more experienced in this art.

3. A weight (*pondus*) is so called because, when balanced on a scale, it hangs (*pendeat*); hence also *pensum*. In an extended sense, a *pondus* is one pound. From this also comes *dipondium*, as though “two weights,” a name that remains in use to this day.

4. A balance (*trutina*) is a pair of pans for weights, hanging with equal equilibrium, made for weighing talents [Note: [Col. 0590D] and hundred-pound weights. Vitruvius uses the word in book 7, chapter 8: “If a hundred-pound stone is placed upon it”; and Pliny, book 7, chapter 20: “Salvius carried two hundred-pound weights with his feet, as many with his hands, and two two-hundred-pound weights on his shoulders against the stairs.” Many such hundred-pound stones remain at Rome, made of the hardest flint, some even inscribed with very ancient letters. In *On Agriculture*, chapter 13, he calls this a *centumpondium*, in these words: “One uncertain hundredweight, and definite weights,” unless you prefer to read *incretum* and *creta* with Chacon, so that *incretum* means “undivided,” as in Festus.]

and hundred-pound weights, just as the *momentana* is used for small and modest sums of money. This is also called a *moneta*. It likewise bears the name *statera*, derived from number, because it consists of two pans and one central rod, balanced so that it stands evenly.

[Col. 0591A] 5. [Note: [Col. 0591C] The *examen* is a thread. From Servius, *Aeneid* 12: “Jupiter himself, with the balance made equal.”]

The *examen* is the central thread by which the balance of the scales is controlled and the pans are made equal. Hence the strap or cord on the pans is also called an *amentum*.

6. The *campana* takes its name from a region of Italy, where its use was first discovered. It does not have two pans; rather, it is a marked rod, graduated in pounds and ounces, and measures by a movable weight.

7. Every weight has a fixed amount, designated by proper names.

8. [Note: [Col. 0591C] The *chalcus* is the smallest part of a weight. It is one-eighth of an obol according to Pollux, book 9, and Cleopatra in the surviving fragment; one-tenth according to Pliny, book 21, at the end; one-sixth according to Diodorus in the *Suda*; and one-third according to Dioscorides. It therefore appears that *chalcus* denoted weights of different sizes.]

The *chalcus* is the smallest part of a weight, one-quarter of an obol, consisting of two grains of lentil weight. It is called *chalcus* because it is tiny, like a small stone (*calculus*), which is so small that it can be stepped on without discomfort.

9. The *siliqua* is one twenty-fourth of a solidus, taking its name from the seed of a tree.

10. The *ceratum* is half an obol, containing one and a half siliquae. Latin calls it a *semiobolus*. The Greek word *ceratum* is translated into Latin as “little horn.”

11. An obol weighs three siliquae and contains two *ceratia* and four *chalci*. In ancient times it was made of bronze in the shape of an arrow. Hence it received its name from the Greeks, meaning “arrow.”

12. [Note: [Col. 0591D] *Scripulus*. This is the reading of the better books; *scripulum*, *scriptulum*, and *scribulum* are found in the oldest manuscripts of other authors, so that the word appears to be derived from *scribere* (“to write”), by analogy with the Greek word γράμμα (*gramma*).]

The *scripulus* consists of the weight of six siliquae. Among the Greeks it is called a *gramma*. *Scripulus* is formed as a diminutive from a small stone, called a *scrupus*.

13. [Note: [Col. 0591D] The drachma … consisting of three *scripuli*. Fannius:

“Among learned Athenians, the silver coin is readily designated by the weight of three scripuli, a drachma.”]

The drachma is one-eighth of an ounce and is the weight of the denarius, a silver coin consisting of three scripuli, that is, eighteen siliquae. The denarius is so called from *dare* (“to give”), because it is counted as ten coins.

14. [Col. 0591C] The solidus is so called because nothing seems to be lacking from it. For the ancients called what was complete and whole *solidum*. It is also called a *nomisma*, because it is marked with the names and images of emperors. [Note: [Col. 0591D] At the beginning it had one form. From Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*.]

At first, one *nomisma* was one silver coin. This originated with the Assyrians. The Jews say that Abraham was the first to bring this form into the land of Canaan.

Among the Latins, the solidus is also called a *sextula*, because six of these make an ounce. [Note: [Col. 0591D] *Sextula* … because six of these make an ounce. Fannius:

“The so-called sextula, for six of these constitute an ounce.”]

As we have said, the common people call it a gold solidus. [Note: [Col. 0591D] The common people call it a gold solidus. Not only the common people, but Apuleius as well, book 10: “And offering one hundred gold solidi as the price.”]

They therefore called one-third of it a *tremissis*, because, when sent three times, it makes a solidus.

15. [Note: [Col. 0591D] Twice taking a sextula makes a *duella*. Fannius:

“When a sextula is doubled, the ancients called it a duella.”]

A sextula taken twice makes a *duella*; taken three times, it produces a *stater*.

16. A stater is half an ounce, weighing three gold solidi; hence it is called a stater, because it equals three solidi. It is also a *semiounce*, because it contains half an ounce. It is also a *semissis*, because it is half a weight, as it were half an *as*.

17. [Col. 0592B] The Hebrews likewise call the quadrant a *codrant*. [Note: [Col. 0592C] The Hebrews similarly call the quadrant a *codrant*. Jerome appears to have intended this in his *Hebrew Names*, under Matthew. Yet Jerome often pretends ignorance of what he knows in that book, as Isidore does here. He interpreted Greek and Latin words as though they were Hebrew.]

It is called a quadrant because it weighs one-quarter of an ounce. [Note: [Col. 0592C] It is called a quadrant because it is one-quarter of an ounce. Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*: “The shekel, which is also called a quadrant, is one-quarter of an ounce, containing half a stater and two drachmas.” But the Greek writer was misled by the Latin word and thereby caused Isidore to fall into the same error. A quadrant is not one-quarter of an ounce but one-quarter of an *as*. Nor can Isidore take refuge in saying that asses were made ounce-weight, for, according to Pliny, they were made half-ounce pieces and thereafter remained in that condition, as we also see in those that now exist in immense numbers.]

18. [Note: [Col. 0592D] The shekel … the weight of an ounce. These are indeed Jerome’s words in his *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 23. Yet, apart from Josephus—who in book 3, chapter 9 of the *Antiquities* states that the shekel weighs four Attic drachmas, that is, half an ounce—Jerome himself, forgetting what he had written, says in *Ezekiel* 4: “The shekel, that is, the stater, contains four drachmas, while eight drachmas make a Latin ounce.” It is surprising that Isidore did not notice this.]

The *sikel*, which in Latin is corruptly called *siclus*, is a Hebrew name and among them has the weight of an ounce. [Note: [Col. 0592D] Among the Latins and Greeks. From Epiphanius.]

Among the Latins and Greeks, however, it is one-quarter of an ounce and half a stater, weighing two drachmas. Hence, when “shekel” is read in the divine Scriptures, it means an ounce; but in pagan authors it means one-quarter of an ounce.

19. The ounce is so called because by its unity it binds together—that is, comprises—the whole of the smaller weights. [Note: [Col. 0592D] It consists of eight drachmas … the year in months. Fannius:

“An ounce is made of twice four drachmas; hence it should be thought that they are called *grammata*, because an ounce contains twenty-four of them. Our speech is marked by that many forms, as many hours as the world completes through night and day; and the ounce is the portion of a pound that corresponds to the months of the year.”]

It consists of eight drachmas, that is, twenty-four scripuli. It is therefore regarded as a legitimate weight because the number of its scripuli measures the hours of day and night, or because, counted twelve times, it makes a pound.

20. A pound is completed by twelve ounces, and thus constitutes a perfect kind of weight, because it contains as many ounces as the year has months. It is called a pound (*libra*) because it is “free” (*libera*) and encloses within itself all the weights mentioned above.

21. The *mna* weighs one hundred drachmas in the system of weights and is a Greek name. [Note: [Col. 0593C] Which amount to siliquae, etc. So most Gothic manuscripts read, although this total is absent from some.]

These are 8,400 siliquae, 225 tremisses, 75 solidi, and 25 staters.

22. [Note: [Col. 0593C] The talent is said to be the greatest weight. The same author, in “On the Talent”:

“What is declared by the learned to be the greatest weight at Athens; for nothing is smaller than an obol, nor anything greater than a talent.”]

Among the Greeks the talent is said to be the greatest weight; for nothing is smaller than a chalcus, and nothing greater than a talent. [Note: [Col. 0593C] Its amount varies among different peoples. Servius, *Aeneid* 5, on “talents of silver and gold,” says: “According to different peoples, the talent is a different weight; but among the Romans a talent is seventy pounds, as Plautus shows in the *Mostellaria*, where he says that two talents are one hundred forty pounds. But Chacon is correct in my judgment: ‘If a talent contains six thousand drachmas, as Fannius asserts, while a pound contains ninety-six drachmas, it follows plainly that a talent weighs only sixty-two Roman pounds, not seventy, as Servius has it; nor does the passage of Plautus suggest otherwise.’ Therefore, since Isidore’s manuscripts consistently have sixty-two pounds and one hundred forty-four pounds, I do not doubt that here, according to the opinion of that most learned man, one must read sixty-two and one hundred twenty-four, and that Servius wrote likewise; for we believe that, through the error of copyists, seventy and forty entered in place of sixty and twenty.]

Its weight varies among different peoples. Among the Romans a talent is seventy-two pounds, as Plautus shows, saying that two talents are one hundred forty-four pounds. It is of three kinds: lesser, middle, and greatest. The lesser consists of fifty, [Note: [Col. 0593D] The middle consists of seventy-two. I write sixty-two.] the middle of seventy-two pounds, [Note: [Col. 0593D] The greatest consists of one hundred twenty. Vitruvius discusses this in book 10, chapter 21, when he says: “Having the weight of a talent of four thousand, which amounts to four hundred eighty thousand pounds.”] and the greatest of one hundred twenty.

23. A hundredweight is a name derived from the number, because it is a weight of one hundred pounds. The Romans established this weight because of the completeness of the number one hundred.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Measures

1. A measure is some object bounded by its proper extent or by time. It is either a measure of body or of time. The measure of a body includes the length or shortness of human beings, pieces of wood, and columns. Geometers also dare to investigate the fact that the sun itself has the proper measure of its orbit. Measures of time include hours, days, and years. [Note: [Col. 0593D] Hence we also speak of measuring the feet of the hours. See Palladius, at the end of each month.]

Hence we also say “to measure the feet of the hours,” that is, to measure.

2. Properly, however, *mensura* (“measure”) is so called because by it crops and grain are measured—that is, wet and dry commodities—such as the modius, artaba, urn, and amphora.

3. The smallest part of measures is the spoon, which is half a drachma, weighing nine siliquae; three of these make a *choncula*.

[Col. 0593C] A *choncula* is filled by one and a half drachmas.

4. A *cyathus* weighs ten drachmas. [Note: [Col. 0593D] It is also called *cuatus* by some. Others read *casatus*, *caulacus*, or *causatus*. The Arabs call this measure *cuatum*. Chacon does not approve *cuatum*, but thinks it was taken from the margin; I pay no attention to Rabanus.]

It is also called *cuatus* by some.

[Col. 0594A] An *oxybaphus* is made when five drachmas are added to ten.

5. [Note: [Col. 0594C] An acetabulum weighs fifteen drachmas. So Pliny says. Isidore’s books have twelve drachmas, an error arising from the similarity of the symbols and η. Rhemnius, on the cyathus:

“Twice five drachmas make this, if you try to weigh it; an oxybaphus will result if five are added to those.”]

An acetabulum is one-quarter of a hemina, weighing twelve drachmas.

[Note: [Col. 0594C] The cotyla … containing six cyathi. Rhemnius:

“But a cotyla receives twice three cyathi in all.”]

A *cotula* is a hemina containing six cyathi. It is called *cotula* because in Greek *cote* means “a cut” or “incision”; and a hemina, being one-half of a sextarius, is divided into two equal parts and makes a cotula. [Note: [Col. 0594C] A hemina is half a sextarius. The same author:

“But the cotylas, which, if you prefer, may be called heminas, one sextarius receives two; taken four times, it becomes, in Greek, a choenix.” And Epiphanius: “The cotyla is half a sextarius; it is called cotyla because the sextarius is cut into two parts.”]

A hemina weighs one pound; doubled, it makes a sextarius.

6. A sextarius is two pounds. Taken twice, it is called a *bilibris*; taken four times, it becomes, in Greek, a *choenix*. [Note: [Col. 0594D] When multiplied fivefold, it makes a *quinar* or *gomor*. Since shortly afterward the *gomor* is said to be fifteen modii, while a modius contains sixteen sextarii—or, according to Isidore in this chapter, twenty-two— I do not see how Isidore’s figures agree. But we know that the finishing hand is absent from these books, and it is clear at nearly every other word that an enormous amount of extraneous material has been added to them.]

Multiplied fivefold, it makes a *quinar*, or *gomor*. Add a sixth, and it yields a *congius*. [Note: [Col. 0594D] For a congius measures six sextarii. Thus below: “because it measures five modii,” he speaks loosely; likewise the jurist, chapter 35, final section, and chapter 36 of *On Buying and Selling* and *On Letting*.]

For a congius measures six sextarii, and from it they also derived the name *sextarius*. [Note: [Col. 0594D] From which the name *sextarius* was also derived. Rhemnius:

“I would believe that the ancients derived the name of sextarius from it.”]

7. A congius is so called from *congiere* (“to grow together”), that is, from increasing by addition. Hence, when money later began to be distributed as a benefit, it was called a *congiarium*. Each emperor, seeking to win the favor of the people in his own time, added something so that he might appear more generous in his gifts.

8. [Note: [Col. 0594D] A congiarium is specifically … From Epiphanius, where it is corruptly read “among the Hebrews.”]

A *congiarium* is specifically a measure of liquids. We find that both the object and the name were assigned by the Romans.

9. A *metreta* is a measure of liquids. It derives its name from a measure, for the Greeks call a measure μέτρον (*metron*), and from this it is called *metreta*. Although an urn, amphora, and other such terms are also names of measures, this one has taken its name from the perfection of the number ten.

A *metron* applies to every kind of measure: μέτρον (*metron*) is Greek for “measure” in Latin. A cyathus is a measure, an amphora is a measure, and anything that holds more or less is a measure. But this term has specially appropriated the name to itself because it is a measure of a perfect number, namely ten.

10. [Note: [Col. 0595D] The modius … is kept. Everything is from Epiphanius.]

The *modius* is so called because it is complete according to its own measure. It is a measure of forty-four pounds, that is, twenty-two sextarii. The reason for this number is drawn from the fact that at the beginning God performed twenty-two works. On the first day he made seven works: formless matter, angels, light, the higher heavens, earth, water, and air. On the second day, the firmament alone. On the third day, four: seas, seeds, sowings, and plantations. On the fourth day, three: the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day, three: fish, reptiles of the waters, and birds. On the sixth day, four: wild beasts, cattle, reptiles of the earth, and human beings. Thus all twenty-two kinds were made in six days.

There are also twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob, from whose seed the entire nation of Israel was born; twenty-two books of the Old Testament, up to Esther; and twenty-two letters, the elements from which the teaching of the divine law is composed. On the basis of these examples, the modius was established by Moses, according to the measure of the sacred law, as twenty-two sextarii. Although different peoples ignorantly add to or subtract from the weight of this measure, among the Hebrews it is preserved by divine ordinance according to this principle.

For *modius* is derived from *modus* (“measure”). Hence *modica*, that is, “moderate.” The word *modius* was imposed on things that are moderate. We use *modica* for small things in an extended, not a proper, sense.

11. [Note: [Col. 0595D] The *satum* is a kind of measure … containing. From Jerome, on Matthew 13.]

A *satum* is a kind of measure which, according to the custom of the province of Palestine, contains one and a half modii. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Its name is derived from Hebrew, etc. This note and what follows to the end of the chapter are from Epiphanius. If there is any fault in them, we do not accept responsibility for it; nevertheless, in view of so great an authority, we consider Isidore sufficiently protected.]

Its name is derived from the Hebrew language. Among them *satum* means “taking” or “lifting,” because the person who measures it takes up and lifts that same measure. There is also another *satum*, capable of holding twenty-two sextarii, like a modius.

12. A *bathus* is called by the Hebrew term derived from an olive mill, which among them is called *bath* or *batha*. It holds fifty sextarii, the amount that is crushed in one turn of the mill.

13. An amphora is so called because it is lifted from both sides. In Greek it is said to have received its name from its shape, because its two handles appear to imitate ears. It holds a square foot of wine or water, but three Italian modii of grain.

A *cadus* is a Greek amphora containing three urns.

14. An urn is a measure which some call a *quartarius*. Properly, however, an urn is a vessel ordinarily used for storing the ashes of the dead, concerning which the poet says:

> He is covered by the sky who has no urn.

15. A *medimna* is a measure of five modii. In Latin it is called *medimna*, that is, “half,” because it measures five modii, which is half the complete number ten.

16. An *artaba* is an Egyptian measure of seventy-two sextarii—a composite number, corresponding to the seventy-two nations, or languages, that filled the world.

17. A *gomor* weighs a burden of fifteen modii.

A *corus* is filled by thirty modii. It derives from the Hebrew language and is called *cora*, from its resemblance to a hill. For in Hebrew *cora* means “hills.” Thirty modii heaped together appear like a hill and make a camel’s load.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Symbols

1. The symbols of weights are unknown to most people and therefore cause readers to err. We shall accordingly set out their forms and characters, as they were marked by the ancients.

2. The letter Z signifies half an obol.

A single horizontal stroke signifies an obol.

A doubled stroke signifies two obols.

The Latin T signifies three obols.

The Latin F signifies four obols.

The Latin E signifies five obols.

3. Six obols have no character, because six make one drachma, which is the weight of a silver denarius.

The letter H signifies eight siliquae, that is, a tremissis.

The Latin N signifies the Greek *nomisma*, that is, a solidus.

[Col. 0596C] IB. An iota added to beta signifies half a solidus.

4. Two strokes diverging from one angle, from left to right, signify a drachma, which they also call a *holce*.

A Latin N joined to a Greek gamma signifies a half-ounce.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] As for gamma, the notation in the Neapolitan manuscript is not displeasing.] A Greek gamma with a Latin o added at its end signifies an ounce.

A Greek lambda with a Latin i added through its middle signifies a pound.

5. Κυ. A Greek kappa, with a Greek upsilon added near the end of its horns, signifies a cyathus.

308 Κo. If it has a Latin o added, it indicates a hemina, which the Greeks call a cotyle.

A Greek character omitted in the supplied text, if joined to a Latin e, signifies a sextarius.

6. [Note: [Col. 0596D] If it has a Latin o added, Paulus adds not o but upsilon.] A symbol omitted in the supplied text, if it has a Latin o added, indicates an acetabulum, which the Greeks call an oxybaphon.

A Greek character omitted in the supplied text, with a Latin n placed above it, signifies a mna.

[Col. 0597A] [Note: [Col. 0597A] A Latin T at the end has a Greek lambda. The form and definition of this symbol make us prefer the symbol for the ounce found in the Neapolitan manuscript.] A Latin T having a Greek lambda at its end signifies a talent.

[Col. 0598A] [Note: [Col. 0598A] Greek Xo; or rather Greek XV. For this is how a choenix is customarily marked.] A Greek Xo, with the letter o joined to its upper right arm, is a choenix.

# BOOK XVII. ON AGRICULTURAL MATTERS

[Col. 0597]

## CHAPTER I. On writers on agriculture

[Col. 0597A]

1. [Note: [Col. 0597C] “The art of writing on agriculture … embraced.” This is drawn almost entirely from Columella, book 1, chapter 1.] Hesiod of Boeotia was the first among the Greeks to contribute the skill of writing on agricultural matters to human learning. Democritus followed; [Note: [Col. 0597C] Mago of Carthage also wrote on agriculture in twenty-eight books. Thus Varro, book 1, *On Agriculture*, chapter 1.] Mago of Carthage also composed a treatise on farming in twenty-eight volumes. Among the Romans, Cato was the first to establish writing on agriculture; Marcus Terentius then polished it, and Virgil soon exalted it by the praise of poetry. [Col. 0597B] [Note: [Col. 0597C] “They deserved no less praise.” Columella: “They earned no smaller praise.”] Cornelius Celsus and [Note: [Col. 0597C] Julius Atticus, who wrote only on vines; Pliny mentions him in books 15 and 17.] Julius Atticus later devoted no less effort to it; [Note: [Col. 0597C] Aemilianus: Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a man of high rank.] Aemilianus, [Note: [Col. 0597D] “Or Columella”: in his usual manner he used a disjunction in place of a conjunction.] or the distinguished orator Columella, who embraced the whole body of this discipline.

2. [Note: [Col. 0597D] “They relate that a certain private man, struck by lightning, was the first to yoke oxen to a plough.” From Augustine, *City of God* 18.6.] They relate that a certain private man, struck by lightning, named Homogyrus, was the first to yoke oxen to a plough. [Note: [Col. 0597D] Some say Osiris, others Triptolemus. From Servius, *Georgics* 1: “And the boy who showed the curved plough.”] Some say that Osiris was the inventor of this art; others, Triptolemus. [Note: [Col. 0597D] “Here too there is a question.” From the same source, on “Ceres first brought iron.”] Here too there is a question how Ceres first instituted the turning of the earth with iron in Greece: it was with iron of some kind, but not specifically with a ploughshare or plough.

3. The method of manuring fields was first introduced in Italy by [Note: [Col. 0597D] A certain man named Stercutius. From Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20. He is also called Sterces and Stercutus in Augustine, *City of God* 18.15, and Sterculies in Macrobius, book 1, *Saturnalia*.] a certain man named Stercutius. [Note: [Col. 0597D] His altar was dedicated by Picus. Macrobius says by Janus, Picus’s father.] His altar was dedicated by Picus. He discovered many agricultural implements and was the first to manure fields. Some thought him to be Saturn himself [Col. 0597C], so as to give him greater distinction by a name that would sound splendid and confer the dignity of a title.

## CHAPTER II. On the cultivation of fields

1. Cultivation is that by which grain or wine is obtained with great labor, and is so called from inhabiting or tending (*incolere*). For the wealth of the ancients consisted in these two things: feeding well and ploughing well. [Note: [Col. 0598C] Cultivation of a field consists of ash, ploughing, fallowing, burning of stubble, manuring, harrowing, and weeding. Servius, at the beginning of the *Georgics*: “Ash, cessation from ploughing, burning stubble, and manuring make land rich; hence he also calls them fruitful. For the manure scattered over fields is commonly called *laetamen*.”] The cultivation of a field consists of ash, ploughing, fallowing, burning stubble, manuring, harrowing, and weeding.

2. Ash is a burning [Note: [Col. 0598C] By which the field sweats out useless moisture. Virgil: “And useless moisture sweats out.”] by which the field sweats out useless moisture.

Ploughing is so called because before the use of iron had been discovered they cultivated the earth with bronze. [Note: [Col. 0598C] There are two kinds of ploughing. From Servius, on *Georgics* 1, “In the new spring.”] There are two kinds of ploughing: spring and autumn ploughing.

[Col. 0598B] Fallowing is that by which a field, left vacant in alternate years, recovers its strength.

3. Manuring is the spreading of *laetamen*. Dung is so called either because it is strewn in fields, or because whatever filth overflows in a city ought to be wiped away; or, more truly, from Sterces, who is also called Stercutus. It is the same as manure (*fimus*), which is scattered over fields. [Note: [Col. 0598C] It is also called *fimus* because it becomes *mus*, that is, dung. Earlier, in book 2, chapter 3, *mus* was interpreted as “earth.” But Chacon judged these matters extraneous, and rightly: I believe that Isidore faithfully copied the words of Servius cited above, and Rabanus does not mention this etymology of *fimus*. Even today Italians call dung *laetame*.] *Fimus* is also so called because it becomes *mus*, that is, dung; it is commonly called *laetamen* because by its nourishment it makes shoots luxuriant and renders fields rich and fruitful.

4. Harrowing is when farmers, after sowing, let loose their oxen and [Note: [Col. 0598D] “Large clods.” Festus: Verrius thinks that *occare* and *occator* are derived from *occaedere*, because one cuts large clods of earth, whereas Cicero most elegantly derives the word from obscuring the sown crops. Here one must read *glebas* (“clods”), not *globos* (“balls”); but Varro used the former etymology, *On Agriculture* 1.31: “To dig or plough young vines, and then harrow, that is, break up, so that there is no clod.” Glossary: *occat*, βωλοκοπεῖ, “breaks clods.”] break up large clods and crush them with hoes. It is called *occatio*, as though *obcaecatio* (“covering up”), because it covers. Thus to harrow is to cover seeds, vines, or trees with earth.

[Col. 0598C] Weeding is the pulling of herbs from the ground. For *rus* means “earth.”

A furrow (*sulcus*) is so called from the sun, because, once cut open, it receives the sun.

*Veruactum* is so called as though “worked in spring,” that is, ploughed in spring.

[Col. 0599A] First ploughing (*proscissio*) is the first ploughing, when the field is still hard.

6. Sowing (*satio*) is so called as though it were the action of seed, or the action of things sown. To sow (*serere*) is so called because this should be done in clear weather, not during rains. Hence Virgil’s saying: “Plough naked, sow naked.” Harvest (*messis*) is so called from reaping, that is, cutting back.

7. A crop (*seges*) is named from seed that we cast, or from cutting.

## CHAPTER III. On grains

1. [Note: [Col. 0599C] Ceres was the first to use crops in Greece. Augustine, *City of God* 18.6: “While Argus was reigning, Greece began to use its own crops and to have grain-fields in agriculture, after seeds had been brought from elsewhere.”] Ceres was the first to use crops in Greece and to have grain-fields, after seeds had been brought from elsewhere. Ovid mentions her, saying:

> Ceres first broke up the clod with the hooked plough;
> 
> Ceres first gave crops and gentle food to the earth.

[Col. 0599B] 2. [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Grains” properly are those that have ears; from Servius, *Georgics* I, on “the pod rattling.”] Grains properly are those that have ears; [Note: [Col. 0599D] “Produce,” on the other hand, means everything else. Yet Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and the produce received”: “Those are mistaken,” he says, “who distinguish grains from produce.”] “produce,” on the other hand, means everything else. Grains, or produce, are named from *frumendo*, that is, from eating. [Note: [Col. 0599D] For *frumen* is called the upper part of the throat. Servius in both places.] For *frumen* is called the upper part of the throat.

3. Firstfruits properly are those that are plucked first from the produce.

4. *Triticum* (“wheat”) is said either from *tritura* (“threshing”), because it is stored in the granary when thoroughly purified, or because its grain is ground and crushed.

5. *Far* (“spelt”) is so called because in the beginning it was broken. [Note: [Col. 0599D] “Among the ancients [there was not yet the use] of grinding.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “and to roast.”] Among the ancients, indeed, there was not yet any use of millstones; instead, they broke the grain after putting it into a mortar, and this was their method of grinding.

6. [Note: [Col. 0599D] A type of wheat. Festus: “*Ador* is a kind of spelt, formerly called *edor*, from eating; or because it is burned so as to become roasted, whence salted meal is made for sacrifice.”] *Adoreum* is a type of wheat, [Note: [Col. 0599D] “Which is also commonly called *semen*.” Pliny, on *zea*, book XVIII, chapter 8: “This too is found in Italy, especially in Campania, and is chiefly called *semen*.”] which is also commonly called *semen*. *Ador* was formerly called from eating, because [Col. 0599C] people first used this kind, or because bread of this type was offered at the altars in sacrifice. Hence sacrifices are called *adoreal*.

7. *Siligo* (“fine wheat”) is named from being selected. For in bread its kind is especially excellent.

8. *Trimestre triticum* (“three-month wheat”) is so called because, once sown, it is gathered after three months; [Note: [Col. 0599D] “For when, because of water or some other cause…” From Columella, book II, chapter 6.] for when sowing at the proper time has been missed because of water or some other cause, recourse is had to this as a remedy.

[Col. 0600A] 9. [Note: [Col. 0599D] *Alica* is a Greek name. Festus considers it Latin: “*Alica*,” he says, “is so called because it nourishes the body.” Charisius, book I: “Verrius reports that *alica* is pronounced without aspiration, and many have said it so; Lucilius, book XV: ‘No one is more of a dealer in *alica* than you,’ used it with aspiration. The matter therefore remains undecided.”] *Alica* is a Greek name.

[Note: [Col. 0600C] *Alicastrum* is like *alica*. Columella, in the same place: “Three-month seed, which is called *alicastrum*, and is outstanding in weight and quality.”] *Alicastrum* is like *alica*, outstanding in weight and quality.

10. [Page 313] *Hordeum* (“barley”) is so called either because, before other kinds of grain, it becomes dry, or because its ear has rows. [Note: [Col. 0600D] “There are three kinds of it.” From the same source, chapter 9, except that he assigned every variety of barley to two kinds.] There are three kinds of it. The first is called *hexastichum*, because its ear has six rows. Some call it *cantherinum*, because it feeds animals better than wheat and is healthier for human beings than inferior wheat. The second is *distichon*, because it has two rows; most people call it *galaticum*. The third is *trimestre* (“three-month barley”), because, when necessity requires, it is sown in spring and gathered quickly.

11. [Note: [Col. 0600D] *Scandula*. Other copies have *scandalia*, or *scandia*. This is what it is called among us.] *Scandula* is named from division. For it is double and is split, that is, divided.

[Col. 0600B] 12. [Note: [Col. 0600D] *Centenum*. Pliny calls it *rye*, book XVIII, chapter 16.] *Centenum* is so called because in most places a sowing of it grows again as a hundredfold increase of the crop.

Hence *millet* (*milium*) too is named from the multitude of its produce.

13. *Panicium* (“millet”) is so called because in many regions people are sustained by it in place of bread, as though it were *panificium* (“bread-making”).

*Pistum* (“ground grain”) comes from *pastus* (“food”).

*Sesamum* (“sesame”) is a Greek name.

14. *Farrago* (“mixed fodder”) is named from *far* (“spelt”). It is a barley plant while still green, before its grains swell to maturity.

15. [Note: [Col. 0600D] “We abusively call the ear [spike] what projects from mature crops.” From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “now the fields are already ear-bearing,” etc.] We abusively call the ear of mature crops a *spica*. Properly, the ear is the part in which, through the sheath of the stalk—that is, through the terminal swelling of the awn—slender parts project while still in the form of a little spike.

[Col. 0600C] 16. [Note: [Col. 0600D] “The awn is so called…” From the same source, *Aeneid* VII, on “would have damaged the awns by his running.”] The awn (*arista*) is so called because it dries first.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] *Culmus*. The same author, *Georgics* I, on “the light stalk and the straw”: “*Culmus* means the stalk itself; the *stipulae* are the leaves that surround the stalk.”] The *culmus* is the stalk itself of the ear, which rises from the roots. It is called *culmus* as though *calamus* (“reed”).

17. The *folliculus* (“husk”) is the grain’s covering, in which the grain is kept inside. [Page 314] [Note: [Col. 0600D] “This forms a barrier above the ear,” etc. Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 8: “Then a rampart is built over the ear itself, so that, like a kind of fortress, it may stand before it, lest the ear be stripped of its fruits by the bites of small birds or be trampled underfoot.” Ambrose reproduced Cicero’s passage from *On Old Age*.] This covering, constructed as a rampart over the ear, provides protection, lest the ear be stripped of its fruits by the bites of small birds or be trampled underfoot.

[Col. 0601A] 18. [Note: [Col. 0601C] “The *stipulae* are leaves.” From Servius and Ambrose, in the same place.] The *stipulae* are leaves, or sheaths, by which the stalk is surrounded and supported, lest it bend under the weight of the crop; these surround the stalk. *Stipula* is said as though *usta* (“burned”), or as though *ustipula*. It is called *stipula* from *ustum* (“burned”), because, after the harvest has been gathered, it is burned for the cultivation of the field. Likewise, *stipula* is so called either because one part of it is burned, while another is sometimes cut for straw.

19. Some say that *palea* (“chaff”) is so called because it is winnowed with a *pala* (“shovel”), so that the grain may be cleaned. The pagans, however, named chaff after a certain *Pale*, the discoverer of crops, whom they wish to be Ceres. Concerning her Virgil says:

“You too, great Pales, and you, memorable one, we shall sing.”

Others say that *palea* was named from *pabulum* (“fodder”), because at first it alone was supplied for feeding animals. [Note: [Col. 0601C] “Its nature is so extremely cold by contrast,” etc. Augustine, *City of God* XXI, chapter 7: “Chaff is so cold that it does not allow snow to melt, and so hot that it compels fruit to ripen.”] Its nature, by contrast, is so cold that it does not allow buried snow to melt, and so hot that it compels fruit to ripen.

## CHAPTER IV. On Legumes

1. [Note: [Col. 0601C] “*Legumina* from *legere* (‘to gather’), as though ‘selected.’ For the ancients gathered whatever was best.” Servius, *Georgics* I, on “whatever was greatest he would gather by hand”: “Hence,” he says, “some want *legumen* to have been so called.] *Legumes* (*legumina*) are named from gathering, as though from selecting. For the ancients gathered whatever was best, [Note: [Col. 0601C] “Or because they are gathered by hand and do not require cutting.” From the same source, on “the pod rattling, the legume.” Varro, *On Agriculture* I, chapter 23, concerning the chickpea: “For this too is a legume, like the others that are pulled from the earth rather than cut down; because they are gathered in this way, they are called *legumina*.”] or because they are gathered by hand and do not require cutting.

2. There are very many kinds of legumes, among which the bean, lentil, pea, *phaselus*, chickpea, and lupine seem more agreeable for human use.

3. The bean (*faba*) took its name from the Greek etymology of eating, as though *phaga*, for in Greek φάγειν (*phagein*) means “to eat.” [Page 315] [Note: [Col. 0601D] “Human beings first used this legume.” Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 12: “Next comes the nature of legumes, among which the bean has the greatest distinction, since even bread was attempted from it.”] Human beings first used this legume. There are two varieties of it, one common and the other Egyptian.

[Col. 0601C] 4. The bean is called *fresa* (“crushed”) because people crush it—that is, break it—and reduce it by grinding.

5. The lentil (*lens*) is so called because it is moist and sticky, [Note: [Col. 0601D] Or because it clings to the ground. Other copies: “Moist…” Some want the lentil to have been called as though *lenis* (“gentle”), on the basis of Pliny’s words: “I find in the authors that those who eat it acquire equanimity.”] or because it clings to the ground.

[Col. 0602A] 6. [Note: [Col. 0601D] “But *phaselus* and *cicer* are Greek. Why he called *cicer* a Greek name requires investigation.”] *Phaselus* and *cicer* (“chickpea”) are Greek names, [Note: [Col. 0601D] “But *phaselus* is an inferior kind.” Virgil called it “the lowly *phaselus*.” The rest is from Servius, in the same place.] but *phaselus* is an inferior kind of legume, because whatever is plentiful is inferior; and this seed is found in abundance.

7. [Note: [Col. 0601D] “*Lupinus* is also Greek. It is said from ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης (‘from distress’), and Virgil seems to have alluded to this as well.”] *Lupinus* (“lupine”) is also a Greek name. Concerning it Virgil says: “And bitter lupines,” because their bitterness makes the face of the person tasting them sorrowful. Hence, because of their bitterness, neither worms nor any other animal eats them.

8. Alfalfa, vetch, and bitter vetch are excellent fodder plants.

9. Alfalfa (*medica*) is so called because it was brought to Greece from the Medes, at the time [Note: [Col. 0601D] “When Xerxes, king of the Persians, invaded them.” Servius, *Georgics* I, on “Then the rotting furrows receive you too, alfalfa”: “This plant was brought from the Medes into Greece,”] when Xerxes, king of the Persians, invaded them.

[Note: [Col. 0602C] “It is sown once and remains for ten years, so that it can be cut four or six times a year.” From Columella, book II, chapter 11.] It is sown once and remains for ten years, so that it can be cut four or six times a year.

10. [Note: [Col. 0602C] “*Vicia* is so called…” Servius, on the words of Virgil quoted by Isidore: “He says *tenues* (‘slender’) remarkably. For vetch scarcely reaches a threefold yield, whereas other legumes have a very fertile and productive growth. From these words Isidore fashioned some sort of etymology. We prefer Varro’s explanation, book I, chapter 31: ‘*Vicia* is so called from binding, because it has tendrils like a vine, with which it climbs in every direction around the stalk of the lupine or some other plant in order to cling to it; this is its way of binding.’”] The vetch (*vicia*) is so called because it scarcely reaches a threefold yield, [Page 316] whereas other legumes have a fertile yield. Hence Virgil too says: “Or the slender fruits of vetch.”

11. The pea (*pisa*) is so called because small pieces of gold were weighed with it. [Note: [Col. 0602D] “For *pis* means gold.” Another copy: “For from this *Pisaurum* is said.” Servius, *Aeneid* VI, on “Look at Torquatus,” and the passage he quotes: “For *Pisaurum*,” he says, “is so called because gold was weighed there.” Chacon rejected this as spurious.] For *pis* means gold.

12. *Ervum* (“bitter vetch”) derives its name from Greek. For the Greeks call it ὄροβον (*orobon*), and although it is harmful to certain cattle, [Note: [Col. 0602D] “It nevertheless makes bulls fat.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 3:

“Alas! how lean my bull is amid the rich bitter vetch!”] it nevertheless makes bulls fat.

## CHAPTER V. On Vines

1. Noah was the first to establish the cultivation of the vine, in the still primitive age. Among the Greeks, however, they call Liber the discoverer of the vine. Hence the pagans also wished him to be a god after his death.

2. [Note: [Col. 0602D] “The vine is so called because it possesses the power of rooting quickly,” from *vita* (“life”), or from *vis* (“strength”).] The vine (*vitis*) is so called because it possesses the power of rooting quickly. Others think vines are so called because they entwine one another with bands (*vittae*) and, by creeping, bind themselves to neighboring trees. [Col. 0602C] [Note: [Col. 0602D] “For their nature is flexible…” Ambrose, *Hexameron* chapter 12, concerning the vine: “Then, because its nature is flexible—or, as it is in an old book, fluid—and drooping, it clasps whatever it has grasped with its tendrils, as though with arms.”] Their nature is flexible, for, like arms, they clasp whatever they have grasped.

3. [Note: [Col. 0602D] “*Labrusca* … of the earth.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 5.] *Labrusca* is a wild vine that grows on the edges [Col. 0603A] of the earth. Hence *labrusca* is so called from the lips and extremities of the earth.

4. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “*Codex* is so called as though *caudex*.” Servius, *Georgics* II: “Even with trunks cut”—he used *caudicibus* for *codicibus*, just as we say *caulem* for *colem* and *sauricem* for *soricem*.] *Codex* is called as though *caudea*. Thus the ancients also said *clodus* for *claudus* (“lame”).

5. [Page 317] *Sarmentum* (“vine shoot”) comes from *serere* (“to plant”), as though *serimentum*.

[Note: [Col. 0603C] “The *malleolus* … provides.” From Columella, book III, chapter 6.] A *malleolus* is a young shoot growing from the previous year’s branch, and it is named from its resemblance to the object: at the part cut from the old vine shoot, a projection extends on both sides and presents the appearance of a hammer.

6. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “*Spadones*.” From the same book, chapter 10.] *Spadones* are shoots without fruit, so called because, as their name indicates, they are unfit for fruitfulness and afflicted with sterility.

7. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “*Sagittam* … it presents.” From chapter 17.] Farmers call the newest part of a shoot a *sagitta* (“arrow”), either because it has receded farther from the mother plant and, as it were, leaps forward, or because, by the slender sharpness of its tip, it resembles a weapon.

8. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “The tips of vines.” So Servius, *Georgics* II, on “Do not seek the highest shoots.” Also Varro, book I, chapter 31.] The tips of vines and shrubs are called *flagella* (“whips”), because they are shaken by the wind.

9. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “*Palmes*, etc.” This is called a derived (*paragogical*) name. Charisius, book III: “There are certain words called *paragoga*, which receive both change and addition from the inflection of a primitive word.”] The *palmes* (“vine branch”) is the soft wood of the vine, sent out through young branches and bearing fruit. Hence farmers call a part of the vine a *palmes*. *Palmes* is a derived name, which is called a *paragogical* name, because it is derived from *palma* (“palm”). For *palma* has a [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Prototype,” which is called the principal form. The same author, book I, chapter on Analogy: “Some nouns are principal; Pliny the Younger calls them *making* nouns, such as *aqua* (‘water’), from which possessives arise, which he calls *suffering* nouns, such as *aqualis* (‘watery’).”] prototype, which is called the principal form, from which something derived from it is made.

10. [Note: [Col. 0603D] “The *pampinus* is a leaf,” etc. From Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 12.] The *pampinus* (“vine leaf”) is a leaf whose aid protects the vine from cold and heat and fortifies it against every injury. In some places it is cut through so that it may both admit the sun for the ripening of the fruit and provide shade. It is called *pampinus* because it hangs from the vine branch.

11. [Note: [Col. 0603D] “*Capreoli*, because they seize trees.” Varro, book I, chapter 51: “On the one hand, *caprea* is so called because it gives birth to a *capreolus*. This is a twisted little vine branch, like a curl; for, so that it may hold the vines, it creeps toward a place to which it can cling. From *capere* (‘to seize’) it is called *capreolus*. More truly, however, we call it *capreolus* because of its tenderness, just as the Greeks call young branches μόσχοι (*moschoi*), that is, ‘calves.’”] The *capreoli* (“tendrils”) are so called because they seize trees. They are curls, or little hooks, with which vines entwine themselves and usually hang from trees. By relying on this support, the vine branches [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Can withstand winds and storms.” This must unquestionably be read on the basis of the older books. He was referring to Virgil’s words on this subject, *Georgics* II:

“By whose strength they may strive and become accustomed to withstand the winds.”] can withstand winds and storms, [Col. 0604A] and [Note: [Col. 0604C] “And sustain their fruits without the slipping of dangers.” All books have “without the slipping of dangers”; some substitute “of stalks,” since stalks are said to belong both to fruits and leaves. Pliny contradicts them, book XV, chapter 28: “Some fruits,” he says, “hang by stalks, such as pears; others by clusters, such as grapes and the date palm; others by both stalks and clusters, such as ivy and elder. What if Isidore said ‘without the slipping of dangers,’ as Catullus says ‘other kinds of dangers’? Chacon wanted ‘without danger of slipping.’”] sustain their fruits without the slipping of perils, and spread themselves out in wandering height.

12. [Note: [Col. 0604C] “*Corymbi* are rings.” Also below, chapter 9: “*Corymbis*, which we call rings, unless perhaps *corynni* should be read. Hesychius: Κορύμνα, a kind of woman’s neck ornament. Since Isidore expressed it in the masculine gender, I do not think this matters greatly.”] *Corymbi* are rings that bind and clasp whatever is nearest, lest the vine branches, loosened too far, be scattered by blasts of wind.

13. The grapes (*uvae*) are so called because inside they are full of moisture, [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Of juice and fatness.” Other copies: “Of the fatness of juice.”] juice, and richness. [Note: [Col. 0604D] “For what is moist is so externally.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 10.] For that is *humidum* (“moist”) which has moisture on the outside, and *uvidum* (“wet”) that which has it on the inside.

14. *Acina* … [lacuna]

*Botrus* … [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0604D] “A *racemus* is part of a *botrio*.” From the same author, *Georgics* II, on “and the ugly clusters bear grapes as prey for birds.”] A *racemus* (“cluster”) is part of a *botrio*, and *botrio* is Greek.

15. [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Suburban grapes.” From Columella, book III, chapter 2. See also Pliny, book XIV, chapter 3.] Certain grapes are called *suburbanae* (“suburban”) because their fruit is sold in cities for eating, like apples. Their appearance and the pleasantness of their flavor recommend them; among them are the early-ripening, the hard-fleshed, the purple, the date-shaped, the Rhodian, Libyan, thunderbolt, wreath-shaped, three-foot, ounce-sized, and quince-shaped varieties. The Venuculan and Numisian varieties, however, remain durable throughout the whole winter.

16. [Note: [Col. 0604D] “*Praecoquae*.” Servius: “*Praeciae*, as though *praecoquae*, because they are ripened by the sun before the others.”] *Praecoquae* (“early-ripening grapes”) are so called because they mature quickly and are ripened by the sun before all others. They call these *lageos*, [Note: [Col. 0604D] “*Lageos*.” Servius, on “and the slender *lageos*: *lageos* is what is called *leporaria* in Latin.”] because they hurry rapidly toward ripeness, like a hare.

[Page 319] 17. The purple varieties are named from their color.

[Note: [Col. 0604D] “*Dactyli*. *Dactylides*.”] The *dactyli* (“date-shaped grapes”) are named from their length.

The Rhodian and Libyan varieties are named from their regions.

The *cerauniae* (“thunderbolt grapes”) are so called because they are red like fire.

[Note: [Col. 0604D] “*Stephanitae*.” The same author: “And, by nature’s play, the *stephanites* have clusters interspersed with leaves like a crown.”] The *stephanitae* (“wreath-shaped grapes”) are named from their roundness.

The *unciariae* (“ounce-sized grapes”) are named from their size.

18. There are very many kinds of vines that serve for wine. Among these, [Note: [Col. 0604D] “*Aminea*, as though ‘without vermilion.’” From Servius, on “There are also Aminean vines,” *Georgics* II, where Pierius discusses the word and the type of wine at length.] the *Aminean* is so called as though “without vermilion,” that is, without redness. For it produces white wine, and although it has one name, it does not produce only one variety. There are two twin Aminean varieties, so called because they produce double clusters.

[Col. 0605A] [Note: [Col. 0605C] “Woolly Aminean.” This is what Columella and Pliny call it.] The woolly Aminean is so called because it becomes more covered with down than all the others.

The Rubellian is so called because its wood is red.

19. The *Faecinian* has grapes with small berries and a tough skin. [Note: [Col. 0605C] “It follows the Aminean in distinction. This concerns the momentary varieties in Columella, who nevertheless joins them with the Rubellian and the Faecenian.”] In distinction it follows the Aminean, but in fertility it surpasses it. It is therefore called *Faecinian* because it produces more sediment (*faex*) than the others.

20. [Note: [Col. 0605D] “The Apian varieties,” etc. From Columella.] The Apian grapes make sweet wine. Unless they are gathered quickly, they are attacked by rains and winds, and especially by bees, whose plundering gave them the name Apian.

[Page 320] 21. The Balanite grapes take their name from their size; for the Greeks call an acorn βάλανος (*balanos*).

22. The Biturican takes its name from its region. It withstands storms, rains, and heat with great strength, and does not fail even in lean soil. The Basiliscan has the same merit.

[Col. 0605B] 23. [Note: [Col. 0605D] “*Argitis* … *Visula* has short wood.” From Columella. We have restored *visula* to its proper place, since it was absent here. Unless someone, following the common reading, prefers to read *vasta* (“broad”) instead of *visula*, so that all these statements refer to the Argitis. I believe, however, that what happened here also happened with the Inerticula that follows immediately: since in Isidore or in Columella the word *materies* (“wood”) preceded *argitis*, while *brevem materiam* (“short wood”) followed *visula*, the scribes copied the following words, which should have been inserted under *argitis*, while omitting the name *visula*. Thus the passage should perhaps be read in full as follows: “The Argitis is a Greek vine of white stock, fertile, luxuriant in broad wood and abundant grapes. The Visula sends out short wood and a broad leaf,” etc.] The Argitis is a Greek vine of white stock, fertile.

The Visula sends out both short wood and a broad leaf. Unless you gather its fruit at the first opportunity, it will either fall to the ground or rot from moisture.

24. [Note: [Col. 0605D] “The Inerticula … dull.” From Columella, in the same place. From him we have restored *amethyston*, against all the books. Chacon said that the word *amaracion*, commonly read here, had been brought over from the Helvolan grapes, which Columella discusses immediately afterward.] The Inerticula is black; the Greeks call it *amethyston*. It produces good, mild wine and derived its name from being considered inactive in testing the nerves, although it is not dull to the taste.

25. [Note: [Col. 0605D] “The Mareotic.” From Servius, on “There are also white Mareotides,” *Georgics* II.] The Mareotic grapes are named from the Egyptian region of Mareotis, from which they first came. There are both white and black varieties.

26. [Note: [Col. 0606C] “The Helvolan varieties.” Pliny calls them *Helvenacae*; among us they are commonly called *hebenes*.] The Helvolan grapes, which some call variegated, are neither purple nor black. They are named from their tawny color, although their must is somewhat whitish. For *helvum* is a color both dark and pale. The tawny color is neither white nor black.

[Page 321] [Col. 0605C] 27. [Note: [Col. 0606C] “The third place … flowing.” There is no place here for this third category. I therefore think it should be deleted.] The third category consists of vines commended solely for their fertility, with abundant productivity and a copious flow of wine.

28. [Note: [Col. 0606D] “*Vitiscionia*, etc.” The name *Vitiscionia* is unknown. Concerning the *Spionia*, Columella says: “But the Spionia is rich in must and more fertile in the size of its grapes than in their number.”] The Vitiscionia has grapes that are larger rather than more numerous. It takes its name from the fact that a great deal of wine flows from it.

[Note: [Col. 0606D] “The Syriac.” Pliny: “There is also a black Aminean to which they give the name Syriac.”] The Syriac is so called either because it was brought from Syria or because it is black.

29. There are many kinds of vines, but through changes of place they lose both their quality and their name.

[Col. 0606A] 30. Among other things, the following especially suit vines: loosening the soil around them, pruning, propagation, and digging.

31. [Note: [Col. 0606D] “To loosen the soil around a vine … they call it.” From Palladius, book II, chapter 1. I see *ablaqueare* written everywhere in authors on agriculture. But why the reading of the Gothic books should be displeasing, in all of which we find *oblaqueare*, if *oblaqueare* means to make a trench around it, I do not know.] To loosen the soil around a vine (*oblaqueare*) is to open the earth around the trunk and make it like a basin. Some call this *excodiacare*.

32. To prune (*putare*) is to cut away an unnecessary branch from the vine, whose shoots grow luxuriantly. *Putare* is said to mean “to cleanse,” that is, to cut off.

33. *Traducere* means “to lead across.” But *propaginare* (“to propagate”) is to lay down a vine shoot buried in the earth and, as it were, plant it farther on. Here [Note: [Col. 0606D] “*Propagines* from *propagare*, that is, to extend.” Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on “the race from the high blood of Teucer”: “*Proderet*,” he says, “means ‘would extend,’ that is, ‘would propagate.’”] *propagines* are so called from *propagare*, that is, from extending.

To dig (*fodere*) is to make a pit, as though *fovere* (“to warm or foster”).

## CHAPTER VI. On Trees

[Col. 0606B] 1. The name of trees, and likewise of plants, is thought to have been altered from *arva* (“fields”), because they cling to the earth with fixed roots. The two are nearly alike for this reason: one is produced from the other. For when you have cast seed into the earth, a plant first arises; then, nourished, it grows into a tree, and in a short time you look upon a young tree where previously you had seen only a plant.

2. An *arbustum* is a young and tender tree in which grafting can be performed, and *arbusta* is said as though “the spear of a tree.” Others [Note: [Col. 0606D] “*Arbustum*, a place … a willow plantation.” These are Servius’ words, *Eclogue* 3.] understand *arbustum* as a place in which trees are found, like a willow plantation. Likewise, *virectum* is a place where shoots and green plants grow.
