3. *Arbor* may be both fruit-bearing and barren; *arbos*, however, is only fruit-bearing. We use *arbores* as a feminine noun, but *poma* (“fruits”) as a neuter noun.

[Col. 0606C] 4. A shrub (*frutex*) is called short because it covers the earth with foliage; its plural is *fruteta*. A tree is tall.

5. A *silva* is a dense and low woodland. [Note: [Col. 0606D] “*Silva* is said as though *xilva*.” Another copy has *xyla*; it is said from ὕλη (*hyle*), with *s* replacing the aspirate.] *Silva* is said as though *xilva*, because timber is cut there. For the Greeks call wood ξύλον (*xylon*). Many Latin names often receive a Greek etymology.

6. *Nemus* (“grove”) is named from divine powers (*numina*), because the pagans set up idols there. [Page 323] Groves are stands of larger trees, shaded by foliage.

7. A *lucus* (“sacred grove”) is a density of trees that removes light from the ground, by the figure called antiphrasis, because it does not shine; or it is named from *lux* (“light”), because torches or candles shone in it on account of the darkness of the groves.

8. A *saltus* (“woodland”) is a tall density of trees. It is called by this name because it leaps upward and rises aloft.

9. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “*Aviaria*.” From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “the aviaries redden with berries.”] *Aviaria* are called secluded groves because birds frequent them.

10. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “*Recidiva*.” From two passages of Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on “reborn by hand,” and *Aeneid* X, on “while the Teucrians [are in] Latium.”] *Recidiva* are trees that sprout again after others have been cut down. Some say *recidiva* comes from falling, because they are born after a fall. Others derive it from cutting back and sprouting again. Thus *recidivum* is found where there is death or a fall.

11. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “Grafting, when a shoot is inserted into a split trunk.” From the same author, *Georgics* II, on “the harsh strawberry tree.” Since this passage and Servius’ manuscript require it, *fisso*, not *infixo*, must be read.] Grafting is when a shoot of a fertile tree is inserted into a split trunk of a sterile one; or it is the placing of buds, when, after the bark has been cut, a bud is inserted into the inner bark of another tree.

[Col. 0607B] 12. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “*Plantae* … *plantaria* … transfer.” From the same author, in the same place.] *Plantae* are shoots taken from trees; *plantaria* are those that have grown from seeds with roots and are transferred from their original soil.

13. *Cespites* (“clumps”) are shrubs, as though *cuspites*, or as though they are “around the feet.”

*Frondes* (“foliage”) are so called because they bear shoots or shade; they are the means of shade.

*Oculi* (“eyes”) are the nodes from which leaves emerge.

14. A root (*radix*) is so called because, fixed in the earth as though by rays, it sinks into the depths.

[Note: [Col. 0607D] “For natural philosophers say,” etc. From the same author, *Aeneid* IV.] Natural philosophers say that the depth of roots equals the height of trees. Others think the root was named from its resemblance to rays, or because, if it is uprooted, it does not sprout again.

[Col. 0607C] 15. The trunk is the stature of a tree standing upon its root.

[Note: [Col. 0607D] “The ancients called the bark *corux*.” I would gladly read *corium* (“hide”), despite the uncertain traces, in the Tarraconensian manuscript: “The trunk is the stature of a tree standing upon its root; the ancients called [the bark] *corux*.”] The ancients called the bark *corux*. It is called *cortex* because it covers the wood like hide.

[Page 324] 16. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “The inner bark.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 10.] The *liber* (“inner bark”) is the inner part of the bark, called *liber* from *liberatus* (“freed”), that is, removed. It is a certain middle substance between wood and bark.

17. Branches are what flow from the trunk, just as other growths flow from the smaller branches.

Shoots are named from being cut by a saw.

18. [Note: [Col. 0607D] “*Virgultum*, because it comes from a *virga*.” Another copy: “because this is a *virga*.”] A *virgulum* is what sprouts from the root; a branch is what comes from the tree’s main wood; a twig is what comes from branches. Properly, however, *virgultum* is what grows at the root of a tree and is cut off by farmers as useless. [Col. 0608A] Hence it is called *virgultum*, because it is taken from a twig. A *virga* (“rod”) is said either from strength, because it contains great force, or from greenness, or because it is an indication of peace, since it restrains force. Hence magicians use it to reconcile serpents among themselves, [Note: [Col. 0607D] “And for this reason they keep the serpents fastened to it.” As we see on Mercury’s caduceus.] and for this reason they keep serpents fastened to it. Philosophers, kings, teachers, messengers, and ambassadors also use it.

19. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “They are called *flagella*.” From Servius, in the passage cited above, chapter 5.] As we said above, the upper parts of trees are called *flagella* (“whips”), because they endure the frequent blasts of the winds.

20. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “They call them *cymae* … as though *comae*.” Also below, chapter 10: *cyma*, as though *coma* (“foliage”).] They call them *cymae* (“sprouts”), as though *comae* (“foliage”).

Leaves are called φύλλα (*phylla*) in Greek; from there the name was transferred to us by derivation.

21. Flowers (*flores*) are so called because they quickly fall from trees, as though *fluores* (“flowings”), because they quickly loosen and fall away. They possess a twofold grace: color and fragrance. For the south wind dissolves flowers, while the west wind produces them.

[Col. 0608B] 22. We call a pregnant shoot a *germen* (“bud”), from *gerere* (“to bear”); hence also *germinatio* (“germination”).

23. The name *fructus* (“fruit”) was taken [Note: [Col. 0608D] “From *frumen*, that is, the projecting part of the throat.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and the produce received.”] from *frumen*, that is, from the projecting part of the throat through which we eat. Hence also *fruges* (“produce”). Fruit properly refers to the produce of fields and trees, which we use. In the case of animals, however, we call offspring “fruit” abusively and metaphorically.

24. Apples (*poma*) are named from *opimus* (“rich”), that is, from abundance and fertility. They are called *matura* (“ripe”) because they are suitable for chewing; likewise, *immatura* (“unripe”) because before they become ripe they are hard to chew.

[Page 325] 25. Wood (*ligna*) is so called because, when burned, it is transformed into light. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “Hence also *lucinium*.” Another copy: *lychnus*, or *ellychnium*.] Hence it is also called *lychnus*, because it gives light.

[Col. 0608C] 26. A small staff (*hastula*) is named from lifting, as though *abstula*. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “*Fomes* is a small staff.” Among us it is commonly called *astilla* (“splinter”). But Festus says: “*Fomites* are small sticks shaken loose from trees when they are cut down.” Opilius thinks that already-burned vines are called *fomites*.] A *fomes* is a small stick shaken from trees by cutting, or a burned stick, or hollowed wood; it received its name from fungi because it catches fire in this way. Concerning it Virgil says: “And he snatched flame from the tinder.”

27. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “A *torris* is burned wood.” Jerome, on Zechariah III: “Why do you try to overwhelm Jesus like a brand, commonly called a firebrand, who escaped from the Babylonian captivity like a half-burned log?”] A *torris* (“brand”) is burned wood, which common people call a firebrand, drawn from the hearth, half-burned and extinguished.

28. [Note: [Col. 0608D] “*Quisquiliae*.” Festus: “*Quisquiliae* is thought to mean whatever small shoots fall from trees, as whatever falls.”] *Quisquiliae* are bits of straw mixed with shoots and dry leaves. They are refuse from the earth.

Rot (*caries*) is decay of wood; it is called by this name because it occurs in wood lacking strength.

[Page 326] ## CHAPTER VII. On the Proper Names of Trees

[Col. 0609A]

1. [Note: [Col. 0609C] “The palm is so called because it is the adornment of the victorious hand.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* III, chapter 13: “The laurel and palm are marks of victory; the heads of victors are crowned with laurel, while the palm adorns the victorious hand.”] The palm is so called because it is the adornment of the victorious hand, or because its branches are spread out in the form of a human palm. It is a tree that is a sign of victory, clothed with a tall and beautiful shoot and long-lasting foliage, preserving its leaves without any replacement. The Greeks call it *Phoenix*, because it endures for a long time, taking its name from that bird of Arabia, which is said to live for many years. Although it grows in many places, it does not bring its fruit to maturity everywhere. It does so especially in Egypt and Syria. Its fruits are dates, named from their resemblance to fingers; their names also vary. For some are called palm-like *myrobalans*. Others are called Theban, [Col. 0609B] [Note: [Col. 0609C] “They are also called Nicolaian.” They are named from Nicolaus the Peripatetic, whose company Augustus enjoyed; but Pliny, Plutarch, Athenaeus, and Suidas report the reason in different ways.] and also Nicolaian. Others are called nut-like, which the Greeks call *caryotae*.

2. The laurel (*laurus*) is named from the verb of praise. For with it the heads of victors were crowned amid praises. Among the ancients it was called *laudea*; afterward, with the letter *d* removed and *r* substituted, it was called *laurus*, as with *auriculae* (“little ears”), which were first called *audiculae*, and *medidies*, which is now called *meridies* (“midday”). [Note: [Col. 0609D] “The Greeks call this tree δάφνη (*daphne*), perhaps because it never loses its greenness.” Some thought he was referring to Hegesippus, who says in book III, chapter 5, that near Antioch there is a grove called Daphne because it is always green.] The Greeks call this tree δάφνη (*daphne*), because it never loses its greenness; for this reason victors are crowned with it rather than with another tree. [Note: [Col. 0609D] “This is also the only tree not struck by lightning.” Pliny, book XIV, final chapter: “It alone is not struck by lightning.”] This tree alone, too, is commonly believed never to be struck by lightning.

3. [Note: [Col. 0609D] “*Malum* is a Greek word.” Thus above, book XII, chapter 1: “The apple, because its form is the roundest of all.”] The apple (*malum*) is so called by the Greeks because its fruit is the roundest of all fruits. Hence those are true apples that are extremely round. [Note: [Col. 0609D] “The Matian apple is named from a place.” Pliny gives a different account, book XV, chapter 14. Yet the same Pliny mentions the town of Matius in book VI, chapter 4.] The Matian apple is named from the place from which it was first brought. [Col. 0609C] For many trees received their names from the provinces and cities from which they were brought. Virgil shows what lovers are accustomed to ask from an apple.

### 4

The quince apples took their name from a town on the island of Crete. The Greeks commonly call Cydonia the mother of the Cretan cities; from its fruit, [*cydonitum*] is made. **[Note: Cydonitum is made from it. See Palladius, in October.]** Wine is also made from it, by which the cravings of the sick are deceived. For in appearance, taste, and smell it reproduces the character of any old wine.

### 5

**[Note: *Melimelum*. Pliny, Book XV, chapter 14: “*Mustea* from the speed with which they ripen; these are now called *melimela* because of their honeyed flavor.]**

*Melimelum* was named from its sweetness, because its fruit has the taste of honey, or because it is preserved in honey. **[Note: Hence also the following verse by someone; Martial, Book XIII, epigram 24.]** Thus someone says:

> If quinces saturated with Cecropian honey  
> Are set before you, say: “These melimela please me.”

### 6

The pomegranate is called the “Carthaginian apple” because its kind was brought from the Carthaginian region. **[Note: It is also called the “many-seeded apple.” Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 19: “Some call it *granatum*.”]** It is likewise called the many-seeded apple because it contains a multitude of seeds within the roundness of its rind. **[Note: Because it contains many seeds within the roundness of its rind. From Jerome, on the final chapter of Haggai.]**

The pomegranate tree is feminine in gender, but its fruit is neuter. **[Note: The flowers of apples are called *cytini* by the Greeks. From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 153.]** The flowers of the apple trees are called by the Greeks κύτινοι (*cytini*). **[Note: The Latins call it *caducum*. Aurelianus, Book V, *On Chronic Diseases*, chapter 2: “The pomegranate’s *caducum*, which the Latins call *ampullacium*.” This, I think, is how the passage should be read in Aurelianus, from the shape of an *ampulla*, or flask. For in Book IV, chapter 3, the same author writes that it is called *ampullagium*. I prefer to read *ampullacium* in both places, with Chacon. I also wish Isidore had said that the pomegranate’s *caducum* is called *ampullacium* by the Latins.] The Latins call it *caducum*.

The Greeks, however, called the flowers of wild apple trees βαλάυστια (*balaustia*). Some are found white, others purple, and others rose-colored, resembling the flowers of the pomegranate. **[Note: The flowers of wild apples are called *balaustia* by the Greeks. From Dioscorides, chapter 155, “On Balaustia.” Pliny mentions *balaustium* in Book XXVI, chapter 3, as does Arnobius in Book VI of *Against the Pagans*.]**

Physicians deny that eating pomegranates nourishes our bodies. Rather, they think that the fruit should be used medicinally, so that it appears to heal rather than to nourish. **[Note: “Physicians deny this.” Dioscorides expressed the point in a single word by calling it ἄτροφον (*atrophon*, “non-nourishing”).]**

### 7

The Persian apple, to which a very short life has been granted, is said to be of three kinds: the *duracinum*, the Armenian, and the Persian. **[Note: Three kinds. Palladius, final book, chapter 6: “Their kinds are these: *duracina*, early-ripening fruits, Persian, and Armenian.”]**

The *duracinum* is so called because its fruit, when tasted, recalls sourness. The Armenian apple is so called because this kind was first brought from Armenia. The Persian apple was so called because Perseus first planted that tree in Egypt; the Ptolemies claimed descent from him. **[Note: “Because Perseus first planted that tree in Egypt,” and so forth. See Pliny, Book XV, chapter 13.]** In Persia it produces a deadly fruit, but among us it is pleasant and sweet.

**[Note: Of these, one is early-ripening. This is what we call *albercoque*, a word not entirely changed from the original.]** Of these, one is called early-ripening, the other summer fruit.

### 8

**[Note: The citron tree, and so forth. These words are from Solinus, in the section on Media.]**

The citron tree, whose name also became famous in the poems of the Mantuan poet, was first brought from the Medes, from whom it also took its name. **[Note: The Greeks call it κεδρόμηλον (*kedromelon*). Dioscorides uses this term in Book I, chapter 167. Although I know that some consider the word doubtful and prefer κετριόμηλον (*ketriomelon*), it should also be known that the interpreter of Nicander calls it νεράντζιον (*nerantzion*), whence our word *naranja*.]**

The Greeks call it κεδρόμηλον (*kedromelon*), and the Latins call it *citrium*, because its fruit and leaves recall the scent of cedar. Its fruit is hostile to poisons. This is also what the same poet intended when he says that the spirit is refreshed by it.

**[Note: “This tree is almost always laden,” and so forth. From Servius, on *Georgics* II.]** This tree is laden with apples almost all the time: some on it are partly unripe, some ripe, and some still set among the blossoms—a rare condition in other trees.

### 9

*Mella*, which the Greeks call λωτός (*lotos*), is commonly called the Syrian bean because of its shape and color. **[Note: “Which is commonly called the Syrian bean,” and so forth. From Servius. Pliny calls the lotus a Greek bean, while Athenaeus calls it an Egyptian bean. I have found no information about *mella*.]**

It is a large tree bearing edible fruit, larger than a peppercorn and sweet in taste; hence it was also called *mella*. **[Note: Larger than pepper. So Dioscorides.]**

### 10

*Coccimela*, which the Latins call a plum because of its color, is called *nixa* by others because of the abundance of its fruit. **[Note: Others call it *nixa* from the abundance of its fruit. In the margin of the Roman manuscript of Saint Peter, Chacon says he found the following addition, written by the same hand: “The Romans call this tree *prunum*, the Spaniards *nixum*, while the Vandals, Goths, Suevi, and Celtiberians call it *cerulea*. The Portuguese and Galicians retain traces of this word today, calling all plums *amexas* or *ameixas*. Aurelianus, Book IV of *Chronic Diseases*, chapter 8, has: ‘For a decoction of *nixae* or licorice.’ I would read *nixarum*. Some argue that *myxa* should be read instead of *nixa*, citing Paul of Aegina, Book VII: ‘The fruit of the *myxa* tree is smaller than that of the *coccymela*, but similar in power.’ This confirms what we said about the Galicians. For we often see that *m* has taken the place of *n*, or conversely, in many words.”]**

Of this kind the Damascene plum is better. It was named from Damascus, the town from which it was first brought. Only this fruit is considered beneficial for the stomach; the others are said to be harmful. **[Note: “This tree alone produces gum.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 175.]** This tree alone exudes a sticky, cohesive gum, which physicians and writers use. **[Note: “Which physicians and writers use,” and so forth. Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 11: “It is very useful to painters and physicians,” and I have changed nothing.]**

### 11

**[Note: “Sweet *elaeomeli*.” These are the words of Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 37, but he is speaking of the oil, not of the tree. Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 7: “It arises spontaneously in the coastal regions of Syria; what they call *elaeomeli* flows from the trees, fatty, thicker than honey, thinner than resin, and sweet in taste.” And in Book XXIII, chapter 4: “*Elaeomeli*, which, as we have said, flows from the olive trees in Syria.” Perhaps the tree itself was also called by this name.]**

*Elaeomeli* grows in Palmyra, a city of Syria, and was so called because oil flows from its trunk with the thickness of honey and a sweet taste.

### 12

**[Note: *Epimelis*. A kind of medlar, as Dioscorides says in Book I, chapter 171. See Macrobius, Book III, chapter 19.]**

The *epimelis* resembles the service tree. It is a medium-sized tree with a whitish flower, and was so called because its fruit combines sweetness with a sharp flavor. This tree lasts only a short time.

### 13

**[Note: *Melosos*. Solinus, chapter 40: “There is also a tree, the *melops*—or, in another reading, *melopos*—from which flows a viscous liquid that we call ammoniacum.” Pliny calls it *metopium*; Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 98, calls it *agasyl­lis*.]**

The *melopos* is a tree called by the Africans in the Punic language. From it flows a viscous juice, which is called ammoniacum from the place.

### 14

**[Note: “The medlar … because its fruits are little balls.” Another reading has *pirulae*.]**

The medlar is a thorny tree, with fruit resembling apples but somewhat smaller; hence it was given its name, because its fruits have the shape of little balls.

### 15

**[Note: “The pear, as if deformed into the shape of fire.” So the Gothic manuscript reads; others have *formata*, “formed.”]**

The pear seems to have been so called because it is shaped like fire. For this kind of fruit begins broad and ends narrow, like fire. The tree is the pear tree, while its fruit is the pear. There are many varieties, among them the Crustumian pears, red on one side and named from the town of Crustumium. **[Note: “The Crustumians are pears,” and so forth. From Servius, on *Georgics* II.]**

The fruits of the pear, when placed upon pack animals—or even in small quantities—are said to be extremely burdensome. **[Note: “The fruits of the pear are burdensome to pack animals.” From Pliny, Book XXIII, chapter 7.]**

### 16

**[Note: “The cherry was named,” and so forth. From Servius, on *Georgics* II.]**

The cherry was named from Cerasus, a city of Pontus. When Lucullus destroyed the city of Cerasus in Pontus, he brought this kind of fruit from there and named it after the city. The tree is called *cerasus*, and its fruit *cerasum*. It existed in Italy even before Lucullus, but was hard; hence it was also called *cornum*. The tree is suitable for spear shafts, which is why Virgil says:

> The cornel wood is good for war.

### 17

The fig tree is called *ficus* in Latin from its fertility, for it is more productive than other trees. It produces fruit three or four times each year, and while one fruit is ripening, another begins to appear.

**[Note: Hence *caricae* were also named from abundance. Caria is exceedingly fertile in figs, according to Strabo. I believe this addition was made by someone to whom *carica* suggested a load, from which the Spaniards formed *carga* and the Italians *carico*.]** Hence *caricae* were also named from abundance.

The Egyptian fig is said to be more fertile. Its wood, when placed in water, immediately sinks; after lying for some time in the mud, it rises again to the surface—a reversal of nature, since once soaked it ought to remain below because of the weight of the moisture.

In former times athletes were nourished on figs, **[Note: “Before Pythagoras trained them,” and so forth. From Pliny, Book XXIII, chapter 7. Pausanias, in the later books of the *Eliaca*, attributes this instead to a certain Dromius, for whom Pythagoras of Rhegium made a statue as a victor. I am very surprised that Laertius omitted this, although he mentions Pythagoras the boxer; thus Pliny may appear to have been deceived.]** before their trainer Pythagoras changed them to the use of meat, which is the stronger food.

Figs eaten more frequently by old men are said to smooth out their wrinkles. **[Note: “Even the fiercest bulls.” So Plutarch, Book XI of the *Table Talk*. Pliny reports this only of the wild fig tree.]** They also say that even the fiercest bulls, when tied to a fig tree, suddenly become tame.

### 18

The wild fig tree was called *caprificus* because it tears apart the walls in which it grows. For it bursts through and emerges from the sides in which it took root. Others think that it was called *caprificus* because the fig tree is fertilized by its agency.

### 19

The mulberry was named by the Greeks; the Latins call it *rubus*, because its fruits are red like those of a shrub. **[Note: “Its fruit is like that of a shrub.” From the Roman manuscript, but I would prefer *arbusti* to *virgulti*.]**

It is a wild mulberry bearing fruit, by which the hunger and deprivation of shepherds in the wilderness are relieved. **[Note: “For it is a wild mulberry bearing fruit.” Jerome, on Amos 7, commenting on “plucking sycamores,” and so forth: “For us, since the solitude in which Amos lived produces no such tree, it seems more likely that he means thornbushes, which bear *mora* and alleviate the hunger and poverty of shepherds.”]**

Its leaves, when thrown over a snake, are said to kill it. **[Note: “Its leaves, thrown over it.” These are the words of Ambrose, Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8.]**

### 20

The sycamore, like the mulberry, has a Greek name. It was called *sycomorus* because its leaves resemble those of the mulberry. The Latins call it *celsa*, “the tall tree,” because of its height, since it is not short like the mulberry.

### 21

The walnut was so called because its shade or the dripping of its leaves harms the neighboring trees. The Latins call it by another name, *juglans*, as if it were “Jove’s acorn.” **[Note: “They call it *juglans*, as if *Jovis glans*, ‘Jove’s acorn.’” From Servius, on Eclogue 8.]**

This tree was consecrated to Jupiter. Its fruit has such power that, when placed among suspicious herbs or mushrooms prepared as food, it draws out, absorbs, and extinguishes whatever poisonous substance is in them.

### 22

**[Note: “Nuts are used generally,” and so forth. From Servius, on Eclogue 2.]**

“Nuts” is the general name for everything covered with a relatively hard shell, such as pine nuts, hazelnuts, walnuts, chestnuts, and almonds. Hence they are also called *nuclei*, because they are covered with a hard shell.

By contrast, all soft fruits are called *mala*, with an additional designation indicating the lands in which they first grew, such as Persian, Carthaginian, Matian, and quince apples.

### 23

Almond is a Greek name. **[Note: “Which in Latin is called the long nut.” Servius, commenting on “when the many nuts clothe themselves in blossom”: “Many,” he says, “that is, long.”]** In Latin it is called the “long nut.”

Others call it *nucicla*, as if “a smaller nut.” **[Note: Others call it *nucicla*; another reading has *nucella*, *nuceda*, or *nucula*.]**

Virgil speaks of it:

> When the abundant nut tree clothes itself in blossom in the woods.

For it is the first of all the trees to clothe itself in blossom and outstrips the other orchards in producing fruit.

### 24

**[Note: “Hazelnuts, named from Avellano, a town in Campania,” and so forth. From Servius, on *Georgics* II, commenting on “the shoots of the sturdy hazel,” and so forth.]**

Hazelnuts were named from Avellano, a town in Campania where they are abundant. The Greeks call them Pontic nuts because they abound around the Pontic Sea. **[Note: “These are called Pontic by the Greeks.” So Macrobius, Book III, chapter 18. But Athenaeus, Book II, calls the chestnut a Pontic nut.]**

### 25

The Latins call the chestnut by a word taken from Greek. The Greeks call it κάστανον (*kastanon*), because its twin fruits are hidden inside a husk in the form of testicles; when they are expelled, they are, as it were, castrated. **[Note: “Because its fruit is twin,” and so forth. Having introduced a Greek word, he thought it safe to indulge in wordplay in the etymology, unless you prefer to regard this as an interpolation. I certainly do not think that the reference is to Castor—that is, the beaver—as some have believed.]**

As soon as this tree has been cut down, it habitually sprouts again from itself like a forest. **[Note: “As soon as it has been cut down,” and so forth. These are the words of Ambrose, Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 13.]**

### 26

The holm oak was called *ilex* from *electus*, “chosen,” because people first chose the fruit of this tree for their food. Hence the poet says:

> The first mortals chewed acorns in their throats.

Before the use of grain, ancient people lived on acorns.

### 27

**[Note: *Suberies*. This word is found in Festus under “Stura.”]**

The cork oak is a tree from which very strong material for swimming is extracted. It was therefore called *suberies* because its fruit is eaten by swine; they are food for pigs, not for human beings. It was called *suberies* as if from *subedies*. **[Note: As if from *subedies*. Festus has *suedies*.]**

### 28

The beech and the aesculus are believed to have been called fruit-bearing trees because people once lived on their fruits, taking them as food and nourishment. The aesculus was named from *esca*, “food.” **[Note: “Aesculus from *esca*.” Servius, commenting on “the aesculus above all,” *Georgics* II: “The aesculus is a tree bearing acorns. Although it is named from eating, it is nevertheless spelled with *ae*, just as *coelatum*, although derived from *caelo*, is spelled with *oe*.]**

The beech, however, took its name from Greek. **[Note: “The beech.” From the same source, on Eclogue 1.]** For φάγειν (*phagein*) means “to eat” in Greek.

### 29

**[Note: *Xyliglycon*. Others call the same tree either ξυλόκερας (*xylokeras*) or κεράτιον (*keration*).]**

The *xyliglycon*, which the Latins corruptly call *siliqua*, received this name from the Greeks because the fruit of its wood is sweet. ξύλον (*xylon*) means “wood,” and γλυκύ (*glyky*) means “sweet.”

**[Note: “The juice expressed from the fruit of this tree is called acacia.” Concerning acacia, see Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 124. In his account it is a tree, or rather a thorn resembling a tree, from whose pods juice is expressed. In Pliny, however, there is nothing in common between the carob and acacia. I therefore think something is missing here.]**

The juice expressed from the fruit of this tree is called *acacia* by the Greeks.

### 30

**[Note: Pistachio. See Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 178, and Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 22.]**

The pistachio was so called because the shell of its fruit recalls the scent of true nard.

### 31

The pine tree, the pitch-producing tree, was named from the sharpness of its leaves. **[Note: The ancients called the pine “sharp.” The same author above, Book XI, chapter 1, and Book XIX, chapter 19.]** The ancients called the pine “sharp.”

The pine is called *pitin* by some, and the Greeks call another kind πέυκη (*peuke*), which we call the pitch tree, because it exudes pitch. **[Note: The Greeks call it πέυκη (*peuke*). From Ambrose, Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 3.]** The two kinds also differ in appearance.

On the islands of Germany, the tear of this tree produces amber. For the falling drop hardens into solidity through cold or warmth and becomes a precious stone, taking a name from its nature: *succinum*, that is, “sap-stone,” because it is the tree’s sap.

**[Note: The pine is believed to benefit all plants sown beneath it, and so forth. From Palladius, in November. See Theophrastus, Book III, *On the Causes of Plants*, chapter 15, although Pliny seems to have held the contrary opinion in Book XVII, chapter 12.]**

The pine is believed to benefit everything planted beneath it, just as the walnut harms everything.

### 32

The fir was so called because it rises far above other trees and projects upward to a great height. **[Note: Its nature is free of earthy moisture. Vitruvius, Book II, chapter 9: “The fir contains a great deal of air and fire, and very little moisture; compared with the lighter parts of nature, it is not heavy.”]**

Its nature is free of earthy moisture, and therefore it is considered manageable and light. Virgil speaks of it:

> And the fir destined to witness maritime disasters,

because ships are made from it. Some call it the Gallic tree because of its whiteness. It is without knots.

### 33

The cedar is called κέδρος (*kedros*) by the Greeks, as if from καιομένης δρυὸς ὑγρόν (*kaiomenēs dryos hygron*), “the moisture of a burning tree.” **[Note: “As if from καιομένης δρυὸς ὑγρόν, ‘the moisture of a burning oak,’” and so forth. From Servius, commenting on “the pines fall forward,” *Aeneid* VI. The passage would better suit *cedria*, which is discussed immediately below.]**

Its leaves resemble those of the cypress. Its wood has a pleasant smell, lasts a long time, and is never destroyed by moths. Persius speaks of it:

> And words worthy of cedar.

That is, because of its lasting permanence. **[Note: Hence ceilings in temples are made from this wood because of its durability. From Ambrose, Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 13, and at the end of the commentary on Psalm 118.]**

The resin of this wood is called *cedria*. **[Note: The resin of this wood is called *cedria*. See Vitruvius, Book II, chapter 9.]** It is so useful for preserving books that books coated with it suffer neither from moths nor from the ravages of age.

It grows in Crete, Africa, and Syria.

### 34

**[Note: The cypress is called so in Greek because of its crown. Servius, on *Aeneid* III, commenting on “the lofty oaks”: “The fruit of the cypress is called a cone, and the tree itself is κωνοειδής (*kōnoeidēs*), cone-shaped. For from roundness it rises to a point.”]**

The cypress is called *cyparissus* in Greek because its crown rises from roundness into a point. Hence it is also called κωνοειδής (*kōnoeidēs*), that is, “a lofty roundness.” Its fruit is therefore also called a cone, because its roundness is such that it imitates a cone. Hence cypresses are also called cone-bearing.

Its wood possesses almost the same qualities as cedar. It is suitable for the beams of temples, and because of its impenetrable solidity it never yields under a load but retains the firmness it possessed at the beginning.

**[Note: “The ancients used branches of the cypress,” and so forth. From the same source, on *Aeneid* VI, commenting on “the funeral cypresses.”]** The ancients used to place cypress branches near the funeral pyre so that, while the corpses were burning, the pleasantness of their scent would overpower the smell of the bodies.

### 35

**[Note: Juniper in Greek. *Janiperus* is a Latin word; in Greek it is called ἄρκευθος (*arkeuthos*).]**

The juniper was called so in Greek either because it narrows from a broad base, like fire, or because it retains fire within itself for a long time. **[Note: “So that if its coals,” and so forth. From Jerome, Letter 126 to Fabiola, section 16.]** Thus, if burning coals are covered with its ashes, they remain until the following year; for πῦρ (*pyr*) means “fire” in Greek.

The juniper is of two kinds, one small and the other large. **[Note: “The juniper is one kind small and another large.” So Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 104.]**

### 36

Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia; once cut, it hardens into stone. Its wood is black and its bark smooth like that of the laurel. **[Note: “But the Indian kind is spotted with yellowish marks.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 130.]** The Indian kind is spotted with small white and yellowish markings. The Ethiopian kind, which is considered superior, has no spots at all; it is black, smooth, and horn-like.

**[Note: “There is a Mareotic marsh in India.” Servius, commenting on “Mareotic white,” *Georgics* II: “Mareotis,” he says, “is a part of Egypt”; and on “India alone produces black ebony”: “Yet it grows in Egypt. But we understand the whole region of Ethiopia as India.”]**

There is a Mareotic marsh in India, from which ebony comes. **[Note: Lucan, Book X.]** Lucan says: “Mareotic ebony.”

Ebony is tied to children’s rattles so that the black object will not frighten infants when they look at it.

### 37

The plane tree was named from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and broad. For the Greeks call πλατύς (*platys*) “broad.” Scripture expresses both the name and the form of this tree when it says:

> Like a plane tree I was spread out beside the water in the streets.

Its leaves are extremely delicate and soft, and it resembles the vine.

### 38

The oak, or *quernus*, was so called because the gods of the nations were accustomed to give responses beneath it to those who sought them. It is a very long-lived tree. **[Note: “As is read concerning the oak of Mamre,” and so forth. Jerome, in the *Hebrew Names*: “The oak of Abraham, which is Mamre, was shown for many centuries, down to the reign of King Constantius—or, in another reading, Constans—and its mausoleum can still be seen today.”]**

Thus we read of the oak of Mamre, beneath which Abraham lived, and which is said to have endured for many centuries, down to the reign of King Constans.

The fruit of this tree is called *galla*, “gallnut.” **[Note: The fruit of this tree is the gallnut. From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 127.]** One kind is wild and is called ὀμφακίτης (*omphacitis*). It is small in size but firm in body and knotty, and is used in medicines and for cauterizations.

Another kind is βάλανος (*balanos*), smooth, soft, and very porous, and is useful only for lamps. **[Note: It is needed only for the uses of lamps. From Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 7.]**

### 39

The ash is said to be called *fraxinus* because it grows especially in rough and mountainous places, in *fragis*. Hence, by derivation, *fraxinus*, just as *montanus* comes from *mons*, “mountain.” Ovid speaks of it:

> And the ash, useful for spears.

### 40

The yew is a poisonous tree, from which toxic poisons are also extracted. The Parthians and other peoples make bows from it. Hence the poet says:

> The Ityrean yews are bent into bows.

**[Note: By “Ityrean” he means Parthian. These are Servius’s words in that passage.]**

By “Ityrean,” he means Parthian.

### 41

The maple is unequal in its colors.

**[Note: *Robur* is a general term. Servius, on *Aeneid* XII, commenting on “in the midst, the hearths”: “*Robur* means every kind of wood, as well as a particular species.”]**

*Robur* is generally used of anything extremely strong, whatever its material.

### 42

The alder is called *alnus* because it is nourished by a river. It grows close to water and does not easily live outside the waves. Hence it is tender and soft, because it is nourished in a wet place.

### 43

The elm received its name because it thrives better in marshy and damp places. In mountainous and rugged regions it is less flourishing.

### 44

**[Note: The larch, from which it receives this name. From Vitruvius, Book II, chapter 9.]**

The larch was given this name from the town of Laricinum. **[Note: “From it boards attached to roof tiles,” and so forth. From Palladius, in November, section 15.]** Boards made from it and attached to roof tiles repel flame and, when burned, do not themselves produce charcoal.

### 45

The poplar was so called because many shoots arise from its base. There are two kinds: one white and the other black.

The white poplar was so called because its leaves are white on one side and green on the other. Thus, being two-colored, it bears, as it were, the marks of night and day, whose times are determined by sunrise and sunset.

It also produces resin near the river Eridanus, or, as others report, in the regions of Syria. **[Note: “It also produces resin.” Dioscorides calls it *electrum*, Book I, chapter 114.]**

### 46

The linden is said to have been so called because it is useful for making weapons, on account of the brightness and lightness advantageous in throwing. It is a very light kind of wood.

### 47

**[Note: “The willow was so called.” From Servius, on Eclogue 1.]**

The willow was called *salix* because it springs up quickly—that is, grows rapidly. **[Note: “A pliant tree, suitable for binding vines.” From Ambrose, Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 13.]** It is a pliant tree, suitable for tying vines.

Its seed is said to have this property: if someone drinks it in a cup, he becomes childless. **[Note: “So that if someone drinks it in a cup, he is deprived of children.” From Jerome, on Isaiah V. See Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 26.]** It also makes women infertile. **[Note: “But it also makes women infertile.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 437. Pliny says that it is a medicine for female sterility.]**

The poplar, willow, and linden are soft woods and suitable for carving. **[Note: “The poplar, willow, and linden.” From Vitruvius, Book II, chapter 9, and Palladius, in November, section 15.]**

### 48

**[Note: “The osier, because it has strength.” More precisely, as if from *vincimen*, “a binding material.”]**

The osier is called *vimen* because it has great strength of greenness. Its nature is such that even if it is dried and soaked, it becomes green again; then, once cut and fixed in the ground, it sends its roots downward into the soil. **[Note: “Its nature is such … that it sends itself down.” From Hilary, on Psalm 136.]**

### 49

The tamarisk, which the Latins call *myrica*, was named from its bitterness. Its taste is exceedingly bitter.

This tree grows in wilderness and rocky soil. From it, by magical arts, hatred is also said to be stirred up—μισήθρα (*misēthra*), that is, “hatreds.” **[Note: “This tree … provokes hatred.” From Jerome, on Isaiah XVII. These remarks concern the wild tamarisk, not the cultivated kind; there are two species. See Pliny, Theophrastus, and Ambrose.]**

### 50

The myrtle was named from the sea because it is more particularly a coastal tree. Hence Virgil says:

> Shores most luxuriant in myrtle groves,

and:

> Myrtle trees that love the shores.

For this reason it is called μυρίνη (*myrinē*) by the Greeks.

Medical books state that this tree is suitable for many women’s ailments. **[Note: “The books of physicians,” and so forth. From Servius, on *Georgics* II, commenting on “the myrtle of solid Paphian wood.”]**

### 51

The mastic tree was called *lentiscus* because its point is pliant and soft. For we call anything flexible *lentum*. Hence we speak of a pliant osier and pliant vines; Virgil says *lentae vites*, “pliable vines,” meaning flexible.

Oil exudes from its fruit, and resin from its bark; this resin is called mastic. The greatest quantity, and the finest quality, is produced on the island of Chios. **[Note: “From its fruit … is produced.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapters 90 and 91.]**

### 52

The terebinth is a tree with a Greek name, producing the finest of all resins. **[Note: Terebinth. From the following chapter of the same author.]**

### 53

Box is a Greek name partially corrupted by the Latins. The Greeks call it πύξος (*pyxos*). It is an evergreen tree, and its smooth wood is suitable for the letters of writing. **[Note: “And because of the smoothness of its wood … write on boxwood.” From Ambrose, Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 3. The scriptural passage is Isaiah, chapter 30.]** Hence Scripture says:

> Write on boxwood.

### 54

**[Note: *Rhododendron*. Dioscorides, Book IV, chapter 8: “Some call the oleander *rhododaphne*; others call it *rhododendron*.” See Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 2. We call it *adelfa*.]**

The *rhododendron*, which is commonly and corruptly called *lorandrum*, has leaves like those of the laurel and a flower like a rose. It is a poisonous tree, for it kills animals, yet it also cures the afflictions caused by snakes.

### 55

The shepherds called it *herbitum* because it serves the place of grass for livestock where pasture is lacking.

### 56

**[Note: *Turbiscus*. The Greeks call it *thymelea*.]**

The *turbiscus* was so called because many shoots rise from a single clump, like a crowd.

The *stipa* was so called because roofs are thatched with it. Hence the diminutive *stipula*, “straw.”

### 57

The reed was called *arundo* because it quickly dries out. The ancients called it *canna*; Varro later used *arundo*. It should certainly be understood that the Latin word *canna* was taken from the Hebrew language. Among them, a reed is called *canna*.

**[Note: “The cicuta is what is between the joints of reeds,” and so forth. From Servius, on Eclogue 2.]** The *cicuta* is what lies between the joints of reeds. **[Note: “Called so because it is hidden.” Below, chapter 9: “The cicuta is so called because, in its jointed stalk, it has hidden knots like a reed, just as a blind ditch is one that is concealed.”]** It was called *cicuta* because it is hidden.

### 58

Reeds and calami are said to grow in the ponds of India. From their roots a very sweet juice is expressed and drunk. Hence Varro says:

> Indian reed does not grow large upon a tree.  
> Its moisture is pressed from tender roots,  
> To which even sweet honey cannot yield in juice.

### 59

**[Note: *Sambucus*. The Gothic manuscripts have *sabucus*.]**

The elder is a soft and easily penetrated tree.

The buckthorn is a kind of thornbush, commonly called the “bear’s thorn.” It is extremely rough and thorny.

### 60

**[Note: “The thornbush was named from *situs*.” He is playing on Virgil’s words, “through places rough with neglect,” *Aeneid* VI.]**

The thornbush was called *sentix* from *situs*, meaning uncultivated ground in which thornbushes and thorns grow. Our ancestors called every thorny tree a *vepres*, because it seizes one with its force.

### 61

The wild olive was called *oleaster* because its leaves resemble those of the olive, though they are broader. It is an uncultivated and wild tree, bitter and fruitless. When an olive branch is grafted onto it, the branch changes the power of the root and transforms the tree into its own nature.

The tear of the wild olive tree is of two kinds. One resembles gum without any biting quality; the other is a drop of ammoniacum gathered by dripping and having a sharp, irritating effect. **[Note: The tear of the wild olive. From Dioscorides.]**

### 62

The olive is called ἔλαιος (*elaios*) in Greek, from which the Latin word *oliva* was derived. **[Note: The olive itself is the tree, the *oliva* its fruit, and *oleum* its juice. From Servius; “the trunks of the olive trees” is the better reading, *Georgics* II.]**

The *olea* is the tree itself, the *oliva* the fruit, and *oleum* the juice. It is the emblem of peace, and its fruit is called by various names.

### 63

**[Note: *Orchades*. I have also found *orchades* in old manuscripts of Virgil, not the common reading *orchites*, as Pierius has pointed out.]**

The *orchades* received their Greek etymology from their resemblance to testicles, which the Greeks call ὄρχεις (*orcheis*).

### 64

**[Note: *Radiolae*. Virgil says:

> *Orchites and radii, and the bitter berry of the Pausia.*

Columella calls it *radiolum* in Book XII, chapter 47, to distinguish it, I believe, from the larger *radius*. Cato, chapter 6, mentions the latter: “In rich, warm soil, plant the preserving olive, the greater *radius*, the Salentina, and the *orchites*.”]**

The *radiolae* were so called because they are elongated in the manner of spokes.

The *Paphiae* were named from the island of Paphos, from which they were first brought.

### 65

**[Note: *Liciniae*. Pliny mentions *liciniae* in Book XV, chapter 2.]**

The *lyciniae* were so called because they give excellent light. For λύχνος (*lychnos*) means “light.” Hence the name *lychnum* was also given to them, because they are suitable for flames and lights.

### 66

The *pausia*, which country people corruptly call *pusia*, is suitable for green and sweet oil. **[Note: “And called *pausia*.” From Servius.]** It was called *pausia* because it is beaten—that is, pounded; hence also the word *pavimentum*, “pavement.”

### 67

The *syria* was so called because it was brought from Syria, or because it is black.

**[Note: “The Crustumian and the Vole­mian as well.” These are kinds of pears placed here among the olives because Isidore, as we said, used Servius’s commentaries without Virgil’s poems; this often led him astray. Anyone who examines Servius’s passage will easily see that this is so.]**

The Crustumians are also called Volemians because they fill the palm of the hand in size—that is, the middle of the hand. Hence we also say *involare*, “to fill the hand.” Some understand *volemum* in the Gallic language to mean “good and large.”

**[Note: “The Colymbades were called,” and so forth. From Pliny, Columella, and Athenaeus; the lacuna can easily be supplied.]**

The Colymbades were called [lacuna].

### 68

Oil is named from the olive. For, as we have said, the *olea* is the tree from which the word *oleum* is derived. **[Note: “The *olea* is the tree, from which *oleum* is derived.” These are Servius’s words.]**

Oil pressed from white olives is called Hispanic oil, and by the Greeks ὀμφάκιον (*omphakion*). **[Note: “But what is pressed from white olives is called …” Pliny, Book XII, chapter 7: “*Omphacion* is pressed from an olive that is still white; oil from the *drupa* is inferior. It is so called before the fruit is ripe for eating, although it is already changing color; the distinction is that the former is green, the latter white. Concerning Hispanic oil, Galen, Book VI of *Simple Medicines*, says: “If oil, when tasted, has something constricting about it, it is considered cold, such as that brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish, that is, Hispanic.” Aurelianus also frequently mentions Hispanic oil, for example in Book III of *Chronic Diseases*, chapter 2.]**

Oil pressed from yellowish olives that are not yet soft is called green oil. That pressed from olives that are excessively ripe is called common oil. Of these, for ordinary use, the first is Hispanic oil, the second green oil, and the third common oil.

69. [Note: [Col. 0620C] “Amurca” is named from “emerging.” Servius: *amurca* is written with *c* but pronounced with *g*.] Amurca is the watery part of oil, named from “emerging,” that is, because it rises out of the oil and is its dregs. The Greeks call it *amorgen*, deriving the word from the Latin language.

[Col. 0619C] 342. 70. Gum is a Greek word; for this is what they call it, **κόμμι** (*kommi*).

71. The Greeks call resin **ῥητίνη** (*rhētinē*), for in Greek **ῥέον** (*rheon*) means whatever flows. It is the tear exhaled as sweat by trees—such as the cherry, mastic, balsam, and other trees or shrubs that are said to sweat—as well as by the fragrant trees of the East. Such are the drop of balsam, the resin of ferulas, and amber, whose tear hardens into a gem. [Note: [Col. 0620D] The first is terebinth resin, etc. From Dioscorides, Book I, chapters 91, 92, and 95.] The first and finest of all is terebinth resin. [Col. 0620A] It is brought from Arabia Petraea, Judaea, Syria, Cyprus, and Africa, and also from the Cycladic islands. The second is mastic resin, which is called *mastic*; it is brought from the island of Chios. The third is pine resin. Of this, one kind is **πιτυΐνη** (*pituinē*), another **πευκίνη** (*peukinē*), another liquid, and another dry; these are brought from Tyrrhenian Colophon. Hence the resin also took the name “Colophonian.”

72. Pitch is a Greek word; they call it **πίσσα** (*pissa*). Some hold that pitch is so called from the pine; [Note: [Col. 0620D] This is called *clonia* by the Greeks. Thus the text in Dioscorides, chapter 95, is corrupt: **Πίσσα ἡ μὲν ὑγρὰ, ἣν ἔνιοι κῶνον καλοῦσι**, which should read **κλῶνον**.] this is called *clonia* by the Greeks. We may call it “branch-pitch,” whose good quality is that it is shining, smooth, and clean. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “Good” means shining, smooth, and clean. Dioscorides: “The good kind is shining, smooth, and clean.”]

73. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “The nature of trees that are to be created” … From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “In the beginning, trees.”] There are naturally three kinds of trees that come into being: some grow of their own accord; some rise from seeds accidentally scattered; and some sprout from roots. Everything else has been discovered by human use, with nature’s assistance.

[Col. 0620B] 74. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “All fruits … composed wood.” From the same source, on Virgil, *Aeneid* II, “With bitter leaves the wild olive.” Some corrections to Isidore’s text are required.] All fruits are said in Latin to be of the neuter gender; trees, however, are of the feminine gender, except for a few, such as *hic oleaster*, “this wild olive,” and *hoc siler*, “this willow,” as Virgil says: “The pliant willow.” Likewise *hoc buxum*, “boxwood,” although *haec buxus*, “the box tree,” is also said. Some people unnecessarily insist on making a distinction, so that *haec buxus* refers to the tree, but *buxum* to wood that has been fashioned.

343. **CHAPTER VIII. On aromatic trees**

1. [Note: [Col. 0620D] Aromatics are fragrant substances brought from India … “Whatever” means “anything whatsoever.”] Aromatics are all things of fragrant odor that India, Arabia, or other regions send us. They seem to have acquired the name *aromata* either because, placed upon altars, they appear suitable for divine invocations, or because they are observed to enter and mingle with the air. For what is scent except air that has been touched?

[Col. 0620C] 2. Frankincense is a tree of Arabia, enormous and branching, with very smooth bark and branches resembling those of the maple. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “With branches resembling the quality of the maple,” etc. From Solinus, chapter 46.] Like the almond, it pours out an aromatic, white sap, which by chewing is reduced as if to powder; [Note: [Col. 0620D] “When it is broken, it is fatty within.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 82.] when broken, it is fatty within and readily catches fire when placed on the fire. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “And among us it is called male.” From Pliny, Book XII, chapter 14.] Among us it is called “male,” because by nature it is round, like testicles. The remainder is flat and almost rough, and of inferior quality. [Note: [Col. 0620D] “It is adulterated by admixture,” etc. From Dioscorides, in the same place.] It is adulterated by the addition of resin or gum, but it can be recognized by its characteristic properties. When frankincense is placed on the fire, it burns; resin smokes; but gum melts when heated.

3. [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Frankincense,” without aspiration. From Servius, on “The soft Sabine frankincense,” *Georgics* II. [Col. 0621D]] Frankincense (*thus*) is said to derive its name from *tundere*, “to pound,” because when drops of gum fall from the tree, they become mixed with clods of earth. When the clods are reduced to powder, the frankincense is gathered and pounded with small sticks, and is then taken up by hand. It is also called “Lebanon,” from the mountain of Arabia where the Sabaeans live. Their mountain is called Lebanon, and frankincense is collected there.

4. [Note: [Col. 0621D] Myrrh: an Arabian tree, five cubits high … From Solinus.] Myrrh is an Arabian tree five cubits high, [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Like a thorn, which they call **ἄκανθος**.” Servius, *Georgics* II: “Acanthus is a tree in Egypt that is always green. It is called **ἄκανθος** because it is full of thorns.”] resembling the thorn that they call **ἄκανθος** (*akanthos*). Its drop is green and bitter, [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Hence it also received its name.” For *myrrh* derives from a Hebrew word, as do *cinnamon*, *nard*, and *saffron*; *agallochum*, or aloe, according to Jerome, likewise.] and from this it received the name *myrrh*. [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Its drop, flowing spontaneously.” From Solinus.] Its spontaneously flowing drop is more valuable; that extracted by cutting the bark is judged inferior. The Arabs feed its branches to fires, and from the highly harmful smoke—unless storax is burned to counteract it—they often contract incurable diseases. [Col. 0621B] [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Troglodytic myrrh.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 180; but perhaps *sinu* should be read instead of *insula*, “island.”] Troglodytic myrrh is named from an Arabian island where a better and purer kind is gathered.

5. [Note: [Col. 0621D] Storax, an Arabian tree. Donatus, on *Adelphoe* I.1: “Storax,” he says, “is named from its fragrance.” The same word occurs in Solinus. Pliny and others have *styrax*.] Storax is an Arabian tree, [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Like a Cydonian apple.” From Dioscorides, chapter 80; Pliny XII.25: “resembling a quince.”] resembling a Cydonian apple. Its small branches, around the rising of the Dog Star, release tears through openings in the bark. Its distillation, falling onto the ground, is not pure; but when it is collected in a hollow of its own bark, it is pure. That which adheres to the branches and reeds is clean and whitish; afterward it becomes tawny from the sun. This is storax calamites: fatty, resinous, pleasantly scented, moist, and emitting something like a honeyed liquid. Storax is so called because it is a flowing and congealed drop of a tree. For the Greeks call a drop *stiria*; the Greek **στύραξ** (*styrax*) is called *storax* in Latin.

[Col. 0621C] 6. [Note: [Col. 0621D] Bdellium. See Dioscorides, chapter 81.] Bdellium is a tree of India and Arabia, whose tear is better when Arabian. It is bright, somewhat whitish, smooth, and fatty, [Note: [Col. 0622C] “Equally waxy,” that is, waxy throughout. Pliny says: “It should be translucent and resemble wax.” [Col. 0622D]] uniformly waxy, easily softened, and, when not mixed with wood or earth, bitter and of good odor. The Indian kind is dirty, black, and in larger lumps. It is adulterated by the addition of gum, which does not make the taste equally bitter.

7. [Note: [Col. 0622D] Mastic. From Dioscorides, chapter 91.] Mastic is the drop of the mastic tree. It is called *granomastic*, because it is in the form of grains. The finest grows on the island of Chios; it has a good odor and [Note: [Col. 0622D] “The whiteness of Punic wax.” Dioscorides has “Tyrrhenian wax,” but this may perhaps derive from Pliny, who says that Punic wax is made extremely white.] the whiteness of Punic wax. Hence it also beautifies the brightness of the skin. It is sometimes adulterated with resin or frankincense.

8. [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Resemblance of the pepper …” From Solinus, his chapter on India.] The pepper tree grows in India and on the side of Mount Caucasus that faces the sun, with leaves resembling those of the juniper. Its forests are guarded by serpents, but when the pepper has ripened, the inhabitants of that region set them on fire. The serpents are driven away by the fire, and black pepper is produced from the flames. By nature pepper is white, [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Its fruit, however, is of different kinds.” From the same source.] but its fruit is of various kinds. The unripe kind is called long pepper; that which remains unaffected by the fire is white pepper; but that which has a wrinkled and rough skin takes both its color and its name from the heat of the fire. If pepper is light, it is old; if heavy, it is new. The fraud of merchants must be avoided: they commonly sprinkle very old pepper with moistened silver dross, or with lead, so that it becomes heavy.

9. Aloe grows in India and Arabia. It is a tree of exceedingly pleasant and noble fragrance. Finally, its wood is burned on altars in place of incense, [Col. 0622B] [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Hence it is also believed to have taken its name.” Or perhaps because the Greek **ἅλως** means “enclosed ground,” and “altar” was read for “enclosed ground” in the glosses, either by Isidore or—more probably—by the person who added these words to his work.] and it is believed to have taken its name from this use.

10. Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender, like a reed. It grows in the regions of India and Ethiopia, as a short shrub only two cubits high, darkish or ash-colored, with extremely slender branches. [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Whatever extends in thickness … is inferior;” from Solinus, chapter 43. See Theophrastus, *History of Plants* IX.5.] Whatever grows to considerable thickness is despised; whatever grows more slender is excellent. When it is broken, it emits a visible breath resembling a cloud or dust.

11. Amomum is so called because it seems to reproduce the fragrance of cinnamon. It grows in Syria and Armenia. [Note: [Col. 0622D] “Its shrub produces clustered seed.” From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 14.] Its shrub produces clustered seed joined together, [Col. 0622C] with a white flower like the violet and leaves resembling those of bryony; it also has a good fragrance and sweetens sleep.

12. [Note: [Col. 0622D] Cassia. From the same source, chapter 12.] Cassia grows in Arabia. It is a branch with thick bark and purple leaves, like those of pepper. Its properties resemble those of cinnamon, but it is less powerful; therefore twice its weight is added to medicines in place of cinnamon.

13. [Note: [Col. 0622D] Aromatic reed. From chapter 17.] Aromatic reed is so called from its resemblance to the ordinary reed. It grows in India, yellow, fragrant, and jointed with many nodes. When broken, it can be split into many pieces, and in taste it resembles cassia with a slight, biting sharpness.

14. [Note: [Col. 0622D] The balsam tree. From Solinus, chapter 48.] The balsam tree once existed in Judaea only within an area of twenty *jugera*. After the Romans gained possession of that region, it was propagated over very extensive hills. Its stem resembles a vine, [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Its leaves resemble rue, but are whiter and always remain.” From Dioscorides, chapter 18.] and its leaves resemble rue, though they are whiter and evergreen. [Note: [Col. 0623C] “The tree, however, is balsam.” From Servius, *Georgics* II.] The tree is called balsam; its wood is called *xylobalsamum*; its fruit or seed, *carpobalsamum*; and its sap, [Note: [Col. 0623C] *Opobalsamum*. This is marked by the added prefix because of what follows. [Col. 0623D] From Hegesippus IV.17.] *opobalsamum*. It is designated with this prefix [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Because, when struck with iron claws …” Dioscorides and Theophrastus say this. Pliny gives a better version: “It hates injury to its vital parts by iron.” Tacitus, *Histories* V: “If you apply the force of iron, the veins shrink.” Hegesippus I: “It grows upon shrubs that the farmers’ boys cut with sharp stones.”] because, when the tree’s bark is struck with iron claws, it distills through openings a drop of exceptional fragrance; for an opening is called **ὀπή** (*opē*) in Greek. Its drop is adulterated by adding Cyprian oil or honey. Genuine balsam is distinguished from honey if it coagulates with milk, and from oil if, when dropped into or mixed with water, it is readily dissolved; furthermore, if woolen garments soiled with it are not stained. The adulterated kind does not coagulate with milk; like oil, it floats on water and stains clothing. [Col. 0623B] [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Balsams, if they are pure.” From Servius, *Georgics* II, on “What shall I tell you of fragrant …?”] If balsams are pure, they possess such power that, when the sun has become scorching, they cannot be held in the hand.

**CHAPTER IX. On aromatic or common herbs**

1. There are also the names of certain herbs that echo some characteristic of themselves and thus contain an explanation of their names. You will not, however, find the etymology of every herb, for names also change according to place.

2. [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Folium,” etc. From Dioscorides, Book I, chapter 11.] *Folium* is so called because it is gathered floating without any root along the shores of India. The Indians pierce it with a thread of linen, dry it, and store it. It is said to be a herb of Paradise, with a taste resembling nard.

348. 3. [Note: [Col. 0623D] Nard. From the same source, chapter 6.] Nard is a spiked herb, and therefore is called by the Greeks **ναρδόσταχυς** (*nardostachys*). One kind is called Indian, another Syrian—not because it grows in Syria, but because the mountain where it is found faces India on one side and Syria on the other. The Indian kind is of many forms, but the Syrian is better: light, tawny, tufted, with a small, extremely fragrant spike, resembling cyperus. If it remains in the mouth for a long time, it dries the tongue. Celtic nard takes its name from a region of Gaul. It grows more often in the Alps of Liguria, [Note: [Col. 0623D] “And in Syria.” I would read *Istria*, from Dioscorides, chapter 7.] and in Syria, as a small shrub whose roots are gathered into a bundle with bindings. Only its flower is prized for its fragrance. Its clusters and little roots are considered useful for our purposes.

[Col. 0624A] 4. [Note: [Col. 0623D] Costus. From chapter 15.] Costus is the root of a herb growing in India, Arabia, and Syria, though the Arabian kind is better. It is white, smooth, and of a sweet, pleasant fragrance. The Indian kind is dark in color and light, like a ferula; the Syrian is heavy, box-colored, and sharply scented, yet the finest is white, light, dry, and burning to the taste.

5. [Note: [Col. 0623D] Saffron is named from a town. From Servius, *Georgics* I, on “The saffron fragrances of Tmolus.”] Saffron is named from a town in Cilicia called Corycium, although it also grows elsewhere, but not in such quantity or of such quality as in Cilicia. Hence it took its name from the superior region. Many things have taken their names from places where they occur more abundantly and in better quality. [Note: [Col. 0623D] “The finest, however,” etc. From Dioscorides.] The finest saffron is fresh, pleasantly fragrant, slightly whitish, elongated, whole rather than broken into pieces, of good inhalation, [Note: [Col. 0623D] “And when it is gathered, staining the hand.” Dioscorides: **Βάπτων ἐν πιέσει τὰς χεῖρας**, that is, “staining the hands by its moisture.” [Col. 0624C]] staining the hand when gathered, and slightly sharp. If it is not of this sort, it is recognized as old [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Or soaked.” Dioscorides: **βεβρεγμένος**, that is, “diluted.”] or soaked. It is adulterated by the addition of saffron residue. Crushed silver dross is also added to increase its weight; this is exposed if it is found to be powdery, [Note: [Col. 0624C] “And boiled.” That is, reduced like fruit syrup. Dioscorides: **Καὶ τὸ τὴν ὀσμὴν ἐψηματώδη τυγχάνειν**. Those who substitute “boiled” here do not sufficiently understand what “boiling” means.] and if, having been boiled, it has lost its natural fragrance.

349. 6. [Note: [Col. 0624D] Saffron residue. Dioscorides, chapter 26, and Pliny XXI.20.] Saffron residue is made from the aromatic substances pressed out of saffron perfume and from the sediment formed into little pieces of cloth; hence it is so called.

7. [Note: [Col. 0624D] Asarum. From Dioscorides, chapter 9.] Asarum grows on shady mountains. [Note: [Col. 0624D] “With leaves resembling cassia.” Rather, resembling ivy. Dioscorides: “Having leaves like ivy.” Pliny XII.13 likewise says “with ivy leaves.” Thus the old translator of Dioscorides, whom Isidore used, seems to have read **cassia** for **ivy**.] Among its leaves is a purple flower near the root, containing seed like grapes. It has many very slender roots, pleasantly fragrant, and its properties resemble those of nard.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Phu. From Dioscorides, chapter 10. Pliny XII.11.] Phu grows in Pontus, with leaves resembling those of the wild olive.

[Col. 0624C] 8. Cyperus is called by the Greeks by this name because it possesses a heated potency. [Note: [Col. 0624D] “It is the root of triangular rush.” Dioscorides applies this description to the stalk: **Καυλὸν γωνιώδη**, “a stalk with angles.”] Its root belongs to the triangular rush; its leaves resemble those of a leek, and its roots are black—or contiguous—and, resembling olives, are extremely fragrant and very pungent. It grows in marshes [Note: [Col. 0624D] “And in empty places.” In contrast, Dioscorides says **ἐν τόποις ἐργασίμοις**, “in cultivated places.” Thus the translator probably erred by reading **ἀργοῖς**, or perhaps **ἀργοσίμοις**.] and deserted places. Another species of cyperus is also said to grow in India and is called in their language *gingiber*.

9. [Note: [Col. 0624D] Illyrian iris. From Dioscorides, chapter 1.] Illyrian iris took its name from its resemblance to the heavenly rainbow. Hence the Latins call it *arcumen*, because the varying colors of its flower imitate that same celestial arc. It is called Illyrian because it is especially abundant and vigorous in Illyria. Its species has leaves resembling those of the gladiolus and an aromatic, pleasantly fragrant root.

10. [Note: [Col. 0625C] Sweet flag. From chapter 2.] Sweet flag has leaves resembling those of the iris and roots of extremely pungent taste, [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Of very pungent taste but pleasant fragrance.” The word “taste” was absent from all manuscripts and has been restored from Dioscorides, who says: **Δρυμίας τῇ γεύσει, καὶ τῇ ὀσμῇ οὐκ ἀηδής**, “pungent in taste and not unpleasant in fragrance.” Pliny likewise says: “Sharp in taste, not unpleasant in odor.”] but of pleasant fragrance; hence it too is aromatic.

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Meu … See Dioscorides, chapter 3.] Meu …

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Cardamom … The same source, chapter 5, and Book II, chapter 185.] Cardamom …

350. 11. [Note: [Col. 0625C] The better schoenus. See Dioscorides, chapter 6. He gives first place to Nabataean schoenus and second to Arabian schoenus, saying that the Libyan kind is useless. The rest agrees.] Squinum—the kind that grows by the Euphrates is better than that of Arabia—is tawny, many-flowered, purple, slender, and rose-scented. When rubbed in the hand, it greatly burns and bites the tongue in taste. Its [Note: [Col. 0625D] “The flower of schoenus is *schoenantos*.” *Squinantos* occurs in Palladius, October, title 14. Aurelianus uses it more than once in a corrupt form, though perhaps that was how it was pronounced and written at the time.] flower is called **σχίνανθος** (*schinanthos*). For **ἄνθος** (*anthos*) is the Greek word for “flower.”

12. Thyme is so called because its flower reproduces its fragrance. Virgil says of it: “And the fragrant honey smells of thyme.”

13. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Epithymum. Dioscorides IV.179: **ἐπίθυμον θύμον ἐστὶν ἄνθος**, “epithymum is a flower of thyme.” See Pliny XXVI.8.] Epithymum is a Greek name, which in Latin means “flower of thyme.” For in Greek the flower is called *thymum*. It resembles the flower of savory.

14. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Sampsuchus. This form also occurs in Aurelianus and Hesychius; others use *sampsuchum*.] Sampsuchus is what the Latins call *amaracus*. Referring this name also to Venus, Virgil says:

> Where the soft amaracus, breathing  
> among the flowers and with sweet shade, embraces him.

This herb is suitable for perfumes. [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Hence it also took the name *amaracus*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Where the soft amaracus …”] It is said to have taken the name *amaracus* from a boy of a certain king, who, having accidentally fallen while carrying perfumes, created a new and very pleasing fragrance through their mixture.

15. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Hyacinth. Servius, *Eclogues* 3, and Ovid, Book X.] Hyacinth is a herb with a purple flower. It took its name from a certain noble boy [Col. 0625C] who was found slain among purple flowers in the woods; thus the accident of the boy’s death gave the herb its name. [Note: [Col. 0625D] “It has the root and flower of a bulb.” See Dioscorides IV.63.] It has a root and flower resembling those of a bulb, and restrains boys from puberty.

[Col. 0626A] 16. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Narcissus. Ovid, Book III.] Narcissus has a name assigned to it by a fable, from a certain boy whose limbs were transformed into this flower. It preserves the name Narcissus in its designation and retains the beauty of his appearance [Note: [Col. 0625D] “In the whiteness of its leaves.” Rather, of its flowers, unless “leaves of flowers” is understood, as shortly afterward with lilies, from Ambrose, whose text says that whiteness is in the leaves. Dioscorides says: “A white flower.”] in the whiteness of its leaves.

17. The rose is named from the appearance of its flower, because it glows red with a radiant color.

18. The lily is a herb with a milk-white flower, and hence it is so named, [Note: [Col. 0625D] “As if *liclia*.” Other manuscripts: “as if *liglia*.”] as if *liclia*, [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Although there is whiteness in the leaves … it shines forth.” These words are from Ambrose, *Hexameron* III.8.] although, while its leaves are white, the appearance of gold shines forth within.

19. [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Violet, because of the force of its fragrance.” All manuscripts read *doloris*, “of pain,” except the Roman manuscript; this is evidently an error. Ambrose says: “In them you would not know whether the beauty of the flowers or the power of their fragrance gives greater pleasure.”] The violet took its name from the power of its fragrance. [Note: [Col. 0626C] “It has three kinds.” Dioscorides lists four: **λευκόν** (*leukon*, white), **μήλινον** (*mēlinon*, yellow), **κυανοῦν** (*kyanoun*, blue), and **πορφυροῦν** (*porphyroun*, purple). Pliny lists three: purple, yellow, and white.] It has three kinds: purple, white, and yellow.

20. [Note: [Col. 0626C] Acanthus. This passage is compounded from three passages of Servius: *Georgics* II, *Aeneid* I, and *Eclogue* 4.] Acanthus is an Egyptian herb that is always green, full of thorns, and has a pliant stalk.

[Col. 0626B] 21. In imitation of it, a garment is ornamented by art; it is called *acanthine* and also *acanthis*.

22. [Note: [Col. 0626C] Ivy. Festus: “Ivy is so called because it clings, or because it seeks elevated places, or because it consumes whatever it has attached itself to.”] Ivy is so called because it clings to trees by creeping over them. Virgil speaks of it:

> Among the victorious laurels, let ivy creep for you.

Others say that ivy was called so [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Because it was given to young goats in abundance beyond milk as food,” etc. Columella VII.6, concerning young goats: “Once they have been born, they are raised in the same manner as lambs, except that the greater playfulness of young goats must be restrained and checked more strictly; then, in addition to an abundance of milk, foliage, or cytisus, or ivy must be provided.”] because in ancient times it was offered as food to young goats in addition to their abundant milk.

23. [Note: [Col. 0626D] “Ivy indicates cold earth.” From Servius, *Georgics* II: “Black ivy reveals its traces.”] According to the natural philosophers, ivy indicates cold earth. It is also an antidote to drunkenness, if a drinker is crowned with ivy.

24. They say that hellebore grows abundantly in Greece around a certain river called Helleborus, and that the Greeks named it from this. The Romans call it by another name, *veratrum*, because when it is taken, it restores a disturbed mind to health. There are two kinds, [Note: [Col. 0626D] White and black. What follows in certain printed editions is absent from all manuscripts. It is, however, taken from Ambrose, *Hexameron* III.9. We therefore reproduce it here: “Experts say that this is food and nourishment for quails, because by a certain natural tempering of their bodies they avoid the force of harmful food …,” and so on up to “health.”] white [Col. 0626C] and black.

25. [Note: [Col. 0626D] Acone is a harbor of Bithynia, famous for the abundance of harmful grasses. From Solinus, chapter 55.] Acone is a harbor of Bithynia so famous for the growth of harmful plants that we call poisonous herbs *aconites* from that place. [Note: [Col. 0626D] “For toxic poisons are named from it.” Pliny XVI.10: “There are also those who say that *taxica* is the source of the name for poisons, which we now call *toxica*.”] For *toxic* poisons are so called because they are extracted from yew trees, especially in Cantabria.

26. [Note: [Col. 0627C] Euphorbium is so named. Isidore, I think, did not wish to recall the etymology, and here, as often elsewhere, something was added by Braulio, or rather by later writers. Pliny thinks it took its name from Euphorbus, physician to King Juba.] Euphorbium is so called because its sap sharpens the sight of the eyes. Its power is so great that, when placed upon tough meat, it compels it to cook more quickly. It grows in many places, but most abundantly in Mauretania.

27. [Note: [Col. 0627C] Laser is a herb native to Mount Oscobagi, or, in another reading, Osabagi. We have never been able to advance beyond conjecture as to which mountain this is.] Laser grows on Mount Oscobagi, where the river Ganges also rises. [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Its sap was first called *lacsir*.” Solinus, chapter 40: “It was first called *lac sirpicum*, because it flows in a milky manner; afterward, through ordinary usage, it was called *laser*.” Columella VI says: ‘The root that the Greeks call *silphion*, common usage in our language calls *laserpitium*.’ *Laserpitium* appears to have been different from *sirpe*. Plautus, in *Rudens*: ‘I ask and beg you, if you hope to have much *sirpe* and *laserpitium* this year.’ See Pliny XIX.3.] Its sap was first called *lacsir*, because it flows like milk; afterward, by a shift in usage, it was called *laser*. This is what some call Cyrenaic opium, since it also grows around Cyrene.

353. 28. [Note: [Col. 0627D] Aloe, an herb with a bitter sap. Dioscorides III.25.] Aloe is an herb with an exceedingly bitter sap.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Panaces. From Dioscorides III.55.] Panaces is an herb of fragrant odor, with a cluster resembling that of a ferula. From it flows a sap called *opopanax*, [Col. 0627B] saffron-colored and fatty, strongly scented, and extremely bitter.

Galbanum is the sap of a ferula.

29. Dicte is a mountain of Crete, from which the herb dittany took its name. Because of it, Virgil says that a wounded hind traverses the Dictaean woods. Its power is so great that it drives iron from the body and casts out arrows; hence wild animals struck by arrows, when they eat it, eject the arrows lodged in their bodies. [Note: [Col. 0627D] Some Latins call this *poleium*. Pliny XX.14.] Some Latins call it *poleium of Mars*, because it casts out weapons of war.

30. [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Mandrake is so called because …” Here too the author did not consider the true etymology.] Mandrake is so called because it has sweet-smelling fruits the size of a Matian apple. [Note: [Col. 0627D] “Hence the Latins call it ‘earth-apple.’” Dioscorides: “The Romans call it *mala canina*, ‘dog apples’; others call it *mala terrestria*, ‘earth apples.’”] Hence the Latins call it “earth-apple.” [Note: [Col. 0628C] “The poets call this *anthropomorphon*.” Columella imitated them: “Although, pregnant with the mad grass of the half-human mandrake, it produces flowers and gloomy hemlock.”] The poets call it **ἀνθρωπόμορφον** (*anthropomorphon*), because its root imitates the form of a human being. [Col. 0627C] [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Its bark, mixed with wine.” From Dioscorides IV.76.] Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink by those whose bodies must be cut open for medical treatment, so that, being rendered drowsy, they do not feel the pain. It has two species: the female, with leaves resembling lettuce, [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Producing fruits resembling plums.” Dioscorides: “Fruits resembling service berries.” [Col. 0628D]] producing fruits resembling plums; and the male, with leaves resembling those of beet.

31. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Poppy. Dioscorides IV.65.] The poppy is a sleep-inducing herb. Virgil speaks of it: “Poppies drenched in Lethean sleep.” For it produces torpor in the weakened. One kind is cultivated; another is wild, from which flows [Note: [Col. 0628D] “The sap called opium.” So Pliny XX.18. Dioscorides: **τὸν ὀπόν**, “the sap.”] the sap called opium.

[Col. 0628A] 32. Colocynth is a wild gourd, exceedingly bitter, which stretches its runners across the ground in the same way as a gourd. [Note: [Col. 0628D] “It is called colocynth because it has a round fruit.” There is no need here to linger over the etymology. Dioscorides: “A round fruit, like a small sphere, exceedingly bitter.”] It is called colocynth because its fruit is round and its leaves resemble those of the ordinary cucumber.

33. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Centaury. From Dioscorides III.9 and Pliny XXV.6.] The Greeks call it centaury because it is said to have been discovered by the Centaur Chiron. It is also called **λιμνήσιος** (*limnēsios*), “marsh-growing,” because it grows in moist places. It is also called “gall of the earth” because of its bitterness.
