34. Licorice is called **γλυκύρριζα** (*glykyrhiza*) in Greek because it has a sweet root; for the Greeks call sweet **γλυκύ** (*glykу*). It is also called **ἄδιψος** (*adipsos*), because it quenches the thirst of those who are thirsty.

35. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Dracontea. From the same source, Book II, chapter 196.] Dracontea is so called because its stalk is variegated like a serpent and imitates the likeness of a dragon, or because the viper fears this herb.

36. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Chelidonia. From the same source, Book II, chapter 211.] Chelidonia is so called either because it seems to burst forth with the arrival of swallows, [Col. 0628B] or because, if the eyes of young swallows are removed, their mothers are said to heal them with this herb.

355. 37. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Heliotrope. See Dioscorides IV.193 and Pliny XXII.21.] Heliotrope first received its name because it flowers at the summer solstice, or because its leaves turn around with the movements of the sun. Hence the Latins call it *solisequia*, “sun-follower.” At sunrise it opens its flowers; likewise, it opens them when the sun has set. It is the plant that the Latins call wild endive. [Note: [Col. 0628D] “It is also called *verrucaria*.” See Pliny.] It is also called *verrucaria*, because, drunk in water, it removes warts, or, applied as a poultice, wipes them away.

38. [Note: [Col. 0628D] *Pentaphyllon*. From Dioscorides IV.42.] *Pentaphyllon* is named from the number of its leaves; hence the Latins call it “five-leaf.” It is such a clean herb that the pagans were accustomed to use it for purification and in temples.

[Col. 0628C] 39. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Hyssop, an herb for cleansing the lungs, etc. From Augustine, on Psalm 50.] Hyssop is an herb suitable for cleansing the lungs. Hence, in the Old Testament, the blood of the lamb was sprinkled with bunches of hyssop upon the person who wished to be cleansed. It grows clinging to rocks, with its roots fixed in stone.

40. [Note: [Col. 0628D] Rhubarb. See Dioscorides III.2.] Rhubarb, or *rheuponticum*, derives its name as follows: the former is gathered beyond the Danube, in barbarian territory; the latter is collected around Pontus. *Rheu* means “root.” Thus *rheubarbarum* means “barbarian root,” while *rheuponticum* means “Pontic root.”

[Col. 0629A] 41. The Greeks call it *hyoscyamos*; the Latins call it “cup herb,” because its capsules grow in the shape of cups, like the fruit of the pomegranate, [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Whose rims are serrated.” Dioscorides. See other sources.] whose rims are serrated and which contain seeds resembling those of the poppy. This herb is also called “insane,” because its use is dangerous. If it is drunk or eaten, it causes insanity or the torpid semblance of sleep. The common people call it *milimindrum*, because it produces mental derangement.

42. Saxifrage is so called because its seed breaks and crushes stones in the bladder.

Gentian, as the physicians report, took its name from its discoverer. Its roots resemble those of aristolochia. It grows beneath the Alps and in Galatia of Asia.

Savory is hot and almost fiery. Hence they believe it was given its name because it inclines people toward Venus.

[Col. 0629B] 43. [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Which the common people call *stingum*.” F. reads *scind cum*. See Dioscorides III.135 and Pliny XXVIII.28.] Satyrion is named from the satyrs because of the inflammation of lust. The common people call it *stingum*; for it arouses Venus. It is also called *orchis*, because its root is shaped like testicles, which the Greeks call **ὄρχεις** (*orcheis*). It is also called “hare’s herb,” because it sends up a soft stalk.

44. Nettle is so called because its touch burns the body. It is entirely of a fiery nature and burns upon contact; hence it also causes itching.

45. [Note: [Col. 0629D] Mugwort. Pliny XXV.7.] Mugwort was consecrated by the pagans to Diana, and hence received its name. For in Greek Diana is called **ἄρτεμις** (*Artemis*).

46. [Note: [Col. 0629D] Chamomile. Dioscorides III.154.] Chamomile is so called in Greek because it has the scent of the Matian apple and is short, lying close to the ground.

[Col. 0629C] 47. Germander is called **chamaedrys** by the Greeks because it is short, spread along the ground, and small, with very small leaves.

48. [Note: [Col. 0629D] Peony. The same source, chapter 157, and Pliny XXV.4.] Paeon was a certain physician, from whom the herb peony is said to have been discovered, as Homer says. Some call it *glycyside*, because it has a sweet taste; others call it *pentorobos*, from the number of its grains; others call it *dactylosa*, because of its resemblance to fingers. It grows in woods.

49. Borage is called **buglossos** by the Greeks because it has extremely rough leaves shaped like an ox’s tongue. [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Which, remarkably, is to be infused in wine for nourishing wisdom,” etc. The meaning is “for cheerfulness”; thus Pliny rendered the **εὐφροσύνη** (“joy”) found in Dioscorides.] The ancients are said to have infused it in wine for the nourishment of wisdom. It is also said to provide convivial cheerfulness. It is used as a vegetable as well.

50. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Arnoglossos*. Dioscorides II.153.] *Arnoglossos*, that is, “lamb’s tongue,” is called *plantago* by the Romans because its sole quickly clings to [Col. 0630A] the earth. Many people eat it as a vegetable.

51. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Herpyllus*. See Servius, *Eclogue* 2.] *Herpyllus*, which among us is called *serpillum*, is so named because its roots creep far and wide. It is also called *matrisanimula*, “little soul of the mother,” because it causes menstruation.

52. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Aristoloch.* Pliny, XXV, chapter 8, and Dioscorides III, chapters 4 and 5.] Aristolochia is so called because it is especially beneficial to women in childbirth. For, applied after delivery, it cleanses the womb by the action of its vapor. There are two kinds of this herb: one is called round aristolochia because it has a round root; the other, long aristolochia, because it has a long root, with longer branches and leaves. It is also called *dactylitis*, because its root is as thick and long as a finger.

53. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Erigeron.* From Dioscorides, IV, chapter 97.] *Erigeron* is a name derived from the Greeks because it grows old at the beginning of spring. Hence the Latins also call it *senecio*. It grows along walls.

[Col. 0630B] 54. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Psyllios.* From Dioscorides and Pliny.] *Psyllios* is so called because it has seed resembling a flea. Hence the Latins call it *flea-herb*.

55. [Note: [Col. 0629D] *Hierabotane.* See Pliny, XXV, chapter 9, and XXII, [Col. 0630D] chapter 2, and Dioscorides.] *Hierabotane* received this name from the Greeks because [Note: [Col. 0630D] “For remedies and embassies.” All the books incorrectly read *ligamentis* (“bindings”). Pliny, book XXII, chapter 2: “Since verbena was used for no other purpose than public remedies and the sacred embassies.”] it was considered by the pagans suitable for human remedies and embassies, and for the purifications of priests. Hence the pontiffs called it *sagmen*, as though *sancimen*—this is *verbena*, because it is pure.

56. [Note: [Col. 0630D] *Paliurus.* From Servius, *Eclogue* 5.] *Paliurus* is an extremely rough and thorny herb.

[Note: [Col. 0630D] *Struthios.* From Dioscorides and Pliny.] *Struthios*, which some call the wool-washing herb because many wash wool with it. It grows in cultivated places.

*Splenos* is so called because it removes the spleen.

57. *Cimicia* is named for its resemblance to a bedbug. Hence the Greeks also called it *korion* (κορίον). It grows in rough and cultivated places.

58. *Marrubium*, which the Greeks call *prasium*, is named for its bitterness. It grows in the fields.

59. [Note: [Col. 0630D] *Pulegium* is more precious than pepper among the Indians. These are Jerome’s words, *Letter* 83, to Evagrius.] Among the Indians, pennyroyal is more precious than pepper. [Note: [Col. 0630D] “It has a warming power,” etc. From Dioscorides, book III, chapter 36. But these words are absent from the older books.] It has a warming power: it heats, draws off, thins, purifies, and digests.

60. [Note: [Col. 0630D] *Absinthium.* From Dioscorides.] *Absinthium* is a Greek name; more probably, the plant is so called because it grows in the region of Pontus, whence it is also called Pontic wormwood.

61. [Note: [Col. 0630D] *Symphyton.* From the same source.] *Symphyton* is named in Greek because its root has such power that, when pieces of meat are sprinkled with it, it coagulates them in a pot.

62. [Note: [Col. 0630D] *Polypodium.* From the same source.] *Polypodium* is an herb whose root is shaggy and hairy, like a polypus, from which it is derived and called *polypodion*. [Note: [Col. 0630D] “It grows in the tender soils of rocks,” that is, on moss-covered rocks. If it is permissible to interpret the words of Dioscorides thus: [Col. 0631C] “It grows on rocks bearing moss” (φύεται ἐν πέτραις βρύα ἐχούσαις). But I would rather read, with Chacon: “It grows in the soft soil of rocks,” or “in soils near oak trees.”] It grows in the soft soil of rocks, [Col. 0630D] or near oak trees.

[Col. 0631A] 63. [Note: [Col. 0631C] *Polion.* From Dioscorides. The printed editions contain much here that is absent from the Gothic manuscripts.] *Polion* is called by the Greeks, and by the Latins *omnimorbia*, because it helps against many diseases. It grows in mountains and hard places.

359 64. [Note: [Col. 0631C] *Scammonia.* From the same source.] *Scammonia*, which the Latins call *acridium*, is an herb full of sap, which is collected beneath a hollowed-out root. They dig the earth in a round hollow; then, after placing shells or walnut leaves beneath it, they collect the sap and carry it away after it has dried. The more reliable kind usually comes from Mysia in Asia. The kind from Syria and Judaea is its opposite and false.

65. [Note: [Col. 0631C] *Daucus* “with fennel-like leaves and a two-palmed stem.” Dioscorides, book III, chapter 76, τὸ δὲ μῆκος σπιθαμῆς, “its length is a span.” Since its old translator rendered *spithamaion* as “two palms,” one will no longer wonder when one notices that Pliny did the same, book XXVII, chapter 4. For what Dioscorides said about *ageraton*, “It is a shrub, brushlike and a span high,” he himself rendered: [Col. 0631D] “Ageraton is like a ferula, two palms in height.” I know that Pliny interprets *spithame* variously: sometimes as a palm, as in books XII, chapter 19; XXII, chapter 21; and XXVI, chapters 7 and 8, and in Dioscorides and Theophrastus; sometimes as half a foot, as in book XXXIV, chapter 4, from Theophrastus, *History of Plants* II, chapter 8, and books XX, chapter 8, and XXVII, the final chapter. At times, however, he renders it correctly as a nine-inch measure, as in book VII, chapter 2, or as twelve fingers, as in book VIII, chapter 21. Unless perhaps all these passages are corrupt in Pliny, where the letters are not very far apart, and one should read *tripalmem* for *bipalmem*, *twelve fingers* for *four fingers*, *half a cubit* for *a slender cubit*, and *half a cubit* for *half a foot.] *Daucus*, with leaves like fennel and a stem two palms high.

*Citocatia* is so called because it quickly cleanses the belly; the common people corruptly call it *citocotia*.

66. [Note: [Col. 0631D] *Lappa* is so called because it has an enormous stalk. Or from ἀπὸ τοῦ λαπίζειν, “to behave arrogantly”? See [Col. 0632C] Pliny, book XXVII, chapter 5.] *Lappa* is so called because it has an enormous stalk [Col. 0631B] spread along the ground. This herb is called *philanthropos* (φιλάνθρωπος) by the Greeks because, owing to its roughness, it clings to people’s clothing. It grows beside walls.

67. *Capillus Veneris* (“Venus’s hair”) is so called either because it restores hair lost after baldness, or because it restrains falling hair, or because it has smooth black twigs with a sheen, like hair. It grows in watery places.

68. [Note: [Col. 0632C] *Rubia.* ἐρυθρόδανον. Dioscorides, book III, chapter 160.] *Rubia* is so called because its root is red; hence it is said to be used for dyeing wool.

360 69. [Note: [Col. 0632C] *Anchusa.* The same, book IV, chapter 25.] *Anchusa*, whose crushed root stains the fingers. It is blood-colored and is therefore also used by painters to produce purple.

70. *Chamaeleon*, which in Latin is called *viscarago*, is so named because it produces birdlime, in which birds become stuck—birds that descend of their own accord for food.

71. *Cicuta* is so called because its jointed stem has hidden knots, like a reed; thus a “blind ditch” is something hidden. Given as a drink, it kills. Socrates drank it in prison and died. Persius:

> Tell me: whom does a draught of deadly hemlock carry off?

Although it is poison to human beings, it makes she-goats fat.

72. [Note: [Col. 0632C] *Trifolium*, with individual leaves arising from each growth. Pliny, book XXVII, chapter 11, calls these *adnata*, which Dioscorides calls παραφυάδες. Others read *adnodationes*.] *Trifolium* is what the Greeks call *triphýllon* (τρίφυλλον), because it has three leaves at each growth.

73. *Phlomos*, which the Latins call the lamp herb, is so named because it is useful for lamps. It is also called *lucubros*, because it provides light in the shadows.

74. *Pyrctron* is called so in Greek because it has a fiery and accumulative root.

75. [Note: [Col. 0632C] *Althea.* Dioscorides, book III, chapter 163: “Althea; some call it hibiscus; it is a kind of wild mallow.” Palladius, in October, title 14: “The leaves of althea, that is, hibiscus.” Today our people call it *malvavisco*.] *Althea* is wild mallow, or the mallow’s “viscus”; but it is called *althea* because it rises high, and *viscus* because it is sticky.

76. [Note: [Col. 0632C] *Origanum*, which is *colina* in Latin. Others read *colerina*; others *colena*. Perhaps *conyla* should be written—the latter, according to Dioscorides, is a species of wild oregano—but the word is not Latin, nor does the etymology concerning coloring fit; everything is full of corruptions and additions.] *Oryganum*, which is interpreted in Latin as *colena*, is so called because, when infused, it colors wine.

[Col. 0632B] 361 77. [Note: [Col. 0632D] *Tithymallum.* This is the fourth kind of tithymallus in Pliny, book XXVI, chapter 8, where he says it is called *helioscopon*. Isidore, in his usual manner, adapted the etymology to the meaning of *helioscopon*.] The name *tithymallum* was given because it turns its leafy crown around toward the sun’s rays. For the Greeks call the sun *titan* (τιτᾶνα) and a crown or head of hair *mallon* (μαλλόν); from these the name *tithymallum* was formed. There are seven species of it, growing in different places.

78. [Note: [Col. 0632D] *Strychnos*, which in Latin is *herba salutaris*. Pliny, book XXII, chapter 31: “Xenocrates declares that there is no bodily ailment for which strychnos is not beneficial.” See Dioscorides, book IV, chapter 69.] *Strychnos*, which in Latin is called *herba salutaris* (“healing herb”), is so called because it alleviates headache and burning of the stomach. It is also called wolf-grape because its seed resembles a grape.

79. [Note: [Col. 0632D] *Polygonos.* Dioscorides, book IV, chapter 4; Pliny, XXVI, final chapter: “Taken as a drink, polygonos brings on menstruation. Others, however, have stated that it stops bleeding.”] *Polygonos*, which the Latins call *sanguinaria* (“blood herb”), is so called because, when placed in the nostrils, it causes bleeding.

80. *Ambrosia*, which the Latins call wild celery. Concerning it Virgil says:

> And the ambrosial locks breathed a divine fragrance  
> from the crown of his head . . . [lacuna]

*Apiago*, because bees especially desire its flowers.

*Portulaca* [lacuna].

81. [Note: [Col. 0632D] *Ros marinus.* From Dioscorides, book III, chapter 87. But where he said that its leaves were rough, he seems to have read τραχύτερα, “rougher,” rather than παχύτερα, “thicker,” as it is commonly read.] *Ros marinus*, which the Latins call *herba salutaris* (“healing herb”) from its effect, has leaves resembling those of fennel, and rough, lying flat on the ground in a circular arrangement.

[Col. 0633A] *Colocasia* [lacuna].

82. Wild mint, [Note: [Col. 0633C] Which the Greeks call *calamintha*. See Dioscorides, book III, chapters 42 and 43.] which the Greeks call *calamintha* (καλαμίνθη) and our people commonly call *nepeta*, is of greater power and strongly heating.

362 83. [Note: [Col. 0633C] *Genicularis*, a healing herb against scorpions. Pliny, book XX, chapter 14, attributes this in the same words to *mentastrum*; and, as far as I know, no one has reported it of *polygonatum*. Nor, unless I am greatly mistaken, did Isidore.] *Genicularis* is placed beneath one to repel the power of scorpions.

*Gladiolus* is so called because its leaves resemble a sword; its stem is a cubit high and its flowers are purple.

84. *Verbascum* [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0633C] “Agaric, a root.” Galen and others indeed thought so, but it has been discovered that it grows attached to trunks, like a fungus. Here there is a great lacuna in the Gothic manuscripts.] *Agaricum*, the root of the white vine.

*Calamites* [lacuna].

*Lappa* [lacuna].

*Lapago* [lacuna].

*Lapella* [lacuna].

*Beneola* [lacuna].

[Col. 0633B] *Orcibeta* [lacuna].

*Mirobalanum* [lacuna].

85. [Note: [Col. 0633D] *Asphodelos*, *albucum*. Others read *albutium*; the glossary has *albucinum*. Dioscorides: “The white asphodel should be cut at the equinox in spring.”] *Asphodelus*, which the Latins call *Albutium* because of its color.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] *Scylla*, because it is harmful. For σκύλλειν means “to trouble,” which Virgil perhaps had in mind when he spoke of Scylla in *Eclogue* 6: “to have troubled the Dulichian ships.”] *Scylla*, because it is harmful, [Note: [Col. 0633D] Concerning the superstition of the pagans. From Dioscorides, book II, and Pliny, XXI, chapter 17.] is the subject of a pagan superstition that, if it is hung whole at the threshold, it drives away every evil.

86. *Chamaepitys* is called so by the Greeks because it clings to the ground and has the smell of pine. The Latins call it *cucurbicularis*, because in part it resembles the smell of a gourd.

87. [Note: [Col. 0633D] *Staphysagria* [lacuna] “in pleasant places.” These are the only words found in the Gothic manuscripts. What is read in addition was inserted in the printed editions by some son of Aesculapius, from Dioscorides, Avicenna, and Averroes.] *Staphysagria* grows in pleasant places.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] *Asplenos.* See Dioscorides, III, chapter 151, and Pliny, XXVII, chapter 5.] *Asplenos* is so called because it removes the spleen, or *scolopendrios*, because its leaves resemble the animal scolopendra. [Note: [Col. 0633D] “It grows on damp rocks.” What follows this in the printed editions is not in the manuscript; it was nevertheless [Col. 0634C] added from Dioscorides and Pliny.] It grows on damp rocks.

88. [Note: [Col. 0634C] *Volvus.* An etymology suited to the spelling. Pliny and others say *bulvus*; the Greeks say βόλβος.] *Volvus* is so called because its root is winding [Col. 0633C] and round.

363 [Note: [Col. 0634C] *Staechas.* From Dioscorides, III, chapter 31.] *Staechas* grows on the Staechad Islands, from which it also receives its name.

89. *Cyclaminus* is called by the Greeks after a certain person named *Kyklos*, who first discovered the power of this herb, or because it has a round root. For the Greeks call a round object *kyklos*. [Note: [Col. 0634C] “If its root or sap is mixed with wine,” etc. From Dioscorides, II, chapter 194; Pliny, XXV, chapter 9: “They report that drunkenness is reproduced when it is added to wine.”] If its root or sap is mixed with wine, it makes people drunk. It grows in wooded places and fields.

[Col. 0634A] 90. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Ampelos leuce*, or bryony. From the same source, book IV, chapter 154.] *Ampelos leuce*, or bryony, which the Latins call white vine, either because of the quality of its color, or because its crushed root, rubbed onto the body, makes the skin softer and whiter. Its berry juice also produces milk in dry breasts.

91. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Ampelos melaena.* From the same source, chapter 185.] *Ampelos melaena*, that is, black vine, also called wild vine, has leaves like ivy; it is larger in every respect than the white vine and likewise bears berries that become black when ripe, whence it received its name.

92. *Viticella* is called by the Latins because, like a vine, it grasps whatever is near it with its tendrils, which we call rings.

93. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Buphthalmos.* From the same source, book III, chapter 156.] *Buphthalmos* has a saffron-colored flower resembling an eye. Hence it received its name from the Greeks. It has a [Col. 0634B] soft stem and [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Leaves of coriander.” *Fennel*—Pliny and Dioscorides.] leaves resembling coriander. It grows beside city walls.

94. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Phlomos.* Discussed shortly above. See Dioscorides, IV, chapter 104.] *Phlomos*, which the Latins call *verbascum*, has one kind that is male, with whiter and narrower leaves, and another that is female, with broader and black leaves.

95. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Ferula*, named from its pith; that is, as though “bearing marrow.”] *Ferula* is named from its pith. For Varro states that the pith of the ferula is what the Greeks call *apoderon*. Some say that *ferula* derives from *ferire*, “to strike.” For boys and girls are accustomed to be beaten with it: [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Its sap is galbanum.” Not the sap of every kind, but that of the *narthex* growing in Syria, as Dioscorides says; that is, a certain kind of ferula that grows in Syria.] its sap is galbanum.

96. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Papyrus.* See Pliny and Dioscorides.] *Papyrus* is so called because it is suitable for fire and candles; for the Greeks call fire *pyr* (πῦρ).

*Juncus* (“rush”) is so called because it clings with joined roots.

[Col. 0634C] 97. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Scirpus*, from which mats are woven. Pliny, XXI, chapter 18, and Festus under *Scirpus*.] *Scirpus* is used to weave mats and has no knot. Concerning it Ennius says:

> They seek in the rush what they were accustomed to call a knot.

And in the proverb: “The man who is hostile looks for a knot even in a rush.”

98. [Note: [Col. 0634D] *Fucus.* From Servius, *Georgics* IV.] *Fucus* is a kind of herb with which clothing is dyed: [Note: [Col. 0634D] “It is so called because it imitates another color,” like that kind of *fucus* which pretends to be a bee.] it is so called because it imitates another color. Hence Virgil also says:

> The wool will learn to imitate colors.

[Col. 0635A] 99. *Alga* grows in standing water. It ultimately received its name from the coldness of the water, or because it binds the feet, since it is thick, with leaves rising partly above the water.

100. *Ulva*, and *typha*, are kinds of herbs that grow around springs, marshes, and ponds. Of these, *ulva*, that is, soft algae and something like a fungus, is so called from dampness.

101. *Typha* is so called because it swells from the water. Hence the swelling of ambitious and self-satisfied people is also called *typhus*.

102. [Note: [Col. 0635C] *Carex.* From Servius, *Eclogue* 3.] *Carex* is a sharp and very hard herb, resembling broom; concerning it Virgil says:

> And feeding on sharp sedge.

103. [Note: [Col. 0635C] *Spartum* [lacuna], “from roughness.” I pay no attention to the etymology.] *Spartus* is a twiggy shrub without leaves, named from its roughness. For the bundles of cordage made from it are rough.

[Col. 0635B] 104. *Gramen* (“grass”) is named rather from its location, because it belongs to many fields. 365 [Note: [Col. 0635C] Hence the Greeks called it ἄγρωστις. Jerome interprets ἄγρωστις in this way in *Letter* 19.] Hence the Greeks called it *agrostis* (ἄγρωστις), although every herb is called *grass* because it sprouts, just as every piece of timber is called *oak* because it is very strong, even though “oak” is also the name of a particular kind.

105. [Note: [Col. 0635D] *Filix* [lacuna] “one produces split leaves.” Dioscorides, book IV, chapter 188, and Pliny, XXVII, chapter 9. The Gothic usage should be noted, since it uses *folia* in the singular more than once. We think, however, that this is more likely due to the error of scribes than to Isidore.] *Filix* (“fern”) is named from the singularity of its leaf. Thus, from a single stalk a cubit high, it produces split leaves, folded back like a feather.

*Oats* [lacuna].

*Darnel* [lacuna].

106. *Zizania* is what poets always call “unlucky darnel,” because it is useless and barren.

*Fenum* (“hay”) is so called because flame is nourished by it; for *phos* (φῶς) means flame.

We call a bundle of hay a *manipulus*. It is called *manipulus* because it fills the hand.

## CHAPTER X. On Vegetables

1. [Note: [Col. 0635D] *Hortus*, named because something is always produced there. Festus: Among the ancients *hortus* meant every country estate, because those able to bear arms arose there. Or, according to Longus: *Hortus* did not originally require aspiration, because herbs arise there, that is, are born, but it nevertheless acquired it through customary usage.] A garden is called *hortus* because something is always arising there. [Note: [Col. 0635D] “For while other earth,” etc. From Servius, *Georgics* IV, under “Hellespontine.”] For while other soil produces something once a year, a garden is never without produce.

2. *Olus* (“vegetable”) is derived from *alere* (“to nourish”), because at first human beings were nourished by vegetables, before they ate grain and meat. They lived only on the fruits of trees and on vegetables, like animals on grasses.

[Col. 0636A] 3. *Caulis* is, generally, the central stalk of herbs or vegetables, commonly called a *thyrsus*, because it climbs upward from the earth. From this it came to be used specifically for a certain kind of vegetable, [Note: [Col. 0635D] “A certain kind of vegetable, *caulis*.” Palladius, in February, title 24: *Brassica*.] because its stalk grows larger than that of other vegetables, that is, it grows. It is a general term: every shrub is a *caulis*.

4. [Note: [Col. 0635D] *Gyma*, as though *coma* (“crown”). Rather, as though κύημα, “offspring,” according to Theophrastus, *History of Plants* VII, and Galen, *On the Powers of Simple Drugs* II, chapter 58. Celsus, Columella, and Pliny use this word.] *Cyma* is so called, as though from *coma* (“crown”). It is the top of vegetables or trees, in which natural vigor is active.

5. [Note: [Col. 0636C] *Malva* [lacuna], because it softens. Pliny, book XX, chapter 21.] *Malva* is partly named from the Greek expression ἀπὸ τοῦ μαλάσσειν, because it has the property of softening and loosening the bowels. [Note: [Col. 0636C] “With whose juice.” From the same source and Dioscorides, book II.] If someone anoints himself with its juice mixed with oil, it is said that bees will not sting him. Its leaves, crushed in oil and applied to scorpions, [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Are believed to cause scorpions torpor.” From Pliny, book XX, chapter 4.] are believed to cause them torpor.

[Col. 0636B] 6. *Pastinaca* is so called because its root is a chief food of human beings. It is pleasant in smell and agreeable as food.

7. [Note: [Col. 0636D] *Rapa*, from *rapere* (“to seize”). Rather, from the Greek word ῥάφυς or ῥάπυς; Columella pronounces *rapum* as neuter.] *Rapa* is so called from *rapere*, that is, “to seize.” It has a larger root than the turnip, a sweeter flavor, and a thinner leaf.

8. *Napus* is named from its resemblance to the *rapa*, except that it has broader leaves and a sharper taste in its root. The similarity of their names is almost common to both because the seed of each is in turn changed into the other. [Note: [Col. 0636D] “For the turnip in another soil.” As Palladius says, book VIII, chapter 2, and Columella, book II, chapter 10.] For, as Aemilianus says, in one soil the turnip changes into the *napus* over two years, while in another the *napus* changes into the turnip.

9. *Napocaulis* has a name composed from two vegetables: although it resembles the *napus* in taste, it does not rise in the root but climbs into a stalk, like *caulis*.

[Col. 0636C] *Sinapis* (“mustard”) is so called because its leaf resembles that of the *napus*.

10. The Greeks call it *raphanos*; we call it *radix* (“root”), [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Because it strives wholly downward.” From the same source, Palladius, in January, title 14.] because it strives wholly downward, whereas the other vegetables project more toward the top. [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Anyone who has soaked his hands in its seed,” etc. From Pliny, XX, chapter 4.] Whoever has soaked his hands in its seed may handle snakes with impunity. [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Even ivory becomes white from its root.” If this is removed, what follows will cohere better, but I believe something is missing. Pliny, IX, chapter 5, on radishes: “They are considered most useful as food in winter, but are always harmful to the teeth because they wear them down; they polish ivory objects perfectly.”] Indeed, even ivory becomes white from its root. It also counteracts poisons when eaten. [Note: [Col. 0636D] “For against poisons its roots,” etc., “should be applied.” From Servius, *Georgics* II, under “Aid came, and to the limbs ...”] For against poisons its roots, nuts, lupins, citron, and celery are beneficial—but against poison that is still to come, not against poison already taken. Hence among the ancients these were customarily placed on the table before other dishes.

[Col. 0637A] 11. [Note: [Col. 0637C] *Lactuca* [lacuna] “may overflow.” These are the words of Palladius, in January, title 14.] *Lactuca* is so called because it overflows with an abundance of milk, [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Or because it fills women who nourish with milk.” See Dioscorides, book II.] or because it fills women who nourish infants with milk. [Note: [Col. 0637D] “Among men this restrains sexual activity.” Pliny, book XIX, chapter 8, reports that a certain kind of lettuce was called *eunuchium*.] In men it also restrains sexual activity.

Wild lettuce is [Note: [Col. 0637D] This is what we call *sarralia*. We call it *cerraja*.] what we call *sarralia*, because its back is shaped like a saw.

12. [Note: [Col. 0637D] *Intubus* is a Greek name. Dioscorides and Galen attest that it is Roman.] *Intubus* is a Greek name. *Intubus* is so called because it has *tophus* (tufa) within it.

*Cepa* (“onion”) is so called because it is nothing but a head.

13. [Note: [Col. 0637D] *Ascalonia*, named from a city in Palestine. Thus Pliny, XIX, chapter 6.] *Ascalonia* was named after one of the cities of Palestine, called Ascalon, from which it was first brought.

14. [Note: [Col. 0637D] *Allium* is so called because it smells. Or because it exhales an odor, as others believe.] *Allium* is so called because it smells.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] *Ulpicum.* See Columella, book XI, and Pliny, XIX, chapter 6. The etymology is uncertain.] *Ulpicum* is so called because it has the smell of garlic.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] *Phaselus.* Cicero, *Against Verres*: “That Phaselis which Publius Servilius captured had not previously been a city of the Cilicians and pirates. Greek Lycians inhabited it.”] *Phaselus* is said to be named after the island of Phaselos in Greece, [Col. 0637B] where Mount Olympus is not far away.

15. *Porrum* (“leek”) has two kinds, headed and cut. The headed kind is larger; the cut kind is small.

368 *Beta* is a kind of vegetable among us, but among the Greeks it is a letter.

*Blitum* is a kind of vegetable with a faint flavor, like an inferior beet.

16. *Cucumeres* (“cucumbers”) are so called because they are sometimes bitter. [Note: [Col. 0637D] “They are said to grow sweet if their seed is infused in honeyed milk.” If in milk and mulsum, Palladius, book IV, chapter 9.] They are said to grow sweet if their seed is infused in honeyed milk.

17. *Cucurbita* [lacuna].

*Apopores* [lacuna].

*Pepo* [lacuna].

*Melipepo* [lacuna].

[Col. 0637C] *Ocymum* [lacuna].

*Olus molle* [lacuna].

*Atriplex* [lacuna].

*Brassica* [lacuna].

*Olisatrum* [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0638C] “*Nasturtium* is named from its flavor,” etc. Pliny, XIX, chapter 8: “Nasturtium received its name from the torment it causes in the nostrils.”] *Nasturtium* is named from its flavor because its sharpness torments the nose.

18. *Fungi* (“mushrooms”) are so called because, when dry, they catch fire and retain it; for *phos* (φῶς) means fire. Hence they are commonly called *esca* (“tinder”), because they are kindling and nourishment for fire. Others say that mushrooms are so called because some of their kind are deadly, whence also *defuncti* (“the dead”).

[Col. 0638A] 19. *Tubera* (“truffles”) reveal a swelling of the earth, and this gave them their name.

*Bulbi* (“bulbs”) are so called because they are winding and round.

*Asparagus* is so called because its shrub is thorny and rough, from which it grows.

20. *Capparis* seems to have taken its name from the Greeks because it has round little heads at the tips of its seeds.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] *Armoraca.* Palladius, book XI, chapter 11: “We shall sow *armoraca*, for this is a wild radish. But *armoracia* is not the same as *lapsana*: Dioscorides discusses the former in book II, chapter 138, and the latter in chapter 142; nevertheless, he says that their leaves are similar.] *Armoracia*, that is, *lapsana*.

*Lapistus* [lacuna].

*Lapathum.* Taken as food, this strengthens the stomach and restrains sexual desire.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] *Carduus*; its juice cures bald patches. Pliny, XXI, chapter 23: “Before it flowers, when crushed and its juice expressed and applied, it fills bald patches.”] *Carduus* [lacuna].

21. *Eruca* (“rocket”) is as though *uruca*, because it has a fiery power and, often eaten, arouses the burning of sexual desire. [Col. 0638B] There are two kinds: one cultivated for use, the other wild and more powerful; both nevertheless arouse sexual activity.

## CHAPTER XI. On Fragrant Vegetables

1. *Apium* (“celery”) is so called because it was used to crown the apex—that is, the head—of ancient triumphing men. Hercules was the first to carry this herb around his head. For at one time he wore poplar on his head, at another wild olive, and at another celery. [Note: [Col. 0638D] “Its roots.” From Dioscorides, book III.] Its roots effectively combat the snares of poisons. The following belong to this kind: *petroselinon*, *hipposelinon*, and *oleoselinon*.

2. *Petroselinon* is so called because it resembles celery and grows on rocks and precipitous mountains. We may call it *rock-celery*, for *selinon* (σέλινον) is the Greek word for celery. But it is the superior and most esteemed Macedonian kind, pleasant in taste and aromatic in smell.

3. *Hipposelinon* is so called because it is hard and austere.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] *Oleoselinon.* I would prefer *oreoselinon*, following Pliny, or even *helioselinon*, which is marshland celery, or certainly *claoselinon*.] *Oleoselinon* is softer in its leaf and tender in its stalk.

4. [Note: [Col. 0638D] *Feniculum*, because it sharpens sight; as though *phenoculum*, from a Greek and Latin word.] The Latins call it *feniculum* because the juice of its stalk or root sharpens the sight. [Note: [Col. 0638D] “Its power is reported.” From Pliny, XX, chapter 23.] Its power is said to be such that snakes cast off their annual old age by tasting it. The Greeks call this vegetable *marathron* (μάραθρον).

5. [Note: [Col. 0638D] *Ligusticum.* From the same source, book XIX, chapter 8, and Dioscorides, book III.] *Ligusticum* received its name from a region. It grows especially in Liguria, with an aromatic smell and a sharp taste.

6. *Aneson*, as the Greeks say, or *anesum*, as the Latins say, is a herb known to everyone and extremely hot in its effect on urination.

*Anethum* [lacuna].

*Cuminum* [lacuna].

7. *Coriandrum* takes its name from the Greek word which they call *korion* (κόριον). [Note: [Col. 0639A] “Its seed,” etc., “nourishes.” From Dioscorides, book III, chapter 71.] Its seed, given in sweet wine, makes people more inclined toward sexual activity; if given in excessive measure, it fosters madness.

[Note: [Col. 0639A] “It also dyes gray hairs from coriander.” Pliny, book XXVI, chapter 15, reports this only of *hypericum*. He also calls it *corion*, but Dioscorides names that kind of hypericum *koris* (κόρις).] It is also reported that gray hairs can be dyed with coriander.

[Col. 0640A] *Abrotanum* [lacuna].

*Ceraefolium* [lacuna].

8. [Note: [Col. 0639A] *Ruta* is so called because it is hot. Is it from *ruere*, “to rush,” or rather from the sound usually produced by boiling liquid? [Col. 0639B] I do not think so; nor did he think about the etymology, but looked to Pliny and Dioscorides, both of whom attribute a hot nature to rue.] *Ruta* is so called because it is extremely hot. One kind is wild and stronger in power, but both are proved to be extremely hot. [Note: [Col. 0640A] “It protects the weasel against poisons.” From Pliny, XX, chapter 13.] Weasels demonstrate that it resists poisons, for when they fight with a snake, they arm themselves by eating it.

9. *Salvia* [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0640A] *Inula*, which country people call *ala*. We retain this name in Spain; concerning *inula*, see Pliny, book XIX, chapter 5.] *Inula*, which country people call *ala*, has an aromatic root, with a powerful smell and slight sharpness.

*Menta* (“mint”). It has six kinds.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN. ON WAR AND GAMES

[Col. 0639]

371 ## CHAPTER ONE. On Wars

[Col. 0639B]

1. [Note: [Col. 0639D] “Ninus first brought war.” From Justin, or perhaps also from Trogus; for this passage is somewhat fuller than in Justin and not of such a kind that it seems to have been expanded by Isidore.] Ninus, king of the Assyrians, first brought war. For, by no means content with his own borders and breaking the bond of human society, he began to lead armies, lay waste to the property of others, slaughter or subjugate free peoples, and conquer all Asia as far as the borders of Libya with a new kind of servitude. From that time the world began to rage in mutual bloodshed and alternate slaughter.

2. There are four kinds of war: just, unjust, civil, and more than civil. A just war is one waged for the recovery of things previously demanded, as stated above, [Col. 0639C] or for repelling enemies. An unjust war is one begun out of fury, not legitimate reasoning. Concerning this Cicero says in *The Republic*: “Those wars are unjust which are undertaken without cause.”

3. No just war can be waged except for the purpose of avenging wrongs or repelling enemies. Tullius likewise added a little later: “No war is considered just unless it has been announced, unless it has been formally declared, unless it concerns things previously demanded.” Civil war is a revolt and stirring up of turmoil among citizens, such as occurred between Sulla and Marius, who waged civil war against each other within one people.

4. More-than-civil war is when not only citizens but also relatives fight, as happened between Caesar and Pompey, when son-in-law and father-in-law fought one another. Indeed, in this struggle brother fought against brother, and a father bore arms against his son. [Col. 0639D] 372 Lucan:

> The prizes of the brother fell upon the brother.

Likewise:

> For whom the severed neck of his father would yield.

5. Wars are therefore called internal, external, servile, [Col. 0640B] allied, and piratical. Piratical wars are the scattered bands of robbers moving across the seas in light and swift *myoparones*, [Note: [Col. 0639D] “Not merely intercepting the traffic of ships,” etc., “but laying waste to islands and provinces.” The words are from Orosius, book VI, chapter 4.] not merely intercepting the traffic of ships but also laying waste to islands and provinces. Gnaeus Pompey first suppressed and defeated them with remarkable speed, after the extensive devastation they had inflicted by land and sea.

6. Just as a war is what is waged against enemies, so a tumult is what is stirred up by civil revolt. [Note: [Col. 0639D] “For revolt.” The same, above, book X, under S.] A revolt is a disagreement among citizens; it is so called because some go apart from others. Others think that a disagreement of minds is called revolt, which the Greeks call *diastasis* (διάστασις).

[Col. 0640C] 7. Cicero explains how the two differ. [Note: [Col. 0640D] Cicero explains it, *Philippic* 8.] “There can be,” he says, “a war without a tumult.” [Note: [Col. 0640D] *Tumultus*, as though *timor multus*, “great fear.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, under “with wretched groaning and tumult.”] But there cannot be a tumult without war. For what is a tumult except such great disturbance that greater fear arises? Hence *tumultus* is also said as though from *timor multus*, “great fear.” A tumult is more serious than a war. For in war leaves of absence are valid, but in a tumult they are not.

8. War, battle, and engagement differ. *War* refers to the whole, as in the Punic War. Its parts are battles, [Note: [Col. 0640D] Such as the battles of Cannae, Trebia, and Termes; all the manuscripts are corrupt.] such as Cannae and Trebia. Again, in a single battle there are many engagements: one is fought on the wings, another in the center, and another on the rear line. Thus war is the whole, battle is the affair of one day, and an engagement is a part of a battle.

9. War was formerly called *duellum*, because there are two sides fighting, or because it makes one the victor and the other the vanquished. Later, after a letter was changed and removed, it was called *bellum*. Others [Note: [Col. 0640D] Others derive it by antiphrasis. From Servius, the same passage.] think it was called so by antiphrasis [Col. 0641A] because it is dreadful; hence the phrase “dreadful wars,” although war is, on the contrary, utterly evil.

373 10. Battles are called *praelia* from *premere*, “to press,” as enemy presses enemy. [Note: [Col. 0641D] “Hence also the press,” etc., “by which grapes are pressed.” From the same source, *Georgics* II.] Hence also the *prelum*, the wooden press by which grapes are pressed.

*Pugna* (“fight”) is so called because the first method used in war was to contend with fists, or because at first they began wars with their fists. Hence a *pugna* is sometimes a contest between two people without weapons.

11. Four things occur in war: battle, flight, victory, and peace. The word “peace” seems to be derived from *pactum*, “agreement.” Peace, however, is understood as following afterward, while a treaty is made first. A treaty is peace established between combatants; the word is derived either from *fides*, “faith,” or from *foediales*, that is, priests. Treaties were made through these men, just as wars were through secular officials. [Note: Others think *foedera* (“treaties”) is derived from a sow (*porca*) foully and cruelly slaughtered, whose death was wished upon anyone who should break away from the peace. From the same source, *Aeneid* IX.] Others think that *foedera* was so called from a sow (*porca*) foully and cruelly slaughtered, whose death was wished upon anyone who should withdraw from the peace. Virgil writes: “And they joined the treaties with a slaughtered sow.” The parts of a treaty are truces. And *induciae* (“truces”) is said as though from *in dies otia*, “rest for a period of days.”

## CHAPTER II. On Triumphs

1. Every kingdom of this world is sought through wars and extended through victories. *Victoria* (“victory”) is so called because it is obtained by force (*vi*), that is, by valor (*virtute*). For this is the law of nations: to repel force by force. Victory obtained by deceit is disgraceful. A definitive victory consists either in the killing of the enemy, in stripping him of his possessions, or in both. [Note: “A victory is not pleasing . . . to have brought back.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on the passage “If also among the Trojans with much glory,” except that in that author the victory is said to be “judged.”] A victory is not pleasing when it is achieved through immense losses. This is what Sallust praises: commanders bringing back victory with a bloodstained army. [Col. 0641C]

2. *Pompa* (“procession”) is said in the Greek sense, ἀπὸ τοῦ πομπεύειν, that is, “to be publicly displayed.” [Note: “Victory precedes it,” that is, the statue of Victory carried in a chariot.] Victory precedes the procession, because for those who are going to this contest the first thing is a vow to Victory.

3. [Note: “Trophy . . . from exultation.” From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “You yourself, Lausus, a trophy.”] *Trophaeum* (“trophy”) is said from ἀπὸ τῆς τροπῆς, that is, from the turning and flight of the enemy. For one who had put the enemy to flight earned a trophy; one who had killed him earned a triumph. The latter is called ἀπὸ τῆς τριάμβης, that is, from exultation. A triumph is owed for a complete victory, a trophy for a half-complete one, because the victor has not yet achieved a complete victory: he did not overcome the army but put it to flight. Writers, however, confuse these names. Suetonius says that *triumphus* was more properly called in Latin because the man entering the city in triumph was honored according to a threefold judgment. First, the army used to judge whether a triumph should be granted to the commander; second, the senate; third, the people.

4. Among the Romans it was customary for those celebrating a triumph to be carried in four-horse chariots, because earlier commanders had been accustomed to enter battles in this attire. Whoever won in close combat was crowned with a golden palm, because the palm has spines. But whoever struck down a fleeing enemy without a fight was crowned with laurel, because this tree is without thorns.

5. [Note: “For they also wore the purple and palm-embroidered toga.” The purple toga differed from the palm-embroidered toga. Festus: “The embroidered garment, now called a toga, was formerly called purple and was without embroidery”; and in the same place: “The palm-embroidered tunic was so called from the width of its stripes, though it is now named from the type of embroidery.” Livy, Book XXX: “Masinissa was presented with an embroidered toga and a palm-embroidered tunic”; and Book XXXI: “Gifts sent to Masinissa: golden vessels, a purple toga.”] Those celebrating a triumph also put on a purple and palm-embroidered toga, and carried in their hand a staff together with a scepter, in imitation of the victory of Scipio, although a *scipio* is also a staff on which people lean. Hence the first Cornelius was called Scipio, because his blind father walked through the forum leaning upon it. [375] An eagle sat upon the staff, as an indication that through victory they were, as it were, approaching heavenly greatness.

6. [Note: “Hence they were also smeared with red color.” Servius, *Eclogue* 10: “Pan is depicted with a red face because of its resemblance to the ether. The ether, however, is Jupiter; hence those celebrating a triumph also possess all the insignia of Jupiter: a scepter, a palm-embroidered toga, and a face smeared with red pigment in imitation of the color of the ether.”] Hence they were also smeared with red color, as though imitating the appearance of divine fire. [Note: “But that they were touched by an executioner.” He did not call him an executioner without reason, though others call him a public slave. I think Pliny had the same point in view, Book XXVIII, chapter 4: “A similar medicine for the tongue, so that fortune, having been entreated from behind, may be the executioner of glory.” This slave used to whisper it to the triumphant man, as Tertullian says in *Apologeticus*, chapter 33: “Look behind you; remember that you are a man.”] That they were touched by an executioner was an indication that those raised to so great a height might be reminded of human mediocrity.

7. An army is destroyed in two ways: either by annihilation or by dispersion. Sallustius says: “The enemies had either been crushed or had scattered.” Virgil likewise gives both examples: annihilation, as in “Bury the submerged ships”; dispersion, as in:

> Or drive them apart and scatter their bodies over the sea.

8. The spoils of the enemy are called *praeda*, *manubiae*, *exuviae*, and *partes*. *Praeda* (“prey”) is so called from *praedari*, “to plunder.” *Manubiae* (“spoils”) is so called because they are taken away by hand. They are also called *exuviae* (“stripped possessions”) from *exuere*, “to strip,” because they are stripped away. They are also called *partes* (“shares”) because of equal division—[Note: “According to the rank of the persons, etc.” See above, Book V, chapter 7. In this passage, however, these words are absent from the older Gothic manuscripts.]—according to the rank of the persons and the just division of labors. [Note: “*Spolia* from cloaks.” In some Gothic manuscripts *exspolia* is consistently read, and the etymology then works better; in the older manuscripts, however, the reading is *spolia*.] *Spolia* (“spoils”) is derived from *pallia* (“cloaks”), as though from *ex pallia*, since they are stripped from the defeated.

[376]

## CHAPTER III. On Standards

1. Military standards are so called because from them the army receives the signal both for fighting, for victory, and for retreat. For the army is either warned by the sound of the trumpet or by a signal. The principal standards of the legions are eagles, dragons, and balls.

2. Eagles are used because that same bird was Jupiter’s auspice in warfare. [Note: “While Jupiter himself . . . was accompanying him.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “Jupiter’s armed standard-bearer with hooked feet.”] For when Jupiter was setting out against the Titans, they say that an eagle appeared to him as an omen. He accepted it as an indication of victory, took it under his protection, and gave it as the legion’s standard; consequently, thereafter it accompanied the standards of the soldiers. Lucan mentions it, saying:

> Equal standards, eagles, and javelins threatening javelins.

3. Dragon standards began with Apollo’s killing of the serpent Python. Thereafter the Greeks and Romans began to carry them in war.

4. Augustus is said to have placed a ball upon the standard because of the nations subjected to him throughout the whole world, so that it might display more clearly the figure of the globe.

5. [Note: “Vexillum . . . through diminution.” From the same source, at the beginning of Book VIII.] *Vexillum* (“standard”), itself a military standard, derives its name through the diminutive form of *velum* (“sail” or “cloth”), as though *velillum*. [Note: “Under Romulus . . .” The same author, *Aeneid* XI, on “And the scattered companies”: “The *manipuli* were called standard-bearers because, under Romulus, when the Roman army was still poor, the Romans tied bundles of hay to spears and carried them as standards. Hence the name remained.”] Under Romulus the soldiers used bundles of hay instead of standards. Hence they are also called *manipuli*. For we call bundles of hay *manipuli* because they fill the hand. The other standards, bearing various images, exist according to military custom; by means of them the army recognizes itself amid the confusion of battles.

## CHAPTER IV. On Trumpets

1. A *buccina* is the instrument by which a signal is given against the enemy. It is so called from its sound, as though *vocina*. For country people and peasants used to be summoned by a *buccina* to crossroads for every purpose. Properly, therefore, this was a signal for peasants. Propertius writes:

> The trumpet was already calling the ancient Quirites to arms.

[Note: “Its blast is called *buccinum*. This may perhaps be something of the sort [sic].” Pliny, *Natural History* XI, chapter 10: “At night there is rest until morning, until one thing awakens them with a double or triple booming, as with some trumpet.” Jerome also seems to have used *buccino oris sui* in the same sense. Yet *buccinum* is also used for *buccina*.] Its blast is called *buccinum*.

2. [Note: “The Tyrrhenians first invented the trumpet.” From Servius, Book VIII, on the passage cited by Isidore.] The Tyrrhenians first invented the trumpet, whence Virgil writes:

> And the Tyrrhenian blast of the trumpet roared through the ether.

They say that it was devised by Tyrrhenian pirates, who, being scattered along the maritime shores, could not easily be summoned by voice or *buccina* whenever an opportunity for plunder arose, since the wind usually made an opposing noise.

3. Later it was employed in battles to announce military signals, so that when a herald could not be heard amid the tumult, the sound of the blaring trumpet might reach the army. [Note: “The trumpet is so called as though *tofa*.” Others read *tova*. Hence we call a certain kind of stone *tovas*, and something porous *fofo*. The digamma is frequent in Gothic in place of *b* and *v*.] The trumpet is called *tuba*, as though *tofa*, that is, “hollow.” Likewise, *tuba* is as though *tibia* (“flute”).

4. The ancients distinguished between the trumpet and the *buccina*. [Note: “For the sounding *buccina* . . . a sound.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI: “It gives the signal for war . . . the *buccina*.”] For the sounding *buccina* announced the alarm for war. Virgil writes: “With which the dread *buccina* gave the signal.” The trumpet, however, indicated battle, as in:

> Then the trumpet gave a terrible sound with its brazen voice.

Its sound is varied. [Note: “Its sound is varied . . . for retreat.” From the same source, *Aeneid* IX, on “The followers of the standards.”] Sometimes it sounds so that battle may begin; sometimes so that the fleeing may be pursued; sometimes for retreat. [Note: “For retreat . . . are called.” From the same source, *Aeneid* XI, on “The plain . . . and a safe retreat.”] A retreat is so called because it is where the army withdraws; hence signals for retreat are said to sound.

5. [Note: “The *classica* are horns.” The same author, *Aeneid* VII: “We call both the trumpet itself and its sound *classicum*”; and in the same book, on the Hortine *classica*: “The Hortine horsemen, who are also called *classici*, whence we call their trumpets *classica*,” and so forth. See also Asconius on *Divinatio*.] The *classica* are horns, made for the purpose of summoning people; they were called *classica* from *calare*, “to summon.” Virgil writes: “And now the *classica* sound.” [Note: “Among the Amazons, etc.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “the queen with the sistrum.”] Among the Amazons, however, the army of women was summoned not by a trumpet, as among kings, but by a *sistrum* sounded by the queen.

## CHAPTER V. On Weapons

[Col. 0644B]

1. [Note: “Weapons in general, etc.” Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Arms and the man”: “Weapons are the instruments of all arts.”] In general, *arma* (“weapons”) are the instruments of all things; hence the places where they are stored are called *armaria*. The term also means weapons and missiles of every kind, but *arma* are the things with which we protect ourselves, while *tela* are the missiles we cast. Weapons are of two kinds: those with which we strike and those with which we shield ourselves.

2. [Note: “Weapons properly so called, because they . . . arms.” From the same source, *Aeneid* IV: “To rise up and the man’s arms,” etc.] Weapons properly so called are named because they cover the *armi* (“arms” or “shoulders”). For *arma* may derive from *armi*, that is, shoulders, as in: “The broad spear, driven through his shoulders, trembles”; or from ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἄρεος, that is, “from Mars.”

[379]

## CHAPTER VI. On Swords

1. In general, a sword in battle is called *ensis*, but *ensis* refers only to the iron, whereas *gladius* refers to the whole weapon. It is properly called *gladius* because it divides the throat (*gula*), that is, cuts the neck. For it was first made for this purpose; the other limbs are more often cut with axes, but the neck only with a sword.

2. The edge of a sword is called *acies* from its sharpness. The hilt is called *capulus*, either because it is the “head” of the sword or because it is where it is grasped so that it may be held. For otherwise the edge of the iron does not permit this. [Note: “The *mucro* is not only a sword’s point.” From Servius, *Aeneid* XI, on “The point stands in the deep wound.”] *Mucro* (“point”) is not only the point of a sword but the sharp end of any weapon. It is so called from its length: the Greeks call long things μακρόν; hence also *machaera*.

[Note: “*Machaera* . . . *framea* . . . *spatha*.” Augustine, on Psalm 149: “That which people commonly call a *spatha* is called a *framea*. Swords sharpened on one side are *machaerae*; these same *frameae* are also called *spathae*. But Augustine perhaps should read ‘on both sides,’ not ‘on one.’”] A *machaera* is a long sword, sharpened on one side.

3. A *framea*, however, is a sword sharpened on both sides, commonly called a *spatha*. It is also a *romphaea*. *Framea* is so called because it is made of iron. For just as an iron tool is called *ferramentum*, so a sword is called *framea*; accordingly, every sword is a *framea*.

4. *Spatha* is said to derive from a Greek word referring to suffering, since in Greek παθεῖν means “to suffer”; hence we say *patior* and *patitur*. Others maintain that *spatha* is a Latin word, so called because it is spacious, that is, broad and ample. Hence also *spatula* (“shoulder blade”) in the chest.

5. A *semispathium* is a sword named from the middle length of a *spatha*, not, as the ignorant crowd says, “without space,” because it is swifter than an arrow.

6. A *pugio* (“dagger”) is so called from stabbing and piercing. It is a small, double-edged sword worn against the side. [Note: “Also *clunabulum*.” Festus: “A *clunaclum* is called a bloody knife either because it divides the haunches of sacrificial victims or because it hangs at the haunches.”] It is also called a *clunabulum* because it is tied to the haunch.

[Col. 0645B]

7. A *chelidoniacus* is a broad iron sword whose double point is formed in a forked shape like a swallow’s tail; hence it is called *chelidoniacus*.

8. *Sica* (“curved dagger”) is so called from *secare*, “to cut.” It is a short sword, used especially by those who practice brigandage among the Italians; from it they are called *sicarii*. Suetonius, however, says: “When the sword of a certain gladiator sent into the training-school had bent away from its straight edge,” one man ran forward to straighten it, and the fighter replied: ‘With this I shall fight thus.’ Hence the name *sica* was derived.”

9. Axes are insignia carried before the consuls, lest they lose either their practice of war or, while idle in peace, the sight of swords. [381] The Spaniards, by derivation from the usage of the Franks, also call them *franciscas*.

## CHAPTER VII. On Spears

1. A spear (*hasta*) is a shaft (*contus*) fitted with iron; its diminutive is *hastile*. The name *hasta* is derived from *astus*, whence also *astutia* (“cunning”).

2. A *contus* does not have iron; it is merely a shaft with a sharp point. Virgil writes:

> And iron-pointed truncheons and *conti* with sharp points.

[Note: “Virgil has *ferratasque trudes*. All books read this way. Pierius notes that *trudes* is also found in some ancient manuscripts of Virgil.] A *contus* is as though *conitus*. For a cone is a sharp rounded form.

3. *Trudes* are spears with crescent-shaped iron, called *aplustria* by the Greeks. They are called *trudes* because they push and thrust away. Virgil writes: “And iron-pointed *trudes*.”

4. [Note: “*Venabula* called as though . . . capable of receiving.” Servius, *Aeneid* IV: “Nets . . . hunting spears.” Perhaps *venabula* were so called because they are suitable for hunting, as though *expia-bula*. I think, however, that Servius wrote: “*Venabula* are so called because they are suitable for hunting, or because they receive what is coming; hence *excipia* or *excipula*, as though ‘capable of receiving,’ or ‘able to receive.’” Glosses: *excipulum*, ἐκδοχεῖον; also ἐκδοχεῖον, “receptacle”; *excipulum*, κρεάγρα; κρεάγρα, “hook”—read perhaps *excipulum*, “grappling hook.”] *Venabula* are so called as though “suitable for hunting,” or because they receive what comes, as though “capable of receiving.” They receive boars, await lions, and pierce bears—provided only that the hand is strong.

5. [Note: “*Lancea*.” A Spanish word, according to Varro, in Gellius, Book XV, chapter 30.] A *lancea* is a spear with a thong attached at its middle. It is called *lancea* because it is balanced on an even scale, that is, is swung with an equally balanced thong.

6. [Note: “*Amentum*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “And they hurl the thongs.”] An *amentum* is the cord of throwing-spears, fitted to the middle of the spears. Hence *amentum* is the thong by which the middle of the spear is bound and the spear is thrown.

7. A club such as Hercules used is called a *clava*, because it consists of iron spikes fastened together, and it is a cubit and a half in length. [Note: “And it is made a cubit and a half long.” Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “Their *aclides* are rounded weapons”: “*Aclides* are certain ancient weapons, so obscure that they are nowhere mentioned in war. Yet it is read that they are clubs a cubit and a half long, with projecting points sharpened on both sides,” etc.] It is also called a *cateja*, which Lucilius calls a *calam*. It is a kind of Gallic weapon made from extremely tough wood. When thrown, it does not fly far because of its weight; but wherever it reaches, it breaks through with immense force. If thrown by a skilled craftsman, it returns to the one who threw it. Virgil mentions it:

> Accustomed, in Teutonic fashion, to hurl the *cateja*.

Hence the Spaniards and Gauls call the Teutons by this name. [Note: “The Spaniards and Gauls call the Teutons so.” These may perhaps be those whom we commonly call *chuzones*.]

8. [Note: “The *phalarica* is a huge weapon . . . could be hurled.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “The hurled *phalarica*.”] A *phalarica* is a huge weapon made on a lathe, with an iron point a cubit long and a round leaden ball, like a sphere, at its very tip. It is also said to have fire attached to it. This weapon is used in fighting from towers, which are clearly called *phalae*. Juvenal writes:

> He consults before the towers and the columns of dolphins.

Thus *phalarica* is derived from *phalae*, just as *muralis* from *murus*. Lucan, indeed, says that a *phalarica* is thrown by twisted cords and by a certain machine:

> The *phalarica*, hurled by twisted cords.

Virgil, however, says that Turnus was able to hurl a *phalarica* by hand.

9. [Note: “*Pila*.” Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “*Pila*,” in a manuscript: “A *pilum* is properly a Roman spear, just as the *gessum* is Gallic and the *sarissa* Macedonian.”] *Pila* are weapons consisting of thrown spears and missiles; they are so called from twisting or hurling. Lucan writes of them:

> Equal standards, eagles, and javelins threatening javelins.

The singular is *pilum*.

10. [Note: “*Telum* . . . can.” From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “Alcides presses from above with weapons.”] According to Greek etymology, a *telum* is anything that can be thrown a long distance, from ἀπὸ τοῦ τηλόθεν, “from far away,” although the word is used improperly for a sword, as in:

> But this is not the weapon which my right hand, with force, wields.

Properly, however, *telum* is derived from distance. Hence also the weasel is called *mustela*, as though “the long mouse,” because it is longer than a mouse.

11. A *cuspis* is a shaft fitted with a thong; it is called from *cespes*, “a turf,” which is a sprout. Virgil writes:

> And a pastoral myrtle fixed upon a spear-point.

[Note: “Properly, *cuspis* is the rear part of the spear.” Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “The spear-point quivering in the middle”: “Strictly speaking, he improperly used *cuspis* for the sword-point of the spear.”] Properly, however, *cuspis* is the rear part of the spear.

[384]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Arrows

1. An arrow (*sagitta*) is so called from a swift throw, that is, a rapid blow. It travels by means of feathers, like a bird, so that death may quickly run through to the human being. The Cretans first used these arrows; as we have said, feathers are attached to them so that they may be light and fly far.

2. *Scaptos* . . .

3. *Spicula* are arrows or short spears, named from their resemblance to ears of grain.

4. [Note: “*Scorpio*.” Vegetius, Book IV, chapter 22: “They were called *scorpiones*, which are now called *manuballistae*, and were so named because they inflicted death with small, fine darts.”] A *scorpio* is a poisoned arrow discharged by a bow or by engines. When it reaches a person, it pours in the poison with which it pierces; hence it received the name *scorpio*. [Note: “Poison, which it injects as it pierces.” Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*: “Hence they also call a war machine that enlivens its missiles by recoil a *scorpio*. That dart is also a tube, broad enough to enter the wound; it pours out the poison with which it pierces.”]

## CHAPTER IX. On Quivers

1. [Note: “*Pharetra*, a case for arrows, and properly for the *coriti*.” Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “The light *coriti*: *Coriti* are properly cases for bows; they are also called cases for arrows, which we call *pharetrae*.”] A *pharetra* is a case for arrows, so called from carrying missiles, just as a *feretrum* is the bier on which a corpse is carried. They share an etymology because a *pharetra* carries death, while a *feretrum* carries the dead.

2. *Coriti* are properly cases for bows, just as *pharetrae* are cases for arrows.

A *vagina* is so called because in it the point or sword is carried.

3. A *theca* is named from the fact that it covers something received within it, with the letter *t* substituted for *g*. Others maintain that it is called *theca* from the Greek word because something is stored there. Hence a *bibliotheca* is a repository of books.

4. [Note: “*Dolones* . . . they display wood.” From the same source, *Aeneid* VII, on “the cruel *dolones*.”] *Dolones* are wooden sheaths within which a dagger lies concealed under the appearance of a staff. They are called *dolones* from *dolus*, “deceit,” because they deceive and cheat with iron while displaying the appearance of wood. The common people call them by the Greek name *oxos*, that is, “sharp.” Hence among physicians an acute disease is called ὀξεῖα. [Note: “An acute disease: ὀξεῖα.” Thus above, Book IV, chapter 6.]

5. A bow (*arcus*) is so called because it wards off an adversary. Hence also *arces* (“fortresses”) are so called, because enemies are warded off from them. The bow is also so named from its appearance, because it is tightly curved.

## CHAPTER X. On Slings

1. A sling (*funda*) is so called because stones are poured from it, that is, thrown. [Note: “Thrown.” Some printed editions insert material after these words, extending to *ballista*; it is absent from the manuscripts, though it appears above, Book XIV, chapter 6, from Servius, *Georgics* I.]

2. A *ballista* is a kind of engine, named from throwing missiles. For βάλλειν in Greek means “to throw.” It is twisted by the force of cords and throws with great power either spears or stones. [Note: “Hence also *fundibalus*.” See Book IV, chapter 6.] Hence also *fundibalus*, as though “pouring out and throwing.” [Note: “A *testudo* is effective against a *ballista*: a line is formed from weapons.” Servius, Book IX, on “They hasten, their formation made a *testudo*: ‘A *testudo* is a connection of shields curved in the shape of a tortoise.’”] A *testudo* is effective against a *ballista*, for a formation of weapons is made, with the bosses joined together.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Battering Ram

1. The battering ram (*aries*) received its name from its appearance, because it strikes the wall with force like fighting rams. [Note: “Rams . . . yield easily.” From Hegesippus, Book III, chapter 11.] The head of a strong, knotty tree is covered with iron; suspended by ropes and handled by many men, it is driven against the wall. Then it is drawn backward and launched with greater force. Thus, by repeated blows, the shaken side of the wall yields, and, hollowed out, makes an opening for those about to break in.

2. A sack full of straw, lowered into the place struck by the ram, is a remedy against its impact. Since the loose interior of the sacks cushions the blow of the ram, the impact is softened. Harder things yield more easily to softer ones.

3. *Plutei* are hurdles covered with rawhide, placed before the enemy while work is being carried out.

4. A *musculus* is made like a tunnel, by which a wall is pierced; hence it is called *musculus*, as though “little wall.” [Note: “*Musculus* . . . as though *murusculus*.” Vegetius, Book IV, chapter 15, thinks that *musculi* were named from sea creatures that assist whales.]

## CHAPTER XII. On Shields

1. [Note: “A *clypeus* is a larger shield.” Servius, frequently.] A *clypeus* is a larger shield, so called because it conceals the body and withdraws it from danger. [Note: “From κλέπτειν.” From the same source, *Aeneid* VII, on “Neither the shields nor the chariots resound.” But it is more correctly derived from γλύφειν, “to carve.” Pliny gives the reason, Book XXXV, chapter 3: “For the shields with which they fought at Troy contained images. Hence they acquired the name *clypei*, not, as the mistaken subtlety of grammarians wished, from *cluere*. Their origin is full of valor: the face of the person who used the shield was represented upon it,” etc.] A *clypeus* is a shield. For, by its protection, it is placed in front of the body and guards it against spears and missiles. [Note: “The *clypeus* belongs to infantry.” From Servius, on “All three hundred shield-bearing men,” *Aeneid* IX.] A *clypeus* belongs to infantry, while a *scutum* belongs to cavalry.

2. A *scutum* is so called because it shakes off the blow of missiles from itself. In order to resist missiles, the shield is held in front.

The *umbo* is the central part of a shield, as though its navel.

3. [Note: “*Ancile* . . . cut away on every side.” Varro likewise: “Or as though ἀμφίχειλον”—Servius adds, *Aeneid* VIII—“that is, having a rim all around.” See Plutarch, *Life of Numa*.] An *ancile* is a short, round shield. Virgil mentions it: “And he carried an *ancile* in his left hand.” It is called *ancile* from *ancisio*, “cutting,” because it is, as it were, cut away and rounded on every side. Ovid writes:

> And they call it an *ancile*, because it is cut away on every side,  
> And wherever you observe it with your eyes, no corner remains.

4. [Note: “*Pelta*.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “The ranks with crescent-shaped *peltae*.”] A *pelta* is a very short shield shaped like a half-moon. The Book of Kings mentions it: “King Solomon made two hundred shields of pure gold and three hundred *peltae* of refined gold.”

5. [Note: “*Cetra* . . . the Spaniards.” From the same source, *Aeneid* VII.] A *cetra* is a leather shield without wood, used by Africans and Moors; concerning it the poet writes: “The *cetra* covers the left side.”

6. [Note: “*Parma*, light arms.” Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “The point passed through the *parma*: ‘A *parma*, that is, light arms, not a *clypeus*.”] A *parma* is a light arm, as though from *parva*, “small”; it is not a *clypeus*. A shield is also called a *testudo*, for a *clypeus* is made in the form of a tortoise. [388] [Note: “A *testudo* is also a connection of shields.” See above, chapter 10.] A *testudo* is also a connection of shields curved into the form of a tortoise. In the various kinds of weapons, soldiers also take their names from animals, as with the *aries* (“ram”). Sallustius says: “In the manner of a military hedgehog.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On Breastplates

1. [Note: “*Lorica* . . . because it lacks thongs, for it is made only of iron rings.” I have no doubt that in Servius, *Aeneid* X, Isidore read that a *lorica* properly means a covering made from leather, which older men were accustomed to use in war. But he adapted the etymology to later breastplates, which are joined by hooks, as Virgil says. Varro, Book IV: “*Lorica* comes from *lora*, because they made breast coverings from rawhide; later the Gauls forged iron under this name, making an iron tunic out of rings.”] A *lorica* is so called because it lacks leather thongs, for it is woven solely from iron rings.

2. [Note: “*Squama* is an iron breastplate, etc.” Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “Nor a breastplate of double scale”: “*Squamae* are the chains of breastplates, arranged in the form of scales. Properly, *squama* also means brightness when derived from fish, and filth when derived from *squalor*.”] A *squama* is an iron breastplate made from iron or bronze plates joined together in the manner of a fish’s scales. It receives its name both from the brightness of the scales and from their likeness. [Note: “Breastplates are polished with haircloth.” From Servius, *Georgics* III, on “Use in the camp and coverings for wretched sailors.”] Breastplates are both polished and covered with haircloth.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Helmets

1. A *cassis* is made of metal plate, a *galea* of leather. For *galerus* means leather. They say that *cassis* was named by the Etruscans. They call a helmet *cassim*, I believe from the head.

2. [389] [Note: “*Apex* is as though the summit of a helmet, etc.” Servius, *Aeneid* XII, on “Yet the crest”: “The projection of a helmet, which the Greeks call a *conus*, where the crest rises”; and Book X: “The *apex*, the height of the cone.”] An *apex* is what projects from the top of a helmet and in which the crest is fixed. The Greeks call it κῶνος. For a *conus* is the curved projection on a helmet above which the crests are placed.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Forum

[Col. 0650A]

1. [Note: “*Forus*. The meal could have been derived without these words, but Braulio thought otherwise. See above, Book XV, chapter 2.] A *forum* is a place for conducting lawsuits, named from *fari*, “to speak.” This place is also called the *rostra*, because, after the Punic War, the prows of ships captured from the Carthaginians were carried off and fixed in the Roman Forum to serve as the emblem of this victory. The Forum consists of a case, a law, and a judge.

2. A case (*causa*) is so called from *casus*, “event,” by which it comes about. It is the material and origin of a matter, not yet disclosed by the examination of a proceeding. When it is brought forward, it is a *causa*; when it is examined, it is a judgment; when it is concluded, it is justice. *Judicium* (“judgment”) is as though *jurisdictio*, “jurisdiction,” and *justitia* (“justice”) as though *juris status*, “the state of the law.” A judgment was formerly called an inquiry. Hence we call those who conduct judgments *actores*, and those placed over them *quaestores* or *quaesitores*.

3. *Negotium* has several meanings: sometimes the conduct of some matter, whose opposite is leisure; sometimes the action in a case, which is litigation in a lawsuit. It is called *negotium* as though *nec otium*, “not leisure,” that is, “without leisure.” In legal cases it is called *negotium*; in commerce, *negotiatio*, where something is given so that greater profits may be gained.

4. *Jurgium* (“dispute”) is as though *juris garrium*, “legal quarrel,” because those who plead a case debate according to law.

*Lis* (“lawsuit”) first took its name from a dispute over a boundary. Virgil writes:

> A boundary had been set to distinguish the fields.

5. A case is established either by argument or by proof.

Argument never provides proof through witnesses or documents; by investigation alone it discovers the truth. Hence *argumentum* means, as it were, “an ingenious discovery.”

Proof, however, is established by witnesses and by the reliability of documents.

6. In every judgment six persons are sought: a judge, an accuser, a defendant, and three witnesses.

[Note: “*Judex* is so called.” The same, above, Book IX, chapter 4.] *Judex* (“judge”) is so called as though “one who speaks the law to the people,” or because he debates according to law. To debate according to law is to judge justly. A person is not a judge if there is no justice in him.

7. An accuser (*accusator*) is so called as though *adcausator*, because he calls to the case the person whom he accuses.

A defendant (*reus*) is named from the matter (*res*) that is sought, because even if he is not conscious of a crime, he is still called a *reus* as long as he is sued in court concerning some matter.

8. [Note: “Witnesses were formerly called *superstites*. Isidore is entirely better here than Servius, who, *Aeneid* III, on ‘Does he survive and feed on the air?’ says: ‘*Superstes* signifies one who is present.’ Festus: ‘*Superstites* signifies present witnesses. Evidence of this is that when those between whom there is a dispute are present, they are ordered to take possession.’ Plautus, in *Artemon*: ‘Now I may say whatever I wish; no witness is present here.’ Chacon read the passage this way: ‘*Superstites* signifies present witnesses.’ This reading, and Plautus’ words, sufficiently confirm this passage of Isidore; Cicero’s words in *Pro Murena* he emended as follows: ‘A composed poem, absurd in other respects and especially because, with neither of the two present as witnesses, [take possession], go on your way.’ He interpreted ‘the two’ as ‘the plaintiff and the defendant,’ and supplied ‘take possession’ from Festus.”] Witnesses were formerly called *superstites*, because they were brought forward as standing over the status of the case. Now, with part of the name removed, they are called *testes* (“witnesses”).

9. A witness is considered according to status, nature, and life. According to status: whether free, not a slave. For a slave often suppresses the truth in his testimony through fear of his master. According to nature: whether a man, not a woman. For a woman is always changeable and fickle. According to life: whether innocent and upright in conduct. For if a good life is lacking, she or he will lack credibility. Justice cannot have fellowship with a criminal.

[391] 10. There are two kinds of witnesses: those who state what they have seen, and those who report what they have heard. Witnesses offend in two ways: when they either utter falsehoods or cover the truth with silence.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Spectacles

1. Spectacles, as I think, are generally called pleasures that do not defile by themselves, [Note: “Which do not defile by themselves.” Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, final chapter: “We have explained above the nature of places: they do not defile us by themselves, but through what is done there.”] but through what is done there. They are called *spectacula* because a public viewing is provided there for human beings. They are also called *ludicra*, because they take place in games or on stages.

2.
