The origin of games is related as follows: [Note: “The Lydians, immigrants from Asia . . . of Father Liber.” From Tertullian, same work, chapter 2.] Lydians who had migrated from Asia settled in Etruria under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, who had yielded the kingdom to his brother after a dispute over royal power. Accordingly, in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also established spectacles in the name of religion. From there the Romans borrowed craftsmen who had been summoned, and from there games were called *ludi*, after the Lydians. Varro, however, says that *ludi* were so called from *ludus* (“play”), because during festivals young men used to delight the people with playful rejoicing. Hence he classifies this play as belonging to young men, festival days, temples, and religious observances.

3. Nothing further need be said about the reason for the word, since the subject itself is idolatry. Hence the games were also indiscriminately called *Liberalia*, in honor of Liber Pater. For this reason the stain of their origin must be considered, lest you regard as good something that received its beginning from evil.

[Note: “[The] stain of origin … received.” From the same passage.] The gymnastic game is one kind; the circus game, the gladiatorial game, and the stage game are others.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Gymnastic Game

1. The gymnastic game is a display of speed and strength. Its venue is called a gymnasium, where athletes train and the speed of runners is tested. Hence it has come about that the exercises of nearly all arts are called gymnasia.

2. Formerly, those competing in the contests were girded, so that they would not be naked. Later, when a certain runner loosened his belt, he suddenly fell prostrate and lifeless. Therefore, by decree of the council, the archon Hippomenes then permitted all competitors thereafter to exercise naked. From this the place was called a gymnasium, because young men exercise naked in the field, where only their private parts are covered.

[Note: “By decree of the council, the archon Hippomenes then …” The authority must be sought.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Kinds of Gymnastic Contests

1. There are five kinds of gymnastic contests: jumping, running, throwing, strength, and wrestling. Hence they relate that a certain king, having as many adolescent sons as there were kinds, ordered them to compete for the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Jumping

1. *Saltus* (“jumping”) is so called as if from *exsilire in altum*, “to leap upward.” For jumping is to leap either higher or farther.

## CHAPTER XX. On Running

1. *Cursus* (“running”) is named from the speed of the legs. For running is the swiftness of the feet.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Throwing

1. *Jactus* (“throwing”) is named from *jacere*, “to throw.” Hence a fisherman’s net is also called a *jaculum* (“throwing weapon”). The practice of this art is to seize a stone and strike from a distance, to hurl spears with measured weight, and to shoot arrows from a bow.

[Note: “To seize a stone and strike from a distance.” Another reading: “to seize stones and carry them far.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. On Strength

1. Strength is the immeasurable extent of power in labor and bodily weight.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Wrestling

1. *Luctatio* (“wrestling”) is named from the clasping of the sides, on which those who compete at close quarters lean. In Greek they are called *athletae*, “athletes.” The place of wrestling is called the *palaestra*.

[Note: “On which those competing at close quarters lean.” Thus the Old Gothic codex. One Roman manuscript has “on which they lean.”]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Palaestra

1. They say that the *palaestra* was named either from Greek ἀπὸ τῆς πάλης (*apo tēs palēs*), that is, “from wrestling,” or from ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν (*apo tou pallein*), that is, “from the movement of the urn” [the transmitted text reads *ruinae*, “of ruin”; this is evidently corrupt]. The latter explanation is given because, when wrestling, they seize one another around the middle and almost shake one another; among the Greeks this is called *pallein*, “to shake.” Some think that the art of wrestling was demonstrated by the struggle of bears. For among all wild animals, bears alone are said to rise when they engage, quickly crouch down and spring back, sometimes trying one another with their paws and sometimes driving each other away by an embrace, after the manner of wrestlers.

[Note: “But the palaestra … of the lot.” Servius, on “and the bodies hardened by the wrestling-school,” *Georgics* II: “The palaestra is named either ἀπὸ τῆς πάλης, that is, ‘from wrestling,’ or ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν, that is, ‘from the motion of the urn’; for they wrestled after being selected by lot.” This passage was in a very bad state in all the Isidorian books.]

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Contest

1. What the Latins call *certamina* (“contests”), the Greeks call ἀγῶνες (*agōnes*), from the crowds with which they were celebrated. Indeed, every gathering and assembly is also called an *agon*. Others think that they were called *agones* because they were presented in circles, or in places that were, as it were, *agōnes*, that is, “without a corner.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Kinds of Contests

1. The kinds of contests included greatness of strength, swiftness in running, skill in shooting arrows, endurance in standing; also, to the accompaniment of the lyre or pipes, the gestures of movement; contests concerning character, appearance, and the modulation of singing; and contests involving endurance of land warfare, naval battle, and punishments.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Circus Games

1. The circus games were instituted for the sake of sacred rites and the celebrations of the pagan gods. Hence those who watch them appear to serve the worship of demons. For equestrian activity was formerly conducted simply, and certainly its ordinary use did not involve guilt; but when natural use was compelled into games, it was transferred to the worship of demons.

[Note: “For equestrian activity …” From Tertullian, *On the Circus*, chapter 6.]

2. These forms are therefore also assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom Stesichorus teaches that horses were distributed by Mercury. Neptune too is an equestrian deity, whom the Greeks call Ἵππιος (*Hippios*), “of horses.” Horses have also been consecrated to Mars and Jupiter in the games, and they themselves preside over the four-horse chariots.

3. The circus games, however, were so called either from *circumeundo*, “going around,” or because, where the turning-posts now stand, swords were formerly placed, around which the four-horse chariots ran; hence they were called *circenses*, from the swords (*enses*) around which they ran. For when driving chariots along the shore beside the banks of rivers, they placed swords in a row on the riverbank, and it was a matter of skill to turn the horses around these dangers. Thus they are thought to have been called *circenses*, as if *circum enses*, “around the swords.”

[Note: “The circus games, etc.” From Servius, at the beginning of *Georgics* III and *Aeneid* VIII, on “when the great circus games had been held.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Circus

1. The circus was principally consecrated by the pagans to the Sun. His temple stood in the middle of the course, and his image projected from the temple’s roof, since they did not think that the god whom they kept in the open ought to be consecrated under a roof. The circus is the entire space around which they customarily ride on horseback.

[Note: “The circus was consecrated to the Sun …” From Tertullian, *On Places*, chapter 5.]

2. The Romans think that it was called this from the circuit of the horses, because the horses run around the turning-posts there. The Greeks, however, assert that it was named after Circe, the daughter of the Sun, who instituted this kind of contest for her father; they derive the name *circus* from her. She was a sorceress, poisoner, and priestess of demons; in the arrangement and activity of this place, magical arts and the worship of idolatry are recognized.

[Note: “The Romans think that it was called this …” Above, Book XV, chapter 2.]

[Note: “The Greeks, however, etc.” From Tertullian, in the same passage.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Ornaments

1. The ornaments of the circus are the eggs, the turning-post, the obelisk, and the starting-gates. The eggs they attribute to the honor of Castor and Pollux, because, believing that they were born from an egg produced by Jupiter in the form of a swan, they are not ashamed of this belief.

[Note: “They attribute the eggs to the honor of Castor and Pollux …” From Tertullian, *On the Circus*.]

2. The Romans, however, contrive that the circus games be referred to the causes of the world, so that under this appearance they may excuse the superstitions of their vanities.

[Note: “They are referred to the causes of the world.” Servius, commenting on “I shall drive a hundred four-horse chariots …”: “That is, he says, ‘I shall present circus games lasting one day.’ For, as Varro says in his books *On the Peoples of the Roman Nation*, formerly twenty-five races were held, twenty-four of them corresponding to the number of hours, while the twenty-fifth was called the ‘money race,’ because it was presented from the people’s contributions. Add twelve victims, representing the twelve signs of the zodiac, and seven turning-posts, representing the seven planets. The circus games were conducted in this order: four-horse, two-horse, or three-horse chariots, four drawn by lot from the four factions—the green, red, white, and blue—were stationed in the starting-gates. Then, when the magistrate presiding over the games sent the cloth—that is, gave the signal—the chariots were released from the gates and completed seven spaces, or circuits, around the turning-posts. When the victor had been crowned, one race had been completed. The same was done in the remaining twenty-four races. Since four chariots ran in each race, Virgil correctly says: ‘I shall drive a hundred four-horse chariots to the river.’ See Suetonius, *Domitian*; Seneca, Book IV of the *Letters*, Letter XXX; Ovid, *Halieutica*; Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, VII; Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 3.]

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Turning-Posts

1. By the designation “turning-posts” they wish properly to signify the boundary and end of the world, from the fact that a limit has been measured out for something, or as a testimony to the rising and setting of the Sun.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Obelisk

1. Mespres, king of Egypt, is said to have been the first to make an obelisk, for the following reason. When at a certain time the Nile had harmed Egypt by a violent flood, the king became indignant, as though he were exacting punishment from the river, and shot an arrow into the waters. Not long afterward he was seized by a grave illness and lost his sight. After recovering his vision following his blindness, he dedicated two obelisks to the Sun. For an obelisk is called an “arrow,” and it is placed in the middle of the circus because the Sun runs through the middle of the world.

[Note: “Mespres, king of Egypt.” Manuscripts have *Messeres* and *Mefferes*; Pliny’s manuscripts have *Mestres* and *Mestires*; printed editions have *Mespheem*; Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, has *Mephres*; Josephus has *Mephes*. Herodotus, Book II, relates this story of Pheron, son of Sesostris.]

2. The obelisk, placed midway between the two turning-posts, signifies the summit and highest point of heaven, since the Sun passes across the middle point between the two intervals at the division of the hours. On the top of the obelisk is placed a gilded object shaped like a flame, because the Sun contains within itself a very great amount of heat and fire.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Starting-Gates

1. In the circus, the places from which the horses are released were called *carceres* (“prisons”), from the same origin as the prison that is in a city: just as condemned and confined men are restrained there, so horses are restrained here lest they come out before the signal is given.

[Note: “In the circus.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, commenting on “He restrains them with fetters and from the prison.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Charioteers

1. The circus profession includes the charioteer and the chariot, horsemen, and footmen. A charioteer is properly so called because he drives and guides the chariot, or because he strikes the yoked horses.

[Note: “For *haurit* means ‘strikes,’ as in: ‘He pierces the exposed side.’ These are Servius’ words, *Georgics* III, on “and fear beating pierces their exulting hearts.”]

2. He is also called an *agitator*, that is, a driver or striker, named from *agere*, “to drive.” Charioteers, however, have two colors with which they clothe a form of idolatry. The green was dedicated by the pagans to the earth, and the blue to the sky and sea.

[Note: “For the green belongs to the earth …” From Tertullian, *On the Art of the Circus*, chapter 6.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Four-Horse Chariots

1. Ericthonius, who ruled at Athens, is said to have been the first to yoke four horses, as Virgil records:

> Ericthonius first dared to yoke four horses to chariots  
> And, victorious, to stand upon the swift wheels.

[Note: From the same passage of Tertullian.]

2. According to the myths, he was born as the son of Minerva and Vulcan from Vulcan’s lust that fell upon the earth: a demonic portent, or rather a devil, who first dedicated a chariot to Juno. With such an originator, four-horse chariots were brought forth.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Chariot

1. *Currus* (“chariot”) is named from *cursus* (“course”), or because it appears to have wheels; hence also *carrum*, as if from *curvum*, “curved.”

[Note: *Carrum* is explained as if from *curvum*, “curved”; another reading explains it as if from *cursum*, “course,” and another as if from *currum*, “chariot.”]

The chariots of four-horse teams formerly had a double pole, continuous along its length, and placed upon all the horses under the yoke.

2. Clysthenes of Sicyon was the first to yoke only the middle horses, attaching each of them separately on either side by a single fastening. The Greeks call these horses σειραφόροι (*seiraphoroi*), “rope-bearers”; the Latins call them *funarii*, “rope-horses,” from the type of fastening by which they were formerly tied.

[Note: “The first was Clysthenes of Sicyon.” Pausanias, *Phocica*.]

[Note: The Latin term *funarii* is used by Suetonius in *Tiberius*.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Horses with Which They Race

1. *Quadrigae* (“four-horse teams”), *bigae* (“two-horse teams”), *trigae* (“three-horse teams”), and *sejugae* (“six-horse teams”) are named from the number of horses and from the yoke. Of these, they consecrated four-horse teams to the Sun, two-horse teams to the Moon, three-horse teams to the underworld gods, six-horse teams to Jupiter, and the riders who leap from horse to horse to Lucifer and Hesperus.

[Note: The words “and Hesperus” are absent from the older Gothic manuscripts.]

They yoke four horses to the Sun because the year turns through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

2. They assign two-horse teams to the Moon because it competes with the Sun in a double course, or because it is seen both at night and by day. They yoke one black horse and one white horse. They assign three-horse teams to the gods of the underworld because they drag human beings to themselves through three ages: infancy, youth, and old age. A six-horse team, the largest chariot, runs for Jupiter, because they believe him to be the greatest of their gods.

3. They say that the four-horse teams run on wheels either because this world passes swiftly along the circuit of its circle, or because of the Sun, since it turns in a revolving circuit, as Ennius says:

> From there the white wheel opened the heavens with its rays.

[Note: “From there the white wheel opened the heavens with its rays.” Some cite this verse from Sidonius.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Seven Circuits

1. The four-horse chariots run seven circuits, referring this either to the course of the seven stars, by which they say the world is governed, or to the course of the seven days of the present life, at the completion of which the end of life is fulfilled. Their end is the chalk, that is, judgment.

[Note: “The end of which is the chalk.” This is found in the best Neapolitan and some Gothic manuscripts. Seneca is entirely correct, Book XIX of the *Letters*, Letter 109: “Then he proceeds to those things that the custom of the age has changed, as Cicero says, since we have been called back by an interruption from the very finish of his speech. What we now call chalk in the circus, the ancients called the finish.” Gloss: *creta*, Greek λευκή (*leukē*), “white.” Lucretius called it “the white chalk”: “[You] … for me as I run, the prescribed white [line] of chalk …”]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Horsemen

1. They say that the individual horsemen run separately because each person individually completes and passes through the course of this life, one following another at different times, yet all along one road of mortality, up to each person’s own turning-post, death.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Riders Who Leap from Horse to Horse

1. They were called *desultores* (“leapers”) because formerly, as each person reached the end of the course, he would leap down, or because he leapt from one horse to another.

[Note: “Leapers.” Hyginus, *Fables* 80: “Hence the Romans also preserve the practice: when they send out a leaper, one man has two horses, a cap on his head, and leaps from horse to horse, so that he performs the role of himself and his brother.” Cassiodorus, *Variarum* III: “The leaping horses, by which the attendants of the circus announce that the races are about to begin, imitate the speed of the herald of Lucifer.”]

## CHAPTER XL. On the Footmen

1. They say that the footmen run on foot for this reason: human beings proceed toward mortality on their feet. Therefore they run from the upper part toward the lower, that is, from east to west, because mortals arise and set. They run naked because a human being in this world has no remains. They run in a straight course because there is no distance between life and death. But they invent these explanations in an attempt to excuse their vanities and sacrileges.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Colors of the Horses

1. In connection with the causes of the elements, these same pagans also associated colors with the horses: red with the Sun, that is, with fire; white with air; green with earth; and blue with the sea. Likewise, they wanted the red horses to run for summer, because they are the color of fire and everything then turns yellow. The white horses were assigned to winter, because winter is icy and everything grows white in the cold; the green horses to spring, because then the vine-shoot becomes dense with green.

[Note: “In connection with the causes.” See Tertullian, *On the Art of the Circus*, chapter 6.]

2. Likewise, they consecrated the red horses to Mars, from whom the Romans arise, and because the Roman standards are adorned with scarlet, or because Mars delights in blood. They consecrated the white horses to the west winds and clear weather; the green to flowers and the earth; the blue to waters or to air, because they are blue in color; the yellow, that is, saffron-colored, to fire and the Sun; and the purple to Iris, whom we call the rainbow, because Iris has very many colors.

3. Thus, while through this spectacle they are profaned by the worship of gods and by the world’s elements, they are unquestionably recognized as worshiping those same gods and those same elements. Therefore you must observe, Christian, how many unclean names the circus possesses. Consequently, the place will be alien to you, since very many spirits of Satan have occupied it.

[Note: “For the devil and his angels have filled the whole of it.” Tertullian, *On Places*: “Satan and his angels have filled the whole world.”]

For the devil and his angels have filled the whole of it.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Theater

1. The theater is the place enclosing the stage, having the shape of a semicircle, in which all the spectators stand and look on. Its form was originally round, as was that of the amphitheater; later, a theater was made from the middle of the amphitheater. The theater was named from the spectacle, ἀπὸ τῆς θεωρίας (*apo tēs theōrias*), “from viewing,” because in it the people, standing above and watching, contemplated the games.

[Note: “The theater.” On the theater, above, Book XV, chapter 2.]

[Note: Ἀπὸ τῆς θεωρίας, “from viewing.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and in the middle of the valley, the theater.”]

2. The same place was also called a *prostibulum*, because after the games had ended, prostitutes stood there for sale. It was likewise called a *lupanar*, from the same prostitutes, who, because of the disgrace of their publicly exposed bodies, were called *lupae* (“she-wolves”).

[Note: “The same place was also called a brothel.” See Tertullian, *On the Theater*.]

[Note: “The same place was also called a brothel.” From Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII, chapter 21, and Lactantius.]

[Note: “Because of the disgrace of their publicly exposed bodies.” Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20: “For she was the wife of Faustulus, and because of the disgrace of her publicly exposed body she was called a ‘she-wolf’ among the shepherds, that is, a prostitute; hence the term *lupanar* is also derived.”]

For prostitutes are called *lupae* from their rapacity, because they drag wretched people to themselves and seize them. Brothels were established by the pagans so that the modesty of unfortunate women might be publicly exposed and made a subject of ridicule, both for those who committed the acts and for those who endured them.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Stage

1. The *scena* (“stage”) was a place below the theater, arranged in the form of a house with a platform. This platform was called the *orchestra*, where comic and tragic actors sang, and actors and mimes danced.

[Note: “The platform was called the orchestra.” Improperly so. Vitruvius clearly distinguishes the orchestra from the platform in Book V, chapter 6: the stage was higher than the orchestra, and among the Romans places were assigned in the orchestra to senators and other distinguished men, but not likewise on the stage. The name *orchestra* can include the platform, but not conversely. The Greeks called the platform *thymelē*, about which Isidore speaks shortly afterward.]

The stage was called *scena* in Greek usage because it was constructed to resemble a house. Hence among the Hebrews the dedication of tabernacles was called *Scenopegia*, “the setting up of tents,” from the resemblance of the structures to dwellings.

[Note: “The stage was so called.” Servius, commenting on “the stage glittering amid the woods”: “*Scena* means shading; it was called *scena* from Greek ἀπὸ τῆς σκιάς (*apo tēs skias*), that is, ‘from shade.’ For among the ancients the theatrical stage did not have a wall, but they sought shade from leafy shelters; later they began to construct wooden panels in the form of a wall.”]

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Orchestra

1. The orchestra was the platform of the stage, where a dancer could perform or two people could dispute with each other. There the comic and tragic poets mounted to compete; while they sang, others performed gestures. The theatrical professions are tragedians, comedians, thymelic musicians, actors, mimes, and dancers.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Tragedians

1. Tragedians are those who sang ancient deeds and crimes of wicked kings in mournful verse before the watching people.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Comedians

1. Comedians are those who sang the actions of private persons through words and gestures, and represented the seductions of virgins and the loves of prostitutes in their plays.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Thymelic Musicians

1. Thymelic musicians were stage musicians who played or sang before the performance on instruments, lyres, and citharas. They were called *thymelici* because formerly they stood in the orchestra and sang upon the platform called the *thymele*.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Actors

1. Actors are those who, dressed in women’s clothing, represented the gestures of immodest women. By dancing they also displayed histories and deeds. They were called *histriones* either because this kind of performance was brought from Istria, or because they represented stories complicated with historical material, as though they were *historiones* (“story-performers”).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Mimes

1. Mimes were so called by a Greek term because they are imitators of human affairs. They had their own author—or, according to another reading, actor—who recited the plot before they performed the mime. For poets composed the plots in such a way that they were especially suited to bodily movement.

[Note: “For they had their own author.” One manuscript reads *actor*, “actor.”]

## CHAPTER L. On Dancers

1. Varro says that dancers were called *saltatores* after Salius of Arcadia, whom Aeneas brought with him to Italy and who first taught the noble Roman youths to dance.

[Note: “Dancers.” From Festus, under *Salii*, except that Festus cites not Varro but Polemo as his authority.]

## CHAPTER LI. Under Whose Patronage Each Performance Is Conducted

1. Clearly, in the theatrical arts Liber and Venus exercise patronage; these are the private and proper concerns of the stage, involving gestures and bodily movement. They sacrificed softness to Liber and Venus: to the former through sexual behavior, to the latter through bodily bending, in a state of dissolution.

[Note: “Clearly.” Everything is from Tertullian, *On Scenic Arts*. We have retained *lyris* (“lyres”) from our manuscripts, where Tertullian’s text reads *litteris* (“letters”).]

2. The activities conducted there with voices, melodies, instruments, and lyres have Apollo, the Muses, Minerva, and Mercury as patrons. You must hate this spectacle, Christian, since you hate its authors.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Amphitheater

1. The amphitheater is a place for spectacles where gladiators fight. Hence it is called a gladiatorial game, because there young men learn the use of weapons through various movements: sometimes competing with one another with swords or fists, sometimes advancing against wild beasts. They enter this deadly contest not from hatred but enticed by a reward.

2. It is called an amphitheater because it is made from two theaters. For the amphitheater is round, whereas the theater is made from the middle of the amphitheater and has the shape of a semicircle.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Equestrian Game

1. There were many kinds of gladiators, the first of which was the contest of horsemen. Two horsemen, after military standards had first been carried before them, proceeded—one from the eastern gate and the other from the western—on white horses with golden helmets and with lighter, more manageable weapons. Thus, with savage perseverance, they entered battle for their honor, fighting until one sprang upon the death of the other, so that the one who fell might have his downfall, and the one who killed him his glory. This armor fought for Mars, for the sake of single combat.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the Net-Fighters

1. The *retiarius* (“net-fighter”) was so called from his type of armor. In the gladiatorial game, while secretly fighting against another, he carried a net—called a *jaculum* (“throwing weapon”)—so that, pursuing his adversary with a pointed weapon, he might cover him and overcome him once entangled.

[Note: “He carried a net, which was called a *jaculum*.” The single word *retejaculum* was also used. A highly learned scholar has recently written on the *retiarius*, *secutor*, and the other kinds of gladiators. See Festus, under *Retiarius*.]

[Note: “Pursuing him with a pointed weapon.” This is the reading of all manuscripts. Chacon preferred *insequentem*, “the one pursuing”; others read *insistentem*, “the one pressing upon him.”]

This armor fought for Neptune, for the sake of the trident.

## CHAPTER LV. On the Pursuers

1. The *secutor* (“pursuer”) was named from pursuing the net-fighter. He carried a pointed weapon and a leaden mass, which hindered his opponent’s throwing weapon, so that, before the other could strike with the net, he might overcome him. This armor was consecrated to Vulcan. For fire always pursues water, and therefore he was matched with the net-fighter, because fire and water are always hostile to one another.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Noose-Fighters

1. The contest of the *laquearii* consisted in pursuing fleeing men in the arena, hindering them by throwing a noose over them, and knocking down those they caught; they were wrapped in a leather shield.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Velites

1. The contest of the *velites* consisted in throwing weapons back and forth. Their combat was varied and more pleasing to spectators than the others. The *velites* were so called either from their flying about, or from an Etruscan city called Veles.

[Note: “The *velites* … either from flying about.” Festus, under *Advolitatio*: “Velites are lightly equipped soldiers, as if *volites*, that is, ‘flyers.’”]

[Note: “Or from an Etruscan city called Veles.” Thus the Gothic codex; other manuscripts have *Veletes*.]

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the Deadly Combat

1. The combat with wild beasts consisted in receiving and fighting against beasts that had been released, competing in a voluntary death—not through guilt, but through madness.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the Abomination of These Things

1. These spectacles of cruelty and this viewing of vanities were instituted not only because of human vices but also at the commands of demons. Therefore a Christian must have nothing to do with the madness of the circus, the immodesty of the theater, the cruelty of the amphitheater, the savagery of the arena, or the luxury of the games. For one who dares such things denies God and becomes a transgressor against the Christian faith, desiring again what he renounced long ago in baptism: the devil, his pageants, and his works.

## CHAPTER LX. On Alea, the Board Game

1. *Alea*, that is, the board game, was invented by the Greeks during the leisure of the Trojan War by a certain soldier named Alea, from whom the art also received its name. The board is played with a *pyrgus*, counters, and dice.

[Note: “By a certain soldier named Alea.” The authority for this statement must be sought.]

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Dice-Tower

1. The *pyrgus* was so called either because the dice pass through it or because it has the appearance of a tower. For the Greeks call a tower πύργος (*pyrgos*).

[Note: “The dice-tower.” A small vessel fashioned in the form of a little tower, from which dice were thrown into a tray, so that no trickery could be involved in throwing them by hand. Martial calls it a “little tower.”]

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Counters

1. The counters were so called because they are smooth and round. Hence a *calculus* is also a short stone, which is trodden upon without inconvenience because of its small size.

[Note: “Because it is trodden upon without inconvenience because of its smallness.” Above, Book XVI, chapter 6, from Servius, *Georgics* II.]

The counters are also so called because they move along ordered paths, as though along little stones (*calculas*).

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Dice

1. The dice were so called because they are square on every side. Some call them “little hares,” because they run about by leaping. Formerly dice were called *jacula*, “throwing weapons,” from *jacere*, “to throw.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Configurations of Dice

1. Some gamblers think that they practice this art according to natural philosophy through allegory, inventing it under a certain likeness to reality. They say that they play with three dice because of the three periods of the world—past, present, and future—since these do not stand still but run their course. They also explain the paths, divided into spaces of six, by the ages of human beings, and by lines of three according to the periods of time. Hence they say that the board is marked out with three lines.

[Note: “Some, through allegory, practice this art according to natural philosophy.” See Eustathius, commentary on the *Iliad*, Book I, at “They delighted their hearts with counters before the doors.”]

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Names of the Dice Throws

1. Among the ancient players, each throw was named from its number: *unio*, “one”; *binio*, “two”; *trio*, “three”; *quatrio*, “four”; *quinio*, “five”; and *senio*, “six.” Later the name of each was changed: they called the *unio* a “dog,” the *trio* a *suppus*, and the *quatrio* a “flat” throw.

[Note: “The *trio* was called *suppus*.” In Greek ὕπτιον (*hyption*), “supine.” See Festus.]

[Note: “The *quatrio* was called *planum*, ‘flat.’ Rather, I think it should be *pronum*, ‘prone,’ which is also Aristotle’s term πρηνής (*prēnēs*). “Prone” is opposed to “supine,” not “flat.”]

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Throwing the Dice

1. The throw of the dice is arranged by experienced gamblers in such a way as to produce what they want—for example, a *senio*, which brings them a favorable outcome by its throw. They avoid the “dog,” because it is disadvantageous; for it signifies one.

[Note: “For example, a *senio*.” This was also called *Venus* and *Cous* whenever four dice fell so that none corresponded with any other.]

[Note: Aristotle, *On the Heavens* II: “It is difficult to succeed either in many things or many times; for example, to cast many knucklebones as a Coan throw (*kōous*) is impossible, but with one or two it is easier.”]

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the Movement of the Counters

1. Some counters move in an ordered manner, others randomly. Therefore some are called “ordered,” others “wandering.” Those that cannot be moved at all are called *inciti*, “blocked.”

[Note: Hence needy people are also called *inciti*. Nonius: “Poverty is called *incitas*.”]

Thus people in need are called *inciti*, because no hope of proceeding farther remains for them.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Prohibition of Dice

1. Fraud, deceit, and perjury are never absent from this art; finally, hatred and loss of property are present as well. Therefore, on account of these crimes, it was at times prohibited by law.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the Ball

1. A ball is properly so called because it is full of hairs. It is also called a sphere, from carrying or striking. Dorcatius gives the following account of the kinds and weight of balls:

> Do not spare to stuff it with the hair of the long-lived stag,  
> Until an ounce has been added to a double pound.

2. Among the kinds of balls are the triangular ball and the arena ball. The triangular ball is one with which three people play.

[Note: “The triangular ball.” Martial, Book XIV, epigram 46:

> If you know that I can drive you away with noble left-hand blows,  
> > I am yours; if you do not, rustic, give me back the ball.

]

The arena ball is one which, after being thrown from within a circle of people standing and watching, they customarily catch beyond the proper distance and use to begin play. They call it “the cubit game” when two people strike the ball face-to-face, from close by, with their elbows nearly touching.

[Note: “He is said to give the shin.” Plutarch, *Cicero*, concerning Cornelius Lentulus, Catiline’s associate, surnamed Sura: “Coming forward very carelessly and contemptuously, he said that he would not give an account but would offer his shin, just as children were accustomed to do whenever they made a mistake while playing ball.”]

He is said to “give the shin” who, extending his leg, offers the ball to his fellow players to be struck.

# BOOK NINETEEN: ON SHIPS, BUILDINGS, AND CLOTHING

## CHAPTER ONE. On Ships

1. I have next undertaken to note, in part, the names of certain arts by which something is manufactured, the tools of craftsmen, and things that perform a service or are of a similar kind.

2. *Artifex* (“craftsman”) is used generally because he makes (*faciat*) an art or product, as a goldsmith (*aurifex*) makes gold. For the ancients used *faxo* for *facio*, “I make.”

[Note: “*Artifex* in the general nominative.” As in the Greek τέκτων (*tektōn*), “craftsman.”]

3. The *nauclerus* was called the owner of a ship, because the ship belonged to his share or lot; for κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek means “lot.” The others on the ship are in partnership.

[Note: “They are in contribution.” The term *contributio* is frequent among the jurists, as in the title *On the Rhodian Law of Jettison*.]

[Note: “The *nauclerus*.” He is also called *navicularius* and *magister navis* by the jurists: one who owns or has hired a ship and receives all its proceeds and revenues. But for Isidore, below, chapter 19, *navicularius* is a builder of ships, just as a *carpentarius* is a builder of a *carpentum*.]

4. The *gubernio*, who is also the helmsman, is so called as if *cohibernator*, “restrainer,” because by his prudence he restrains the winter storms of the sea.

[Note: “The *gubernio*, who also governs.” Gloss: *guber*—I believe the word is mutilated—Greek κυβερνήτης (*kybernētēs*), “helmsman.” Laberius is said by Aulus Gellius, Book XXI, chapter 7, to have used *gubernium* for “helmsman” in *Anna Perenna*. One also finds *archigubernius*, or *archigubernus*, in the Digest, Book XXXVI, title 1, chapter 46. Lucretius likewise used *guberna* for “rudders”:

> The great sea is accustomed to scatter benches and rudders;

and Lucilius, cited by Nonius:

> Strip the prows and knock off the rudders.

]

5. *Nauta* (“sailor”) is derived from *navis*, “ship.” *Navita* is used poetically for *nauta*, just as *Mavors* is used for Mars. The correct form is *nauta*.

[Note: “*Navita* for *nauta*.” From Servius, *Georgics* I and *Aeneid* VI. Thus the Greeks use both ναύτην (*nautēn*) and ναυάτην (*nauatēn*).]

6. The *remex* (“oarsman”) is so called because he carries an oar. It is formed like *tubex* in the nominative case.

[Note: “Like *tubex*.” One manuscript reads “like *obex*”; concerning this type, see Servius.]

7. *Epibata* is called in Greek the person who in Latin is called “one who comes aboard.” He has no business, but, after paying the fare, intends to cross to other lands.

[Note: “*Epibata*.” Hence *epibatēgoi*, “transport ships.” *Epibatae* are also those taken on board for protection. See Pollux.]

8. Some say that a ship was so called because it seeks a *gnavus* (“skilled”) pilot—that is, one who is knowledgeable, wise, and energetic, who knows how to contain and steer amid maritime dangers and accidents. Hence Solomon’s saying: “The intelligent will possess the helm.”

[Note: “Because it seeks a skilled pilot.” Thus the Gothic manuscripts, correctly. The editor also assigns *navus* its own etymology, as though it meant “one who knows”; I attach no importance to this, although the glossaries interpret *navus* in the same way: “*Navus*, knowledgeable”; “*navus*, active, nimble, mobile.”]

The Lydians were the first to construct a ship; seeking the uncertainties of the open sea, they made the sea traversable for human use.

[Note: “The Lydians first made a ship.” This seems to have been taken from Hister, a Greek writer whom some think Jerome translated into Latin.]

9. A raft (*rates*) was the first and most ancient kind of vessel, joined together from rough beams and planks.

[Note: “Rafts were first.” Pliny, Book VII, chapter 56: “Danaus first came to Greece from Egypt by ship; before that, people sailed on rafts invented in the Red Sea.”]

Ships built in imitation of it were called *ratariae*.

[Note: “*Ratariae*.” Aulus Gellius mentions them, Book X, chapter 25; but some prefer the form *ratiariae*.] Nowadays *rates* is used improperly for “ships.” Properly, *rates* are beams joined together.

[Note: “*Rates*, abusively ‘ships’ … beams joined together.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, at “and scattered the raft.”]

10. A *trieris* is a large ship, which the Greeks call a *durcon* [Note: [Col. 0664C] “Which the Greeks call *durcon*”; another reading has *durchonem*. Perhaps these words are rightly absent from the Seguntine manuscript. Further investigation is needed, for that codex is often mutilated elsewhere as well.], concerning which it is said in Isaiah: “No large ship passed through it.”

[Col. 0664A] 11. A *carpasia* is a ship named from the island of Carpathos, just as a *Rhodian* is named from Rhodes and an *Alexandrian* from Alexandria.

12. [Note: [Col. 0664C] *Liburnae.* These too seem to derive from Hister. But just as in his text *Liburnia* should be read for *Libya*, so here I would substitute *Libyans* for *Liburnians*. See Appian, *Illyrian War*; Lucian, *The Loves* (ἐν τοῖς ἔρωσι); and Vegetius, book IV.] *Liburnae* are so called from the Libyans; for they are merchants’ ships. Horace speaks of them:

> You will go in Liburnian ships among the tall vessels.

13. *Rostratae* (“beaked ships”) are so called because they have bronze beaks at the front [Note: [Col. 0664C] “So that they may not strike against the reefs.” Hister: “For the beaked ships themselves, raised high toward the open sea like a more prominent peak of a sandbank, have beaks at the front because of the reefs, so that, since they possess such force as they move and hurry along, they may not perhaps strike or collide.”], so that they may not strike against or collide with the reefs.

14. *Longae* (“long ships”) are those which we call *dromones*. They are so called because they are longer than the others; their opposite is the *musculus*, a short vessel. *Dromo* derives from “running down” (*decurrendo*); for the Greeks call a course *δρόμος* (*dromos*).

15. [Note: [Col. 0664C] “A fleet is so called … they carry.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “Shall Pallas burn the fleet?”] *Classis* (“fleet”) is named from the Greek expression ἀπὸ τῶν κάλων, that is, “from pieces of wood,” [Col. 0664D] whence also *calones*, the men who carry wood for the soldiers. 417

[Col. 0664B] 16. An *ancyromagus* is so called because, by reason of its speed, it is suited to carrying anchors and the other equipment of ships.

17. A *phaselus* is a vessel which we incorrectly call a *baselus*. Virgil mentions it:

> And [uncertain: *putisque*] little *phaseli*.

18. [Note: [Col. 0664D] A *scapha*, also called a *catascopus*. See Vegetius, book IV, chapter 37, and Gellius, book X, chapter 25, where *catascopium* is a diminutive form. *Catascopus* occurs in Hirtius, *On the African War*.] A *scapha*, which is a *κατάσκοπος* (*kataskopos*), is a vessel called in Latin a “scouting vessel” (*speculatorium*); for *σκοπεῖν* (*skopein*) is rendered in Latin by *intendere*, “to observe” or “to direct one’s attention.”

19. A *barca* is a vessel that carries all a ship’s cargo to the shore. On the open sea, because of the excessive waves, the ship takes it into her own bosom. But when she has approached the harbor, the *barca* returns to the ship the service that the ship rendered to it at sea.

20. [Note: [Col. 0664D] A *paro* is a vessel suited to pirates. That is, it is equipped and, as it were, prepared; for he is seeking this sort of derivation. Unless one prefers to suppose that *apertum* (“open”) was written *aptum* through a Gothic abbreviation. This is supported both by *fluctigeri* for ἐπίθελοι in Cicero’s verse and by the fact that open ships, called ἄφρακτα (*aphrakta*) by the Greeks, are contrasted with decked ships. Livy, book XXXVI: “Gaius Livius, commander of the Roman fleet, set out from Rome for Naples with fifty decked ships, where he had ordered the allies of that coast to assemble; the open ships which were owed under the treaty,” and so forth.] A *paro* is a vessel suited to pirates, and is so called from this circumstance. Cicero says:

[Col. 0664C]

> Then he gives himself to the wave-bearing vessel and entrusts himself to the *paro*.

And elsewhere:

> He plays by the shore in swift little *parunculi*.

[Col. 0665A] 418

21. A *myoparo* is, as it were, a small *paro*. It is a skiff made of wickerwork which, covered with rawhide, provides a type of vessel such as German pirates use along the shores of the Ocean or in the marshes because of its agility. Concerning these vessels, the *History* says: “The people of the Saxons rely on *myoparones*, not on strength; they are prepared for flight rather than for battle.”

22. *Celoces*, [Note: [Col. 0665C] Which the Greeks call *celetes*. Suidas: Κέλης, ὁ μόνος ἵππος καὶ ὁ ἐπὶ τούτου φερόμενος, “a single horse and the rider carried upon it”; and shortly afterward, Κέλης εἶδος πλοιαρίου μικροῦ, “a kind of small boat”; and the interpreter of Thucydides: Μικρὸν πλοιάριον ὑφ’ ἑνὸς ἐρεττόμενον, ἀπὸ μεταφορᾶς τοῦ κέλητος ἵππου, ᾧ εἷς ἀνὴρ ἐπικάθηται, “a small boat rowed by one man, named metaphorically from the racehorse on which one man sits.”] which the Greeks call *κέλητες* (*keletes*), are swift biremes or agile triremes, suitable for the service of a fleet. Ennius:

> The oiled hull of a *celox* glides over the gray waters.

23. Biremes are ships having a double row of oars.

Triremes and quadriremes have three and four rows; similarly, *penteres* and *hexeres* have five or six rows.

[Col. 0665B] 24. [Note: [Col. 0665C] *Actuariae* are so called because they can be driven swiftly, says Nonius.] *Actuariae* are ships driven both by sails and by oars.

[Note: [Col. 0665C] *Hippagogus.* Festus reports that *hippago* is the Latin form.] An *hippagogus* is a vessel customarily used to transport horses.

[Note: [Col. 0665C] *Pontonium.* A diminutive word; for *pontones* is the primary form. [Col. 0665D]] A *pontonium* is a river vessel, slow and heavy, which can advance only by rowing.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Hence also *trajectus*. Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “the dove stretched across the line”: “*Trajecto*,” he says, means “stretched across”; hence *transenna* is called a stretched rope. I cannot sufficiently see how these remarks can be fitted to this passage.] Hence also *trajectus*, that is, “stretched across.” For it is broad, and hence *transenna* is also called a stretched rope.

25. A *lembus* is a short boat, also called by another name a *cymba*, 419 and a *caupilus* [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Et caupilus.* Another reading has *caupolus*. Gellius, book X, chapter 25, has *capulica*.], as is also a *linter*, that is, a *carabus*, of the kind used on the Po and in marshes.

26. A *carabus* is a small skiff made of wickerwork which, covered with rawhide, provides a type of vessel.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] *Portemia.* All the books have this form, and the etymology argues that Isidore wrote it so. It is nevertheless a Greek word; in Diodorus Siculus the same vessels are called now πορθμεῖα (*porthmeia*), now πορεῖα (*poreia*).] A *portemia* is a broad vessel of the Syrian type, without a keel, named from carrying. Such vessels are used in Pannonia.

[Col. 0665C] 27. [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Trabariae.* Festus: “A *trabica* is a ship fastened together with beams.”] *Trabariae* are river vessels hollowed out of individual beams; they are also called *littorariae*. [Note: [Col. 0665D] These are also called *caudicae*, and *caudicariae* or *codicariae*. Nonius, Festus, Gellius. For just as, according to Festus, a *trabs* properly consists of two pieces of wood joined together, so a *caudex* is a structure made by joining several boards, as Seneca says in *On the Brevity of Life*.] These are also *caudicae*, made from a single hollowed-out tree, and are called *caudicae* because they can hold from four to ten men.

## CHAPTER II. On the Parts of Ships and Their Equipment

[Col. 0666A]

1. The *puppis* is the rear part of a ship, as though from *post*, “behind.” The *prora* is the front, as though from *priora*, “the forward parts.”

[Note: [Col. 0665D] *Cumba.* Commonly *gomba*.] The *cumba* is the lowest part of a ship, because it rests upon the water.

The *carina* is named from *currere*, “to run,” as though *currina*.

420 2. [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Fori.* This passage is pieced together, more or less, from Servius and is also somewhat expanded. But Charisius says: “*Fori* are in ships where sailors sit while rowing,” ἐδώλια (*edolia*).] The *fori* are the concave sides of ships, named from carrying a burden, or else the ship’s decks, which are laid down. They are so called because they bear people walking upon them, or because they project outward. Virgil says of them:

> And he loosens the decks.

3. [Note: [Col. 0666C] *Columbaria.* See Philander on Vitruvius, book IV, chapter 2.] *Columbaria* are concave spaces in the upper sides of ships, through which the oars project. I think they are so called because they resemble the hiding places of doves, in which they nest.

4. [Note: [Col. 0666C] *Agea*: “pathways.” Festus: “An *agea* is a passage in a ship, so called because the largest matters are accustomed to be managed there.”] *Agea* are passages or spaces in a ship through which the exhorter approaches the rowers. Ennius says of it:

> He will place many things upon the deck, and the long *agea* will be filled.

5. *Transtra* are the boards on which the rowers sit; they are so called because they lie crosswise. [Note: [Col. 0666C] These are what Virgil calls *juga*, *Aeneid* VI:

> Then other souls, who were sitting along the long ridges.

[Col. 0666D] Servius there says: “He calls them *juga* in Greek, for they call the boards we call *transtra* ζυγά (*zyga*).”] Virgil calls them *juga*.

6. [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Tonsae*, oars. From Servius, *Aeneid* VII:

> … they struggle with the oars in the sluggish marble.] The *tonsae* are oars, so called from removing and beating away the waves, just as *tonsores* are named from cutting and beating away the hair.

7. [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Palmula.* See Festus and Servius, *Aeneid* V. By the same derivation the Greeks used *ταρσός* (*tarsos*) for the palm of the hand and for the broad part of oars, as Aelius Dionysius says in Eustathius, *Odyssey* I, on “the palms of oars.”] The *palmula* is the broad end of an oar, named from *palma*, “palm,” by which the sea is driven.

[Note: [Col. 0666D] “The *antennae* are so called because they are placed before the river,” from Servius, *Aeneid* VII. Festus says nearly the same under *Amnenses*. But he is speaking not of a part of ships, but of cities situated near a river.] The *antennae* are so called because they are placed before the river. 421 For the river flows past them. [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Cornua.* From the same source, *Aeneid* III, on “the horns of the sails facing the antennae.”] The *cornua* are the outer ends of the *antennae*, named metaphorically.

8. [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Malus*, “tree.” From the same source, *Aeneid* V, except that Servius reads *malis*, not *malleolis*.] The *malus* is the ship’s mast, by which the sails are supported. The mast is called *malus* because at its top it has the appearance of an apple, or because it is encircled, as it were, by certain wooden mallets, whose rotation makes it easier to raise the sails.

9. The *modius* is the fitting on which the mast rests; it is named from its resemblance to a measuring vessel.

The *carchesia* are at the top of the mast. [Note: [Col. 0666D] Cinna: “They shine brightly.” The verse attributed here to Catullus may have been common property, since it appears in Nonius.] Cinna:

> The shining *carchesia* gleam at the top of the tall mast.

10. [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Trochleae*, as though from the letter Φ. Philander, in his notes on Vitruvius, reads “as though from the letter Θ.” Athenaeus also lists *trochleae* among a ship’s equipment, in his account of Hiero’s ship. The Glossary: *trochleae*, ἐπιδρόμιδες (*epidromides*).] *Trochleae* are, as it were, shaped like the letter φ; ropes are drawn through them. They are called *trochleae* because they have wheels, for τροχός (*trochos*) is Greek for “wheel.”

11. *Parastatae* are paired upright posts by which the mast is supported. Cato says: “The mast tied down, the *parastatae* bound.”

12. [Note: [Col. 0667C] *Clavus.* Servius, *Aeneid* V, interprets *clavum* as the tiller, the shaft of the rudder.] The *clavus* is the means by which the rudder is controlled. Ennius says of it:

> So that I may hold the straight tiller and steer the ship.

13. [Note: [Col. 0667C] *Porticulus.* Festus and Nonius have the same form, except that they write *portisculus*. Isidore is supported by the Glossaries, which have *porticulus*, κελευστής (*keleustes*), “the boatswain.” [Col. 0667D]] The *porticulus* is a mallet carried in the hand, by which a signal and measure are given to the rowers. Plautus says:

> For speaking and for keeping silent, you yourself should have the *porticulus*.

It is therefore called *porticulus* from *portare*, “to carry.”

422 14. A *tonsilla* is an iron or wooden hook, fixed on the shore, to which ships’ ropes are fastened. Ennius says of it:

> They seize the hooked *tonsillae* and fix them in the shore.

15. An *anchora* is an iron tooth. Its name derives from Greek, because it grasps either like a human hand, or grasps reefs or sand. For “hand” is χείρ (*cheir*) in Greek. [Note: [Col. 0667D] In Greek the word has no aspiration. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “the anchor does not fasten with its hooked bite.”] In Greek it is written without aspiration, for it is called ὄγκυρα (*onkyra*); hence among the ancients it too was pronounced without aspiration.

16. *Pulvini* are machines by which ships are hauled down and drawn into the harbor.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] *Pons scala.* From the same source, *Aeneid* X: “He sets them out on bridges.”] A *pons* is a ship’s ladder.

## CHAPTER III. On Sails

1. Sails [Note: [Col. 0667D] The Greeks call sails ἄρμενα (*armena*), following Homer, as Eustathius says. The word itself is much broader, encompassing all equipment—not only nautical equipment but every kind of apparatus. According to the Etymologist, it derives from ἄρω, “to fit together,” from ἁρμόζω, “to join,” and from ἀραρημένον, “fitted together,” contracted into ἄρμενον.] the Greeks call ἄρμενα (*armena*), because they are moved by the air. Among the Latins, sails are called *vela* from flying. Hence the expression:

> We spread the wings of the sails.

2. [Note: [Col. 0667D] The types of sails are discussed by Pollux, Hesychius, and Suidas, though they do not mention the *artemon*.] The types of sails are the *acation*, *epidromos*, *dolon*, *artemon*, *siparum*, and *mendicum*. Of these, the *acation* is the largest sail and is set in the middle of the ship.

3. The *epidromos* is second in size, but is placed toward the stern.

The *dolon* is the smallest sail and is fixed toward the prow.

[Col. 0668A] [Note: [Col. 0667D] *Artemon* is chiefly for steering the ship. Correct. See Chrysostom, Acts XXVII.] The *artemon* was devised more for steering the ship than for speed.

423 4. The *siparum* is a type of sail one foot wide, by which vessels are customarily assisted during a voyage whenever the force of the wind slackens. Lucan says:

> And, stretching the upper sail,  
> he gathers the winds that will perish among the *sipara*.

They think it was named from “separation.” [Note: [Col. 0667D] The *pes* is the outer corner of a sail. Servius, *Aeneid* V, on “all together they made a *pes*: ‘*Podia*,’ he says, ‘that is, the rope by which a sail is stretched.’ The interpreter of Apollonius, book II, likewise calls the ropes by which sails are either turned or slackened *podes*. Hence in Lucan, book V: ‘He slants the canvas with the left *pes*,’ that is, with the left rope. Regarding the *mendicum*, Festus says: ‘They think a *mendicum* is called a sail because it is placed at the prow.’] The *pes* is the outer corner of a sail, as sailors call it.

## CHAPTER IV. On Ropes

1. Ropes [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Ropes are so called as though from having been surrounded with wax for use as lights.” Does he therefore wish *funem* to be derived from ἀπὸ τοῦ φαίνειν, “to shine”? I do not think so; rather, he has not sufficiently noticed the passage of Servius from which this material is taken. [Col. 0668D]] are so called because formerly they were coated with wax for use as lights; hence also *funalia*, “torches.”

They are called *restes*, either because they hold ships together or because nets (*retes*) are stretched upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] *Rudentes.* Servius, *Aeneid* I: “and the creaking of the ropes.” “Properly,” he says, “for there is creaking in ropes.”] *Rudentes* are ships’ ropes, so called from their excessive creaking.

2. *Spirae* are ropes used in storms, which sailors in their own terminology call *cucurbae*. [Note: [Col. 0668D] Most Gothic manuscripts have *cucurbas*; others have *curcubas*. See Festus under *spira*.] *Spirae* are so called from *spartum*, “broom” or “esparto grass.” [Note: [Col. 0668D] “*Spirae* from *spartum*.” Perhaps Pacuvius’ verse gave occasion for this derivation:

> Why do you delay, comrades, casting out the esparto ropes?

Rather, *spira* is derived from σπειράομαι (*speiraomai*), “I coil into a circle.”]

424 3. A *propes* is a rope to which the foot of a sail is fastened, as though “near the feet.” Turpilius says:

> As when a favorable wind carries a ship out to sea, if someone has cast out a *propes*, if [he has cast it] to the left side of the sail [Note: [Col. 0668D] *Si veli sinistrum*: Lilius Giraldus reads *in veli sinistrum*, “to the left side of the sail.”].

4. A *tormentum* is a long rope in ships by which the prow is extended toward the stern, so that they may be drawn more tightly. *Tormenta* are named from twisting, as are ropes and cables.

5. A *saphon* is a rope placed at the prow. Caecilius says of it:

> With a favorable course I came, with foot extended, all the way to the *saphon*.

6. *Opisphorae* are ropes stretched from the right and left horns of the *antenna*, and toward the rear.

A *prymnesium* is a rope by which a ship is tied to a post on the shore.

A *mitra* is a rope by which the middle of a ship is secured.

7. An *anquina* is so called because it is fastened to the mast and the *antenna*. Cinna says of it:

> And may the strongest *anquina* guide the steadfast course.

8. [Note: [Col. 0668D] *Remulcum.* See Festus under *remulcus* and *promulcus*.] A *remulcum* is a rope by which a tied-up ship is towed in place of an oar. Valgius says:

[Col. 0669A]

> Here my prow, following me by a long *remulcum*,  
> brings me, rejoicing, to rest in a hospitable place.

9. [Note: [Col. 0669C] *Struppi*, bindings by which oars are fastened to the rowlocks. Vitruvius, book X: “The oars were also fastened around the rowlocks with *strophi*”; the more learned read *struppis* there, whereas *stuppis* for *struppis* is found much more incorrectly in Gellius, book X, chapter 3. According to Festus, *struppi* were also bundles of herbs made for cushions, which were placed before the heads of the gods.] *Struppi* are bindings made of leather or flax, by which oars are fastened to the rowlocks. Livy says of them: “Then he ordered the oars to be untied from the *struppi*.”

10. [Note: [Col. 0669C] *Catapirates.* I read this form from the oldest manuscripts—the Roman, Complutensian, Salmanticensian, and one marked “On.” The interpretation being tested also requires it. I think the others, who prefer *cataproraten*, should be heard rather than obeyed. See Festus under *rodus*.] A *catapirates* is a line with a leaden weight, by which the depth of the sea is tested. 425 Lucilius says:

> Let the boy bring this oiled *catapirates*,  
> a little lump of lead, a coil of line, and a bundle of cord.

## CHAPTER V. On Nets

1. Nets [Note: [Col. 0669D] “They are called *retes*.” This is the reading of all the manuscripts. Charisius also calls them *retes*, as do the Glossaries, which have *retes augurales*.] are called *retes*, either from holding fish or from the ropes (*restes*) on which they are stretched.

A smaller net is called a *simplagium*, from *plagae*. [Note: [Col. 0669D] Properly, *plagae* are those ropes … the part … From Servius, *Aeneid* IV, on “the sparse meshes of the nets.”] Properly, we call *plagae* the cords by which nets are stretched around their lower and upper edges.

[Col. 0669B] 2. A *funda* is a type of fishing net, so called because it is thrown to the bottom. [Note: [Col. 0669D] It is also called a *jaculum*, or *rete-jaculum*. Servius. Turnebus reads it this way here, *Adversaria* XVIII, chapter 26, but I make no change. For Isidore above, book XVIII, chapter 54, says: “The *retiarius*, from the type of weapon used in the gladiatorial contest, secretly carried a net with which he fought against another; it is called a *jaculum*.”] It is also called a *jaculum* from throwing. Plautus says:

> Surely you were formerly a good thrower.

3. A *tragum* is a type of net, named from being dragged; it is also called a *verriculum*. For *verrere* means “to drag.”

A *nassa* [lacuna]

A *cassis* is a type of hunting net, because it catches. [Note: [Col. 0669D] Hence the expression *in cassum*, “in vain.” From Servius, *Georgics* III.] Hence we also say *incassum*, that is, “without cause,” as though “without nets,” without which hunting is fruitless.

4. A *conopeum* is a net in the form of a tent, by which gnats are kept out. The Alexandrians use it especially, because there abundant gnats are born from the Nile; hence it is called *conopeum*, for *Canopea* is Egypt. 426

## CHAPTER VI. On Smiths’ Furnaces

[Col. 0669C]

1. *Faber* (“smith”) derives its name from making iron. [Note: [Col. 0670C] He followed the same view in the monastic rule, saying that Joseph was a *faber ferrarius*, “a blacksmith,” perhaps addressing his brother Leander in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 33. It is not surprising, since Hilary and Bede held the same opinion. Ambrose, however, seems to have made him both a metalworker and a carpenter; for he writes in book III of his commentary on Luke: “The Father of Christ works with fire and spirit, and, like a good craftsman of the soul, cuts away our vices, quickly applying the axe to barren trees,” and so forth: “to soften the rigidness of minds with the fire of the spirit.”] From this the word was extended to craftsmen and workshops dealing with other materials, but with an added specification, such as *faber lignarius*, “a carpenter,” and the like, because of the firmness of the work. [Note: [Col. 0670D] Specifically, because of the solidity of the work. *Ferrarius*, “metalworker,” made *faber* its own specific general designation.]

[Col. 0670A] 2. [Note: [Col. 0670D] “In the smiths’ furnace.” The same material appears above, book VIII, chapter 11.] In the smiths’ furnace, the pagans figuratively say that Vulcan is the originator, signifying fire through Vulcan, without which no kind of metal can be melted and extended. For there is almost nothing that cannot be produced by fire. In one place it produces glass, in another silver, in another lead, in another minium, in another pigments, in another medicines. By fire stones are dissolved into bronze; by fire iron is produced and tempered; by fire gold is perfected; by fire, when stone has been burned, mortar and walls are joined.

3. [Note: [Col. 0670D] “Fire turns black stones white …” From Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chapter 7.] Fire makes black stones white by baking them; by burning it darkens white wood; from glowing embers it makes black charcoal; from hard wood it makes fragile wood, and from rotten wood it makes wood that does not rot; it loosens what is tight, tightens what is loose, softens what is hard, and makes what is soft hard. It also has medicinal uses. [Col. 0670B] [Note: [Col. 0670D] “It is often beneficial to burn.” From Pliny, book XXXVI, final chapter.] For it is often beneficial to burn. It is also certain that it assists against the pestilence contracted through the obscuration of the sun. Moreover, in a work one thing is produced by the first fires, another by the second, and another by the third.

4. [Note: [Col. 0670D] “Fire also contains another diversity in itself; it erupts.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48: “Philosophers know the difference between hidden fire and public fire; so different is the fire intended for human use from that which appears at God’s judgment, whether it draws lightning from heaven or erupts from the earth through the mountain peaks.”] Fire also contains another diversity in itself. For one fire is for human use, another obeys divine judgment, whether it is the fire that draws lightning from heaven or that erupts from the earth through mountain peaks.

5. Fire is so called because nothing can be produced from it. For it is an inviolable element, consuming everything it seizes.

A workshop consists of two things: winds and flame.

6. Flame is properly the fire of a furnace, so called because it is stirred by the blowing of the bellows.

[Col. 0670C] A *fornax* (“furnace”) is named from fire: φῶς (*phos*) is Greek for “fire.”

[Note: [Col. 0670D] A *caminus* is a furnace. From Servius, *Aeneid* III.] A *caminus* is a furnace; the word is Greek, derived from *cauma*, “heat.”

*Favilla* is a spark left behind by fire.

7. [Note: [Col. 0670D] *Pruna.* From the same source, *Aeneid* XI.] A *pruna* is so called while it is burning; when it has been extinguished, it is called *carbo*, “coal.” *Pruna* derives from *perurere*, “to burn thoroughly,” whereas *carbo* is so called because it lacks flame. [Note: [Col. 0671C] “Although it is believed to have perished.” From Pliny, book XXXVI, final chapter, and book XXXIII, chapter 5.] Although it is believed to have perished, it becomes stronger. For when it is kindled again, it glows with a more powerful light. Its force is so great, and its solidity even without fire so considerable, that it is corrupted by no moisture and overcome by no age. Once extinguished, it endures incorruptibly for so long 428 that those who mark boundaries place it beneath the earth in the trenches and set stones above it, so that, after however many centuries, they may recognize the fixed stone as the boundary and convict the litigant.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Tools of Smiths

1. An *incus* (“anvil”) is the place where iron is hammered; it is named from *cudere*, “to hammer,” because there we hammer something, that is, shape it by striking. For *cudere* means “to cut” and “to strike.” [Col. 0671B] The ancients did not call it *incus*, but *intudem*, because metal is hammered on it—that is, stretched— [Note: [Col. 0671C] “Hence also *tudes* is said.” These words are not in the Roman manuscript.] whence also *tudes*, “hammer,” is named from *tundere*, that is, *tendere*, “to stretch.”

2. A *malleus* (“hammer”) is so called because, while something is hot and soft, it cuts and shapes it.

A *marcus* is a large hammer; it is called *marcus* because it is larger and stronger for striking.

[Note: [Col. 0671C] *Martellus.* More recent books have *Marcellus*. See Caprarius, *Grammar*.] A *martellus* is medium-sized; a *marculus* is a small hammer. Lucilius says:

> Just as, while the iron is hot in the workshop, a small hammer beats it with many great blows.

3. *Forcipes* (“tongs”) are, as it were, *ferricipes*, because they seize and hold glowing iron; or because with them we take and hold something hot, as though *forvicapes*. [Note: [Col. 0671D] For *forvum* means “hot,” from which come *fervidus*, “hot,” and *formosus*, “beautiful,” since the heat of the blood creates beauty through redness. From Servius, *Aeneid* VIII, on “and with tenacious tongs they turn the mass.” See above, book X, under *formosus*.]

4. A *lima* (“file”) is so called because it makes something smooth. For *limum* means “smooth.”

429 [Note: [Col. 0671D] *Coelum.* Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “and embossed in gold”: “*Caelata*,” he says, “means engraved. For *coelum* is the iron itself with which silversmiths work.” Isidore says below, book XX, chapter 4: “*Caelata* vessels are named from *coelum*, which is a kind of iron tool that is commonly called a *cilio*.” Therefore *cilum*, through the common word *cilio*, entered our manuscripts. The same tool is called a *celte* in Job XIX. In an extremely old and amusing inscription of the parasite Sertius, at Salona, a city of Dalmatia—which I shall not hesitate to transcribe—we read: “It pleases me to speak with you and to hold you hanging from my mouth. This stone calls you. What do I mean? Alive, knowingly or unknowingly, and dead as well, I deceive you. For that which lacks a mouth does not call you, but he whose ashes lie hidden here. Once, when he was able, he wished you to be called here, and achieved this. Such was once his wish: that you should willingly read this writing. Ah! What am I saying? Rather, what has been engraved. How difficult it still is for truth to reconcile itself with me! For here there is neither ink, papyrus, nor any parchment, but the flint has been lettered with a hammer and a chisel.”] A *coelum* is the tool with which silversmiths work; from it *caelata* vessels also receive their name.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Construction of Walls

1. In the construction of walls and ceilings, the Greeks assert that Daedalus was the inventor. He is said to have first learned the craft from Minerva. The Greeks call craftsmen or artisans τέκτονες (*tektones*), that is, builders. *Architecti* (“architects”) are masons who arrange the foundations. Hence the Apostle says of himself: “As a wise architect, I laid the foundation.”

2. [Note: [Col. 0672C] *Machiones*, from *machinae*. Here *machinae* means the platforms on which those who work stand. [Col. 0672D] Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 10, speaking of the painter Amulius: “He painted in a few hours, and with dignity, because he was always dressed in the toga, although on the platforms.”] *Machiones* are so called from *machinae*, the platforms on which they stand because of the height of the walls. 430

## CHAPTER IX. On Design

1. The parts of buildings are three: design, construction, and beauty.

*Dispositio* (“design”) is the description of the building site, the ground, and the foundations.

## CHAPTER X. On Construction

[Col. 0672B] 1. *Constructio* is the building of walls in height. *Constructio*, or *structio*, is so called because it binds and makes things adhere—stones to mortar, and wood and stones to one another. [Note: [Col. 0672D] The dipping of iron into water is also called *strictura*. The old manuscripts erroneously have *instructura*. Gothic scribes frequently add or remove an *i* in words beginning with *s*, as in *instoria* for *historia* and *Spania* for *Hispania*. All of this is relevant because *constructio* is as though *constrictio*, and *instructio* as though *instrictio*, or rather because *structura* is as though *strictura*, discussed above, book XVI, chapter 21.] For the dipping of iron into water is also called *strictura*. Unless glowing iron is dipped, it cannot be tightened and made to cohere. Likewise, *constructio* is named from the multitude of stones and timbers, whence also *strues*, “a heap” or “structure.” For *aedificatio*, “building,” is one thing, and *instauratio*, “restoration,” another. A *aedificatio* is a new construction. *Instauratio* [Note: [Col. 0672D] “*Instauratio* is that which is repaired.” From Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “equal in size to a mountain.”] is what is repaired to resemble the former structure. For the ancients used *instar* in the sense of “resemblance”; hence they also said *instaurare*.

2. Construction consists of foundations, stones, lime, sand, and wood.

A *fundamentum* (“foundation”) is so called because it is the bottom (*fundus*) of a building. [Col. 0672C] It is also called *caementum*, from *caedere*, “to cut,” because it rises from roughly cut stone.

3. [Note: [Col. 0672D] Stones suitable for structures. From Palladius, book I, chapter 10. Pliny discusses this class of stones in book XXXVI, chapter 22. It should be examined whether Isidore agrees sufficiently with him.] Stones suitable for construction are white stone, Tiburtine stone, dove-colored stone, river stone, *sphungia*, red stone, and others.

4. White stone is of two kinds, hard and soft. Soft stone is cut with a toothed saw. 431 It is workable in construction, so that letters can be written in it as though in wood.

5. Tiburtine stone is named from a place in Italy. Although it is strong for construction, [Note: [Col. 0672D] Nevertheless, it bursts from heat. From Pliny, who took the passage from Vitruvius; Vitruvius, book II, chapter 7, says: “All Tiburtine stone withstands everything, but cannot be protected from fire; as soon as it is touched by fire, it bursts apart.”] it nevertheless bursts from heat.

[Col. 0673A] 6. [Note: [Col. 0673C] *Tophus* is useless for buildings. Pliny also described this from the same passage of Vitruvius. But the passage is badly corrupted in the common manuscripts of Pliny; in the Toledo Church manuscript it reads: “Among the remaining mass of stones, *tophus* is useless for buildings.” What follows there, “in mortality, softness, and defect,” is from Isidore’s “mortality and softness.” Finally, instead of *exercetur halitu maris*, A. Covarrubias prefers *exestur*, “is eaten away,” but *ex aestu* (“by the heat”) can be defended from Isidore.] *Tophus* is useless for buildings, though suitable for foundations, because of its friability and softness. It is worn away by the heat and breath of the sea [Note: [Col. 0673D] “It is struck.” Pliny has “rubbed by the wind and beaten by rain.” Salmasius, the *Onomasticon*, and the oldest Complutensian manuscript have *feritur*, “is struck”; Valentinus has *friatur*, “is rubbed away,” agreeing with Vitruvius.], and is beaten by rains.

7. *Arenatius* is stone compacted from sea sand; it is also called *bibulus*, “absorbent.” For it retains the moisture it receives. The same kind is found in Baetica, where it is called Gaditanian, from the island in the Ocean where it is quarried in great quantities.

8. [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Piperinus* is hard and extremely strong. It is not so hard at Rome, but it is extremely hard and strong at Toledo, where many columns and arches of it can be seen in the fortress and other buildings.] *Piperinus* is somewhat whitish, with black spots, hard and extremely strong.

*Conchleatius* is compacted from shells, pebbles, and sand; it is very rough and sometimes full of cavities.

9. *Columbinus* (“dove-colored”) is named from the color of a bird; by nature it is related to gypsum and is very similar to it in softness.

10. [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Molaris* is useful for walls. Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 23, on lime: “It is more useful for millstones, because its nature is somewhat fatter.”] *Molaris* is useful in walls because its nature is somewhat fatter, hard, and rough; millstones are also made from it, whence it derives its name. It has four kinds: white, black, mixed, and hollow.

11. [Note: [Col. 0673D] *Sphungia.* See above, book XII, chapter 6.] *Sphungia* [Note: [Col. 0673D] “A stone created”; another reading has “compacted.” It now forms at Tibur from the water of the Anio. [Col. 0674C]] is a stone formed from water, light and porous, and suitable for vaulted chambers.

432 12. *Silex* (“flint”) is a hard stone. Of its varieties, black flints are the best; in some places they are also reddish.

[Note: [Col. 0674C] White flints resist age. From Pliny.] White flints are imperishable against the passage of time. They are also carved for monuments and remain undecayed; not even fire harms them. For molds are also made from them, in which [Note: [Col. 0674C] Bronze is cast. From Vitruvius, book II, chapter 7. The Gothic manuscript erroneously has “sand is cast.”] bronze is cast.

Green flint also resists fire vigorously, but it is nowhere abundant; where it is found, it is a stone rather than a rock.

Pale flint is rarely useful in mortar.

13. [Note: [Col. 0674D] *Globus.* I would read *globosus*, “rounded,” following Pliny.] A *globus* is strong against damage but unreliable in construction unless it has been secured with much bracing. [Col. 0673C]

14. River flint is always, as it were, wet. [Note: [Col. 0674D] “This should be exposed in summer.” Our books consistently read this way; I would prefer to extract it from Pliny and Vitruvius.] It ought to be exposed in summer and not inserted into the structures of houses before two years have passed. [Note: [Col. 0674D] “Clay constructions for walls, and so forth.” This is sketched from Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 12. How it came into this place someone else may conjecture.] Clay works for walls and foundations are made with baked bricks; roofs, with curved tiles and roofing tiles.

15. *Tegulae* (“tiles”) are so called because they cover buildings, and *imbrices* (“curved tiles”) because they receive the rain. *Tegula* is the name for the first laying; *tigillum* is its diminutive.

16. *Laterculi* (“small bricks”) are so called because they are formed broadly by means of four boards turned around them on every side.

[Col. 0674A] *Lateres* (“bricks”) are unbaked; they too receive their name from being made broad in wooden molds.

17. Their *crates* are the frames in which they customarily carry mud for these unbaked bricks. For they are interlacings of reeds, called *crates* from ἀπὸ τοῦ κρατεῖν (*apo tou kratein*), “from holding,” that is, because they hold one another.

18. Some think *lutum* (“mud”) is so called by antiphrasis, because it is not clean. For everything that has been washed is clean.

433 19. [Note: [Col. 0674D] *Calx viva*, “quicklime.” The same discussion appears above, book XVI, chapter 3.] Quicklime is so called because, although cold to the touch, it contains hidden fire within; hence, when water is poured over it, the concealed fire immediately bursts forth. Its nature produces something marvelous. For after it has burned, it is kindled by water, which normally extinguishes fire; it is extinguished by oil, which normally kindles fire. Its use is necessary in building construction. For stone cannot adhere more firmly to stone unless joined with lime.

20. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Gypsum is related to lime. From Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 3.] Gypsum is related to lime, and its name is Greek. It has several varieties. The best of all comes from specular stone. [Note: [Col. 0674D] “For it is especially fine and pleasing.” From the same source, chapter 24.] It is especially pleasing in the figures and cornices of buildings.

21. [Note: [Col. 0674D] *Arena.* See above, book XVI, chapter 3.] *Arena* (“sand”) is named from dryness, not, as some maintain, from adhering in construction. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Testing it. From Palladius, book I, chapter 10.] It is tested if, when pressed in the hand, it grates, or if, when scattered on a white garment, it leaves no dirt.

22. Columns are so called from their length and roundness; on them the weight of the entire structure is raised. [Note: [Col. 0674D] The ancient proportion of columns. The whole passage is from Pliny and Vitruvius.] The ancient proportion was that the width of columns was one third of their height. There are four kinds of round columns: Doric, Ionic, Tuscan, and Corinthian, differing from one another in the measurement of their thickness and height. A fifth kind consists of those [Col. 0674C] called Attic, with four or more angles and equal intervals between their sides.
