23. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Bases. See above, Book XV, chapter 8.] Bases are the supports of columns, rising from the foundation and bearing the weight of the superimposed structure. *Bases* is also the Syriac word for a very strong stone.

24. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Capitals—*capitula*, in Vitruvius. Pliny uses both words.] Capitals are so called because they are the heads of columns, as it were a head above a neck.

Epistyles are the members placed above the capitals of columns; the word is Greek.

[Col. 0675A] 25. Pavements derive the origin of their workmanship from the Greeks. They are called *pavimenta* because they are *paviantur*, that is, “cut” or “beaten”; hence also *pavor* (“terror”), because terror strikes the heart.

26. [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Ostracus*. I would prefer *ostraceum*, on the authority of Pliny, chapter 25, and Vitruvius, Book VI, chapter 4.] *Ostracus* is a pavement made of tiles, so called because it is beaten down from broken potsherds mixed with lime. The Greeks call a potsherd ὄστρακα (*ostraka*).

434 27. [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Rudos*. Above, Book XVI, chapter 3.] Builders call *rudos* crushed stones mixed with lime, which they pour over pavements when making them; hence they are also called *rudera*.

28. A canal is so called because it is hollowed in the shape of a reed. [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Canalem*. Above, Book XV, chapter 8.] It is certainly better to pronounce *canalis* in the feminine gender than in the masculine.

29. Water pipes are so called because they pour out and convey water. For in Greek, στέλλειν (*stellein*) means “to send.” Their forms are made according to the quantity and capacity of the water, and through them water is divided into fixed measures, [Note: [Col. 0675D] Among these are the *uncia* and the *quinaria*. See Pliny, XXXI, chapter 6; Vitruvius, VIII, chapter 6; and Frontinus, *On the Aqueducts*] among which are the *uncia*, the *quinaria*, the square digit, the round digit, and [Note: [Col. 0675D] “And the other measures, each.” Other copies have *cujusque* (“of each”); others, “and the other measures for each purpose.” Chacon reads, “and all the other measures,” or “and the other measures up to one hundred.” Frontinus discusses the measures from the *quinaria* up to the *centenaria*.] the other measures, each in its own form.

## CHAPTER XI. On Beauty

1. Thus far we have discussed the parts of construction; next comes the beauty of buildings. Beauty is whatever is added to buildings for the sake of ornament and elegance, such as gilded and patterned ceilings, veneers of precious marble, and paintings in various colors.

## CHAPTER XII. On Ceilings

1. Ceilings [Note: [Col. 0676D] *Laquearia*. The whole chapter is found above, Book LI, chapter 8.] are those elements that cover and adorn a vaulted chamber. They are also called *lacunaria*, because they have certain square or round recesses [Col. 0675C] depicted in wood, plaster, or colors, with figures gleaming between them. Properly speaking, a *lacus* is a recess, as Lucilius says: “The halls and the recesses resound.” Its diminutive is *lacunar*, as in Horace:

> Nor does the golden  
> Ceiling shine in my house.

From this comes the further diminutive *lacunarium*, and by a change of letters, *laquearium*.

435 ## CHAPTER XIII. On Veneers

1. Veneers are slabs of marble. Hence marble-covered walls are called *crustati*, “veneered.” Who first devised the method of cutting marble into veneers is not known. [Note: [Col. 0676D] Who cut marble. From Pliny, Book XXXVI. Nowadays the saw is made not of iron but of bronze; Toledo sand is especially praised for this work.] They are made with sand and iron, by means of a saw pressing the sand along an extremely fine line and cutting through the motion itself; but the coarser the sand, the more marble it will wear away. Fine sand, however, is suited to finishing and polishing.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Mosaic Floors

1. Mosaic floors are paintings skillfully worked out with small veneers and little tesserae colored in various hues. [Note: [Col. 0676D] Worked out by the art of painting. From the same source, above, Book XV, chapter 8.] *Tesserae* are so called from *tesserae*, that is, square little stones, by diminution.

## CHAPTER XV. On Plaster Modeling

1. *Plastice* is the fashioning and impressing of figures and images on walls with plaster, and painting them with colors. The Greek word πλάττειν (*plattein*) means “to model in earth or plaster” likenesses, which in Latin is *pingere* (“to paint”). For making some form by pressing clay is *plasta*. Hence the human being is called *protoplastus*, because he was first formed from clay.

436 ## CHAPTER XVI. On Painting

1. Painting is an image expressing the appearance of some thing which, once seen, brings it back to the mind’s memory. *Pictura* (“painting”) is so called as if from *fictura* (“fashioning”), for it is a fashioned image, not reality. Hence also *fucata* means “smeared with an artificial color,” possessing no faithfulness or truth. Thus there are paintings that surpass real bodies through the ambition of their coloring and, while attempting to increase credibility, advance into falsehood—for example, those who paint the Chimera with three heads, or Scylla with a human form above and surrounded below by canine heads.

2. [Note: [Col. 0676D] Painting was devised by the Egyptians. From Pliny, XXXV, chapter 6.] The Egyptians first devised painting by tracing the outline of a human shadow with lines. Thus at first it was of this kind; next, single colors were added; afterward, different colors. Gradually the art itself differentiated its features and discovered light, shadows, and distinctions of color. Hence even now painters first draw certain shadows and lines of the image they are about to make, then fill them in with colors, preserving the order in which the art was discovered.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Colors

1. Colors are so called because they are brought to perfection by the heat of fire or by the sun, or because at the beginning they were strained so that they might become extremely fine.

2. Colors either arise naturally or are made. Natural colors include sinopis, red ochre, Paretonium, Melian white, Eretrian earth, and orpiment. The rest are fabricated either by art or by mixture.

3. Sinopis was first discovered in Pontus. From the city of Sinope it received its name. There are three varieties: red, less red, and intermediate between these.

4. Red ochre is so called because it is red and close to the color of blood. It is produced in many places, but the best is from Pontus, and therefore it is also called Pontic.

437 5. Syrian red is a pigment from which the headings of books are also written. It is the same as Phoenician red, so called because it is collected in Syria along the shores of the Red Sea, where the Phoenicians live.

6. Seric silk and Syrian red are different. *Sericum* is wool sent by the Seres; *syricum* is the pigment that the Syrian Phoenicians collect along the shores of the Red Sea. It is also among the manufactured colors, for it is often made by mixing sinopis or sandyx with it. [Note: [Col. 0677C] “With sinopis or sandyx.” A disjunction used for a conjunction. See Pliny.]

7. [Note: [Col. 0677C] The first discovery of minium. Pliny, XXXIII, chapter 7, and Vitruvius, VII, chapter 8.] The Greeks are said to have first discovered minium in the territory of Ephesus. [Note: [Col. 0677C] Spanish minium. Justin, Book XLIII: “A portion of Gallaecia is called Amphilochi, a region extremely rich in copper and lead, and also in minium, which gave its name to a neighboring river.”] Spain abounds in this pigment more than other regions, and it even gave its name to one of its own rivers. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Its distillation produces liquid silver. From Pliny, XXXIII, chapter 8.] Its distillation produces liquid silver. Some, however, say that this minium is cinnabar.

8. [Note: [Col. 0677D] *Cinnabaris* from *draco* and *barrus*. Above, Book VIII, chapter 11; Pliny, XXXIII, chapter 7; Solinus, chapter 38.] Cinnabar is named from *draco* (“dragon”) and *barrus* (“elephant”). For they say that it is the blood of dragons, when they entwine themselves with elephants. The beasts fall, and the dragons are crushed; their blood, flowing out, stains the earth, and whatever the soil has tinged becomes pigment. It is a powder of red color.

9. Prasine, that is, green earth, although it is produced indiscriminately in certain lands, is nevertheless best in Libyan Cyrenaica. [Note: [Col. 0677D] The best is in Libya, in Cyrene. But Vitruvius, VII, chapter 7, says: “Green earth is produced in many places, but the best is at Smyrna.” Thus the source of this statement must be investigated.]

438 10. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Chrysocolla. From Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 5, and Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 4.] Chrysocolla is green in color. It is so called because its vein is said to contain gold. It is also found in Armenia, but a good quality comes from Macedonia. It is dug from copper mines, whose discovery also reveals silver and indigo, for its veins share a natural relationship with them.

Cyprian is named from the island of Cyprus, where it is found in great abundance.

11. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Sandarac. From Pliny, XXXV, chapter 5.] Sandarac grows on the Red Sea island of Topaz, cinnabar-colored and sulfur-scented. It is found in gold and silver mines, and is better the redder it is and the more strongly it smells of its poisonous substance. White lead, however, if roasted in a furnace, becomes sandarac, and hence it has a flame-colored appearance. If it is roasted with an equal portion of red ochre mixed in, it produces sandyx.

12. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Arsenic. From the same source, XXXIII, chapters 4 and 8, and Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 55.] Arsenic, which the Latins call *auripigmentum* (“orpiment”) because of its color, is collected in Pontus from gold-bearing material, where sandarac is also found. The best is that which turns the color of gold, is pure, and is fissile, with a fine branching of veins. That which is paler or resembles sandarac is judged inferior. There is also a third, scaly variety, with which golden color is mixed. Its properties are like those of sandarac, but sharper.

13. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Ochre also. Everything is from Pliny, XXXV, chapter 6.] Ochre too is produced on the Red Sea island of Topaz, where sandarac is also found. [Note: [Col. 0677D] Red ochre is also made from burned ochre. The passage of Pliny reads in the Toledo manuscript: “Ochre is produced in iron mines; from it, when burned, red ochre is made.” This reading is confirmed by this passage of Isidore and by Dioscorides, *On Artificial Red Ochre*: Γίνεται τῆς ὄχρας καιομένης (“It is made from ochre when it is burned”). Theophrastus, *On Stones*, likewise says: Γίνεται ἐκ τῆς ὄχρας, ἀλλὰ χείρων (“It is made from ochre, but is inferior”); shortly afterward his text has the corrupt readings λενὰς for καινὰς and πολὺν for πῆλον.] Ochre is also made into red ochre by burning it in new pots coated around with clay; the more intensely it has burned in the kiln, the better it becomes. Venetian [lacuna].

14. [Note: [Col. 0678C] Mixing blue. The Segovia manuscript reads continuously: “Venetian blue is mixed with blue,” which could be supported by Vitruvius, Book VII, chapter 11. But the better manuscripts have *Venetum* without an interpretation.] Alexandria first discovered how to temper blue. [Note: [Col. 0678D] In Italy, from sand. At Puteoli, as Vitruvius and Pliny relate.] In Italy they make the same pigment from sand dust and the flower of soda. But if you add roasted Cyprian copper to this mixture, [Col. 0678B] it will resemble Vestorian blue.

439 15. [Note: [Col. 0678D] *Purpurissum*. From Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 6; anything that appears lacking should be supplied from that source.] Purpurissum is dyed together with purple from silver-bearing chalk, and it absorbs that color more quickly than wool does. The finest, however, is that which [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Still in the vessel.” A. Covarruvias read *aheno in vase* (“in a bronze vessel”), from Pliny.] is still steeped in a vessel with the raw substances. Next in quality is that from which the material has been removed and to which chalk has been added in the same liquid; and each time this is done, the quality of the most precious purple is diminished. The reason is that it is especially stained by *hysginum* and red dye.

16. [Note: [Col. 0678D] Indigo. From the same source, Book III, chapter 6.] Indigo is found in Indian reeds, as foam adhering to mud. It is a deep-blue color, producing a marvelous mixture of purple and blue. There is another kind in the purple-dyers’ workshops: foam floating on bronze cauldrons, which the dyers remove and dry.

17. Black pigment (*atramentum*) is so called because it is black; the kind necessary both for painting and for everyday use belongs among the manufactured colors. [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Built as a small chamber.” Pliny says, “For this reason they also built workshops.” Vitruvius, Book VI, chapter 10: “A place is built like a Laconicum, and its furnace is carefully sealed so that the flame does not escape outside.” Columella also uses the word *lacusculus*, in Book XII, chapter 50.] Painters mix glue with it and water, so that it may shine more brightly. [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Painters use this.” So Pliny; Vitruvius says “plasterers.”]

18. To hasten the work, charcoal from old vine shoots, ground with glue and applied to walls, produces the appearance of ink. [Note: [Col. 0679C] Some use wine sediment. From Pliny, XXXV, chapter 3.] There are also those who burn dried wine sediment and maintain that, if the sediment came from good wine, this ink gives the appearance of indigo. But if you burn the shoot of a black grapevine, which has been soaked in excellent wine, after it has dried through desiccation, and then grind it with added glue, it will produce the sheen of indigo.

19. [Note: [Col. 0679C] Burnt pigment. From Pliny, XXXV, chapter 6.] Burnt pigment, which is very necessary, is produced without difficulty. [Note: [Col. 0679C] “For if you burn a lump of good *sil*.” Pliny’s manuscripts incorrectly read *silicis boni* (“good flint”) at this point.] If you burn a lump of good *sil* in fire and extinguish it by pouring very sharp vinegar over it, it yields a purple color when a sponge is moistened with it. Once you have ground it, it will be burnt pigment. All ink, however, is perfected by the sun.

20. All colors are spoiled by the admixture of lime.

[Col. 0679B] 21. [Note: [Col. 0679C] The name *melinum*. From Vitruvius, VII, chapter 7, and Pliny, XXXV, chapter 6.] Melian white is so called because one of the Cyclades, the island named Melos, is rich in this mineral. It is white, but painters do not use it because of its excessive oily quality.

22. [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Annular … glass gems.” Pliny adds “from ordinary rings,” whence *annulare* was named. 23. [Note: [Col. 0679D] Ceruse. [Note: [Col. 0679D] “After thirty days.” Pliny has “for ten days.”] After thirty days the vessel is opened, and ceruse is found floating on the distillation from the sheets. It is removed and dried, ground, and then divided into pellets with vinegar added; it is dried in the sun. [Note: [Col. 0679D] This procedure. From Vitruvius, VII, chapter 12. See Pliny, XXXIV, chapter 11, and Dioscorides, V, chapter 47.] By this procedure, [Col. 0679C] if you place sheets of copper over the vine shoots, they produce verdigris.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Chalcanthum. The best manuscripts contain no interpretation. In only one manuscript, the Gothic College copy at Oviedo, nearly the same words as in the printed editions are found. If anyone considers it worthwhile, these would permit reading *chalcus* instead of *calcis*, or, as it appears in the Gothic manuscript, *chalcitis*, and *anthos* instead of *thymum*. Yet Isidore also interprets *thymum* as a flower above, Book XVII, chapter 9. But what has chalcanthum to do with thyme? 441 ## CHAPTER XVIII. On Building Instruments

[Col. 0680A]

1. The masonry of walls ought to be made according to the square and to correspond with the plumb line.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] *Norma* comes from the Greek word γνώμων (*gnōmōn*).] *Norma* is named from a Greek word, and nothing straight can be made without it. [Note: [Col. 0679D] “It is composed … this will be the square.” These words seem to have been taken from Vitruvius, Book IX, chapter 2. But the example here is not equally exact, although it is not far off. For if you convert two feet—that is, one side—into unciae and square them, they produce 576 square unciae. Adding another similar side, the two together produce 1,152 square unciae. But the square of the third side, which is two feet and ten unciae—that is, thirty-four unciae—contains 1,156 square unciae. It therefore exceeds the squares of the other two sides by four unciae.] It is composed of three rulers, two of them two feet long, while the third is two feet and ten unciae long; these, polished to equal thickness, join one another at their pointed ends so as to form the figure of a triangle. This is the square.

2. A ruler is so called because it is straight, as though *rectula*, and has no obstruction.

[Note: [Col. 0680C] Plumb line. “The plumb line,” says Ascanius, “is a line that tests the equality of the sides in width from top to bottom.”] A plumb line is so called because it is always suspended. [Note: [Col. 0680D] “Finally, in a building … the structures collapse.” The entire passage is expressed from Lucretius’ elegant verses, Book IV:

> Finally, as in a building, if the first ruler is crooked  
> And the square …]

Finally, unless everything in a building is made according to the plumb line and a fixed rule, all of it must be constructed incorrectly: some parts will be crooked, some leaning, some sloping downward, others sloping upward, and consequently everything constructed will collapse.

3. A line is so called from its material, because it is made from flax.

The name *trulla* is formed from *trudere* (“to push”), because it encloses stones with lime or mud.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Hammer. This is found in all the Gothic manuscripts. Glossary: *martellus*, σφύρα (*sphyra*, “hammer”); another copy has *marcellus*. Likewise the glossary has *marculum*, σφύριον σιδήρου (“iron hammer”), and *marculus*, *malleolus*, *malleus*, Σφύρα σιδηρᾶ καὶ κόπανον (“iron hammer and mallet”).] Hammer [lacuna].

Machine [lacuna].

4. Stairs are called *scalae* from *scandere* (“to climb”), [Note: [Col. 0680D] “For stairs cling to walls.” These are Virgil’s words, not especially suitable for supporting the etymology; I think they migrated here from the margin.] for they cling to walls. *Scalae* are called those that are either one or several, [Note: [Col. 0680D] Because the word is plural only. From Servius, *Aeneid* II. A jurist uses it in the singular, in the chapter “Let it first be,” *Digest* on theft, and Jerome uses it in his *Questions on Genesis*.] because the word is plural only, like *litterae*, which signifies a letter.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Carpenters

1. A *lignarius* is generally called a worker in wood.

2. *Carpentarius* is a specific name. For he makes only a *carpentum*, just as a *navicularius* is so called because he is exclusively a builder and craftsman of ships.

3. [Note: [Col. 0680D] *Sarcitector*. This is found in nearly all the books, and the etymology seems to fit; the eminent Jacobus Cujacius does not reject the word. Only one manuscript, the especially old Salamanca copy, has *arcitector*, but the preceding chapter had spoken of an architect.] A *sarcitector* is so called because he patches together into one body of a roof the many boards joined here and there.

4. The same person is also called a *tignarius*, because he applies plasterwork to wood.

[Col. 0681A] 3. [Note: [Col. 0681C] The Greek etymology of *lignum*. Varro, however, says: “From *legere* (‘to gather’) come *ligna* (‘wood’), because fallen pieces were gathered in the field for use on the hearth.”] *Lignum* is named by a Greek etymology because, when burned, it is changed into light and flame. Hence it is also called *lychnion*, because it gives light.

4. *Materia* is the name given to every piece of wood because something is made from it; or, if you refer it to a door or statue, it will be the material. Material must always be understood in relation to something, just as we say that the elements are the material of things, because we see that existing things are made from them. *Materia* is called so as if from *mater* (“mother”).

5. Beams are called *trabes* because, placed crosswise, they hold both walls together.

Timbers and beams, however, are different. [Note: [Col. 0681C] “For joined timbers make a beam.” Festus: “Properly, a beam is two pieces of wood fastened together.”] Joined timbers make a beam. [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Beams are when they have been hewn.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX, on “These Dardanian …” It should be noted that timbers are not called beams unless they have already been cut and assembled.] Beams are what they become once they have been hewn.

6. [Note: [Col. 0681C] *Tholus*. From the same source, *Aeneid* IX, “from the suspended dome.” Glossary: *tholus*, τριπτήρ (“dome”).] Properly, a dome is like a short shield, located in the middle of the roof, where the beams meet.

[Note: [Col. 0681C] *Cuplae*. Another copy has *coplae*. Italians today call a half of a vaulted shell a *cupola*; Vitruvius calls it a hemisphere.] *Cuplae* are so called because they join together opposing elements.

They are called “opposing” because, standing upright, they hold one another in the manner of wrestlers.

[Note: [Col. 0681C] *Agrantes* [lacuna]. Other copies have *agentes* (“acting”) or *conantes* (“striving”), with the words attached to the preceding sentence: “acting or striving in the manner of wrestlers.” Chacon thought *Atlantes* should be read, followed by a lacuna. For Vitruvius, Book VI, chapter 10, says: “If figures in a male form support modillions or cornices, our people call them *telamones*. The reason why or how this came about is not found in the histories; the Greeks call them *Atlantes*. For Atlas is represented in myth as supporting the world.” Servius gives the following explanation, *Aeneid* I: “Ennius says that the Nile is called Melas and Atlas Telamon. For those ancient Romans who could not pronounce Greek words correctly were accustomed to say *Telamon* instead of *Atlas mons* (‘Mount Atlas’). The glossary reads: ἄγλαστὸ ὄρος; perhaps it should read ἄτλας τὸ ὄρος (‘Atlas, the mountain’).] *Agrantes* [lacuna].

7. [Note: [Col. 0681D] *Asseres*, from *as*. I would read *asso*. In Nonius, *assa* is a word meaning “a human voice alone, without any other sound.” Festus gives another explanation: “*Asseres*, because they sit against the wall and beams.” Others think *asseres* was formed from *axeres*, according to the ancient declension *axer, axeris*, like *pulver, pulveris*.] *Asseres* are so called from *as*, because they are laid singly and are not joined together.

[Note: [Col. 0682C] *Scindulae*. This is also found in Rabanus. In other authors the same objects are called *scandulae*. Perhaps Isidore’s form has remained uncorrupted.] *Scindulae* are so called because they are split, that is, divided.

[Note: [Col. 0682C] “*Epigri* are nails.” They are called *epiri* in Augustine, Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 27. I think this passage was taken from there. “Unless perhaps,” he says, “wood could not be joined to wood by wooden pegs, *epiri*, nails, and bitumen glue, so that the ark could be built.” Perhaps the word “nails” is a gloss on *epiros*; alternatively, one might prefer to read *epigros*.] *Epigri* are nails by which wood is fastened to wood.

Nails are called *clavi*, as if from *chalybes*, because they are made of *chalybs*, that is, iron. For *chalybs* means iron.

8. The ancients called boards *tagulae*, from *tegere* (“to cover”), whence also *tegulae* (“tiles”).

[Col. 0681C] A joint is the joining together of boards.

[Col. 0682A] 444 A section is so called from following what one has begun. [Note: [Col. 0682C] For *secare*, *sectari*, and *sequi* are related. Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “the hope which each one cuts”: “*Secat*,” he says, “means ‘follows.’”] For *secare* means *sectari* and *sequi*—to cut, pursue, and follow.

9. The name *serra* (“saw”) is formed from a sound, that is, from a rasping noise.

A certain young man named Perdix invented the saw and compass. [Note: [Col. 0682C] Perdix. From Servius, *Georgics* I. See Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.] As a boy, he had been entrusted to his mother’s brother Daedalus to be thoroughly instructed in his studies. The boy is said to have possessed such great ingenuity that, while seeking a convenient means of dividing wood, he imitated the spine of a fish, sharpening a strip of iron and arming it with the biting points of teeth. Artisans now call this a saw. Because of the invention of this craft, his teacher Daedalus, moved by the dark jealousy of envy, threw the boy headlong from the citadel. Then, having gone into exile, [Note: [Col. 0682C] “He went into exile.” Victor uses the same expression, Book II of *The Vandal Persecution*: “He likewise drove his brother Theodoric, naked and abandoned, into exile.”] he went to Crete, and remained there for some time, as the stories relate. From Crete he flew on wings and came to Cilicia.

10. [Note: [Col. 0682C] The compass is so called. Ovid described the compass most elegantly:

> First he joined two iron arms from a single hinge,  
> So that, standing apart at an equal distance,  
> One part would remain fixed while the other traced a circle.] The compass is so called because, by bending, it produces a circle. Its method is made by doubling a line that had previously been extended in a single breadth. The point in the middle of the compass is called *centrum* (“center”) by the Greeks, toward whose middle everything converges.

11. An axe is called *securis* because trees are cut down with it, as though *succuris* (“that which cuts down”). [Note: [Col. 0682D] Likewise *securis*, as if *semicuris*. From Servius, *Aeneid* I, on “with Remus as companion.”] Likewise, *securis* is as if *semicuris*. For it is sharp on one side and digging on the other. Among the ancients this was also called a *penna*; when it has an edge on both sides, it is a *bipennis*. [Note: [Col. 0682D] It is called *bipennis* because it has an edge on both sides. So Nonius, under *bipennis*.] A *bipennis* is so called because it has a sharp edge on both sides, like two wings. The ancients called anything sharp *pennum*. [Note: [Col. 0682D] Hence the feathers of birds are also called *pennae*, because they are pointed. Quintilian, Book I, chapter 6: “Let no one wonder why *scabellum* comes from *scamnum*, or why the sharp part of an axe is called *penna*, an axe having an edge on both sides being a *bipennis*. Let him not follow the error of those who, because they think the name comes from two *pennae* or *pinnae*, maintain that birds’ feathers are called *pinnae* or *pennae*.”] Hence the feathers of birds are also called *pennae*, because they are pointed. [Note: [Col. 0682D] “And here is the ancient name preserved.” Servius, *Aeneid* II, on “with a lifted double axe”: “I have preserved this name from antiquity, because the ancients said *pennae*, not *pinnae*.”] Here too is the ancient name preserved, because the ancients said *pennae*, not *pinnae*. It is also called a *dolabra*, because it has two *labra* (“lips” or “edges”); a simple axe has only one.

[Col. 0683A] [Note: [Col. 0683D] *Dextralis*. Victor uses this word, Book I of *The Vandal Persecution*: “When they found the doors of the venerable hall closed, they vied with one another in opening an entrance by blows from their *dextralia*.”] *Dextralis* means suitable for the right hand.

12. An adze is called *ascia* from the small shafts (*hastulae*) which it removes from wood; its diminutive is *asciola*. It has a short handle and, on the reverse side, resembles either a simple hammer, a hollowed one, or a two-horned rake.

13. A chisel is called *scalprus* because it is suited to carving and making holes, as though *scalforus*. Its diminutive is *scalpellus*.

14. A drill is called *terebra* from a woodworm called *terebra*, which the Greeks call τερηδών (*teredōn*). Hence *terebra* is so called because, as the worm bores by wearing away, it is as though *tere-fora* (“it bores by wearing”), or as though *transforans* (“boring through”).

15. [Note: [Col. 0683D] *Taratrum*. Commonly *taladro*.] *Taratrum* is as though *teratrum*; a rasp is called *scofina* because, by clinging, it makes a *scofen*.

[Note: [Col. 0683D] *Cantherium*. Glossary: *cantherius*, καβάλλης μηχανικός (“mechanical horse”).] *Cantherium* [lacuna].

[Col. 0683B] [Note: [Col. 0683D] *Galla* [lacuna]. It is absent from most books. Perhaps it was a Gallic drill, called *bibrequi*.] *Galla* [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0683D] *Guvia* [lacuna]. The same name remains in use among us today.] *Guvia* [lacuna].

446 ## CHAPTER XX. On the Invention of Woolworking

1. The gentiles praise a certain Minerva as possessing many talents. [Note: [Col. 0683D] “A certain Minerva.” Other copies have “a certain person.”] They say that she first demonstrated the use of woolworking, and that she also first set up the loom and dyed wool. [Note: [Col. 0683D] “She was the first of woolworking.” Servius, *Aeneid* VII, on “the warlike … of Minerva”: “She is both the goddess of arms and of woolworking.”]

2. [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Also of the olive.” Virgil, *Georgics* I: “Minerva, discoverer of the olive.”] They also call her the discoverer of the olive, of craftsmanship, and of many arts. Therefore artisans commonly pray to her. But this too is a poetic fiction. [Note: [Col. 0684D] “For Minerva is not the originator of all these arts.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 2.] Minerva is not in fact the originator of these arts; rather, because wisdom is said to reside in a person’s head, and Minerva is imagined to have been born from Jupiter’s head—that is, from intellect—and because the understanding of the wise person who discovers everything is in the head, Minerva is also called the goddess of the arts. Nothing is more excellent than intellect, by which everything is governed.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Priestly Garments in the Law

1. There are eight kinds of priestly garments in the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0684D] *Poderis*. In Hebrew, *chethoneth*.] *Poderis* is a priestly linen garment, fastened closely to the body and descending to the feet, from which it receives its name. It is commonly called a shirt.

2. *Abaneth* is a round priestly belt, woven in a figured design from scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-colored threads, so that flowers and gems appeared to be set into it.

[Col. 0684A] 447 3. [Note: [Col. 0684D] *Pileum*. Hebrew, *miznepheth*.] The *pileum* is a round linen cap, like half a sphere, covering the priestly head and fastened at the back of the head with a band. The Greeks and our people call it a tiara or [Note: [Col. 0684D] “They call it a *galeria*.” Jerome, *galerus*.] *galeria*.

4. *Mahil*, which is an ankle-length tunic, entirely hyacinth-colored, having at its feet seventy-two bells and an equal number of interspersed and hanging pomegranates.

5. *Ephod*, which in Latin means [Note: [Col. 0684D] “*Ephod … supergarment*; for it was …” These words are absent from the Gothic College manuscript at Oviedo.] “supergarment.” It was an upper shoulder garment, woven from four colors and gold, having on each shoulder two emerald stones enclosed in gold, on which the names of the patriarchs were engraved.

6. [Note: [Col. 0684D] *Logion*. Hebrew, *chosen*.] *Logion*, which in Latin is called the *rationale* (“breastpiece”), was a double cloth woven with gold and four colors. It was a span square and had twelve precious stones woven into it. [Col. 0684B] This cloth was fastened to the shoulder garment opposite the high priest’s breast.

7. [Note: [Col. 0684D] *Petalum*. Hebrew, *ziz zaab*.] *Petalum* was a golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, bearing the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, written in Hebrew letters.

8. [Note: [Col. 0684D] *Badim*, and more properly by the name *michnesi*.] *Badim*, or undergarments, were linen breeches reaching to the knees, by which the priest’s private parts were covered.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Names of Other Garments

1. The variety of garments includes *tegmen*, *tegumen*, *indumentum*, *vestimentum*, and the rest.

*Tegmen* is so called because it covers the limbs, as do *tegumen* and *tecta*, things that cover bodies.

*Indumentum* is what is put on beneath, next to the body, as though *intumentum*.

448 2. A *vestimentum* is what extends down to the footprint, as though *vestigimentum*, such as an ankle-length tunic. But the usage of authors also confounds these distinctions.

*Amictus* [lacuna].

3. Clothing (*vestitus*) is distinguished from dress (*cultus*), since dress is understood to be more elegant. Dress is likewise distinguished from habit (*habitus*). For habit pertains to nature, while dress pertains to human beings.

4. Most garments are named either from the time when they are especially in use, from the places where they were first made or are most extensively sold, from their kind of color, or from the names of their inventors.

5. The oldest garment of human beings was the *perizoma*, [Col. 0685A] that is, a loincloth, by which only the genitals are covered. [Note: [Col. 0684D] *Perizoma*, that is, a loincloth. For what it was like, see Augustine, Book V *Against Julian*.] The first mortals made this garment for themselves from the leaves of trees when, after the transgression, they blushed and covered their private parts. Certain barbarian peoples still retain its use, remaining naked otherwise to this day. [Note: [Col. 0685C] “These are also called *campestria* … they cover.” The words are Augustine’s, *City of God* XIV, chapter 17. Horace:

> A cloak in summer, a loincloth against snowy winds.]

These are also called *campestria*, because young men who exercise naked in the field cover their private parts with them.

6. The tunic is called the oldest garment because it makes a sound when a person in motion walks. *Tonus* means “sound.” At first, however, tunics were made of skins, in which Adam and Eve were clothed after the offense and expulsion from paradise.

7. [Note: [Col. 0685C] Ankle-length tunic. From Jerome, on Ezekiel IX.] An ankle-length tunic is so called because it descends to the ankles and falls to the feet, [Note: [Col. 0685C] “Like a chest garment.” In Greek, ἐξωμίς (*exōmis*), which, as Gellius says, was tight and short and ended above the shoulder.] just as a chest garment was so called because among the ancients it was short, covering only the chest, although now it is more ample.

8. [Note: [Col. 0685C] *Manicleata.* Thus all books read it. Rabanus has *manucleata*. I read *manuleata*, for that is how it is found in Plautus, in the *Pseudolus*, and Suetonius, in *Caligula*. Cicero used *manicatis tunicis* in the *Second Catiline*. Gloss: *manulea*, “sleeve” (χειρίς).] A *manicleata* tunic—that is, a sleeved tunic—is so called because it has sleeves, which the Greeks call a “sleeved garment” (χειριδωτόν).

449 9. The *dalmatica* was first woven in the province of Dalmatia in Greece; it is a white priestly tunic [Note: [Col. 0685D] *The dalmatic tunic.* It is clear that this was in use among the Romans from Lampridius’ account of Heliogabalus, whom he says was often seen in public after dinner wearing a dalmatic; Sylvester established it as the garment of deacons during the offering of the sacrifice.] with purple stripes.

10. [Note: [Col. 0685D] *Russata.* If we believe Thylesius, *russus* is indeed a Latin word, but more a word of farmers than of orators.] *Russata*, which the Greeks call *phoenicea*, we call scarlet; [Note: [Col. 0685D] *Discovered by the Lacedaemonians.* So Philostratus says in his letters.] it was discovered by the Lacedaemonians for concealing the appearance of blood whenever someone was wounded in battle, so that the enemy looking at him would not gain courage. The Romans used it for their soldiers under the consuls, and hence they were also called *russati*. [Note: [Col. 0685D] *For they used to be displayed on the preceding day.* Plutarch, in his accounts of Fabius, Brutus, and Pompey.] They also used to display them before the headquarters on the day before battle, as a warning and indication of the coming fight.

[Col. 0685C] 11. *Laculata* is a garment that has certain square compartments woven into it with decoration, or added with the needle.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] *Hyacinth-colored garment, the color of bronze.* Jerome, to Fabiola: “Hyacinth is attributed to bronze because of the similarity of its color.”] A hyacinth-colored garment shines with a bronze-like color.

12. [Note: [Col. 0685D] *Molochinia, which is made with mallow fiber.* Better, I think, [Col. 0686C] Nonius: “*Molochinum* comes from the Greek; it is a color resembling the flower of the mallow.”] *Molochinia* is made with the fiber of mallows; some call it *molocina*, others *malvella*.

13. *Bombycina* is made from the silkworm, which produces extremely long threads from itself; the fabric woven from them is called *bombycinum*, and it is made on the island of Cos.

*Apocalama* [lacuna]

450 14. *Serica* is so called from *Sericum*, or because the Seres first sent it.

*Holoserica*: entirely silk—for ὅλον means “whole.”

*Tramoserica*: with a linen warp and a silk weft.

[Note: [Col. 0686C] *Holoporphyra.* The first kind of *trabea* among the three discussed by Servius, *Aeneid* VII: “They themselves in the Quirinal robe …”] *Holoporphyra* is entirely purple.

15. [Note: [Col. 0686C] *Byssina, from a certain kind of flax.* Others read “wood.” This is wrong, although someone is not lacking who insists that this reading is correct, on the basis of Philostratus, book II of *The Life of Apollonius*. They say that *byssus* grows on a tree equal in height to poplars and resembling a willow in its leaves. But is it therefore true that garments are made from thicker wood? Byssus is discussed again below, chapter 27.] *Byssina* is white and made from a certain kind of coarser flax. Some also believe that *byssus* is a particular kind of flax.

16. *Fibrina* has a weft made from the wool of the beaver.

*Aprina* [lacuna]

*Masticina* [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0686C] *Mena … Masticina …* See below, chapter 28.] *Mena* [lacuna]

[Col. 0686B] *Linea* is made solely from flax.

17. *Linostema* is a garment woven from wool and flax. It is called *linostema* because it has flax in the warp and wool in the weft.

18. [Note: [Col. 0686D] *Recta.* From Festus, under *Recta* and *Regilla*.] A garment is called *recta* when it is woven by people standing upright and working upward.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] *Segmentata.* See Servius, *Aeneid* I, on the verse “a necklace upon her neck.”] *Segmentata* is adorned with certain bands and, as it were, cut-out pieces. For small pieces cut from any material are also called *praesegmina*.

19. [Note: [Col. 0686D] *Levidensis.* I pay no attention to the various readings or conjectures of others in Cicero, letters 12, book IX.] *Levidensis* is so called because it is made with sparse thread and lightly compacted.

*Pavitensis* is the opposite of *levidensis*, being heavily pressed and trodden.

451 20. [Note: [Col. 0686D] *Citrosa.* Festus: “A *citrosa* garment, from its resemblance to citron.”] *Citrosa*, as though tightly curled in the manner of a citron. [Note: [Col. 0686D] Naevius: “and a beautiful garment of gold, and a citron-colored garment.” See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III, chapter 19.] Naevius:

[Col. 0686C] “[lacuna] beautiful and golden, and a citron-colored garment.”

21. [Note: [Col. 0686D] *Velensis.* Others read *Velenensis*. What if it is *Melensis*, from *melos*, one of the Cyclades? Or *Melitensis*, mentioned by Cicero, book II against Verres: “I say that you have a very large quantity of gold, silver, ivory, and purple, a very large quantity of Melitene cloth, coverlets, and so on.”] A *velensis* tunic is one brought from the islands.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] *Exotica.* Nonius: “*Exoticum*, foreign.” Plautus, *Mostellaria*: “Not everyone can smell of foreign perfumes.”] An *exotica* garment is foreign, arriving from abroad, as from Greece into Spain.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] *Polymina*, multicolored. Pliny: “Alexandria first established weaving with many threads what they call *polumina*.”] *Polymina* is multicolored. For *polymitus* means a fabric of many colors.

[Col. 0687A] 22. An *acupicta* garment is woven with the needle or decorated with the needle. [Note: [Col. 0687C] *Also Phrygian.* From Servius, *Aeneid* III, or Pliny, book VIII, chapter 48.] It is also called *Phrygian*. For all those skilled in this craft are called Phrygians, either because it was invented in Phrygia. Hence the artisans who practice it are called *Phrygiones*. Virgil: “a Phrygian cloak for Ascanius.”

23. [Note: [Col. 0687C] *Trilicis.* So all books read it. I would prefer *trilex* or *trilix*. But in this work such oblique forms are frequently used for the nominative, as *calcis* for *calx*.] *Trilicis* comes from three threads, because it is single-layered, [Note: [Col. 0687C] *And bilex.* Virgil, *Aeneid* XII: “and he tears the breastplate of two threads, fixed upon him.” Gloss: *bilex*, δίπτυκτον, δίμιτον.] and also *bilex*.

[Note: [Col. 0687C] *Ralla*, commonly called *rasilis*. But Nonius says: “A *ralla* garment, so called from its sparseness.” Plautus, *Epidicus*: “A thin tunic, a dense tunic.”] *Ralla* is what is commonly called *rasilis*.

[Note: [Col. 0687D] *Interpola.* Martianus, chapter 45, discussion of sale and purchase: “Labeo writes in the *Later Books* that if someone buys used clothing as new, Trebatius holds that the seller must make good the difference if the buyer purchased the used clothing in ignorance.”] A garment is called *interpola* when, although old, it is reworked into the appearance of a new one.

24. [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Pannutia.* Persius called the old woman Baucis *pannutia*.] *Pannutia* is so called because it is covered with various pieces of cloth.

[Note: [Col. 0687D] *Colobium … they used it.* From Servius, *Aeneid* IX: “and sleeved tunics.” See the notes on Cassian.] *Colobium* is so called because it is long and without sleeves. The ancients used this garment more frequently.

452 [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Lebitonarium.* Jerome, preface to the *Rule of Saint Pachomius*: “The monks have nothing in their cells except a mat, two *lebitonaria*,” which is a type of sleeveless garment among Egyptian monks. Suidas: λεβητονάριον, μοναχικός χιτών, “a monastic tunic.”] A *lebitonarium* is a sleeveless *colobium*, such as the Egyptian monks wear.

25. [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Lumbare.* See Jerome, on Jeremiah XIII, and in the preface to his commentary on Hosea.] A *lumbare* is so called because it is tied around the loins or because it clings to the loins. In Egypt and Syria not only women but also men wear it. Hence Jeremiah carried his loincloth across the Euphrates and hid it there in a hole in the rock, later finding it torn. Some also call it *renale*, because it is tied around the kidneys.

26. [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Limu* is a garment. From Servius, *Aeneid* XII: “clothed in linen,” or *limus*, and the accompanying words.] *Limu* is a garment extending from the navel to the feet. At its lower edge this garment has a purple *limus*, that is, a winding or undulating border. Hence it received its name. For we call something oblique *limus*.

27. It is called *licinum* because its weave is entirely bound together, as though the word were *ligninum*, with *c* substituted for *g*.

[Col. 0687C] 28. [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Armelausa.* Paulinus uses this word.] *Armelausa* is the common name for a garment divided and open in front and behind but closed only at the shoulders, as though it were *armiclausa*, with the *c* removed.

29. We call them *camisas* because we sleep in them, in *camis*, that is, on our beds.

They are called *femoralia* because they cover the thighs. They are also called *brachae*, because they are short and cover the body’s private parts.

30. [Note: [Col. 0688C] *Tubrucos.* Others read *tubricos* or *tubraicos*.] They are called *tubruci* because they cover the shins and the breeches.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] *Tubraci … reach.* This is absent from the Valencia manuscript and could have been omitted without loss.] *Tubraci* are so called because they extend from the breeches to the shins.

453 **CHAPTER XXIII. On the distinctive dress of certain peoples**

1. Certain nations each have their own distinctive garment: [Note: [Col. 0688C] *For the Parthians, the sarabara.* So reads the common Greek edition, which Isidore usually follows, Daniel III: “And their sarabaras were not altered.” Aquila, Theodotion, and Jerome instead have *saraballa*, which is better. For in Syriac it is *sarbal*.] the Parthians have the *sarabara*, [Note: [Col. 0688C] *For the Gauls, the lenae.* So Strabo says in book IV, concerning the dress of the Helvetii and Arverni.] the Gauls the *lenae*, [Note: [Col. 0688D] *For the Germans, the rhenones.* Caesar, book IV of *The Gallic War*.] the Germans the *rhenones*. The Spaniards have *stringes*. The Sardinians have *mastrucae*.

2. *Sarabara* are loose and flowing garments, concerning which we read in Daniel: “And their sarabara were not altered.” Publius also says: “Why then have the Parthians hung *sarabara* in your belly?” Among some peoples, however, *sarabara* is the name for certain head coverings, such as we see painted on the heads of magi.

3. *Lenae* are square, soft cloaks. Concerning them Plautus writes:

“Gaul is covered with a woven *lena*.”

4. *Rhenones* are coverings of the shoulders and chest extending to the navel, and so bristling with twisted hairs that they repel rain. These hairs are commonly called *repti*, because the length of the hairs seems, as it were, to creep. Sallustius writes of them: “The Germans cover their uncovered bodies with rhenones.” They are called *rhenones* from the Rhine, the river of Germany, where they frequently use them. [Note: [Col. 0688D] *Rhenones from the Rhine, the son of Germany.* Others derive it ἀπὸ τῶν ῥηνῶν, that is, “from sheep.” Servius, *Georgics* III: “As Sallustius says in his histories, garments made from hides are called *rhenones*.”]

5. [Note: [Col. 0688D] *Mastruca, a Sardinian garment.* So read Tarracina, Simancas, Seville, and Mejorada. Several Gothic manuscripts instead have *mastruga*, “a German garment”; this reading could be accepted if the passage cited from Cicero did not stand in the way. Prudentius:

“Recently a Getic tyrant tried to destroy

Italy, coming from the Danube, sworn

To level these citadels, dissolve golden roofs

In flames, and clothe senators in togas with mastrucae.”] *Mastruca* is a Sardinian garment made from the skins of wild animals; Cicero speaks of it in his defense of Scaurus: “The man whom royal purple did not move, the Sardinian *mastruca* changed.” *Mastruca* is so called as though from *monstruosa*, “monstrous,” because those who put it on are, as it were, transformed into the appearance of wild animals.

6. [Note: [Col. 0688D] *Peoples are distinguished in this way by dress and language.* He seems perhaps to have had in mind Virgil’s words:

“[lacuna] the conquered peoples advance in long procession,

As diverse in language as in dress and arms.”] Peoples who differ in language are also distinguished in this way by their dress. The Persians cover their arms and legs with linen wrappings and their heads with a tiara. The Alans stand out with pointed, conical headgear; the Scots bristle, poorly clothed, with barking tongues; the Alemanni wear cloaks; the Indians linen garments; the Persians jewels; the Seres silk; the Armenians quivers.

7. Some peoples also claim certain distinctive features as their own marks, not only in clothing but in the body itself, [Note: [Col. 0689C] *Each claims certain things as distinctive marks.* Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*. Virgil: “They too ought to defend certain marks of distinction for themselves: the plumes of the Garamantes, the barbarian tufts, the cicadas of the Athenians, the curls of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons.”] as we see in the curls of the Germans, the *grani* and cinnabar markings of the Goths, and the tattoos of the Britons. The Jews circumcise their foreskins; the Arabs pierce their ears; the Getae have blond hair and go bareheaded; the Albanians gleam with white hair. The Moors have the dark night of their bodies; the Gauls white skin; the Alans appear inert when without horses; nor is the name of the Picts absent from their bodies, since an artisan’s needle, with its tiny punctures, and the expressed juice of a native plant mark them, so that their nobility bears these scars as signs of their identity, their tattooed limbs mottled.

8. Sex too has an established appearance of dress: [Col. 0689B] [Note: [Col. 0689D] *Men with shorn hair.* “If a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him.” 1 Corinthians.] men wear their hair shorn, while women have an abundance of hair. This is especially characteristic of virgins, whose adornment is specifically arranged so that the gathered circumference of their hair covers the crown at the top of their head.

**CHAPTER XXIV. On men’s cloaks**

1. The *pallium* is what covers the shoulders of attendants, so that while serving they may move about freely. Plautus:

“If you are about to do something, hang your cloak upon your shoulders,

And let the nimbleness of your feet proceed as far as it is able.”

The *pallium* is called this from *pelles*, “skins,” because in earlier times people wore it over leather garments, as though it were *pellea*; or it derives by formation from *palla*.

[Col. 0689C] 456 2. The *chlamys* is worn on one side; it is not sewn together but fastened with a brooch. Hence it received its Greek name.

3. The *toga* is so called because it covers and conceals the body with its covering. [Note: [Col. 0689D] *It is a pure cloak.* “Pure toga” was said of one without purple; I do not see who would have called a plain cloak *purum pallium*. Therefore Chacon deleted τὸ *purum*. But “pure garments” are used in another sense by Festus and Servius in the fragments.] It is a pure cloak, more broadly rounded in shape, with a fold spreading and, as it were, flooding outward; coming from beneath the right side, it is placed over the left shoulder. We see something similar in the coverings of statues or paintings, and call such statues *togatae*.

4. The Romans used the toga in peace, but in wartime they used *paludamenta*. [Note: [Col. 0689D] *The proper measure of a toga is six cubits.* Horace, in the *Epodes*:

With a toga twice three cubits long,

5. [Note: [Col. 0689D] *The palm-bearing toga.* Servius, *Eclogue* 10: “With the blood-red berries of the elder … The palm-bearing toga, which was worn by those who had earned the palm.”] The *toga palmata* was so called because it was awarded to those who brought back palms from the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0689D] *It is also called the toga picta.* See Festus, under *Picta*.] It was also called the *toga picta*, because it had victories woven into it together with palms.

6. The *toga candida*, also called *cretata*, was worn by candidates—that is, by those seeking office—when they canvassed for support; chalk was added to make it whiter and more distinguished. Cicero titled the speech he delivered against his competitors *In the White Toga*.

7. [Note: [Col. 0689D] *The Gabine cincture.* See Servius, *Aeneid* VII:

“He himself in the Quirinal trabea and Gabine cincture.”

8. [Note: [Col. 0690C] *The trabea was a special kind of toga.* Servius, *Aeneid* VII: “The *trabea* is the augurs’ toga, made of scarlet and purple.”] The *trabea* was a kind of toga made of purple and scarlet, in which the kings of Rome, covered with it, proceeded in the earliest period. [Note: [Col. 0690C] *Romulus first introduced it.* Pliny, book IX, chapter 39: “I see that purple was always used at Rome, but by Romulus in the trabea.”] Romulus is said to have devised it first, to distinguish royal dress. The *trabea* is so called because it would *transbeare* a man—that is, make him blessed with a higher and more lasting dignity of honor. [Note: [Col. 0690C] *Transbearet.* Thus the Gothic manuscript reads; others have *transveheret*, “would carry across.”]

9. The *paludamentum* was the distinctive cloak of emperors, marked with scarlet, purple, and gold. Sallustius speaks of it: “He changed his toga for a military cloak.” It was a military cloak, called this, as some think, because the emperor, dressed in it, publicly declared that war was about to take place.

10. *Circumtextum* is what is called in Greek κύκλας, concerning which Virgil writes:

[Note: [Col. 0690D] *And a cloak bordered all around.* Servius: “The covering—understand *circumtextum*—signifies a *cyclas*. It is not that *velamen* is an apposition to *circumtextum*, as someone thought, but that the covering is bordered all around with saffron acanthus. For *circumtextum* is a participle no less than *pictum*, especially since the same verse is repeated shortly afterward by Maro with a slight alteration:

“And a mantle and a covering embroidered with saffron acanthus.”

Although *circumtextum* may also be used substantivally, whether for a type of garment or rather for a part of a garment. Varro, book IV: “*Amictus* is said from *amjectus*, that is, ‘thrown around’; hence what garments wrap themselves in is also called *circumjectum*, and what they have as purple around the *amictus* they call *circumtextum*.”] “And a cloak bordered all around with saffron acanthus.” *Circumtextum* is so called because it is a round cloak.

11. [Note: [Col. 0690D] *Diplois.* Servius, *Aeneid* V: “Having spoken these words, the double …” That is, an *abolla*, which is double, like a *chlamys*. Horace:

“Against whom patience veils wisdom with a double cloth.”] *Diplois* is a Greek name, from the fact that it is a double cloak. Horace:

“Against whom patience veils wisdom with a double cloth.”

[Note: [Col. 0691C] *It is a military garment.* It is clear that this passage has been wrongly assigned to *diplois* in all the books.] It is a military garment, whose use began during Gallic campaigns, from booty taken from the enemy. Concerning it comes that expression of the Senate: [Note: [Col. 0691C] “Having laid aside your togas, Quirites, to the military cloaks.” Some manuscripts add *iverunt*, “they went”; others have *fuerunt*, “they were,” *fugerunt*, “they fled,” or *conversi fuerunt*, “they turned.” All these are certainly interpolations. The established words in a time of disturbance were: “Having laid aside your togas, Quirites, to the military cloaks.” Or perhaps: “Having laid aside your togas, Quirites, go to the military cloaks,” which I consider more likely. For the *ite* that followed *Quirites* was omitted by scribes who, as often happens, did not repeat the same syllable. Cicero frequently uses *ire* and *redire ad saga*, “to go” and “return to the military cloaks.” Likewise, *saga sumere*, “to take up military cloaks,” and *togas deponere*, “to lay aside togas.” See *Philippics* 5, 6, 8, and 14.] “Having laid aside your togas, Quirites, (go) to the military cloaks.”

458 13. *Sagum* is a Gallic word. It is called a square *sagum* because among the Gauls it was originally square or fourfold.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] *Paenula is a cloak with long fringes.* Cicero’s words in the speech for Milo strongly confirm this: “What could be less ready for a fight, when he was entangled in a *paenula*, hindered by a carriage, and almost bound by his wife?” The *paenula* itself was also tight and narrow, according to grammarians and rhetoricians. Tacitus, *On the Causes of the Corruption of Eloquence*: “How much indignity do we think these *paenulae* have brought upon eloquence, in which, constrained and almost enclosed, we speak with judges?”] A *paenula* is a cloak with long fringes.

“This *lacerna* is woven for your camps.”] A *lacerna* is a fringed cloak, once worn only by soldiers. [Note: [Col. 0691D] *Hence *lacernae*, as though their heads were cut off.* Festus, under *Lacerare*: “A *lacerna*, because it has a smaller opening at the neck.”] Hence *lacernae*, as though the heads of the fringes had been cut off, and they are not as loose as those of *paenulae*.

17. A *casula* is a hooded garment, called by diminutive formation from *casa*, because it covers the whole person, as though it were a small house. Hence also *cuculla*, as though a small cell. Hence the stars are also called *planetae*, that is, “wanderers,” because they move about in their wandering course and motion.

18. *Birrus* derives its name from Greek; for they call *birrum* *bibrum*.

19. *Melotes*, also called a *pera*, is a goatskin hanging from the neck and fastened around the loins. It is a garment especially necessary for carrying out work. The edges of garments, that is, their ends, taking their name from Greek. For the Greeks call a boundary ὅρον.

1. [Note: [Col. 0692C] *Regillum.* See Festus and Nonius.] *Regillum* is a very elegant mantle of queens, from which it received its name. 460 [Note: [Col. 0692C] *Peplum.* Servius, *Aeneid* I: “Properly, a *peplum* is a woman’s embroidered cloak dedicated to Minerva. But the same Varro, in his books *On the Latin Language*, says: “It is called *palla* because it is visible, just as *intusium* is so called because it is inside.”] *Palla* is also said to derive from πάλλειν, “to move,” that is, from the movement around the lower edge of such a garment, or because it is made wavy and curled by vibrating folds.

[Col. 0692B] 3. The *stola* is a matron’s covering which, with the head and shoulder covered, is thrown from the right side over the left shoulder. It is called *stola* in Greek because it is placed over something.

The *amiculum* deserves further investigation.] among the ancients this was a mark of a prostitute’s garment; now in Spain it is a mark of respectability.

To this day the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia veil themselves with it, and by it are protected in the heat by a very safe shade. Isaiah speaks of it.

1. [Note: [Col. 0693C] *Stragula garment.* All the Gothic manuscripts have *stragula*, not *stragulata*.] A *stragulum* is a multicolored garment, distinguished by the craftsman’s hand in varied patterns. [Note: [Col. 0693D] *Fulcra are:* “*Fulcra* are the supports of beds, by which we support ourselves,” says Servius, *Aeneid* VI.] *Fulcra* are ornaments of beds, so called because we are supported by them, that is, sustained; or because they support the couches or the head. [Note: [Col. 0693D] *Culcitrae … because they are stuffed.* So Varro, book IV.] *Culcitrae* are so called because they are *calcentur*, that is, stuffed with feathers or padding, so that they may be softer and warmer.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] *Curtains are leather *aulaea*.* It is strange that he departed from Servius, who says in *Aeneid* III: “A *cortina* is the place from which an oracle proceeds, either because Apollo’s tripod is woven from the hide of Python, or because certain responses are given there, as though from *certina*, or—and this is more accurate—because the heart of the prophet is held there.” He adds in book VI: “Or certainly according to the Greek etymology, because it stretches the pupil” (ὅτι τὴν κόρην τείνει), and so on. **CHAPTER XXVII. On wool**

1. *Lana* is so called from *laniendo*, that is, “pulling out.” Hence *vellus* is also so called, because wool was originally pulled out, not shorn.

[Col. 0694C] *Linum* grows from the earth, and its name is derived from Greek. For the Greeks call flax λινάριον [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Greeks call it λινάριον. Rather, probably λίνον, or λινάρια, “nets” in Pamphylia, according to Eustathius, *Odyssey* β.]—or because it is soft and smooth.

[Col. 0695A] 2. *Stuppa* is hemp or flax. [Note: [Col. 0695C] This follows ancient orthography. From Servius, *Aeneid* V.] According to ancient spelling it is called *stippa*, because cracks in ships are *stippantur*, “caulked,” with it.

[Note: [Col. 0695C] *Hence *stippatores* … put it together.* From the same source, *Aeneid* III: “And they caulk the hulls.”] Hence those who put it into ships are called *stippatores*. [Note: [Col. 0695C] *Who work on ships.* Others read *vallibus*, “in valleys”; F has *navalibus*, “in naval works.”]

3. [Note: [Col. 0695C] *Tomentum.* Others read *tumentum*.] *Tomentum* is so called because it swells either in thread or in cloth and lacks fineness.

*Cannabum* is named from its resemblance to a reed, or from Greek etymology. For the Greeks call hemp κάνναβιν.

4. [Note: [Col. 0695C] *Byssum … they call *papates*.* This material is absent from the Gothic-Toledo manuscript.] *Byssum* is a kind of flax, exceedingly white and very soft, [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Which the Greeks call *papates*.* For πᾶππος ἀκάνθης is “the white blossom of a thistle,” as Eustathius says. Festus likewise says: “The *pappi* are the flowers of thistles.”] which the Greeks call *papates*.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] *Fibrinum.* Above, chapter 22.] *Fibrinum* is the wool of animals called *fibres*, which they also believe to be beavers. When hunters pursue them, the animals tear off their own testicles.

[Col. 0695B] [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Aranea.* Above, book XII, chapter 5.] *Aranea* is so called because it is nourished on leaves by an infusion of air.

5. [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Sericum.* From Servius, *Georgics* II, on the verse “and fleeces like leaves … the Seres.”] *Sericum* is so called because the Seres first sent it. Worms are said to be born there, and from them these threads are drawn around trees. The worms themselves are called in Greek βόμβυκες.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] *Placium.* Or rather *plathium*, as though from τὸ πλήθω, “I fill,” and “I stuff.”] *Placium* is tow, and, as it were, the [Note: [Col. 0695D] *And, as it were, the thickness.* Commonly *seda cadarca*.] coarseness of silk; it is a Greek name.

**CHAPTER XXVIII. On the colors of garments**

1. *Tinctura* is so called because something is dipped and colored into another dyed appearance for the sake of brilliance. [Note: [Col. 0695D] *The Greeks call it *coccum*.* In the Septuagint κόκκινον is more frequent than κόκκος. Jerome sometimes renders it *vermiculum*, sometimes *coccum*, or leaves *coccinum*. He usually interprets φοινικοῦν as “red.”] The Greeks call it κόκκον; we call it red or scarlet. For it is a little worm found on woodland foliage.

2. [Note: [Col. 0695D] “Conchylion … is extracted.” From Vitruvius, Book VII, chapter 13.] “Conchylion” is so called because its color is collected from marine shellfish [Col. 0695C]. It is also called “oyster-purple” (*ostrum*).

3. Oyster-purple, which is prepared for the color purple, is produced in many places, but the finest grows on the island of Cyprus, or in those regions that the sun’s course illuminates more directly.

4. Shellfish are creatures of the sea which, when cut around with iron, emit tears of purple color. After these are collected, the purple dye is prepared; and they say that *ostrum* was subsequently [Col. 0696A] named from this, because it is extracted from the moisture of the shell.

5. [Note: [Col. 0695D] “Purple … from the purity of light.” He perhaps had Virgil’s words in mind, *Aeneid* I: “And the purple light of youth.” For although *purpura* is πορφύρα, he himself does not seem to doubt that the word is so.] Among the Latins, *purpura* is said to derive its name from the purity of light. Among the Greeks, however, it is called πορφύρα, with aspiration; among us, *purpura*, without aspiration.

6. [Note: [Col. 0696C] “Ferrugo is a color … in Spain.” Servius, *Georgics* I: “When the head … with ferrugo”: “Ferrugo is a darker Spanish purple”; elsewhere, “And bright with Iberian ferrugo,” where the gloss “Spanish” belonged to the word “Iberian.” For Servius himself, in the passage he cites from *Aeneid* IX, intends “Iberian ferrugo” to mean Pontic, not Spanish, purple. Thus, in Isidore’s time, as now with everything, certain copies of Servius were corrupted.] *Ferrugo* is the color of a nearly black purple, which is made in Spain, as in: “Bright with Iberian ferrugo.” It is called *ferrugo* because all purple, in its first dyeing, has this kind of color.

7. [Note: [Col. 0696D] “Glaucus is the color of ferrugo.” Above, in the discussion of the colors of horses, Book XII, chapter 1.] *Glaucus* is a ferruginous, nearly black color.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] *Elbum*. Above, Book XII, chapter 5.] *Elbidum* is named from the color *elbum*. For *elbum* is an intermediate color between white and black, and *elbum* is derived from *album*.

8. [Note: [Col. 0696D] “Luteus.” From Servius, *Eclogue* 4.] *Luteus* is a reddish color, which is saffron-colored; for saffron is the color of *luteus*, as in: “He will change the fleece with saffron-yellow dye.”

[Col. 0696B] [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Menum*. Other copies have *melum*; others, *melium*; perhaps *melinum*, mentioned elsewhere.] *Menum* is so called because it is black in color. For the Greeks call black μελαν.

*Masticinum* is so called because it has the color of mastic.

*Blatteum* … *blavum* … *mesticium* … [lacuna]

9. [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Osticium*, because it derives from something burned.] *Osticium* is so called because it derives from something burned. It is made from the soot expelled from the hanging surfaces of roofs by continual fires; hence its color, when dyed, is fiery.

1. [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Tela*, “loom,” from length, from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ τηλόθεν, that is, “from afar.”] *Tela* is so called from the length of the warp threads; its derivative is *telaria*.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] *Insula*. Glosses have *insubula*, ἀντίον καὶ ἀντία, “opposite,” and elsewhere ἀντίον ἔνθα ὑφαίνουσιν αἱ γυναῖκες, “opposite, where the women weave.” Lucretius, Book V:

“Shuttles, spindles, and sounding weaving reeds,”

where some read *iusubula*, without concern for the length of the syllable. Jerome calls it a “weaving instrument” in 1 Chronicles.] *Insubuli* are so called because they are below and above, or because they are inserted beneath.

*Radii*, “weaving reeds,” are so called because they are made by scraping.

[Col. 0696C] *Pectines*, “combs,” are so called because they return and press the combed (*pexa*) threads.

2. *Colus*, “distaff,” is so called because it is long and rounded, like a column.

*Fusus*, “spindle,” is so called because through it what has been spun is poured out.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] *Alibrum*, as though “in which they are balanced,” that is, wound. The Gothic copies have *liberantur*, “are loosened.”] *Alibrum* is so called because on it the threads are balanced, that is, wound.

3. *Calathus* is a light carrying vessel made of wood, reed, or rush, in which either skeins of wool are placed or flowers are gathered. [Note: [Col. 0697C] For the Greeks call wood κᾶλον, as Servius says more than once. See the beginning of *Aeneid* VI. Festus also says: “*Calones* are shoes made of wood.”] κᾶλον in Greek means “wood,” from which *calathus* is derived. [Note: [Col. 0697C] “For in Latin it is called *quasillum* … gold.” These are Servius’s words, *Eclogue* 4.] For in Latin it is called *quasillum*. Cicero, in the *Philippics*: “But in this man’s house gold was hung among the wool-baskets.”

4. The women’s *pensum*, “task,” is so called from hanging, whence come *pensa* and *impensa*.

*Netum* … [lacuna]

5. *Fila*, “threads,” are so called either because they are made from the hair of animals, or because wool-working consists of fine threads in the manner of hairs, that is, like filaments.

6. [Note: [Col. 0697C] *Mataxa*. Commonly *madexa*. Glosses: *mataxa*, σειρά, “cord,” and *mataxa*, ἡνία, “reins.” Vitruvius uses the word in Book VII, chapter 3, and Martianus in Book XXXIX, in the title *On Pledges and Mortgages*. Hence *metaxarii* in Justinian, Book VIII, under the same title.] *Mataxa*, as though *metaxa*, is named from the winding of the threads. For *meta* means “a circuit,” or because it is transferred.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] *Gubellum*. Other copies have *lubellum*, *jubellum*, or *globiellum*. In Spanish, *ovillo*, and among some writers, *jovillo*.] *Gubellum* is a corrupt diminutive of *globus*, “ball,” as though *globellum*.

[Col. 0697B] 7. [Note: [Col. 0697D] *Panuliae*, or *panuclae*. The two final words are absent from the Gothic copies. See the notes of learned men on Varro’s words in Book IV: “*Pannus* is Greek; *panuclum* is called from *pannus* and from the winding of the thread.”] *Panuliae* (or *panuclae*) are so called because cloth is woven from them. For they move back and forth through the loom.

*Stamen*, “warp,” is so called because it stands straight.

*Trama*, “weft,” is so called because it is transmitted in a straight path through the loom. It is the thread running within the warp.

*Licia* are the cords by which the warp threads are tied, as though *ligia*, “ties.”

*Ordiri* … [lacuna]

*Texere* … [lacuna]

**CHAPTER XXX. On ornaments**

1. Thus far concerning clothing; let us now proceed to the rest of personal adornment.

*Ornamenta*, “ornaments,” are so called because through their adornment the faces and countenances are beautified. The first ornament is the crown, a mark of victory or a sign of royal honor. It is placed on the heads of kings to signify the peoples spread throughout the world, by whom he is encircled, so that his head is, as it were, crowned. Lucilius called it *corolla*, “little crown,” and Homer στεφάνη, “crown.” [Note: [Col. 0697D] “Its beginning was from Liber.” See Athenaeus, Book XV, chapter 5.] The Gentiles believe that its origin came from a certain Liber, because he began, while drinking, to bind people’s heads with little bands moved by wine. For this reason the crown was formerly made of linen and wool, [Note: [Col. 0697D] “As it was among pagan priests,” for example, among the flamines. They were called *flamines*, as though *filamines*, from *filum*, “thread,” according to Festus. The same was true of ambassadors. Livy, Book I: “When an ambassador comes to their borders, from which restitution is demanded, with his head veiled”—a woolen thread is the veil—“Hear, Jupiter,” and so on. That he also says that crowns were made of linen derives from Virgil’s verse, *Aeneid* XII:

“With linen veils and their temples bound with sacred branches,”

although Servius, Capro, and Hyginus, against this interpretation, prefer to read *limo* in that passage.] as was customary among pagan priests.

2. [Note: [Col. 0698C] The name *corona*. Festus: Although it appears to derive from *chorus*, “dance,” it nevertheless lacks aspiration.] The name *corona* was given for this reason: at first people ran around altars, and it was formed and named after the image of a circuit or a chorus.

469 3. [Note: [Col. 0698C] Roman emperors and kings. See Pliny, Aulus Gellius, and Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*.] Roman emperors and certain kings of foreign peoples use golden crowns. The Persians wear tiaras, [Note: [Col. 0698C] “But kings wear them upright.” Xenophon, Book VIII of the *Cyropaedia*: “Cyrus, standing on a chariot and wearing his tiara upright.” And Hesychius: “A tiara, the so-called *kurbasia*; the Persian kings alone wore it upright, while the generals wore it tilted.”] the kings upright, the satraps tilted. The tiara was discovered by Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians. That people has retained this type of ornament ever since.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] “The Athenians wore cicadas.” For this reason they were called τεττιγοφόροι, “cicada-bearers.”] The Athenians wore golden cicadas, some on the crown of the head, others on the forehead. For the insignia of all kingdoms are not the same. The pagan prophets used the *infula*, *apex*, *pileus*, or *galerus*.

[Col. 0698B] 4. [Note: [Col. 0698D] *Infula*. From Servius, *Aeneid* X. See Festus.] An *infula* is a white priestly headband, in the form of a diadem, from which ribbons hang on both sides and bind the *infula*. Hence they are called *vittae*, “bands,” because they bind; the *infula* itself is generally twisted and made of white wool and scarlet.

5. [Note: [Col. 0698D] *Apex*. From Festus.] An *apex* is a sewn cap worn by pagan priests. It is called from *apiere*, “to fasten,” that is, “to tie.” [Note: [Col. 0698D] “For the little rod.” Servius, *Aeneid* II: “The *apex* pours forth light.”] The little rod that was in the cap was fastened with a thread made from the wool of the sacrificial victim.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] *Galerum*. The same author, *Aeneid* VII: “*Galerus* is a type of cap,” which Fronto gives in the neuter: *hoc galerum*. Other copies have *galerium* or *galearium*. Festus: “*Galearia* is so called from its resemblance to helmets.”] A *galerum* is a cap made from the hide of a slaughtered sacrificial victim. A *pileus*, “cap,” is likewise named from the hide of the victim, from which it was made.

6. [Note: [Col. 0698D] *Cydaris*. From Jerome, on Zechariah III and Ezekiel XII.] The *cydaris* also belonged to priests; most people call it a *mitra*.

470 **CHAPTER XXXI. On women’s head ornaments**

[Col. 0698C] 1. Women’s head ornaments are the diadem, nimbus, *capitulum*, and mitre.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] *Diadema*. Festus cites the following words from Cato, under *Rusca*: “Women covered with gold and purple … a diadem, golden crowns,” and so forth. But since Jerome, on Ezekiel XII, and others say that a diadem is not an ornament of married women but an insignia of a king’s head, the learned editor read *anadema* here, from Lucretius, Book V: “Diadems and mitres are made.” Isidore’s great fondness for this poet is evident from many passages of this work.] A *diadema* is a head ornament of married women, woven of gold and gems. Its ends are brought around and fastened at the back; it is therefore called in Greek from the fact that it is bound on.

2. A *nimbus* is a transverse band sewn with gold onto the linen garment worn across women’s foreheads. Plautus:

“The more I look at her, the more nimbate she appears.”

[Note: [Col. 0699C] “For the light also that is painted around angels’ heads.” Servius, *Aeneid* X: “When she had spoken these words … she sent forth winter, girded with a cloud”: “Girded with a cloud”—he says—“because she sent winter ahead; otherwise we would receive the radiance that surrounds the bodies of the gods.”] The light painted around angels’ heads is also called a *nimbus*, although *nimbus* may also mean a dense cloud.

3. [Note: [Col. 0699C] *Capitulum*. I read *capital*. Varro, Book IV: “Likewise, a woven band with which they bound their hair on the head; it was called *capital* from *caput*, ‘head,’ because priestesses still commonly wear it on the head.” Festus: “*Capital*, a certain linen cloth used in sacrifices.”] *Capitulum* is what people commonly call *capitulare*. It is also called a *cappa*, either because the letter *cappa* has two peaks, or because it is a head ornament.

471 4. [Note: [Col. 0699C] “The mitre is a cap.” Servius, *Aeneid* IV: “A mitre is a curved cap, from which a covering of beads hung.”] A *mitra* is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as is worn as the head ornament of consecrated women. [Note: [Col. 0699D] “But *pileus* belongs to men … to women.” From Servius, *Aeneid* IX.] The *pileus* belongs to men, whereas the *mitra* belongs to women.

5. *Redimicula* are the bands with which a mitre is tied. As we said above, the *pileus* was made from hide. The mitre, however, is made of wool.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] *Ricula* is a mitre for a virgin’s head. See Varro, Festus, and Nonius.] A *ricula* is a mitre for a virgin’s head.

[Col. 0699B] 6. *Vittae* are bands woven into the hair, by which the flowing locks are tied back. They are called *vittae* because they bind.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] *Taenia*, the end of the bands. From Servius, *Aeneid* VII: “The band of the long ribbon is made.”] A *taenia* is the hanging end of bands of various colors.

A *vitta* is also the band with which a crown is bound; a *taenia*, however, is the end of the *vitta* that hangs down from the crown.

7. [Note: [Col. 0699D] *Retiolum* … “so that it may retain the hair.” Varro calls it *reticulum*, Book IV.] A *retiolum* is what gathers the hair. It is named from the fact that it holds the hair back so that it does not spill out.

472 8. [Note: [Col. 0699D] *Discriminalia*. Jerome, on Isaiah III, calls it *discriminale*; for Varro and Nonius it is *discerniculum*, that is, a pin that separates the hair from the middle of the forehead. What is called *discrimen* in the glossaries, I think, belongs here among ornaments: *discrimen*, διάκριμα, “separation.”] Women’s head ornaments are called *discriminalia* because they divide the head with gold. [Note: [Col. 0699D] For *discriminare* means “to divide.” Virgil, *Aeneid* XI: “And widely divides the fields.”] For *discriminare* means “to divide.”

[Note: [Col. 0699D] *Antiae* are curls. Festus: “*Antiae* are women’s locks hanging down over the forehead; they seem to be named from the Greek, since what we call *contra*, ‘opposite,’ they call ἀντί. I do not see why Isidore derives them from the ears. Tertullian uses this word in *On the Pallium*.] *Antiae* are curls hanging near the ears, named by a Greek term from the ears.

[Col. 0699C] 9. [Note: [Col. 0699D] “So that the hair may not be scattered.” Jerome’s words, on Isaiah III.] *Acus*, “pins,” are used by women to hold together the structure of their arranged hair, so that it does not flow too loosely and the scattered hair does not come apart.

10. Earrings (*inaures*) are named from the openings of the ears, [Col. 0700A] [Note: [Col. 0700C] “From which precious grains of stones hang.” Thus Tertullian, *On the Adornment of Women*: “So that from them certain grains, I know not what, born for the iron, might hang.”] from which precious gems hang. [Note: [Col. 0700C] “The use of earrings in Greece.” Other copies have “Their use.” Both, I think, derive from the margin.] Their use in Greece was as follows: girls wore them in both ears, [Note: [Col. 0700C] “Boys only in the right.” Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, concerning Achilles: “He was made effeminate by having even his ear pierced.”] while boys wore them only in the right ear.

11. *Torques* are golden rings hanging from the neck down to the chest. *Torques* and *bullae* are worn by men, whereas women wear necklaces and chains. *Torques* are so called because they are twisted; *bullae* because their rounded shape resembles bubbles inflated by wind in water.

473 12. [Note: [Col. 0700C] *Monile*, an ornament made of gems. From Jerome, on Ezekiel XVI.] A *monile* is a gemmed ornament that usually hangs from a woman’s neck; it is named from a gift.

[Note: [Col. 0700C] “This is also called that of serpents.” Thus the Gothic copies; and Pollux, Book VI, counts ὄφεις, “serpents,” among women’s ornaments. Other copies have *serpetum*; the Greeks likewise have ἑρπετόν; and so does Festus. “*Serpula*,” he says, “from *serpere*, ‘to creep’; Messalla says *serpens*, ‘creeping in.’”] This is also called a serpent ornament, because it consists of certain small golden vessels and various gems arranged in the form of a serpent.
