[Note: [Col. 0700D] “Some call this a *segmentum* as well.” From Servius, *Aeneid* I: “And a beaded necklace around her neck.”] Some also call this a *segmentum*, as Juvenal says: “Bands and long garments,” although we also speak of *segmentatae vestes*, “banded garments,” as he himself writes:

“And the little girl had slept in banded cradles.”

13. [Note: [Col. 0700D] “Usually, however, all ornaments are also signified by *monile*.” From Jerome, on Isaiah III.] More generally, all the ornaments of married women are signified by *monile*, whatever is given to them as a gift.

14. [Note: [Col. 0700D] *Muraena* … is woven. From the same author, Letter 15, to Marcella, on the praises of Asella.] What is commonly called a *muraena* is a chain woven from gold drawn into flexible rods and arranged in a winding pattern, in the likeness of the serpent called a moray eel, and fitted around the neck as an ornament. [Note: [Col. 0700D] “This is sometimes woven from rods of gold and silver.” From the same author, on Isaiah III.] Sometimes it is woven from rods of gold and silver. Hence in the *Song of Songs* it is said: “We will make golden *muraenulae* for you, worked in silver.”

15. *Catellae* are little chains of the neck, each clasping the next in the manner of a chain; hence their name.

16. [Note: [Col. 0700D] “The right-hand ornaments are common.” I read *dextralia communia*, “right-hand ornaments in common.” What the Septuagint calls περιδέξια, Jerome translates as *dextralia*; Ambrose and Julius Capitolinus, in their account of Maximinus, call them *dextrocheria*.] Right hands are common to men and women, [Col. 0700C] because both sexes have right hands.

474 [Note: [Col. 0700D] “Armlets properly belong to men.” See below.] *Armillae*, however, properly belong to men. They were awarded to soldiers for victory, in recognition of their courage in arms. Hence they were once commonly called [Note: [Col. 0700D] “*Viriolae* were the name.” *Viriolae* are frequently read in the *Pandects*, and in the glossaries: *viriolae*, ψέλλια, “bracelets.” *Viriola* is a diminutive of *viria*, a word used by Ambrose, *On Abraham the Patriarch*, chapter 9: “He had these in his ears, which did not weigh down his ears; these *viriae*, which adorned the hand not with material gold but raised it through spiritual action.” Tertullian likewise uses it in *On the Pallium*: “Just as the *viria* occupied the traces of boxing gloves.”] *viriolae*. In its meaning, an *armilla* does not differ from a circle, since it too constricts by encircling the place where it is worn. But an *armilla* extends more broadly, whereas a circle is round.

17. [Note: [Col. 0701C] *Fibulae*. On these, see below, chapter 32.] *Fibulae* are fasteners with which women’s breasts are adorned, or by which men hold their cloaks at the shoulders, or their belts at the waist.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] *Lunulae*. From Jerome, on Isaiah III. The word is also familiar from Plautus.] *Lunulae* are women’s ornaments: little golden disks hanging down in the likeness of the moon.

18. [Note: [Col. 0701C] “Mirrors … *periscelides*.” From the same author.] *Specula*, “mirrors,” are so called because women look at their faces in them. A mirror is called *speculum* either because it reflects through its brightness, or because women, looking into it, examine the appearance of their faces and add whatever ornament they see to be lacking.

19. *Periscelides* are women’s leg ornaments, by which their steps are adorned.

*Olfactoriola* are women’s little vessels in which perfumes are carried.

475 **CHAPTER XXXII. On rings**

1. [Note: [Col. 0701C] “The first was Prometheus.” Pliny, in the preface to Book XXXVII. Yet in Book XXXIII, chapter 1, he had identified this story as fictitious.] Prometheus is said to have been the first to surround his finger with an iron ring containing a stone, [Note: [Col. 0701D] “He put it around.” An old manuscript has “he put it around.”] placing it upon his finger.

[Note: [Col. 0701D] “By this custom people …” From Hyginus, Book II, chapter “Sagittarius.”] Following this custom, people began to wear rings. [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Rings are named by diminution.” Varro, Book V: “The period from one winter solstice to the next, while the sun returns, is called a year; just as small circles are called *annuli*, so large circles are called *anni*. According to Festus, *circites* are circles made of bronze.”] Rings (*annuli*) are named by diminution from *circuli*, “circles,” and from *ani*, which are around the arms and legs. Hence their engraved devices are also called *sigilla*, “little seals,” by diminution. For *signa* are larger, while *sigilla* are, as it were, smaller signs.

2. People first began to wear rings on the fourth finger from the thumb, because a certain vein runs from it all the way to the heart. The ancients thought that this finger ought to be marked and adorned with some distinguishing ornament.

3. [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Among the Romans, rings were given from public funds.” Pliny says, Book XXXIII, chapter 1, that they were given only to those who were about to go as envoys to foreign peoples.] Among the Romans, rings were given from public funds, and not without distinction. [Note: [Col. 0701D] “For men distinguished by rank.” The source of this statement must be investigated.] For men distinguished by rank received gemmed rings, while the others received plain ones. A free man wore a gold ring in public; neither a slave nor a freedman did so, but [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Freedmen used gold rings, freedmen silver, slaves iron.” I think not all free men used gold, except senators or equestrians; nor did slaves alone use iron, but soldiers also.] free men wore gold rings, freedmen [Col. 0702A] silver, and slaves iron, although many men of the highest respectability also wore an iron ring.

4. Among the ancients, it was considered disgraceful for a man to wear more than one ring. Gracchus, speaking against Maenius: “Consider, Quirites, his left hand, whose authority you follow: because of his desire for women, he is adorned like a woman.” Crassus, who perished among the Parthians, had two rings in old age, claiming as his justification that his wealth had grown immeasurably. Many Romans likewise refrained from wearing a ring on their finger out of dignity. Women did not use rings except those sent to them by a fiancé, and they customarily wore no more than two gold rings on their fingers. [Note: [Col. 0701D] “But now, because of gold, no limb is light or free.” These are Tertullian’s words, in the *Apologeticus*.] But now, because of gold, no limb of women is light or free from adornment.

5. The types of rings include the *ungulus*, *samothracius*, and *thynnius*.

[Note: [Col. 0701D] “*Ungulus* is gemmed.” Pliny: “Although I see that there is uncertainty even about the name itself, the Greeks named it from the fingers. Among us the ancients called it *ungulum*.”] The *ungulus* is gemmed, and is so called because, just as a hoof surrounds flesh, so the gem of a ring is enclosed by gold.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] “The Samothracian, although … with iron.” Pliny: “Even slaves now encircle iron with gold, while others adorn objects separately with pure gold; the origin of this license is revealed by the name itself, which shows that the practice began in Samothrace.”] The *samothracius* is indeed gold, but has an iron setting; it is named from the place.

6. The *thynnius* is plain and was first fashioned in Bithynia, [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Which they once called Thynna.” Thus Acron, Ode 3, Book III.] which they formerly called Thynna. [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Flaccus, mourning.” The verses of Flaccus, as they appeared in the Gothic books, have been left uncorrected. They may be read from Alciatus as follows: “My life, shining—do not send me emeralds, beryls, bright gems, or dazzling pearls,” and so on. Or, with very little risk and excellent sense, following Antonius Covarrubias, they may be restored in full as: “To me in mourning, my life, do not send emeralds, beryls, or shining pearls. Not white …” For after *mihi*, “to me,” the scribes probably omitted *mitte*, “send,” because of the similarity—which is even greater in Gothic characters—between the words. It also seems clear that *Flacce* is out of place. He forbids precious stones to be sent to him in mourning, because, as the other Flaccus says, their use cannot soothe a grieving person.] Flaccus writes:

“In mourning, my life, I seek neither emeralds nor beryls for me, Flaccus, nor gleaming, dazzling pearls; neither rings polished by the Thynnian file, nor little jasper stones.”

**CHAPTER XXXIII. On belts**

1. [Note: [Col. 0702D] *Cinctus* is a broad girdle. Varro: “*Cinctus* and *cingulum* derive from *cingere*, ‘to gird’; the former is assigned to men, the latter to women.”] A *cinctus* is a broad belt; a *semicinctium* is narrower; and the narrowest of all, for both sexes, is a *cingulum*. For *cingulum* is a diminutive of *cinctus*. With the *cinctus*, young men modestly covered themselves during athletic exercises in the Campus; hence it was also called a *campestre*.

2. [Note: [Col. 0702D] *Balteus*. Varro: “A *balteum* was a belt made of leather and studded with bosses; hence it was called *balteum*.”] A *balteus* is a military belt. It is so called because signs hang from it, to show the total number of a military legion, namely six thousand six hundred men, of which number they themselves consist. [Note: [Col. 0703C] “Hence *balteus* … hang.” From Servius, *Aeneid* V.] Thus *balteus* refers not only to what is girded but also to that from which weapons hang.

3. *Zona* is a Greek word; the Greeks call it ζωνάριον, “little belt,” while we call it *cingulum*, “belt.”

A *strophium* is a golden, gemmed belt, concerning which Cinna writes: “With a *strophium* encircling her swelling breasts.” [Note: [Col. 0703C] “*Lactentes*, ‘swelling.’” Other copies have *luctantes*, “struggling.”] Prudentius likewise writes: “This name of the gem has been bound to the *strophium*.” [Note: [Col. 0703C] The same occurs in Prudentius, *On the Crowns*, hymn 4. Tertullian uses *strophium* for a head ornament at the end of *On the Crown of the Soldier*: “Why do you condemn the headband or serpent-shaped ornament destined for a diadem?”]

4. [Note: [Col. 0703C] *Limus*. Above, chapter 22.] A *limus* is the garment worn by public slaves. It is called *limus* because it has transverse purple stripes, that is, *limae*.

[Note: [Col. 0703C] *Caltulum*. All the Gothic copies have this form except one from Salamanca, which has *catulum*. We reject neither form. Plautus, in *Epidicus*:

“An indusiate, bordered *caltula*, or saffron-colored garment.”

The same words are cited by Varro, Book IV. But concerning *catulus*, Festus says: “*Catulus* is a kind of fastening, sometimes called a dog”; and Plautus: “So that you may recline with an iron *catulus*.”] *Caltulum* is a type of belt, named from a leather strap that has been compressed.

[Col. 0703B] [Note: [Col. 0703D] *Fibula* is Greek. In place of θλίβειν, “to press,” the Aeolians said φλίβειν.] *Fibula* is Greek; the Greeks call it φιβλήν, because it fastens.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] *Suffibulum*. *Subligabulum*. I would prefer to read these separately, without interpretation, as they occur in certain books, rather than take one as a gloss on the other. Some have conjectured this from Varro’s words, Book V: “No one may enter except Vestal Virgins and the public priest. When he goes, let him not have a *suffibulum*.” It is said to have been written, as *subligaculum*, from *suffire*, “to blow beneath.” See Festus.] *Suffibulum*, *subligaculum*.

5. [Note: [Col. 0703D] *Redimiculum*. The entire passage is taken from John Cassian, *On the Institutes of Monastic Life*, chapter 6.] A *redimiculum* is what we call a *succinctorium*, or *brachile*. Descending through the neck and divided at the sides of the neck, it surrounds the hollows of both armpits and girds them on either side, so that, by constricting the breadth of the garments, it draws them toward the body and joins and arranges them. It is commonly called *brachile*, as though *brachiale*, [Note: [Col. 0704C] “Although now it is not a belt of the arms but of the kidneys.” Monks who follow the rule of Saint Bernard now wear these doubled woolen straps.] although nowadays the belt is not for the arms but for the loins. It is called *succinctorium* because, as stated, it is drawn beneath the arms, surrounds the hollows of the armpits, and girds them on either side.

6. [Note: [Col. 0704C] *Fascia* is … “is tightened.” From Jerome, Letter 47, concerning the avoidance of suspicious cohabitation.] A *fascia* is used to cover the breast and compress the nipples, while the breast is made narrower by a tightening, crimped belt. It is called *fascia* because it binds the body in the manner of a bundle. Hence also come the little bandages with which wounds are bound.

[Col. 0704A] 7. A *vitta* is so called because by it the breast is bound like a vine that clings.

[Note: [Col. 0704C] *Limbus*. From Servius, *Aeneid* IV.] A *limbus* is what we call an ornamental border.

8. A *fasciola* is a border that surrounds the edge of garments or cloaks, woven either from threads or from gold and sewn onto the outside at the garment’s or cloak’s edge. Concerning it Virgil writes:

“Having surrounded the Sidonian cloak with a patterned border.”

**CHAPTER XXXIV. On footwear**

1. Shoemakers are so called because, inserting pig bristles as thread, they stitch—that is, sew—almost as though they were called *setores*.

2. A *caligarius*, “shoemaker,” is named not from the callus of the feet but from *calus*, that is, “wood,” without which footwear cannot be sewn. [Note: [Col. 0704C] “Which the Greeks call *calopodia*.” Other copies have *calopodion*. Both are correct. The Latins call them *formae*. Horace: “If you do not know lasts and forms, you are no shoemaker.” Acron likewise interprets *formae* by the Greek word καλόποδια.] The Greeks call these καλόποδας. They were formerly made only from willow; hence footwear is also called *calceamenta*, either because it is made on a *calus*, that is, on wood, or because it is fitted to the foot.

3. [Note: [Col. 0704C] “The Greeks used *crepidae*.” The word itself is Greek. Aulus Gellius, Book XIII, chapter 21: “Almost all footwear of this kind, in which only the soles of the feet are covered underneath while the rest is nearly bare and joined by smooth straps, they called *soleae*; sometimes, using the Greek term, *crepidulae*.”] The Greeks were the first to use *crepidae*. It is a type of footwear with a single form, suitable for either foot, right or left. *Crepidae* are so called either because they are fastened with a noise, or from the sound made by the feet while walking.

4. [Note: [Col. 0704C] “Kings used shoes.” Perhaps *auratis* or *gemmatis*, “gilded” or “gemmed,” is missing. We know that Gothic kings and certain emperors used such footwear. Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 2, concerning Caligula: “Above all his feminine luxuries, he wore slippers covered with pearls.” Lampridius, concerning Heliogabalus: “He had gems in his shoes, and indeed engraved gems, which provoked everyone’s laughter, as though the work of noble craftsmen could be seen in gems attached to the feet.”] Kings and Caesars used shoes.

Their form was as follows:

Romulus invented the patrician shoe with four straps and a sewn-on crescent. Only patricians used it. The crescent on them did not signify the shape of a heavenly body but the mark of the number one hundred, because at the beginning there were one hundred patrician senators.

[Col. 0704C] 5. [Note: [Col. 0704D] *Ocreae*, because they cover the leg. Varro: “*Ocrea*, because it was placed against the leg.” Festus gives a very different explanation from Ateius Philologus: “The ancients called a rugged mountain *ocris*; from this *ocreae* were named, because they are unevenly swollen.”] *Ocreae* are footwear covering the shins, so called because they cover the legs.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] *Cothurnus*. As Servius says, *Aeneid* I, *cothurnus* is also a type of hunting shoe, by which the calf is likewise bound, and it fits either foot. For this reason Maro used the singular:

“And bind the calves high with the purple cothurnus.”] *Cothurni* are worn by tragedians who were to speak in the theater and sing their verses in a high, resounding voice. It is a type of footwear resembling a *crepida*, used by heroes, but fashioned so that it fits either the right or the left foot.

6. [Note: [Col. 0705B] *Baxeae* were the footwear of comic actors. Tertullian: “If a philosopher may wear purple, why may he not also wear Tyrian *baxae*, unless gold is entirely unsuitable to Greek ways?” Apuleius, Book II of *The Ass*: “Dressed in palm-leaf *baxae*.”] *Baxeae* were the footwear of comic actors, just as *cothurni* were that of tragedians. Some also call them *calones*, because they were made from willow. For, as we said, the Greeks called wood κᾶλον.

7. *Talares* are slipper-like shoes, apparently so named because they are shaped to touch the ankle, just as *subtolares* are so called because they are beneath the ankle, as though *subtalares*.

8. [Note: [Col. 0705B] *Obstrigilli*. Pliny calls the straps of shoes *obstragula*, Book IX, chapter 35, concerning pearls: “They add them to the feet—not only to the straps of sandals but also to entire slippers.”] *Obstrigilli* are sewn across the soles, and a strap is drawn across the upper part so that they may be tightened; hence their name.

9. I think *ossae* were originally made from bone, and although they are now made from another material, they retain their original name.

[Col. 0705B] 10. [Note: [Col. 0705B] *Mullei*. See Festus.] *Mullei* resemble *cothurni* in having a high sole; in the upper part, however, they have little bone or bronze hammers to which the straps were tied. [Note: [Col. 0705B] “They are named from their red color, like that of the fish called the *mullus*. Unless rather the fish received its name from the shoes. Pliny, Book IX, chapter 17: “Fenestella thinks they received their name from the color of the *mullei* footwear.”] They are named from their red color, like that of the fish called the *mullus*.

11. [Note: [Col. 0705C] *Soleae*. See the passage from Aulus Gellius cited above under *crepidae*.] *Soleae* are shoes that cover only the soles of the feet, named from the sole of the foot. There are also *soleae materiales*, [Note: [Col. 0705C] “*Soleae materiales*.” Pliny would have said *materiariae*, as in Book VII, chapter 56.] “wooden sandals,” made of wood covered with leather.

12. *Socci*, whose diminutive is *socelli*, are so called because they have a sack into which part of the sole is inserted.

*Caliculae* … [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0706B] *Caligulae*. Other copies have *galigulae*.] *Caligae* are named either from the callus of the feet or because they are tied. For *socci* are not tied but merely slipped on.

13. [Note: [Col. 0706B] *Cernui*. Festus: “*Cernuus* is a type of footwear.” Perhaps Lucilius’s verse, cited by Nonius, may be referred to here:

“Immediately, stooping, he covers his honorable soles.”

Yet it may also be understood as “inclining,” as Nonius wishes.] *Cernui* are slippers without a sole.

*Lingulati*, [Note: [Col. 0706B] “Which we call *folleati*.” Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium: “Among them everything is affected: loose sleeves, baggy leggings, and thicker clothing.” A little earlier: “All their concern is with clothing—whether it smells good, whether the foot does not bulge through loose leather.”] which we call *foliati*.

*Clavati*, as though *chalybati*, “steel-studded,” are fastened to the sole of the *caligae* with small nails, that is, pointed studs. [Note: [Col. 0706B] “Only to the soles of the *caligae*.” Thus one manuscript. There is mention of shoemaker’s nails. Pliny, Book IX, chapter 17.]

[Note: [Col. 0706B] *Perones*. Servius, *Aeneid* VII: “*Perones* are rustic footwear.” See Festus, under *mullei*.] *Perones* and [Note: [Col. 0706C] *Sculponeae*. Cato, *On Agriculture*: “It is proper to provide good *sculponeae* every other year.” See also Nonius.] *sculponeae* are rustic footwear.

[Col. 0706B] *Baxeae* are women’s footwear.

*Corrigiae*, “straps,” are named either from leather (*corium*) or from tying, as though *colligiae*.

**BOOK XX. ON PROVISIONS AND DOMESTIC AND RUSTIC IMPLEMENTS**

[Col. 0705]

483 **CHAPTER I. On tables**

[Col. 0705C]

1. Daedalus was the first to make a table and a chair. [Note: [Col. 0705D] “The equipment of the kitchen: Apicius.” Seneca, *To his mother Helvia*, chapter 10, speaks of him.] A certain Apicius was the first to devise kitchen equipment; after squandering his property on it, he perished by voluntary death—and deservedly, because one who serves gluttony and voracity destroys both soul and body. The word *mensa*, “table,” is derived from eating and feasting. For it has no other use.

2. [Note: [Col. 0705D] *Torus*, from twisted herbs. From Servius, *Aeneid* II.] A *torus* is so called from twisted herbs, which are placed beneath the shoulders of those reclining.

484 [Note: [Col. 0705D] *Stibadium* is said to derive from *stipites* (“trunks”), against which diners reclined. The books of better quality, however, have *stipibus* (“stumps”).] The word *stibadium* is derived from *stipites*, as though *stipadium*; for this is how it was first begun. *Accubitum* (“reclining place”) is named from eating, as though *ad cibatum* (“for food”). [Note: [Col. 0706D] As though *ad cibitum*. Others read *ad cubitum* (“at the elbow”) or *ad cibatum* (“for food”).]

### 3. [Note: [Col. 0706D] *Convivium* among the Greeks. From Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book I.] 

Among the Greeks, *convivium* (“banquet”) comes from drinking together, *συμπόσιον* (*symposion*). Among us, however, it is more correctly called from *convictus* (“living together”), or because it involves conversation about life. Likewise, *convivium* comes from the multitude of those eating together; for a private meal is merely sustenance, not a banquet. There are three aspects of a banquet: reclining, eating, and drinking. Reclining, as in:

> “I was ordered to recline on embroidered couches.”

Eating and drinking, as in:

> After the first rest from the feast and the tables had been removed,  
> they set up great mixing bowls and crown the wine.

## CHAPTER II. On Foods

[Col. 0706D]

### 1.

*Cibus* (“food”) is so called because it is taken by the mouth; likewise *esca* (“food”), because the mouth takes it.

What properly retains life is called *victus* (“nourishment”); hence *ad cibum vocare* (“to call to food”) also means *invitare* (“to invite”).

### 2.

*Alimonia* (“nourishment”) is so called because by its expense the body is nourished. The young receive it for growth, the old for endurance. For the flesh cannot persist unless it is strengthened by nourishment. *Alimentum* (“nourishment”) is what nourishes us. [Note: [Col. 0707C] *Alimonium* is the care of nourishing. Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 8: “Where nature is moist, the vine must be raised higher, because in bearing and nourishment wine, unlike in a cup, seeks not water but the sun.”]

### 3.

*Affluentia* (“abundance”) is so called as the outpouring of something excessively overflowing, beyond what is enough, without any limit.

### 4.

*Opulentia* (“wealth”) is derived from *ops* (“resources”); if you examine it, you will find that it observes moderation. For how can something that is excessive be helpful, when it is often more harmful than too little?

### 5.

*Epulae* (“feasts”) are named from the abundance of provisions. Simple feasts, however, are divided into two necessities, bread and wine, and two superfluities, those things sought from land and sea for the sake of eating.

485 ### 6. [Note: [Col. 0707C] *Dapes* are the meals of kings. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book I, on the verse “who with banquets.”] 

*Dapes* (“banquets”) belong to kings, whereas *epulae* belong to private persons.

[Col. 0707B] *Deliciae* (“delicacies”) are so called because people take pleasure in them and desire them agreeably.

### 7.

*Pulmentum* (“relish” or “accompaniment”) is named from *puls* (“porridge”); whether only porridge, or something else mixed with it, is consumed, it is properly called *pulmentum*.

### 8.

*Satietas* (“satisfaction”) and *saturitas* (“fullness”) differ from one another. *Satietas* can be said of a single food, meaning that there is enough; *saturitas*, however, takes its name from *satura*, which is composed of a varied arrangement of foods. [Note: [Col. 0707D] *Saturitas* is derived from *satura*. See Festus under *Satura*.]

### 9.

*Crapula* (“gluttony”) is immoderate voraciousness, as though *cruda epula* (“raw food”), whose rawness weighs down the heart and makes the stomach incapable of digestion. Immoderate voraciousness is indeed a vice, but health consists in as much food as is sufficient for sustenance and for nature.

[Col. 0707C] ### 10. [Note: [Col. 0707D] *Jantaculum*. Thus the better books, and Festus under *Silatum*. Likewise in the manuscript of Paul the Abbreviator, not *jentaculum* as in the printed editions.]

*Jantaculum* (“breakfast”) is the first food by which the fast is broken, and hence it receives its name. Nigidius says:

> We ourselves pollute our fasts with light breakfasts.

### 11.

*Prandium* (“midday meal”) is named from the preparation for eating. Properly, however, the ancients called the meal of all soldiers before battle *prandium*; hence the saying of the commander:

> Let us dine as though we were to sup among the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Hence the saying of the commander—Leonidas, commander of the Spartans, in Justin and Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I.]

### 12. [Note: [Col. 0707D] *Merenda* is food, as though “food that is taken.” Nonius: “*Merenda*: food given after midday.” Glossary: *merenda*, *ἄριστον δειλινόν* (“late-day meal”). Calpurnius: “When the late hour of the afternoon meal has come.”]

*Merenda* (“afternoon meal”) is food taken as the day declines, as though food to be eaten after midday, and is near to supper. Hence some also call it *antecoenia* (“before-supper meal”). [Note: [Col. 0707D] Likewise *merendare* (“to take an afternoon meal”), as though “to eat at midday.”]

Likewise, *merendare* means “to eat at midday.”

### 13. [Note: [Col. 0707D] *Annona* is derived from the time, etc. Suidas is no better under the word *Νόνναι*: “They seem also to have arisen from the *Nonae*, as though being distributed on the Nones.”]

*Annona* (“provisions”) is derived from the time when the ancient Romans were summoned to meals, as Martial writes:

> The Ninth commands that the lofty couches be broken,

which the Persians still do to this day.

### 14.

*Coena* (“supper”) is so called from the fellowship of those eating, for the Greeks call what is common *κοινόν* (*koinon*). Hence also *communicantes* (“sharing together”), because they meet communally, that is, together. [Note: [Col. 0707D] Among the ancients it was customary to eat in public and to feast communally. Valerius, book II, chapter 1, and Macrobius, book II, chapter 17.]

Among the ancients it was customary to eat in public and to feast together, so that individuality would not generate luxury. *Coena* is an evening meal, which the ancients called *vesperna*. [Note: [Col. 0707D] The ancients called *vesperna* what we now call *coena*. Festus: “Among the ancients *coena* was what is now *prandium*; *vesperna* is what we now call *coena*.” Likewise under *Vesperna*: “In Plautus, *vesperna* means supper.”] [Note: [Col. 0708C] For midday meals were not customary. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book IV, on the verse “Now, as the day declines, she seeks the same banquets.”] Midday meals were not customary.

### 15.

*Panis* (“bread”) is so called either because it is set down with food, or because every animal desires it: for in Greek *πᾶν* (*pan*) means “everything.”

*Cibarius* is bread given to slaves for food, and is not delicate. [Note: [Col. 0708D] *Fermentatius*. Thus most Gothic manuscripts, as also *clibanitius* and *focatius*.] *Fermentatius* is made with leaven. *Azymus* is unleavened. For *ἄζυμος* (*azymos*) means “without leaven,” “pure.” *Acrozymus* is lightly leavened, as though *acroazymus*.

*Siligineus* bread is named from a kind of grain. *Siligo* is a type of wheat. [Note: [Col. 0708D] *Rubidus*: baked again and reddened. Festus: “In Plautus, bread is called *rubidus* when insufficiently baked,” though the passage from *Casina* cited by him rather supports Isidore.] *Rubidus* is baked again and reddened. *Subcineritius* is baked in ashes and turned over again. [Note: [Col. 0708D] It is also *focatius*. In common speech, *hogaza*.] It is also called *focatius*. *Clibanitius* is baked in a baking vessel.

### 16. [Note: [Col. 0708D] *Spongia*: bread kneaded in water for a longer time. This is also found in the better books, and the word *malaxare* (“to knead”) is cited by Zanchius from Varro.]

*Spongia* is bread kneaded for a long time in water. It receives a small amount of fine flour and a small amount of leaven, and contains more moisture than any other bread. Hence it received the name *spongia* (“sponge”).

[Col. 0708C] ### 17.

*Placentae* (“cakes”) are made from *far* (“spelt”); some call them *liba*, because they please and are pleasing.

*Laganum* is broad and thin bread, first fried in water and afterward in oil.

### 18. [Note: [Col. 0708D] *Dulcia*. Others read *dulciamina*, not without merit. Jerome, *Life of Saint Pachomius*: “As he distributes sweetmeats to the brothers going out before the doors of the banquet, let him meditate, in the act of giving, on something from Scripture.” Hence *dulciarii*. In the Glossary: *γλυκεροπράκτης* (*glyceropractes*), “seller of sweets”; and *πλακουντάριος* (*plakountarios*), “maker of cakes, seller of sweets.”]

*Dulcia* (“sweetmeats”) are kinds of baked pastry, named from their taste. They are eaten with honey sprinkled over them.

[Note: [Col. 0708D] *Crusta* is the surface of bread. On *crustum* and *crusta*, see Servius, *Commentary on the Georgics*, book III, and *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book VII, and Varro, book IV. Here we have retained only what we found in the older books.] *Crusta* (“crust”) is the surface of bread. It is also called *fragmenta* (“fragments”), because it is divided, as something broken.

[Col. 0709A] *Simila* … [lacuna]

### 19.

*Amolum* is the finest flour of meal, expelled from the mill because of its lightness; hence its name, as though derived from *mola* (“mill”).

*Farina* (“flour”) and *furfures* (“bran”) are named from *far* (“spelt”), whose waste products they are.

*Pollis* … [lacuna]

*Fermentum* (“leaven”) is named from *fervere* (“to boil”), because it cannot be contained for more than one hour. By increasing, it overflows.

### 20.

*Carnes* (“meat”) are so called because they are dear, or from *creare* (“to create”); hence the Greeks call meat *κρέας* (*kreas*).

[Note: [Col. 0709C] *Crudum* (“raw”) because it is bloody. Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book X: “Let him drive the sword through the ribs, raw”—that is, “cruel, bloody.”] *Crudum* is bloody, for it is accompanied by blood.

### 21.

*Coctum* (“cooked”) is as though *coactum* (“forced”), that is, driven by fire and water in a violent manner and made suitable for eating. [Col. 0709B] [Note: [Col. 0709C] Something cooked for a long time is also called *coctum*. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book XI, on “accustomed to knots and hardened by fire.”] Something cooked for a long time is also called *coctum*.

### 22. [Note: [Col. 0709C] *Assum* (“roasted”), as though *arsum* (“burned”). Correct, although Varro prefers the explanation that *assum* is named from becoming dry through fire.]

*Assum* is so called because it burns, as though *arsum*.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] *Elixum* (“boiled”). *Lixa* means water. Nonius: “*Elixum* is anything softened in water, for the ancients called water *lixa*. ”] *Elixum* is so called because it is boiled in water alone. *Lixa* means water, from its being loosened; hence *solutio* (“release”) is also used for sexual indulgence, and limbs moved out of place are called *luxa* (“dislocated”).

### 23.

*Frixum* (“fried”) is named from the sound made when it burns in oil.

*Salsum* (“salted”) is as though “sprinkled with salt,” with three syllables removed from the middle.

*Rancidum* (“rancid”) is named from its defect, because it makes things harsh-voiced.

### 24.

*Succidia* are meats stored for use, named from *succidere* (“to cut down”).

[Note: [Col. 0709D] *Lardum* (“bacon”), because it is preserved by being stored in the house. But Macrobius, book VII, chapter 8: “I think we call it *lardum* as though *longe aridum* (‘very dry’).”] *Lardum* is so called because it is stored and preserved in the house. For the ancients called houses *lares*.

[Col. 0709C] [Note: [Col. 0709D] *Taxea*. Hence perhaps our words *tocino* and also *tassaio*.] *Taxea* is the Gallic word for bacon. Hence Afranius, in *The Rose*:

> A Gaul in a sagum, fed on rich bacon.

### 25.

*Axungia* (“lard”) is named from *ungere* (“to anoint”).

*Sebum* (“tallow”) is named from *sus* (“pig”), as though *suebum*, because this animal has more fat.

### 26. [Note: [Col. 0709D] *Offa* …, with the diminutive *ofella*. Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book VI: “A morsel steeped in honey and in medicated grain.” Hence the diminutive *ofella*; but the *f* is not doubled, for diminutives often change many things.]

*Offa* is properly a morsel for the teeth; its diminutive is *ofella*. Hence *offarii* (“offa-cooks”) are cooks who prepare food bit by bit, that is, *offatim*.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Now *offa* is used of barking animals. In the glosses of Placidus: “*Offa* is what barking animals receive”; its diminutive is *offella*, which, if thrown into a dog’s mouth, immediately satisfies it, causing it to stop and become silent.] Now *offa* is used of barking animals, because if it is thrown into a dog’s mouth, the dog is immediately satisfied, stops, and becomes silent.

489 ### 27.

*Frustum* (“piece”) is so called because it is taken from the *frumen*. For the *frumen* is the uppermost part of the throat.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] *Pulpa* (“flesh”) is so called because it was eaten mixed with porridge. Pliny, book XVII, chapter 8, says that it is evident that the Romans lived for a long time without bread, on porridge; hence dishes are still called *pulmentaria*.] *Pulpa* is so called because it was formerly eaten mixed with porridge; hence it is also called *pulmentum* and *pulmentarium*.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] *Pulpa* is flesh without fat … sticky. From the same work, above, book XI, chapter 1.] *Pulpa* is flesh without fat. It is so called because it throbs, for it often springs back. Many call it *viscum* (“birdlime”), because it is sticky.

### 28.

*Lucanicae* (“sausages”) are so called because they were first made in Lucania.

*Farcimen* (“sausage filling”) is chopped and minced meat with which the intestine is stuffed, that is, filled, together with a mixture of other things.

### 29. [Note: [Col. 0710C] *Minutal*. Juvenal, satire 14: “He was accustomed to save yesterday’s *minutal* for mid-September.”]

*Minutal* is so called because it is made from fish, *isicia* (forcemeat), and vegetables chopped into small pieces.

[Note: [Col. 0710C] *Afratum*. Others read *Afrotum*. *Africia* also occurs in Arnobius, book VII. It seems to be a kind of cake, or at any rate a kind of porridge.] *Afratum*, which is called *spumeum* (“foamy”) in Latin; for in Greek *ἄφρος* (*aphros*) means “foam.”

[Note: [Col. 0710D] *Martisia*. From this passage, I think, a certain Alphonsus of Palencia included *Martifrium* in his lexicon; how much authority should be granted him, others may judge. It is certain that he copied many things from Isidore. Thus he says: “*Martifrium* is a kind of condiment made from fish.” Someone might therefore think *Martyphrium* to be a Greek word, for *ἀφρύη* (*aphrye*) is a small fish mentioned by Athenaeus, book VII.] *Martisia* is made from fish in a mortar, and is named accordingly.

### 30. [Note: [Col. 0710D] *Isocen* … *Isicia*. Arnobius, book VII: “What do these things mean, I shall explain: *isicia*, *silicernium*, *longano*? These are names and kinds of sausages, some made from goat’s blood, others stuffed into lungs with a mixture.”]

They call a certain fish *isocen*, from which *isicia* were first made. Although they are now made from another kind of fish, the name of the original fish nevertheless gave the dish its beginning.

### 31.

*Galaticae* (“Galatian cakes”) are named from their milky color. For the Greeks call milk *γάλα* (*gala*).

490 *Sphaera* (“sphere”) is named by a Greek word from its roundness. Whatever is formed into a round shape is called *σφαῖρα* (*sphaira*) by the Greeks.

### 32.

The masters of the kitchen called *jus* (“sauce” or “broth”) by that name because it is the law of its seasoning. The Greeks call it *ζωμός* (*zomos*).

[Col. 0710C] ### 33.

*Caseus* (“cheese”) is so called because it lacks whey, as though *careus*. For all the whey is drawn off from it, [Note: [Col. 0710D] So that this may be demonstrated by weighing it: no whey remains.] so that this may be demonstrated by weighing it.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] *Colostrum* is new milk. Servius, *Eclogue* 2: “It is praiseworthy that someone has new milk, that is, *colostrum*, which is neuter in gender.”] *Colostrum* is new milk, a neuter noun.

### 34.

*Lac* (“milk”) is derived from a Greek expression referring to whiteness. For the Greeks call white *λευκόν* (*leukon*). Milk and blood are both what nourishes and what is nourished: we are nourished by milk and live by blood. [Note: [Col. 0710D] “We are nourished by milk and live by blood.” The same author, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book III: “And we consign the soul to the tomb.” The body is nourished by milk after the union with the soul, and the soul is never without blood.]

[Col. 0711A] ### 35.

*Quactum* (“curdled”) is as though *coactum* (“congealed”) and as though coagulated. Once another substance has been received, it coagulates together with it.

### 36.

*Mel* (“honey”) is a word of Greek origin, and is evidently named from bees. For the bee is called *μέλισσα* (*melissa*) in Greek. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Formerly honey was thought to come from dew. From the same author, at the beginning of the *Georgics*, book IV.] Formerly, however, honey was thought to come from dew, and it was found on the leaves of reeds, whence Virgil writes:

> Immediately, the heavenly gifts of airy honey.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] This is still gathered in India. From Dioscorides, book II.] Indeed, it is still gathered in India and Arabia, clinging to branches in the likeness of salt. All honey is called sweet. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Sardinian honey, however, is bitter. From the same source.] Sardinian honey is bitter because of wormwood, in abundance of which the bees of that region are nourished.

### 37.

*Favus* (“honeycomb”) is so called because it is eaten more than it is drunk: for the Greeks call eating *φαγεῖν* (*phagein*).

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Physicians say that it is beneficial … From Jerome, letter 10, to Furia, *On Preserving Virginity*.]

Physicians, and those who have written about the nature of human bodies—especially Galen, in the books entitled *περὶ ὑγὶας puerorum et juvenum, ac perfectae aetatis virorum mulierumque* (“On the health of children and young people, and of men and women of full age”)”—say that the bodies of children and young people, and of men and women in the prime of life, burn with an inborn heat. Foods that increase heat are harmful to people of these ages, while cold foods are conducive to health when taken as nourishment. The opposite is true of the elderly, who suffer from phlegm and cold: hot foods and old wines benefit them.

## CHAPTER III. On Drink

### 1.

*Potio* (“drink”) is named by derivation from Greek. For the Greeks call it *πότον* (*poton*).

[Note: [Col. 0711D] *Aqua* … because its surface is level. Varro likewise says: “*Aqua*, because its top is even.”] *Aqua* (“water”) is so called generally because its surface is level; hence also *aequora* (“level waters”). We call it *recent* (“fresh”), because, unlike wine, old water is not useful; it is to be drawn at once from a river, spring, or well, for old water becomes foul.

### 2.

*Vinum* (“wine”) is so called because drinking it quickly fills the veins with blood. Others call it *Lyaeus* (“Liberating”), because it releases us from care. The ancients called wine *venenum* (“poison”). But after the poisonous juice that causes death was discovered, wine was called *vinum*, and that poisonous juice *venenum*. Hence Jerome, in the book he wrote *On Preserving Virginity*, said that young women ought to flee wine as poison, lest, by drinking it in the fervor of their age, they drink and perish.

Hence among the ancient Romans women did not use wine except on certain days for the sake of religious rites. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Among the ancient Romans … on certain days. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book I, on the verse “And, having poured a libation, she touched it only with the tips of her lips.”]

### 3.

We use *merum* (“pure wine”) when we mean unmixed wine. For we call anything pure and unadulterated *merum*, including pure water, entirely unmixed with anything.

Hence also *merenda* (“afternoon meal”), because in ancient times bread alone was given at that hour to working children, or because they ate at midday at the same time—*meridies*—that is, alone and separately, not as at breakfast or supper, at one common table. From this we also believe that the period after midday is called *meridies* (“midday”), because it is pure. [Note: [Col. 0711D] That *meridies* is so called … because it is pure. The same author, above, book III, chapter 41; book V, chapter 30; and book XIII, chapter 1.]

### 4.

*Mustum* (“must”) is wine immediately drawn from the vat. It is believed to be called *mustum* because it contains mud and earth mixed within it. [Note: [Col. 0711D] For *mus* means earth. Likewise in book XII, chapter 3.] *Mus* means earth, whence also *humus* (“soil”). Its force of fermentation is so great that, if vessels—even large ones—are filled with it and left without a vent, it immediately bursts them.

### 5. [Note: [Col. 0711D] *Roseum*. Our people call it *rosete*.]

*Roseum* wine is wine with redness. For a rose is red.

[Col. 0712B] [Note: [Col. 0711D] *Amineum* … is white. From Servius, *Commentary on the Georgics*, book II, on the verse “There are also Aminean vines.”] *Amineum* is as though “without minium,” that is, without redness, for it is white.

*Succinatium* resembles the gemstone amber, that is, it is tawny in color.

### 6.

*Limpidum* wine is clear, that is, transparent; it is named from the appearance of water, as though *lymphidum*. For *lympha* means water.

*Turbidum* is as though *terbidum*, that is, mixed with earth; it is wine containing sediment.

*Falernum* wine is named from the Falernian region of Campania, where the finest wines are produced.

493 ### 7. [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Colatum* is properly a vessel. Servius, *Commentary on the Georgics*, book II, on “You, with thick wicker, the strainers”; and *Commentary on the Georgics*, book II, on “the wine strainers”: “Strainers through which wine flows, themselves also named from straining.”]

*Colatum* is the name given to a vessel in which wine is carried.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] *Gazetum*. Sidonius Apollinaris: “The wines I have are not Gazetan, Chian, or Falernian.”] *Gazetum* is named from the region from which it is transported. Gaza is a town of Palestine.

[Col. 0712C] [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Infertum*. All books have this reading. But a very learned man read *inferium*, a word mentioned by Festus, Arnobius, book VII, and Cato, chapter 34. On *ferctum* or *fertum*, see above, book VI, chapter 19.] Wine is called *infertum* when it is poured out and offered on an altar.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] *Spurcum* (“impure”), because it may not be offered. From Festus.] *Spurcum* is wine that may not be offered, or wine to which water has been added, as though *spurium*, that is, impure.

### 8. [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Honorarium*. Cicero also mentions *honorarium* grain in the *In Pisonem*.]

*Honorarium* wine is offered to kings and powerful men as a mark of honor. Cato, *On His Own Innocence*: “When I was serving as a legate in the province, many people gave honorific wine to praetors and consuls; I never accepted it, not even as a private citizen.”

### 9. [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Crucium* wine. Festus: “*Crucium*, because it torments; hence Lucilius called unpleasant wine *crucium*.”]

*Crucium* wine is unpleasant wine, which slaves drink.

*Acetum* (“vinegar”) is so called either because it is sharp, or because it is watery. Wine mixed with water quickly changes into this taste. Hence also *acidum* (“acid”), as though *aquidum* (“watery”). [Note: [Col. 0712D] And *acidum*, as though *aquidum*. Chacon thought that what follows in the printed editions was an interpretation of *lorea*, whose explanation is left bare somewhat later; we have agreed with him.]

[Col. 0712D] *Conditum* (“spiced wine”) is so called because it is not simple but composed by mixing spices.

### 10. [Note: [Col. 0713C] *Lactatum* is a drink made from milk. Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 2, says that moray eels grow fat on *lactatum*.]

*Lactatum* is a drink made from milk.

*Mulsum* is mixed with honey. It is a drink made from water and honey, which the Greeks call *μελίκρατον* (*melikraton*).

### 11. [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Oenomelum*. See Palladius under October.]

*Oenomelum* is must mixed with honey and vigorously shaken and stirred.

*Hydromelum* is made from water and Matian apples.

494 [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Saccatum* is a liquid of water mixed with wine sediment, expressed through a sack. Some think that two kinds of wine have been confused here and therefore read: “*Saccatum*, expressed through a sack. *Faecatum*, a liquid of water mixed with wine sediment.” For they deny that water is mixed with *saccatum*, and Cato and Pliny mention *faecatum*.] *Saccatum* is a liquid of water mixed with wine sediment and expressed through a sack.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] *Lorea*. It is a cheap drink suitable for slaves, because the grapes are washed with water in the winepress after the wine has been expressed. Chacon thought that this lacuna should be filled with these words, borrowed from elsewhere.] *Lorea* … [lacuna]

### 12.

*Oxymeli* is so called because it is made by mixing vinegar and honey; hence it retains both sweetness and sourness.

*Rhodomeli* is so called because honey is mixed into rose juice.

[Col. 0713B] *Melicratum* is wine mixed with honey.

### 13.

*Medus* is as though *melus*, because it is made from honey, just as *calamitas* is used for *cadamitas*.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] *Faecula* … useful for the stomach. Horace, book II of the *Satires*, satire 8:

> Such things as refresh an exhausted  
> stomach—skirret, fish-sauce, Coan sediment …]

*Faecula* is a rich grape, boiled down to the thickness of honey and, once cooled, useful for the stomach.

### 14. [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Passum*. From Palladius, under October, chapter 19.]

*Passum* is whatever flows out when dried grapes are pressed. It is called *passum* from *patior* (“to undergo”), because the drier grape is beaten and boiled, and from it *passum* is made.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] *Defrutum*, *carenum*, *sapa*. From the same author, chapter 18. Isidore seems to have read “from *defraudare*” (“to cheat”) rather than “from *defervescere*” (“to boil down”).] *Defrutum* is so called because it is reduced, as though it “suffers fraud.”

### 15.

*Carenum* is so called because, by boiling, it becomes short of part of itself. When a third part of the must has been lost, what remains is *carenum*. Its opposite is *sapa*, which is reduced by boiling to a third.

### 16. [Note: [Col. 0714C] *Sicera* is every kind of drink. From Jerome, letter 2, to Nepotianus. Thus it is not ineptly read for “drunkenness” in Tertullian.]

*Sicera* is every drink other than wine that can intoxicate. Although its name is Hebrew, it nevertheless has a Latin sound, because it is made from the juice of grain or fruit, or because the fruit of palms is pressed into liquid; and when cooked grains are strained, a thicker water, like juice, is produced, and the drink itself is called *sicera*.

[Note: [Col. 0714C] “Thicker water,” as though juice is strained out. Jerome: “The thicker water is colored.”]

### 17. [Note: [Col. 0714D] *Cervisia* … *caelia*. A Hispanic word. Pliny, book XXII, at the end: “From the same things are made the drinks called *zethum* in Egypt, *caelia* and *ceria* in Spain, *cervisia* and many kinds in Gaul.”]

*Cervisia* is named from Ceres, that is, from grain. It is a drink made in various ways from grain seeds.

### 18.

*Caelia* is named from heating. It is a drink skillfully made from wheat juice. The fiery force of the soaked grain’s germ is awakened, then dried, reduced to flour, and mixed with a mild juice. Once this has fermented, a flavor of harshness and the heat of intoxication are added. It is made in those parts of Spain that are not fertile in wine.

*Faex* (“sediment”) is so called because, emerging from the vessels, it clings to them.

### 19.

*Garum* is a salty liquid made from fish. In former times it was prepared from a fish the Greeks called *γάρον* (*garon*); although it is now made from an unlimited variety of fish, it retains the original name from which it began.

### 20.

*Liquamen* (“fish sauce”) is so called because the little fish dissolved in brine liquefy the same fluid; this liquid is called *salsugo* (“salt liquor”) or *muria* (“brine”).

[Col. 0714B] Properly, *muria* is water mixed with salt and made, in taste, like the sea.

### 21.

*Succi* (“juices”) are so called because they are expressed through a sack, as with *ptisanae*.

*Ptisanae*, *zema*, and *opozema* are Greek words.

## CHAPTER IV. On Eating Vessels

### 1.

*Vas* (“vessel”) is named from *vesci* (“to eat”), because food is placed in it. Its diminutive is *vasculum*, as though *vesculum*.

### 2.

*Fictilia* (“earthenware”) are so called because they are made and shaped from earth. *Fingere* means “to make,” “form,” and “mold”; hence potters are also called *figuli*. A vessel is called *fictile* not in the sense of something fictitious, which is a lie, but something formed so as to exist and possess a shape. Hence the Apostle says:

> Does the thing molded say to the one who molds it, “Why have you made me this way?”

### 3. [Note: [Col. 0714D] Earthenware vessels on the island of Samos. From Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 12.]

Earthenware vessels are said first to have been invented on the island of Samos. They were made from clay and hardened by fire, and hence were called Samian vessels.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Later, the addition of red pigment was invented. Pliny: “It was the invention of Dibutades to add red pigment, or to shape clay from red pigment.”] Later, people invented the addition of red pigment and the shaping of vessels from red clay.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] That it was older. From the same source.] They say that the use of earthenware vessels was older than the casting of bronze or silver.

497 [Note: [Col. 0714D] Among the ancients … as for wine. Pliny: “Even earthenware vessels were devised for wine and for water.”] Among the ancients there were neither golden nor silver vessels, but earthenware ones: wine was kept in storage jars, water in amphorae, and water for baths in hydriae; the remaining vessels used by human beings were made either on a wheel or shaped by hand.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Amphorae for water. Thus Pollux, book X, chapter 5, and Hesychius. Hence the translator of the common edition rendered *κεράμιον* (*keramion*) as “amphora of water.” That wine was also stored in amphorae is widely known. Horace:

> You are sparing to remove from the storeroom  
> the amphora of the consul Bibulus, growing old.]

### 4.

Clay, once fired, takes the name *testa* (“potsherd” or “earthen vessel”), because while it was soft it becomes *testa*; it no longer shares the name of its former kind, because what it was, it is no longer.

### 5. [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Aretine vessels*. On these, see Martial, book XIV, epigram 98.]

*Aretina vasa* (“Aretine vessels”) are named from the Italian municipium of Arretium, where they are made; for they are red. Concerning them Sedulius writes:

> Because the red earthenware supplies the vegetable placed before us.

### 6.

Some think that Samian vessels take their name from the town of Samos in Greece. Others say that *samia* is a clay of Italy, obtained not far from Rome, [Note: [Col. 0715D] Which is called *samia*. Because he had mentioned the Samians shortly before, some substituted *Samnia* here. The Samnites lived not far from Rome.] and that it is called *samia*.

### 7.

*Caelata* (“chased”) vessels are silver or gold vessels with raised figures embossed inside or outside. They are named from *caelum*, a kind of tool that is commonly called a *cilio*. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Commonly called a *cilio*. Others read *cilicio*. We call it a *sinzel*.]

### 8. [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Chrysendeta*. Bayfius says: “Silver vessels fitted with golden plates.”]

*Chrysendeta* are gilded vessels; the word is Greek.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] *Anaglypha*. Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book V, on “rough with figures”: “That is, sculpted, *anaglypha*.”] *Anaglypha* are vessels sculpted in relief above the surface. For the Greeks call “upward” *ἄνω* (*ano*) and “sculpture” *γλυφή* (*glyphe*): that is, “sculpted upward.”

### 9. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Hence also *scutella*. And Martial’s *scutula*: “And light shallow dishes and hollow platters.”]

*Discus* (“dish”) was formerly called *iscus*, from its resemblance to a shield; hence also *scutella* (“small shield,” or small dish). Later it was called *discus* because it gives food, that is, sets it down. Hence those reclining at table are called *discumbentes*, or from the Greek *ἀπὸ τοῦ δίκειν* (“from throwing”), that is, because they throw or cast.

### 10. [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Messorium*. *Missorium*. Collected from the Oviedo manuscript.]

*Messorium* is so called by derivation from *mensa* (“table”), as though *mensorium*.

498 *Parapsis* is a quadrangular, four-sided vessel, that is, one with equal sides.

[Col. 0715C] *Patina* (“dish”) is so called because it has broad and open mouths, like platters.

### 11. [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Gabata*. Martial:

> Dishes rush past, and platters fly.]

*Gabata* is as though *cavata* (“hollowed”), with the letter *g* substituted for *c*. Hence also *concha* (“shell”); the former is hollowed, the latter concave. The Greeks likewise call these vessels by this name.

*Scutella* is derived from *scutum* (“shield”) by diminutive formation, for it resembles a shield.

### 12. [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Apophoreta*. It appears that not only gifts or leftovers carried away from banquets, but also vessels, were called *apophoreta*.]

*Apophoreta* are named by the Greeks from carrying away fruit or something else; the vessel is flat.

*Salinum* is a vessel suited to such things. [Note: [Col. 0716C] It is also called *sulzica*. We have found no other trace of this word.] It is also called *sulzica*, as though *salzica*.

*Acetabulum* (“vinegar vessel”) is as though *acetaferum*, because it holds vinegar. Also:

> Amphorae have learned to drink smoke,

under the consul Tullus.

### 13. [Note: [Col. 0716D] An ancient distich. Martial, book III, epigram 121.]

*Cochlear* (“spoon”) was first named from its use with snails. Hence the ancient couplet:

> I am useful for snails, and no less useful for eggs.  
> Do you know why I am rather called a *cochleare*?

### 14. [Note: [Col. 0716D] *Trisceles*. Greek *Τρισκελεῖς*.]

*Trisceles* is Greek; in Latin, *tripedes* (“three-footed”). Those that stand on four feet are improperly called by the same name.

### 15.

In small vessels, three things are sought that give pleasure: the craftsman’s hand, the weight of the silver, and the brilliance of the metal.

499 ## CHAPTER V. On Drinking Vessels

### 1.

*Poculum* (“cup”) is named from drinking. Every vessel in which there is a practice of drinking is a *poculum*.

*Phyalae* (“bowls”) are so called because they are made of glass. For glass is called *ὕαλος* (*hyalos*) in Greek.

### 2.

*Paterae* (“libation bowls”) are called *phyalae*, either because we customarily drink from them or because they are broad and have widely spread lips.

### 3.

*Cratera* (“mixing bowl”) is a cup with two handles and is a Greek name; among the Greeks it is declined as masculine, *crater*. [Note: [Col. 0716D] In Latin, however, *cratera* is feminine. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book I.] In Latin it is called *haec cratera*. Hence Persius:

> If you have silver mixing bowls …

and Virgil:

> They set up great mixing bowls and crown the wine.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] At first they were made by joining together branches. These may have been called *craterae*, concerning which see Nonius.] At first they were made by joining together branches, and hence they were called *craterae*, from *ἀπὸ τοῦ κρατεῖν* (“from holding”), that is, because they hold one another together.

### 4.

*Cyathi*, *scyphi*, and *cymbia* are likewise kinds of cups. [Note: [Col. 0716D] *Cymbia* … a ship. From Servius, *Commentary on the Aeneid*, book V.] *Cymbia* were called cups because of their resemblance to the boat *cymba*.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] *Amystis*. Hence the Greeks say *ἀμυστὶ πίνειν*, “to drink in one draught, with the lips not closed.” Horace:

> Lest many a draught of unmixed wine  
> should defeat Bassus by a Thracian *amystis*.]

*Amystis* is a kind of cup from which one drinks in a continuous draught, that is, in a single breath.

[Note: [Col. 0716D] *Baccea*. Others read *Bacchia*. Commonly *bazia*.] *Baccea* was first named from Bacchus, which means wine; afterward it passed into use for water.

### 5. [Note: [Col. 0716D] *Calathi*. Virgil, *Eclogue* V:

> I shall pour new Arisian nectar into baskets.]

*Calices*, *calathi*, and *scalae* are kinds of drinking vessels, formerly made of wood and named accordingly. For the Greeks called every kind of wood *κᾶλον* (*kalon*).

500 *Ampulla* (“flask”) is as though *ampla bulla* (“large bubble”); for in its roundness it resembles bubbles formed from water’s foam and inflated by the wind.

## CHAPTER VI. On Wine and Water Vessels

### 1.

*Oenophorus* is a vessel carrying wine; *οἶνος* (*oinos*) means “wine.” Hence the verse:

[Note: [Col. 0716D] “The bottom turns in the wine-carriers, according to our judgment.” We said in book I that Nonius cites this verse in *Sententia*, from Lucilius, book III of the *Satires*.]

> The bottom turns in the wine-carriers, according to our judgment.

[Col. 0717A] ### 2. [Note: [Col. 0717C] *Phlascae* are named from a Greek word. Or perhaps from *φιάλων ἄσκοι*, that is, “skins of bowls.” We commonly say *frascos*.]

*Phlascae* are named from a Greek word. They were first made for transporting and storing bowls, and were named accordingly. Later they passed into use for wine, while retaining the Greek word from which their name originated.

### 3.

*Lagena* and *sicula* are Greek names adapted in part so that they might become Latin. The Greeks say *λάγηνος* (*lagenos*), while we say *lagenam*; they say *sicile*, while we say *siculam*.

*Cantharus* … [lacuna]

### 4.

*Hydria* is named by derivation as a kind of water vessel, for the Greeks call water *ὕδωρ* (*hydor*).

[Note: [Col. 0717C] *Situla*. Festus: “The Greeks call a low, hollow water vessel *nanos*, commonly called a bearded *situlus*. Hence dwarfs are called *nani*, and so forth.”] *Situla* is so called because it is suitable for thirsty people to drink from; the Greeks call this vessel *cadus*. [Note: [Col. 0717D] The Greeks call it *cadus*. For *cadus* is not a vessel of only one kind.]

### 5. [Note: [Col. 0717D] *Catinum* is an earthen vessel. See Varro, book IV, and book I of *On Agriculture*, chapter 43.]

*Catinum* is an earthen vessel. It is better spoken in the neuter gender than the masculine, just as *salinum* is called a vessel suitable for salt.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] *Orca* is an amphora. Varro suggests that the word is Spanish, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 13: “In Spain amphorae burst from the heat of the must, and in Italy the large storage jars likewise.”] *Orca* is a kind of amphora; its diminutive is *urceus*, and the diminutive of that is *urceolus*.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] *Scyphus*, in which we wash our hands. Plutarch, *Life of Antony*: “And to a boy putting water into a silver *scyphus* to bring it, etc.” That it was also a drinking vessel is known to everyone.] *Scyphus* is a vessel in which we wash our hands.

6. *Seriola* is a straight row of *orcae*, or an earthenware wine vessel, first devised in Syria, just as [Note: “As *cilicises.” Other readings: *silicisses, silicenses, cilises, cilicienses, cilici*.] *cilicises* were so called from Cilicia, from which they were first imported.

*Dolium* . . .

7. They hold that *cupos* and *cupas* were named from *capere*, that is, “to receive,” water or wine; hence also *caupones*.

*Utres* [“wineskins”] from *uter* [“womb”].

[Note: A *mulgarium* is a vessel into which livestock are milked. The same is *mulctrum*, because milk is milked into it. Georgics III, however, has:

“Like their fathers, the cows will fill the snow-white milk-pails,”

as Pierius pointed out after finding it in the oldest manuscripts; and before Valgius the same word was used:

“But we before the cottage [have] warm milk-pails.” [Col. 0718C]]

A *mulgarium* is a vessel into which livestock are milked. The same is *mulctrum*, because milk is milked into it.

8. A *labrum* is so called because it was customarily used for washing infants; its diminutive is *labellum*. It is also called an *alveus*, because washing was customarily done in it. [Col. 0717C]

[Note: *Pelvis*. Varro, Book IV: “*Pelvis* derives from washing the feet, as *pedelvis*.”]

*Pelves* are so called because feet are washed in them.

9. A *siphon* is the name given to a vessel because it pours out water by blowing; the Orientals use it for this purpose. For when they notice that a house is burning, they run with siphons full of water and extinguish the fires, and [Note: “They also clean the ceilings by forcing water upward.” The ceilings were decorated with figures in slightly raised plasterwork, or divided into coffers; when they became dirty, they were cleaned with siphons, since their height made them otherwise inaccessible.] they also clean the ceilings by forcing water upward.

## CHAPTER VII. On vessels for oil

1. [Note: *Hemicadium*. Pollux, Book X, chapter 20.]

*Hemicadium*, an oil vessel.

[Note: *Scortea*. Festus, or Paulus, under *Scorta*. For everything made from hides is called *scorta*.]

*Scortea*, an oil vessel, so called because it is made of leather.

2. *Alabastrum*, a vessel for perfume, named from its characteristic stone, called *alabastrites*, which preserves unspoiled perfumes.

3. *Pyxides*, small perfume vessels made from boxwood. For what we call *buxum*, the Greeks call πύξον (*pyxon*).

4. [Note: *Lenticula*. Jerome, on Habakkuk III: A small earthenware vessel is so called, that is, φακός (*phakos*); and Apuleius, Book II of the *Florida*, indicates that *lenticula* was named from the shape of a lentil: “An oil flask which he carried, of lentil-like shape, with a smooth circumference and compressed roundness.” Both also seem to have been water vessels. For in 1 Samuel 26, where David takes the spear from Saul’s tent, the ancient translation—which Lucifer of Cagliari cites in Book I of *For Athanasius*—renders φακὸς ὕδατος (*phakos hydatos*) as “water-lentil.”]

*Lenticula*, a small oil vessel made of bronze or silver, is named from *linire* [“to smear”]. For kings and priests were anointed with these.

## CHAPTER VIII. On kitchen vessels

[Col. 0718B]

1. All vessels prepared for cooking are called *cocula*. [Note: *Cocula*. Festus: *Cocula* are bronze vessels suitable for cooking. Others say they are small pieces of wood with which food is easily cooked.] Plautus:

“With bronze eyes all my compassion has been boiled out of me.”

[The quotation is apparently corrupt in the source.]

2. An *olla* is so called because water boils in it when fire is placed beneath, so that it gives off steam more vigorously. Hence it is also called a *bulla*, which is sustained in water by the inward spirit of air.

A *patella*, as though *patula* [“open”]. It is a pot with a more open mouth.

3. *Cacabus* and *cucuma* are named from the sound of boiling. These names are common to Greek and Latin, but it is uncertain whether the Latins borrowed these words from the Greeks or the Greeks from the Latins.

4. [Note: *Lebetes* are bronze vessels. Servius, on *Aeneid* III, “the bronze Dodonian cauldrons”: “He means bronze pots.”]

*Lebetes* were called by a Greek term; they are smaller pots prepared for cooking. [Col. 0718C]

5. A *sartago* is named from the clatter of the sound produced when oil burns in it.

*Tripedes* are so called because they consist of three feet; the Greeks call them *tripodes*.

6. [Note: “*Mola* as *mala* [apples] of fruit.” In other words, he confuses μῆλον (*melon*, “apple”) and μύλον (*mylon*, “mill”).]

A *mola* is named from its roundness, like the apples of fruit; the Greeks use the same term.

[Col. 0719A] A *cribrum* [“sieve”], because grain runs through it, as though *currifrum* [“that which makes things run”].

[Note: *Rotabulum*. All books read this. Festus: “A *rutabulum* is what country people use to thrust forward a fire for the purpose of baking bread.” As regards the etymology, however, it makes no difference whether one writes *rotabulum* or *rutabulum*, since below, in chapter 12, he derives *rota* from *ruere*. Glossary: *Rotabulum*, ἐνοκάλης [sic].]

A *rotabulum* is so called from thrusting forward dung or fire for the purpose of baking bread.

## CHAPTER IX. On storage vessels

1. [Note: “The treasury . . . are sent.” Words of Augustine, on Psalm 63.]

A *gazophylacium* is a chest in which those things are collected in the temple that are sent for the needs of the poor. The word is compounded from the Persian and Greek languages.

[Note: *Gaza* means “treasure” in Persian. From Servius, on *Aeneid* I and V.]

For *gaza* means “treasure” in the language of the Persians, while φυλακή (*phylakē*) means “guard” in Greek.

2. [Note: *Arca* from *arcere* [“to ward off”]. Varro: “An *arca* is so called because, when closed, it keeps thieves away from it.”]

An *arca* [“chest”] is so called because it keeps sight away and prevents access. [Note: “Hence also *arcivum*. The Greeks call it ἀρχεῖον (*archeion*). See the *Suda*.”]

Hence also *arcivum*; hence *arcanum*, that is, “secret,” since others are kept away from it.

3. *Cibutum* is a Greek word; we call it an *arca*. [Col. 0719B]

A *loculus* is a place made for putting something into the ground, or for keeping clothing or money; hence it is also used as a diminutive.

4. *Mozicia*, as though *modicia*; hence also *modicum*, with *z* substituted for *d*, just as Italians customarily say *ozie* for *hodie* [“today”].

*Scrinia* . . .

5. A *saccus* is named from *saggus*, because, when sewn together, it becomes something like a *sagus* [cloak].

A *marsupium* is a small money-bag, which the Greeks call μάρσυπον (*marsypon*). For certain Greek names are slightly inflected in Latin on account of Roman usage.

6. [Note: *Sitarciae* are sailors’ provisions. Apuleius, Book II of *The Golden Ass*: “For this voyage the ship of Venus needs only this *sitarcia*.” The word is extended to other provisions as well, as in 1 Samuel 9: “The loaves have failed from our provisions.”]

*Sitarciae* are sailors’ provisions, so called because they are sewn together.

[Col. 0719C] An *involucrum* is so called because it holds something wrapped up within itself.

7. [Note: “The *fiscus*, a small bag . . . are called.” From Augustine, on Psalm 146.]

A *fiscus* is a public money-bag; hence *fiscellae* and *fiscinae* are also so called. Tax collectors possess it, and into it they put the public payment that is rendered to kings. *Fiscus* is the primary form; *fiscina* is derivative, and *fiscella* diminutive.

8. [Note: “The *canistrum* . . . others assert it is Greek.” Not incorrectly. For, according to Pollux, κάναστρον (*kanastron*), or also κάνιστρον (*kanistron*), is used.]

A *canistrum* is woven from rushes (*fisci*), whence it receives its name; others assert that the word is Greek.

A *cistella* is named from the ribs—*costae*—of reed or wood with which it is woven.

9. [Note: *Cophinus*, a vessel made from slender branches. Another reading: *virgultis*, “brushwood.”]

A *cophinus* is a vessel made from slender branches, suitable for clearing away dung and carrying earth. [Col. 0719D] Concerning it the Psalmist says of Israel: “His hands served in the basket.” [Note: It is called *cophinus*, as though *covus*. The explanation arose from the spelling *covinus* with digamma.]

It is called *cophinus*, as though *covus*, as though *cavus* [“hollow”].

10. [Note: “*Corbes* . . . because they are woven from bent branches.” Unless one prefers ἀπὸ τοῦ κορμοῦ (*apo tou kormou*, “from the trunk”), as Pollux has it in Book X, chapter 24.]

*Corbes* are so called because they are woven from bent branches.

[Note: *Sporta*, either because it is made from *spartum* [“esparto grass”]. The second explanation, which corrects the first, is absent from some old books. The other explanations found in printed editions, concerning the plant *spartum*, have been brought here from Book XVII, chapter 9.]

A *sporta* is so called either because it is customarily made from *spartum*, or because it carries something out. (*Sporta* is derived from *spartum*, not from “carrying out,” as some maintain. For it was originally made from *spartum*.) [Col. 0720B]

## CHAPTER X. On vessels for lights

1. [Note: “The ancients called the kitchen *culina* from tending the fire.” [Col. 0720C] All the manuscripts corruptly read: “From tending the fire, and wood.” Varro, quoted by Nonius, Book I of *The Life of the Roman People*: “What is the front and what the rear? In the rear part was the kitchen, called so because they tended the fire there.” There is no doubt that these are Nonius’s words: “The ancients called the kitchen *colina*, not, as the common people now suppose, *culina*, evidently. For his sole purpose is to establish by testimony that the ancients said *colina*, not *culina*. There was also *culigna* (as Festus says), a drinking vessel. But why is the drinking vessel written *culigna* with *gn*, rather than *culina* for the hearth, if we trust Varro’s etymology? I think that *culina* was in fact an ancient original name, and that this same part of the house—because, as Varro says, it was at the rear—was called *culina* from the rear part of an animal. But the ancients, serving propriety, changed its first vowel; Varro himself saw this and deliberately concealed it, even covering up with an elegant etymology that unpleasantness which might offend more modest ears, and diverting minds elsewhere. In this he acted more as a philosopher than as a grammarian. Thus what Nonius wished will also prove true: that the ancients said *colina*. The more obscure point is that Festus says *culina* means the place where funeral banquets are burned.”]

The ancients called the hearth *culina*, from tending the fire. A *focus* [“hearth”] is so called because φῶς (*phōs*) is “fire” in Greek, from which, according to certain philosophers, all things are produced. Indeed, nothing is born without heat, so much so that concerning the North the poet says [Note: “Nothing is born in sterile cold.” From Lucan, Book IV.] “nothing is born in sterile cold.” [Col. 0720D]

But Varro says that *foci* [“hearths”] were so called because they nurture fires. For fire itself is the flame; whatever nurtures fire, however, is called a *focus*, whether it is an altar or anything else in which fire is nurtured.

2. [Note: “*Lucerna* from *lychnos* . . . the verse would not scan.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I, at “the lamps’ chains hang down.”]

A *lucerna* [“lamp”] is named from *lychnos*, whence its *lu* is also short, as Juvenal writes:

“The arranged lamps vomited forth a thick cloud.”

For if it were said to derive from *lux* [“light”], the verse would not scan. *Lychnus* is, as it were, *lucinius*. A *cicindela* is a kind of lamp. [Col. 0721A]

3. A *candelabrum* is named from *candela* [“candle”], as though *candelaferum*, because it carries a candle.

A *cereus* [“wax candle”] takes its name by derivation from *cera* [“wax”], from which it is formed; concerning it someone writes: [Note: Concerning this, someone has written. Martial, Book XIV, epigram 42:

“Here this candle will provide you with nocturnal fires;

For your boy’s lamp has been taken away.”

Nevertheless, the agreement of the Isidorian manuscripts permits us to change nothing, since these lines too can be understood in this way.]

“Here this candle will provide you with nocturnal fires.

With one light withdrawn, I am another light for you.”

4. [Note: “*Candela* . . . ceilings.” These lines are found in some Gothic manuscripts but are absent from the better ones.]

A *candela* [“candle”] is so called from *candere* [“to shine white”], because it is consumed by shining.

*Lacunaria* are hanging lights, as though *lucanaria*, that is, “things shining in the air.”

5. [Note: “*Funalia* . . . are called *funera*.” From Servius, at the same passage.]

*Funalia* are what are inside wax. They are named from *funes* [“cords”], which our ancestors, before the use of papyrus, used to surround with wax before employing them; hence they are also called *funera*. The Greeks call *funalia* *scolaces*, [Note: Because they are σκόλιαι (*skoliai*), that is, twisted. Hence the common word *antorchas* [“torches”].] because they are *scoliae*, that is, twisted. The Romans called these cords *funes* and *funalia*. [Note: “*Funalia*, that is, . . .” *Funus* (says Donatus, on *Andria*) is named from *funalia*, and from the *cunei* or wedges of candelabra into which cords coated with wax, or waxen wicks, are inserted.]

Among the ancients, *funalia* were candelabra into which cords coated with wax or a similar fuel for light were fixed. Thus sharply pointed stakes were likewise called *funalia*.

6. [Note: “*Lampas* . . . because it appears to show the movement of something licking.” I think he had in mind Virgil’s words, “the flame licking their hair,” although it was otherwise clear that the word is Greek.]

A *lampas* is a flame shining at the top, so called because it appears to display the movement of something licking.

A *fax* [“torch”] is so called because it makes *foci* [“hearths”]; its diminutive is *facula*.

7. A *laterna* [“lantern”] is so called because it has light enclosed inside. It is made of glass, with the light shut within so that a gust of wind cannot reach it; it can therefore easily be carried about everywhere for providing light.

8. A *lucubrum* is so called because it shines in shadow. It is a small fire, customarily made from thin tow and wax.

9. [Note: “A *pyra* . . . is customarily made.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* VI: “And the altar of the tomb.”]

A *pyra* is a structure that is customarily built of wood in the form of an altar, so that it may burn; for πῦρ (*pyr*) means “fire.” [Note: “But a *pyra* is the pile of wood itself . . . they call it burned.” From the same source, on *Aeneid* XI, at “They set up pyres.”]

But a *pyra* is the pile of wood itself, when it has not yet begun to burn; it is a *rogus* [“funeral pyre”] when it has begun to burn; a *bustum* [“burned burial place”] is what they call it once it has been burned.

10. [Note: “A *pharus* is a tower, etc.” The same work above, Book XV, chapter 2, drawing on Hegesippus, Pliny, and Solinus.]

A *pharus* is a very large tower, which Greeks and Latins alike, from the use of the thing itself, called a *pharus*. It is so called because sailors can see it from far away by the indication of its flames, as we said above. Ptolemy is reported to have built such a tower near Alexandria at a cost of eight hundred talents. Its purpose is to show fires to ships sailing at night, indicating shoals and the entrances to harbors, so that sailors deceived by the darkness may not strike the rocks; for Alexandria has treacherous approaches with deceptive shoals. Hence in harbors they call the structures built to shine ahead *phari*. For φῶς (*phōs*) is “light,” while [Note: Ὅρος (*horos*) means “sight.” More properly, ὅρασις (*horasis*).] ὅρος (*horos*) is said to mean “vision”; hence the bringer of light is called φωσφόρος (*phōsphoros*) in Greek.

## CHAPTER XI. On beds and seats

1. [Note: “*Lecticae* from gathered herbs. Varro says that *lectica* is so called because they gathered the straw and herbs from which they made it. Festus: “*Lectus* is so called either from collected leaves, for lying down, etc.”]

*Lecticae* [“litters”] are named from gathered herbs.

A *stratus* [“bed”] is named from *sternere* [“to spread”], as though *storiatus*. In ancient times people reclined for sleeping only on these, before woolen bedding had been invented.

A *storia* is so called because it is earth spread out.

2. A *cama* is short and close to the ground. [Note: For the Greeks call χαμαί (*chamai*) “short.” The same author, Book XII, chapter 1: “The camel received its name either because, when loaded, it lies down so as to become shorter and lower, since the Greeks call χαμαί ‘low’ and ‘short.’”]

For the Greeks call χαμαί (*chamai*) “short.”

A *cubile* is a place for lying down.

[Note: *Grabatum* is Greek: κράββατον (*krabbaton*).]

A *grabatum* is Greek.

A *bajonola* is a bed carried during a journey, from *bajulare* [“to carry”], that is, to transport.

3. A *pulvinar* is the bed of the wealthy; hence also *pulvillus* [“small cushion”].

[Note: “*Spingae*, on which there are *spingatae* images.” Chacon read “*spingae*, *spingatae*.” It should be considered whether the word derives from *sphinxes*, concerning which Book XII, chapter 2, says: “Sphinxes are hairy in their manes.”]

*Spingae* are beds on which there are images of *spingae*, which we call *gryphes* [“griffins”].

[Note: Punic beds. Concerning these, see Cicero, *For Murena*, Valerius Maximus, Book IX, chapter 3, and Seneca, Letter 96.]

*Punicani* beds are small and low; they were first imported from Carthage and named from that origin.

4. *Lecticae*, or *plutei*, are beds concerning which Rutilius [Note: Rutilius Rufus, *On the Life of Scipio*.
