Appian mentions him in his work on the Spanish War: “Rutilius Rufus, the writer of these events, who at that time was commander of a thousand.” Cicero, *Brutus*: “I remember hearing at Smyrna from Publius Rutilius Rufus, when he said that as a young man he had happened to be present when, following a decree of the Senate, Publius Scipio and Decimus Brutus (as I think), the consuls, were deliberating about a grave and important matter,” etc.] Rufus writes in *On the Life of Scipio*: “First, contrary to the custom of generals, he himself used litters instead of beds.”

5. [Note: “The *sponda* is the outer part of the bed.” Correct. For Caesar’s statement, according to Suetonius in *Julius*, that the inner *sponda* of a royal litter was called this by Dolabella makes the insult particularly harsh.]

The *sponda* is the outer part of the bed, while the *pluteus* is the inner part.

[Note: Nuptial beds. The same work above, Book VIII, final chapter.]

*Nuptial beds* properly are those spread for girls who are marrying; they are so called from the begetting of children.

6. [Note: “*Cunabula* . . . give birth.” From Servius, on Eclogue 4.]

*Cunabula* are little beds in which infants customarily lie. They are so called because they are used for childbirth, as though *cynabula*; for κύειν (*kyein*) is Greek for “to give birth.”

7. [Note: “*Pheretrum* . . . near the bier.” From the same source, on *Aeneid* XI. [Col. 0723C] For that which is carried above men’s heads Chacon regarded as foreign to the passage, and I have no doubt that he was right, especially since Servius adds: “And *capulus* is so called because it holds the body.” Festus likewise says: “*Capulum* derives from *capere*.”]

A *pheretrum* is so called because the dead are carried in it, [Col. 0723A] and the name is Greek. For φέρετρον (*pheretron*) is derived ἀπὸ τοῦ φέρειν (*apo tou pherein*), that is, from *ferre* [“to carry”]. In Latin it is called a *capulus*, because it is carried above men’s heads. Thus Plautus writes: “An old man fit for the bier,” that is, near the *capulus*.

8. [Note: “*Scamna* . . . *scabellum*.” Varro, Book IV: “By this simple climbing they climbed into a low bed, using a *scabellum*; into a higher one, a *scamnum*.”]

*Scamna* are placed beside higher beds; they are so called from *scandere* [“to climb”]. Hence also *scabelli*, which are placed beside small beds or seats to enable one to climb up. A *scabellum* is also called a *suppedaneum*. For what the Greeks call ὑποπόδιον (*hypopodion*), the Latins call a *scabellum*, while others call it a *suppedaneum*, because it is beneath the feet.

[Note: “*Scansilia* . . . cling to the seats.” Another reading: “cling to the buildings.”]

*Scansilia* are steps where honored persons sit in places of honor.

9. *Sedes* [“seats”] are so called because among the ancient Romans there was no custom of reclining; hence they were also said to *considere* [“sit down”]. Later, as Varro says in *On the Life of the Roman People*: [Note: “Men began to recline, women to sit.” Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter 1: “Women dined sitting while the men reclined.”]

Men began to recline and women to sit, because reclining was considered an indecorous sight in a woman. In the singular, *sedes* properly refers to a throne, which is called θρόνος (*thronos*) in Greek.

*Subsellia* [“benches”], however, are for others; [Note: “*Cathedrae* are for teachers.” Cassiodorus, on Psalm 1: “A *cathedra* is properly given to teachers.] *cathedrae* are for teachers.

10. [Note: “The *solium* . . . is called.” From two passages of Servius, on *Aeneid* I and VII.]

A *solium* is the seat on which a king sits for the protection of his body. According to some, it is named from its solidity, as though *solidum*; according to others, by transposition of letters, as though *sodium*, from *sedere* [“to sit”]. Hence *sella* [“seat”] is also said to derive from *seda*, and *subsellia* [“benches”] from *subsedia*.

11. *Sellae curules* were seats on which magistrates, while seated, administered justice. They were called *curules* because in ancient times praetors and consuls, on account of the great distance involved, were conveyed to the forum by chariot; the seats carried behind them, on which they customarily sat while administering justice, were named *curules* from the chariot.

22. [Note: “*Tripodes*, little steps.” Thus in Vitruvius, Book III, chapter 3, and Book V, chapter 9. In the common editions, however, the reading is *scamilli*; other books have *scabelli* and *scamnuli*.]

*Tripodes* are little steps with three feet; candelabra are also *tripodes*, because they likewise have three feet.

## CHAPTER XII. On vehicles

1. A *carrum* [“cart”] is named from the axle (*cardo*) of its wheels; hence *currus* [“chariots”] are also so called, because they appear to have wheels.

A *rota* [“wheel”] is so called because it rolls (*ruat*), and *rotundum* [“round”] is named from *rota*.

2. A *rheda* is a kind of four-wheeled vehicle. The ancients called these *retae*, because they had wheels.

3. [Note: “*Carpentum* . . . as a ceremonial cart.” Ovid:

“For formerly Italian matrons were carried in *carpenta*.

I think these too were named from Evander’s mother.”

Thus *carpentum* is as though *carmentum*, from Carmenta, Evander’s mother.]

A *carpentum* is a kind of ceremonial vehicle, as though a ceremonial cart.

[Note: *Plaustrum*, as though *pilastrum*. Varro: “A *plaustrum* is so called because it is open on every side,” or rather from *palari*, that is, “to spread out.”]

A *plaustrum* is a two-wheeled vehicle for carrying loads. It is called *plaustrum* because it rolls, as though one said *pilastrum*.

*Caracutium* is a vehicle with extremely high wheels, as though an “acutely shaped cart.” [Note: Gothic manuscripts have *carrucium*; among us the same vehicle is called a *carricoche*.]

[Note: *Capsum*. Festus uses this word in *Ploxemum*. The Glossary has *capsum*, πλίνθιον (*plinthion*).]

A *capsus* is a carriage covered on every side, as though a *capsa* [“box”].

4. [Note: *Pilentum*. From Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII.]

A *pilentum*, or *petoritum*, is a covered four-wheeled vehicle formerly used by matrons. Virgil:

“Mothers in soft *pilenta*.”

Horace:

“More drivers and horses to be fed,

And more four-wheeled wagons to be hauled.”

Formerly *pilenta* were Venetian in color, not reddish as they are now; only chaste matrons were permitted to use them, just as they alone could wear fillets.

5. [Note: *Basterna*. Jerome also mentions it, on Isaiah 66.]

A *basterna* is a traveling vehicle, as though *viae sternax* [“a spreader of the road”], fitted with soft bedding and carried by two animals.

## CHAPTER XIII. On other things used in daily life

1. *Baculus* [“staff”] is said to have been invented by Bacchus, the discoverer of the vine, so that people overcome by wine might lean upon it. Just as *baculus* comes from Bacchus, so *bacillus* is its diminutive.

2. [Note: *Fustes*, as though *stent* [“they stand”]. Above, Book V, chapter 27: “*Fustes*, because, fixed in ditches, they stand.”]

*Fustes* [“clubs”] are so called because, fixed in the ground, they stand. Country people call them *pali* [“stakes”]; young men are beaten with them for offenses.

[Note: *Vectes*. The same book, chapter 27.]

*Vectes* [“levers”] are so called because they are carried by hand; hence doors and stones are pried loose with them.

3. [Note: *Forfices*, according to the etymology. Vel. Longus, in his work *On Orthography*: “There is a question in pronunciation concerning *forcipes* and *forpices*, and *arcesso* and *accerso*. In these cases it is especially difficult to determine how they are pronounced. Therefore, when I say a form, you will write it for me; nevertheless, we have noted that the ancients said *forcipes* by transposing the syllables. Virgil also writes: ‘And they turn the mass with tenacious tongs.’ We say *forcipes* because they seize (*capiant*) something hot (*formum*), that is, warm.”]

*Forfices* [“shears”]: if they are named from *filum* [“thread”], the *f* is used, as in *forfices*, which belong to tailors; if from *pilus* [“hair”], *p* is used, as in *forpiceps*, which belong to barbers; if from *accipere* [“to take”], *c* is used, as in *forcipes*, because they seize something hot, and belong to smiths. For the ancients called something hot *formum*; hence also *formosus* [“beautiful”].

4. A *novacula* [“razor”] is so called because it renews the face.

A *pecten* [“comb”] is so called because it makes hair *pexus* [“combed”] and arranged.

[Col. 0725A] [Note: *Calamistrum*. From Servius, on *Aeneid* XII, at “hair curled with hot iron.”]

A *calamistrum* is a needle which, when heated and applied, heats and curls the hair. Hence those who curl their hair are called *calamistrati*.

5. A *clavis* [“key”] is so called because it closes and opens. [Note: *Catenatum*. Because we say *candado* [“lock”].]

A *catenatum* [“lock”] is so called because it holds by seizing.

A *horologium* [“sundial”] is so called because we read, that is, gather, the hours from it. It is set on a solar dial, where the shadow moves from a peg along lines, so that it indicates whichever hour of the day it may be.

## CHAPTER XIV. On agricultural implements

1. [Note: “*Vomer* . . . or from vomiting out the earth.” Varro: “The plow is so called because it plows the earth; its iron is the *vomer*, because it vomits out more earth with it.”]

A *vomer* [“plowshare”] is so called because it violently tears up the soil, or because it vomits out the earth. Concerning it Lucretius writes:

“The iron hook of the plow

Grows smaller, the plowshare, in the hidden fields.”

[Note: “And through wear takes on brilliance.” Perhaps “luster.” He may have alluded to Virgil’s words: “And worn by the furrow, the plowshare shines.”]

“And through wear takes on brilliance.”

2. An *aratrum* [“plow”] is named from *arare* [“to plow”] the earth, as though *araterrium*.

[Note: “*Buris* . . . an ox’s tail.” From Servius, on *Georgics* I.]

A *buris* is the curved part of a plow, called as though βοὸς οὐρά (*boos oura*), “an ox’s tail,” because it is made in the likeness of an ox’s tail.

[Note: *Dentale*. From the same source, except that there the part is introduced, whereas here it is enclosed.]

A *dentale* is the foremost part of the plow, into which the plowshare is inserted, as though it were a tooth.

3. *Cultelli* [“knives”] are named from *cultura* [“cultivation”], because in former times people used them for pruning trees and vines before sickles had been invented.

4. [Note: A *falx*. Palladius, Book I, final chapter: “Pruning sickles used in trees and vines.”]

A *falx* [“sickle”] is used to prune trees and vines. Sickle blades were so called [Note: “Because soldiers first used these.” Chacon rejected *milites* as having been taken from a verse of Martial, since Palladius, whose words these are, does not mention soldiers. He says: “Likewise, very short sickles with which we usually cut fern.” The distinguished scholar believes that *falx* derives from the Syriac *palca*.] because soldiers formerly used them to cut fern.

[Note: Hence the following line: “Certain peace.” Martial, *Apophoreta*.]

Hence the following:

“Certain peace has bent me, the commander, to peaceful uses.

Now I belong to the farmer; before, I belonged to the soldier.”

5. A *falcastrum* is named from its resemblance to a sickle. It is a curved iron tool with a long handle, used for cutting through dense brambles. [Col. 0725C] [Note: These are also called *runcones*. Palladius, in the same passage: “*Runcones*, with which we cut through thickets.”]

They are also called *runcones*, with which brambles are cut; the name derives from *runcare* [“to cut”].

6. A *serrula* [“small saw”] is a very thin sheet of iron that cuts trees or branches by the biting action of its teeth.

[Note: *Rastra*. From Servius, on *Georgics* I.]

A *rastrum* [“rake”] is named either from *radere* [“to scrape”] the earth or from the sparseness of its teeth.

*Ligones* [“hoes”] are so called because they lift the earth, as though *levones*.

7. [Note: *Scudicia*. Perhaps we call it an *escoda* [“pickaxe”].]

A *scudicia* is so called because it opens the earth around the trunk of a tree. Although it is used for other tasks as well, it retains its name from the trunk. Others generally call it a *fossorium* [“digging tool”], because it makes a pit, as though *fovessorium*.

8. [Note: *Sarculi*, either single-pronged or two-pronged. From Palladius, in the same passage.]

*Sarculi* [“hoes”] are either single-pronged or two-pronged.

[Note: *Pastinum* . . . are dug up again. From Columella, Book III, chapter 18.]

Farmers call a *pastinum* a two-pronged implement with which seeds are planted. Hence old vineyards that are dug up again are called *repastinatae*.

9. [Note: *Cylindrus*, a stone. From Servius.]

A *cylindrus* is a smooth, cylindrical stone, which received its name from its capacity for rolling. Concerning it Virgil writes:

“First, the threshing floor must be leveled with a massive cylinder,

And turned by hand.”

10. [Note: *Tribula*. From the same source.]

A *tribula* is a kind of vehicle with which grain is threshed, and for this reason it is so called.

[Note: *Pala*. Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine use this word.]

A *pala* [“shovel”], commonly called a *ventilabrum* [“winnowing shovel”], is named from winnowing (*ventilare*) chaff.

11. [Note: *Furcillae*. From Servius, on *Georgics* II.]

*Furcillae* [“little forks”] are so called because grain is moved with them. Hence *oscilla* [“little faces”] are also so called because their faces are moved; for *cillere* means “to move.”

12. [Note: *Tesserae* are used to mark the number of grain measures. Servius, on *Georgics* I: “Or he impressed numbers upon the heaps,” that is, either he makes marks by which cattle are branded, or tablets by which the number of grain measures is indicated. For he used *numeros* [“numbers”] for the letters in which numbers are contained.]

*Tesserae* [“tokens”] are used to indicate the number of grain measures.

[Note: *Trapetum*, an olive mill. From the same source, on *Georgics* II.]

A *trapetum* is an olive mill.

[Note: *Prelum*. From the same source.]

A *prelum* is a beam with which crushed grapes are pressed; it is named from *premere* [“to press”], as though *pressorium*.

A *prelum* is also used to press oil.

A *lacus* [“vat”] is where the liquid flows out, and where wine and oil are extracted by pressing grapes or olives.

13. *Verennes* are named from *vehere*, that is, “to carry out” or “export.”

[Note: *Qualus*. From the same source.]

A *qualus* [“straining basket”], through which must flows, is named from *colare* [“to strain”].

[Note: *Fisclum*. Either read *fiscellum* here, or, in Columella, Book XII, chapter 38, read *fisclum*.]

A *fisclum*, as though *fisculum*, is named from straining oil, or as though an oil *fiscella*.

## CHAPTER XV. On garden implements

1. [Note: *Rota*. See Vitruvius, Book X, chapter 11.]

A *rota* [“wheel”] is so called because it rolls, as it were. It is a machine by which water is drawn from a river. Lucretius:

“As we see wheels turn the rivers and the water-scoops.”

[Note: *Haustra*. Nonius: *Haustra* properly refers to wheels, just as in Greek ἀντλήματα (*antlēmata*).]

*Haustra*, that is, a wheel, are so called from drawing up water.

2. A *girgillus* [“windlass”] is so called because it turns in a circle. It is a piece of wood movable on a transverse pole, from which a rope with a bucket or wineskin is lowered into a well for drawing water.

3. [Note: “Gardeners call it a *telon*.” Isidore’s etymology shows that this is what he wrote, but he should have said *tollenon*. Festus: “A *tolleno* is a kind of machine by which water is drawn, one end being weighted with a counterweight; it is named from *tollere* [‘to lift’].” Livy, Pliny, and Vegetius use this word.]

Gardeners call a *telon* a long piece of wood with which they draw water. It is called a *telon* from its length, for τέλον (*telon*) in Greek means anything long. [Note: Hence *mustella*, as though “long mouse.” These are Servius’s words.]

Hence also *mustela* [“weasel”] is named, as though “long mouse.” The Spaniards call this implement a *ciconia* [“stork”], because it imitates the bird of that name, raising and lowering its beak while it cries.

[Note: *Hama* . . . an hooked iron implement for controlling fires. Pliny, Letter 250: “And besides, there is nowhere in public a fire pump, no *hama*, and, finally, no implement for restraining fires.” Also Paul, chapter 3, *Digest*, “On the Duties of the Prefect of the Watch”: “It should be understood that the prefect of the watch must remain vigilant throughout the night and go about shod with *hamae* and mattocks.” Also Ulpian, chapter 12, *Digest*, “On the Establishment of Estates.”]

*Hama* . . . .

4. A *lupus*, also called a *canicula*, is an iron grappling hook. It is called *harpax* because, if anything falls into a well, it seizes and pulls it out; for ἁρπάζειν (*harpazein*) means “to snatch” in Greek.

## CHAPTER XVI. On equipment for horses

1. *Phalerae* are ornaments for horses, and the word is Greek. [Note: *Phaler* is a Greek term. From Servius, on *Aeneid* IX.]

*Frena* [“bridles”] are so called because they compel horses to snort, or because horses gnash these—that is, press and bite them—with their teeth. Hence *nefrendes* are called the suckling piglets that have not yet gnawed anything, that is, crushed anything with their teeth. [Note: Hence also *faba fressa* [“crushed bean”]. Festus: “*Frendere* means ‘to break’; hence *faba fressa*, and hence we say *frendere* of the teeth.” Glossary: *Faba frensa*.]

Hence also *faba fresa*, a bean that has been ground.

2. [Note: *Lupata*. From Servius, on *Georgics* III.]

*Lupata* are extremely harsh bridles. They are called *lupata* from the teeth of wolves, which are uneven; hence their bite is especially harmful.

*Chamus* . . . .

3. [Col. 0728A] *Habenae* [“reins”] are named from *habere* [“to hold”], because with them we hold horses, that is, restrain them; hence horses are also called *habiles* [“manageable”]. [Note: These are also *retinacula* [“restraints”]. He alluded to Virgil’s words: “Straining the restraints in vain,” *Georgics* I.]

These are also called *retinacula*, from *retinere* [“to restrain”].

*Lora* . . . .

4. A *capistrum* [“halter”] is named from the head (*caput*) of beasts of burden.

A *sella* [“saddle”] is named from *sedere* [“to sit”], as though *sedda*.

[Note: *Antella* . . . *postella*. Read *antillena* and *postillena*, despite all the manuscripts. The error undoubtedly arose from the etymological explanations. Glossary: *antillena*, εἰστέτηρ [sic]. *Postillena* is also found in Plautus’ *Casina*.]

An *antella* is as though “before the saddle,” just as a *postella* is as though “behind the saddle.”

[Note: *Cingulum* [“belt”] for human beings is neuter. From Servius, on *Aeneid* IX.]

*Cingulum* is neuter when referring to human beings; for animals we use the feminine *cingulae*.

5. A *sagma*, which the common people corruptly call a *salma*, is named from the bedding of pack-saddles. Hence *caballus sagmarius*, “a packhorse,” and *mula sagmaria*, “a pack mule.” [Note: “A packhorse . . . a pack mule.” The same reading should be adopted in Servius, on *Aeneid* I, at “They exhale with fresh garlands,” not *saginarius*. See the *Suda*, under Σάγμα (*Sagma*).]

A *capulum* is a rope, named from *capere* [“to seize”], because untamed beasts of burden are captured with it.

6. *Calcaria* [“spurs”] are so called because they are fastened to a person’s heel, that is, the rear part of the foot, to spur horses that must either fight or run, because of the animals’ sluggishness or fear. For they are named from fear, *stimuli* [“goads”], although there are also goads of lust.

7. *Strigiles* [“scrapers”] are named from *tergere* [“to wipe”], because horses are rubbed down with them.

A *character* is a heated iron with which marks are branded onto livestock. χαρακτήρ (*charaktēr*) in Greek means *forma* [“form”] in Latin.

8. A *cauterium* [“branding iron”] is called as though *cauturium*, because it burns, and because a prudent and severe precaution is taken in its use, so that when ownership is visible, greed may be restrained. It is applied sometimes as a mark and sometimes as a treatment, so that the force of a disease may be dried up by the heat of fire.

[Col. 0729A]

**Verse 1.** I described the Regiovatican Codex in which these verses are prefixed to the *Etymologies*, marked number 1953, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 32, no. 101. There is some conjecture that this poem is by Saint Ildefonsus.

**5.** This verse is corrupt, like many others, and is one foot too long.

**9.** I restored *poterit* (“will be able”) in place of *poteris* (“you will be able”), which stood in the manuscript.

**11.** The Codex had *que* instead of *quas*, and *dignatae matri* (“to the honored mother”) instead of *dignam te matrem* (“you, a worthy mother”).

**15.** It had *polus* (“pole”); perhaps it should be read: “The rejoicing heavens rise up; the stars accompany them.”

Holy Mother of God, perpetual virgin after childbirth,

Star of the sea, sovereign of the world by the command of your Son,

Even if the whole world, rightly eloquent in speech,

Were to produce, under countless conditions, fitting expressions,

[5] Striving, according to the better nature, in human fashion,

What the stars cannot penetrate in their highest dwellings,

And the fiery sun itself, sweating beneath its swift chariots,

Cannot gaze upon, lowering its beautiful face,

Could it in any worthy manner offer you the smallest rites,

[10] Or speak in any ordered way of the praises

Which the almighty Creator won, and then the Son himself,

By everlasting right, exalting you as a worthy mother,

Carried you today to the heavenly citadels of the Father.

He decreed that you should ascend among the angelic ranks:

[15] [Col. 0729B] The rejoicing city rises up, and the stars accompany it,

And with divine praise behold their queen.

O you who remain the door, also the cause of our salvation,

Virgin’s glory and most chaste virtue of mothers,

Full of all [grace], you with whom the grace of the Son is always present,

[20] Now extend your merciful gifts abundantly to those freed from guilt,

And to the wretched sufferer bound in fetters.

And, pitying the foul wound of care in his breast,

Lest livid sores spread over his entire body

And stain it with the loathsome intake of corruption.

[25] I confess you as mistress, mistress; you have pity on your foster-child:

Great as you are, grant aid; and at last, when my bonds have been removed,

### 501

Command me to follow your dewy [steps] across the grass as you walk,

Although I may trace a path far too long.

For, just as the shining rising dawn

[30] Dispels darkness, so your path gives immense light.

Hence they say that the sun and moon possess no brightness of their own;

You surpass the thousand orbs of light poured forth.

## APPENDIX II  
### To Book I of the *Etymologies*, Chapter 17: A Little Work on Feet

[Col. 0730A]

[Note: [Col. 0729C] **Appendix II, no. 1.** This little work is attributed to Isidore in Codex Regiovaticanus 112, which I examined in *Isidoriana*, chapter 99, no. 9. Its beginning indicates that it is a fragment excerpted from some more extensive work.] 

**1.** The composition of feet is now to be discussed; we have already made some mention of them. There are, therefore, disyllabic feet, trisyllabic feet, and tetrasyllabic feet. We shall explain from where their names are derived and how many patterns they have. From doubled disyllabic feet arise tetrasyllabic feet, whose names and patterns we shall also append. From disyllabic and trisyllabic feet combined arise five-syllable feet; and from doubled trisyllabic feet arise six-syllable feet. Concerning these, I think it necessary now to labor carefully.

[Note: [Col. 0730C] **2.** In *asserimus*, the first syllable is long, the following two are short, and the last is long if the following word begins with a consonant, but short if it begins with a vowel.]

**2.** There are therefore four disyllabic feet, eight trisyllabic feet, and sixteen doubled feet, since one syllable has two patterns: it is either long or short. Two syllables have four patterns, for either both are short, or both long, or one is short and one long, or one long and one short. Feet possess arsis and thesis—that is, elevation and lowering—through the heavy sound of syllables; thus, as we assert, two long syllables and two short syllables are placed. There is also time, in which syllables are lengthened and shortened. Resolution proceeds from a foot into a syllable, and from a syllable into a letter. For a letter is an atom, that is, indivisible, or a cutting. We shall explain according to the measure of all the feet.

[Note: [Col. 0730C] **3.** The manuscript had *Exstuant ardentes* (“the burning Tyrians surge forth”); I altered it to *Instant ardentes* (“the burning Tyrians hasten”), from Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 427. In the manuscript, *Troes* seemed to have been written instead of *Tyrii*. Concerning the pyrrhichius and pyrrhicha, and their origin, see Quintilian, book IX, chapter 4; Diomedes, book III, p. 471 of Putsch; Pliny, book VII, chapter 57; Solinus, chapter 11 [or 16], *On Crete*. The Codex had *primus tetensium* instead of *primus Cretensium*, or, as I printed it, *primus Cretenses*. The spondee was used in libations; hence *spondeus*, from the Greek σπονδή (*spondē*), “libation.” Compare Diomedes, book III, p. 472 of Putsch.]

**3.** Some say that the pyrrhichius was so called from Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, who, they say, first danced armed upon his father’s tomb as an act of honor. Aristotle, however, says that Achilles was the inventor of this game. Some think that this foot received its name from ardor—that is, from the very speed of its sound—ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρός (*apo tou pyros*), “from the fire,” that is, from the swiftness of a flame. For ardor and speed are related; hence: “The burning Tyrians hasten,” that is, “make haste.” The pyrrhichius took its name from the *pyrrhicha*, a kind of game, because soldiers use this sound to begin their exercises under arms. The *pyrrhicha* itself is said to derive its name from *pyrrhiacha*, that is, “a game,” or from Pyrrhichia, the daughter of Pyrrhichus, or from Pyrrhichus, who first established that the Cretans should dance armed to the rhythm of this foot. The spondee, however, took its name from sacrifice, because *spondeon* in Greek means “sacrifice”; to this sound they sang hymns, that is, praises, to the immortal gods. Hence Homer also says: “Make your libation, Crete.”

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **4.** Concerning *Iambe*, who discovered the iambus, some say that she was the servant girl of Celeus, and the story itself is narrated in different ways. The manuscript had *licosas* instead of *jocosas*.]

**4.** The iambus was named from Iambe, the daughter of Celeus, who, by uttering playful jests in the rhythm of this foot, aroused love most pleasing to herself. Hence it is also said that the meter of this foot was adapted to comedians—that is, to the most cheerful subject.

**5.** The trochee was named from the speed of a wheel, which it imitates by its sound. Others call it the *chorius*, because the chorus contains a suitable principle of melody; hence the foot composed of this trochee and an iambus is called the choriambus.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **6.** The passage is obscure.]

**6.** The tribrach was named from the quality of its syllables, because it consists of three short syllables, which in Greek are called *brachya* (“short”); for in this he preserved the rule and began with three syllables.

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **7.** What the Greeks call *anapaestin* could be corrected to ἄναπαίειν (*anapaiein*). In the *Etymologies*, Isidore generally follows explanations of feet that differ from these; they should be compared with one another.]

**7.** The molossus was so called because it was discovered by the Molossians of the Cretan region; some also called it the Cretic, among them Aristophanes. The anapest was called the opposite of the dactyl; it received its name because what belongs to the dactyl is thrown back—that is, struck back—which the Greeks call *anapaestin*.

**8.** The dactyl was named from a finger, whose joints give it its shape: it begins with a long syllable and ends with two short ones. For “finger” is called *dactylus* in Greek. The amphibrach was so called because it receives shortness from both sides, which the Greeks call *brachyn* (“shortness”).

**9.** The amphimacrus is called so, like the antipast, because it receives from both sides a long syllable, which the Greeks call *macron* (“long”). This foot was nevertheless called the Cretic because on the island of Crete the Corybants, in order to conceal Jupiter’s cries from Saturn, made a sound that was heavy, short, and heavy.

[Col. 0731C] [Note: [Col. 0731D] **10.** Different origins are given for the proceleusmatic or proceleumatic foot in the *Etymologies* and the notes. *Procelosis* and similar Greek words as they are usually transmitted are wholly corrupt. The matters that may seem more necessary have already been explained in Book I of the *Etymologies*.]

**10.** The bacchius was so called because the rhythmic pattern of this foot, received from Bacchus—that is, Liber Pater—was composed for its sound. The antibacchius, or palimbacchius, is so called because it is the opposite of the bacchius. The proceleumatic is so called because the Corybants, stirring up their dances in order to celebrate the dancing more quickly, urged one another on; for in Greek an exhortation is called *proceleosis*.

**11.** The dispondeus was so called because it consists of two spondees. The diiambus was so called because it is composed of two iambuses. The ditrochee was so called because it is formed from two trochees. The antipast was so called because it is raised from both sides, which in Greek is called *antesponi*, that is, “raising.”

**12.** The choriambus is so called because it consists of a chorius and an iambus. There are two Ionics, the greater and the lesser, named from their inventor Ion, who composed Ionic lyric meters using these feet.

[Col. 0732A] **13.** The paeons received their name from the poet Paeon. The four epitrites were given this name because they consist of three long and one short syllable of equal measure.

## APPENDIX III  
### To Book I of the *Etymologies*, Chapter 27

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND ORTHOGRAPHY  
### From the Albanian Codex

[Note: [Col. 0731D] **Appendix III, no. 1.** I discussed the Codex of the distinguished Albanian family’s library in *Isidoriana*, chapter 107, where, at no. 27, I spoke of this addition to the *Etymologies*. The unusual methods of writing that are explained here need not be treated with excessive concern; they should nevertheless be kept before one’s eyes, so that the extent of medieval freedom in this matter may be understood and so that one may more easily arrive at the correct readings in ancient manuscripts.]

**1.** *Ara* (“altar”) is written with *a* alone; *harena* (“sand”) with *h* and *a*. *Aurit* (“raises water”) is written with *a* and *u*, that is, “raises water”; *haurire* (“to see”) is written with *h*. *Aescas* [perhaps *aestas*, “summer”] is written with *a* and *e*. *Aerat*, *aequitas*, *aedes*, *Aeneas*, and *Aesculapius* are written with the diphthong. *Alite* (“with a wing”) with *a* alone. *Halitus* (“breath”) with *h*. *At*, which signifies “truly,” is written with *a* and *t*; the preposition *ad* with *a* and *d*, as in *ad amicum vado* (“I go to my friend”).

[Col. 0732B] [Note: [Col. 0732D] **2.** There is no reason, as it appears, for *apparet* to be written with two *p*’s, while *adponit* is written with *d* and *p*. Both may be written in either way. It may be questioned whether those who write *adparet* at one time and *apparet* at another are sufficiently consistent. I would certainly not dare condemn those who allow themselves this freedom, using words that are pronounced variously by approved authors—such as *seculum* and *saeculum*, *litera* and *littera*—sometimes in one spelling and sometimes in another, just as, since either form may be said, one does not sin by saying sometimes *amarunt* and sometimes *amaverunt*.]

**2.** *Assiduus* and *assecutus* are written with two *s*’s. *Accumulatus* with two *c*’s. *Aggeruus* [perhaps *aggeratus*] with two *g*’s. *Apparet* with two *p*’s; *adponit* is written with *d*, because the preposition *ad* is joined to the verb. *Ammonitus* has two *m*’s. *Annuit* and *annuntiat* have two *n*’s. *Ademptus* is written with *m* and *p*.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] **3.** The error of writing *b* for *v*, and conversely *v* for *b*, became widespread in the Middle Ages among many nations and is even now common among some Spaniards, who use and pronounce *b* and *v* interchangeably, although Antonio de Nebrija’s *Hispanist Latin Art* appropriately prescribes that the distinction should be observed.]

**3.** *Apud* is written with *p* and *d*. *Austus* [perhaps *auctus*, “increased”] is written with the diphthong, but *austio* [*auctio*, “sale”], which means “a sale” [something may be missing]. *Birtus*, *boluntas*, *bita*, and similar forms, by which Africans corrupt the spelling of *virtus*, *voluntas*, and *vita*, must be entirely rejected and written not with *b* but with *v*.

**4.** *Cedo* is written with *c*, meaning [obscurely] “I consent”; *caedes* with *a* and *e*; *caesaries*, *caelum* [perhaps *cesaries*, *celum*], *centenarius*, *ceterum*, *cere*—the word we use for “hail”—and *celeritas* with *e*. *Commentarius* has two *m*’s. *Competit* [something may be missing]. *Clangor* is written with *c*, not *g*. *Caelebs* is written with *b*; hence we say *caelibem*. *Coire* is written without *h*. *Cymbalum* is written with *y*. *Corax* is written with *c*, not *g*.

**5.** *Commentatio* is written with *c*. *Caetus*, that is, “a multitude,” with the diphthong *a* [perhaps *ae*]. *Cete*, which means “a sea monster,” with *e*. *Commercium*, which means “business,” with two *m*’s. *Clanculum* with two *c*’s. The preposition *cum* is written with *c*, but if it is an adverb, with *q*; for we say *quum lego* (“when I read”).

**6.** *Deus* is written with *e* alone. *Daemon* with the diphthong. *Dilabitur* and *disterminat* with *i*. *Dogma* with *g*, not *c*. *Delubra* with *e*, not *i*. *Dictatus* with *i*, not *e*. *Erus*, meaning “master,” with *e* alone. *Externa*, meaning “foreign,” with *e* and *x*; if it speaks of a day, with *h*. *Effecta*, *effigi* [perhaps *effingi*], *effudit*, *efficit*, and *effluit* have two *f*’s. *Erebus* is written with *e*.

**7.** *Fabor* is written with *b*. *Flagra*, which are two [perhaps “whips”], with *f* and *l*; *fragra*, which means “fragrant things,” with *f* and *r*. *Fero*, meaning “I endure,” with *e* alone. *Gerosus* [perhaps *generosus*, “noble”] with *e*. *Gaeometres* with *a* and *e*. *Gnarus*, meaning “knowing,” with *g* and *n*; *gnatus* likewise. *Grassator*, meaning “servant” [perhaps “savage”], with *g*. *Glaber*, meaning “smooth-faced,” with *b*.

**8.** *Haec*, the pronoun, is written with *h* and the diphthong *ae*, and all pronouns with *h*, except possessive, subjunctive, and relative pronouns. For whenever we place the conjunction syllable *ac*, we write it with *a*, so that the conjunction may be distinguished from the preposition. *Hic*, the pronoun, is written in the same way as the adverb of place; but they differ in that we pronounce the adverb of place with a lengthened syllable, and the pronoun with a shortened one. *Hiat* and *honor* are written with *h*; *onus* with *o*. *Haud*, meaning “not,” with *h* and *d*; the conjunction [is written] with silent *t*. *Hausit*, meaning “he drank,” with *h*. *Hisco*, meaning “the opening of the mouth,” with *h*. *Heremus*, *hispidus*, and *hereos* [perhaps *heros*, “hero”] are written with *h*, as are any similar words requiring aspiration.

[Note: [Col. 0733C] **9.** There are still some who approve this spelling: *inmaculatus*, *inmortalis*, and so on.]

**9.** *Impedit*, *impius*, *immanitas*, *immemor*, and *imperator* are written with two *m*’s [something may be missing]; likewise *inmaculatus* and *inmortalis* with *i* and *n*, because when the preposition *in* is added, it either completes or empties [the following word]. *Irritum* has two *r*’s. The *t* must be placed at the end of *inquit*, for if it has *d*, it is a question, as if one were to say, “Into what does he send?” The pronoun *id* is written with *d*.

### 505

**10.** *Karitas*, *Kalendae*, and any similar nouns that follow *a* and *c* [sic] are to be written with *k*. *Laetus* with the diphthong *ae*; *laethalis*, meaning “mortal,” likewise with *ae*. *Levare*, meaning “to assist,” with *e*. *Lixa*, meaning “low” or “luxurious,” is written with *i* and *x*. *Mecum*, meaning “I and you,” with *e* alone; *moechum*, meaning “an adulterous man,” and *moenia* with *o* and *e*. *Mussitas* has two *s*’s. *Mos* and *mors* are likewise to be written as they are. *Mysterium* is written with Greek *y*.

[Note: [Col. 0733C] **11.** *Notus*, meaning “the south wind,” is also written without *h*; *nothus*, meaning “illegitimate,” with *h*.]

**11.** *Nexae*, meaning “joined” [read “bound together”], is written with *x*; but when we say *nec fecerit* (“nor will he have done”), it is written with *c*. *Nanctus* is written with *n* and *c* in the middle. *Naenia* with *a* and *e*. *Nomenculator*, meaning “one who calls a name,” with *c* and *u*. *Notus* with *t* alone; *nothus*, meaning “the south wind,” with *h*.

**12.** *Ostium*, which is opened and closed, is written with *o*; *hostia* with *h*. *Occipitium*, which is the back part of the head, with two *c*’s. *Occulum* [perhaps *occultum*, “hidden”] with two *c*’s. *Obpilat* with *b* and *p*. *Offendit*, *offulsit*, *officiat*, and *officium* with two *f*’s. *Occursa* with two *c*’s. *Oppulit* and *opperior* with two *p*’s. *Osores*, meaning “those who exercise hatred,” with *o*. *Olympum* with Greek *y*.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **13.** I do not know what is concealed in the words *presum* and *prestant*. Compare no. 27.]

**13.** *Paenis* is written with the diphthong *ae*; *poena* and *poenitudo* with *o* and *e*. *Peculatus*, meaning “theft of property,” with *e* alone. *Penum*, meaning “a storeroom,” with *e*. *Precator*, *presum*, meaning “companion,” and *pretestant* with *e*. *Praecipuus* and *praevius* with *a* and *e*. *Quum* with *q*, because it is not the preposition governing an ablative, but an adverb. *Quae*, when preposed or when it is a feminine pronoun, is written with the diphthong; *que*, when it is a conjunction, as in *fecitque* (“and he did”), with *e* alone. *Quaerit* with the diphthong *ae*; *quaeque* with the original diphthong, while the final syllable has *e* alone. *Quod*, the neuter pronoun, is written with *d*; when it refers to number, with *t*, for we say *quot panes* (“how many loaves”) or *quot pisces* (“how many fish”). *Quassat* with two *s*’s. *Revehit* with *h*.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **14.** For *studei*, *istud* should perhaps be read. See no. 30. Other passages occur throughout that require correction.]

**14.** *Reus* is written with *e* alone; *raeda* with *a* and *e*; *seminat* with *e* alone. Similar words lack *y*. *Studei* is written with *i* and *s*. *Suppetit* has two *p*’s, just as *succedit* has two *c*’s. *Sosyma* [*sophysma*] with Greek *y*. *Scapham* with *p* and *h*. *Scropulam* with *p*, not *b*. *Suggerit* with two *g*’s. *Succumbit* with two *c*’s. *Syrtes* with *y*. *Suggestus* with two *g*’s, like *successus* with two *c*’s. *Severitas* with *e* alone. *Taedet* with *a* and *e*. *Thema*, meaning “matter,” with *t* and *h*. *Vae*, a monosyllable, with the diphthong, as in *vae misero mihi* (“alas for wretched me”). *Subjunctiva* is written with *e* alone. *Volumptas* with *m* and *p*.

[Col. 0734B] **15.** *Xerras*, *Xenophontes*, and *Xenium* are to be written with *x*. *Ylion*, *Ydros*, *Yterius*, and so forth are written with *y* [or are to be written so]. The letter *z* was admitted because of foreign names; with it one writes *Zelans*, *Zabulon*, *Zoticus*, *Zenon*, and the rest.

## GLOSSARY ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WORDS

### From Codex Vaticanus 6018

[Note: [Col. 0733D] **16.** In *Isidoriana*, chapter 56, no. 21, I discussed this work, where I showed that *Agroecius* seems to be read with *o* and *e*, not with *y*, as some think. My conjecture at no. 25 was also that the subject is Agroecus, a comedy by Plautus; from that word perhaps arose the invention of some author named Agroecius or Agroetius.]

**16.** *Acrocius* is written with *c* and *o*, not *y*, as some think. In *ad illum vado* (“I go to him”) and *ad me venit* (“he comes to me”), *ad* is written with *d*. *Assiduus* and *assecutus* are written with two *s*’s, so that the preposition may not be joined to the noun [perhaps “because the preposition is not joined to the noun”]. *Accommodus* has two *c*’s. *Aggestus* has two *g*’s. The same applies to similar words. *Ammonitus* has two *m*’s. *Annuit* has two *n*’s. *Atque* has *t*, not *d*. *Ademtus* is written without *p*, because they think the letter *m* can suffice. The same applies to the rest. *Aequus*, when it concerns equity, is written with *a*; *equus*, when it concerns animals, without *a*.

[Col. 0734C] [Note: [Col. 0733D] **17.** Not *d* and *s*, but, etc. Perhaps read “not *o* and *s*, but, etc.” The Codex is Vaticanus 6018, not Regiovaticanus, as had been printed in the note to no. 29, chapter 27 of the *Etymologies*. It belongs approximately to the tenth century. At the beginning is a glossary that someone believed to be Isidorian, but Lucas Holstenius notes that it is plainly different from Isidore’s. It begins: “*Abstrusa*, hidden,” etc. Another work on grammar follows: “We have heard many,” etc. “The letter *A*,” etc. Then *On the Letter*, from the book of Donatus: “A letter is an element of speech,” etc. After other glossaries and an epact with figures comes the work that I now publish. On the first page a large cross is painted, bearing on both sides this inscription: “In the name of the Most High God begins the book of the glosses [the manuscript has *glossemate* for *glossemata*] of Saint Isidore the Bishop, On the Difference between Words. This standard of the cross shines in heaven; now it saves us through the upright wood.” It begins: “*Acrocius* with *c*,” etc. Another little work follows, entitled “Here begins the synonymy of Cicero’s words: *tenebo*, I shall hold; *possidebo*, I shall possess; *obtinebo*, I shall obtain,” etc. It ends: “*Emissarius*, raider. The synonyms of Cicero are complete; amen, successfully.” Immediately afterward: “Here begins the book of the Chronicles of Saint Isidore the Bishop: *Breve temporum*,” etc. As I think, this work too, *On the Difference between Words*, having been collected as if from Cicero’s works, was attributed by the scribe to our Isidore. Other fragments and little works of Saints Damasus, Jerome, and Augustine are found in the same Codex.]

**17.** If the word *apostolus* (“apostle”) must be divided into syllables, it should not be divided between *d* and *s*, but the *s* and *t* should remain joined. The same applies to *constans* and the rest, whenever it comes before the letter *t* [perhaps, “whenever the letter *s* comes before *t*”]. *Apud* was written with *d*. *Aras* with *a*. *Harena* (“sand”), *hauri* (“draw water”), *halitus* (“breath”)—all these with *h*. *Aures* (“ears”), from hearing, without *h*. *Araem* [perhaps *aera*, “bronzes”], *aescas* [perhaps *aestas*, “summer”], *aequor* (“sea”), *aetas* (“age”), *aesus* [perhaps *aestus*, “heat”], *aedis* (“temple”), and *Aeneas* are all written with *a* and *e*.

### 507

**18.** *At*, which signifies “truly,” was written with *a* and *t*. The preposition *ad* governing the accusative, as in *ad amicum vado* (“I go to my friend”). *Aliter* [perhaps *alitus* or *alitur*] with *a* alone. *Accumulatus* with two *c*’s. *Apparet* with two *p*’s. *Adpomo* [perhaps *adpono*] with *d*, because the preposition *ad* is joined to the verb. *Ammonuit* and *ammonitus* with two *m*’s. *Annuit* and *annustra* [sic] with two *n*’s. *Ademptus* with *m* and *p*. *Auctio*, meaning “sale,” requires *e*. *Aggestus* with two *g*’s, meaning [something is perhaps missing] “greedy.”

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **19.** The words *quod est negotium* (“which means business”) seem to stand in the wrong place after *quum lego*; nevertheless it is not sufficiently clear whether *quod est negotium* should be read.]

**19.** *Cedo*, meaning “concession”; *cementarius*; *ceterum*; *cere*; *celeritas*; and *celebs* with *b* [perhaps written with *e*]. *Caesaries*, *caelum*, and *caetus*, meaning “a multitude,” are written with *a* and *e*. *Cete*, meaning “a sea monster,” is likewise written with *a* and *e*. *Cepit*, from “taking,” is written with *e*; *coepit*, from “beginning,” with *o* [perhaps *o* and *e*]. *Commentarium* with two *m*’s. *Commestio* [perhaps *commercium*], meaning “business,” with two *m*’s. *Clangor* with *c*. *Competens* with *m*. *Coire* without *h*. *Cymbalum* and *cymbala* with Greek *y*. *Commercium* and *caput* are written with *c*. *Clanculus* with two *c*’s. The preposition *cum* governing the ablative was written [or written by them] with *c*; if it is an adverb, with *q*, for we say *quum lego*, meaning “when I read,” which means “business” [the final gloss is probably misplaced].

**20.** *Deus* is written with *e* alone; *daemon* with *a* and *e*. *Dogma* with *g*, not *c*. *Dilabitur* and *disterminat* with *i*. *Delubra* with *e*, not *i*. *Dixistis* with three *i*’s. *Erus*, meaning “master,” with *e* alone. *Externa*, meaning “foreign,” with *e* and *x*; if we speak of the previous day, *hesterna* is written with *h* [perhaps *h* and *s*]. *Effectus* with two *f*’s. *Exemptus* with *m* and *p*. *Essentia* with two *s*’s. *Effosa*, *effecit*, *effodit*, *effugi*, and *effluit* with two *f*’s.

**21.** *Fedus*, meaning “deformed,” with *e* alone; *foedus*, meaning “a judgment of peace,” with *o* and *e*. *Fabor* was written with *f*; hence also *faber Deus* (“God the craftsman”). *Fabis* [sic] with *v*, meaning “fruits.” *Flagra*, which are whips, with *f* and *l*; *fragra*, which are fragrant things, with *f* and *r*. *Fero*, meaning “I endure,” with *f* alone.

**22.** *Gerolus* was written with *e* alone. *Gnarus*, meaning “knowing,” with *g* and *n*. *Gnatus*, meaning “son,” with *g* and *n*. *Grassator*, meaning “robber,” with *g*. *Glaber*, meaning “smooth-faced,” with *b*. *Gryphes*, not *gryphi*. *Haec*, the pronoun, is written with *h*, *a*, and *e*, for *h* is written with all pronouns except possessive, subjunctive, and relative pronouns. Whenever we place the conjunction syllable *ac*, it is written with *a* alone, so that the conjunction may be distinguished from the preposition [perhaps “from the pronoun”]. *Hic*, the pronoun, is written like the adverb of place; but they differ in that we pronounce the adverb of place with a lengthened syllable and the pronoun with a shortened one. *Hiat* and *honos* with *h*; *onus* with *o*. *Haud*, meaning “not,” with *h* and *d*, with the mute letter placed last. *Hausit*, meaning “he drank,” with *h*. *Hisco*, meaning “I open the mouth,” with *h*. *Heremus* with *h*. *Hispidus* with *h*. *Heroes* with *h*. The same applies to any similar words requiring aspiration. *Hactenus* is written with *h* and *e*.

**23.** *Impedit*, *impius*, *immemor*, *imperator*, *impendit*, *implet*, and *immanitas* were all written with *m*. *Inmaculatus*, *inmortalis*, and *innocens* with *n*. The *t* must be placed at the end of *inquit*; for if it has *d*, it is a question, as if one were to say, “Into what does he send?” *Id*, the pronoun, was written with *d*. *It*, the verb, was written with *t*. *Ideo* [something is missing]. *Irritum* with two *r*’s. *Karitas*, *Kaput*, *Kalendae*, and any nouns following *a* and *c* [perhaps “*a* after *c*”] are written with *k*.

**24.** *Laetus*, *laesus*, *laetitia*, and *laeva*, meaning “left,” are all written with *a* and *e*. *Lethalis*, also called “mortal,” is written with *e* alone. *Levare*, meaning “to assist,” with *e* alone; that which is “low” [a noun is missing, namely *lixa], or “luxurious,” is written with *i* and *x*. *Mecum* with *e* and *c*. *Moechum*, meaning “adultery” [perhaps “adulterer”], with *o* and *e*. *Mos* and *mors* are simply to be written as they are. *Mysterium* with Greek *y*.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **25.** This little work and the preceding one have much in common, including the same errors, such as what is said above about *notus* and *nothus*, in no. 11.]

**25.** *Nexae*, meaning “bound together,” is written with *x*. *Nanctus* with *n* and *c*. *Naenia* with *a* and *e*. *Nomenculator* [something is missing]. *Nubo* and *nubit* with *b*. *Nupsit* with *p*. The vocative of *nomen* is written with *c* and *v*. *Notus*, meaning “known,” is written with *t*; *nothus*, meaning “the south wind,” with *t* and *h*.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **26.** The manuscripts read “of adversaries . . . of sacrifice.”]

**26.** *Ostium*, which is opened and closed, is written with *o* alone; *hostium*, referring to adversaries, with *h* and *o*; *hostia*, referring to sacrifice, likewise with *h* and *o*. *Occipitium*, the back part of the head, with two *c*’s. *Olympus* with Greek *y*. *Obpilat* with *b* and *p*. *Offendit*, *officium*, *offulsit*, and *officit* with two *f*’s. *Occultum* with two *c*’s. *Opplet* with two *p*’s. *Occurrat* with two *c*’s. *Opperior* with two *p*’s. *Osores*, meaning “those who exercise hatred,” was written with pure *o*.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] **27.** *Pressum* could be read instead of *presum*, but the explanation “which means eaten” suggests that *presum* stands for *peresum*, as if by syncopation. For *prestut*, it may be useful to read *prensat*, *prester*, or *pressat*.]

**27.** *Paenes* and *paenitudo* are written with *a* and *e*. *Poena* with *o* and *e*. *Peculatus*, meaning “theft of property,” with *e*. *Penum*, meaning “storeroom,” with pure *e*. *Praecipuus*, *praecisus*, and *praemium* are all written with *a* and *e*. *Precatur*, *presum*, meaning “eaten,” *prestat*, *presbyter*, and all such forms are written without *a*.

**28.** *Qur* was written with *q*. *Quum* was written with *q*, because it is not a preposition governing the ablative, but an adverb. *Quae*, when preposed or when it is a feminine pronoun, is written with the diphthong. *Quaeque*, however, is written with *a* and *e*, the final syllable with *e* alone. *Quod*, the neuter pronoun, was written with *d*; when it refers to a neuter number [perhaps “to number of the neuter gender”], this syllable is written with *t* [many words may be excessive here]. We say *quod scrinium* (“which chest”), *quod nomen* (“which name”), written with *d*. *Quot petens* [perhaps “asking how many”], as in *quot pisces* (“how many fish”). The former belongs to number, the latter to the neuter gender: the latter is written with *d*, the former with *t*. *Quassat* has two *s*’s.

[Col. 0736C] **29.** *Religio* is so called because it binds (*religit*, perhaps *religat*) souls to divine worship. *Reus* is written with *e* alone. *Reda* [perhaps *rhaeda*] was written with *a* and *e*.

[Note: [Col. 0736D] **30.** Instead of *scena*, the author of this little work may have written *scina*, since *e* was formerly easily changed into *i*. I do not see, however, why it is mentioned here, since the beginning of the word is *i*, not *s*, unless perhaps some people then wrote *stud* for *istud*. The Greek *y* should be rejected from *sophisma* and *sophista*, as is prescribed in the preceding work. The preceding little work has *scropulam* instead of *stupulum*, and perhaps *scrupulus* should be read.]

**30.** *Saevit*, *saepe*, and *saeries* are written with *a* and *e*. *Semel*, *semina*, and *severitas* with *e* alone. *Spissa*, *scena*, *stimulus*, and similar words lack *y*. *Istud* is written with *i* and *s*, and ends in *d*. *Suppetit* has two *p*’s. *Succedit*, *succubuit*, and *successus* have two *c*’s. *Sophysma* and *Sophysta* are written with Greek *y*. *Suggerit* with two *g*’s. *Scapha* with *p* and *h*. *Stupulum* with *p*, not *b*. *Syrtes* was written with *y*. *Suffectus* has two *f*’s. *Successus* has two *c*’s. *Severitas* [perhaps *serenitas*] with *e* alone. *Saerites* with *a* and *e*.

**31.** *Taedet* is written with *a* and *e*. *Thema*, meaning “matter,” with *t* and *h*. *Vae*, expressing grief, as in *vae misero mihi* (“alas for wretched me”), with *a* and *e*. *Subjunctivum* with *e* alone, as in *casusve*, *deusve*. Write *vafrum*, not *fabrum* [perhaps *bafrum*]. *Vultus* has two *v*’s. *Volunt* is written with *v*, not *u*. *Volumptas* with *m* and *p*.

**32.** *Xerxes*, *Xenophontes*, and *Xenium* are written with *x*. *Z* was admitted because of obscure foreign names [or “because it is foreign to names”]; with it one writes *zona*, *zelus*, and similar words, for *z* is a double Greek letter.

[Col. 0737A] Fragment from the Albanian Codex.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] **33.** This fragment too, found in the aforementioned Albanian Codex, can be referred to the same orthographic subject, although it largely contains other grammatical controversies. Even in these, however, we should not follow the author’s opinion without caution.]

**33.** One should say *somnio* (“I dream”), not *somnior*, and *somniavi* (“I dreamed”), not *somniatus sum*. One should say *illud scamnum* (“that bench”), not *ipsud*, but *ipsum*. *Pauper vir* (“a poor man”) and *mulier pauper* (“a poor woman”), not *paupera*; *baculum hoc* (“this staff”), not *hunc*. *Balnea* and *balneas*, not *balneum*. *Clunes hae* (“these buttocks”), not *hi*.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] **34.** Perhaps *ficedulae* should be read instead of *ficidulae*, and shortly afterward *coturnices* instead of *cotturnices*. In *coturnix*, the first syllable is more often shortened. The *querquedula* appears especially in cold and wintry weather; therefore some think it was named from *querquerus*, that is, “cold.”]

**34.** *Ficidulae*, not *ficedulae*, that is [perhaps “because of this”], because they eat figs; similarly *querquedulae* from *quercus* (“oak”) [perhaps from *querquerus*]. *Cotturnices*, not *coturnices*. *Arbor* denotes every kind of wood; *arbos* only a fruit-bearing tree.

**35.** *Hora* means the hours of the day; *ora*, boundaries. *Pignera* are pledges of things; *pignora*, pledges of children. *Columbae* are doves that can be tamed and accustomed to houses; *palumbes* are wild and inhabit rocks and forests. *Rubor* is the color red; *robur*, strength. *Veniunt* is like *vendunt* (“they sell”); *veneunt* is like *venduntur* (“they are sold”) [the two *quasi*’s are unclear, and *veniunt* is written instead of *veneunt*]. *Dilectum* comes from *diligere* (“to love”); *electum* from *eligere* (“to choose”); *delictum* from sinning [perhaps from *delinquere*, “to sin”].

**36.** We say *pinnas* of walls, *pennas* of birds. “Every animal is *pecus*, except man” [six corrupt words follow], they said in this manner. *Culleus*, *pluteus*, *latens* [perhaps *lacus*], *cuneus*, *laqueus*, *postis*, *margo*, *veper*, or *vepris* are masculine.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] **37.** Some further material is added concerning the distinction between *hic sol* (“this sun”), *has sales* (“these jokes”), and *hos sales* (“these salty men/things”), but it is so corrupt that I judged it should be omitted entirely.]

**37.** *Carbo*, *axis*, *modius*, *sextarius*, *congius*, *orbis*, *gladius*, *sanguis*, *venter*, and *aqualiculus* are masculine; likewise *restis*, *flos*, and *pons* [some corrupt words follow]. *Radius* is masculine, not neuter *radium*.

## APPENDIX IV  
### To Book III, Chapter 9, of the *Etymologies*, from Codex Ottobonianus 6

## ALSO ON ISIDORE’S NUMBERS

[Note: [Col. 0737D] **Appendix IV, no. 1.** I described Codex Ottobonianus 6, from which these few passages concerning numbers are attributed to Isidore, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 105, nos. 2 and 3. Nothing else occurs that seems especially worthy of note.]

**1.** Cardinal numbers are such as one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and the rest in sequence.

**2.** Ordinal numbers are such as first, second, third, fourth.

**3.** Adverbial numbers are such as once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, six times.

**4.** Distributive numbers [the term is obscure] are such as singly, in pairs, in threes, in fours, in fives, in sixes, in sevens.

**5.** Ponderal numbers are such as single, double, triple, quadruple.

**6.** Denunciative numbers are such as alone, the other, or another.

**7.** There are also multiplicative numerical forms, such as simple, double, triple, and so forth; but these nouns are known to belong to three genders.

**8.** There are likewise adverbial forms arising from these, such as simply, doubly, triply.

## APPENDIX V  
### To Book IV of the *Etymologies*, Chapter 4: Specimen of an Interpolation, from Codex Chisianus

[Note: [Col. 0737D] **Appendix V, no. 1.** In this specimen of an interpolation in the Chisian Codex, the author wished to indicate the peculiar way in which medical matters are explained. In that Codex, after the final words of chapter 4 of Book IV of the *Etymologies*, the following occurs: “The logicians add reasoning,” etc.]

**1.** The logicians add the reasoning and particular causes of the foregoing. Letter concerning Asclepius. Asclepius, or Aesculapius, having been born a boy as the son of Apollo by Coronis, the daughter of Flavia, was handed over to the Centaur Cero to acquire medical knowledge, etc. A letter concerning Hippocrates follows. Hippocrates’ lineage derives from Asclepius; on his father’s side he was born of Heraclides, etc.

**2.** A chapter follows entitled: “That not every human nature is suited to receiving instruction.” Also: “What sort of person a student of medicine ought to be.” Also: “On the physician’s entering the sick person.” Also: “How the physician should visit the sick person.” Also: “On the names of philosophers who wrote medical books.”

**3.** A discussion of medical books follows, or Book 10 from the editions. Then follows: “Why medicine is not included among the liberal arts,” or chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 0738D] **4.** On *esinamidia*. This passage seems corrupt. I restored *criticus* in place of *creticus*.]

**4.** A letter of Galen concerning the nature of the human body follows. Galen’s second letter concerning the effects of pigments and concerning their *esinamidia*. Then follows: “That every quality and power of the four elements is demonstrated in four ways.” A discussion of scents and ointments follows, or chapter 12, then one concerning physicians’ instruments, or chapter 11. Then follows: “Whence the term *Criticus* is derived. A day is called *Criticus*,” etc. Chapter 9 follows.

5. Chapter 5 follows, but plainly altered; then [the text treats] the four seasons of the year, the fourfold division of the human body, the ages of life, the four corners of the head, and the resources of the human body; the components of the eye, diseases of the eyes, cataracts, health and disease, and the sources from which they flow—namely, chapter 5 beginning with the words “health” and continuing to “phlegm.” To these words the following is added: “And by these things the healthy are governed, and from them the sick are made so”; the healthy are governed if they remain according to the course of nature; whenever something occurs beyond the course of nature, they produce illnesses.

[Note: [Col. 0738D] 6. Vindician’s letter to Pentadius also occurs in other old manuscript codices.]

6. The discussion of the four humors and the reasons for their names follows—that is, the same chapter 5, from the words “whether, however, four” to the end of the chapter. Chapter 6 follows, then chapters 7 and 8 under a single title: “On chronic diseases.” Then follows Vindician’s letter to his nephew Pentadius on the nature of each kind of body; likewise, a letter on the functioning of the abdomen and internal organs; Galen’s book on pulses; his book on urine; Hippocrates’ book of signs; and Galen’s letter on phlebotomy.

## APPENDIX VI

To Book V, chapter 36, of the *Etymologies*.

### ON THE INDICTION

From the Albanian Codex.

[Col. 0738C]

[Note: [Col. 0738D] APP. VI, n. 1. Although in the Albanian Codex this fragment on the indiction is inserted after Book I, chapter 34, its proper place is nevertheless in Book V, chapter 36. It was written in the same hand as the book of the *Etymologies*, or perhaps in one slightly older. Others have a different view of the indiction and do not attribute such great antiquity to it. Compare Du Cange, under the word *Indictio*.]

1. “Indiction” (*indictio*) is so called as though from *valde dictio*, “a very great declaration.” For after Octavian Augustus had subjected the whole world, he divided it into three parts, namely Europe, Asia, and Africa. Then he ordered every person throughout the whole world, and throughout the three regions of the earth, to pay a census-tax for the support of the state.

2. This first levy was instituted so that every person might pay tribute to Caesar. From a child of seven years up to an old man with white hair, every person paid a coin to Caesar in honor of the state. This first levy was imposed in Europe for five years, and for five years the tribute was conveyed to Rome (perhaps “to the city of Rome”), and the city of Rome was illuminated with lamps.

[Col. 0739A]

[Note: [Col. 0739C] 3. Isidore says this—specifically, in chapter 6 of *On the Nature of Things*, though not in the same words: “The lustrum,” says Isidore, “is a period of five years among the Romans. It is called a lustrum because the census was conducted for five years in the state. Then, after the census had been completed and a sacrifice performed, the city of Rome was purified.”]

3. That year was called a *lustrum*. Isidore says of it: “Among the Romans, a lustrum is called a period of five years, because the census was paid to the state over a five-year period” (perhaps, “because the census was collected”). Hence, after the census had been completed, the city of Rome was illuminated. In the sixth year the census was collected from Africa, specifically over a period of five years; then in the fifth year the tribute was again delivered in Rome, and that year was called a *lustrum*.

[Note: [Col. 0739C] 4. The manuscript had “through all five years”; I have restored “through three times five years.” In this fragment the use of the ablative for the accusative is observed more than once. I do not recall where Macrobius uttered the words attributed to him concerning the indiction. The earlier Latins, it seems, called it an *indiction* when something was publicly announced as payable outside the ordinary course and anew.]

4. In the eleventh year the levy went to Asia, and the census was collected for five-year periods for Caesar. When the five years had been completed, in the fifteenth year the census was again poured into the treasury of the Capitol, and that year was called an *indiction*, because the census was collected for three periods of five years from the three parts of the world. For this reason the indiction does not proceed beyond fifteen years; and when fifteen years have been completed, another indiction begins. Macrobius says of this: “Indiction is called the collection of the state”—that is, the census of the whole world was completed in the city of Rome; and then, after the fifteen years had been completed, the city of Rome was illuminated for seven days.

## APPENDIX VII

To Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 39.

### CONTINUATION OF THE ISIDORIAN CHRONICLE

From the Chisian Codex.

[Col. 0739B]

[Note: [Col. 0739C] APP. VII, n. 1. Isidore’s *Chronicle*, inserted in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, is sometimes found continued in manuscript codices beyond his own time, as appears from the specimen that I present from the Chisian Codex. In the Ottobonian Codex the *Chronicle* is also interpolated toward the end: “In the fourteenth year of his reign Heraclius subdued Judaea. The Spaniards became Christians,” and so forth. More is added concerning the restoration of the cross in the time of Heraclius. It continues and ends: “Anastasius, who was also called Artemius, in the second year. Theodosius for one year. The remaining period of the sixth age is known to God alone. The seventh book ends. The eighth begins, on the Old and New Testament.” Evidently a different order of books is preserved, unlike that of the printed editions.

“In Codex Ottobonianus 477 the *Chronicle* is likewise interpolated, as follows: ‘Diocletian, in the twentieth year. He . . . did this; and he was the first to put gems on garments. In his time the Theban legion was killed . . . . He persecutes Christians throughout the whole world; he orders all church temples to be destroyed to the ground. Later, Benedict, teacher of monks, became renowned . . . . Heraclius is in the seventeenth year of his reign. In his fifth year, and in the fourth year of the most devout prince Sisebut, the Jews in Spain became Christians, and the Persians were defeated by the Romans. V. DCCCLXVI. Likewise, Heraclius with his mother,’ and so forth. It continues to: ‘Leubrandus, king of the Lombards, transferred the bones of Saint Augustine from Sardinia to Ticinum and buried them with great honor. V. DCCCCXLIX. The remaining period of the sixth age is known to God alone.’

“The Regiovatican Chronicle 112 ends: ‘D. DCCCIV. Phocas, in the seventh year. The Romans are slaughtered by the Persians. V. DCCCXXXI. Heraclius, in the twenty-seventh year . . . . In his fifth year, and in the fourth year of the most devout prince Sisebut, the Jews in Spain become Christians. The remaining period of the sixth age, and so forth, up to the tenth year of the present glorious prince Reccesuinth, which is year DCLXVI of the era, V. DCCCLVII.’

“Codex Regiovanicanus 1953, in which the *Chronicle* is written in Roman capital letters, reads as follows: ‘Phocas, VII. V. DCCCVII. The Romans are slaughtered by the Persians. Heraclius, VII. He is in his tenth year, V. DCCCXXIIII. The Jews in Spain, and so forth. The tenth year of Reccesuinth, which is year DCLXVI of the era, V. DCCCLVII.’

“Codex Vaticanus 624: ‘V. DCCCV. Phocas, in the eighth year. The Romans are slaughtered by the Persians . . . . Heraclius, in the twenty-sixth year. In his fifth year, and so forth, up to the present tenth year of the glorious prince Reccesuinth, which is year DCXCVI of the era, V. DCCCXXXII.’

“Palatinus 281: ‘Phocas, in the eighth year. The Romans are slaughtered by the Persians. V. DCCCVI . . . . Heraclius, in the thirty-second year. In his fifth year, and so forth.’ It has nothing else distinctive.

“Palatinus 282: ‘Heraclius, in the twenty-seventh year,’ and so forth, up to the tenth year of the glorious Reccesuinth, which is year DCXCVI of the era, V. DCCCL I.

“Palatinus 283 agrees with Reg. 112, but has year DCLXVI of the era and, at the same time, V. DCCCCLVIII.

“Urbinas 100: ‘Phocas, in the seventh year. The Romans are slaughtered by the Persians. DCCCI’ (so). ‘Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, whose fame’s splendor penetrated the whole world,’ and so forth. Much is inserted concerning the conversion of the Britons. It ends: ‘From the fellowship of pagan depravity. DCCCXXII’ (so). ‘Heraclius, in the twenty-seventh year . . . . V. DCCCXXII.’

“Urbinas 474: ‘Phocas, in the eighth year . . . . V. DCCCVIII. Heraclius is in his twenty-seventh year. The Jews,’ and so forth, ‘V. DCCCXXXIII . . . . up to the present year, which is year DCXCVI of the era, V. DCCCLVII.’ This is how I read it. In the codex it reads: ‘Which is the era in years 5857696.’”]

1. Theodosius, in the fourth year. Theotonia received the grace of baptism. Leo, in the sixteenth year. In his time the crown of Greece fell to Italy. The Lombards held it. Charles Martel conquered the Gauls. His son Pippin sat with his father. At the request of Pope Stephen, he came to Italy and, by freeing the Church and the Romans from the yoke of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, became patrician of the Romans.

2. Charles the Great, in the forty-sixth year. At the request of Pope Adrian, he came to Italy, conquered the Lombards, captured their king Desiderius, and received the imperial crown upon the altar of Saint Peter. Then he hastened with a large army to Greece to claim the right to the crown. The emperor of Constantinople, fearing him, then made a pact with him and arranged that each should be called the other’s brother and that they should jointly possess the empire.

3. Louis I, in the thirty-seventh year. He greatly honored the Church. Lothair, in the fifteenth year. At that time Harald, king of the Danes, received baptism. Gaul appointed a king for itself. Louis II, in the seventeenth year. He held the territory as far as Tharum [uncertain]. Charles II, in the second year. Charles III, in the fourth year. Charles IV, in the second year. These three accomplished nothing worthy of remembrance.

4. Aniubous, in the second year. Arnulf reigned for seven years. Then Cendebubous, the illegitimate son of Arnulf, reigned for one year; but he did not receive the imperial crown. He is said to have struck Bishop Agrippinus, or the bishop of Cologne, with a staff. Louis the Child, in the third year, the brother on his father’s side of Cendebubous; and he was the last of the Carolingian line.

5. Conrad I reigned for sixteen years. He subdued the Illyrian sea and the Italians. Henry I, in the seventeenth year. He wished to bear the imperial crown. Otto I, in the forty-sixth year. On the day of holy Easter, after he had judged that a certain soldier ought to be killed without prior legal proceedings, the condemned soldier leapt upon him and, throwing him to the ground, would have strangled him had the soldiers not rescued the king. The king later pardoned that soldier and confessed that, because he had denied him justice, he had justly received such contempt from the Lord.

6. Otto II, in the twenty-sixth year. When the Italians broke the peace that he had imposed upon them and began wars among themselves, he returned to Italy in anger. Having summoned the nobles and counts of Italy before Rome, he ordered their heads to be placed before him among the dishes. Otto III, emperor, in the nineteenth year. Henry II, in the seventeenth year. He is said to have remained a virgin, and to have built a thousand churches.

7. Conrad II, in the eighth year. Henry III, in the seventeenth year. Henry IV, in the fiftieth year. He was born in a place called Guebelinger, and this is the surname of all the Henries. While he was oppressing the Italians and Germans with excessive ferocity, despoiling and selling churches, he was anathematized by Pope Gregory VII. Against him, Rudolf the Saxon was appointed emperor, and the imperial crown was transferred to him; upon it this verse was inscribed:

> The Rock gave [the crown] to Peter, Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf.

Rudolf was killed in the war that he had begun, and thus the victorious Henry remained excommunicated.

8. Henry V, son of the aforesaid [Henry], in the eighteenth year. While he was wearing the crown in the City, Robert Guiscard—who during the disturbance that had arisen in the empire against Henry, his father, had occupied the kingdom of Sicily with his brothers—dared to set fire to the Lateran gate. This Henry captured Pope Paschal, who later rebuilt the Church of the Four Saints, which Robert Guiscard had destroyed.

[Col. 0741B]

9. Lothair, of the Saxon race and not descended from the Carolingians, ruled as emperor for twelve years. At that time there was a schism in the Church and in the empire: two popes were made, Innocent and Anacletus; and Conrad, of the imperial line, fought against Lothair. King Roger was then crowned. Conrad III, of the Carolingian line and uncle of the emperor Frederick, in the twelfth year.

[Note: [Col. 0741C] 10. Frederick II was elected emperor in the year 1212. See Petavius, *De ratione temporum*, concerning the varied fortunes of the succession of the Western Empire.]

10. Frederick I, emperor, in the thirty-sixth year. He destroyed Milan, had a dispute with Pope Alexander, and died overseas. Henry VI, in the eleventh year. He recovered the kingdom of Sicily. Otto IV, in the seventh year. He was deposed by Innocent, and Frederick II was elevated in his place; he is now emperor.

## APPENDIX VIII

To Book VI, chapter 17, of the *Etymologies*.

### THE CAESAREAN SYNOD ON EASTER

[Note: [Col. 0741D] APP. VIII, n. 1. In the year of Christ 198, or thereabouts, a council was held in Palestine, or at Caesarea, which Theophilus, metropolitan bishop of Caesarea, convened on the authority of Victor, bishop of Rome. A truly golden fragment of it, as Labbe calls it, survives in Bede’s work on the spring equinox, and thence in Baronius and in the work cited by Labbe, volume I of the *Councils*, column 596. The acts of this same council, differing considerably from those presented by Bede, have been preserved in many very ancient copies of the *Etymologies*, perhaps inserted there by Isidore himself—namely, in the Albanian Codex, in the more recent Malatesti Codex, in Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive, and in Ottobonianus 122. Muratori also published the same acts in volume III of the *Anecdota*, in a work on computation. In Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive the prologue is omitted. The more recent Malatesti Codex, like the Albanian, begins: “After the resurrection,” and so forth. The Ottobonian Codex begins with the words: “When all the apostles.” In the Albanian Codex it read “that it was good”; in the Malatesti Codex, “that it is good.”]

1. After the resurrection or ascension of the Lord and Savior, the apostles could establish nothing concerning how Easter ought to be observed, because they were scattered and occupied throughout the whole world. When all the apostles had passed from this world, different fasts were practiced throughout the world. All Gaul observed Easter on one day of the year, namely 8 Kalends of April [25 March], saying: “What have we to do with observing Easter according to the reckoning of the moon together with the Jews?”

[Note: [Col. 0742C] 2. In the Albanian Codex: “just as,” with *sed* (“but”) omitted. The Ottobonian Codex omits *venisset* (“had come”) after “the fourteenth moon.”]

2. But just as the Lord’s Nativity is observed on 8 Kalends of January [25 December], regardless of the day on which it falls, so also we ought to observe Easter on 8 Kalends of April, when Christ’s resurrection is said to have occurred. The Easterners, however, as the history of Eusebius of Caesarea relates, celebrated Easter on whatever day of March the fourteenth moon had come.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 3. In the Albanian Codex, *celebrabant* (“they celebrated”) occurs instead of *jej u n a b a n t* (“they fasted”). In the Ottobonian Codex, *concluditur* (“it is concluded”) occurs instead of *conditus dicitur* (“is said to have been created”), although the latter reading itself is obscure in the Albanian Codex. The Malatesti Codex generally agrees with the Ottobonian.]

3. In Italy, some fasted the full forty days, others twenty days (a marginal variant reads thirty), and others said that it was sufficient for them to fast for eight days, during which the world is said to have been created. Others held that, because the Lord had fasted for forty days, they ought to abstain for forty hours.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 4. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “Since, therefore, the observance was so varied and diverse, there was sorrow among the priests, so that where there was one faith,” and so forth. It soon has *jej unia* (“fasts”). “At that time Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, chose this, so that . . .”]

4. When such observances were maintained in the individual provinces, there was—as the obscure text says—sorrow among the priests at Rome, because, where there was one faith, the fasts differed. Then Pope Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, sent word that authority should be given to Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine—for at that time Caesarea was called the metropolis of Jerusalem—that the regulation of Easter might proceed from that place where Christ had lived in the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 5. The Ottobonian Codex adds *spiritualibus* (“spiritual”) after *Scripturis* (“Scriptures”).]

5. Having received authority, Theophilus understood that such a task had been entrusted to him, one that was to be transmitted as an observance throughout the world—not only to his own country but also to neighboring provinces. He summoned all the bishops and learned men to a council. When that great multitude of priests and learned men, instructed in all the Scriptures, had been gathered together, Bishop Theophilus produced the authority of Pope Victor that had been sent to him and disclosed what task had been entrusted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 6. The Ottobonian Codex reads *responderunt* (“they replied”) instead of *edicunt* (“they declare”).]

6. Then all the bishops together said: “We must first inquire how the world was created in the beginning; and when this has been investigated with greater care, a salutary regulation of Easter may proceed from it.” The bishops therefore said: “Which day do we believe was created first in the world?” They declared: “The Lord’s Day.”

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 7. For “Bishop Theophilus said,” the Ottobonian Codex reads: “But they said.”]

7. Bishop Theophilus said: “How can you prove that the Lord’s Day was made first?” The bishops replied: “According to the authority of divine Scripture: ‘AND THERE WAS EVENING, AND THERE WAS MORNING, THE FIRST DAY.’ Then came the second, then the third, then the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh, on which God rested from all his works; this day he called the Sabbath. Since the Sabbath is the last, what can be first except the Lord’s Day?” They said: “So it is, and otherwise it is not.”

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 8. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “What is said about the seasons?” and later: “Which season do you believe was made first?”]

8. Bishop Theophilus said: “You have proved concerning the Lord’s Day that it is the first. What is your opinion concerning the season? There are four seasons of the world in the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Which season, then, do we believe was made first?” The bishops replied: “Spring.”

[Note: [Col. 0742D] 9. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “But they replied: It is written.” It gives the words of Scripture as follows: “Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree according to its kind, bearing fruit.”]

9. Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.” They replied: “When Scripture says: ‘LET THE EARTH BRING FORTH THE GRASS OF HAY ACCORDING TO ITS KIND, AND A FRUIT-BEARING TREE, PRODUCING FRUIT WITHIN ITSELF,’ we see these things taking place in spring.” They said: “It is true.”
