[Note: [Col. 0742D] 10. The Ottobonian Codex has “It is written” instead of “When Scripture says.” So it is in several other places.]

10. Bishop Theophilus said: “Since spring is reckoned as three months, where is the beginning of the world believed to lie—in the first part, in the middle, or at the end?” The bishops replied: “At the equinox, that is, on 8 Kalends of April [25 March].” Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.” They replied: “As Scripture says: ‘AND GOD MADE THE LIGHT, AND CALLED THE LIGHT DAY. AND GOD MADE THE DARKNESS, AND CALLED THE DARKNESS NIGHT. AND GOD DIVIDED THE LIGHT AND THE DARKNESS INTO EQUAL PARTS.’” They said: “This is truly so.”

[Note: [Col. 0743C] 11. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “Whether it was created waxing, full, or perhaps waning? The bishops said: Full.”]

11. Bishop Theophilus said: “You have now proved your point concerning the day and the season. What is your opinion concerning the moon? When do we say that it was created—waxing from the beginning, full, or waning?” The bishops replied: “Full.”

[Note: [Col. 0743C] 12. The words of Scripture in the Ottobonian Codex are: “God made the greater luminary for the illumination of the day, and the lesser luminary at the beginning of the night.” In the Malatesti Codex: “And God made two great luminaries and placed them in the firmament of heaven, so that they might shine over the earth: the greater luminary at the beginning of the day and the lesser luminary at the beginning of the night, so that they might shine over the earth.”]

12. But he said: “Prove what you say.” The bishops replied: “As divine Scripture says: ‘AND GOD MADE TWO GREAT LUMINARIES AND PLACED THEM IN THE FIRMAMENT OF HEAVEN, SO THAT THEY MIGHT SHINE OVER THE EARTH.’ Since it shines over the earth from the beginning of the night and throughout the whole night, it could not have been otherwise than full.” They said: “This is true.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] 13. “Therefore now,” and so forth. The Ottobonian Codex has instead: “Now, therefore, we shall investigate how the world was created in the beginning—that is, on the Lord’s Day, in spring, at the equinox, which is 8 Kalends of April, with the moon full. Thus it is now established how the world was created in the beginning, and how through the Lord’s resurrection it was redeemed from sin.”]

13. “How, then,” they asked, “do we find that the world was created?” They replied: “On the Lord’s Day, at the equinox of spring, which is 8 Kalends of April [25 March], with the moon full.” They said: “Just as the world was created in the beginning and the elements arise, so through the Lord’s resurrection it was redeemed from sin.” Thus our Lord Jesus Christ rose on the Lord’s Day, in spring, at the equinox, with the moon full; it is only during that season that the elements arise.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] 14. “They said,” and so forth. The Ottobonian Codex has a shorter version: “Theophilus said: Now we must deal with the regulation of how we ought to observe Easter. The bishops said: Can . . . ?”]

14. They said: “Behold, we have investigated how the world was made and how it was redeemed from sin. Now we must also address the observance of Easter. What is your opinion concerning the Lord’s Day?” The bishops said: “Can the Lord’s Day be passed over so that Easter is not celebrated on it, since it has been sanctified by so many and such great blessings?”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] 15. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “He said: Tell us, then, by what and by how many blessings it was sanctified, so that we may know.” It then has “The first blessing,” and thereafter “for it” instead of “for them.”]

15. Bishop Theophilus said: “Tell us more clearly by what or by how many blessings you assert that it was sanctified, so that we may know.” The bishops said: “Its first blessing is that on it the darkness was removed and the light appeared.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] 16. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “That the people were freed from the land of Egypt, as from the darkness of sins, through the baptismal font and through the Red Sea. The third . . .”]

16. “Its second blessing is that the people of Israel were freed from Egypt, the land of darkness, as though through the baptismal font and through the Red Sea, from harsh servitude. Its third blessing is that on the same day manna was given to human beings as heavenly food.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] 17. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “Moses commanded the people: Let the first and the last day be observed by you.”]

17. “Its fourth blessing is that Moses gives the people this command: ‘LET THE FIRST AND THE LAST DAY BE OBSERVED BY YOU’—that is, the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath.”

[Note: [Col. 0744C] 18. The Ottobonian Codex gives the whole psalm concerning the Passion: “They surrounded me . . . like bees the honeycomb,” and so forth. It also adds other material from the sacred writings.]

18. “Its fifth blessing is that Psalm 117 [118], concerning the resurrection and the Passion, is sung. It says:

> THEY SURROUNDED ME, YES, THEY SURROUNDED ME, AND IN THE NAME OF THE LORD I SHALL AVENGE MYSELF UPON THEM. THEY SURROUNDED ME LIKE BEES, AND THEY FLARED UP LIKE FIRE AMONG THORNS.

“And after intervening verses:

> THE STONE THAT THE BUILDERS REJECTED HAS BECOME THE HEAD OF THE CORNER.

“These words concern the Passion. Concerning the resurrection it says:

> THIS IS THE DAY THAT THE LORD HAS MADE; LET US REJOICE AND BE GLAD IN IT.

“And after intervening verses:

> APPOINT THE FESTAL DAY WITH THE MULTITUDE, UP TO THE HORNS OF THE ALTAR.

19. “Its sixth blessing is that on it the Lord rose. You see, therefore, that the Lord’s Day of resurrection is specially commanded to be observed at Easter.”

[Note: [Col. 0744C] 20. The Ottobonian Codex reads “all thirty” instead of “the whole thirty.” It continues: “It is established that all thirty days were consecrated by the Lord for Easter. The bishops replied: Above we have already given the answer concerning the beginning of the world,” and so forth.]

20. Theophilus said: “Can the day and the season be understood [in this way]?” The bishops replied: “The season could be understood if divine Scripture had not elsewhere fixed it, when Moses says: ‘THIS MONTH SHALL BE FOR YOU THE BEGINNING OF MONTHS; CELEBRATE EASTER IN IT.’ He did not say ‘on the first day of the month,’ or ‘on the tenth,’ or ‘on another day,’ but he sanctified all thirty days for Easter.”

[Note: [Col. 0744C] 21. “Therefore from 8.” The Ottobonian Codex reads: “From there up to 8 Kalends of May we read that all the days of Easter were consecrated.”]

21. Theophilus said: “Which are these thirty days?” The bishops replied: “We have already said that the beginning of the world is the equinox on 8 Kalends of April [25 March]. Therefore, from 8 Kalends of April to 8 Kalends of May [25 April], these are the thirty days sanctified for Easter.”

[Note: [Col. 0744D] 22. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “So that the Lord’s Passion and the mystery of so great a sacrament might be excluded beyond the boundary? For our Lord suffered from 11 Kalends of April, on which night he was betrayed by Judas, and he rose on the 8th. How, then . . . ?”]

22. Bishop Theophilus said: “Is it not impious that those three days of the Lord’s Passion should be excluded beyond the boundary? For on 11 Kalends of April [22 March], the fifth day of the week—which we call the Lord’s Supper—when he had reclined with his disciples, he foretold that he would be betrayed by Judas (perhaps, “that Judas would betray him”), and this is known to have been fulfilled. How, then, are these three days excluded beyond the boundary?” (Earlier the reading was *excludantur*, “should be excluded.”)

[Note: [Col. 0744D] 23. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “All the bishops . . . so that the Passion might not be excluded; but these three days should be brought within the boundary, and it should be drawn back both above and below. It was therefore established in that synod that Easter should be observed from 11 Kalends of April to 7 Kalends of May, and that no one should have the power to cross the boundary either before or afterward.”]

23. The bishops said: “There is no reason why so great a sacrament should be cast beyond the boundary of the Passion. Rather, these three days must be brought into the Easter sequence and drawn back from the end.” And so it was established in that council that Easter should be celebrated neither before 11 Kalends of April [22 March] nor after 7 Kalends of May [25 April]. Thus the rule concerning the day and the season was established.

[Col. 0744C]

[Note: [Col. 0744D] 24. “To have been consecrated.” It is clear that *fuisse consecratas*, or something similar, must be supplied, as frequently happens in other ancient documents. The Malatesti Codex explicitly has *constat*, “it is established.”]

24. “What is your opinion concerning the moon?” They replied in the same way: “The divine command must also be observed concerning the moon, as Moses says: ‘LET IT BE OBSERVED BY YOU FROM THE FOURTEENTH TO THE TWENTY-FIRST.’ Therefore these seven moons were consecrated for Easter.”

[Note: [Col. 0744D] 25. The Ottobonian Codex reads: “Within that boundary, from 11 Kalends of April to 7 Kalends of May, when the Lord’s Day and one moon among these eight sanctified moons coincide, we are commanded to observe Easter in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.” Up to this point the Ottobonian Codex extends.]

25. Therefore, when within that established boundary the Lord’s Day coincides with one moon among those seven, it seemed right to us to celebrate Easter from 11 Kalends of April to 7 Kalends of May. Within these thirty-four days holy Easter must thus be sought and found, from the fourth day before the Nones of March [4 March] to the fourth day before the Nones of April [2 April].

[Note: [Col. 0745D] 26. After the words “let it be counted on the first day,” the following occurs in the codices of the *Etymologies*: “The word Easter, however,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.]

26. Within these days the moon is born on the twenty-eighth day; in that lunation holy Easter is celebrated from the twelfth moon to the twenty-first. From this lunation it must be found—although the passage is obscure—that the first day is counted in holy Easter.

## APPENDIX IX

To Book VI, chapter 19.

### ON VARIOUS WORDS

[Note: [Col. 0745D] APP. IX, n. 1. Bignaeus brought this fragment forward at the beginning of his edition of Isidore, from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Denis in France. He says that it appears to belong to Isidore’s books of the *Etymologies*. No more suitable place can be assigned to it than Book VI, chapter 19. On the acclamation *Hosanna* there is a French dissertation in the *Trivultian Journal* for February 1706.]

1. *Alleluia* sounds in Latin as “praise the Lord.” For *Ia* is one of the ten names of God among the Hebrews. *Amen*: truly, or faithfully. *Diapsalma*: always—that is, whatever it is attached to, it makes eternal. It signifies neither a change of meter, as some think, nor a renewal of the prophetic spirit. There are also those who think that *diapsalma* is inserted so that from it one may understand a change either of persons or of meanings. *Osanna*: save, or make safe. For *osia* is interpreted as “save,” while *anna* is an interjection of one making a supplication. Thus the complete form is *osianna*, but when shortened it sounds corrupted. *Osanna* means “save,” with either the people of Israel or the whole world understood.

2. *Rama*: lofty. In the Gospel: “A voice was heard in Rama,” that is, “in lofty places.” Yet there is also a city called Rama. *Racha*: empty or vain. *Rabbi*: my teacher; *Abba*: Father; this too is Syriac. *Man*: what? *Manna*: what is this? *Anathema*: betrayal. *Maranatha*: our Lord has come; this is Syriac. *Anathema maranatha*: as some say, “betrayal at the coming of the Lord.” *Mammona*: riches.

3. *Theraphim*: figures or images, better than “fires.” *Seraphim*, or *Ceruphim*: burning or setting alight, according to the passage: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire.” Therefore they affirm that the seraphim are powers in heaven who praise the Lord and are sent on various ministries. *Cherubim*: a multitude of knowledge. In the Holy of Holies, however, *cherubim* signifies only two living creatures. In other places where this name is read, it indicates either some picture or a variety.

## APPENDIX X

To Book VIII, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] This appendix contained a catalogue of heresies, to which Arevalus appended the following profession of faith. We have assigned this catalogue a more suitable place among the Isidorian materials, at chapter 86, no. 29, since it is attached there to the preliminary notices of Muccioli and Hugh Menard. See *Patrologia*, volume LXXXI, column 636.]

[Note: [Col. 0745D] A. X.—In the profession of faith that I append to the catalogue of heresies, some things perhaps require correction, such as “who is of one nature with the Father” and “is of one substance”; and below, “so that he may be perfect in his own things and true in the human.” For *secuturos*, which the manuscript had, I restored *consecuturos*. After the final words “and the reward,” the manuscript adds: “Book VIII ends. The chapters of Book IX begin.”]

### PROFESSION OF FAITH

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and in God the Holy Spirit. We worship and confess not three gods, but one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet we do not understand “one God” as though he were solitary, nor as though he were the same person who is himself Father to himself and himself Son. Rather, the Father is he who begot; the Son is he who was begotten; and the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, neither created nor made, but proceeding from the Father and the Son, coeternal and coequal with the Father and the Son, and their co-worker.

For it is written: “AND BY THE BREATH OF HIS MOUTH ALL THEIR POWER [or, ‘all their host’].” And elsewhere: “SEND FORTH YOUR SPIRIT, AND THEY WILL BE CREATED, AND YOU WILL RENEW THE FACE OF THE EARTH.” Therefore, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, we confess one God. For “God” is a name of power, not of personal distinction. The proper name of the Father is “Father”; the proper name of the Son is “Son”; and the proper name of the Spirit is “Holy Spirit.”

And in this Trinity we believe one God. He who is from the one Father is of one nature with the Father, of one substance, and of one power. The Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity, but by nature. In the final age, the Son descended from the Father to save us and to fulfill the Scriptures. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born from the Virgin Mary in flesh, soul, and sensation—that is, he assumed a complete human being. He did not lose what he was, but began to be what he was not. He was not a changeable God, but a God who remained [what he was], yet in such a way that he is perfect in his own [things] and true in those of the human being [reading uncertain].

For, being born as a human being, he acts as God; as a human being he dies; as God he rises again. Having overcome the dominion of the devil, with the flesh in which he had been born, suffered, and died, he rose again and ascended to the Father, and he sits at his right hand in glory. He has always possessed what he now possesses.

In his death and blood we believe that we have been cleansed, and that on the last day we shall be raised in this flesh in which we now live and which we possess. From him we shall receive either eternal life, the reward of good merit, or, in accordance with our sins, the punishment of eternal suffering. Read this law; retain it; subject your soul to this faith and to Christ the Lord; and you will attain both life and the reward.

## APPENDIX XI

To Book IX, chapter 5.

### FRAGMENT FROM AN OLD EDITION

[Note: [Col. 0746D] APP. XI, II. 1. In an old edition, without place or year, after the words “great-grandfathers” and “great-great-grandfathers,” the fragment beginning “At this point” is added; it is absent from most other copies. It also occurs in Codex Ottobonianus 336, where it is noted that it was taken from Justinian’s *Institutes*.]

1. At this point it is necessary to explain how the degrees of kinship are counted. In this matter we must first be advised that some kinds of kinship are counted upward, some downward, and some transversely; the latter are also called lateral relationships. The upper relationships are those of parents; the lower, those of children. Transverse relationships are those of brothers and sisters and of those descended from them, and consequently of paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts. The upper and lower relationships begin with the first degree, whereas those counted transversely begin with the second. In the first degree, upward is the father; downward, the son and daughter.

[Note: [Col. 0746D] 2. The Greek names had been corrupted, and I have therefore restored them to their correct readings. From Greek *theios*, some pronounce the word in Latin as *Thios*; hence the Spaniards say *Thio*.]

2. In the second degree upward are the grandfather and grandmother; downward, the grandson and granddaughter; transversely, the brother and sister.

In the third degree upward are the great-grandfather and great-grandmother; downward, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter; transversely, the son and daughter of a brother or sister; and consequently the paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt.

A paternal uncle is the father’s brother, called in Greek *patrōs* [πάτρως]. A maternal uncle is the mother’s brother, properly called among the Greeks *mētrōs* [μήτρως], and commonly *theios* [θεῖος]. A paternal aunt is the father’s sister, while a maternal aunt is the mother’s sister; both are called *theia* [θεία], or among some peoples *tēthis* [τηθίς].

3. In the fourth degree above are the great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the nephew and niece of one’s brother or sister [Col. 0746D]; and thereafter the great-granduncle and great-grandaunt—that is, the brother and sister of one’s grandfather; likewise the great-granduncle and great-grandaunt on the maternal side—that is, the brother and sister of one’s grandmother.

A male or female cousin (*consobrinus*, *consobrina*) is one descended from brothers or sisters. Some, however, correctly hold that *consobrini* properly denotes those descended from two sisters, as though they were *consororini* (“co-sisters’ children”). Those descended from two brothers are properly called *patrueles*. If sisters are born to two brothers, they are called *sorores patrueles* (“paternal cousins”). Those descended from a brother and a sister are properly called *amitini*. The sons of your paternal aunt call you *consobrinus*; you call them *amitini*.

4. In the fifth degree above are the great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the grandnephew and grandniece of one’s brother or sister; and thereafter the great-great-granduncle and great-great-grandaunt—that is, the brother and sister of one’s great-grandfather; the great-great-granduncle and great-great-grandaunt on the maternal side—that is, the brother and sister of one’s great-grandmother.

Likewise, the son or daughter of a male or female paternal cousin, of a male or female cousin descended from two sisters, or of a male or female cousin descended from a brother and sister is called a *propior sobrinus* or *propior sobrina*. These are the son and daughter of the great-granduncle, great-grandgrandaunt, great-granduncle on the maternal side, and great-grandgrandaunt on the maternal side.

5. In the sixth degree are, above, the great-great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter; collaterally, the great-nephew and great-niece of one’s brother or sister [Col. 0747B]; and thereafter the great-great-great-granduncle and great-great-great-grandaunt—that is, the brother and sister of one’s great-great-grandfather; and the great-great-great-granduncle and great-great-great-grandaunt on the maternal side—that is, the brother and sister of one’s great-great-grandmother.

Likewise, *sobrini* and *sobrinae* are those descended from male or female paternal cousins, from male or female cousins descended from two sisters, or from male or female cousins descended from a brother and sister.

[Note: [Col. 0747C] 6. The printed edition had *denotari*, *numerentur*, and *infigitur*.]

6. It is sufficient thus far to have shown how the degrees of kinship are counted, for from these examples it is clear how we should count each further degree. Indeed, it is always necessary to add a degree for each person mentioned; or, much more easily, one may answer in which degree someone stands than designate each person by the proper name of the relationship. The degrees of agnatic kinship are counted in the same way. But since truth is impressed upon the minds of human beings more by what is seen with their own eyes than by what enters through their ears, we have therefore considered it necessary, after describing the degrees, to have them written in the present book as well [Col. 0748A], so that 537 young people may attain a most complete knowledge of the degrees both through hearing and through seeing them.

## APPENDIX XIII

To Book IX, chapter 6, of the *Etymologies*.

### ISIDORE ON THE SEVEN DEGREES OF CONSANGUINITY

From Ottobonian Codex 1968.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Appendix XIII, no. 1. In Gratian, caus. 35, quaest. 5, canon 6, these matters are reported from Isidore. The notes observe that they were taken from Book IX, chapter 5, of the *Etymologies*; from the *Sentences* of Julius Paulus, Book IV, title 11, “On Degrees”; from Hugh of Saint Victor, part 11, Book II, chapter 14; from Burchard, Book VII, chapter 28; from Ivo, part 9, chapter 64; from Panormitanus, Book VII, chapter 89; and from Anianus’ translation of Paulus. Most of the material certainly appears in Isidore at the cited place.]

1. In the first degree, the father and mother are contained in the upper line; the son and daughter in the lower line. No other persons are joined to them.

2. In the second degree, the grandfather and grandmother are contained in the upper line; the grandson and granddaughter in the lower line; and the brother and sister in the transverse line. These persons are doubled. For grandfather and grandmother are understood both on the father’s side and on the mother’s side; and in the following degrees these persons are likewise doubled, according to the substance of those who subsist in the second degree and in the same order.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] 3. In Gratian: “Because there are two grandfathers, paternal and maternal.” And so forth.]

3. These persons in the second degree are therefore called double because there are two grandfathers, paternal and maternal. There are likewise two kinds of grandchildren, whether begotten from a son or from a daughter. The brother and sister come in the transverse line—that is, either the father’s brother or the mother’s brother, who is called either *avunculus* or *patruus*. These too are doubled in the same order.

4. In the third degree come, above, the great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter. Obliquely come the son or daughter of one’s brother or sister; the paternal uncle and paternal aunt—that is, the father’s brother and sister; and the maternal uncle and maternal aunt—that is, the mother’s brother and sister.

5. In the fourth degree come, above, the great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; obliquely, the grandson and granddaughter of one’s brother and sister; and the male and female paternal cousins—that is, the son or daughter of one’s paternal uncle.

[Col. 0749C] [Note: [Col. 0749D] 6. “The great maternal uncle, the maternal aunt,” and so forth. These have been transposed in Gratian.]

6. The male and female cousins descended from the maternal uncle or aunt—that is, their son or daughter. The male and female cousins descended from the paternal aunt—that is, her son or daughter. The great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the grandmother, whether paternal or maternal. Likewise, the cousins born from two sisters, to whom are added the great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the grandmother, whether paternal or maternal.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] 7. In Gratian’s *Decree*: *propior consobrinus*, *propior consobrina*, in place of *proconsobrinus*, *proconsobrina*. And shortly thereafter: *propatruus*, *proamita*. These are the brother and sister of the paternal great-grandfather, and so forth.]

7. In the fifth degree come, above, the great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; obliquely, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of one’s brother and sister; the son 540 or daughter of a male or female paternal cousin, of an *amitinus* or *amitina*, or of a *consobrinus* or *consobrina*; and the male and female *proconsobrini*—that is, the son or daughter of the great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt. To these are added the great-great-granduncle and great-great-grandaunt, the *proamitini*—obscure—the brother and sister of the great-grandfather on the maternal side, and the great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt. These are the brother and sister of the paternal or maternal great-grandmother. This category can be explained neither through other degrees nor by other terms than those written here.

[Col. 0750A] 8. In the sixth degree come, above, the great-great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter; obliquely, the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of one’s brother and sister; the son and daughter of a male or female paternal cousin; the *amitini* and *amitinae*; the male and female cousins descended from two sisters; the sons and daughters of the great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt; the grandson and granddaughter of the great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt; and the son or daughter of the nearer cousin, who are called the son or daughter of a cousin.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] 9. In the same place: “This too cannot be explained more fully than as the author [Anianus] himself expounded it.”]

9. On the collateral side are added the son or daughter of the *propatruus*, *proamita*, *proavunculus*, or *promatertera* (the great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt); the *adpatruus* and *adamita*—these are the brother and sister of the paternal grandfather; and the *abavunculus* and *abmatertera*—these are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-grandmother and of the maternal great-grandfather. These too cannot be explained more fully than the author himself expounded them.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] 10. Gratian added: “How many degrees of consanguinity or affinity there are, how they are to be counted, and by what names they are also called, has been sufficiently demonstrated on the authority of Isidore, Gregory, and Alexander.”]

10. Those who are related in the seventh degree in the direct line, both above and below, are not called by their own proper names; rather, they are included under the transverse line: the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter of one’s brother or sister, and the sons and daughters of one’s cousins. The degrees of succession were therefore established as seven, because beyond this, by the nature of things, neither names can be found nor can life be extended to those who succeed one another. Within these seven degrees all the names of relationships are contained; beyond them affinity cannot be found, nor can succession be propagated any further.

## APPENDIX XIV

Fragments from Gothic Toledan Codices and others.

### FIRST FRAGMENT

From the Gothic Toledan Codices and older editions; differing from our edition in Book II of the *Etymologies*, chapter 29.

[Note: [Col. 0750D] Appendix XIV consists chiefly of additions that have been inserted or interpolated into the ancient Toledan copies, unless one prefers to believe that certain such fragments are from Isidore’s own hand, since he published many titles of the *Etymologies* separately, perhaps in versions somewhat different from those found in most copies of the *Etymologies*. The first fragment is presented so that the different order of the definitions from that preferred by Grialius may be viewed.]

1. The tenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *kat’ elleipes plērous homoiou genous* (“according to the omission of a complete thing of the same genus”), which the Latins call “through the lack of a complete [definition] from the same genus,” as when one asks, “What is a thesis?” and the answer is: “That which lacks the force to be an *arsis*.” The eleventh species of definition is what the Greeks call *kat’ analogian* (“according to analogy”), which the Latins call “according to reason” [otherwise, “according to proportion”], as when one asks, “What is an animal?” and the answer is: “Like a human being.” The example given has clarified the thing being sought. This, however, is the proper function of a definition: to declare what the thing being asked about is.

2. The twelfth species of definition is what the Greeks call *kat’ epainon* (“according to praise”), that is, “through praise,” as Cicero says in defense of Cluentius: “Law is the mind, counsel, spirit, and judgment of the state.” Another example is: “Peace is tranquil liberty.” It may also be made through blame, which the Greeks call *psogos*, as in: “Slavery is the last of all evils, to be repelled not only by war but even by death.” The thirteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *kata to pros ti*, which the Latins call “relative” or “in relation to something,” as in: “A father is one who has a son.” “A master is one who has a slave.” The fourteenth species of definition is *kata ton horon*, in Latin “general.” Cicero says in the *Rhetorics*: “A genus is that which embraces several parts.” Likewise: “A part is that which lies beneath a genus.”

3. The fifteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *kat’ aitiologian*, which the Latins call “according to the explanation of the thing”: “Day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth.” We should understand that the aforesaid species of definitions are rightly associated with the *Topics*, since they have been placed among certain arguments and are mentioned in some passages of the *Topics*. Now let us come to the *Topics*, which are the seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions.

### SECOND FRAGMENT

From a very ancient Toledan Codex, chapter 6 of Book III of the *Etymologies*.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] 4. There is great variation in the presentation of the divisions of number, since different copies report them in different ways. I present a specimen of this discrepancy from the first Toledan Codex, which is the oldest; another codex largely agrees with it. The Gothic Toledan Codex also agrees with it, although it is not equally ancient. Both codices have in the same way “or O considered in itself,” and so forth, which is not easy to understand. Where the codices agree with Grialius’ edition and ours, the sequence of the discourse does not continue. Nor is there time to linger over correcting errors or obscure passages.]

4. Every number is primary, or is considered as O in itself. A secondary number is relative to something. I. This is divided as follows. I. Some are equal, others unequal. III. But it is divided as follows: four by four, five by five, and by the others . . . And another one, which is said to be a fourth part of the number four, and other such numbers. A subsuperparticular number is a smaller number which is contained in a stronger number together with one of its parts, whether a half, third, fourth, or fifth; for example, II in relation to III, III in relation to IIII, in relation to IIIII, and so forth. A superpartient number [follows].

5. And its four other parts. A superpartient number is one which . . . A multiple-superparticular number . . . for example, five compared with three: when compared, they contain within themselves twice two, four, and one part of it . . . twice four, eight, and one part of it. A submultiple-subsuperparticular number is one which, when compared with the number stronger than itself, contains it as a multiple together with one of its parts; for example, two compared with five, when compared, is contained in it twice together with one of its parts. A multiple-superpartient number is . . . with two of its parts: XIV compared with XVI, when compared . . . sixteen compared with four, when compared, contains it twice together with two of its other parts. XXII compared with VII, when compared, contains within itself twice eight together with its other three parts.

6. A submultiple-subsuperpartient number with three of its parts is one which, when compared with the number stronger than itself, is contained in it as a multiple together with some of its parts; for example, three compared with eight is contained twice together with two of its parts; four compared with XI is contained twice together with three of its parts.

From the second Gothic Toledan Codex, chapter 7 of Book III of the *Etymologies*.

7. A superficial number is one that is contained not only in length but also in breadth, such as a triangular, square, pentagonal, or circular number, and others that are always contained on a plane surface, that is, on a surface. The triangular number is as follows. The square number is as follows. The pentagonal number is as follows. The circular number is one which, when multiplied by itself beginning from itself, returns to itself; for example, five times five, six times five, and so on; and so on.

8. A solid number is one that is contained in length and height, such as pyramids, which rise in the form of a flame, as follows. A cube is like dice, as follows. Spheres have equal roundness on every side, as follows. A spherical number is one which, multiplied by a circular number, begins from itself and returns into itself. Five times five, twice five. This circle, when multiplied by itself, produces a sphere—that is, five times XXV, CXXV.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] 9. These matters belong to chapter 8 of the same Book III of the *Etymologies*.]

9. There is this difference among arithmetic, geometry, and music. To find the mean in arithmetic, you first proceed in this way: you join the extremes, divide, and produce the mean. Suppose, for example, that the extremes are VI and XII. Joining them together, they make X and VIII; dividing the middle, you produce IX, which is the arithmetic proportion, so that the number of units by which the mean exceeds the first is the number by which it is exceeded by the extreme. For nine exceeds six by three units, and by these it is exceeded by twelve. According to geometry, you proceed in this way: the multiplied extremes produce as much as the doubled means; for example, six multiplied by twelve produces seventy *dipondii*, while the means VIII and IX, multiplied, produce the same amount.

10. According to music, you proceed thus: by as many parts as the mean exceeds the first, by the same parts the mean is exceeded by the extreme. For example, VI and VIII exceed by two parts; by these two parts the third, middle eighth (sic) is exceeded by the final ninth. Solid figures. Plane figures are those contained in length and breadth. According to Plato there are five of them. A numerable magnitude is one that can be divided by the numbers of arithmetic. Rational magnitudes are those whose measurable quantity is not known.

### On Figures

[Note: [Col. 0752D] 11. These correspond to chapter 12 of Book III, which concerns the figures of geometry. The circle, as it is drawn in the codex, is number 8 on the table; at its center the codex writes “that is, a circle,” which the table likewise represents in the following figures.]

11. Solid figures are those contained in length, breadth, and height, such as a cube. Of these, five kinds are [represented] on a plane. The first is the circle, a plane figure called “circumducted,” in whose middle is a point toward which all things converge; this is called the center of geometry. The Latins call it the point of the circle.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] 12. The quadrilateral figure is number 9. *Danatheton grammon*, or, as others write it, *Dianatheton*, number 10. *Orthogonium*, number 11. In the manuscript there was “a full rectangular figure.”]

12. A quadrilateral figure is a plane figure. A square figure is a plane figure squared, lying upon a plane surface beneath four straight lines. *Danatheton grammon* (“diagonal line”) is a plane figure on a plane surface. *Orthogonium*, that is, a right-angled figure, is a plane figure; for it is a right triangle.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] 13. *Isopleros*, or, as others have it, *Isopleuros*, number 12. Sphere, number 13. Cube, number 14. In the codex one reads *continetur in solibum*, “is contained in solibum,” but perhaps *in solidum*, “as a solid,” is a correction of the preceding *in solibum*. In the printed editions *in solidum* is attributed to the cylinder, whose definition Grialius questioned. See the note.]

13. *Isopleros* (“equal-sided”) is a straight plane figure, established beneath on a plane surface. A sphere is a figure formed into roundness, equal in all its parts as a solid. A cube is a solid figure contained in length and breadth as a solid.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] 14. Cylinder, number 15. Cone, number 16. Pyramid, number 17.]

14. A cylinder is a square figure having a semicircle above. A cone is a figure that terminates from broad to narrow, like an *orthogonium*. A pyramid is a figure that rises like fire, from broadness to a point. For fire is called *pyr* in Greek.

[Col. 0753A] [Note: [Col. 0753C] 15. This circle is the one represented by number 18; but the words “the circumference of all figures” are not present in the figure of the codex.]

15. Just as every number lies below ten, so the circumference of all figures is enclosed within this circle.

[Note: [Col. 0753C] 16. Compare chapter 13 of the cited Book III. The printed editions have “in the figures above,” omitting “ten.” The ten figures above are the circle and those that follow. The circumference of all figures comprises these ten, but lies outside their number.]

16. The first figure of this art is the point, which has no part. The second is length without breadth: a line. A straight line is one that lies evenly through its points. A surface has only length and breadth. Surfaces are the boundaries of lines. Their forms have not been placed among the ten figures above because they are found within them.

[Note: [Col. 0753C] 17. For *septuagies dipondios* in the printed editions there is *LXXII*.]

544 17. You seek numbers according to geometry in this way. For its multiplied extremes produce as much as its doubled means; for example, VI multiplied by XII produces seventy *dipondii*; the means, eight and nine, multiplied, produce the same amount.

### Explanation of the Figures

From two Toledan Codices.

[Note: [Col. 0753C] 18. These are entirely absent from the printed editions. The inscription in the manuscripts is: “Explanation of the figures written below,” or, incorrectly, “of the figures written beneath.” Perhaps one should read *id est*, “that is,” or *aut superferens*, “or superimposing,” or *aut circumfertur*, “or is carried around.”]

18. A similar method in the motion of the stars is likewise gathered into eight figures: either because they are diametrical, or square, or triangular, or hexagonal, or unconnected, or together, or superimposing—that is, supporting—or carried around.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] 19. In place of *particula* another reading is *partiuncula*. In the codex the figures are arranged so that the tetragonal figure is first, the hexagonal second, the unconnected third, the triangular fourth, and the diametrical fifth. On the copperplate table these figures are distinguished by their names, as in the manuscript codex, namely numbers 19, 20, 21, 22, and 23. Seven other figures follow without definite names, represented in the table by numbers 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, and 30. After figure 27 there is this note: “According to Porphyry and Plato this formula is explained in this way”; a figure follows, distinguished as number 30 in our table. After figure 30 another note follows: “On a plane surface let the mean and extremes be joined in the number XXVII.” But the number XXVI is expressed in the figure, as in our table; XXVII, however, seems more correct.]

19. They are diameters when five signs intervene. Tetragonal, when two; hexagonal, when one; unconnected, when none; together, when they are in the same small part. *Superferens* (“superimposing”), when one comes over another or performs an action. *Superfertur* (“is superimposed”), when it precedes. Triangular, when there are three intervening signs. According to another method, there are eight differences: sign, parts, boundaries, conjunction, retrogression, whether on a straight course, breadth, and length.

### The Inner Form’s Principle

[Note: [Col. 0753D] 20. After the five figures just mentioned—namely 24, 25, 26, 27, and 30, for this is their order in the codex—the title “The inner form’s principle” follows. For *posset*, etc. In place of *hinc prius*, another reading is *hic prius*. In place of *vicibus*, another reading is *cubus*, perhaps *bicubus*.]

20. A question of this sort might arise at this point: since there are first VIII in the numerical order, why did he then place nine first, when in the arithmetic or geometric proportion VIII is greater than IX? For VIII is a number of times, or a solid—that is, a body—which cannot find anything greater; IX, however, is a surface, that is, a thing that is not complete but requires perfection. Here two cubes—that is, two solidities—are found in the following manner.

[Note: [Col. 0754C] 21. In the manuscript: *bis ternis sexis*; perhaps *sexies*. In the same place: *non invenies*; another copy omits *non*. In the same place: *quod a proposito*; I omitted *a*. For *facitque*, Burriel or Bayer conjectures *fac itaque*. In the same place, “with two,” etc.; another reading has “two,” to which one is first in order. After the words “another together XXVII,” there are two figures, which our table presents as numbers 28 and 29. In the older Toledan Codex there follows a large figure, filling the page, belonging to the next chapter, chapter 15, on music. At the beginning of the page are the words: “According to some, who explain this ratio through *labdo* in the same way.” We have reproduced this figure on page 135. In the more recent Toledan Codex, which transmits the other figures in nearly the same manner, this large figure concerning music was omitted, but a blank place was left for it; and the following note, concerning the same subject, was added: “According to musical proportion it happens that either those born in seven months or those born in nine months can live, but never those born in eight months, because in seven or nine all the harmonies are found, and when these are complete the things are firmly stable. Five multiplied by six produces both seven months and nine months. Thus five times six is thirty. Taking this seven times produces seven months, and taking it nine times produces nine months.”]

21. The number six is the first perfect number, for it is divided by equal numbers in this way. A sixth, through these, into a third, through *dipondii*, three times two, six. Into a half, that is, twice three, six. You will find no other number that can be divided in this way by equal numbers and that agrees with the proposition among the first order, that is, X. Therefore, multiplying the first perfect number by the first sequence, six times nine gives LIV, and nine times six gives LIV. The material is thereby understood, not without reason, to have had so many parts: two, to which it has one in this order: I, II, III, IV, IX, IX, VIII, another together XXII.

26. The most blessed Jerome says the following in his commentaries on Zechariah: “The feast days in the Old Law are these: the Day of Unleavened Bread, the Passover, is on the fourteenth day of the first month; when the moon is completely full, after the leaven has been removed, the lamb is sacrificed.”

27. The day of Pentecost is the day on which the law was given to Moses on the summit of Mount Sinai, and on which they offered showbread from the first fruits.

28. The day of Sabbaths is the day on which rest is celebrated according to the law, and on which it was not permitted to gather manna in the desert.

29. The day of the New Moons is observed by celebrating the new moon. For the Jews always kept a feast at the beginning of the months—that is, at the first moon. They did this at the beginning of the month because, when the moon fails, time comes to an end, and when it is born again, time begins anew.

30. The day of Trumpets is the beginning of the seventh month, when the Jews celebrated a solemnity at which they sounded the trumpet and offered more sacrifices than in each of the individual months.

### CHAPTER II

On the Position and Appearance of the Human Body
Source preparation: Embedded Greek text recovered from the supplied local archive; translated as part of this section. Supplied textual variants, notes, and column references retained.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Appendix XV, note 1. Concerning Codex Regiovaticanus 1850, what I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 101, no. 29, may be consulted. As a specimen of the allegorical expositions contained in that codex under the title *Etymologies of Saint Isidore*, I present these two chapters, which in that codex are placed as Book VI after chapter 1 of Book XI. In the Vulgate: “He found the girl lying on the bed.”]

1. To stand signifies that human beings stand firm in faith, as in the Apostle: “Stand firm in the faith” (1 Cor. 16:13). To walk signifies to advance toward the Lord, as in the Psalms: “And I walked in the breadth” (Ps. 118:45). To sit signifies to rest humbly in God, as in the Gospel: “But you, remain seated in the city” (Luke 24:49), and in the Books of Kings concerning David: “And he sat before the Lord” (2 Sam. 7:18). To lie signifies to succumb to vices and temptations; hence it is read in the Gospel: “And he found her lying on the bed” (Mark 7:30). To run signifies to prepare oneself for good works; in the Apostle: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24). It may also have a bad sense: “Their feet run to evil” (Prov. 1:16).

[Col. 0755D] [Note: [Col. 0755D] 2. In the Vulgate: “The children of Israel from the land of Egypt.” [Col. 0756D] And in Isaiah: “Woe … to those who walk, so that they may descend into Egypt.”]

2. Ascent signifies progress toward the Lord; in the Psalms: “He arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83:6). And in Exodus: “The children of Israel went up from Egypt toward the sea” (Exod. 13:18). In a bad sense, however, ascent signifies the presumption of pride; in the Gospel: “Whoever does not enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs up by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Descent signifies falling away from God; in the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke 10:30). And in Isaiah: “Woe to you who mount horses in order to descend into Egypt” (Isa. 30:2).

## CHAPTER III. How human limbs are attributed to the devil

[Col. 0756C]

[Note: [Col. 0756D] 3. The words of the Vulgate are: “His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing upon one another.” And shortly afterward: “From his mouth proceed torches.”]

3. It must be understood that the limbs of a human being and human actions are attributed to the devil, not according to the historical sense, but are to be understood allegorically, since such figures are found in many places in Sacred Scripture. For the devil is the head of all evils; hence it is read in Habakkuk: “You struck the head from the house of the wicked” (Hab. 3:13). The devil’s heart, however, signifies reprobate human beings; hence concerning Behemoth it is read in the book of blessed Job: “His heart is like cast shields” (Job 41:6). His teeth signify mad heretics (*dementes haeretici*), as they do all wicked teachers; the source’s connecting *vel* (“or/even”) is ambiguous. As it is written in the aforesaid book: “His eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn. Around his teeth is terror” (ibid., 5, 9).

4. The devil’s nostrils signify his wicked inspirations: “From his nostrils smoke proceeds” (ibid., 11). The devil’s mouth signifies his words, by which he addresses human hearts through hidden thoughts, as it is stated in Job: “From his mouth [Col. 0756D] flame proceeds” (ibid., 10). The devil’s tongue signifies the wisdom of this age, or the doctrine of heretics, as it is stated in Job: “And with a rope you shall bind his tongue” (Job 40:20).

[Note: [Col. 0756D] 5. Vulgate: “His bones are like tubes of bronze; his cartilage is like plates of iron.” The reading is obscure in the manuscript and perhaps corrupt: *eamdem faciat*.]

5. The devil’s bones signify all who are powerful and strong in wickedness, such as heretics, as it is stated in Job: “His bones are his tubes” (ibid., 13). His cartilage signifies those less powerful than the ones called bones, as it is stated in Job: “His cartilage is like an iron plate” (ibid.). The devil’s breath signifies his hidden inspiration through human hearts, or perhaps [the text is corrupt] “let it be made by the carnal love of sinners.”

[Note: [Col. 0756D] 6. [Line 5.] In the Vulgate: “Joined together with him.”]

6. The devil’s face signifies the coming of Antichrist, or his open [Col. 0757A] wickedness, as it is stated in Job: “Poverty goes before his face” (Job 41:13). The devil’s flesh signifies those who are weak in his heart and less strong in sins, as it is stated in Job: “The members of his flesh cling together” (ibid., 14). The devil’s testicles signify either heretics or wicked thoughts, subtly binding through the bonds of sins, as it is stated in Job: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined” (Job 40:12). The devil’s tail is Antichrist, or the habit of sinning, as it is stated: “He tightens his tail like a cedar” (ibid.). The devil’s sleeping signifies resting in the heart of the reprobate, as it is stated in Job: “Under the shade he sleeps in the secret place of reeds” (ibid., 16). The devil’s feeding signifies delighting in the sins of the wicked, as it is stated in Job: “For him the mountains bear herbs” (ibid., 15).

Addition from the most ancient Toledo Codex to chapter 2 of Book XII of the *Etymologies*, numbers 3 and following

1. For *leo* is Greek, and in Latin means “king.” It has three [Col. 0757B] characteristics: when it walks and makes its way through the sand, [the text is corrupt or incomplete: “the scent of hunters”], and it covers its tracks with its tail so that hunters cannot follow it.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] 2. The manuscript reading is obscure, and it might be better to read: “Thus also our Savior, the lion from the tribe of Judah.”]

2. Thus also our Savior, from the tribe of Judah, sent by the Father, covers his tracks—that is, his divinity—so that he might appear to all while … descending with the Father into the Virgin’s womb to save what had perished; and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” And people, not understanding this, while he descended from heaven and ascended, said: “Who is this King of glory?”

[Note: [Col. 0757D] 3. It would be better to cite the Song of Songs; but perhaps the author of the addition wrote what is found in the manuscript, since, as the Middle Ages progressed, the titles of books were commonly cited in approximately this manner.]

522 3. Its second characteristic is that, while it sleeps, its eyes remain vigilant, for they are open. In the Song of Songs it is said concerning it: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). For he neither sleeps nor slumbers who guards Israel.

4. Its third characteristic is that, when it has begotten its cub, it gives birth to it dead; and the lioness guards her offspring until its father comes on the third day, breathes into its face with a mighty roar, and raises it up.

5. Thus the almighty Father raised up his Only-Begotten [Col. 0757C] on the third day; hence Jacob says: “A lion’s cub is Judah.”

## Addition from the same Toledo Codex to chapter 7 of Book XII of the *Etymologies*

[Note: [Col. 0757D] 6. The Codex does not indicate to what passage this addition, written crosswise in the margin, belongs. Nevertheless, it should not be detached from the chapter beside which it stands. The *charadrius* is mentioned in Deuteronomy, chapter 14, verse 18. What is related here about this bird can to some extent be confirmed from Aldrovandi’s *Ornithology*, Book XX, chapter 27, where Albertus and Aelian are cited as authorities. In the Toledo manuscript it is written *Curadrius*, or, [Col. 0758D] as I rather think, *Caradrius*. Perhaps one should read: “It heals the sick, whose …”]

6. By nature the *charadrius* is born entirely white, having no blackness; and in Deuteronomy it is written concerning it that its entrails heal the sick whose eyes are dim.

7. It is found in royal courtyards, and by it one can recognize whether a sick person will live or die. If the person is destined to die, it turns its face away; if destined to live, it looks at the sick person, and the sick person looks at it.

8. When it flies upward against the rays of the sun, it burns away the illness and scatters it, and the sick person will be healed. It bears the figure of Christ, who is wholly snowy and pure, having no blackness, coming from the Father above, while his own people did not receive him.

9. He turned his face away from the Jews, but in his divinity [Col. 0758A] he looked upon the Gentiles, taking away the sickness of sins. “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our diseases,” so that he might be lifted up upon the wood: “ascending on high, he led captivity captive.”

10. But you say: “The *charadrius* is unclean as food. How can it bear the figure of Christ?” The serpent is also unclean. Hear the evangelist John: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). For when the children of Israel looked upon the bronze serpent, they were made well.

# APPENDIX XVIII

To Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, number 7

## Fragment concerning natron

From a manuscript codex in Vulcanius

[Col. 0758C] [Note: [Col. 0758D] Appendix XVIII. In Vulcanius’s edition it is noted that in a certain manuscript, before the word *Aphronitrum*, the following occurs: “For just as salt …” It ought not to have been omitted by us.]

For just as the heat of the sun produces salt on the seashore by hardening seawater into stone—water that a stronger force of winds, or the heat of the sea itself, has thrown onto the farther shores—so in Nitria, where during summer prolonged rains saturate the earth, such heat of the heavenly body burns that it cooks the rainwater itself, spread across the breadth of the sands, into a stone very similar in appearance to salt or ice, but possessing no hard rigidity and no salty taste. Nevertheless, in accordance with the nature of salt, it customarily hardens in hot weather and flows and melts in cloudy air. The natives collect and preserve it, and whenever necessary use it as a cleansing agent [the reading *lumento* is uncertain]. Hence the prophet says to sinful Judea: “Though you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the herb *borith*, you are stained in your iniquity, says the Lord” (Jer. 2:22). It crackles in water like quicklime; it itself disappears, but makes the water suitable for washing.

# APPENDIX XIX

To Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 20, number 9, from Codex Vaticanus 1343

[Col. 0759A]

## ON BELLS AND SMALL BELLS

[Note: [Col. 0759B] Appendix XIX. I thought that these materials concerning bells, which I found in Codex Vaticanus 1343, should be added here, so that some information might thereby be extracted concerning the manner in which the faithful were formerly summoned to church. Many modern writers have treated this subject.]

Concerning cast vessels, or also vessels drawn out into thin sheets, which are simply called signals because, when their sound is produced by certain strokes, they signify the hours at which the appointed services are celebrated in the house of God, this, it seems, should be said: their use was not so widespread among the ancients, because they did not have such a multiplicity of frequent assemblies as exists today. Among some peoples, devotion alone compelled people to gather at the appointed hours; others were invited by public announcements and learned in advance of the solemnity that was soon to take place. Among some, the hours were announced by tablets; among others, by horns. The use of the vessels under discussion is said to have first been discovered among the Italians. Hence, from Campania, which is a province of Italy, these larger vessels are called *campanae*, “bells”; [Col. 0759B] the smaller ones, which from their sound are called *tintinnabula*, “little tinklers,” are called *nolae* after a city of the same Campania, where such vessels were first altered [perhaps “made”; the reading is uncertain].

# APPENDIX XX

To Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25, number 11

## FRAGMENT OF SAINT ISIDORE CONCERNING WEIGHTS

From a manuscript codex in Bignaeus

[Note: [Col. 0759B] Appendix XX. Bignaeus published this fragment at the beginning of his edition from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Denis, [Col. 0759C] as well as the fragment of the following appendix, [Col. 0760B] which, as the title indicates, I do not believe to be Isidore’s.]

A talent has a weight of 63 pounds, which make 80 Attic pounds. A *mina* is one pound and a half-ounce. A talent contains 60 minae. The Greek *mina* is called *mna* in Latin. A drachma contains 3 scruples; a didrachm, [Col. 0760A] two drachmas. Hence the mina—just as in the book of *Hebrew Questions* a half-ounce is written; the phrase is textually corrupt.

A stater, as some assert, is one ounce—that is, six gold pieces; according to others, three. In the Gospel the name “stater” is given to two didrachms.

A *sekel*, which in Latin is corruptly called *siclus*, as is indicated in the Questions mentioned above, has the weight of an ounce and, as I found written elsewhere, six scruples—which I myself also think correct. For *siclus* itself, from *secle*, because of the closeness of its weight, sounds almost like *sicilicus*. An obol is half a scruple, which makes three *siliquae*. In Ezekiel a shekel contains twenty obols.

# APPENDIX XXI

To Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 26, number 17

## FRAGMENT CONCERNING MEASURES

From a manuscript codex in Bignaeus

[Note: [Col. 0760B] Appendix XXI. These two fragments are corrupt and ought to be entirely emended from Isidore’s teaching in the cited Book XVI, so that a true account of measures and weights may be inferred. Bignaeus printed them in the form in which they have been published [Col. 0760C] by us.]

A *corus* is 30 modii. A *bath* is one amphora, that is, three modii. A *cadus* is a Greek amphora. An *ephi* has, for dry goods, [Col. 0760B] the measure which a bath has for liquids. A *metreta*, as some say, contains 100 sextarii. “Measure” in Greek is *metron*, whence *metreta* is also called so. It must be noted, however, that “measure” is a Hebrew word.

In Isaiah, the Egyptian measures that make three modii—ten *sata*—are the same as an *ephi*, that is, three modii. A *gomor* is an Attic measure, containing, as some think, three *congii*, that is, 12 or 13 sextarii. Some say that a *gomor* is a little less than five sextarii; I follow this view as well, since it is a tenth of an *ephi*. Some think that a *gomor* contains three modii; the remaining words are corrupt: “it is to be clearly examined into sextarii.” A *cotyla* is a mina in Ezekiel: “Ten cotylae are a gomo[…]”

[Col. 0759]

# VARIOUS READINGS OF THE *ETYMOLOGIES*

Selected from many ancient manuscript and printed copies, interspersed with several shorter fragments not previously published

[Col. 0759C] When I already had at hand an immense forest of variant readings, collected from almost innumerable ancient manuscript codices and early editions, it seemed sufficient—so that the work might not grow without limit—to select only those that could be held in greater esteem, leaving aside the others, which may perhaps at some future time be useful to those who, having obtained copies of them, wish to illustrate more fully the *Etymologies of Saint Isidore* separately from his other works.

[Col. 0759D]

In indicating these various readings, I shall follow this order: I shall first give the text of my edition, which generally agrees with Grialius’s; then I shall record the discrepancy from other copies, usually without naming them. Among the copies collated, a special place is occupied by the first edition of the *Etymologies*, without place or year; the Venetian edition of 1483; Vulcanius’s edition, with which the editions of Bignaeus, Breulius, and Gothofredus agree; two manuscript codices of the Vatican archive; the codex of the Most Excellent Albanian family; two Caesenate codices of the Malatesta; the Lucan codex; the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark; the Modenese codex from Book III onward; two Gothic Toledo codices; and several other Vatican codices, such as Vat. 624; Palat. 281, 282, 283; Ottob. 336, 343, 345, 352, 404, 427, 477; Urb. 100, 479; Regiovat. 102, 1953; and so forth.

## BOOK I

### CHAPTER I

1. *qui discit* (“who learns”). Others: *quod discit* (“that which he learns”); others: [Col. 0760C] *qui didicit* (“who learned”).

2. *consistat* (“may consist”). Others: *constat* (“consists”).

3. *voluerunt* (“they wished”). Others: *dixerunt* (“they said”). In the same place, *disciplinam vero esse* (“but that it is discipline”). Others: *disciplina vero est* (“but discipline is”).
