### CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0763B]

1. *ex Graeco nomen accepit* (“it received its name from Greek”). Some omit these words.

4. *ut ars* (“as *ars*”). In Palatinus 281 the variant is *ut res* (“as *res*”). *ut Romanus* (“as Roman”). Others: *ut Metellus* (“as Metellus”). *et ultimam brevem* (“and the final short [syllable]”). Others: *et obliquam brevem* (“and the oblique short [syllable]”).

5. *trisyllaborum retinentur* (“they are retained among three-syllable words”). Others: *trisyllabarum retinetur* (“it is retained among three-syllable words”). *est, ut armipotens, omnipotens* (“it is, as in *armipotens*, *omnipotens*”). Others: *est, ut malesanus* (“it is, as in *malesanus*”); others: *est, ut malesanus, ut armipotens* (“it is, as in *malesanus*, as in *armipotens*”).

6. *producta me* (“lengthened by me”). Others omit *me*. *conjunctio est* (“it is a conjunction”). Others: *conjunctionem significat* (“it signifies conjunction”); others: *in conjunctionem transit* (“it passes into a conjunction”).

### CHAPTER XIX

2. *a summo sinistrae in dexteram* (“from the top of the left [side] to the right”). Others: *a summo dexterae in sinistram* (“from the top of the right [side] to the left”).

6. *connectit* (“it connects”). Others: *conjungit* (“it joins”). *versui* (“to verse”). Others: *verui*; others: *verbi* (“of a word”).

7. *versui* (“to verse”). Others: *verui*.

8. *ultima vocalis* (“the final vowel”). Others: *ultimas vocales* (“the final vowels”).

11. *si conjungas has, facis* (“if you join these, you make”). Others: *si jungas has, fecisti* (“if you join these, you have made”).

### CHAPTER XX

2. *prima positura* (“the first position”). Others: *prima posituris* (“the first positions”).

3. *enim in initio* (“for at the beginning”). Others: *enim initio* (“for at the beginning”). *pars sensus est* (“it is a part of the sense”). Others: *pars sensui est* (“it is a part for the sense”). *respirare oportet* (“one must draw breath”). Others: *respiramus* (“we draw breath”). *ad imam* (“to the bottom”). Others: *ad unam* (“to one”).

4. *puncto notamus* (“we mark with a point”). Others: *punctum notamus* (“we mark a point”); others simply: [Col. 0763C] *punctum* (“a point”). *fit colon* (“a colon is formed”). Others: *fit cola* (“cola are formed”).

5. *separavit* (“it separated”). Others: *separat* (“it separates”).

6. *quia … facta est* (“because … was made”). Others omit this.

### CHAPTER XXI

1. *scripturarum notae* (“marks of writings”). Others: *sententiarum notae* (“marks of sentences”). *ad demonstrandum* (“for demonstrating”). Others: *ad demonstrandam* (“for demonstrating,” feminine object).

2. *omissa sunt* (“were omitted”). Others: *amissa sunt* (“were lost”). *asteriscus est* (“it is an asterisk”). Others: *asteriscus, stellula, est* (“it is an asterisk, a little star”).

4. *appunctus* (“marked with a point”). Others: *punctus* (“pointed”); *punctatus* (“marked”); *appunctatus* (“marked with a point”). *necne* (“or not”). Others: *necne apponi* (“whether or not it is to be placed”). The most ancient Toledo copy: “Whether or not it is to be placed is marked as false.”

5. *sed diversis* (“but with different [ones]”). Others: *et diversis* (“and with different [ones]”).

7. *hac proprie* (“properly with this”). The Gothic copies: *hanc* or *hunc* (“this,” accusative), as elsewhere I use the accusative.

9. *sicut ille* (“as he”). Others: *sicut illa* (“as she”).

10. *quaestio dura* (“a difficult question”). Others: *quaestio dubia* (“a doubtful question”). *solvi non potest* (“cannot be solved”). Others: *solvi non potuit* (“could not be solved”); *solvi non poterit* (“will not be able to be solved”); *solvi potuit* (“could be solved”).

11. *sic et in* (“thus also in”). Others: *sicut et in* (“just as also in”).

14. *apposuit* (“he placed beside”). Others: *posuit* (“he placed”).

15. *aut permutaverat* (“or had changed”). Others omit this.

17. *aversa quoties* (“turned away whenever”). Others: *versa obelismene quoties* (“turned with the obelus whenever”).

18. *aversa cum obelo* (“turned away with an obelus”). Others: *adversa cum obelo* (“turned toward with an obelus”).

20. *quoque esse* (“also to be”). Others omit this.

23. *Phi et Rho, id est, Φροντις* (“Phi and Rho, that is, *Φροντις*—*phrontis*, “thought” or “care”). Others: *Phietro, id est fortis, vel frontes* (“Phietro, that is, strong, or foreheads”).

24. [Col. 0763D] *omnino est* (“is entirely”). Others: *omnino non est* (“is not at all”).

26. *nota* (“a mark”). Others omit this.

27. *nota ad* (“a mark toward”). Others: *Nota, quae ad* (“a mark which [is] toward”).

28. *fiunt et aliae librorum notulae* (“other little marks of books are also made”). Others: *fuerunt et aliae librorum notae* (“there were also other marks of books”).

### CHAPTER XXII

1. *pro concione* (“before the assembly”). Others: *pro contentione* (“for contention”); *per contentionem* (“through contention”). Others omit *pro concione*. *in judiciis* (“in judgments”). Others: *apud judices* (“before judges”).

2. *Vipsanius*. Others: *Vipsannius*; others: *Tertius Persanius*. *Philargius*. Others: *Philargyrus*. In the same place, *Maecenatis, alius alias* (“of Maecenas, one [copy] one way, another another way”). Others: *Maecenatis alias*, omitting *alius* (“one”).

### CHAPTER XXIII

1. *celeris, breviorque* (“swift and shorter”). Others: *celeris, brevisque* (“swift and short”); others: *celebris brevior* (“more celebrated, shorter”). *per b et f* (“by b and f”). Others: *per b et per f*, and likewise below.

*per supinam III litteram* (“by the inverted letter III”). Most copies have *per supinam m litteram* (“by the inverted letter m”). One of the two Gothic Toledo copies has *per supinam a litteram* (“by the inverted letter a”). Ottobonianus 427 has *me litteram* (“the letter me”), but above it, in the same hand, quite clearly has the letter III.

*verso capite* (“with the head turned”). Others: *averso capite* (“with the head reversed”).

2. *plurimae … inveniuntur* (“very many … are found”). Others: *plurimas … invenimus* (“we find very many”). *per has* (“through these”). Others: *per haec* (“through these things”). In the same place, [Col. 0764A] *in legibus litteras* (“letters in laws”). Others: *in apicibus litterarum* (“in the strokes of letters”). *demonstrent* (“they demonstrate”). Others: *demonstrarunt* (“they demonstrated”).

### CHAPTER XXIV

1. *bello cecidissent* (“had fallen in war”). Others: *in bello occisi sunt, aut essent* (“were killed in war, or would have been”). *t nota* (“the mark t”). Others: *tau nota* (“the tau mark”). *in capite versiculi* (“at the head of the verse”). Others: *incipiente versiculo* (“at the beginning of the verse”). *posita* (“placed”). Others omit this. *Θ vero* (“but theta”). Others: *theta vero*.

2. *impuritiam* (“impurity”). Others: *in pueritia* (“in childhood”); *impueritiam*; *pueritiam* (“childhood”); *peritias*; *imperitiam* (“inexperience”). *lambda littera* (“the letter lambda”). Others omit *littera* (“letter”).

### CHAPTER XXV

1. *Scriptura* (“Scripture”). Others: *in scripturis* (“in the Scriptures”). *mutuo* (“mutually”). Others: *mutue* (“mutually,” feminine). *usus iis litteris* (“the use of those letters”). Others: *in his litteris*, omitting *usus* (“in these letters”).

2. *incidunt* (“fall into”). Others: *accidunt* (“happen”). *scribi ad alterutrum oportet* (“they ought to be written in relation to one another”). Others: *scribi alterutrum oporteat* (“one of the two ought to be written”). *ergo* (“therefore”). Others omit it. *scribebant* (“they wrote”). Others: *scribunt* (“they write”).

### CHAPTER XXVI

1. *consentiat* (“may agree”). Many excellent copies: *consentit* (“agrees”).

2. *quasi in choro, etc.* (“as if in a chorus, etc.”). Almost all codices disagree in reporting these verses. The adverb *datatim* is found in many copies, and in some is the result of correction. In the same place, *quasi* (“as if”). Others: *quae* (“which”). *alii adnutat* (“another nods”). [Col. 0764B] Others: *alii nutat* (“another nods”); *alium admittit* (“he admits another”); *alii innuit* (“another gives a sign”); *alii annuit* (“another assents”); *alii adnotat* (“another notes”); *alii adnictat* (“another winks”).

In the same place, *alibi manus* (“elsewhere, hand”). Others: *alibi manibus, seu manu* (“elsewhere, by hands, or by hand”). *annulum spectandum* (“the ring to be looked at”). Others: *annulum exspectandum* (“the ring to be awaited”); *aspectandum* (“to be looked at”). *et a labris* (“and from the lips”). Others omit *et* (“and”). *Salomon* (“Solomon”). Others: *Salomon ait* (“Solomon says”).

## CHAPTER XXVII

1. “It is a conjunction.” Another copy: “it is conjunctive.”

2. “It is aspirated at the beginning.” Another copy: “it has aspiration at the beginning.”

3. “Just as” [*sicut*] “to” [*ad*]. Another copy omits this. In the same place, “*apud* instead of *ad*.” Another copy: “*ad* instead of *apud*.”

4. “Instead of *Pirrho* we say *Birrhum*.” This is how it is read in some copies of Grialius; in others: “Instead of *Birro* we say *Pirrum*.” It seems that one should write: “Instead of *Pyrrho* we say *Birrhum*,” or, as I printed it, “instead of *pirrho* we say *birrhum*.” See Facciolatus, s.vv. *Birrus*, *Byrrhus*, and *Burrus*, which derives from the Greek πυρρός.

Others correct it as follows: “Instead of *burro* we say *pyrrum*.” In the same place, “*porro* between *c* and *q*.” Another copy omits “between.”

5. “By *e*.” Another copy: “by *e* alone.” In the same place, “it must be written.” Another copy omits this.

6. “Because it was not … made.” Another copy: “because the name was made from *aqua* [water].” This seems corrupt.

9. “Because it is called from *forma* [form].” Thus Grialius reads in some copies, together with Vulcanius. In others: “because it is from *formo*, that is, hot”; for the heat of the blood produces beauty. The manuscripts vary: another copy has, “because it is called from *forma*”; another, “because it is called *forma*, or even from *formo*, that is, hot”; “for *color* [colour],” etc.

In the same place, “*facit generatus*.” Another copy: “*facit agnatus*.”

10. “A sign.” Another copy: “a letter.” In the same place, “*humus*.” Another copy adds: “*humus*, *humilitas* [earth, humility].”

11. “*Troiia*, *Maiia*.” In some manuscripts only one capital *I* is written, as *TroIa*, *Mala*. In the same place, “for the double [letter].” Another copy: “for the doubled [letter].”

13. “Everything … must be written.” Another copy omits this.

14. “To which it is contrary.” The Gothic witnesses: “of which, on the contrary.” In the same place, “it assumed the name.” Another copy: “it takes its name.”

15. “He handed [him] over, Caesar.” The Lucanian manuscript has: “he handed [him] over to Caesar”; this should be noted.

16. “By one.” Another copy: “by one *l*.” “By two *ll*.” Another copy: “by two *ll*.”

17. “Or *ossum*.” Another copy: “or *ossa*.”

19. “By *e*.” Another copy: “by *e* alone.”

20. “Is prefixed.” Another copy: “is placed.” In the same place, “follows.” Another copy: “follows afterward.”

21. “With *a*.” Another copy: “by *ae*.” In the same place, “without *a*.” Another copy: “by *e*.”

23. “Communion.” Another copy: “commonality.”

24. “*Sēdum*.” Another copy: “but *sēdum*.”

25. “*Tamtus*.” In the middle, *m*. Another copy: “*tantus* … with *n* in the middle.” But the appended reasoning conflicts with this.

26. “With *a*.” Another copy: “by *ae*.” In the same place, “without *a*.” Another copy: “by *e*.”

28. “Just as *militia*.” Another copy: “thus *militia*.”

29. Above *sicilicos*. Another copy: “above *sicilicum*.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

1. “So that they are uncertain.” The Gothic witnesses, with Lucanus, as elsewhere often happens, have: “and uncertain.”

2. “If indeed.” The Lucanian manuscript has: “if anything,” which seems correct. In the same place, “by chance.” Another copy: “of chance.”

4. “That it is.” Another copy: “that it is the same.”

“*Pistrilla*.” Another copy: “*pistrella*.” In Grialius there was a mistake: *pristinum* instead of *pistrinum*.

In the same place, “from the position … to infer.” Another copy: “From the exposition—that is, the primitive declension—and from diminution to infer the gender”; another: “that is, the primitive declension, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

1. “With the example proposed.” Grialius printed this way in some copies, but omitted “with the example proposed” in others. Other copies have *posito* instead of *proposito*.

In the same place, “because it grew by flowing.” Another copy: “what flows grew.”

3. “Kings from acting rightly.” Here too the copies of Grialius vary. Some have this wording; others add: “Kings from ruling, that is, from acting rightly.” Some manuscripts: “Kings from ruling and acting rightly”; others: “Kings from acting rightly.”

In the same place, “from washing mud.” Another copy: “from washing, *lotus* [washed].”

4. “*Graculus*.” Another copy: “*garrulus*.” In the same place, “into Latin.” Another copy: “in Latin.” In the same place, “in Greek.” Another copy omits this.

5. “From different ….” Another copy: “from the ….” In the same place, “unknown names.” Another copy: “names, and unknown [names].”

## CHAPTER XXX

1. “Word for word.” Another copy: “adverbially.”

In the same place, “about which inquiry is made.” Another copy: “about which [something] is sought”; another: “about the matter concerning which inquiry is made”; another: “about whose quality inquiry is made.”

2. Likewise: “Latus.” Another copy: “Virgilius Latus.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

1. “Let there be between the king.” Another copy: “let there be a distinction between the king.” In the same place, “let both be.” Another copy: “let there be between both.” In the same place, “thus, and so forth.” Another copy omits this.

## CHAPTER XXXII

1. “Or by sound.” Another copy: “or by number.”

“Deeds of the Romans with their resources.” Another copy: “deeds subjected to the Romans, with their resources.” Some have: “with their works.”

2. “Likewise, when.” Another copy: “again, when.”

3. “Aspirations.” Another copy: “annunciations.”

4. “Into another syllable.” Another copy: “in another syllable.”

5. “*Metacisms*.” Another copy: “*motacisms*”; another: “*miotacisms*.”

6. “But this too.” Another copy: “but this.”

7. “The sound is doubled, as in *Troiia*, *Maiia*.” Another copy: “it is doubled, as in *Troia*, *Maia*.”

8. “If … they are pronounced.” Another copy: “whenever … they are pronounced.” In the same place, “which is contrary.” Another copy: “which is the opposite.”

9. “Mother earth.” Another copy: “mother earth is”; another: “*matertera* [maternal aunt].”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

1. “Grant pardon.” Another copy: “grant pardon” [plural or imperative variant].

2. “From the Cilicians.” Another copy: “from Cilician citizens.” In the same place, “among others.” Another copy: “among Italians.”

In the same place, “inconsequently.” Another copy: “and inconveniently.”

4. “Or by parts.” In Grialius there was the error: “or by by parts.”

In the same place, “through accidents.” Another copy adds: “through the accidents of the parts of speech.” In the same place, “it comes about in speech.” Another copy omits “it comes about.”

In the same place, “they occur.” The Gothic witnesses: “they are made to occur.” In the same place, “with parts, so that.” Another copy: “with parts of speech, so that.” In the same place, “figures.” Another copy: “a figure.”

5. “Lucilius.” Another copy: “Lucius.” In the same place, “he ought … he strives.” Another copy: “they ought … they strive.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV

1. “*Cacephaton*.” Another copy: “*cacephaton*, *pleonasmos* ….”

2. “As when … in forgiving.” Another copy omits this material.

3. “As when … among human beings.” Another copy omits this material.

5. “The Doric camp.” Virgil. Another copy: “To see the Doric camp.” In the same place, “it becomes.” Another copy: “it became.”

In the same place, “he had finished.” Another copy adds: “It is finished. But if in any other way whatsoever an uncomposed expression is uttered, it is called *cacephaton*.”

6. “As in *Hactenus*.” Another copy: “as in Virgil: *Hactenus*.”

7. “Provided that it is not.” Another copy: “since it is not.” Thus elsewhere *dum* and *quum* vary in the manuscripts.

In the same place, “not to die.” Others add: “*not to die*. And in Isaiah: ‘With the ear you have heard.’ And in John: ‘What we have seen with our eyes.’ Since we do not see in any other way except with our eyes. And: ‘I have spoken with my tongue.’”

9. “The same expression.” Another copy: “the same repeated utterance.”

10. “It was.” Lucanus adds: “it was.” To these are added *hypallage*, *onesis*, *anacolaton*, that is, “incomparable”; *pathos*, that is, “passion”; *ecphonesis*, the first exclamation; *energia*, that is, “exclamation—it was.”

The Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark omits “*pathos*, that is, passion,” and adds: “the second exclamation—it was.”

11. “Humility, etc.” Another copy: “humility, an inferior expression of a great matter, as ….” In the same place, “vast.” Another copy adds “Virgil.” The same occurs in other examples.

13. “*Amphibolia*.” Another copy: “*amphibologia*.” In the same place, “it arises either through case.” Another copy omits “either.” In the same place, “in it.” Another copy: “in that.”

14. “It also arises through.” Another copy: “*amphibologia* also arises through.” In the same place, “distinction.” Another copy: “definition.”

15. “The verb: *Deprecatur*.” Another copy: “the verb, as in *Deprecatur*”; another: “the verb, as when someone says *Criminatur*.”

In the same place, “Cicero accuses.” Another copy: “Cicero goes to court.”

In the same place, “nor is it shown … to accuse.” Another copy has:

“Nor does he add whom, or by whom. For Cato the philosopher was criticizing the crimes of others. Cicero was a defender of cases; for *vades* are those who conduct legal cases. But in this ambiguity it is not shown whom Cato accuses, or on whose behalf Cicero acts. For *vadat* means ‘he conducts a case,’ and he does not say whose case it is.”

Others agree with us, but somewhat differently: “Whether they themselves entreated others, or were themselves entreated by others, etc.”

16. “Through *homonymia*, when.” Another copy: “through homonyms, by which.”

## CHAPTER XXXV

1. “In Latin.” Another copy: “Latin.” In the same place, “which comes about.” Another copy: “which comes about” [feminine agreement].

2. “Of a word.” Another copy adds: “of a word, letter, or syllable.”

In the same place, “and *tetulit* instead of *tulit*.” Another copy omits this.

In the same place, “as in *reliquias* … *imperator*.” Another copy omits this; another adds: “And let descendants remain in religion,” instead of “for religion.”

3. “As *magis* instead of *mage*.” Another copy: “as *admittier* instead of *admitti*.”

4. “Lengthening.” Another copy: “prefixing.”

In the same place, “so that … it ought.” Another copy adds: “once he has done this, an exile”; Virgil. And: “Diana exercises the choruses.”

In the same place, “watery Orion.” Another copy: “as when we say *Orion*”; another omits “watery Orion”; another adds: “and the city Fidena.”

In the same place, “to be pronounced with length.” Another copy: “to be lengthened.”

In the same place, “the splitting of one.” Another copy omits “one.”

In the same place, “*Albai*, *longai*.” Others give examples in *pictai*, *aulai*.

5. “As *Phaeton*, etc.” In other examples there are *janva* instead of *janua*, *genva* instead of *genua*, and *parjete* instead of *pariete*.

In the same place, “of those joined.” Another copy: “joined”; another: “united.”

6. In Grialius there was the error “collision of the vowels.”

In the same place, “and on the lands.” Others add: “tossed about and elsewhere.”

In the same place, “counter-position.” Another copy: “first position.”

In the same place, “instead of another letter.” Another copy omits this. Thus others too omit the examples *Olli*, *Evandre*, etc.

7. “*Lexin*.” Another copy: “figures.”

In the same place, “is a *metaplasmus*.” Another copy: “to be a *metaplasmus*”; another: “they say it is a *metaplasmus*.”

In the same place, “it comes about through reason.” Another copy: “it comes about through speech.”

In the same place, “*phrasin*.” Another copy: “*schema*.”

In the same place, “through faulty reasoning.” Another copy: “through faulty speech.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI

1. “Adornment.” Another copy: “ornament.”

In the same place, “although there are many.” Another copy: “since there are many”; another: “although many are.”

Others have: “By the forms of both expressions they remove weariness from the thoughts and adorn the utterance. These, then, are the kinds among grammarians.”

2. “Ought to follow.” Another copy: “they say they ought to follow.”

In the same place, “as an ornament.” Another copy: “as an ornament of poetry.” In the same place, “and afterward.” Another copy: “and afterward” [shorter form]. In the same place, “from there.” Another copy: “and then.”

3. “*Oenophoris*.” Another copy: “*oenophori*.”

5. “Completed.” Another copy: “is completed”; another: “finished.”

In the same place, “Soft chestnuts.” Another copy omits this.

In the same place, “above … milk.” Another copy omits this.

6. “Parts.” Another copy: “parts of speech.”

13. “With a certain circuit of expression.” Another copy omits this. In the same place, “clouds.” Another copy: “mist.”

14. “But this is good.” Many manuscripts: “but this is good”; another: “but these things are good.”

In the same place, “now in the middle … thickets.” Many omit this entire passage.

15. “Or lifting [it] with his hand.” Another copy: “and lifting his hands.” Thus others read it in Virgil.

17. “To nothing.” Another copy: “into nothing.”

18. “That.” Another copy: “that: ‘From above.’”

## CHAPTER XXXVII

1. “Latin modes.” Another copy: “in Latin, either manners or modes.”

In the same place, “to be handed down.” Another copy: “in handing down”; another: “to be handed down” [plural].

2. “Just as when.” Another copy omits “when.” In the same place, “placed.” Another copy omits this.

3. “He will have asked.” Another copy: “he asked.”

6. “This from that.” Another copy: “this and from that.” In the same place, “bestows.” Another copy: “bestows something else.”

In the same place, “and: *Now*.” Another copy: “and: *Centaur*. *Now*.”

In the same place, “only.” The Gothic witnesses: “just as much.”

7. “Indicating from what precedes what follows: *Inque*.” Another copy: “from what precedes what follows, as in: *Inque*.”

8. “Proximity.” Another copy: “by proximity.”

9. “Mixed, etc.” The first edition: “Vulcan sends the mingled spark to the stars.”

12. “The noun: it is prefixed.” Another copy: “the noun placed: it is proposed.”

In the same place, “or we show.” Another copy: “or we offend”; another omits this.

13. “But the species is a part, whereas the genus is the whole.” Another copy: “but the species is its own whole genus”; another omits this.

15. “Through the limbs, sleep.” The Gothic witnesses omit this.

In the same place, “avoids.” Another copy: “avoids completely.”

16. “In order.” Another copy omits this.

17. “*Synchesis*.” Thus Grialius and most others. Another copy: “*synthesis*”; another: “*synchrisis*.” But *synchisis* is better, as I restored at note 20.

In the same place, “*hysteron proteron*.” Another copy: “*proteron*, or *hysterologia*.”

18. “The judgment.” Another copy: “our judgment.” In the same place, “for it is … Achates.” Another copy omits this.

20. “The gods by whom this command had stood. Hence.” Another copy: “the gods. Hence,” with the other words omitted.

21. “By which they are indicated.” Another copy: “which are indicated.”

22. “The Punic [wars], or the three Punic wars are signified.” Another copy: “the Punic [wars] are signified, or the three Punic wars.”

23. “Is stated.” Another copy: “must be stated.”

24. “Through excessive.” Another copy: “because of excessive.”

In the same place, “and the *Manes*, etc.” Another copy: “and the *Manes*, that is, the gentle ones, although they are fierce; and the moderate ones, although they are terrifying and savage.”

25. “Signifies.” Another copy: “calls.”

26. “The force of allegory is twofold.” Another copy: “allegory is doubled twice.”

In the same place, “under another matter.” Another copy: “under other matters.”

In the same place, “an obscure … shadowed meaning.” Another copy: “it obscures … with an obscure sense.”

Others add after “shadowed”: “For example: ‘A certain daughter, mother of her mother, and mother of the daughters of her daughter.’”

27. “As when one responds to those asking questions.” Another copy: “as when we respond to those asking questions.”

In the same place, “fortune.” Another copy omits this.

28. “The wolf first.” Another copy: “the wolf earlier.” In the same place, “this.” Another copy: “that.”

30. “As that.” Another copy: “as this.”

31. “Of the matter through its likeness.” Another copy: “its likeness of the matter.”

In the same place, “is laid open.” Another copy: “is placed.”

33. “Settled down.” The Gothic witnesses, together with the ancient editions: “sat down,” as it is also read in the *Art* of Saint Julian of Toledo.

In the same place, “a likeness from a foreign kind.” Another copy: “a comparison from another kind.”

34. “Appropriate to it.” The Gothic witnesses: “appropriate to him.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

1. “To signify.” Another copy: “to be signified.”

In the same place, “may rush forth.” Another copy: “may come forth.”

2. “Moreover, so much.” Another copy: “therefore it must be understood that so much.”

In the same place, “*Syrius*.” Another copy: “*Syrus*.”

In the same place, “he wrote in unbound discourse.” Another copy: “he wrote unbound discourse.”

In the same place, “from then on, and the rest strove in prose eloquence.” Another copy: “from then on they composed prose.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX

1. “Because.” Another copy: “which.”

In the same place, “established.” Another copy: “established” [feminine form].

2. “Arranged.” Another copy: “arranged” [plural agreement].

In the same place, “which … are called.” Another copy: “whom they call.”

In the same place, “could.” Another copy: “may.”

6. “For it is, etc.” Another copy: “for animal is common and general to all.”

7. “To the mute.” Another copy: “and to the mute.”

In the same place, “when mortal.” Another copy: “when ‘mortal’ is said.”

8. “Occur.” Another copy: “approach.”

In the same place, “full of meaning.” Another copy: “full of a sentence.”

In the same place, “and differences.” Another copy: “and teachings.”

In the same place, “which this same.” Another copy: “which are common.”

9. “And a fiction.” Another copy: “and fictions.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

2. “That is.” Another copy: “namely.”

3. “Of several.” Another copy: “of very many.” In the same place, “gives.” Another copy: “give.”

4. “Denominatives.” Another copy adds: “that is, derivatives”; another: “and derivatives.”

5. “That is.” Another copy: “namely.”

6. “Principally.” Another copy adds: “to subsist.”

In the same place, “species.” Another copy: “omits.”

7. “Either … or.” Another copy: “whether … or.”

In the same place, “nor a slave.” Another copy adds: “the former.”

In the same place, “the other.” Another copy: “the other” [masculine form].

8. “Moreover … may lie.” This passage is omitted.

In the same place, “in the forum.” Another copy: “as in the forum.”

In the same place, “they have two.” Another copy adds:

“They have two: position and time. Position, as ‘far away’ and ‘near.’ Time, as ‘today’ and ‘yesterday.’ Moreover, position, etc., ‘may lie,’ as at the beginning of this note.” Another copy: “Moreover, position is so called from placement, as in: ‘What is that man doing?’ Either he is sitting or he is lying down.”

9. “Something.” Another copy: “from elsewhere.”

10. “Since … since.” Another copy: “when … when.”

11. “Orator.” Another copy: “preacher.”

In the same place, “by arguing.” Another copy: “by preaching.”

In the same place, “*usia* … the rest.” Another copy: “But *usia* is substance, that is, a property, which belongs to the rest”; another: “that is, a property belonging to substance, which [belongs] to the rest.”

13. “Three.” Another copy omits this.

In the same place, “there are: quantity.” Another copy: “there are, namely, quantity.”

14. “From subjects.” Another copy: “from substances.”

In the same place, “to man.” Another copy: “to a name.”

15. “It must be read attentively: *quoniam*.” Another copy: “it must be understood: *quando*,” or “thus: *quando*.”

In the same place, “ten.” Another copy: “these ten.”

In the same place, “are applied.” Another copy: “are appended.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

1. “Most cautious in repetitions.” Another copy: “most acute in reasonings.”

In the same place, “he kept writing.” Another copy: “he wrote.”

In the same place, “he dyed.” Another copy: “he held.”

In the same place, “the preface to the *Perihermeniae*.” Another copy omits this.

2. “Is signified by one.” Another copy: “signifies by one.”

In the same place, “they interpret the whole.” Another copy: “they interpret; for he uses these things—the whole.”

In the same place, “interpreter of the mind.” Another copy: “interpreted by the mind.”

3. “And in making speeches.” Another copy omits this.

In the same place, “we call [it] *hermenia* ….” Another copy: “he demonstrated it in the most eloquent speech”; another has *perihermeniam* instead of *hermeniam*.

In the same place, “uttered.” Another copy: “proved.”

In the same place, “*cataphasis* and *apophasis*.” Another copy: “*cataphrasis* and *apophrasis*.”

5. “Of those things which … he thinks.” Another copy: “of something among those things that are said about another, noted as ‘he thinks’”; another: “things are said, as in ‘he notes, he thinks.’”

In the same place, “signifying.” Another copy adds: “by convention.”

7. “All these things … an explanation is found.” Another copy omits this.

In the same place, “This is the usefulness of the *Perihermeniae*.” Another copy: “This is the account of the *Perihermeniae*”; another: “intention” instead of “account.”

### Chapter XXVIII

Note 1: “of that art.” Another reading: “of the dialectical art.” In the same place, “to the greatest extent.” Another reading: “first.” “Let him be absent.” Another reading: “let it be absent to him.”

Note 2: “that is.” Some copies omit *id est* (“that is”), while others add it elsewhere.

Note 3: *directim* (“directly”). Another reading: *directum* (“direct”), and likewise below.

Note 4: “in the dedicative [affirmative] propositions.” Another reading: “in the dedicative and abdicative [negative] proposition.” In the same place, “therefore no.” Another reading: “therefore none”; there is a similar variation below.

Note 6: “the dedicative and universal abdicative [propositions]—the abdicative.” Another reading: “the dedicative and universal abdicative—the dedicative.” Below also, *dedicativa* occurs for *dedicativo*, or conversely.

Note 9: “in the dedicative [propositions].” Another reading: “in the dedicative [proposition].” And similarly elsewhere.

Note 12: “of the formula of the second mode.” Another reading: “of the formula of the second mode.”

Note 15: “the abdicative.” Another reading: “the dedicative.”

Note 16: “of the formula of the third.” Another reading: “of the formula of the third [mode].”

Note 19: “from universal propositions.” Another reading: “from the universal [proposition].”

Note 22: “to be able fully.” Another reading: “to know clearly.” In the same place, “and what has been treated more subtly. He will recognize.” Another reading: “and he will recognize what has been treated more subtly.”

Note 26, [Col. 0772C]: “so that they may be able,” etc. Another reading: “so that they may clearly display the manifestations of judgments and certain indications of expressions”; another reads *judiciorum* (“of judgments”) for *indiciorum* (“of indications”).

### Chapter XXIX

Note 1: “not of what sort.” Another reading omits *non* (“not”). In the same place, “the nature of the thing.” Another reading omits *rei* (“of the thing”). In the same place, “into fifteen parts.” Another reading: “into fourteen parts.”

Note 2: “laughter.” Another reading: “sense.”

Note 3: “in conception, and.” Another reading omits *et* (“and”). In the same place, “he did not say here.” Another reading: “for he did not say.” “By saying.” Another reading omits this. “He calls away.” Another reading: “having been called away.” “For in this [case], and in the others.” Another reading: “for this [case], and the others.” “Because.” Other copies read “and because” or “but because.” “Substantial.” Another adds *est* (“is”).

Note 4: “qualitative.” Another reading: “quality.” “What sort it is.” Another reading: “what sort [of thing] it is.” “That which exists.” Another reading: “that which is sought.” “It ought.” Another reading: “it ought to.”

Note 5: “is called.” Another reading: “is named.” “What each thing is.” Another reading: “what the thing is.” “All things.” Another reading: “of the whole.” “And burdensome.” Another reading: “and of honor.” “Inclined toward lust.” Another reading: “ready for lust.” “These and other things.” Another reading: “these and such things”; another: “these sorts of things.” “Breadths.” Another reading: “breadth.” “In a similar manner.” Another reading: “likeness.”

Note 6: “word for word.” Another reading: “adverb.” In the same place, “concerning whose matter.” Another reading omits *re* (“matter”); another reads “concerning which”; another, “concerning whose account.” “Is asked.” Another reading: “is required.” “He declares one thing by another.” Another reading: “he declares another thing.”

Note 8: “is that by which he eludes the waves.” Another reading: “is because he strikes down the waves.” In the same place, “so that he may warn.” Another reading: “so that he may move.” “And rebuke.” Another reading: “or rebuke.” “Virtue.” Another reading: “virtues”; another: “of virtue.” “Of the greater.” Another reading: “of the modes.” “Is the head.” Another reading: “is the summit.”

Note 11: “The Greeks say *hōs typos* [ὡς τύπος], the Latins *exemplum* [‘example’],” etc. Another reading: “the Greeks say *kat’ elleipes* [κατ’ ἔλλειπες],” etc., as in the following note; for what is the eleventh species for us is the tenth for others.

Note 12: “The Latins say *per* [‘through’].” Another reading: “The Latins say, according to the rule, that is, ‘through lack,’” etc. In the same place, “to whom a *bes* [two thirds of a unit] is lacking.” Codex Albanianus: “to whom a *dodrans* [three quarters of a unit] is lacking.”

Note 14: “They say according to the rule.” Another reading: “they call [it] relative.” In the same place, “but this happens,” etc. Here some place the following species, “the relative,” etc. Thus all these matters are confused with one another.

Note 16: “beneath the earth.” Another reading: “under the earth.”

### Chapter XXX

Note 1: “are called affected things, which.” Another reading: “are called effected things, which,” [Col. 0773A]; another omits *quae* (“which”).

Note 4: “is elicited.” Another reading: “is chosen”; another: “is said.” In the same place, “he says.” Another reading: “I say.”

Note 5: “affected things.” Another reading: “effected things.” “Into another inflection of the word.” Another reading: “in another inflection of the word.”

Note 7: “suggest.” Another reading: “to suggest.”

Note 8: “is derived.” Another reading: “is said.”

Note 9: “to open.” Another reading: “or to open.”

Note 11: “from joined things.” Another reading: “from conjugated forms.” In the same place, “when probably.” Another reading: “when, on the contrary, probably.”

Note 13: “by imputation.” Another reading: “by opposition.”

Note 14: “The Greeks.” Another reading: “in Greek.” In the same place, “all testimony … in five ways.” Another reading: “testimony, however, consists in a matter and is divided in five ways.”

Note 15: “from tortures. A person.” Another reading adds:

> “From tortures. The third, therefore, higher mode, which is from circumstances, is divided into eight species: I, natural ability; II, resources; III, age; IV, fortune; V, skill; VI, use; VII, necessity; VIII, the concurrence (another reading: concussion) of accidental circumstances. All testimony is what is taken from some external matter in order to produce belief. A person, etc.”

Thus read the Gothic manuscripts and the older editions.

Note 16: “especially in virtue.” Another reading: “with the greatest virtue.” In the same place, “circumstances.” Another reading: “testimonies”; another: “testimonies from circumstances.” [Col. 0773B] “They bring forward.” Another reading: “let them bring forward.”

Note 17: “in time.” Another reading: “with time.” In the same place, “belongs.” Another reading: “belong.” “To pertain.” Another reading: “to belong.”

Note 18: “mobility.” Another reading: “nobility.” “He concluded.” Another reading: “he has concluded.” “May fall.” Another reading: “so that it may fall.”

### Chapter XXXI

Note 1: “because.” Another reading: “on account of which.” “Which belong to it.” Another reading omits *sibi* (“to it”). “All contraries.” Another reading: “all things in opposition.” “Contrary.” Another reading: “different”; another: “differently.” “Only contrariwise.” Another reading: “only contrary.”

Note 2: “some of them.” Another reading: “some of it”; another: “some such things”; some omit *quaedam* (“some”) or *ex eis* (“of them”), reading instead “of it” or “of such things.” “Both.” Another adds: “both of the contraries.” “May create.” Other readings: “believes,” “may believe,” “may hand down,” or “may lack.” “White and black.” Another reading has the neuter forms: “white and black.” “They have.” Another reading: “it has.”

Note 3: “They have—not happily. According to.” Another reading: “They have, namely, neither happy in its entirety nor unhappy in its entirety. According to.”

Note 4: “This alone.” Another reading: “this alone of these.” “Is greater.” Another reading: “there is a greater [one].” “May be referred.” Another reading: “is referred.” “To the double.” Another adds: “or to the thing opposed to it.” “Relative.” Another reading: “to the relative itself”; another: “or relative.” “That which is opposed.” Another reading: “that which is opposed, however it may be opposed.” Another reading omits “or that it belongs to the thing to which it is opposed.”

Note 5: “so that they do not belong … namely.” Another reading: “so that they do not belong to those things that are opposed. Namely”; another: “again, so that they do not belong to the things to which they are opposed. Namely.”

Note 6: “because it shows.” Another reading: “by which it shows.” “Vision. In the place.” Another reading: “vision in the eyes. In the place.”

Note 7: “therefore they differ.” The Gothic manuscripts read: “that differs”; for which I would prefer “that they differ,” since *id* in the sense of “in that respect,” with *differre*, is characteristic of the age of Isidore. “Individually.” Another reading: “separately.”

Note 8: “its third.” Another reading omits *ejus* (“its”).

## Book Three

### Preface

“Separating.” Another reading: “we separate.” “Geometry, music.” The Gothic manuscripts and the older editions read: “music and geometry”; and immediately afterward they explain music before geometry. “Countable.” Another reading: “numerical.” “The magnitude of forms.” Another reading: “the magnitude and forms.” “We shall indicate.” Another reading: “we indicate.” “The causes … may.” Another reading: “the cause … may.” “To be shown.” Another reading: “to be recognized.”

### Chapter I

Note 1: “since it itself, so that it may be.” Another reading: “because it itself, so that it may be so”; another: “by which it itself may be.”

### Chapter II

Note 1: “of number.” Another reading: “numbers,” or “of number.” “They assert.” Another reading: “they name”; another, apparently corruptly, “they pursue.” In the same place, “arranged.” Another reading: “composed.”

### Chapter III

Note 1: “not a number.” Another adds: “they wish.” “Whence are numbers so called? From *numero* [‘number’], *numus* [‘coin’],” etc.

Note 3: “in many.” Another reading omits *in* (“in”).

Note 5: “hence also the thousands, which.” Another reading: “hence also the thousands, as though *milatia*.” In the same place, “which the Greeks.” Another reading omits *quae* (“which”). “The letter *myria* [μυρία].” Another reading: “the letter, namely *r* in place of *l*; they call them *myriades*.” A manuscript note in the old Bignaean edition reads:

> “It would be more correct to read *chilian* [χιλίαν], for it is certain that *myriada* [μυριάδα] signifies ten thousand.”

### Chapter IV

Note 1: “of the holy.” Another reading: “of the sacred.”

Note 3: “knowing this art.” Another reading: “the knowledge of this art,” omitting *noti* (“knowing”); another has “of knowledge” for “knowingly”; another, “being acquainted with” for “knowing.” In the same place, “they can.” Another reading: “we can.” “From a great.” Another reading: “from some.” “We calculate the courses of the months.” Another reading: “we discuss the course of the months.”

Note 4: “in matters.” Another reading: “in matters.” “Take away.” Another reading: “you take away.” “In the age.” Another reading: “in calculation”; another: “a calculation”; another: “the calculation of reckoning.” “He who does not know calculation.” Another reading: “those who do not know calculation.”

### Chapter V

Note 1: “An even number … a third, intermediate [kind].” Another reading: “an even number, etc.: evenly odd and oddly even. An odd number is divided here into first, simple; second, composite; third, etc.” Another reading has “intermediate” instead of “intermediate [masculine].” In the same place, “incomposite.” Another reading: “composite.”

Note 2: “and the rest.” Another reading: “and so with the others.”

Note 3: “half.” Another reading: “the middle.”

Note 4: “indivisible.” Another reading: “unseverable.” In the same place, “VI, X, XVIII.” Some copies omit X; others omit VI and X; others arrange the matter differently.

Note 5: “into half.” Another reading: “in the middle.”

Note 7: “they measure by unity.” Another reading: “they counterfeit unity”; another: “they perceive unity.” In the same place, “by another number.” Another reading: “from another number.” “And XXI, etc.” Another reading: “and twenty-one.”

[Col. 0774B] “For we say three times three, and seven times three; three times five, and five times five. Intermediate [numbers], etc.”

Note 8: “only of the second and.” Another reading omits “of the second and.”

Note 9: “others diminished.” Another reading: “diminutive.” In the same place, “which is two.” Another reading: “which is two”; and similarly below.

Note 10: “drawn together.” Another reading: “joined together”; another: “drawn together.” “Multiplied together, when reduced to parts they result in a lower total.” Another reading: “they amount to a smaller total.”

Note 11: “a third and a half.” Another reading: “a third half.” “Three together.” Another reading: “and three together.” In the same place, “within the denary.” Another reading: “between the ten”; and likewise below, *inter* (“between”) occurs for *intra* (“within”).

### Chapter VI

Note 1 and following: There is great variation in the wording here and in the following chapters, which can be observed in the fragments of the Gothic manuscripts among the appendices. In this first note, however, it should be observed that some read:

> “Either it is referred to something else. That which is according to itself is divided thus … That which is referred to something else is divided thus.”

Others read: “There are greater [things],” etc.

### Chapter VII

Note 1: “superficial III.” Another reading: “superficial things, such as three.” “Solid.” In the same place, “solid. Discrete.” Another inserts:

> “Solid. For the ternary is the first number that unfolds breadth: solids, such as eight. For it is the first cube. Discrete.”

Note 2: “if in.” Another reading omits *in* (“in”). In the same place, “is understood as a line, or space, or solid.” Another reading: “is understood, that is, as a line (or in a line), or a space, or a solid.” “Likewise.” Another reading: “likewise as.”

Note 3: “up to.” Another reading omits *usque* (“up to”). “For designation.” Another reading: “for marking.” In the same place, “among the Greeks.” Another adds: “among the Greeks; this is a linear figure.”

Note 4: “but also.” Another reading omits *et* (“also”). In the same place, “are contained.” Another adds:

> “A triangular number is as follows,” etc., approximately as in Codex Toletanus T A, a fragment of which was included among the appendices.

Note 5: “while for themselves.” Another reading: “while similarly.” “Five. Solid.” Another reading: “five times. Thus. Solid.” This indicates that a figure should be added, which most copies omit.

### Chapter VIII

Note 1: “analogical.” Another reading: “analogy.”

Note 2: “and the means multiplied.” Another reading: “and the means doubled.” In the same place, “make LXXII.” Another reading: “make seventy-two.”

Note 3: “thus.” Another adds:

> “The middle exceeds [the others] by a part. First, the middle is exceeded by the extreme by the same part; for example, six and eight exceed [it] by two parts, and these two parts are a third.”

In the same place, “for example, etc.” Another reading: “for example, six, eight, twelve. For the first, that is, six, is exceeded by its third part—that is, where it is exceeded by the middle, namely eight—which the middle, twelve, surpasses by a third part of itself, namely four.”

In the same place, “from the last.” Another adds “twelfth”:

> “The arithmetic mean: VI, IX, XII. The musical mean: V, VIII, XI. The geometric mean: VI, VIII, IX, XII.”

### Chapter IX

Note 1: “I do not say that the very same.” Another reading: “I do not say that it is possible.” Another: “I do not say the very same.” In the same place, “however great it may be.” Another reading omits this. “Of numbers.” Another reading: “number.”

### Chapter X

Note 1: “The discipline of geometry.” Another reading: “the discipline of geometry.” In the same place, “because, when it overflowed.” Another reading: “because of the overflowing.” “And with mud, the possessions of all.” Another reading: “and with its mud, all possessions.” “Advanced by the wise.” Another reading: “proceeded from the wise”; another: “was produced by the wise”; another: “was perfected by the wise.”

Note 2: “students.” Another reading: “study thus.” “He would spread out.” Another reading: “he will have spread out.”

Note 3: “has been named.” Another reading: “is named.”

[Col. 0775A]

### Chapter XI

Note 1: “into plane figures.” Another reading: “into a plane.” In the same place, “countable.” Another reading: “numerical.” “Into a rational magnitude.” Another reading omits this; another reads “into a reasonable magnitude.”

Note 2: “There are things which.” Another reading: “as geometers call them, which.” In the same place, “are contained.” Another adds:

> “These are, according to Plato, five in number: triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal, and heptagonal. The octad now proceeds into a cube, that is, into a solid figure. Countable.”

Note 4: “figures … five.” Another reading omits this.

### Chapter XII

Note 1: “On the plane, etc.” Another reading: “solid figures are, etc.,” as in Codex Toletanus, with which Albanus and many others agree in this chapter, including the figures explicitly.

### Chapter XIII

Note 1: “the principles of this art.” Another reading: “but the first figure of this art.” In the same place, “line.” Another reading: “the second is the line.” “Lies.” Another reading: “lies …”

Note 2: “forms.” Another reading: “formulas.” In the same place, “figures.” Another reading: “ten figures.”

### Chapter XIV

Note 1: “the means multiplied.” Another reading: “the means doubled.” In the same place, “LXXII.” Another reading: “seventy-two.”

### Chapter XV

Note 2: “is.” Another reading: “is, and.” In the same place, “into past time.” Another reading: “in past time.” “Of Memory.” Another reading: “of Minerva”; another: “of Juno.”

### Chapter XVI

Note 1: “Jubal.” Another reading: “Tubal.” “Struck by extension.” Another reading: “by the striking of extended [strings].”

### Chapter XVII

Note 1: “is revolved.” Another reading has *revolvi* (“to be revolved”) without another verb, as elsewhere.

Note 2: “consoles.” Another reading: “solidifies.”

Note 3: “aroused.” Another reading: “aroused.” In the same place, “music excites dolphins.” Another reading: “music excited dolphins.” “We are moved.” Another reading: “we move.”

### Chapter XVIII

“Parts.” Another reading omits this. In the same place, “discerns.” Another reading: “decides.”

### Chapter XIX

Note 1: “sound.” Another reading: “the sound of music.” “By a beat.” Another reading: “by an impulse.”

Note 2: “through a trumpet.” Another reading: “through a small trumpet.” “By a beat.” Another reading: “by an impulse.” “Sonorous.” Another reading: “sounding.”

### Chapter XX

Note 1: “harmonic.” Another reading: “harmony.”

Note 2: “by the spirit.” Another reading: “through the spirit.” In the same place, “properly, etc.” Another reading: “properly, however, the voices of human beings are rational, or of animals.” “A sound is called a voice.” Another reading: “a sound is called a voice,” without another verb. “Harmony.” Another reading: “harmonic.”

At this point the manuscript copies add other headings, such as “On the second division of music, which is called harmonic,” or “There are many kinds of voice.”

Note 3: “the sense of hearing.” Another reading: “the sense of the hearer.”

Note 6: “of passing from one sound into another.” Another reading: “passing from one sound into another.”

Note 7: “from which.” Another reading: “from which the first [is derived].”

Note 8: “sound makes song.” Another reading: “sound makes a chant.”

Note 9: “position.” Another reading: “deposition.”

Note 10: “continuous.” Another reading: “continuously.”

Note 12: “when.” Another reading: “when.” In the same place, “it emits sounds.” Another reading: “it emits a sound.” “Is struck.” Another reading: “strikes.”

Note 13: “A harsh voice is hoarse.” The Gothic manuscripts read: “A harsh voice is faint.” “Vinnola.” Another reading: “vinnolated.” “The voice is soft.” Another reading: “the voice is a voice, light, soft.”

Note 14: “may fill.” Another reading: “may completely fill.” In the same place, “may charm the minds.” Another reading: “may charm the spirits.”

### Chapter XXI

Note 1: “with the breath blowing back.” Another reading: “with the breath blowing.” “Pandura.” Another reading: “pandoria.”

Note 2: “is customary.” Another reading: “is the custom of the Greeks.”

Note 3: “praises.” Another reading: “of praise.” “Distinguished.” Another reading: “distinguished [feminine].” “At the beginning.” Another reading: “in the beginning.”

Note 4: “then through.” Another reading: “whence through.” In the same place, “the singer.” Another reading: “the song is.”

Note 5: “from *calendo* [‘calling’].” The Gothic manuscripts read: “from *canendo* [‘singing’].” “Called.” Another reading: “called [neuter].”

Note 6: “from Idi.” Another reading: “from Ide.” Codex Palatinus 281, in the margin: “from one.” In the same place, “*phos* is a word.” Another reading: “*phos*, in Latin ‘voice.’”

Note 8: “Pandura, etc.” Another reading: “Pandorius … called, concerning whom.” “First.” Another reading: “first [adverbially].”

### Chapter XXII

Note 1: “and a beat.” Another reading: “and a beating.” “Struck.” Another reading: “struck back.” “Of this kind.” Another reading: “of this sort.”

Note 2: “Jubal.” Another reading: “Tubal.” “Is handed down.” Another reading: “is believed.”

Codex Mutinensis adds:

> “It is believed. But the pagan Plato, Aristotle, and others, likewise moved by the truth of things, condemned this with a common judgment, saying that the confusion of things is rather generated by such a persuasion. For just as the human race is pressed by the necessity of birth toward various actions, since the good deserve praise while the wicked receive the punishment of the laws, and although they have not been harmed, those devoted to heavenly wisdom nevertheless rightly struck down their errors by the testimony of truth.”

These words are foreign to this passage.

Note 3: “*barbiti*.” Another reading: “*barbitae*”; another: “*barbita*.” In the same place, “*pectides*.” Another reading: “*pectines*.” [Col. 0776A]

Note 4: “or a lyre.” Another reading: “or a lyre-player.” In the same place, “agree.” Another reading: “agrees.”

Note 5: “may render a sound.” Another reading: “may render a voice.” “or because.” Another reading: “because”; another: “and because.”

Note 6: “he tightened the strings into sound.” Another reading: “he established the sound in the strings” (or “on the strings”).

Note 7: “concavity.” Another reading: “on the contrary, concavity.” In the same place, “the psaltery, etc.” Another reading: “they used the psaltery … with ten strings.” “Decalogue.” Another reading: “of the Decalogue.”

Note 8: “within the leather.” Another reading: “between the leather.”

Note 9: “is judged.” Another reading: “is considered.” In the same place, “to have attracted.” Another reading: “to have applied.”

Note 10: “stretched out.” Another reading: “extended.”

Note 11: “for thus.” The Gothic manuscripts read: “for when”; I do not know what they intend.

Note 12: “a woman.” Another reading: “a woman came into being.”

Note 14: “stretched.” Another reading: “extended.”

### Chapter XXIII

Note 1: “you seek.” Another reading: “you will seek.” “and XII.” Another reading: “and twenty”; another: “and twenty.” “You multiply.” Another reading: “multiplied.” “You join.” Another reading: “you will join.” In the same place, “XXXVI.” Another reading: “thirty-six times.” “Is produced.” Another reading: “produces.” In the same place, “namely VI, that is, six times.” Thus elsewhere *sexies* (“six times”) occurs for “six,” and similar adverbs occur for numerical nouns.

Note 2: “does not consist.” Another reading: “is not established.” [Col. 0776B] “They consist.” Another reading: “they are established.”

### Chapter XXV

Note 1: “author.” Another reading omits this. In the same place, “asserts.” Another reading: “explains.”

Note 2: “of the soul.” Another reading: “of the mind.” “Fixed.” Another reading: “rotated.” “Which, by defining.” Another reading: “and by defining.”

### Chapter XXVI

Note 1: “Ptolemy.” Another adds: “king of Alexandria.” In the same place, “may be found.” Another reading: “may be found” [singular].

### Chapter XXVII

Note 2: “of the stars, and definite times.” Another reading: “definite [positions] of the stars and of times.” “Signs.” Another reading: “signs of heaven.” “To predict.” Another reading: “to proclaim.”

### Chapter XXVIII

Note 1: “the axis of heaven.” Another reading: “the axes of heaven.”

### Chapter XXIX

Note 1: “is he who.” Another reading: “is he.” In the same place, “both on land and at sea.” Another reading: “on land and sea”; another: “from land and from sea.” “For that reason.” Another reading: “therefore.”

### Chapter XXX

Note 1: “formation.” Another reading: “form.” In the same place, “is demonstrated.” Another reading: “is shown.”

### Chapter XXXI

Note 1: “revolving and fiery.” The Gothic manuscripts read: “revolving [masculine], and fiery [masculine],” and likewise in the following note *eum* (“him”) for *id* (“it”). In the same place, “has impressed signs.” Another reading: “may have impressed figures.”

Note 1: “beneath the earths.” Another reading: “beneath the earth”; another: “beneath the earths.”

Note 2: “but when.” Another reading: “but when.” In the same place: “To whom, therefore, God … leaves [it] to the winter cold.” The Gothic manuscripts omit this sentence. “In the same [places].” Another reading: “in those same [places].” “All things would be consumed.” Another reading: “the earth would be consumed”; another: “it would consume everything.” “Just as.” Another reading: “but so that.” “Receives.” Another reading: “received.” “By which the air.” Another reading: “whose air.” “Is administered.” Another reading: “may be administered”; another: “the administrator.” “And the order of changes is preserved.” Another reading: “may be preserved”; another: “it receives the movement of changes”; another: “it received [it].” “The highest [part] of heaven.” Another reading omits “of heaven.” “Descending.” Another reading: “departing.” “In autumn.” Another reading omits this. “It returns.” “Returns” is erroneous in Grial’s edition; in the book *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 17, the reading is “it will have returned.” In the same place, “of the winter cold.” Another reading: “of winter and cold.” [Col. 0777B]

Note 1: “will have dyed.” Another reading: “will have stained”; another: “will have joined.”

Note 2: “may interpose itself.” Another reading: “may intervene.”

### Chapter LXXI

Note 3: “from heaven.” Another reading: “out of heaven.” “As was stated above.” Another reading: “as was mentioned above.”

Note 4: “direct, etc.” Another reading: “direct their course toward the purpose of the courses.” In the same place, “elsewhere.” Another reading: “in another place.” “And their radiance.” Another reading: “and its radiance.”

Note 5: “for foreseeing.” Another reading: “for seeing beforehand.”

Note 6: “which, because.” Another reading: “which, since.”

Note 7: “as though *terriones*.” Another reading: “as though *teriones*.” In the same place, “are in it.” Another reading: “are fixed in it.”

Note 8: “the same.” Another reading: “whence.” “They said.” Another reading: “they had said.”

Note 9: “Arcturus is.” Another reading omits this. “Placed.” Another reading: “placed as an associate.”

Note 10: “Orion.” Another reading: “Urion.” In the same place, “the star.” Another reading: “toward the south.”

Note 11: “like a sword.” Another reading: “like a sword” [nominative]. “If they shine.” Another reading: “if these things shine.” “Their sharp points.” Another reading: “the edge of this.”

Note 12: “for rain … is called.” Another reading: “for rains … are called.” In the same place, “because when.” Another reading: “because when.” “The Hyades. They are.” Another reading: “the Hyades and the twin Triones. They are.”

Note 13: “because … they call.” Another reading omits this. “Which is spring, when.” Another reading: “which truly”; another: “which is spring, when.”

Note 14: “are called the Dog-stars.” Another reading omits “the Dog-stars.”

Note 15: “may affect: Sirius.” Another reading: “may affect, or”; another: “or may affect.”

Note 16: “when.” The Lucensian, or Lucanian, Codex almost always has *quum* (“when”) for *quando*; and in manuscripts the connection of the letters in *quum* and *quando* is often ambiguous.

Note 17: “comets.” Another reading: “cometes.” In the same place, “in Latin … because.” Another reading: “the Latins call them ‘long-haired,’ because.” This variation is also quite common: *quod* (“because”) for *quia* (“because”), or conversely.

Note 18: “may bear: it is.” Another reading: “may bear. For Lucifer is.” “One of.” Another reading: “one [feminine] of.” “This properly.” Another reading: “he properly.” “The locks of light.” Another reading: “the radiance of light.” “May pour forth.” Another reading: “may pour forth from itself.” “In the manner of a lock.” The Gothic manuscripts read: “in the manner of radiance”; another reading: “in the manner of radiances.” “May be extended.” Another reading: “are extended.”

Note 19: “Hesperus … to Hesperus.” Another reading: “Vesperus … to Vesperus.” In the same place, “one is lost.” Another reading: “moisture is suspended.”

Note 20: “Of which … Stilbon.” Some copies omit this; others read “of whom” for “of which.” The Greek names themselves are corrupt in most copies.

Note 21: “The Romans [call] these.” Another reading: “these Romans.” “Jupiter, etc.” Another reading: “Saturn, the Moon, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury.” “Flattery, which attributes something to itself.” Another reading: “by flattery, which [attributes] something to.” [Col. 0778B] “of the age.” Another reading omits this.

Note 22: “conforming.” Another reading: “confirming.”

Note 23: “Jupiter for that reason.” Another reading: “that is, Jupiter”; another: “Jupiter’s, for that reason.” In the same place, “on whose head.” Another reading: “because on his head.” “They fix.” Another reading: “they fashion.”

Note 24: “to pursue its course.” Another reading: “to complete its course.”

Note 27: “The etesian winds produce.” Another reading: “The winds and heat produce greater [effects] than in the whole rest of the year.”

Note 28: “within the stars.” Another reading: “among the stars.” This discrepancy also occurs throughout: *intra* (“within”) for *inter* (“among”).

Note 31: “therefore they formed.” Another reading: “therefore they fashioned.” In the same place, “of the same time.” Another reading: “of the same month.”

Note 32: “and fishes.” Another reading: “and a fish.” In the same place, “into heaven.” Another reading omits this.

Note 34: “among the stars of heaven.” Another reading: “into the stars of heaven”; another: “into the stars.” “Quadrigae.” Another reading: “a quadriga.”

Note 35: “of the king.” Another reading omits this. “Turned.” Another reading: “turned around.” “Arctophylax.” Another reading: “Arctophylax” [variant form].

Note 36: “into heaven.” Another reading: “in heaven.” In the same place, “will have nourished.” Another reading: “had nourished.”

Note 37: “these things of superstition.” Another reading: “these superstitions,” which is plausible.

Note 38: “and of faith.” Another reading: “which belong to faith.”

Note 39: “into falls.” Another reading: “in a fall.” In the same place, “to be able to know beforehand.” Another reading omits “to be able.” “of things, by truth.” Another reading omits “of things.” “by persuasion.” Another reading: “by persuasion” [variant form].

Note 40: “as they say.” Another reading omits this. “is pressed.” Another reading: “would be pressed.”

Note 41: “would lead away.” Another reading: “would lead toward.”

In Codex Albanianus and others, the book *On Laws* follows.

Note 2: “from it.” Another reading: “from her.” “They would demonstrate.” Another reading: “they demonstrate.” “Leads.” Another reading: “produces.”

### Chapter VI

Note 1: “as pleuritis.” Other readings: “pleurisis”; “pleuresis.” In the same place, “delays.” Another reading: “is mentioned.”

In the same place, the Gothic and Lucensian manuscripts insert:

> “Phlegmon is a restless condition with redness, pain, tension, hardness, and swelling. For when phlegmon begins to develop, fever and restlessness follow. Hence it is called *phlegmon*, from the Greek *phlegein* (φλέγειν), that is, ‘to inflame.’ For it is felt in this way, and from this it received its name. *Febris* [fever] comes from *fervor* [heat], etc.”

These manuscripts omit “But certain [illnesses] … received.” The printed editions discuss phlegmon below, in note 7. Instead of “is an inflammation,” the Lucensian manuscript reads “is a restless disease.”

Note 3: “they gnash.” Other readings: “they gnash”; “they will gnash.” In the same place, “disturbance.” Another adds: “disturbance of the mind.”

Note 4: “cardiace.” Another reading: “cardia.” Grialius has *cardiace* in the text and *cardiaca* in the note; since this appears erroneous, I changed it to *cardiace*. In the same place, “is affected.” Another reading: “is produced.”

Note 5: “lethargy.” Another reading: “lethargus.”

Note 7: “phlegmon.” Another reading: “phlegmon.” In the same place, “and pain. For when it begins.” Another reading adds:

> “And pain: that is, phlegmon is a restlessness with redness, pain, extension, hardness, and swelling; when this begins …”

Another:

> “And pain; when it begins to develop, fever follows.”

Note 8: “with fever, etc.” Codex Albanianus reads:

> “with fever, coughing, bloody sputum, and purulent discharge. If one of these signs is absent, it cannot be called pleuritic.”

Note 9: “hence also.” Another reading: “therefore also.”

Note 11: “violent.” Another reading: “excessive.”

Note 12: “of the greater.” Another reading: “greater.”

Note 14: “from the torment of the intestines.” Another reading: “because of torments of the intestines.”

Note 15: “hence also … they call it.” Another reading omits this. In the same place, “from its.” Another reading: “from the air.”

Note 17: “although this.” Another reading: “although this” [neuter].

Note 18: “each.” Other readings: “whom”; “whatever.”

Note 19: “inguinal.” Another reading: “inguinia.” In the same place, “which so much.” Another reading: “which so greatly.”

### Chapter VII

Note 1: “chronic.” Another reading: “chronic.” In the same place, “delays.” Another reading: “is renewed.” “Phthisis.” Another reading: “cough,” here and below, instead of “phthisis.”

Note 2: “from a cause.” Another reading: “from the head.” “For the Greeks.” Another reading: “and the Greeks.”

Note 3: “from an accident.” Another reading: “from occurring.” “May ingest.” Another reading: “ingests.” “Sends around in a circuit.” Another reading: “moves in a circuit.”

Note 5: “grasping.” Another reading: “hanging.” In the same place, “they call.” Another reading: “they name.” “When it has overflowed.” Another reading: “when it has abounded.” “Turned.” Another reading: “hostile.” “Spasms.” Another reading: “spasm”; another, apparently as a correction, “foams.”

Note 6: “for the course of the moon.” Another reading: “through this course.” “May madness accompany them.” Other readings: “may the snares of demons accompany them”; “may the madness of demons accompany them.” The same applies to *larvatio* (“demonic possession”). “The same, greater, and divine.” Another reading: “that is, greater and long-lasting.” “Of which.” Another reading: “to which.”

Note 7: “the third day before the Kalends of January.” Another reading: “on the Kalends of January” (*in Kalendis Ianuariis*); another: “toward the Kalends of January” (*in Kalendas Ianuarias*).

Note 8: “from emptiness.” Other readings: “from iniquity”; “from antiquity.” In the same place, “they called.” Other readings: “they call”; one omits the entire phrase “or from emptiness … they called.”

Note 10: “fevers.” Another adds: “which are improperly [so called],” etc. These words, cited by Grialius in a note and rejected as having been introduced here without any rationale, I would not so readily assert were not introduced by Isidore himself. Certainly, the very words occur in the oldest manuscripts. In the same place, “or from recedings.” Another reading omits this.

Note 11: “which, while.” Another reading: “who, while.”

Note 12: “influx.” Another reading: “infusion.” In the same place, “provocation.” Other readings: “suffocation”; “choking.”

Note 13: “from the cold.” Another reading: “with the cold.” In the same place, “around which.” Another reading: “around whom.” “Branchiae.” Other readings: “branchia”; “brancia.”

Note 14: “from injury to the arteries.” One copy omits this; another reads: “from injuries to the arteries.” In the same place, “suffocation.” Another reading: “asphyxiation.”

Note 15: “from the lungs.” Another reading: “from the lung.”

Note 16: “he took.” Another reading: “he received.”

Note 17: “which [occurs] in young people.” Another reading: “which [occurs] in young people.” “To occur.” Another reading: “to come.” “Consumption.” Another reading: “completion.”

Note 18: “the uvula drips.” Another reading: “the uvula tickles.” The reading *distillat* (“drips”) must be retained. Martial, Book X, epigram 56:

> *Non secat et tollit stillantem Fannius uvam*  
> “Fannius neither cuts nor removes the dripping uvula.”

That is, the little fleshy projection at the end of the palate, hanging near the throat, which can be seen when a person gapes.

Note 19: “abscesses.” Another reading: “abscesses” [variant form].

Note 20: “in sputum and purulent matter.” Another reading: “in foam and purulent matter.”

Note 22: “they call.” Another reading: “they say.”

Note 23: “nephritis.” Another reading: “nephresis.” “From the kidneys.” Another reading: “from the renal organs.”

Note 24, [Col. 0780A]: “paralysis,” etc. Codex Albanianus reads:

Note 26: “in a bad condition.” Other readings: “through injury”; “in a bad condition or through injury”; “through injury or from licking.” In the same place, “from.” One copy omits this. “The evil treatment of the healer.” Other readings: “the bad medicine”; “the bad medication”; one omits “bad.” “By resumption.” Another reading: “resumption.”

Note 28: “sarcia.” Other readings: “sarcian”; “sarcina”; “sarcoma.” In the same place, “by which.” Another reading: “which.”

Note 29: “ischias.” Other readings: “ischiasis”; “sciasis.” In the same place, “of the vertebrae.” Another reading: “of the vestibules.” “Of which.” Another reading: “by which.” “Of the ilia.” Another reading: “of those.” “It is made from phlegm.” One copy omits “from phlegm”; another: “phlegm is produced from it.” In the same place, “has descended.” Another reading: “descends.”

Note 31: “arthritic.” Another reading: “arthritis.”

Note 32: “is a stone.” Another reading: “is a stone” [using another term].

Note 33: “may constrict.” Another reading: “may strain.” In the same place, “with difficulty.” Another reading: “difficulty.”

Note 34: “from satyrs.” The Gothic manuscripts add:

Note 36: “For *dys* [δύς] is division.” Another reading: “For *dys* [δύς] signifies difficulty.” In the same place, “which.” Another reading: “whom.”

Note 37: “through the smooth intestines.” Other readings: “through the smooth part of the intestine”; “through the line of the intestine.” In the same place, “may produce.” Another reading: “produces.”

Note 39: “fissures.” Other readings: “ragadiae,” or “rhagadinae”; “ragadia.” In the same place, “fissures.” Another reading: “clefts.” “These are also hemorrhoids.” Another reading: “this and hemorrhoids.”

## CHAPTER VIII

No. 1, “with the hairs trimmed around it.” Another reading: “with the tawny hairs trimmed around it.”

No. 2, “parotides.” Another reading: “parotidae.” Likewise, “hardnesses.” Another reading: “hardness.” Likewise, “or from something.” Another reading: “or from some cause.” Likewise, “nearness.” Another reading: “nearnesses.” Likewise, “in Greek they are called little ears.” Another reading: “the Greeks call it an ear”; another: “in Greek it is called an ear.”

No. 4, “the skin reddens with a fiery redness.” Another reading: “fiery redness; the skins redden.” Likewise, “with the redness having been moved.” Another reading: “with mutual redness”; another: “with much redness.”

No. 7, “by burning.” Another reading: “by itching,” as a correction or gloss.

No. 8, “is restored.” Another reading: “is given back.”

No. 9, “satyriasis.” [Col. 0780C] Another reading: “phthiriasis.” Likewise, “one by one.” Another reading: “individually.” Likewise, “one is stronger.” Another reading: “another is stronger.” Likewise, “more are found.” Another reading: “itching caused by scaling.”

No. 10, “scabies and leprosy, etc.” Another reading: “but scabies and leprosy are a thin roughness and scaling.” Likewise, “which is thus.” Another reading: “which swiftly.”

No. 11, “like the lepidi.” Another reading: “like the herb alepis”; another: “like the herb alapidis”; another: “like the herb lepida.” Likewise, “into blackness.” Another reading: “into black coloration.” Likewise, “into whiteness, now into redness.” Another reading: “in whiteness, now in redness.” Likewise, “adulterine.” Another reading: “adulterous.”

No. 12, “of elephants.” Another reading: “. . . of elephants.”

No. 13, “of bile.” Another reading: “biliary”; another: “biliary, that is, black.” Likewise, “the Latins.” Another reading: “in Latin.” Likewise, “they call.” Another reading: “they say.” Likewise, “by resemblance.” Another reading: “from resemblance.” Likewise, “more easily.” Another reading: “more quickly.”

No. 14, “as physicians.” Another reading: “thus physicians.” Likewise, “or.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “somewhat.” Another reading: “a little”; another: “to some extent.” Likewise, “for a longer time.” Another reading: omitted.

No. 15, “*furunculus* (boil), etc.” Others insert “*hordeolus* (stye), etc.,” as in the following number. Likewise, “fiery.” Another reading: “fires.”

No. 16, “in the hairs.” Another reading: “in the hair.” Likewise, “of the eyelids.” [Col. 0780D] Another reading: “on the eyelids.” Pal. 281 has “of the eyelid” as a variant reading. Likewise, “resembling a grain.” Another reading: “like a grain.”

No. 17, “which.” Another reading: “in which.”

No. 19, “vi. And an ulcer.” Another reading: “vi, an ulcer. And an ulcer.” Likewise, “which smells, as though it were *olcus*.” Another reading: “which hurts, like an ulcer.” Likewise, “as though it were an olcus.” Another reading adds: “whence also ulcers.”

No. 20, “swollen.” Another reading: “swelling.”

No. 21, “as a small pimple (*pupula*).” Another reading: “as a pupil.” Likewise, “sirimpio.” Another reading: omitted.

No. 23, “may blind.” Another reading: “blinds.”

## CHAPTER IX

No. 2, “by kinds.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “which the Latins.” Another reading: “which the Latins.” Likewise, “medicines.” Another reading: “a medicine.” Likewise, “call.” Another reading: “name.” Likewise, “of the law.” Another reading: “of death,” as a correction.

No. 3, “power.” Another reading: “force.” Likewise, “that is, strength.” Another reading: “and strength.”

## CHAPTER XI

No. 2, “incision in Greek.” Another reading: “incision in Latin, in Greek.”

No. 3, “similar.” Another reading: “similars”; another: “similar things.”

No. 4, “guva.” Another reading: “guvia”; another: “guna.” Likewise, “calls forth.” Another reading: “calls.” Likewise, “clyster . . .” The Codex Albanus adds in the margin: “A clyster is an instrument by which an enema is injected.”

No. 5, “Pila, etc.” Another reading: “Pisa, from seeds to be pounded and ground”; another: “from seeds that adhere,” instead of “ground.” Likewise, “pilagmenta.” Another reading: “piligmenta.” Likewise, “to be made.” Another reading: “to be struck”; another: omitted. Hence also “pigmenta” down [Col. 0781B] to “are usually cut up.”

No. 6, “Pilumnus.” Another reading: “Pilumnius.” Likewise, “presided over fields being pounded.” The Lucanian Codex has, as a correction, “provided the art of pounding,” which is also found in the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, which often agrees with the Lucanian. Likewise, “is pounded.” Another reading: “will be pounded.” Likewise, “called.” Another reading: “is called.” Likewise, “into a mortar.” Another reading: “in a mortar.”

No. 8, “coticula.” Another reading: “citicula.”

## CHAPTER XII

No. 1, “called.” Another reading: “is called.”

No. 5, “which means ‘to flow.’” Another reading: “which means ‘to flow excellently.’” Another reading derives it from the Greek ΠΑΡΑ ΤΟ ΣΤΑΖΕΙΝ ΣΤΑΚΑΝ (another reading: ΣΤΑΚΤΗ), “from dripping, *stakē*” (or “*staktē*”), that is, *oltritum*, “myrobalan.” Thus the Gothic codices.

No. 6, “oil . . . mixed in.” Another reading: omitted.

No. 7, “telino.” Another reading: “telinio,” from which Vulcanius incorrectly conjectured “delinio.” Likewise, “we anoint.” Another reading: “we are anointed.” Likewise, “Telo.” Another reading: “Delo.” Likewise, “there is one.” Another reading: omitted “one.”

No. 9, “another.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “of Cyprus; hence also properly.” Another reading: “of Cyprus, and therefore also properly”; another: “of Cyprus; hence also properly.”

No. 10, “whence also . . . worshipped.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “they lead.” Another reading: “they introduce.”

No. 11, “chalasticum, calcasticum”; another: “calesticum.” [Col. 0781C] Likewise, “martiatum.” Another reading: “marciacum”; another: “marciatum.”

## CHAPTER XIII

No. 1, “liberal disciplines.” Another reading: “liberal arts.” Likewise, “is contained.” Another reading: “is held.”

No. 2, “because of the number of hours.” Another reading: “of the numbers,” with “because of . . . hours” omitted.

No. 3, “because of the qualities.” Another reading: “because of the number of qualities”; another: “because of the quality.” Likewise, “what each person.” Another reading: “what each person ought to observe”; another: “what it is proper for each person to observe.” Likewise, “among the sick.” Another reading: “among the Greeks.” Likewise, “it is read concerning David.” Another reading: “it is found concerning David.” Likewise, “because from a.” Another reading: “who from a.”

No. 4, “change.” Another reading: “changes.” Likewise, “for just as . . . of themselves.” Another reading: omitted.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I

No. 1, “to the Hebrew nation.” Another reading: “of the Hebrew nation.” Likewise, “in the sacred writings.” Another reading: “the sacred writings”; another: “written writings.”

No. 2, “legal rights.” Another reading: “the rights of the laws.”

No. 3, “into the kingdom.” Another reading: “in the kingdom.” Likewise, “created.” Another reading: “decreed.” Likewise, “of Solon.” In the Gothic copies there is the error “of Solomon.” Likewise, “explained.” Another reading: “published.”

No. 4, “Appius, etc.” [Col. 0781D] Another reading omits the given names and lists Sextius in sixth place, whereas for us he is in third place.

No. 5, “to establish.” Another reading: “to decree.”

No. 7, “new.” Another reading: “new laws.” Likewise, “and they were.” Another reading: “for they were.”

No. 1, “these.” Another reading: “this.”

No. 2, “through another’s.” Another reading: “through another’s field”; another: “through another’s property.”

## CHAPTER III

No. 3, “treated just as much.” Another reading: “treated only”; another: “treated just so much.” I think the Isidorian reading has *tantumdem* for *tantum*; similarly, others of his contemporaries use *tantumdem*. Likewise, “when also the law.” Another reading: “when, or even by law.”

No. 4, “everything now which.” Another reading abbreviates it as “everything, that.”

No. 1, “is held.” Another reading: “is held” [present passive]. Likewise, “acceptance.” Another reading: “succession.”

No. 1, “or a state.” Another reading: “or any state.”

No. 1, “servitudes.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “treaties.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “of things to be violated.” Another reading: “of violent things.”

No. 2, “decision.” Another reading: “division.” Likewise, “and labors.” Another reading: “and labor.” Likewise, “likewise.” Another reading: “and.”

No. 1, “and to the priests.” Another reading: “and among the sacred matters.”

No. 1, “of the Quirites.” Another reading: “of the Quirites” [alternative inflection]. No. 2, “by senatorial decrees.” Another reading: omitted.

## CHAPTER XI

No. 1, “decrees.” Another reading: “they constitute plebiscites”; another: “to constitute.” Likewise, “called decrees.” Another reading: “called thus.” Likewise, “he consults.” Another reading: “he asks”; another: “he inquires”; another: “he investigates.” Likewise, “just as it was asked.” Another reading: “and he asks that it be done”; another: “and he asks that they be done”; another: “and he asks that he do it.”
