“They decide by advising the peoples.” Another reading: “the peoples dedicated [it] by deliberation.”

## CHAPTER XIII

No. 1, “he proclaims.” Another reading: “he publishes.”

## CHAPTER XIV

No. 2, “of equity.” Another reading: “of truth.” “Civil.” Another reading: “civil matters.” Likewise, “and disputes.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “they might calm.” Another reading: “they might be calmed.”

[Col. 0782B]

## CHAPTER XV

“Certain laws also.” Another reading: “certain laws exist.” Likewise, “they brought forward.” Another reading: “they contributed.” Likewise, “of the fathers.” Another reading: “first.”

No. 2, “he might leave more by will.” Another reading: “he might leave more to outsiders by will”; another: “he might leave more to outsiders in his will.” Likewise, “has been formally named.” Another reading: “is formally named.” Likewise, “is formally named.” Another reading: “is called.” Likewise, “Aquillius . . . is formally named.” Another reading: omitted.

## CHAPTER XVI

No. 1, “he expresses himself.” Another reading: “he speaks.” Likewise, “from fullness.” Another reading: “from satiety.” Likewise, “and to write satire.” Another reading: “and to write a satura.” Likewise, “of Persius.” The Gothic copies and the older Caesenas copy add: “The New Law.”

## CHAPTER XIX

“For his.” The older editions read “or indeed,” which gives a clearer sense; another reading: “for his reward and punishment.”

## CHAPTER XX

“Let him be restrained.” Another reading: “he would be restrained.”

No. 1, “according to the custom of the fatherland.” Another reading: “through the custom of the fatherland.” Likewise, “into capture.” Another reading: “in capture.” Likewise, “contains.” Another reading: “obtains.”

No. 1, “pragmata.” Another reading: “pragmatica.” Likewise, [Col. 0782C] “and the plaintiff.” Another reading: “and the author.”

No. 2, “nor be confirmed.” Another reading: “nor be strengthened.” Likewise, “what is in it.” Another reading: “what in it.”

No. 1, “is called.” Another reading: “has the name”; another: “received the name.”

No. 6, “or if he has tortured.” Another reading: omitted.

In some codices, a book on Medicine is found here, followed by Book VII, *On Times*, which for us is part of Book V.

No. 1, “lest it be unbecoming.” Another reading: “lest it be contrary in that respect.” Likewise, “might be consoled.” Another reading: “might be consoled” [plural]; another: “might be comforted”—namely, passively, which I could easily believe to be from Isidore’s own hand. Likewise, “all.” Another reading: “human beings.”

No. 2, “might moderate.” Another reading: “may moderate.”

No. 3, “to occur.” Another reading: “they say occurs”; another: “we say occurs.” Likewise, “reaches.” Another reading: “will have reached.” Likewise, “weakened.” Another reading: “wasted away”; another: “wasted away” [singular]. Likewise, “is compelled.” Another reading: “compels.” Likewise, “brought forth above the earth.” Another reading: “brought forth beneath the earth.” [Col. 0785A]

No. 4, “dawn.” Here others insert “twilight . . . and darkness,” as somewhat later.

No. 5, “the evening . . . is called.” Another reading: “the evening . . . was called.” Thus the older Toledan codex, with the following notes in Gothic cursive script:

“*Vesper* is so called when the sun or moon is covered by clouds at any hour of the day or night, and this name produces *vesperis*. *Vespera*, however, begins from the ninth hour, when the sun begins to descend; but this word has no declension. *Vesperus* is when, with the sun setting, the day declines, and it is declined thus: *vesperus, vesperi, vespero*, and so on. *Vespera* (in the manuscript, *vespere*) is when the night ends at the dawn’s rising, and it is declined thus: *vespera, vesperae, vesperae*.”

No. 6, “but darknesses were called.” Another reading: “but darkness was called.”

No. 8, “everything.” Another reading: “all.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII

No. 1, “for the vacant [ones].” Another reading: “for those who call.”

No. 2, “did not yet exist.” Another reading: “did not yet exist” [singular]. Likewise, “is called.” Another reading: “was called.”

No. 3, “it was sounded by trumpets.” The Gothic copies and Caesenas I read: “the trumpets were sounded”; the same is also found in Codex 1 of the Vatican Archives.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

No. 1, “which they follow.” Another reading: “which follow one another”; another: “which they always follow.”

No. 2, “loving.” Another reading: “he loves.” Likewise, “with the ear pierced.” Another reading: “with the ear perforated.” Likewise, “is subjected.” Another reading: “subjected.”

No. 4, “the last.” Another reading: “the extremity”; another: “the final end.” Likewise, “is known.” Another reading: “is born.”

No. 5, “of Judah.” Another reading: “of Juda.” Likewise, “Babylonia.” Another reading: “Babylon.” Likewise, “up to.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “in the flesh.” Another reading: “from the flesh”; another: “into the flesh.”

No. 6, “and kingdoms.” Another reading: “and kingdoms; thus it is examined,” and omits: “The first among our people . . . may be recognized as belonging to the age.” Likewise, “Julius.” Another reading: “Julian.” Likewise, “of the canons.” Another reading: “the canon.”

No. 8, “of the past.” Another reading: “past” [feminine]. Likewise, “may be recognized.” Another reading adds: “The course of these things through generations and kingdoms is thus examined.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX

No. 1, “in the lights.” Another reading: omits “in.”

No. 2, “Adam in the year.” Another reading: omits “in the year.” Another reading: “in years,” and likewise thereafter. Likewise, “Seth . . . 205.” Another reading: “202.” Likewise, “who began.” Another reading: “who first began.” Likewise, “of the Lord, 435.” Another reading: “of the Lord, 432 . . .” Likewise, “Malaleel . . . 715.” Another reading: “Malalael . . . 815”; another: “795.” Isidore generally follows the Septuagint translators. The Vulgate gives the lower number.

No. 3, “Jared . . . 172.” Another reading: “162”; another: “166.”

No. 5, “Shem . . . in the second year.” Another reading: “in the year 102.” Likewise, “Arphaxad . . . 135.” Another reading: “225.” Likewise, “from whom the Samaritans and Indians came.” Another reading: “from whom the ancient Samaritans and Indians,” omitting “came.”

No. 6, “the kingdom of the Scythians begins.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “the tower.” Another reading: “then the tower.” The Mutina Codex states: “At this time the languages were divided, and throughout the world a dispersion took place in the building of the tower.”

No. 7, “Serug . . . 79.” Another reading: “89.” Likewise, “magic.” Another reading: “the art of magic.” Likewise, “3184.” Another reading: “3183.”

No. 3, “Isaac. For earlier, also Ishmael.” Another reading: “Isaac and Ishmael, from whom”; another: “Isaac from Sarah the free woman. For earlier, also Ishmael.” Likewise, “Jacob . . . 91.” Another reading: “40.” Likewise, “Phoroneus . . . 3435.” Another reading: “3434.”

No. 9, “Joseph . . . 110.” Another reading: “105.” Likewise, “the servitude of the Hebrews in Egypt.” Another reading: omits “in Egypt.” Likewise, “he discovered 3689.” Another reading: “3758”; another: “at this time astronomy was discovered.” Likewise, “he ruled the people in the wilderness.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “they began 3729.” Another reading: “3728,” and so thereafter.

No. 10, “in Greece.” Another reading: “in Troy.” Likewise, “first.” [Col. 0786B] Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “he discovered the art of medicine.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “he found . . . 3916.” Another reading: “3923.”

No. 11, “he established the lyre.” Another reading: “he discovered the lyre and handed it over to Orpheus.” Instead of 3956, other copies have 3906, 3933, 3955; and there is generally this kind of disagreement in the years.

No. 12, “was captured.” Another reading adds: “and Aeneas came to Italy”; instead of the year 4025, another has 4024. Likewise, “he founded.” Another reading: “he founded a city, from which came the Albans.” Likewise, “Eli the priest.” Another reading omits “the priest.” Likewise, “Samuel.” Another reading: “Samuel and Saul.” Likewise, “is thought.” Another reading: “is reckoned”; instead of the year 4125, another has 4128.

No. 13, “Gad . . . prophesied.” Another reading: omitted.

No. 14, “Asa . . . Ahijah, Amos, Jehu, Joel, and Azariah prophesied.” Another reading: “Asa . . . Isaiah, Amos, Nahum, and Joel prophesied.” Likewise, “Elijah, Obadiah.” Another reading: “Elijah, and Elisha, Obadiah.”

No. 15, “Athaliah.” Another reading: “Gotholiah.” Likewise, “Jonadab the priest.” Another reading: “Jonadab son of Rechab the priest.” Likewise, “flourished.” Another reading: “flourished, and Jehoiada the high priest.”

No. 16, “Elisha.” Another reading prefaces it with: “The prophet Zechariah is killed between the temple and the altar. Elisha.” Likewise, [Col. 0786C] “Carthage was founded.” Another reading: “Some assert that Carthage was founded at this time, others not, as above.” Likewise, “is established.” Another reading adds: “and the kingdom of the Assyrians is transferred to the Medes.” Likewise, “Romulus is born.” Another reading: “Remus and Romulus are born.”

No. 17, “Rome is founded.” Another reading: “the Senate is established at Rome.” Likewise, “a census is first conducted, 4556.” For this year others have 4555; another has 4552.

No. 18, “Sappho . . . flourished.” Another reading: omitted.

No. 19, “is written.” Another reading: “is written down.” Likewise, “is released.” Another reading: “is dissolved.” Likewise, “are celebrated.” Another reading: “notable things are celebrated.”

No. 20, “he renews.” Another reading: “he recalls.” Likewise, “who is also called Nothus.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “Plato and Gorgias, the first rhetorician.” Another omits “and Gorgias, the first rhetorician”; others read “Plato, the first rhetorician”; another: “Plato and Gorgias,” omitting “the first rhetorician.” Likewise, “is completed.” Another reading: “is written.”

No. 22, “Alexander the Macedonian.” Another reading omits “the Macedonian”; instead of the year 4874, others have 4873 or 4884. A note is added in Codex 1 of Toledo: “From this point the kings of Alexandria begin.” Likewise, “are recognized.” Another reading: “are found.”

No. 23, “The history of the Second Book of Maccabees is composed” (another reading: “is written”). [Col. 0786D] Another reading omits these words and gives in their place: “Forty thousand armed Jews, defeated in that battle, fell.” Then the words “The history . . . is composed” are placed before “the Romans [defeat] the Greeks,” etc. Likewise, “he conquered.” Another reading: “he conquers.”

No. 24, “he subdued.” Another reading: “he subjected.”

No. 25, “he captures.” Another reading: “he captured.” Likewise, “Caesar.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “first.” Another reading: “earlier.” Instead of the year 5155, others have 5154, 5064, or 5160.

No. 26, “he is born, 5211.” Others give the year 5210, 5220, or 5215. From this point there is similar variation.

No. 28, “under Trajan, for nineteen years.” Others have fourteen or eighteen. Likewise, “he rests.” Another reading: “he rested.”

No. 29, “Antoninus Pius, [in his] year.” Another reading: “Antoninus Verus Pius.” Likewise, “Antoninus.” Another reading: “Antoninus Pius.”

No. 30, “Theodotion the translator.” Another reading: “Theodotion, the third translator.” Likewise, “Symmachus the translator.” Another reading: “Symmachus, the fourth translator.”

No. 31, “Caracalla.” Another reading: omitted. Likewise, “has an account of his deeds.” Another reading: “his deeds are recorded”; another: “he has a history.” Likewise, “Aurelius Antoninus.” Another reading omits “Antoninus.” Likewise, “the heresy of Sabellius.” Another reading: “Sabellius.”

No. 32, “Origen.” [Col. 0787A] Another reading: “Origen of Alexandria.”

No. 33, “Gallus.” Another reading: “Gallerius.” Likewise, “he founds.” Another reading: “he founded.”

No. 34, “the brevity of his life lacks a preliminary notation.” Another reading: “his brief life has nothing recorded in history”; another: “he did nothing memorable”; another: omitted.

No. 35, “arose.” Another reading: “arose” [with an additional prefix]. Likewise, “of this . . . he contributed.” Another reading: omitted; another: “he contributed nothing worthy of history,” with the rest omitted.

No. 37, “Valentinian, eight years.” Another reading: nine years; another: nineteen years.

No. 38, “heresiar­ch.” Another reading: “heresiar­ches.”

No. 39, “arose.” Another reading adds: “The body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of Matthew were discovered.”

No. 40, “are extinguished.” Another reading: “are extinguished by Belisarius.”

No. 41, “were made.” Another reading: “are made.” Likewise, “by the Persians.” The Lucanian Codex adds:

“Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, whose fame’s radiance has penetrated the whole world, brings the nation of the Angles, that is, of the Saxons, to the faith of Christ. He sent twelve [men] from himself to Britain, through whose ears [sic]—which the Saxons themselves now call ‘Sectis’ [sic]—the division from that island, or rather, I should say, from the smaller world to the greater, after nearly all the Britons had been brought under their power, returns from pagan estrangement.”

Codex Ottobonianus 345: “Maurice, twenty-one years. Pope Gregory was pope. The Angles are converted to the faith. The Goths become Catholics. Phocas, etc.”

No. 42, “Heraclius, seventeen.” Another reading: twenty-seven; another: “the tenth.” Likewise, “now he is carrying out, etc.” Another reading: “in the fifth and fourth year of this most religious prince Sisebut, the Jews in Hispania are baptized and become Christians.” Likewise, “the remainder of the sixth age, etc.” Another reading: “the remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone.”

Vulcanius adds: “The whole period from the beginning of the world up to the present, the tenth year of the glorious prince Heraclius, is calculated as 5857.” But, as is clear from this number of years, the passage cannot concern Heraclius; rather, it must be understood of Recceswinth, king of Hispania, who is named here in many ancient codices. It was certainly added after Isidore’s death by Ildefonsus, as I think, who held the see of Toledo in the tenth year of Recceswinth.

In Codex Ottobonianus 352, after “it has been known,” the following is added: “The whole period from the beginning of the world up to the present tenth year of Prince Recceswinth, which is the year 666 of the era, is calculated as 5856.” Thus Codex Ottobonianus 404, but it adds “up to the present generation,” followed by the combined number of years, 5957. Codex Ottobonianus 336: “Era 665, years 5857.” Codex Ottobonianus 343: “Era 646, years 5858.”

No. 11, “or human beings.” Another reading: “or from human beings”; another: “what from human beings.” Likewise, “announced beforehand.” Another reading: “announced.”

Nos. 5 ff.: In the first nineteen-year cycle, the following variation exists between our edition and the most ancient Toledo codex:

- Edition: “B. com. ann., II Idus April., XX (lunae)” (“Common year, 12 April, 20 [of the moon]”).
- Codex: “Com., III Id. Apr., L. XX” (“Common year, 11 April, lunar 20”). Thus “L” is inserted for *luna* (“moon”).

- Edition: “C., VI Kal. April., XVI” (“C., 27 March, 16”).
- Codex: “B. com., VI Kal. Ap., XVI” (“Common year, 27 March, 16”).

- Edition: “BC., IX Kal. Ap., XV” (“BC., 24 March, 15”).
- Codex: “B. com., X Kal. Ap., XVI” (“Common year, 23 March, 16”).

- Edition: “BC., V Id. Ap., XV” (“BC., 9 April, 15”).
- Codex: “B. com., VI Id.” (“Common year, 8 April”).

- Edition: “BC., V Kal. Ap., XVII” (“BC., 27 March, 17”).
- Codex: “B. com., VI” (“Common year, 27 March”).

- Edition: “E., XVI Kal. Maii, XVIII” (“E., 16 April, 18”).
- Codex: “E., XIV Kal. Maii, XIII” (“E., 18 April, 13”).

- Edition: “C., IX Kal. Ap., XVII” (“C., 24 March, 17”).
- Codex: “E., IX Kal. Ap., XVIII” (“E., 24 March, 18”).

- Edition: “BE., XI Id. Apr., XVII” (“BE., 3 April, 17”).
- Codex: “B. com., II Id. Apr. XII” (“Common year, 12 April, 12”).

- Edition: “C., Non. Apr., XX” (“C., 5 April, 20”).
- Codex: “com., II Non. Apr., XX” (“Common year, 4 April, 20”).

- Edition: “E., VIII Kal. Maii, XXI” (“E., 24 April, 21”).
- Codex: “E., VIII Kal. Apr., XXI” (“E., 25 March, 21”).

Second lunar cycle: everything agrees, except that the edition has “E., IV Id. Apr., XV” (“E., 10 April, 15”), while the codex has “C., IV” (“C., 10 [April],” etc.).

Third lunar cycle:

- Edition: “C. IV, Non. Apr., XX” (“C. 4, 5 April, 20”).
- Codex: “C., III Non.” (“C., 3 April,” etc.).

The remainder agrees.

Fourth lunar cycle:

- Edition: “C., III Id. Apr. XIX” (“C., 11 April, 19”).
- Codex: “C., IV Id. Apr., etc.” (“C., 10 April, etc.”).

There is no other variation either in this cycle or in the following one. It would be of no use to record similar discrepancies between our edition and other manuscript or printed copies. It should, however, be noted that in Ottob. 345 the first cycle begins: “Common year, 12 April, lunar 21,” an indication of year 21, which some judge preferable. Other codices agree: Palat. 283, Regiovat. 112, and Urb. 479.

No. 14: “of emperors.” Another reading: “of an emperor.” The same passage: “for the army.” [Col. 0805A] Another reading: “for the armies.”

No. 15: “also the rest.” Another reading: “also the rest of Caesar’s [people].” The same passage: “among the Persians, the Arsacids.” Another reading: “among the Persians, Artaxerxes.”

No. 16: “first.” Another reading: “at first.”

No. 17: “dishonorable.” Another reading: “honorable from this point onward”; in Toledo Manuscript 1, in the margin, there is the note: “fabricated flatteries.” The same passage: “as a sign.” Another reading: “as a man.” “by an edict.” Another reading: “by a saying.” “but it was.” Thus the Gothic manuscripts and others; Grialius printed “for it was.”

No. 18: “as bases.” A note in Toledo Manuscript 1 states: “Bases are the supports of columns.” The same passage: “the people.” Another reading: “the peoples.” “they have crowns.” Another reading: “they crowned.”

No. 19: “concerning whom the Lord speaks: ‘Through me.’” Another reading: “concerning those of whom the Lord speaks, saying: ‘Through me.’”

No. 20: “luxurious, etc.” Another reading: “luxurious men exercising dominion with the cruellest desire.”

No. 21: “the prince and of dignity.” Another reading: “the prince and dignity.” The same passage: “but he was called.” Another reading: “or he was called.” “with which at first.” Another reading: “which previously.”

No. 22: “to be named.” Another reading: “ought to be named.” The same passage: “in battle.” Another reading: “into battle.” “himself.” Another reading: “to be.”

No. 28: “because of someone’s.” Another reading: “as though belonging to someone’s.”

No. 30: “they preside.” Another reading: “they preside over soldiers.” The same passage: “we name.” Another reading: “we call.” [Col. 0805B]

No. 35: “called.” Another reading: “are called.” The same passage: “let them sit.” Another reading: “let them sit upon.” “he serves.” Another reading: “they serve.”

No. 36: “they are de-iguntur.” Another reading: “they are delegated”; another: “they are selected.” “those who are called.” Another reading: “each of those called.” “they may have been asked.” Another reading: “they may have been approved,” or “are approved,” or “may have been approved.”

No. 39: “they may have contracted.” Another reading: “they may have constructed.”

No. 44: “a soldier may have stood.” Another reading: “soldiers may have stood.”

No. 45: “from thousands.” Another reading: “from soldiers.” The same passage: “from moletia.” Another reading: “from moleatia.”

No. 46: “from the levy.” Another reading: “from the chosen man.”

No. 46: “of the Macedonians.” Another reading: “in the language of the Macedonians.”

No. 49: “strioti.” Another reading: “structi.” The same passage: “under him.” Another reading: “under the second.”

No. 51: “thirty horsemen.” Another reading: “three hundred horsemen.” The same passage: “and it was made.” Another reading: “and they were made.”

No. 55: “it occurs in tumult.” Another reading: “it occurs in tumult.” The same passage: “and tumultuous in anger.” Another reading: “and a tumultuous military force.”

No. 56: “they borrow.” Another reading: “they imitate.”

No. 58: “called.” Another reading: “is called.” Here many old manuscripts insert: “A wedge is a gathered [formation], etc.,” as below at No. 61.

No. 59: “and a fleet.” Another reading: “and a naval force.”

No. 64: “in length.” Another reading: “into length.”

## CHAPTER IV

No. 2: “may they live.” Another reading: “they live.”

No. 3: “the family lineage.” Another reading: “the lineage of the family,” which Vulcanius printed; but in a marginal note he remarks that he prefers “lineage, family,” since *domus* (“house”) is used both for lineage and for family. The same passage: “of the husband and wife.” Another reading: “of the husband and woman.” “For the Greeks call roofs/houses δώματα (*dōmata*).” Another reading omits this; another has “they say” instead of “they call.”

No. 4: “but lineage.” Another reading: “or lineage.” “from the definition.” Another reading: “from divination.” “of certain [things].” Another reading: “of the others.” “such as nations.” Another reading: “or nations.”

No. 5: “assembly.” Another reading omits this. The same passage: “of the state.” Another reading omits this.

No. 6: “but a people, etc.” Vulcanius conjectures: “But the people is called from the Greek πολίτων ἄθροισμος, that is, ‘an assembly of citizens.’”

No. 7: “divided.” Another reading: “separated.”

No. 10: “they had.” Another reading: “they nourished.”

No. 13: “the name of censor, a judicial dignity.” Another reading: “censor, the name of a judicial dignity.”

No. 14: “to debate.” Another reading: “to discuss.”

No. 17: “the leaders of the state.” Another reading: “the leaders of the citizens,” or “of the state.” “let them precede.” Another reading: “let them proceed.” “prominent walls.” Another reading: “processed walls.” “they stand out above the rest of the multitude.” Another reading: “they stand out from the rest of the multitude”; another: “they are preeminent over the rest of the multitude.”

No. 18: “so that it gives rights to the plebs.” Another reading: “so that it either gives rights to the plebs”; another: “so that it gives the plebs either rights.” The same passage: “they grant.” Another reading: “they may grant.” “then the plebs themselves [appoint] tribunes.” Another reading: “then they [appoint] tribunes.”

No. 22: “and into the place.” Another reading: “and into the places.”

No. 25: “they belong to an order.” Another reading: “they are orders.” The same passage: “because they are first.” Another reading: “because they preside.”

No. 26: “magistrates.” Another reading: “magistrati.”

No. 26: “Duumviral …” Another reading adds: “The duumviral officials, who have authority over two men.”

No. 27: “porter.” Another reading: “carrier.” The same passage: “because it.” Another reading: “who it.”

No. 28: “the name of a people.” Another reading: “the name of a nation.”

No. 31: “that is, weak.” Another reading: “and weak.”

No. 32: “who … who.” Another reading: “because … because.”

No. 33: “governance.” Another reading: “governor.” “administration.” Another reading: “administrator.” “administrator of villages.” Another reading: “see *dispensator*”; another: “see *dispensatorum*.”

No. 35: “in place.” Another reading: “by way of.”

No. 36: “those who cultivate.” Another reading: “those who hold.” “those who owe.” Another reading: “those who defend.” “auxiliaries.” Another reading: “helpers.”

No. 38: “they emigrate.” Another reading: “they migrate.”

No. 40: “he indicates.” Another reading: “they indicate.”

No. 42: “they were called.” [Col. 0806A] Another reading: “they are called.” The same passage: “the city of Rome alone.” Another reading: “Rome, the only city.” “the other towns.” Another reading: “the other towns” [with feminine agreement].

No. 43: “they might be able.” Another reading: “they may be able.”

No. 45: “are thought to be slaves.” Another reading: “are said to be slaves.”

No. 46: “who are in the lineage.” Another reading: “who are from the lineage.”

No. 47: “of freedmen.” Another reading: “of freeborn persons.”

No. 48: “whenever they were freeing slaves.” Another reading: “when they were being freed by hand.” Another reading: “when they were being released from the hand.”

No. 49: “it is said.” Another reading: “it is.”

No. 52: “because by a will.” Another reading: “because by testament.” The same passage: “there was access.” Another reading: “access was added.” “to remain.” Another reading: “having remained.”

## CHAPTER V

No. 7: “they consider.” Another reading: “they think.”

No. 8: “hence she is called *materfamilias*.” Another reading: “hence she is called *materfamilias*.”

No. 10: “above the grandfather.” Another reading: “above the great-grandfather.”

No. 11: “called.” Another reading: “are called.”

No. 12: “for from the thigh.” Another reading: “for the thigh.” “lineage and stock.” Another reading: “lineage as the stock.”

No. 13: “called.” Another reading: “is called.” The same passage: “because generated.” Another reading: “as though generated.”

No. 14: “divided into four parts.” Another reading: “divided into four.” “only begotten, after whom no one [is born].” Another reading omits this; another: “who is unique, with no one before or after.”

No. 15: “when they are called.” Another reading omits “when.” “not born.” Another reading: “not named or not born.”

No. 16: “by human custom.” Another reading: “human custom.”

No. 17: “from this it also results.” Another reading: “between the sons also.”

No. 18: “for sons.” Another reading: “for freedmen.” The same passage: “they are of servile condition.” Another reading: “they are sterile by condition.”

No. 20: “of whom.” Another reading: “into whom.” The same passage: “through emancipation.” Another reading: “through mancipation”; another: “through mancipations.” “of both.” Another reading: “because of both.” “Fabius.” Another reading: “Flavius.” “Paulus.” Most old manuscripts read “Paulinus.”

No. 21: “by one abortion.” Another reading: “by one abortive child.”

No. 22: “he receives.” Another reading: “he received.” The same passage: “from the deceased.” Another reading: “after the deceased.” “let it be called.” Another reading: “it is called”; another: “it might be called.”

No. 23: “just as from a concubine.” Another reading: “or from a concubine.”

No. 24: “with an uncertain father.” Another reading: “and from an incestuous father.”

No. 25: “having drunk.” Formerly the reading was *austro* or *haustro*; Vulcanius restored *hausto*. The same passage: “they are thought.” Another reading: “they were thought.” “But in Latin.” Another reading: “But the Latins.”

No. 26: “so that we may say *neptis*.” Another reading: “so that we may say *nepotis*.” The same passage: “admitted.” Another reading: “admitted” [feminine].

No. 17: “from a grandson.” Another reading: “from a granddaughter.”

No. 28: “and ancestors who are also progenitors.” Another reading: “and ancestors, who are also progenitors.”

## CHAPTER VI

No. 1: “paternal uncle. Relations.” Another reading: “paternal uncle by relationship of kinship. Relations.”

No. 4: “as an image.” Another reading: “and as an image.”

No. 5: “are.” Another reading: “may be.”

No. 6: “flowing forth.” Another reading: “flowing forth by birth.”

No. 7: “and from one womb.” Another reading: “from one womb.”

No. 8: “a brother.” Another reading: “your brother.”

No. 9: “whom the Latins.” Another reading: “whom, in Latin.” The same passage: “between your shepherds and my shepherds.” Another reading: “between my shepherds and your shepherds.” “because we are all brothers.” Another reading: “because we are brothers,” omitting “all of us.”

No. 10: “spiritual.” Another reading: “special,” which is contrasted with “common” twice. “they are called.” Another reading: “we are called.” “common, since all.” Another reading: “in common, which also all”; another: “in common, since also all”; another: “likewise common, etc.” “in brotherhood.” Another reading: “in shared brotherhood.”

No. 13: “called cousins.” Another reading: “the sons of paternal uncles are called cousins.”

No. 14: “from a sister and a brother.” Another reading: “from a sister or brother.”

No. 15: “*thius* is Greek.” Vulcanius writes *tius* and notes in the margin: “For θεῖος (*theios*) means ‘paternal uncle.’”

No. 16: “and with the father departing.” Another reading: “and with the father descending”; another: “and with the father dying.”

No. 20: “*novitricus*.” Another reading: “*novitricius*.” Toledo Manuscript 1 contains this note: “A stepfather is the son of one’s own wife, and no other.”

No. 21: “*privigenus*, or as it were.” Another reading: “*privigenus* because.” After these words, or shortly afterward, the same Toledo manuscript contains this annotation or addition: “*Oppieteres*, that is, those who are born while their grandfather is alive and their father dead.”

No. 22: “brothers, sisters.” In some copies there is added: “This consanguinity … would be terminated by so many degrees,” as below at Nos. 20 and 30.

No. 23: “my father’s great-grandfather … or a great-great-granddaughter.” Another reading omits this.

No. 29: “this consanguinity, etc.” Others place these words after No. 22, approximately as follows: “This is consanguinity, while it … divides, finally …” Grialius, who produced only two tables—the first entitled “The Tree of Law,” the second “The Degrees of the Human Race”—attached the words “This consanguinity, etc.” to the lower part of the cross in the second table. In Ottobonian Manuscript 336, [Col. 0807A] there is inserted: “Likewise, from Book Three, Chapter Six of Justinian’s *Institutes*: On the Degrees of Kinship. At this point it is necessary … to acquire a knowledge of the degrees”; this was taken from an old edition and included among the appendices.

## CHAPTER VII

No. 5: “it is granted, because marriage.” Another reading: “it is granted, and marriage.”

No. 7: “from *procando*, that is, seeking.” Another reading: “from *precando* and *praetendendo*”; another: “from *precando* and *petendo*”; another: “from *procando* and *petendo*.”

No. 8: “which alludes to the name of the bride.” Another reading: “which also alludes to the name of the bride.”

No. 12: “as though *unxores*.” Another reading: “as though *unxiores*”; another: “as though *junxiores*.” The same passage: “they would anoint.” Another reading: “they would be anointed.”

No. 13: “because now.” Another reading omits “now.” “they have passed over.” Another reading: “they have passed over. One law is called …”

No. 14: “to one, two.” Two Toledo manuscripts read “of one.”

No. 15: “a bigamist.” Another reading: “a digamist.” The same passage: “by two or three.” Another reading: “of two or three”; another: “by two or three women,” omitting “husband.”

No. 16: “when there have been two with one man.” Another reading: “when there have not been two with one man”; another: “when there has been one with one man”; another: “when there has not been a second with one man.” The Albani manuscript reads: “when there had long been one man.” The same passage: “the partnership of a husband.” Another reading: “the partnership of another husband.”

No. 20: [Col. 0807B] “which in weddings.” Another reading: “which in weddings.”

No. 22: “who is first.” Another reading: “who was earlier”; another: “because he is first.” The same passage: “because the membranes.” Another reading: “which membrane.”

No. 25: “whenever.” Another reading: “whenever indeed.” The same passage: “that is, ways.” Another reading: “that is, roads”; another: “that is, a way.”

No. 26: “*trivolum*.” Another reading: “*fribolum*.” The same passage: “having flowed out.” Another reading: “having flowed.”

No. 27: “he blessed them.” Another reading: “he blessed them” [with a different grammatical construction]. The same passage: “similar.” Another reading: “similar to itself”; another: “similar to it.”

No. 28: “affection.” Another reading: “effect.”

No. 29: “Nevertheless, it is better, etc.” Another reading: “Nevertheless, it is better if in her character morals are sought rather than beauty.”

No. 30: “Therefore, however … to consist in guardianship.” Some omit this.

# BOOK TEN

### A

No. 1. In some copies the title is: “Here begins [the discussion] of certain names arranged alphabetically.” Many old manuscripts preface it with: “The origin of certain names—that is, where they come from—is almost” (perhaps, “well”) “known to everyone. Therefore, for the sake of knowledge, we have inserted certain matters into this work. Concerning certain names” (another reading: “of human beings”). “Although the origin, etc.”

The same passage: “whence it comes.” Another reading: “whence they may come”; another: “whence they come.” “as a man.” Another reading: “as a man through derivation.” “properly, a man.” Another reading omits “a man.”

No. 2: “they think it cannot be.” Another reading omits “they think”; another has “it cannot be” instead of “they think it cannot be.” “in the feminine.” Another reading: “in the feminine gender.” “an actor from acting.” Another reading omits this.

No. 3: “called.” Another reading: “is called.” The same passage: “yet he who nourishes.” Another reading: “yet he who is nourished.”

No. 4: “of the spirit.” Another reading: “of friendship”; another: “of the soul.” The same passage: “properly, *amicus* (‘friend’) from *hamus* (‘hook’), etc.” Toledo Manuscript 1 arranges it thus: “Properly, *amator turpitudinis* (‘a lover of disgrace’), because he is tormented by love of lust. *Amicus* (‘friend’) from *hamus*, that is, from a chain, etc.”

No. 5: “*amasius* … to love.” Another reading omits this. Thus, in this book, some derivations of names are absent from certain manuscripts, while others are inserted in another place.

No. 6: “which is.” Another reading: “who is.” The same passage: “of a man.” Another reading: “of a name.”

No. 7: “equality.” Another reading: “equity.” “fastidious.” Another reading: “very fastidious.” “spirited, because.” Another reading: “spirited, insofar as.”

No. 8: “raised up.” Some write *aelatus*, so that, because of the diphthong, it could belong here; Vulcanius remarks in the margin that *elatus* should instead be referred to the letter E. The same passage: “himself above.” Another reading: “he himself above himself.” “his own table.” Another reading omits “his own.”

No. 9: “called.” Another reading: “named.” The same passage: “for what is it to be greedy?” Another reading: “for some have said that it is to be greedy.” “neither avarice nor abundance.” Another reading: “neither avarice [nor] abundance”; another: “nor the abundance of avarice.” “is diminished.” Another reading: “may be diminished.”

No. 10: “may pollute.” Another reading: “*odlluit*” [uncertain reading].

No. 11: “here and there.” Another reading: “here and there.” The same passage: “into which direction.” Another reading: “in which part.”

No. 14: “enormous.” Another reading: “*aenormis*,” as above *aelatus*.

No. 15: “clad in black and clad in white.” Another reading: “*atramus* and *albatus*.” Two Toledo manuscripts read: “*atramiste albatus*.” The same passage: “likewise, an alien, … where he is.” Another reading omits this; another: “likewise, an alien, because he is of foreign stock, and not of the place where he is”; another: “likewise, an alien, because he is from a foreign region and not from the place where he is.”

No. 16: “someone.” Another reading: “something.”

No. 17: “he was.” Another reading: “he presided”; another: “he was present.” The same passage: “it must be written.” Another reading: “it must be written” [impersonal form].

No. 18: “let him hold.” Another reading: “let him be held.”

No. 19: “stupefied.” Another reading: “astounded.” The same passage: “by lightning or by touch.” Another reading: “by lightning and by touch.” Perhaps: “by lightning and touch.”

No. 20: “he was openly desired.” Another reading: “he was openly adopted”; another: “he was exhorted”; another: “he was urged,” without “openly”; but in both “exhorted” and “urged” there is probably an error.

No. 21: “having been changed.” Another reading: “having been altered.” “from two.” Another reading: “he is called from two”; another: “he is called by two.” “called.” Another reading: “is called.” “he uses.” Another reading: “let him use.”

### B

No. 22: “he wishes nothing evil.” Another reading: “he wishes no evil.”

No. 28: “whom the brother.” Another reading: “against whom the brother.” The same passage: “Junius.” Toledo Manuscript 1 adds: “Burrus, red and black.”

### C

No. 34: “divinities.” Another reading: “names.” The same passage: “in marriages.” Another reading: “among spouses.” “is called.” Another reading: “was called.”

No. 35: “and containing, because.” Another reading: “and is called containing, because.” The same passage: “he abstains from evils.” Another reading: “he abstains wrongly.”

No. 36: “because he cleanses.” Another reading: “because he washes away.”

No. 37: “*concors* (‘harmonious’) from conjunction.” Another reading: “*consors* (‘sharing’) from conjugation.” “who is joined in heart.” Another reading: “because he is joined in heart”; another: “who joins the heart.”

No. 38: “he applies.” Another reading: “he may apply.”

No. 40: “called.” [Col. 0808B] Another reading: “is called.” “to decline.” Another reading: “he would decline.” “you have.” Another reading: “using.”

No. 44: “had mixed together.” Another reading: “mixed together.” The same passage: “and when the compiler.” Another reading omits “and when.”

No. 46: “he swells with words.” Another reading: “he swells with words.” “something.” Another reading: “something” [feminine].

No. 47: “or because.” Another reading: “or who.”

No. 49: “may bring about.” Another reading: “may affect.”

No. 50: “who by one.” Another reading: “because by one.”

No. 51: “of lot.” Another reading: “by lot.”

No. 52: “*confinalis*.” Another reading: “*confinialis*.”

No. 53: “*curator* … *cognitor*, etc.” In some manuscripts these and certain other items have been transposed.

No. 54: “he falls away from him.” Another reading omits “from him.” The same passage: “by legal experts.” Another reading: “by learned men.”

No. 57: “may be.” Another reading: “are.”

No. 58: “from bodily fattening.” Another reading: “from a marked body.”

No. 59: “white, etc.” Another reading: “white, good, shining. *Canus* (‘gray-haired’) is called from *candidus* (‘white’), and *candidus* is as though derived from *candor* (‘brightness’).”

No. 60: “*clodus* …” Another reading: “*clodus*, that is, *clopus*. *Curvus* (‘curved’), that is, hunchbacked.” The same passage: “*crispus* …” Another reading: “*scrispus*, having curled hair arranged with a curling iron.” “called.” Another reading: “is called.”

No. 61: “from confusion.” Another reading: “from confession,” which seems appropriate to the matter.

No. 62: “a ship battered.” Another reading: “battered ships.” The same passage: “whose prominence.” Another reading: “to which prominence.” “are taken away.” Another reading: “is taken away.” “whence also Virgil.” Another reading: “as Virgil.”

No. 63: “the body.” Another reading omits this. “a prostitute.” Another reading: “a *laeno*.”

No. 64: “collegiate.” Another reading: “bound together”; another joins the words: “collegiate, carpenter.”

### D

No. 65: “let him preside.” Another reading adds: “let him preside and rule over the whole household.”

No. 66: “learned from teaching, hence also teacher.” Another reading: “learned, so called from teaching,” omitting “hence also teacher”; another: “teacher from speaking, hence also speaker.” The same passage: “called from learning.” Another reading: “is called from learning.”

No. 67: “administrator, because first he who.” Another reading: “administrator of money, first he who.”

No. 68: “from bronze.” Another reading: “from possessing.” “called.” Another reading adds: “called, or one who eats for a long time.” “from ten.” Another reading: “is said from ten.” “called.” Another reading: “is called.” In the lower margin of Toledo Manuscript 1 there is this addition: “*Dapsilis*, or generous, and also excellent or noble.”

No. 70: “with *ceroma*.” Another reading: “with a contest.” The same passage: “poured over.” Another reading: “poured over on top.”

No. 73: “degenerate, or ignoble.” Another reading: “degenerate, because he is ignoble.”

No. 74: “because of death.” Another reading: “because of death” [with a different grammatical form]. The same passage: “may turn.” Another reading: “may crack.”

No. 75: “into it.” Another reading: “induced into it.”

No. 76: “gaping, very much gaping.” Two Toledo manuscripts read: “unaware, very knowing.” The same passage: “to love intensely, to desire.” Another reading: “to love intensely, to desire.”

No. 77: “may uncover.” Another reading: “will uncover.” “*reses*.” Another reading: “*resides*”; another: “*residens*.”

No. 78: “into which all the crop runs.” Another reading: “into which the crop runs through every furrow”; another: “in which furrow all the crop runs.”

No. 79: “which she was accustomed to.” Another reading: “which she used to.”

### E

Nos. 81–82: “Raised up … Enormous.” Another reading omits these, since they were already stated under the letter A, namely in *aelatus* and *aenormis.

No. 85: “as though across the soil.” Another reading: “because across the soil.”

No. 86: “driven out, and with terror.” Another reading: “having been driven out, and with terror.” “driven from his own land.” Another reading: “expelled from his own land”; another: “driven outside his own land.”

No. 88: “from the boundaries.” Another reading: “outside the boundaries.”

No. 89: “in need.” Another reading: “in need and destitute.”

No. 90: “as though utterly consumed.” Another reading: “because utterly consumed.”

No. 95: “he restored.” Another reading: “he restores.”

### F

No. 96: “from modesty and temperance.” Another reading: “from the temperance of modesty.”

No. 97: After *Fenerator*, etc., Gothic Toledo Manuscript 1 has this addition at the bottom of the page: “*Femellarius*: devoted to women, whom the ancients called *mulierarius*.”

No. 98: “who [possesses] happiness.” Another reading: “which [possesses] happiness.”

No. 99: “easy.” Another reading: “doable.”

No. 100: “from *formus*.” Another reading: “from *forma*.”

No. 101: “may be broken.” Another reading: “can be broken.”

No. 102: “he sat back.” Another reading: “he withdrew.”

No. 103: “to the vital organs.” Another reading: “or from the vital organ.” Another reading: “or from the vital organs”; perhaps: “from the skin, or from the vital organs.”

No. 105: “he soothes.” Another reading: “he smears.”

No. 106: “roaring.” Another reading: “roaring, resounding, becoming angry”; another: “roaring, that is, shouting with fury.”

No. 107: “a thief from *furvus*.” Another reading: “a thief from *furere* (‘to rage’), or from *furvus*.” The same passage: “of night.” Another reading: “of nighttime.” “seditious.” Another reading: “seditious” [accusative]. “when [he is] seditious.” Another reading: “when [he is] a seditious man.” “gracious and powerful, as though.” Another reading: “gracious, powerful, and as though.”

No. 109: “from masters, of disgrace.” Another reading: “to the disgrace of the name.”

No. 111: “*fornicarius* … *fornicatrix*.” Another reading: “*fornicarius* and *fornicatrix*.” The same passage: “these women prostituted themselves beneath vaulted structures.” Another reading: “these women were prostrated beneath vaulted structures”; another: “were thrown down.”

No. 112: “as though abounding in offspring.” The Gothic manuscripts and others read: “as though fertile.” Toledo Manuscript 1 has this marginal note: “*Feta*: at one time ‘full,’ at another ‘one who gives birth.’” The same passage: “fertile … weeping.” Another reading: “fertile, pregnant; weeping.” “with tears.” Another reading: “tears.” “or from a school.” Another reading: “or from schools.” “she may have departed.” Another reading: “she departed.”

### G

No. 113: “but fixed.” Another reading: “but faithful.”

No. 114: “slender.” Another reading omits this. Toledo Manuscript 1 reads: “slender, fragile, thin”; other manuscripts omit entirely the words “large, slender.” The same passage: “because it is.” Another reading: “as though it is.” “who more.” Another reading: “which more.”

No. 115: “called.” Another reading: “is called.” The same passage: “neither able nor willing.” Another reading: “neither able nor willing” [plural]. “and as though.” Another reading: “and although.”

### H

No. 116: “hero … strong.” Another reading omits this. “sloping upward.” Another reading: “steep.” The same passage: “for honor.” Another reading: “in honor.”

No. 117: “humanity, which.” Another reading: “humanity, so called, which.”

No. 118: “*honorosus* is more than *honoratus*.” The Gothic manuscripts and others read *honerosus plus est quam honeratus*, namely for *onerosus* and *oneratus*, with an *h* added, as was customary in that age. [Col. 0809C]

No. 119: “from the Greek.” Another reading has “Greek,” without *e*.

No. 120: “images.” Another reading: “an image.” The same passage: “of the mouth.” Another reading: “outside.” “and necks.” Another reading: “and a neck.”

No. 121: “of an argument.” Another reading: “from arguments.”

### I

No. 123: “ingenious.” Another reading: “called ingenious.”

Note 280, “insane, not properly sound.” Another reading: “insane, moreover sound.” Note 282, “from a hunting spear.” Another reading: “from hunting.” In Toledo Manuscript 2, after “pressers” is added: “Here ends happily the tenth book of the first part. Book eleven of the *Etymologies*, of the second part.” Toledo Manuscript 1 has similarly: “Likewise, the second part, book eleven.” For, as I already observed in the Isidorian material, chapter 48, note 16, the ancients divided the *Etymologies* into two parts, the first comprising the first ten books and the second the last ten. We therefore reserve the second part of the *Etymologies* for the following volume.

## CHAPTER V

No. 2, *in sua arte* (“in its own art”). Alternatively, *in suo labore* (“in its own work”).

No. 3, *vel ibi uspiam adhaerescit* (“or adheres anywhere there”). Alternatively, *vel ubi uspiam adhaeserit*, which is perhaps better (“or wherever it may have adhered”).

No. 4, *cauda figat* (“let it fix [it] with its tail”). Alternatively, *caudam figat* (“let it fix its tail”). Ibid., *scorpioni* (“to the scorpion”). Alternatively, *scorpionis* (“of the scorpion”).

No. 5, *qui humano corpori statim ut fuerit* (“which, as soon as it has [touched] the human body”). Alternatively, *qui dum humano corpori tactu fuerit* (“which, when it has touched the human body”).

No. 6, *qui contactus* (“which, when touched”). Alternatively, *qui contra ictum contractus* (“which, when drawn together against the blow”). Ibid., *in globulum* (“into a little ball”). Alternatively, *in globum* (“into a ball”).

No. 10, *importuno* (“inopportunely”). Alternatively, *inopportuno* (“inopportunely”).

Note 28: “sea.” Another reading: “the sea.”

Note 29: “it was an ancient custom.” Another reading: “it was a custom of antiquity”; another: “it was the custom of the ancients.” In the same place: “many together.” Another reading: “together with many.” In the same place: “to seize.” Another reading: “they seized.”

The same passage: *armaverit* (“will have armed”). Alternative: *armavit* (“armed”). The same passage: *exsulatus* (“having been exiled”). Alternative: *exsulatum* (“exiled”). The same passage: *et in Ciliciam venit* (“and came to Cilicia”). Alternative: *et inde Ciliciam venit* (“and from there came to Cilicia”).

No. 10: *hujus modus* (“the manner of this”). Alternative: *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”). The same passage: *circini* (“of a compass”). Alternative: *circuli* (“of a circle”). The same passage: *in cujus medium* (“into the middle of which”). Alternative: *in cujus medio* (“in the middle of which”).

No. 11: *quasi succurris*. Alternative: *quasi sucuris*. The term is uncertain. *pennum* (“feather”). Alternative: *pinnum* (“fin” or “wing”).

No. 12: *dicebant pennas, non pinnas* (“they called them *pennae*, not *pinnae*”). Alternative: *pinnas dicebant, non pennas* (“they called them *pinnae*, not *pennae*”). The word *nomen* (“name”) is omitted in the alternative. The same passage: *ex aversa* (“from the reverse side”). Alternative: *ex adversa* (“from the opposite side”).

No. 13: *scalprus* (“a chisel”). Alternatives: *scalprum*; *scalptrus*. The same passage: *sit aptus* (“may be suitable”). Alternative: *sit aptum* (“may be suitable”). The same passage: *diminutivum* (“a diminutive”). Alternative: *diminutivus* (“diminutive”).

No. 15: *scobina* (“a file”). Alternative: *scofina* (“a file”). The same passage: *terendo* (“by rubbing”). Alternative: *haerendo* (“by clinging”). The same passage: *faciat* (“may make”). Alternative: *facit* (“makes”). The same passage: *galla* (“gall”). Alternatives: *Gallia* (“Gaul”); omission. The same passage: *guvia*. Alternatives: *gulvia*; *gulbia*.

## Chapter XX

No. 1: *ordisse* (“to have begun”). Alternative: *ordinasse* (“to have arranged”).

No. 2: *invenit omnia* (“he discovered everything”). Alternative: *invenit haec omnia* (“he discovered all these things”).

## Chapter XXI

No. 1: *est sacerdotalis linea* (“it is a priestly linen garment”). Alternative: *est tunica sacerdotalis linea* (“it is a priestly linen tunic”). The same passage: *nuncupatur* (“it is called”). The alternative adds:

> “For the Greeks call feet *podes*; this is commonly …”

Another alternative: *et nuncupata, quam vulgo* (“and called, which commonly …”). The same passage: *camisia vocatur* (“it is called a shirt”). Alternative: *camisiam vocant* (“they call it a shirt”).

No. 2: *viderentur* (“they might seem”). Alternative: *videantur* (“they may seem”).

No. 3: *est ex bisso* (“it is made of byssus”). Alternative:

> “It is what the Greeks call a *tiara* and the Latins a *galea*, made of byssus.”

The same passage: *sphaera media caput* (“the sphere covers half the head”). Alternative: *sphaera medium caput* (“the sphere [covers] the middle of the head”). The same passage: *galeriam* (“a head-covering”). Alternative: *galeam* (“a helmet”).

No. 7: *Dei tetragammaton* (“God’s tetragrammaton”). Alternative: *Dei illud ineffabile tetragrammaton* (“that ineffable tetragrammaton of God”).

No. 8: *feminalia* (“breeches”). Alternative: *femoralia* (“thigh garments”). The same passage: *velabantur* (“were covered”). The alternative adds: *velabantur; badin enim Hebraice linum dicitur* (“they were covered; for *badin* is the Hebrew word for linen”).

## Chapter XXII

No. 1: *sicut tegumen* (“like a covering”). Alternative: *quasi tegumenta* (“as coverings”). The same passage: *quasi intumentum* (“as a swelling or padded covering”). Alternative: *quasi intumentum amictus* (“as a padded covering of a cloak”).

No. 2: *sed et haec* (“but also these”). Alternative: *sed et hoc* (“but also this”). The same passage: *sermonis* (“of speech”). Alternative: *sermones* (“speeches”).

No. 3: *lautior* (“more splendid”). Alternative: *lautius* (“more splendidly”).

No. 4: *venditantur* (“are hawked for sale”). Alternative: *vendicantur* (“are claimed”).

No. 5: *perizoma* (“a loincloth”). Alternative: *perizomatum* (“a loincloth”). The same passage: *e foliis* (“from leaves”). Alternative: *de foliis* (“from leaves”). The same passage: *velarunt* (“they covered”). Alternatives: *velabant* (“they covered”); *velaverunt* (“they covered”).

No. 6: *ejectionem* (“casting out”). Alternative: *dejectionem* (“casting down”).

No. 7: *profusior sit* (“may be more excessive”). Alternative: *profusior est* (“is more excessive”).

No. 8: *manuleata* (“with sleeves”). Alternative: *manicleata* (“with sleeves”).

No. 9: *clavis ex purpura* (“stripes of purple”). Alternative: *clavis et purpura* (“stripes and purple”).

No. 10: *animus augesceret* (“the spirit might grow”). Alternative: *animos augeret* (“he might increase courage”). The same passage: *proponi* (“to be set forth”). Alternative: *poni* (“to be placed”).

No. 11: *laculata est* (“it is lacunated” or “ornamented with hollows”). Alternative: *lacuna est* (“it is a hollow”). The same passage: *aerio* (“of bronze”). Alternative: *aereo* (“of bronze”).

No. 12: *quae malvarum* (“which [is] of mallows”). Alternative: *quae e malvarum* (“which [is] from mallows”). The same passage: *malvellam*. Alternative: *maloelam*.

No. 15: *byssum esse* (“to be byssus”). Alternative: *byssinum esse* (“to be byssine”). The same passage: *existiment* (“they may consider”). Alternative: *existimant* (“they consider”).

No. 16: *aprina* (“of boarhide”). Alternative: *caprina* (“of goatskin”). The same passage: *masticina . . . mena*. Alternative:

> “*Mena*, because it is black in color; for the Greeks call black *melum*. *Masticina*, because it has the color of mastic.”

Another alternative:

> “*Masticina* … *Mela* from the black color; for the Greeks call black μέλαν (*melan*).”

No. 18: *segmentata* (“segmented”). Alternative: *segmenta* (“segments”). The same passage: *abscissas* (“cut off,” feminine plural). Alternative: *abscissae* (“cut off,” feminine plural). The same passage: *praesegmina* (“cuttings”). Alternative: *praesegminas* (“cuttings”).

No. 21: *velensis*. Alternative: *velenensis*. The same passage: *ut in Hispaniam* (“as into Spain”). Alternative: *ut in Hispania* (“as in Spain”).

No. 23: *et bilex* (“and twofold”). Alternative: *et biplex* (“and double”).

No. 24: *sine manicis* (“without sleeves”). Alternative: *lineum sine manicis* (“linen, without sleeves”). The same passage: *utuntur* (“they use”). Alternative: *utebantur* (“they used”).

No. 25: *renibus* (“for the kidneys”). Alternative: *in renibus* (“on the kidneys”).

No. 26: *producitur* (“is extended”). Alternative: *ducitur* (“is led”). The same passage: *flexuosam* (“winding”). Alternative: *fluxuosam* (“flowing”).

No. 29: *camisas* (“shirts”). Alternative: *camisias* (“shirts”). The same passage: *vocamus* (“we call”). Alternative: *vocari* (“to be called”).

No. 30: *tubrucos vocatos dicunt, quod* (“they say that they are called *tubrucos* because”). Alternative: *tubralicos vocatos quod*, with *dicunt* (“they say”) omitted. The same passage: *tubraci quod* (“*tubraci* because”). Alternative: *tubruci quod* (“*tubruci* because”).

## Chapter XXIII

No. 1: *sarabara*. Alternative: *sarabarae*. The same passage: *lenae*. Alternative: *linnae*. The same passage: *stringes*. Alternative: *striges*. The same passage: *mastrucae*. Alternative: *mastrugae*.

No. 2: *sarabara . . . immutata* (“the *sarabara* … changed”). Alternative: *sarabarae . . . immutatae* (“the *sarabarae* … changed”). The same passage: *sarabara suspenderunt* (“they hung up the *sarabara*”). Alternative: *sarabarum suspenderunt* (“they hung up the *sarabarum*”). The same passage: *nuncupantur* (“they are called”). Alternative: *nuncupabantur* (“they were called”). The same passage: *in capite* (“on the head”). Alternative: *in capitibus* (“on the heads”).

No. 3: *saga quadra* (“a square cloak”). Alternative: *sagae quadrae* (“of a square cloak”).

No. 5: *vestis. Sarda* (“a garment. Sardinian”). Alternative: *vestis germanica* (“a Germanic garment”). The same passage: *induuntur* (“they are clothed”). Alternative: *induantur* (“let them be clothed”). The same passage: *transformentur* (“let them be transformed”). Alternative: *transformantur* (“they are transformed”).

No. 6: *linamentis* (“with linen materials”). Alternative: *liniamentis* (“with linen threads”). The same passage: *et male tecti cum latratoribus* (“and badly covered with barkers”). Alternatives: *et malis tecti cum latrantibus* (“and covered with evil things, with barking creatures”); *et male tecti cum latratricibus* (“and badly covered with female barkers”). The same passage: *sagati* (“cloaked”). Alternative: *sacrati* (“consecrated”). The same passage: *linteati* (“clad in linen”). Alternative: *lineati* (“lined”).

No. 7: *expressus* (“expressed”). Alternative: *expressos* (“expressed,” masculine plural). The same passage: *succus* (“juice”). Alternative: *succos* (“juices”). The same passage: *illudit* (“deceives”). Alternative: *includit* (“encloses”). The same passage: *specimen* (“sample”). Alternative: *speciem* (“appearance” or “kind”). The same passage: *ferat* (“may bear”). Alternative: *ferant* (“they may bear”).

No. 8: *ut concumulatus* (“as heaped together”). Alternative: *ut cumulatus* (“as heaped together”). The same passage: *ambitus* (“circumference”). Alternative: *ambitu* (“by circumference”).

No. 1: *est quo* (“it is by which”). Alternative: *est, in quo* (“it is in which”). The same passage: *ministrantium* (“of those serving”). Alternative: *administrantium* (“of those administering”). The same passage: *utebantur* (“they used”). Alternative: *induebantur* (“they were clothed”).

No. 5: *intextas* (“woven in”). Alternative: *intextis* (“woven in”).

No. 17: *Graeci* (“the Greeks”). Alternative: *Graece* (“in Greek”). The same passage: *planetas dictos* (“called *planetae*”). Alternative: *planetas dictas* (“called *planetae*”). No. 19: *aestimant* (“they estimate”). Alternatives: *existimant* (“they consider”); *aestimat* (“it estimates”). The same passage: *et melotae* (“and *melotae*”). Alternative: *et melotes* (“and *melotes*”).

No. 20: *orae* (“of the edges”). Alternative: *ora* (“edges”). The same passage: *vocabulum trahentes* (“drawing the word”). Alternatives: *vocabulum trahunt* (“they draw the word”); *vocabulo trahunt* (“they draw from the word”).

No. 3: *cooperto* (“covered”). Alternative: *operto* (“covered”). The same passage: *vocatur* (“it is called”). Alternative: *vocata* (“called”). The same passage: *supermittatur* (“is placed above”). Alternative: *superemittatur* (“is placed over”).

No. 3: *fulciant* (“let them support”). In Grialius’s edition it appeared to read *fulciat* (“let him support”).

> “They were provided, or *mandelia*, from *mandere*, ‘to chew.’ *Mappae*.”

No. 3: *propius* (“nearer”). Alternatives: *propior* (“nearer”); *proprie* (“properly”).

No. 1: *staminum* (“of threads”). Alternative: *staminis* (“of thread”). The same passage: *derivativum* (“a derivative”). Alternative: *derivatum* (“derived”). The same passage: *insubuli quia* (“*insubuli*, because”). Alternative: *insubuli dicti quia* (“called *insubuli* because”).

No. 2: *colus quod* (“*colus*, because”). Alternative: *colum quod* (“*colum*, because”). The same passage: *fusus quod* (“*fusus*, because”). Alternative: *fusum quod* (“*fusum*, because”). The same passage: *per ipsum* (“through it”). Alternative: *per eum* (“through it”).

And so again.

## Chapter XXX

No. 1: *dicta quod* (“called because”). Alternative: *dicta eo quod* (“called because of the fact that”). The same passage: *quae in capite* (“which on the head”). Alternative: *quae ideo in capite* (“which therefore on the head”). The same passage: *ad significandum* (“to signify”). Alternative: *ad significandos* (“to signify”). The same passage: *corona fuit* (“was a crown”). Alternative: *coronas fuisse* (“to have been crowns”).

No. 2: *vocatum quod* (“called because”). Alternative: *vocatum eo quod* (“called because of the fact that”). The same passage: *est formata, et nominata corona* (“a crown is formed and named”). Alternative: *et formatam, et nominatam coronam* (“both formed and named as a crown”).

Alternative: *plerumque lata erat, plerumque tortilis* (“it was usually broad, usually twisted”). The same passage: *de albo* (“from white”). Alternative: *ex albo* (“from white”).

No. 5: *sutile* (“stitched”). Alternative: *subtile* (“fine”). The same passage: *appellatus* (“called”). Alternative: *appellatur* (“is called”). The same passage: *a ligando* (“from binding”). Alternative: *alligando* (“from tying”). The same passage: *connectebatur* (“was connected”). Alternative: *contexebatur* (“was woven”). The same passage: *galerum* (“head-covering”). Alternative: *galerium* (“head-covering”). The same passage: *fiebant* (“they were made”). Alternative: *fiebat* (“it was made”).

No. 6: *cidaris et ipsa sacerdotum* (“the *cidaris* itself [is] of priests”). Alternatives: *cidaris insigne sacerdotum* (“the *cidaris* is an insignia of priests”); *cidarim et ipsum sacerdotum* (“the *cidaris* itself [is] of priests”). The same passage: *quae a plerisque* (“which by most people”). Alternative: *quod a plerisque* (“which by most people”).

No. 1: *nimbus* (“halo”). Alternative: *nimbum* (“halo”).

The same passage: *viriolae*. Alternative: *viriliae*. The same passage: *armilla non discrepat* (“the name *armilla* does not differ”). No. 1: *circa brachia* (“around the arms”). Alternative: *circum brachia* (“around the arms”).

No. 4: *in Maenium*. Alternative: *in Maevium*. The same passage: *gestare* (“to carry”). Alternative: *portare* (“to carry”). The same passage: *miserat* (“he had sent”). Alternatives: *mittebat* (“he was sending”); *mittere praeferebat* (“he preferred to send”).

## Chapter XXXIII

No. 1: *nam a cinctu* (“for from girding”). Alternative: *nam a cincto* (“for from the girded garment”). The same passage: *nominatur* (“is named”). Alternative: *nominatum* (“named”). Alternative: *et campestris* (“and the *campestris*”).

No. 3: *lactantes* (“suckling”). Alternative: *lactentes* (“suckling”). The same passage: *et Prudentius* (“and Prudentius”). Alternative: *sed Prudentius* (“but Prudentius”). The same passage: *illigatum* (“tied on”). Alternative: *illigatae* (“tied on”).

No. 4: *limus*. Alternative: *lunus*. The term is uncertain. The same passage: *publici habebant* (“they had publicly”). Alternative: *publice habent* (“they have publicly”). The same passage: *id est, limas* (“that is, *limas*”). Alternative: *id est, lunas* (“that is, *lunas*”). The same passage: *caltulum*. Alternative: *calculum* (“little stone”). The same passage: *quam illi* (“which they”). Alternative: *quia illi* (“because they”).

No. 5: *nuncupamus* (“we call”). Alternative: *nuncupatur* (“it is called”). The same passage: *descendens* (“descending”). Alternative: *dividens* (“dividing”). The same passage: *alarum sinus* (“the hollow of the wings”). Alternative: *alarum sinum* (“the hollow of the wings”). The same passage: *vestes ad corpus contrahat* (“let it draw the garments toward the body”). Alternatives: *vestiat corpus, contrahat* (“let it clothe the body and draw [the garments together]”); *vestium corpus contrahat* (“let it draw the body of the garments together”). The same passage: *dicunt* (“they say”). Alternative: *vocant* (“they call”).

No. 6: *alligat* (“he ties”). Alternative: *alliget* (“let him tie”).

No. 7: *vincitur* (“is bound”). Alternative: *vinciatur* (“let it be bound”).

No. 8: *Virgilius* (“Virgil”). Alternative: *Virgilius dicit* (“Virgil says”).

## Chapter XXXIV

No. 1: *nuncupati sunt* (“they have been called”). Alternatives: *nuncupantur* (“they are called”); *nuncupatos* (“called”). The same passage: *insertis filo* (“with thread inserted”). Alternative: *incertis filis* (“with uncertain threads”).

No. 2: *caligarius vero non a callo* (“but *caligarius* is not from *callus*”). Alternative: *caligarios viros non a calce* (“*caligarii* are not men named from *calx*”). The same passage: *vocatus* (“called”). Alternative: *vocatos* (“called,” masculine plural). The same passage: *quas Graeci* (“which the Greeks”). Alternative: *quod Graeci* (“because the Greeks”). The same passage: *calceamenta* (“footwear”). Alternative: *calciamenta* (“footwear”); Grialius printed it this way.

No. 3: *crepidae autem dictae* (“but *crepidae* are called”). Alternative: *crepidas autem dictas* (“but [they] called *crepidas*”). The same passage: *in ambulando* (“in walking”). Alternative: *in ambulandum* (“for walking”).

No. 4: *iis soli* (“to them alone”). Alternative: *quos soli* (“whom alone”). The same passage: *centum fuerint* (“there were a hundred”). Alternative: *centum fuerunt* (“there were a hundred”).

No. 5: *cantaturi* (“about to sing”). Alternative: *canturi* (“about to sing”). The same passage: *ut dextro* (“as on the right”). Alternative: *ut in dextro* (“as on the right”). The same passage: *pedi* (“to the foot”). Alternative: *in pede* (“on the foot”).

No. 6: *baxeae* (“*baxeae*”). Alternative: *baxea* (“*baxea*”). The same passage: *fierent* (“might become”). Alternative: *fuerunt* (“were”).

No. 7: *sicut subtolares* (“like *subtolares*”). Alternative: *sicut subtalares* (“like *subtalares*”). The same passage: *quasi subtalares* (“as though *subtalares*”). Alternative: *quasi subcalares* (“as though *subcalares*”).

No. 8: *consuti* (“sewn together”). Alternative: *contusi* (“bruised” or “crushed”).

No. 9: *ossas puto ab osse* (“I think *ossas* comes from *os*, bone”). Alternative: *osas puto ab oso* (“I think *osas* comes from *osum*”).

No. 10: *vel aeneis* (“or bronze”). Alternative: *vel aereis* (“or bronze”).

No. 12: *quod saccum habeant* (“because they have a sack”). Alternative: *quod soccum habeant* (“because they have a sock”). The same passage: *injicitur* (“is put on”). Alternative: *injiciatur* (“let it be put on”). The same passage: *ligantur* (“they are tied”). Alternative: *ligentur* (“let them be tied”).

No. 13: *lingulati* (“tongued”). Alternative: *lingulati* (“tongued”). The same passage: *folleatos* (“bellows-shaped”). Alternatives: *foliatos* (“leaf-shaped”); *foleatos* (“bellows-shaped”). The same passage: *chalybati*. Alternatives: *calviati*; *callivati*; *calivati*. The term is uncertain. The same passage: *sola caligis vinciantur* (“let them alone be fastened with boots”). Alternatives: *solea caligis vinciatur* (“let the sole be fastened with boots”); *solea caligis vinciantur* (“let the soles be fastened with boots”); *sola calcis vinciantur* (“let the soles of the heel be fastened”). The same passage: *sculponeae*. Alternatives: *culponei*; *culponiae*. The same passage: *braxeae*. Alternative: *braxea*.

# Book Twenty

## Chapter I

No. 1: *mensam et sellam fecit* (“he made a table and a chair”). Alternative: *mensas et sellas fecit* (“he made tables and chairs”). The same passage: *factum vocabulum* (“a word formed”). Alternative: *factum dicitur vocabulum* (“the word is said to be formed”).

No. 2: *quasi ad cibatum* (“as though for eating”). Alternative: *quasi ad cubatum* (“as though for lying down”).

No. 3: *convivium a multitudine* (“*convivium* from a multitude”). Alternative: *convivium dicitur a multitudine* (“*convivium* is so called from a multitude”). The same passage: *nam privata mensa victus est, convivium non est* (“for the food of a private table is not a banquet”). Alternative: *nam privatae mensae victus convivium non est* (“for the food of a private table is not a banquet”).

No. 1: *vocatur* (“is called”). Alternative: *vocatus* (“called”).

No. 4: *parum* (“little”). Alternative: *parvum* (“small”).

> “*Simila* is the finest flour.”

Another alternative adds:

> “It is flour, said from *far*, whose impurities it contains.”

No. 19: *tenuissimum* (“the finest”). Alternative: *tenuissimus* (“the finest”). The same passage: *egestum* (“removed”). Alternative: *ejectum* (“cast out”). The same passage: *poliis*. Alternative:

> “*Pollen* is a kind of very white flour.”

The same passage: *una hora* (“one hour”). Alternatives: *prima hora* (“the first hour”); *plurima hora* (“a very long time”).

No. 21: *violenti* (“violent”). Alternative: *violento* (“violently”).

No. 23: *quando ardet in oleo* (“when it burns in oil”). Alternative: *cum ardeat in oleo* (“since it burns in oil”).

The same passage: *unde Afranius* (“whence Afranius”). Alternative: *unde dicit Afranius* (“whence Afranius says”). The same passage: *in Rosa*. Alternative: *in prosa* (“in prose”). No. 29: *quod fiat* (“because it is made”). Alternative: *quod fit* (“because it is made”). The same passage: *isiciis* (“forcemeat”). Alternative: *insiccatis* (“dried”). No. 37: *favus vocatur* (“it is called a honeycomb”). Alternative: *favum vocari* (“to be called a honeycomb”). The same passage: *fervere* (“to boil”). Alternative: *fervescere* (“to grow hot”). The same passage: *sanitatique* (“and to health”). Alternative: *sanitatemque* (“and health”). The same passage: *sicut e contrario* (“just as conversely”). Alternative: *sicut contrario* (“just as conversely”).

No. 2: *vapor emittatur* (“let vapor be emitted”). Alternative: *vaporem emittat* (“let it emit vapor”). The same passage: *patentioribus* (“more open”). Alternative: *patentibus* (“open”).

No. 4: *scrinia*. The alternative adds:

Alternative: *in reliquis operiatur* (“let it be covered in the remaining works”). The same passage: *fossorium* (“digging tool”). Alternative: *fossoriam* (“digging tool,” feminine).

No. 8: *sarculi sunt vel simplices, vel bicornes* (“hoes are either simple or two-pronged”). The alternative reads:

> “A *sarculum* is an iron digging tool having two teeth, named from *sarriendo*, that is, digging.”

The same passage: *pastinum* (“dibble”). Alternative: *pastinatum* (“dug over”). The same passage: *panguntur* (“are planted”). Alternatives: *sparguntur* (“are scattered”); *punguntur* (“are pierced”); *purgantur* (“are cleared”).

No. 11: *cilluntur* (“are shaken”). Alternatives: *cillentur* (“let them be shaken”); *celluntur*. The same passage: *moveantur* (“let them be moved”). Alternative: *moventur* (“they are moved”).

No. 12: *profluit* (“flows forth”). Alternative: *profluat* (“let it flow forth”).

No. 13: *exportare* (“to carry out”). Alternative: *portare* (“to carry”). The same passage: *qualus per quem* (“a basket through which”). Alternatives: *qualus corbes, colaque praelorum, per quem* (“baskets and press-baskets, through which”); *quales, per quos* (“what sorts, through which”); *qualos, corbesque praelorum, perquos* (“baskets and press-baskets, through which”); *qualus, corbiculae quoque praelorum per quos* (“a basket, and also little press-baskets, through which”).

## Chapter XV

No. 1: *a flumine* (“from a river”). Alternative: *ex flumine* (“from a river”).

No. 2: *gyrgillus, quod* (“*gyrgillus*, because”). Alternative: *gyrgillus dictus, quod* (“*gyrgillus*, so called because”). The same passage: *in gyrum* (“into a circle”). Alternative: *in gyro* (“in a circle”). The same passage: *pertica* (“pole”). Alternative: *parte* (“part”).

No. 3: *telonem*. Alternative: *tolonem*. The same passage: *Graece* (“in Greek”). Alternative: *juxta Graecos* (“according to the Greeks”). The same passage: *dicunt* (“they say”). Alternative: *vocant* (“they call”). The same passage: *quod imitetur* (“because it imitates”). Alternative: *propter quod imitetur* (“because of which it imitates”). The same passage: *levantem, ac deponentem* (“raising and lowering”). Alternative: *levantis ac deponentis* (“of the one raising and lowering”).

## Chapter XVI

No. 1: *vel quod haec equi* (“or because these [belong] to a horse”). Alternative: *vel quo equi* (“or by which horses”). The same passage: *lactentes* (“suckling”). Alternative: *lactantes* (“suckling”).

No. 2: *lupata sunt* (“they are wolf-toothed”). Alternative: *lupati sunt* (“they are wolf-toothed”). For *freni asperrimi* (“very harsh bits”), *frena asperrima* (“very harsh bits”) would be better.

The same passage has the following addition:

> “*Chamus* is a kind of harsh bit, by which proud horses are usually restrained. It is called from its curvature; for the Greeks call a curved thing *chamos*.”

No. 3: *habenae ab habendo dictae* (“reins, called from holding”). Alternative: *habenas ab habendo dictas* (“reins, called from holding”). The same passage: *a retinendo lora* (“straps from restraining”). Alternative: *a retinendo ora* (“from restraining the edges”).

No. 4: *capistrum* (“halter”). Alternative: *capistria* (“halters”). The same passage: *dictum* (“called”). Alternative: *dictam* (“called,” feminine). The same passage: *quasi ante sellam* (“as though before the saddle”). Alternative: *quasi antesella* (“as though *antesella*”). The same passage: *quasi post sellam* (“as though behind the saddle”). Alternative: *quasi postella* (“as though *postella*”). The same passage: *cingulum* (“girdle”). Alternative: *cingula* (“girdles”).

No. 7: *caloratum* (“heated”). Alternative: *coloratum* (“colored”).

No. 8: *ardore siccetur* (“let it be dried by heat”). Codex Lucanus adds:

> “The Book of the Etymologies of the lord Isidore, bishop, ends here. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

[Column 0849]

# Semleri’s Notes on the Etymologies

For these, see *Isidoriana*, chapter 52.

[Column 0849A] The index of all the chapters of the books, which Gothofredus prefixed, is not found in A and B. In its place there are six letters of Isidore and Braulio, which pertain to the history of these books. The chapters are numbered, but not entirely as in Gothofredus’s edition. For what is chapter 4 in that edition still belongs in A and B to chapter 3, although I do not approve this arrangement. For chapter 2 is entitled “On Common Letters”; therefore there must also have been a heading “On Latin Letters,” and from that point chapter 4 should be numbered.

## Chapter I

No. 2: *artis praeceptis*, that is, *arctatis* (“by the precepts of an art,” that is, “things tightened”), where one thing is tightened against another. See Festus under *Artus*. Servius, in his interpretation of the second edition of Donatus—which is in the edition of the twelve grammarians by Ascensius, Paris, 1516, folio, fol. 47 verso—explains the term, from which Isidore took this material, as “short, narrow.” Diomedes has similar material at the beginning of Book II. Hence in those times grammarians were called *artistae* and *artigraphi*. Priscian calls the works of Herodian “arts,” in his letter to Sulianus; thus *ars Phemnii* and *ars Donati* are used for grammar, ἐξόχως (“especially” or “preeminently”).

[Column 0849B]

## Chapter II

No. 1: *loquendi peritia* (“skill in speaking”). A [reads] “speaking correctly.” Asper defines it almost in the same way in *The Art*.

## Chapter III

No. 1. Varro has *litteratio*. Asper: “Terentius Varro first called it *litteratura*, as he says that it was still rudimentary”; so too Diomedes: “grammar, *litteratura*”; and this reading is preferable. No. 3. *Legiterae*. Diomedes: “as if *legitera*, because it is read, or because it shows the way to readers, or from the erasure (*litura*) it undergoes, or because it is repeated in reading.” Add Priscian also. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book I, chapter 7: “*legere*, because letters are read by the eyes.”

No. 4. “The same among the Latins.” B has “therefore,” which is better. In the same place: “twenty-two.” All the holy Fathers count in this way; hence it is certain that the passage in Irenaeus, book II, is corrupt, where ten Hebrew letters are said to exist—a mistake by which Schukford was deceived. See the *Acts of the Society for Latin Studies at Jena*, vol. I, p. 70.

In the same place: “They have twenty-three elements.” A counts twenty-three, and thus agrees with other grammarians, although some omit the Greek zeta and ypsilon and count twenty-one; see Diomedes, book II, p. 415 of Putsch’s edition, Priscian, book I, and others. In Gothofred’s edition twenty-two was mistakenly printed.

No. 5. “Having begun from the law.” These words are taken from Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, chapter 39; but I do not know how it happened that here they appear to convey another meaning, as though letters were then invented, although Augustine is arguing against this opinion and merely reports it in these words, immediately refuting it. I think there was here a sign indicating a quotation, or something similar, referring to Augustine’s entire argument; for it is clear from what follows that Isidore, along with many others, believed letters to have been invented before Moses.

In the same place: “Isis … handed them down.” Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 37: “Before Isis handed letters over to the Egyptians.” Isis is reported to have been the daughter of Inachus; hence these words. On the various accounts of the Egyptian letters, see Diodorus Siculus, book III, and Porphyry, *Life of Pythagoras*. Add the *Universal History*, written by very learned men in England, in its German translation from Halle.

In the same place: “priestly.” Thus Rufinus in his *Ecclesiastical History*: “Who, indeed, can enumerate the impious superstitions of Canopus? Under the pretext of priestly letters, there was almost a public school of magical art.”

In the same place: “The Phoenicians invented them.” Pliny, *Natural History*, book V, chapter 12: “The people of the Phoenicians themselves possess great glory for the invention of letters.” See also Athenaeus, book I, and elsewhere.

No. 6. “The headings are described.” A and B read “are written,” and this is better. *Describere* means to write much, whereas the titles of chapters consist of only a few letters or words.

In the same place: “Cadmus from Phoenicia.” Victorinus likewise relates this, in Putsch’s edition, p. 1944. Add Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, at the beginning, and Chisullus on the Sigean inscription.

Ancient writers do not agree in their threefold enumeration of the inventors of letters. Eusebius and the *Paschal Chronicle* state that letters were first used in the sixteenth year—not, as here, the seventeenth; Irenaeus, book I, chapter 12, agrees. Aristotle counts the ancient letters as ten and eight; consequently the number of those added by Palamedes and Simonides also necessarily varies. In such diversity Isidore certainly could not agree with everyone.

In the same place: “Palamedes.” Victorinus counts four: ν, ψ, φ, χ. Monsieur Du Breul prefers to follow Servius, who, in his commentary on book II of the *Aeneid*, says that ο, φ, χ belong to Palamedes. But Aristotle agrees with Isidore that ο is not Palamedes’ but Epicharmus’; and Servius himself indicates that it is more certain that χ belongs to Palamedes, while the others are doubtful. Irenaeus likewise supports Isidore. Therefore Isidore assigns these three letters to Palamedes, and not without considerable authority.

In the same place: “Simonides the soldier, likewise three.” *Miles* is absent from B; “likewise” should probably be read instead. Ancient grammarians frequently cite the poet when they are discussing metres and their principles. A has “added”; B has “put in.”

No. 7. “Pythagoras.” These words come from Servius on book VI of the *Aeneid*, with some additions and alterations. Here *formavit* does not belong with *ad primus*, so as to mean “he invented,” but refers to the model of human life; for the letter in question is certainly older than Servius’ account. The same words occur in Peter the Deacon’s book *On the Deeds*, addressed to Emperor Conrad.

No. 8. “By punishment.” A has “by death and punishment.”

No. 9. “The shape of the cross.” Many of the Fathers affirm this through a consistent tradition and piety. See Montfaucon’s *Palaeography* and others. In Henry Bentzel’s *Collection of Dissertations*, vol. I, p. 110 of Kapp’s well-known edition, there is a philological essay on *tau*, or the pious mark on the forehead, Ezekiel 9:4.
