This opinion of the ancients rests on their understanding of the words “mark them with the sign of tau” as referring to the letter, although *signa* may simply mean “mark them with a sign,” just as many names in the sacred text are simultaneously names of letters in the alphabet and of things.

In the same place: “and the end.” The manuscript has “itself and the end.” Immediately, “alpha,” not “from *a* alone.”

In the same place: “Coming together in one another.” A has “among themselves.” This is to be understood of the manner of writing: when α and ω are placed at the beginning of a book or folio, the lines are extended through the middle in various forms.

No. 11. “Except those which.” One manuscript has: “except certain ones, which indicate numbers by their shape, such as i for one, c for one hundred … and X for ten, a letter which also has the shape of a cross,” and so forth. The reading therefore differs somewhat from that collected in the notes to Isidore by Johannes Grial. There the most learned editor looks for a knot in a reed; but Isidore himself says that the Latins do not count by letters, except for certain signs which are not counted but signify and indicate.

“To count by letters” does not mean to count individual letters, but to count with them. Isidore therefore observes that this is a kind of resemblance, not the same method of counting by letters; the Greeks used letters for counting. Nor is it an objection that he repeats the point concerning X and the cross, since one seemed not to exclude the other.

Some of the most ancient writers held that the Greek chi corresponded to the shape of the cross. Hence certain learned men believe that the chi-shaped form used in the Jewish anointing of kings was based on this, on the authority of some rabbis, and seek in it an image of Christ’s cross. Many other grammarians, such as the *Breviloquus*, the *Catholicon*, and Solomon of Constantinople, agree with Isidore and say that χ is written in the shape of Christ’s cross. Yet they have no other source for this, and the form may therefore have existed in older manuscripts, which appear to have been variously truncated for the sake of brevity. An example occurs in Solomon of Constantinople, under the word “Letters,” where he copies Isidore with several alterations. I refer the reader there.

## Chapter IV

No. 1. “Carmentis.” Servius appears to have taken this from Hyginus, who writes: “Evander, an exile from Arcadia, brought [the letters] to Italy, and his mother Carmenta changed them into Latin ones.” Livy also discusses Evander and Carmenta, book I, chapter 7.

No. 2. “Either common or liberal.” Johannes Grial’s notes explain these words. Solomon of Constantinople had almost led me into error, since he reads *litterae librales*. Augustine speaks similarly, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 52: “Did he not himself persecute the Church, who forbade Christians to teach and learn the liberal letters?” Add the *Catholicon*, and note 41. Most of what follows agrees with the ancient grammarians and is also copied by Solomon.

No. 12. “Sallustius.” Solomon of Constantinople and A and B have *Salvius*. In Peter the Deacon’s book *On the Signs of Letters*, addressed to Emperor Conrad, in Gothofred’s collection, p. 1498, the reading is *Saulius magister*. Instead of *in sono*, Constantinople has incorrectly read *in se*. I think Saulius, or Salustius, was probably an obscure grammarian of the fifth or sixth century who counted this among the letters as a Latin and useful one.

In the same place: “Karta, Kalends.” The first word is absent from A and B. Solomon has *Karthayo*, but it is also absent from Peter’s little book. The ancient grammarians give various and uncertain accounts of the use of the letter K; there is no need to cite them here.

No. 13. “Because the ancients wrote everything with c.” These words are absent from A. This passage too seems to have been variously interpolated.

No. 14. “Up to the time of Augustus,” and so forth. In Solomon, the following is interpolated after these words: “And deservedly at this time the name of Christ became known,” and so forth. What I have cited above is a striking example of the ways in which these books were altered and of the fact that more foolish material was introduced by foreign hands. In Solomon, too, the order of chapters 3 and 4 has been disturbed.

No. 15. “From the Greeks.” A adds *autem*. In the same place: “*hilarissat*.” A adds that instead of *HILARIZAT* they wrote *HILARISSAT*.

No. 16. “Three things occur.” Add Diomedes, book II.

In the same place: “the power which.” A has *qua … qua*, and this is better.

In the same place: “among those being born.” Constantinople incorrectly has “among those who do not know.”

No. 17. “After they had them.” I read *eos*, so that it refers to the sounds of the mouth. I do not know what *eas* could refer to, but no one has noticed this.

No. 18. “And the apex.” A has *apicum*, namely “the shape,” which I prefer. *Apicis* is a better genuine etymology, supplied by Isidore, book XIX, chapter 30, from *apiendo*; nevertheless countless lexicographers play with this word.

Scaurus says: “Apexes should be placed wherever the same letters designate different things.” That is how it ought to be, but craftsmen often heap them onto inscriptions without any fixed principle. B and Gothofred read “they oppose”; Solomon has *a* instead of *in*, while A reads *apponatur*. Add the *Breviloquus*: “Apexes: letters written on the façades of walls or churches, and at the beginnings of books and in titles of laws”—in another sense.

In the same place: “for it is a lying line.” This passage appears to have been interpolated from Solomon: “… but a drawn figure by which the whole letter is written.” A reads similarly. The distinction here is therefore between the letter, or figure, and the apex. Above, instead of *dixerunt*, I would prefer *distinxerunt*; otherwise the sentence scarcely flows.

## Chapter V

No. 1. “The foundation of the liberal arts.” A has “of letters.” Solomon of Constantinople: “a grammarian … a teacher of the liberal letters.”

In the same place: “but this.” *Autem* is absent from A and B.

In the same place: “of speaking.” A adds “and of dictating.”

No. 4. “The divisions of grammar.” I confess that I have not found the number thirty explicitly given by any ancient grammarian. Yet, if the items that follow are counted, that number results.

“Articulate sound.” Priscian, or the author of *On Accents*, in Ascensius’ edition, fol. 122: “The element is the smallest part of the parts of articulate speech.”

In the same place: “faults.” Understand the ten faults enumerated by Donatus, Ascensius’ edition, fol. 46.

In the same place: “metres.” Priscian, *On the Twelve Poems*, fol. 111: “There are nine general metres.”

In the same place: “fables.” Priscian, *On Preliminary Rhetorical Exercises*, translated from Hermogenes.

## Chapter VI

No. 1. “The principal matters are referred back.” B has “are turned back.”

No. 2. “But the conjunction ‘and.’” *Vero et* is absent from A.

## Chapter VII

No. 1. “The noun is so called.” These words are taken from Servius’ commentary on the second edition of Donatus, but *quasi notamen* is absent there. It is nevertheless cited with the other material from Donatus in Cledonius’ *Art*, in Putsch, p. 1861. In Gothofred’s edition *res* is wrongly absent.

No. 2. “But a surname commonly.” A and B add “called.” In the same place: “is added above”; both manuscripts have “should be added above.”

No. 3. “Appellative nouns.” See Priscian, book II, p. 579 of Putsch, and Asper, p. 1728.

In the same place: “and among many.” They add: “and among them corporeal terms are similarly named.”

No. 6. “Specific.” They add “are,” that is, “are called.”

No. 9. “Are diminished.” A has “diminish the meaning.”

No. 11. “Calisto.” B adds “Calypso,” which seems more correct; the other may be a variant reading. Diomedes uses the same example, book I.

No. 13. “But among the Latins.” A reads “among us” instead of “among the Latins.”

No. 14. “Polyonymous.” A and B have the incorrect form *plurinomia*.

No. 17. “In relation to something, otherwise.” A has “in what manner.” Diomedes likewise, book I, p. 309 of Putsch. I would therefore read: “But such things, namely, are …,” not “those things.”

No. 20. “Patronymics.” See Diomedes, p. 310: “From ancestors, as Bellides; from mothers, as Latous Apollo,” and many others.

No. 21. “Possessives of *vhetica*.” The reading must be corrected; I am astonished that it was so often printed instead of *aetica*—already corrected by Grial. A has that form; B, incorrectly, has *eretica*.

No. 22. “Placed underneath.” A and B have “placed above,” as does Solomon of Constantinople; so too Donatus, *On Tropes*, p. 1776 of Putsch.

In the same place: “add.” A and B have “you add”; Constantinople has “with the same things added,” and this is nearly preferable.

No. 27. “The comparison is called.” A and B have simply “comparison,” which is more correct.

No. 28. “The remaining nouns are not genera.” A and B read more correctly: “the remaining are not”; they have *haec* in place of *hoc*.

In the same place: “one common … communicates one name.” A and B read *nominum*; Constantinople nevertheless preserves the singular.

No. 29. “Skill in meaning.” A and B have *tantum*; Constantinople reads likewise. I would therefore prefer that reading.

In the same place: “and in common.” A and B have “common and every.”

No. 32. “Of this teacher.” A adds “Iona.” These statements about case come from Diomedes.

No. 33. “Diptotes, such as Jupiter.” From Diomedes, book I, p. 288.

## Chapter VIII

No. 1. “Thus.” A and B have *sicque* in place of *varietas*; in Gothofred, *varietas* was incorrectly printed as *varietates*.

No. 2. “Finished.” A and B have “either finished.”

In the same place: “is said concerning absent things.” A and B have “are said,” which is better.

No. 4. “Are compressed.” A has “are tightened”; B has “are compressed.” The simpler reading is certainly preferable.

## Chapter IX

No. 1. “The verb is so called.” It is better to derive this from the Greek ἐρέω, “I say,” with the addition of the doubled Aeolic digamma.

No. 2. “Present, past.” A and B reverse the order: “past, present … he made, he makes.”

No. 3. “Meditative forms.” B adds “are”; A has “is.”

In the same place: “I meditate on reading.” A has “I wish to read”; so does Cledonius’ *Art*.

In the same place: “as an indication of beginning.” This is how A and B read. Some printed editions have *indicio*, which I do not approve. Diomedes has “the force of beginning.”

In the same place: “forms.” Other grammarians call them species or qualities.

No. 4. “Of the modes, in what manner.” A has “according to the mode.” No ancient writer explains these words, and they do not seem to be quite sound. Perhaps the meaning is “the manner of acting in their significations”? It would have been easy to make a mistake in abbreviated writing.

In the same place: “of commanding.” A has “of the one commanding.”

No. 5. “I shall read.” Nevertheless, it is clear that verbs were not infrequently transferred from the third conjugation to the second. See Nonius, chapter 10: *dicebo*, *vivebo*, or *fidebo*, as it is printed.

No. 7. “Common.” See Nonius, chapter 7, *On Opposing Classes of Verbs*.

## Chapter X

No. 1. “May occur.” A and B have “may approach,” correctly.

In the same place: “therefore called.” The word “called” is absent from A and B. Solomon adds: “Because it clings to the verb as to its husband.”

## Chapter XI

No. 1. “As though it takes a share.” A and B have *particapium*, which should be read in that form; otherwise *quasi* is meaningless. Add Diomedes, Ascensius’ edition, fol. 41, and Servius, p. 1794 of Putsch.

## Chapter XII

No. 2. “The forum itself.” In Gothofred and others this is incorrectly joined, but B separates it as “to the forum, itself,” and the meaning is thereby improved. So Servius, p. 1796. “I and these men shall go”: in this expression both the words and the sense are joined.

In the same place: “we do not say … to the king.” The words are missing, or rather absent, from A and B.

No. 3. “They are placed everywhere before and after.” A alone has “they are placed everywhere.”

No. 4. “The reason is.” These words are absent from A and B.

## Chapter XIV

No. 1. “Has been called.” A has *exsulat*.

In the same place: “with an exultant ‘eia.’” A reads *vah*. Certainly *eia* is said by Alcuin and Probus to be an exhortation. Diomedes calls *vah* an expression of pleasure. I think *evax* should be read, not *eia*.

## Chapter XVI

No. 2. “Because it has various durations of sound.” A and B have “through various.” Read *simpla*, not *simplicia*, as in Gothofred.

No. 3. “But among our ancestors.” For example, *utei*, *sibei*, and similar forms. See the laws of the Twelve Tables and ancient inscriptions.

In the same place: “individual forms.” A has “singular forms.”

## Chapter XVII

No. 1. “They consist in the tenses.” A and B have “they insist in the tenses.”

No. 2. “Pyrrhichius.” See Scaliger’s books *On Poetic Composition*. As for this dance, or contest, the interpreters of antiquities seem to derive it from Servius on book V of the *Aeneid*: “And now the boys [play Troy],” and so forth.

In the same place: “either from fire.” This is more or less Scaliger’s opinion; these words are absent from B.

In the same place: “spondeus.” They have not yet ceased incorrectly writing this as *spondaeus* instead of *spondeus*, Greek σπονδηος; hence Solomon also writes *spondius*.

In the same place: “of those sacrificing.” This touches on the true origin of the word σπένδειν, “to pour a libation.”

In the same place: “spondial.” Turnebus used this testimony to explain Cicero, *On the Orator* II, chapter 46, where he wishes to read *spondialia* instead of *spondalia*. But I cannot believe that *spondiales* was ever heard among the Latins. Marius Victorinus, p. 1284 of Putsch, has: “Hence those who are accustomed to blow such long pipes are called *spondulae*.” No one will doubt that, with one letter added, the reading should be *spondaules*, as in *Onoraules*. Similarly, in Diomedes, p. 472 of Putsch, we read amid corrupt and disjointed material: “And he ordered the player to play a spondalic melody with an equal sound, so that, with two long melodies, as though with doubled and continuous vows, the favorable will of the gods might be confirmed”; I would prefer *spondaulam*. Hence here I would prefer *spondaules*. In Diomedes one might also read *spondaulium … juberetur*. Thus in Cicero, *spondaulia*.

[Col. 0853]

## Father Anton Zaccaria’s Notes on Chapters IV, V, and VI of Book VIII of the *Etymologies*

### Chapter IV

No. 4. “The books of Moses.” The Lucerne manuscript has this reading, which Honorius of Autun appears to have found in his own manuscripts.

No. 5. The old edition of Rabanus, together with the Venetian edition of Isidore of 1483 and Bignaeus’ Paris edition, supported by the Lucerne manuscript, reads *Efnei*.

No. 6. “Masbothaei.” The Venetian and Paris editions just cited incorrectly have *Marbonei*, and the old edition of Rabanus and the Lucerne manuscript are no better with *Marbonei*.

No. 7. “Genistae.” This is found in the old edition of Rabanus, in the manuscript of Antonius Vion of Herovall, and in other manuscripts of the Royal Paris Library cited by Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, col. 761. The Paris edition of Isidore has *Genistaei*, and the Madrid edition agrees.

No. 8. “Meristae.” The Roman manuscript cited by Grial, the Lucerne manuscript, and the manuscripts used by Cotelerius have this form; the old edition of Rabanus agrees. Bignaeus’ and the Madrid editions of Isidore have *Meristaei*.

In the same place: Rabanus omits this entire clause: “for μέρος …,” and so forth.

In the same place: “separation.” The Lucerne manuscript has this instead of “part.”

No. 9. “Let them guard.” The Venetian edition of 1483.

### Chapter V

No. 1. “Of their own authors.” The Lucerne and Pistoia manuscripts.

No. 2. “He would have wished.” The Lucerne manuscript adds: “He lived at this time under Nero and died in the twenty-third year after Christ’s crucifixion”; perhaps “thirty-third” should have been written. Simon certainly died in the year 65.

No. 3. “A magician.” *Magno* was printed incorrectly in Bignaeus’ edition. The name is omitted in the Pistoia manuscript.

No. 4. “Called.” The Pistoia manuscript has this instead of “named.”

In the same place: “there are those who.” The Lucerne manuscript.

In the same place: “denies.” The Lucerne and Pistoia manuscripts.

No. 5. “Saint Stephen.” The Malatesta manuscript.

In the same place: “by Peter the Deacon.” The Lucerne manuscript.

In the same place: “you have the good.” The Pistoia manuscript.

In the same place: “which you hated.” The Lucerne and Pistoia manuscripts.

No. 6. “Who has the soul.” The Lucerne manuscript.

In the same place: “and the good.” The Pistoia manuscript.

In the same place: “to have created God.” The Malatesta manuscript, which consequently attributes an entirely different position to the doctrine of the Basilidians.

In the same place: “they fashion doctrines.” The Lucerne manuscript.

No. 8. Gratian has the reading *Millenarii*, as does the Madrid edition. But I have no doubt, with Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, col. 765, that Isidore wrote *Milliastae*, as in Bignaeus’ edition. Rabanus also has *Milliastae* in book II of *On the Instruction of Clergy*, and several manuscripts display a corruption that can be corrected only by restoring the name *Milliastae*. Thus *Milliasti* occurs in the Herovall manuscript cited by the same Cotelerius; *Militiasti* in the Pistoia manuscript; and *Miliciastae* in the Lucerne and Malatesta manuscripts and in the Venetian edition of 1483.

No. 10. “The virtue of knowledge.” The Pistoia manuscript.

No. 12. I cannot agree with the most learned men, Chacon and Grial. Not only the manuscripts I consulted—the Malatesta, Lucerne, Pistoia, and others—but also those used by Rabanus and Honorius of Autun present this passage in the same way. We therefore have no reason to doubt the integrity of the text. Rather, we should say that Isidore did not correctly grasp the meaning of Apelles.

No. 13. Chacon read *archonton*. Nothing should be changed, since the manuscripts of Rabanus, Honorius, and our own oppose the alteration.

No. 14. “Who.” The Pistoia manuscript; others have “which.”

In the same place: “imitate.” The Pistoia and Lucerne manuscripts.

No. 15. “The Cainites are mentioned” in the Lucerne manuscript.

No. 21. “Of creation.” Correctly so. The Venetian and Bignaeus editions and the Lucerne, Pistoia, and Malatesta manuscripts have “of the Creator.” In the margin of the Malatesta manuscript, however, an ancient hand has written the genuine reading, which we restored from the Madrid edition.

No. 25. One edition of Bignaeus has: “They abhor meats.”

No. 27. “The province of Phrygia.” Apart from the Madrid edition, this is found in the Lucerne, Pistoia, and Herovall manuscripts, and in the three Royal manuscripts cited by Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, p. 773. The Venetian and Bignaeus editions have *provinciae Cataphrygiae* (“of the province of Cataphrygia”); the Malatesta manuscript, however, has *provinciae a Frigia* (“of a province from Phrygia”), from which this too could easily be brought back to the genuine reading.

In the same place: “Priscilla.” The Lucerne manuscript; others have “Prisca.”

In the same place: “of God, and of the Holy Spirit.” The Pistoia manuscript; the Venetian edition has “of the Holy Spirit.”

No. 31. “They receive.” Bignaeus’ edition adds: “They are called Anomians, that is, in Latin, ‘without law’—a reading also found by Honorius of Autun in his manuscripts.”

No. 33. “Heraclitaes.” The Venetian and Bignaeus editions and the Lucerne, Pistoia, and Malatesta manuscripts have this form. The Malatesta manuscript also has *Heraclio* instead of *hierarcha*.

No. 34. One edition of Bignaeus has “the pontifical chair,” just as shortly afterward it has “to receive apostates.”

No. 36. “For Christ.” The words from here through “they were called because of their poverty of understanding” are omitted in the Pistoia manuscript. In the Malatesta manuscript they are absent as well, except for “because of their poverty of understanding they were called.”

No. 40. “From heaven.” The Pistoia manuscript.

In the same place: “the world.” This is the reading of the Venetian and Madrid editions and of the Lucerne and Pistoia manuscripts. Bignaeus has “that the world had been made.”

No. 53. “Contopites.” The Maurist Corbie manuscript has this form, as they note in connection with Augustine’s letter 53. Fabricius and others prefer *Campites*, not *Cotopites*. See also what we said concerning Jerome’s catalogue.

No. 61. “To be celebrated.” The Malatesta manuscript; others have “to be observed.”

No. 64. “By Nestorius.” He was substituted for Saint Sisinnius in the year 428, as Cuperus establishes in his *Chronological History of the Patriarchs of Constantinople*; see that work. Fabricius surveys the ancient and modern authors who have discussed Nestorius and his heresy, *Greek Bibliography*, vol. IX, pp. 236 ff. Add our Doucin’s French *History of Nestorianism* (1698); Johannes Sartorius’ two dissertations on Nestorius the heresiarch; Paul Ernst Jablonski’s historical-theological study of Nestorianism, especially the Nestorian phrase by which they used to call Christ’s human nature the temple of Divinity; and Joseph Simon Assemani’s dissertation on the Nestorian Syrians, vol. III of the *Oriental Library*, p. 2.

No. 65. “By Eutyches.” On this, consult Liberatus the Deacon’s *Breviary* and the other authors cited by Fabricius, vol. VIII of the *Greek Library*, p. 350.

No. 66. Why he calls these “the Chalcedonian chapters,” when they were treated at the Fifth Synod; and why Saint Isidore should or should not be regarded as a defender of these same chapters—see the notes of the bishop of Segovia on chapter 4 of the book *On Illustrious Men*.

No. 67. “Bishops who had been ordained.” See Sollerius, *History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria*, nos. 340 ff.

In the same place: “They say the nature.” The Pistoia manuscript.

In the same place: “They contend.” This heresy had nevertheless broken out earlier, under Timothy III, bishop of Alexandria, through Severus the monk, whom Timothy himself favored, teaching that Christ’s body was corruptible, while Julian of Halicarnassus taught that it was incorruptible. See Liberatus’ *Breviary*, chapter 19; Sollerius, cited work, no. 337; and Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book I, chapter 16, no. 30 and following.

No. 68. On the Agnoites (*Agnoiti*), consult Petavius.

### Chapter VI

No. 8. “Pisanactian.” This is the reading of the old books. The printed editions have *Pisanaction*; in fact, it is established that the portico was called by both forms. See Diogenes Laërtius on Zeno and Plutarch on Cimon.

No. 10. “Of continence, which they deny to exist.” I added these words in Jerome’s catalogue and in Cotelerius, vol. I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, col. 719, because the sequence of the argument itself requires them. Just as it was altogether ridiculous among the Stoics that they should pursue eternal glory while admitting that they were not eternal, so in this case it was supremely absurd that they should profess to love the virtue of continence while denying that it existed.

No. 15. Some writers, including the learned Guaseus, absolve Epicurus entirely from so infamous an accusation.

No. 17. “Gymnasium.” The same author, book XVIII, chapter 17.

No. 19. “As Pythagoras.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I.

In the same place: “as Maro.” This is the reading of the Madrid and Bignaeus editions, supported by two Malatesta manuscripts and the Lucerne manuscript. The Venetian edition of 1483 and other books, however, have “Varro.”

No. 23. These matters are treated fully and carefully by Massuet, dissertation 1 on the books of Irenaeus. See also Abbot Longuerue’s discussion of the origin of heresies.

[Col. 0855]

## Arevalus’ Notes on the *Etymologies* of Saint Isidore of Seville

### Preface

Some manuscripts and printed editions place before the work letters from Isidore to Braulio and from Braulio to Isidore, in which the *Etymologies* are mentioned. We shall publish them together with Isidore’s other letters. The *Etymologies*, their editions, and their manuscript copies were discussed at length in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 49 and following.

The preface to Braulio is said in some manuscripts to have been addressed to Sisebutus; in others, either to Braulio or to Sisebutus, or to both. Among the additions, or appendices, to the *Etymologies*, we shall first place certain hexameter verses in praise of the Mother of God, which in Vatican Royal Manuscript 1953 are inserted between those letters and the index of chapters of the first book.

Semler’s annotations on the opening chapters of the first book will be presented after the appendices to the *Etymologies*. They correct many passages already treated by Grial, because, although Semler praises Grial’s notes, I believe he had read them in Breul, not in the royal Madrid edition.

## Book I

### Chapter I

No. 1. “*Disciplina* from *disc.*” [the abbreviation is unresolved]. Others think that *disciplina* is an abbreviation of *discipulina*, from *discipulus*; and the word *discipulina* does indeed occur on ancient coins.

No. 2. “Because of the precepts of the art.” Becman explains the etymology of *ars* at greater length, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, p. 886, under the word *Pulcher*. Isidore repeats these same words in chapter 4, no. 2, and before him Cassiodorus, in the preface *On Grammar*: “The art, however, is so called because it constrains and binds us with new rules”—perhaps the reading should be *nos*, “us,” rather than *novis*, “new.”

Others say that the word was taken from the Greeks, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς, that is, “from virtue,” meaning the virtue of learning, which they call the knowledge of every good subject possessed by an eloquent person.

### Chapter III

No. 1. “Calculators.” Add Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 164, who cites these words from Augustine, *Confessions*, book I, chapter 13: “Those first lessons, in which one learns to read, write, and count.” Semler would prefer *litteraturam* instead of *litterationem*; but *litterationem* occurs not only in Augustine but also in Martianus Capella, book III, shortly after the beginning: “And Romulus gave me the name *litteratura*, although he wished me, as an infant, to be called *litteratio*.” See also the notes to Isidore’s *Glossary*, under *Magister ludi* and *calculo*.

Grial printed *introducunt*, which is better than the reading of the other printed editions, *introducuntur*. The subject is letters, which introduce words through the eyes.

No. 4. “Among them the alphabet.” Grial: “The same among the Latins.” I have restored “therefore” with the others. One might also read *id est*, “that is,” since *idem* and *id est* are frequently confused in manuscripts.

No. 5. “The letters of the Hebrews.” Verses on the inventors of letters, cited by Crinitus, occur among the poems of Saint Eugenius of Toledo, part I, poem 21, and in treatise 1 *On Grammar* by Saint Julian of Toledo. See also Burmann’s *Latin Anthology* and vol. IV of the Pisaurian edition of the *Latin Poets*, where the verses are arranged in a different order but otherwise agree.

Many writers discuss the inventors of letters; some are listed by Fabricius in *Bibliography of Antiquity*, chapter 21, no. 11. There he attributes the verses I mentioned from Eugenius of Toledo to Ennodius of Pavia; but I do not find them among Ennodius’ poems.

No. 6. “With Phoenician color.” Red. Ovid, *Tristia*, book I, elegy 1, verse 7:

> Let neither title be marked with vermilion, nor the paper with cedar.

See Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, Canaan I, 20.

No. 7. I restored *diduxit* instead of *deduxit*, as found in Grial and others. Some say that υ was invented not by Pythagoras but by Palamedes. More on this may be found in Muncker’s notes on Hyginus, fol. 277.

No. 8. Similar expressions with the infinitive occur frequently in Isidore, especially in manuscripts: “But there are five …,” and so forth. In my opinion, the name of the author who transmitted the statement was written in an abbreviated form of letters, and was later overlooked or misunderstood by the scribes.

No. 9. “Showing the shape of T, the Lord’s cross.” Ezekiel’s words in the Vulgate are:

> And the Lord said to him: “Pass through the middle of the city, through the middle of Jerusalem, and mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and lament.”

I have collected further material on the significance of the letter tau in the *Prudentiana*, chapter 20. You may add other material from Cotelerius’ edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, with notes, vol. I, p. 29, Antwerp, 1698. It should be written *tau*, not *thau*, as in Grial’s edition and in some Bibles.

No. 11. “But only words compose.” In Grial’s edition the chapter ends with “words compose,” but I do not think the material found even in our oldest manuscripts should be omitted. Compare Semler’s notes. Concerning the letter X, Ausonius’ verse in *Idyll* 12, “On Letters,” should be noted:

> In Latium the number ten is the Argive X.

### Chapter IV

No. 8. “The same, and the digamma.” Vulcanius’ note on this passage must not be omitted: “Why V is called digamma is clear from German pronunciation, in which—perhaps the reading should be *quae*, ‘which,’ rather than *qui*, ‘who’—v is pronounced like f, which is established by the double gamma. From this it is also understood why in many manuscripts, especially Gothic ones, v is frequently found instead of f, as *veritas* for *feritas*, and so forth.”

No. 14. “The letter X.” On the antiquity of the letter X, Matthew the Egyptian should also be consulted, in his explanation of the senatorial decree concerning the Bacchanalia, under the word *Exdeicendum*. The words “And deservedly …,” about which Grial writes, also occur in two Toledo manuscripts of excellent quality, whose variant readings were sent to me, as I noted in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 107, no. 32 and following.

No. 15. Tobias Gutberlethus, *On the Salii*, chapter 26, citing Velius Longus, reports that z occurs in the Saliar hymn. “If that is true,” he adds, “Isidore is wrong.” It must be observed, however, that Isidore is speaking of the ordinary practice of writing, which is not contradicted by a few exceptional examples.

### Chapter VII

No. 27. “The second part of the noun.” In some manuscripts the title is: “The second part of the noun: comparison.”

No. 33. “Diptotes, such as Jupiter.” Grial denies that *Juppiter* has two variant forms. Isidore, however, defends himself by the authority of Priscian, who, in book VI, p. 695 of Putsch, says that *Juppiter* has the proper genitive *Juppiteris* or *Juppitris*, whereas *Jovis* derives from the ancient nominative *Jovis*. Today only the genitive *Jovis* is in use.

### Chapter IX

No. 1. Some printed editions contain material concerning the perfect form, as Grial says; see Grial’s note there. But below, at no. 3, after the words “what we do,” this can be recognized from the variant readings.

### Chapter X

No. 1. “May approach.” Grial and other printed editions have *accidat*, “may occur”; and in manuscripts i is frequently found for e, just as e is found for i. Here I prefer *accedat*, with Semler, since an adverb more properly “approaches” a verb than “occurs” to it.

### Chapter XIII

No. 1. “*Loquelares*.” Julian of Toledo also calls these prepositions *loquelares* in the work on grammar now being published. He takes much from Isidore there, but also explains it.

### Chapter XIV

No. 1. “From the exultant ‘vah.’” On the interjection *vah*, compare Semler’s notes. One may conjecture that Isidore wrote “from the insulting *vah*,” following Jerome, letter 20, to Damasus: “In the Latin language we have certain interjections, as when, in insulting, we say *vah*, in expressing wonder *papae*, and in sorrow *hei*.” But Augustine’s passage cited by Grial favors the Vulgate reading, as do certain examples commonly brought forward from Terence. Add Augustine, *Tractate 51 on John*, which Grial may perhaps have intended to indicate, since the words seem to be identical.

### Chapter XVII

No. 2. “Pyrrhichius.” Meursius, *On Ancient Dancing*, observes that Servius confused the pyrrhichic dance with the Trojan game; he infers this from Capella and from this passage of Isidore. Many think that *pyrrhicha* was named after Pyrrhichus of Crete, who first taught the Cretans to dance in armor to the rhythm of the pyrrhichic foot.

No. 13. “To the song of those singing the *celeuma*.” The more common spelling is *proceleusmaticus*, like *celeusma*; but *celeuma* is also found in the best ancient books, and Julian of Toledo likewise used *proceleumaticus* in his work on grammar.

No. 26. “The islands … Achates.” I corrected the Grial edition, corrupted by an interchange of letters: *insulaees, Achat* instead of *insulae, Achates*.

No. 30. “Metres acquire effects from feet.” In the old Vatican Royal Manuscript 212 there is a short work attributed to Isidore, with the title: “Here begin little inventions concerning feet necessary to us.” I shall publish it as Appendix 2 to the *Etymologies*. Perhaps this work was published by Isidore before he completed the *Etymologies*, and he later arranged book I, chapter 17, from it.

### Chapter XVIII

No. 6. “Accents, however, were discovered.” Riccioli discusses accent at length in the eighth part of his *Prosody*, which is “On Accent in Pronunciation and Writing,” where he cites several other authorities.

In the same place, Grial printed: “and with *meta* not lengthened,” and the manuscripts are more or less the same. Some prefer Vulcanius’ reading: “and with the *me* not lengthened,” that is, with the first syllable of *meta* short. Some have *producte* instead of *producta*.

### Chapter XIX

No. 6. “For the verse.” In the oldest Toledo manuscript, *verui* appears here instead of *versui*, and likewise in the following note. In both places the figure is represented in another manner, as will be shown together with the notes on the *Sentences*, chapter 21, in the table.

### CHAPTER XX

**No. 1.** There was an ancient custom of punctuation, but it was neither universal nor observed by everyone. Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning*, book I, says:

“But so that you may seem to add ornament to all these matters, place at the individual heads the punctuation marks which the Greeks call θέσεις (*theseis*), that is, very short, simultaneously rounded and perfectly smooth points, except in the translation of Saint Jerome, which consists of passages and commas adorned with such marks.”

See also Diomedes, book II, p. 432 in Putsch, and what I noted from Sergius in the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*, no. 171. In a later age, a certain Peregrinus, a scribe whom I cited in *Isidoriana*, chapter 108, no. 26, listed more signs for distinguishing and punctuating.

**No. 2.** *The first punctuation mark.* Cassiodorus, in the passage cited, explains it differently: “The first is medial; the second is the subdistinctive mark; the third is the full stop.” But Isidore agrees with Diomedes; this seems to be approved by Lipsius in his letter to Hubert Audeiantus, *On Distinction and Punctuation*, *Miscellaneous Letters*, century 3, letter 39, where he observes that people in that age varied among themselves. The subject is discussed learnedly in the *Proceedings of the Academy of Barcelona*, vol. I, chapter 2, pp. 436 ff. In vol. I of the *Göttweig Chronicle*, prologue, book I, chapter 1, pp. 20 ff., much material is collected concerning the most ancient use of punctuation, where Isidore’s explanation is easily preferable to the others, especially in view of the Cassiodorean testimony cited.

### CHAPTER XXI

**No. 1.** In the cited *Göttweig Chronicle*, vol. I, pp. 24 ff., this and the following chapters on signs are presented from a twelfth-century Göttweig manuscript; but it is not stated whether this is a manuscript of the *Etymologies*. There are, however, a few divergences.

**No. 2.** *The asterisk.* Augustine, Letter 10 to Jerome:

“You marked with asterisks what is in the Hebrew and absent from the Greek; but with obelisks what is found in the Greek and not in the Hebrew.”

From this it is clear that ancient writers sometimes used the signs of their texts according to their own discretion, not according to any definite and consistent rule. We should be little concerned about the form of the signs, whether those printed in the cited *Göttweig Chronicle* or others displayed by different scholars from ancient manuscripts, since there is great variation in manuscripts and printed editions. What must be observed is that the form should agree with the definition supplied by Isidore. Other variations which, while preserving that definition or description, commonly occur should be attributed to scribes, just as among us the same Latin or Greek letters are formed differently by different people. Compare the copperplate table added by us. (You will find this table at the end of this volume. **Editor**.)

**No. 22.** *Chrismon* (χρήσιμον, “useful”). The Reverend Thomasius, in the preface to the Psalter, vol. II of Vezzosi’s edition, p. 23, describes five signs used in the Psalter, among them the *chrismon*, as he calls it, which is placed at the writer’s discretion to signify something. It is well known that by this sign the name of Christ is expressed, and for that reason it is called a monogram. Grialius follows a different etymology. Fortunius Licetus should also be consulted, *On Lamps*, book VI, chapter 47. In Ciampini, vol. II of *Ancient Monuments*, p. 172, plate 19, certain ancient monuments display a sign which some regard as a *chresimon* and others as a *ceraunium*.

**No. 23.** *Phi and rho.* Grialius printed Φ and ρ; but it is better to print the names of these letters, *phi* and *rho*, as Vulcanius conjectured, with the following annotation: “I emend to PHI and RHO.” For the sign seems to be composed of these two letters. Since Isidore himself says that this sign is customarily placed out of concern, I would indeed believe that it signifies φρονητέον (*phronēteon*), that is, “the passage is obscure, and therefore one must think about it more carefully.” Scribes joined *phi et rho*, from which *phietro* arose in manuscripts and printed editions. In the Gothic Psalter still preserved at Toledo, this very sign appears, although in a somewhat different form, as is observed in the extremely learned preface to the new edition of the Isidorian, or Mozarabic, Breviary, p. 20.

### CHAPTER XXII

**No. 1.** *Ennius was the first to introduce common signs.* Many writers have written much about common signs. I shall present certain matters especially relevant to illustrating or defending Isidore. Lipsius, in his letter to Leonard Lessius, *On the Signs and Notaries of the Ancients*, book I, letter 27, observes that Isidore is the first to call these signs “common,” in order to distinguish them from juridical and military signs. He then thinks that Isidore did not write *Ennius primus* (“Ennius was the first”), but *Persannius primus* (“Persannius was the first”), since nothing of this kind is read concerning Ennius. Perhaps, however, he was not thinking of the later Ennius, about whom Grialius speaks.

Lipsius took the name *Persannius* from old editions. For he reads as follows: “He devised signs, but only for prepositions. After him, Tertius Persannius, Philargyrus, and Aquila,” etc.; and he emends it: “After him, Persannius,” etc., since the word *Tertius* is absent from the manuscripts. In place of *astantes* (“those standing”), Lipsius suspects that *audientes* (“those listening”) should be read, because he had found *addentes* (“those adding”) in one manuscript; nevertheless, he does not condemn *astantes*. Indeed, I alone think this reading is correct. It seems to have been characteristic of notaries, as may be gathered from Prudentius’ hymn in honor of Saint Cassian, where the boys who worked with their styli addressed him thus, *Peristephanon*, hymn 9, verse 71:

“We return to you, behold, so many thousands of signs,

as, while standing and weeping, under your instruction, we received.”

Unless we say that the boys, because they were under their teacher’s discipline, were accustomed to receive the signs while standing.

Samuel Petit observes that the passage should be punctuated as follows: “He devised signs. But only signs for prepositions were added after him by Tertius Persannius, Philargyrus, and Aquila,” etc. That is, Tiro invented signs composed of distinct characters, separate from Ennius’ common signs made with letters. Philargyrus and Aquila received Tiro’s system. Persannius, third after Tiro, added signs only for prepositions.

Peveratus thought that the signs attributed by Gruterus to Tiro were spurious; he claimed to possess Tiro’s genuine signs, as I said in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 9, verse 23. Perhaps Isidore understood the matter as follows: Ennius the first—namely, the Younger—invented 1,100 signs for different words; and Tiro likewise was the first to devise signs only for prepositions, about which Ennius had said nothing. After Tiro, Vipsanius—or Persannius, as some printed editions have it—or Samnius or Saninius, as some manuscripts read—together with Philargius or Philargyrus and Aquila, each added different signs. There would be nothing wrong with reading, “each added different signs.”

Grialius seems to make Vipsanius and Philargius one and the same person; but we should distinguish them better: “Vipsanius, Philargius.” Since the ancients themselves disagree greatly about the inventors of signs, I think that Isidore, following one authority, made Ennius the first author and then, following another, Tiro. It was easy for scribes to omit the names of authors indicated in the margin by abbreviated letters, as I have already observed in *Isidoriana*.

More may be seen concerning signs in the *Proceedings of the Academy of Barcelona*, vol. I, p. 427; in vol. I, prologue, book I, of the *Göttweig Chronicle*; and in Fabricius, *Bibliography*, chapter 16, no. 15, and *The Library of Ancient Latin Authors*, book II, chapter 9, no. 8, and book IV, chapter 6. There he lists various editions and explanations of the ancient signs, as well as the authors who discuss them. The Vatican Library, Ottobonian collection, no. 2971, preserves an outstanding manuscript work of great value, namely Giovanni Battista Guazzeroni’s interpretation of the ancient signs of the Romans, etc. The signs number 6,400; their explanations, 10,720. Among the ancient Vatican parchments there are also some short works of our Isidore written in the ancient signs of the Romans.

**No. 2.** *Then Seneca.* Lipsius, in the letter to Lessius cited above, thinks that Isidore means Seneca the Elder, who composed a work of five thousand signs. Fabricius calls this a plausible conjecture in his note to book II, chapter 9, no. 8, of *The Library of Ancient Latin Authors*, although Bernard of Mallinckrodt, chapter 24 of *On the Nature and Use of Letters*, prefers to understand the philosopher Seneca. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 110, seems unwilling to accept either interpretation. From Seneca’s words about signs, Letter 40—“Such contrivances belong to the most worthless slaves”—he concludes that Isidore is reporting something false. But why could Seneca not have considered a contrivance which belonged to the most worthless slaves worthy of being expanded by himself, or by any other freeborn man?

In the text and notes of Grialius’ edition one reads *contractu omnium* (“by the contraction of all”); Varro used *contractu* for *contractione* or *contractura* in book I of *On Agriculture*, near the end. But, as with others, *contracto* seems preferable, namely, “collected, arranged, and increased in number,” etc., as in the example produced by Grialius from Suetonius, and in Suetonius himself, *Augustus*, chapter 31: “He burned two thousand books collected from every quarter.”

### CHAPTER XXIV

**No. 1.** *In little booklets.* In the note to Pollux, vol. II, book VIII, chapter 9, it is conjectured that *in matriculis* (“in registers”) should be restored here in place of *in breviculis* (“in little booklets”). Scaliger says that the V from *ferale sonans* in Ausonius, *Idyll* 12, is so called because the word *ululare* (“to howl”) begins with it; thus he interprets the passage. It is certainly established that in surviving ancient monuments V is used for *vivit* (“he lives”). Among others, Marini collected examples in *The Acts of the Arval Brethren*, pp. 610 ff.

What, then? Should V be restored in Isidore in place of T? The manuscript copies oppose this. Rutgersius, *Various Readings*, book V, chapter 17, defends T as representing “surviving,” from the Greek verb τηρέω (*tēreō*, “to preserve”). Barthius follows Rutgersius, book XLIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 6. He says that Latin too supplies reasons for defending this letter as the sign of the blessed cross, since the letter which Ennodius, *Epigrams*, 17, calls “the guide of righteousness” denotes an upright person using his arms properly and therefore someone healthy and vigorous.

Rutgersius’ conjecture did not please Nicholas Antonio, *The Old Spanish Library*, book V, no. 97. Against Lipsius, who wished to substitute V for T in *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, chapter 14, Antonio instead adopts the observation of Thomas Reinesius, who argues in book I of *Various Readings*, chapter 7, that Υ should be read in Isidore in place of T. For Υ is the initial letter of ὑγεία (*hygeia*, “health, soundness, well-being”), a reading confirmed by the notable testimony of Galerius.

One may also add, from Isidore himself above, chapter 3, no. 7, that Υ was formed as an example of human life, and at no. 8: “There are five mystical letters among the Greeks. The first is Υ, which signifies human life, about which we have just spoken. The second is Θ, which signifies death.” It was certainly easy for Υ, with its little horns lowered, to pass into T in the hands of copyists. I would nevertheless like some such example to appear in the ancient little booklets of soldiers. Perhaps this usage began after the Roman Empire passed to Greek emperors.

Grialius and other editors punctuate the passage thus: “It has a weapon through the middle.” That is, “the sign of death.” I prefer: “a weapon, that is, the sign of death,” as in Grialius himself above, chapter 3, no. 8. Otherwise theta too is called the sign of death, as in Martial, book VII, epigram 36:

“You know the deadly sign of the quaestor, Castricius.”

“It is worthwhile to learn the new theta.”

In Persius’ verse the reading was *est* (“is”), for which I restored *es* (“you are”). Montfaucon, *Greek Palaeography*, book 4, chapter 2, observes that the ancients wrote Θ with a little line through the middle, whereas the more recent custom is to write it differently, namely θ. Bottarius should be consulted concerning the funerary inscription which he discusses in vol. I of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 74, where Θ is visibly written.

**No. 2.** *But when impurity.* See at its proper place the various readings *imperitia* (“inexperience”), *impuritia* (“impurity”), and *peritia* (“expertise”).

### CHAPTER XXV

**No. 1.** *Also the signs of letters.* Besides Trithemius, several writers have transmitted instructions on the art of secret writing, or steganography, and on the art of deciphering and reading hidden writings. They are listed by Fabricius in *Ancient Bibliography*, chapter 21, no. 11. Emmanuel Friedrich Gregorius also concludes that Cicero used letter-signs in his dissertation *On the Style of Writing by Means of Signs, Especially among the Ancient Latins*, which is found in vol. II of the *Proceedings of the Latin Society of Jena*.

**No. 2.** *But in place of z, double aa.* Caesar’s words perhaps begin with *cum*, and therefore *incidant* (“may fall”) should be read, not *incidunt* (“fall”), as Grialius has it. Grialius thinks the words *Pro z autem*, etc., should be read as follows: “But for X,” etc. Suetonius, however, speaks in the same way in *Augustus*, chapter 88: “For z, double aa.”

Nor does Isidore state in chapters 3 and 4 that in Augustus’ time the final letter was x. Rather, he says that y and z were not written among the Romans until Augustus’ time, and he taught the same concerning the letter x. That Caesar changed letters in a different manner when writing to others is shown by Suetonius, *Julius Caesar*, chapter 56: he changed the fourth letter of the alphabet, that is, d for a, and likewise the remaining letters. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVII, chapter 9, praises a commentary by the grammarian Probus, carefully composed, on the secret significance of the letters in Caesar’s epistles.

### CHAPTER XXVI

**No. 1.** *By the movement of swords.* I discussed the signs made with the fingers, and counting or speech by finger gestures, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 86, no. 15. In the text Grialius printed *gladiorum motu* (“by the movement of the swords”), but in the notes he seems to have intended *gladiorum nutu* (“by the sign of the swords”), which the recent Madrid editor adopted. Indeed, Grialius himself appears to have done so while preparing the edition. For although the text in my copy reads *motu*, in another copy of the very same edition I found *nutu*. Thus copies of one and the same edition sometimes differ among themselves. I see no reason to change *motu* to *nutu* against most of the ancient manuscripts.

**No. 2.** *Ennius concerning a certain shameless man.* Since Festus establishes that these verses belong to Naevius, I safely restored *Naevius* in place of *Ennius*, although Grialius and the other editors and manuscripts consistently read *Ennius*. It was easy for the first scribes to substitute Ennius for the name Naevius, perhaps abbreviated by a sign.

I likewise changed *dotatim*, which appeared in Grialius’ and other editions, to *datatim*, since my first edition, without date, supports it, as do several manuscripts. Plautus likewise has, *Curculio* II.3.18: “Those who play ball by giving it back and forth,” that is, by passing it among themselves. Those who played ball in this fashion were called *pilicrepi*, concerning whom see Seneca, Letter 56, and Lipsius’ note. Manilius’ verses on ball play are elegant, book V, verses 165 ff.

The verses in manuscript copies are generally transcribed corruptly, as will be clear from the various readings. A trace also remains of the verb preserved by Festus, *adnictat*, and it certainly ought not to have been omitted by Isidore. In the Vulgate, in Solomon, one reads “He winks with his eyes,” not “with his eye.”

### CHAPTER XXVII

**No. 5.** *He exults.* As I have already observed in *Isidoriana* and in these notes, and as I shall often observe, it seems to me that Isidore placed on the margin, in abbreviated letters, the names of the authors from whom he took words or statements. Scribes later omitted these names through negligence or ignorance. (See Grialius’ note at the passage.) It should therefore not seem surprising if two contrary statements are sometimes presented, as happens here.

**No. 26.** *The interjection vae.* I have not found in Aulus Gellius either the words or the statement that Grialius attributes to him. In the cited book V, chapter 12, he does not even mention the word *vetus* (“old”), in which *ve* is certainly short, though not in *vecors* (“foolish”). Gellius’ statement in the cited passage and in book XVI, chapter 5, is that the particle *ve* has a twofold and, indeed, opposite meaning: it serves both to increase and to diminish. It increases, as in *vehemens* (“violent”) and *vetus*, which he thinks was named from the great length of age; it diminishes, as in *vaecors* (“foolish”).

**No. 27.** *And likewise Xrisma.* The name of Christ is commonly written in manuscripts as Χρῖς, following the Greek idiom, from which the monogram is formed. Others also wrote *Xps*, because the Latin p resembles the Greek r. When all the letters were written out, the form was pronounced or written *Xristus*. This spelling continued down to the latest times, as may also be observed in many printed books, in which words relating to Christ or Christians are placed by the indexes under the letter x. In Christian alphabetic poems, the name *Xristus* is frequently inserted in place of x, as I observed concerning Sedulius in the alphabetic hymn, verse 81, where I restored *Xristo myron post Sabbatum* in place of *Xeromyrrham post Sabbatum*, which had previously been read contrary to the meter.

**No. 29.** *Place the sicilicus above.* The sicilicus was certainly placed above a vowel which the ancients doubled, as Marini demonstrates from ancient inscriptions in *The Acts of the Arval Brethren*, p. 39: namely, in RÚFA, SURA, MÚSA, etc. Marini suspects that Victorinus confused the sicilicus with the little line still seen in inscriptions as a sign for doubling consonants, as in COMISSVM, etc.

Victorinus, however, speaks of books, not inscriptions: “As is still apparent,” he says, “in many ancient books written in this way.” We should therefore not too readily suspect that he was mistaken. Indeed, in the inscriptions cited by Marini, p. 37, the line placed to double the following consonant is not very unlike the sicilicus, as in VÉTIO for Vettio.

I would rather believe that the sicilicus was formed in two ways: either like an apostrophe, as in MÚSA, etc., or like a grave accent, as in VETIO. But since Victorinus says, “They placed the sicilicus above the letter which ought to be doubled,” and Isidore says, “They placed the sicilicus above …; they did not double the letters, but placed them above the sicilici,” Grialius was wrong to print *sel’a, ser’a, as’eres*. They should be written SEL’A, SER’A, AS’ERES. Thus we understand what Festus says: “It is called *sicilicus* because it cuts a half-ounce.” For it cuts the letter whose doubling it indicates.

In ancient stones one of the two consonants to be doubled is often absent. In appendix 3 to the *Etymologies* I shall present three other short works on orthography. The first is inserted in the *Etymologies* in the Albanian manuscript; the second, bearing Isidore’s name, is found in the old Regio-Vatican manuscript 6018; the third I shall publish from the *Etymologies* manuscript Vat. Arch. 1.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

**No. 1.** Isidore—or at least this chapter of his work—is criticized by Grialius. (See Grialius’ note at the passage.) Why? “Among Quintilian’s works,” he says, “the comparison of like things is a part of analogy, whereas among Isidore’s it is the genus.” But nothing prevents some part of analogy from being called “comparison” by a special name; indeed, Isidore calls one of the eight parts of analogy *comparatio positivorum* (“comparison of positives”). Nevertheless, analogy in general may be called a comparison or proportion of like things.

“More correctly,” says Grialius, “Sergius called it the relation of like things.” But what will he set against Cicero, whom our Isidore followed? Cicero says in *On the Universe*, chapter 4, at the end:

“He best achieves this, which in Greek may be called ἀναλογία (*analogia*) and in Latin—one must dare to use the term, since these names are first being introduced by us—*comparatio* or *proportio*.”

The word *comparatio* seems to have been new in Cicero’s time, at least in the sense of analogy. For that reason he says, “one must dare,” etc., and did not wish to employ the usual word *ratio*.

**No. 2.** *They differ accidentally.* Here I do not think Isidore is rightly criticized by Grialius. Certainly he ought not to be criticized. For even if the resemblance is lacking, it is enough that the hare and the wolf differ accidentally.

**No. 4.** *Pistrinum, pistrilla.* It should be observed that *pistrilla* is more properly derived from *pistrina, pistrinae* than from *pistrinum*.

### CHAPTER XXIX

**No. 4.** *As “silva.”* If we wish to follow the Greek etymology, we ought rather to write *sylva* than *silva*. Some indeed write *sylva*, but most authorities on orthography disagree.

### CHAPTER XXX

**No. 1.** *This the philosophers call “word for word.”* It should be written as two words, *ad verbum* (“word for word”), as among the Greeks. Grialius seems to have preferred *adverbum*, or *ad-verbum*. Isidore’s description of a gloss should be understood in its more proper sense, although in a broader sense a more extensive interpretation might also be called a gloss. In the same way Isidore explains, in book II, chapter 29, no. 6, from Marius Victorinus, the fifth kind of definition, which in Latin we call *ad verbum*. The Isidorian Glossary appears to conform exactly to this definition of a gloss: in it, almost always, the meaning of one word is made clear by one word.

### CHAPTER XXXI

**No. 1.** *There is a difference.* Two books of Isidore belong here: one entitled *Differences of Words*, the other *Differences of Things*. We shall bring them forward after the *Etymologies*.

### CHAPTER XXXII

**No. 8.** *Labdacism.* Saint Julian of Toledo defines labdacism in a similar manner and in nearly the same words in his work *On Grammar*, book I, no. 115. He took much from this book of Saint Isidore.

**No. 9.** *As “mother earth.”* I did not hesitate to restore *mater terra* (“mother earth”) in place of *mater tera*, which Grialius and the other commonly printed editions have. The description of the collision requires two words; *mater terra* is found in my old edition without place or date, and in another Venetian edition of 1483, and several manuscripts support it.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

**No. 2.** *With Cilician garments.* Grialius has *e cilicibus* in his note and *a cilicibus* in the text, as most other editions present it.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

**No. 5.** *Cacephaton, an obscene expression.* Vossius, *Institutions of Oratory*, book IV, chapter 6, §10, denies that the term appears to have been derived from an obscene matter:

“Their minds were roused by these words, especially since Maro was called *Parthenias* because of his virginal modesty.”

Grammarians explain these terms in various places.

### CHAPTER XXXVI

**No. 13.** *Clouds, snow, hail.* I think a conjunction is missing: “Clouds, snow, and hail,” so that the hexameter verse may stand correctly.

**No. 15.** *Or lifting with his hand.* From Virgil I restored *tollentemve manu* (“or lifting with his hand”), which the scribes had changed to *tollentemve manus* (“or lifting his hands”), as it also appears in the printed editions.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

**No. 8.** *Metonymy.* From Charisius.

**No. 9.** *Vulcan sends.* Grialius enclosed the word *mittit* (“sends”) in parentheses, although it occurs in most manuscripts and printed editions, and also in Julian of Toledo, no. 183. The poet perhaps wrote:

“Vulcan sends the mingled ash to the stars.”

The old edition reads:

“Vulcan entrusts the mixed ash to the stars.”

I thought the reading might be:

“When Vulcan sends the mixed ash to the stars.”

**No. 13.** *Synecdoche.* Grialius printed *synedoche* more than once. I restored *synecdoche*. Usage and the etymological derivation from the Greek words require this. In Julian, synecdoche is “a signification capable of complete understanding,” etc.

**No. 20.** *Synchysis.* Some manuscripts and printed editions have *synthesis*; Grialius, with others, has *synchesis*, as it is also read in Servius in the edition of Pierre Daniel. I restored *synchysis*. See Alciatus, book X of *Legal Miscellanies*, chapter 11, and Gerhard Johannes Vossius, book IV of *Institutions of Oratory*, chapter 1, §14.

**No. 28.** *Paroemia.* *Paroemia*—“kicks against the goad”—means resisting a contrary thing, as Charisius says; accordingly, perhaps *adversis resisti* (“to resist adversities”) should be read in Isidore.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

**No. 6.** *And calls them long.* Gellius, book XVIII, chapter 15: “In long verses, which are called hexameters.” Turnebus, in Cicero’s *On the Laws*, book II, near the end, observes that Isidore took from Cicero—“not an altogether bad authority,” as he says—the statement that Ennius called hexameters “long.” Giraldus places Livius Andronicus earlier than Ennius, but adds that writers disagree about his period and the number of years involved. Some hexameter verses occur among the fragments of Livius; therefore he must be said to have composed hexameters before Ennius. Compare Aulus Gellius, book XVII, chapter 21.

**No. 9.** *For heroes are [called] aerial.* In Isidore’s age, *aeros* seems to have been the customary spelling for *heros* (“hero”), for the alphabetical vocabulary of nouns begins: “*Aeros*, a brave and wise man.” This corresponds to the words of this paragraph: “Heroes are called men, as if aerial,” and similar passages in book VIII, chapter 11, no. 96. The spelling cannot properly be defended, but the etymology is not altogether absurd. Some think that *heroes* were named from ἀήρ (*aēr*, “air”), because they have no taste for earthly things but tower above them like the air. See Becman, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, p. 525.

**No. 16.** *And Diana’s rustic chorus.* Grialius seems, by conjecture, to have preferred *Agrestis Dianae* (“of rustic Diana”), or the dative *Agresti Dianae* (“to rustic Diana”).

**No. 17.** *The prophet David … Mnemia.* In printed editions and manuscripts I find *propheta* (“prophet”), but *prophetam* (“the prophet”) should be read, as in book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 6: “It is clear that he, the same prophet, first composed and sang hymns, and afterward other prophets [did so].”

The manuscripts disagree among themselves concerning the nymph Mnemia and Timotho; no certain reading can be extracted. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 97, no. 19, from Vatican manuscript 4498, I mentioned a certain nymph Idvomea Marica, who was the mother of Rhythmus, from whom rhythm is believed to have been named. I suspected that this might be Cymothoe, or Timothoe, concerning whom Isidore says:

There may also be some conjecture concerning Phemonoe, about whom Fortunatianus reports in his *Art*, in the chapter on the dactylic meter:

“This [the dactylic meter] Ennius calls long; the Greeks call it Deliac, because Phemonoe, the prophetess of Apollo, prophesied in this meter.”

Gottfried Olearius published at Leipzig in 1708 a dissertation *On Greek Poetesses*, which I have not yet seen.

**No. 19.** *And likewise now.* Nevertheless, this had been prohibited by the Third Council of Toledo, held in 589, canon 22:

“The bodies of all the religious who depart this life through the divine calling are to be carried to their graves only with the voices of those singing psalms. For we altogether prohibit the funeral song which is customarily sung for the dead, or the beating of breasts by those who are near them or belong to their families … If a bishop can prohibit this among all Christians [another reading: ‘prohibit all Christians from doing this’], let him not delay to do so. We decree, however, that among religious persons it must by no means be done otherwise.”

Perhaps the bishops could not secure the cessation of such funeral songs at the funerals of all Christians. Those who interpret “the bodies of all the religious” as meaning “the bodies of all the faithful” are clearly mistaken, as is shown by the following words, which distinguish between religious persons and Christians. The meaning therefore seems to be this: if a bishop can prohibit a funeral song at the funeral of any member of the faithful, let him not delay to do so; but it is decreed that funeral songs must be altogether prohibited at the funerals of religious persons.

**No. 25.** *Centos.* Tertullian’s passage is in chapter 39. Grialius had printed *facilitatis* (“of facility”); today, from Virgil, the reading is *fabula in totum* (“a story in its entirety”). I restored the words as they now appear in corrected editions. Others also print *plenissime exsuxit* (“he sucked out most completely”), and shortly afterward: “They are also commonly called Homeric centos,” etc.

**No. 26.** *Proba, the wife of Adelphus.* I discussed Proba’s cento in appendix 5 to Sedulius, no. 52, concerning the Decree of Gelasius, where a cento on Christ, composed from Virgilian verses, is listed among the apocryphal books. I explained the laws of the cento in the same work, appendix 1, note 88.

### CHAPTER XLI

**No. 1.** *History, from ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱστορεῖν (“from investigating”).* Gellius, book V, chapter 18:

“Some think that history differs from annals in this respect: although both are narratives of things done, history properly concerns those things in which the person narrating participated; and Verrius Flaccus reports this to have been the opinion of certain people in the fourth book of *On the Meaning of Words*. He says that he himself is uncertain about the matter, but thinks that there may be some reason in this opinion, because in Greek *historia* signifies knowledge of present things.”

**No. 2.** *A sequence … from garlands of flowers.* Others derive *series* (“sequence”) from *sero* (“I join”), just as *congeries* (“heap”) comes from *congero* (“I heap together”). Thus *series*, as Becman observes, p. 965 of *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, properly pertains to gardeners and farmers, who sow; from there it is transferred to other things that proceed in a fixed order.

### CHAPTER LXIV

**No. 3.** *Things were recorded in commentaries.* I do not know whether Grialius understood Isidore’s meaning. Isidore does not say that commentaries were composed from official records; rather, he teaches that annals were so called from annual deeds, because whatever deeds were worthy of remembrance were written down year by year in commentaries. Nor is it unusual to speak of “commentaries of deeds” or of “deeds in commentaries.”

**No. 4.** *But between history and annals.* Gellius, in the passage cited, reports, on the authority of many, that all annals are history, but not all history is annals. For history is either an exposition or a demonstration of things done; annals are history in which the order of each year is preserved.

The following distinctive passage, which Gellius attributes to Sempronius Asellio in this genre, is also relevant:

“But there was this difference between those who wished to leave annals and those who attempted to set forth the deeds of the Romans. Annalistic books merely demonstrated what had been done in each year—that is, they did what those who write a diary do, which the Greeks call an *ephemeris* (a daily record). I believe that it is not enough for us merely to state what was done; we must also demonstrate with what intention and by what reasoning it was done.”

See also Cicero, *On Oratory*, chapter 20.

**No. 5.** *Between history, argument, and fiction.* Servius, commenting on *Aeneid* I.239, “recalled from Teucer’s blood,” in the Leiden edition of 1680, says:

“And it must be understood that the difference between a fable and an argument—that is, history—is this: a fable is an account contrary to nature, whether the events happened or did not happen, as in the story of Pasiphae. History is an argument in which whatever is said is according to nature, whether it happened or did not happen, as in the story of Phaedra.”

Perhaps the reading should be: “History and argument are whatever is said according to nature,” etc.

In manuscript codices this is also the end of book I, with the heading *Explicit*, or “The first book ends.” In some, however, the final four chapters are presented under a separate title, with the heading *On History*. In the oldest Toledan manuscripts, these four paragraphs are listed under that title:

1. On the word “history.”
2. On the first authors of histories.
3. On the usefulness of history.
4. On the kinds of history.

But the chapter headings are not inserted, as they are in the printed editions.

## BOOK II

### CHAPTER II

**No. 2.** *For with the parchments retained as before.* Ildefonsus seems to have imitated this passage of Isidore when praising Isidore’s eloquence, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 5, no. 9.

### CHAPTER VII

**No. 2.** *Benivolum.* The established spelling *benevolus*, like *beneficium*, *benedico*, etc., may be retained, as Cellarius and others demonstrate. Compare the note to book X, under the word *Benevolus*.

### CHAPTER IX

**No. 3.** *Although the Apostle.* I think *licet Apostolus* (“although the Apostle”) is Isidore’s own wording. He means that the Apostle too sometimes used the arts of dialectic and rhetoric, a point he supports with Jerome’s words. Many manuscripts have *syllogismos … utuntur* (“they use syllogisms …”).

**No. 14.** *From the assumption alone.* In most codices only this is read: “From the assumption alone, as in the statement, ‘if he is an enemy,’” etc.

**No. 15.** *From the conclusion alone.* Vossius, *Institutions of Oratory*, book III, chapter 5, §5, observes that this was taken from Victorinus and adds that orators argue in this way when the conclusion has preceded.

**No. 16.** *Then follows the epicheireme … a broader and more fully worked-out rhetorical syllogism.* Vossius, in the same place, §4, wishes *epicherema* to be written. He explains the expansion of the discourse by saying that the orator adds proof of the major and minor premises. In many Gothic manuscripts one reads: “broader and more fully worked out than rhetorical syllogisms.”

### CHAPTER X

**No. 2.** *Reason commends it.* This passage is praised by Atto, Letter 1, vol. II, p. 298: “Since blessed Isidore says, ‘Custom is law,’” etc. There *per legem* (“through the law”) should be corrected to *pro lege* (“in place of law”).

### CHAPTER XVI

**No. 2.** *Unless he says what he says, and says it gracefully.* Vatican Archival manuscript 1 reads *nisi id quod dicat et facere* (“unless he says what he should say and to do”), which may be preferable. For Isidore had prefaced this, chapter 3, no. 1:

“An orator, therefore, is a good man skilled in speaking. The good man consists in nature, morals, and the arts.”

Vatican Archival manuscript 1 agrees with Toledan manuscript 2. One may also read: “unless he does what is fitting,” so that the meaning remains the same.

### CHAPTER XVIII

**No. 2.** *And thus … a period is formed.* The matters I discussed concerning punctuation, or the method of inserting stops, in book I, chapter 20, belong here. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book II, chapter 17, understands a period to be those lines by which works were formerly divided, as sacred Scripture still is.

### CHAPTER XX

**No. 4.** *It suggests height.* Our manuscripts read *altitudinem imaginis* (“the height of the image”), and V, A, and I, with other words omitted, have: “Lowered, fallen by a rope, [it] suggests an image.” Perhaps the reading should be: “It suggests an image of height.”

### CHAPTER XXI

**No. 3.** *As in that passage of Africanus.* Africanus may perhaps be that Africanus, an eloquent man and constant advocate of cases, who was killed by Valens. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions him in these words in book XXIX, chapter 3. Another Africanus was a jurist.

**No. 4.** *Youth, a disgrace to old age.* The word *dedecoramentum* (“disgrace”) is omitted from Forcellini’s Latin Lexicon, where *inhonestamentum* is nevertheless restored, with this passage of Gracchus cited. *Dehonestamentum* is more common than *inhonestamentum*; see Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon*, appended to the *Lives of the Fathers*.

**No. 5.** *Compelled by force and against his will.* I do not agree with Grialius, who asserts that *coactus* (“compelled”) is an explanatory gloss. The Latin expression *vi coactus* (“compelled by force”) is correct, as is *necessitate coactus* (“compelled by necessity”), and Nepos, *Themistocles*, chapter 4, says: “So that all were compelled against their will to fight it out.” Why, then, should *vi atque ingratiis coactus* be rejected?

**No. 6.** *Finally, from this … with iniquity, luxury, and sloth.* In the printed editions of Cicero, *hinc* (“from this”) is absent before *denique* (“finally”); and shortly afterward *cum* (“with”) is added—namely, “with luxury, with sloth.”

### N. 7. “Two and two”

Our Vulgate reads: “Good is against evil, and life against death; so also the sinner against the righteous man. And so look upon all the works of the Most High. Two and two, one against one.”

### N. 27. “Of one who weeps … of one who admonishes”

Examples are lacking for *flentis* (“of one weeping”), *admonentis* (“of one admonishing”), etc.; but in some manuscripts *ut* is added—namely, *flentis ut*, *admonentis ut*, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXII

### No. 1. “Which is called logic”

Gerardus Johannes Vossius, *On the Nature of the Arts*, book III, chapter 4, says that the ancients learned mathematics even before logic; later, some departed from this order, as is clear from these books of Isidore. Barbarian writers followed them in the *trivium* and *quadrivium*. Vossius does not approve this. Plausible arguments can be offered on both sides; and Cassiodore preceded Isidore in this matter.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### No. 2. “And immovable”

Others read less suitably in Lactantius *et mobile* (“and movable”), or *et immortale* (“and immortal”), instead of *et immobile* (“and immovable”). On this subject see Copernicus, Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, and others, cited in the note on Lactantius, edited by Jean-Baptiste Le Brun and Nicolas Lenglet.

### No. 4. “Having contemplated the reason”

The passive use of *contemplatus*, meaning “examined” or “considered,” was also employed more than once by Ammianus Marcellinus; therefore the manuscript reading *contemplata ratione* (“with the reason contemplated”) should not be disturbed.

### No. 8. “For which our manuscripts have *theoretical*”

Isidore explains the disciplines of the three kinds in the same way in the prefaces to the title *On the Books of Solomon*. Compare the note on that passage. Instead of *theoricam* (“theoretical”), some manuscripts have *theologiam* (“theology”).

### No. 15. “Astronomy is a discipline, etc.”

This description is repeated in book III, chapter 24. It is taken from Cassiodore, *On Astronomy*, from which one might read: “It follows the courses of the heavenly stars and contemplates their figures.”

## CHAPTER XXV

### No. 9. “Boethius published”

*Boetius* and *Boethius* are commonly written. V. C. Marini, in *Acta Arvalia*, p. 395, showed that the true spelling is *Boethus*, as it is read in the most ancient inscriptions. Yet, as he himself admits, by the fifth and sixth centuries *Boetius* and *Boethius* were already being written.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### No. 3

The annotations on Cassian, which Grialius praises (see Grialius, there, in the note), are by Pedro Chacón, from whom Grialius received a great many notes for his edition of Isidore.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### No. 3. “Who concludes”

In manuscripts, *cl* and *cd* are frequently confused, as in *Eradius* for *Eraclius*. Hence I suspected that here and in the following passages one should read *concludit* (“concludes”), a word proper to the syllogistic art and used by Cassiodore and others from whom Isidore learned.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### No. 6. “Which the Greeks call *kat’ antilexin*”

This is how the term is explained in the glossary, book I, chapter 30, no. 1.

### No. 12. “So that it is *assis*”

*Assis* in the nominative case, used for *as*, is also found in the old scholiast on Persius, satire 2, verse 59, and in Donatus on Terence’s *Phormio* I.1.9.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### No. 1. “Which, according to Cicero, is called contrary”

The work of Saint Julian of Toledo, entitled *Antikeimena*, is well known. It deals with passages of Sacred Scripture that appear to be contradictory and brings them harmoniously into agreement through an appropriate explanation of each.

### No. 6. “Not to call an infant toothless”

Isidore says that an infant whose tender age has not yet given it teeth should not be called *edentulus* (“toothless”) or “without teeth,” as though deprived of teeth, since it has never possessed them.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I

### No. 1. “For the Greeks”

In Grialius’s edition there is a note-mark before the words “for the Greeks,” but nothing is supplied in the note itself; perhaps the annotation fell out during printing. I think the note was intended to warn us that this material was taken from Boethius or someone else. Boethius proves at length, *On Arithmetic*, book I, chapter 3, that arithmetic is prior to the other mathematical disciplines.

## CHAPTER II

### No. 1. “The discipline of number”

Vossius, *On the Nature of the Arts*, chapter 10, observes that Cassiodore erred in *On the Mathematical Disciplines*, in the chapter on arithmetic—which Isidore copies here—when he says that the first of the Latins to write on arithmetic was Lucius Appuleius, or Apuleius, of Madaura; for Terentius Varro preceded him.

## CHAPTER III

### No. 1. “Not *numerus*”

Most people think that *numerus* (“number”) is derived not from *numus* (“coin”) but from Greek *nomē* (νομή), meaning “distribution.”

### No. 2. “Four from the square figure”

Others think that *quatuor* (“four”) derives from Greek *katera*, for *kai hetera* (“and another”), because the Aeolians said *tria* (“three”) and, for “four,” *kai hetera* (“and another”).

### No. 3. “But *octo* by translation”

*Octo* (“eight”) is so called by translation because the same letters in Greek spell ὀκτώ.

### No. 4. “Moreover, *viginti* … because they are twice-born tens”

From Isidore, Papias gives: “*Viginti*, as if *decem bis geniti* (‘twice-born tens’).” Becmann does not reject this, p. 1139; but he adds that *ginti* or *ginta* has the flavor of the Greek *konta*, which in compounds denotes the number ten, as in *triginta*, Greek *triakonta*, and so on.

### No. 5. “But *centum* from *canthus*”

Others think that *centum* (“one hundred”) is derived from the Greek ἑκατόν. Some explain the etymology of *mille* (“thousand”) in this way: *mille* derives from the Greek χίλιοι or χιλιάς, or from the Hebrew [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], meaning “fullness” or “multitude.” *Miles* (“soldier”) was formed from *mille*. Isidore returns to these matters in book IX, chapter 3. Most prefer the spelling *mille* with a double *l*, but *milia* with only one.

## CHAPTER IV

### No. 1. “The nature of number”

Moved by this consideration, Isidore wrote a book on numbers, or their mysteries; I discussed it in chapter 63 of my *Isidoriana*.

### No. 3. “Known to those skilled in this art”

Isidore uses *cognitum* with a similar meaning in his letter to Braulio: “Because I am unable, etc., I asked you to send me the sixth decade of Saint Augustine; I ask you somehow to make me known to him.” Perhaps this means “make it known to him,” namely, the *decade*. I discuss this again in the note on that letter.

## CHAPTER V

### No. 8. “Nine measures three times three”
