Perhaps one should read: “Nine measure three times three.” The meaning is this: the number three, multiplied three times, is the measure of the ninth number, and the number three, multiplied five times, is the measure of the fifteenth number.

## CHAPTER VI

### No. 1. “Others unequal. This one”

In Grialius it read: “unequal. This one is divided thus.” Other printed editions differ greatly. “Unequal. That one is divided” would seem better, and so forth.

### No. 14

The various readings of this chapter, differing greatly among themselves, can be read separately in the several editions.

## CHAPTER VII

### No. 2

In the manuscripts and old editions, diagrams of the numbers are reproduced. They must not be passed over, even though Grialius omitted them. See chapter 13, no. 2, and the copperplate with numerical and geometrical figures to be appended to chapter 12.

## CHAPTER VIII

### No. 2. “According to the geometrical [mean]”

Perhaps Isidore indicates that the two means of geometry are to be found in such a way that one is taken from arithmetic and the other from music, as he explains more clearly in chapter 23. They are proved to be means when, after multiplication, they produce the same result as the multiplication of the extremes themselves.

## CHAPTER IX

### No. 2

In Codex Ottobonianus 6 I find a fragment with this title: “Likewise, on Isidore’s number.” It can in some way be referred to this passage and will be placed in Appendix 4; strictly speaking, however, it belongs more to grammar than to arithmetic.

## CHAPTER X

### No. 1

Cassiodore, whom Isidore otherwise usually follows, discussed music first and then geometry.

## CHAPTER XII

### No. 2

In the editio princeps, which gives neither place nor year, and in the oldest parchment manuscripts, geometrical figures are printed. From the following chapter, no. 2, it is argued that they ought to be restored according to Isidore’s intention.

### No. 4. “Cylinder”

I present the figure of the cylinder, together with other numerical, geometrical, and musical figures engraved on copper, from the oldest manuscript codices. Fuller explanations of the figures will be given among the appendices.

## CHAPTER XIII

### “In the figures above”

Grialius, who omitted the figures of the preceding chapter, does not seem to have paid attention to these words.

## CHAPTER XV

### No. 1. ἀπὸ τοῦ μῶσθαι

Gerbertus included these chapters of Isidore in his collection of ancient writers on music, as I observed in chapter 55, no. 35, of my *Isidoriana*. Before Grialius, Vulcanius had already printed *mōsthai* (μῶσθαι). In his manuscript Gerbertus had *apo tou muson*; but in Cassiodore, *On the Arts*, chapter 5, he read ἀπὸ τοὺ μασενεῖν, which is unusual, from *maō* (μάω). The matter comes to the same thing.

## CHAPTER XVI

### No. 3. “And laments were sung to the pipes”

Juvencus, at the cited passage in Matthew, mentions not pipes but trumpets; similarly, the old Vercelli version has not *tibicines* (“pipe-players”) but *tubicines* (“trumpeters”). Sedulius retained the reading of our Vulgate. See the note on Juvencus, book II, verse 400, and on Sedulius, book III, verse 134.

For *conviviale* (“festive” or “banqueting”) *convivale* would be better, as Gerbertus has it; but since *convivialis* is also read in Macrobius, the doubtful reading *conviviale* may be retained. Quintilian, or Quinctilian, who wrote on music and is cited by Grialius, is Quintilianus Aristides, whose work appears among other works on the same subject edited by Meibomius.

## CHAPTER XVII

### No. 3

“Whatever we say, etc.” is from Cassiodore, at the cited passage, no. 2. In his manuscript Gerbertus seems to have found *venarum impulsu* (“by the impulse of the veins”) instead of *venarum impulsibus* (“by the impulses of the veins”).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### No. 2

Fabricius, in his usual thorough manner, gives a full catalogue in his *Bibliography*, chapter 4, no. 15 and following, of authors who wrote on music and its parts, as well as of those who published separate treatises on many musical instruments. I wished to note this here so that it may also be kept in view in the following chapters, especially since musical instruments will be discussed. To the more recent writers one may add Martini, Eximeno, and others.

## CHAPTER XX

### No. 2. “The voice of the trumpet thundered”

Perhaps: “The voice of the trumpet, as it thundered.” The following words are Virgil’s, *Aeneid* III, verse 556, and are cited as another example of an improperly used word.

### No. 3. “Symphony is a tuning of melody, etc.”

Cassiodore says nearly the same in his *On Music*. I reproduce the musical figure from an old Codex Toletanus.

### No. 13. “Vinnola”

Many approve Isidore’s etymology of *vinnula*. From *villus*, which is a kind of tuft of hair, comes *vinnus*; or, as others think, *villus* comes from *vinnus*. Nor are there lacking those who derive *vinnulus* not from *vinnus* but from *vinum* (“wine”). It is written *vinnolus*, *vinnulus*, or *vinulus*.

## CHAPTER XXI

### No. 1

Many people have written works on musical instruments, both in general and individually, and, as I said, they have been catalogued by Fabricius. Among them is Bonanni, whose later edition bears this title: *Description of Harmonic Instruments of Every Kind, Second Edition, Revised, Corrected, and Enlarged by the Abbé Giacinto Ceruti, Adorned with 140 Engravings Engraved by Arnold van Westerhout*. Rome, 1776, quarto.

### No. 2. “The word *organum* is general”

I made several observations on the organ in my note on Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 148.

### No. 4. “Hence also the pipe-player”

There were pipe-players at sacred ceremonies, mentioned in ancient inscriptions preserved by Reinesius, Gruter, and others. Johann Zacharias Hilliger published a dissertation on pipe-players employed at funerals. Wittenberg, 1717. I also made some observations on this subject in my notes on Juvencus, book II, verse 400, and Sedulius, book III, verse 134. Compare also Vulpes’s note on Catullus, poem 62, where he discusses the material of pipes.

### No. 5. “*Calamus* is properly a tree”

Isidore—or whoever authored the etymology—perhaps intended *calamus* (“reed”) to be derived from *clamando* (“crying out”). But *calamus* is also said in Greek in precisely this form: κάλαμος.

### No. 6. “But *fistula* is so called”

Others think that the name *fistula* was coined from its sound, or was derived from the Greek φυσάω, “I blow.”

### No. 7. “Sambuca”

Festus and others say that the *sambuca* was a type of organ. It seems to have been the very instrument that we call a harp. For this reason Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 81, wonders why Isidore introduces a discussion of pipes here. I think Isidore shifted from the musical instrument *sambuca* to the elder tree *sambucus*, as though he were saying: “The elder is a kind of fragile wood,” and so forth. In any case, many think that *sambuca* is a Syrian name and that the instrument was invented by the Syrians.

### No. 8. “Pandura”

Lampridius, *Life of Heliogabalus*, chapter 32: “He played on the pipes, blew the trumpet, played the *pandura*, and performed on the organ.” Casaubon, in his note on Lampridius, p. 112, line 34, says: “*Pandura*, as if *pandouris* (πανδουρίς), which Isidore also suggests.” Some report that it was a three-stringed instrument; others, that it consisted of several pipes joined with wax, which agrees with Isidore. For Spaniards, *pandero* is a type of drum; the name perhaps passed from one musical instrument to another. Here, however, Isidore is speaking of organ instruments, not rhythmic instruments. The same may be supposed of the *bandurria*, which for Spaniards is a rhythmic instrument and which some derive from *pandura*: this can be understood only if, over time, the word migrated from an organ instrument to a rhythmic one. Bottarius, *Subterranean Rome*, volume II, p. 44, argues against Isidore and others that the *pandura* was a three-stringed lyre; thus the word can more readily be connected with the *bandurria*.

## CHAPTER XXII

### No. 3. “As the barbarian [calls it] a psaltery”

Pollux, book IV, chapter 9: “The tortoise-shell lyre, the psaltery, the *trigon*, the *sambycae*, the *pyctides*—or *pektides* (πηκτίδες)—the *phorminges*, the *phoenix*, the *spadix*, etc.” Pollux enumerates these and other instruments that are played by striking or plucking. Stephanus, in his lexicon, has *pektis* (πηκτίς), with further information about this instrument.

For *indicae*, Delrius preferred *scindapsi*; Jungermannus, in his note on Pollux, preferred *jambycae*; Salmasius thought that *indicae* should be retained, in accordance with the oldest manuscripts, either because the instruments may have come from India or because Indians used them extensively. Pollux, in the cited passage, does indeed list *jambyce*, *scindapsus*, and so on.

### No. 6. “But strings are so called from *chorda*”

The true origin of *chorda* (“string”) is the Greek χορδή, meaning “intestine.”

### No. 7. “Above he has, etc.”

The same account is given by Eusebius in his preface to the Psalms, Basil in his commentary on Psalm 1, Ambrose in his preface to Psalm 1, and Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 56.

### No. 8. “The lyre is so called, ἀπὸ τοῦ λυρεῖν”

Becmann thinks that *lyra* (“lyre”) was so called from the somewhat harsh thinness of its sound, *lir, lir*, and says that Isidore indicates this here. Certainly *lyreîn* (λυρεῖν) means nothing other than “to play the lyre,” unless it expresses the sound *lyr, lyr*; and one may conjecture that Isidore wrote that it came from *lir* or from *lyr*. Isidore returns to the lyre in book VIII, chapter 7, no. 4. Blanchinus, *On the Music of the Ancients*, and Bottarius, *Subterranean Rome*, volume II, pp. 42 and following, catalogue various kinds of lyres.

### No. 11. “Cymbals and *acitabula*”

In the text Grialius printed: “Cymbals, *acitabula*, are certain things”; but in the note he retains the reading of other printed editions: “Cymbals and *acitabula* are certain things.” I prefer the reading of the text, and substitute *acetabula* for *acitabula*, changing *i* to *e*, as frequently happens in manuscripts.

Strictly speaking, an *acetabulum* is a vessel for vinegar, and by catachresis the word is used of any vessel. Its shape is round; without any breadth at the rim, it gradually narrows on every side, like a cup, down to the bottom. The characteristic sound of drums was called a “bellowing,” in contrast with the ringing and rattling of cymbals; Seneca noted this distinction, *Natural Questions* II.27.

For *ballematia*, see Du Cange under *balare*, a word that Saint Augustine also used for “to dance.” Salmasius, in his note on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 211, line 6, says that Isidore, as usual, is mistaken because *ballematia* are dances and *ballematica* are cymbals—not because they are called that from being struck, but because people dance to their sound.

Yet critics often declare that Isidore is mistaken because they twist his words into a different meaning. Isidore asserts that cymbals are so called not because they are struck, but because they are struck together with *ballematia*, that is, while dancing. Nor could Isidore have been ignorant of what *ballematia* or *ballematium* means, since the title of canon 23 of the Third Council of Toledo is: “That *ballematia* and shameful songs are to be prohibited from the solemn celebrations of the saints.” Others write *balemanthiae* or *ballimanthiae*. Whether the etymology of *cymbalum* derives from *ballematia* is another question, and hardly worth deciding.

### No. 12. “The *sistrum* was named after its female inventor”

Others think that *sistrum* derives from σείειν, “to shake,” but many retain Isidore’s etymology. Hieronymus Bossius, *On the Sistrum*, says that Isidore must be refuted because he said that women strike the sistrum—as though, he adds, women rather than human beings played it.

But Isidore does not deny that men play the sistrum; he merely suggests that it is more particularly a woman’s instrument than another. Apart from the Amazons, Virgil writes of Cleopatra, *Aeneid* VIII.696: “She summons her troops with the ancestral sistrum”; and Lucan, *Pharsalia* X.63:

> “She terrified, if such a thing may be said, the Capitol with her sistrum.”

### No. 14. “Symphony”

Isidore described the *symphonia* in chapter 20, no. 13, in opposition to *diaphonia*. As a distinctive instrument, he asserts that it is a drum with a full body; for shortly before, no. 10, he said that the drum is the middle part of the *symphonia*, in the likeness of a sieve. Papias agrees.

Saint Jerome, in the passage cited by Grialius, not only denies that the *symphonia* is a kind of organ but also seems to affirm that *symphonia* means nothing other than consonance, which is the meaning of the Greek word.

The very learned Mazochius, in *Biblical Spicilegium*, volume I, part II, dissertation “On the Origin of Musical Instruments,” shows that *symphonia* in Daniel is not understood as consonance but as a certain kind of musical instrument. He does not agree with those who say that the *symphonia* is a lyre. He explains Isidore’s view and concedes that Isidore’s *symphonia*, as it was commonly called in his age, may be called a kind of drum.

But he endeavors, by many examples from the ancients, to establish that *symphonia* can mean a trumpet and, more frequently, a pipe or flute. He adds that *symphonia*, when it denotes a particular musical instrument, is Chaldean in origin—namely *siphonia*—which was rendered by interpreters in the Greek manner as *symphonia*.

He concludes that among the Latins *symphonia* sometimes does not signify a particular instrument but any leading instrument by which rhythm was directed, and perhaps at times a drum, trumpet, or lyre; but most often it means a curved pipe or flute.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### No. 2

In Appendix 5, after the *Etymologies*, I shall present an excerpt on *rhythmomachia* found appended to these chapters of Isidore on music in a manuscript Codex Vindobonensis, edited by Gerbertus, as I mentioned in *Isidoriana*, chapter 55, no. 35.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### No. 1

Compare the note on the cited passage, book II, chapter 24, no. 15.

## CHAPTER XXV

### No. 1. “Astronomy”

Vossius, Riccioli, and other writers on astronomy are catalogued by Morhof, *Polyhistor*, volume II, book IV, chapter 1, no. 8. Concerning Riccioli, Morhof makes the following observation:

> “As for learning, Giovanni Battista Riccioli deserves praise above all others in the *New Almagest*, in which, like a kind of *Pandects*, he embraced the whole of astronomical learning up to his own time; he alone can serve as a library. For he reviews and evaluates everything, both ancient and modern. There one may see everything concerning the various systems of the world, collected according to the opinions of different authors.”

So Morhof. But nowadays later writers prefer whatever is more recent.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### No. 1. “But astrology”

Superstitious astrology, called genethliacal and judicial astrology, has rightly been condemned, although some utterly foolish people dare not only to follow it but also to defend it.

## CHAPTER XXVIII AND FOLLOWING

Pliny, book II, chapter 4: “What the Greeks called *kosmos* (κόσμος), using the word for ornament, we call *mundus*, from perfect and complete elegance.”

Becmann calls Isidore’s etymology novel: “Rather, old,” he adds, “from Varro.” Hence animals also seem to Varro to be elements, since they move by themselves. Festus too agrees with the same etymology. Varro also accepts the earlier derivation from cleanliness, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 29, where he speaks of women’s adornment, which, he says, is called *mundus* from *munditia* (“cleanliness”).

## CHAPTER XXX

### No. 1. “Toward the northern region”

Lucan called the northern part the lowest, as will be clear in chapter 41, and again in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 9, where Isidore explains *imus* as “last” and “extreme,” not “depressed,” whereas the world is rather said to rise toward the northern region. *Imus* is often taken to mean “extreme” and “last” by Horace, Ovid, Martial, and others. Since the passages are readily available in the lexicons, I omit them.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### No. 1. “Heaven, etc.”

See also Phurnutus, chapter 1 of his commentary *On the Nature of the Gods*.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### No. 1. “They say”

The word *dicunt* (“they say”), or some similar word, is often missing in manuscripts. This suggests that Isidore sometimes indicated the names of authors whose opinions he was reporting by means of abbreviated letters. As I pointed out long ago, it was easy for such sigla, once no longer understood by scribes, to drop out; hence we frequently find an infinitive without the verb governing it. Printed editions supply *dicunt*, *constat*, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### No. 2. “From polishing”

The true etymology is from Greek πολέω, “I turn”; hence Greek πόλος and Latin *polus* (“pole”).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### No. 1. “And they are called pivots”

Becmann, under *cor* (“heart”), reports from Servius, Isidore, and others that *cardo* (“pivot,” “hinge”) is said in Latin from Greek καρδία (“heart”), either because of its shape like a heart or because it is, as Servius says, like the heart of a door by which it moves.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### No. 1. “Convex”

Strictly speaking, the outer part of a circle is called convex and the inner part concave. Poets use *convexa* substantivally for the vault of heaven; Claudianus also uses *convexa* simply for “the heavens” more than once.

## CHAPTER XLII

### No. 3. “Midday … because it is the middle of the day”

Varro, Cicero, and others support the etymology of *meridies* (“midday”) from *medius dies* (“middle of the day”). Others, however, do not reject the derivation of *meridies* from *merus*, meaning “full” and “pure,” because at that time no further addition to the daylight occurs. See Joachim Camerarius, *Etymological Problems*, decade 1, and below, book V, chapter 28, no. 15.

### No. 4. “The third, Catachoras”

Cassiodore, from whom nearly all the words of this section come, has the following: “The first is Merobis”—in the manuscripts, *Meroe*—“the second Syene, the third Catuchoras, that is, Africa, the fourth Rhodes,” and so forth. In the best editions of Cassiodore, the passage appears in this form, without any variation in spelling.

In the Gothic manuscripts of the Toletan codices, one finds *Merohis* for *Meroe* or *Merobis*, as it is read in Cassiodore; *Soinis* or *Soynis* for *Syene* or *Siene*, as Grialius printed it; and *Brastenus* for *Boristhenes*. Other codices also give *Brastenus* or *Brustenus* for *Boristhenes*, and similarly vary or go astray in writing these names. Their variation may nevertheless perhaps assist in discovering the true reading.

## CHAPTER XLIII

### No. 1. “The hemisphere, etc.”

From Cassiodore.

## CHAPTER XLIV

### No. 4. “The fifth circle”

Much the same material concerning these five circles occurs in book XIII, chapter 6, and in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 10.

## CHAPTER XLVI

### No. 1. “The Milky Circle”

Concerning the Milky Circle, which Cicero calls the *orbis lacteus* (“milky orb”), one may consult Macrobius, book I of his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 15. He also discusses the zodiac, in which he recognizes three lines, and the other celestial circles.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### No. 1. “The earth is stronger”

Cassiodore similarly says: “The sun is stronger than the earth; the earth is stronger than the moon by a certain quantity.” The claim that the sun, at the very moment when it rises, appears equally to the east and to the west requires explanation. Astronomers infer that the earth is smaller than the sun because the earth’s shadow ends in a point; for, except for the moon, the other planets are not darkened by the earth’s shadow. Isidore reports this same matter at greater length from Ambrose in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 16.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### No. 1. “Whose fire, they say, is nourished by water”

I discussed this ancient opinion—that there is a fire in heaven nourished by water—in my notes on Dracontius, book I, verses 24 and 25.

## CHAPTER L

### No. 1. “The sun by itself”

Hyginus, *Astronomical Poetry*, book IV, chapter 13, uses nearly the same words: “Since we see that the days are unequal, and that the sun will set today in one place and set yesterday in another.” Isidore copied the same passage in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 17, from Aratus and Hyginus.

## CHAPTER LI

### No. 2, note. “The remainder … is absent from the manuscripts”

Grialius says that the words “For which reason …,” through the end of the chapter, are absent from the manuscripts. But in fact they exist in many old parchments, in the Albanian Codex, in Codex Vaticanus Arch. 1, and in others.

Although the same words are read in *On the Nature of Things*, this does not prove that they were brought here by someone other than Isidore. Many things said in this book on astronomy are repeated in book XIII and in *On the Nature of Things*. It was Isidore’s practice to collect and repeat much material both from his own works and from those of others.

## CHAPTER LIV

### No. 1. “The seventh, two-horned”

In the oldest manuscripts and in some editions one reads *bicornis est* (“is two-horned”); a figure of the two-horned moon is also added, and the same is done in what follows.

## CHAPTER LIX

### No. 2. “The shadow of the obstructing earth”

Saint Martin of León, volume III, p. 98, in his sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, presents chapters 55 and following through this chapter 59. Some passages there can be corrected from Isidore; nevertheless, Martin’s variant reading is not to be despised: “May he emerge from the shadow of the intervening earth, see the sun, and be seen by the sun.”

## CHAPTER LX

### No. 1. “Stars and heavenly bodies”

Macrobius, book I of his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 14, distinguishes between *stellae* (“stars”) and *sidera* (“constellations” or “heavenly bodies”), as Isidore does. He adds: “Thus also among the Greeks *astēr* (ἀστήρ) and *astron* (ἄστρον) have different meanings. For *aster* is one star, and *astron* is a sign formed from a group of stars, which we call *sidus*.”

## CHAPTER LXI

### No. 1. “The stars do not possess their own light”

Most people assert that the stars called fixed shine with their own light. The matter is different with the planets, such as the moon. Isidore maintains the same position in chapter 24 of *On the Nature of Things*. Compare the note.

## CHAPTER LXVI

### No. 2. “Pyrois”

Grialius says that Isidore should be corrected in book V, chapter 30; but since the passage does not correspond, I think he was speaking of *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 23, where the manuscripts likewise have *vesper* (“evening star”) instead of *Pyrois*.

## CHAPTER LXVII

### No. 1. “Certain stars are therefore called planets”

These matters are also treated in chapter 23 of *On the Nature of Things*; but there the planets are called “wanderers,” not because they themselves wander, but because they make us wander. Compare the note on that passage.

Among the ancient Latins one will scarcely find anyone who used the word *planeta* apart from Julius Firmicus, book 2, chapter 2, and an ancient inscription in Fabretti, chapter 10, no. 307, as Forcellini observes. He could have added Martianus Capella, who uses it frequently in book VIII.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### No. 1. “Antegradation”

Cassiodore also uses the word *antegradatio*, which is proper to this discipline and should not have been omitted from the best Latin lexicons. In the same way Forcellini admitted *retrogradatio* on the authority of Apuleius.

## CHAPTER LXXI

### No. 1. “The sun was so called”

The etymology of *sol* (“sun”) is taken from Varro and Cicero.

### No. 3. “The stars were so called from standing”

Capella, in the chapter on the five parallels of book VIII, records that the stars were called *stellae* from *stare* (“to stand”), constellations *sidera* from *considere* (“to sit together”), and heavenly bodies *astra* from Astraeus.

### No. 4. “The constellations were so called”

For the etymology of *sidus*, see the preceding note. Others derive *sidus* from εἶδος (“form”), because it is a figure visible in the sky, or from σύν (“together”) and εἶδος, because several stars are seen together.

### No. 7. “Because they wear down the earth, etc.”

This is from Varro, book VI of *On the Latin Language*. From him I restored *quasi terriones* (“as if earth-wearers”), whereas Grialius has *quasi teriones*.

### No. 9. “As if *arktou oura*”

That is, “as if the tail of a bear”; this is what the Greek words properly mean.

### No. 10. “And Orion was called from urine”

In Greek, urine is called οὖρον. Others have other ideas.

### No. 11. “The Latins call this the *jugula*”

Corrected editions of Varro, book VI of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 3, midway through, have *inter quas* (“among which”), whereas Grialius printed *inter quae* (“among which things”). Some, following Festus, derive *jugula*, the star of Orion, from *juglans* (“walnut”), because it is larger than the walnut.

Hyginus, *Astronomical Poetry*, book II, chapter 24, tells the story of Orion, whom he says was first called *Urion* from *urina* (“urine”), and was later received among the constellations.

### No. 12. “The Hyades were so called”

Gellius, book XIII, chapter 9, says that the Hyades were called *suculae* (“little pigs”), not from *sues* (“swine”), as Tullius Tiro wrote in his commentaries, but because the ancient Latins first called them *syades* and then *suculae*, just as we say *super* where the Greeks say ὑπέρ.

He further denies that these stars are in the head of Taurus, as Tiro also taught. Rather, he shows that the head of Taurus consists solely of them.

### No. 23. “On account of Jupiter Ammon”

I have punctuated the passage in this way; in the printed editions I find: “On account of Ammon, they called him Jupiter.” Isidore says that the first sign was named for Jupiter Ammon, on whose head makers of images attach—or, in another reading, fashion—horns, and call him a ram. The story of horned Jupiter Ammon is well known.

### No. 25. “Castor”

Varro, *On Agriculture* II.1, teaches that the Twins in the zodiac are not Castor and Pollux but Apollo and Hercules, as Vulpius observes in his learned note on Catullus, p. 25.

### No. 27. “Annual blasts: the Etesian winds”

That is, the Etesian winds, which are annual or recurring each year.

### No. 35. “Jupiter with his son”

*Jovis* in the nominative case is also found in Apuleius, in fragments of Caecilius and Accius, on ancient coins, in Hyginus, *Fables* 54, and elsewhere in Isidore.

### No. 38. “The other superstitious matters, etc.”

This is from Cassiodore. In some editions of his work one reads: “They join them to the knowledge of the stars,” that is, “to knowledge of events.”

### No. 39. “Which is called *mathesis*”

Concerning judicial astrologers, Tacitus, *Histories* I.7, says: “A class of people faithless to those in power”—some restore *petentibus*, “to those who seek power”—“deceitful to those who hope; it will always be prohibited and always retained in our state.” These people were commonly called *mathematici*, just as the harmful calculations themselves, which Isidore names *mathesis*, were so called.

### No. 41. “The seven secular disciplines”

Isidore explained these further. In the later age, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic were called the *trivium*; arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy the *quadrivium*. Du Cange provides abundant examples of this meaning under *Trivium* and *Quadrivium*, or *Quatrivium*, extending even to the time of Boethius.

The order was not observed identically by everyone. Capella arranged the seven disciplines as follows: grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, and music. Isidore followed Cassiodore’s order, except that Cassiodore discussed music first and then geometry.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER II

### No. 1. “From *modus*”

Learned men approve this same etymology, namely, that *medicina* (“medicine”) comes from *medius* (“middle”), and *medius* from *modus* (“measure”), as can be seen in Becmann under *Medium*. This ought to be much more acceptable than the opinion of others that *medeor* (“I heal”) derives from the Greek μέδω or μεδέω, “I rule,” because it is the physician’s role to command.

## CHAPTER III

### No. “Of the medical art”

The history of the medical art is explained by Conringius in his introduction to the medical art, and by Lindenius with Mercklin’s additions. Sigebert Havercamp, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 23, observes that in Tertullian’s Fulda manuscript *Aesculapius* appears as *Aescopius*, and that this form is always found in Isidore and others in the manuscripts, as Schoppius testifies.

In some old parchments of Isidore I find *Scolapius*, both here and in book VIII, chapter 1. Some report Hippocrates as the fourteenth after Aesculapius. See Hardouin’s note on Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 1. In Grialius, at the following number, it read book IX; I corrected it.

## CHAPTER IV

### No. 1. “And so, three men”

Marcellus gathered the three medical schools into this verse in his poem *On Medicine*, verse 6:

> “What logos, or methodos, or simple empiricism fashions,  
> This book contains.”

Some attribute this poem to Vindicianus, others to Serenus Sammonicus. The fact that the Methodic school pursued verses may be explained either by the reference to Apollo or by the incantations that some ancient physicians prescribed, as Serenus says under “For driving away the *Hemitritaeus*”:

> “You write upon a sheet what is called *Abracadabra*  
> Repeatedly, and underneath you repeat …”

Those people called *ensalmadores* are well known in Spain. Homer too mentions healing by means of incantations, and for this reason Galen wrote an entire little book on Homeric healing. Compare Morhof, *Polyhistor*, volume II, book III, chapter 1, no. 17.

Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 1, pursues the history of medicine; and in no. 4 he says: “Another faction—called the Empiric from its experiments—began in Sicily,” and so forth. I cannot find where he wrote *medicina experimentosa* (“experimental medicine”), nor does that expression appear in Hardouin’s very extensive index.

### No. 2

In Appendix 5, after the *Etymologies*, I shall present a specimen of interpolation in the Chisian Codex, in which many additions are made to this book of Isidore on medicine.

## CHAPTER V

### No. 1. “Health”

Strictly speaking, *sanitas* (“health”) derives from *sanus* (“healthy”); and *sanus*, like *salus* (“well-being”), derives from the Greek σάος or σόος.

### No. 2. “Disease … the force of death”

Some say that *morbus* (“disease”) means “the road of death”; others derive it from Greek μόρος βίου, “the fate of life.” See J. C. Scaliger, in his notes on Theophrastus, *On Plants*, and Plautus. Perhaps in Isidore one should restore *mortis viam* (“the road of death”).

### No. 4. “The Greek etymology of *sanguis*”

The etymology of *sanguis* (“blood”) may also be Greek, from σαίειν γυῖα, “because it preserves and invigorates the limbs of the body.” Others less correctly think it is Latin, from *sancio*, as though *sancuis*. Again, at no. 6, another etymology of *sanguis* is given.

Concerning *cholera*, Caelius Aurelianus, book III, chapter 19, reports from Asclepiades that it is “a swift flow of humor lasting a short time.” Perhaps Isidore’s words allude to this, since the condition ends within the space of one day.

N. 8. “Which the Greeks call *chronic*.” The causes of chronic diseases are expressed in Latin, as I showed in my note on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verse 20:

> You seek the causes of the suppliants, which pour forth remedies.

In Spanish we say *achaques*.

## CHAPTER VI

### No. 1. Pleurisy, phrenitis

I printed *pleuritis*; for that is how physicians write it, from the Greek term. Grialius has *pleurisis* in the text, but indicates *pleuresis* in the notes. The matter of *phrenesis* is different; for among the ancients one finds *phrenesis* (φρένησις) and *phrenitis* (φρενῖτις).

### N. 3. “It is a disturbance accompanied by [exag.].”

Retain the true derivation from the Greek name.

### N. 4. Cardiac disease

Coelius, book II, chapter 31, reports, on the authority of Artemidorus and the followers of Asclepiades, that cardiac disease is a swelling beside the heart. It may therefore be preferable to read in Isidore “from some swelling,” although Isidore seems to have intended “from fear”; for he repeats “with fearful dread,” which he may perhaps have taken from Coelius himself, who, among the many and varied causes of cardiac disease, lists sadness or fear.

### N. 5. Lethargy

Lethargy is said to derive from forgetfulness rather than from sleep. Coelius observes that the continuous sleep which most people attribute to lethargic patients is not truly sleep, but oppression.

[Col. 0879A]

### N. 6. Synanche

Grialius, together with the other printed editions, published συνάγχειν; but Coelius in the Lyons edition of 1566 has: “For the Greeks call containment συνέχειν,” which is correct.

### N. 7. Phlegmon

More recent physicians define *phlegmon* as a form of deeper external inflammation.

### N. 8. “With bloody sputum,” although this is not always present.

### N. 13. “A weapon”

Rutilius also seems to have referred to disease as a “weapon” when he wrote, book I, verse 451:

> Weapons of pain.

In the edition of Samonicus that I use, the marginal note says that *telum* means pleurisy, but adds: “Others understand a stabbing pain.”

### N. 17. Pestilence

Theophilus Raynaudus argues, with many testimonies and arguments from the ancient Fathers, that pestilence is generally brought about through aerial powers, though not without God’s governance, in his philological work entitled *Vitae et mortis terminalia*, point 6, p. 224 ff.

[Col. 0879B]

### N. 18. “It is called pestilence”

*Pestilentia* derives from *pestis* (“plague”) and *pestilens* (“pestilential”). Nor is the etymology of *pestis* sufficiently certain.

### N. 19. “Itself and the inguinal disease”

The inguinal plague was once fairly common, especially in the Middle Ages; that many people were carried off by this disease is also evident from epitaphs.

## CHAPTER VII

### N. 4. “Hence also vertigo”

*Vertigo* derives from *verto* (“I turn”), because to a person afflicted with this disease everything seems to turn. *Vertex* (“crown of the head”) also derives from *verto*, because at that point the hair turns in a circle.

### N. 6. “According to the course of the moon,” etc.

I believe this reading to be not only genuine but also taken by Isidore from Juvencus, as I observed in my note on book I of this work, verse 482:

> And madness of mind accompanying the moon’s course.

Samonicus also contributes the following concerning epilepsy:

> The god himself mentions one conceived under the phases of the uncertain moon,  
> Whom such a collapse has often struck down.

Coelius says that epilepsy is called the sacred disease, either because it is thought to be sent by divine agency, etc. Perhaps for this reason Isidore called it the “divine disease,” which others call “sacred.”

[Col. 0879C]

### N. 7. “It was, however, among the Romans, a matter of the elections”

Samonicus plainly mentions the *comitia*, at which voting took place:

> There is a kind of sudden disease whose name comes from this:  
> That we refuse to conduct proper voting.  
> For often, when the limbs have collapsed in black illness,  
> A dreadful plague has cut short the council of the people.

### N. 10. “The *typoi* are cold fevers”

Chacon’s opinion is confirmed by the *typos* of Constans—namely, the notorious edict by which silence was imposed concerning one or two wills in Christ. In the posthumous work of Vazquez, through I know not whose fault, *typos* was named among the Monothelites as though it were some heretical person. This hallucination, first noticed by Theophilus Raynaudus, subsequently gave others occasion to criticize Vazquez most sharply, although he perhaps deserved nothing of the kind.

In any case, *status* should be retained in Isidore; and, as I think, the reading should be: “The *typoi* are cold fevers.” For among physicians *typos* means the form, state, mark, or character of recurrent fevers. Coelius, book I of *Acuta*, chapter 14, reports from Asclepiades that a quotidian fever is produced by the stationary position of larger corpuscles, a tertian by smaller ones, and a quartan by the smallest. Apuleius, *On Herbs*, chapter 102: “For chills and all types of fever.”

[Col. 0879D]

### N. 11. “From the nostrils”

Perhaps “from the nostrils” should be deleted. Certainly Coelius, book II of *Tardae*, chapter 7, has:

> An influx occurs—now toward the nostrils, which is called coryza; now toward the throat, which is called branchos; now toward the chest or lung, which is called ptysis.

For πτύσις some have φθύσις.

### N. 12. “Coryza … whenever there is an influx”

In Greek, *coryza* means a head-cold, fluid flowing from the head; it derives from κάρα (“head”) and ζέω (“I boil”), because it seems to boil out of the head.

### N. 13. “Branchos”

I would readily read βρόγχος; for this is what the Greeks call the throat, from which comes *bronchos*, hoarseness.

[Col. 0880A]

### N. 24. Nephritis

Nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys accompanied by continuous fever.

### N. 25. “Paralysis, so called from the impediment of the body”

Perhaps Isidore wrote “from the loosening of an impeded body.” *Paralysis* literally means “loosening.” Some manuscripts have “from the impairment of the body.”

### N. 26. Cachexia

In Greek, *cachexia* means a bad bodily condition.

### N. 30. Podagra

*Podagra* is as if from ποδὸς ἄγρα, that is, “capture of the foot.” Isidore reported two etymologies from Coelius. Podagra is said to arise from the knot-like constriction of the feet. Ovidius, book I of *Letters from Pontus*, letter 1, verse 255:

> Medicine does not know how to lift knotty podagra.

### N. 36. “Which the Greeks …”

In Grialius and the other printed editions there was *quam Graeci* (“which the Greeks”); I restored *quem* (“whom”) from Coelius, whom Isidore transcribes.

### N. 39. Rhagades

Celsus, book VI, chapter 17, distinguishes *rhagadia*—for that is what he calls them—from hemorrhoids:

> Rhagades occur when the skin around the anus is frequently, and indeed in several places, split [others: torn]. Hemorrhoids are the mouths of veins, rising as though from certain little heads, which often pour forth blood.

Celsus calls *rhagadia*, or *rhagades*, recent fissures; accordingly, perhaps *scissurae* (“tears”) should be read instead of *fissurae* (“fissures”). The Greek ῥαγὰς means “rupture.”

## CHAPTER VIII

### N. 1. “Having the quality of air”

I would suppose that one should read “having the quality of a bald patch.” Alopecia is a kind of bald patch. Celsus, book VI, chapter 4:

> There are also two kinds of bald patches. What they have in common is, etc. But the condition called ἀλωπεκία spreads in any shape; it occurs both on the hair of the head and on the beard.

The opinion that *alopecia* was named not because of its resemblance to a little fox, but because foxes frequently suffer from this disease, is the more accurate. Concerning the other kind of bald patch Celsus continues in the same passage:

> But that which is called ὀφίασις (“snake disease”) because of its resemblance to a serpent begins at the back of the head, etc.

Perhaps someone, and consequently Isidore, inferred from this that *alopecia* too was named from its resemblance to a fox.

[Col. 0880C]

### N. 4. Erysipelas

Various etymologies of *erysipelas* are given by different authors: either from ἐρείδω, “I draw,” and πέλας, “near,” because it draws the neighboring parts toward itself; or from ἐρυθρὸς, “red,” and πελός, “black” or “livid,” etc.

### N. 6. “He calls it *sarna*”

The Spaniards still use this term, and it seems to be, and to have been, a specifically Spanish word. Papias took it from Isidore: “*Sarna*, impetigo.” Semler, in his note on the *Isidorian Glossary*, under the word *Scaturrio*, thought *sarna* in this passage was a monster; and, not understanding what it meant, conjectured *scarra*, which is a German word.

In Ducange’s supplement, from the Biturician manuscript of Papias, there is:

> Dry impetigo, a scab protruding with roughness and roundness of form; this is commonly called *sarreuma*.

A suspicion is added that *sarna*, as found in the printed edition, was wrongly formed by contraction from *sarreuma*. But on the authority of Isidore and the Spanish idiom, *sarna* should be retained.

### N. 7. Pruritus

It is derived directly from *prurio* (“I itch”), which may itself be derived from *prouro*.

[Col. 0880D]

### N. 12. Elephantiasis

Aretaeus, book II, chapter 13, explains the correspondence between elephantiasis and the elephant.

### N. 13. “Arquatus”

Nonius, chapter 5, no. 14:

> Those are called *arquati* whose complexion and eyes are green, as though in the likeness of an *arquus*.

He had previously stated that a suspended arch is called a *fornix*, whereas *arquus* refers only to the phenomenon that appears in the sky, which poets called Iris. Nevertheless, many write *arcuati* and *arcuatus morbus*, and this was the reading in Grialius’s text. Grialius likewise gives *icteris* in the text, but *icteron* in the notes.

### N. 14. Cancer

When Celsus discusses cancer, he calls it an ulcer, not a wound. At times, however, “ulcer” and “wound” are confused. From the words “Or else,” etc., the sense seems either incomplete or at least obscure.

### N. 19. Ulcer

It derives from the Greek ἕλκος, from which some write it with aspiration, *hulcus*.

[Col. 0881A]

### N. 21. “As a little pap”

Festus:

> The nipples are called the little heads of the breasts because they resemble little swellings.

If *quasi papilla* (“as a nipple”) is read, one should rather say that the swellings were so called because they resemble nipples. This seems preferable; for *papillae* were so called because infants treat them almost as *papae* (“things to suck”), as Isidore says in book XI, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER IX

### N. 2. “Diet: observance of a rule and of life”

For the various meanings of the word *diaeta*, one may consult Janus Dousa, *Praecid.*, chapter 10; Joannes Wouweren, on Petronius; and Vossius, in his *Etymological Dictionary*.

### N. 6. “These two also,” etc.

Isidore refers to what he has said: that every treatment is applied either from opposites or from similars. These two principles are commonly signified by the very names of remedies.

### N. 11. Pessaries

Apuleius, *On Herbs*, chapter 121, calls it *pessum*; Plinius Valerianus, book I, chapter 1, at the end, uses the masculine *pessus*. Theodorus Priscianus, book III, chapter 5, uses *pessarium*.

## CHAPTER XI

### N. 4. “Guva”

Theodorus Priscianus, book II, part II, chapter 16, calls *guva* a “cupping gourd.” But Isidore suggests that it is simply called a “cupping vessel”; and this is now the specifically Spanish word *ventosas*.

[Col. 0881B]

### N. 6. “He presided over the fields to be pounded”

I am not persuaded that “fields to be pounded” means the same as “by pounding grain.” If *arvis* (“fields”) is retained, I would prefer to understand it as saying that Pilumnus presided over the threshing of fields; he also invented the *pilum* and *pila*, with which grain is pounded. I suspected that the reading should be “he presided over grain to be pounded.”

### N. 7. Mortar

Some etymologists wish it to have been called *moretarium*, as if from *moretum*, because *moretum* was made in it.

### N. 8. Coticula

Add Pliny, book XXXVII, chapter 10:

> Physicians make whetstones from agate.

What follows in Isidore, “for it will be smooth,” should perhaps be changed to *laevis* (“smooth”), or, as others write, *levis*. Nevertheless, *lenis* can have the same meaning.

## CHAPTER XII

### N. 1. Odor

It derives its origin from the Greek ὄζειν, “to smell” or “to give off an odor.”

### N. 3. Incense

The word *incensum* is an older term for frankincense than some believe. See *Prudentiana*, note A, under no. 151.

[Col. 0881C]

### N. 4. Tetraidos

Perhaps *tetraides* or *tetrades*. I miss this word in the lexicons of both early and medieval Latin.

### N. 7. “Perfumes … from places, such as telinum”

Because some perfumes are named from places, Augustine, Theophylact, and others have thought that the *pisticum* perfume mentioned in the Gospel of John, chapter XII, verse 3, was named from Bista or Pista, a city of Caramania, or from a province of Kabul among the Indians, or from some other place. See the note of Petrus Lazeri on Bruno of Asti, in his commentary on Matthew.

Others think that *telinum* was not named from a place but from Greek fenugreek, which in Greek is called τῆλις; for fenugreek is one of the principal ingredients from which *telinum* is compounded. Some read *Corpus suavi* without the conjunction *-que*; even so, the senarius verse can stand with the trisyllabic *suavi*.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I

### N. 1. “Phoroneus … established laws and judicial procedures”

These and many other passages from this book were incorporated among the canons of Gratian’s *Decree*. They may be seen collected by Berardus in my *Isidoriana*, chapter 32. But since Berardus did not use the royal Madrid edition, he sometimes attempted to emend the wording of the *Decree* from corrupt copies.

### N. 2. “The Lacedaemonians received laws from Apollo”

Berardus, in the passage cited, says that, in accordance with the commonly circulated manuscripts of Isidore, one should read: “The laws of Lacedaemon, laws from Apollo,” rather than “The Lacedaemonians received laws from Apollo,” as in Gratian. In Grialius’s edition, however, this very reading of Gratian is printed, except that Grialius’s text contained the error *Appollinis*.

### N. 4. “These ten decemvirs”

The names of the decemvirs are reported somewhat differently in Gratian.

### N. 5–6. “They have fallen out of use in books”

The Roman correctors of the *Decree* write *in libros* (“into books”) as a variant reading. Gratian has *obsoleverunt* (“have become obsolete”) instead of *exoleverunt* (“have fallen out of use”).

[Col. 0882A]

## CHAPTER II

### N. 1. “Of divine nature”

Berardus explains this in the passage cited, so that, according to Isidore’s understanding, the distinction between natural and divine laws may be recognized. Suárez, book I *On Laws*, chapter 3, no. 9, shows on the authority of Saint Thomas and Saint Augustine, book II *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 9, that natural law may also be called divine. For who, except God, writes the natural law in human hearts? Isidore calls this law divine even more explicitly in book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2.

### N. 2. “Fas, divine law”

Suárez explains the distinction between *fas* and *ius* in the same work, book I, chapter 2, no. 11, bringing forward Isidore’s words, whom he frequently praises.

## CHAPTER III

### N. 1. “But *ius* is so called because it is just”

Hieronymus Magius, *Miscellanies*, book IV, chapter 1, asserts that *ius* derives from *iubere* (“to command”), not from *iustitia* (“justice”), as Ulpian holds, nor from *iustus* (“just”), as Isidore holds, whom the authors of Pontifical Law follow. He also criticizes Isidore for asserting that *iustitia* was so called because *ius* stands within it.

I have often warned that neither Isidore nor other learned men should be readily criticized for this kind of etymology. I myself believe that *iustum* derives from *ius*, and *iustitia* from *iustum*. But many deny that *ius* comes from *iubeo*; they rather derive *iubeo* from *ius*. Others therefore trace the origin of *ius* to *iuvo* (“to help”), others to Jupiter, as if *Jous* or *Jovis os* (“the mouth of Jove”), and others to the cry ἰοὺ, from which *ejulare* (“to wail”) arose. See Becmannus and the other etymologists.

Nor are there lacking those who assert that *ius*, meaning “what is equitable,” was named from *ius coquinae* (“cooking broth”), because the broth was customarily distributed in equal portions. The etymology of *iustitia* which Magius condemns may perhaps be the one found in book XVIII, chapter 15: “Justice is, as it were, the state of the law.”

### N. 2. “Law from reading”

Andreas Cirinus, *On the City of Rome*, chapter 39, denies that this etymology should be accepted—namely, that *lex* (“law”) was so called from *legere* (“to read”): “For,” he says, “if this were true, an unwritten law would not exist.” Yet the origin of this name could very suitably be sought in the fact that at first a law was written and publicly read, as many say, although later the same name was applied to an unwritten law.

To make this etymology applicable to every law, some theologians explain it as an inward reading and writing, since natural law is said by Saint Paul, Romans II, to be written in our hearts. Others think that *lex* was called from *legere*, that is, “to choose,” because, as Cicero says in book I *On the Laws*, “we place the force of selection in law.” Others, with Saint Thomas, derive the etymology of *lex* from *ligare* (“to bind”).

### In the same place. “But custom,” etc.

These words are also quoted by Ivo in letter 79. Isidore frequently uses *tantumdem* for *tantum*. AREV.

## CHAPTER IV

### N. 1. “The receiving of children”

Berardus considers both readings—*susceptio* (“acceptance”) and *successio* (“succession”)—excellent, provided that *successio* is not understood as hereditary succession, but personal succession, whereby a son naturally succeeds his father through the power of generation.

### N. 2. “Or the restoration of what was lent”

The Gothic manuscripts read: “or the restoration of money entrusted.” But *pecuniae* (“of money”) may safely be omitted, since *rei* (“of the thing”) has already preceded it. The reading *commodatae* (“lent”) is also preferable, with Grialius.

## CHAPTER IX

### N. 1. *Ius Quiritium*

Both *Quiritium* and *Quiritum* are used. Grialius retains this in his note, and the old editions likewise print it. But *decretionibus* as written in these editions is an obvious error, and must be entirely distinguished from *cretionibus*, which is explained more clearly afterward.

## CHAPTER XI

### N. 1. “Or because the plebs knows it,” etc.

Berardus agrees that the reading admitted by Grialius into the text—“because the plebs knows it, or because it asks for it, just as it was requested”—better accords with the ancient formulas of plebiscites. The wording in the other printed editions, “or because it is asked for and requests that it be done,” should be corrected to *rogatur* (“it is requested”), if the sense is to proceed properly.

Some hold that *plebiscitum* was so called because the plebs was summoned or cited, namely, when, after the proposal of a law, it was called to vote. But the more convincing etymology seems to derive it from *scisco* (“to inquire” or “to decree”).

## CHAPTER XV

### N. 1. *Papia Poppaea*

In the old printed editions *Pompeia* was wrongly read for *Poppaea*. The same error is found in some editions of Suetonius and in other authors, as Isaeus noted in his annotation on Lactantius, book I, chapter 16.

[Col. 0883A]

## CHAPTER XVI

### N. 1. “Whence also to write *satyra*”

Andreas Schottus, *Observations on Human Affairs*, book I, chapter 2, confirms that there was no *lex saturae* (“saturated law”); Festus, Diomedes, and Isidore were deceived by some corrupt copy of Sallustius into accepting such a law.

I do not see why what is added—“to write *satyra*,” etc.—should be considered extraneous. For *satura*, *satira*, or *satyra* was said of a poem filled with many and varied subjects, such as the satires of Horace. Casaubon, book II *On Satire*:

> Thus, in very similar fashion, the short poems in which many people were briefly attacked were called *saturae*, or, as pronunciation later came to have it, *satirae*.

Scaliger, however, book I *Poetics*, chapter 12, contends that *satira* was named from the Satyrs, not from *satura*, whether the word be understood as a law or a dish; indeed, he thinks that these too were called after the Satyrs. They came forth with platters and baskets full of every kind of fruit, with which they might entice the nymphs. But Casaubon is supported not only by these words of Isidore, but also by similar words of Porphyrion on Horace. See below, book VIII, chapter 7, no. 8.

## CHAPTER XXI

### N. 1. “But a law will be honorable,” etc.

Suárez explains these matters splendidly in the cited book I *On Laws*, where he entitled chapter 9: “Whether it belongs to the nature of law that it be just and justly enacted.” There he discusses the other conditions of law set out by Isidore. He confirms each of the conditions of law transmitted by Isidore through the judgment of the ancient Fathers and theological arguments.

## CHAPTER XXII

### N. 1. *Pragma*

Among the Greeks, and later also among the Romans, those who practiced in the courts were called *pragmatici*. For a fee, they advised litigants ignorant of law and court procedure, suggested what they should say, and taught them how to conduct a case; they were quite distinct from advocates.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### N. 1. “To conceal”

The Gothic manuscripts have *insimulare*, with the gloss *accusare* (“to accuse”).

### N. 2. “Witnesses … because of a testament”

The more accurate origin of *testamentum* is from *testatum* (“attested”) and *testamen*, which etymologists derive from *testis* (“witness”). They hold that *testis* comes from the ancient Greek word θέστορ.

[Col. 0883C]

## CHAPTER XXIV

### N. 1. “By will”

Perhaps *voluntarie* (“voluntarily”) or *voluptate* (“with pleasure”) should be read. The matter comes to the same thing: the disposition of legal instruments is called a “will” because it is made by willing.

### N. 2. “Called a testament”

I recently gave the etymology of *testamentum*. Many jurists say that *testamentum* is, as it were, a *testatio mentis* (“attestation of the mind”). This etymology, and the one used by Isidore, explain something distinctive about a testament, but do not reveal the true origin of the word. For *-mentum* derives neither from *mens* (“mind”) nor from *monumentum* (“monument”), but is an extension of the word, or a paragogic formation, as in *cognomentum* (“surname”), etc.

The true origin of *testamentum* is from *testes* (“witnesses”) or *testor* (“I testify”). Isidore himself indicates this clearly enough in book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 11. Gellius should also be compared, book VI, chapter 12, where he criticizes the jurist Servius Sulpicius, the most learned man of his age, for having written that *testamentum* was a compound word formed from *mentis testatio*. “What, then,” Gellius asks, “of *calceamentum*, *paludamentum*, *pavimentum*, *vestimentum*, and a thousand other words extended in this fashion?”

[Col. 0883D]

### N. 6. “A testament according to praetorian law,” etc.

Justinian distinguishes the presence of witnesses, subscription, seals, and number as follows, *Institutes*, title 10, § 3:

> Thus this law appears to be divided into three parts: witnesses and their presence, for the purpose of executing the testament in a single proceeding, derive from the civil law; the subscriptions of the testator and witnesses are required by the observance of the imperial constitutions; and the seals and number of witnesses derive from the praetor’s edict.

### N. 14. “As the ancients [used] a codicil,” etc.

*Ut* (“as”) may be omitted, or it is clear that something must be supplied; for *codicillus* soon occurs in the masculine gender, and is used in that way by the others. But what does Isidore mean when he says: “Just as a codicil takes the place of a testament, so a letter takes the place of codicils”?

Lipsius, chapter 2 *On the Institution of Letters*, proves that a letter is a written message of the mind to absent persons, or persons who are as if absent; but that *codicilli* are properly so called when persons who are present are addressed in writing. This seems to be Seneca’s meaning in letter 56:

> I see you, my Lucilius, most vividly; I hear you, and I am so completely with you that I wonder whether I should begin writing you not letters but codicils.

Perhaps, then, Isidore means that when one writes to absent persons, a letter is used in place of codicils. Or he means that, before the use of paper and parchment, conversations in the form of letters were customarily written in codicils, as he says in book VI, chapter 8, at the very end.

In any case, some observe that *codicilli* are occasionally used generally for a letter. Brissonius discusses codicils at length in book VII *On Legal Forms*.

[Col. 0884A]

### N. 16. “It is called *cretio*”

Nicolaus Antonius, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, book V, no. 95, includes this among the etymologies criticized in Isidore: namely, that *cretio* is said to derive from *decretio*, or “deciding.” But, following Alciatus, he observes that these two words, *cernere* and *decernere*, are used interchangeably by the very authors of the law, as in the laws *Is qui heres*, near the end, and *Pupillus*, *On Acquiring an Inheritance*.

[Col. 0884B]

### N. 17. *Fideicommissum*

Many wish to derive *fides* (“trust”) from the Greek πίστις (“faith”). Isidore follows Cicero’s view, book I *On Duties*, chapter 7:

> Although this may perhaps seem rather harsh to someone, let us nevertheless dare to imitate the Stoics, who diligently seek the origin of words, and let us believe that *fides* was so named because what is said is done.

Saint Augustine, letter 109, and Isidore again, book VIII, chapter 2, no. 4, are relevant here.

### N. 18. “*Pepigi* is from *pango*”

As Quintilian teaches, book I, chapter 6, or section 10 in some editions.

### N. 19. *Placitum*

In Latin, *placitum* means a judgment or opinion. As a legal term, however, it belongs to a later period. At times *placitum* meant an agreement or pact; examples of this sense are found in Ducange. At other times it meant a lawful term established by common agreement of the parties or by judicial decision, from which the Spaniards derive *plazo* (“term” or “deadline”). This is the second meaning Isidore suggests. Others say, etc.

[Col. 0884C]

### N. 20. “He gave his hand”

Perhaps *manu dabat* (“he gave with his hand”) or *in manum dabat* (“he gave into the hand”) should be read. The etymology of the verb *mando* (“I entrust” or “I command”) is customarily explained in this way.

### N. 24. “Sale, as if *venundinatio*”

*Vendo* (“I sell”) derives from *venum* (“for sale”), and *venditio* (“sale”) from *vendo*.

### N. 25. Donation

The etymologies of *donatio* (“donation”) and *dos* (“dowry”) used by Isidore explain some characteristic of the matter, as often elsewhere, but do not disclose the true origins of the words. From the Greek δῶ (“I give”) come *do* (“I give”), *dos*, *dono* (“I present”), and *donatio*.

### N. 26. “For the ancient marriage [contract]”

Albert Dieterich Trekell, in his note on Brissonius’s book *On the Rite of Marriage*, p. 289, conjectures that the origin of marriage tablets is to be sought in the agreement of *in manum* marriage through *coemptio*. On p. 298, against those who assert a mutual purchase by husband and wife, he argues that only the husband purchased the woman and her property, even though both parties carried out the *coemptio*.

In this passage Isidore joins those who maintain a mutual *coemptio*. In book IX, chapter 5, he calls marriage tablets instruments of purchase; Dieterich explains this as an *in manum* agreement through *coemptio* without mutual purchase.

[Col. 0884D]

### N. 29. Conditions

I have followed the common spelling and used *conditiones*, although Grialius preferred *condiciones* even in the text. Both forms occur in ancient documents.

### N. 30. “Stipulation from *stipula*”

Others believe that *stipulatio* was named from *stipula* (“straw”), which they held in their hands in agricultural contracts as a representation of the intact field. Varro, at the end of book IV *On the Latin Language*, and Festus, under *Stipes*, derive *stipulatio* from *stips* (“small coin” or “contribution”). Someone derives it from *stipulae*, twisted in the manner of a knot, by which sheaves of grain were bound and secured. Those who say that *stipulum* among the ancients meant “firm” suspect that it descended from *stipes* (“stalk” or “trunk”). Brissonius, book V *On Legal Forms*, should be consulted.

As for what Chacon considered spurious—“The ancients … acknowledged”—I do not know how he could have persuaded himself of this, since the oldest copies agree. Indeed, why should we not believe that the custom which we see observed in Spain by children—breaking a straw, joining it again, and scattering it to the winds, which they call *pajitas a volar* (“little straws to fly”)—was derived from an ancient custom? The Spaniards also say *hechar pajas* (“to cast straws”) of the game in which they seek a lot by means of straws.

[Col. 0885A]

### N. 31. “An oath is the pledge of a promise”

Petrus Pithoeus, book I *Adversaria*, chapter 18, says that Isidore learned from some better author that a lawful pledge of a promise is an oath. Certainly Isidore collected from older—and, if you wish, better—authors nearly everything he presents, including matters that seem absurd to overly severe critics.

Among the ancients, a *sacramentum* was money which litigants, or those contending over some matter, deposited in a sacred place or before a priest. The money of the victor reverted to him; that of the loser was spent on sacred things. See Varro, book IV *On the Latin Language*, and Festus, under *Sacramentum*.

Isidore, however, moves from this first meaning to another, in which *sacramentum* is understood as an oath, which was regarded as especially sacred.

[Col. 0885B]

## CHAPTER XXV

### N. 1. “Hence *heres*”

Perhaps *herus* should be read; for many wish *heres* (“heir”) to derive from *herus* (“master”), while others derive it from *haereo* (“I cling”). See book IX, chapter 5, no. 1. Whether it is written *heres* or *haeres*, the matter is the same with respect to its etymology.

### N. 3. “He uses his own [property] badly”

Read *suis utitur* (“he uses his own [property]”) instead of *sua utitur*. For *utor* (“I use”) often occurs with the accusative in the ancient copies of Isidore, although it is sometimes given differently in the printed editions. Vulcanius, like the other printed editions, used the ablative here: *suis male utitur*; but in the following section he retained the accusative: “that people may use good things.”

### N. 5. “To manage as his own”

That is, “to administer as his own.” The jurists discuss this kind of peculium extensively in the *Digest*, book XV, title 1, entitled *On the Peculium*.

### N. 8. “Because his heirs”

I suspect that one should read “because heirs [come] from them.” Ulpianus, *Book of Rules*, title 17, *On Forfeited Legacies*:

> Whatever someone has been left in a testament in such a way that he could take it under the civil law, but for some reason has not taken it, is called *caducum*, because it has, as it were, fallen away from him.

In Fabretti, chapter 10, no. 319, an ancient inscription reads:

> D. Laberius Secundus, procurator of forfeited legacies.

[Col. 0885C]

### N. 9. *Familia herciscunda*

More clearly, *familia herciscunda* means “an inheritance to be divided.” See title 2 of book X of the *Digest*.

### N. 10. *Communi dividundo*

Title 3 of book X of the *Digest*: *On Dividing Common Property*.

### N. 11. *Finium regundorum*

Title 1 of book X of the *Digest*: *On Establishing Boundaries*.

### N. 19. Deposit

It is obvious that *depositum* derives from *de* and *positum* (“placed down”). But Isidore, or whoever he took this from, wished to express that a deposit is a thing entrusted for a time, which he indicated by the adverb *diu* (“for a long time”).

### N. 21. Earnest money

*Arra*, or *arrha*—for both spellings are used—has a Hebrew origin. The Italians say *caparra* and *arra*. See book IX, chapter 9, no. 6.

### N. 32. “Against the truth”

Should one read: “against the will, he agrees with the other”?

### N. 33. Interdict

Justinianus, book IV of the *Institutes*, title 15, § 1, says that interdicts are so called because they are pronounced between two parties. The Isidorian etymology is more appealing, since it touches upon the substance of the matter.

### N. 34. Price

Some foolishly derive *pretium* (“price”) from *peritus* (“experienced”); others from *proco* or *posco* (“I ask”); others from elsewhere. Vossius should be consulted in his *Etymological Dictionary*, to omit the others.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### N. 1. “Crime from *carere*”

*Crimen* (“crime”) is better derived from κρίνω (“I judge”) or κρίμα (“judgment”).

### N. 3. Offense

Others say that the origin of *flagitium* (“disgraceful act”) is *flagrum* (“whip”), or *flagrare* (“to burn”), so that *flagitare* would mean “to demand ardently.” Perhaps Isidore wrote: “*Flagitium* from burning, the corruption of lust,” etc.

The statement is taken from Augustine, book III *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10:

> What unruly desire does to corrupt the mind and its own body is called *flagitium*; what it does in order to harm another is called *facinus* (“crime”).

Plautus, *Rudens* III, 4, 28, seems to allude to the etymology of *flagitium*:

> Do you even reproach violence with the burning shame of disgrace?

[Col. 0886A]

### N. 7. Deceit

The word is Greek: δόλος. The other etymologies brought forward are concerned with explaining the nature or properties of the thing. Who this Petronius was, whose words Isidore has preserved for us, is uncertain.

### N. 9. Falsity

Properly, *falsitas* derives from *falsus* (“false”) and *fallo* (“I deceive”), which arise from the Greek forms σφάλλειν and φάλλειν.

### N. 10. “Among comic writers”

I would prefer “among the Comic Poet,” that is, Terence, whose *Hecyra* I, 1, 15 has:

> But it is unjust to take revenge on one’s adversaries.

### N. 14. Sexual violation

Some ancient manuscripts join the words as follows:

> *Stuprum raptus proprie est illiciti coitus a corrumpendo dictum.* “Stuprum, or rape, properly means illicit intercourse, and is so called from corrupting. Hence he who obtains a rape enjoys *stuprum*”; others: “obtains by rape.”

Gratian cited this statement in two places. Canon 48, cause 27, question 2:

> Rape is illicit intercourse, so called from corrupting. Hence he who obtains by rape enjoys *stuprum*.

And canon 1, cause 36, question 1:

> Rape too is illicit intercourse, and is so called from corrupting. Hence he who obtains by rape enjoys *stuprum*.

The Roman correctors observe that the printed Isidore reads:

> *Stuprum raptus proprie est illicitus coitus, a corrumpendo dictus.* “Stuprum, or rape, properly means illicit intercourse, and is so called from corrupting. Hence Virgil: ‘He obtains what was seized,’ that is, he enjoys *stuprum*.”

It does indeed seem that Isidore wished to join *stuprum* with *raptus*, following Servius’s interpretation of Virgil, book IV, verse 217:

> “HE OBTAINS WHAT WAS SEIZED”: he enjoys *stuprum*.

### N. 18. “*Internecivi*”

Some write *internicivum*, others *internecinum*. The more common and accurate spelling is *internecivum*. Becmannus explains an *internecivum bellum* (“war of extermination”) as one that kills both combatants; others, more accurately, as a war undertaken for the extermination of one party. In compounds, *inter-* sometimes strengthens the force of the word; this is true in *interbibo* (“drink up”), *interneco* (“kill utterly”), etc.

### N. 19. “Before the penalty of fourfold damages”

According to Gellius, in the passage cited, the law of the decemvirs permitted a thief to be killed if either it was night when he committed the theft, or if during the day he defended himself with a weapon when apprehended. Later this law was abandoned, and an action for fourfold damages was granted if someone wished to proceed lawfully and formally concerning manifest theft. For other thefts, which are not called manifest, they subsequently imposed a penalty of double damages.

[Col. 0886C]

### N. 24. “He took”

I corrected *cepit* (“he took”) in place of *coepit* (“he began”), as it appears not only in Grialius but also in the other printed editions.

### N. 27. “The offenses committed,” etc.

Perhaps he referred to Virgil, book VI, verse 568:

> Whatever sins anyone, rejoicing in futile theft,  
> Has committed before the gods above and deferred until late death.

Servius: “OFFENSES COMMITTED”—on account of which expiation is owed.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### N. 4. “Eight kinds of punishment”

Augustine mentions the law of retaliation from Cicero; accordingly, it is not inappropriate to assign this passage among Cicero’s fragments. Fabricius explains who wrote about punishments and penalties, and about the various kinds of torture, in chapter 15 of his *Bibliography*.

[Col. 0886D]

### N. 9. Chains

The second etymology may perhaps refer to the claim of some that *catena* (“chain”) comes from the Greek καθ’ ἕνα (“one by one”), because it links and joins various rings. Others derive it from κάθεμα (“necklace”).

### N. 11. Shackle

The printed editions read:

> A *nervus* is an iron bond by which the feet or necks are restrained.

See the variant readings.

### N. 12. *Boia*

I discussed *boiae* in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verse 46:

> The prison restrains necks bound with harsh *boiae*,

where I included an engraving of an ancient *boia* from the Borgian Museum; it is appropriate to reproduce it here as well.

[Col. 0887A]

[Col. 0887B]

### N. 13. “Only in the plural number”

From Varro, book IV *On the Latin Language*, chapter 32:

> *Arx* (“citadel”) comes from *arcere* (“to restrain”) … *carcer* (“prison”) from *coercere* (“to confine”), because those in it are prevented from going out.

This is more convincing than the explanation offered by others, that *carcer* derives from *cancer*, *canceris*, the word now used for “barriers.” Besides Virgil, some others use *carcer* in the singular for the place from which the four-horse chariots are released. More commonly, however, *carceres* is used in the plural with this meaning. See book XV, chapter 2, no. 46.

[Col. 0887C]

### N. 14. Blow

It is Greek, as is *plecto* (“I strike”), from which it derives: πλήττω, πληγή, and, in the Doric form, πλαγά. *Flagrum* (“whip”) derives from *flagro* (“I burn”), because a person struck with whips burns or is scorched.

### N. 15. *Anguilla*

The words of Hesychius are relevant here:

> Σκυτάλαι ὄφεών εἰσι φλαγέλλια, λῶροι.  
> “*Skytalai* are whips or thongs of serpents.”

### N. 16. Stakes

For “stakes,” the best authors use *sudes*; for “clubs,” the Spaniards still use this word.

### N. 17. Lever

It is a staff by which something suspended is carried; therefore the conjecture of Antonius Augustinus is highly probable.

### N. 18. Rods

I discussed rods and scorpions in my commentary on Prudentius, hymn 1, verse 44:

> That one, rods and axes and two-pronged claws.

There also, and in other places, I discussed the *fidiculae*, or “little strings,” about which Isidore speaks shortly afterward.

N. 20. Claws. After my commentary and index to Prudentius, I appended to Gallonius’s illustrations on this same subject a plate reproduced from the actual instruments with which the martyrs were tortured. I explained it in my commentary on *Peristephanon*, hymn 11, verse 57. I shall not hesitate to reproduce the same plate here, adding a brief explanation. No. 1 depicts an iron glove, a type of claw, found in the cemetery of Calepodius. No. 2 is an iron hook driven into the head of a certain martyr, from the cemetery of Saint Agnes. No. 3 is an iron comb preserved among the sacred relics of the monastery of the Dominican nuns of Saint Mary Magdalene on the Quirinal Hill. Nos. 4 and 8 are two instruments taken from the Vatican Sacred Museum, which appear to belong among the claws. No. 5 shows bifurcated claws preserved in the basilica of Saint Peter. No. 6 shows lead-weighted scourges from the Vatican Sacred Museum. Nos. 7 and 9 are two cauldrons engraved on the tombs of Saints Victorina and Exuperantius. I have discussed all these at greater length in the place cited.

[Col. 0888A] [Col. 0888B]

N. 21. The little horse. Sagittarius, in *On the Tortures of the Holy Martyrs*, chapter 17, corrected this passage as follows: “The *eculeus* was so called because the accused was stretched upon it as upon a horse.” See my commentary on *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, verse 109.

N. 22. Instruments of torture. *Tormentum* derives from *torqueo* (“I twist”) and *tortum* (“twisted”), and perhaps from *tormen*, or *tormina* (“pain,” “torment”); the word is formed by lengthening the vowel, as was observed in chapter 24, note 2, under the word *Testamentum*.

N. 23. *Latumia*. Grialius printed *latomia* and *latomias* in the text, but *latumia* and *latumias* in the notes. Festus wrote *latumiae*, as the order of the letters in his work requires. Varro, book 4 of *On the Latin Language*, has *latomiae*, and says that the word was transferred from *Latonia*, because there too there were stone quarries. It is Greek, λατομίαι (*latomiai*), which in the Sicilian language means “a place where stones are cut.” That the Latins changed *latomias* into *lautumias* is sufficiently clear from the passage of Seneca cited by Grialius, which nevertheless reads as follows in the more accurate editions: “When the defendant requested that he be transferred to the *lautumiae*, Sabinus said, ‘Let none of you be deceived by the name of luxury; in my mind, that is a luxurious thing.’” Many follow this spelling. Perhaps the ancients used different forms.

24. Verses of Juvencus, book 1, verses 584ff.:

“You hold the precepts of the law long made known;

Let a similar vengeance always follow the one who causes harm.”

It is unclear from where Isidore took the notion that *talio* (“retaliation,” “requital”) could also be understood in a favorable sense. In Ducange, from a donation to the abbey of Saint Giles dated 1038, this example is found: “In requital, heavenly things are due to us.” Ducange assembles numerous further examples to show that *talio* was understood as reciprocal punishment; but for this meaning there was no need at all to resort to medieval writers.

N. 25. *Ignominium*. This corresponds to what Nonius says in chapter 1, note 93: “*Ignominia* is a mark upon one’s name.” The *Onomasticon* states the matter more clearly: “*Ignomines*, ἀνώνυμοι (*anōnymoi*), anonymous, without a name.” Commodianus used *ignominium* in the neuter gender in *Instructions*, 19: “It is not a dishonor for a prudent man to be led astray.”

N. 26. *Infamium*. Or *infamia* (“infamy”). It is something worse than *ignominia* (“dishonor”); for, as Cornelius Fronto says: “Dishonor is imposed by one who has the power to censure; infamy arises from the talk of many.” Nevertheless, the two words are ordinarily used indiscriminately. In the printed verse of Virgil they give *malum quo* (“the evil by which”), which seems preferable, although Grialius thinks otherwise. In Tertullian too, whom Isidore had before his eyes, the reading is *quo*.

N. 27. “But certain fame.” This may perhaps have to be emended on the basis of Tertullian, who in the cited chapter 8, or chapter 7, of the *Apology* has the following: “It lives as long as it is not proved. For once it has been proved, it ceases to be […] From then on the matter is held, the matter is named […] Fame, the name of what is uncertain, has no place where the matter is certain.”

N. 28. “Whence *postliminium*.” Title 15 of book 49 of the *Digest* is “On Captives and *Postliminium*, etc.” Isidore may perhaps have alluded to this, although his words are not sufficiently complete.

N. 31. “They are assigned to the mine […].” Sigebert Havercampus, in his commentary on chapter 9 of Tertullian’s *Apology*, conjectured that *deportantur* (“are deported”) should be read instead of *deputantur* (“are assigned”); this is the reading of the Neapolitan manuscript.

N. 34. “As though carrying the head.” These words suit the fork, not the crossbeam. The origin of this word is sought in *patior* (“I suffer”) or *pateo* (“I am exposed”). Consult Lipsius, *On the Cross*.

N. 35. “Even within the same category of death.” Havercampus, in his commentary on chapter 9 of Tertullian’s *Apology*, observes that Isidore took this from Tertullian but, in his usual manner, concealed the name of the author from whom he drew, while slightly rearranging the wording. He adds further discussion of this very statement, explaining a different kind of death. Barthius, book 32 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 8, shows that the punishment of beheading is now generally regarded as more honorable than the others; he says that this results from a profound imitation of antiquity, citing Xenophon and this authority of Isidore. In my commentaries on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verse 93, and hymn 14, verse 63, I considered why the martyrs, although they had sometimes overcome other tortures, succumbed always, or almost always, to the sword or iron. Fabricius observes that the Hebrews regarded death by the sword as exceedingly disgraceful, in chapter 15, note 14, of the *Bibliographia*, where he surveys the writers on the forms of capital punishment customary among the Hebrews.

N. 36. *Cuiteus*. I discussed the *culleus* in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, verse 458.

[Col. 0889C] CAP. XXIX. Note 2. After this chapter Grialius once again assigns the following chapter the number XXVIII, and continues in this way thereafter. For this reason, up to chapter 66 of book 3, note 2, I thought that the chapter cited as 30 did not correspond to the chapter cited by Grialius.

CAP. XXX. Note 3. “Thus it is also customary, etc.” Mazochius, in volume 1 of the *Biblical Spicilegium*, on Genesis 7:4, adduces numerous examples in which writers, following the proper meanings of the words, expressed days and nights together in order to designate a fixed period: “forty days and forty nights,” “five days themselves and an equal number of nights,” “five days and five nights,” “for three days and three nights,” and so forth. Isidore discusses these matters again in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 1.

N. 4. “According to the Athenians, from the sixth hour of the day.” Perhaps Servius attributed to the Athenians what Gellius reports from Varro concerning the Umbrians, or certain people in Umbria—namely, that they began the day at the sixth hour. Prudentius has a hymn for cockcrow in the *Cathemerinon*, hymn 1, where I made several observations. *Mesonyctium* (“midnight,” literally “the middle of the night”) is read in the Lyon *Taurobolium* inscription in Muratori, page 333. In *Acta Inscriptionum Francicarum*, volume 2, pages 503ff., the word *mesonyctium*, or *mesonyctius*, is explained from the same inscription; some Greeks use the latter adjectivally. Something may perhaps be missing from Isidore’s wording.
