N. 8. “Ridiculous fictions.” Sedulius, book 1, verse 17:

“While the gentile poets strive after their own fictions […]”

N. 12. “Holidays from *fari*.” Some derive *feriae* (“holidays”) from *festum* (“festival”); others from striking the sacrificial victims; others from carrying out banquets, because feasting took place during the holidays.

N. 15. “Midday, etc.” The same matter, in almost the same words, appears in book 3, chapter 42, note 3.

N. 22. “The day after tomorrow.” Isidore does not express the meaning of *perendie* with sufficient clarity. It means “the day following tomorrow,” the third day, as though from a day having passed away or from passing through one day.

CAP. XXXI. Note 1. “Night is so called, etc.” This should be compared with *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 2.

N. 3. “The sun grows weary on its long journey.” On the sun’s course, see chapter 17 of *On the Nature of Things*, with the notes.

N. 4. “The divisions of the night.” In *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 2, they are reported in a somewhat different manner.

N. 6. “Darkness.” The etymology of *tenebrae* (“darkness”) is given in the same way in book 13, chapter 10. Some think that darkness is so called because people are held by it, preventing them from seeing or acting freely.

N. 12. “Morning.” There is a morning hymn of Prudentius in the *Cathemerinon*, hymn 2, which perhaps was the same as the hymn for cockcrow in the Gothic office. See the observations I made on it in that place.

N. 14. “Now dawn is […].” Some derive *aurora* (“dawn”) from *aurea hora* (“golden hour”).

CAP. XXXII. Note 1. “For morning […].” On the meaning of *mane* (“morning”), see above, chapter 30, note 14.

CAP. XXXIII. Note 1. “The name of the month.” On the months and their correspondence, see chapters 4 and 5 of *On the Nature of Things*, where certain matters are explained differently from here.

[Col. 0890B] N. 12. “The Kalends.” Most think that *Kalendae* derives from καλεῖν (*kalein*), which is also expressed in Latin by *calare*, that is, “to call.” On the Kalends the people were summoned so that the days of the Nones of each month might be proclaimed; these days were also said to be *calari*. See Varro, book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 4, and Macrobius, book 1, chapter 15. The Ides are more likely called from *iduare*, “to divide,” than from *edere*, “to eat,” since the Ides generally divide the month. See Macrobius, same book, *Saturnalia*, chapter 15. Macrobius says there that the Nones were called as though they marked the beginning of a new reckoning, or because from that day nine days were always counted to the Ides. He adds in chapter 16, drawing on Rutilius, that the Romans established the market-days so that country people would work in the fields for eight days, but on the ninth day, leaving their rural labor aside, would come to Rome to attend the market and receive the laws. Thus *nundinae* are as it were *novendinae*, “nine days,” which is almost the same etymology as that of the Nones. In any case, the derivations indicated by Isidore appear to have been taken from an older author, although it is unclear who that author was.

[Col. 0890C] CAP. XXXIV. Note 2. “There are two solstices.” Ancient writers generally understood the summer solstice when they used the term *solstitium*; they called the winter solstice *bruma*. The dates of the solstice and the *bruma*, as well as those of the equinoxes, differ for us from those of the ancients according to the Gregorian Calendar, as explained in the note on *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 8, which also treats of the solstice and equinox.

CAP. XXXV. Note 1. “The seasons from […] tempering.” *Temperamentum* (“tempering”) should rather be derived from *tempus* (“season,” “time”) than *tempus* from *temperamentum*.

N. 3. “Because it is green.” From Varro, book 5, chapter 2, who suggests another etymology from Greek, except that he says: “The Ionians say βῆρ.”

N. 7. “As though *hiemevernus*.” Grialius’s note read: “Alternative reading: *hibernus*.” I restored: “Alternative reading: *hievernus*,” since *hibernus* is not a different reading unless we understand Grialius to have supplied all these words as variant spellings: “Alternative reading: *hibernus*. Thus it would mean ‘winter that is early.’” *Hibernus*, meaning the season between winter and spring, will scarcely be found elsewhere. In the neuter, *hibernum*, and perhaps also in the masculine, *hibernus*, Saint Ambrose and other later writers use it simply for “winter”; hence the Spanish *invierno* and Italian *inverno*.

CAP. XXXVI. Note 1. “A year is […].” This should be emended or explained from Varro, book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 2: “The period from one winter solstice to the next, while the sun returns, is called a year; and just as small circles were called rings, so large circles were called the circles of years; hence *annus*.” Thus *annus* is derived from *annulus* (“ring”) rather than *annulus* from *annus*.

N. 4. “The eras of individual years.” Although *era* may have its origin in *aes* (“bronze,” “money”), as Isidore says, among the Spaniards, who used this word most frequently, it is regularly written without the diphthong in ancient monuments. I follow this usage, although I do not reject the spelling *aera* used by others. These matters concerning the era, along with others explained in this chapter, are repeated in chapter 6 of *On the Nature of Things*. Critics disagree greatly among themselves about the origin of the word *era*. Sepúlveda’s opinion, in his book *On the Correction of the Year*, was that it was formerly customary to write A. ER. A., that is, “the year of Augustus” or “from Augustus,” from which *aera* was later corruptly formed. Joseph Scaliger refutes this opinion in book 5 of *On the Emendation of Time*, where he observes that in the ancient monuments of Spain *aera* is never written, but rather *era*. Scaliger himself derives *era* from *aes* and says that it signifies a number, for Faustus of Riez—or Reiensis—in his book *On the Holy Spirit* (now believed to have been written by Paschasius) uses it in this way: “Three hundred in the era, or reckoning, of the Cross.” Isidore likewise more than once used *era* in book 6, chapter 15, for a number. Becmanus cites the old *Breviary of the Theodosian Code*: “The emperor Theodosius, era 22,” that is, “title 22,” and from Hilderic the Gaul, *eras dierum*, “numbers of days.” Earlier writers used *aera* in the plural for numbers; the examples cited by Grialius from Nonius and Cicero belong here. Salmasius, in *Plinian Exercises*, page 686, proves that later writers accepted *era* for a number assigned, as they say, in some reckoning.

In the councils of Spain, *era* is used for a number, canon, or chapter, as in Pueyus, page 688: “The Council of Ilerda was also reopened, in which it is ordered, etc. For era seven reads as follows: ‘Whoever has bound himself by oath, etc.’” And on page 690: “From the Council of Chalcedon, era eighteen.” The meaning of *era* as a fixed and notable point from which years are counted—what they call an epoch—is better known among the Spaniards, and Isidore explains it in this sense. On the Spanish Era there is an excellent work by the Marquis of Mondéjar, reprinted at Madrid in 1795: *The Spanish Era, the Origin of Its Name, etc.*

In Vatican Codex 20, after the table listing the Roman pontiffs, these verses occur:

“To know the era, to the present years of the Lord

add thirty years and twice four;

and however many these shall be, know that they will constitute the whole era.”

That manuscript had *fuerunt* (“were”) for *fuerint* (“may have been”), and *usque* (“and up to”) for *bisque* (“and twice”); for this is the method by which thirty-eight years are added to the years of the common era, so that the year of the Spanish Era may be determined. In the same manuscript, *era* is explained as a measure of land that the Romans imposed upon the provinces; I find nothing about this in other authors.

There is a remarkable disagreement among chronologers about the year of the common era in which Christ was born, or whether he was born before it. Fabricius explained it in chapter 7 of the *Bibliographia*, arranging a catalogue of the various opinions by year. In this subject the distinguished scholar Henricus Sanclementius, Camaldolese abbot, was exceptionally learned; a work of his, printed in folio at Rome a few years ago, treats the matter with erudition. In the Albanian Codex, after the middle of chapter 34 of book 1 of the *Etymologies*, certain material has been inserted concerning the census that Augustus Caesar ordered to be taken throughout the whole world. Although this material is not Isidore’s, it will nevertheless have a place among the appendices, no. 6.

CAP. XXXVII. Note 2. “There are still consuls, etc.” From this Grialius concludes that Isidore seems not to have considered Virgil’s words. I do not see the reason. Isidore could, using Servius’s words, have observed that before the consuls the Romans reckoned by eras, lustrums, and Olympiads. Because of the Olympiads, *per olympiadas* (“by Olympiads”) may perhaps have to be restored. It should be observed that *lustrum* is often understood as a completed period of five years, as Savaro notes on Sidonius, poem 13, and Christian Gottlieb Schwarz on Mamertinus’s second panegyric to Maximian, chapter 1.

CAP. XXXVIII. Note 4. “And *aetas* is said as though *aevitas*.” According to Arnobius, book 2, *aevitas* (“age,” “eternity”) is a contracted form of *aetas*.

N. 5. “The ages […] of the world.” Isidore took this distribution of the six ages of the world from Augustine, the final book and chapter of *The City of God*.

N. 6. “Whose course.” Vulcanius and the other printed editions conclude this chapter as follows: “Whose course through generations and kingdoms is thus surveyed.” At the end of the following chapter of the *Chronicle* they add: “Whose course through generations and kingdoms Julian, the first of our people, […]” —“so that the sum of the past age may be known”—with this note by Vulcanius: “The following material is found in a certain printed codex before the title ‘On the Division of Times,’ but it is not found in manuscript copies.”

N. 8. “Up to the emperor Heraclius.” At the beginning of the fuller *Chronicle* one reads: “Up to the emperor Heraclius and the reign of Sisebut, king of the Goths.” This indicates that the *Chronicle* was published before the final hand was applied to the *Etymologies*. For Sisebut was succeeded by Reccared II, and Reccared—who reigned only three months—by Suinthila. I corrected *praeteriti saeculi* (“of the past age”) for *praeterita saeculi* (“of the past of the age”), which was read here in Grialius and other printed editions; in the opening of the *Chronicle* mentioned above, *praeteriti* is correctly given. The older Cesena Codex inserts here Isidore’s fuller *Chronicle* itself, of which this text, found in most manuscripts of the *Etymologies*, is an abridgment.

CAP. XXXIX. Note 1. “The first age, etc.” Grialius passed over this chapter without any note, perhaps because the learned notes of Loaisa are found in the fuller *Chronicle*, and because many scholars—Scaliger, Petavius, and others—have admirably illuminated this subject. Nevertheless, some matters deserve particular observation. The statement that the angels were created on the first day under the name of light perhaps suggests that they were created together with the world, which is Augustine’s opinion and that of theologians generally. Yet not a few Fathers maintain that the angels were created before the world, and some that they were created after the world. See Pererius, *Commentary on Genesis*. Several opinions concerning the beginning and end of the world may be found in Cotelerius, volume 1 of the *Apostolic Fathers*, page 44.

N. 6. “Heber, etc.” The reading is IIM.DCXLIII, not IIM.DCXLVII, as Grialius printed it in the fuller *Chronicle*; I shall correct the passage there.

N. 13. “Carthage.” Again, in note 16, under Amasia: “Carthage founded.” This results from differing opinions among the writers, which he expressed more clearly in the *Chronicle* under Amasia: “Some assert that Carthage was founded at this time; others, earlier.” For under David he had previously written: “Carthage is built by Dido.” See the variant readings on note 16.

N. 22. “Evergetes, year 26.” This too should be read in the *Chronicle*, where Grialius’s text incorrectly gives year 36, as can be inferred from the note itself, which indicates year 26.

N. 24. “Evergetes, year 29.” Loaisa observes in his note on the *Chronicle* that in the Bignaean edition of the *Etymologies* the reading “year 24” is erroneous. The same error had appeared earlier in Vulcanius’s edition.

N. 37. “Valentinian, year 8.” Loaisa observes in his note on the fuller *Chronicle* that the manuscripts variously indicate six or seven years, and occasionally eight or nine, in the *Etymologies*. He himself printed “in the eighth year,” which he considers preferable on the basis of the consular reckoning. I have followed him, although Grialius printed “year 7.”

N. 42. “Known to God alone.” Vulcanius and the other printed editions continue as follows: “It is known to God alone. All time from the beginning of the world up to the present tenth year of the most glorious prince, namely Heraclius, is reckoned as VM.DCCCLVII.” Vulcanius adds this note: “In other copies I find the following words added after ‘Heraclius, year 27’: ‘In his fourth and fifth years, the Jews in Spain were baptized under the most religious prince Sisebut.’ One copy, however, has *sepulti* (‘buried’) instead of *Sisebuti* (‘of Sisebut’). Another adds material here, as I said under note 6 of chapter 38. In the Chisian Codex, the continuation of this *Chronicle* is found; it will be reported among the appendices, no. 7. Among the variant readings, other details will be indicated concerning the different ways in which the *Chronicle* ends in many manuscripts, including a mention of King Recceswinth, who lived many years after Isidore.”

CAP. I. Note 1. “The Old Testament, etc.” The matters explained in this chapter correspond for the most part to those in the book of *Prefaces*.

N. 7. “That is, *Paralipomena*.” On these matters, compare Cotelerius’s notes on the *Apostolic Fathers*, page 7, column 2. The words that Grialius says were added in the printed editions are these: “*Paralipomenōn*, which is also called the *Chronicle*, divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins. Ezra is the eighth, etc.”

N. 11. “The whole of both Testaments is divided in three ways.” Isidore explains this threefold meaning of sacred Scripture more fully in book 1 of the *Sentences*, chapter 18: “The divine law is to be understood in three ways: first, historically; second, tropologically; third, mystically, etc.”

CAP. II. Note 1. “The Old Testament, etc.” This chapter too corresponds to what Isidore transmitted in the book of *Prefaces* and in book 1 of *The Offices*, chapter 12.

N. 23. “Which are not lamentations.” Grialius incorrectly argues that Jeremiah’s *Lamentations* were once customarily sung in the offices for the dead. Isidore is speaking of the type of poem itself that was used at funerals and was called a *threnus*, or lament, not of Jeremiah’s *Lamentations* specifically. See book 1, chapter 39: “A *threnus*, etc. They were used at funerals and in laments, and likewise they are used now.” Also chapter 19 of this book 6: “Opposed to the hymn is the *threnus*, which is a poem of lament and mourning.” Several learned dissertations on the meters of the Jews are extant, including those by Xaverius Matthaeus and others whom I listed in my dissertation on ecclesiastical hymns, no. 17.

N. 26. “These are the four prophets, etc.” In the prologue to the book of *Prefaces*, Isidore appears to follow the opinion of the Greeks and Latins, who maintain that all the books of the prophets were composed by the prophets whose names they bear. See Mariana’s note on the words of the prologue: “Of these there are four, etc.”

N. 28. “Because the second, third, and fourth, etc.” Mariana, in his note on the prologue to the book of *Prefaces*, considers the words “because the second, third, and fourth, etc.” to be manifestly corrupt. For if the statements of Ezra and Nehemiah are said to be contained in one book—which Isidore may perhaps be following here—then only two books remain to be numbered among the apocrypha, those commonly called the Third and Fourth Books of Ezra, by writers who divide the statements of Ezra and Nehemiah into two books. Natalis Alexander, volume 2 of *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, in the sixth age, dissertation 7, article 3, says that Isidore, joining the Third and Fourth Books under the name of Ezra, distinguished only two books of Ezra: one canonical and the other apocryphal. Yet, as the words of this note show, Isidore clearly distinguishes four books of Ezra. Accordingly, Isidore’s assertion, as it now appears, can be true only if he included the First and Second Books of Ezra, as we now call them, under the name of the First Book, while dividing what we call the Third and Fourth Books into three books and naming them the Second, Third, and Fourth.

N. 30. “They assert that it belongs to Philo.” This should be maintained rather than what Isidore himself taught in the prologue to the book of *Prefaces*, namely, that the Book of Wisdom was—or was said to have been—published by Jesus son of Sirach. See Mariana’s note. Mariana understands the Philo to whom Jerome also attributes the Book of Wisdom not to be Philo of Alexandria, but the biblical Philo, who is frequently mentioned by Eusebius. Others rashly confuse the two Philos, the Alexandrian and the biblical.

[Col. 0893D] N. 45. “To the Hebrews.” On the Epistle to the Hebrews, see what I noted on Sedulius’s Appendix 5, page 405. Isidore’s words should perhaps be emended to: “It is said to be uncertain.”

N. 46. “Peter wrote, etc.” See the note on the *Apostolic Fathers*, pages 6, 7, and 12.

N. 49. “The Apocalypse.” Vincent Fassinius of the Order of Preachers defends the authority of the Apocalypse, which Abarizitius of Geneva, a Calvinist, had attempted to undermine. Bruno Brunus explained several points of this controversy in the preface to volume 2 of the works of Saint Bruno of Asti. See also my note on the Decree of Gelasius, Sedulius’s Appendix 5, page 405, note pp. I discussed the various meanings of *apocryphal* in my note on the Decree of Gelasius, cited above, page 419. See also Mariana’s note on the prologue to the book of *Prefaces*, note 1, and Cotelerius, volume 1 of the *Apostolic Fathers*, page 6, column 2.

N. 53. “By canonical authority, etc.” Isidore is referring, I think, to the Decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received and not to be received.

CAP. III. Note 2. “The library.” I discussed the use of *bibliotheca* for the sacred Scriptures in *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, notes 8ff. The illustrious prelate Simon de Magistris adorns his description of the Alexandrian Library with every kind of learning in dissertation 5, appended to Daniel’s edition of the Septuagint from Origen’s *Tetrapla*. Regarding the number of books, Gellius says in the passage cited by Grialius: “Afterward, an immense number of books was collected or produced in Egypt by the Ptolemaic kings, amounting to nearly seven hundred thousand volumes. It is said that all of these were burned in the first Alexandrian war.” Livy and Seneca report that forty thousand books burned; from this the distinguished prelate de Magistris concludes, in dissertation 1, note 6, that three hundred thousand volumes escaped the fire, including the sacred Scriptures. Lipsius, in his *Treatise on Libraries*, chapter 2, argues from Gellius’s words that Isidore should read *septingenta* (“seven hundred”) rather than *septuaginta* (“seventy”).

CAP. IV. Note 2. “Indeed, sing. [uncertain abbreviation].” Among recent writers who discuss the history of the Septuagint translation, the first to consult is the distinguished de Magistris, whom I mentioned shortly before.

N. 5. “That common translation.” This is the version called the Itala; perhaps the reading should be *vulgaris Itala interpretatio* (“the common Itala translation”), unless someone instead concludes from this passage that in Saint Augustine, book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 15, the reading should be *illa*, not *Itala*, so that it may be said that no version was formerly called the Itala—a position maintained by some. This controversy is well known, and various scholars have repeatedly treated it.

CAP. V. Note 1. “Then Lucullus […].” Plutarch agrees with Isidore about Lucullus. Lucullus’s library was in a certain sense public and open to all learned people; nevertheless, he retained ownership and control of it, as Lipsius notes in his *Treatise on Libraries*, chapter 5.

N. 2. “The first in Rome.” In Pliny, one should read *prima in Urbe* (“the first in the City”), not *in orbe* (“in the world”), as Grialius has it. Isidore agrees: “The first at Rome,” or, as Lipsius gives it in the cited passage, “The first.” Lipsius’s chapter 10 concerns images in libraries: “Images of learned men were placed in them by an honorable custom whose origin goes back to Asinius.” Consult my *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, note 5. The printed editions incorrectly punctuate the passage after “with the images of authors added in the atrium,” as though the images had been placed not in the library but in some separate atrium. Asinius therefore established the libraries in the Atrium of Liberty, as Suetonius states in the *Augustus*; he furnished it from the spoils of the Dalmatians whom he had conquered. Lipsius, chapter 5, prefers the verb *publicavit* (“made public”) to *exstruxit* (“built”), which is the verb used by Suetonius. For the Atrium of Liberty had been built long before the age of Augustus and Pollio. Ovid speaks of this Atrium in *Tristia* 3, elegy 1:

“Nor did Liberty allow me to touch her Atrium,

which was the first to lie open to learned books.”

CAP. VI. Note 2. “Jerome and Gennadius.” Isidore indicates that Jerome and Gennadius discussed in their catalogues those writers whose works they had in their own libraries; I think this is true for the most part. Barthius, book 22 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 18, observes that *studia* (“studies”) is used by Optatianus Porphyrius for books or writings, as it is here by Isidore: “They pursued them and their writings, etc.” He reads this, along with some printed editions, as *prosecuti sunt*, not *persecuti sunt*, which Grialius preferred.

CAP. VII. Note 1. “As many […] as.” In place of *tot […] quot* (“as many […] as”); this phrase was introduced into usage in the later period and passed into the vernacular languages.

N. 3. “Augustine wrote so much, etc.” The same thought is expressed in the verses for Isidore’s library concerning Saint Augustine:

“He lies who claims to have read you entirely;

Or who could possess all your works as a reader?”

Perhaps *An quis* (“Or could anyone?”) should be restored.

CAP. VIII. Note 2. “Homily.” Properly, “conversation” or “intercourse.”

N. 3. “They sowed.” Some less correctly read *ferebant* (“they bore/carried”) for *serebant* (“they sowed”) in Virgil, since there is an allusion to the etymology of *sermo* (“speech”), from *sero* (“I sow”), or, as Varro says in book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 7, from *series* (“a series”), which itself derives from *sero*. For, Varro says, speech cannot exist in one person alone, but only where discourse is joined with another.

N. 4. “Treatises.” Among ecclesiastical writers, *tractatus* means the same as *homily*. Augustine, letter 4 to Quodvultdeus, prefixed to the book *On Heresies*: “Popular treatises, which in Greek they call *homilies*.” Hence *tractatores*, *tractare*, and so forth are used in the same sense.

N. 8. “Books of the *Fasti*.” *Fasti* is immediately derived from *fasti dies* (“lawful days”), while the origin of *fasti dies* is from *fari* (“to speak,” “to declare”).

N. 12. “The seer Martius.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book 14, chapter 1, discusses the seer Martius, or Marcius: “Amphiaraus and Martius, illustrious seers.” Macrobius likewise says in book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 17: “From the prophecy of the seer Martius, etc.” It is reported that in the poems of the seer Martius—two volumes of which were brought into the Senate—it was found written as follows: “[…]”

N. 17. “A letter […] sent.” Some interpret *epistolam* as “a letter sent.”

N. 18. “Dialogues.” Jerome writes: “They used to send one another the mutual conversations of letters.” Hence also the bearers of them, etc. Lipsius reproduces Isidore’s words almost exactly in chapter 1 of his *Institution of Letter-Writing*: “Conversations of letters were written on tablets. Hence also the bearers, etc.” *Portitor* (“bearer”) is the more genuinely Latin word.

CAP. IX. Note 1. “They themselves give ingenuity, etc.” A distich of Dracontius occurs in his elegy, which I published in full after his poem *On God*, from old Vatican parchment manuscripts; from these I restored *prosit littera* (“may the letter be useful”) instead of *praestet* (“may it provide”). See the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 8. The passage could elegantly be restored, if conjecture is permitted, from Rivinus’s emendation of Dracontius:

“Wax tablets, molds for letters, nurses of little children.”

Hilary of Arles may perhaps allude to this in his *Life of Saint Honoratus of Arles*: “When blessed Eucherius had received his letters from the desert on tablets coated with wax, as is customary, […] ‘You have returned his honey to the wax,’ he said.” For the whole method of writing, Hermann Hugo should be consulted, especially his second edition with Trotzius’s notes, in addition to the other authors cited by Fabricius in chapter 21, note 10, of the *Bibliographia*.

N. 2. “As Atta indicates.” Only this fragment of Quintus Atta is transmitted among the fragments of the ancient poets, along with another from Servius on Virgil’s *Eclogue* 7, verse 33: “Of course, at table, where conversation customarily begins to arise from the bosom.”

CAP. X. Note 1. “The use of sheets.” Fabricius carefully investigated and listed the writers who discussed the paper and papyrus of the ancients in chapter 21, note 10, of the *Bibliographia*. In the corrected editions, Lucan’s verse reads:

“A Memphian boat is woven from absorbent papyrus.”

It is uncertain how long wax tablets remained in use. I made several observations on this subject in *Isidoriana*, chapter 11, note 10.

N. 2. “But *charta* is so called.” *Charta*, like *character*, has a Greek origin. Vulcanius’s note is as follows: “Pliny, book 13, chapter 12, assigns the first kind of paper to the Augustan, the second to the Livian, named from Livia, the wife of Augustus, the third to the amphitheatric, the fourth to the Saïtic, and the fifth to the Taeniotic. From this passage of Pliny, the conjecture concerning Livian paper, which I shall now mention, was not difficult. On royal paper, which the Greeks call μακρόκωλα (*makrōkōla*, ‘long sheets’), see Cicero, book 13, *Letters to Atticus*, letter 25, and book 16, letter 3.”

N. 3. “Livian, in honor of Livia.” In many printed editions and in many ancient manuscripts, such as Vatican Codex 2 of the Archives, *Libiana* was read, “in honor of the province of Libya,” or the same idea was expressed in other words. Without noting any difference in the written form, Grialius printed: “The second, Livian, in honor of Livia.” Joseph Scaliger, in his *Annotations on Guilandinus*, on section 19, likewise thinks that the name of the province should be deleted and that Isidore understood Livia Augusta. “Although,” he adds, “I would not dare to alter it completely, because Isidore teems with many such trifles.” But since copyists have generally introduced the trifles from their own store, fairness requires that, whenever the context permits, we restore the errors that have crept in to the truth and intention of the writers from whom Isidore derived his material.

CAP. XI. Note 1. “The kings of Pergamum, etc.” Pliny, book 13, chapter 11, drawing on Varro, and Saint Jerome, letter 43 to Chromatius. The adjective is ordinarily expressed in the phrase *pergamena charta* (“parchment paper”), etc. The Spaniards retain from this the word *pergamino*. Nor is *membranum* in the neuter gender readily found among earlier writers. Apuleius, in book 6 of the *Metamorphoses*, used *tenue membranulum* (“a thin little parchment”). In any case, Lampius, on Psalm 45, page 86, argues that the use of parchment for writing existed long before the time of Eumenes and Ptolemy. Isaac Vossius, on Catullus, pages 50ff., maintains that the use of parchment codices, or square books, began with Attalus.

N. 2. “Of yellow color.” On yellow parchment, Tibullus writes in book 3, elegy 1, verse 9:

“But let yellow parchment enclose a snow-white little book.”

The Marquis Maffei, in volume 3 of *Illustrated Verona*, chapter 4, drawing attention to this statement of Isidore, vigorously attacks certain recent forms of library decoration that harm the eyes. On *Carystean*, or *Carystian*, marble—both forms are used—see Isidore again, book 16, chapter 5, where he says that it is pleasing to those who carve gems, since its greenness refreshes the eyes.

N. 4. “It is saffron-colored.” The verb *crocatur* (“is saffron-colored”) is unusual; nevertheless, Pliny used *crocatum* (“saffron-colored”) in book 16, chapter 34. In the editions of Persius, the reading is *et bicolor positis* (“and, when placed, two-colored”).

N. 5. “But the purple one.” Some add “red parchments,” but Isidore seems to have intended to count these among the purple ones.

## CHAPTER XII

### Note 1. “On the elephant’s entrails”

Lipsius, in his letter *On Distinction and Punctuation*, infers from this passage of Isidore that books were composed according to fixed measures, so that the number of verses or lines in each work might more easily be determined. For the ancients counted works by verses and were accustomed to note how many thousands of verses a book contained. See below, chapter 14, note 7.

But, as he observes, a verse may also explain short divisions, and the sections may have been arranged in this way, almost as in our Bibles. Many understand “a book of ivory,” or one ornamented and embellished with ivory, to be the book about which Vopiscus writes in *Tacitus*, chapter 8: “The Ulpian Library has in its sixth cabinet an ivory book in which this senatorial decree has been written out in full.”

Others think that Isidore’s “ivory books” were so called because they were made from elephants’ entrails. Others believe that the name was given to enormous books because of their size and bulk. The practice of writing on mallow leaves is attributed to the Hebrews, and that of writing on palm leaves to the Egyptians. Compare Hermann Hugo with Trotzius’s notes, and the *Acts of the Academy of Barcelona*, p. 309.

### Note 2. “We know the airy…”

The subject is, I think, Aratus’s poems translated into Latin. A smooth, or rather *laevis*, mallow is flat, not rough. Thus in Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 157, a smooth cabbage is one with extended leaves, as opposed to a curly one.

A Prusian little boat seems to be one from Bithynia, whose king was Prusias. Silius, book XIII, near the end:

> Until he was carried sluggishly to the Prusian shores.

In the oldest Vatican manuscript, no. 5764, concerning which see the *Prolegomena*, chapter 98, no. 13, one reads *quas ignes novimus aerios* (“which we know as airy fires”), apparently an allusion to lamps. But the sense requires something else.

Vulcanius published *quae ignes novimus aeres* (“which we know as bronze fires”) and *Persica vexi* (“I carried Persian [boats]”); but he added this annotation:

> “The old manuscripts read: *Queis ignes novimus aereos*; and shortly afterward, in place of *Persica*, an old manuscript has *Prusiaca*; others have *Pruxaica*.”

### Note 3. “To whom shall I give it,” etc.

More recent editions now read Catullus’s verses:

> To whom shall I give … [lacuna]  
> just now with dry pumice, etc.

They consider this more elegant. See Vulpes’s notes.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Notes 1–2. “Codex, book, volume”

These terms are often confused with one another. The following distinction may be used, if one wishes.

A *codex* is something that contains one work, several works, or even some portion of a large work. A *volume*, strictly speaking, was a written text rolled up in parchment; but the word is found used indiscriminately either for a codex or for some portion of a work divided into several books, just as we now say “in book twenty of the *Etymologies*,” whereas formerly one might say “in volume twenty.”

*Book* sometimes had the meaning it has today, namely, a portion of the many divisions into which a work was separated; at other times it meant the work as a whole. Thus one might say “in the tenth book of the work *Etymologies*,” or “in the tenth volume of the *Etymologies*.” It would be pointless to cite examples from ancient authors, since they are apparent in the lexicons. See Forcellini, under *volumen*.

### Note 3. “Volumes of books made from trees”

Montfaucon, in *Antiquity Explained*, book V, chapter 5, volume III, part II, says that he does not approve what Isidore asserts here: that books made from trees are older than books made from parchment. For, he says, the antiquity of parchment is so great that its origin cannot be investigated.

But he could have observed that this very thing had been transmitted before Isidore by Jerome, Pliny, and Varro. See note 1 to chapter 11 of this book.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Note 1. “The same, and antiquarians”

In printed editions and manuscripts one encounters *idem* for *iidem*, a usage that I have also noticed in the works of others. Poets indeed commonly use *idem* as a contraction for *iidem*. But I believe *iidem* to be more appropriate to prose.

On the antiquarian art, one may consult Jerome, letter 6, to Florentius. In the Theodosian Code, book 4, title 8, law 2, the emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian prescribe as follows:

> We order that four Greeks and three Latins skilled in writing be selected as antiquarians to prepare the books of the library, or to repair them because of their age.

Sometimes, however, *antiquarius* means any librarian or copyist, as in Augustine, Sidonius, and others.

### Note 3. “Reed pen and quill”

In Ducange’s *Supplement*, *penna*, meaning a writing reed, is, following Mabillon’s opinion in the *Supplement to the Diplomatic Arts*, p. 51, assigned to the reign of Louis the Pious, in the ninth century, as though its use in writing seems to have begun at that time. This is very surprising, since Isidore’s words are so clear.

It is not established that Latins older than Isidore used the word *penna* in this sense; for in some of the passages cited, *penna* means not a writing instrument but wings. The paintings in which a quill is placed in the hands of ancient authors merely show that the painter fashioned the image according to the custom of his own time.

A passage from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, provides clearer evidence for the antiquity of the writing quill:

> Then the sacred scribe comes forward, having quills on his head, a book in his hands, a little vessel containing writing ink, and a reed with which they usually write.

The quills on the head may perhaps derive from a custom that still survives and is described by John in the *Life of Saint Odo*, book I, no. 20:

> He saw a quill, as is the custom of a scribe, hanging above his ear and sharpened to a point as though by the skill of a teacher, etc.

I am still uncertain, however, whether Clement meant something else; for besides the quills on the head he mentions a reed with which they usually write. Consult the aforementioned Hermann Hugo with Trotzius’s notes, and the *Acts of the Academy of Barcelona*, p. 372.

### Note 4. “Reed pen”

The word is Greek. Among older Latin writers, *calare* meant “to call,” “to name,” or “to invoke”; among later writers it meant “to place,” “to lower,” “to loosen,” or “to descend.” In Italian, *calare* is used for “to descend” and “to lower.”

### Note 5. “The quill, however, from hanging”

Others derive *penna* from the Greek word πτερόν (*pteron*, “wing”), or πετεινός (*peteinos*, “flying”).

### Note 6. “Leaves of books”

You will not easily find *folia* used among the ancients, except that Hardouin, from manuscripts, restored in Pliny, book XXXVII, chapter 7, *chartarum folia ad se rapere* (“to draw the leaves of the papers toward himself”), where previously *fila* (“threads”) was read instead of *folia* (“leaves”).

In Isidore, *folium* comprised at least two parts joined to each other, which he calls pages; and most of the other testimonies concerning pages can probably be referred to this.

### Note 7. “Verses”

Here the word is understood as a line of writing. *Versus* has another meaning when it refers to the shorter divisions of a text, as in the sacred Scriptures; I discussed these verses in chapter 12, note 1.

There exists a dissertation by Peter Holmius on writing and on the various methods of writing—to the right, to the left, from above, or in any other direction—published at Lund in Scania in 1670, in octavo, and reprinted in the *Philological Miscellanies* edited by Thomas Crenius in the Netherlands in 1699, in octavo. Consult also Bochart, book I of *Canaan*, chapter 20.

### Note 8

What Isidore has so far discussed concerning writing and books has provided others with material for treating the entire subject at greater length and composing works of considerable scope.

Fabricius accurately lists such writers in his *Bibliography*, chapter 21, no. 8: namely, those who write about the writing of the ancients; ancient Roman scribes and notaries; chartularies; keepers of book-chests; librarians; antiquarians; booksellers; the arrangement of volumes; the books of the ancients; the various equipment of the book trade; the ornamentation of ancient codices; diptychs; libraries; and so forth.

## CHAPTER XV

### Note 1. “Canons”

The Venetian cardinal Thomasius, volume I of the Vezzosian edition of his works, pp. 315 ff., published the Eusebian canons, translated by Saint Jerome, from Roman manuscript codices, with various readings and notes appended.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Note 1. “By Braulio, who interpolated this work”

I do not at all agree with Grial, who believes that Braulio interpolated this work, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 51, no. 12.

Isidore himself, therefore, composed this chapter from the preface to the genuine collection of the councils of Spain, whether he himself was the author of that collection, or at least of its preface, or whether he was not.

When note 10 says that the acts of the councils are contained in this work, it does allude to the collection of canons itself. But the words were either carelessly inserted by Isidore’s copyist while transcribing the entire passage, or Isidore likewise intended them not to be removed from the surrounding context because, as I believe, he indicated the place from which he had drawn the words. In this way anyone could easily understand that the acts of the councils were contained not in the *Etymologies* but in the collection of canons.

I believe that this indication was omitted through the negligence of copyists. See *Isidoriana*, chapter 51, no. 16.

What Gratian took from this chapter, in canon 1 and 2 of distinction 3 and canon 1 of distinction 15, Berardus has already compared; he is cited in *Isidoriana*, chapter 32, no. 30. In Gratian’s decree, instead of *pravumque quid corrigat* (“and correct whatever is wrong”), a different reading is added: *pravum quiquid corrigat*.

### Note 5. “The four Gospels”

Isidore himself compared the four Gospels with the four rivers of Paradise in the prefaces, under the title “On the Four Gospels.”

### “Showing that there remain,” etc.

Thus the Roman correctors read it in Gratian’s decree, although in some manuscript copies one found *manere in Christo duas naturas, et unam Domini nostri Jesu Christi personam* (“that two natures and one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remain in Christ”).

### Note 10. “Whose acts,” etc.

Why Grial considered these words alien to this passage, I explained at note 1. Most codices agree in this reading. The Vatican manuscript 5764, discussed in *Isidoriana*, chapter 98, no. 13, differs slightly:

> Whose acts, begun in this body, are contained in it.

### Note 12. “They treated. Hence also the council”

Between *tractabant* (“they treated”) and *unde* (“hence”), Grial placed an asterisk, moved by some reason unknown to me.

The Roman correctors of Gratian’s decree, in distinction 15, canon 1, note that this passage is corruptly read in the *Etymologies*. They then produce the words of the preface to the Paris edition of the councils, which is the interpolated preface of Isidore Mercator. Finally, they observe that there are many variations in Gratian’s manuscripts, from which the reading that seemed better was retained, although perhaps something is still missing.

Grial referred to this in his note. Gratian’s canon, compared with our text, reads as follows:

> The name of a council, however, … they treated. Hence *CONCILIUM* (“council”) is said from common intention, as though *CONSILIUM* (“counsel”); *CONCILIUM* as though *CONSIDIUM*, with *d* passing into the letter *l*; or *CONCILIUM* is said from common intention, because all direct the gaze of their minds toward one point. For the eyelashes belong to the eyes; hence those who disagree among themselves do not hold a council, because they do not consent to one thing. Therefore it is also called a gathering, because people gather together there; just as a group is named from gathering, so also a council is named from the association of many into one.

In the preface to the genuine collection of the canons of Spain, in Vatican manuscript 1341, these words are given more briefly:

> The name of a council is derived from common intention, because all direct the gaze of their minds toward one point. For the eyelashes belong to the eyes. Hence those who disagree among themselves do not hold a council, because they do not perceive one thing. “A gathering,” etc.

As in our text, this continues up to *nuncupatus* (“called”), followed by:

> because everyone gathers there, just as a gathering is a group, or a council is the association of many into one.

The preface ends.

In Vatican manuscript 5764, the variant reading is:

> Hence *CONCILIUM* [is] *CONSILIUM*, with *c* passing into the letter *s*;

instead of which most manuscripts have:

> Hence *CONSIDIUM* [is] *CONSILIUM*, with *d* passing into the letter *l*.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Note 1. “The paschal cycle”

The Alexandrian Church was regarded in a certain sense as the mother of the doctrine of the paschal cycle, since among the Egyptians expertise in this calculation seemed to have been handed down from ancient times, as Saint Leo the Great says in letter 64, to the emperor Marcian.

Our friend Raimundus Diosdado confirms this with many arguments in his excellent work, still in manuscript, *Critical Marcology*, in the dissertation on the Alexandrian catechetical school.

Braulio commends the diligence of Isidore and others in arranging the paschal cycle in letter 22, volume XXX of *Hispania Sacra*, where he discusses the paschal feast:

> For thus our ancient forefathers prescribed: Theophilus to the emperor Theodosius; his successor Cyril; Dionysius; Proterius to Pope Leo; likewise Paschasinus [perhaps Paschasius]; and the others, whose mention would be lengthy. But also the distinguished man of our own time, Isidore of Seville. Nor do I believe that in so great and necessary a matter they could have gone wrong through neglect of diligence and labor.

Many have written much about Hippolytus, bishop, and his cycle. But above all one should consult the most illustrious prelate Simon de Magistris in his work *Acts of the Martyrs at Ostia on the Tiber under Claudius Gothicus*, from a manuscript of the Royal Library of Turin, Rome, 1795. It is preceded by fifteen dissertations on Saint Hippolytus and his works.

The seventh dissertation is entirely devoted to Hippolytus’s paschal cycle. In dissertation 13, chapter 5, the episcopate of Portus is asserted for that same Saint Hippolytus. See also the two dissertations of Francesco Bianchini of Verona, on Caesar’s calendar and cycle, and on the paschal canon of Saint Hippolytus the martyr.

### Note 3. “The cycle”

Joannes Vander Haagen, volume II, p. 239, describes and explains Isidore’s paschal cycle from Vulcanius’s edition. He observes that this cycle begins in the year 627 and ends in 721.

He notes that the signs of the leap year, which are the letters *B*, are advanced by one year. He also notes an error in the first year of the first cycle: moon 20 instead of moon 21; and in the first year of the fourth cycle: the third day before the Ides of April instead of the fourth day before the Ides of April.

In the very old Toledo codex there is indeed this variation, namely the fourth day before the Ides of April instead of the third, as in the printed editions, including Grial’s. In some manuscripts I found, in the first year of the first cycle, moon 21 instead of moon 20.

Nevertheless, I retain the cycle table as Grial presents it, so that more knowledgeable readers may judge after comparing the various readings that will shortly be given.

### Note 4. “Cyclic works”

Bentley likewise wishes Horace’s verse to read *scriptor cyclius*, not *cyclicus*; this is supported by the writing of Rabanus, who was copying Isidore. There are nevertheless some who think that *Cyclicus* was a proper name for the poet in Horace.

The ancient scholiast Acron explains his interpretation in these words:

> *Cyclicus*: one who does not know how to vary the order, or one who circulates his poems, like a street performer or mountebank.

Another explanation is that a poet is called *cyclicus* if he composed an entire body, or cycle, of tales or history. See Casaubon, in Athenaeus, book VII, chapter 3.

Isidore’s words, “made in simple form,” refer to the idea that the cyclic poet was one who did not know how to vary the order, as Acron says.

Salmasius, p. 850 of the *Plinian Exercises*, attempts to prove that the epic cycle was a mythological composition gathered from various poems and heroic poets, who had set out mythology in simple form and historical fashion. Hence, he says, a poet was called cyclic if he composed a similar poem.

Andreas Schottus, book II of the *Human Observations*, chapter 1, shows that cyclic poems were so called because one could begin from any verse, whereas the cycle was a particular poem called by that name, concerning which Horace writes:

> Nor will you linger around the cheap and wide-open circle.

Concerning the calendars of the paschal festival, see chapter 5 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. That *laterculum* is neuter in this meaning can scarcely be inferred from anywhere else than Isidore’s words, which correspond to the Greek of Cedrenus, where λατέρκουλον is written.

### Note 5. “Com. … Em.”

The explanation of the common year and the embolismic year—for the latter is indicated by the letters *C* and *E*, or *Com.* and *Em.*—is given in notes 21 and 22.

### Note 10. “The years counted are VMDCCCCXX”

In Grial’s note it was written *computantur anni DXCII* (“the years counted are 592”), for which I corrected it to *anni VMDCCCCXX* (“the years counted are 6,920”); that is how it is read in the printed editions.

After the final words of this note, “the Lord’s Day would not be omitted,” the acts of the Council of Caesarea concerning the equinox are found in the Albanian codex. Baronius and Labbe published them from Bede. They agree with the printed texts in substance and opinion, but are explained by a very different method. We shall therefore present them as Appendix 8, collated with the Ottobonian Codex 122, the more recent Caesena codex, and the copy that Muratori published in his anonymous work on the paschal cycle among the *Anecdota*.

### Note 11. “The word Pascha”

Becman, under *Pascha*, says:

> Its origin, he says, is not Greek, from πάσχω (“to suffer”), as the monks sang, or as others have contrived from some play on words, but Hebrew, etc.

There is certainly no reason to say that the monks contrived a Greek origin for *Pascha*. The words of the Gospel in the Vulgate are:

> Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.

### Note 12. “Therefore it is observed through the night”

Grial’s note had *dicitur* (“is said”), which I changed to *ducitur* (“is observed” or “is conducted”).

I discussed the most celebrated paschal vigil among the ancients in chapter 12 of the *Prudentiana*, where I explained the title of hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, “On the New Light of Holy Saturday.” But in note a to no. 147 I asserted that Lactantius’s passage was not indicated in the notes to this passage of the *Etymologies*. I now discover that this is certainly false. Perhaps I meant to say that it was not transcribed.

Lactantius’s words are:

> And this is the night that we celebrate by a vigil because of the coming of our King and God. The reason for this night is twofold: on it he received life again when he suffered, and afterward he will receive the kingdom of the whole world.

### Note 14. “Purging out the old leaven”

The Apostle’s words are:

> Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.

### Note 22. “Embolism”

It seems to be derived from ἐμβάλλω, “to insert” or “to interpose,” because in an embolismic year certain days are inserted, or intercalated.

### Same passage

Joannes Vander Haagen, in the place cited, explains Isidore in such a way that embolismic years supply the number of days missing from common years in relation to the solar year.

### Note 28. “To lower”

The verb *calare*, meaning “to place,” was discussed in chapter 14, note 4.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Note 1. “From *sollus*, that is, firm”

Others derive *sollemne* from ὅλος (“whole”) and σεμνός (“venerable”); others from *solus* (“alone”) and *annus* (“year”).

On ancient inscriptions and in the best authors, the word is written *sollemnis*, *solemnis*, and *solennis*. See Noris, *Pisan Cenotaph*, dissertation, and the final chapter.

Fabricius lists in his *Bibliography*, chapter 10, those who have illuminated the question of which Christian festivals were celebrated.

### Note 2. “Celebrated, from celestial”

The etymology is uncertain. But what Scaliger and other critics say—that *celebris* is perhaps *calabris*, from *calare*, “to call,” “to assemble,” and so forth—is perhaps no more correct.

### Notes 6–7. “Epiphany”

The Church celebrates these three events on the same day of Epiphany, as is clear from the liturgy: Christ’s adoration by the Magi, the sacrament of the Lord’s baptism, and the miracle of the water changed into wine.

Isidore discusses these same solemn feasts at greater length in book I of *On the Offices*, beginning with chapter 10, “On the Nativity of the Lord,” and so forth. There one may observe—as I have often noted—that Isidore continually draws both ideas and words not only from the works of others but also from his own.

### Note 9. “Scenopegia”

The same etymology of *scenopegia* is found in book XVIII, chapter 43.

### Note 10. “Neomenia”

In the Vulgate the psalm reads:

> Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the appointed day of your solemn feast.

### Note 12. “Encaenia”

In nearly the same words, *encaenia* is explained in book I of *The Offices*, chapter 36.

### Note 14. “Capitilavium”

Brissonius, who frequently uses Isidore’s authority in relation to the law of Dominicus concerning spectacles, observes on p. 269, from Saint Ambrose, that it was customary for the heads of those baptized to be anointed. From this he explains the custom that had become established in Spain of washing the heads of infants who were to be anointed.

The following verses by an uncertain author, concerning the baptism of Bebianus, may perhaps refer to the same washing, volume VI of the *Collection of Poets of Pesaro*, p. 250:

> He believed the one who prayed, and the bishop, girded with a pure stream,  
> poured over him, thirsty, the rivers of life.

From the words of Saint Augustine, to be cited in the note to chapter 28 of book I of *The Offices*, it is clear that the same custom prevailed in Africa, but on a different day.

In the Roman Order, Palm Sunday, as in Spain, is called *capitilavium*. Compare also Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, Papias, and others.

### Note 15. “On this day, the symbol of the competentes”

In the Roman Order, Palm Sunday is also called *Pascha petitum* (“the requested Passover”) and *Dominica Competentium* (“the Sunday of the Competentes”).

### Note 19. “The Lord’s Day”

Brissonius gathers much learned material concerning the Lord’s Day in his commentary on the law of Dominicus concerning spectacles in the Theodosian Code, drawing on Isidore and other Fathers.

## CHAPTER XIX

### Note 4. “If any catechumen,” etc.

Cotelerius infers from the author of the *Life of Saint Martial*, volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 259, that it was the duty of deacons to address the people in this way.

Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 23, seems to indicate that the *missa* properly meant the action by which the catechumens were sent outside. I therefore understand canon 1 of the Council of Valence of the year 546 as follows:

> When we were discussing ecclesiastical discipline and rereading the ancient canons, among other things we judged this to be observed: that the sacred Gospels be read after the Apostle, before the offering of the gifts, or at the dismissal of the catechumens, in the order of the readings, so that the saving commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ, or the sermon of the priest, might be heard not only by the faithful but also by catechumens, penitents, and all those who come from different conditions. For we clearly know that, after hearing the preaching of the pontiffs, some were drawn to the faith.

Flórez, volume III of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 226, says that, following the older editions, one should read *ante munerum illationem in missa catechumenorum* (“before the offering of the gifts, in the dismissal of the catechumens”), or else delete *catechumenorum* if one reads, with Loaysa, *ante munerum illationem, vel missam* (“before the offering of the gifts, or the dismissal”).

He thinks that Isidore here understands *missa* as referring to the sacraments of the altar, which catechumens cannot attend. But from the context it is clear that the dismissal of the catechumens was called *missa*. Subsequently, the name *missa* became attached to the remaining portions and, specifically, to the first prayer, which is an exhortation addressed to the people to urge them to pray to God.

See Lesleus’s note on the Isidorian Missal, p. 509.

### Note 5. “Others derive *chorus* from harmony”

It is perhaps not unreasonable to derive *chorus* from *corona* (“crown”), since among the ancients a crown was called στέφανος χορωνός (*stephanos choronos*). Although this rather proves that *corona* comes from *chorus* than that *chorus* comes from *corona*. Compare chapter 3 of book I of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, and the note there.

### Note 6. “In Latin, *sincinium*”

It is written *sincinium*, *sicinium*, and *sicinnium*. The word’s etymology is derived from *sine* (“without”) and *cano* (“I sing”), because it was singing without accompanying pipes. Others derive it from *se* and *cano*.

In the Arabic-Latin glossary, *sicinium* is a word meaning a kind of solitary song—that is, when one person sings—which the Greeks call *monody*. In Aelfric’s Saxon glossary:

> *Monodia*, *latersicinium*, as though *solicinium*.

From this it may be inferred that *sicinium* is something like *solicinium*.

### Note 13. “The first assistant cantor”

In book VII, chapter 12, the *praecentor*, *succentor*, and *concentor*, who is the *accentor*, are arranged in this order. The *praecentor* also seems to be the same as the *incentor*. Certainly, the conjecture is strongly confirmed by that chapter 12.

### Note 14. “Some wish *diapsalma* to be Hebrew”

*Diapsalma* is indeed a Greek word. But perhaps Isidore, or someone before him, intended to say that the Greeks corruptly derived *diapsalma* from the Hebrew word *sela*, meaning “always.”

Becman discusses at greater length the various meanings of *sela*, or *saelah*, on p. 932. See also Nicolas du Mortier, in the *Sacred Greek-Latin Etymology*, under *diapsalma*.

### Note 17. “A song of those praising”

I prefaced my *Hymnody of Spain* with a dissertation on ecclesiastical hymns.

### Note 18. “A lament”

On laments, see book I, chapter 39, no. 19.

### Note 19. “Alleluia … praise of God”

At the beginning of the Bignaean edition are certain fragments of Saint Isidore that seem to belong to his *Etymologies*. The last of them begins:

> “Alleluia” means in Latin, etc.

Certain Hebrew words are explained, such as *alleluia*, *amen*, *diapsalma*, and *hosanna*, or *osanna*. The same fragments are repeated by Braulio after the *Etymologies*. The fragment beginning “Alleluia,” which pertains to this chapter, will be placed among the appendices as no. 9.

### Note 22. “Osianna”

In the Vulgate it is written *Hosanna*. Thomas Malvenda is said to have composed a dissertation on the Hebrew word *hosanna* in the *Hispanic Library* of Nicolás Antonio.

Peter Lazerus discusses the various meanings of the same word in his note on the commentary of Saint Bruno of Asti on Matthew, no. 85.

### Note 26. “Gifts properly divine”

This distinction between *donum* (“gift”) and *munus* (“offering” or “service”) is not generally recognized; certainly both words are used interchangeably.

Paulus, in the *Digest*, final book, penultimate title, law 194, and Marcianus, in the same place, law 214, distinguish *donum* and *munus* as genus and species. They say that a *munus* is a gift given for some reason, whereas a *donum* is offered voluntarily, without necessity, legal obligation, or duty.

The *donaria*, however, discussed in the following note, are usually understood specifically as gifts offered in temples. Isidore seems to express the opinion of the grammarian Donatus, who, commenting on Terence’s words in the *Eunuch*—“whatever gift and reward you wish from me”—writes:

> A gift is a reward, and an offering is a reward; but a gift is a reward given to the gods, while an offering is a reward given to human beings.

### Note 30. “That which is dedicated”

From Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4, no. 121:

> *Dedicare* is *dicere* (“to say”).

From Cornelius Fronto, column 1329 of the *Latin Authors*:

> It is dedicated to God; it is consecrated, as though it were made holy.

That is, something is dedicated to God when it is owed to him; it is consecrated when what is profane is made holy. For other distinctions, see Forcellini, under *dedico*.

### Same passage

A. Augustinus’s conjecture is pleasing, since Festus derives the word’s etymology from *mola*:

> To immolate is to sprinkle a victim with *mola*, that is, ground spelt, and salt, and to consecrate it.

But it would be better to restore the passage as follows: “because on the *mola* placed upon the altar,” etc.

### Note 33. “Victims among the ancients”

Barthius refers here to the remarkable statement of John Scotus, who used *hostiae* to mean hostile forces or resources:

> And he carried away splendid furnishings from the slain enemies.

See the *Adversaria*, book LVII, chapter 12, column 2704.

The etymology Isidore uses is taken from Servius on *Aeneid* I, verse 338, as Grial indicated. But Servius himself, on *Aeneid* II, verse 155, also derives *hostia* from *hostire*, because *hostire* means “to appease.” Others, with Festus, derive it from *hostire*, meaning “to strike.”

Moreover, Ovid, *Fasti*, book I, verse 335, distinguishes the terms as follows:

> The victim that fell by the victorious right hand is called *victima*.  
>   
> Once the enemies have been removed [another reading: “subdued”], it receives the name *hostia*.

### Same passage

In volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 56, in the canonical letter of Saint Barnabas, the words are taken from Isaiah, chapter 1, verse 11:

> I am full of the holocausts of rams and the fat of lambs.

Compare the note in Ducange’s *Supplement*, under *holocaustoma*, and Du Mortier, under *holocautoma*; for that is how he writes it.

### Note 36. “Ceremonies”

Some write *cerimoniae*, others *ceremoniae*, and others *caeremoniae*. On some inscriptions it is engraved as *caerimonia*.

Prudentius wrote it without a diphthong in the preface to book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 5:

> So that the pagan people might reject, once God was acknowledged,  
> their savage ceremonies.

When Forcellini says that Prudentius, a generally poor observer of prosody, shortened the first two syllables of *ceremonias*, this should be understood as meaning that Prudentius followed the usage of his own time, which differed in many respects from the ancient custom.

The shortening of the first syllable in *cerimonia* is also supported by the etymology from *carere* (“to lack”), as confirmed by Masurius Sabinus in Gellius, book IV, chapter 9; Servius Sulpicius in Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 3; and Augustine, book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 37.

Those who derive *ceremoniae* from Ceres support the same view, since the first syllable is short both in *carere* and in *Ceres*. There is no time to pursue the other etymologies devised by others.

### Note 38. “Sacrifice, so called as though ‘a sacred act’”

Heretics have invented the claim that this passage of Isidore has been corrupted, as though Catholics had omitted certain words contrary to their doctrine of the Eucharist. I refuted that slander in *Isidoriana*, chapter 30.

Catholic doctrine concerning the Eucharist is confirmed by a document recently brought to light: the Theban fragment on the real presence of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Eucharistic sacrifice, from the distinguished codex of the Borgian Museum concerning the *Lives of the Fathers*. It appears in the work *On the Miracles of Saint Coluthus*, etc., edited by the learned P. Augustine Antonius Georgius, Rome, 1793, p. 57.

### Note 39. “The sacrament is in some celebration”

Heretics also abuse these words, concluding that there are only two sacraments. I answered them in the cited chapter 30 of the *Prolegomena*.

### Note 40. “Which are therefore called sacraments”

Varro, book V of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 16:

> *Sacramentum* comes from *sacrum* (“sacred”).

See book V, chapter 24, final section, and Havercamp’s note on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 2.

Isidore indicated another etymology, from hidden powers, in the title of his *Exposition of the Old Testament*. Ildefonsus refers to this in his eulogy of Isidore:

> He also collected from various authors what he himself calls “expositions of the secrets of the sacraments.”

### Note 42. “Hence, whether through good or bad ministers”

Theologians distinguish the matter as follows: the sacrament is valid even when conferred by an unworthy minister, but the minister confers it unlawfully if stained by mortal sin.

See Saint Thomas, part III, question 64, articles 5, 6, and 9, and Suárez there, section 4, where he asks whether the holiness, goodness, or faith of the minister is necessary for the conferral of a sacrament.

### Note 50. “Chrism”

Here it is plainly shown that the sacrament of baptism is distinguished from the sacrament of confirmation, contrary to the opinion of the heretics who perversely twist Isidore’s words to support their heresy.

Yet he does not explain all the sacraments distinctly in this passage. Although he mentions chrism, or anointing, he does not explicitly include extreme unction.

Theologians have already noted that the Fathers sometimes omitted explanations of those sacraments about which there was no controversy at the time. Some people were surprised that the surviving monuments of the Gothic Church contain no clear mention of extreme unction.

But this is not at all surprising. Since no question had been raised, they prescribed nothing particular concerning this sacrament in their canons, especially since the genuine collection of the canons of the Gothic Church contained the letter of Innocent I to Decentius of Gubbio, in which Catholic doctrine concerning the sacrament of extreme unction is clearly transmitted.

Isidore also cites some words from this letter in book II of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 27.

### Note 53. “And the one who is not said to have been a sinner”

Rabanus, as I believe, read these words of Isidore—“and the one who is not said to have been a sinner,” etc.—but since many people held the opinion that Mary Magdalene and the sinful woman were the same person, an opinion which Rabanus himself may perhaps also have held, he wished those words to be omitted.

Some distinguish three Marys, whom others regard as one and the same woman: Mary the sister of Martha, Mary Magdalene, and the Mary who is called a sinner in the Gospel.

### Note 55. “Conjuration,” etc., and the following note, “to conjure”

In some places *adjurare* (“to adjure”) may perhaps be read with the same meaning. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXII, chapter 6, observes that Peter Pithaeus, book II of the *Adversaria*, chapter 8, noted from Isidore that a later age explained *adjurare* as “to exorcise.” Barthius shows that the word was drawn from deep antiquity from Gratius’s *Cynegeticon*, where he writes:

> And they adjure the herbs with magical songs.

Barthius adds that in this passage of Isidore the published books read *conjurare*, not *adjurare*, and that his own manuscript agrees with this, together with two very ancient editions, which he possessed in his cabinets as faithfully as though they were parchment originals.

Pithaeus perhaps intended to indicate book VII, chapter 12, no. 31:

> Exorcists are called *ADJURANTES*, or “those who rebuke,” from the Greek translated into Latin.

In the words of Zachariah, the Vulgate adds *Dominus* (“the Lord”):

> And the Lord showed me Jesus, etc.

### Note 59. “To pray is to ask”

Suárez explains in what sense we are forbidden by Christ to pray in public in *On Religion*, volume II, book III, chapter 7, where he discusses the circumstances to be observed in vocal prayer, such as place, time, and so forth.

### Note 62. “For first,” etc.

I discussed the three hours at which prayer is to be offered—the third, sixth, and ninth—in my commentary on Prudentius, hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 86:

> You, best Father, at the new morning, etc.

There, following the opinion of the learned Giovenazzi, I noted that this passage of Isidore appears to require correction: *communitatis omnis* (“of the whole community”) instead of *communicationis* (“of communication”).

Isidore is describing Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 25, which Muratori published among his miscellanies, volume III. Tertullian’s words are:

> As for the time, there will also be an outward observance that is not useless, even of certain hours—I mean those common hours that mark the intervals of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth, which are found to be more solemn in Scripture. First [I correct *primum* from Isidore], the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the assembled disciples at the third hour. Peter, on the day when he experienced the vision of the whole community [Isidore’s copies less correctly have *communicationis*] in that vessel, had gone up at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer. Likewise, with John, he went to the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to health.

Perhaps Isidore encountered a copy of Tertullian in which *communicationis* stood instead of *communitatis omnis*. But the latter is certainly better.

### Note 63. “Let us worship three times a day”

The *Apostolic Constitutions*, 24:

> Pray three times a day.

That this was done in honor of the Most Holy Trinity may be inferred from Theodoret, letter 145:

> But also food, etc.

See the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, “Before Food.”

### Note 65. *Jejunium* … *jejunum*

Celsus, book IV, chapter 1, says this about the empty intestine: “It has this name because it never retains what it receives, but immediately passes it on to the lower parts.” Thus *jejunium* (“fasting”) was not named from the empty intestine; rather, the intestine is called *jejunum* because it is, in a certain sense, empty and vacant.

### Note 66. “But also fasting and the station”

Ambrose, sermon 25: “Our fasts are our camps, which defend us from the devil’s assault. Hence they are called ‘stations,’ because by standing and remaining in them we repel the enemies lying in wait.”

### Note 67. “Some distinguish between fasting and the station”

At times *jejunium* and *statio* are used interchangeably. Tertullian distinguishes them in book II *To His Wife*: “So, if a station is to be held, let the husband arrange to go to the baths during the day; if fasts are to be observed, let the husband hold banquets on that same day.” Against the Psychics, the same Tertullian says in chapter 14: “Why do we call the fourth and sixth days of the week stations, but the day of Preparation fasts?”

The theological questions of the priest Auxilius are said to exist in the Casinensian library; in them he asks what difference there is between a station and a fast. Stations were also called “half-fasts.” I do not know where Isidore obtained the claim that fasting on the fourth and sixth days of the week had been commanded by the Old Law. The Pharisees certainly fasted twice in the Sabbath, that is, every week, as may be gathered from Luke; but neither is it established that they fasted on fixed days, nor was that fasting prescribed by the Law. See Sigonius, book IV *On the Republic of the Hebrews*, chapter 18.

Peter of Alexandria, chapter 15, gives the reason why the ancient Christians observed the fourth and sixth days of the week as stations: “The fourth day, because the Jews then began their plot to betray the Lord; the sixth, because he himself suffered for us.” Saint Augustine’s *Letter 86 to Casulanus* agrees with this. See Selvaggius, *Institutions of Christian Antiquity*, book II, part II, chapter 8, § 3.

[Col. 0905B] ### Note 69. “Around the boundary of the Lord’s Passion”

Thus some, especially the Greeks. By others, the week of the Passion is included within Lent. See Cotelerius, on the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 316.

### Note 71. “Penance”

Penance is treated more fully in book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 13.

### Note 75. “Exomologesis”

See volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 98. Cotelerius, in his note on book II of the *Shepherd of Hermas*, Mandate 10, divides *exomologesis* into confession of sins and praise; concerning this second sense he explains the words of Hermas: “And he does not make *exomologesis* beforehand.”

### Note 80. “But litanies,” etc.

These words are cited by the Council of Mainz of the year 813, canon 32, up to the words “it is found in the designation.” The canon reads *agantur* (“let them be performed”) and *indicantur* (“let them be indicated”). Saint Martin of León, volume III, p. 3, copies these same words through the end of the chapter, with some changes, such as: “Litanies, however, are commanded to be performed in order to entreat God and obtain his mercy in some matter.”

The same Martin treats the institution of litanies, or rogations, in the same work, pp. 37 and 40, where he says: “In certain churches during those three days a figure of a dragon is carried in the litanies, sometimes before the cross, sometimes behind the cross, etc.” A nearly identical custom is still retained in certain churches of Spain during the processions performed on the feast of the Most Holy Body of Christ.

[Col. 0905C] ### Note 82. “For the *feriae* are either lawful,” etc.

Understand this as meaning that supplications—or, which amounts to the same thing, *supplicia*—are so called from *supplex* (“suppliant”). But because, when a citizen was put to death, his property became sacred and the king of sacred rites went out into the forum for the purpose of making supplication, *supplicium* thereafter came to mean a capital punishment, and every more severe form of chastisement or torture.

# BOOK SEVEN

## Chapter I. Number 1. “Interpretations of Hebrew names”

The Hieronymian interpretations of Hebrew names, which Isidore excerpted, have been learnedly elucidated by Martianaeus and Vallarsius. At times, as often happens in the etymologies of Latin words, we must admit that they are forced; but not to such an extent that either Jerome or Isidore can properly be blamed, since they followed the practice of other learned men.

For the names of God, one should consult, among the ancients, Irenaeus, Origen, Epiphanius, Evagrius, Theodoret, and Photius; among more recent writers, Petavius, Ludovicus of León, and the others listed by Fabricius in chapter 8, number 8, of the *Bibliography*.

### Note 9. “Quintus Elius … exalted”

In composition, *ex-* sometimes signifies increase and perfection, as in *exclamo* (“I cry out”) and *exaudio* (“I hear fully”), but not always.

### Note 10. “This name … does not have death”

Isidore truly took this passage from Jerome, Letter 136. Petavius, volume I, book I of the *Theology*, chapter 6, number 8, doubts whether the derivation of the proper name from Exodus is sufficiently solid. Ambrose, after all, thinks that it is not the name of God but the reality expressed by the name that is meant.

### Note 11. “For when he asked what his name was”

The words of Exodus are: “God said to Moses: ‘I am who I am.’ He said: ‘Thus you shall say,’” etc.

### Note 18. “Immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable, eternal”

On these attributes of God, as theologians call them, compare the first chapters of book I of the *Sentences*, together with the notes.

### Note 23. “No one has ever seen God”

The same words also occur in the Gospel of John, chapter 1, verse 18.

### Note 35. “There are also certain terms”

This same doctrine is transmitted in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 1, to which Loaisa’s fuller notes are appended.

### Note 39. “Psalm 103”

“Deep waters, like a garment, are his covering”: thus the Vulgate. And in Psalm 138: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there.”

## Chapter II. Numbers 1 and 2. “Christ may also be called by many names”

I have partly indicated and partly transcribed the ancient verses concerning the titles of the Savior in my note on Sedulius’s *Elegy*, verse 104. The verses of Silvius, which I then said existed in Goldast’s *Biblical Manual*, are found under the name of that same Silvius in Vatican Codex 553.

[Col. 0906B] In his book *Differences of Things*, distinction 7, Isidore also explains certain names attributed to the Son of God. In the Isidorian breviary, p. CX of the second edition, there is a hymn “At the Ordination of a King,” in which chrism is mentioned:

> But, O Christ, by chrism …  
> Advance the kingdom of the faithful  
> Prince to glory;  
> Let him shine with sacred unction …

### Note 3. “For they were gathered together”

In the Vulgate: “For they truly gathered together in this city against your holy servant, whom you anointed.”

### Note 8. “You shall call … because he himself”

In the Vulgate, *ipse enim* (“for he himself”) occurs instead of *quia ipse* (“because he himself”).

### Note 9. “This word does not exist in the Latin language”

Saint Martin of León gives these same words from Isidore, volume II, p. 3. Baronius should also be consulted on the name of the Savior in the *Roman Martyrology*, 27 November; there he criticizes those who prefer to say *Servator* rather than *Salvator*.

Saint Augustine, book XIII *On the Trinity*, chapter 10, preceded Isidore: “In Hebrew, Jesus; in Greek, Σωτήρ (*Sōtēr*), and in our speech, *SALVATOR*.” “This word did not previously exist in the Latin language, but it could exist, just as it did when it wished to.” Before Augustine, the name *Salvator* was used by Tertullian, Lactantius, Juvencus, and others. The same word occurs in an inscription in Gruter, p. 19, no. 5: “To Jupiter Custos Quirinus Salvator, for the safety of Caesar Nerva Trajan,” etc.

### Note 14. “Homousios”

The Greek adverb ὅμως or ὁμοῦ means “together, as one”; and *homousius*, or *homusios*, means “of the same essence, consubstantial.” The Catholics defended three persons in the Trinity as *homousioi* against the Arians, who asserted that the Son was *heterousios*, that is, of a substance different from the Father; and against the Macedonians, who rejected *homousios* but admitted *homoiousios*—that is, “of similar substance”—in a heretical sense, and especially affirmed that the Holy Spirit was a creature.

### Note 29. “Mediator”

This word too is particularly proper to Christians. Apuleius nevertheless used it in book IX of the *Metamorphoses*.

### Note 34. “Angel of the great counsel”

From Isaiah, I think, chapter IX, verse 6, where the Vulgate has: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God,” etc. In the Roman Missal, however, at the third Mass of the Nativity of the Lord, the following is taken from Isaiah chapter IX: “And his name shall be called the Angel of the great counsel.”

### Note 35. “And I came into this world”

In the Vulgate, *hunc* (“this”) is absent before *mundum*: “I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father, and came into the world.”

### Note 40. “For, coming humbly”

Such nominatives absolute used in place of ablatives absolute are not uncommon among medieval writers, including Isidore, especially in old manuscripts. In printed editions, however, correction has generally been applied against the authority of the manuscript codices.

### Note 44. “Eagle”

Isidore omitted certain names of Christ that are mentioned by others. See what I noted on verse 104 of Sedulius’s *Elegy*.

[Col. 0907A] ### Note 46. “Because the Father”

In the Vulgate: “Because the Father is greater than I.”

### Note 48. “Thus the human nature was joined to the Son of God”

In the synodal letter of the Council of Frankfurt of 794, in Labbe, volume VII, column 1039: “Isidore too, in his book of the *Etymologies*: ‘Thus,’ he says, ‘human nature was joined to the Son of God,’ etc.” In our copies, the reading is *conjuncta* (“joined”).

### Note 49. “This is what theologians call the communication of idioms”

Theologians explain this at length.

## Chapter III. Number 1. “The Holy Spirit,” etc.

The whole of this chapter was inserted by Saint Ildefonsus into his book *On Knowledge of Baptism* and divided into several chapters, from chapter 57 through chapter 71. Ildefonsus does not explicitly name Isidore, either because this was then the customary method of excerpting, or because, as we may conjecture, he placed Isidore’s name in the margin and the copyists’ negligence later omitted it.
