Theodulf of Orléans also takes much from this chapter of Isidore in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, volume II of Sirmond’s works, column 1011; so does Saint Martin of León, volume III, pp. 311 ff., though he does not suppress Isidore’s name. Ildefonsus adds: “He himself is the Father, that is, God.” See also chapter 15 of book I of the *Sentences*, which is “On the Holy Spirit,” where much is repeated from this third chapter.

### Note 2. “It is related to something”

Martin has: “The one who breathes is related to something, and certainly,” etc. Ildefonsus has: “That which breathes is related to something; and what breathes certainly breathes by the spirit,” etc.

### Note 3. “That the Spirit”

Perhaps *quod* (“that”) is superfluous.

### Note 4. “Incorporeal nature”

The soul is explicitly taught to be incorporeal in this passage. Some discussion of this occurs in book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24, and book II *On Differences*, chapter 26.

### Note 6. “Lest there be two Fathers,” etc.

Augustine and others present this very argument; Petavius cites them in volume II, book VII of the *Theology*, chapter 14, number 11. Otherwise, if there were no danger of error, the word *ingenitus*, whether understood as “uncreated” or as “not begotten,” could be applied to the Holy Spirit.

### Note 7. “I still have many things that”

Theodulf reads: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” Martin of León, together with the Vulgate, has: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” This is less suitable for proving the procession of the Holy Spirit.

### Note 8. “But whoever”

The Vulgate: “But if anyone,” etc. This very clear testimony of Isidore for the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was not omitted at the Council of Florence, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 31, number 14.

### Note 11. “Then the children will mourn,” etc.

The Vulgate: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

### Note 13. “Sevenfold”

These are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit mentioned by Isaiah, chapter XI, verses 2–3: “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” On these matters, see the theologians, together with Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* I–II, question 68.

### Note 14. “God is spirit”

The Vulgate has John’s words: “God is Spirit.” In Psalm 50: “Have mercy on me, O God,” etc. Verse 12: “And renew a right spirit within me.” Verse 13: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” Verse 14: “Strengthen me with your principal Spirit.” Many understand all these expressions of the third person of the Trinity, so that the same Spirit is called “right,” “holy,” and “principal.”

Lorinus lists the Fathers who understand the Trinity in the “principal Spirit,” the “right Spirit,” and the “Holy Spirit”: Cassiodorus, Haimo, both Brunos, and Bernard, who may perhaps have learned this from Jerome in chapter IV of the Epistle to the Galatians.

[Col. 0908A] ### Note 17. “Are given”

*Donantur* is used by approved writers instead of *condonantur*. Hence the word *perdono* (“I forgive”) in certain vernacular languages. The sanctification of the just is attributed to the Holy Spirit in Sacred Scripture and by the holy Fathers.

But whether indwelling in the just through charity, and personal presence, belong specifically to the person of the Holy Spirit or are common to the three persons is asked by Petavius, volume II of the *Dogmatic Theology*, book VIII, chapter 6, number 5. He concludes that the Holy Spirit is joined to, and present within, those whom he makes holy in a proper and singular manner.

Elsewhere. In the Vulgate: “In the Spirit of God I cast out demons.”

### Note 22. “It lacks gall”

I discussed this popular belief in my note on book II of Sedulius’s *Paschal Poem*, verse 171: “Through the bird that lacks gall.”

### Note 24. “For the instruction of the faithful”

In Grialius and other printed editions, the reading was *eruditione* (“by instruction”); I restored *eruditioni* (“for the instruction”), which the sense requires, since *e* and *i* are often interchanged in manuscripts.

### Note 26. “As many … so great, instead of as many, so many”

Grialius wondered why mention of hair had been introduced here, because he did not attend to the usage of the ancient Latins, especially the poets, who also attributed hair and locks to fire. Valerius Flaccus, book I, verse 205:

> When fire, struggling through the pliant entrails,  
> brought forth a lock of hair …

I have indicated examples of others in my note on book III of Dracontius’s *On God*, verse 171:

> With fiery locks it supplies scant nourishment.

### Note 27. “In the name of water, the Spirit”

The Vulgate: “If anyone thirsts … If anyone believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this, however, about the Holy Spirit, etc.

### Note 30. “And you have no need”

The Vulgate: “And you have no need … he teaches you about everything.”

## Chapter IV. Number 2. “The same, and three”

See the commentary on the first verse of Prudentius’s *Apotheosis*:

> God is one in supreme being, threefold in form, one in power.

[Col. 0908C] ### Note 3. “Another, not another thing”

Thus Orientius, poem *On the Trinity*: “Not the same, but altogether the same.” Compare the note on Dracontius, book II, verse 105, and on Sedulius, book I, verse 319.

### Note 11. “Three hypostases”

There was formerly a major controversy concerning the word *hypostasis*, namely, whether three hypostases were to be admitted in God. The Latins understood by *hypostasis* nothing other than substance, whereas the Greeks, knowing that *hypostasis* could also mean a suppositum, admitted three hypostases without difficulty.

Certainly, if *hypostasis* is taken to mean that which underlies accidents, it cannot in any way be said of God; nor can *substance* when taken in the same sense. Accordingly, Augustine, book VII *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, taught that God is abusively called a substance. In chapter 9 he adds: “Because our customary way of speaking has now established that what we understand when we say ‘essence’ is understood when we say ‘substance,’ we do not dare to say ‘one essence, three substances,’ but ‘one essence,’ or ‘substance,’ and three persons.”

In the course of time it became established that the word *hypostasis* was not understood by Catholic Greeks as essence or substance, but as person, subsistence, or suppositum. Consult Petavius, book IV *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, number 10 and following.

## Chapter V. Number 1. “Angels are called in Greek”

Much is repeated here about angels from chapter 10 of book I of the *Sentences*. Loaisa’s notes on that chapter 10 are also relevant here.

### Note 3. “For whom, therefore, the license of painters”

On the wings of the winds, see Vulpius on Catullus, poem 65; verses of poets attributing wings to the winds are familiar to everyone. In our Vulgate the reading is: “You who walk.”

### Note 4. “There are nine orders”

The order of the angelic hierarchy is not explained in the same way by everyone, as may be seen in Petavius, volume III of the *Theology*, book II, chapter 3.

### Note 7. “Run and speak”

In the Vulgate: “Run, speak.”

### Note 15. “All of this—Uriel … was commanded—is omitted”

All of this—“Uriel … was commanded”—is omitted in Vatican Codex 5764, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 98, number 16. But since it is read in most codices, including very ancient ones, it is preferable to believe that it was deliberately omitted somewhere by a copyist who thought that Uriel’s name ought to be excluded from the company of the angels.

There was an extremely ancient opinion that Uriel should be admitted among the angels, although some of the ancients attempted to overturn it. I have explained this controversy as far as necessary in my note on number 53 of Appendix 5 to Sedulius. More may be seen in the very learned work of the distinguished Cancellieri, *On the Secretaries of the Ancient Christians*, pp. 1009 ff.

### Note 21. “The thrones are hosts”

Thus many of the ancients cited by Petavius in the place mentioned, number 5.

### Note 30. “Let there be a firmament, and it was called”

In the Vulgate, verse 6: “Let there be a firmament”; and verse 8: “And God called the firmament heaven.”

## Chapter VI. Number 1

Certain matters treated in the books *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* and *Allegories* are relevant here.

### Note 5. “For *calamitas* took its name from falling”

Properly, *calamitas* is the breaking of a crop of reeds or stalks, and a disaster caused by hail or another cause. Thus *calamitas* was derived from *calami* (“stalks, reeds”).

### Note 6. “But others say”

In his *Elegy*, verses 7–8, Sedulius establishes a comparison between Eve and the Mother of God, deriving the origin of death from Eve and that of life from the Mother of God:

> She alone was the woman through whom the gate to death was opened,  
> and she alone was the woman through whom life returns.

### Note 7. “His father said; rather, his mother”

The words of Genesis are: “Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying: ‘I have acquired a man through God.’”

### Note 10. “Then the invocation of the Lord’s name began”

The Vulgate: “This man began to call upon the name of the Lord.” The Jews whom Isidore follows interpret the words of Genesis in this way: “Then the name of the Lord began to be profaned.” Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, prologue 3, follows them. See the explanations of others in Calmet’s *Dictionary*, and in the notes to the French translation of the Bible drawn from various English authors.

### Note 13. “Methuselah is interpreted”

Braulio, Letter 44, volume 30 of *Hispania Sacra*, copies this passage, prefacing it with praise of Isidore: “In our own times, the man of incomparable learning Isidore, bishop of Seville, when he wished to settle the origin of this name, declared as follows: ‘Methuselah,’” etc. For that is how it is written there.

It should also be observed that Grialius in the text, and other printed editions, omit *eum* (“him”) after *enim* (“for”), which I restored from Braulio, and because Grialius himself reports these words in his notes: “For some [say] him with his father.”

### Note 15. “This man will rest”

In the Vulgate: “This man will comfort us from the works and labors of our hands.”

### Note 22. “To build a tower of impiety”

Saint Martin of León likewise has this from Isidore. Saint Augustine, book XVI *On the City of God*, chapter 4, says of the same Nimrod: “He was raising a tower with his peoples against the Lord.” This too is the opinion of others. Compare Calmet’s dissertation on the tower of Babel.

### Note 29. “Sarai”

The Vulgate: “You shall not call Sarai your wife SARAI, but SARAH. And I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son; I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from her.”

### Note 32. “Ishmael”

The Vulgate, verse 11: “You shall call his name ISHMAEL, because the Lord has heard your affliction.” And verse 15: “And Hagar bore Abram a son, whom he called ISHMAEL.” Some write *Ismahel*.

### Note 36. “For very many sorrows”

Perhaps *plures* (“more, many”) should be read instead of *plurimos* (“very many”).

### Note 45. “Mambres”

Calmet, in his literal translation of Hebrew names following the *Biblical Dictionary*, interprets *Mambres* as “sea with poverty” and asserts that the word is Egyptian, not Hebrew. Vallarsius would prefer Jerome’s “clear sea,” but he observes that the Greek nomenclator likewise translates it as “leathern sea.”

[Col. 0910A] ### Note 60. “Ophni, barefoot”

The Vulgate: “And your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace.”

### Note 61. “How beautiful are the feet”

The words of Isaiah in the Vulgate are: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and preaches peace, who announces good things!” etc. The same thought occurs in Nahum, chapter 1, verse 15: “Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of him who evangelizes and announces peace.” From these words the Apostle, Romans X, 15: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things!”

### Note 65. “Trinomius”

Thus Grialius has it in the text; but in the notes he took *tribus nominibus* (“by three names”) from other printed editions.

### Note 69. “Ochozias”

Others, and Grialius in the text, have *Achazias*.

### Note 70. “Joash, breathing”

Vallarsius defends *Joas sperans* (“Joash, hoping”).

## Chapter VII. Number 2. “Abram”

The Vulgate: “Your name shall no longer be called ABRAM, but you shall be called ABRAHAM, because I have established you as the father of many nations.”

### Note 5. “Behold, a second time”

The Vulgate has *en altera vice* (“on another occasion”) instead of *ecce secundo* (“behold, a second time”).

### Note 6. “I saw the Lord”

In the Vulgate: “I saw God face to face, and my life was preserved,” etc.

### Note 7. “Because God saw”

The Vulgate: “Saying: ‘The Lord has seen my humiliation.’”

### Note 8. “Because he heard”

The Vulgate: “Because the Lord has heard me.”

### Note 9. “Now my husband will be with me”

The Vulgate: “Now also my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.”

### Note 10. “Now because of this”

The Vulgate: “Now I will confess to the Lord.”

### Note 11. “God has given me my reward”

The Vulgate: “God has given me a reward.”

### Note 12. “He dwelt with me”

The Vulgate has the future: “Even this time my husband will be with me.”

### Note 13. “He made me dwell”

The Vulgate: “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.” And she called his name NAPHTALI.

### Note 14. “He judged me”

The Vulgate: “The Lord has judged for me and has heard my voice, giving me a son.”

### Note 15. “In fortune”

In the Vulgate, *feliciter* (“successfully”) occurs instead of *in fortuna* (“in fortune”). It can also be explained as referring to the outcome and the undertaking.

[Col. 0910C] ### Note 16. “Blessed am I”

The Vulgate: “This is for my blessedness. For women will call me blessed”; therefore she called him ASHER.

## Chapter VIII. Number 2. “Let us go to the seer”

After the words “Let us go to the seer,” the following is added: “For the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.”

### Note 8. “I have appointed you over”

The Vulgate: “I have appointed you today over nations and over kingdoms.”

### Note 9. “Certain signs”

From the various readings it is argued that the passage may be read as referring to certain abbreviations.

### Note 13. “Nahum, groaning”

Isaiah’s words are reported somewhat differently in chapter 6, note 61, and in the Vulgate, as I said there. Volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 9, column 2; p. 12, column 2; and p. 40, column 2, discusses the name *Naum*, or *Nahum*, which means “comforter,” not “shoot.” Jerome, at the end of his book *On Hebrew Names*, referring to the Catholic Epistle of Barnabas, interpreted *Nahum* as “shoot.” But the passage appears corrupt, and *Nave* should be read, since Barnabas mentions Nave, not Nahum. See also the note in Vallarsius’s edition of Jerome.

### Note 14. “Why in human affairs”

This is the question that Claudian pursued in vigorous language at the beginning of book I *Against Rufinus*:

> Often a thought has drawn my mind into doubt:  
> why should the gods above care for the earth …

### Note 16. “To the prophet”

“Prophets” would seem better, since *ipsi sciunt* (“they themselves know”) follows. In some printed editions, *prophetas* does indeed occur. But the manuscript codices oppose it. In the Vulgate, *dedi te* (“I have given you”) occurs instead of *te posui* (“I have placed you”). And in Amos: “For the Lord God does nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.”

### Note 19. “Now I know”

The Vulgate: “Now I know by this,” etc., and “the word of the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0911A] ### Note 22. “The taking up of the word”

The Vulgate: “The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachi.”

### Note 27. “Or ascent”

Grialius gives *acsensus* in the text, but in the note he seems to prefer *ascensus*.

### Note 32. “I have placed you”

The Vulgate has *dedi te* (“I have given you”) instead of *posui te* (“I have placed you”).

### Note 35. “Do not stretch out”

The Vulgate: “Do not stretch out your hand over the boy.”

### Note 37. “Three kinds of visions”

Benedict XIV gathers much concerning prophecy and its kinds in book III, chapter 45 and following, of *On Beatification*, after many others whom he lists there.

### Note 41. “To have prophecy … evil”

This is the opinion of the theologians, together with Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 172, article 4. It is transmitted from Saint Augustine in canon law, in the canons *Multae autem* and *Prophetavit*, 1, question 1, where the same example is cited: “Saul too, the evil king, prophesied.”

## Chapter IX. Number 2. “You are Peter,” etc.

The boldness of those who chatter against the first see of Peter is well known in their interpretation of this text of Matthew. They reject the common exposition of the holy Fathers and cling tenaciously to the interpretation of one or two individuals, which Isidore also indicates here, as though it alone were valid.

I have explained my judgment on this matter in my commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 1, verse 63. Since the same scriptural text can have two literal senses, as many writers teach, there is no objection to considering the interpretation of a few of the ancients probable—namely, that the words “upon this rock” indicate Christ—provided, however, that the interpretation of the others is held as certain, an interpretation which the Church has in a certain way confirmed by her authority in the hymn of Saint Ambrose, which all the faithful sing at Sunday Lauds:

> The very rock of the Church, singing this, washed away guilt.

The hymn of the Gothic office for the Chair of Saint Peter agrees with this:

> O Peter, rock of the Church.

[Col. 0911C] ### Note 3. “Cephas … because it means ‘in the head’”

Isidore plainly teaches in this passage that Peter was appointed by Christ as the head of the apostles.

### Note 6. “Obedient”

Grialius printed in the note: “Simon … hearing”; but since *obediens* (“obedient”) appears in the text, I restored that same reading in the note.

### Note 9. “For which I chose”

The Vulgate: “For which I took them.”

### Note 10. “The last of the apostles”

Either, from the passage cited, it means “the least of the apostles,” or it comes from 1 Corinthians IV, 9: “He has displayed us apostles as the last.” The other passage, from the Epistle to the Ephesians, is in the Vulgate: “The least of all the saints.”

### Note 20. “And they received the reward”

The Vulgate: “And they received thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price was set, whom they priced on behalf of the children of Israel.” The words of Zechariah that correspond in some way to this passage are from chapter XI, verse 13: “And they weighed out my reward, thirty pieces of silver.” Matthew names Jeremiah, but in Jeremiah the words are not found as clearly as in Zechariah. I discussed this controversy in my note on Juvencus, book IV, verse 638.

## Chapter X. Note 6. “Glorious leathern”

The printed editions distinguish *pelliceus, gloriosus* (“leathern, glorious”); but the etymology from Greek is “glory of the skin.”

## Chapter XI. Number 2. “Witnesses”

The Latin noun *testes* (“witnesses”) is also sometimes used for martyrs, as by Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verses 21–22:

> Christ, who is good, has never denied anything to his witnesses,  
> witnesses whom neither chains nor harsh death have terrified.

### Note 4. “There are two kinds of martyrdom”

The martyrdom that does not consist in open suffering but in hidden strength of soul, as Isidore says, is not properly martyrdom, even if someone loses his life while ministering to those afflicted by plague. For according to the common understanding of the Church, only those are called martyrs who, in struggle and combat with a tyrant, lay down their lives without resistance.

The work of Theophilus Raynaudus, *On Martyrdom through Plague*, is well known; the controversies that arose from it may be seen in Benedict XIV, book III *On Beatification*, chapter 11.

Since the heroic virtue of the saints is compared with martyrdom, two kinds of martyrdom are consequently distinguished. Although at first only true martyrs were received with public honor, later veneration began to be offered in the Church to other holy men whose extraordinary integrity had been demonstrated. Hence both confessors and martyrs are entered in the Martyrology. Compare my commentary on Prudentius, *Preface*, verse 42.

## Chapter XII. Number 3. “Psalmist”

In accordance with current usage in the churches of Spain, *psalmistae* (“psalmists”) now means singers or chanters, concerning whom see below, number 28. For in Spanish the *praecentor* is called *chantre*, and sometimes *capiscol*, that is, “head of the choir school”; the *succentor* is called *sochantre*; and those who sing together, or join in singing, are *psalmistae*.

### Note 4. “The fourfold order of bishops”

A similar division, and these same names—patriarchs, metropolitans, and archbishops—are read in the third letter of Anacletus, which, together with the two preceding letters, is now generally considered apocryphal.

[Col. 0912B] ### Note 13. “Pontiff”

Following the custom of the ancients, Isidore calls every bishop a high priest and *pontifex maximus*. In the same sense, the episcopate was formerly called the high priesthood, the presbyterate the second, and the diaconate the third.

You can read the words of the ancients who spoke in this way in Theophilus Raynaudus’s *Pontifical Onomasticon*, under “*Pontifex maximus*” and “High Priest.” In both places he concludes that the designation “high priest,” just like “high pontiff,” has long been restricted to the highest of all bishops, namely, the Roman bishop.

### Note 14. “Hence the Roman emperors too”

The Roman emperors, even after becoming Christians, wanted to be the high priests of paganism, lest anyone, abusing that supreme power, stir up disturbances in the empire. For among the Romans the authority of the high priest was notable, even above that of the consuls, as may be seen in Gutherius, *On the Pontifical Law of the Romans*.

### Note 15. “*Vates* from strength of mind”

In Varro’s words, Scaliger suspects that *vates* were said to derive from uttering verses and that *vagendis* should be read. Others think that *vates* was derived from *fari* (“to speak”), so that Φάτης (*phátēs*) would mean *vates*. The word *vates* is used in the sense of “priest” in the verses of Isidore’s library: “Leander the priest.” Isidore explains the etymology of *vates* again in book VIII, chapter 7, number 3.

### Note 20. “The same men are bishops and presbyters”

That bishops are superior to presbyters by divine law is the Catholic doctrine, against which certain heretics abuse Jerome’s authority. The theologians do not all explain Jerome’s words in the same way in order to restore them to their true meaning, as may be seen in Valentia’s book *On the Distinction between the Priestly and Episcopal Order*, chapter 3.

There can be no doubt about Isidore’s meaning, since in explicit words he asserts a distinction between bishops and presbyters in the following number. Compare book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7, with its notes, and chapter 27.

### Note 21. “But for this reason,” etc.

These matters are expressed more fully in the cited chapter 27 of book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

### Note 26. “Two kinds … it corresponds”

Compare book VI, chapter 19, number 13, with its notes.

[Col. 0912D] ### Note 30. “Then the lamps are lighted”

I discussed the use and abundance of lights in churches among the ancients at length in the *Prudentiana*, chapter 11.

### Note 31. “Those who adjure”

Thus Saint Augustine, in his book *On the Blessed Life*, chapter 12: “They are said to exorcize, that is, to drive him out by adjuring him through divine things.” See the notes on book VI, chapter 19, number 55.

### Note 32. “Doorkeepers”

According to Ezra II, XII, 25, there were in the temple guardians of the gates and vestibules before the doors. Hence certain additions occur in some copies of Isidore.

### Note 33

Isidore had already treated these ecclesiastical orders in book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, from which he transferred much material here.

## Chapter XIII. Number 1. “Monk”

More about monks and their various kinds is found in the cited book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

### Note 4. “Desert”

Vulcanius noted that ἔρημον means “desert.” This is what Isidore meant when he called the desert *eremum*, as though it were “remote,” that is, removed from human sight.

## Chapter XIV. Number 2. “By the Jews,” etc.

Christians were also contemptuously called Nazarenes and Nazaraeans by the gentiles. See the commentary on verse 25 of Prudentius’s *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, and on verse 45 of hymn 10: “If he does not reject the Nazarene discipline.”

### Note 5. “Doxa”

The Greek word δόξα (*doxa*) signifies both “opinion” and “glory.” Isidore seems to suggest that one should be called *orthodox*, “right-believing,” who both thinks correctly and lives gloriously—that is, as he believes and as befits a man of right glory.

### Note 7. “Catechumen”

Properly, a catechumen is one who is instructed in the elementary principles of some field of knowledge; in this sense he is called a hearer or disciple. All these matters, however, are explained more fully in book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

# BOOK EIGHT

## Chapter I. Number 1. “Church”

Isidore discusses the Church in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 16, where Loaisa elucidates many matters in his notes that are also relevant here. See also chapter 1 of book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book I, chapter 1, takes certain material from this chapter 1 of book VIII of the *Etymologies*, as well as much other material from Isidore’s books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, without naming Isidore.

### Note 2

The Vulgate adds: “To my God through Jesus Christ for all,” etc. In the Gospel of Luke the same Vulgate reads: “He who does not gather with me scatters.” And in Matthew XII, 30: “He who does not gather with me scatters.”

### Note 3. “And it fell away”

In the Vulgate, the conjunction *et* (“and”) is omitted before *excidit* (“fell away”) in the words of Proverbs.

## Chapter II. Number 2. “Religion”

Other discussions of the etymology of *religio* (“religion”) may be found in Gellius, book IV, chapter 9. That the force of the word extends more broadly, and that it is used for every form of piety toward one’s country, parents, friends, and others, is shown by Carolus Fridericus Walchius in his essay “On the Religion of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius,” in volume I of the *Proceedings of the Latin Society of Jena*, p. 213.

### Note 4. “That thing comes to be”

In Grialius and other printed editions the reading was *sit illud* (“let that be”); I restored *fit illud* (“that thing comes to be”). For the etymology of *fides* (“faith”), see the note on book V, chapter 24, number 17. Various derivations of *foedus* (“covenant”) are explained in book XVIII, chapter 1.

### Note 5. “Hope … because it is *pes*”

Varro, book V *On the Latin Language*, chapter 7, thinks that *spes* (“hope”) may be declined from *sponte* (“of one’s own accord”).

### Note 6. “The fullness of the law”

Paul’s words are: “Therefore the fullness of the law is love.”

## Chapter III. Number 2. “From this, therefore, heresy … word … to introduce”

The sentence is taken from Tertullian, the cited book *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 6, though not in exactly the same words. In the corrected editions of Tertullian, *inducere* (“to introduce”) is now read; Grialius had observed that it should be substituted for *indulgere* (“to indulge”).

N. 6. Superstition. Lactantius sharply refutes Cicero’s opinion, in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, that those were called superstitious who prayed and sacrificed all day long so that their children might survive them. Lactantius, in Book IV of *On True Wisdom*, chapter 28, concludes instead that they were called superstitious who, having survived their parents, honored their images at home as household gods. What Isidore says—“which those ignorant of ancient things adopt”—alludes to Virgil’s verse:

> Vain superstition, ignorant of the ancient gods;

for those who worshiped the ancient gods were not considered superstitious.

## CHAPTER IV

### No. 1. Jews

Saint Martin of León, vol. I, pp. 432 ff., brings forward and expands this chapter of Isidore against the Jews. The notes that Zaccaria had prepared on this and the following two chapters, intending to insert them into his collection of authors who wrote catalogues of heresies, will be presented separately after the *Etymologies*.

### N. 2. *Transitores*

Martin of León reads *transeuntes* (“those who pass by”) instead of *transitores* (“passers-by”).

### N. 3 and 4, note on Isaiah XIX

Grialius’s note had *Isid. XIX*, for which I have restored *Isaiae XIX*.

### N. 5. Essenes

The names of heretics of this kind are generally corrupt in Martin of León.

[Col. 0914A] ### N. 7. Genistae

Grialius printed *Genistaei*, and in the following note *Meristaei*.

## CHAPTER V

### No. 1. Certain persons

This catalogue of heretics is also found separately from the *Etymologies* in some manuscripts, for example Vatican MS 3791, under the title of a letter of Isidore, as I stated in chapter 75 of the prolegomena. I collated that manuscript with the Breulian edition. You will find there, in chapter 32, various readings collected from Gratian’s *Decree* by Berard.

I shall present, as the tenth item among the appendices, the catalogue attributed to Jerome concerning the heresies of Jews and Christians, which I mentioned in *Isidoriana*, chapter 86, nos. 21 ff., together with a certain profession of faith appended to it in Vatican Archive MS 2, as I stated in *Isidoriana*, chapter 107, no. 9.

Zaccaria, whose notes I shall publish after the *Etymologies*, used the manuscript of the bishopric of Pistoia, which contains a collection of canons. He recorded the different wording of this Pistoian manuscript in the margin of Grialius’s 1753 edition.

### N. 4. Basilidians

Concerning the Basilidians, Hugh Menard’s note on the Letter of Barnabas is learned; see vol. I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 60. Barnabas says there: “And for this reason, the Lord endured suffering for our soul, etc.”

### N. 8. Millenarians

Zaccaria had intended to print *Milliastae* instead of *Millenarii*.

### N. 11, note on Tertullian

The passage of Tertullian occurs in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter XXX: “Where then was Marcion, the Pontic shipmaster, a devotee of Stoicism, etc.”

### N. 22. Artotyrites

At the Third Council of Braga—or, according to others, the Fourth—in the year 675, the error of certain persons is noted: in the Lord’s sacrifices they brought milk instead of wine, offered a bunch of grapes instead of wine, and believed that the Eucharist, drenched with wine, ought also to be distributed to the people as a completion of communion.

### N. 35. Montanists

See vol. I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 99. The Montanists, so called from Montanus, are described by Cotelerius, who says that the words of the catalogue of heresies attributed to Jerome concerning the Montanists are very corrupt but readily curable.

### N. 36. Ebionites

Or Ebionaeans. Since they followed Jewish superstitions, they worshiped Jerusalem as though it were the house of God, just as the Jews placed more than sufficient confidence in the Jerusalem Temple. See the Letter of Barnabas, together with Cotelerius’s note, cited above, vol. I, p. 48.

### N. 37. Photinians

Photinus, born in Lesser Galatia, or Galatograecia, presided over the church of Sirmium. Accordingly, *Sirmii* (“of Sirmium”) seems to be the reading that should be adopted.

### N. 38. “These despise offering sacrifice”

The Church’s judgment that sacrifice should be offered for the dead has always been so constant.

### N. 49. “I am the Lord”

Isaiah’s words are:

> Forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil: I am the Lord, doing all these things.

### N. 50. “God made”

The passage in Genesis reads:

> And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.

Saint Julian of Toledo explains how these two statements are mutually consistent in Book I of *Antikeimena*, answer 7, or 16.

### N. 52. Bonosians

Grialius’s conjecture—that the Bonosians were perhaps introduced here by someone—is not persuasive to me. They occur in all the oldest parchment manuscripts, and Isidore likewise shows that this heresy was not unknown in Spain. In *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 33, while describing the book of responses by Justinian, bishop of the Church of Valencia in Spain, he says:

> The second response is against the Bonosians, who say that Christ is an adopted Son and not the proper Son.

It is not clear whether *Circumcelliones* should precede *Bonosiaci* or *Bonosiani*. For perhaps the Bonosians too belonged to the Donatist flock, as did the Circumcellions. The founder of the Bonosian heresy was Bonosus, bishop of Sardica. On him, see Baronius under the year 389, no. 72, together with Pagi’s note.

### N. 53. “Whom the Cotopians”

Grialius’s note read: “But since the Cotopians …”

### N. 55. Luciferians

Saint Martin of León argues against the Luciferians in vol. I, p. 576, describing them in Isidore’s words. There, in place of “the bishop of Syria,” *the bishop of Sardinia* has rightly been corrected in the margin.

Isidore himself can, however, be corrected on the basis of Martin. Martin reads: “They chose to return to the Catholic Church.” In Isidore’s printed editions and manuscripts, *ecclesiam* (“the Church”) had been entirely omitted. The complete works of Lucifer of Cagliari were published at Venice in 1778, under the care of the Coleti.

[Col. 0915A] ### N. 56. “Of marriages”

I would prefer *nuptarum* (“of married women”). For a comparison is being made between married women and virgins, just as between those who abstain and those who feast.

### N. 62. “Divine laws, who …”

This phrase is occasionally used by good authors for “the laws of God, who …” Isidore describes the Nyctages in almost the same words in Book I of *The Offices*, chapter 22, at the end.

### N. 64. Nestorians

Alvarus of Córdoba, in his letter to John of Seville, vol. XI of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 127, cites these words: “The Nestorians, as our light (sic) Isidore says, from Nestorius, etc.” He reads *hominis asseruit* (“he asserted of the man”) and *Christum Verbo, et alterum Dei*, omitting only *et*, *in*, and *filium*.

### N. 68. “The day of judgment”

The words of the Vulgate are:

> For the day of vengeance is in my heart.

## CHAPTER VI

### No. 1. Philosophers

On the philosophical sects, one should consult above all Jacob Brucker’s *Critical History of Philosophy, Traced from the Beginnings of the World Down to Our Own Age*, Leipzig, 1742.

### N. 22. “These errors of the philosophers”

I regard it as sacrilegious to restore Tertullian’s text with Chacon, since Tertullian’s words in chapter 7 of *On the Prescription* are perfectly clear:

> Hence aeons, and I know not what forms, and among Valentinus’s doctrines the trinity of man: he had been a Platonist. Hence Marcion’s better god, derived from tranquility: he had come from the Stoics. And for the soul to be said to perish is an Epicurean observance, etc.

The name of Arius was inserted into Isidore by some unskilled person who did not understand what “the trinity of man” meant. In Isidore’s printed and manuscript copies the passage reads:

> Hence αἰῶνες (*aiōnes*, “aeons”), and I know not what forms; hence, among Arius’s doctrines, a trinity of names, and among Valentinus’s, Platonic madness.

Grialius did not wish to change this, even though Chacon had pointed it out. On the trinity that Valentinus fabricated—of the material, animal, and spiritual man—see Irenaeus, Book I, *Against Heresies*, chapter 1.

### N. 23. “Epicurus is observed”

Here too it would be better to restore Tertullian’s wording, “is observed by the Epicureans”; and shortly afterward, where something concerning the fiery god is alleged: “then the same substances … are tossed about.” Nevertheless, what occurs in Isidore’s copies can to some extent be tolerated. Tertullian uses “restoration of the flesh” for “resurrection of the flesh.”

## CHAPTER VII

### No. 2. “Therefore, just as temples”

That poetry increased idolatry is also demonstrated by Prudentius, Book II against Symmachus, lines 45 ff.:

> Thus Homer, keen Apelles, and Numa alike  
> follow one path and conceive empty dreams of things;  
> and the kindred evil—paints, Muses,  
> idols—the triple power of deception, has grown strong.

Compare the commentary on Prudentius, the note on Sedulius, Book I of the *Paschal Poem*, line 280, and below, chapter 11 of this book, nos. 2 and 29.

### N. 3. Seers

On the derivation of *vates* (“seer”), see the note on Book VII, chapter 12, no. 15. In Grialius, *antiquis* occurred senselessly in place of *antiqui*. In other printed editions, *antiquis* is supplied by those who print *vincire*. Concerning *divini*, “soothsayers” in Spanish (*adivinos*), see again chapter 9.

### N. 4. Lyre

Where the word is derived from is explained in Book III, chapter 22, no. 8. Because of his lyric poetry, Prudentius is described in the verses of Isidore’s library as follows:

> That man, sufficiently renowned for varied songs …

And in an epigram from Vatican Alexandrian Codex 321, chapter 28 of the prolegomena to Prudentius, no. 243, his book *Peristephanon* is described thus:

> The final Muse resounds with varied song.

That now seems to be the correct interpretation, although in note A I had asserted that *finali musa* and *vario canore* indicated a final ditrochaeus.

### N. 6. “Comic poets … from revelry”

Festus likewise derives *commessatio*, or *commissatio* (“revelry”), from *vici* (“villages”), which the Greeks call κῶμαι (*kōmai*).

[Col. 0916A] ### N. 7. “There are, moreover, two kinds of comedy”

Johannes Gerardus Vossius, *Institutions of Poetics*, Book III, chapter 9, admits that Old Comedy preceded satire in its use of abusive language. But he does not accept Isidore’s division of comic poets into two classes, one Old Comedy and the other satirists, nor Isidore’s statement that Plautus, Accius, and Terence wrote Old Comedy.

Certainly this distinction is not found in other writers, nor are satirists counted among comic poets. Old Comedy was rich in biting statements and enjoyed great freedom; New Comedy followed it and possessed greater artistry and elegance. Plautus and Terence flourished in this latter genre, and in this sense they should not be said to have written Old Comedy. Accius was a writer of tragedies.

### N. 8. “But satirists are called …”

On satire, its derivation, and its meaning, I have spoken in the note on Book V, chapter 16. *Quae per vinolentiam dicunt* (“what they say in drunkenness”) seems to be the reading required.

## CHAPTER VIII

### No. 1. Sibyls, etc.

See the note on the *Apostolic Fathers*, vol. I, p. 78.

[Col. 0916B] ### N. 4. The fourth, the Cimmerian

Joseph Isaeus, in his note on Lactantius, Book I, chapter 6, observes that Isidore appears to have borrowed all this from Lactantius. Yet in Lactantius—in the twelve prophetic books, in all the other manuscripts, and in the printed editions—the reading is “the fourth, the Cumaean, in Italy,” whereas Isidore calls her Cimmerian.

After naming the Cumaean Sibyl in Italy, Lactantius names another Cuman Sibyl from Cuma in Ionia, as Isaeus believes. The Cimmerian people are placed in Italy between Baiae and Cumae. This Sibyl, therefore, could also have been called Cumaean by Lactantius and could have been distinct from the other Cuman Sibyl, named from Cumae. Isidore, however, places the Cimmerian and the Cuman Sibyls in Italy not far apart from one another.

### N. 5. “From the city of Cumae”

In some copies I find *in civitate Cumas* (“in the city Cumas”), and this reading is not objectionable. For names of cities were sometimes pronounced indeclinably in the accusative or ablative. See the note on *Prudentiana*, chapter 24, no. 212, and Bochart, *Canaan*, Book I, chapter 25.

## CHAPTER IX

### N. 5. Lycaeus

Mount Lycaeus is in Arcadia and is sacred to Jupiter and Pan, or Faunus. Hence both Jupiter and Pan were called the god Lycaeus. In Valerius Flaccus, Book VI, line 533, Lycaeus is Pan or Faunus.

### N. 11. “To whom they should summon the dead”

Grialius printed *sciscitandos* in the text and *suscitandos* in the note. I think he wished either to prefer the latter or to print it exclusively, although in the following number the phrase *adhibito sanguine inferos sciscitari* occurs.

### N. 13. “Varro says that divination was brought from the Persians, etc.”

As is clear from his note, Grialius wished to print: “Varro says that it was brought from the Persians. There are four kinds of divination: earth, etc.” The verb *constat* (“it is established”) would then be understood.

In fact, however, he left the passage in the text as it appears in the other printed editions: “It is said to have been brought from the Persians. Varro says that there are four kinds of divination, etc.” This is certainly how I read it in two copies of the Royal Madrid edition, and the error was not corrected in the recent Madrid edition.

Grialius’s note has *fertur* (“is reported”) instead of *dicitur* (“is said”), which is found in the text and in the other editions. Augustine’s words are: “This kind of divination Varro said had been brought in from the Persians.” It might therefore be preferable to restore *illatum* (“brought in”) in Isidore as well, instead of *allatum* (“brought”).

After *genera* (“kinds”) I added *constat* in parentheses, so that the sense would be immediately clear to the reader. Grialius customarily does this when Isidore speaks through infinitives, at least in the manuscript copies that have come down to us.

### N. 14. Diviners

Cicero, *On Fate*, chapter 8: “He hopes that the Chaldaeans and the other diviners may be mistaken.”

### N. 16. Soothsayers

Many write *hariolus* with an aspirate and derive it from the earlier form *fariolus*, from *fari* (“to speak”). Isidore perhaps had Tertullian in mind, *Apology*, chapter 23:

> Let one of those who are thought to suffer for God be brought forward—those who, breathing upon altars, conceive the divine power from the odor.

Desiderius Heraldus compares Isidore with Tertullian.

### N. 17. Diviners of entrails

Some hold that *aruspex* was named from *ara* (“altar”); others derive it from *haruga*, a sacrificial victim kept in a stall. This derivation favors the opinion of those who write *haruspex* with an aspirate. The same origin is indicated either by Isidore or by another writer who derives the word from *horae* (“hours”).

### 24. A constellation is properly called a configuration of stars, and a certain disposition of the heavens gathered from it for various purposes.

### N. 26. “He might interpret”

In the cited work of Tertullian, chapter 9 according to Grialius’s note, the reading is *interpretetur* (“let him interpret”); but perhaps Isidore changed it to *interpretaretur* (“he might interpret”).

### N. 28. The term *sortilegus* encompasses every kind of divination by lots; but Isidore seems chiefly to have intended those Christians who practiced the superstitions associated with lots. I believe the “Lots of the Saints” was a book entitled *The Lots of the Apostles*, which is declared apocryphal in the Gelasian decree on books to be received and not to be received. Fabricius discusses it in *Codex Pseudepigraphus*.

### N. 29. Jumpers

Marcellus Empiricus, chapter 21: “The beating of the heart, or a jumping.” Tobias Gutberlethus, *On the Salii*, chapter 2, says that this passage of Isidore should be used to correct Augustine, *On the Nature of Demons*, where one should read *Salisatores* (“jumpers”) instead of *Salitores* (“leapers”). Beckmann does not seem to reject this, deriving *salitores* from *salitum*, *salio* (“to leap”); from the same root come *saliso*, or *salisso*, and *salisator*, or *salissator*. The supplement to Du Cange mentions *salisatores* on the basis of Isidore, Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, and John of Salisbury, Book II of the *Policraticus*, chapter 12.

### N. 30. “Whether in characters”

I refer *phylacteria* (“amulets”) to the *characteres* (“characters” or “inscribed signs”). I discussed them in Appendix 5 to Sedulius, on the words of the Gelasian decree, no. 53: “All amulets, etc.”

### N. 34. “From mouths”

I think *exoriens* (“arising” or “springing forth”) should be read instead of *ex oris* (“from mouths”). What follows confirms the conjecture. On this story of Tages, see Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, lines 553 ff.; Lucan, Book I, line 637; as well as Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*, chapter 23, and Columella, Book X, line 345.

Martianus Capella, Book II, after the middle, says:

> Tages sprang forth from the furrows and immediately revealed the rite of the people and sleep (*sypnum*; reading uncertain).

Compare Muncker’s note on Fulgentius, *Exposition of Ancient Terms*, under *Manales lapides* (“Manalian stones”), where he strains himself while attempting to restore the passage of Isidore already emended by Grialius, reading *artem* (“art”) for *autem* (“but”), and *Tages* for *Stages*.

## CHAPTER X

### No. 1. Pagans

The gloss of Iso on Prudentius, hymn 10 of the *Peristephanon*, line 296, deserves attention:

> “Are you not ashamed, fool, devoted to the village?” says Iso: “*PAGO*: to a village, or to paganism. Villages, as Isidore says”—Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2—“are places suited to buildings, for those living among the fields. Hence ‘devoted to the village,’ without the discipline of cities. *Villa*—perhaps also *page*—in Greek means *villa*; hence we call them ‘rustic pagans,’ as though removed from the city of God.”

Consult my commentary on that passage, and Isidore’s *Glossary*, with its notes, under *pagae*: “memories without idols.”

Joannes Franciscus Masdeu, a highly learned historian, in his *Defense of the Acts of Saint Emygdius of Ascoli*, 1794, imputes to our Isidore the explanation of the etymology of *pagans* in such a way that he asserts they were called pagans because, after peace had been restored to the Church by Constantine, the number of idolaters was greater in the villages than in the cities.

Many indeed hold this view. But Isidore derives the word *pagans* from the Athenian villages, an etymology that is not so commonly found elsewhere. I have shown that Sedulius adopted it in Book I of the *Paschal Poem*, line 280. Compare also the note on line 42, “Athenians, abandon the shame of the villages,” where I cited similar verses of Iscanus.

Grialius prefers Festus’s etymology because he did not attend to the fact that Isidore is speaking of *pagans* insofar as the word is used for idolaters.

### N. 2. Gentiles

The Jews called those *gentes* and *gentiles* who did not observe their religion. Following this custom, Christians called those *gentes* and *gentiles* who were neither Jews nor had embraced the Christian faith. Hence the books of Arnobius and others *Against the Gentiles*.

### 3. Lazerus

In his note on Bruno of Asti’s commentary on Matthew 5:27, Lazerus remarks that Bruno gives a far-fetched and false origin for the name *ethnici* (“ethnics” or “gentiles”):

> “Ethnics,” Bruno says, “whether they are so called from *ETHNA*, or, as seems more likely, from the valley of ENNON, from which *GEHENNA* is named, signify hypocrites and sinners.”

### N. 2. “The poets also contributed”

I observed, in chapter 7, no. 2 of this book, that poets contributed greatly to the expansion of the worship of idols. It is well known that many have written on the origin of idolatry: Gerardus Johannes Vossius, Banier, Pluche, Poupart, Elias Amato, Calmet, and others. See Fabricius’s *Bibliography*, chapter 8.

### N. 5. “Having been received into heaven”

Havercamp, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 25, read *in coelum receptae, et se terris* (“received into heaven, and themselves to the earth”) in the old editions of Isidore, but restored *receptorum, et se in terris* (“of those received, and themselves on earth”). The latter reading now occurs in most editions.

In place of *receptorum*, *receptis* (“having been received”), as Grialius printed it, is correct. Muncker, in his note on Book I, chapter 1 of Fulgentius’s *Mythology*, read *se daemones colendi* (“that demons should be worshiped”) and emended it to *colendos* (“that they should be worshiped”), a correction Grialius had also already made. Muncker discusses there at greater length the origin of idols, drawing on Minucius, Lactantius, and others.

### N. 9. Cecrops

Atto of Vercelli, commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, vol. I of his works, p. 180:

> Among the Greeks, Cecrops is said to have first made an image—perhaps “first” is the correct reading—built altars, offered a victim, and accomplished many other things that had never been seen or heard of in Greece.

Sedulius, Book I of the *Paschal Poem*, line 40:

> The teaching of Cecropian Attica creeps forth like poisonous venom.

Lactantius, however, Book I, chapter 22, asserts that Melissus, the most ancient king of the Cretans, father of Melissa and Amalthea, was the first to sacrifice to the gods and to introduce the rites and processions of sacrifice. In the note on Atto, Melissa is called king of the Cretans.

### N. 11. Idolatry

In Grianus and other printed editions I find *idolatria*. This spelling is common in old, even ancient, parchment manuscripts. I restore *idololatria*, since I believe Isidore wrote it that way.

### N. 13. “He makes a little image”

That is, a small image. As I understand it, at the beginning the representations of the gods were genuinely *idola*, that is, little images and diminutive forms. Even now, most of those that remain are represented in reduced form.

Beckmann, however, argues against these words of Isidore—or rather of Tertullian—on p. 1136, maintaining that *idolum* is not a diminutive word but derives directly from εἴδομαι (*eidomai*, “to appear” or “to be seen”).

### N. 17. “The devil is the prince”

Most people use *daemon* and *diabolus* indiscriminately; but *diabolus* is the proper title of the prince of demons. See the interpreters of Sacred Scripture, Maldonado and others.

### N. 18. “Devil. Hebrew.”

The etymology invented by some—that *diabolus* was so called as if from “two boluses”—is ridiculous. In the Vulgate one reads “before the sight of God.”

### N. 19. “Satan, etc.”

On these matters, compare the note on the *Apostolic Fathers*, vol. I, p. 56, column 1.

[Col. 0918D] ### N. 20. Antichrist

One may read some curious material concerning the Antichrist in Saint Martin of León, vol. IV, pp. 378 ff., from the book *On the Life of the Antichrist*, attributed to Adso, abbot of the monastery of Derbensis. It circulates, however, under the names of Augustine, Alcuin, and Rabanus.

### N. 21. “The Antichrist will claim to be Christ, because he will usurp Christ’s name”

Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 19:

> This is the one who is called Antichrist; but he will falsely claim to be Christ and will fight against the true Christ.

See Prudentius, hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 110, with its commentary.

### N. 22. “For he will also restore the Temple, etc.”

This was the madness of Alambert—such was the name he himself gave it in letters 180 and 183 of volume XIV of the posthumous works of King Frederick II of Prussia—that he ardently desired the Temple of the Jews at Jerusalem to be rebuilt and tried to accomplish this through Frederick, King of Prussia. In this way he attempted to prove false a prophecy that was exceedingly famous among Christians.

### N. 23. Bel

Beckmann discusses at length the etymology and meaning of this idol, *Bel* or *Beli*, on p. 284.

### N. 24. “It was the idol of Moab”

Grialius printed *idolum fuit Moabitarum* (“it was the idol of the Moabites”) in his note; I have restored *Moab* (“Moab”), since that is how he and others give it in the text.

Prudentius tells the story of Priapus differently in Book I against Symmachus, lines 102 ff. Calmet should be consulted, in the dissertation prefixed to the Book of Numbers and in the *Biblical Dictionary*; also Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*; the commentators on the Book of Numbers; and others.

### N. 26. Beelzebub

Joannes Drusius, *Praeterita*, Book I, says that the Jews write *Beelzebul* as an insult and disgrace to the idol, as though it meant “lord of dung.” Beckmann, p. 708, under *Musca* (“fly”), retains *Beelzebul*, which means “lord” or “prince of flies.” He adds, citing Gregory of Nazianzus, that Satan appeared in the form of a fly.

“As even today,” he continues, “he is said to be seen in the same form in glasses or crystals. In pagan antiquity he was also worshiped for the purpose of driving away troublesome flies, and evidence of this was provided by the fact that he ensured that no fly remained in his temple. Similarly, it is said that today none are found in the Venetian palace, and only one in the palace at Toledo. If that report is reliable, we must conclude that some idol had been buried beneath the palace threshold.”

I consider this story wholly uncertain and entirely false. For more on Beelzebub, see Sanctius’s commentary on 2 Kings 1:5 and Calmet’s *Biblical Dictionary*.

### N. 28. Leviathan

I think the question marks, which were absent from the printed editions, are necessary. Corderius shows in his commentary on Job 2:8 that *Leviathan* means in Hebrew “their association” or “their society”: “Those who are ready to stir up Leviathan.” Theodotion translates this as “the dragon,” while others render it “a great whale.”

Corderius thinks that, in the literal sense, Leviathan is understood in that passage as the devil. He adds further material on the tropological sense from Gregory the Great and other Fathers.

### N. 29. “But this was done by poets”

The poets, as promoters of the worship of the gods, were discussed above, in chapter 7 of this book, no. 2.

### N. 30. “The Latins derive this from sowing”

Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 10: “And Saturn was called from sowing, etc.” Cicero, Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 24: “Saturn was so called because he is filled with years.”

Both explanations of the name conflict with the quantity of the first vowel, which is long in *Saturnus*. Others have recourse to Hebrew or Greek in seeking the origin of the word.

### N. 32. “He holds a sickle”

On Saturn’s sickle, see Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 8.

### N. 33. “In certain cities, etc.”

Hercules introduced the custom that sacrifices made to Saturn should use agricultural produce instead of a human victim, and that thirty statues fashioned in human likeness should be thrown into the Tiber. See Ovid, Book V of the *Fasti*, line 621.

### N. 34. Jupiter

In the nominative, as in no. 1 and elsewhere in Isidore and other authors. *Praestare* is often used by Isidore’s contemporaries in the sense of *juvare* (“to help”).

### N. 37. “To the four regions of the world”

In antiquity only four regions of the world were understood: east, west, south, and north.

### N. 38. Neptune

Cicero, Book II, chapter 26, and Book III, chapter 25, of *On the Nature of the Gods*, derives *Neptunus* from *nando* (“swimming”); others derive it differently.

In Cicero, some read *a nubendo* (“from covering”) instead of *a nando*, so as to agree with Varro, who says in Book IV of *On the Latin Language* that Neptune was so called because he covers the earth with clouds, from *nuptus*, that is, “covering.” From this it may perhaps be preferable to read in Isidore “as though covering with a cloud.”

### N. 39. Vulcan

He is also written *Volcanus*. Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 10, says that he was so called from the greater force and violence of fire. Vossius and others derive the name from Tubal-cain, who was a hammer-worker, etc., from Genesis 4:22.

### N. 41. “Lame, etc.”

For this reason Catullus calls Vulcan the “slow-footed god” in poem 36.

### N. 42. “Pluto, in Latin, Diespiter”

Isaeus, in his note on Lactantius, Book I, chapter 13, conjectures that Lactantius should read *Pluto Latine est Dis pater* (“Pluto in Latin is Dis Pater”), not *Diespiter*. He supports his conjecture from this passage of Isidore.

Accordingly, Isidore too ought to be restored to *Latine Dis pater*, or *Ditis pater*. Certainly *Diespiter* is a proper name of Jupiter. *Pluton* is more common than *Pluto*.

### N. 44. “From a mountain of India”

Some call the Indian mountain on which Liber is said to have been raised Merus. The city of Nysa was nearby. On these matters consult Mela, Pliny, Justin, Curtius, and others.

### N. 45. “For this reason Mercury”

In Arnobius, Book III, p. 118, Mercury is said to have been called *medicurrius*, as it were, for the reason Isidore suggests: speech runs midway among human beings and is exchanged back and forth. Others prefer to derive *Mercurius* from *merces* (“goods” or “merchandise”).

### N. 47. Poisons

I thought *bella* (“wars”) should be read instead of *venena* (“poisons”), on the basis of the explanation that follows and of the story itself, which Hyginus, Book II of *Astronomy*, chapter 7, relates as follows:

> When he was setting out for Arcadia, he saw two dragons with their bodies joined, one attacking the other, as though they were fighting among themselves. He placed his wand between them, and they separated. Having done this, he said that the wand had been appointed for the sake of peace.

See Passerius, vol. II of the *Astronomical Treasury of Gems*, pp. 35 ff. In the Borgia Museum at Velletri there is a bronze caduceus found in the territory of Tarentum in 1795 and recently engraved. On it two intertwined serpents bear ram-like heads.

### N. 48. “Peace was made through caduceator-envoys”

For this reason it came about that on coins even all the divinities thought to bring peace carry a caduceus in their hand: Felicitas, *Felicitas Saeculi* (“the Happiness of the Age”), *Saeculum Frugiferum* (“the Fruitful Age”), *Mars Pacifer* (“Mars the Peace-Bringer”), and others, which Carolus Fridericus Walchius lists in his treatise on the religion of the emperor Marcus Aurelius as represented on coins, vol. I of the *Acts of the Jena Latin Society*.

### N. 49. Trismegistus

Several Mercuries were distinguished in antiquity. One of them is said to have been born from the Nile and was regarded as a most powerful king, a supremely wise philosopher, and a high priest; hence he was also called Trismegistus.

Nearly all the deeds of the various Mercuries, however, are customarily attributed to a single Mercury, the son of Maia. The Egyptians called their Mercury, or Trismegistus, Anubis and represented him with a dog’s head. For *Anubis* means “dog” in the Egyptian language. Hence Virgil and other poets call him “barking Anubis.”

Why the Egyptians worshiped the dog is not reported by all authorities in the same way. Walchius, in the work cited, and Octavius Rossi, *Brescian Memoirs*, pp. 235 ff., may be consulted.

### N. 50. “So that Mars may be *maris ars*”

Some think *mas* (“male”) was formed from Mars, while *Mars* itself derives from the Greek Ἄρης (*Ares*).

### N. 52. “Among the Thracians”

Vulcanius printed *apud Graecos* (“among the Greeks”) instead of *apud Thracas* (“among the Thracians”), and noted in the margin that the words “among the Greeks” seemed superfluous.

### N. 53. “The Titan himself”

It would be better to read *ipsum Titanum*, *ipsum Titana*, or *ipsum Titanem*. Both *Titan* and *Titanus* are used.

Servius, on Book VI of the *Aeneid*, line 580, says that one of the Titans refrained from harming the gods and for that reason earned heaven. *Facere adversus aliquem* (“to act against someone”) is indeed a Hispanicism, as Grialius notes, but it derives from Latin usage, as in Cicero, *For Quintus*, chapter 1, and Nepos, *Life of Eumenes*, chapter 8.

The opposite is *facere ab aliquo*, or *facere cum aliquo*, meaning “to favor” or “to stand with someone.”

### N. 54. “Phoebus, as though *ephebus*”

Vulcanius, in his marginal note, thinks that *Phoebus* was more likely named from φοιβᾶν (*phoiban*), “to purify.” This is supported by the view of others that *Phoebus* comes from φοῖβος (*phoibos*), “pure” or “bright.” Properly speaking, *phoebus* is an adjective and an epithet of the sun; hence Homer and Virgil speak of Phoebus Apollo.

For more on the names of the sun, see Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 17. It is well known that Apollo is represented with uncut hair and beardless. Gisbert Cuper, *On the Apotheosis of Homer*, in the chapter on the image of Harpocrates, confirms from the philosopher Albricus that the sun was represented as a boy.

### N. 56. “Diana also”

Diana was formerly called *Jana*. Hence *dea Jana* and *diva Jana*, then *Dejana* and *Diviana*, and finally *Diana*. Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 10, thinks she was called *Diviana* because she proceeds along a double road (*divia*, that is, “by a twofold way”).

[Col. 0921A] ### N. 57. “The same goddess, and Trivia”

On why Diana is called Trivia, besides Varro and others, see Raderus, p. 23, on Martial. Muncker beautifully elucidates this entire passage of Isidore in his notes on Albricus, chapter 7, drawing on Augustine, the scholiast of Germanus, and others.

### N. 58. “She was the daughter of Latonia”

Grialius and Vulcanius read *Latonis*. Muncker, in the work cited, corrected this to *Latonae*. Isidore perhaps wrote *Latonas* in the genitive, just as *familias* is used; and in Priscian, Book VI, p. 679, one finds *filius Latonas* (“son of Latonas”).

### N. 59. Ceres

Muncker, in the work cited, conjectured *a gerendis frugibus* (“from bearing crops”), since *Ceres* is said to be equivalent to *geres*, as also in Cicero. But afterward he found in Probus that Ceres was said to derive from *creando* (“creating”).

### N. 61. “Vesta, because of vegetation”

Ovid, Book VI of the *Fasti*, line 299:

> She stands by her own power: from standing she is called Vesta.

Cicero gives a different explanation in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 27:

> The name Vesta comes from the Greeks. She is the one whom they call ἑστία (*hestia*).

Perhaps the punctuation should instead be: “They represent the Great Mother as turreted, etc.”

### N. 64. “Not being moved”

The verb *constat* (“it is established”), or something similar, is understood.

### N. 65. “They signify”

Perhaps the reading should be *significant* (“they signify”) instead of *significat* (“it signifies”).

### N. 66. “That they boast of themselves before her”

Lampridius and Ulpian, Book I of *On the Aedilician Edict*, speak of “boasting one’s head”; Varro says “to toss one’s hair.” See Casaubon’s note on Lampridius, p. 103, line 23.

Isidore suggests that the ancients worshiped the earth when bronze had been discovered, before iron was invented. Consult Bochart, Book I of *Canaan*, chapter 19.

### N. 68. “Nor do you, Vesta, have anything else”

For more on Vesta and Terra, the mother of the gods, the universal mother, the revered mother of the gods, and so forth, see Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 21; Reinesius; Spanheim; and others.

### N. 69. “May she open the gates of mothers to their offspring”

Havercamp, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 24, quotes this passage from the old editions as:

> May she open the gates of mothers to their offspring, that is, of women marrying husbands.

He corrects it to:

> May she open the gates of nature,

or:

> May she open the gates to offspring and to the husbands of women marrying.

I believe he would have attempted nothing if he had seen Grialius’s edition, where *Natura* occurs. *Natura*, corresponding to the Greek φύσις (*physis*), is used by Cicero and others for the generative organs.

Some derive *Juno* from *juvando* (“helping”); others from *Jove*. Cicero, in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, understands the air by Juno and the ether by Jupiter.

### N. 71. Minerva

Isidore seems to ground the derivation of *Minerva* in her gift of the various arts, but this is not a sufficiently suitable etymology. The explanations offered by others are no better: either from “she diminishes” or “she threatens,” with Cicero, or from *meminerva*, as though from *memoria* (“memory”), with Arnobius.

*Ingenium* (“genius” or “talent”) is used in the sense of an ingeniously devised thing by Pliny the Younger, Tacitus, and others.

### N. 73. “In whose breast …”

Perhaps the phrase should read “in the middle of the breast, a cuirass.” Servius, on Book VIII of the *Aeneid*, line 435:

> If that defensive covering is on the breast of a divinity, it is called an aegis; if on the breast of a human being, as we see in ancient statues of emperors, it is called a cuirass.

See Muncker’s note on Albricus, chapter 8.

[Col. 0921D] ### N. 74. Triton

There is a river in Africa which empties into the Tritonian marsh. Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, discusses it. Festus—or rather Paulus, excerpting Festus—says:

> Minerva is called Tritonia from the bank of the river Triton, where she was first seen.

Others say that she was born there, including Mela, Book I, chapter 7, and Silius, Book I, line 322, and others.

### N. 75. Pallas

As Paulus, excerpting Festus, reports, Minerva was called Pallas because she killed the giant Pallas, or, as they believed, because she was born in the marsh of Pallas. So uncertain are the origins of myths.

### N. 76. “They consequently call her Venus”

No more acceptable is the etymology of Venus given by Cicero, Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 24:

> Venus, because she comes to everything.

### N. 90. “Therefore *fatum* is from *fando*”

Many ask whether the word *fatum* (“fate”) may be used by Christians. Picus Mirandolanus, Lipsius, Beckmann, and others affirm that it may.

### N. 95. Furies

They are said to derive from *furo* (“to rage”), or both words derive from the Greek φονία (*phonia*) or φόνος (*phonos*), “slaughter” or “murder.”

[Col. 0922A] ### N. 97. Nymph

This is a Greek word and means “bride.” Virgil called the Muses nymphs in *Eclogue* 7, line 21:

> Nymphs, my love, Libethrian nymphs, grant me a song  
> such as you grant to my Codrus.

### N. 98. “Heroes … of the dead”

The etymology of *heros* (“hero”) was explained in Book I, chapter 39, no. 9.

### N. 99. “They were called Penates”

They were also called *dii penetrales* (“inner gods”), as Vulpius observes from Seneca’s tragedy *Thebaid*, line 340, in his note on Catullus, poem 67, line 102.

### N. 100. “Apuleius, however, says”

Apuleius likewise relates this in part I of his *Apology*: “But to you, Aemilianus, etc.”

### N. 101. “Larvae, etc.”

Saint Augustine, Book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 11, speaks somewhat differently about the Manes, following Plato:

> He says that human souls are demons, and that from human beings they become Lares if they have deserved well; Lemures, or Larvae, if they have deserved ill; but Manes when it is uncertain whether their merits were good or bad.

Apuleius, in *On the God of Socrates*, teaches that the human soul, stripped of the body, is called a Lemur. He distinguishes among the Lemures the Lares, Larvae, and Manes, in approximately the same way as Plato.

Isidore suggests that the Manes are gods of the dead, just as other gods are gods of the living; the latter are called *genii*. Andreas Cirinus’s *On the City of Rome*, chapter 37, should be consulted.

N. 102. Lamiae. This is a Greek name, λάμιαι, from λαιμός, “throat” or “crop,” or from λήμη, which means “the filth of the eyes.”

N. 103. The hairy ones, who are called Panites in Greek. Cicero called them Panisci more than once, as it were “little Pans,” woodland gods, just as from satyrus comes satyriscus. Jean Bodin, *De daemonomania*, book II, chapter 7, says that neither *Inui* nor *Inivi* should be read, but *Innui*, although this is displeasing to most other scholars. The same Bodin wishes *Drusios* to be substituted for *Dusios*, interpreting them as woodland devils. But *Dusius* is also found in Saint Augustine, in Papias’s vocabulary, and in Isidore’s Glossary: “Dusius, a demon.” Compare the notes.

Hincmar likewise says in *On the Divorce of Lothair*, p. 654:

> Certain women, too, were found to have endured intercourse with Dusii in the form of men, whose love inflamed them.

I believe that the Spanish Duendes were called *Duendes* from *Dusii*. Augustine’s words, which differ somewhat from Isidore’s, are these:

> They assert that certain demons, whom the Gauls call Dusii, both continually attempt and accomplish this unclean act; many persons of that sort affirm it, etc.

N. 104. This one the Romans called Faunus. The Fauns, whom others called Incubi, were called *Incubones* by Servius in his commentary on *Aeneid* VI, verse 776. Mazochius wrote an erudite short commentary on the Ficarii Fauns, in volume II of the *Spicilegium biblicum*, p. 275, on Jeremiah 50:39: “Dragons shall dwell with Ficarii Fauns.” In several editions of Isidore he corrects the error *Sicarios*, which also found its way into certain recent editions of the Bible. In the *Miscellaneous History*, book XII, the form *Phicarios* is written. In Isidore’s glosses, *Ficarius* and *Faunus* appear as two synonyms, not as though the Fauns were called *Ficarii* as a surname.

Rejecting the conjectures of others, Mazochius thinks that the Fauns were called *Ficarii* because of their lustfulness, a view that he confirms by Isidore’s authority. Grialius indicates that Servius calls the Ficarius Faun *Fatuus Fatuelus*; others read the same in Servius, in his notes on *Aeneid* VI, verse 776, and *Aeneid* VII, verse 47, so that the same god is *Fatuellus* as *Fatuus* and *Inuus*. I see that Godofredus Schutzius’s dissertation on the sacrifices offered by the pagan Germans to ward off incubi is commended.

# BOOK NINE

## CHAPTER I

### No. 1. From one language, many peoples.

Here *people* is not taken in its broader sense, in which it denotes all the inhabitants of a given region—for example, the German people, the Indian people, and so forth—but in its more proper sense, as a multitude of human beings composed of several families, or as the entire population of a city or province.

### N. 3. There are, however, three languages, etc.

Much has been set forth concerning the usefulness of the Greek and Hebrew languages, especially by those who insist that sacred literature ought to be explained or illuminated from the original sources themselves. Nor should those disagree greatly who attribute more than sufficient authority to the Vulgate translation. In the Clementine regulations concerning teachers in public schools, it is prescribed that not only professors of Hebrew but also of Chaldean be appointed, namely, on account of the Chaldean paraphrase, or Targum.

### N. 4. Greek, however, is the more illustrious language.

Besides several other discussions by Erasmus, Michael Neander, and others on the excellence of the Greek language, there is a speech by Matthew Bresserus, book III, p. 25, and a dissertation by Cresollius in the *Mystagogue*. Julian of Toledo, in his recently published work *On Grammar*, book I, no. 16, transcribes these words of Isidore:

> The Greek language is regarded as more illustrious than those of the other peoples, etc.,

continuing through no. 8, but with some variation:

> as it is divided into five parts . . . the Egyptians and Syrians . . . which Evius . . . and Cicero poured forth, or the other peoples.

Some include the mixed language, or common language, among the other ancient Greek dialects; Salmasius refutes them in part II of his *Commentary on Hellenistic Language*. For he argues that it is not properly a dialect, since among the Greeks the common language only gradually prevailed.

### N. 6. Latin, which, etc.

Since writers have explained the origin, growth, and decline of the Latin language in different ways, why should Isidore have been forbidden to set forth the various states of the language in this manner? Grialius seems to suspect some fault here, though I do not know what. But Christian Falster, in *Roman Questions*, book I, chapter 1, commends and learnedly elucidates Isidore’s method of division. Becmanus also employed the Isidorian division for his own purposes in *Introduction to the Latin Language*, chapter 6.

Other divisions of the Latin language, and the authors who wrote more fully about them, are reported by Johann Georg Walchius in *A Critical History of the Latin Language*, chapter 1, which concerns “The Origin and Fate of the Latin Language.” I discussed the twelve kinds of Latin, which were not commonly known, from very ancient manuscripts that I believe I was the first to publish, in appendix 5 to Sedulius, p. 426. Tobias Gutberlethus discusses the hymns of the Salii from Isidore and others in *On the Salii*, chapter 19. See also, for example, Marini in his work *On the Acts of the Arval Brothers*, p. 596 and following, where he suspects that the name *Salii* was applied indiscriminately to the Arval Brothers.

### N. 8. All the peoples of the East, etc.

After others, but surpassing them by far, the learned Lorenzo Hervás wrote on the origin, diversity, and affinity of languages in volumes XVIII and following of *The Idea of the Universe*, which first appeared in Italian and is now being reprinted in an enlarged edition by the Madrid press. He is also now laboring energetically to arrange and elucidate a vast collection of alphabets, including those of foreign peoples.

### N. 11. But what sort of language, etc.

The language that was common to human beings before the diversity and confusion of languages is thought to have been the language now called Hebrew, and to have received that name from Heber. Many therefore think that the language which was first common and afterward called Hebrew supplied the words that we read as spoken—whether by God, Adam, Eve, or the serpent—in the first three chapters of Genesis. See Pererius on Genesis 2:20.

### N. 12. Not that of the angels, etc.

This is the solution to the question. Many indeed assert that the Apostle used hyperbole; consequently Theodore Beza, in his commentary on that passage of the Apostle, calls those who debate the languages of angels in this passage utterly foolish. But the Fathers and other interpreters are not really to be censured. Although they do not acknowledge a language, properly so called, among angels, they nevertheless infer from the Apostle’s words that there is a certain conversation among angels, which the Apostle calls a language.

Thus Chrysostom, on the cited passage of the Apostle:

> Here he calls it the language of angels, not attributing a body to angels, but meaning something like this: “Even if I speak as angels speak with one another.”

For what the Fathers and theologians thought concerning the manner of angelic speech, see Petavius, *On the Angels*, book I, chapter 12.

### [Col. 0924A] N. 13. It is nowhere found.

He answers the question and adds, on the authority of the Apostle, that languages will cease. Nevertheless, some believe that the blessed will use the Hebrew language in heaven after the resurrection.

### N. 14. Isidore says that peoples arose from languages.

He says this because the division of peoples, who already existed, had its origin in the division of languages.

## CHAPTER II

### No. 2. The peoples, however . . . seventy-three.

Why do Isidore and Augustine say that there were seventy-two languages, when the total comes to seventy-three? The reason is that, as Saint Augustine says, Heber and Peleg, who are distinctly included in this number, neither formed two different peoples nor possessed two different languages. Therefore the number of those peoples and languages is rightly said to have been seventy-two.

But Pererius’s opinion in his *Commentary on Genesis*, book XVI, disputation 10, should be observed. He says that two things must be distinguished. The first is what the Fathers, extracting it as certain from the history of Moses, stated: that as many peoples and human families as there were at that time, so many languages were assigned to them. The second is what they reported as celebrated among the Hebrews and commonly repeated even among Christians, not as certain but as widely known: that there were seventy-two peoples and an equal number of corresponding languages. He insists that this is highly doubtful and uncertain.

To avoid repeating what has already been done, we willingly refer the reader to Fabricius, who, with his characteristic learning, indicates in *Ancient Bibliography* the authors who have elucidated the origins of the individual peoples.

### N. 3. *Ludi*, from whom the Lydians.

Lydia is a region of Asia Minor, formerly called Maeonia. But since the Tuscans were descended from the Lydians, Tuscany, or Etruria, was also called Lydia. From the Lydians came the names *Ludii* and *Ludiones*. Consult Bochart, *Phaleg*, book II, chapter 12, besides more recent geographers.

### N. 11. He is called Phut.

Calmet, in his *Biblical Dictionary*, believes that from Phut, or Phuth, came the region called Phtemphu, Phtemphuti, or Phtembuti, whose metropolis was Thara in Lower Egypt toward Libya. He adds that Phut was at least the father of the inhabitants of Phtenotes, whose metropolis was Buthus. The aforementioned Bochart should be consulted on these matters, *Phaleg*, book IV, chapter 33.

### N. 19. The Phuthaeans.

For the Phuthaeans, compare no. 11.

### N. 20. The Philistines.

On the Philistines, see no. 58 and book XV, chapter 1, no. 17.

### N. 25. From whom Edessa.

It is not Edessa but Syria itself that is called *Coeles*, or, as others write it, *Coele*. Hence Coele-Syria, a part of that same Syria. See Pliny, book V, chapters 12 and 20; Livy, book XLII, chapter 29, and book XLV, chapter 11; Bochart, *Phaleg* IV.36; and others.

The passage could be read as “the noble city of Coelesyria,” omitting *which is called*; or *which* may be understood to refer to Syria, not to the city. In the manuscripts the word *Edessa* is absent; some wish to substitute *Emessa* for it.

### N. 26.

Galatia is the same as Gallograecia, a province of Asia Minor. Many think it was so called from the Gauls who migrated into those regions.
