The Greeks call the Gauls Γαλαταί, *Galatae*, from the milky complexion of the people. Others seek a different derivation of the name. On the Galatians again, see no. 68 and book XIV, chapter 3, no. 39.

### [Col. 0924D] N. 27. Magog.

Isidore, below, no. 89, and in the prologue to his *History of the Goths*, expresses this very opinion of certain people, namely, that the origin of the Goths is to be traced to Magog. Some think that they were so called from *Gut*, or *Gott*, whom the Goths once worshiped as a god.

### N. 31. Tiras.

Interpreters agree that Tiras was the father of the Thracians. See Bochart, *Phaleg*, book III, chapter 2.

### N. 32. Grandsons.

Johann Schefferus, in *On Naval Warfare*, book VII, chapter 2, read *nepotis* in certain printed editions, and corrected it to *nepotes*, as it is in fact found in Grialius.

### N. 33. The Phrygians.

Another origin of the Phrygians is explained in book XIV, chapter 3, no. 39.

### N. 36.

Schefferus thinks that one should read “the city Citium of Cyprus,” as in Jerome, or in another author of the *Questions on Genesis*.

### [Col. 0925A] N. 39. Yet many names of peoples were changed.

The same opinion concerning the alteration of names occurs in book XIV, chapter 1, at the beginning. In Grialius’s text there was the error *inludit*.

### N. 40. “Unknown in appearance.”

It is not now known who the author of the verse beginning “Unknown in appearance” was.

### N. 42. The Hyrcanians . . . from the Hyrcanian Forest.

I shall discuss the Hyrcanian Forest in book XIV, chapter 2, no. 33.

### N. 43. Zoroastes.

In Grialius and other printed editions, the form here was *Zoroaster*.

### N. 46. Of Pelias.

Munckerus, in his notes on Hyginus, fable 191, thinks that *Jolciaci*, or *Peliae Jolci*, should be read instead of *Peliaci*. He observes, however, that Pelias was Jason’s uncle, not his brother.

In some copies the word *invenimus* is written with such an abbreviation of the letters that *Hieronymus* could also be read. In that case *ait*, or something similar, would have to be supplied. But since Isidore refers back to no. 28 of this chapter, where Madai is mentioned, from whom the Medes are thought to have arisen, the words *invenimus in Genesi* must be understood as indicating that this opinion is found in Genesis, not as expressing it plainly. Isidore speaks similarly of the Saracens below, no. 57. On the origin of the Medes, as also of many other peoples whom Isidore lists, see Calmet in his *Biblical Dictionary*.

### N. 49. The Sabaeans.

Raderus, p. 32, should be compared with Isidore concerning the Sabaeans.

### N. 57. Or because.

Perhaps one should read *vel quod*, as below; or *praedicant* instead of *praedicent*. Yet *quia* is sometimes found with the subjunctive in place of *quod*. The name of the Saracens is not explicitly found in sacred Scripture. The Arabs, Hagarenes, and Ishmaelites merged into one people with the Saracens. See above, no. 46, where Isidore speaks of the Medes.

### N. 71. “And of Callisto.”

Other printed editions have *et Calystae*. Munckerus, in his note on Lactantius Placidus, fable 10, book II, corrects this to *et Callistus*. The name is written *Callisto* and *Calisto*; in the genitive, *Calistonis* or *Calistus*. Grialius printed *Calystonis* with a *y*.

### N. 74. The Pelasgians.

They wandered about like storks. See Strabo, book 9. Servius, in his note on *Aeneid* I, verse 628, says that Pelasgus was the son of Jupiter and Larissa; but in his note on book II, verse 83, he calls him a son of Earth. Others report that he was the son of Jupiter by Niobe, daughter of Phoroneus.

### N. 80. The Dorians.

Cicero and others call them *Dores*, not *Doros*. But *dorus* is also an adjective. Vitruvius, book IV, chapter 1, calls Dorus the son of Hellen and the nymph Optica. Grialius printed *Ellepis* in the text and *Ellopes* in the note; others have *Ellopis*.

### N. 81. “From the mark of their mother’s virginity, Parthenians.”

Justin, book III, chapter 4:

> Those born from them were called Parthenians because of the mark of their mother’s virginity.

Here *pudor* seems to mean disgrace arising from illicit intercourse. The Tarentines who came from Lacedaemon called themselves, as many think, *Partheniae*, as though born of virgins, in order to conceal the disgrace of their birth. In Isidore it was formerly read: “They were called Spartans.” Isaeus, in his note on book I of Lactantius, chapter 20, thought that Isidore had been misled by an error. But this is a scribal error, which Grialius corrected long ago in his edition and replaced with: “They were called Parthenians.”

### N. 83. The Histri . . . who were sent.

On the Istri, or, as others write, Histri, see Livy, book XLI, chapter 11, and Pliny, book III, chapter 19. They were a people at the far end of Italy, bordering on the Liburnians.

### N. 85. The Sicani from Sicanus.

Others say that the Sicani were a people of Spain, so called from King Sicanus. Before the Trojan War they migrated to Sicily under the leadership of Sicanus and gave the island the name Sicania. See Servius, on verse 293 of book V of the *Aeneid*:

> From every side the Teucrians gather, mingled with the Sicani,

and in other passages; also Silius, book XIV, verse 34, and Bochart, *Phaleg*, book I, chapter 30.

### N. 86. The Tuscans.

The Greek derivation of the name argues that it should be written *Thusci*, as Grialius wrote it; but common usage favors the contrary form.

### [Col. 0926A] N. 87. The Umbrians.

Servius has similar remarks concerning the Umbrians in his note on *Aeneid* XII, verse 753.

### N. 88. “Called from Marsyas, the companion of Liber.”

Silius’s verse was corrupted in Grialius as follows:

> When [he] was fleeing the Phrygian lands, the sea Marsya Crenos [corrupt text].

Others, in the passage of Pliny cited by Grialius, read not *Marsya*, the daughter of Circe, but *Marsus*, her son, as also in Solinus, chapter 2, or 8 in another numbering.

### N. 89. The Goths.

On the Goths, see above, no. 27. Isidore more clearly asserts the origin of the Goths from Magog in the *Recapitulation in Praise of the Goths*, which Labbe published.

### N. 91, note. “But the poem of Saint Paulinus.”

The verses of Paulinus, poem 17, are:

> The Getae run, and both Dacians:  
>   
> he who dwells in the middle of the land, or that  
>   
> cap-wearing inhabitant of the shore rich in many cattle.

Paulinus had earlier mentioned the Bessi:

> And his Bessi, harder than snow.

Aurelian Victor called the Dacians “wearing caps,” chapter 13, *On the Caesars*. Martial calls the Parthians “wearing caps” in book X, epigram 72:

> To the Parthians, far away, wearing their caps.

### N. 93.

Martial, *On the Spectacles*, epigram 3:

> And the Sarmatian comes, nourished by drinking the blood of his horse.

Raderus illustrates Martial’s passage in his note, p. 30. I believe *inquietabant* should be read, following Florus, book IV, chapter 12, in Gryphius’s edition:

> The Sarmatians harass the open plains, and it was enough for that same Lentulus to keep them from the Danube.

### N. 94. The Alemanni.

Most reject the etymology of the Alemanni from *Lemannus*, asserted by Servius. On the origin of this word, more may be seen in the work of the Germans themselves, or Alemanni, as in Becmanus, p. 250, under the word *Ascenas*.

### N. 95. The Langobards.

Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Langobards*, book I, no. 9:

> It is nevertheless certain that the Langobards, from the length of their beards, untouched by the razor, were afterward so called, although at first they were called WINILI. For in their language LANG means “long,” and BART means “beard.”

### [Col. 0926C] N. 97. The peoples of Germany.

Becmanus discusses at length the origin and etymology of the Germans in *Introduction to the Latin Language*, chapter 5, and in the work cited above, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *Ascenas*.

### N. 98. The Suebi . . . “founds.”

On the basis of Lucan’s text I have substituted *Fundat* for *Fundit*. Caesar, book IV of *The Gallic War*, chapter 1, says of the Suebi:

> They are said to possess one hundred districts, etc.

See also Tacitus, *Germany*, chapter 38, and Cellarius, book II of his *Geography*, chapter 5.

The Bollandists, under 18 July, after the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, by an author whom they believe to be Ummo, cite two fragments from an old Lombard manuscript of the chancery of Vicenza, in which that Life precedes. There one reads:

> It seems to those not ignorant of history that the SUEBI are related to the SABAEANS, and they strive to establish this by their proximity [perhaps *nominis*, “of the name,” is missing], as Isidore testifies in the books of the Etymologies.

The Bollandists note that they themselves found no such statement in the books of the *Etymologies*. This passage would be the most suitable place for that etymology to be expressed, or no. 14, where the Sabaeans are discussed. But since the opinion attributed to Isidore is found neither in these passages nor anywhere else, one must believe that the author of the fragment encountered an interpolated copy of the *Etymologies*.

### [Col. 0926D] N. 99. The Burgundians, etc.

From Orosius, book VII, chapter 32. *Burgus* is a word of declining Latin, of uncertain origin. It also passed to the Spaniards; hence perhaps *briga* for a town, as in Flaviobriga and Juliobriga. In Ducange’s supplement, however, *briga* is said to be a Celtic word meaning “bridge” or “mountain.” Compare the same dictionary under *Burgus*, and below, chapter 4, no. 28.

### N. 101. The Franks.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLVI, chapter 1, says that Isidore here marks the ferocity of the Franks. I do not know whether he printed *called a delay to the truth* through error or deliberately. In ancient manuscripts *v* frequently occurs for *f* because of their affinity. For this reason Juretus, as I said in my note on Sedulius’s prose, book I, after verse 195, in Eumenius’s *Speech for the Schools*, chapter 19, substituted *feritate Francorum* for *veritate Francorum*.

Isidore’s words, “from the ferocity of their customs,” are sufficiently supported not only by the context but also by the manuscript evidence, which agrees in this reading. Isidore likewise mentions Gallic ferocity in book XV, chapter 1:

> And, defending themselves with arms against Gallic ferocity, they founded Massilia.

See also below, no. 106.

### [Col. 0927A] N. 102. The Britons.

Isidore plainly states that they were also called *Britauni* and *Britones*, and this is confirmed by Ausonius’s epigram 110:

> This Silvius is a good man. Which Silvius? That Briton.  
>   
> Either this Briton is not Silvius, or he is a bad man.

Some explain Ausonius as referring to the Britons of Gaul; for that is generally what the peoples living along the British Ocean are called, whose region is called Britannia Minor. But no reason compels us to accept this explanation.

### N. 103. The Scots.

Scotland may perhaps be named from σκοτία, a Greek word meaning “shadow” or “darkness.”

### N. 105. The Gauls are naturally fierce.

It seems established, and nearly everyone thinks so, that differences in climate produce a certain diversity in the bodies, customs, and minds of human beings. In Stephen de Terreros’s *Spanish Paleography*, or rather in that of Andrés Burriel, there is a fragment by Diego de Campos, chancellor of Castile, taken from the prologue to a work entitled *The Planet*, which he dedicated to Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo. There he praises Rodrigo as follows:

> He corrects, or commends, the Galicians in speech, the people of León in eloquence, the Campesinos at table, the Castilians in battle, the Sarranos in endurance, the Aragonese in steadfastness, the Catalans in cheerfulness, the Navarrese in *leloa*, and the people of Narbonne in hospitality. He corrects, or commends, the Britons in instruments, the Provençals in rhythms, the people of Tours in meters, the Franks in vigor, the English in cleverness, etc.

The author wrote in the year 1218. It must nevertheless be admitted that for various reasons it sometimes happens that the character of people and of different provinces passes from one set of customs to another.

### [Col. 0927C] N. 107. Vacca.

This was the name of a river in Lusitania, mentioned by Pliny, book IV, chapter 21, and of a town in Africa, mentioned by Sallust in the *Jugurthine War*, chapter 51, and by Hirtius in *The African War*, chapter 74. Sallust calls its citizens *Vaccenses* in the same work, chapters 70 and 72.

The Virgilian verse, as cited by Isidore and Jerome, could perhaps be understood in some such way:

> And the Vaccaei wander far and wide.

Virgil’s manuscripts, however, give:

> And the Barcaei rage far and wide.

Florus, book IV, chapter 12, mentions the Vaccei as neighbors of the Cantabri. But Virgil is speaking of Africans.

### N. 110. The Gallaeci.

The name is written *Gallaecia*, *Gallaetia*, *Gallecia*, *Callaecia*, and, apparently especially in later times, *Gallicia*. The word *Gallaeci* likewise varies. A Greek origin from γάλα, “milk,” more strongly requires the spelling with *g* than with *c* or *k*. Florez, volume XV of *Sacred Spain*, rejects a Greek derivation from milk, both because he denies that the Gallaeci were fairer than the other peoples of Spain and because the Greeks, when they name the Gallaeci, write *Kallaikoi* with *k*, not *Gallaikoi*.

### [Col. 0927D] N. 111. “They are said to have granted.”

Grialius omitted *ferunt* after *concessisse*, because it is absent from the ancient copies. But since this word, or something similar, is necessary to complete the sense, I took it from the printed editions and enclosed it in brackets.

### N. 112. The Astures.

Florus, book IV, chapter 12:

> The Astures, etc., by the river Astura, etc.

### N. 113. The Cantabrians.

Florez, volume XXIV, p. 126, observes that earlier writers do not mention the city *Canta*, which Isidore indicates as the source of the city’s name and of the Iberus, etc. Braulio, chapter 26 of the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, called Cantabria a city. Some think that *Cantabria* means something like κατὰ Iberum, “along the Iberus”; others offer other conjectures. A city called Cantabria is believed to have existed near Logroño, where the name remains attached to the place called Cerro de Cantabria.

### [Col. 0928A] N. 114. The Celtiberians.

Lucan, book IV, verse 9:

> And the Celts, refugees from the ancient race  
>   
> of the Gauls, mingling their name with the Iberians.

### N. 115. The Africans.

On Africa, see book XIV, chapter 5, no. 1 and following.

### N. 118. The Gaetuli.

The word is also written without the diphthong as *Getuli*, but in such a way that the first syllable is always long, whereas in *Geta* it is short. This change of quantity nevertheless does not prevent *Gaetulus* from being derived from *Geta*.

### N. 123. Massylia.

In Grialius and other printed editions it is written with an *i*, *Massilia*; but when the peoples of Africa are meant, orthography requires *y*: *Massyli*, and so forth.

### N. 124. Gauloe.

Solinus calls it an island *Gauloe*; Pliny calls it *Gaulos*. An uncertain author writing on geography says: “The island Gaulea lies in the southern ocean of western Ethiopia.” “What he means, I do not know,” says Salmasius, p. 384 of his *Plinian Exercises*.

### [Col. 0928B] N. 125. The Garamantes.

On the Garamantes, see Pliny, book V, chapter 5, and Solinus, chapter 42, in whom, in my edition, the chief city of the Garamantian region is called *Garamana*. Some interpret Virgil’s “the farthest Garamantes” as meaning “the most remote from us.” They were called the farthest because the Romans had not yet extended their arms beyond them.

### N. 130. “Producing.”

That is, “the things that are produced”; the same explanation applies to “the revolving years” and similar expressions.

## CHAPTER III

### No. 4. Such was the proverb.

The proverb that Isidore says was taken from children’s play is gathered from Horace, whose words are found in book I, *Epistle* 1:

> But the boys, playing, say, “You shall be king  
>   
> if you do what is right.”

He then calls it a children’s nursery rhyme, which offers kingship to those who do what is right.

### N. 6. Benevolence.

I write *benevolentia*, not *benivolentia*, as Grialius does. Although Isidore sometimes says that it should be written with *i*, namely in book X under *Benivolus*, the contrary spelling with *e* is more common. Isidore also often speaks not so much from his own opinion as from that of others, and changes his view.

### N. 8. “They might perform the office.”

Isidore and his contemporaries liked to use *utor*, *fungor*, and similar verbs with the accusative in this way.

### N. 11. Masters of the people.

Some think that the dictator was so called from the office of dictating letters to pupils in schools. Hence Julius Caesar jokingly said, according to Suetonius, chapter 77, that Sulla did not know his letters, since he had resigned the dictatorship. Juvenal may perhaps allude to this, *Satires* 2, verse 28:

> If three schoolboys should speak against Sulla’s statute.

Other editions have, not improperly, *Unde et edicta*, “whence also proclamations.” I prefer *Unde et dictata*, “whence also dictations,” for this is what teachers dictate to boys in schools for them to learn. See Varro’s words in Grialius’s note.

### N. 12. “Caesar, however, was called so.”

I understand this of the first person who was called Caesar, not of Julius Caesar.

### N. 19. “Through me kings reign,” etc.

I indicated in the margin the passage from Proverbs to which, I think, Isidore was referring. The Vulgate words are:

> Through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just.  
> Through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice.

I discussed the various meanings of the word *tyrant* in *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, no. 25. On the etymology of *tiro*, or, as others write it, *tyro*, see below, no. 36.

### N. 27.

Cicero asserts that praetors were called from *praeire*, “to go before,” in *On the Laws*, book III, chapter 3.

### N. 29. Tribunes.

Jacobus Gutherius, in *On the Offices of the Household of Augustus*, book III, chapter 9, asserts from Dionysius and Varro that tribunes were called not from *tribuere jura*, “to assign rights,” but from the tribes themselves. Among the Romans, tribunes initially presided over the tribes; later other kinds of tribunes were added.

Pomponius, *Digest*, book I, title 2, law 2, near the beginning:

> They were called tribunes because formerly the people were divided into three parts, and one was created from each; or because they were elected by the votes of the tribes.

### [Col. 0929A] N. 32. “Liber first taught the ordering of military service.”

The etymology of *militia* from *mille*, “a thousand,” and from multitude was explained in book III, chapter 3, at the end of the chapter, and recurs in this chapter, no. 45. The tradition that Liber first taught the order of military affairs may perhaps be explained by the fact that Bacchus fought for the freedom of Boeotia, conquered the Indians, and celebrated a triumph over them; or because some regard that same god as identical with Mars, as Macrobius demonstrates, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 19.

### N. 36. “Recruits are called strong,” etc.

He alludes to the etymology of the name that he had given in no. 19. For *tiro* means “strong”; here he perhaps followed the spelling used by some, and adopted by Grialius in that passage, namely *tyro*, from which he derived *tyrannus*. But the common spelling is *tiro*. Some etymologists derive this word from τείρω, “to wear down,” so that *tiro* means “unskilled,” “tender,” and so forth.

Claudius of Turin, at the end of his *Questions on the Books of Kings*, copied from this passage of Isidore the etymology of *tiro* and several other words. The following note is attached to it:

> I beg the reader to examine this etymology carefully.

### [Col. 0929B] N. 42. In the porticoes.

I prefer *in portis*, “at the gates,” since guards were usually stationed before the gates themselves or at the gates. Watches were only nocturnal; sentry duties and guard stations were both nocturnal and diurnal. Guard stations consisted of entire troops or cohorts, while watches and sentry posts consisted of four men. See Lipsius, book V, *On Roman Military Affairs*.

### N. 43. “From these Velites, therefore, elephants were once . . . killed.”

Isidore discusses the battle of the Velites in book XVIII, chapter 57, where he again treats the derivation of the word.

### N. 45. Military service.

On the etymology of *militia*, see above, no. 32.

### N. 49. The reserve troops.

Festus:

> To reinforce a century means to supply or add men in order to complete it.

What Isidore adds, “Hence also for lying in ambush,” seems to have been taken from Terence’s metaphor, *Phormio*, act I, scene 4, at the end:

> Now you go ahead first; I shall be here in ambush,  
>   
> as a reserve, if you should fail in anything.

### N. 53. In which.

Havercampus, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 2, orders that *in quod* be read, not *in quo*. I nevertheless would not venture to alter it.

### N. 59. Classes.

Paul, drawing on Festus:

> An army was called a *procincta classis* when it was girded with the Gabinian girding, ready to fight immediately.

For in earlier usage a multitude of men, rather than a multitude of ships, was called a *classis*.

### N. 60. Knot.

The meaning of *nodus* as a dense mass of infantry is scarcely found anywhere except in Servius and Isidore. See my commentary on Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, verse 210:

> The knot and delay of battle.

### N. 64. Column or marching force.

Becmanus, p. 204, under *Ago*, argues that *agmen* is a broad term and that Servius improperly narrows it:

> No one will readily believe him, unless perhaps he is a slave to another’s opinion.

There are, however, many considerations by which it can be shown that Servius correctly expressed the proper meaning of the word, even though it is commonly used of any multitude, whether marching or otherwise. Livy, book XXXIII, chapter 9, suggests the same specific meaning:

> The phalanx that had arrived had more the appearance of a marching column than of a battle line, and was better suited to travel than to battle; it had scarcely yet reached the ridge.

### N. 12. Of the first rank, etc.

This distinction belongs to a later age. Among Pliny the Younger and other contemporaries, any senators, and the consuls as a mark of honor, were called *clarissimi*, “most illustrious.” Thus in Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, chapter 18, *clarissimus ordo* means the senatorial order. *Clarissimus* was also a term of rank. See Bottari, volume I of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 35 and following, where he explains an ancient inscription in which Junius Bassus is called *v. c.*, “most illustrious man”; and see my *Prudentiana*, p. 33 and following.

### N. 16. Praetors.

The discussion here concerns the urban praetors. The derivation of the word was given in the note on chapter 3, no. 27.

### N. 18. Tribunes.

On the etymology of *tribuni*, see the note on chapter 3, no. 29. Isidore’s words, “But now certain overthrowers, etc.,” may perhaps have been spoken because, although there were no tribunes at that time, he nevertheless wished to mark the calamity of the age in which overthrowers had been substituted for defenders of the plebs.

### [Col. 0930A] N. 19. The accountants.

There is a title concerning the *numerarii* in book XII, title 50, of the Justinian Code. See also book VIII, title 1, of the Theodosian Code. Forcellinus, in his *Lexicon*, under *Numerarius*, says that one should read in Isidore, “those who bring the public account into the treasury”; this does not please me.

### N. 23. Decurions.

According to the opinion of others, they are called from *decem*, “ten,” or from *decuria*, which itself comes from *decem*. From this number arose the original meaning of *decuriae* and *decuriones*.

### N. 25. “Let the first be magistrates.”

Most printed editions have *praesint magistratibus*, “let them preside over magistrates.” Grialius has *primi sint magistratibus*. I prefer *primi sint magistratus*, “let them be the chief magistrates.”

### N. 27. The *tabellio*.

The meanings of the terms should be distinguished as follows: a *tabellarius* is a carrier of tablets or documents; a *tabellio* is one who draws up public instruments or public documents; an *exceptor* is a scribe who takes down dictation, and was called a *notarius* because he usually wrote it in notes; a *scriba* is one who, in the name of the emperor or magistrates, writes out laws, acts, accounts, or anything else.

### [Col. 0930B]

The private secretaries of individuals were not called *scribae*.

### N. 28. The *burgarii*, from *burgi*.

On the *burgi* and the Burgundians, see above, chapter 2, no. 99. Title 14 of book VII of the Theodosian Code concerns the *burgarii*, who seem to have been those stationed in *burgi*, or fortified settlements, to guard the province.

### N. 29. The *collegiati*.

This is certainly a difficult passage. For, as is clear from certain inscriptions, *collegiati* were those who belonged to some college. But Isidore understands something else: men born of an unknown father and assigned from their group to those who had committed some crime.

Ducange observes that in King Theodoric’s edict, chapter 69, the *collegiati* are placed among slaves and those bound to the curia:

> Whoever has possessed a curial, a *collegiatus*, or a slave for fifty years, etc.

He adds that the *collegiati* in the Theodosian Code, in the title *On the Collegiati*, seem to be different persons. There they are so called because they provided some manual craft, labor, or service to the public. Their sons followed their condition and were therefore not only of servile status but, for the most part, slaves by birth. On these persons Jacobus Gothofredus should be consulted in his note on that title.

Yet these explanations do not fully illuminate our Isidore, nor does the fact that in Papias a carpenter is also called *collegiatus*. We must seek a very degraded class of people.

I therefore think that Isidore calls *collegiati* those who in book XI of the Justinian Code, title 17, sole law, are called *decani* or *collegiati*. In title 8 of book II, law 4, the number of the *decani* of the Church of Constantinople is established. These *decani* and *collegiati* were *vespillones*, whose duty it was to bury the bodies of the dead; they were also called *copiatae*.

Even today this is a very degraded class of people. From Isidore we learn that formerly, and in certain places, men assigned to this sad service were drawn from the *custodiae* of those who had committed some crime and were of unknown parentage. They were perhaps called *collegiati* because they too formed a college of *vespillones*, or *decuriones*.

### 31.

Lilius Gyraldus, in *Dialogism* II, 12, explains the word *barones* by means of these words of Isidore, “a pontiff distinguished for holiness and learning,” which he compares with other passages of Cicero and Caesar—or rather Hirtius—in whom some read *berones* or *verones*. Manuscripts also vary in Cicero.

Formerly the word was an insult meaning “log,” “fool,” and so forth. Cornutus, in his note on Persius, *Satire* 5, verse 139, says that in the language of the Gauls *barones*, or *varones*, were called the soldiers’ servants, who were certainly extremely foolish—namely, the servants of fools.

From this, the name *barones* also adhered to those who were devoted to the obedience and service of princes; this seems to have been the earliest origin of the dignity of barons. On the etymology of the word, see Vossius in his *Etymology*, and Ducange together with his supplement.

### Note 33

“Which is, etc., a steward.” The sense does not proceed correctly, unless something is supplied. Some printed editions have *dispensator* instead of *dispensatorem*; I would prefer *id est* (“that is”) for *quod est* [Col. 0931A]. Thus the sentence coheres properly: “It signifies, that is, the steward of all possessions and estates.”

### Note 35

“Procurators.” The distinction between a *procurator* and a legal representative (*cognitor causae*) is excellently explained in Book I of the *Differentiae*, no. 123. Although some printed editions correctly have *vice fungantur* (“let them perform the function”), the Isidorian reading seems to be *vicem*, as has been noted elsewhere.

### Note 38

“Difference between a tenant and an immigrant.” The distinction between a tenant, a resident, and others is also explained in Book I of the *Differentiae*, no. 323.

### Note 41

“Foreigners.” *Peregre*, *peregrinus*, and related words seem to have been formed from *ager* (“field,” “country”). The final words concerning “a distant region” belong here.

### Note 42

“For Rome alone is the city.” Rome is called “the City” by excellence, just as among the Greeks Athens is called ἄστυ (*asty*, “the city”). Quintilian, Book VI, chapter 3: “It has become customary to understand Rome by the designation ‘the City,’ even when no proper name is added.” This is what Isidore means, as do others who speak similarly.

Forcellinus, in his *Lexicon*: “It is false [Col. 0931B],” he says, “that only Rome is called *urbs* in Latin, while other places are called *oppida*; for some people asserted this on the basis of Quintilian, whose words we have not yet seen.” It is certainly true that other towns too are called *urbes*; it is equally certain that Rome is also called an *oppidum*. But this does not prevent Rome from being called “the City” by excellence, as I have said, and from the Romans’ common usage of calling other cities *oppida*, especially in order to distinguish them from the City, that is, Rome. This distinction applies particularly between *urbani* and *oppidani*: the *urbani* were Romans, whereas the *oppidani* were other, non-Roman people.

### Note 44

“Female servants.” Some hold that *ancillae* derives from the ancient verb *anculare*, that is, “to serve”; perhaps someone in turn derives that word from *ancon*. I am uncertain, however, whether Isidore is referring to the city of Ancona when he says, “Hence we also say *Anconem*,” or to *ancon*, or *ancones*, a term familiar to Vitruvius and other architects for the parts of a carpenter’s square which, joined together, form a right angle, or for something else.

I think it more likely that Isidore is speaking of the city of Ancona, which was also named from the elbow (*cubitus*) of a curving shore. For the place where it stands resembles the shape of an elbow.

### Note 47

“But now *libertinus*, etc.” Some time after the period of Appius Claudius Caecus, the distinction between *libertus* and *libertinus* was as follows. The two words did have the same meaning, but *libertus* referred to the patron, whereas *libertinus* designated the person’s status without reference to the person whose slave he had been. Thus one correctly says that Tiro was a *libertinus homo* (“a freedman”) and at the same time a *libertus Ciceronis* (“Cicero’s freedman”).

### Note 48

“They led them around, etc.” Seneca likewise says, Book I, Letter 8, to Lucilius: “You must serve philosophy, so that true freedom may fall to your lot. The person who has subjected and surrendered himself to it is not kept waiting for a day. He is immediately led around.”

Sedulius alluded to the blow of a slap when, speaking of the blows with which the Savior was struck, he said in Book V, verse 103:

> By these slaps the greatest freedom applauded for us.

Isidore took the account from Cornutus, the commentator on Persius, on Satire 5, verse 75. Fabricius, chapter 15 of the *Bibliographia*, no. 17, notes:

“Manumission of slaves did not have one single ritual. They were manumitted either into full freedom, so that they became Roman citizens, by the *vindicta*, that is, by the praetor’s rod, and by the infliction of a slap and the leading around in a circle; or by the census, or by a will . . .; or in such a way that they obtained incomplete freedom and became Latins under Latin law rather than citizens under Quiritary law, by letter; or among friends and by admission to a banquet.”

Ducange, under the entry *Manumissio*, records especially many other forms of manumission among Christians.

### Note 49

“*Dedititii*.” All who surrendered themselves to the victor in war were called *dedititii*. By another kind of surrender, freedmen were called *dedititii* when, after having committed crimes, they had been publicly beaten so that marks remained impressed on their face or body. Those manumitted in this manner were called *dedititii*. On them, see Gaius, *Institutiones*, title 1. In Justinian’s Code, Book VII, title 5, is *On Abolishing Deditician Freedom*, where deditician freedom is called a worthless name. The legal interpreters debate this matter extensively.

### Note 51

“Latins were made among Latins before the founding of Rome.” Freedmen are understood, or the passage should be read: “Latin freedmen before, etc.,” as Grialius expresses it in his note. In the text he omitted *liberti*, as did some other printed editions and manuscript copies.

Although the Latin freedmen known to us from the Norban law differ from the Latin freedmen whom Isidore describes, Isidore may have traced the original origin of the Latin freedmen to some ancient author who no longer survives. In Justinian’s Code, Book VII, title 6, Justinian asserts that Latin freedmen seem to have been introduced in imitation of the ancient Latin status that was granted in the colonies. “It is sufficiently absurd,” he adds, “that, after the thing itself has been abolished at its origin, its image should be left behind. Since, therefore, the status of Latins was introduced in many and almost innumerable ways, and different laws and senatorial decrees were introduced, etc.” Everything will therefore fit correctly if the periods are distinguished.

### Note 52

“To these the first access was granted, etc.” Isidore is speaking of the earliest times [Col. 0932B]. “But no one ever said this,” remarks Antonius Augustinus. How did Antonius Augustinus discover that? The writers who described all Roman antiquities have not all come down to us. Nor may an argument properly be drawn from later periods to earlier ones.

## Chapter V

### Note 1

“The name *haeres*.” On the etymology of *haeres*, see Book V, chapter 25, no. 1.

### Note 2

“For it is.” The word *enim* frequently occurs in Isidore with a meaning that is not entirely suitable. Perhaps it was inserted by scribes in place of *item* (“likewise”), or perhaps it arose from some connection of letters.

### Note 3

“And they accomplish what was well acquired.” Most people read this in Lucretius:

> And the well-acquired possessions of fathers become the fillets of the mitre.

Andreas Schottus likewise prefers *patrant* in accordance with Isidore’s interpretation, Book V of the *Observations on Human Matters*, chapter 9: “Hence *patrantes* eyes, *patrans* pleasure, etc.”

### Note 5

“Growth.” Perhaps *crementum* derives from *creo* (“I create”), as though it were *creamentum*. Otherwise *crementum* means “increase”; Barthius supplies examples in his *Adversaria*.

### Note 6

“Mother, as it were, matter.” It is generally thought that *materia* derives from *mater*, not *mater* from *materia*.

### Note 8

“Documents of purchase.” See the notes on Book V, chapter 24, no. 25. The following passage of Gellius, Book XVIII, chapter 6, should not be omitted. From the grammarian Melissus he quotes:

“*Matrona* is a woman who has given birth once; a woman who has given birth more than once is *materfamilias*, just as a sow which has given birth once is a *sus*, and one which has given birth more than once is a *porcetra*.”

Gellius continues:

“Whether Melissus himself invented and conjectured this concerning *matrona* and *materfamilias*, or whether he read it written by someone else, is certainly a matter for fortune-tellers; for concerning *porcetra* he does indeed have Pomponius as an authority . . . That explanation is much more probable which competent interpreters of ancient words have handed down: *matrona* properly denoted a woman who had entered into marriage with a man, for as long as she remained in that marriage, even if children had not yet been born; and she was so called from the name *mater*, not yet possessed, but with the hope and presage of soon possessing it. Hence the marriage itself is also called *matrimonium*. A *materfamilias*, however, was only a woman who was under her husband’s authority and ownership, or under the authority and ownership of the person under whose authority and ownership her husband stood, since she had entered not merely into marriage but also into her husband’s family and the position of a *sui heres*.”

What Isidore says, that a *matrona* is as it were a mother of one who has been born, others explain better: the *-ona* in *matrona* indicates lengthening, just as *patronus* is formed from *pater*. Manutius discusses the various meanings of *materfamilias* carefully in his note on Book V of Cicero’s *Letters to Friends*, Letter 10. See also below, chapter 7, no. 13.

### Note 9

“Grandfather.” Others derive *avus* from *abba*, a word that originates in the Syriac language.

### Note 13

“Offspring.” I write *soboles*, as most people do. Whether it derives from *suboleo* or from *substitutio*, the interchange of letters is sufficiently common, especially for the sake of euphony.

### Note 14

“The same, and the youngest, from *monas*.” *Minimus* derives from *minor*, and the latter perhaps from *minuo* (“I lessen”).

### Note 19

“The same, and children, from *pubes*.” This perhaps belongs to another place. Whether *puer* derives from *pubes*, from *purus*, or from Greek παῖς (*pais*, “child”), and in the Doric dialect ποίρ, is uncertain.

### Note 21

“*Vopiscus*, etc.” From Pliny, Book VII, chapter 10, and Solinus, chapter 1, or 4.

### Note 23

“*Nothus*.” The distinction between *nothi* and *spurii*, as Isidore explains it, is not found among earlier writers. Festus says: “The Greeks call one born from an illegitimate wife *nothus*; among us he is said to have been born of a *spurius* father.” Those born of an uncertain father were called *spurii*; hence the ancients wrote *spurius* and “without a father” with the same letters, *sp*.

### Note 26

“But the grandson of both was king.” The masculine *nepos* is indeed found in some places for a female granddaughter, but Cicero and others commonly use *neptis*.

### Note 27

“Descendants.” It is not clear from where Isidore drew this material concerning *progenies*. In ordinary usage, however, *progenies* is also said of children. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, chapter 35: “A hostile hand killed Priam, deprived of such a great line of descendants.” The word *progenitor* properly indicates one who comes before the father or begetter.

### Note 31

Berardus explains the material that Gratian quotes from Isidore; this may be seen in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 32, nos. 35 and 50. After the words “and the term *tritavus*,” an old edition adds the heading “On the degrees of kinship,” suitable for explaining the genealogical diagram of consanguinity which follows immediately. I shall reproduce it in Appendix 11. That same old edition presents only one genealogical diagram, which in our edition bears the heading “On the degrees of the human race.”

## Chapter VI

### Note 5

“Brothers are called.” To make clear that two people are brothers by the same father and the same mother, one must say *frater germanus* (“full brother”). Spaniards and Italians commonly express this by *frater carnalis* (“brother by flesh”).

### Note 8

“But if you purchase.” The Vulgate has: “When your Hebrew brother has been sold to you, etc.” In the Apostle’s words: “For I myself was wishing to be accursed, etc.”

### Note 9

“Let there be no quarrel.” The Vulgate has: “Please, let there be no strife between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds; for we are brothers.”

### Note 10

“Brothers called by affection.” On the ancient custom by which all Christians called one another brothers, I spoke in the note on verse 73 of Hymn 2, *Peristephanon*, concerning Saint Lawrence: “Then the brothers’ greatest care is this.”

Isidore passes from the masculine gender to the neuter and from the singular to the plural: “They are called brothers by affection, and they are divided into two kinds, the spiritual and the common. The spiritual, etc.” But this may perhaps be a scribal error: “They are called brothers by affection, which is divided into two kinds, the spiritual and the common. The spiritual, etc.”

The neuter plural *duo* sometimes occurs instead of masculine plural *duos*. This may have caused the scribes to err: after *duo* they thought that *spiritale* and *commune* necessarily had to follow. I do not find the words in Scripture, unless Isidore was perhaps referring to Isaiah, chapter 66, verse 5: “Your brothers who hate you have said, etc.”

### Note 14

“*Consubrini*.” Grialius followed the spelling *consubrini*, *subrini*. Usage retains the *o*: *consobrini*, *sobrini*. Nor should old manuscripts be an obstacle, since in them *o* is very often changed into *u*.

### Note 15

“*Thius*.” Among the Spaniards, both *patruus* and *avunculus* are called *tio*; among the Italians, *zio*. The Arabic-Latin glosses have: “*Thius*, uncle.” Likewise *thia* means “aunt” in the Second Council of Braga, held in 563, chapter 15. Cerda did not take this into account when he wrote in his Isidorian glossary that *tius*, meaning “uncle,” was an addition inserted by some ignorant person. See the *Isidoriana*, chapter 57, no. 5.

### Note 20

“*Vitricus*.” Others say that *vitricus* derives from *patricus*. Isidore’s glosses have: “*Vitricus*, stepfather.”

### Note 21

“As if *privigenus*.” Perhaps the reading should be *privigenitus*, that is, “born privately, separately, and apart,” before the mother had married the stepfather.

### Note 27

After this no. 27, Grialius’s edition contains only two genealogical diagrams, namely the first and the second. Other printed editions and manuscripts contain three, almost as they are presented by us in the three following figures.

Although Grialius omitted the third diagram because, as he says, there are only two in the oldest books, I nevertheless considered that it should be restored, persuaded by the authority of other copies. The notes corresponding to nos. 28 and 29, however, are expressed in the first and final genealogical diagrams and are prefixed here.

### Note 29

“This genealogy of consanguinity . . . fleeing.” The Second Council of Douzy, in 874, in its synodal letter to the bishops of Aquitaine, Labbe, volume IX, column 261, cites Isidore’s words as follows:

“Thus Isidore speaks concerning consanguinity: ‘Its sequence is separated into seven degrees in this manner: son and daughter; grandson and granddaughter; great-grandson and great-granddaughter; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter; and the son and daughter of the great-great-great-great-grandchild. This genealogy of consanguinity, as it gradually . . . withdraws itself from the degree, etc., as far as “fleeing.”’”

#### Same place

“Therefore only as far as the sixth.” Regino, page 288, and others discuss consanguinity as far as the sixth degree. Berardus, in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 32, no. 35, says that learned men dislike this restriction, “as far as the sixth degree.” Several verses on the degrees of consanguinity, found in certain old manuscripts of the *Etymologiae*, and a fragment entitled *On the Seven Degrees of Consanguinity*, attributed to Isidore and inserted in Codex Ottobonianus 1968, will be presented as Appendices 12 and 13.

## Chapter VII

### Note 5

“On the *arra*,” Book V, chapter 25, no. 21. From *arrabo*, Greek ἀῥῥαβὼν (*arrabōn*, “pledge” or “security”), *arra* was formed by apocope. Isidore derives *arrabo* from *arra* in order to serve his interpretation.

### Note 8

Venantius Fortunatus, Book VIII, poem 5, verse 303:

> Thereupon the angel, as bridesman, recounting your honors.

The *paranymphs* are also mentioned by the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 13, in Regino, Book II, chapter 153. See Ducange.

### Note 9

“Spouses, etc.” Isidore treats married people more fully in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 20.

Brissonius, *On the Marriage Rite*, page 313, does not dare to accept what Servius, in his commentary on *Aeneid* IV, verse 16, and Isidore after him, report here concerning the marriage yoke. Albert Dietericus, who added notes, observes that Grialius cites Augustine, *On Marriage*, chapter 11, but found nothing there. He himself adduces Festus, Ulpian, and Statius in support of the same view, although, as he says, their words allow another interpretation. Nevertheless, he does not consider improbable the rite which some understand as a veil resembling a yoke.

He himself suspects that the following passage from Servius, on *Aeneid* IV, verse 374, may be relevant: namely, that concerning two yoked seats, which perhaps represented a yoke or were joined together in the manner of a yoke. Ivo of Chartres discusses the whole of Isidore’s opinion at greater length in Letter 173.

The explanation concerning the marriage yoke, insofar as it concerns Christians, must be taken from Isidore himself, in the place cited:

“But after the blessing, the newly married are joined by the levite with a single bond, plainly so that they may not break apart the structure of marital unity. But the same band is interwoven with white and purple color: white, indeed, is applied to purity of life, and purple to the succession of blood, etc.”

### Note 10

“Let them veil their faces.” This veil was thin and yellow in color. Catullus calls it *flammeum* in poem 60. From Genesis 20:16, Vulpius concludes that the custom of using the *flammeum* seems to have been handed down from the Hebrews.

### Note 12

“They would anoint with oil.” Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 9, reports that anointing was customarily performed with fat. Arnobius, Book III *Against the Nations*, speaks of “fatty ointment” when he mocks the goddess who presided over such anointings. Brissonius explains other reasons why newly married women were forbidden to step over the threshold, *On the Marriage Rite*, pages 327 and following.

### Note 16

“Widow.” On widows, see Book II of the *Offices*, chapter 19, where it is explained more clearly that a woman who has been bound to several husbands does not properly possess the name of true widowhood. In Grialius the reading was *iduere* instead of *iduare*; I have adopted the form from Macrobius and others. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 15, says that a widow is so called as though she were “very much divided,” or “divided from her husband.”

### Note 17

“A brother’s wife, *fratrissa*.” In Isidore, as in others, one may also read *fratria*, not *fratrissa*. Forcellinus says that the wives of two brothers were called *janitrices*, not because they knocked at the same door, but because they made their beds opposite one another at the door and customarily slept there as if to keep watch.

Among the Romans there was a custom that the wife who had first entered into her husband’s authority made a bed for herself in the atrium of the house, directly before the door. Propertius refers to this, Book IV, final elegy, verse 81:

> Or if the door should nevertheless change the bed opposite it,  
> and the cautious stepmother should sit beside our couch.

Some think that *janitrices* is a corrupt form derived from the Greek εἰνατέρες, *inateres*, which means *fratriae* (“wives of brothers”).

### Note 20

“Marriage.” On the yoke of spouses, see above, no. 9.

### Note 21

“Marriage union.” Ulpian, *Rules*, title 6: “Roman citizens have *connubium* with Roman citizens; with Latins and foreigners, if it has been granted; with slaves there is no *connubium*.”

### Note 22

“*Hymenaeus*.” Hymen, or Hymenaeus, was the god of weddings; the mythographers tell many stories about him.

### Note 23

“*Contubernium* was also called the marital union of slaves, between whom in former times there was no true marriage.”

### Note 24

“Divorce.” Modestinus explains the distinction between *repudium* and *divortium*, *Digest* L, final title, law 101: “A *divorce* is said to take place between husband and wife; a *repudiation* seems to be the dismissal of a betrothed woman, although the term may not improperly be applied to a wife as well.” *Repudium* is commonly used for *divortium*.

### Note 26

“It is frivolous.” Grialius and other printed editions have *Fribolum est*, etc., but shortly afterward Grialius has: “For it is *frivolum*.” The *Pandects* do indeed read *fribusculum*, but this arose because *b* was often used for *v*; many think that *frivusculum* should also be read in Ulpian. The attempt of others to restore *frigusculum* is not satisfactory. Isidore certainly seems to have read either *frivolum* or *frivusculum*.

### Note 27

“And he blessed.” The Vulgate has: “And God blessed them and said: ‘Increase,’ etc.”

### Note 29

“Likewise, in choosing a wife, four things.” In Codex Vaticanus Palatinus 282, this note occurs at the passage:

Chrysostom, on Matthew 1: “Those who choose wealth and not character, beauty and not faith, desire in wives what is ordinarily sought in prostitutes. Therefore they do not beget children subject either to themselves or to God, so that their children are not the fruit of a righteous union but the deserved punishment of irreligion.”

## Alphabet of Definite Words

In old manuscripts, different titles of this book appear, such as: “Book X, arranged alphabetically”; “Chapter of Book X, that is, concerning certain names distinguished alphabetically”; “Concerning certain words of names according to derivation”; “Concerning the remaining names according to the order of the elements”; “Book X, according to derivation,” and so forth.

Codex Urbinas 100, in which the *Etymologies* are divided into twenty-two books, gathers titles of this kind under the following rubric:

“Book Twelve of Isidore, concerning certain names distinguished alphabetically, concerning the remaining names according to the order of the elements or letters, concerning certain words for persons [or, in another copy, names] according to derivation, begins.”

# Book Ten

### Note 2

“*Aeros*.” Below, under H, *heros* appears in its proper place. The reason why *aeros* is placed under A and written in this way may be sought in the claim that *heros* is said to come from the Greek, as though it meant “heavenly, belonging to the air.” See below, no. 116, and Book VIII, final chapter, no. 96.

Barthius, Book XXVI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, says: “No one could have conjectured how *heros* can agree with the letter A, which ought to be the beginning of the word. Nor should Isidore be thought so clumsy as to have confused the Greek eta with A.”

In his old book he found *aros* instead of *aeros*, and conjectures *Amos*, which, according to Saint Pagninus, means “a strong and wise man.” Thus Papias says: “Amos means powerful, strong, modest.”

I can confirm Barthius’s suspicion from the spelling of Codex Vaticanus 623, as I indicated in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 93, no. 29. In that codex *Amos* is clearly read instead of *aeros*. Nevertheless, I would not dare to alter the common and widespread reading, which, as I have said, can be defended to some extent.

Isidore himself interprets the word *Amos* in Book VII, chapter 8, no. 12: “A people torn away,” which is far removed from “a strong and wise man.”

Concerning the word *heros*, as it is sometimes applied to saints, I spoke in my commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 6, verse 114, where I observed that Avitus, Book V, used the phrase *heros impius* (“impious hero”) concerning Pharaoh. Bembus, on the other hand, is criticized by Scaliger, Book VI of the *Poetics*, chapter 4:

“When Bembus calls the Lord Jesus *hero*, he greatly disturbed me. The word is certainly impious and unworthy of him in either respect, lest someone make a clever argument that he is half God and half man.”

Regarding what is added in this same number—“But they think that the author . . . cannot”—Barthius, in the place cited, observes that *autem* is absent from his manuscript, while others have *etiam* (“also”), followed by *existimant*. Grialius denies that the passage is complete because in *cursor* the derivation is different from that in *auctor*. But, as I think, Isidore’s meaning is that *auctor*, when it refers to authority, should be taken as common gender, although in another meaning it can be inflected into the feminine *auctrix*. At the same time he observes that certain nouns cannot in any way be inflected into the feminine, such as *cursor*.

### Note 4

“*Amicus* is from *amor*; *amor* itself can properly be derived from ἅμα (*hama*), ‘together’ or ‘as one.’”

### Note 7

“The derivation of *aemulus* may perhaps be from αἱμύλιος, αἱμύλος (*haimýlios*, *haimýlos*), ‘pleasant’ or ‘flattering.’”

### Note 8

“*Elatus*, etc.” These very words occur below under E, no. 81. They should not be inserted here unless the spelling is *aelatus*, which is contrary to orthographic rule.

### Note 12

“*Aerumnosus* from *rumen*.” Perhaps what Arnobius says in Book VII belongs here: “The first parts in the throats are *aerumnae*, by which nature has assigned to ruminating creatures the task of lowering and bringing back food through their gullet.”

Plautus, in Festus, calls *aerumnulae* the little forked poles to which travelers’ bundles were tied and carried. *Ruma*, *rumis*, or *rumen* formerly meant “breast”; *rumen* is also a part of the neck, or something like its stomach. Isidore’s words, “through lack,” may be referred to these senses. Others propose different etymologies for the word.

### Note 13

“*Astrosus*.” In Isidore’s glossary it is also said to mean “lunatic.” In the ordinary Spanish language its meaning is *desafortunado*, that is, “unfortunate.”

### Note 14

“*Enormis*.” This does not belong here unless it is written with *ae*, which is contrary to the rule. *Abnormis* could be substituted, but that means “without a standard” or “without a law.” See below, the note on no. 81, where *enormis* is correctly placed under E.

On cattle thieves, see Paulus, Book V of the *Sentences*, chapter 18. On cattle rustlers, Ulpian, *Digest* XLVII, title 14, law 1.

### Note 17

“The expense of the treasury.” Grialius printed *aerarium expensum* in the text, which he condemns in his note.

### Note 22

“Blessed.” It is clear that *beatus* derives from *beo*, which some derive from βίω (*biō*, “I live”).

### Note 26

“*Benivolus*.” The accepted spelling *benevolus* and *benevolentia*, as well as similar examples, supports the customary way of writing the word: *beneficus*, *benedico*, and so forth. Lipsius, Vossius, and Dausquius, together with the earlier Eutyches, Bede, and others, approve *benivolus*.

### Note 28

“*Brutus*.” Others say that *brutum* derives as though from βρωτόν (*brōton*), “something that can be eaten,” “edible.”

### Note 30

“*Bucco*.” Barthius, Book VI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 14:

“That Isidore in the *Origins*, Book X, and another compiler of glosses gathered from various sources call *buccones* foolish people because they are accustomed to say many and great things is certainly also in accordance with the teaching of the ancients.”

He cites the following from Dionysius Cato, Book II, chapter 21: “Little trust should be granted to those who speak much,” and elsewhere: “Many say many things where many are foolish, whereas the wise are few.”

### Note 31

“*Biothanatus*.” From the Greek, *biothanatus* means “one who has died by force or violently,” such as those who take their own lives. In some printed editions the reading was *bis mortuus* (“twice dead”), which some explained as meaning that the souls of those who died violently are not received into their proper origin until, wandering about, they have completed the allotted period of fate, as Servius says; poets refer this to burial.

But Grialius’s reading, “one who died by force,” must be retained. The pagans called our martyrs *biothanati* because they voluntarily met death for Christ’s name. Ducange supplies examples.

### Note 33

“Abstinence from lust.” It should be noted that *abstinentia libidinis* means “self-restraint” or “temperance.”

### Note 36

“*Clientem*.” The etymology of *cliens* is not sufficiently clear. Properly, *cluere* means “to hear”; by metalepsis it means “to be named,” and from this comes “to be” or “to exist.” It is also taken to mean “to cleanse.” According to Donatus, *clemens* means “one who cultivates the mind”; according to others, it is as though it were *clinimens*, from *clino* and *mens*.

### Note 44

“The Mantuan poet, etc.” Perhaps this comes from Jerome, in the preface to his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.

### Note 47

“*Contemptibilis*.” In *contemptibilis*, as in *laudabilis*, *visibilis*, and similar words, the lengthening belongs to *-bilis*; there is no need to resort to *habilis* or *vilis* for the etymology.

### Note 52

“*Confinalis*” also means “belonging to a boundary,” as in *lineae confinales* (“boundary lines”) in Varro’s *On Boundaries*, page 310.

### Note 55

“*Colomis*.” I write *columis* with the other printed editions, although Grialius prefers *colomis*. *Columis* is also taken to mean “unharmed.”

### Note 57

“*Calamistratus* from *calamistrum*.” Pignorius, *On Slaves*, page 195, confirms Isidore’s statement that a *calamistrum* was an iron needle, citing Ovid, Festus, and Juvenal. Nonius, chapter 15, no. 27, calls it a *fistula* (“tube”) because inside it is hollow like a reed. In Isidore, *acu ferreo* (“with an iron needle”) is perhaps a scribal error for *acu ferrea* (“with an iron needle”), and so forth. For the ancients use *acus* in the feminine gender.

### Note 58

“From *creando* (‘creating’) flesh.” That is, from the Greek κρέας (*kreas*, “flesh”); perhaps Isidore used a Greek word in place of *creando*.

### Note 62

“Shaken by the waves, etc.” Others interpret this as “shaken and scattered.”

### Note 64

“*Circumforaneus* . . . *Collegiatus*.” Latins say *circumforaneus*. The *collegiati* here are perhaps the *vespillones*, discussed in Book IX, chapter 4, no. 29.

### Note 65

“From *disserendo*.” From Festus and Varro, although the short *i* in *disertus* seems to suggest something else.

### Note 66

“*Discipulus* from *disciplina*.” *Disciplina* derives from *discipulus*, as was stated in the note on Book I, chapter 1, no. 1.

### Note 67

“They hung up.” Hence *pendere* can mean “to pay.” See Varro at the end of Book IV of *On the Latin Language*.

### Note 71

“*Debilis*, because through bile.” *Debilis* derives from *de* and *habilis*.

### Note 72

“*Desperatus*.” On the word *desperatus*, Georgius, in his dissertation *On Monograms*, chapter 10, page 64, should be compared with Isidore.

### Note 74

“*Decrepitus*.” Festus: “*Decrepitus* is one whose life is already hopelessly *crepera*; or because, owing to old age, he can neither move himself nor make any *crepitus*.” Thomas Gataker, *Miscellaneous Adversaria* II, chapter 14, says that it may be uncertain which *crepitus* Festus intended. He notes that Isidore’s interpretation—that they had ceased *crepare*, that is, speaking—is taken from Donatus’s commentary on Terence.

Becmann explains *decrepitus* from the slower gait which produces a creaking or rattling sound. Joseph Scaliger derives it from a lamp or candle which, as it expires for the last time, is accustomed to make a crackling sound.

### Note 75

“*Depretiatus*.” Hence the Spaniards say *despreciado*, and the Italians use a nearly similar form. Festus explains the etymology of *dirus*: “*Dirus*, born from the anger of the gods.” Servius takes *dirus* to mean “great” in his commentary on Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 37, *dira cupido* (“great desire”). So also *dira religio*, and so forth.

### Note 77

“*Delator*.” *Delator* derives from *defero* (“to bring or report”). Raderus, page 34, discusses the word and office of the *delator* in his commentary on Martial.

### Note 78

“*Lira*.” Festus and Nonius call *lirae* “furrows.” Isidore also, in Book XV, chapter 15, distinguishes *lira* from *porca*: *lira* is the furrow, or what is dug down during plowing; *porca* is what rises during plowing, from which water runs down into the *lira*, or furrow. The two are easily confused because both are produced together during plowing. Compare the note on the alphabetical book of the *Differentiae of Words*, no. 140.

### Note 85

“*Exsul*.” In Book I, chapter 27, Isidore prefers the spelling *exsul* over *exul*. Grialius’s edition varies. See the note on that passage.

### Note 96

“*Facetus*.” According to the opinion of others, it derives from *fari* (“to speak”).

### Note 97

“*Foenerator*, or *fenerator*, derives from *foenerare*, *foeneratum*.” Properly, it is one who lends money at interest. But since *foenero* and *foeneror* can also mean “to repay and receive money at interest,” *foenerator* may likewise be taken to mean one who borrows money.

### Note 99

“*Fidelis* . . . *Firmus* . . . *Formosus*.” The etymology of *fides* is explained in a similar manner in Book V, chapter 24, no. 17, and Book VIII, chapter 2, no. 3. *Formosus* is better derived from *formo* in the following number; or the passage should be read: “*Firmus* from *formo*, whence also *formosus*.” Others derive *firmus* from ἕρμα (*herma*, “support” or “foundation”).

### Note 100

“The Greeks call *forma* μορφή (*morphē*), from which *forma* is produced by metathesis.”

### Note 102

“*Fessus* . . . *Fatigatus*.” Some believe that *fessus* is a participle from *fatiscor* (“I become weary”). *Fatigatus* certainly derives from *fatigo* (“I weary”); the latter perhaps comes from *fatim ago* (“I act abundantly”), for *fatim* means “fully,” “very much,” or “greatly.”

### Note 103

Gellius, Book IX, chapter 12, lists certain nouns that have both active and passive meanings.

### Note 104

“*Fatuus*.” In Justinus, at the place cited by Grialius, Book XLIII, chapter 1, most people read *fatuari dicuntur* (“they are said to speak foolishly”). In ancient times seers were called *fatui*, and the word *vates* itself derives from φάτης (*phatēs*, “speaker”). Some think that people who speak many useless things were called *fatui*, as in Isidore’s glossary, where *effatui* means “empty talkers without effect.”

### Note 105

“*Fictores*.” They belonged among the duties of household servants. The name *fictor* is also read among divine offices, as Petrus Scriverius observes in his note on the inscription of Volaterra, *On the Priesthoods of the Romans*. There he reads Isidore’s passage as *linit, et pertrectat* (“he smears and handles”), and conjectures that it should read *leniter pertrectat* (“he handles gently”).

The *fictores* of the pontiffs, mentioned in ancient inscriptions, seem to have been those who assisted the pontiffs in decorating or making images of the gods [Col. 0938C]. Those who made sacrificial cakes were also called *fictores*.

### Note 111

“These under the arched structures.” Brissonius, *On the Law of Marriage*, page 354, reports the passage in this form: “These women were prostituted under the arches.”

### Note 115

“*Glutto*.” Hence the Spaniards say *gloton*.

### Note 116

“*Heros*.” On the word *heros*, see above, no. 2. Some have *acclivis* instead of *acclinis*. But *acclinis* is correct, just as *reclinis* occurs more than once in Prudentius. In *honorabilis*, the lengthening belongs to *-bilis*, as I have already said of similar words.

### Note 118

“*Honorosus*.” You will scarcely find a certain example of the word *honorosus*; nevertheless, *honroso* remains in the Spanish language. It may be questioned whether the reading should be *honerosus*, “more than burdened,” from the old error of writing *honus* instead of *onus*. On the phrase “bristling with hair,” from the resemblance to the hair of wild animals, Barthius has much to say in Book XXI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11.

### Note 124

Some derive *interpres* and *interpretator* from *pretium*; others from *paro*; others from the obsolete *prator*; others, with Isidore, from *pars*; and others from still different sources.

### Note 126

“*Innox*.” Instead of *innoxius*, the form *innox* is found in ancient Christian inscriptions collected by Reinesius. Barthius, in Cyprian, *On the Discipline of Virgins*, chapter 16, corrected *quarum innox lavatio est* (“whose washing is harmless”) for *quarum in vos pudica lavatio est* (“whose chaste washing is in you”). He thinks that *pudica* (“chaste”) was a gloss explaining *innox*, in place of which the corruption *in vos* arose. In the Oxford edition from the Sheldonian Theatre, the reading is “whose chaste washing is,” with *in vos* omitted.

### Note 129

“*Infirmus*.” It repeats the derivation from *formo*, which was followed for *firmus* in no. 99.

### Note 133

“*Impius* . . . for *infidelis*, etc.” Hence the holy Fathers placed between the pious and the impious a middle group, namely sinful Christians.

### Note 136

“*Improbus*.” It means “not *probus*.” According to Festus, *probi* are *prohibi*, those who restrain themselves from wrongdoing. Hence *labor improbus* is labor that is not restrained.

### Note 137

Festus: “*Importunum* is that in which there is no assistance, as is often the case with a harbor for sailors.”

### Note 140

“*Inveterator*.” Most printed editions have *inveteratus*. But just as *veterator* is said, *inveterator* may also be retained.

#### Same place

“*Immunis* as ‘not generous.’” I do not know whether this can be confirmed by an example from a good author. The proverb “The citizens exempt from duties,” etc., fits perfectly one who does not perform public services.

### Note 143

“*Ignarus*.” Others derive *gnarus* from γνορίζω (*gnōrizō*, “I make known”). Gellius, Book IX, chapter 12, noted that *ignarus* can also be taken passively, meaning “unknown.” There are many ancient examples. The Spaniards use *olfecisse*, “to have smelled,” nearly in the sense of “to investigate.” See Book XI, chapter 2, no. 47.

### Note 149

“*Impudicus*.” It means “not *pudicus*.” *Pudicus* itself may be derived from *paedor* (“filth”), although according to the opinion of others it derives from *putor* (“stench”), because the senses turn away from foul things. Some printed editions have *impudicus a pudice*; perhaps it should be *a podice* (“from *podex*”), since *o* and *v* are frequently confused in manuscripts, as many have already noted.

### Note 150

“*Internicida*.” I write *internecida* and *internecivum*. Grialius’s edition has *internicida* and *internicivum*. In manuscripts, *i* frequently appears in place of *e*.

### Note 152

“*Incincta*.” Italians also use *incincta* of a pregnant woman; Spaniards say *encinta*, which some divide as *en cinta* (“in a band”).

### Note 153

“*Iscurra*.” Here this is used for *scurra*, which recurs below in its proper place under S and is explained more clearly there.

### Note 154

“*Katholicus*, etc.” These words are now written with *c*, not *k*.

### Note 155

In Virgil, some printed editions have *concita*, but others, better, have *consita*. The subject is a group of closely packed islands, or Cyclades, which are in a sense scattered throughout the sea.

#### Same place

In Grialius the reading was *multaeque dictione*. I restored the reading from Nonius, whose words Isidore transcribes: *multaque ditione* (“and with extensive authority”). Iso, in his glossary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 171: “Rich, full of places.”

[Col. 0939C] **157. Liberal.** It is from *liber* (“free”), which some prefer to derive from *libet* (“it pleases”), because free men do whatever pleases them. The only possible objection would be the quantity of the first syllable, which is short in *libet* but long in *liber*; yet this argument does not always hold.

**Note 157. Longus.** Many think that *longus* is derived from the Greek λόγχος, “lance, spear,” or from ὄγκοι, “bulk, magnitude.” Perhaps it would be preferable to read, “*Longus*, derived from *lancea*.”

**Note 162. Lymphaticus.** *Lymphae* (“waters”) are said to have been named from the nymphs, as Festus says. He adds that tradition records that those who had seen the image of a nymph in a spring did not cease raving; hence they were called *lymphati*.

**Note 163. Luridus.** *Lura* is a leather vessel, or, as Festus says, the skin of a *culeus*, or also of a *uter* (“wineskin”). Hence *luridus* and *lora*. Others derive *luridum* not from the color of *lura* or *lorum*, but from the beating with a *lorum*, as though it meant “bruised” or “livid.”

**Note 164. Luscitiosus.** *Lusciosus* and *luscitiosus* mean the same thing. Varro and Nonius support Isidore’s interpretation, and Ulpian follows them in the *Digest*, book XXI, title 1, law 10, according to Torrentinus’s edition; and apparently Pliny does so as well, book XXVIII, chapter 11. Besides Fulgentius Placciades, Seneca supports Festus, *On Benefits*, book III, chapter 1, although some there read *vitiosi* (“vicious”) instead of *luscitiosi*.

**Note 165. Mactus.** Ludovicus Carrion, *Emendations*, book II, chapter 3, thinks that Servius should be corrected from Isidore at the verse “*Macte nova virtute*”: namely, *MACTE* means *MAGIS AUCTE* (“increased still more”), with *affectata gloria* (“glory sought after”) instead of *affectatae gloriae* (“of glory sought after”), for Isidore took his words from Servius: “*Mactus*, increased more greatly in glory.” Nor will one easily find elsewhere an example in which *auctus* is joined with the genitive case.

**167. Munifex.** It is from *munus* (“service, gift”) and *facio* (“I make/do”). Isidore’s glossary reads: “*Munifer*, one who carries gifts.”

**Note 170. Memoriam tenet.** Perhaps it should read *memoria tenet* (“it retains in memory”) instead of *memoriam tenet*.

**Note 173. Caeterum rationabilis.** Namely, because *modicus* properly means one who observes a measure: moderate, restrained. Perhaps *caeterum rationabilis, moderatus, a modo*, etc., should be joined together, so that *modi* may be understood as deriving from *modus*.

**Note 176. Mendax.** In Cotelerius, volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, page 257, column 2, the explanation of this word should be consulted.

**Note 178. Ab acie oculorum.** Grialius and other printed editions give *a facie oculorum* (“from the face of the eyes”). I have restored *ab acie oculorum* (“from the sharpness of the eyes”) from the old Palatine Codex 281. In the text it agrees with the others, but in the margin it prefers *ab acie*, which I consider more correct, or uniquely correct.

**Note 179. Mulcator.** Among the ancients, *mulcare* means “to strike, beat, flog.” Althelmus used it for *mulcere* (“to soothe”) in *On the Seven Deadly Sins*:

> Thus he was able to beat the hosts of heaven.

Hence *mulcator*, in the sense explained by Isidore, is a word of a later age.

**B. 180. Hesperios audax.** In the printed editions Lucan’s verse now reads:

[Col. 0940B]

> Bold surveyor, I shall enter the western fields.

**184. Morio.** It is of Greek origin, from μωρὸς, “foolish.”

**Note 187. Nugas.** The ancient grammarians teach that *nugas* may be used indeclinably, like *nequam*, *fas*, and *frugi*. Perhaps one should read *alium nugas existimantes* (“thinking another [person] to be *nugas*”), as shortly afterward: “that is, *nugas*.” See below, note 192.

**Note 189. Alias nefarius, etc.** In other printed editions *alias nefarius* is lacking. Although Grialius does not place punctuation between *nefarius* and *nefandus*, he nevertheless seems to have intended this, judging from the distinction he employs—not that one should say *alias nefarius nefandus* (“otherwise wicked, accursed”). *Nutritor* is from *nutrio* (“I nourish”) and *nutritum* (“nourished”). The phrase “as though an educated person by a nod” is a kind of description produced by a play on words, as often elsewhere, and is not an etymology.

**Note 190. Nuntius.** Vulpius defends *nuntium* as neuter, against Laurentius Valla, Joseph Scaliger, and others, in his commentary on Catullus, poem 62: “Bringing new messages”; he also adds Lucretius and Varro.

**Note 192. Nugas autem.** Hebrew. From Jerome, on Zephaniah III. It is, however, a Hebrew word.

**Note 196. Rectae gloriae.** Vulcanius’s marginal note reads: “Rather, *rectae sententiae* (‘of a correct judgment’).” Both meanings are expressed by *doxa*: “glory” and “judgment,” or “opinion.”

**Note 201. Orbus.** Sedulius used *orbum* simply for “blind,” book III, verse 195. Italian preserves this word and meaning.

**Note 203. Perfectus, cui nihil adjici potest.** Nevertheless, *perfectior* (“more perfect”) is in use. Cicero, *Against Verres*, book VI, chapter 56: “more perfect doors,” etc.

**Note 204. Te multo plus.** Cicero’s words are: “For the figure and features of his hostess delighted him much more.”

**Note 205. Pellax.** Again *pellax*, note 225, and *pellex*, note 229.

**Note 207. Quod pueros agat.** Vulcanius reads *pueros agat*, “that is, may teach,” and notes in the margin: “Rather, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγωγῆς, that is, from instruction.”

**Note 211. Antiqui enim viciam.** *Vicepota*, “Victorious,” is derived from *vicia* in Seneca’s *The Play on the Death of Claudius*: Diespiter, son of Vicepota, as Lipsius notes, *Epistolical Questions*, book II, letter 11. Joseph Scaliger had wished to read in Seneca “son of Nicephora.” *Vicia* is a kind of leguminous plant useful as fodder for beasts of burden.

**Note 214. Petulantes.** That it is derived from *petendo* (“seeking, assailing”) is established by Festus and Nonius as well. But Isidore, using another author unknown to us, adds something else.

**Note 219. Praecinctus.** In the Vulgate: “He began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.”

**Note 221. Piratae.** *Pirata* comes from the Greek πειράω, “I attempt, try.”

**Note 222.** *Pugillator* and *pugillones* are scarcely found anywhere except in glossaries. There is no evidence that earlier writers used these words.

**Note 224. Varum.** *Varus* is also used by Apuleius for “very crooked.” The passage of Pliny is cited by Grialius as book VIII, and by others as book XVIII.

[Col. 0941A]

**Note 225. Pellax.** It is from *pellicio* (“I entice”) and *pellex* (“mistress”). See notes 205 and 229.

**Note 226. Parracida.** Grialius printed *parracida* even in the text, which is unacceptable and will scarcely be found in other authors. Common usage has *parricida*, sometimes *paricida* and *patricida*. *Parricida* appears to have been derived from *parenticida* by syncope.

**Note 227. Persecutor.** It also signifies one who pursues his legal right, or one who accompanies another, unless perhaps *prosecutor* should be substituted for *persecutor*.

**Note 228. Peccator.** Some derive *peccare* (“to sin”) from *pecus* (“cattle”), as though it were *pecuare*, that is, “to act like cattle.” Others foolishly derive it from *pedem capere* (“to catch the foot”).

**Note 229. Prosedendo.** Bar­thius praises, book LX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 7, the reading he found in his own Codex: “*Prosiduae meretrices*, from *prosidendo*.” Plautus calls them *prosedae* in *The Carthaginian*, 1.2.53:

> Or do you wish to linger there among those  
> courtesans, the bakers’ mistresses?

Grialius divided the words at *sub dolositate* (“under deceitfulness”), unless this should be attributed to the printer.

**Note 231. Pisinnus.** Grialius had *pisinus*. Most others write *pisinnus*, a word belonging to Labeo and perhaps also to Martial.

**Note 232. Quaestuosus.** *Quaestuosus* (“profitable”) is the customary form, but not so *questuosus* (“complaining”), and *querimoniosus* (“lamenting”) derives from *queror* (“I complain”) and *querimonia* (“complaint”).

**Note 234. Religiosus.** The derivation of the name *religiosus* and of *religio* is also given in book VIII, chapter 2, note 2.

**Note 244. Superstitiosos ait.** On the etymology of *superstitio*, see book VIII, chapter 3, notes 6 and 7. Concerning *sedulo*, Nonius, chapter 1, note 171: “*Sedulo* means ‘without deceit.’” He gives examples from Lucilius and Cicero. There are also examples from Plautus, Terence, and others, and Donatus likewise transmits the same etymology. Nevertheless, Perottus, Forcellinus, and others disagree.

**Note 245. Socii.** Some think *socius* (“companion”) was derived from *sequor* (“I follow”), through *secta* (“following, faction”); others from *seco* (“I cut, divide”), that is, “I divide.”

[Col. 0941C]

**Note 246. Ego me esse, etc.** Some think these words belong to Afranius.

**Note 247. Sine cura id est.** Perhaps *sine cura* (“without care”) should be restored. *Idem* (“the same”) is intended, for in manuscripts *idem* and *id est* are frequently confused. Thus the text may proceed without parentheses.

**Note 248. Superbus.** Others derive *superbire* (“to be proud”) from *super ire* (“to go above”), or *superbus* (“proud”) from *super* alone.

**Note 249. Susurro.** Perhaps from this passage of Isidore Atto of Vercelli, commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter I, page 15, volume I, wrote: “A whisperer is one who slanders not to the face but in the ear; hence he received his name from the sound of the ears, because he sounds beneath the ear.”

**Note 251. Simulator . . . a simulacro.** Rather, *simulacrum* (“image”) and *simulator* (“imitator”) derive from *simulo* (“I imitate”), which itself derives from *similis* (“similar”).

**Note 257. Secundus.** According to the opinion of others, it derives from *secando* (“cutting”), because in *secundus* the cutting and division begin.

**Note 258. Stipulator.** On the etymology of *stipulatio*, see book V, chapter 24, note 30.

**Note 259. Sanus et salus.** *Sanus* (“healthy”) and *salus* (“health, safety”) are of Greek origin, from σάος or σόος.

**Note 262. Sepultus.** Isidore, together with Servius, explains the description of a buried person through an allusion to the letters, whereas the certain derivation of the name is from *sepelio* (“I bury”), whose true origin is unknown.

**Note 263. Saio.** In the *Supplement to Cangianus’s Glossary*, after rejecting the etymology of *saio*, or *sagio*, from *exigendo* (“exacting”), and another devised by Hickesius, from the Scanian Gothic verb *sakan*, it is more plausible that the *Saiones*, or *Sagiones*, were named from *sagum*, their distinctive garment.

**Note 276. Venustus.** Properly, it derives from *Venus*. Cicero, Macrobius, and others think Venus was so called because she comes to everything, or because everything comes from her.

**Note 279. Vanus a Venere.** The etymology of *vanus* (“empty, vain”) from *Venus* is not appealing; but perhaps it is no better than the alternatives others propose, deriving it from *ve* (“empty”).
