In some manuscripts the *Etymologies* are divided into two parts, and [Col. 0942A] at this point the first part ends after book ten, as will become clearer in the fuller account of the variant readings. Before the variant readings, however, several appendices relating to the books of the *Etymologies* reviewed thus far must be prefixed. They have been drawn from ancient copies of the *Etymologies*, especially from Vatican and Toledan manuscripts, which contain more material than the printed editions.

# BOOK ELEVEN

**Book eleven.** Although, as I noted at the end of the preceding book, the *Etymologies* are divided into two parts in some manuscripts, the books nevertheless continue in the same numerical order; thus this book, which is the first of the second part, is called book eleven.

## Chapter I

**Note 3. Vita.** The origin of *vita* (“life”) is more correctly derived from the Greek βίος.

**Note 4. Et creavit, etc.** The Vulgate, Genesis 2:7: “Then the Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth.” Isidore discusses the same meaning in book I of the *Sentences*, [Col. 0942B] chapter 12, where Loaisa’s note is excellent.

**Note 13. Nam et memoria, etc.** Isidore repeats some of this in the book *On the Differences of Things*, when he explains the difference between *anima* and *animus*, and between *anima* and *spiritus*.

**Note 14. Corpus . . . quod corruptum.** Perhaps the opinion of those who think *corpus* (“body”) means “the work of flesh,” or derive it from *cor*, “heart,” is no better. Others say *caro* (“flesh”) is so called because it lacks life; I would prefer deriving it from the Greek κρέας.

**Note 17. Caro autem et corp.** Those who derive *caro* from the fact that it lacks life think that *caro* properly refers to a dead person. Certainly flesh is something that lives or has lived.

**Note 19. Unde et praesentia.** From *praes* and *sum* the ancients formed *praesesse*, from which *praesentia* (“presence”) remains. Otherwise, however, it is correct that those things are called *praesentia* which are before the senses.

**Note 21. Visus . . . quod vivacior.** This is a similar etymology, which merely explains the property of the thing; for *visus* (“sight”) was not properly so called because it is more vivid than the other senses. The true origin of the name is from ἰδεῖν (“to see”), as Gataker notes in his dissertation *On the Style of the New Testament*, chapter 38. He believes Isidore correctly judged the matter itself, although he rejects the etymology of the name offered by Isidore. Gataker says more there about *visus* in the sense of intellect and of every kind of perception.

**Note 27. Capitium.** It is a woman’s covering for the breast; Nonius interprets it less accurately as a covering for the head.

**Comae . . . Unde et cirri.** Adrian Junius, in his commentary *On Hair*, chapter 1, says that Isidore and Merula manifestly err in interpreting *cirri* as the cut hair of the head, from the Greek κείρεθαι (“to cut”). He himself explains *cirrus* as something twisted around, as if from *circum*. The printed editions have it from the Greek κυρεῖν (“to meet” or “encounter”). Instead of μαλλὸν (“a fleece”), Vulcanius printed *mallonem* and suspected μαλλοὺς (“fleeces”).

**Note 31. Discriminalia.** This word occurs in the Vulgate, Isaiah chapter 3, verse 20. Compare Du Cange and the note to book XIX, chapter 31, notes 8 and 9.

[Col. 0942D]

**Note 42. Cilia.** Bar­thius, book XLIX, chapter 9, is not pleased with the derivation of *cilia* (“eyelashes”) from *celent* (“they conceal”); but he offers nothing better. *Intercilium* is not found among the ancient Latins; hence the Spaniards say *entrecejo*.

**Note 44. Malae.** The Greeks call apples μῆλα; hence, because of a similar roundness, they also call the cheeks or jaws μῆλα. See below, note 74.

**Note 45. Barbam.** Others offer additional etymologies for *barba* (“beard”), but none is suitable.

**Note 47. Nares . . . nare non desinit.** Isaeus likewise observed, in his note on Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 11, that *manare* (“to flow”) is incorrectly read in Isidore instead of *nare* (“to swim”); the words are the same in Lactantius. The etymology was explained from *nares* (“nostrils”) by one ignorant of its origin in book X, note 143. In some printed editions of Terence I read *at non, et caeperit*. But Priscian, book X, page 879 of Putsch’s edition, agrees with Isidore in having *caeperet*, from the ancient word *coevio*. The more common spelling is with *ae*.

[Col. 0943A]

**Note 50. Labia . . . labra.** Others say, conversely, that the upper one is called *labrum*, and the lower one *labium*. In prose, *labrum* is used more frequently than *labium*. In the oldest Toledan Codex this note has been added in the margin: “*Granon*, the hair above the lips.”

**Note 51. A ligando cibo.** Isaeus, in his note on Lactantius, book X *On the Workmanship of God*, attributes to Isidore the statement that it comes from *lingendo cibo* (“licking food”), because he had not seen Grialius’s edition but another in which the reading is *a lingendo cibum*. Avitus compares the tongue to a plectrum in book I, verse 88. See the note on Dracontius, book III, verse 633.

**Note 52. Colomellos.** The Spaniards now call them *colmillos*. Ugutio, Papias, and others took both the explanation and the name from Isidore; but some write *columellos*, others *columnellos*.

**Note 53. Dentium autem.** Salmasius discusses this passage at length in his *Plinian Exercises*, page 33.

**Note 55. Palatum . . . sicut coelum.** Iso, in his glossary on Prudentius, hymn 10, *Peristephanon*, verse 932: “He says ‘under a vaulted covering’ because *URANON* in Greek is called *PALATUM* in Latin, since it is curved in the likeness of the sky, which is also called *URANON*.” The Spaniards call the palate *el cielo de la boca* (“the sky of the mouth”).

**Note 57. Toles.** Grialius’s text had *tolles*, while the note had *toles*, which is also the more common spelling among others. Some prefer *tolae*, *tolarum*.

**Note 59. Rumen.** On *rumen* and *ruminatio*, see again book XII, chapter 1.

**Note 61. Cervix.** Before Hortensius, Pacuvius and Ennius had used *cervix* in the singular. The distinction Isidore adduces from Servius on book II of the *Aeneid*, verse 507—namely, that *cervix* in the singular means the neck, or the limb itself, but in the plural means pride—is not pleasing to others. Many deny that Cicero ever used *cervix* in the singular.

**Note 65. Subhircos.** Guibertus, *On His Life*, book III, chapter 22: “And of the armpits, which they call *subhirci*.”

**Note 66. Unde manupretium.** Brissonius, book IV, chapter 23 of the *Select Antiquities*, says that in Isidore and others one should read *manupretium*, not *manuspretium*. The annotator Trekellius approves both forms on the basis of manuscript copies.

[Col. 0943C]

**Note 74. Quasi malae.** Perhaps *quasi mala* should be restored. Since apples are round, the name *malae* (“cheeks”) and *mamillae* (“breasts”) is derived from their roundness. On the origin of *malae*, see above, note 44.

**Note 78. Incisio.** Vulcanius’s note on the word *incisio* is as follows: “Perhaps he alludes to the etymology of δέρματος. For δέρμα is said to derive from δέρω, which means ‘I cut’ or ‘I strike.’” Vulcanius reads: “For skin in Greek is called *incisio*.” Grialius substituted “κοπτὴ (‘a cutting’) enim,” etc. The two Gothic Toledan manuscripts place numbers 78 and 79 afterward and prefix number 80.

**Note 79. Corium.** Julius Caesar Scaliger, in exercise 127, *On Subtlety against Cardanus*, argues that those who delight, as he says, in Latin purity never use *corium* (“hide”) for *tergum* (“back”). Vulpius rightly refutes Scaliger in his note on Catullus, poem 62, not only because Catullus, Ovid, and other suitable authors used *corium* for “back,” but also because Scaliger himself did not refrain from the word *puritas* (“purity”), which no authoritative Latin writer used.

**Note 82. Ab arctando.** Grialius’s *ab artando* (“from tightening”) could be retained, but I prefer to represent the common spelling.

**Note 87. Quod madefaciant, etc.** Dracontius has the same in book II, verse 613:

> When moisture has first entered the exhausted marrow.

See the note.

**Note 90. Laevus.** It is better derived from the Greek λαιὸς (“left”).

**Note 94. Palae.** This word for the two broad bones of the shoulder blades occurs in Caelius Aurelianus, book III *On Acute Diseases*, chapter 3, and elsewhere in the same author.

**Note 99. Umbo.** It is anything that projects from a flat surface into the shape of a cone, from the Greek ἄμβων (“projection, boss”).

**Note 101. Longao.** Some have *ongabo* in Varro.

[Col. 0944A]

**Note 103. Virus.** It is indeed used of the seed of an animal, and may be used of a man’s seed; but properly it means the vital juice of anything, and is sometimes taken for something harmful.

**Note 106. Femora et femina.** They derive from *femur*, whose genitive is *femoris*, and more frequently *feminis*. Nor is any genuine distinction found between *femora* and *femina*.

**Note 107. Suffragines.** The knee (*genu*) is a bend or curvature made above; opposite to it is the *suffrago*, bent below, as also occurs in the arms.

**Note 108.** *Genu* is correctly derived from the Greek γόνυ.

**Note 111. Talus . . . tholus.** I write *tholus*, although Grialius and others have *tolus*. In the Gothic manuscripts it is *talus*, said to derive from *talo*.

**Note 114. Calcis prima.** Isidore, I think, wrote *calces*; from this the scribes produced *calcis*, changing *e* into *i*, as often happens in manuscripts.

**Note 115. Solum dicitur.** On the meaning of *solum*, see the commentary on Prudentius in many places, as indicated in the index.

**Note 116. Viscera.** Barthius notes, book XLIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 12, that in the homilies commonly attributed to Eusebius of Emesa the tongue is also counted among the internal organs.

**Note 131. Jejunum . . intestinum, unde et jejunium.** Isidore gave this same etymology of *jejunium* (“fasting”) in book VI, chapter 19, note 65.

**Note 135. Hinc et uter.** Namely, *uter*, genitive *utris*, as in book XX, chapter 6, where Isidore also derives *utrem* (“wineskin”) from *uterus* (“womb”).

**Note 138. Lotium.** Others agree that *lotium* (“urine”) comes from *lotum* or *lotu*, although the quantity differs; but some derive the explanation from the fact that the body’s inner parts through which urine passes are washed by this fluid. The use—or abuse—of urine for washing and cleaning garments is certain. Catullus, poem 36, addressed to Egnatius, and Apuleius, in the *Apology*, also indicate that the Spaniards once habitually rubbed their teeth with urine so that they would be whiter.

**Note 147.** In the Regiovatican Codex 1850 there is an *Etymologies* with an allegorical exposition. As an example, I shall include among the appendices, at note 15, chapter 2 of this book, [Col. 0944C] a chapter which in the manuscript is entitled book VI: “On the Position and Condition of the Human Body”; and chapter 3: “How Human Limbs Are Assigned to the Devil.”

## Chapter II

**Note 4. Ad gignendum adulta.** Again, note 15: “A young person . . . for procreation.” Eugenius of Toledo lists six ages of human life, though with some difference, in his recapitulation of Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*. See my prolegomena to Dracontius, pages 18 and 21.

**Note 11. Puer natus est nobis.** In the Vulgate: “For a little child is born to us.” And in Jeremiah, at the passage cited: “Do not say, ‘I am a child’ . . . Do not be afraid,” etc. Isidore appears to be referring to this passage.

**Note 12. Pupilli autem dicti, quasi.** Perhaps one should read: “*Pupilli* are called *orbi* (‘orphans’), as though without eyes.” I restored *decesserunt* (“they departed”) from the Gothic manuscripts in place of *discesserunt*.

**Note 14. Laudantur simili prole puerperae.** In the ancient editions: “The woman who has given birth to her first child is praised”; Munckerus thought this had been written by Isidore through an error, in Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book I, chapter 26, page 61. Grialius restored Horace’s actual words.

**Note 20. Et formavit.** The Vulgate: “And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman.”

**Note 23. Vira.** Festus, under *Querquetulanae virae*: “The ancients called women *virae*, whom we now call women; hence *virgines* and *viragines* still remain.” Mariana, on Genesis 2:23, explains that play on words from the Hebrew idiom: “She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from a man.”

**Note 25. Quo jure.** Since Terence’s words come from the prologue to *The Mother-in-Law*, where Donatus explains the meaning of *adolescentior* (“younger”), discussed in the following note, they seem to belong below, after the words “like an older man, less an old man.” Terence has: “With what right I have acted as a younger man”; where the comparative degree, etc.

**Note 28. Quasi annosa. Nam si commune.** Saint Martin of León, book II, page 484, sermon for the Second Sunday after Easter, quotes this entire passage of Isidore, namely notes 27, 28, and 29. Saint Martin reads *quasi annosa* (“as though aged”). Hence also *vetula* (“old woman”), etc., while entirely omitting the words “For if it is common . . . an old woman?”—which confirms Chacon’s conjecture. Catullus uses the word *anilitas* (“old age”) elegantly, poem 60:

> Until, moving her trembling  
> white hair, old age  
> assents to everything for everyone.

**Note 30. Senectus autem.** Horace, in *The Art of Poetry*: “Many troubles surround an old man.”

**Note 31. Mors dicta.** Saint Julian of Toledo reads this passage as follows in book I of the *Prognostics*, chapter 4: “Death is so called” (in my old manuscript *est* is lacking), “because it is bitter, or is named from the bite of the first man. For when the first father of the human race touched the forbidden tree through disobedience, by the bite he incurred death. Hence *mors* itself is certainly called from *morsus* (‘bite’). There are three kinds of death,” etc. I follow my old Codex, since the editions vary.

The note of the most learned editor of the works of the Toledan Fathers must not be omitted, however, volume II, page 11: “From this passage the reading of some manuscript Codices of Saint Isidore is confirmed, in which this other etymology of *mors* from *morsus* is contained in precisely the same words. Although the Paris edition of Saint Isidore (the Bignaean edition based on Vulcanius), which is older than our royal edition, had indicated this reading, we do not see why in the latter it was not only rejected from the text but entirely omitted from the margin. We could often ask the same question concerning Grialius, who pursued the praise of brevity so zealously that he deliberately passed over entirely many variant readings not to be despised, which he had before him in the Bignaean edition. In this respect the two very old Gothic Toledan Codices agree for the most part with the Bignaean edition, as I shall say in the account of the variant readings.”

Nevertheless, I would not dare reject the reading of Grialius’s edition, which is found in very ancient parchment manuscripts. I would point out, however, that Julian of Toledo, who lived almost at the same time as Isidore, saw a different copy of the *Etymologies*. For, as I have often noted, before Isidore sent the entire work to Braulio, several parts of it circulated as separate publications. Isidore expressed the etymology of death from *Mars* in book VIII, chapter 11, note 51. Others, for their part, prefer to derive *mors* (“death”) from the Greek μόρος, “a destructive fate.” See Vossius, Martini, and William Junius in the dissertation published at Leipzig in 1743, *On the Cult Once Offered to the Goddess Death*. Caesellius Vindex reported that one of the three Parcae was named *Morta*, which Gellius, book III, chapter 16, does not seem to approve.

**32.** Barthius, book XIX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, cites from Apuleius and Virgil the bitter death and bitter funeral of infants.

**Note 35. Cadaver.** Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 18: “And indeed it is flesh that is overthrown by death, so that thereafter it is called *cadaver* from *cadendo* (‘falling’).” This is what Isidore implies, because it can no longer stand; nor do I see why Barthius, book LIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 26, calls this foolish. I consider more foolish what he himself reports: that *cadaver* was so called because all its form and appearance have collapsed.

## Chapter III

**Note 3. Monstra vero a monitu, etc.** In volume I of Cotelerius’s *Apostolic Fathers*, page 60 of the edition, much is explained concerning signs and portents.

**Note 7. Alii magnitudine partium, etc.** Salmasius discusses these matters in his *Plinian Exercises*, page 32.

**Note 14. Praevaricatores angelos, etc.** See the note on line 235 of the *Song on Genesis*, appendix 1 after Juvencus.

**Note 21. Satyri.** Rosweydus’s *Onomasticon*, following the *Lives of the Fathers*, under “Faunus, Satyr, Incubus,” etc., should be consulted for Jerome’s passage which Isidore reproduces.

**Note 24. Octonos.** Grialius printed *octenos*.

**Note 31. Quia fluctus Venerem creav.** The poets imagined Venus as having arisen from the sea, whence she was called *Aphrodite*, *Pontia*, *Marina*, *Pelagia*, and so forth.

**Note 32. Vorticibus.** It is also written *verticibus*.

**Note 34. Dicunt et hydram.** The same account, in nearly the same words, is given of the hydra in book XII, chapter 4.

[Col. 0946A]

**Note 37. Centauris autem.** The two Gothic Toledan Codices give the passage as follows: “The word *species* gave the Centaurs their name, that is, a man mixed with a horse, whom indeed,” etc.

**Note 38. Semibovemque, etc.** Seneca gives a curious account, in *Controversies*, book II, controversy 10, at the end, of the verse of Ovid which his friends wanted removed.

# BOOK TWELVE

## Chapter IV

**Note 2. Herbarum veneficio.** Grialius’s edition has *herbarum beneficio* (“by the aid of herbs”).

**Note 3. Concava littorei, etc.** Ovid’s verses read:

> If you remove the hollow arms of the shore-dwelling Crab,  
> and place the rest beneath the earth, from the buried part  
> a Scorpion will leap forth and threaten with its hooked tail.

**Note 6. Animalia, quae eduntur.** This property of the name is unknown to other authors. Likewise many derive *pecus* (“cattle”) from the Greek πόκος, “fleece,” rather than from *pascendo* (“feeding”).

**Note 9. Mactant lectas.** In Grialius there was *mactant laetis* (“they sacrifice joyfully”) in the note, which I corrected from book IV of the *Aeneid*, verse 57; I think it is an error.

**Note 10. Vervex.** Iso, in his glossary on Prudentius, hymn 10, *Peristephanon*, verse 187: “A *vervex* is so called from the *vermis* (‘worm’) which it has in its forehead; by agitating it, the worm rouses it to battle.” From Isidore’s glossary we learn that this worm is called *simultus*. Compare the notes on this word.

**Note 13. Erit ergo haedus.** Grialius had printed *hoedus*, and some indeed write it that way; but the etymology requires *haedus*, as Varro proves in book IV of *The Latin Language*, chapter 19: “*Hircus* (‘he-goat’), because among the Sabines it is *fircus*; and what there is *fedus*, in the rural districts of Latium is *hedus*, which in the city, as in many cases, becomes *faedus* through the addition of *a*.” Grialius himself, as is clear from his note, wanted *ederae*, or *hederae*, printed in the text; but *edere* remained, which, in accordance with Grialius’s intention, I changed to *hederae*. See Grialius’s preface to our Isidorian edition, chapter 51, note 9. Isidore thought that just as *hedera* (“ivy”) could be derived from *edo* (“I eat”), so *hedus* or *haedus* (“kid”) could be derived from the same verb *edo*.

**Note 14. In transversum, etc.** Hence Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, verse 8: “With the he-goats looking askance.” Grialius’s text has *ciniphii*.

**Note 17. Spiritu narium, etc.** See the note on verses 639–640 of book I of Dracontius’s *Song on God*:

> From their tree-like foreheads stags lose their antlers for snakes to take up,  
> but soon they grow again, palmate.

**Note 21. Hinnulus.** Whether *innulus* or *hinnulus*, “fawn,” it is derived, according to the opinion of others, from ἴννος, “offspring.”

**Note 22. Damula . . . damae.** Others derive *dama* (“doe”) from δεῖμα, “fear.”

**Note 23. Lepus.** Gellius, book I, chapter 18, gives other words of Marcus Varro from book XIV of *Human Affairs*, where he says that Lucius Aelius was mistaken several times:

“For he gave false explanations of several ancient Greek words, as though they were native words of our own . . . In this I not only do not criticize Aelius’s talent, but praise his diligence; for fortune follows success, while praise follows experience.”

Gellius shows that Varro likewise seems to have been mistaken concerning *fur* (“thief”), but adds: “In this matter, concerning a man of such outstanding learning, I am not competent to judge.” Thus learned men, even when they disagree with others about such derivations of names, nevertheless do not behave arrogantly. In volume I of Cotelerius’s *Apostolic Fathers*, page 31 and following, many notes are given concerning the hare and other animals mentioned here.

**Note 24. Cuniculi.** Others say that Spain was named from *cuniculi* (“rabbits”), because these animals are called *Spania* in Punic. This etymology is rejected by the delightful writer Joseph Francis de Isla, in his note on part I of Duchesne’s *Compendium of the History of Spain*, published in French and translated by him into Spanish.

**Note 25. Sus . . . quod pascua subig.** Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, chapter 4: “*Sus* (‘pig’) is called ὖς in Greek, formerly *thysus*, from the verb they call θύειν, which means ‘to sacrifice.’ For the beginning of sacrificing seems first to have been taken from the swine species of livestock.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV, verse 111:

[Col. 0947A]

> The pig is thought to have been the first victim  
> worthy to die, because with its curved snout  
> it had dug up the seeds.

Compare Johann Philipp Cassel’s dissertation *On the Pig in the Sacrifices of the Gentiles*.

**Note 30, note. Syri fratris.** In Grialius read *Satyri fratris* (“of the satyr’s brother”).

**Note 34. Ex eis gerulae.** Solinus used *gerula* adjectivally, namely “bearing drinks”: *cornua potuum gerula*, “drink-bearing horns.” As a noun, according to Hofmann, *gerulae* are vessels capable of holding wine or any liquid. Today the people of Burgundy call large wooden vessels for carrying milk or water *gerlas*. See the enlarged dictionary of Du Cange and Salmasius, page 230 of the *Plinian Exercises*.

**Note 35. Camur.** Vulcanius printed *camor* instead of *camur* and conjectured that one should read καπρύλον. On *camurus* (“curved”), see the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 53:

> Then it ran in varied curved arcs through brilliant crystal.

[Col. 0947B]

**Note 36. Dromeda.** The manuscript Glossary of Camberon, in Rosweydus’s *Onomasticon* following the *Lives of the Fathers*: “*Dromedus*, *dromas*, and *dromedarius* are the same animal, smaller than a camel but swifter and faster in running; hence certain long, swift ships are also called *dromones*.” See there further material about dromedaries. The older Latins said *dromas*, genitive *dromadis*; Saint Jerome called them *dromedarii*. On *dromones*, the ships, see book XIX, chapter 1.

**Note 37. Ruminatio.** On *rumen*, see above, book XI, chapter 1, note 59.

**Note 48. Badius.** This is Vulcanius’s note: “ἀπό των βαὶων, that is, from palm branches, which display a dark reddish-brown color; today the Spaniards call this color *bayo*. They also call a horse of dark reddish-brown color *un bayo*.”

**Note 50. Nam veteres glaucum alb . . . Melinus.** That the ancients called *glaucus* (“bluish-gray”) “white” is again suggested in chapter 6 by the Greek etymology. *Melinus* is a naturally bright-white kind of color. *Melinus* is also used for a yellow or tawny color.

**Note 53. Myrteus est pressus in purpura.** Forcellinus, under *myrteus*, interprets Isidore’s words—“which is *pressus* in purple”—as “darkish, or brown without brightness,” in Italian *baio scuro* (“dark bay”). Servius, on book III of Virgil’s *Georgics*, verse 82: “Those which they call *phoeniciatos*, *pressos*, *myrteos*: they are the same as *badii*.”

**Note 54. Dosinus . . . equiferos.** Salmasius, page 250 of the *Plinian Exercises*, applies Virgil’s words to a *dosinus* horse: “the worst color among whites, and also dun,” book III of the *Georgics*, verse 82. Grialius printed *dosinus* in the text and *dossinus* in the note. Isidore appears to have intended *dosinus*, since he derives it from *de asino* (“from an ass”). Another etymology from *dorsum* (“back”), which the ancients called *dossum*, would require *dossinus*, as in *dossuarius*. Pliny mentions *equiferi*, “wild horses,” in book XXVIII, chapters 10 and 13.

**Note 57. The Jews maintain that Ana [was] a great-grandson . . .** In the oldest Gothic Toledan manuscript one reads: “The Jews assert that Hanaan, the grandson of Esau,” and in the variant readings Bayerius, or Burrielius, noted: “*Hanaan* instead of *Chanaan*, as is habitual among the Goths, such as *amihi* for *amici*, *maicus* for *magicus*, and *loicus* for *logicus*.”

**Note 60. Hanc enim feminarum dicunt.** I supplied *dicunt* (“they say”), which is absent from Grialius’s text but present in the note and in other printed editions. The sense would require *earumque satiata, et species earum* (“and having been filled with them, and their appearance”), unless one understands “the appearance of their faces.”

**Note 61. Dux gregis.** Some very ancient Codices, such as Vatican 623 and Ottobonian 477, add *dux gregis* (“leader of the flock”). *Lycisca* is from *lupus* (“wolf”) and *catula* (“female puppy”). In the following chapter, note 28: “*Lycisci*, as Pliny says, are called those born from wolves and dogs.” The following verses of Eugenius of Toledo are relevant, book I, poem 22:

> These are creatures of mixed stock, produced by unequal mating.  
> A *burdo* is produced when a stallion mates with a she-ass.  
> A mule is created from an Arcadian sire and a mare for its mother.  
> The *tityrus* arises from sheep, with a he-goat as its father.  
> The *musmo* is produced by a goat from the seed of a ram.  
> The *hybris* is born hairy from boars and a sow.  
> But a wolf and a female puppy, mating, produce the *lycisca*.

Perhaps *vervecis semine* (“from the seed of a ram”) should be read instead of *verveno*; strictly speaking, however, *vervex* cannot be used for a ram.

## Chapter II

**Note 6. Scymnique leonum.** Properly, *scymnus* is a lion’s cub; and perhaps Isidore expressed the entire passage of Lucretius:

> And the cubs of lions  
> with claws and feet, already then, and with their bite, resist,  
> scarcely even when their teeth and claws have been formed.

See Appendix 16.

**Note 12. Rhinoceros . . . monoceros.** Montfaucon, volume III of the *Supplement to Antiquity*, book I, chapter 9, understands Isidore’s words as explaining that the rhinoceros and the monoceros are two different animals. That is, he takes “the same, and the monoceros” to mean that just as the rhinoceros is so called because it has a horn on its nose, so the monoceros is so called because it bears a single horn in the middle of its forehead. Perhaps it would be preferable to read *item et monoceros* (“likewise the monoceros”), since *item* and *idem* are frequently confused in manuscripts.

Robert of Sorbonne offers a different explanation in his glosses on the book of Numbers, volume II of Menochius’s Venetian edition, 1743, page 473: “*Rhinoceron* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as ‘horn on the nose.’ The same beast is called *monoceron* in Greek and *unicornis* in Latin because it has one horn in the middle of its forehead, and it is four feet tall.” Raderus discusses the rhinoceros in his commentary on Martial, pages 37 and following and 51 and following; he distinguishes it from the monoceros. Breulius refers in the margin to Pinto on Isaiah chapter 51 and to Pipinus, sermon 10, *On the Secrets of Secrets*.

**Note 13. Virgo puella proponitur.** Montfaucon, at the cited place, displays an image from a gemstone of a girl with an open breast embracing a unicorn.

N. 14. For in Greek, a mountain is λόφος (*lophos*). Gisbert Cuper, in *Exercitation* I, chapter 1, discusses elephants and their trumpeting; from Bochart he says that in Isidore one should restore *mons ὁ λόφος* (“the mountain, the crest”) in place of *mons Clifio*, as it was formerly read incorrectly. From Thomas Hyde he notes that the most common Indian name for the elephant is *bari*, or *bri*. Bochart lists the writers who mention the word *barrus*, [Col. 0948C] *Hierozoicon*, part I, book II, chapter 23. That *ebur* (“ivory”) was derived from *barrus*, as Isidore again asserts, is agreed by most authorities. The Arabs call the elephant *fil*, and its tooth *cenalfil*; from this, I think, the Spaniards derived *marfil*. See Becmann, *On the Origins of the Latin Language*, under *Ebur*, and Vossius, in his *Etymology*, who rejects Isidore’s etymology of *cinnabaris* (“cinnabar”) from *draco* and *barrus* somewhat improperly, because *barrus* is a Latin word, whereas *cinnabaris* had already been used by the Greeks. Isidore himself suggests that *barrus* is an eastern word, and many others confirm this. Whether the trunk is called *rostrum proboscis* or *promuscis*, as Grialius printed it, matters little: manuscripts vary in Isidore and elsewhere, but the more common spelling is *proboscis*, which I prefer to follow. The etymology of the elephant’s name—that it has the appearance of a mountain—can be supported by the fact that many others compare it to a mountain, as Dracontius does in book I of *On God*, line 286:

> It walks with the bulk of its body like a mountain;

where perhaps *molem* should be read instead of *mole*.

[Col. 0948D] N. 15. *Boves lucas* (“Lucanian oxen”). Varro, book VI of *On the Latin Language*, thinks that elephants were called *boves lucas* (“Lucanian oxen”) not so much from Lucania, or from Libya, as some believe, but from *lux* (“light”), because they shone from afar on account of the royal shields, gilded with gold, with which their towers were decorated.

N. 16. *Nunc sola India* (“Now India alone”). It is not sufficiently clear why Isidore denies, or from what source he derived, the claim that now—that is, in his own time—India alone produced elephants, as he again asserts in book XIV, chapter 3, no. 12. Africa still produces them. An accurate description of elephants, as also of the other beasts mentioned by Isidore in this chapter, is found in the French *Dictionary of Animals*, Paris, 1759.

N. 17. *Gryps vocatur* (“It is called a gryps”). Grialius printed in the text *Gryphes vocantur* (“they are called gryphes”), while in the notes he has *Gryphs vocatur* (“it is called gryphs”). Other printed editions have *Gryphes vocatur*. Perhaps Isidore wrote *Gryphis*, as *lyncis* occurs below in the manuscripts instead of *lynx*, or *gryphus*, as others render it. For the present we retain *Gryps* [Col. 0949A], which is the more common spelling. The animal is believed to be fabulous.

N. 18. *Chamaeleon*. The name comes from χαμαί (*chamai*), “on the ground,” and λέων (*leon*), “lion,” as though “little lion.” Grialius and other printed editions write *cameleon*, a spelling supported by the etymology from *camelus* (“camel”) and *leo* (“lion”), though that etymology is otherwise false and perhaps not Isidore’s either. For the words “because it is like a camel,” etc., are absent from the Albanian manuscript, Vatican Archive manuscript 1, and others; and the sense seems to be: “But it is called thus: ‘the little body of this chameleon,’ etc.,” so that *chamaeleontis* is indicated as a genitive.

N. 19. *Camelopardus*. It is also called *camelopardalis*, as by Isidore in book XIV, chapter 5, no. 15; Capitolinus and Vopiscus call it *camelopardalus*.

N. 20. *Numeratur* (“is counted”). From Solinus, chapter 2: “Lynxes too are counted among this class of animals.” Salmasius, however, on page 88 of *Plinian Exercises*, preferred, with the manuscript books, *nominantur et lynces* (“lynxes too are named”). He also refutes Solinus’ opinion, because the lynx resembles the *lupus cervarius* (“deer-wolf”) only in that it too is marked with spots.

[Col. 0949B] N. 21. *Cicero in the Scaurian speech*. Cicero’s *Scaurian Speech*, or *For Marcus Aemilius Scaurus*, is lost. Some fragments of it survive, preserved by Asconius Pedianus in his commentaries. Compare Cicero’s fragments with the notes of Andrea Patricius. Juvenal’s verses are as follows:

> … imitating the beaver, which  
> makes himself a eunuch, wishing to escape the loss  
> of his testicles—for he knows the groin has been treated.

Virgil’s verse, *Georgics* I, line 58, cited by Grialius, should be read as follows:

> But the naked Chalybes send iron, and Pontus manly castoreum,  
> of course.

Hence beavers were called “Pontic dogs.”

N. 22. *Sic format* (“Thus it forms”). The verse beginning *Sic format*, etc., is not found in Dracontius’ poem, which I committed to print from a Vatican manuscript and which, for the most part, had not previously been published.

N. 28. *Lycisci*. On *lyciscus*, or *lycisca*, see the note on the final number of the preceding chapter. Others omit *indiae*, or *Indiae*. They say that *insiliri* (“to be leapt upon”) and *nasci* (“to be born”) should be supplied, or something similar.

N. 29. *Quasi volupes* (“as though swift-footed”). Or *volipes*. Some more recent writers dislike this etymology, although it was adopted by the most ancient learned men, and seek another in the Greek name.

N. 37. *Ichneumon*. Isidore encountered a corrupted copy of Dracontius; for Dracontius is not speaking of the ichneumon, or *suillus* (“swine-like animal”), but of the African people called the Psylli, book I of *On God*, line 515. See the note and prolegomenon, no. 7. Salmasius, on page 446 of *Plinian Exercises*, had not found the verse in Dracontius’ poem and wrongly asserted that Isidore read *suillus* instead of *sullus*. But on page 1315 he reports that the *silurus* is called *suillo* by the Spaniards—perhaps he intended *sollo*—and observes from Isidore that in his day the sea-pig was commonly called *suillum*. Yet, apart from the fact that Isidore, as I have said, had read a corrupted copy of Dracontius in which *suillus* stood for *Psyllus*, he did not understand *suillum* or *sullum* [Col. 0949D] of the sea-pig, but of the ichneumon, commonly called the Indian mouse; concerning this see Pliny, book VIII, chapters 24 and 25.

Whether Isidore called the ichneumon *enhydros* on the basis of an earlier edition of Solinus, as Salmasius says on page 446, may be doubted. For what Pliny reports about the ichneumon—namely, that after rolling itself in mud, when crocodiles open their mouths it leaps into their bellies, and so forth—Isidore attributes to the *enhydros*. Yet in this way *enhydros* can also be distinguished from the ichneumon. Solinus, chapter 45, on Egypt, says:

> The trochilus is a small bird. While seeking scraps of food, it gradually scrapes the mouth of this beast—the crocodile—and, little by little, through the pleasant stimulation of the scraping, makes its way into the throat. When the *enhydros* sees this, it enters the beast as another kind of ichneumon; after ravaging its vital organs, it emerges through the abdomen it has eaten away.

Concerning the *enhydros*, or *enhydris*, Pliny says, book XXX, chapter 3, and book XXXII, chapter 7: “The Greeks call *enhydris* a snake that lives in water,” and so forth.

[Col. 0950A] N. 38. *Catum … catat*. Grialius’ text had *cattum* and *cattat*. That spelling is supported by the word *captura* (“capture”) and by Salmasius’ interpretation, on page 1009 of *Plinian Exercises*, who thinks that *cattat* was formed from *captat* (“seizes”). More often *catus* is written; Varro’s words support this, as does the fact that the first vowel in *catus* is short.

N. 40. *Melo*. Also *melis* in some authors; it belongs to the class of wild cats. Salmasius, in the passage cited, rejects the interpretation taken from Capro, according to which it is so called because it catches honey, or because it has an extremely rounded limb.

## Chapter III

N. 1. *Minuente luna* (“as the moon diminishes”). On this phrase and the matter itself, see the note on Dracontius, book I, lines 735–736:

> And let the waters, the liquids, diminish as the moon diminishes.

See also below, chapter 6, no. 48, of this book.

N. 3. *Mustela*. It is also written *mustella*, as Grialius printed it; but the more common spelling is *mustela*, which is supported by the etymology. Cotelerius, in *Apostolic Fathers*, vol. I, p. 35, lists authors who report that the weasel conceives through its mouth and gives birth through its ear, and adds that learned men labor in vain when they disturb Isidore’s familiar reading. Others, by contrast, assert that the weasel conceives through its ear and gives birth through its mouth.

N. 4. *Aranea* (“spider”). What is missing here concerning the spider can be supplied from chapter 5 of this book and chapter 27 of book IX. Other printed editions present the text as follows: “The shrew, by whose bite the spider dies. It is an animal found in Sardinia,” etc. Otherwise, among the Latins the *mus araneus* is an animal the size of a mouse, with a weasel-like appearance, found in Britain.

What Isidore says about the *solifuga* (“sun-fleeing creature”) is taken from Solinus, chapter 4, or 10, where one reads *occultim reptat* (“it crawls secretly”), etc. But learned men note that Solinus encountered corrupt manuscripts, or himself wrongly described and named the little creature, which others commonly call *solipunga*, *solipuga*, *salpuga*, and *solpuga*. See Festus and Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 4, etc., and the following chapter of this book with Grialius’ note, no. 33.

N. 6, note. *Tota mihi*, etc. These are Martial’s verses [Col. 0950C], *Tota mihi*, etc. Grialius could also have cited another verse from the most ancient Gothic manuscript of Toledo, which reads:

> They come back to life.

Hence some say:

> Dormice sleep through an everlasting winter.

## Chapter IV

N. 1. *Pro Geniis locorum* (“for the genii of places”). Most printed editions incorrectly read *pro Geniis lucorum* (“for the genii of groves”), followed by “and the grove is sacred.” Perhaps *habiti saepe* (“often held”) would be better than *habiti semper* (“always held”). On the genii of the ancients, who were assigned to each individual place, see Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, lines 444 and following, with commentary. On serpents, see Beger, *On Serpent-Bearing Coins*, and Spanheim, *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, pp. 216 and 219.

N. 4. *Omnium animantium* (“of all living creatures”). One may conjecture *omnium reptantium super terram* (“of all creeping things upon the earth”).

N. 5. *Esse necessaria* (“to be necessary”). Supply *traditur* (“it is reported”), or something similar. Solinus, chapter 38, describes the battle between dragons and elephants. Vossius, *On the Theology of the Gentiles*, book IV, chapter 52, produces two coins of Julius Caesar: [Col. 0950D] one depicting a battle between an elephant and a dragon, the other a dragon crushed by an elephant.

I think that Isidore took from Solinus the statement: “It is produced in Ethiopia and India amid the very fires of the unbroken heat”; and perhaps one should read “even amid the fires of the unbroken heat.” Solinus says:

> Ethiopia, etc. On the southern side a mountain rises above the sea, perpetually hot with its natural fire and, even in repose, continually blazing; amid these fires of the unbroken heat there is a great abundance of dragons.

Then he continues: “But as for true dragons,” etc. Isidore understood this to mean that amid the fires of the unbroken heat there was a great abundance of dragons. Solinus, however, after completing his description of the mountain perpetually hot with fire, adds that there is a great abundance of dragons in Ethiopia—not that they are produced amid the fires of the unbroken heat themselves. In antiquity, moreover, the name Ethiopia often included the Moors and all the inhabitants of Africa.

N. 10. *Vipera … Nam cum venter ejus*, etc. Prudentius gives an extensive account of this ancient opinion concerning the conception and birth of the viper in *Hamartigenia*, line 582:

> Thus the viper, as they say, etc.

N. 11. *Pastilli* (“lozenges”). Concerning the lozenges, Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 4, says: “Lozenges are made from a viper; the Greeks call them *theriaci*, after the intestines have been removed,” etc. Add the Salisbury author, book 7, chapter 10.

N. 12. *Fertur autem aspis* (“The asp is also said”). The sense would proceed more clearly as follows: “It is said, however, that the asp….” Saint Martin of León, vol. IV of his works, p. 205, in his exposition of the Epistle of Saint James, copies out this entire passage, but reads it in the same way as the printed editions. The editor notes that Calmet has a dissertation on bewitched serpents, which is certainly learned.

N. 13. *Latine situla* (“in Latin, *situla*”). Martin likewise has this, in the passage cited. Again concerning the *dipsas*, see no. 32.

N. 15. *Per sanguinem evocet* (“summon through blood”). Solinus uses this verb, chapter 40, or 27: “He summons it through blood”—that is, the *haemorrhois* summons it.

N. 16. *Prester*. I write *prester*, not *praester*, as Grialius [Col. 0951B] and others do. Isidore’s and Solinus’ passage do not seem to require alteration. Solinus says in chapter 40: “Whomever the *prester* strikes becomes distended and dies, swollen with an enormous bulk.”

N. 17. *Seps*, etc. Much the same is repeated below, no. 31: “The *seps*, a small serpent.”

N. 18, note. *From Solinus 40*. Solinus’ words from chapter 40 should be quoted. Grialius cites chapter 30 and often changes the order of the chapters in Solinus; I have sometimes restored it to that of the more familiar editions. Solinus therefore says:

> The *cerastae* display four little horns; by showing them, as though they were alluring bait, they kill birds that have been enticed. For the rest of their bodies they deliberately bury in the sand and give no sign of themselves except that part by which, offering food deceitfully, they lie in wait for the death of the winged creatures.

Some read *passibus* (“steps”) instead of *pastibus* (“food”). Salmasius, on page 339 of *Plinian Exercises*, conjectures that Isidore read in Solinus *invitatis dolo passeribus* (“sparrows enticed by deceit”); he himself corrects the passage to *nisi ex ea parte quae invitantis dolo pastus necem praepetum aucupetur* (“except on that part which, as food for the one who entices by deceit, seeks the death of the winged creatures”), with *pastus* in the genitive.

[Col. 0951C] N. 19. *Scytale*. Salmasius, in *Plinian Exercises*, p. 339, denies the variation in the back that Isidore, together with Solinus, recognizes in the *scytale*.

N. 20. *Amphisbaena*. Many think that the *amphisbaena* was not named from having two heads, but because it moves in both directions, forward and backward. They also deny that it has two heads, although its tail is not easily distinguished from its head.

N. 23. *Hydra*. The *hydra* was discussed in book XI, chapter 3, no. 34.

N. 27. *Parias*. It is also written *pareas*.

N. 30. *Ammodytes*. In Lucan, following Grotius’ emendation, I read: “Though marked with very small spots,” etc., and shortly afterward *ammodyes*. Most write *ammodytes*; some *hammodytes*, others *ammodites*.

N. 32. *Dipsas*. Compare above, no. 13, concerning the *dipsas*.

N. 33. *Solpunga*. In the preceding chapter, no. 4, the *solifuga*, or *solpunga*, was discussed. Concerning *caecula*, it should be observed, from Grialius’ note, no. 19, that the interpreter of Dioscorides calls the *scytale* *caecilia* [Col. 0951D]. Pliny also discusses the *caecilia* in book IX, chapter 51.

N. 35. *Βάτραχον* (*batrachon*). The printed editions had βότραχον (*botrachon*) instead of βάτραχον (*batrachon*), which is the more correct spelling. Perhaps *batr[a]x* should also be read instead of *botrax*. *Batrachus* is a kind of spiny sea fish, concerning which Pliny speaks in book XXII, chapter 11. I find nothing about *botrax* in other authors, not even in those who discuss serpents, nor in the Greek lexicographers.

N. 38. *Stellio*. Festus, following Verrius, reports that the *stellio* was rather so called because its venom drips onto food than from its resemblance to stars. I do not find this satisfactory.

N. 39. *Frigidae sunt* (“they are cold”). In Vatican Archive Codex 1, instead of *frigidae sunt* and *sunt frigidae*, the word *frigidescunt* (“they grow cold”) occurs twice; this seems to me genuine. On similar, less common verbs in *-escere*, see the commentary on Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, line 913.

N. 43. *Serpens autem*, etc. The words of the Vulgate are: “But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth.”

[Col. 0952A] ## Chapter V

N. 2. *Aranea*. The spider is discussed again in book XIX, chapter 27. In the most ancient Gothic manuscript of Toledo, after *suspendium* (“hanging”), the following is added:

> For they too are changed together with the web.

Hence some say:

> Wild moths—for the observation is known to farmers—  
> change their shape together with the deadly butterfly.

Perhaps *immutatur* (“is changed”) should be read.

N. 8. *Bombycinum*. In the plural, *bombycina* (“silks”) is used absolutely for “silken garments.” Isidore uses *bombycinum* in approximately this sense for “silken fabric.”

N. 11. *Tinea*. Some think that *tinea* derives from φθίνω (*phthino*), “I corrupt.”

N. 13. *Hemicranius … Costi*. Both *hemicranium* and *hemicraneum* are written; *Cossi* is preferable to *Costi*.

## Chapter VI

N. 2. In the Vulgate it reads: “and spacious in the hands; there,” etc. A short work by Paolo Giovio on Roman fish is extant.

N. 5. *Nigri merulae* (“black female blackbirds”). From Grialius’ note it appears that he intended to print *meruli* in the text; but in fact *merulae* is read. Not only grammarians but also examples from Pliny, Ovid, and others show that this is how it should be said. *Merula* is also the name of a species of bird, whether male or female. Nevertheless, the author of the poem on the nightingale, line 13, says:

> And the singing blackbird joins in with such beautiful songs.

Ibid. *Albouarii* and *alvouarii* perhaps signify the same thing, since in manuscripts *b* is often confused with *v*. *Albouarius* means “white and variegated,” as *albogilvus* does, etc., but in such a way that the white color predominates. *Alvouarius* could be taken as “variegated in color on the belly.” The former, however, fits the subject better; and perhaps that marine thrush is the one that Ray, among other marine thrushes, calls *turdus major varius* (“the large variegated thrush”). Among fish whose names derive from resemblance, Quintilian, book VIII, chapter 2, and Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 12, list the *turdus*, along with the other authorities cited in the French *Dictionary of Animals*, under *Tourd*.

[Col. 0952C] N. 6. *Orbis … calceamentorum soleis* (“a circle … with the soles of shoes”). In Pliny, in the passage cited by Grialius, the corrected editions read *orbis*, not *orchis*. I wrote *calceamentorum soleis* (“with the soles of shoes”) according to the more common usage; Grialius has *calciamentorum soliis*. I would also prefer *instar calceamentorum soleae* (“like the sole of a shoe”), since *instar* governs the genitive.

N. 8. *Exaudivit me*, etc. Jonah’s words in the Vulgate are: “And he heard me; from the belly of hell I cried.”

N. 11. *Delphines certum habent vocabulum* (“Dolphins have a definite name”). Solinus’ words are found in chapter 12, or 22, in Grialius’ chapter 18: “They have a definite name; when called by it, they follow, for they are properly called *simones*.” Solinus took this from Pliny, book IX, chapter 8: “Dolphins are called *SIMONES*, because they have a snub snout.” What is related here about crocodiles is found again below, no. 19.

Ibid. Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 336, copies out the words of this number and adds: “It could not have been restored better.” Salmasius corrects *sulli* in place of *suilli*, prompted by Dracontius’ verse, where formerly one read “*Praecidit suillus*”; to make the meter work he himself emends it to [Col. 0952D] “*Praecidit sullus*.” But in chapter 2 of this book, no. 37, I have already shown that Dracontius should be read:

> Psyllus foretells the force of every poison.

N. 17. *Tradunt*, etc. The same material is repeated below, no. 51.

N. 18. *Aure feriat* (“let it strike with the ear”). I do not sufficiently understand what Isidore means. Grialius’ note had *de ferendo* (“concerning carrying”); I restored *de feriendo* (“concerning striking”), for Isidore seems to be referring to the words *aure feriat*.

N. 20. *Pisces quidam* (“certain fish”). He said in no. 11 that these were dolphins. But perhaps there are others as well. Here these fish are said to have a saw-toothed crest; there, the dolphins of the Nile have a saw-toothed back.

N. 23. *A similitudine capitis* (“from the resemblance of the head”). Rondelet, book XV, chapter 9 and following, describes a certain species of sea hare that resembles the land hare in its snout. But this sea hare appears to be different from the one discussed by Pliny and other ancient writers.

N. 24. *Denique reti* (“finally, by a net”). Others have *rete* in the ablative, a form that can be retained on the basis of the usage of certain ancient writers. See the note on Sedulius, book II, line 62:

> He remained, and God rested in a narrow manger.

N. 25. *Mullus in vino … affert* (“the mullet in wine … brings”). Many old copies present the passage as follows: “A mullet killed in wine: those who drink from it develop an aversion to wine.” I would believe that this arose from the usage of Isidore’s age, since the nominative was often used for the ablative absolute.

N. 28. *Glaucus*. In chapter 1 of this book, no. 50: “The ancients called *glaucus* white.”

N. 30. *Scarus*. Spaniards commonly place an *s* before an initial vowel; this usage appears to have been current already in Isidore’s time, for he derives *scarus* from *esca* (“food”), as though it were written *escarus*.

N. 33. *Hamia*. Grialius printed *hamio*, but in the note he says that *hamia* should be written; I have therefore substituted it.

N. 36. *Ostendit* (“it shows”). Grialius had *designat* (“it indicates”) enclosed in parentheses, indicating that this word, or something similar, was absent from the manuscripts. The first Gothic manuscript of Toledo has *ostendit*, which I restore.

[Col. 0953B] N. 41. *Anguilla vino* (“the eel in wine”). Here again, in ancient copies, the nominative absolute occurs in place of the ablative: “Eels killed in wine: those who drink from it develop an aversion to wine.”

N. 43. *Muraenam*. In vol. I of *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 31, in the notes, there is a discussion of the *muraena*. Some deny that it mates with the viper, others assert it, and others remain doubtful.

N. 44. *Polypus*. In vol. I of *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 32, many observations on the *polypus* are recorded from Athenaeus and others.

N. 45. *Torpedo*. A beautiful poem by Claudian on the *torpedo* is extant.

N. 46. *Sepia*. It is called σηπία (*sepia*) in Greek, not *saepia*, as Grialius printed it. In vol. I of *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 32, it is noted that when pursued by a fisherman the cuttlefish emits ink from its belly in order to elude him.

N. 48. *Incremento lunae* (“as the moon increases”). Compare chapter 3 of this book, no. 1, concerning the alteration of certain bodies during the moon’s waning and waxing.

N. 49. *Celae*. Salmasius, on page 1127 of *Plinian Exercises*, says that *caelae*, not *celoe*, should be read here; but neither is *coelae* correctly derived from *coelum* (“sky” or “heaven”), as Isidore suggests. For *coelae* in Greek is κοῖλαι (*koilai*), that is, “hollows.”

N. 51. *Tradunt quidam*, etc. This is repeated from no. 17.

N. 52. *Ostrea dicta est a testa* (“The oyster is called from its shell”). It would be permissible to restore the passage as *Ostrea dicta a testa*, without *est*; or *dicta sunt a testa*; or, better, *a testa qua* (“from the shell by which…”). For the relative *quibus* has no antecedent with which it can agree.

N. 54. *Angusta ab sede*. Virgil’s editions have *angusta a sede* (“narrow from its seat”), but Isidore may have found *ab sede*.

N. 56, note. *Also from Pliny*. Salmasius observes that Pliny should be emended on the basis of this passage of Isidore, p. 1122 of *Plinian Exercises*.

N. 58. *Grandiores cunctarum* (“larger than all”). This is a phrase common in the later period, used for *grandiores cunctis* (“larger than all”).

N. 59. *Agredulae*. Salmasius, p. 1318 of *Plinian Exercises*, reads *acredulae* and observes that Isidore here explains *acredulae* as little frogs, while elsewhere—chapter 7, no. 37—he explains the word as a nightingale, but nowhere touches the truth; for an *acredula* is an owl, so called from its sharp and piercing voice.

There are, however, several opinions concerning the bird *acredula*: some think it is an owl, others a nightingale, others a lark, and others a *ravarinus*. Nor is it established for everyone that there is not also a kind of frog called *acredula*, or *agredula*. Some indeed take Cicero’s Latin verse from Aratus’ Greek, book I of *On Divination*, chapter 8, as referring to a frog, since Aratus’ Greek word ὀλολυγών (*ololygon*) also signifies a frog:

> And the *acredula* insists with its morning voices.

This interpretation seems foolish to many, but from Isidore one can infer that it is ancient.

N. 60. *Spongia*. Grialius has *sfungia*, and shortly afterward *fungiis*. I restored the common spelling *spongia* everywhere; it is a Greek word. Nor is the etymology from *fingere* (“to fashion”) an obstacle, since it indicates the use of the object rather than the origin of the word. Cicero’s words, in the passage cited, are: “to sponge blood out of the Forum,” as many read them with Servius on book VIII of the *Aeneid*, line 634. The common reading is *effundi* (“to be poured out”) instead of *effingi* (“to be sponged out”).

Ibid. Grialius had written *pennicilli* (“little brushes”).

N. 63. *Loliginum*. Here Grialius printed *luliginum*; above, no. 47, he had *lulligo*. The more common spelling is *loligo*, or *lolligo*.

## Chapter VII

N. 1. *Aliae enchoriae* (“other native species”). *Encorius*, meaning “native” or “regional,” is also used by Philargyrius on *Georgics* IV, line 298. Salmasius, p. 170 of *Plinian Exercises*, reads *aliae enchorae* and cites from Frontinus *enchores lapides* (“native stones”), and from the *Lives of the Fathers* *unus enchoris* (“one native [person/thing]”). Saint Jerome, letter 104, used *enchoria avium genera* (“native species of birds”). Some write *incores* or *encores* instead of *enchores*, and *enchorii* is preferable. See Ducange.

N. 5. *Pulli*, derived from the Greek πῶλοι (*poloi*, “young animals”). The other explanations that Isidore frequently offers, intended to explain some property of a thing through alliteration, do not concern the true etymology.

N. 13. *Avis … tarda*, now *avutarda*, or *abutarda*, in Spanish. Some say that this is the bird the Italians call *gallo di montagna*, “mountain cock”; others call it *starda* in Italian and *outarde* or *otarde* in French. See the already cited French *Dictionary of Animals*.

N. 18. *Cygnus*. Since in the following number Isidore says that *cygnus* is a Greek name, while here he says that it derives from singing, he merely intends the bird’s characteristic to be recalled through an allusion in the letters, not to acknowledge a true etymology. This point must be repeated regularly, lest etymologies be mocked as foolish.

N. 19. *Cygnus in auspiciis* (“the swan in augury”). Saint Martin of León, vol. I, sermon 2, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, p. 444, copies out this entire passage on the swan and reads: “because it plunges itself into the waves.” Servius, on book I of the *Aeneid*, line 397, reports these two verses as follows:

> The swan, in auguries, is a bird most welcome to sailors.  
> They always desire it, because it never sinks beneath the waves.

The reading explained from Saint Martin seems less correct; for swans portend favorable things to sailors because, although they swim extensively, they never sink, as Aldrovandus explains these verses from Isidore, *Ornithology*, vol. III, p. 26.

N. 20. *Struthio*. Hence the Spanish *avestruz*.

N. 23. *Cinnamolgus*. In Grialius’ note one should read or understand: “*Cinnamum* is the same as *cinnamomum*; for *cinnamolgus* is a bird,” as Isidore explains. Concerning it, see the note on Dracontius, book I of *On God*, line 326, where I observed that nests resembling those reported by Isidore are now purchased at great cost and exported from the Philippine Islands to be served at the tables of luxurious people.

N. 24. *Psittacus*. Especially after the discovery of the West Indies, many species of parrots have been listed. Besides Solinus, Aristotle, Pliny, Apuleius, and others should be consulted concerning the parrot of the ancients. As for what is meant by the claim that parrots once knew how to utter *ave* (“hail”) or χαῖρε (*chaire*, “greetings”) without a teacher, the interpreters of Martial at the cited passage and of Persius at the prologue to this work, line 8, explain it: “Who taught his *chaire* to the parrot?”

[Col. 0954D] N. 25. *Cyaneus*. It denotes something that reflects a blue color. Accordingly, *ales oceanea* (“ocean bird”) would seem more correct, since the words that follow refer to the Ocean, not to the color blue. Grialius indeed indicates in his note that he wrote *oceanea*, but in the text there appears *ales cyanea*. Pliny, book X, chapter 32, writes that halcyons are for the most part *cyaneus* in color. But others report that halcyons vary in color according to how they turn toward the light or the sun.

Ibid. On the pelican, Eusebius and pseudo-Jerome on Psalm 101 should also be consulted. Grialius wrote *pellicanus*, but the correct spelling is *pelicanus*, or, as others prefer, *pelecanus*, from πελεκάν (*pelekan*), because it has a broad beak. Many think that the pelican is the *onocrotalus*, concerning which Pliny speaks in book X, chapter 47; accordingly Saint Jerome translated the *onocrotalus* in Leviticus 11 from the Greek as “pelican.” Others wish the word *pelican* to denote different birds, as Calmet explains in his *Biblical Dictionary*, where he observes [Col. 0955A] that the stories of pelican offspring restored to life by their parent’s blood are believed only because of the prejudice of ancient philosophy. The *onocrotalus* is discussed in no. 32.

N. 27. *Stymphalidae*. Stymphalus is a lake and also the name of a very high mountain in the Peloponnese, in Arcadia. On the Stymphalian birds, see Hyginus, fables 20 and 30, and Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, line 300. Muncker, in his note on Hyginus, fable 30, defends the spelling *Stymphalidae* rather than *Stymphalides*, just as *heroidae* is used for *heroides*, etc. But what is said—that Breulius rashly corrected *Stymphalides*—is false; for Breulius’ first edition reads *Stymphalidae aves a Stymphadibus insulis* (“Stymphalidae birds, from the Stymphades Islands”).

N. 32. *Onocrotalon*. See the note on no. 26. Pliny also discusses the *onocrotalus*, book X, chapter 47.

N. 34. *Coredulus*. Since I find the name *coredulus* nowhere else, I wondered whether someone had formed *coredulus* from *carduelis*, discussed in no. 74. Some think that Isidore wrote *coredulus* for *corydalus*, which is a lark.

N. 36. The old printed editions read *brachiorum membris* (“with the limbs of the arms”); Grialius correctly restored *membranis* (“with membranes”), although some maintain that *membris* can be retained for *membranis*. The Gothic manuscripts of Toledo read *membranis*, and in the oldest of them the following addition appears in the margin:

> For, just like mice, this creature produces its young from its own offspring.

N. 37. *Acredula*. Compare what I said concerning *acredula* in the preceding chapter, no. 59.

N. 39. *Bubo*. On the bad omen of the owl, see Pliny, book X, chapters 12 and 13.

N. 41. *Nycticorax*. Others believe it to be an owl; the word properly means “night-raven.” Bochart, *On the Animals of Sacred Scripture*, part II, book II, chapter 20, thinks that the Hebrew word *cos*, which the Vulgate and the Septuagint interpret as *nycticorax*, is the *onocrotalus*.

N. 43. *Stridet* (“it shrieks”). Ovid likewise has this, *Fasti* VI, line 128:

> They are called *striges*; but the reason for this name is  
> that they commonly shriek horribly at night.

Others read *horrenda* (“horrible things”), and others *horrenda stridere voce* (“to shriek with a horrible voice”). Pliny, book XI, chapter 39, at the end, says: “I consider it fabulous that *striges* suck milk from the breasts of infants.” Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 59, line 1044:

> Moreover, if the black *strix* should happen to press upon children,  
> offering poisonous breasts to their outstretched lips.

Ovid, in the passage cited, line 125:

> They fly by night and attack children deprived of their nurse,  
> and ravage the bodies they have snatched from their cradles.  
> They are said to tear the nursing entrails with their beaks,  
> and to have throats full of the blood they have drunk.

Isidore says: “It is said to provide milk for infants,” because, according to popular belief, it lured them in order to suck out their blood. Virgil, book XII, line 862, seems to describe the *strix*:

> Suddenly gathered into the form of a little bird …

Others understand this as a screech-owl.

N. 44. *Cornix*. In Greek, κορώνη (*korone*). Horace, book III, ode 17, line 16:

> The aged crow, an augur of the water.

N. 45. *Quidam voluit* (“Someone wished to claim”). This was Varro, whose name Isidore spared, unlike Quintilian, whose words he reproduces from book I, chapter 6, or 10:

> Who would grant pardon after Varro? He tried to persuade Cicero that *ager* (“field”) was so called because something is done in it, and *graculi* (“jackdaws”) because they fly in flocks, although the first word is plainly derived from Greek and the second from the cries of birds.

Pliny, book XI, chapter 37, section 79, and chapter 47, says that *graculi* are named from the sound of their cry, *gra, gra*. Festus thinks that *graculi* derive either from the sound of their mouths or from carrying seeds or berries, as though they were called *geraculi*.

N. 46. *Picae … poetricae* (“magpies … poetic”). In Persius’ prologue, most read *poetrias picas* (“poetic magpies”).

N. 47. *Diu haerere* (“to remain for a long time”). Pliny explains this in book X, chapter 18:

> There are also small birds with hooked claws, such as the woodpeckers, distinguished by the surname *Martius* and highly significant in augury, etc. They alone raise their young in hollows [of trees]. It is popularly believed that when wedges driven into their cavities by a shepherd are touched with a certain herb, they slip out.

N. 49. *Argiva primo*. In Martial’s verse, some have *Argiva primum* (“Argive first”).

N. 50. The priests of Cybele were mutilated, or castrated; but they were called *Galli* (“Galli”) from the river Gallus, not because they were castrated.

N. 51. *Anas*. Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 13: “*Anas* comes from *nando* (‘swimming’).”

N. 52. Pliny, book X, chapter 22:

> And the goose, with its vigilant care—as the defense of the Capitol proved—exposed the danger at a time when the silence of the dogs had revealed the situation.

See Livy, book V, chapter 47. In Breulius’ edition, this note was accidentally inserted by the printer into Isidore’s text. It reads: “He was discovered. As Livy reports in book V, Plutarch in *Camillus*, and Florus in book I, chapter 13.” These words are absent from the Bignaean edition, which Breulius followed.

N. 53. *Leporinam sapiat* (“it tastes like hare”). Grialius printed in the text, together with the old editions, *leporinam sapit* (“it tastes like hare”), that is, “hare meat”; in the note, *leporem sapit* (“it tastes like a hare”).

N. 54. *Ab assiduitate mergendi* (“from the frequency of plunging”). See Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 13.

N. 55. *Accipiter*. Concerning the *accipiter*, Cotelerius noted some interesting matters in vol. I of *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 30, in connection with the words of Barnabas. The Gothic manuscripts of Toledo have in the Apostle’s words: “If anyone takes.” The Apostle’s words are:

> For you tolerate it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes you, if someone exalts himself, etc.

In Isidore’s glossary, *accipiter* is also called *acceptor*: “a fledgling, *accipiter*, *acceptor.” Lucilius used *acceptor* for *accipiter* in Charisius, book I, p. 76 of Putsch.

N. 59. *Ossifragum*. The Spaniards use *Quebrantahuesos* with the same meaning, “bone-breaker.”

N. 62. *Titos vocant* (“they call them *Titi*”). Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 15:

> The *Sodales Titii* were so called from the birds called *TITII*, which they customarily observe in certain auspices.

Some call the wood-pigeon not chaste but lustful. In saying “after bodily companionship had been lost,” Isidore follows the usage of others who use *consortium* for “partner” and *conjugium* for “spouse.” See the note on Juvencus, book IV, line 16.

N. 63. *Perdix*. It is also called this in Greek. On its nature, compare Pliny, book X, chapter 33, with Isidore.

N. 66. *Cujus sanguine*, etc. These statements are fabulous.

N. 67. *Cuculos*. Instead of *cuculos*, the two often-cited Gothic manuscripts of Toledo repeatedly have *ciculos*; perhaps that was once their name.

N. 69. *Merula*. In Achaia it is white. Pliny says in book X, chapter 30:

> White blackbirds are born around Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, and nowhere else.

And Solinus, speaking of Arcadia, chapter 12:

> While the blackbird is tawny in other places, around Cyllene it is exceptionally white.

Arcadia is part of Achaia, in the middle of the Peloponnese.

N. 70. *In aere capiat escas* (“it catches food in the air”). The basis of the etymology—that it catches and eats food in the air—is not sufficiently apparent; but no other suitable derivation of the name presents itself. The attempt by some to derive *hirundo* (“swallow”) from the Greek χελιδών (*chelidon*) is unconvincing. Pliny says much about the swallow in book X, chapters 24 and 33.

N. 71. *Turdela*. I find nowhere else the claim that *turdela* is a larger *turdus*. Some authorities list *turdelix* and *turdillus* for a small thrush.

N. 72. *Furfurio*. This name too, like many others in Isidore, is absent from the lexicons.

N. 74. The printed editions had ἀκάνθοις (*akanthois*). In Virgil’s verse, others more correctly read *et acanthida*.

N. 78. *Auguriantur*. Instead of *auguriantur*, one could restore *augurantur*, which is more Latin. In the words “has no credibility,” one should understand: “the third kind has no credibility”—that is, even among the ancients themselves, who considered the first two kinds of augury certain and valid.

N. 81. *Ovorum vim* (“the force of eggs”). Salmasius, in his note on Aelius Spartianus, p. 243, line 26, observes from the commentator on Juvenal that glass is also customarily solidified with sulfur. On ductile and flexible glass, compare book XVI, chapter 16, no. 6.

## Chapter VIII

N. 1. *Quod sine pedibus* (“that which is without feet”). This etymology was sufficiently accepted among the ancients; nevertheless, Julius Caesar Scaliger opposed it.

N. 3. **Costros.** I believe, with Chacon, that the discussion here concerns *oestri*; nevertheless, I change nothing on that account. For I think that errors of this kind arose because Isidore, or some earlier writer, came upon corrupt manuscripts, was deceived by them, and sometimes divided one and the same thing into two because of two different names. Pliny, concerning *oestri*, Book XI, chapter 16: “At the outermost parts of the honeycombs bees are born that are larger and drive away the others; this pest is called an *oestrus*.”

N. 4. *Crabro*, as some think, is so called from its unpleasant buzzing, or from *craceo*, meaning “to be slender.” *Scarabaeus* is a Greek name, and there is no need to derive it from *crabro*.

N. 6. **Cicindela.** Festus: “*Cicindela*, a kind of fly that shines at night, evidently from its brightness.” Grialius wrote *cicendela*; Vulcanius and others, *cicendula*.

N. 9. **With long feet, like a spear.** This etymology is ridiculed by Becmann and others. Rightly so, if one is seeking only the true origin of the word; but the ancients attempted, not without some usefulness, to express the characteristic of a thing through the word itself—as in the word *locusta*, since the locust is furnished with long feet, like a spear. Nor can the derivation which Becmann offers from the verb *uro* be defended in any other way: locusts are so called because they seem to scorch every place on which they settle and consume every kind of crop.

N. 10. **Cicadas.** Pliny discusses cicadas at greater length in Book XI, chapters 26 and 27. Understand this as meaning “nor anywhere else in such numbers.”

N. 13. **Culex.** Becmann approves Isidore’s etymology: “*Culex*,” he says, “as if *aculex*.” He observes that Tertullian attributes a tube and a lance to the mosquito.

N. 15. **Oestrus.** It is used in both ways, in the masculine and neuter genders: *oestrus* and *oestrum*; but *oestrus* is more frequent. Compare no. 3. Varro also uses *tabanus* for *asilus* in Book II of *On Agriculture*, chapter 5. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 28: “Some of the remaining creatures have a sting in the mouth, as with the *asilus*, or, as some prefer, the *tabanus*; likewise mosquitoes and certain flies.”

[Col. 0957C] N. 16. **Bibiones.** Salmasius, in his note on Spartianus’s *Hadrian*, chapter 16, read *bibones* and interpreted it as “mosquitoes.” But *culex* is the genus, whose species is the *bibo* born from wine. Nor is there any reason why we should prefer *bibo*. From the old vernacular term *mustiones*, the name *mosquitos* passed to the Spaniards.

N. 17. **Gurgulio.** The proper name of the little worm is *curculio*, which, as Servius wishes in his note on Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 185, is so called from *gurgulio*, that is, “throat.” Nevertheless, because of the similarity of the letters, among the ancients the little worm is also called *gurgulio*. In the old Vatican-Palatine Manuscript 281 of the *Etymologies*, I find a certain fragment concerning the sounds of birds and other animals. For the benefit of scholars, and to illustrate this book, I shall place it among the appendices to the *Etymologies*, section 17.

## BOOK THIRTEEN

### CHAPTER I

**No. 1. And the world was made through him.** In the Vulgate: “And the world was made through him.”

### CHAPTER II

**No. 2. To some small particle.** Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 10: “We see particles of dust in the sun when it has admitted its rays through a window.” Isidore uses the word *atomus* in both the masculine and feminine genders, since it can be used in either way; but it is more frequently employed in the feminine, which most later writers accordingly retain.

### CHAPTER III

**No. 1.** *Hyle*, “matter,” and *silva* are also transferred to the literary apparatus. The philologist Atteius, in Suetonius, *On Grammarians*, chapter 10: “Remember to commend our *hyle* to others: as you know, we have gathered material of every kind into eight hundred books.”

**No. 3. All things contain it.** Supply “the Greeks say,” or something similar.

### CHAPTER IV

**No. 2. Now this in Greek.** Grialius, together with the other printed editions, published *Hoc autem Graece* (“Now this in Greek”); but in the text he has *Hic autem Graece* (“Here, however, in Greek”). I do not know whether he varied the wording deliberately. Saint Martin of León, who transcribed this entire chapter in volume II, sermon 2, on Septuagesima, pages 17–18, gives: “Now this in Greek,” etc. In other words he differs slightly, as in no. 1, where he has *luminaria* and *luminaribus* instead of *lumina* and *luminibus*.

**No. 3. The birds of heaven.** Saint Martin, in the passage cited, reports: “The Lord also in the Gospel calls them the birds of heaven.” Here the learned editor added the following note: “Isidore reads: ‘And the Psalm calls them the birds of heaven.’” But the birds of heaven are often mentioned both in the Psalms and in the Gospel, as can be seen in Psalms VIII and CIII, and in Matthew chapters VIII and XIII, Mark IV, and Luke VIII, IX, and XIII.

### CHAPTER V

**No. 1. Aether.** Saint Martin of León, in the passage cited, pages 30 and following, describes chapters 5 and 6 as follows: “Therefore the outstanding teacher Isidore says: ‘The aether is a place,’” etc. The editor rightly observed that one should read: “The aether is a place.”

**No. 2. And with its motion.** Grialius had *et cum mora ejus* (“and with its delay”), which, on the basis of manuscripts and other printed editions, I changed to *et cum motu ejus* (“and with its motion”).

[Col. 0958B] **No. 5. The poles, etc.** These statements are for the most part repeated in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 12, just as many other passages of this book are related in that work, where anyone wishing to find fuller notes may do so. *Polus*, however, ought not, according to its true etymology, to be derived from *polire* (“to polish”), but from the Greek *πολέω* (*poleō*), from which comes *πόλος* (*polos*), “pivot” or “pole.”

### CHAPTER VI

**No. 2. Of the constellations.** Saint Martin of León, in the passage cited, also gives *arctorum*, or, as it was printed there, *artorum*; this reading is therefore ancient.

**No. 7. The zodiac, etc.** These words are entirely omitted by Saint Martin of León, who stopped at the words “they dwell in the regions of the south wind.” It appears that he read nothing else in his copy of Saint Isidore, for he immediately adds: “After these brief statements by blessed Isidore concerning the sphere of heaven and the five zones,” etc.

### CHAPTER VII

**No. 1. Of whom Virgil writes.** Virgil, in the passage cited:

> Having followed it through the long void with a light javelin;

Grialius omitted this. Therefore change nothing.

[Col. 0958C] ### CHAPTER VIII

**No. 2. It simultaneously represents flashes of lightning.** I would prefer *simul et fulgur emicat* (“and at the same time the lightning flashes”); this is certainly clearer. Pliny the Elder likewise used *fulgetra* for *fulgetrum*.

### CHAPTER IX

**No. 2. From the wind, etc.** Among the ancient effects of lightning, in addition to others, Seneca lists these in Book II of the *Natural Questions*, chapter 31, and Pliny in Book II, chapter 51.

### CHAPTER X

**No. 4. And to the clouds.** I would suppose that one should read *et ad nimbos* (“and to the rain clouds”), since these belong to rain. See Servius on *Aeneid* I, verse 747: “Whence rain and fires,” and on *Aeneid* III, verse 194, and V, verse 10:

> A blue rain cloud stood above his head.

**No. 13. Air deprived of the sun.** Others commonly describe shadow in this way; but Becmann, under the word *Umbra* (“shadow”), observes that shadow is not air. Properly, shadow is in the air *ἀπουσία φωτός* (*apousia phōtos*), “the absence of light.” This is also what Isidore soon indicates: “We take light away from it.”

### CHAPTER XI

**No. 3. The Vulturnus.** Salmasius, page 1245 of the *Plinian Exercises*, denies that the Vulturnus is on the right side of the Subsolanus, since for most writers the Vulturnus is the same as the Eurus, which is placed on the left side of the Subsolanus. Others, however, place the Eurus midway at the equinoctial pivot of the east, as Favorinus does in Gellius. Yet, as Gellius himself says, among the ancients there was generally no agreement either about the names of the winds, their boundaries, or their number. Pliny contradicts Favorinus, saying in Book II, chapter 47: “From the equinoctial east comes the Subsolanus; from the winter east, the Vulturnus.” Seneca says the same in Book V of the *Natural Questions*, chapter 16. Isidore, following I know not whom, treats the Vulturnus as a wind distinct from the Eurus and the Euronotus, and thinks it is the same as the Caecias, as is clear from *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 37: “The Vulturnus itself, which is also called the Caecias, is to the right of the Subsolanus.” The verses on the winds, transcribed after the cited chapter in certain manuscripts and printed editions, correspond to this:

**No. 6. It corrupts the air.** Gellius gives a different account in Book II, chapter 22: “In Latin it is called the Auster, in Greek *Νότος* (*Notos*), because it is cloudy and moist; for *νοτίς* (*notis*) in Greek means ‘moisture.’” Thus Gellius follows Favorinus’s opinion.

**No. 8.** In the first Toledo Manuscript, of remarkable antiquity, the following is added: “It was named Favonius because it fosters the crops and flowers. Hence in Greek, Zephyrus, because it generally blows in spring; whence comes the following:

> And by the Zephyr the yielding clod is loosened …  
> Zephyrus, by its Greek name …  
> By the Zephyr they are made …

**No. 10. Corus.** It is written *Caurus* and *Corus*, and, with an inserted aspiration, *Chaurus* and *Chorus*. But the true explanation of the name is not thereby established—that it is so called because it supposedly makes a *chorus*. Isidore adds this in his customary manner, so that through an allusion to the letters we may understand that the Corus is last in the enumeration of the winds and, as it were, closes the chorus; for in *On the Nature of Things* he begins from the north and ends with the Caurus, or Corus.

**No. 12. Circius.** Perhaps this is the wind called *Cierzo* in Spanish, namely one that comes from the region of the north. Gellius, in the passage cited, observes that the Circius, a wind blowing from the region of Gaul, is called by Varro, when he writes about the Spaniards, the *Cercius*. Pliny, Seneca, Favorinus, and others appear to regard the Circius as a special wind of Gallia Narbonensis; this may be supported by the readings *Gallicum* and *ex parte Galliae*. Compare, however, Salmasius, page 1258 of the *Plinian Exercises*, and Vossius on Pomponius Mela, Book II, chapter 5; they contradict one another.

### CHAPTER XII

**No. 2. Water.** This was the more common opinion of the ancients: that waters stand in heaven. It is confirmed by clear testimonies of Holy Scripture.
