See the note on Dracontius, Book I, verses 25 and 137. Isidore perhaps wrote *quibus igni et aqua interdicitur* (“to whom fire and water are forbidden”).

**No. 4. They carry away with them.** The reading found in the Gothic Toledo Manuscripts, *rapiunt et secum* (“they carry away and with them”), would not be bad.

### CHAPTER XIII

**No. 2. From Lake Clitorius.** Pliny, Book IV, chapter 6; Livy, Book XXXIX, chapter 35; and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, verse 322, agree concerning Lake Clitorius, or its spring, which makes people abstain from wine. *Clitor*, or *Clitorium*, is a city of Arcadia, beside which Lake Clitorius is situated. It seems certain, therefore, that Isidore is speaking of the Arcadian lake, not the one in Italy. This entire chapter could be illuminated by the dissertation of Johann Heinrich Schmid, published at Leipzig in 1738, *On Springs Famous for Their Medicinal Properties*.

**No. 3. On the island of Chios.** Vulcanius notes that Pliny has the different reading *In Cea insula* (“on the island of Cea”). Cea, also called Ceos and Cia, is one of the Cyclades, near the island of Helena, famous for its abundance of water. Pliny discusses it in Book IV, chapter 12, and Book XI, chapter 22; Harduinus should be consulted there for his notes and emendations.

**No. 7. Of Marsyas.** In the text Grialius, together with the other printed editions, has *Marsidae*; in the note, *Marsyae*. Vulcanius observes that Pliny has a different reading, “in Arcadia”; and in fact the Styx is found in Arcadia, which is part of Achaea.

### CHAPTER XIV

**No. 1. And the gatherings.** The Vulgate: “And he called the gatherings of the waters seas.”

**No. 4. That it has no color.** Supply “it is evident,” as elsewhere, or “Servius says,” or something similar.

[Col. 0959D] ### CHAPTER XV

**No. 1. It vomits back.** In the printed editions and most manuscripts one reads *removet* (“removes”) instead of *revomit* (“vomits back”). I restore *revomit* from the most ancient Toledo Manuscript, where the form is *revomet*, since *i* is often changed to *e* in manuscripts.

**No. 2. Of the great sea.** That is, of the Mediterranean, as Grialius explains in the following chapter, no. 1. The Latins called the Ocean the “outer sea” and the Mediterranean the “great sea,” in order to distinguish it from the other seas—apart from the Ocean—and from the gulfs within the Mediterranean. Lexicographers have failed to observe this.

**No. 3. Near the Greeks and Illyricum.** For these words, someone conjectured *juxta Xestum et Abydum* (“near Xestus and Abydos”).

**No. 5. The Aegean.** The etymology of the Aegean Sea is explained in more than one way by the ancient writers Strabo, Varro, Paulus, Suidas, Ptolemy, and others. Solinus and Isidore refer to Pliny and should be corrected on the basis of his account. Pliny, Book IV, chapter 11, says that it was named after a reef between Tenos and Chios, which sailors call *αἶγα* (*aiga*), “goat,” because those viewing it from a distance believe it resembles a goat.

**No. 10. Plagia.** Gregory the Great, Isidore of Seville, and others used *plagia* in the same sense as Servius; their words can be read in Ducange’s dictionary. The Italians likewise derive *spiaggia* from it.

### CHAPTER XVII

**No. 1. Persian, Arabian.** The Erythraean, or Red, Sea is divided into two gulfs, the Persian and the Arabian. The Arabian Gulf is assigned to the Ocean. See Pliny, Book VI, chapter 23, and Mela, Book III, chapters 16 and following.

**No. 2. But it is called the Red Sea.** Curtius, Book VIII, chapter 9: “It received its name from King Erythras, which is why the ignorant believe that the waters are red.” Some think that this King Erythras was Esau, who had reddish hair.

### CHAPTER XVIII

**No. 3. Rhegium.** Justin, Pliny, Festus, and others provide the same account of the origin of the name Rhegium for the strait.

**No. 4. As if it had a shape, etc.** The reading of the first Toledo Codex seems better: “As if it had the form of a human being, its heads girded with canine heads.”

**No. 5. And from there where.** Grialius printed *inde ibi* (“from there, there”), as found in the other printed editions. In the note he indicates *ubi* (“where”) instead of *ibi*; and the sense certainly requires *ubi*: namely, from there ships emerge—or emerge again—after suffering shipwreck, where, or after, they have been torn apart.

### CHAPTER XIX

**No. 1. In the great sea.** That is, in the Mediterranean, as I have already said.

**No. 2. They flow into rivers.** Perhaps: “They flow into the rivers.”

**No. 3. It is illuminated.** Saint Martin of León, who transcribes this passage in volume II, sermon on the beginning of the fast, page 109, also reads *illustratur* (“is illuminated”). Grialius conjectures *incrustatur* (“is encrusted”); but, in view of Justin and Eusebius, whom he cites, he could more correctly have conjectured *illinatur* (“is smeared” or “is coated”).

**No. 4. Five hundred and eighty.** Saint Martin, in the passage cited, also gives “seven hundred and eighty”; but Grialius’s emendation seems worth retaining, since numbers are easily altered in manuscripts. In Grialius’s note there was *Salinarum* (“of the saltworks”). I restored *Hieron.* in place of *Vere*, unless one prefers *Beda*.

**No. 5. Healthier, etc.** Perhaps for this reason, on coins of the city of Tiberias struck under Trajan, the goddess Health (*Sanitas*) is seen encircled by the coils of a serpent and seated beside a mountain from which a rich stream of water flows. By this emblem the baths too may be understood to be health-giving. The lake of Tiberias, which, as can be gathered from Grialius’s note in the following number, had several names, was called *Genereth* or *Kinnereth*, *Genesareth* or *Genesar*. It extended one hundred stadia in length and forty in breadth, according to Josephus, *The Jewish War* III, chapter 18.

**No. 6. One hundred and forty.** It may be corrected to “one hundred,” as I was just saying, with “forty” omitted. Compare Calmet in the *Biblical Dictionary*.

**No. 7. Benacus.** It is now called *Lago di Garda* by the Italians. See Pliny, Book II, chapter 103.

**No. 9. A pond.** Others, with Varro and Festus, think that *stagnum* (“pond”) is derived from the Greek *στεγνός* (*stegnos*), because it holds water so that none can flow away.

### CHAPTER XX

**No. 1. Whence it is also called the abyss.** Forcellini infers from this passage of Isidore that *abyssus* is derived from the Greek intensive prefix *a-* and *βυσσός* (*byssos*)—Ionically used for *βυθός* (*bythos*), “depth.” But since *βυθός* also means “bottom,” it is better to take *a-* in *abyssus* as meaning “without,” that is, “without a bottom.” Isidore suggests this as well: “an impenetrable depth of waters.” Isidore makes *abyssus* masculine; most writers make it feminine.

**No. 3. A wave.** Many think that *unda* (“wave”) is called so from *udus* (“wet”) and from the Greek *ὕδωρ* (*hydōr*), “water.”

### CHAPTER XXI

**No. 2. Of which.** This can be retained, provided it is understood as referring to the word “torrent,” etc.

**No. 3. River.** Others derive *amnis* from the Greek words *ἀμφί* (*amphi*) and *νεῖν* (*nein*), because it flows around.

**No. 7. The river Gihon of Paradise, etc.** On the four rivers of Paradise, commentators on Genesis and Calmet in the *Biblical Dictionary* should be consulted. We shall touch briefly on what is more necessary for explaining Isidore’s words. More recent writers maintain that the Gihon of Paradise is different from the Nile. Since the Tigris and Euphrates are two certain rivers among the four of Paradise, the Nile—whose source lies extremely far from the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates—cannot be counted among the rivers of Paradise. The opinion of the ancients might be supported by the fact that even in our own age the Nile is called Gihon by the inhabitants of the kingdom of Gojan. The Greeks call the Nile *Melas*, that is, “black” or “muddy.” Virgil alludes to this in *Georgics* IV, verse 491:

> And black sand makes green Egypt fertile.

And Servius, commenting on this passage: “For previously the Nile was called *Melo*.” Yet *Melo* means “full” in Hebrew, which may suit the Nile because of its inundations. Concerning Lake Nilis, Solinus, chapter 45: “Then immediately it forms a lake, which they call the Nilis.” I do not agree with Grialius, who wished to restore, on the basis of Solinus, “from which, toward the south, the Egyptian sea receives it”; for Solinus said this of the Nile as it enters the sea. Isidore had read other authorities besides Solinus. Indeed, according to reliable historians, the Nile empties into the enormous Lake Zaire, which, I think, Solinus and Isidore call the Nilis; from there it emerges and flows in a long circuit toward the south, watering several regions before spreading into Egypt. Whether Isidore’s reading, *aquis retro luctantibus* (“with the waters struggling backward”), is preferable to Solinus’s *aquis in arcto luctantibus* (“with the waters struggling in a narrow channel”) may be questioned. For my part, I find Isidore’s reading far from objectionable. Raderus, in his notes on Martial, pages 28 and following, brings together much material about the Nile and points to the holy Fathers among whom the river Gihon of Paradise is identified with the Nile, although Pererius disagrees.

**No. 8. Phison.** A river of Paradise. Many believe it to be the famous Phasis, the river of Colchis, not the Ganges, which lies far from the Euphrates and the Tigris, which Moses’s testimony establishes as flowing from the region of Paradise.

**No. 9. Tigris.** Genesis II:14: “The name of the third river is the Tigris; it flows toward Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates.” In the Hebrew of Moses, *Chidkel* appears in place of Tigris. This word means “arrow” in the language of the Medes, to indicate the river’s speed. In Grialius and others one read “flowing into the Dead Sea”; I corrected it without hesitation to “flowing into the Red Sea.” Isidore is describing Jerome from Jerome’s *Onomasticon of Sacred Places*. Jerome’s words are: “The river Tigris, issuing from Paradise according to the testimony of Scripture and proceeding toward Assyria, after many windings, as Josephus holds, flows into the Red Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, running with the extraordinary swiftness of a beast.” In reality, the Tigris, joined with the Euphrates, flows into the Persian Gulf. Although, according to the usage of Holy Scripture, the Persian Gulf is not called the Red Sea, that name being assigned only to the Arabian Gulf, other historians and geographers nevertheless call both the Arabian and Persian gulfs the Red Sea, as Bonfrerius confirms in his notes on Jerome’s *Onomasticon*.

[Col. 0961D] **No. 10. The Tigris and Euphrates from one source, etc.** The ancients—Lucan, Boethius, and others—assigned common sources to the Euphrates and Tigris. Calmet, however, now asserts in the *Biblical Dictionary* that they were mistaken, and Pererius proves this at greater length in his commentary on Genesis II:10. Clericus, in his notes on Jerome’s *Onomasticon*, argues from these words of Isidore that Jerome’s passage is now abridged. Perhaps so; but Isidore may also have drawn his statement simultaneously from Jerome and Sallust, or from another writer who had reproduced Sallust.

**No. 12. The Indus with its vast waters, etc.** Lucan’s verses, Book VIII, verse 227, are:

> Where the swift Ganges and the Nysaean Hydaspes  
> Approach the sea, nearer now to the fire  
> Of the rising Sun than I was to Persia.

From this Isidore’s text may be corrected by reading *Nysaeus* instead of *Medus*: the Hydaspes is called Nysaean from the city of Nysa, which it waters. But since Isidore had stated beforehand that Hydaspes was a king of the Medes, perhaps he himself read in Lucan, or in another writer drawing on Lucan, *Medus Hydaspes*. Virgil certainly wrote in *Georgics* IV, verse 210:

> Lydia, nor the peoples of the Parthians, nor the Mede Hydaspes.

Some think that the Nysaean Hydaspes, which Lucan places in the kingdom of Porus, was a different river from the Median Hydaspes mentioned by Virgil. Perhaps for this reason Horace called the Hydaspes fabulous in Book I, Ode 22, verse 27, since nothing certain about it was established among the ancient geographers. Others believe that the ancients, misled by the similarity of the names, called the Choaspes the Hydaspes; the Choaspes is discussed below, in no. 15.

**No. 14. Bactrians.** Pliny, Book VI, chapter 16: “The Bactrians, whose city is Zariaspe, later called Bactrum after the river.” See Curtius, Book VII, chapter 4. They are called both *Bactri* and *Bactriani*, and the city is *Bactra*, “the city of the Bactrians.”

**No. 15. Choaspes.** Tibullus, Book IV, poem 1, verse 140:

> Nor where the Nile, nor Choaspes, the royal stream,  
> Flows forth.

Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 3, reports that the kings of the Parthians were accustomed to drink only from the waters of the Choaspes and the Eulaeus, and that these waters accompanied them even when they traveled far away.

**No. 17. Which is called the Orontes.** Baluzius, in chapter 5 of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, published *in Orientem praecipitata est* (“it rushed toward the East”). In a note, Joannes Columbus, following Cuperus, says that this reading should be excused, for Hegesippus, *Destruction of Jerusalem* III, chapter 5, and Isidore in this passage clearly show that the Orontes was also called the Orient. In the ancient editions of Isidore one reads: “which is called the Orontes … the ancients called the East *Orientem* in Latin.” Grialius reads *Orentem* in both places, as though the Orontes had been named from the East. Isidore’s habit is not foreign to etymologies of this kind.

**No. 19. Whence it is also named.** These words were added by someone who found *Eusis* or *Euxis* written in place of *Phasis*, and consequently thought that the Euxine Sea had received its name from it. But what if Isidore himself had read *Euxis* for *Phasis* in Saint Ambrose or another author? I know that he often encountered corrupt manuscripts, and it is not surprising if, being intent only on excerpting rather than judging, he adopted an error from an old manuscript. Pliny discusses the Phasis in Book VI, chapter 4. As I indicated in no. 8, some think that it is one of the four rivers of Paradise called the Phison.

**No. 22. Hermus.** Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 137:

> Nor the beautiful Ganges, nor the Hermus turbid with gold.

**No. 23. Of which Ovid writes.** In the printed editions of Ovid one reads:

> And he who plays amid the winding waters of the Maeander.

The poets frequently mention the windings of the Maeander.

**No. 24. Tanais.** Properly, it flows into the Maeotian Marsh, which is joined to the Euxine Sea. See Pliny and Mela.

**No. 25. The beginning of Argive nobility.** Solinus says: “He first gave rise to Argive nobility.”

[Col. 0962D] **No. 26. Around Ravenna.** These words are absent from Solinus. Pliny gives a more exact description of the Padus in Book III, chapter 16.

**No. 27. Tiber.** I have retained the common spelling, which also appears on ancient inscriptions: *Tiberis*, with the first Latin *i*. Grialius printed *Tyberis*; others would prefer *Thyberis*. Isidore’s characteristic explanation that *Albula* derives from its white color is not incompatible with his usual method, and others still maintain it.

**No. 32. Because it has a great deal of that in it.** Perhaps: “because it has the greatest amount of it,” unless *qui color* (“which color”) is understood. Florez, volume XV of *Sacred Spain*, pages 37 and following, discusses the river Minius carefully and proves at length that the Minius is not the river now called the Miño, but another river called the Sil, which is joined by the river now called the Miño. As for his assertion that *minium* is a Latin word, others, by contrast, think it is Spanish; Vitruvius may perhaps allude to this in Book VII, chapter 9: “Minium and indigo indicate by their very names the places in which they are produced.” Isidore again reports that the river Minius was named from the pigment *minium* in Book XIX, chapter 17, as does Justin in Book XLIV, chapter 3.

**No. 33. Durius.** Florez, volume XIII, pages 49 and following, thinks that the Durius was rather so called from the Phoenician Dorians, that is, from the inhabitants of the city of Dor or Dori, than from the Greek Dorians. On the Durius and the other rivers of Spain, Cellarius, *Ancient Geography* II.1.1, should be consulted.

**No. 34. Wools are dyed with a beautiful color.** This should be understood of the natural color, not of coloring produced by human craft. See Pliny and the other ancient writers who discuss Baetican wool.

### CHAPTER XXII

**No. 2. On distant mountains, shells and oysters, etc.** This is certainly a strong argument in confirmation of the reality of the Flood, whose force some more recent critics attempt to weaken.

**No. 4. The third.** Nonnus also enumerates three floods in Book III of the *Dionysiaca*. Compare Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II, chapter 11.

## BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 0963B]

### CHAPTER I

**No. 2. Sallust.** Sallust’s words are read in different ways in the old copies. I would prefer: “When winds had been driven through the hollow places of the earth, several mountains burst apart and hills subsided.” Isidore repeats the same passage in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 45. Grialius’s assertion that a hemistich is contained in these words together with a complete hexameter cannot be admitted unless *sedere* is infinitive. Besides, it would be no wonder if a hemistich had slipped from Sallust, without his intending it, alongside a complete hexameter. Lartius, Bagomarsinus, and others have carefully collected similar examples.

### CHAPTER II

**No. 1. Little wheel.** *Rotula* is more in keeping with Latin usage than *rotella*. Now that a new world has been discovered, four parts of the earth are reckoned, America having been added to the former three.

**No. 3. The great sea.** Isidore often uses *mare magnum* simply for the Mediterranean; he expressly explained this in Book XIII, chapter 16, no. 1. In the *Isidoriana*, chapter 82, I discussed the Itinerary falsely circulated under Antoninus’s name, or rather the old register of provinces wrongly attributed to Antoninus, which is much later. The same work is attributed by some to our Isidore because it was taken from the collection of canons of Pseudo-Isidore; accordingly, it must not be confused with the matters which Isidore discusses in this book concerning the world, its parts, and its regions. See Pithoeus, *Adversaria* II, supplementary chapter 1. Between this second chapter and the following third chapter, two Gothic Toledo manuscripts display a sphere of the world; in the older manuscript its interior is inscribed with Arabic words.

### CHAPTER III

**No. 1. Asia.** Some wish it to have been named from the nymph Asia, others from Asius, son of Maneus the Lydian.

**No. 3. The flaming rhomphaea.** Grialius, with the other printed editions, published *romphaea flamma*. I restore *romphaea flammea*. Genesis 3:24: “And he placed before the paradise of delight Cherubim and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.” Isidore calls the flaming and turning sword a *romphaea*, or *rhomphaea flammea*, and shortly afterwards mentions the rhomphaea’s burning. Yet his interpretation of a fiery wall by which Paradise was enclosed on every side does not please everyone. The interpreters’ opinions about that flaming and turning sword differ greatly. See Pererius on that passage of Genesis.

**No. 4. Cherubim, that is, a guard of angels, etc.** The aforementioned Pererius shows that here the word *cherubim* signifies many angels; for although the name properly belongs to the eighth order of angels, it is nevertheless extended to all orders of angels.

**No. 5. India . . . Tylon.** Mela too should be consulted on India. Grialius printed *Tylen* in the text, *Tylon* in the note. Solinus: “Tylos is an island of India . . . every tree that grows there never lacks foliage.” Moreover, anyone wishing to know more fully what Isidore discusses in these chapters must consult the writers who have elucidated ancient geography and chorography. Fabricius lists them in a long sequence in chapter 5 of his *Bibliography of Antiquities*.

**No. 6. The monoceros beast.** Perhaps: *monocerotem bestiam*. The Latin forms are *monoceros*, *monocerotis*.

**No. 9. Arachosia.** There was both a town and a river of that name. Compare Pliny, Book VI, chapter 23. It is now a region of the Great Mogul. Parthia, discussed in the preceding number, taken in its broader sense includes Parthia proper, which is now being described.

**No. 10. From Assur, son of Shem.** Saint Augustine teaches this in *The City of God* XVI, chapter 3. For the rest concerning Assyria, see Pliny, Mela, and Solinus. Solinus on perfumes: “From there Roman luxury first made its entry into foreign fragrances.”

**No. 11. Media.** On Media, see Pliny, Book VI, chapter 26. Solinus’s chapter 59 is wholly devoted to the Median tree. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 126:

> Media produces bitter juices and the lingering taste
> Of the blessed apple.

Grialius and the other printed editions had *Perso* for *Perseo*, which I restored, because the man from whom the Persians derived their origin is called Perseus or Perses.

**No. 12.** Both *Persis* and *Persia* are said; but *Persis, Persidis* is more usual. The statement that Nimrod—or, as others have it, Nemroth or Nembrod—taught the Persians to worship fire may perhaps have been drawn from Eutychius, patriarch of Alexandria. See Calmet’s *Biblical Dictionary*.

**No. 13. Εὐδαίμων (*eudaimōn*).** In no. 15 below the Greek word εὐδαίμων is explained, namely Arabia Beata, or Felix—“Blessed” or “Happy Arabia.”

**No. 15. It is interpreted.** In a passive sense. Yet I would prefer to restore from Solinus: “Arabia was named, that is, ‘sacred’; for that is what they interpret it to mean.” Saint Jerome, Bochart, and others think that Arabia Felix was called Saba. Josephus, whom Grialius cites for this view, if Book I, chapter 7, and Book II, chapter 5, are compared, rather holds that the Saba frequented by Saba, son of Cush, was an island famous under the name Meroë. Hence there is also controversy whether the Queen of Sheba ruled in Ethiopia or in Arabia Felix.

**No. 17. Commagena.** Grialius always has *Commagena* with double *m* in the text, and always *Comagena* with a single *m* in the note. Dausque prefers *Commagene* or *Commagena*.

**No. 19.** Ascalon was a city in the region of the Philistines, between Ashdod and Gaza; but I cannot establish that it was called *Philistin*. The Philistines were also called *Philisthiim* and *Philisthini*. The common opinion is that Palestine was named from the Philistines. Grialius writes *Palestina*.

**No. 21.** On these matters Bochart should above all be consulted in his learned work entitled *Chanaan*. Jerusalem has several names, contained in this distich:

> Solyma, Luca, Bethel, Hierosolyma, Jebus, Aelia,
> The holy city, Jerusalem, and Salem are its names.

It appears in the *Ephemerides* of George Gemnicensis, in Pez, volume II, column 575. Perhaps *Helia* is written for *Aelia*. Isidore again treats Jerusalem and its names in Book XV, chapter 1, no. 4. Some modern writers do not acknowledge in the land of promise the degree of fertility praised even by the ancient pagans. It is nevertheless certain that many traces of its former fertility still remain, although certain fields now bristle with barrenness because they are not cultivated through the inhabitants’ neglect.

**No. 22. Sebastia.** Or, more commonly, *Sebaste*: it means Augusta. Herod gave it this name. See Josephus, *Antiquities* XV, chapter 11.

**No. 23. Galilee.** The derivation of Galilee is from the city Galgala, a Hebrew name meaning the turning of a wheel. Isidore adapts a Greek etymology from milk, as in *Galati*, Gauls, and so forth.

**No. 25. Nabaioth.** The printed editions, including Grialius, also had *Nabath*. I restored *Nabaioth*, for that was the name of Ishmael’s firstborn son. Nabath was the father of Jeroboam, the first king of Israel; another man of the same name was a cousin of the elder Tobias.

**No. 27. Egypt.** Solinus’s words are: “Egypt retreats inland from the south as far as the Ethiopians extend.” Grialius cited chapter 33 of Solinus; he corrected this to the end of chapter 53. In my edition it is chapter 45; elsewhere it is chapter 32.

**No. 28. Canopaea.** Perhaps one should read *Canopus* or “the Canopaean region.” Solinus, chapter 44: “What extends from Atlas as far as the Canopic mouth, where Libya ends and Egypt begins, is named from Canopus, Menelaus’s helmsman, who was buried there. On the island which forms the mouth of the Nile,” etc. Ammianus, Book XXII, chapter 41, bears on this. Tacitus is clearer: in *Annals* II, in the year of the City 772, chapter 6, he calls Canopus the captain of the ship in which Menelaus was carried. The city of Canopus is believed to have been founded by Menelaus. Pliny, Book V, chapter 31, has only this: “The first of the islands before Asia lies at the Canopic mouth of the Nile, and is said to be named after Canopus, Menelaus’s helmsman.”

**No. 29. Silk kind.** Perhaps *genus* is superfluous, for *sericum* is said simply of silk fleece or a silk garment. Solinus, chapter 63, on the Seres: “This is that silk which, to general use, was admitted at the cost of strictness,” etc.

**No. 30. The region of Bactria.** On the Bactrians, see above, Book XIII, chapter 21. Solinus’s words, chapter 62, are: “The Bactrians moreover have as their own river the Bactros, from which also comes the name of their town, Bactrum. The peoples lying beyond them are enclosed by the ranges of the Paropamisus; those facing them are bounded by the sources of the Indus; the Oxus river encloses the rest.” Curtius, Book VII, chapter 4, calls the mountain Paramisus. Grialius has Paropanisus.

**No. 31. Magog.** Josephus, Jerome, Theodoret, Eustathius, and many others think that he was a son of Japheth and the father of the Scythians or Tartars. Certainly, among the Getae, Goths, Massagetae, and so forth, there are many names indicating an origin from Gog and Magog. The name Scythians, however, must be sought elsewhere. Some think that the Scythians were named from Scythes, son of Hercules.

**No. 32. The Phasis of the Moschi.** Grialius quotes Solinus’s words with punctuation between *Moschorum* and *Phasidem*, and Isidore appears to have understood them in that sense. In my edition of Solinus I read: “The mountains of the Heniochi give rise to the Araxes; those of the Moschi, to the Phasis,” so that there are two rivers, the Araxes flowing from the mountains of the Heniochi—or rather Heniochi—and the Phasis from those of the Moschi. In fact, the Phasis rises among the Moschi. See Pliny, Book VI, chapter 4.

**No. 33. Hyrcania named from a forest.** It is more reasonable to believe that the Hyrcanian forest was so named from Hyrcania than the reverse. The forests of Hyrcania are famous. Lucan, Book III, verse 268: “and the vast Hyrcanian forests.” Valerius Flaccus, Book VI, verse 114: “Hyrcanian groves.” Servius wrongly interprets Virgil’s cited verse, “and Hyrcanian tigresses offered their udders,” as referring to Arabia, where he asserts that a Hyrcania—a forest so called—exists.

[Col. 0965D] **Note 34. “From the complexion of the people.”** Compare the following chapter: “the Gauls, from the fairness of the people,” and chapter 5: “the Moors, from the complexion of the peoples.” Therefore *capilli* (“hair”) is not acceptable in place of *populi* (“people”).

**Note 32. Armenia.** Strabo writes that Armenia was named from Armeus, or Armenius the Thessalian, a companion of Jason; Stephanus, following Antipater’s opinion, says it was named from Armenus of Rhodes. Armenia is divided by some into Greater and Lesser Armenia: Greater Armenia lies beyond the Euphrates and is now Turcomania and Kurdistan; Lesser Armenia lies between Cappadocia and the Euphrates and is now Anatolia. See Pliny, book VI, chapter 9.

**Note 36. Iberia.** It is now called Georgia, or in Italian *Giorgia*. It is also written *Iberia*; that spelling is likewise the proper name of Spain. Hence some ambiguity has occasionally arisen in explaining ancient authors.

**Note 37. “Cappadocia.”** The name Cappadocia was taken from a small river called the Cappadocus, mentioned by Pliny, book VI, chapter 3. Others derive the name from Cappadocus, son of Ninus. Forcellinus distinguishes two rivers called Halys among the ancients: one enormous river, which separates Paphlagonia from Cappadocia, mentioned by Pliny, book VI, chapters 2 and 3; the other in Lydia, of which Lucan, book III, line 272, writes: “Where the Halys, fatal to Croesus, flows.” But in reality the Halys is one and the same river: the river of Paphlagonia that forms the boundary of Lydia. See Cellarius, book III, chapter 8, no. 57.

**Note 40. “The Galatians.”** On the origin of the Galatians, see the same work, book IX, chapter 2, no. 68.

**Note 41. “Phrygia.”** Concerning the Phrygians, compare what is said in book IX, chapter 2, no. 33. According to the opinion of others, the name Phrygia is derived from the river Phrygius, or from a town called Phrygium in Macedonia, from which a colony is believed to have been led into Phrygia, or from Phrygia, daughter of Cecrops. From the name of Dardania, or of the town of Dardanus, there remains the designation Dardanelles, as it is commonly called.

**Note 43. “From Lydus, the king’s brother.”** Perhaps it should read “from Lydus, the brother-king,” since the preceding passage says “two brother-kings,” and so forth.

[Col. 0966B] **Note 45. “From a certain Cilix.”** Some think that he was the son of Agenor. See Servius, on *Aeneid* III, line 88. Raderus, page 30, on Martial’s line,

“And here the Cilician cloths were drenched by their own storms,”

indicates the authors who report that Cilicia was named from Cilix, son of Agenor the Phoenician. Isidore is copying Solinus.

**Note 46. Lycia.** It is believed to have been named either from Lycus, son of Pandion, or from the nymph Lyce. Isidore wishes the name Lycia itself to recall that it was joined to Cilicia on the east.

**CHAPTER IV, no. 2. “A third part,” etc.** Ovid, *Fasti*, book V:

“The Bull begins the heavens; Jupiter fills you, Sidonian girl,  
And a third part of the earth bears your name.”

The abduction was elegantly described by Theocritus, *Idyll* 20. Pliny, Strabo, and others discuss Europa at length.

**There. “The first region of Europe,” etc.** Mela likewise says in book I: “There is another Scythia of Asia.”

**Note 4. “Because of fertility,” etc.** Becmann investigates various other derivations of the word *Germania* in his *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *Ascenas*, page 249 and following. Solinus calls the Callaic gem *callaica*; Pliny calls it *callais*, or *callain*. See Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, page 236 and following.

**Note 5. “Moesia, from the yield of the crops,” etc.** This means nothing other than that from the word *Moesia* we can recall the yield of the crops, and so forth. On Moesia, see Pliny, book III, final chapter. Bulgaria and Serbia are now situated there. Concerning the two Mysias, Greater and Lesser, see the same Pliny, book V, chapter 32. Moesia, adjoining Pannonia, was also called Mysia; but the Latins more often pronounced it *Moesia* in order to distinguish it from the Mysia of Asia.

**Note 6. “From the savagery of the inhabitants.”** In Greek, τραχύς (*trachys*), “harsh, rugged.” Others hold that Thrace was named from Thrax, son of Mars.

**Note 7. “From a Greek king,” namely, of Thessaly.** See Pliny, book IV, chapter 7: “And two in the sea,” that is, two provinces; but in this way there are eight. It could be corrected to *Hellas*, that is, Thessaly. Compare Pliny, in the passage cited. What stands against this is that shortly afterward Hellas is clearly distinguished from Thessaly. Illyricum, or Illyria—called *Esclavonia* by the Spaniards and *Schiavonia* by the Italians—includes Liburnia and Dalmatia. Others assign broader boundaries to Illyricum. Pliny, book III, chapters 20 and 21, divided Illyricum into three judicial districts; Augustus divided it into two provinces, Upper and Lower.

**Note 8. “From Delmi.”** We may safely read “from Delminium.” For Isidore took this from Velius Longus, or rather from Cassiodorus, who in his little work *On Orthography*, drawing on Velius Longus, reports as follows: “It is also preferable that we write *DELMATIA*, not *DALMATIA*, because the name is thought to have been derived from Delminium, the greatest city of that province.” This spelling is confirmed by ancient inscriptions and coins. Usage, however, prevailed, so that *Dalmatia* is now retained everywhere. In one of the Gothic Toledo manuscripts, the following words are added after *clauditur*: “Illyria is a region beside the Adriatic Sea, in which the Dardani have their settlements. It is also Dardania,” and so forth, as Grialius indicates in his note on this passage. In the manuscript, instead of *efferati* (“savage”), there is *efferata* (“savage,” feminine).

**Note 9. “Epirus, from Pyrrhus.”** Others think that Epirus was named by the Corcyraeans for the neighboring mainland, because in Greek ἤπειρος (*ēpeiros*) means “mainland.” Others subsequently used this same name.

**Note 10. “From Hellen,” etc.** That is, from the king of Thessaly, after whom Thessaly was properly called Hellas. The name of Hellas was also applied to all Greece, and especially to the part that is more extensive and lies farther from the sea, excluding the Peloponnese. See Pliny, book IV, chapter 7; Mela, book II; and Solinus, *Plinian Exercises*, page 142. Solinus observes that later writers also included the Peloponnese under the name Hellas, as is clear from Isidore. Cellarius discusses Hellas in book II, chapter 13. In note 5 to that section, Schwartzius observes that the origin of the opinion concerning the Hellenes as a common stock and kindred people is to be sought in Apollodorus, book I, chapter 7. There it is taught that Hellen divided the Peloponnese among his son Xuthus, the lands beyond the Peloponnese among Dorus, and the lands adjoining Thessaly among Aeolus—and perhaps Achaea among Achaeus.

Concerning the etymology of the region of Attica, some think that Attica was named from ἀκτή (*aktē*), “shore,” because most of it is coastal; it is also called Acte. See Pliny, book IV, chapter 7. In Codex 1 of the Vatican archives, and in other ancient copies, instead of “where the city of Athens was,” I find “where the city of Athenas was.” This reading is not to be dismissed, so that *Athenas* may be indeclinable. Similar names occur elsewhere, such as *Centumcellas*, a town in the nominative, and *Veios*, a colony. Nepos, in *Miltiades*, chapters 4 and 5, among others, describes the famous battle of Marathon between Athens and the coastal shore.

**Note 11. “And the Peloponnese.”** This is according to the opinion of certain writers; for, as I said, others excluded the Peloponnese from Hellas. Ovid narrates the story of Thebes in Boeotia, founded by Cadmus, at the beginning of book III of the *Metamorphoses*. Others think that Boeotia was named from Boeotus, son of Neptune, as Hyginus relates, *Fable* 186. Before Solinus, Pliny taught that Thebes had been the homeland of Liber and Hercules, book IV, chapter 7.

It is commonly believed that Apollo was born on the island of Delos. But perhaps Isidore spoke according to the opinion of Aristotle and others, who maintain that Apollo and Liber were one and the same god, as Macrobius proves at length, book I, chapter 18, and Servius, on *Eclogue* 5, line 66, and on *Aeneid* VI, line 78. Isidore’s words, “where formerly the civil wars thundered,” do not refer to Thebes or Boeotia, but to the Pharsalian fields in Thessaly, concerning which Solinus, chapter 13, writes: “The Pharsalian fields are in Thessaly, where the storms of civil wars thundered.” Grialius has in his note: “It is also Aonia,” but in the text he omits *et* (“also”), as other writers likewise omit it.

Gellius, book XIV, chapter 6, places among kinds of knowledge that neither delight nor are useful the knowledge of changed names of cities and regions—such as that Boeotia was formerly called Aonia, Egypt Aeria, and so forth. Yet it is certainly useful to know such things at times; nor are many other matters more useful that he himself gathered into his *Noctes*. Isidore, however, should be explained as follows: Aganippe was called the Aonian spring from the Aonian mountains; from the Aonian spring—or rather from the mountains themselves—Boeotia was called Aonia.

The Peloponnese is, as it were, the νῆσος (*nēsos*)—that is, “island”—of Pelops. It is in fact a peninsula, and in a broader sense an island; it is now called the Morea. Pelops, its king, was the son of Tantalus, king of the Phrygians. Conrad Samuel Schurzfleisch, in *Disputationes Historicae Civiles*, disputation 48, no. 2, says in a note that Isidore defines the circuit of this peninsula as 363,000 paces, although its circumference extends to 550,000 paces. I cannot find where Isidore expressed that opinion. In the Gothic and Toledo manuscripts, the words of this note, “where formerly . . . that Theban,” are moved to the following note, after the words “Thessalonica and Thebes.”

**Note 12. Thessaly.** Solinus mentions Thessaly and Thebes as cities in Thessaly; therefore perhaps Isidore should be read in the same way, not *Thessalonica*, which is a city of Macedonia, so called as though it meant “victory over the Thessalians,” Θεσσαλῶν νίκη (*Thessalōn nikē*), because Philip, king of Macedonia, defeated the Thessalians in battle in that region. Nor am I otherwise aware of any famous city called Thessaly in the province of Thessaly. Since Solinus and Isidore place Thebes in Thessaly, this must be understood of Thebes in Phthia; for the other, more celebrated Thebes in Boeotia was correctly placed by Isidore in the preceding note. Geographers agree that Parnassus also does not lie in Thessaly, as Isidore again asserts in chapter 8, no. 11, following Servius—perhaps confusing Parnassus with Pindus—but in Phocis, a region of Achaea.

**Note 13. “From King Emathius.”** Solinus makes Emathius an unknown king, virtually a son of the earth. Others call him Emathion, son of Aurora and brother of Memnon. Emathia properly formed part of Macedonia; but especially among poets the name is commonly used for all Macedonia, and even for Pharsalia and Thessaly. Hence Lucan:

[Col. 0968B] “Wars more than civil through the Emathian fields,” etc.

**Note 14. Achaea.** Servius, on *Aeneid* I, line 442, says that the Achaeans were named from Achaeus, son of Jupiter and Pithia. Another account derives the name from Achaeus, son of Xuthus, who, accused of homicide, fled to Laconia. Achaea is often taken to mean all Greece, but properly it is a region of the Peloponnese whose chief city is Corinth.

**Note 15. “And Calista.”** Isidore perhaps wrote *Calistus*, or *Calistonis*, as Servius does on *Georgics* I, line 67; scribes who did not understand this changed it to *Calistae*. The Peloponnese, in whose center Arcadia lies, is said by Mela, book II, to resemble a plane-tree leaf. I do not know that Arcadia was called Sicyonia, or that the kingdom of the Sicyonians was named from King Sicyon; for in the ancient geographers I find only that Sicyon was a city of the Peloponnese in Achaea, whose inhabitants were called Sicyonians.

**Note 16. Pannonia.** On Pannonia, see Pliny, book III, chapter 25. Since Isidore says that Pannonia was named from the Paenine Alps, there can scarcely be any doubt that the reading below should be “from the African wind, the Paenine Alps,” not the Apennine Alps, or, as Grialius printed it, the Appennine Alps. The Paenine Alps, or, as others write, the Pennine Alps, lie on the boundary of Narbonese Gaul and Italy, and Hannibal is believed to have crossed them when he made war on the Romans. The name Alps is commonly applied to many mountain ranges, such as the Rhaetian, Noric, Bastarnic, and Graian Alps. Livy, book XXI, chapter 38, calls them the Pennine Alps, not the Paenine, because they received their name from the god Penninus, not from the passage of the Carthaginians. Compare Cellarius, book II, chapter 9.

**Note 20. Tuscia.** Pliny, book III, chapter 5: “The Lydians, from whose king the Tyrrheni were named, were later, from their sacrificial rite, called Tusci in the language of the Greeks.” Add Servius on *Aeneid* II, line 781. This etymology would suggest that it should be written *Thuscia*, as Grialius and others wrote it. But the more common spelling lacks the aspiration, as in *tus*. Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, line 4: “The ancients used to say *thus* and *orchus*, from which a later age removed the aspiration.” There are innumerable examples of this kind. In note 22 the discussion of Tuscia recurs.

**Note 21. “Called by a Greek name.”** Solinus omits *Graece* (“in Greek”), for he writes: “Marcus Antonius asserts that these same people, because they survived the watery disaster and the rains, were called Umbri.” Isidore added *Graece* because *imber* (“rain”) derives from the Greek ὄμβρος (*ombros*).

**Note 22. “The brother of Lydus.”** Here Grialius called him *Lydius*, although in chapter 3, no. 43, he repeatedly called him *Lydus*. Isidore denies that it ought to be called *Tascia*, perhaps because *Tuscia* is not readily found among the ancients, who instead speak of the region of the Tusci, or use something similar.

**Note 23. Apulia.** It is written *Apulia* and *Appulia*, and likewise *Brundusium* and *Brundisium*; but in ancient monuments *Brundisium* is more frequent.

**Note 25. “From the fairness of the people.”** Compare chapter 3, no. 34, with the note. Becmann examines other etymologies of the Gauls on page 492.

**Note 26. “But among the Belgians there is a city.”** It is unclear from other sources what city was called *Belgae*. Caesar likewise does not call Belgium a city, but a province or region, which was part of Belgica and properly the native land of the Belgians.

**Note 30. “There are two . . . Hispaniae.”** Isidore does not explain what *Hispania Citerior* and *Hispania Ulterior* are, but attempts to investigate the etymology of *citra* (“on this side”) and *ultra* (“beyond”), or to provide some explanation. The true derivation is from *cis* and *uls*, forms used by the ancients for *citra* and *ultra*, as Gellius reports, book XII, chapter 13.

**CHAPTER V, no. 1. Libya.** Hyginus, *Fable* 160, says that Libya was the daughter not of Epaphus but of Palamedes—unless *Epaphus* should be restored in Hyginus in place of *Palamedes*, as Muncker suspected. Others think that Libya was so named from Libys, son of Hercules. See Martianus Capella, book VI.

**Note 2. Africa.** Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapters 12 and 23, calls Afer, or Apherus, the grandson of Abraham through his son Midian; Solinus, chapter 37, calls him Libys, son of Hercules. Some think that Africa was named from the Greek privative α (*a*) and φρίκη (*phrikē*), as though it meant “without the horror of cold.” Bochart, *Canaan*, I.25, should be consulted on Africa, in addition to Cellarius, book IV, introduction, where he explains Africa’s various names.

**Note 4. Greater Syrtes.** In the first Gothic-Toledo manuscript, the old gloss above, “Greater Syrtes,” is *mountains* or *cliffs*.

**Note 5. Teuchira.** Grialius printed *Teuchira* in the text, but *Theuchira* in the note. The correct spelling is *Teuchira*, or *Tauchira*, which was also called by the name of the queen Arsinoe.

**Note 6. Bizacium.** Here Grialius printed *Byzantium*, and shortly afterward *Byzatium*. But in no. 3, although he placed *Bizacium* in the text, he correctly preferred *Byzacium* with Chacon. Bochart, *Canaan*, I.24, reads: “of the cities Oea and Sabratha.” The old editions are very erroneous in these names.

**Note 7. The Byzacene region.** Bochart discusses the Byzacene region in *Canaan* I.24–25, and Cellarius in book IV, chapter 4. The metropolis of the province of Byzacena was Hadrumetum, or Adrumetum.

**Note 8. “Zeugis, where Carthage is,” etc.** Victor of Vita agrees with Isidore. Salmasius conjectures, on page 318 of his *Plinian Exercises*, that Pliny should be understood in no other way; Solinus perhaps misunderstood him, placing the province of Zeugitania between Numidia and Africa. Hardouin, and with him Cellarius, understand Pliny’s words from Isidore and others as follows: “The region of Zeugitania, and that which is properly called Africa”—that is, the region of Zeugitania, which is also properly called Africa.

**Note 9. Hippo Regius and Rusicade.** One must beware of the common spelling, including Grialius’s, *Hipponem, Rhegium*, etc., as though there were two cities, Hippo and Rhegium or Regium. Grialius has *Rhegium* in the text and *Regium* in the note, but places the punctuation between *Hipponem* and *Regium*. Hippo Regius, made famous by the episcopate of Saint Augustine, was so called in order to distinguish it from other cities named Hippo. Silius writes of it, book III, line 259:

“Then Vaga, and Hippo, beloved by ancient kings.”

The Greeks call the Numidians *Nomades* from νομή (*nomē*), “pasture,” either because they frequently move their pastures, because they trade in livestock, or because they live on grass like cattle. Vulcanius notes that Pliny places the river Ampsaga in Tingitana, but does not indicate the passage. Pliny, book V, chapter 2, considers Ampsaga the boundary of Caesarean Mauretania; and in chapter 3 he says: “From Ampsaga begins Numidia, famous for the name of Masinissa.”

**Note 10. “Gaul, from the fairness of the people.”** So also in chapter 3, no. 34. “Albania, from the fairness of the people.” See below, no. 14.

**Note 12. “Which India alone now produces.”** I stated in book XII, chapter 2, no. 16, that elephants are still not produced only in India, but also in some parts of Africa.

**Note 13. “Of the Garamantian region.”** In my old edition of Solinus: “The chief city of the Garamantic region is Garamana.” But other writers call the city *Garama*. Isidore perhaps wrote *of the Garamantid region*, although *Garamas, garamantis* is also in use.

**Note 14. “From the complexion of the peoples.”** As in no. 10.

**Note 15. Camelopardalis.** See book XII, chapter 2, no. 19.

The animal called *camelopardus* is here called *camelopardalis*. Compare the note.

**Note 21. Gallaecia.** Formerly, as a province, it included the Cantabri and Astures. Orosius, book VI, chapter 21: “The Cantabri and Astures are parts of the province of Gallaecia.” The same conclusion follows from the *Itinerary of Antoninus* and from Pliny, book XIX, chapter 1. See Flórez, volume XV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 12.

**Note 22. Territory.** Others think that *territorium* was named from *terrere*, “to frighten,” because it frightens enemies away. Vossius discusses the matter at greater length in his *Etymology*. Servius, in my edition, on *Aeneid* V, line 755, writes: “Hence *territorium* was also named as though from *tritorium*, ground worn down by oxen and the plow.” Crellius, in his dissertation on the ceremony by which cities were founded, supports Isidore’s opinion: the ancients marked out with the plow not only the boundaries of cities but also the limits and boundaries of their territories.

**CHAPTER VI, no. 1. “That they lie in the open sea.”** This appears to have been taken from Festus, under *Insulae*: “And they are situated in the open sea.”

**Note 3.** In corrected editions of Solinus, including editions earlier than Grialius, the reading is *Thanatos*, not *Athanatis*. Salmasius corrected the corrupt passage in Isidore, “from Britain is separated varied, slender,” on page 247 of his *Plinian Exercises*, from Solinus; but Grialius had already anticipated him.

**Note 4. Thule.** In my edition of Solinus the words are: “Many [days], etc.; at the winter solstice the day is so shortened that sunrise and sunset are joined.” Grialius wrote *Thyle*; I retain *Thule*, which is the more common spelling. On this island, Pliny, Mela, and others should be consulted. More recent geographers do not agree among themselves about which island the ancient writers mean. Cellarius, book II of *Ancient Geography*, chapter 4, no. 87, thinks that Thule is the island now called Shetland, Schetland, or Hitland, or perhaps one of the Faroe Islands. Most assert that Thule is Iceland.

[Col. 0970C] **Note 5. Orkneys.** Pomponius Mela, book III, says that the Orkneys number thirty; Ptolemy says approximately thirty; Pliny, forty. Many write *Orcades*.

**Note 6. Scotland.** Scotland is now the northern part of Great Britain. Formerly the name Scotland was applied to Ireland. I discussed this usage of the ancients in the prolegomena to Sedulius, chapter 1, no. 11.

**Note 7. “Setting out from the Red Sea.”** Solinus has: “Setting out from the Red Sea”; and it is certainly easy for scribes to have changed *mari* into *mare*, since in manuscripts *e* and *i* are frequently confused. But *mare* may also be retained as an ablative, like *praesepe*, and so forth. On Gades, see Bochart, *Canaan*, book I, chapter 34, where he reads *Gadir* in its own language, correcting *Gades*, as Grialius had already corrected it.

**Note 8. The Fortunate Islands.** They are now called the Canaries, because one of them was called Canaria from the dogs of enormous size found there. On this island, see Pliny, book VI, chapter 22, and Solinus near the end of his work; he concludes that the qualities of the islands do not entirely correspond to their name, “the Fortunate.” Hardouin’s note on Pliny should be consulted.

**Note 9. The Gorgades.** Other printed editions of Mela, Solinus, Pliny, and others read “the Gorgon Islands,” not *Gorgades*, as Grialius printed it. In place of *Hersperuceras*, my Solinus reports *Hesperionceras*. Perhaps it is also preferable to read in Isidore “which we call,” not “which is called.” Vulcanius noted that in Pliny *Hesperion ceras* is read in another form instead of *Hespuceras*. Pliny used both forms, *Hesperion ceras* and *Hesperu ceras*; thus he wrote in Latin letters the Greek Ἑσπέρου κέρας (*Hesperou keras*), “the horn of Hesperus.” The promontory now called Cape Verde is believed to be Hesperu Ceras.

**Note 10. The Hesperides Islands.** Pliny discusses the Hesperides Islands in book VI, chapter 31. On the explanation of the story of the dragon, see the same author, book V, chapter 1, and Solinus, chapter 24, or 36. The islands and gardens of the Hesperides received their name from the three daughters of Hesperus, brother of Atlas. Isidore derives the etymology from the city of Hesperis, which was first called Hesperis and afterward Berenice, situated in the province of Cyrenaica.

**Note 12. Taprobane.** Others pronounce it *Taprobane*. Some now believe it to be Sumatra, but most, more correctly, identify it with Ceylon; many geographers, ancient and modern, discuss it.

**Note 13. “Tylos . . . bearing leaves at all times.”** Perhaps the reading of the ancient manuscripts is correct: “green, bearing leaves at all times.” This reading is also found in the two frequently cited Gothic-Toledo manuscripts. For a later age said *folia*, *foliae*, from which the Italian and Spanish vernacular forms *foglia* and *hoja* have descended. Unless one prefers *folio* (“leaf”) with Solinus, chapter 65: “Tylos is an island of India . . . whatever tree grows there is never without a leaf.”

**Note 14. “In the Great Sea.”** That is, in the Mediterranean, as I have often observed. Paphos was a city; but whether Cyprus itself was also called by that name is not clear from other sources. Isidore returns to Cyprian bronze in book XVI, chapter 20. Meursius’s book on Cyprus, published at Amsterdam in 1675, should be consulted.

**Note 15. “Macaronesus . . . Crete, from Crete.”** *Macaronesum*, more correctly *Macaronesos*, means “blessed island.” Solinus, chapter 16: “Dosiades says that it was named from Crete the nymph, daughter of Hesperus; Anaximander says that Crete, formerly called Aeria, and afterward Curetes, was named from Crete, king of the Curetes; while some have reported that it was called Μακαρόνησον (*makaronēson*) because of the temperateness of its climate.”

**Note 16. “He fixed the laws.”** Isidore perhaps took the expression from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 622: “He set laws for a price, and repealed them.” In Pliny and Celsus *phalangium* occurs in the nominative; Vegetius, in *On Veterinary Medicine*, book III, chapter 81, has *sphalangios*, for so he writes. In Isidore one may read *phalangios*.

**Note 17. “Abydos and Sestos are now called the Dardanelles.”** Isidore incorrectly makes Abydos an island. There was another city called Abydos in Egypt, and in it a splendidly built palace of Memnon and a famous temple of Osiris.

**Note 18. Coos.** In my edition of Solinus the reading is *Coos, Ceos*; but Isidore seems to have read *Ceos, Coos*, as Salmasius observes in his *Plinian Exercises*, page 143. Finding *Ceos, Coos* in Solinus, Salmasius corrected it to *Coos, Ceos* and observed that Isidore shares with Solinus the error of saying that Coos lies opposite Attica. *Coos* is also written *Cos*, and *Ceos*, *Cea*. On the confusion of these names and islands, consult Hardouin’s notes and emendations on Pliny, book XI, chapter 22, no. 42, and Cellarius, book III, chapter 2, no. 26.

**Note 19. “Around the same one.”** That is, Delos. I would nevertheless prefer “around the same ones.” The meaning is certainly that the Cyclades were so called because it is necessary to sail around them in a long circuit, according to Servius, in the passage cited by Grialius. Pliny, book IV, chapter 12: “Situated in a circle from Cape Gerestus around Delos—and from this they also derived their name—are the Cyclades.”

**Note 20. Fifty-three.** Hyginus counts only nine, *Fable* 276. Strabo, book X: “At first twelve were counted—the Cyclades—but more were added.” See also Velleius, book I, chapter 4, and Muncker’s note on Hyginus.

**Note 21. “That after the flood,” etc.** Taken from Solinus, chapter 17.

**Note 22. “The head of the rose.”** Gisbert Cuperus, in *The Apotheosis of Homer*, section “Serapis,” corrects *rosa e capitulum*, or *capitolium*, as it is read somewhere, to: “the head of the rose was formerly called,” and so forth. Isidore seems to call the cup of the rose its head; properly, however, the head of a rose is the lower globule filled with down. On the colossus dedicated to the sun by the Rhodians, see Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book VIII, chapter 24. On other colossi, see Paulus Voetius on Herodian, page 186 and following, and Raderus on Martial, page 23. On Rhodes, see Bochart, *Phaleg* III.6. Diodorus, in book V of his *Grammar*, derives the name Rhodes from a girl named Rhodos; others derive it rather from the roses said to have grown there in great abundance.

**Note 23.** Isidore reads *Tenedos*, and Ampelius, chapter 6, also counts Tenedos among the Cyclades. Muncker disagrees in his note on Hyginus, *Fable* 276, where he corrects *Tenedos* to *Tenos*. Artemidorus, Strabo, Ovid, Stephanus, and Pliny also call it *Tenos*. There is another Tenedos, a city and island opposite the Trojan territory, of which Virgil writes in *Aeneid* II, line 21. Isidore attributes to Tenos what most writers relate about Tenedos, and confuses the two islands.

Different accounts are given concerning Tene, son of Cycnus and founder of Tenos. One says that he established the rule that anyone caught in adultery could immediately be killed by the person who caught him. The “Tenedian axe” became proverbial; Erasmus discusses it in his *Adages*. Tenes was regarded as a most holy god among the Tenedii, as Cicero says in *Against Verres* III, chapter 19, and in book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “Indeed, in Greece they have many gods who were originally human beings: Alabandus among the Alabandians, Tenedos among the Tenedii,” and so forth.

**Note 24. Carpathos.** It is said to have received this name because of the rapid ripening of its fruits, since καρπός (*karpos*) in Greek means “fruit.” Bochart, *Canaan* I.7, calls this as futile as the following claim, that the large and spacious ships called *Carpasian* were named from this island. He himself thinks that Carpathos was named from *carpath*, because it lies along the coast of Caria.

**Note 25. Cythera.** *Cythera* and *Cytherae* occur for the island in Tacitus, *Annals*, chapter 69: “So that he might rather concede Cythera.” But others tamper with this reading. Cellarius confirms with suitable evidence that the island of Cythera lies opposite the town of Boeae and Cape Malea, with a town and harbor of the same name, in book II, chapter 14, and book III, chapter 7.

**Note 26. The island of Icaria.** Solinus and Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, call it *Icaros*, and Pliny also lists it among the Sporades. Mela, book II, calls it *Icaria* and likewise lists it among the Sporades. Strabo and Ptolemy also call it Icaria.

**Note 27. Naxos.** On Naxos, see Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, and Bochart, *Canaan* I.30. In my Solinus the reading is *Dyonisia*, not *Dyonisias*. Pliny calls it *Dyonisias*. Coins bearing the inscription ΝΑΞΙΩΝ (*Naxiōn*) survive and seem to belong to this island.

**Note 28. Melos.** Mela places it among the Sporades in book II. Its inhabitants are called *Melii*; hence Diagoras of Melos, about whom Minucius Felix writes in chapter 8.

**Note 29. The sardian stone.** Taken from Solinus, chapter 20.

**Note 30. Chios.** It is reported that Chios alone among the islands produces mastic. See Pliny, book V, chapter 31. Others derive the etymology from Greek, because of the abundance of snow, or from the nymph Chione, or from the daughter of Daedalion. Bochart, *Canaan* I.9, demonstrates that the name Chios is Syrian, but derives it from *Chivia*, “serpent,” because the histories of the Chians report that a dragon of enormous size once lay hidden beneath Mount Pelinaeus on that island and for some time terrified the islanders with its hissing. He denies, however, that the Syrians called mastic *chion*.

**Note 31. “The island is sea.”** Perhaps it should read, “It is in the sea.”

**Note 32. “Trinacria . . . in Latin, Triquetra.”** In corrected editions of Quintilian, book I, chapter 6, or 10, the reading is not *Triquadra* but *Triquedra*. He derives the etymology of the word from three seats or places, since ἕδρα (*hedra*) means “seat.” Perhaps, therefore, Isidore should read: “In Latin it is called *triquedra*, as though divided into three *hedrae*.” Bochart, *Canaan* I.30, discusses at length the first or earliest inhabitants of Sicily and rejects the ancient stories preserved by Thucydides and others. He derives the name Sicily from Hebrew.

**Note 37. Hephaestias.** Solinus, chapter 11, says: “In the Sicilian strait are the islands called ἠφαιστίαι (*hēphaistiai*),” and so forth. Perhaps *Hephestias* was introduced into Isidore from this source, and one could read *Ericusa Hephaestica*, so that there would be only one island. The Greeks call these islands the Hephaestiades. *Hephaestia*, or *Hephaestias*, is also the metropolitan city of the island of Lemnos. See Pliny, books III, chapters 8 and 9, where he teaches that Lipara was named from Liparus, son of Auson, who succeeded Aeolus. Others say that Aeolus succeeded Liparus. Consult Cellarius, book II, chapter 12.

**Note 38. The Stoechades Islands.** They are now called the Hyères Islands; there are three of them. See Pliny, book III, chapter 5. But smaller or less famous islands are counted alongside the three better-known ones.

**Note 39. “Sardus, begotten by Hercules.”** So say Solinus, chapter 10, Strabo, Silius, and others. Earlier the Greeks called it Ἰχνοῦσα (*Ichnousa*), from its resemblance to the sole, or the lower part of the human foot. Bochart, *Canaan* I.31, considers the story told by Isidore and other earlier writers about Sardus, son of Hercules Maceris, just as suspect as the derivation by Isidore and Servius of Corsica’s Greek name, Cyrnos, from Cyrnus, likewise a son of Hercules. He devises a Hebrew origin for the name Sardinia.

**Note 40. “But the sun-fleeing creature . . . unless it is a plant.”** Solinus, in the passage cited, discusses the *solifuga* and the Sardonian or Sardoa herb, which kills people as though they were laughing.

**Note 41. The island of Corsica.** Bochart discusses Corsica in *Canaan* I.31–32. He asserts that the name Corsica is Punic and denotes a wooded place, because no other island is more densely forested. Eustathius, on Dionysius, line 458, and the Byzantine chorographer, under Κορσίς (*Korsis*), favor Isidore. Seneca more plausibly considers the island’s various inhabitants, *To Helvia*, chapter 8.

**Note 42. “In Greek Κύρνη.”** More correctly, Κύρνος (*Kyrnos*). Pliny also writes *Cyrnos*, book III, chapter 6, as do the epigrams attributed to Seneca, in opposition to Corsica. Servius, on the Virgilian passage cited, calls it *Cyrne*. See the note on no. 39.

**Note 43. Ebusus.** Also *Ebusus*, *Ebosia*, or *Ebusia*; it is now Ibiza. Bochart, *Canaan* I.35, derives its origin from the Hebrew *Jebuso*, “of the dried fig,” that is, dried figs, for which Ebusus was famous.

**Note 44. The Balearic Islands.** Isidore describes the Balearic Islands in such a way that Majorica appears to have been called Aphrosiade and Minorica Gymnasie. Grialius indicates in his note that both were called Aphrosiades, or Aprosiades, and conjecturally Aphrodisiades; both were also called Gymnasides. Pliny, book III, chapter 5, testifies that the Greeks called these islands Gymnasiae because their inhabitants exercised themselves naked in summer by throwing the sling. Bochart, *Canaan* I.35, derives the etymology of *Balearic* not from Greek but from Punic or Phoenician: “skilled in throwing missiles.” Eustathius, on Dionysius, line 457: “Therefore they are called BALEARES, that is, SLINGERS, according to their native language.”

**CHAPTER VII, no. 1. “And their places.”** Perhaps it should read, “and their necks.” In the following chapter, no. 19: “Hills are the more prominent ridges of mountains, as it were their necks.”

**Note 2. Sigeum.** Grialius wrote *Sigaeum* with a diphthong; this cannot be approved. In Greek, Σίγειος (*Sigeios*), or *Sigeus*.

**Note 3. Maleum.** *Malea* is the name of a promontory; *maleum* is an adjective. Statius describes Malea in *Thebaid* II, lines 32 and following, among other passages.

**Note 4. Pelorum.** In Orosius, book I, chapter 2, *Pelorum* is also read as a neuter, namely, “the promontory.” It is usually called *Pelorus*, that is, “the mountain”; sometimes in the feminine form *Peloris* and *Pelorias*. That it was called Pelorum from Pelorus, who commanded Hannibal’s fleet, is confirmed by Mela, book II, and Valerius Maximus, book IX, chapter 8, who recounts the story of Pelorus, who was killed and buried on this promontory.

**Note 5. Pachynum.** This promontory is called both *Pachynum* and *Pachynus*, or *Pachynos*.

**Note 6. Lilybaeum.** The city is now Marsala. Cicero discusses it in *Divination against Verres*, chapter 17.

**Note 7. Borion.** Grialius, along with other printed editions, gave *Borio* in the text and *Borion* in the note. Solinus’s words are: “We shall furnish proof from places and cities that very many foreigners settled in it [Africa]. The Greek newcomers gave the name Borion to the promontory struck by the north wind. Greek horsemen founded the most famous towns: Hippo, afterward called REGIUS, and another Hippo, called DIARRHYTUS from the strait flowing between them.”

Just as the Greeks called the promontory *Borius* or *Borion* from Boreas, or the north wind, so they named the two Hippones from horses; when the Latin word was added, one was afterward called *Hippo Regius*. Isidore—or whoever he took the material from—because of the faulty punctuation in Solinus, still found in some printed editions, understood that Borion was afterward called Hippo Rhegium, and added an explanation of the Greek word *Rhegium*, as is said of Rhegium in Calabria: that it was once torn away from Sicily by the force of the waves and the breaking apart of the land. On Hippo Regius, see chapter 5, no. 9, of this book.

**CHAPTER VIII, no. 2. Caucasus.** On the Caucasus, compare Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*. Raderus, in his commentary on Martial, pages 36 and 584, also indicates the authors who wrote about the two-peaked Caucasus mountain.

**Note 3. Taurus.** The Caucasus itself is part of Mount Taurus.

**Note 4. Lebanon.** Calmet, in his *Biblical Dictionary*, thinks that Lebanon was named from the Hebrew *leban*, or *laban*, meaning “white.” For it gleams with perpetual snows, concerning which Jeremiah, Tacitus, and others write.

### Note 5. Ararat

John Struys, in his travels, relates that he climbed to the summit of Mount Ararat and was assured that relics of Noah’s ark still remain there. Tournefort, who visited the place, testified that nothing of the sort was to be found there; other learned men likewise agree that the summit of the mountain is covered by perpetual snows. See Calmet, *Dictionary of the Bible*, and Bochart, *Phaleg*, book I, chapter 3, who observes that Arab and Hebrew writers assert that the remains of the ark were preserved in the mountains of the Gordyaeans, Ararat.

### Note 6. Acroceraunian

This is an adjective; the substantive is *Acroceraunia*, or *Ceraunia*. In place of “the cast of the thunderbolts,” I would prefer “the strike of the thunderbolts.” Servius likewise has *jactus* in my edition, in his note on *Aeneid* III, verse 506. The Ceraunian Mountains of Epirus were named from the frequent lightning strikes caused by their height. Hence Horace more precisely said *Acroceraunia*, on account of both their height and the cast of the thunderbolts.

### Note 7

Pliny places the Hyperborean peoples in book IV, chapter 12, behind the Riphaean Mountains and beyond the north wind, or north. Whether, however, there are mountains properly called Hyperborean is uncertain to me, except that Ptolemy distinguishes the Hyperborean Mountains from the Riphaeans. Cellarius, by contrast, supports the opposite view, book II of *Ancient Geography*, chapter 6, no. 27.

### Note 8. *Impetus* and ὀρμή

Ῥιφή and ὁρμή signify “impetus” or “force of attack.”

### Note 10. Athos … Lemnos

Solinus, chapter 21, in my edition, reads: “When Athos is separated from Lemnos by eighty-six thousand paces.” Pliny, book II, chapter 7, reads: “From it [Imbros] to Lemnos are 22,000 paces; Lemnos is 87,000 paces from Athos. Its circuit extends for 120,000 paces.”

### Note 11. Parnassus

I said in chapter 4, no. 12, that Parnassus is not a mountain of Thessaly. Parnassus is in Phocis, not far from Delphi; concerning its twofold summit, see Cellarius, book II, chapter 13, section 9.

### Note 12. The Ceraunian … Mountains

These are the very Acroceraunian, or Ceraunian, Mountains discussed in note 6.

### Note 13. The Apennine

Some want it written *Apoeninus*, implying an origin from the Carthaginian Hannibal. Common usage opposes this. The Poenine Alps were discussed above, in chapter 4, no. 16.

### Note 14. Gehenna

Isidore was not unaware that this is a Hebrew word; in chapter 9, no. 9, he explains the matter itself from Saint Jerome. Nevertheless, by the alliteration of *Aetna* and *Gehenna*, he wanted to bring the fire of hell to people’s minds.

### Note 16. Solorius

Pliny, book III, chapter 1, mentions a very high mountain in Spain, but Mariana does not designate it by this name among the more celebrated mountains of Spain.

### Note 17. “He filled Atlas”

Lucan, in my edition, reads “he filled Atlanta.” Calpe is now called Gibraltar in Spanish.

### Note 18. “The lofty Alps”

Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 226: “and the lofty Alps.” Many use *Alps* and *Alpen* in the singular of any lofty mountain—Silius, Prudentius, Sidonius, Ausonius, Fortunatus, and others, collected in abundance by Ducange in his *Dictionary*. Bochart, *Canaan*, book I, chapter 42, no. 7, observes that most people have thought *Alps* was named from the whiteness of the snows. Nevertheless, it is not without basis that others explain *Alpen* as “a lofty mountain,” since *al* means “high” in French and *pen* means “hill” or “mountain summit.”

### Note 19. Hills

Others think they are called *colles* from *colere*, “to cultivate.” Statius confirms Isidore’s etymology when, by way of comparison, he called the ridges of Parnassus beneath its summit “leafy necks” in *Thebaid* IX, verse 643. See the note on the preceding chapter, no. 1. In place of *praeminentiora* or *praeeminentiora*—for both forms are written—I would prefer *prominentiora*, “more prominent”; and this is how it is written in book I, no. 376, of the *Differences*.

### Note 20. Ridges

This term is used especially of the continuous crest of a mountain. Caesar, *Civil War* I, chapter 70: “So that, after changing his route, he might reach Octogesa along the ridges.”

### Note 21. Mound

Because it is often used for a grave, Isidore points out that a *tumulus* can also be piled-up earth where there is no memorial. See book XV, chapter 11, no. 2, and Vulpius’s note on Tibullus, book IV, poem 1, verse 204:

> Indeed, when a mound shall have covered my bones.

### Note 22. “As though torn away”

Because a valley is withdrawn from, and as it were cut apart from, a mountain; hence *reducta vallis*, “a withdrawn valley,” in Virgil, Horace, and others.

### Note 23. Plain

Becmann explains other etymologies of *campus* at length.

### Note 25. “Trees leap upward”

Others, following Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 4, infer that *saltus* is so called because cattle leap in it. Others derive the name from the Greek ἄλσος, “grove.”

### Note 27. “Where the winds were breaking”

Perhaps the reading should be “where the winds were broken.” In Festus, some read *conflant* instead of *confluunt*. *Confluges* are something else; concerning them, see Nonius, chapter 1, no. 311, and Livy, quoted by him: “Confluges, where they soak the entire assembly-ground.” Another reading has “where, at an assembly.”

### Note 30. Grove

One may consult John Rhodius’s *Description of a Grove Devoted to Ancient Sacrifices*.

### Note 33. “Which is without a gift”

Because formerly *moenia* and *moenera* were written for *munia* and *munera*.

### Note 35

The etymology proposed by others is not a bad one: *opacum*, “shaded,” is derived from Ops or Opis, who is Earth, daughter of Caelus and Vesta, as the myths relate.

### Note 36. “And it is called slippery, not because …”

Isidore perhaps wrote: “It is called slippery not only because it slips, but …” Grialius, however, defends the received reading.

### Note 38. Naval yards

*Navale* is metaphorically called a weaving shop, because ships are, as it were, woven there. Servius, in his note on *Aeneid* XI, verse 326, cites a verse of Ennius to this effect.

### Note 39. Station

All sorts of places, even uncultivated ones, suitable for ships to rest in were called *stationes*. See Scheffer, *On Naval Warfare*, page 210.

### Note 40. *Baia*, *baias*

I do not find *baia*, *baias*, in the lexicographers. Yet Isidore took it from some earlier source. Ducange’s supplement has *baia*, “bay,” from a thirteenth-century document.

### Note 42. “The margin is a part”

Perhaps *extrema* is missing: “The margin is the outermost part of anything,” and so forth.

## Chapter IX

### Note 5. Tartarus

This is a Greek word, later adopted by the Latins.

### Note 11. “Hence there”

Some printed editions read *hinc illic*, “hence there.” The genuine reading appears to be *hinc ibi*, although *ibi* for “there,” “in that place,” or “to that place” is less Latin. The ancient Vatican Codex 623 has, in place of *eo*, *dicuntur, quod animae hinc ibi feruntur*: “they are said to be so called because souls are carried from here to there.” Petavius supports Isidore’s view that the abode of the underworld is in the middle of the earth, volume III of *Theology*, book III, chapter 5, no. 6.

# Book Fifteen

## Chapter 1

### Note 1. Sallust

In the cited passage he says: “The city of Rome … the Trojans, who, as exiles, under the leadership of Aeneas wandered with uncertain abodes, and with them the Aborigines.”

### Note 2. “Nor the historians, etc.”

Isidore took not only this statement but also the material preceding it in no. 1 from Servius; the same statement appears in book IX, chapter 1, no. 38.

### Note 4. Babylon

Secular writers assign Babylon another origin, as may be seen in Calmet’s *Dictionary of the Bible*. Rader, in his commentary on Martial, page 19, collects and compares various opinions of authors concerning the founder, or founders, of Babylon.

### Note 5. Salem

Concerning the names of Jerusalem, see the note on chapter 3 of book XIV, no. 21. Learned men have said much about its true etymology, but there is no room to pursue it here. See the *Dissertation* of Georg Caspar Kirchmaier, published at Wittenberg in 1676, book V; several of its opening chapters concern the affairs and customs of the Jews.

### Note 6. Dionysus, also called Liber

Justinus, book XII, chapter 7, calls Bacchus the founder of Nysa. Others assert that Bacchus was born in that city and was therefore also called Dionysus.

### Note 7. Media

Media is the region discussed in book XIV, chapter 3, no. 11. Concerning the city of Media, Bochart, *Phaleg*, book III, chapter 14, should be consulted. He observes that it was a city in the province of the same name, also called Medena and Hammedena, now Hamadan.

### Note 8

Persepolis, or Persaepolis, was the capital of Persis proper. I do not find the term *Persidae* among the earlier geographers.

### Note 10. Susa

In Latin it is usually called *Susa*, genitive *Susorum*. Pliny, book VI, chapter 27, reports that Darius, son of Hystaspes, was the new founder of this city. What Isidore says, *oppidum Susis*, “the town at Susa,” may be understood in the sense in which, in a later age, city names were sometimes pronounced as indeclinable in the sixth case, or in the fourth, as in *oppidum Centumcellis*, “the town at Centumcellae.” See my *Prudentius*, page 185, no. 212, in the note.

In Grialius’s notes, the reading from the Gothic manuscripts was *Menonis patrem*, “the father of Menon”; but *Menonis* is perhaps a typographical error, and I have therefore restored *Memnonis*, “the father of Memnon.” The present name of Susa is Tousther, or Schousther, the metropolis of Khuzistan.

### Note 11. Bactra

Concerning Bactra, see book XIV, chapter 3, no. 30.

### Note 12. Carrhae

The name more commonly occurs in the plural, *Carrhae*, genitive *Carrharum*. Concerning Carrhae, a city of Mesopotamia, see Lucan, book I, verse 107. Pliny, book V, chapter 24, speaks of a city of Arabia called Carrhae: “Arabia, mentioned above, has the towns of Edessa … Carrhae, famous for the slaughter of Crassus.” He understands this as a part of Mesopotamia inhabited by Arabs, to which, he says, the prefecture of Mesopotamia was joined—that is, Mesopotamia properly so called.

In Holy Scripture it is written *Charan* or *Charran*, and in the Vulgate *Haran*. Nevertheless, many deny that Haran is the Carrhae of Mesopotamia. Cellarius examines the various opinions on the matter, book III, chapter 15.

### Note 12. Edessa … Philadelphia

Jerome attests in his *Chronicle* that Edessa was founded by Seleucus the Great, king of Syria. Some believe that Arach, the city founded by Nimrod according to Genesis 10:10, was Aracca in Susiana on the Tigris. Some learned men think Chalanne was Callinicum.

Philadelphia is assigned at one time to Arabia and at another to Coele-Syria; it was the metropolis of the Ammonites. The Rephaim were giants against whom Chedorlaomer led an army in Abraham’s time, according to Genesis 14. Why Isidore says that this nation of Rephaim was killed by the sons of Lot, I do not see.

### Note 15. Damascus

The report concerning the founder of Damascus is uncertain. Justinus, book XXXVI, relates that this city was founded by Damascus, to whom Abraham succeeded as second in the administration of the kingdom. Others say that Abraham was the founder and that he gave the city its name from Damascus, the son of his steward or household administrator, concerning whom Genesis 15, verse 2, says: “And Abram said … This Damascus Eliezer is the son of the steward of my house.”

Others conjecture other things, as may be seen in the dissertation of the aforementioned Kirchmaier. It is also written *Laodicea* and *Apamea*.

### Note 16. Gaza

The name is the Hebrew *Aza*, or *Haza*, from which *Gaza* was formed.

### Note 17. “Of which above”

Where? Perhaps Isidore took these words from some source whose name has been lost, as I often suspect happened with him.

*Philistim*, or *Philisthiim*, is not the name of a city; rather, this is what the Philistines are called, designated by the Seventy Translators as *allophyles*, “people of another race.” Ashkelon was a city in the region of the Philistines.

Grialius had *Cesloim*; I restored *Chasluim*, following the Vulgate, Genesis 10:14: “and Pathrusim, and Chasluim, from whom the Philistines and Caphtorim came forth.” See book IX, chapter 2, nos. 20 and 58.

### Note 18. Dor

Jerome mentions this city in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “She admired the ruins of Dor, once a most powerful city.”

### Note 19. Joppa

Some think it was founded by Cepheus, who gave it its name from his wife Joppa. Jerome, in his note on Jonah 1 and in the *Epitaph of Paula*, also bears witness to the traces of Andromeda’s chains. Josephus, Mela, Pliny, and others confirm this in a similar manner, though in such a way as to acknowledge that the story is mythical.

### Note 20. “Uzzah of Bethel”

Bonfrerius, in his note on Jerome, observes that it is incorrect to call him Uzzah of Bethel: he was Hiel of Bethel, according to 1 Kings 16:34.

### Note 21. Shechem

In the Gospel it is called *Sychar*, a corrupted form. *Emor* is elsewhere written *Emmor*, and in the Vulgate *Hemor*, Genesis 34:2. Jerome, in the *Onomasticon*, indicates that Neapolis was situated at some distance from ancient Shechem; some more recent writers agree with him.

### Note 22. “Truly, here is a house”

The Vulgate reads: “This is no other place but the house of God and the gate of heaven.” Bonfrerius, in his note on Jerome’s *Book on Hebrew Places*, or *Onomasticon*, thinks that there were two neighboring places: Bethel, formerly called Luza, perhaps in the tribe of Ephraim; and Bethel in the tribe of Benjamin, where Jacob had the vision of the ladder.

### Note 23. “Bethlehem is a name, etc.”

Bonfrerius, in his note on Jerome’s *Onomasticon*, conjectures that this name was given after Bethlehem, the son of a man of Ephrathah, who is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2 and 4.

### Note 24. “It is itself also Mamre”

It was not the city of Chebron, or Hebron, itself that was called Mamre, but the valley beneath it, as Bonfrerius and others think.
