See the interpreters on Genesis 35:27: “He also came to Isaac his father at Mamre, the city of Arba; this is Hebron.” The city was called *Ciriatharbe*, which means “the city of Arba,” or “the city of three.”

### Note 25. “King Sennacherib, etc.”

These statements must be corrected. Samaria was founded by Omri, king of Israel, who purchased the mountain from Shemer, its owner, and gave the city its name, as is clear from 1 Kings 16:24 and Josephus, book VIII of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 18.

In place of *Sebastiam*, one may restore *Sebastem*, since *Sebaste* is the Greek name given for *Augusta*. See Calmet’s *Dictionary of the Bible* and Bonfrerius’s note on Jerome’s *Onomasticon*.

### Note 26. Tiberias

It was founded by Herod Antipas. See Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book XVIII, chapter 3.

### Note 27. Tyre

It was founded after Sidon, mentioned in the following note, by the Sidonian Phoenicians themselves.

### Note 29. Sidon

Pliny, book V, chapter 19: “Sidon, inventor of glass and parent of Boeotian Thebes.”

### Note 30. Carthada

Servius’s words on *Aeneid* IV, verse 670, are: “Carthage was first called BYRSA, then TYROS, and afterward CARTHAGE, from the town of Cartha.” Solinus suggests something else: namely, that when it was first founded by Elissa it was called Carthada, or “new city.” He adds: “Then, once the language had been changed into a Punic term, the former was called ELISSA and the latter CARTHAGE.”

### Note 31. “Traces of error”

He perhaps means the pyramids of Memphis. Rader, in his commentary on Martial, page 18 and following, draws from Bellonius and others much material concerning the form and purposes of the pyramids.

### Note 32. Tanis

The miracles of Moses in the field of Tanis are mentioned in Psalm 77:12 and 43. Bonfrerius, in his note on Jerome’s *Onomasticon*, asserts that Tanin is the same city as Taphnis, concerning which Jeremiah speaks in 43:9. Calmet, in his *Dictionary of the Bible*, maintains that they are two different cities.

### Note 33. City of the Sun

Because it had a temple of the Sun, as Strabo says in book XVII. Ptolemy, Stephanus of Byzantium in *On Cities*, Pliny, and others speak of it, apart from the sacred writers.

### Note 35, note. “From Solinus, chapter …”

Grialius cited the passage of Solinus as chapter 45; in the list of errata he noted that it should be read as 35, as I state in his note. But in my edition the passage itself is chapter 45, which Grialius ordered to be changed. Concerning Cadmus, founder of Thebes, see above, no. 29, and below, no. 46.

### Note 39. “The fatherland of the poet Homer”

Most poets think so: Lucan, Silius, Claudian, Sidonius, and others. The people of Smyrna indeed dedicated a shrine to Homer in their town. But many other peoples of Greece claim Homer as their fellow citizen, and the dispute still remains undecided. There is a book by Leo Allatius on Homer’s birthplace.

### Note 42. “That it might become a refuge for him, etc.”

Orosius, book III, chapter 13, reports these same words concerning Philip, king of the Macedonians: “Thinking Byzantium, a maritime city, necessary for useful advantage, he judged the noble city most suitable to become a base for himself by land and sea; and, when it resisted, he at once enclosed it with a siege.”

Orosius, in the cited passage, has a little more about Constantinople than Grialius gives. Concerning the name Byzantium, see Eustathius on Dionysius, verse 804. Byzas, leader of the Megarians, is believed to have been the founder of Byzantium; and on some ancient Byzantine coins the name BYZAC appears with an aged, helmeted head.

### Note 47. Sparta

The city is also called Lacedaemon; hence the state is called Lacedaemonian. In Orosius these words precede: “It must nevertheless be understood that this is especially Sparta itself, etc.”

### Note 48. Pelops

The Peloponnese was indeed named from Pelops. Whether, however, some city founded by him was called *Peloponnensis* is unclear; nor have I happened to find the term *Peloponnensis* as a city-name among the ancient geographers.

Strabo, book XIV, reports that Rhodes was founded around the time of the Peloponnesian War by the same architect who built the Piraeus; nearly all the citizens of Ialysus, Camirus, and Lindus gathered there.

Concerning Thessalonica, see book XIV, chapter 4, no. 12. I have encountered no city named Thessalia that was founded by Thessalus. The only distinction worth noting is that *Thessaly* sometimes signifies the entire region and sometimes the part properly called Thessaly and Thessaliotis.

### Note 49. Brundisium

Concerning Brundusium, or Brundisium, see book XIV, chapter 4, no. 23.

### Note 51. “Who was victorious”

It would be preferable to read, with Solinus, chapter 8, “because he was victorious,” etc. Solinus says that the town of Pompeii was so called from a procession of oxen; under the emperor Nero it sank because of an earthquake, and under the emperor Titus it was completely buried beneath the ashes of Vesuvius.

### Note 55. “Then King Evander”

Virgil says, “then King Evander”; Isidore likewise has this reading in no. 1 of the present chapter.

### Note 56. “That he might delay the enemy”

Perhaps because some write *Hostia*. But the more correct spelling is *Ostia*. At first, it seems, it was called only *Ostia*, *Ostiorum*; later the feminine forms *Ostia*, *Ostiae* were also used.

### Note 58. “Afterward changed”

Perhaps *versae postmodum*, “afterward changed,” and so forth. Servius, in his note on *Aeneid* VIII, verse 9, reports that the part of Apulia held by Diomedes was called Messapia and Peucetia after two brothers. Pliny, book III, chapter 11, suggests that Calabria was called Peucetia after Peucetius, brother of Oenotrus.

### Note 59. Manto … Mantua

Others say that Ocnus, son of Manto, founded Mantua. See Virgil, book X, verse 199, and Servius there. Ocnus was also called Bianor; Virgil, *Eclogue* 9, verse 59:

> For the tomb of Bianor begins to appear …

In manuscript codices, *m* and *in* are easily interchanged and confused; hence *manes* for *inanes*, and the reverse. In this passage, however, the etymology of Manto, or Mantua, requires *manes* rather than *inanes*, which is found in the printed editions.

### Note 60

The city’s customary name was Parthenope, after one of the Sirens, Parthenope, from whom it was so called. The name Neapolis was added when the city was enlarged by new colonists; corresponding to it is Palaepolis, apparently a part of ancient Parthenope, concerning which Livy speaks in book VIII, chapter 22.

### Note 62. Phalantus

From Servius, on *Aeneid* III, verse 551, the statement should be corrected or explained as follows: “Phalantus, eighth in descent from Hercules, led the Parthenii, or Partheniae, into the town that Taras, son of Neptune, had built; from him it was thereafter called Tarentum.” Concerning the Parthenii, see book IX, chapter 2, no. 81.

### Note 63. The Phocaeans

The printed books had *Phocenses*; I restored *Phocaeenses*. Although Lucan more than once confuses *Phocaeentes* or *Phocaeos* with the Phocians, and attributes the origin of Massilia to the Phocians, most ancient writers clearly assign this distinction to the Phocaeans—that is, to the citizens of the Asian city of Phocaea in Ionia. See Valesius on Ammianus, book XV, chapter 9; Cellarius; and others.

Christian Wilhelm Franz Walch’s treatise *On the Trilingual Massilians* was published in volume III of the *Acts of the Jena Latin Society*. In this passage Isidore notes the fierceness of the Gauls, or of Gaul. In book IX, chapter 2, no. 101, he speaks of the fierceness of the Franks; and in no. 105 the Gauls are said to be naturally fierce.

### Note 65. “Tarraco, etc.”

From Solinus, chapter 36.

### Note 66. Caesaraugusta

In some of our manuscripts as well, this description of Caesaraugusta is absent. I consider it probable that Braulio added it in the margin of his copy, after which others inserted it into the text.

Two Toledo codices agree with Grialius’s edition, as do Palatinus 281, which is very ancient, Palatinus 282 and 283, Urbinas 100, and others. The description of Caesaraugusta is absent from Regiovat. 212 and 1953, Urbinas 479, and Ottob. 343 and 404.

The statement that Caesaraugusta was flourishing because of the burials of holy martyrs appears to have been taken from Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 4, where eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta are celebrated together.

### Note 67. “Under Hannibal”

Florez corrected this to “under Hasdrubal,” as I said in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 17, no. 23, where I explained the entire passage. The manuscripts consistently read “under Hannibal.”

### Note 69. “Are called”

I corrected *dicuntur*, “are called,” in place of *dicunt*, “they call,” which, I think, Grialius printed through an error.

### Note 70. Olyssipona from Ulysses

In ancient inscriptions collected by Gruter it is written *Olisipo*. Others prefer *Ulyssipo*, since, with Solinus, they maintain that it was founded by Ulysses. *Olyssipona*, or *Ulyssipona*, belongs to a later period.

### Note 71. Hispalis

Isidore appears to derive the name *Hispalis* from *pali*, “stakes.” Florez, volume IX of *Sacred Spain*, page 8, together with Arias Montanus and Bochart, prefers deriving *Hispalis* from the Phoenician word *sephela*, or *spelu*, “plain.” Formerly it was written *Spalis* for *Hispalis*, just as *Spania* was written for *Hispania*.

### Note 72. Gades

Bochart, *Phaleg*, book III, chapter 7, observes that Pliny, Solinus, Avienus, and Hesychius explain *Gadira* as *septum* or *saepes*, “enclosure” or “fence.”

### Note 74. Sala

Solinus, chapter 37: “The town of Sala overlooks the river Sala.”

### Note 77. Cyrene

Battus is believed to have been the founder of Cyrene, according to Strabo, Pausanias, Justinus, Silius Italicus, and others. See Cellarius. It is also called *Cyrenae*, genitive *Cyrenarum*.

## Chapter II

### Note 3. “From the circumference, etc.”

From Servius, on *Aeneid* I, verse 16.

### Note 4. “For this reason, etc.”

There is a dissertation by Crellius on the public ceremony by which cities were founded, published at Leipzig in 1745; it elucidates both Isidore and this subject.

### Note 5. “From the opposition of the walls”

From Servius, on *Aeneid* IX, verse 608.

### Note 6. “A town, however, by its size, etc.”

From Servius, in the passage cited. Varro, Tullius, and others teach the same. Varro and the jurist Pomponius also support the derivation of *oppidum* from *ops*, “aid” or “resources.”

### Note 10. Municipality

The ancient writers—Festus, Gellius, and others—do not agree sufficiently among themselves in defining a *municipium*.

### Note 12. Village

More recent writers investigate a Hebrew or Greek origin for *vicus*; Varro derives it from *via*, “road.”

### Note 13. “A high hut”

I am no more persuaded by the opinion of others that *castrum* derives from *casus*, “a fall,” in order to indicate a dwelling that is not permanent.

### Note 16. Suburban districts

I would prefer *suburbia*, “suburbs,” and *civitati*, “to the city.”

### Note 18. Walls

Servius, on *Aeneid* XI, verse 567: “It must be understood that *moenia* is used improperly for everything,” and so forth.

### Note 19. Towers

This is also a Greek word.

### Note 22. “A gate is called, etc.”

Compare Cato’s words in no. 3.

### Note 26. *Subvolamina*

Grialius also printed *Subvolamina* in the text, which he thinks should be restored conjecturally in the note. The old printed editions have *subvolumina*; others, *subvelamina*. Papias writes: “Either because they are beneath a covering.” Ducange says that *imbolum*, or *embolum*, is a narrow street of a city. The Byzantines generally used this word for the colonnades scattered throughout the city; later the word itself was applied to the districts in which those colonnades stood.

### Note 27. “The forum … from Phoroneus; read … ‘before the Rostra’”

Bignaeus defends this definition of the forum, as is clear from his words reproduced in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 35, no. 8. Nearly the same passage is repeated in book XVIII, chapter 15, where mention of King Phoroneus is omitted and *Prorostra* is written.

Grialius, in his note, presents the reading *Rostra vocantur*, “they are called the Rostra,” although in the text he printed *Prorostris*. The noun is *Rostra*; but the preposition *pro* is sometimes added and should be written separately, as in *sedens pro Rostris*, “sitting before the Rostra.” Likewise: *in Rostra*, “onto the Rostra”; *e Rostris*, “from the Rostra”; *de Rostris*, “concerning the Rostra,” and so forth.

Schwartzius, in his dissertation on the Rostra of the Roman Forum, argues from this passage of Isidore and from other writers against those who think that saying *pro rostris* is not the same as saying *in rostris*, or “upon the Rostra.” He also illustrates the form of the Rostra, or of the place called *Rostra*, from an ancient coin.

### Note 34. Theater

Concerning the theater, see the cited book XVIII, chapter 42.

### Note 37. Lighthouse, etc.

The same material is repeated in book XX, chapter 10. Montfaucon, volume III of the *Supplement to the Explanation of Antiquities*, book IV, chapter 3, argues against the etymologies of *Pharus* offered by Isidore, Licetus, and Isaac Vossius. He maintains that the tower was called *Pharos* from the island of Pharos, which bore that Egyptian name before any tower or fire was seen upon it.

Homer mentions the island of Pharos. Nicholas Antonius, book V of *The Old Library of Spain*, no. 95, shows—following the opinion of Martini—that Isidore’s etymology of *Pharus*, criticized by John Scheffer, book III of *On Naval Affairs*, *Addenda*, page 337, should not be dismissed.

### Note 38. “Spiral … such as is at Rome”

The more celebrated column at Rome is Trajan’s Column. Eutropius, speaking of Trajan, says: “His bones, placed in a golden urn in the forum which he built, lie beneath his column, whose height is 140 feet.”

Isidore appears to be speaking of the Column of Antoninus, to which most ancient and modern writers assign precisely 175 feet, as Eschinard notes in his *Description of Rome*, part II, chapter 1. They are called *cochleae*, “spirals,” because the Greek κοχλίας means “snail.”

### Note 40. Baths

Joachim Kuhn, in his dissertation *On the Washings and Baths of the Greeks*, rejects the etymology of *balneum* offered by Augustine and Isidore. In his view, the Greeks ought to have said βαλάνιον (“bath”) rather than βαλανεῖον. Compare Suidas.

### Note 42. Tavern

Others think *popina* was named from *popa*, a minor priest who sold sacrificial victims. Certainly *propino* is the Greek προπίνω: “I drink beforehand,” “taste the wine lightly beforehand,” and “offer it to another.” A discussion of the taverns of the ancients appears in volume III of the *Acts of the Jena Latin Society*, page 268.

### Note 45. Customhouse

The word *telonium* also occurs in Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 12, and *On Baptism*, chapter 12. Some, however, read *teloneum*, as in Nonius, chapter 1, no. 65, who has *telonearius*, while others have *telonarius*.

### Note 46. Prison

Servius derives *carcer* and its etymology from *arcere*, “to restrain,” in his note on book V, verse 145: “The *carceres* … are gates by which the horses are held back; hence *carceres*, as though *arceres*, according to Varro.”

Isidore combined both explanations in book V, chapter 27, no. 13.

## Chapter III

### Note 2. Temple

Becmann writes: “*Aedes* is derived by Servius from *edere*, ‘to eat’; by Varro, in book IV, from *aditus*, ‘entrance’; by Festus, from *editus*, ‘elevated’; and by others, from the fact that one’s life (*aevum*) is spent there.” He rejects these and does not himself produce better explanations from Hebrew and Greek.

### Note 4. Atrium

Florez, volume XIII of *Sacred Spain*, treatise 41, chapter 9, nos. 9 and following, observes that *atrium episcopi* is often used by Paul the Deacon for an episcopal residence. He confirms this meaning, which Ducange overlooked, from this passage of Isidore.

By synecdoche, *atrium* also means an entire house in Ovid, *Heroides* 16, verse 184:

> Nor will our halls contain Phrygian daughters-in-law.

Strictly speaking, the *atrium* was a place within a spacious or noble house, enclosed by porticoes and having an open area beneath the sky. Servius explains, on *Aeneid* I, verse 730, that there was a kitchen in the atria: “There was also a kitchen there, from which it was called *atrium*, because it was black (*atrum*) from smoke.”

Isidore added “and from the lamp,” perhaps because Servius shortly afterward explains this word; for he interprets the verse:

> Lamps hang from the high ceilings of the atria.

I further think that the atria were blackened by the fire that servants lit during winter to warm themselves. This may be inferred from Mark 14:54: “But Peter followed him from a distance, even inside, into the atrium of the high priest; and he was sitting with the servants at the fire and warming himself.”

Rader, in his commentary on Martial, page 25, explains that, in the opinion of some, the atrium was called *atrum* because it became black from the smoke of the hearth and kitchen, which among the Romans were located in the atrium.

### Note 5. Palace

Strictly speaking, this was Mount Palatine, concerning whose origin Varro, Servius, Scaliger, and others say much. The more sumptuous houses built upon it gave their name to the word *palatium*, “palace.”

### Note 6. Bridal chamber

This is a Greek word. There is remarkable disagreement among the ancients concerning Talassus, or Talassio. Some think that he was the presiding god of marriage. Some write *Thalassus* with an aspirate.

### Note 8, note. “The basilica itself”

In Servius’s words I restored *ipsam basilicam*, “the basilica itself,” from my edition. Grialius printed *ipsum*, “itself,” in the masculine.

### Note 9. “Called a cell”

Grialius had *cellas appellaverunt*, “they called cells”; in my edition of Servius, the reading is *cellam*, “a cell.” *Cubile* sometimes denotes the room in which we lie and sleep; *cubiculum* sometimes also means the chamber in which we remain during the day.

### Note 10. Lodging

In one of my two copies of Grialius’s edition there is *hospitum*, as also in the copy against which the Gothic Toledo manuscripts were collated. In my other copy, however, the correct reading is *hospitium*. This confirms the diversity among copies of Grialius’s edition in several places, as I indicated earlier.

The etymology of *metor, metaris*, “to measure out,” is more correctly derived from *metior*, “to measure.” For a *metator*, going ahead of an army, measures out a place for setting up camp.

### Note 11. Maenian balconies

These are nearly what the Romans now call *mignani*. Isidore takes *materies*, or *materia*, “material,” and shortly afterward *materia*, to mean wood, as is clear because he distinguishes it from stone. The Spaniards call it *madera*. This meaning of *materia* can be found in Pliny, Columella, and others.

### Note 12. “Washing”

That is, “washing himself.” For *lavo*, “I wash,” is often used in the active voice with passive meaning, as the examples of the ancients show.

### Note 13. “With illnesses and starvation”

In Grialius, Jerome’s words were displayed as follows: “I, compassionate, might cherish the limbs afflicted by illness and starvation.”

## Chapter IV

### Note 5. Monastery

Isidore gives the distinction between a monastery and a coenobium from Cassian in book II, chapter 16. Saint Jerome, Saint Anastasius, and Saint Nilus agree; Ducange cites them.

### Note 7

Others seek a Greek etymology for *templum*; others derive it from *tueri*, “to protect.” For *contemplatio*, “contemplation,” rather derives its origin from *templum*. After idolatry was destroyed, the name *templum* was applied to the churches of Christians.

The form of Christian temples was ordinarily the same as that described by Vitruvius. Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 20: “The more common practice, and the one closer to reason, was to turn toward the East when praying.” This is relevant to chapter 57 of book II of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

Those who explain Christian antiquities prove by examples that not all the churches of the ancient Christians were built in that form.

### Note 8. “From Fauns”

Perhaps for this reason Christians did not wish to impose the term *fanum*, “shrine,” on their churches. Although Varro and Festus derive *fanum* from *fari*, “to speak,” because at the dedication of a temple the pontiff customarily pronounced certain words beforehand.

### Note 9. Shrines

In explaining the etymology of *delubrum*, Varro, Festus, Cornelius Fronto, Asconius, and others offer various opinions. Certainly Christians almost always avoided the name *delubrum* when naming their churches.

Schurzfleisch, *Dissertation on Civil History* 53, no. 1, says that in Isidore, as in Asconius Pedianus and Servius, one should read *a deluendo*, “from washing away,” rather than *a diluendo*, “from dissolving,” as other codices have. The prepositions *de* and *di* are frequently confused in compounds, and it is often impossible to insist on one rather than the other.

The practice of placing basins before the entrances of temples continued among Christians, so that those about to worship God might wash their hands beforehand. These basins were later replaced by lustral, or blessed, water.

### Note 10. “In shrines”

On the occasion of *delubrum*, he discusses the baptismal font, or baptistery, which some called a *delubrum*, as appears from Ducange’s dictionary.

In the cited passage in Grialius, book II of the *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 25—Grialius incorrectly had chapter 24—the words *in delubris* are missing. The remainder of the sentence, as is clear from the note on that passage, was taken from Jerome’s letter to Rusticus of Narbonne concerning the seven grades of the Church, volume IX; thus there is no need to appeal to Tertullian.

I have indicated certain matters concerning the baptisteries of Christians in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 8, and elsewhere in connection with Prudentius. Isidore, following Jerome, maintains that there were three steps in the descent to the baptistery.

### Note 11. Basilicas

Some think that the name *basilica* became attached to churches because Constantine granted many basilicas for ecclesiastical use.

### Note 12. Martyrium in Greek

In Latin, *memoria* was a church built over the tomb of one or more martyrs. Properly, however, the place itself beneath the principal altar, where the bodies of holy martyrs rest, is called a *martyrium*, or *confessio*. Hence the confession of the holy apostles in the Vatican church, the confession of Saint Lawrence, and so forth. See my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 2, verses 527–528.

### Note 13. “The altar … imprecation: κατάρα (‘curse’)”

The reading formerly was: “The imprecation is called *satura*.” Grialius restored the passage as it appears in Servius; nor was there any reason for Arntzenius, only in our own time, to labor at correcting the old editions of Isidore, together with Joseph Wase, in his note on Sallustius’s historical fragment, page 224, *Miscellanies*, chapter 6.

But most people, unaware of Grialius’s edition, sometimes undertake a useless task and do work that has already been done.

Becmann proves, from Tertullian and together with Joseph Scaliger in his note on Ausonius, book II, chapter 22, that *ara*, “altar,” can sometimes be understood as the height and elevated position of a place. Compare chapter 13, no. 16, of this book.

### Note 16. “From the Tribune its seat was called the tribunal”

Hence the tribunal of the priest or bishop in churches, concerning which Isidore speaks here, as does Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 11, verse 225:

> Before the facing front, the lofty tribunal  
> Is raised high on steps; from there the bishop proclaims God.

See my commentary on this passage.

## Chapter V

### Note 1. Lectisternia

Servius, on book XII of the *Aeneid*, verse 199: “Where people sit in the temple,” and so forth. Properly, however, a *lectisternium* was a sacrifice at which couches or beds were spread for the gods and a banquet was set out. I do not see Servius’s opinion confirmed by any more authoritative witness. Compare Ezekiel Spanheim, *On the Use of Coins*, volume II, page 193, and Filippo della Torre, *Ancient Antium*, page 318.

### Note 2. Votive offerings

They were also called *dona*, “gifts,” especially those offered to temples.

### N. 4. Armarium

Hence the Spanish and Italian word *armario*, with nearly the same meaning. *Armamentarium* is used especially of a place where naval arms or naval equipment are stored. In the words by which they are exercised, *arma* must be supplied or understood. Servius, on *Aeneid* IV, line 495 [Col. 0983A]: “Properly speaking, *arma* are those things that cover the shoulders.”

### N. 6. Promptuarium

It is also written *promptarium*; but among earlier authors of good Latin it is found in neither form as a neuter noun, except adjectivally. Apuleius, Ausonius, and other writers of the same period use it substantivally.

### N. 7. Ministeria mensarum

By this name Lampridius, chapter 34 of his *Life of Alexander Severus*, and Paulus, *Sentences* III, chapter 7, call the eating and drinking vessels used in serving at table. Servius, on *Aeneid* I, line 708, assigns a distinction not between *promptuarium* and *cellarium*, but between *penus* and *cellarium*.

### N. 8. Entheca

It is used not only for the substance of a stored object but also for the place itself in which it is stored. Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 42, *On Various Matters*: “We are not permitted to have an *entheca* for ourselves. For it is not the bishop’s office to keep gold.” Here *entheca* appears to mean a repository for money.

## CHAPTER VI

### No. 1. Ergasterium

In the *Theodosian Code* it is a workshop of craftsmen at work.

[Col. 0983B]

### No. 2. Ergastula

The words of Lipsius, cited by Grialius at the indicated passage, should not be omitted; they correct and explain Isidore’s statement:

“First, not only criminals but also harmless purchased slaves were assigned to the *ergastulum*. Then, never gladiators. Nor do I agree concerning exiles. Finally, the principal purpose of the *ergastulum* was agriculture; but also labor in quarries, mills, and perhaps drawing water. It was characteristic of those detained in an *ergastulum* that they were kept in chains.”

Apuleius, in the *Apology*: “Fifteen free men constitute the populace; as many slaves, the household; as many chained men, the *ergastulum*.”

### No. 3. Gynaeceum

It was the more private part of a house, in which women lived apart from men; Isidore indicates another, specialized meaning.

### No. 4. Clibanus

The word is Greek. A certain kind of portable oven made of bronze, iron, or earthenware was called a *clibanus*. Isidore explains the name from its shape: the *clibanus* was wider at the bottom and narrower at the top, and thus narrowed as it rose and resembled the form of a slope:

[Col. 0983C]

### No. 6

According to the opinion of others, it is an oven, from *formus*, since the ancients called something hot *formum*.

### No. 8. Lacus

It comes from Greek λάκκος (*lakkos*), “a pit.” In its transferred sense it denotes a large vessel into which pressed must is received, or into which the dregs are collected during the making of oil.

## CHAPTER VII

### No. 2. Vestibulum

Aulus Gellius discusses at length the meaning and etymology of *vestibulum*, *Attic Nights* XVI, chapter 5. Relevant to our subject is the following:

“*Vestibula* were called the spaces—as we have said—large areas left before the doors of houses, where those who had come would stand before they were admitted into the house.”

Gellius had prefaced this by explaining that the particle *ve* signifies both intensification, as in *vetus* and *vehemens*, and diminution. Servius explained *vestibulum* in the opposite way, through the notion of diminution.

### No. 5. Fenestrae

Servius, on these words of Virgil, *Georgics* IV, line 298—“It has only windows admitting slanting light”—says: “Those which pour in light obliquely, as we see in granaries.” Isidore perhaps thought that *fenestrae* properly meant windows that admit light obliquely; for [Col. 0983D] after the description he adds, “because they lend out light.”

### No. 7

*Limen* is a Greek word, from which some derive *limes*. Compare below, chapter 14, note 2.

### No. 8. Postes et antae

Grialius printed *Postes et antae* in the text, but *Postes et antes* in the notes. Yet *antae* must be distinguished from *antes*. *Antae* are stone piers, or square-built columns, at the sides of doorways on the fronts of houses.

## CHAPTER VIII

### No. 1. Idem et caementum

The Spaniards use *cimiento* for “foundation.” Among the Latins, however, *caementum* did not properly mean a foundation, but stone cut in quarries, or fragments cut from larger rocks, for building or filling walls. Nonius, chapter 2, no. 179: “*Caementa*: stones of no great size, by which buildings rise.”

### No. 2. Paries

According to some, it derives from *paro*; according to others, from *pareo*. Some trace its origin to Greek.

[Col. 0984A]

### No. 5. Camerae

Or *camarae*. The word is Greek, and in Latin it is written in both ways.

### No. 7. “It is interpreted in Latin as LUCIDA”

Salmasius denies this, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1219, although he admits that the apse of churches—that is, the sanctuary—received light through an arch. Certainly in Greek ἁψίς (*hapsis*) means “a joining,” and hence the curve of a wheel, or the wooden circle into which the spokes are fixed. But Isidore perhaps derived it from ἅπτω (*haptō*), “I kindle.”

Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 6, and the manuscript Cambrai Glossary cited by Rosweyde in the *Onomasticon* appended to the *Lives of the Fathers*, reproduce Isidore’s interpretation and nearly his very words. The latter discusses this word *absis* at length and explains its four meanings: the curve of a wheel; an arch bearing an inscription; the elevated place where the bishop sits; and the chamber in which the relics of the saints are deposited.

Paulinus was uncertain whether it should be called *absis* or *absida*, in Letter 12 to Severus, whom Isidore perhaps consulted:

“In which he likewise indicated that an *absis* had been made. But concerning this, whether I should more properly say *ABSIdam* or *ABSIdem*, you must judge. I confess that I do not know, since I do not remember having read this form of the word.”

Both forms were used by ecclesiastical writers, but *absis* appears preferable.

### No. 8. “Others [call it] a vault, etc.”

This too was taken from Servius, who quotes Cicero’s words in the *Brutus* and adds: “Some wish a *testudo* to be a place in a part of the atrium opposite those entering.” The editions of Isidore, including Grialius’s, read *in partem* instead of *in parte*. In my edition, Servius has left Cicero’s passage incomplete. Cicero, in the *Brutus*: “Having composed [something] in a …”; and “Some, etc.” is added, as though these words too belonged to Cicero.

Cicero, *Brutus*, chapter 22: “With everyone else excluded, I had composed [my work] in a certain vaulted chamber with literate slaves.”

Arntzenius, on Sedulius IV, line 233—

> “While he sits in the middle of his own temple’s vault”—

criticizes Isidore as though he were passing off under his own name what he owed to Servius. Arntzenius therefore had not read Isidore’s preface, [Col. 0984C] or dedicatory letter, to the *Etymologies*. It should be noted, however, that Sedulius, in prose, explains “the middle vault of the temple” as “the walls of the temple.”

### No. 9. Arcus

As others prefer, from *arceo*, “because it drives back.”

### No. 11. Ostraci

I find no example for “a pavement of baked brick.” In Ducange, *ostracarii* are those who make tiles from clay, suitable for covering roofs.

### No. 13. Bases

Its etymology is usually sought in the Greek language.

### No. 15. Epistylia

They are not placed above a door but above columns, from Greek ἐπί (*epi*), “above,” and στύλη (*stylē*), “column.” An *epistylium* is a beam laid transversely above the capitals of columns; it supports the other beams of a roof, and in stone architecture it is the stone corresponding to such a beam.

### In the same place. Capitella

Varro, *On the Latin Language* VII, near the end, denies that the word *capitellum* belongs to ordinary Latin usage. Apuleius and the elder Pliny subsequently used it, although some read *capitula* instead of *capitella* in Pliny.

[Col. 0984D]

## CHAPTER IX

### No. 1. Munitum

From *munio*, formerly *manio*, which is derived from *manus*, unless this itself comes from *manio*. *Cors*, or *cohors*, may also be derived from *coerceo*, “to restrain.” Others derive it from Greek.

### No. 2. “The rampart … from *vallis*”

This is a better and clearer explanation than Varro’s, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 31: “*Vallum* comes from *volatus*, because when they throw it, the light objects fly away.”

### No. 4. Maceriae

Others derive it from Greek μάκελλα (*makella*), “enclosures made of rubble walls.”

### No. 5. Earthen walls

If they are made solely of earth, the Spaniards call them *tapias*; if made of small stones mixed with lime, *hormigon*, apparently a corruption of the Latin *formatio*. In a certain copy of the *Etymologies* I find a marginal note stating that, in the territory of Siena, country people use such earthen walls.

[Col. 0985A]

### No. 6. Saepes

And *sepes*. It is written in the same way as *saepio* and *sepio*. Both spellings have their supporters.

### In the same place. “With the C removed”

Servius, on *Aeneid* IX, line 6, reads in my edition *c detracto*, “with the c removed.”

## CHAPTER X

### No. 2. Tentorium

Lipsius discusses tents in the fullest detail in *Roman Military Matters* V, Dialogue 5.

### No. 3. Papiliones

Vegetius, Pliny, Lampridius, Trebellius Pollio, Tertullian, and several others call military tents *papiliones*. The same word, somewhat corrupted, passed into the vernacular languages.

## CHAPTER XI

### No. 1. “That admonishes the mind”

Servius, on *Aeneid* III, line 486: “*Monumenta* are so called from the admonition of the mind.”

On the custom of burying within or outside the City, see my commentary on Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, line 190. The common people, who possessed neither fields nor estates, were buried in a common place designated for burial; this was called a common tomb. In another sense, *loci communes* meant tombs customarily made for an entire family and its descendants. Tombs intended for private individuals or married couples, however, were more commonly called *requietoria*, or simply *loci*. See Taubmann, on Plautus, *Casina*, p. 365 ff.; Kirchmann; and others.

### No. 2. Tumulus

On *tumulus*, see XIV, chapter 8, no. 21. Barthius, *Adversaria* IV, chapter 3, confirms the etymology from Fulgentius, on Chalcidius: “Where the place would swell, hence *tumulus*.” He corrected this from his own manuscript, since it had previously been corruptly read “whence Rutilius.” *Sarcophagus* is the name of the stone from which tombs were customarily made. See Book XVI, chapter 4.

### No. 3. Mausolea … from a mausoleum

Perhaps “from Mausolus,” for this king is usually called Mausolus, and his wife Artemisia. On the mausoleum, see Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV, chapter 5; Gellius, *Attic Nights* X, chapter 18; and Raderus, on Martial, pp. 22 and 371, where he also discusses the mausoleum of Augustus.

### No. 4. Pyramis

The purpose of pyramids and columns in tombs was to rise above other mortals, as Pliny teaches, *Natural History* XXXIV, chapter 6. Raderus, on Martial, p. 16 ff., detected a double error in Pliny’s measurement of the [Col. 0985C] pyramid.

Concerning the shape and size of the pyramids, and the fact that, although extremely high, they did not cast a shadow, Fabricius, chapter 23 of the *Bibliographia*, cites John Greaves, Norden, Kircher, Pietro Bellon, and others. Munckerus, with Scheffer, on Hyginus, fable 223, interprets the statement that the pyramids in Egypt cast no visible shadow as referring to the time of the solstice and the middle of the day.

## CHAPTER XII

### No. 1. Tueri

It is also used passively by Varro and the ancient jurists.

### No. 2. “They call it a *capanna*”

Thus, more or less following Isidore, do Papias and John of Genoa write. I find no examples among the older authors; Ducange supplies examples from later writers and, with some others, suspects that *capanna* derives from Greek καπάνη (*kapanē*).

### No. 3. Tesqua

Varro, *On the Latin Language* VI, chapter 2, says that *tesca* are rural places belonging to some god, deriving the word from *tueor*, “to protect.” Festus teaches that *tesca* are places designated by augury. Others understand *tesca*, or *tesqua*, as rough, shady places difficult to enter.

### No. 4. Magalia

In Plautus, prologue to *Poenulus*, line 86, *Magaria* is the proper name of a place in the city of Carthage. Bochart, *Canaan* I, chapter 24, teaches that *magalia* is a corrupt form of *magaria*, and that, once Carthage’s harbor and citadel are excluded, it denotes the remainder of the city assigned for the habitation of its citizens. He derives the word from the Hebrew *magur*, “dwelling.” The Albanian manuscript and several others read *cellam dicunt*, “they call it a cell,” instead of *villam dicunt*, “they call it a farmhouse.”

## CHAPTER XIII

### No. 1. Ager

The word is Greek. It can also be derived from *ago*, “I drive” or “I do”; but Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 4, gives another explanation: “*Ager* was called the land in which they carried on some activity and from which they obtained something for the sake of its fruits; the Greeks call it ἀγρός (*agros*).”

### No. 3. Possessiones

Festus says: “Because they were held not by formal conveyance but by use, and whatever each person had occupied was pleasing to him.” Compare Brissonius, *Selected Antiquities* IV, chapter 1.

### No. 5. Praedium

It is better derived from *praes, praedis*, “surety,” which Varro says comes from *praestare*, “to provide” or “to guarantee.”

[Col. 0986A]

### No. 7. “The ancients called [them] *rura*, etc.”

This comes from Servius on *Georgics* II, line 412, who cites Cato as his authority.

### No. 9. “A common-pasture field, etc.”

From Festus.

### No. 10. “Alluvial land, etc.”

From the anonymous author of *On the Limits of Fields*, in Goes, p. 293.

### No. 11. Arcifinius

On *arcifinius*, or *ager arcifinalis*, see Siculus Flaccus, *On the Classification of Fields*, p. 3, and Aggenus Urbicus, p. 45, in Goes’s edition. The discussion returns shortly afterward to *subseciva*.

### No. 12. Novalis ager

The field first broken by the plow is not the same as the field that lies fallow in alternate years. A field first broken by the plow is one into which the plow has been introduced for the first time, when previously it had been woodland or uncultivated land. This is the proper meaning of *novalis*, which Servius explains, *Georgics* I, line 71: “Properly, *novales* are fields plowed for the first time and producing their first crop.”

But *novale* and *novalis* are also used for a field that rests in alternate years and is renewed, as Varro reports, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 4. After the words *semel vacua*, the first Gothic manuscript has this marginal note or addition:

“Thus Virgil:

> ‘Will the impious soldier possess these fields, so carefully cultivated, now lying fallow?’”

### No. 13. Squalidus

Festus and others derive the explanation of *squalor* and *squalidus* from their resemblance to *squama*, “scale.”

### No. 14. Uvidus

Servius, on *Georgics* II, line 184, reads in my edition: “Always moist: *uvidus* is what at some time becomes dry.” Others read: “Always damp: *uvidus* is what at some time becomes dry.” No distinction is usually observed between *uvidus* and *humidus*.

### No. 15. “Subseciva, etc.”

Forcellini cites these words as though they came from an ancient author *On the Limits of Fields*, in Rigaltius, p. 299; but perhaps this is not a different author from our Isidore. Ancient writers on agriculture, who discuss this subject in Goes’s collection, speak frequently of *subcisiva*, or *subcesiva*.

### No. 16. Area

Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV:

“Where grain that has been cut is threshed and dried, [it is called] an *area*. Because of the resemblance of these [places]—perhaps *harum* should be read—places in the city are called *areae*. From this it is also possible that the gods’ *ara* is so called because it is pure. Unless perhaps it is rather from *ardor*, ‘heat,’ toward which an *ara* is made, from which the *area* itself is not far removed; for what dries something is the sun’s heat.”

On the etymology of *ara*, see above, chapter 5, no. 13.

### No. 18. Paludes

Becmanus investigates a Hebrew and Greek derivation of *palus*; this has no bearing on our subject.

## CHAPTER XIV

### No. 1. Fines

There are some who derive *finis* from *funis*, “rope.” See Becmanus. Others derive it from *fio*, “I become.”

### No. 2. Limites

These matters were briefly discussed in chapter 7, no. 7, of this book. To the meaning of *limes*, add Festus. On *limus*, the servants’ girdle, see below, Book XIX, chapters 22 and 33.

Servius differs somewhat in my edition from Grialius’s text: “From the navel to the feet they were almost completely covered. This garment, etc.” See Petrus Pithoeus, *Subseciva* I, chapter 2, and Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 29, who argues from a Greek inscription that certain slaves were called *limocincti*, “girded with a *limus*.”

### No. 3. Termini

They were stones or posts, concerning which see Ovid, *Fasti* II, line 641, and Tibullus I, elegy 1, line 17, where Vulpianus’s note should be consulted.

[Col. 0986D]

### No. 4. “For undoubtedly, etc.”

He perhaps alludes to Servius, who explained the two *limites* in the opposite manner, on *Georgics* I, line 126. Salmasius pursues this argument at length, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 676.

### No. 5. Arca

Among ancient writers on agriculture, it is a square boundary constructed in the form of a chest. Varro and several others agree that *arca* is derived from *arceo*, “to restrain.”

## CHAPTER XV

### No. 3. Pertica

Some think that *pertica* is called *pertiga*, as though from *pertingo*, “I reach.” In Spanish we say *pertiga*. Ezekiel’s measuring reed, or *kanna*, was ten feet and three inches, as Calmet calculates in the *Biblical Dictionary*. Isidore cautiously says “in the likeness of a reed,” so that there is no reason for Georgius Agricola to say that Isidore is mistaken here, *On Measures*, p. 227.

Compare Mariana, *On Weights and Measures*. Burrielius, in his work *Report of Toledo on the Standardization of Weights*, no. 89, p. 227, observes that the *pertica* was the old Toledan *estadal*. This suggests that the ancients used the measure for measuring fields, as Isidore indicates in chapter 13 of this book: “Fields left over, divided according to the *pertica*, etc.”

### No. 4. Arapennis

Isidore took the substance of what follows from Columella, though he did not reproduce the exact words and also altered some things. Columella indicates that *arepenna* is a Gallic, not a Baetican, word. In either case, its Latin derivation from *aro*, “I plow,” is less satisfactory, although perhaps foreigners formed a new name for themselves from a Latin verb.

In writers of the later period it is written *arpennum*, *arpentum*, and *agripennus*. See Vossius, *Etymology*. Raderus discusses *jugera* learnedly in his notes on Martial, p. 17 ff., and shows that two hundred feet should be assigned to a *jugerum*.

### No. 6. Porca … lira

“What is dug down is a *lira*.” Isidore follows Festus and Nonius I, chapter 62; [Col. 0987B] but Columella seems preferable. He says, *On Agriculture* II, chapter 4:

“Farmers call those same ridges *lirae* when the land has been plowed in such a way that, between two furrows set farther apart, the mound in the middle provides a dry resting place for the grain.”

Columella explains it in this way more than once. Therefore what stands above the ground in plowing is called both *porca* and *lira*; what is dug down is the *sulcus*, “furrow.”

### No. 7. Centuria

On *centuria*, see Grialius’s note on chapter 13, no. 15, of this book.

## CHAPTER XVI

### No. 1. Gallic *leucae*

Hence the Spanish call it *legua*.

### No. 3. “One thousand five hundred”

In some printed editions *quingentis*, “five hundred,” is an error. See Bochart, *Canaan* I, chapter 16, who was correcting an error already corrected by Grialius, and Vossius, *On the History of Language* III, chapter 19, who derives the origin of *leuca* from the English.

Now a *leuca* is longer than one thousand five hundred paces, with differing measurements in different regions. Concerning what Isidore relates here about Hercules, Gellius, *Attic Nights* I, chapter 1, reports as follows:

“For since it was generally agreed that the length of the stadium-course at Pisa, which is sacred to Olympian Jupiter, had been measured by Hercules with his own feet, and that he had made it six hundred feet long, etc.”

### No. 4. Via

Some derive it from *eo*, “I go”; others from *veho*, “I carry.” Isidore combines both: “to go by vehicle.” Grialius printed *nam duos actus* in the text, but the note indicates that he preferred *duo*. Other editions read *duos*, which I approve: namely, “a road accommodates two *actus*.” See below, no. 13.

### No. 6. Strata

Clearly from *sterno*, “I spread” or “I pave.” Authors of ancient Latin said *via strata*, or *strata*, *stratorum*, and poetically *strata viarum*. In the later period, *strata*, *stratae*, began to be used by Eutropius and others. Hence the Italian *strada*. See my notes on Juvencus I, line 325.

The word *delapidata* is taken from Festus: “*Delapidata*: paved with stone.”

### No. 7. Agger

Servius says: “An *agger* is the raised middle of a road, paved with stones heaped together.”

### No. 8. Iter

Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 3: “From where they went, they called it *iter*, from *itus*, ‘going.’”

No distinction between *iter* and *itiner* is recognized by the earlier authors; rather, *itiner* is the complete inflected form, while *iter* is produced by syncope. Both mean both the act of going and a road, and properly a narrower one, along which a person can go only on foot.

Pliny, in the preface to the *Natural History*: “Moreover, an *iter* is not a road trodden by authorities.” Instead of *appellamus* and *itum*, perhaps *appellamus exitum* should be read.

[Col. 0987D]

### No. 9. Semita

Phaedrus, preface to Book III, line 38:

> “I have made his footpath into a road.”

For Aesop had composed only a few fables, whereas Phaedrus invented more. Thus other writers commonly distinguish between *semita* and *via*.

Cicero, *Against Verres* II, chapter 23: “You will now understand that this money, which a moment ago seemed to have gone out from him by the road, returned by that same path.” I would prefer to read: “which a moment ago seemed to have gone out from him by the road, returned by the same footpath”; that is, what had been taken openly was returned secretly. This is certainly what Cicero means, even if the received reading is retained.

### No. 13. “An *actus*, along which cattle are usually driven”

Above, at no. 4, Grialius said, following Servius, that an *actus* accommodates two vehicles. But Isidore, following more authoritative writers, establishes that a *via* is what accommodates two vehicles, while an *actus* is half a road, accommodating only one vehicle—or two draft animals.

Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 4: “Just as the place along which they drove was called an *actus*, so the place along which they traveled by vehicle was called a *via*.”

Pomponius’s statement is clear, *Digest* VIII, title 1, law 13:

“If, after a path so narrow that neither a vehicle nor an animal could enter it has been described, a *via* has been granted, an *iter* rather than a *via* or an *actus* will appear to have been acquired. But if an animal can be led along it, though not a vehicle, an *actus* will appear to have been acquired.”

Forcellini proves that the other jurists who spoke differently had regard not to the native force of the word but to popular usage. Grialius distinguished *clivosum* and *iter flexuosum*, as though *clivosum* were a substantive; this is unsatisfactory.

In the first Toledo Gothic manuscript there is the following note or addition, placed after the word *cognoscantur*: “*Boscionium*, *borcionium*: a place between two walls.” It is incorrectly written *inter duabus parietibus*, “between two walls.”

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 0988B]

## CHAPTER I

### No. 1. Pulvis

Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV, chapter 13, says that dust is the worst part of earth, and that it is therefore called *pulvis*. He also discusses Puteolan dust there.

### No. 2. Limus

Some assert a Greek origin for *limus* and think it was called in opposition to *favilla*, “ash,” because it nourishes fire. But it is not part of our purpose to pursue at greater length what others have said, especially in a matter so uncertain.

### No. 3. “*Gleba*, because it is a *globus*”

Becmanus says that this is not inept.

### No. 4. “From *labe*”

It is better derived from *labor, laberis*, “to slip” or “to slide.” Saint Jerome uses this word, as do others cited by Ducange under *lavina*; for some write it in such a way that it is derived from *lavo, lavas*, “to wash.” According to the opinion of others, *lutum*, “mud,” is so called because earth has been washed, or dissolved by water, from Greek λύειν (*lyein*), “to loosen.”

[Col. 0988C]

### No. 5. Volutabra

In *volutabrum*, the vowel of *-abrum* is long; there is no need to relate it to *aper*, “boar.” But Isidore reproduces Servius, on *Georgics* III, line 411: “*Volutabra* are places in which boars roll themselves.” Yet pigs also roll themselves there.

### In the same place. “Sabulum, etc.”

Rosweyde gives these very words in the *Onomasticon*, from the manuscript Cambrai Glossary, which cites other passages of writers. Italians call *sabulum* *sabbia*. See Varro, *On Agriculture* I, chapter 9, where he uses *sabulon* for *sabulo*.

### No. 6. Argilla

In Greek it is ἄργιλλος (*argillos*), which may derive either from barrenness or from its white color. That *creta*, “chalk,” was named from the island of Crete may be confirmed by Horace, Book I, Ode 36:

> “So that the beautiful day may not lack its Cretan mark.”

Bentley discusses this passage further. Crete is called *Cimolia* from Cimolus, an island in the Cretan Sea. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, line 463: “and the Cimolian fields of Crete.” Pliny, *Natural History* IV, chapter 12, also discusses this Crete.

Vulcanius reproduced the following words of Pliny from Book XXXV, chapter 17, in his notes:

“Cimolian earth softens genuine and precious colors and brightens with a certain luster those darkened by sulfur.”

For Pliny had previously said that it was fumigated with sulfur and scoured with Cimolian earth.

### No. 7. Samian earth

Pliny discusses Samian earth again, *Natural History* XXVIII, chapters 12 and 19, and XXXI, chapter 10.

### No. 8. Puteolan dust

In Italian, *pozzolana*. It is similarly praised by Vitruvius, Seneca, and Sidonius. It is still transported from the Roman territory to distant regions.

### No. 9. “The living thing that is dug out”

The printed editions formerly read *unum, quod foditur*, “one thing that is dug out.” Vulcanius observes from Pliny that “living sulfur” is called what is dug out, etc.

### No. 10. “The fourth for lamp-wicks”

To correct this passage as well, Vulcanius, in his notes, quoted Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV, chapter 15:

“But it is especially the fourth [kind] that is used for making lamp-wicks. Its power is otherwise so great [Col. 0989A] that, when placed on a fire, it detects epileptic illnesses by its odor. Anaxilaus also made use of it: glowing in a new cup, with a coal placed beneath it, its reflected flare cast a dreadful pallor, like that of corpses, over the banqueters.”

## CHAPTER II

### No. 1. “Bitumen … useful for joining ships”

Bochart, *Phoenician History* I, chapter 11, observes that Isidore took from Josephus the statement that the nature of bitumen makes it useful for joining ships; he also gathers much additional material about bitumen.

### No. 2. Alumen

Better derived from Greek ἅλς (*hals*), “salt.”

### No. 3. Sal

From the Greek word just mentioned, ἅλς (*hals*), by metathesis. Hence *salum*, not conversely *salum* from *sal*.

### No. 7. Nitrum

Pliny discusses *nitrum* at length, *Natural History* XXXI, chapter 10, where he says that it is collected among the Medes, in valleys whitened by dryness.

*Nitria* is also discussed in Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 21, in Rosweyde, from Palladius. There the name *Nitria* is derived from *nitrum*, not the reverse:

“We also came to Nitria, a place famous throughout all the monasteries of Egypt, situated about forty miles from Alexandria. It takes its name from the neighboring village, in which *nitrum* is collected, and from this derives the name *Nitria*. Divine Providence, I believe, was already looking ahead to the fact that in those places human sins, like filth, would have to be washed away and abolished.”

Vulcanius produced from a certain manuscript a fragment concerning *nitrum* that is absent from other copies; we have relegated it to the appendices, no. 18.

[Col. 0989B]

### No. 8. Aphronitrum

Isidore reproduced Martial’s genuine reading, which Joseph Juvencyus of the Society of Jesus also retained in his edition of Martial, in the work cited, Book XIV, but epigram 54 in his edition. Other printed editions have, as Grialius notes, “I am called *Aphronitrum*” (*dicor Aphronitrum*).

Grialius also omitted the question mark after “You are a rustic” and after “You are a Greek,” although these marks are necessary for explaining the sense.

### No. 9. Aeris flos

Salmasius notes that this was taken from Dioscorides, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1078.

### No. 10. “It is made in hollowed bricks, etc.”

Salmasius, at the passage cited, p. 1159, observes that Isidore explains this much better than Pliny.

## CHAPTER III

### No. 1. Lapis … saxa

Cornelius Fronto distinguishes *saxum* and *lapis* as follows: “*Saxum*: natural rock. *Lapis*: stone cut from rock.”

### No. 2. “Or from a covering”

J. C. Scaliger observes in his *Book on Plants* that the primary meaning of Greek σκέπειν (*skepein*) is “to cover.” Grialius printed *rupis*, but the more common spelling is *rupes*, although in manuscripts *e* and *i* are often interchanged.

A *spelunca* differs from a *caverna* in that a *spelunca* is an excavated rock, whereas a *caverna* is an empty and dark hollow in the earth.

### No. 5. Scrupus

Grialius printed *cui contrarius est scrupus* in the text and *scrupulus* in the notes. But *scrupus* should be retained, on the authority of Servius.

### No. 6. “*Cotis* from the Greek language”

Vulcanius conjectures Greek κόμμα (*komma*). Others derive it from ἀκή (*akē*), “the edge of iron.” Grialius, in his notes, refers to some earlier passage that I cannot identify. On oil used for sharpening iron, see below, chapter 20.

### No. 7. “When placed in a vessel”

Here too, as in other passages, a nominative is used instead of an ablative absolute: namely, *missus*, “having been placed,” instead of *misso pumice*, “with pumice having been placed.”

### No. 8. Rudos

I would prefer *rudus* to *rudos*, since in manuscripts *u* is easily changed into *o*, and *rudi* or *rudos* is not found elsewhere. Nor should it be an objection that Isidore says *rudera* is derived from it; perhaps he merely distinguishes the plural from the singular.

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIV, chapter 25, observes that Isidore explains what *rudus* is better than Nonius, who, chapter 1, no. 65, says: “*Rudus*: manure that is thrown down.”

### No. 9. “From *lapis specularis*”

In Grialius and others, the excellent reading is *lapis specularis*. I restored *e lapide speculari*, as Grialius indicates in his notes.

Pliny, at the passage cited by Grialius: “Gypsum is a substance related to lime. It has several varieties, for it is also made by baking stone, etc. The use of gypsum in the white plastering of buildings, in seals, and in ornamental moldings is especially agreeable.” Perhaps in Isidore *sigillis*, “seals,” should be restored in place of *signis*, “signs.”

## CHAPTER IV

### No. 1. Indian stone

Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1103, insists that one should read *lapis Idicus*, “Idaean stone,” and *in Ida*, or *Lydicus*, “Lydian,” and *in Lydia*, since, he says, it is certain that the stone received its name from its homeland Magnesia, not from its discoverer.

But Isidore had regard not only to Pliny but also to Augustine, who, after discussing the diamond and the magnet, says in *The City of God* XXI, chapter 4: “India sends these stones.” Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVI, chapter 16, asserts in the best copies that the stone was found on Mount Ida and named after its discoverer. Lucretius, Book VI, lines 909, 1044, and 1062, derives the name *magnes* from the Lydian city of Magnesia.

### No. 2. “The liquid of glass also, etc.”

For these marvels of the magnet, one may consult the ancient writers Prosper, Part III, chapter 38, *On the Promises and Predestination of God*, and Bede, *On the Nature of Things*. Gisbert Cuperus, *On the Image of Harpocrates*, mentions in this connection the ark of Muhammad suspended in the temple at Mecca. Tevenotius and Tabernerius, however, classify this among fables, as does Athanasius Kircher concerning the earlier accounts. See chapter 21 of this book, no. 4.

[Col. 0990B]

### No. 3. Fictilia

Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVI, chapter 19: “Objects made of it, when inscribed, cannot be erased.” Much of what is related about *gagates* is fabulous.

### No. 4. Asbestos

From the stone asbestos is made asbestos linen, which they call “living.” Once set alight, it can indeed be extinguished, but it is not consumed while burning. In our own age paper made from this linen has been devised, and some books have already been printed on it; fire, naturally, cannot harm them. See the *Acts of the Academy of Barcelona*, p. 361, and *German Library* 14, p. 190. On the similar stone *amiantus*, see below, no. 19.

Ampelius mentions a perpetually burning lamp in the temple of Venus, chapter 8: “At Argyros there is a temple of Venus above the sea; there a lamp is placed upon a candelabrum, shining toward the sea under the open sky. Neither wind scatters it nor rain extinguishes it.”

Munckerus, in his notes on Lactantius Placidus, Book XIV, fable 4, thinks that *coelo* should be deleted after *divo* and that *dispergit*, “scatters,” should be read instead of *aspergit*, “sprinkles.”

### No. 5. Pyrites

Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 718, says that Isidore confuses the stone with the gem discussed by Pliny and Solinus; he names Persia as its homeland. From some manuscripts he corrects *fulvus* to *furvus* in Solinus. Pliny likewise says: “The *pyrites* is indeed black.”

Isidore partly reproduced Augustine, at the passage cited by Grialius: “The Persian *pyrites* burns the hand holding it if it is squeezed too hard; for this reason it received its name from fire.”

Solinus too, when about to speak of the *pyrites* and other notable stones, says in advance, chapter 50: “In Persia there is such an abundance and such a variety of stones that it would almost take too long to linger over their very names.”

Below, at no. 14, Isidore says that *memphitis*, listed among the stones, is of a gem-bearing nature. For this reason he also places certain notable stones among the gems.

There is indeed a *pyrites* that is a millstone, discussed by Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVI, chapter 19. There is another *pyrites* resembling bronze, discussed by Pliny in the same place. Another *pyrites*, also discussed there by Pliny, is commonly called “firestone,” in Italian *pietra focaia*. The characteristic property of the *pyrites* gem, however, seems to be that it burns the hand holding it when squeezed too hard.

[Col. 0990D]

### No. 6. Selenites

On *selenitis*, see Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVII, chapter 10.

### No. 7. “And what is remarkable in that burning”

Solinus, in the chapter cited, 50: “And what is remarkable in that arrangement, etc.” This does not seem absurd. See again the discussion of gems, chapter 11.

### No. 10. “The Syrian stone, from Syria”

Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVI, chapter 17: “From the island of Scyros,” or, more correctly, “from the island of Syros,” which is one of the Cyclades near Delos. In Isidore it would be better to read *Syrius lapis a Syro*, “the Syrian stone from Syros.” In this sense Pherecydes is called *Syrius*, with the first syllable of *Syrius* long. See Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, line 175.

### No. 15. Sarcophagus

On *sarcophagus*, see above, Book XV, chapter 11, no. 2. Many manuscripts add after *corpora*:

> “But [it is] gentler for preserving bodies, not for consuming them.”

In the Albanian manuscript, *absumendis* seems to have been written. Perhaps Isidore wrote:

> “But *chernites* is gentler for preserving bodies, not for consuming them.”

[Col. 0991A]

### No. 17. “Hence it also took its name”

Because by its hardness it subdues men, from ἄνδρας δαμάζειν (*andras damazein*), “to subdue men.” This is a different stone from the *androdamas* gem, discussed in chapter 15, no. 11.

### No. 18. Schistos

Psellus numbers *schistum* among those stones whose names alone we possess, in his little book *On the Powers of Stones*. Some printed editions read *ischistos* or *iscistos*, through faulty pronunciation. See Munckerus’s note on Fulgentius, *Explanation of Ancient Expressions*, under *Sculponeas*.

### No. 19. Amiantos

Bochart, *Phoenician History* I, chapter 6, should be consulted on *amiantus*.

### No. 21. Obsidius

Pliny calls it *obsidianus lapis*, saying that it was discovered in Ethiopia by a certain Obsidius. It is also found by the Ocean in Spain and in Egypt, as may be seen in the work published at Velletri in 1794 by Gregorius Wad, *Egyptian Fossils of the Borgian Museum*, where several stones mentioned by Isidore are learnedly described and illustrated.

[Col. 0991B]

In Isidore we can read: “The *obsidianus* stone, black, etc.” See chapter 16 of this book, no. 5.

### No. 21. Mitridax

*Mitridax*, or *mithridax*, appears to be corrupt for *mithrax*; for that is how it should be read in Pliny. *Mithras*, or *Mithra*, is the name of the sun among the Persians.

### No. 22. Aetitae

Solinus, chapter 50, on *aetites*: “Bound beneath, it protects the womb from abortive discharges.”

Isidore’s statement appears contrary to Solinus and Pliny. Pliny, *Natural History* XXX, chapter 14, says: “The *aetites* stone, found in an eagle’s nest, protects pregnancies against every danger of miscarriage.” This is why it was tied to pregnant women. But it could not be removed until they had begun to give birth; otherwise the wombs would fall out—or so the ancients believed. Nowadays such claims and similar ones are commonly ridiculed.

### No. 24. Chernites

Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1205, reports that the Plinian manuscripts call this stone *chermites*, not *chernites*. But the best old [Col. 0991C] and recent books prefer *chernites*.

### No. 27. Smyris

Dioscorides and Hesychius discuss the stone *smyris*.

### Note 28. Chrysites

It is a stone of golden color, concerning which Pliny writes in Book XXXVI, chapter 22; and it is also a gemstone resembling Attic ochre, about which the same Pliny writes in Book XXXVII, chapter 10. It is also called *phloginos* and is found in Egypt.

### Note 29. Hammites

In Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, it is a small gemstone resembling fish eggs, and it is named from the Greek ἄμμος (*ammos*), “sand.”

### Note 32. Molotius

See whether the subject is the *molochite* gemstone, about which Pliny writes in Book XXXVII, chapter 8, and Isidore, chapter 7, number 12, of this book. Pliny says that *molochites* is thickly and densely green and grows in Arabia.

### Note 35. Siphnius

From Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 22, where *siphnius* is read, not *siphinius*, as Grialius printed it. Other printed editions have *sifnius*.

[Col. 0991D] **Note 36. Thebaicus**

Gregorius Wad, in his description of the Egyptian fossils in the Borgian Museum, p. 27, thinks that the *Thebaic stone* of the ancients—which formed entire portions of mountains and was used to make mortars, since by a certain natural quality it was suitable for grinding collyria—is to be identified with a darkly greenish-black steatite, concerning which Pliny writes in Book XXXVI, chapter 8. Since, according to the same Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 22, the Thebaic stone is soft, the reading of others may perhaps be preferable, [the words] “releasing themselves” [or “yielding of their own accord”]. See the following chapter, note 10.

## Chapter V, number 1. Marbles

A stone is the genus; marble is the species. In Greek, marble is μάρμαρος (*marmaros*), from the verb μαρμαίρω (*marmairō*), meaning “to shine.”

### Note 3. Ophites

Lucan, Book IX, line 714:

> The Theban ophite, stained with tiny spots.

He means Egyptian Thebes.

### Note 4. Augusteum

Concerning Augustan and Tiberian marble, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7. He calls it *marmor augustum*, not *augusteum*, or, as Grialius less correctly writes it, *augustaeum*.

### Note 6. Basaltes

*Basal* means “iron” in Ethiopian. On the origin of basalt there is a letter from the Commander Dolomieu to Baron de Salis-Masklin in the French *Journal de physique*, September 1790.

### Note 7. Alabastrites

Onyx, or *onychites*, is a marble from which alabasters—that is, perfume vessels—were customarily made; for this reason it is also called *alabastrites*. There is also a gemstone called *alabastrites*, because it grows around Alabastron, a city of Egypt. It has a whiteness interspersed with various colors, as Pliny reports in Book XXXVII, chapter 10.

### Note 8. Parius … lychnites … lygdinus

The Parian stone called *lychnites* was quarried by lamplight in underground passages, as Pliny teaches from Varro in Book XXXVI, chapter 4. Concerning the *lygdinus* stone, Pliny writes in the same book, chapter 8; in him most read *in Tauro* (“in Taurus”) instead of *in Paro* (“in Paros”), although from Isidore it appears that *in Paro* should be read. Martial, Book VI, epigrams 13 and 43, mentions the white marble *lygdon*, which should not be distinguished from the *lygdinus* stone. The exceptional whiteness of Parian marble is celebrated throughout the poems of the poets.

### Note 9. Coraliticus … alabandicus

Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 8, discusses the *coraliticus* stone, a type of white marble so called from the River Coralios in Phrygia. Alabanda is a city of Caria. Hence come the *alabandic* stone and the *alabandine* gemstone, concerning which see chapter 14 of this book.

### Note 10. Thebaicus

Concerning the Thebaic stone, see the preceding chapter, note 36.

### Note 11. Syenites

Concerning syenite, see Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 8.

### Note 12. Thasius

Seneca, *Letter* 86, near the beginning:

> Thasian stone, once a rare spectacle in some temple, surrounded our pools.

Thasos is an island of Thrace in the Aegean Sea.

### Note 13. Lesbius

Pliny also lists this among the spotted marbles, Book XXXVI, chapter 6.

[Col. 0992C] **Note 14. Corinthaeus**

*Corinthius* is more usual than *Corinthaeus*, and *repertus Corinthi* than *repertus Corintho*. Corinthian columns are those made according to the Corinthian manner or order, as it is called. Whether Corinthian marble was famous, however, is uncertain. Certainly it is not praised as commonly as Corinthian bronze and Corinthian vessels, which were simply called “Corinthian.”

### Note 15. Carystium

Concerning Carystian marble, see Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 7. Because the green color refreshes the eyes, skilled architects in former times placed neither golden ceilings in libraries nor any other floors than those made of Carystian or Carystean marble, as Isidore has taught us in Book VI, chapter 11. See the note to chapter 7, number 1, of this book.

Salmasius, in his commentary on Julius Capitolinus, p. 164, observes that some formerly wrote *charisteum* for *Caristeum* or *Carysteum*; consequently, he thinks that Isidore, deceived by the corrupt spelling, supposed that the marble was called *charisteum* because it was pleasing to those who used it, and so forth. Isidore is indeed accustomed to play upon similar alliterations, but I certainly do not think [Col. 0992D] that he was unaware that the marble was called *Carystean* from Carystus, a town of the island of Euboea.

### Note 16. Hence it also received its name

Perhaps these words should be placed after “Numidia sends.” Concerning Numidian marble, see Pliny, Book V, chapter 3, and Book XXXVI, chapter 6. Grialius omitted *tantum* (“only”) in the text, although in the note he orders that the word be inserted. Seneca likewise praises Numidian veneers in *Letter* 86.

### Note 17. Luculleum

Grialius printed *Lucullaeum*; others have *Luculleum*. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapters 2 and 6, mentions this marble, found on an island in the Nile.

### Note 18. Lunensis … tephria

Luna marble, quarried in the territory of the city of Luna, is praised by Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapters 6 and 18. *Tephrias*, or *tephria*, comes from τέφρα (*tephra*), “ashes.” See Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 7.

### Note 19. Ivory

It ought not to have a place among marbles, since it is the elephant’s tooth; concerning it, see Book XII, chapter 2.

## Chapter VI, number 2. Kinds of gemstones

Some assert that *gemmae* properly refers to the eyes on trees and on the vine, because they swell, from the Greek γέμω (*gemō*), “I am full.” Others, following the opinion of Quintilian and Cicero, think that the proper meaning of *gemma* is precious stones, especially translucent ones; thus the etymology given by Isidore need not be rejected. Theophrastus, Joannes de Laet, Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt, Gimma, Calmet, in the *Dictionary of the Bible*, and others discuss gemstones specifically.

## Chapter VII, number 1. Emerald

A bitter or harsh color is a dark, blackish, excessively saturated, gloomy color. See Salmasius, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 201. Something is called *smaragdinus* from the color of the emerald. Apicius, Book III, chapter 1:

> Every vegetable will become emerald-green if it is cooked with natron.

See Barthius, Book XL of the *Adversaria*, chapter 2. He observes that an emerald color was judged extremely beneficial to the eyes, citing Marcellus the Rhapsode, chapter 8:

> A scarab of emerald color is said to provide such benefit to the eyes that it makes the sight of anyone who gazes at it continually exceedingly sharp.

Compare chapter 5, number 15, of this book.

### Note 3. Chalcosmaragdus

Concerning *chalcosmaragdus*, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 5; from him one may read *aereis venis* (“with veins of bronze”), especially since the manuscripts of Isidore vary.

### Note 4. Prasius

It is so called from its leek-green color.

### Note 5. Beryllus

Concerning beryl and its kinds, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 5.

### Note 6. Chrysoberyllus

Isidore understood Pliny’s meaning more correctly than Solinus concerning *chrysoberyl*, as Salmasius observed, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 1103. Pliny’s words are:

> And they are somewhat greener, but their radiance passes into a golden color.

Solinus, however, says:

> They shine more faintly and are surrounded by a golden cloud.

### Note 7. Chrysoprasus

Grialius printed *chysoprasus* in the text and *chrysoprasius* in the note. Salmasius, p. 406 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, observes that Isidore uses *chrysoprasius*, or *chrysoprasus*, for Solinus’s *chrysopastum* and Pliny’s *chrysolampis*, although *chrysoprasus* is a different gemstone. He adds that Solinus thought the *chrysopastum* and *chrysolampis* were the same stone. *Chrysolampis* is counted among the kinds of chrysolith, and Isidore mentions it in chapter 15, number 4; he also mentions *chrysoprasius* again in chapter 14, among the “fiery” gemstones, number 8. Salmasius may perhaps have had that passage in mind.

### Note 8. Jasper … pina

From the Hebrew, Becmann, p. 543, interprets *jasper* as a green gemstone. *Pina*, or *pinna*, is a marine shell. Salmasius, p. 1125 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, observes that Isidore calls it the shell in which the pearl is found in Arabia and India; but Pliny recognizes different shells in which pearls are produced, and in Acarnania the shell is called *pinna*, not in the other regions.

### Note 9. Topazion

Perhaps *topazios*, since *topazion* is neuter. *Topazios* was found on Topaz Island in the Red Sea. Consult Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 8.

### Note 10. Callaica … Germania

Pliny distinguishes two kinds of *callais*: one in Book XXXVII, chapter 8, resembling topaz and pale green; the other, in the same book, chapter 10, sapphire-colored but whiter. In the same chapter he teaches that gemstones are called *callaides* when they have the cloudy color of *callais*. Solinus, chapter 30 or 33, calls *callaica* a *callais* resembling topaz.

Vossius gives a different account of the color *callainus* in his *Etymologies*. Salmasius, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 237, maintains that the gemstone should be called not *callaica*, as Isidore reads, but *callaina*, from the color *callainus*. He criticizes Isidore for deriving *callaica* from gold. Grialius, however, had already observed that Isidore derives *callaica* not from gold but from the Greek καλὸν (*kalon*), “beautiful.”

Salmasius says that the error *Germania* for *Carmania* in Solinus is similar to errors in corrupt manuscripts of Pliny. But perhaps the copyists who transcribed Solinus or Isidore were mistaken, since an ignorant scribe could easily change *Carmania* into *Germania*.

### Note 12. It changes the rays of the sun

Vulcanius, in a note, reports from an old manuscript: “It imitates the rays of the sun by a bloody reflection”; and from Pliny:

> When thrown into a vessel of water, by a bloody reflection it changes the radiance approaching that of the sun.

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, it may be gathered that when this gemstone is put into water it increases the sun’s radiance by a bloody reflection; outside water, however, it turns away the rays or radiance and presents the sun as though in a mirror, and consequently detects an eclipse by showing the moon passing across it. Isidore’s words should be evaluated in accordance with this explanation.

### Note 14. Myrrhites

Or *myrrhitis*. In Solinus it is masculine. In the edition I use, chapter 50, we read: “If you examine it thoroughly and stimulate it toward color, it gives off the fragrance of nard.” *Ad calorem* (“toward heat”) is better, in agreement with Isidore, who first says *dicta est* (“it is called”), understanding *myrrhites* as a gemstone, and afterward uses the masculine form *compressus*.

## Chapter VIII, number 1. Coral

It is written *corallium*, *coralium*, *corallum*, and *curalium*, and there is a similar variation among the Greeks. *Corallium* is said to be named ἀπὸ τῆς κουρᾶς ἐν ἁλὶ, “from cutting in the sea,” that is, because it is cut or pruned in the sea. Others give a different derivation from Greek.

### Note 2. From Sardis

It appears that *a Sardianis*, or *a Sardis*, should be read—that is, from the inhabitants of Sardis. Marbodus, in his *Dactyliotheca*, writes:

> Sardius is from Sardis, by whom it was first discovered.

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7, lists the *sarda* gemstone, first discovered at Sardis, the chief city of Lydia. It does not appear to differ from the *sardius* stone mentioned by Tertullian in Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 10. In Isidore, it would be preferable to read *primum reperta sit Sardibus* (“was first discovered at Sardis”), not *a Sardibus* or *a Sardis*, as others have it with Marbodus.

### Note 3. India or Arabia

That is, *vel* (“or”) is used in the sense of *et* (“and”).

### Note 4. And *sardo*

Better *et Sardio*, or *Sarda*.

### Note 6. Succinum, which

*Succinum quod* (“amber, which”) would be more correct. *Succinus lapis* (“amber stone”) may be understood adjectivally. It is also written *sucinus*, but less correctly. Amber is discussed in chapter 24 of this book, where it is again repeated that poets call the sun *elector*. Compare also Book XVII, chapter 7, note 31, concerning the pine. In Greek, ἠλέκτωρ (*ēlektōr*) means “the sun.” *Succinum* is the sap of trees of the pine kind, as Pliny says. Some think it is the sap of earth or rocks. See Libanius, who published a book on amber, and Hyginus, [manuscript reference] 152. In Grialius, read Ἰλ. ζ … Πριάμοιο … ἄκρης.

### Note 7. By coldness or warmth

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7:

> In Syria women make spindles from it and call them *harpaga*, because they snatch leaves, straw, and the fringes of garments.

A spindle-whorl is an instrument used with a spindle so that it may turn more easily.

### Note 8. Lyncurius

In 1795 there appeared *Memoria sul lincurio del cavaliere Carlo Antonio Napione*, published by Antonio Fulgoni, Rome, quarto. Napioni refutes those who reduce *lyncurium* to the hyacinth gemstone. He thinks it is a certain kind of amber, which was called *ligurium* from Liguria, and hence, through corruption, *lyncurius*. From this corrupt word arose the fabulous etymology from the lynx’s urine, which Pliny at times accepts and at other times rejects.

## Chapter IX, number 2. Sapphire, etc.

From this passage Salmasius corrected Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9, which had been corrupt in the older editions. Isidore gives *sapphirum* in the masculine gender; others use the feminine. Grialius printed *saphirus*.

### Note 3. Hyacinthus

Pliny also discusses hyacinth in Book XXXVII, chapter 9.

### Note 4. Hyacinthizon

Pliny discusses *hyacinthizon* in Book XXXVII, chapter 6.

### Note 5. Amethystizon, etc.

See Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7.

### Note 8. Rhodites, etc.

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11. It is also written *Rhoditis*.

## Chapter X, number 1. Paederos, etc.

See Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9.

### Note 3. Asterites

Martianus Capella, Book I, calls it *astrites*; Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9, calls it *asteria*. Salmasius, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 756, thinks Pliny was mistaken in deriving the name *asteria* from the sun, since *aster* is never used of the sun. *Asteria* is called so from ἀστήρ (*astēr*), “star,” or “sparkling ray,” because it reflects rays of brightness toward the sun. Pliny also suggests this.

### Note 4. White with the taste of milk

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, one may restore: *album, ac lactis saporem* (“white, and with the taste of milk”). But Isidore copied Solinus, whose reading, Salmasius says in the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 137, some stubborn person might defend. Salmasius emends it to *album, ac lactis sapore* (“white, and with a milky taste”).
