### Note 5. Chalazias

From Solinus, chapter 50, and Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11. See below, chapter 13.

### Note 6. The appearance of the sun

Isidore is better than Solinus, who has *sideris* (“of a heavenly body”) instead of *solis* (“of the sun”). See Salmasius, p. 756 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*.

### Note 7. Each day

From Solinus, chapter 50, where it is read: “either diminished or increased each day.”

### Note 8. Cinaedia

Concerning *cinaedia*, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10. *Cinaedus* is a fish of yellow color, in whose brain *cinaedias*, or *cinaedia*, is found. It should not be written *cynaedia*, as Grialius and others do.

### Note 9. Belus’s eye

Grialius joins the words as *Belioculus*. It is commonly called “cat’s eye”; according to Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, it is a gemstone of whitish color surrounding a black pupil that shines with a golden radiance from the center. Accordingly, I have corrected Isidore to read: “it surrounds a black pupil, shining with a golden radiance in the middle,” whereas others had read: “it surrounds a pupil, black with a golden radiance in the middle.” The copies of Grialius vary: some, incorrectly, follow the printed editions; others have the reading I have adopted.

### Note 10. Epinielas

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, discusses the word *epimelas*, which may be applied to any white gemstone whose upper surface is blackish.

### Note 11. Exhebenus

Concerning *exhebenus*, or *exebenus*, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10.

## Chapter XI, number 1. It is black, etc.

Grialius thinks that this was added to Isidore. But I am little persuaded by the argument he gives. For that author of glosses, who wrote only after Hugutio—that is, not before the thirteenth century—could certainly not distinguish what Isidore had originally taught from what Papias and Hugutio had added. There exist copies of Isidore older than Hugutio and Papias, who flourished in the eleventh century, in which these same words are found, such as the Alban manuscript, Vatican Archive manuscript 1, and others.

Although what Isidore says about agate is found neither in Solinus nor in Pliny, Isidore could have obtained it from another source. Bochart, *Chanaan*, Book I, chapter 29, discusses several matters concerning agate that are relevant here.

### Note 2. Heated

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, where *excalfacta* is read. Pliny uses this form of the word more than once. I find neither *excalefactus* nor *excalefacio* elsewhere, nor perhaps did Isidore use them, since he follows Pliny.

### Note 3. Aegyptilla

Pliny, in the same place, says that *aegyptilla* is frequently found in Egypt.

### Note 5. At Veii

In Pliny, in the same place, it is “found at Veii,” not “from Veii,” since Veii is a town of Etruria whose inhabitants were called Veientes. In Isidore, Grialius reads *a Veiis* (“from Veii”); others have *a Vegenis*. But *Veiis* should be read, as in Pliny, or *a Veientibus* (“from the Veientines”), as in the margin of the Breulian edition.

*Baroptis* is also called *baroptenus* and, by another name, *barippe*. See Pliny, in the same place, where *baroptenus* and *baroptis* are read.

### Note 6. Mesomelas

Grialius distinguishes the words as: “*Mesomelas*, black, with a vein, whatever, etc.” It is better to follow the edition of Pliny, in the same place: “*Mesomelas*, a black vein, whatever, etc.” There too *per mediam* (“through the middle”) is read, not *per medium*.

### Note 7. Black from the root

Harduinus has this from the manuscripts. Thus he reads in Pliny, in the same place:

> At the root, nitre; in the middle, blood; at the top, ochre.

Ochre is earth of a yellow color.

### Note 8. Dionysias

Grialius printed *Dionysia* in the text and *Dionysias* in the note, as in chapter 4, number 7. In the same place, number 5, the discussion concerns pyrite.

## Chapter XII, number 1. Orca

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10. Harduinus, from the manuscripts, reads *olca*; others have *orca*.

### Note 2. Mitridax, etc.

See chapter 4, note 21. Here Grialius had printed *mitrydax*. Breulius notes in the margin *mitrax*, from Pliny.

[Col. 0996A] **Note 3. Opalus**

Pliny discusses opals at length in Book XXXVII, chapter 6. “India alone,” he says, “is the mother of these also.”

### Note 4. With golden drops

Salmasius, p. 187 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, corrects Pliny to *aureis guttis* (“with golden drops”), since Solinus likewise calls them “golden stars,” or “golden drops.” From Isidore, however, he corrects Solinus: “they are not sprinkled with drops, but are streaked with long lines of colors,” that is, “marked with lines.” Previously the reading had been *liniuntur* (“they are streaked”). In Isidore he read *aliae habentes stillas* (“others having drops”) instead of *stellas* (“stars”). Again, concerning the Pontic gemstone, chapter 15: “having red stars,” or, in another reading, “red drops.”

### Note 5. Hexecontalithus

Concerning *hexecontalithus*, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, and Solinus, chapter 31 or 34. Some write *hexacontalithus*, but the Greek ἑξήκοντα (*hexēkonta*), “sixty,” more strongly requires *hexecontalithus*.

### Note 6. Murrhina

*Murrha* is the stone under discussion here. Vessels, or other objects made from *murrha*, were called *murrhina*. The words “its variation,” etc., are an obscure abridgment of Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 2, who writes as follows:

> But its variation of colors is highly prized, with spots surrounding one another, passing into purple, whiteness, and a third color arising from both, as though the color were passing into purple or into reddish milk. There are those who especially praise the edges and certain reflections of color, such as are seen in the celestial rainbow.

Harduinus discusses *murrha* and *murrhina* at greater length in his notes to the preface of Book XXXIII.

## Chapter XIII, number 1. It is said that snow

Saint Martin of León, who copies this passage, reads:

> It is said that snow is ice hardened over many years.

See his sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, vol. III, p. 147. Marbodus, in the book of Evax on gemstones, expressed Isidore in chapter 41:

> Crystal is ice hardened over many years.

But Isidore perhaps took the half-line from Dracontius, as I conjectured in my notes to Book I of the *Poem on God*, lines 712–713, where there is a fuller discussion of the origin of crystal.

### Note 2. Diamond, etc.

Salmasius, p. 205 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, observes that not every diamond is exactly like crystal, but especially the Indian and Arabian kinds. As for what the ancients believed—that diamonds yield to not even iron—modern writers have shown this to be false. See Vossius in his *Etymologies*.

### Note 3. But if the magnet, etc.

These words may be understood from the wording of Solinus, chapter 65:

> Or if, when a magnet is brought near, it draws iron as a kind of prey, whatever has clung to the magnet, let the diamond seize and carry away.

### Note 4. Chalazias

Concerning *chalazia*, see above, chapter 10, note 5. In ancient copies it is written:

> Even when placed in fire, it retains its coldness.

As often happens in Isidore and his contemporaries, an absolute nominative is used instead of an ablative absolute. *Chalazias* is indeed masculine, although in the cited chapter 10 it is given in the feminine, because *gemma* (“gemstone”) is understood; unless, perhaps, that passage too should be corrected by a similar restoration of the text.

### Note 5. Which Germany sends

Isidore had Solinus before his eyes, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. But since Salmasius, p. 240 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, insists that *Carmanica*, not *Germanica*, should be read in Solinus, although the common editions prefer the latter, it may likewise be restored in Isidore to “which Carmania sends.”

### Note 7. In whose center is a star

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9:

> Inside, from the center, as though a star.

Thus we may restore the reading in Isidore.

### Note 9. For it exudes water

The older printed editions have *exundat* (“overflows”), which Salmasius, p. 770 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, taught should be changed to *exudat* or *exsudat* (“exudes”), following Solinus. But our Grialius had already corrected the passage. Yet, as I think, this does not agree with Pliny’s meaning. Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11, says:

> The *enhydros* is a gemstone of perfectly rounded form, smooth in its whiteness, but when moved there is something inside it that ripples, like liquid in eggs.

## Chapter XIV, number 1. Of all, etc.

In some printed editions this chapter is improperly joined to the preceding one.

### Note 2. Anthracites

Concerning *anthracites*, see Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 21, and Book XXXVII, chapters 7 and 11; but Pliny may perhaps be mentioning different stones in these passages. Solinus calls the gemstone which Pliny calls *anthracites* *anthracias*.

### Note 3. Sandasirus

The copies of Pliny vary, but the more correct reading is *Sandaresus*, which is the name of the place where this gemstone grows. Breulius reads in Pliny *Sandactros* and *in translucido stellantes* (“sparkling in translucence”), where Isidore has *in translucido igne* (“with translucent fire”). Grialius, in the text, has *stellarum* (“of stars”).

### Note 4. It tests part of the wax

Vulcanius, from an old manuscript, notes *partem carpere tentat* (“it tries to seize part”), from Pliny, *partemque cerae in signo tenent* (“and they hold part of the wax in the image”). He himself printed *partem cerae temptat* (“it tests part of the wax”).

### Note 5. Carchedonia

Understand “gemstone,” since *carchedonius* in Greek means “Carthaginian.” Carthage abounded in this kind of carbuncle. See Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7.

### Note 6

Pliny, in the passage cited, calls those carbuncles *alabandici* which are born in the rocks at Orthosia and finished at Alabanda. Isidore is speaking of the same stones.

### Note 8. Chrysoprasus

In Grialius, the text has *Chrysophrasius*; in the note, correctly, *Chrysoprasus*. Concerning *chrysoprasus*, or *chrysoprasius*, compare chapter 7, number 7, of this book.

### Note 9. Phlogites

In some copies Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11, also names *philogitis*. The distinction between this and similar names is that *phlogites* is masculine, from *phlogites, -ae*, except where *gemma* (“gemstone”) is understood; *phlogitis* is feminine, from *phlogitis, -idis*. Solinus, chapter 37 or 50, writes:

> *Phlogites* displays what appear to be flames burning among themselves.

For *ex Persida* (“from Persida”), *ex Perside* or *ex Persia* should be read.

### Note 10. The first is in one part

Isidore has combined the words of Solinus and Pliny, as he often does elsewhere. One might read: “the first is,” and afterward, “also in Lucania.”

### Note 11. Hormesion

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, describes *hormesion* in similar words.

## Chapter XV, number 2

Harduinus also reads *chrysopis* in Pliny, from the manuscripts. Pliny gives *chrysolithus* in the feminine gender, perhaps because he understands *gemma* (“gemstone”).

### Note 3. Chryselectrum

Pliny calls *chryselectrum* neuter in Book XXXVII, chapter 3.

### Note 4. Chrysolampis

Concerning *chrysolampis*, compare what was said in chapter 7, number 7.

### Note 6. Leucochrysus, etc.

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9. There is another *leucochrysus*, “in the manner of crystal,” concerning which the same Pliny writes in Book XXXVII, chapter 10. The statement that pure honey shines through gold suggests the ancient custom of serving honey at banquets in golden vessels. I discussed this in my notes to Sedulius, Book I, line 14, in the preface:

> And the golden vessels shine together with their honeycombs.

### Note 7. Except that it increases

The sense will be clearer if we read:

> Except that it is said to glue gold together.

In Greek, κόλλα (*kolla*) means “glue.” Concerning *argyritis*, see Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 6.

### Note 8. Almost a diamond

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, has “like a diamond.” Salmasius, p. 565 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*, suspects that Pliny should read *vi adamas* (“a diamond in strength”), not *ut adamas* (“like a diamond”). Otherwise he thinks Pliny, and with him Solinus and Isidore, were mistaken, since *androdamas* has nothing resembling a diamond. Concerning *androdamas* marble, see above, chapter 4, note 17.

### Note 9. Chalcites

*Chalcites*, *chalcitae*, and *chalcitis, chalcitidis* is also the name of a stone from which bronze is made by firing. Concerning the *chalcitis* gemstone, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11. In chapter 10 he discusses *chalcophonos*.

### Note 10. Cutting through the middle

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, where it is read: “a fiery vein cutting through the middle.”

### Note 13. Ethiopian

Concerning Ethiopian carbuncles, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 7.

### Note 14. Zmilampis

Harduinus reads this form in Pliny, from all his manuscripts. Salmasius, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 703, thinks that *zenilanthis* should be restored from the manuscripts of Isidore. In Solinus, some editions have *zmilanthis*, others *zmilaces*, as Grialius printed it.

### Note 16. Ostracites

The *ostracias*, or *ostracites*, gemstone discussed here by Isidore is described by Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, where *scalpantur* (“are scraped”) is read, not *sculpantur* (“are carved”), as some read it in Isidore; the latter, however, could also be defended. Pliny also mentions the *ostracites* stone in Book XXXVI, chapter 19.

### Note 18. Echites … Carcinias

Concerning *echites*, see Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 2. Concerning *carcinia*, the same book, chapter 11.

### Note 19. Scorpitis … Myrmicites … Taos … Hieracites … Aetites … Aegopthalmos

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11, discusses *scorpites*, *myrmicites*, *taos*, *hieracites*, *aetites*, and *aegophthalmos*.

### Note 20. From the ruddy [stone], blood-red … Meconites

From Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 11, it appears that one should read: “from the ruddy [stone], and blood-red, with black in the middle surrounded by white.” The same writer, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, explains *meconites* in a similar manner.

### Note 22. Lipara suffita, etc.

Thus Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10. Grialius and others read *liparia* in Isidore. In place of *hydromantia*, some printed editions have *necromantia*; but Grialius restored *hydromantia*, which Harduinus also defends from the manuscripts in his edition of Pliny. From Pliny I likewise read *synochitis*, not *synocitis*, as Grialius has. *Aiunt* (“they say”) may also be omitted after *teneri* (“to be held”), since in Pliny it is governed by *dicunt* (“they say”), which precedes it.

### Note 23. Chelonites

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, distinguishes *chelonitides*, which are gemstones resembling tortoises, from *chelonia*, which is the eye of an Indian tortoise.

### Note 24. Brontia

Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, distinguishes *brontia* and *bronte*: the latter is said to fall from tortoise heads during thunder, while the former is said to fall with rain and lightning.

### Note 25. Hyaenia

The *hyaenia* is discussed in volume I of Cotelerius’s edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 33 and following; Pliny also discusses it in Book XXVII, chapter 10.

### Note 26. Stars

Grialius printed *stellas* (“stars”) in the text; in the note he assumes *stillas* (“drops”), perhaps from other editions.

## Chapter XVI, number 3. With Cyprian added; others have “with copper”

Pliny has *aere Cyprio* (“with Cyprian bronze”). He likewise says that glass, like bronze, is melted.

### Note 5. Obsidianus

Concerning obsidian stone, or *obsidio*, see chapter 4 of this book, note 21.

### Note 6. Someone said that glass is solidified with sulfur

See the note to Book XII, chapter 7, number 81.

## Chapter XVII, number 1. Of investigating

That is, investigating metals. “And iron, which subdues everything,” perhaps comes from some poet. Concerning metallurgy there are works by G. Agricola, I. Gotsch, V. Vallerius, Bomarius, Cellertius, and others.

## Chapter XVIII, number 1. Hence also *aurarii*

See the commentary on Prudentius’s *Hymn* 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 22, and there the old gloss:

> *Aurora* is so called from its radiance; hence *aurarii* are called those who favor it.

### Note 2. Refined gold

Isidore’s contemporaries, and even earlier writers, customarily used *d* for *z*, as *trapedia* for *trapezia*. This is relevant to the etymology of *obryzum*: “because it shines forth.” See Salmasius on Capitolinus, p. 20, line 32. Others derive the origin of the word *obryzum* from Greek; others from the island of Ophir.

### Note 3. From rattling

Virgil, Book VI, line 209:

> Thus the gold leaf rattled in the gentle wind.

### Note 4. From Saturn, etc.

Cassiodorus, Book VII, letter 32, says of coinage:

> It is said that King Servius first stamped it in bronze.

### Note 6. Treasury

The entire word is Greek, from “putting away for tomorrow.” For this reason, they say, the Latins called gold *aurum*. *Auraria* absolutely, in Book XII of the Theodosian Code, title 6, law 29, is used for a gold tax, or payment in gold. But Isidore appears to understand *auraria* as a gold mine, as Tacitus also does in Book VI of the *Annals*, chapter 19.

### Note 7. So that those who were in charge

In Servius’s commentary on Aeneid V, line 560, it is read:

> So that even those who were in charge of the individual divisions, etc., named them.

### Note 9. Nomisma

Concerning the etymology of *nomisma*, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 2 of the *Peristephanon*, line 50. Isidore repeats the same point below, chapter 25, note 14. It is also written *numisma*. Lucretius used *effigiae* in the plural.

### Note 10. Coins from Numa

Gisbert Cuper, in his letter to Otto Sperling, which begins *Inter febres*, denies that bronze was stamped by Numa. He thinks that Suetonius and Isidore, who report this, were deceived by the false etymology of *nummus*. Against Harduinus, he maintains that Pliny, Book LIV [apparently corrupt], chapter 1, did not teach this. Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 33, suggests that *nummus* is a Sicilian word. Festus derives its origin from the Greek νόμισμα (*nomisma*). Vossius discusses the matter more fully in his *Etymologies*.

### Note 11. Bags

For a purse, which is usually made from leather or hide. Vegetius, Book II of *On Military Matters*, chapter 20, Juvenal, Satire 14, line 281, and others use *follem* for a money pouch.

### Note 12. Three things in a coin

Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 36:

> Just as metal, figure, and weight are examined in a coin, so in every teacher, etc.

Compare the note.

### Note 13. Dies or forms

*Forma* is a technical term among bronze-workers, since the form of a coin is the mark impressed upon it. Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus, chapter 39:

> Twofold forms—that is, coins worth two gold pieces.

See Casaubon and Salmasius on this passage.

## Chapter XIX, number 3. A hundredweight stone

Concerning the hundredweight, see below, chapter 25, final note. Here and elsewhere Grialius commonly writes *scripulum* for *scrupulum*.

## Chapter XX, number 3. Aurichalcum

Concerning the etymology of *aurichalcum*, or *orichalcum*, see Vossius in his *Etymologies*. Annayus published a French commentary on the *orichalcum* of the ancients at Brussels in 1780.

### Note 4. Thus Corinthian objects were produced

Objects made from Corinthian bronze were simply called “Corinthian.” Cicero, Book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*, chapter 14:

> If you should lose anything of your Corinthian objects.

Concerning the origin of Corinthian bronze, Isidore agrees with Pliny and Florus; Muretus should nevertheless be consulted, Book III of the *Various Readings*, chapter 5.

### Note 6. And it imitates flames

Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, line 2:

> And pyrope, imitating flames.

Perhaps Isidore wrote “*Pyropus dicitur*” (“it is called pyrope”), or he means *aes pyropum* (“pyrope bronze”).

### Note 9. Campanian, etc.

Hence the name of bells, concerning which Becmann says something and Ducange more. In old Vatican manuscript 1343, which contains certain fragments from Saint Isidore’s work *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, I find a chapter on bells, perhaps not yet published; for that reason it may be worthy of placement among the appendices, section 19.

### Note 11. The flower of bronze

From Dioscorides. See Salmasius, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 1078.

### Note 14. And thus, dripping

The genuine reading appears to be *atque ita distillantes* (“and thus dripping”), since *superpositae* (“having been placed above”) precedes it, and the nominative used for an ablative absolute frequently occurs in Isidore and his contemporaries in manuscript books.

## Chapter XXI, number 1. From the River Chalybes

Now the river Cabe in Galicia, which Justinus and Silius Italicus mention. Flórez, however, observes in volume XV of *España sagrada*, p. 51, that *chalybs* was so called from the peoples of Asia called Chalybes, and that perhaps the Chalybes River of Galicia was named after them.

### Note 3. A fitting name imposed from “binding”

Salmasius approves this reading on p. 1083 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*. Nevertheless, others retain in Pliny: “from binding the sword-edge, a name, etc.” Concerning the forging of iron, see below, Book XIX, chapter 10, note 1.

### Note 4. More pleasing … for it touched

I think *delectatior* (“more pleasing”) has crept in for *delicatior* (“more delicate”); perhaps *delecatior* was written, since *i* and *e* are often confused in manuscripts. “For it touched,” namely, with blood. Concerning the image which seemed to hang in the bronze by the force of the magnet, see already chapter 4 of this book, note 2.

### Note 5. Rust

Others derive *rubigo* (“rust”) from *rubeus* (“red”) and do not approve deriving it from *rodere* (“to gnaw”). Isidore’s view appears to be that *rubigo* is also called *aerugo*; but in fact *aerugo* is a defect of bronze, as it were “the rust of bronze.”

### Note 6. Scoria

From the Greek σκωρία (*skōria*).

## Chapter XXII, number 1. Lead

Some think *plumbum* was formed as though from *pelumbum*, from πηλὸν (*pēlon*), “mud,” because it is of a muddy and earthy nature. Pliny also uses *auraria metalla* (“gold-bearing metals”) for gold mines, as Isidore does *auraria metalla*.

[Col. 1000A] **Note 3. From the skin of the earth**

That is, it is extracted from the upper crust and surface of the earth.

## Chapter XXIII, number 1. Of tin

Semler, in his note to the *Isidorian Glossary*, under the word *stagnare*, or *stannare*, cites this passage and insists that ἀποχωρίζον (*apochōrizon*) should be read, that is, “as though it makes a pool.” The reading ἀπὸ χωρίζων (*apo chōrizōn*), “separating,” should be retained, with the words divided, not joined as in the printed editions: ἀποχωρίζων.

## Chapter XXIV, number 1. Amber

The gemstone amber was discussed in chapter 8, number 6; here the subject is electrum as a metal. The gemstone *electrum* is also called amber, as the following note makes clear. See Muncker’s note to Hyginus’s fable 152.

N. 2. Three kinds of this. Servius, in his note on verse 402 of Book VIII of the *Aeneid*, distinguishes from Pliny three kinds of electrum. Servius, in the edition I use, says: “which parts, even if you resolve its nature,” etc. Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapters 2 at the end and 3, and Book IX, chapter 40, discusses these three kinds of electrum at length: he says that the nature of metallic electrum is such that it shines by lamplight more brightly than silver and that, when native, it can even detect poisons.

[Col. 1000B] **CHAPTER XXV.** No. 1. *Of weights and measures.* Graevius collected learned works, both ancient and modern, on weights and measures in his *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*.

N. 3. *That it . . . should hang.* So many read it; but others instead derive *pendere* (“to hang”) from *pondus* (“weight”).

N. 4. *Scales.* The correct form would be *lanx*, but Isidore commonly uses similar nominative forms. Lexicographers of Latin are profoundly silent about the words *momentana* and *moneta* in the sense of a balance. *Statera* is sometimes used for a balance with two pans, but properly it is the steelyard, mentioned shortly afterward. A *trutina* is a category containing various species under it, such as the steelyard, the ordinary balance, and so forth.

N. 5. *Whence also on the scales, etc.* These words are not found in Servius, and are absent from many manuscripts of Isidore.

N. 6. I do not find the word *campana* used by the ancients in this sense. Anastasius the Librarian uses it. [Col. 1000C] See Ducange. Papias combines this section of Isidore with the following one. Rosweyd, in his *Onomasticon* following the *Lives of the Fathers*, gathers together much learned material about the steelyard (*statera campana*).

N. 8. *Chalcus.* This is a Greek word and among the Greeks is also the name of a weight. Compare Hardouin’s note on Pliny, Book XXI, final chapter.

N. 9. *From the seed of a tree.* That is, from the seed of the Greek carob tree.

N. 10. *Ceratum.* In the following section the plural is *ceratia*. Some have *cerates* here and below. I prefer *ceratium* and *ceratia*. It should also be noted that the Greek carob is called in Greek κεράτιον (*keration*, “ceratium”), because it resembles a curved little horn. Perhaps Joseph Scaliger had this in mind when, on page 55 of *On Money*, he asserts that the carob pods are called *cornus* by Isidore and *al-charub* by the Arabs, from which the Spaniards say *algarrobas*. The modern Greeks corruptly say *charouba*, while the Italians say *caruba* and *caroba*.

N. 11. *Obolus.* At the beginning of the Bignaean edition there is a fragment concerning the obol and other weights, which will form Appendix 20.

[Col. 1000D] N. 12. *Gramma.* Marsilius Cognatus correctly emended *gramma* for *drachma*, which he had found in some copies. Isidore, like many others, derives *scrupulus* from *scrupus*, not from *scribere* (“to write”).

N. 13. *Drachma.* Grialius printed and punctuated the passage as follows: “The drachma is the eighth part of an ounce and the weight of a denarius of silver, consisting of three scruples.” Pliny, Book XXI, final chapter, says: “The Attic drachma has the weight of a silver denarius; and it makes six obols.” From this I restored Isidore’s passage. Instead of saying that it was named *a dando* (“from giving”), it would be better to derive it from *decem* (“ten”), or *denus*/*deni* (“ten each”).

N. 14. *The solidus . . . the coin.* What is said here about the coin is repeated from chapter 18 of this book, section 9, where *effigiisque* (“and images”) is likewise read. Although *effigies*, *effigiei* is frequently used, Plautus nevertheless used *effigia*, *effigiae*, and Lucretius used *effigiae* in the plural. Barthius discusses the solidi in Book XI, chapter 20 of his *Adversaria*, and derives from them the name *soldatorum*.

N. 18. *The weight of an ounce.* Some would prefer to read in Jerome “the weight of half an ounce.” Whether the sanctuary shekel was worth twice as much as the ordinary shekel is not agreed among interpreters of Holy Scripture. Some, in fact, think that the sanctuary shekel was the same as the ordinary one, but was called “of the sanctuary” to indicate that it was a just and exact weight.

N. 19. *Ounce.* This is a Sicilian word, οὐγκία (*ounkia*).

N. 20. *Pound.* It is also derived from the Sicilian word λίτρα (*litra*). On the complete pound, see the note on Book IV of Sedulius, verse 154. It was a gold pound.

N. 21. *Mina.* Pliny, Book XXI, chapter 34: “The mina, which our people call *mina*, weighs one hundred Attic drachmas.”

N. 22. *Talent.* Servius likewise assigns a weight of seventy pounds to the talent in Book IX of the *Aeneid*, on verse 265: “Two great talents of gold.” Marsilius Cognatus, Book IV, chapter 6 of his *Observations*, censures Isidore for saying “among the Romans,” since the Romans were not accustomed to use the word *talent*, and Plautus is speaking about Greeks. Isidore took his wording from Servius. Cognatus adds that the error may seem to be that of a copyist, with LXX substituted for LX and CLX for CXX; but he does not doubt that it is the author’s error to have placed two minas above sixty in the talent, since in Plautus four minas above 120 were owed as interest. Joseph Scaliger, on page 30 of *On Money*, declares that *great talent* and *small talent*, and in Isidore *lesser, middle,* and *greatest*, are inventions of grammarians and, as he says, utterly foolish. Concerning Plautus’ words in the *Rudens*, however, he admits that he is perplexed. Yet Scaliger cannot deny that the matter is found among the ancients without having been sufficiently investigated, nor that modern scholars have labored considerably to explain the value of the talent—Salmasius, *On Ancient Money*; Vossius, in his *Etymologies*; and others.

As for Isidore, it should be noted that some wish to substitute *minas* for *pounds* in Servius, from whom Isidore borrowed his material. Fannius says:

[Col. 1001C]

“After this, it remains to teach the Cecropian talent:

Sixty minas, or, if you will, six thousand drachmas.”

A pound contains 96 drachmas, and therefore sixty pounds would amount to only 5,952 drachmas. Sixty-two pounds, which Chacon wanted retained in Servius and Isidore, would amount to 6,072 drachmas. And Plautus does indeed speak of minas. Festus enumerates different kinds of talents:

“There is not one single kind of talent. The Attic talent is six thousand denarii. The Rhodian and Cistophoric are four thousand five hundred denarii. The Alexandrian is twelve thousand denarii. The Neapolitan is six denarii. The Syracusan is three denarii. The Rhegian is a victoriatus.””

There was also a greater Attic talent, containing 83 minas and 4 ounces, of which Livy speaks in Book XXXVIII, chapter 38.

N. 23. *The name of the number.* Scaliger correctly says, in the work cited, page 64, that this term is used to distinguish it from the weight, which the Arabs call by the corrupted name *kintar*, and the Spaniards and Aquitanians *quintal*. In the Middle Ages the names *quintale* and *quintallus* were in use; Ducange discusses them at greater length. The Spaniards call a weight of one hundred pounds a *quintal*. Compare Mariana, *On Weights and Measures*, chapter 9, where from Isidore’s words he concludes that at a later period the Latins began to signify a talent by the name *centenarius*, with the weight altered to some extent.

**CHAPTER XXVI.** No. 3. *Spoon.* Writers disagree vehemently among themselves in explaining measures, just as they do in explaining weights. The ancients generally spoke obscurely; and sometimes they understand Greek measures by the same name, sometimes Latin ones. Forcellinus, together with others, says that a spoon is one quarter of a *cyathus*; but from Isidore it may be inferred that it is one twentieth of a *cyathus*, while from Fannius it is one twenty-fourth. For a *cheme* is one twelfth, and a spoon is half a *cheme*. Fannius’ words are:

> “The *mystrum* is a quarter of a *cyathus*, and a third of a *mystrum*;
>
> this they call a *cheme*, and it holds two spoons.”

[Col. 1002A] Mariana, speaking of Greek measures, says: “The *concha* is half a *cyathus*. The *mystrum* is a quarter of a *cyathus*. The *cheme* is a fifth of a *cyathus*. The small spoon is one tenth of a *cyathus*.” But when he discusses Roman measures, he explains as follows: “The spoon, or *ligula*, is a quarter of a *cyathus*, one twenty-eighth of a *sextarius*, whereas in Greek measures the spoon is one tenth of a *cyathus*. The *ligula* in water or wine weighs three drachmas, or one scruple.”

N. 5. *Cotyla.* Grialius printed *cotula* in the text and *cotyla* in the notes. It is written both ways: *cotula* in the Latin manner, *cotyla* in the Greek manner. On this passage of Isidore, Guillelmus Bodaeus should be consulted, Book V of *On the As*, although he shows himself a less than fair judge of Isidore: “After these monuments of antiquity, since I greatly desired to ascertain the systems of measures, I undertook to test the matter by weight. When neither those verses nor Pliny yielded an answer, I ultimately found nothing preferable to what is read in Isidore, himself not the best author even on these matters: ‘The hemina weighs,’ etc.”

There is a celebrated controversy over the wine-hemina in the rule of Saint Benedict. Menardus in his *Concordance of Rules*, Martenius in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, Joannes Pelletier in his French dissertation on the pound of bread and the wine-hemina in the Rule of Saint Benedict, Monsieur Lancelot in his dissertation on the wine-hemina, and others have dealt with its explanation. The measure may perhaps have varied according to time and place. See Ducange together with his supplement.

N. 6. *Quinarem.* This appears to be a Spanish word proper to the language, for Ducange asserts that *quinalis* is a measure of liquids among the Spaniards and cites examples from Spanish documents. Perhaps in Isidore one should read “it makes a *quinalis*, or *gomor*.” The difficulty raised by Grialius against this passage of Isidore is easily dissolved if two measures are distinguished: one, the *gomor* or *ghomer*, which Isidore is discussing here; the other, the *chomer*, or *chorus*/*corus*, which he discusses below, section 17. The *gomor* or *ghomer* is one tenth of an *ephah*, according to Exodus 16:36. Mariana, in *On Weights and Measures*, concludes that the *gomor* amounts precisely to six Toledan *sextarii*, but to four Roman *sextarii* and four fifths of another; and he cites the words of our Isidore, by which it is proved that the *quinalis*, or *gomor*, consists of five Roman *sextarii*. Whether a further distinction must be made between *chomer* and *corus*, we shall see later.

N. 7. *Congius.* In some editions *congium*, neuter, is given instead of *congius*, less correctly; the same fault occurs in old glossaries. Fabrettus reproduced the form of the *congius* in chapter 7, page 526. I find the verb *congiendo* nowhere else. In the Middle Ages *congiare* or *congeare* meant “to grant permission to depart,” which the Italians call *congedare*.

N. 9. *The number of denarii.* This confirms that in Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 82, one should read that the *metreta* is a measure of ten *congii*; others read eight, others twelve. The *metreta*, which is mentioned in the sacred writings, is said to correspond to the Hebrew *bath*.

N. 10. *Of sextarii.* Perhaps Epiphanius and Isidore are speaking of Hebrew *sextarii*, which are one third smaller than Roman ones; but, as Mariana observes, the text should then say that a *modius* contains twenty-four *sextarii*. It must always be kept before one’s eyes, however, that measures and weights change according to differences of place; perhaps Epiphanius generally means Samaritan measures, since he himself was of Samaritan origin. Isidore defends himself by Epiphanius’ authority.

N. 11. *Satum.* In the glosses on the Old Testament, which I intend to publish from Codex 1 of the Vatican archives among the appendices wherever the appropriate place appears, the *satum* is said, at Genesis 16, to contain one and a half *modii*.

N. 12. *Bathus.* Grialius printed *batus*; the common spelling is *bathus*, but it is also called *badus*. Mariana says approximately this about the measure in the work cited: the *bathus* contains 48 Roman *sextarii* and 72 Hebrew ones. Or certainly there were two kinds of *bathus*: the smaller equal to the *ephah*, and the larger one and a half times the smaller.

[Col. 1003A] N. 13. *Let it be taken up on both sides.* This is because, by syncope, *amphora* is said to come from ἀμφιφορεύς (*amphiphoreus*). The Roman amphora was called a *quadrantal*, because it consisted of a Roman foot squared. Volusius Maetianus, *On the As*, says: “The *quadrantal*, which most people now call an amphora, contains two urns, three *modii*, etc.” A Greek or Attic amphora contained three urns. Fannius:

> “Moreover, for us the Attic amphora must be called
>
> either a *cadus*; you will make it so if you add our urn.”

N. 15. *Medimna, medimnus,* or *medimnum* is a measure of six *modii*, as may be inferred from Cornelius Nepos, Fannius, and others, in Rosweyd’s *Onomasticon*. Ausonius, in his *Riddle of the Ternary*, used “Sicilian medimna” in the plural. As for Isidore’s statement that the *medimna* consists of five *modii*, the same answer applies: almost everything reported about the measures of the ancients is uncertain; measures also varied under the same name according to differences of place and time.

N. 16. *Artaba.* Rosweyd, in the work cited, after presenting several mutually inconsistent ancient testimonies about the *artaba*, concludes: “But the *artaba* was altogether a variable measure.” Mariana, having first stated that according to some opinions the *artaba* corresponded to 80 *sextarii*, according to Epiphanius to 72, and according to Fannius to 53⅓, adds that these varying opinions cannot be reconciled except perhaps by a variation in the *sextarius*: Fannius may have been speaking of Roman measures, Epiphanius of Attic measures, and others of Hebrew measures.

N. 17. *Chomer.* Since it was said above, section 6, that the *gomor* consists of five *sextarii*, here, at least for the sake of distinction, one should write *chomer*, not *gomor*, as Grialius and others printed it. Certainly the subject here must be a large measure; and the only doubt can arise from the fact that *chomer* or *homer* and *corus* or *chorus* are commonly used for the same measure. Nor does anything occur that can be offered in reply, unless perhaps the name *chomer* was given in some places to half a *corus*. Certainly, according to the common opinion, Hebrew measures preserve the following order. The *corus* or *chomer* is the largest of all, containing ten *ephahs*, as many *bathus*, thirty *sata*, one hundred *gomor*, and one hundred eighty *cadi*. We shall present a short appendix on Hebrew measures, section 21, from fragments printed at the beginning of the Bignaean edition.

**CHAPTER XXVII.** No. 1. *Signs of weight.* Perhaps from signs of this kind for weights and measures, formerly found in manuscript books, arose the confusion observed in explaining the weights and measures of the ancients.

N. 4. *Gamma.* Grialius printed *gammae* in the note; I have restored *gamma*, which appears in the text, so that it remains indeclinable.

**BOOK SEVENTEEN**

**CHAPTER ONE.** No. 1. *Agricultural matters.* The best edition of the writers on agriculture is that prepared by Gesner, Leipzig, 1735. The ancient *Geoponica* may also be consulted, edited by Johann Nikolaus Niclas, Leipzig, 1781. The number of modern writers is immense. Among the Spaniards, Herrera is famous; I see that he had already been translated into Italian at Venice in 1608.

N. 2. *But with iron of whatever kind, etc.* This can scarcely be understood unless Servius’ words on Book I of the *Georgics*, verse 147, are read: “Ceres first revealed every kind of agriculture to human beings; for the commentators raise a needless question when they say that Osiris or Triptolemus invented the plow. For it is one thing to invent a single object and another to teach all agriculture, which Ceres did. By saying ‘iron,’ he comprehends generally all the implements of farmers.” In place of *fulminatum* (“thunderstruck”), the collations of the Gothic manuscripts of Toledo had *Fulmi natum* (“born of Fulmi”).

N. 3. *Stercutius.* Grialius printed *Stercutius* in the text but indicates *Sterculius* in the note. In Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 9, some read *Stercutius*, while Hardouin, from the manuscripts, reads *Stercutus*. Prudentius, *Hymn 2 of the Peristephanon*, verse 449:

> “The senate worships two-faced Janus
>
> and Sterculus.”

Some likewise read *Sterculum* in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 25. Below, in the following chapter, section 3, there is again discussion of *Sterculius* or *Sterculus*.

**CHAPTER II.** No. 1. *Of bronze.* That is, of instruments made of bronze. For the particle *de* has this force. In any case, the verb *aro* (“I plow”) is Greek and is not derived from *aes* (“bronze”).

N. 3. *From stercus, which is also Stercutus.* This comes from Augustine, as Grialius observed above. But some read Augustine as follows: “Some called him Stercen, others Sterculius.”

N. 5. *Runcatio.* It truly comes from the Greek ῥύγχος (*rhynchos*), “snout.” Hence *runco*, *runconis*, and *runco*, *runcare*, from which the Spaniards say *arrancar*. Likewise, *sulcus* (“furrow”) should be derived from the Greek ὁλκός (*holkos*). For *veruactum*, the Spaniards say *varuecho*.

N. 6. *Satio.* It comes from *satum*, as *actio* comes from *actum*, and so forth. Becmanus, page 966, asserts a Hebrew origin for the verb *sero* (“I sow”). Isidore perhaps had Servius in mind, who, on the cited passage of Virgil, says: “That is, under such a clear sky that you do not need clothing.”

[Col. 1004B] **CHAPTER III.** No. 2. *But crops and the rest.* Isidore does not deny that grain is also *fruges* (“produce”), but asserts that *fruges* is applied not only to grain but also to other things; therefore he is not contrary to Servius, who concludes from Cicero that grain too is called *fruges*. Grain and *fruges* are consequently distinguished as species from genus, not as one species from another. Whether the verb *frumendo*, or *frumere*, meaning “to eat,” is found elsewhere, I have no knowledge at all. See Book XX, chapter 2, section 27.

N. 3. *First fruits.* These are the first things in any category; but from the common usage of writers it seems possible to conclude that the word properly refers to crops offered to a deity and, by metaphorical extension, to other things.

N. 4. *Wheat.* Varro, *On the Latin Language*, chapter 22: “*Triticum* [wheat], because it is threshed from the ears.”

N. 6. *Ador.* There is an old gloss on *ador*, or *adoreo*, among those I published in my notes on Prudentius, *Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, final verse; it indicates the etymology of this word from *adoro* (“I worship”), an explanation supported by Priscian, Book IV, page 628 of Putsch. I do not find elsewhere an explicit statement that sacrifices were called *adorea*. *Adorea*, feminine, is ordinarily understood as “glory” and “praise.”

N. 7. *Siligo.* In Greek it is similarly called σίλιγνις (*silignis*).

N. 8. *Three-month wheat.* Some explain four-month wheat by the words that the Savior said to his disciples: “Do you not say that there are still four months, and the harvest comes?” See my notes on Juvencus, Book II, verse 313.

N. 12. *Centenum.* The word *centeno* remains among the Spaniards; I do not find it among other ancient writers in this sense. Concerning millet, Festus says: “Some think that *milium* [millet] took its name especially from the sum of money that is a thousand.”

N. 13. *Panicium.* Pliny and Caesar call it *panicum*. But Isidore appears to have written *panicium*. I have no certainty about *pistum frumentum*, unless it is the adjective *pistum*, “ground,” from *pinsere*, “to pound.” See Festus. On sesame as a summer grain, see Pliny, Book XVIII, chapters 7 and 10.

N. 14. *Farrago.* Varro, Columella, Pliny, and others discuss *farrago*.

[Col. 1004D] **CHAPTER IV.** No. 4. *Crushed bean.* *Fressus* and *fresus* are participles of *frendeo*, or *frendo*, which is also used in the sense “to break.” Celsus, Book V, chapter 18, section 21, mentions a crushed bean.

N. 6. *Faselus . . . chickpea.* Some derive the etymology of *cicer* (“chickpea”) from the Hebrew language. Virgil speaks of the *faselus* in the *Georgics*, verse 227:

> “You will sow vetch and the worthless bean.”

N. 7. *And the bitter lupine.* *Triste* (“bitter” or “sad”) is commonly taken to mean “bitter.” See my commentary on verse 50 of Prudentius’ *Dittochaeon*.

**CHAPTER V.** No. 1. *In the still-primitive age.* In the world newly established after the Flood. *Rudis* (“primitive”) is commonly used of something new. Prudentius, Book II against Symmachus, verse 277:

> “Whatever custom prevailed
>
> in the primitive years of the newborn world,” etc.

Compare the index to Prudentius.

[Col. 1005A] N. 3. *At the ends of the earth.* Servius, on verse 7 of Eclogue 5: “At the ends of the fields.”

N. 5. *Sarmentum from serere.* Festus derives *sarmentum* (“branch or vine shoot”) from *sarpere*, since the ancients used *sarpere* for “to cleanse.”

N. 9. *Let it be derived from palma.* Paulus, from Festus: “The shoots of vines are called *palmites*, because they produce little hooks resembling the fingers of human hands, in the manner of palms.”

N. 11. Festus also derives *capreoli* (“tendrils”) from *capere* (“to seize”). Others derive the word from the fact that they resemble the horns of young goats.

N. 13. *It is humid, etc.* Servius, on verse 20 of Eclogue 10: “That is *humidum* which has some moisture on the outside, whereas *uvidum* is moist within; hence grapes are so called.” Grialius printed in the text “that which is humid on the exterior”; in the note he indicates *extrinsecus* (“on the outside”).

N. 16. *Called early-ripening . . . these they call lageoi.* Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 3, asserts that the *lagea* vine—for that is what he calls it—is foreign. It is therefore not established that the ancients called every early-ripening grape *lageos*, or, as others write, *praecoques* or *praecoces*. Virgil clearly distinguishes them in Book II of the *Georgics*, verse 93:

> “And the raisin-bearing Psythia is better, and the slender Lageos,
>
> which will one day try the feet and bind the tongue,
>
> the purple and early-ripening grape,” etc.

Servius, in my edition, reads *praeciaeque*: “These ripen quickly; hence they are also called *praeciae*, from *praecoquae*, because they ripen before the others,” with *sole* (“sun”) omitted.

In Codex 2 of the Vatican archives these matters are presented in another order: “These the Greeks call *lageoi* . . . like the hare. *Purpureae* are so called from their color; *unciariae* from their size; *dactyli* from their length; *stephanitae* from their roundness; *Rhodiae* and *Libycae* from their regions; but *cerauniae* because they are red like fire. The kinds of grapes, however, are,” etc.

N. 18. *Ammineae.* Servius, on *Georgics* II, verse 96, writes: “There are also *ammineae* vines”; most critics prefer this spelling. Grialius printed *aminea* in the text, as he writes in the note. The name is better derived, with Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, chapter 11, and others, from the region of Amminea, where Falernian wine was produced—or, as others read, Salernian or Salentine wine.

N. 19. *Faecinia.* In Grialius it read *faeciniam vocat* (“he calls it *faecinia*”), through an error, I think; other copies have *vocant* (“they call it”).

N. 22. *Basilica.* In Grialius and other printed editions it was *basilisca*; I restored *basilica*, as it is read in Pliny and Columella.

N. 23. *The *visula* requires wood.* In Grialius it read: “*Visula*, the wood, and the short and broad leaf,” which perhaps entered against his intention. Other printed editions have: “the wood, and the short and broad leaf.” Anyone wishing to judge the entire matter must keep Columella’s words before his eyes:

“Next, the *visulae* and the smaller *argitis* thrive in moderately rich soil. In rich soil they grow luxuriantly with excessive vigor; in poor soil they become thin and bear no fruit. They prefer a trellis to trees, but the *argitis*, even when trained high, is fertile, with large wood and abundant grapes, while the *visula* is better suited to very low trellises. The *visula* requires short wood and a broad leaf, whose breadth effectively protects its fruit from hail; nevertheless, unless the grapes are gathered as soon as they ripen, they fall to the ground. They also rot from moisture before they drop.”

N. 25. *Mareotic.* Servius’ words on verse 91 of Book II of the *Georgics* are: “‘White Mareotides.’ Egyptian, for Mareotis is a part of Egypt. By saying ‘white,’ he shows that there are also purple grapes or grapes of another color.” But Columella, Book III, chapter 2, lists the Mareotic among Greek vines. Some understand this as referring to a part of Epirus called Mareotis, where excellent wine is produced.

N. 26. *Helvolae, etc.* This comes from Columella in the cited passage, where he says that they were called *helvolae*, if he is not mistaken, from their color. Pliny also calls them *helvolae* and *varianae* in Book XIV, chapter 2. The *helvenacae*, which Grialius cites from Pliny—namely, from the same book, chapter 12—belong to another species. Columella calls these *helvenaciae* and distinguishes three varieties of them.

N. 27. *The third class, etc.* This too comes from Columella; [Col. 1006A] there is no reason to reject it as superfluous. “Celsus,” says Columella, “assigns third place to those vines commended solely for their fruitfulness, such as the three *helvenaciae*, etc. But as for the *spionia*, etc.”

N. 28. *The *spionia* vine.* Grialius and others had *vitiscionia*. From Columella I have safely restored *vitis spionia*.

N. 31. *Oblaqueare.* Even in writers on agriculture, Cato and Columella, old editions and manuscripts have *oblaqueare*, not *ablaqueare*. In this sense both verbs derive from *lacus* (“basin” or “hollow”), not from *laqueus* (“snare”).

N. 33. *Hence the propagines.* Grialius had: “Here the *propagines*.”

**CHAPTER VI.** No. 2. *Like the shaft of a tree.* This does not come from Servius and has no connection with the true etymology.

N. 3. *But *arbor*, etc.* This comes from Agraetius: “Every piece of wood is called *arbor*; *arbos* only refers to a fruit-bearing tree.” But no distinction is generally recognized except that *arbos* is poetic.

N. 4. *It was called a short shrub.* Neither the etymology of *frutex*, nor the claim that *fruteta* is its plural, nor the claim that *fruteta* means a tall tree can be confirmed by suitable authority. From *frutex* come *fruticetum*, *frutectum*, and *frutetum*, a place abounding in fruits.

N. 5. *Woodland.* Grialius, with some others, wrote *sylva*, because the Greek etymology requires that spelling. Stones and old books prefer another form; and Latins often used *i* for *y* in words borrowed from Greek.

N. 6. *Nemus* is a Greek word. The statement that *nemora* are larger trees, etc., can be understood only by synecdoche. It is certain that pagans customarily established idols in groves. They also honored the trees themselves with pagan worship.

N. 7. *Grove.* Torches also burned in the grove, because it was customary for sacred rites to be celebrated there at night. Others explain it tropologically, by antiphrasis.

N. 9. *Aviaries* also existed in which birds raised for food were kept and fed. Perhaps one should read *frequentent* (“they frequent”).

[Col. 1006C] N. 10. *Recidiva.* On *recidiva*, see the note on Book I of Dracontius, verse 558.

N. 14. *Is submerged.* Grialius has *dimergitur* (“is plunged under”).

N. 19. *As we said above.* Namely, in the preceding chapter, section 8.

N. 20. *Cymes.* This is a Greek word that has also passed into the vernacular languages. Some write it in Latin as *cimae* and *cumae*.

N. 23. *From *frumen*.* See above, chapter 3, section 2.

N. 25. *Whence *ellychnium*.* Grialius printed *lychnum* in the text but gives *lychnus* or *ellychnium* in the note, although he offers this only as a conjecture in place of *lucinium*, which appears in other editions. I do not know whether the matter mentioned below, chapter 7, section 65, belongs here: olives called *lyciniae* or *liciniae*, which give the best light. See the note and Book XIX, chapter 19, section 3; from the latter, *ellychnium* appears preferable.

N. 26. *Fomes is a splinter.* This passage of Isidore is illustrated, with notes by Mazochius, in the collection of works on the *Dedication under the Axe*; but the old editions’ errors are corrected there in the manner already emended by Grialius. Servius, on the cited passage of Virgil, says: “Properly speaking, *fomites* are splinters that fall from trees when they are cut, because they nourish fire.” Clodius writes: “. . .” Elsewhere he says: “Burnt splinters, hollowed-out pieces of wood, taking their name from fungi.” Clearly, the best tinder is made from fungi. The word is written both *assula* and *hastula*; hence the Spanish *astilla* or *hastilla*. Vulcanius’ note is: “Thus today the Spaniards call *hastillas* what the Greeks call κάρφη (*karphe*).” In Pliny’s manuscripts, according to Hardouin, *hastula* is also found where others have *assula*.

N. 27. *A firebrand.* Varro, Celsus, Apuleius, and others use the word *tition*. Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 14, also indicates that it was taken from popular usage: “The common people call a half-burned log drawn from the hearth a *tition*.” The vernacular languages retain the same name.

**CHAPTER VII.** N. 1. *Palmula* is used by some of any fruit of the palm. *Caryota* is a kind of *palmula*, as in Caelius Aurelianus, Book II of *Acute Diseases*, chapter 37: “The nut-bearing *palmulae*, which they call *caryotae*.” Properly, *myrobalanum* is the nut of a certain Egyptian tree, from which an ointment, likewise called *myrobalanum*, is made.

N. 2. *From a word of praise.* Servius, on Eclogue 8, verse 13, says: “The reason why triumphant men are crowned with laurel is this: among the ancients it derived its name from *laus* (‘praise’), for they said *laudum*.” They think that in Greek laurel was called *daphne* because it resounds when burned. Perhaps it would be useful to punctuate Isidore as follows: “They call it [laurel], which never lays aside its greenness; therefore victors are crowned with it.” Among the ancients laurel was regarded as possessed of a good genius, for many reasons reported by Bodaeus in his notes on Theophrastus, pages 185ff., and Meursius, volume IV of the *Sacred Arboretum*, page 9. Compare Georg August Langguth in the little book he published at Leipzig in 1738, entitled *Antiquities of Funereal Plants among the Greeks and Romans*, page 17.

N. 3. *Virgil, for lovers, etc.* Perhaps he refers to verse 64 of Eclogue 3:

> “The wanton girl Galatea pelts me with an apple,”

about which the commentators say more.

[Col. 1007B] N. 5. *The taste of honey, etc.* Nevertheless it is written *melimelum* with a single *l*, because it is derived from the Greek word μέλι (*meli*), “honey.” In Martial’s epigram some read: “You may call these *melimela*, if you wish.”

N. 6. *Pomegranate.* Some doubt whether *malogranatum* can properly be said. The ancients seem to have said only *malum granatum*. Pliny simply calls pomegranates *granata*; the Spaniards adopted this name as *granadas*.

N. 7. *Duracinum.* Hence the Spaniards say *durazno*, which derives from the Latin *durus* (“hard”). Brissonius, Book II of *On the Kingdom of Persia*, section 236, together with Pliny, Book XV, chapter 13, refutes the error of Columella, verses 403ff., and of Isidore in this passage, who believed that Persian apples were poisonous in Persia. There is another tree, the *Persea*, which many say is poisonous in Persia but harmless in Egypt. Pliny discusses it in Book XIII, chapter 9, and Book XV, chapter 13. Grialius writes *Armenicum* in the first place and *Armeniacum* afterward.

N. 8. *He became renowned.* Because Virgil devoted himself exclusively to this one tree, as Servius notes. In place of *ex illa foveri animam* (“from it the soul is nourished”), Codex 1 of the Vatican archives has *ex illa tueri animam* (“from it the soul is protected”), so that *tueri* may be understood passively; this may perhaps be the Isidorian reading.

N. 9. *Syrian bean.* Isidore, together with Servius on verse 84 of Book II of the *Georgics*: “They express the common name of the lotus in the Syrian bean.” On the lotus, an Egyptian plant resembling a bean, see Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 17. Salmasius discusses the lotus tree at greater length, page 1039 of his *Plinian Exercises*.

N. 10. *Nixa.* Salmasius, page 1324 of his *Plinian Exercises*, observes that for some people *myxa* is the Sebesten plum and that Isidore confuses it with the Damascene plum. He himself thinks that the *myxa* of the ancient Greeks is the *musa*, a fruit close to the fig, which the Spaniards call *higuera banana*, that is, “the fig tree bearing bananas.” Rosweyd, in his *Onomasticon*, under *Nixae siccae* (“dried nixas”), cites many ancient passages about *nixae* or *myxae*, which were also called *myxaria*.

N. 11. *Elaeomeli.* This is an indeclinable neuter, as Pliny uses it. Isidore perhaps wrote *elaeomelis* to make it refer to a tree.

N. 13. *Melopos.* Grialius indicates *melosus* in the note but printed *melopos* in the text. Salmasius, page 351 of his *Plinian Exercises*, correctly says that Pliny calls it *metopon*. In Pliny, Book XII, chapter 23, most read *metopium*.

N. 14. *Mespilus.* Grialius writes *mespila* in the note and *mespilus* in the text, which is correct. *Mespilum* is the fruit of the *mespilus* tree.

N. 16. *Suitable for spear shafts.* This comes from Servius, in the cited passage of Virgil.

N. 17. *Hence also the Carian figs.* Grialius leaves me uncertain whether he considers all these words spurious: “Hence also the Carian figs, named from abundance.” I accept all of them as genuine. Isidore says that Carian figs were so called from abundance, presumably because Caria abounded in them. Cicero, Book I of *On Divination*, chapter 40: “A man selling Carian figs brought from Caunus in the harbor was loudly proclaiming, ‘Caunean figs!’” Other writers used *Caricae* for any kind of fig. Ovidius, Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 674:

> “Here is the nut, here the fig mixed with wrinkled palms.”

Pliny does the same.

N. 18. *Caprificus.* Martial, almost playfully, derives the etymology of *caprificus* (“caprifig”) from *caprus* (“goat”) and *ficus* (“fig”), in Book IV, epigram 52. Becmanus, Vossius, and other etymologists may be consulted. On the remedy, or *caprification*, by which the fig tree is fertilized, see Pliny, Columella, and Palladius.

N. 20. *Let it be similar in its leaves.* Some old copies read *sit folia similis* (“let it be similar to leaves”), with *folia* feminine. This appears to have been said in that way during the Middle Ages, from which the vernacular name developed. Isidore perhaps hints—remaining faithful to his usual method—that *sycomorus* was so called as if it meant “like a mulberry.” In reality, however, it is composed of συκή (*syke*), “fig,” and *morus*, “mulberry.” The fruit of the sycamore approaches the fig in shape and size.

N. 25. *Chestnut.* Some think it was called *castanea* from Castana or Castanea, a city of Thessaly where chestnuts abound.

N. 26. *Ilex from electus.* That is, as if it were *elex*, from *eligere* (“to choose”), an etymology also favored by other etymologists.

N. 28. *Aesculus.* Grialius printed *esculus* in the text and *aesculus* in the note.

N. 29. *Siliqua.* Salmasius, page 461 of his *Plinian Exercises*, observes, against Isidore, that *siliqua* (“carob pod”) was so called because it was inside a *siliqua*; that it is not the fruit but the woody shell that is sweet; that *acacia* is obtained from the seed or fruit of the Egyptian thorn, whose fruit is also found in pods; and that the Egyptian thorn, from which gum is obtained, is likewise called *acacia*. This is approximately Salmasius’ account. Acacia is indeed obtained from a thorny shrub likewise called *acacia*; see Pliny, Book XXIV, chapter 12, and Celsus, Book VI, chapter 6.

N. 30. *Of pistic nard.* Isidore derives the etymology of *pistacia* from *pistic nard*, which the evangelist John mentions. Some nevertheless think that scribes transcribed *pistici* for *spiked nard*, as Mark calls it at 14:3.

N. 31. *Pitin.* Some think that *picea* (“fir”) is not πεύκη (*peuke*), but *pytin*. See Matthiali’s notes on Dioscorides and Langguth in the cited work, pages 28 and 39. On electrum, or amber, see Book XVI, chapter 8, section 6.

N. 32. *Let it go far.* That is, “let it extend far upward”; I see that this etymology is also favored by more recent writers. That the Gallic fir is so called because of its whiteness is clear from the fact that *Gallia* is said to derive its name from whiteness, as was already explained in Book XIV, chapter 4, section 25. In the fir, the lower part is knotless and the upper part knotty.

N. 33. *Cedria.* Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 3, discusses *cedria*, with which books are coated and preserved.

N. 34. *Cypress.* Festus assigns another reason why the cypress—*cypressus*, *cupressus*, or *cyparissus*—was customarily placed at houses and around a funeral pyre as a sign of mourning: namely, because once cut down it does not grow again. Scaliger should be consulted on this passage.

N. 36. “With white and tawny distinctions.” Salmasius, [Col. 1008D] p. 1033 of the *Plinian Exercises*, observes that Dioscorus’s word διαφύσεις should be explained not as “spots,” as Isidore seems to interpret it, but as lines of the veins running lengthwise. Salmasius likewise, ibid., p. 1030, criticizes Isidore for placing Lake Mareotis in India; but Isidore follows Servius’s explanation, whose words Grialius brought forward. I approve Salmasius’s correction, by which in Lucan’s verse he emends *ebenus Meroetica* to refer to Meroe, the chief city of Ethiopia. For the same Lucan, in Book X, verse 303, says:

> Meroe, fertile in black inhabitants, is surrounded,  
> Glad with the branches of ebony . . .

In the first Gothic-Toledo manuscript there is this note: “Ebony is a tree which heat does not burn.”

N. 37. “Spread out like an exalted plane tree.” In the Vulgate: “I have been exalted like a plane tree.” Perhaps from the Greek πλατύς, “broad.”

N. 38. “In encaustic paintings.” Concerning the proper restoration of encaustic works according to ancient practice, Petrus Garzia de la Huerta, following Requeno, likewise a Spaniard, published a most learned commentary in the royal press at Madrid. [Col. 1009A]

N. 40. “They are twisted.” In Virgil, *curvantur* (“are bent”) is read instead of *torquentur* (“are twisted”). Pliny, Book V, chapter 23, teaches that Ituraea, or Ityraea, is a province of Coele-Syria. Concerning the poisonous substances which, according to Pliny and others, were formerly called *taxica*, see the commentaries of the physician Johannes Gorraeus on Nicander’s *Alexipharmaca*.

N. 47. “Which quickly leaps”; Cincius also has this reading. Nevertheless, Festus and later authorities regard it as ridiculous.

N. 48. “Vimen.” Some think it was so called because it is easily *vietur*, that is, bent. *Viere* means “to bend by force.”

N. 50. “Myrtle.” The word derives from the Greek μύρτος, *myrtos*; some derive μυρσίνη, *myrsinē*, from *myrrha* because of the similarity of scent. Grialius, with other printed editions, writes μυρίνη, but the usual word is μυρσίνη, or in Attic μυρρίνη.

N. 52. “More excellent.” For *praestantissimam*, “most excellent”; this expression was also familiar to Isidore’s contemporaries and to earlier writers.

[Col. 1009B] N. 53. “Write on boxwood.” The Vulgate: “Write upon it, on boxwood.”

N. 54. *Medeor* is found with an accusative in some ancient writers, but under a varied and uncertain reading.

N. 56. “Stipa.” Concerning *stipa*, see Festus, under the word *Stipatores*.

N. 57. “Canna.” Properly this is a smaller and more slender reed. Columella, Book VII, chapter 9: “The degenerate reed which the common people call *canna*.” Writers generally confuse the two. Agroetius: “*Arundo canna* is so called from its dryness.” Isidore derives the etymology of *cicuta* as though it were called *caecuta*, as can be gathered from the passage cited by Grialius. Concerning the plant itself, see Servius, *Eclogue* 2, verse 36. “*Cicuta* is the space between the nodes of reeds.”

N. 58. “Indian, not large.” In Grialius and other printed editions it read:

> The Indian reed does not grow large on a tree.  
> Of that and the pliant . . . .

In my note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 199, I observed [Col. 1009C] that the reading I have recorded here is the true one, and many critics adopt it. Salmasius, p. 1018 of the *Plinian Exercises*, wondered whether one ought to restore: “For Indian reeds grow too large on the tree,” and so forth, since Strabo affirms that those reeds are large. Nevertheless, he judged that nothing should be changed. Certainly reeds can be large in their own kind without thereby being called a large tree.

The same Salmasius observed that those Indian canes whose roots, when pressed, yielded a honey-like moisture are precisely the same as the canes that produce our sugar; for the ancients had a different kind of sugar. Again, on p. 1021, he discusses ancient natural sugar and modern manufactured sugar, and conjectures that our sugar may be attributed to the Arabs’ discovery of Indian canes. It should be considered whether in the third verse it would be preferable to read, as in some printed editions, “to yield to the juice of honey.”

N. 59. “Rhamnus.” Rhamnus is discussed in Volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 23, column 2, with Cotelerius’s notes. Langguthius provides more, *Antiquitates plantarum feralium*, p. 13. [Col. 1009D]

N. 63. “Orchades.” Becmanus considers *orchites* more correct, p. 902. Isidore takes this from Servius, on *Georgics* II, verse 86.

N. 65. “Lyciniae.” Grialius has *lyciniae* in the text and *liciniae* in the note. Other printed editions have *lychniae*. Nor is the reading of many copies displeasing: “From this the wood also received its name,” although Isidore, chapter 6, number 25, teaches the contrary—that *lychnus* derives from *lignum*.

N. 66. “Pusiam.” In the prologue to chapter 49, number 13, I observed that Burriel wanted to derive the Spanish name *bujía* from *pusia*, as though Isidore were speaking of a lamp, whereas he is speaking of an olive.

N. 67. “Crustumian pears . . . Volemian pears.” It can be sufficiently gathered from Servius’s own commentaries that he is speaking of pears. Virgil’s verse 88 of Book II of the *Georgics* is:

> With Crustumians, Syrian pears, and heavy Volemian pears.

Servius’s words are: “*Crustumia* are pears partly red, named from the town Crustumium. ‘And heavy Volemian pears,’ that is, large pears. For *volema* was also so called because it fills the palm (*vola*). Hence we also say *involare*.” Perhaps Isidore followed another author who explained these names as olives.

Forcellinus, otherwise a careful scholar and one who is usually very useful to me, asserts that Servius adds at this passage that *volema* means “good and large pears” in the Gallic language. “If that is so,” Forcellinus continues, “the word should not be derived from Latium but from the Gallic language, which was once the same as the Germanic.” I do not find these words of Servius in my edition; nor does Ducange cite any other author for the Gallic etymology of *volemum* except Papias, who took it from our Isidore. That *involare* is derived from *vola* is also reported by Iso in his gloss on Prudentius, verse 860 of the *Apotheosis*: “*Vola* is half the palm; hence we say *involare*, because whatever we seize we conceal in the palm.”

N. 69. “Amurca.” The Latins probably derived this word from the Greek rather than the reverse.

N. 70. “Gumen.” *Gummi* is said to be indeclinable, and also *gummis, gummis*. Palladius used *gumen*, as Isidore does here.

N. 71. “Resin.” Bochartus, *Chanaan*, Book I, chapter 8, offers some observations relevant to resin. Pliny has more, Book XVI, chapter 11, and Book XXIV, chapter 6; he lists various medicinal uses of resin.

N. 72. “Light.” Grialius printed *laevis* in the text and *lenis* in the note. Dioscorus’s Greek word can be translated in either way, either “gentle” or “smooth,” and *levis* has the same meaning. Others: *cui probatio* [reading uncertain].

N. 74. “And this is boxwood.” Servius reads that we should say *haec buxus* of the tree, but *buxum* of something made from the wood; this perhaps displeased Grialius, but it certainly should not be dismissed. For something made from boxwood, such as a flute, may be called both *buxum* and *buxus*.

## CHAPTER VIII

N. 1. *Quisque*, for *quicumque* or *quisquis*, occurs in Plautus, Ausonius, Prudentius, and others, as I have often observed in my commentaries on Prudentius. *Aroma* is a Greek word; there is no need to resort to a Latin derivation from *arae* (“altars”) or *aer* (“air”). [Col. 1010C]

N. 2. “Frankincense.” Grialius writes *thus* with aspiration in the text, but in the note to number 3 he writes *tus* without aspiration; the latter is the more common spelling, although many think *tus* derives from the Greek θύειν, “to sacrifice.” Others, in the following text, number 3, write *tus* without aspiration, deriving it from *tundere*, “to pound.”

N. 3. “Frankincense from pounding.” Charisius also derives it in this way. *Tus Libanum* is used adjectivally, as in Sedulius, Book IV, verse 55, *libana cedrus*, “Lebanese cedar.” Compare Bochartus, *Phaleg* II.18.

N. 4. “Myrrh.” Salmasius, p. 1268 of the *Plinian Exercises*, emends the passage: “But myrrh among the Troglytes, from an island of Arabia,” and so forth. Yet there is no doubt that Isidore is speaking of Trogodytic myrrh, which Pliny calls by that name in Book XII, chapter 16. The same Pliny, Book VI, chapter 29, and Scribonius Largus, *Compositiones* 90, call it “myrrh of the Trogodytes.” Langguthius should be consulted on myrrh, *Antiquitates plantarum feralium*, p. 22; he discusses the property by which myrrh prevents corpses from decaying.

[Col. 1010D] N. 5. “Storax.” Salmasius, p. 1026 of the *Plinian Exercises*, observes that liquid storax and calamite storax, or *storax*, are distinguished by Actius and others, whereas Isidore confuses the characteristics of both. The adjective *mellosus*, “honey-like,” is used for *melleus*, “of honey,” by Caelius Aurelianus. The Spaniards say *meloso*. Isidore seems to make *storax* feminine; but perhaps he means the tree. In fact, it is masculine. *Stiria*, meaning “a drop,” is Latin, not Greek, although *stiria* is of Greek origin.

N. 7. Grialius printed *mastix* in the text and *mastyx* in the note. The name commonly found among good authors is *mastiche* or *mastice*.

N. 9. “Aloe.” I wrote *aloe*, as ancient writers present the name, although Grialius and other printed editions have *aloa*. Compare the following chapter, number 28.

N. 11. “Amomum.” The word derives from α privative and μῶμος, “blemish,” as though meaning “pure” and “without stain.” Langguthius, at the cited place, p. 23, says that there is uncertainty not only about what *amomum* is but also whether it exists at all today. Salmasius, p. 400 of the *Plinian Exercises*, criticizes Pliny and Isidore for having believed that *amomum* was a grape, owing to a misunderstanding of Dioscorus, who speaks not of a grape-like seed but of a grape-like shrub, or one twisted and interwoven with itself like a cluster. Grialius also seems to interpret Dioscorus as speaking of a grape-like seed. Pliny speaks of a fruit resembling a grape, or grape-cluster; see Book XII, chapter 13, and Book XVI, chapter 22.

N. 12. “Cassia.” Langguthius, at the cited place, p. 23, says that cassia is either especially closely related to cinnamon, discussed above, or is entirely identical with it.

N. 13. “Aromatic cane.” Dioscorus wishes κίρρον to be the aromatic cane, as Salmasius observes, p. 1053 of the *Plinian Exercises*. Isidore rendered it “tawny.” Pliny says: “The remaining criterion is that it should not be black.”

N. 14. “The Romans gained possession of the same region.” Solinus used the ablative: “But when we gained possession of Judaea,” and so forth. Yet many good authors also occasionally use *potior* with the accusative. By force of its origin, *opobalsamum* denotes the tear or juice of a tree; but Langguthius, at the cited place, p. 24, observes that writers sometimes used *balsamum* for the tear and *opobalsamum* for the tree. [Col. 1011B]

## CHAPTER IX

N. 2. “Leaf.” Concerning the fragrant leaf, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 119:

> And the leaf exhales its fragrance, which a river,  
> Licking it from its hidden spring, carries outward.

At that passage I also supplied an old gloss: “The leaf is a most precious herb, said to come from paradise.” Salmasius, p. 1054, says that *malabathrum*, or *folium*, is called the herb of paradise to indicate its excellence. Thus aloe is called the tree of paradise because of its outstanding fragrance; birds of paradise are so called because they come from distant places; and today we likewise have “apples of paradise,” and so forth.

Again, on p. 1071, he observes that *malabathrum* does not readily grow in places far from the sea; it clings to and winds around trees. Hence the story that it floats on water without any root. Pliny also discusses *malabathrum*, or *malobathrum*, in Book XII, chapter 26, where he teaches that it grows in the marshes of India.

N. 3. “Nard.” Concerning spiked or spike-bearing nard, see above, the note on chapter 7, number 30. In two Gothic-Toledo manuscripts it reads: “It is Indian, multiform, but better is the Syrian: smooth, tawny, tufted, small in its spike, most fragrant . . . Celtic nard.” Some printed editions also have here and below, number 8, “most fragrant” and “most fragrant” in the corresponding forms.

N. 5. “Which is called Corycus.” This should be read in that form, not, as in most printed editions, *Coricium* or *Corycium*. *Corycius* is an adjective from *Corycus*; hence *corycium crocum*, “Corycian saffron,” frequently occurs among the poets. Salmasius, p. 773, translating from a corrected text of Dioscorus, gives: “Which stains the hands when it is rubbed and pressed,” where Isidore has “and when it is plucked, staining the hands.”

[Col. 1011D] N. 8. “Triangular rushes.” Celsus, Book III, chapter 21, and Book IV, chapter 20, calls *cyperus* a square rush.

N. 11. “Squinum is better.” Grialius has *squinum melius* in the text and *flos σχινάνθος*; in the note, *Schoenos melior* and *flos schoenanthos*. The Greek words are σχοίνου ἄνθος, “flower of the rush,” and, if correctly written, *schoenuanthos*. In Vegetius, Book I, *On Veterinary Medicine*, chapter 59, this word is likewise corrupted as *scinoanthos*.

N. 13. “Epithymum.” Salmasius, p. 1296 of the *Plinian Exercises*, distinguishes different *epithyma*, which, he says, authors confuse. One is Dioscorus’s *epithymum*, the flower of spiked thyme; another is Oribasius’s, the flower of headed thyme; and another *epithymum* is dodder, which grows upon and winds around spiked thyme.

N. 14. “Sampsuchus.” Grialius printed *samsucus* in the text and *sampsuchus* in the note; the latter is the correct spelling, derived from the Greek word.

[Col. 1012A] N. 15. “Like bulbs.” Grialius correctly has this in the text, although in the note he wrote *volui*, which occurs in some copies but should be rejected.

N. 20. “Acanthus . . . Egyptian.” Salmasius, p. 537 of the *Plinian Exercises*, observes that Isidore, following Servius, confuses the topiary plant with Egyptian acanthus, which is a herb; and that he thinks the *acanthine* garment was named from that Egyptian acanthus, although it was called after *acanthus*, a thorn or kind of thistle. He adds that there was not just one kind of thorn in Egypt.

*Acanthium* must also be distinguished from *acanthus*: garments were made from the cobweb-like down covering the leaves of *acanthium*; Pliny discusses these in Book XXIV, chapter 12. *Acanthion* is a shrub resembling a white thorn. *Acanthus* is a herb, one variety of which is wild and resembles a thistle, while another is cultivated; its form was commonly represented on the capitals of Corinthian columns, on embossed vessels, and in elaborate garments. *Acanthus* was also the name of a certain thorny Egyptian tree, which some believe to be the Egyptian thorn, whose juice is called *acacia*.

[Col. 1012B] N. 24. “White and black.” Grialius, who undertook to copy words added in some editions, left them incomplete; these will be presented among the variant readings from the old first edition of the *Etymologies*.

N. 26. “Euphorbium.” It is called *euphorbium, euphorbii*, and *euphorbia, euphorbiae*. Isidore uses both genders, in *dictum* and *plurima*, wherever this herb may be understood. As for Isidore’s etymology, there is no reason for us to labor over it.

N. 27. “Laser.” Properly, this is the juice of *silphium*, but it is sometimes used for the *silphium* itself. In Isidore it may perhaps be necessary to read *lac sirpis* for *lacsir*, as Grialius printed it in the text; in the note, however, he indicates *lac sirpicum*. In fact, Isidore is copying Solinus.

It should be observed that Solinus confuses *lac sirpicum*, or *laserpitium*, with *ladanum*, the thick, dewy substance of *lada*, a plant belonging to the species of *cistus* and found in Cyprus. Pliny discusses *ladanum* in Book XXVI, chapter 8.

The distinction between *sirpe* and *laserpitium* is that *sirpe* is the plant itself, whereas *laserpitium* is the juice pressed from it, although the latter word is also used for the plant itself. *Laserpitium* was held in the highest esteem by the ancients and was strongly recommended by physicians, as Vulpius observes in his note on Catullus, poem 7: “Cyrene lies rich in laser-bearing plants.”

N. 28. “Aloe.” Here Grialius correctly writes *aloe*, whereas in chapter 8, number 9, he printed *aloa*. There, aloe is listed among aromatic trees, although the features described belong to the herb aloe. See Pliny, Book XXVII, chapter 4.

The printed editions, including Grialius in the text, have *panace* for *panaces*, as Grialius indicates in the note. One may say *panacea, panaceae*; *panax, panacis*; and *panaces, panacis*. *Galbanus* is less usual than *galbanum*, which is found in our Vulgate.

N. 29. “Called . . . Dictamnus . . . Mars’s pennyroyal.” For *Dicta*, *Dictis* or *Dicte* would be better. Grialius incorrectly writes *Dicta*, *dyctamnum*, and *dyctaeos* with *y*. Instead of *dictamnum*, the masculine form *dictamnus* may also be used. [Col. 1012D] *Dictamnum* is a herb resembling pennyroyal; for this reason some call it “Mars’s pennyroyal,” as Grialius indicates in the note, although in the text, with other editions, he printed *poleium*.

N. 30. “Mandrake.” Pliny and other ancient writers use *mandragoras, mandragorae* in the masculine gender. Isidore perhaps means “the mandrake herb,” and so forth. Mandrakes are mentioned in Genesis, chapter 30, where the interpreters offer several observations. Some special remarks on mandrakes occur in the manuscript glosses on the Old Testament, to be published among the appendices.

N. 31. “The juice which they call opium.” Grialius printed this, although in the note he reports *quem opion vocant*, “which they call *opion*.” Pliny completes his description of poppy juice with “they call it *opion*”; but Isidore sometimes alters the wording.
