N. 33. “Centaurea.” Grialius often writes the word one way in the text and another in the note; here he has *centauriam* in the text and *centaurium* in the note. Among good authors one finds *centaureum, centaurei*; *centaurion, centaurii*; and *centaurea, centaureae*. [Col. 1013A]

N. 34. “Glycyrrhiza.” Pliny discusses glycyrrhiza in Book XXII, chapter 9.

N. 38. “For purification and temples.” Perhaps this refers to the custom, also practiced among the pagans, of scattering flowers and foliage in temples. See my *Prudentiana*, chapter 14, number 158, p. 135.

N. 40. “Rheu.” Grialius printed *reu*; but it should be written *rheu*, *rheo*, or *rha*. The name *rha* was taken from a river of Sarmatia bearing that name, on whose banks grows a root called Pontic rhubarb, and by Celsus, Book V, chapter 23, *radix pontica*, “Pontic root”; it was sometimes formerly called simply *rha*. Later another, different root, *rheo*, became known; to distinguish it from Pontic *rha*, it was called “barbarian *rheo*,” namely our rhubarb. Isidore and other authors, such as Salmasius, p. 797 of the *Plinian Exercises*, did not sufficiently distinguish these things.

N. 41. “A serrated edge.” Grialius’s edition had *ora serata*; other printed editions have *ora serrata*. Apuleius, chapter 4, discusses the herb *calycularis*; this is the preferable spelling, rather than *calicularis*, used by Grialius and others. The *calyx* and *calyculus* of flowers and herbs are the little globule in the middle of the leaves that contains the seed.

N. 42. “From its discoverer.” That is, from Gentius, king of the Illyrians. See Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 7. That savory makes people inclined to sexual love is not certain; for neither Pliny nor Columella attributes this power to it, while Ovid and Martial perhaps speak not of savory but of *satyrion* or *satyreum*.

N. 43. “Stingum.” Perhaps *stigum*. In Johannes de Janua, *stiga* means “a thorn, a goad,” and so forth. Hence *instigare*, “to incite.”

N. 46. “Chamaemelos.” *Chamaemelon* is better, as though meaning “small apple tree.”

N. 47. “Chamaedrys.” As though “small oak”; in Latin it is called *trixago*. Pliny and others discuss these plants.

N. 51. “Serpillus.” Latin writers use *serpillum* in the neuter gender. Varro, Pliny, and others derive it from *serpo*, “I creep,” as *herpillum* is derived from the Greek ἕρπω, “I creep.”

N. 54. “Psyllion.” Grialius has *psyllios* in the text and *psyllion* in the note; the latter is more correct. The herb called *psyllion* is meant. It is also called *cynomyia*, which Pliny discusses in Book XXV, chapter 11.

N. 55. “Embassies.” Grialius printed *ligamentis* in the text, which he rejects in the note. The public remedies mentioned by Pliny were purifications and expiations. Others agree concerning the use of vervain in embassies: Martianus in the *Digest*, Livy, and Festus. Festus’s words are: “*Sagmina* are called vervains, that is, pure herbs, because they were taken—or perhaps summoned—from a sacred place by a consul or praetor, or by ambassadors setting out to make a treaty and declare war; or from *sancire*, that is, ‘to confirm.’”

N. 56. “Struthius.” *Struthion* would be more correct. Pliny also calls this herb *radicula*, which displeases Salmasius, p. 1162 of the *Plinian Exercises*. Yet not only Pliny but also Columella and Celsus call certain edible herbs *radicula* and *radix*, since their power and use lie chiefly in the root and bulb. For *splenos*, Pliny uses *splenion*, Book XXV, chapter 5: “It cures disorders of the spleen, and is said to have been discovered in this way: when entrails were thrown upon it, they adhered to the spleen and emptied it. For this reason some call it *splenion*.” It is believed to be the same herb as *asplenum*, which Pliny discusses in Book XXVII, chapter 4.

N. 58. “Marrubium.” Pliny and Columella discuss *marrubium*.

N. 63. “Polion.” Grialius had *polios* in the text, but gives *polion* in the note, as Pliny writes it. It should be observed that it is called *polion* because its leaves resemble the gray hair of human beings; for πολιός means “gray-haired.” Isidore suggests something else when he renders it *omnimorbia*, “all-disease herb,” which the Spaniards call *sánalo todo*, “heal-all.” The other material added here in the printed editions is relegated to the variant readings.

N. 64. “Scammony.” Grialius has *scammonia* in the text and *scammonea* in the note. Both forms are used.

[Col. 1014A] N. 65. “With a two-palm-long thyrsus.” This, I think, is what Grialius intended, as is clear from the note, although in the text, with the other printed editions, he published *thyrso bipalmis*.

N. 68. “Madder.” See also Pliny and Vitruvius on *rubia*.

N. 69. “Alkanet.” Pliny also discusses *anchusa*, or *ancusa*.

N. 70. “Chamaeleon.” It is also called *ixia*. See Pliny, Book XXII, chapter 18.

N. 71. “Thus it is called,” and so forth. The explanation given—“Thus a blind ditch is called one that is hidden”—suggests that Isidore wrote *cecuta* or *caecuta*. Certainly Isidore derives *cicuta* from *caecus*, “blind,” to explain that it contains hidden nodes.

N. 72. “Clover.” Perhaps it is the herb now called “trinity.”

N. 73. “Phlomos.” In Latin it is called *verbascum*, according to Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 10.

N. 74. “Pyrethrum.” Pliny describes *pyretrum*, or *pyrethron*, in Book XXVIII, chapter 9. [Col. 1014B]

N. 75. “Marshmallow.” The word is Greek, from ἁλθαίνειν, “to heal” or “to cure,” because it has many medicinal uses. For this reason Pliny, Book XX, chapter 21, says that *althaea* was named from the excellence of its effects. It is written *althaea* with a diphthong, although Grialius and other printed editions have *althea* without one.

N. 76. “Oregano, which in Latin is *colina*.” Pliny, Book XX, chapter 17: “Oregano, which rivals the kitchen in flavor.” Vulcanius’s note is: “Pliny makes every herb resemble oregano.” For *colena*, which Grialius gives in the text, Vulcanius indicates *colora* in the margin as a variant reading.

N. 77. “Tithymallum.” It is usually written *tithymalus* or *tithymallus*.

N. 79. “Polygonus,” or *polygonos* or *polygonium*, is described by Pliny in Book XXVII, chapter 12, and is mentioned by Scribonius Largus, *Compositiones* 103.

N. 80. “Ambrosia.” The name *ambrosia* is common to many herbs. For *apiago*, which Grialius printed, *apiacon* should be read. Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 157: “There is another cabbage, curly; it is called *APIACON*.” Pliny calls it *apiaca brassica*, that is, “celery cabbage,” from *apium*, “celery,” which itself is said to derive from *apes*, “bees.” Vulcanius gives *apiacum*.

N. 81. “Rosemary.” According to Apuleius, *On Herbs*, chapter 79: “Having leaves like fennel, but rough, and lying prostrate on the ground.”

N. 82. “Celsus lists *nepeta* among herbs of harmful juice in Book II, chapter 21. *Calamintha* is a useful mint.” It is also written *menta* without aspiration. The Greek word in Grialius and other printed editions was written καλαμίθην; this should have been corrected.

N. 84. “Mullein.” Isidore discusses some of the herbs mentioned here elsewhere. *Verbascum* is *phlomos*, discussed in numbers 73 and 94. I think *calamites* should be read as *calaminthes*, concerning which see number 82. For *lappa*, see number 66.

N. 85. “Albucum.” This seems to be what Grialius intended, although his text nevertheless shows *albutium*. Apuleius, *On Herbs*, chapter 32: “By the Greeks it is called *asphodelus*, by the Latins *hasta regia*, and by some *albucus*.” Pliny, however, Book XXI, chapter 17, distinguishes *albucum* to some extent from *asphodelus*. The name of the herb *scilla* is written with an *i*. Grialius gives *scylla* both in the note and in the text, perhaps to explain Isidore’s indicated etymology.

Concerning the pagan superstition of hanging herbs at doorways, one might perhaps understand chapter 73 of the collection of canons of Saint Martin of Braga: “It is not permitted to practice wicked observances at the Kalends . . . or to encircle houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All such observance is paganism.”

N. 86. “Chamaepitys.” As though “dwarf pine.” Pliny, Book XXIV, chapter 6.

N. 87. “Concerning *asplenum*, see number 56.”

N. 88. “Bulbus.” Grialius printed *volvus*, in keeping with the etymology. See number 19 of the following chapter.

N. 95. “Ferula.” Some classify it among trees. See the old glosses on *ferula* in my edition of Prudentius, in the note on the prologue, verse 8.

N. 96. “Papyrus, called . . .” The correct forms would be *papyrus dicta . . . apta*, or *papyrum dictum . . . aptum*. Guilandini’s *Papyrus*, or *Commentary on Three Chapters of Pliny Concerning Papyrus*, published at Venice in 1572, is an excellent and not easily obtainable work. [Col. 1015A]

N. 97. “I restored from Festus *quod dicere* for *quid dicere* in Grialius, or *praedicere* in other editions.”

N. 101. *Typhus* is frequently used by Arnobius, Augustine, and others for pride and mental arrogance, because *typhus* in Greek means “smoke.” Isidore indicates another explanation: the proud swell and inflate themselves, like the herb *typha*. It is familiar among ecclesiastical writers to explain pride by swelling.

N. 103. “Spartus.” Bochartus discusses *spartum* in Book V of the *Chanaan*, chapter 35. *Spartum* is ordinarily used in the neuter gender. Harduinus, in his note on Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 2, observes that *spartum* derives from σπείρω, “to sow, bind, or interweave,” because it is chiefly useful for tying ropes.

N. 104. “In Grialius’s note, *cum sit* perhaps dropped out in place of *licet sit*, as he printed it in the text with other editions.”

N. 105. “Leaves.” In ancient copies of Isidore I have repeatedly found *folia* in the feminine gender instead of *folium*; perhaps this corruption had already begun in Isidore’s time.

N. 106. “Tares . . . unlucky.” Juvencus, Book III, verse 7: “But unlucky darnel.”

## CHAPTER X

N. 3. “Thyrsus.” The Spanish *troncho* and the Italian *torso* derive from *thyrsus*.

N. 4. “Concerning *cyma*, see above, chapter 6, number 20.”

N. 7. Scribonius Largus uses *rapa* in the feminine gender, as does Columella occasionally. *Rapum* is more usual.

N. 9. “Not in the root, but into a thyrsus.” Perhaps: “Not in the root, but in,” and so forth. Others have: “Not in the root, but in the thyrsus.” Pliny, Book X, chapter 8, lists a kind of mustard with leaves resembling those of the turnip. The Greek word, however, is σίναπι.

N. 11. “Lettuce.” Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 8, teaches that the name *lactuca* was taken from a certain kind of lettuce formerly known only in Italy, which abounded in a quantity of soporific milk like that of the poppy and was called *meconis*. In Greek, μήκων means “poppy.”

[Col. 1015C] N. 12. “Endive.” *Intubus* is masculine, while *intubum* is neuter. It is also written with *y*, since the Greeks say ἔντυβον. *Caepa* is more often found with a diphthong than without one. There are two kinds: one used chiefly as a seasoning and almost without a head, and another headed variety, which swells out into a head. On the etymology, compare Becmanus, Vossius, and others.

N. 15. “From *beta*, because it has a soft stalk.” Augustus was accustomed to use *betisso* or *betizo* for “to languish,” as Suetonius relates in his *Life of Augustus*, chapter 87. The Greeks also call it *bliton*. That Isidore here and elsewhere uses a genus for a species is a matter of common usage. Others explain more distinctly the classes, genera, species, and families of herbs.

N. 18. “Tinder.” Vulcanius notes: “Even today the Spaniards call tinder suitable for lighting a fire *yesca*.” The Italians retain the actual name *esca*. Others give a more suitable derivation for *fungus*, namely from the Greek σφόγγος or σπόγγος, “sponge.”

N. 19. “Bulbs.” Grialius has this here, although in the preceding chapter, number 88, he preferred *volvus* on etymological grounds. Although *v* and *b* were easily interchanged in antiquity, Isidore could nevertheless have written *bulbus* and still derived the word from something rolling or winding.

N. 20. “Horseradish.” Pliny calls it *armoracia*, while Columella has *armoracium*. In Palladius some read *armoraceam*, not *armoracam*. Nothing concerning *carduus* appears in Grialius’s text, although he supplies an explanation in the note for certain words found in other editions. Compare the variant readings.

N. 1. “Rocket is derived from *uro* or *erodo*, for it gnaws the tongue with its sharpness.” Some write *aeruca*. Columella, Book X, verse 110:

> So that rocket may rouse sluggish husbands to love.

Martial and Ovid have similar lines, which Langguthius cites in *Antiquitates plantarum feralium*, p. 4.

## CHAPTER XI

N. 1. “Celery.” It is said to derive from *apes*, “bees,” for whom it is especially pleasing. See number 80 of chapter 9 of this book. The etymology Isidore gives here has Marcellus Empiricus as its source; in the chapter on celery he teaches:

> Celery was so called because the apex [ritual cap] used to bear it  
> When, according to ancient custom, a victor’s triumph was celebrated.

In the same passage he reports that Hercules was the first to be presented with such a crown.

N. 6. “As the Latins say, *anisum*.” This is how I read it. Grialius had *ut Latini, anesum*. Other printed editions have: “*Annison*, as the Greeks say, or, as the Latins say, *anneson*.”

N. 7. “Coriander.” The Greeks also call it κορίανδρον, perhaps from κόρις, “bug,” because it smells like a bug. *Corion* is the same herb as *chamaepitys*, or *hypericum*. Isidore confuses the two. Most write *abrotonum* rather than *abrotanum*. For *cerefolium*, or, as it stood in Grialius’s text, *ceraefolium*, the more usual spelling is *caerefolium*, a corrupted form of the Greek χαίρεφυλλον, *chaerephyllum*. The names of herbs circulating in the mouths of country people were easily corrupted. [Col. 1016B]

N. 9. “Concerning *mentha*, or *menta*, see the preceding chapter, number 82.”

## BOOK EIGHTEEN

### CHAPTER ONE

N. 2. “From the aforesaid.” Because war must be announced and proclaimed. Others prefer *ex edicto*, “from an edict.” See the variant readings.

N. 4. “More than civil.” See what I noted on Book II of Dracontius’s *On God*, verse 294:

> Nor is merely civil strife enough.

The character of a war “more than civil” must be sought in opposing commanders who are otherwise related and connected by kinship.

N. 7. “So that greater fear may arise.” In Cicero’s words some read *major tumor oriatur*, “so that greater swelling may arise.” Cicero adds: “Hence the name *tumultus* was also derived . . . That a tumult is more serious than a war can be understood from this: exemptions are valid in war, but not in a tumult.”

N. 9. “War.” In the old edition we read: “After the letter *D* was removed and *V* changed into *B*, it was called *bellum*”; this was given as the first etymology. [Col. 1016C]

N. 10. “Battles.” Others give different accounts of the derivation of the name *praelium*, and there is not sufficient agreement about its spelling. Most write *proelium*, others *praelium*, and some *prelium*, although the latter is less approved by those who teach orthography.

N. 11. “A treaty is peace,” and so forth. Festus: “*Foedus* was so called because, when a treaty was made, a sacrificial victim was killed.” Virgil:

> . . . And with the slaughtered sow they joined the treaties.

Or because *fides*, “trust,” is inserted into a treaty. Servius, on *Aeneid* I, verse 66: “But *foedus* was so called either from the *fetiales*, who were formerly called *foedales*, that is, priests through whom treaties are made; or from the sow being killed *foede*, ‘foully,’ that is, with stones.”

Etymologists do not agree about the derivation of *induciae*, or, as others write it, *indutiae*, “truce.” Some derive it from *in* or *indu* and *otium*, “leisure”; others from *induco*, or *inductae*, because rest is introduced among weapons; others derive it from elsewhere. See Gellius, Book I, chapter 25. Isidore’s etymology pleases me more than the others. Instead of *resilisset*, perhaps *resiliisset* or *resiluisset* should be read.

### CHAPTER II

N. 1. “Victory.” The derivation of *victoria* from *vis*, “force,” is not accepted by many. Grialius printed *reportasse* in the text and *deportasse* in the note. Servius’s words on verse 421 of Book XI are: “And this is why Sallust praises commanders: because they brought back victory with an unbloodied army.”

N. 3. “Tranquillus . . . triumph.” Joannes Nicolaus, in his work *The Roman Triumph*, chapter 1, defends, with many others, the derivation of *triumphus* from a Greek word.

N. 5. Instead of *accederent*, “they might approach,” *ascenderent*, “they might ascend,” would perhaps be better.

N. 6. “Rufus.” Grialius writes *ruffo*, which is displeasing to sound critics. Havercampus, in his commentary on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 33, says that Isidore rather comically calls a public slave an executioner. Fabricius, chapter 17 of the *Bibliography*, number 10, observes that Isidore used *carnifex*, “executioner,” for “public slave” because he misunderstood a passage of Pliny. See Ferrarius, Book I of the *Electa*, chapter 11, and Casaubon on Suetonius, p. 281.

N. 7. “By annihilation.” This is how I write it, although Grialius and some others printed *internicione*. In editions of Virgil one reads, “Or drive them apart,” namely the ships. But Isidore follows his Servius: “‘Or drive them apart’; that is,” says Servius, “scatter them in different directions, so that they do not come to Italy. An army is destroyed in two ways: either by annihilation or by dispersal.”

N. 8. “The spoils of the enemy.” On military spoils, see Lipsius, Book V of *Roman Military Matters*, chapter 17. That work contains much that could illuminate this book of Isidore, besides innumerable other authorities I pass over.

### CHAPTER III

N. 2. Isidore frequently uses *Jovis* in the nominative.

N. 3. “The standards of the dragons.” Just as eagles were the standards of the legions, so dragons were those of the cohorts. See my commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 55 and following:

> . . . And the standards of war  
> They display, renowned for their swollen dragons.

See also the work of Michael Angelo Causseus, or de la Chausse, *On Military Standards*.

N. 4. A *pila* is a ball with which one plays, but the word is used for any ball or sphere; because it is round, it sometimes denotes a circle or globe. Zeilichius presents ancient coins on which a ball can be seen set upon standards, in *Observations from Coins*, Wittenberg, 1745, p. 10 and following. Compare also the coins of Probus and Maximianus in André Morell’s *Specimen of Numismatics*, plate 22, number 10.

N. 5. “Vexillum.” Gisbertus Cuperus, letter 44 to Sperlingius, observes that when authors distinguish *vexillum* from other standards, they understand the banner or cloth about which Isidore speaks here and in Book X, chapter 22. Such a *vexillum* was a purple tunic when the republic was free. Festus and Priscian also say that *vexillum* is a diminutive of *velum*, “cloth” or “sail.” Cicero, however, in *Orator*, chapter 45, teaches that *velum* was formed from *vexillum*.

## Chapter IV

**No. 1. Bucina.** It is also written *buccina*, especially by those who derive it from *bucca*, “mouth.” The etymology supplied by Isidore is usually preferred.

**No. 3.** Some derive *tuba* from *tubus*, “tube,” and likewise *tibia*. See Lipsius, *De militia Romana*, book IV, dialogue 10. *Tofus*, or *tophus*, is a porous stone.

**No. 4. At tuba, etc.** Virgil’s verse from *Aeneid* IX reads:

> But the trumpet, with its brazen mouth,  
> Blared from afar a terrible sound with sonorous bronze . . .

**No. 5. Classica.** Caesar clearly explains why the *classicum* was the signal for entering battle, *Civil War* III, chapter 92: “It is a certain arousal of the spirit,” etc. See Vulpian’s note on Tibullus I, elegy 1, verse 4:

> Whom the martial trumpets, once sounded, drive from sleep.

On *sistra*, see my remarks in the commentary on book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 527. [Col. 1017D]

## Chapter V

**No. 1.** *Tuemur* is used passively, as Isidore also uses it elsewhere.

**No. 2. Ab armis.** Festus likewise has this form.

## Chapter VI

**No. 1. Gladius . . . ensis.** Some distinguish *ensis* and *gladius* in this way: *ensis* is generally used of a military sword, *gladius* of a civilian one. In fact, however, these distinctions are either nonexistent or not observed. Forcellinus says that *ensis* means a military sword; but afterward, under *gladius*, he asserts that those who make this distinction are saying nothing. The more certain point is that *ensis* is a poetic word. Varro derives *gladius* from *clades*, “slaughter,” in book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 24. Many have illuminated the more noteworthy arms of antiquity in their observations; among them Fabricius, frequently praised, records no small number in *Bibliography*, chapter 18.

**No. 2.** *Machaera* may perhaps better be derived from Greek μάχομαι (*machomai*), “I fight.”

**No. 3. Framea.** In Augustine’s time among the Africans, *framea* was used for “sword,” as may be gathered from letter 120, chapter 16. [Col. 1018A] Earlier Latin writers called a spear *framea*, using a Germanic word. Tacitus, *Germania*, chapter 6:

> They carry spears, or, in their own language, *frameae*, with a narrow and short iron point, but so sharp and suited to use that they fight with the same weapon, as circumstances require, either at close quarters or from a distance.

Compare Becman, who also discusses *romphaea*, p. 920.

**No. 4. Spatha.** Greek σπάθη (*spáthē*) properly means a broad, elongated instrument with which medicines and other substances are mixed. By analogy with it, a broader sword is called a *spatha*; the word then passed into the vernacular languages. *Spatula*, and more correctly *spathula*, in the context of the chest, is a broader rib; thus Apicius, book IV, chapter 3, has *spathula porcina*, “pork rib.” Hence the Spanish *espalda*, “back.” Consult Bochart, *Canaan*, book I, chapter 42.

**No. 5. Semispathium.** Vegetius uses the word *semispatha*. Isidore indicates that *semispathium* was a missile weapon.

**No. 6. Idem et clunabulum.** Grialius, along with other printed editions, has *item*; but *idem*, which should be retained, appears in the note. In the old copies *item* and *idem* are frequently confused. [Col. 1018B] In place of *clunabulum* I would prefer *clunaculum*: for Gellius, book X, chapter 25, lists among the names of swords *machaerae, spathae, pugiones, lingulae,* and *clunaculae*. Others give *clunacula* in the neuter gender. In the Isidorian Glossary we find: “*Sica*, *cluniculus*, *machaera*.” Compare the notes.

**No. 8. Sica a secando.** This is likewise found in book X, under *sicarius*. Although *sica* and *seco* differ in vowel quantity, the etymology should not therefore be judged false. In the words of Tranquillus, “With this I shall fight,” the old editions had admitted the error “I shall fight with a dagger,” which Brissonius corrected from manuscript codices in *Select Antiquities*, book II, chapter 11. Barthius investigates the form of the *sica* in *Adversaria*, p. 2634, and Lipsius in *Roman Military Science*, book III, chapter 3, where he also discusses the *pugio*.

**No. 9. Secures.** Isidore discusses the axe again in book XIX, chapter 19. In the bundles of rods carried before magistrates there were also axes, to inflict punishment on criminals when necessary. The name *francisca* given by the Spaniards to axes seems also to have been adopted by the Franks themselves, as may be inferred from the authorities cited by Ducange. There Papias is reported as saying that the Spaniards called them *franciscos*, not *franciscas*, as Isidore’s copies read. [Col. 1018C]

## Chapter VII

**No. 1.** *Hasta* was formerly written *asta*. Varro gives another etymology in book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 24: “*Hasta*, because it usually bears one who is standing” (*stans*, or alternatively *astans*).

**No. 2. Conus acuta rotunditas.** Varro, in the passage cited, has: “*Conus*, because it is forced toward a point.” Perhaps the reading should be *conus*.

**No. 3. Trudes.** The spelling *trudes* in Isidore is confirmed by Virgil and by Tacitus, *Annals* III, chapter 46:

> Some sought to overthrow the inert mass with poles or forks.

As in many other cases, *trudis* may derive from *trudo*, “I push,” with a short initial vowel, although *u* in *trudo* is long. Thus *lucerna* comes from *luceo*, and so forth. It is not sufficiently clear why *trudes* should have been called *aplustria*. For *aplustre* properly meant a ship’s ornament, made of boards, at the upper part of the stern; its shape can be seen on Trajan’s Column and is reproduced by Schefferus in book II of *Naval Warfare*, chapter 6. [Col. 1018D]

**No. 4. Excipiunt enim apros, etc.** From Martial, book XIV, epigram 30, entitled *Venabula*:

> They will receive the boars and await the lions;  
> They will enter against bears, provided the hand is firm.

In my copy Servius has *apta venatui*, “suited to hunting,” as though the word were *excipiabula*.

**No. 5. Lancea.** Sisenna, as quoted by Nonius, chapter 18, no. 26, reports:

> The Gauls strike with *materes*, the Suebi with spears.

Festus says: “*Lancea* is named from the Greek word which they call λόγχη (*lonchē*).” Isidore wished to discover a Latin derivation.

**No. 7.** Horace calls it *caia*. Grialius conjecturally printed: “Lucilius calls it *calam*.” Although this is supported by Servius’ authority, the reading of all the copies seems to be retained: “Horace calls it *caiam*.” For it is not established [Col. 1019A] that Isidore had in mind the passage of Servius in which he discusses Lucilius and *cala*. Whatever the truth about the author of the word *caia*, Salmasius believes that it should be retained, p. 207, verse 22, in Trebellius Pollio, against the very learned man—Grialius, I suppose—who corrected it to *calam*. For from *caia*, “staff” or “club,” came *caio*, *caias*, and *caiatio*. Fulgentius, *Continuation of Virgil*:

> Among the ancients, *caiatio* was called the beating of a boy.

Hence Plautus also says in the comedy *Cistellaria*—perhaps *Clitellaria*:

> Why are you afraid of your mistress, lest she strike you with a hand-held club?

Papias has:

> *CATEIA*: in the language of the Persians, a spear or weapon. *Cateia*, which Horace calls *CAIA*. It is a kind of Gallic weapon; if thrown by a skilled practitioner, it returns again to the one who threw it.

Servius explains this at the cited verse of Virgil, “in Teutonic fashion,” etc.:

> When they hurled it at the enemy, they made it return by means of the cords with which they had fastened it.

This, I believe, is the “deceitful bow” mentioned in Hosea, chapter VII, verse 16. See Mariana’s note on book I of Isidore’s *Against the Jews*, chapter 19, where the old edition gives *sagitta reciproca*, “returning arrow.” Some wrongly explain this as an arrow that rebounds against the very person who drew the bow. [Col. 1019B]

**No. 8. Phalarica is a huge weapon.** It is written both *phalarica* and *falarica*. There was a larger *phalarica*, launched by a catapult, and a smaller one, thrown by hand.

**No. 9. Pila sunt arma jaculorum.** Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 24: “Likewise from *omen* comes *pilum*, because it strikes the enemy, as in *perilum*.” Others derive it from Greek πῖλος (*pilos*). See Lipsius, *Roman Military Science* III, dialogue 4.

**No. 11.** Properly, *cuspis* is the rear part of a spear. That *cuspis* does not properly mean the point of a spear but its rear part cannot easily be confirmed by the authority of the ancients, although the word is sometimes used by synecdoche for a spear or staff. Properly, however, the point is the *mucro* of a sword, while *cuspis* is the point of a spear or *contus*, and so forth. Becman’s claim that *cuspis* derives from *aspis* appears foolish.

## Chapter VIII

**No. 1.** *Sagitta* and *spiculum* are sometimes confused; but the distinction used by Isidore should be approved: an arrow (*sagitta*) is shot from a bow, whereas a *spiculum* is a short lance, also called a *pilum*. [Col. 1019C]

**No. 3. Scorpio.** The war machine called a *scorpio* was of two kinds, larger and smaller, as appears from Livy, book XXVI, chapters 47 and 49. Its form also varied according to the period. Ammianus gives a detailed description of the *scorpiones* of his own time in book XXII, chapter 4, alternatively numbered chapter 8. Rigaltius, in his note at the beginning of Tertullian’s *Scorpiace*, charges Isidore with error for calling a *scorpio* an arrow, since it is rather a machine that shoots arrows. Nicolaus Antonius defends Isidore in book V of *Bibliotheca veterum*, no. 95, on the authority of Stewechius’ commentary on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* IV, chapter 22, which supports Isidore. *Scorpio* is also used for an arrow shot by a *scorpio* in Hirtius, *African War*, chapter 29: “An arrow being more accurately discharged by the *scorpio*, and their centurion being killed.”

## Chapter IX

**No. 1. Feretrum, where a funeral is carried.** The same etymology of *feretrum* is repeated in book XX, chapter 11. *Pharetra* is a Greek word, but according to some it is nevertheless derived from φέρω (*pherō*), “I carry.” [Col. 1019D]

**No. 2.** A *vagina* is so called because in it . . . the sword is carried. Others think *vagina* comes from *vaco*, as though *vacina*, because it is empty and suitable for receiving a sword or weapon.

**No. 4. Oxos.** Ducange apparently intended to note something concerning *oxos*, for under *oxa* he says, “See *dolo*.” But the word *dolo* is missing; perhaps he intended to record there the words of our Isidore concerning *dolones*.

**No. 5.** A bow is properly so called of the instrument with which arrows are shot, because it restrains or drives them away (*arcet*, that is, *propellit*). From this, *arcus* also became a term in architecture.

## Chapter X

**No. 1. Fundibalus.** In book XIV, chapter 6, at the end, *fundibalum* is given in the neuter gender. Another instrument is the *fustibalus*, concerning which see Vegetius, as is clear from Grialius’ note on that passage.

## Chapter XI

**No. 4. Musculus.** A description of the larger *musculus* may be found in Caesar, *Civil War* II, chapter 10. [Col. 1020A]

## Chapter XII

**No. 1. Clypeus est scutum.** The following distinction between *clypeus* and *scutum* is usually made: the *clypeus* was bronze and round, while the *scutum* was wooden and rectangular, with an elongated form. The *parma*, discussed in no. 6, was generally made of leather or hide, but was round. Nevertheless, writers easily confuse these terms and use them interchangeably.

**No. 2.** Some derive *scutum* from *cutis*, “skin,” with a change in the quantity of the syllable, because it was often covered with leather. It is more easily derived from the Greek σκῦτος (*skytos*), “hide, leather.” Likewise *umbo* comes from the Greek word ἄμβω (*ambō*); hence *umbilicus*.

**No. 3.** *Ancile* comes from *am*, “around,” and *caesus*, “cut,” as though *amcisum*. See Bochart, *Canaan*, book II, chapter 11. Some, with Nonius, chapter 18, no. 11, write *ancyle*. The form of the *ancile* is preserved on certain old coins.

**No. 4.** The Vulgate has: “shields of the purest gold.”

**No. 5. Afri et Mauri.** This is found in the old copies; Grialius likewise printed it in the text, although in the note he indicates *Hispani* in place of *Mauri*. [Col. 1020B] Indeed, Servius says, “Africans and Spaniards.” Tacitus, *Life of Agricola*, chapter 26, also reports that short *cetrae* were in use among the Britons. Bochart, *Canaan*, book I, chapter 42, may be consulted for the elucidation of this passage of Isidore.

**No. 6.** Varro thinks that *parma* is so called because it is equal (*par*) from the middle in all directions, *On the Latin Language*, chapter 24. Bochart should be consulted at the same place, chapter 42.

## Chapter XIV

**No. 1. Galea de corio.** Becman, pp. 489 ff., confirms that this is the true origin—namely, from γαλέη (*galē*), “cat” or “weasel.” The ancients generally made coverings or helmets from leather or the skins of animals, as Becman demonstrates at length. Tacitus clearly distinguishes *cassis* and *galea*, but other writers frequently use them indiscriminately.

## Chapter XV

**No. 1. Forus.** For the etymology of *forus*, see book XV, chapter 2, no. 27, where we read: “These places are also called *pro rostris*,” which is better than *prorostra*. Perhaps, however, in the Middle Ages the name *prorostra* became established. I certainly cannot agree with Grialius, who attributes this passage to Braulio. [Col. 1020C] Why could Isidore, who constantly repeats himself, not have discussed the *forum* twice when the opportunity arose?

**No. 2.** *Justitia* comes from *justus*, “just,” as *laetitia* comes from *laetus*, “joyful,” and so forth. Isidore discusses law and statutes in book V, *On Law and Laws*.

**No. 4.** *Jurgium* comes from *jurgo*, “I quarrel”; Varro derives the latter from *jus* and *ago* in book V of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 6.

**No. 7. Reus a re qua petitur nuncupatus.** *Reus* is said to be named from the matter that is claimed. Grialius printed *a re quam petitur*, perhaps because the copies vary and *peto* sometimes occurs with two accusatives. But apart from the fact that the similar passages usually cited have uncertain readings, Isidore shortly afterward says *pro re aliqua petitur*, “it is claimed on behalf of some matter,” with the same meaning. To accord with Grialius’ sense, the passage could be corrected to *a re quae petitur*, “from the matter that is claimed,” namely, by the claimant.

**No. 10.** In Vatican Codex 623, which I described in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 93, nos. 19 ff., after this chapter—which ends in silence—the indication is given that some begin book XX at this point, as I explained more fully in the same place, no. 32.

## Chapter XVI

**No. 1. Voluptates.** I showed in my commentary on Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 1125, and *Hymn* VI of the *Peristephanon*, verse 66, that the entertainments of the pagans were called *voluptates*, “pleasures,” in a special sense. [Col. 1020D] Numerous works on spectacles and the various kinds of ancient games can be read in Gronovius’ *Thesaurus of Greek Antiquities*, volumes VII and VIII, and in Graevius’ *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*, volume IX.

**No. 2. Inde Romani accersitos, etc.** See Livy, book VII, chapter 2. Hence they were called *ludii* and *ludiones*, as though *Lydii* and *Lydiones*, “Lydians,” because they performed games.

**No. 3. Idololatria.** I restore *idololatria*, since *idolatria*, the form frequently found in ancient manuscripts and retained by Grialius, may be attributed to copyists.

## Chapter XVIII

**No. 1. Virtus.** It should be observed that *virtus* here means boxing.

## Chapter XIX

**No. 1. Saltus.** *Saltum* comes from *salio*, “I leap,” and from it *saltus*. The other remarks concern the explanation of *saltus*.

## Chapter XX

**Cursus.** It comes from *curro*, “I run.” Some investigate a Hebrew etymology for the verb *curro*.

[Col. 1021A]

## Chapter XXIII

**No. 1. Innituntur.** Grialius’ text has *innitent*, which is meaningless. Perhaps Isidore wrote *innitunt* actively, or perhaps *imminent* should be read.

## Chapter XXV

**No. 1. Agona dici.** It is clear that something must be supplied here, or something similar. Ovid investigates the origin of the *agonalis* festival in book I of the *Fasti*, verses 317 ff. The character of the Greek word indicates a circle, or a place without angles.

## Chapter XXVII

**No. 1. Daemonum cultibus inservire videntur.** Mariana splendidly elucidates this entire subject in his treatise *On Spectacles*, chapter 12, adducing testimonies from Tertullian, Cyprian, Salvian, John Chrysostom, and our Isidore.

**No. 3. Circenses.** No one will deny that they are named from the *circus*. The other explanations which Isidore and others derive from Servius concern learning and erudition, not the true derivation of the name. Compare Vossius, *Etymologies*.

## Chapter XXIX

**No. 1. Ova honori Castoris.** Codex 1, Gothic Toledo, adds several things here, but not in sufficiently orderly form:

> Eggs in honor of Pollux and Castor. It is said that Jove (for *Jupiter*), in the likeness of a swan, had violated Leda, the mother of Castor and Pollux; therefore they think that they were born from an egg, and they attribute to them the likeness of a bird, since they say that they were born from an egg, etc.

## Chapter XXXI

**No. 1. Obeliscum.** The old copies preserve a variant reading that should not be dismissed: “he had harmed Egypt by a violent inundation,” although *Aegypto* is more Latin. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVII, composed the account of the transfer of the obelisk consecrated to the sun from the city of Hieropolis to the Circus Maximus at Rome. I discussed another obelisk of the sun, erected in our own time before the Innocentian Curia, in my commentary on Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 309.

## Chapter XXXIII

**No. 1. Haurit apertum.** Servius, commenting on these words, says: “*Haurit* here means *ferit*, ‘strikes.’” Aspiration was formerly easily neglected, and *aurit* was written for *haurit*. In any event, the etymology of *auriga* is better explained from Festus:

> *Aureax*, “charioteer.” For the *bit* was called *aureas*—perhaps *dicebant*, “they called”—because it was fastened to the horses’ ears; *orias*, by which the mouths were restrained. [Col. 1021C] [Col. 1021C]

**No. 2. Aurigae . . . coloribus.** From this passage Salmasius corrects Tertullian’s words, *aurigis coloribus idololatriam vestierunt*, “they clothed idolatry in the colors of the charioteers.” For this he restores: *aurigas coloribus*, that is, “they clothed idolatry in the charioteers.”

## Chapter XXXIV

**No. 1. Erichthonius.** Servius, commenting on the cited passage of Virgil, and Hyginus, fable 166, recount the myth of Erichthonius.

## Chapter XXXV

**No. 1. Currus.** Some printed editions have: “either because it appears to have many wheels.” But, says Schefferus in *On Vehicles*, book II, chapter 15, chariots had only two wheels, so that Isidore must have slipped. Schefferus therefore had not seen Grialius’ edition, in which *multas* is omitted. See book XX, chapter 12, no. 1.

Salmasius, p. 897 of the *Plinian Exercises*, thinks that the reading should be: “and because it was imposed on all, upon the yoke. The first . . .” Against him Schefferus argues in book II of *On Vehicles*, chapter 10, and himself reads: “and which was imposed on all. First upon the yoke . . .” He explains the matter as follows: the pole was formerly double and continuous—that is, one joined to the other. [Col. 1021D] Clysthenes removed the second pole and added two other horses, tied by a simple bond, to the yoked horses; all four then proceeded abreast in an even line. Previously, in the three-horse team, there was a trace horse, or *funalis*, which did not proceed abreast with the two yoked horses but went ahead of them.

All this fits perfectly with Grialius’ reading, which I retain: “For that double and continuous pole was imposed upon the yoke of four horses.” I do not accept Schefferus’ *injiceretur*. “First upon the yoke . . . he yoked.” The words “and which,” etc., proceed correctly; and since they occur in all the manuscripts, as Schefferus confirms, they should not be changed to “and because,” etc., as Salmasius wished.

**No. 2. Eosque singulos.** Salmasius, in the passage cited, corrected this to *eisque singulos*, “and to each of them,” which is sufficiently plausible. In place of *equo funario*, or *funali*, Ausonius poetically used *funem*, “rope,” in his *Funeral Poem for Phosphorus,” as poets use *habenae*, “reins,” for horses.

[Col. 1022A]

## Chapter XXXVI

**No. 1. Desultores.** Nicolaus Calliachius explains the pagan symbolism of the two-horse and three-horse teams, and so forth, from Isidore and other ancient monuments, in his dissertation *On Circus Games*. In place of *desultores* I would prefer *desultorios*, namely, “horses.” For a *desultor* is one who leaps from one horse to another, as is explained below, chapter 39. Cassiodorus, *Variae* III, letter 51, calls them *equi desultatorii*, “desultory horses”; some instead read *desultorii*.

**No. 3. Volubili ambitu.** Prudentius, in the preface to his poems:

> The pole turns the year while we enjoy the revolving sun.

In *pateficit* the second syllable is lengthened; Lucretius does the same in book I, verse 345, although I do not know whether any other ancient poet does so.

## Chapter XXXVII

**No. 1. Creta . . . judicium.** Salmasius, p. 1073 of the *Plinian Exercises*, criticizes Isidore for ineptly explaining *creta* as “judgment,” since in Greek κριτής (*kritēs*) means “judge.” This practice, however, belonged not only to Isidore but also to other very learned men, who constructed similar allegories on every slight occasion. The turning-post in the circus was marked with chalk (*creta*) so that it could easily be seen [Col. 1022B]; hence the turning-post itself was called *creta*. Pliny discusses it in book VIII, chapter 42:

> When the prescribed course had been completed, to stop at the chalk.

## Chapter XXXVIII

**No. 1. Equites singulares.** Calliachius, already cited, discusses the *equites singulares* and the *desultores* at greater length in his dissertation *On Circus Games*.

## Chapter XXXIX

**No. 1. Desultores.** Hyginus, in the passage cited by Grialius:

> Hence the Romans also . . . on the head, from horse to horse, etc.,

with *de* omitted through ellipsis. See Muncker’s notes on that passage.

## Chapter XLI

**No. 1. Roseos soli . . . roseos aestati.** I think *rosseos*, or *russeos*, should be read, as some read it in Cassiodorus, *Variae* III, letter 51, where he explains the same symbolism of the colors. See Salmasius, p. 98, on Lampridius, and my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* XI of the *Peristephanon*, verse 130:

> He had played with a little blood-red gore.

Add Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, chapter 9, and Sirmond’s note [Col. 1022C] on Sidonius, poem 23. After *densatur*, something appears to be missing concerning the *veneti* and autumn.

**No. 2. Cocco decorantur.** In the republican period the standard was a purple or scarlet tunic, as I said above, chapter 3 of this book, no. 5. *ALBOS ZEPHYRIS*: Horace, book III, ode 7, calls the west winds (*favonios*) white. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 120:

> White among the blessed west winds of the flocks.

## Chapter XLII

**No. 2. Ibi prostarent.** The old copies read *ibi prosternerentur*, “there they might prostitute themselves.” Thus the Vulgate, Jeremiah II:20: “You prostituted yourself as a harlot.” Lipsius likewise reads this in book I of the *Electa*, chapter 11. He says that Isidore is elegantly treating the custom of bringing prostitutes onto the stage. He adds much more on the same subject from Plautus, Livy, Statius, and Tertullian. Other examples could easily be collected if there were time.

It should be observed that among reputable authors *prostibulum* does not mean a brothel but a prostitute who sat or stood before the establishment for the sake of daily and nightly profit; hence she was called *prostibulum* or *prostibula*. [Col. 1022D]

## Chapter XLIII

**No. 1.** Julius Caesar Bulengerus, who wrote a learned work on the theater, confirms from Pollux, book X, chapter 13, the distinction between the orchestra, the *pulpitum*, and the stage: the platform was called the *orchestra*.

## Chapter XLVII

**No. 1. Musici scenici.** They served the theatrical *thymele*, or platform. Properly, the *thymelici* differed from the *scenici*: the *scenici* performed a drama on the stage, while the *thymelici* played musical instruments in the orchestra, or on the platform.

## Chapter XLVIII

**No. 1. Histriones.** Festus says: “They were called *histriones* because they first came from Histria.” Livy, Valerius Maximus, and others more correctly think that both the name and the art of the *histriones* originated with the Etruscans, among whom *hister* meant “dancer.”

## Chapter L

**No. 1. Adolescentes nobiles.** Festus’ reading, “Italian youths,” is more correct, since, according to common opinion, there were no Roman adolescents in the time of Aeneas. Varro teaches that the *Salii* were so called from *salio*, “I leap,” in book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 15.

[Col. 1023A]

## Chapter LI

**No. 2. Quorum odisti auctores.** The old copies have *odire debes*, “you must hate,” which could be retained. The phrase *quorum* should also be noted; I would not readily change it to *cujus*, although that reading occurs in some codices.

In Tertullian, chapter 10 of *On Spectacles*, Pamelius’ edition reads:

> Through the flowing of the body . . . through flowing . . . and lyres . . . they have Mercuries as managers. You must hate, Christian, those whose authors you cannot help hating.

We are warned that certain passages in Tertullian were corrected from Isidore in this book. In Isidore, *fluxu et fluxum*, meaning “softness,” might have been read from Tertullian.

## Chapter LII

**No. 1. Amphitheatrum.** Raderus, in the *Prolegomena to Martial*, chapter 5, offers several observations on the amphitheater that help explain this passage of Isidore.

**No. 2.** Some began book XXIII here, before the chapter on equestrian games. See the *Prolegomena*, chapter 93, no. 32 [Col. 1023B], where other similar divisions of books or titles are indicated.

## Chapter LIV

**No. 1. Retiarius.** I do not see why Grialius remained silent about the name of the very learned man who wrote on the *retiarius*, and so forth. Fabricius lists quite a few authors who wrote on gladiatorial games in *Bibliography*, chapter 18, no. 12: Petrus Faber, Hieronymus Mercurialis, Octavius Ferrarius, Nicolaus Calliachius, Lipsius, Maffei, and others. I have also noted some matters in my commentary on book II of Prudentius’ *Against Symmachus*. I have scarcely any doubt that Chacon’s conjecture is correct: “pursuing the opponent with a point,” as becomes clearer from the following chapter.

## Chapter LV

**No. 1. Feriret reti.** The old copies give *rete*, which could be retained, as in *mare*, *praesepe*, and so forth; I have already discussed this elsewhere.

## Chapter LVI

**No. 1.** *Consecutos* is passive, following the example of Varro as quoted by Priscian, book VIII.

## Chapter LVII

**No. 1. Velites.** More concerning the *velites* is given above, book IX, chapter 3, no. 43.

[Col. 1023C]

## Chapter LVIII

**No. 1. Ferarum pugna.** Raderus discusses the contest of wild beasts in the *Prolegomena to Martial*, chapter 7 and p. 37, and explains the entire beast-fight from Martial and other writers.

## Chapter LIX

**No. 1. Haec quippe spectacula.** These matters, like many others concerning this subject, are taken from Tertullian’s *On Spectacles* and *Apology*, chapter 38, where he says:

> We have nothing to say, see, or hear in common with the madness of the circus, the indecency of the theater, the savagery of the arena, or the vanity of the exercise-ground.

Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, verse 361:

> The circus’ fevered madness.

## Chapter LX

**No. 1. Alea, id est ludus tabulae.** *Tabula* and *alea* are used of the same thing. The Council of Elvira, canon 79: “If any believer has played at dice, that is, at the board,” etc. See Savaron’s note on Sidonius, p. 17.

Becman, p. 523, sought a Greek origin for *alea*; Vossius in *Etymologies* and Senftlebius, *On Ancient Dice*, chapter 2, follow him. In chapter 3 Senftlebius asserts that all later writers followed Isidore’s opinion concerning *alea* and the soldier.

In chapter 11, no. 1, he charges Isidore with error for saying, “the board is played by means of the *pyrgus*,” since one did not play *with* the *pyrgus* but *through* it. We leave this dispute to the grammarians, since the fact itself is clear: Isidore reports in the following chapter that the dice proceeded through the *pyrgus*. [Col. 1023D]

## Chapter LXII

**No. 1. Per calculas.** This appears to be a derivative of *calces*. *Calces* is also found for “piece” in Priscian, book VI. Isidore seems to understand *ordinales viae* as “regular paths,” referring to the ordinary pieces, or those moved in sequence; he discusses them again below, chapter 67.

I therefore do not sufficiently understand what *quasi per calculas* means. For the moment, it occurs to me that *quasi per caulas*, “as though through enclosures,” should be read. Martial calls the various squares of the game board *mandrae*, “enclosures,” in book VII, epigram 71:

> Shut up among enclosures with a glass thief.

The author of the *Panegyric to Piso*, falsely attributed to Lucan, who gives an extensive description of the game of pieces [Col. 1024A], says at verse 191:

> So that, swift, it may break through the shattered ranks of the enclosure.

*Mand­ra* and *caula* have the same meaning.

## Chapter LXIII

**No. 1. Tesserae.** Andreas Senftlebius, *On Ancient Dice*, chapter 5, no. 1, asserts that Isidore suffered a lapse of memory and frequently confused the things he describes, such as *tesserae* with *tali*, and the latter with the former.

* Tali* and *tesserae* did differ. *Tesserae* were square on every side; *tali*, although they had six sides, could rest on only four, because the remaining two were curved. But since the throw from the *pyrgus* into the receptacle was similar in both games, writers sometimes use one term for the other.

Nor is it clear that Isidore confused *tesserae* with *tali*: he always speaks of *tesserae* and never mentions *tali*. J. A. Ernst explains the difference between *tali* and *tesserae* in *Ciceronian Key*, under *Talus*. The number of pieces also differed: four *tali* were normally used in play, whereas there were generally two *tesserae*, at most three. [Col. 1024B]

## Chapter LXIV

**No. 1. Aleatores.** Senftlebius, in the passage cited, chapter 5, prints the entire chapter and adds: “Laugh at whatever nonsense there is in the work of the man from Seville. Which gambler was concerned with anything other than acquiring profit?” Senftlebius himself deserves laughter. Who taught him that everyone who played dice thought about acquiring profit? Or that those who did think about profit did not admit some allegory in the game itself?

Compare what Isidore explains from Cassiodorus and others in chapters 36 ff. concerning horses, horsemen, foot soldiers, and the colors of horses—things invented by the pagans to excuse their vanities.

Salmasius, p. 245, verse 36, on Flavius Vopiscus, observes that Isidore calls the figures in the dice game *viae*, “paths,” which the Greeks call ὁδόν (*hodon*), and an old epigram calls it “the players’ track” (*scriptorum tramitem*)—namely, the lines along which the pieces ran.

## Chapter LXV

**No. 1. De vocabulis tesserarum.** Senftlebius, in the cited work, chapter 5, criticizes Isidore for placing *quinio* among the *tali*, contrary to Julius Pollux. [Col. 1024C]

But there is no explicit mention here of *tali*, and the title of the chapter clearly names *tesserae*. The names of the throws that Isidore explains can apply both to *tesserae* and to *tali*; indeed, as he himself observes, the terminology varied according to period.

Senftlebius, in the cited work, chapter 4, no. 10, notes that the sides of the *tali*, which others call *supina* and *plana*, are called by Isidore *suppi* and *plani*. Festus says: “The ancients called *suppum* what we now call *supinum*.” On these words Scaliger notes that the side of the gaming die called ὕπτιον (*hyption*), “supine,” was called *suppum* when the *talus* fell so that this side was uppermost.

What Isidore calls *trio* and *quatrio*, others call *ternio* and *quaternio*. Octavius Ferrarius, book I of the *Electa*, chapter 16, teaches that *Venus* was the throw in which all four *tali* fell with different faces showing; *senio* was the throw in which all the *tali* fell on their concave side, or two on the convex and two on the concave side; and *canicula* was the throw in which all four *tali* stood upright.

[Col. 1024D]

## Chapter LXVI

**No. 1. Componitur, etc.** Martial, book XIV, epigram 16:

> The wicked hand seeks to throw the dice once they have been arranged.

For *voluerit*, perhaps *voluerint* should be read.

## Chapter LXVII

**No. 1. Calculi partim, etc.** Senftlebius, who had in a certain sense made it his project to scold Isidore, says in the cited work, chapter 11, no. 11: “At last Isidore is occasionally correct, and he explains the doctrine contained in this chapter.”

Salmasius, p. 246, verse 19, on Flavius Vopiscus, reports that everything Isidore writes about regular, wandering, and impetuous pieces is to be referred to *latrunculi*. Very learned men wrongly refer these matters to the game of *duodecim scripta*, which the Spaniards call *damas*.

*Calculi inciti* are *scacco matto*, “checkmate.” Isidore’s Glossary has: “*Mattum*, wet,” etc. Cicero, letter 12 of book XVI to Atticus: “And the *via matta*.” The manuscripts consistently read this, as Salmasius testifies. The printed editions have *via inepta*, “foolish path.”

From *calculi inciti* [Col. 1025A] arose the proverb *ad incitas redigi*, “to be reduced to extremity,” that is, to the lines beyond which the pieces could not move at all. Although Charisius, book I, teaches that *incitas* has only one case, like *inficias* and *suppetias*, the expression *ad incita redigi* is also found, meaning “to be reduced to places”; and the boundaries beyond which one could no longer advance were called *inciti*.

Thus *incitus*, like several similar words, has two contrary meanings: it is used for “agitated” or “impetuous,” and, from the privative *in-*, for “motionless.” Compare the Isidorian Glossary, under *Incitae*, with the notes.

## Chapter LXVIII

**No. 1. Interdicta legibus.** Not only by ecclesiastical laws but also by civil laws. See, among others, Ferdinand Mendoza on the Council of Elvira in Labbe, volume I, pp. 1361 ff.

## Chapter LXIX

**No. 1. Pila.** On the game of ball, see Hieronymus Mercurialis, Petrus Faber, Octavius Ferrarius, Vossius, and others listed by Fabricius, *Bibliography*, chapter 22, no. 6.

*Sphaera* is a Greek word, and Becman is engaged in investigating its Hebrew origin. Like many other things, Isidore has preserved for us both the name and two verses [Col. 1025B] of Dorcatius, whom Fabricius admits in *Bibliotheca medii aevi* to have been otherwise unknown to him; there he transcribes the verses inaccurately from some old edition.

**No. 2.** Pliny, book VII, chapter 56, distinguishes four kinds of balls: the *trigon*, the *paganica*, the *follis*, and the *harpastum*. The *pila arenata*, “sand ball,” is perhaps the one called *harpastum*. Martial, book IV, epigram 19:

> Whether you rub the slow *ceroma* and the warm *trigon*,  
> Or seize the dusty *harpasta* in your hand.

In the game of *harpastum*, victory belonged to the side that drove the *harpastum* beyond the boundaries of the opposing side. Some have *qui pilam* instead of *qui pila*; I would prefer *qui illam*, “those who did that.” That is, those who fouled in the game of ball offered their shin to be struck.

# Book Nineteen

## Chapter One

**No. 1. De navibus.** Writers on the naval affairs of the ancients may be consulted in the *Thesaurus of Greek Antiquities* by Gronovius and the *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities* by Graevius. [Col. 1025C]

**No. 2.** *Faxo* for *fecero* or *fecerim*, “I shall have done” or “I may have done,” is found in many reputable authors, just as *faxim* is used for *faciam*, “I shall do.”

**No. 3. Nauclerus.** The etymology of *nauclerus* may perhaps indicate the nature of the thing rather than the true origin of the word. *Nauclerus* could come from *navicularius*, just as *nauta* comes from *navita*. Nevertheless, some maintain that Isidore’s etymology is genuine. See Becman, p. 726, and Savaron on Sidonius, book VI, letter 8. This is supported by the fact that in Greek it is likewise ναύκληρος (*nauklēros*, “ship-owner”).

**No. 4. Quasi cohibernator.** Our critics will certainly not accept this etymology, except insofar as it explains some part of the ship’s helmsman’s function. Many think that in Laberius *gubernium* should be understood not as “helmsman” but as “steering.” In the *Digest*, some prefer *archigubernus* to *archigubernius*. The verb cited by Isidore is repeated by Papias and occurs in the ancient Glossaries; I think it was taken from no other source than Isidore himself. [Col. 1025D]

**No. 5. Navita.** Festus contradicts Servius and Isidore. From Festus’ view, supplemented by Fulvius Ursinus, one may infer:

> According to uncorrupted usage, they were called *navitae* whom we now call *nautae*.

**No. 8. Gnavum.** Grialius retained *gnavum* in the text, although in the note he appears to prefer *navum*. Many indeed write *navum* for *gnavum*; nevertheless, *gnavus* may be retained, even while accepting Isidore’s etymology, or saying with Festus that *navum* is named from the speed of ships. In Isidore I would prefer *noverit* for *novit*.

**No. 9. Rates primum, etc.** Quintilian, book I, chapter 2:

> If no one had achieved more than the man he followed, we would still be sailing on rafts.

Servius, on *Aeneid* I, verse 47:

> *Rates*: improperly used for ships . . .

Hence small boats with oars are called *ratiariae*.

**No. 10. Non transibit.** The Vulgate reads:

> Nor shall a great trireme pass beyond it.

*Trieris* is a Greek word; in Latin the form is *triremis*. *Trieris* occurs in many old inscriptions, but not in reputable Latin authors except in one or two passages where the reading varies between *trieris* and *triremis*. [Col. 1026A]

**No. 12. Liburnae.** Isaac Vossius published a dissertation on the construction of triremes and Liburnian ships.

**No. 13. Rostratae.** Mention of beaked ships occurs frequently in ancient writers. The *rostra* were generally three-pronged, which is why poets often call bronze tridents *tridentia*. Fabrettus gives an image of a trident-shaped *rostrum* in chapter 4 of *On Trajan’s Column*, p. 115. Schwarzius discusses this subject at greater length in his dissertation *On the Rostra of the Roman Forum*.

### Note 14

Concerning *dromones* there is an old gloss, cited in the note to Book XII, chapter 1, no. 36, where the etymology of *dromon* is less suitably derived from *dromedarii*. The noun *musculus*, used for a ship, is missing from the Lexicons. Ducange drew this word from ancient glossaries and observes that, among other terms for vessels, it occurs in the Tironian notes. [Col. 1026B]

### Note 15

“Whence also *calones*.” In Vulcanius and other old copies one reads: “Whence also *calones*, small boats that carry wood for the soldiers.” Pignorius, p. 120 and following, in his work *On Slaves*, where he discusses *calones* and *caculi*, emended Isidore’s corrupt text—“defective,” as he says, through no fault of Isidore himself—in this way: “Whence also *calones* and *caculae*, who carry wood, etc.” This is a sufficiently judicious conjecture. He observes that the wood consisted of poles and clubs. Juvencus, Book IV, verse 514:

> Some with drawn swords, others trusting in the weight of a club.

Compare chapter 34 of this book, nos. 2 and 6.

### Note 16

*Ancyromagi.* This word, as I think, occurs in ancient glossaries derived from Isidore, but it is written—or corrupted—in several forms: *anchiromagus*, *anquiromagus*, *anguiromagus*, *angromagus*. Compare Ducange.

### Note 17

“Corruptly *baselum*.” Hence the Spaniards call it *baxel*. Perhaps Isidore wrote *pictis phaselis*, for the verse is Virgil’s:

> And in painted *phaseli* he is carried around his own fields. [Col. 1026C]

Achilles Statius insists that *phasellus* should be written with double *l*, while others oppose him, as Vulpius explains in his note to Catullus, p. 18.

### Note 18

“*Scapha*, which is κατασκοπος (*kataskopos*, ‘watch-boat’).” Johann Scheffer, Book II of *On Naval Warfare*, chapter 2, citing glosses on the Old Testament mentioned by Heinsius in *Sacred Exercises*, reports the following: “A *scapha*, or *catascopus*, is a light boat made of wickerwork and covered with raw hide.”

### Note 19

“*Barca*.” Saint Paulinus of Nola, poem 21, formerly 13, to Cytherius, verse 95:

> So that presently the boat might serve as a healthy means of rescue  
> for the survivor of the wrecked stern.

You will not easily find other earlier writers who speak of a *barca*. The word itself passed into the vernacular languages.

### Note 20

“*Paro*.” Isidore preserved for us these verses of Cicero, which do not survive elsewhere. Some think that *parones* were named from the island of Paros. [Col. 1026D]

### Note 21

“*Myoparo*.” Some hold that *myoparones* did not differ in form from *phaseli*. I cannot discover which history Isidore is citing at this point. I restore *contecta crudo*, etc., in place of *contexta*. See note 26.

### Note 22

“*Celoces*.” In Ennius’s verse some incorrectly read *celonis* instead of *celocis*. Scheffer, *On Naval Warfare*, Book II, chapter 2, explains *biremes* and *triremes* not as vessels with two or three banks of oars, but as vessels with two or three oars. Others say that the *celoce* was a ship steered either by one oar, or by several, but in such a way that each man handled a single oar.

### Note 24

“*Hippagogus*.” Grialius’s text had *hippopagus*; in the note it correctly had *hippagogus*. Ships of this kind were called either *hippagogi*, *hippagi*, or *hippagines*. Concerning the *pontonium*, Scheffer, Book IV of *On Naval Warfare*, chapter 1, thinks the reading should be: “It can advance only by being towed.” The ship was secured by a rope whose ends, extending to both banks, were fastened to stakes, so that, when the rope was pulled, the ship followed—as we see done even today. Accordingly, Isidore’s words that follow, “Hence also a crossing,” etc., should be understood as referring to this method, although Servius, from whom Isidore took them, applied those words to another matter. [Col. 1027A]

### Note 25

“*Lembus … caupilus*.” In some copies of Isidore *limbus* is written, either because it derives from the Greek λίαν (*lian*, “very much”), as Scheffer says in the cited work, Book II, chapter 2, or rather because in manuscripts *e* and *i* are frequently confused. The same Scheffer thinks that *capulus* should be read, on the evidence of Vulcanius’s Arabic-Latin glosses: “*Lembus*, etc.” In Gellius some read *caupuli*, others *capuli*, and others *capulici*. Perhaps this last form is what Grialius intended to write in his note.

### Note 26

“*Carabus … portemia*.” After Forcellinus had quoted Isidore’s words concerning the *carabus*, he added: “But he offers no example from a competent Latin author bearing on this matter.” Yet how many works of the ancient authors whom Isidore used have perished—even where he names no author? Concerning the *carabus*, see above, no. 18, Rosweyd’s *Onomasticon*, [Col. 1027B] and Ducange. Before Isidore, Saint Gregory the Great also used the same word.

Some printed editions give, in Isidore, *contexta crudo corio*, as they do also in no. 21 concerning the *myoparo*. Grialius has *contecta* here and *contexta* in no. 21, but in both places *contecta* should be read. For *portemia*, Martini thought that *porthmium* should be written, on the basis of Hesychius. Papias retained *portemia* with Isidore. In the supplement to Ducange it is read with the same meaning as *portenna*, from Nicolaus Specialis. Semler conjectured *Scythici* or *Sarmatici generis*, because in the printed editions he found *Syriatici generis*. See his notes to Isidore’s Glossary.

### Note 27

“*Caudicae*.” Perhaps *caudiceae* would be more correct, as some read it in Gellius, Book X, chapter 25.

## Chapter II

### Note 1

“*Cumba*.” Rosweyd, in his *Onomasticon*, under *Cuba*, quotes from the manuscript Camberon Glossary: “*Cuba* is called the end of a ship because it rests upon the waters. A *cumba*, however, is a litter, from lying down.” Latins more often write *cymba*, from the Greek κύμος (*kymos*), “a hollow recess.”

[Col. 1027C]

### Note 3

“*Columbaria*.” Festus, under the word *Navalis*, says: “Either because the parts of a ship called *columbaria* are those by which they row,” etc.

### Note 4

“*Agea*.” Scheffer, *On Naval Warfare*, Book I, chapter 6, orders Isidore’s text to be emended as follows: “*Agearia* are places in a ship through which the encourager approaches the rowers,” from a manuscript Latin-German glossary: “*Agiaria* are certain places in ships, through which the encourager approaches by the oars,” which seems to have been taken from Isidore, as many other passages were.

But Festus supports our reading. Some read Ennius’s verse, either from Isidore’s manuscripts or by conjecture, in different ways:

> Placing many things on the deck, and the long *agea* is filled;

or:

> He places many things on the deck, and the long *agea* is filled.

Scaliger, in his note to Festus:

> Placing many things on the deck, and bridges, and the long *agea* is filled.

Cerda, in *Sacred Adversaria*, chapter 173, no. 6, cites from an old glossary, relevant to this matter: “*Egeator*, the encourager of a ship.” [Col. 1027D]

### Note 6

“*Tonsae*.” Servius’s words on Aeneid VII, verse 28, are these: “*TONSAE*: Oars, so called from striking away the waves, just as *tonsores* are so called from cutting and striking away the hair.” Scheffer, in the cited work, Book II, chapter 5, emended or supplemented Isidore’s words as follows: “*REMI*, from removing, and *TONSAE*, from cutting and striking away the waves, just as *tonsores*, etc.”

### Note 7

“*Palmula*.” Pollux explains precisely what a *palmula* is in the *Onomasticon*, Book I, chapter 9. *Antenna* is written more frequently than *antemna*, whatever the etymology may be.

### Note 8

“*Maleolis*.” Grialius, along with others, published *malleolis*; but it seems that *maleolis* should be written, with Scheffer, in the cited work, Book II, chapter 5, from the resemblance to *mali* or apples. For the *malus*, so that it could be raised more easily together with the sails, had certain circular pieces of wood wrapped around it, shaped like apples. Servius is relevant here; Isidore copied his words, except that, as Grialius observes, Isidore wrote *maleolis* instead of *malis*.

[Col. 1028A]

### Note 9

“*Cinna: Lucida*.” Nonius, chapter 15, no. 28, reports the following verse of Catullus of Verona, as he says:

> Brightly shine the *carchesia* of the highest mast.

### Note 10

“*Trochleae*.” Pollux, in the *Onomasticon*, vol. II, p. 1117, discusses the *trurocheae* of the ancients. An example of them can be seen in certain wells in Italy for raising water. Vitruvius, Book X, chapter 2, explains that a pulley was called a *rechamus*.

### Note 13

“*Portisculus*.” Becman, p. 866, following Perottus and others, derives *portisculus* or *porticulus* from *portus*, “harbor.” The usual spelling is *portisculus*, and I retain it, although Grialius gives *porticulus*.

### Note 14

“*Tonsilla*.” In Ennius’s verse I would think that *configunt littore aduncas* should be read. Festus: “A *tonsilla* is a stake brought to a point and shod with a tip, which is driven into the shore for the purpose of mooring a ship.” He gives examples from Accius and Pacuvius. In place of *delatus*, *dolatus* seems to be the correct reading.

[Col. 1028B]

### Note 15

“*Ancora*.” In the time of Servius and Isidore, the custom perhaps prevailed of writing *anchora* with an aspiration. Now, certainly, *ancora* is normally written, which is more correct and should be retained.

## Chapter III

### Note 3

“*Artemon*.” Baïf, *On Naval Matters*, p. 121, thinks that the *artemon* was the larger sail of a ship. Scheffer, on the contrary, agrees with Isidore that it was a small sail; he correctly confirms this by the testimony of Labeo, *Digest*, Book L, title 16, law 242. Labeo and Isidore also use *artemon* in the nominative case above, but in this passage the copies had *artemo*. I wished to change it to *artemon*, as it is also said in Greek.

### Note 4

“In most copies there is *siparum*; indeed, some write it in this way from the Greek σίφαρος (*sipharos*). But the common spelling is *supparum* or *supparus*. Some, following Festus, identify *supparum* with the *dolon*, discussed in no. 3. Others, with Isidore, think that the foot of a sail is the sail’s extreme corner; and perhaps that name was first given to the sail’s farthest corner, then to the rope by which the sail is stretched and to which its extreme corner is attached. The rope to which the foot of the sail is fastened is called *propes* by Isidore in the next chapter, no. 3.

## Chapter IV

### Note 1

Servius’s words on Aeneid I, verse 731, are:

> *FUNALIA*: These are within wax; they are called from the cords which, before the use of papyrus, our ancestors encased in wax before using them. Hence they are also called *funera*.

### Note 2

“*Cucurbas*.” Papias, Ugutio, and John of Genoa call them *curculiae*. In an Arabic-Latin glossary there is *corcuba*, “a thong.” The same word seems to occur in Vegetius, Book II of *Veterinary Medicine*, chapter 33, and in the Emperor Leo, Book and title XI of the Justinian Code, where *curcuma* or *curcumia* is usually read for a bridle and halter.

### Note 3

“*Si veli*.” In Turpilius’s verse others have *si velis*, “if you wish,” or *sinistrum*, “left.”

### Note 5

“*Saphon*.” Fabricius, in Part 3 of his *History of His Library*, reports from Crenius that in this passage Isidore has *Saphon* instead of *Safon* or *Savon*, which is a river of Campania between the city of Sinuessa and the river Vulturnus, now called the Saone. But Isidore certainly understood *saphon* as a rope, and nothing in Caecilius’s verse suggests that the subject is a river.

[Col. 1028D]

### Note 6

“*Prymnesium*.” In ancient copies *prosnestium* was incorrectly read for *prymnesium*, as Paulus Leopardus already observed long ago in Book I of his *Emendations*, chapter 18.

### Note 7

“*Anquina*.” Nonius, chapter 13, no. 16, quotes Lucilius:

> For the rope is quickly cut, and the *anquina* loosened.

Some think that *anguina* or *angina* should be read. In some editions of Ponium [reading uncertain] there is *ancora soluta*, “the anchor loosened.”

### Note 8

“*Valgius*.” A very celebrated poet of the Augustan age, about whom Vulpius says much, among others, in his note to Tibullus, Book IV, poem 1, verse 180:

> No other is closer to eternal Homer than Valgius.

[Col. 1029A]

### Note 10

“*Catapiratem*.” Vulcanius notes as follows. In an old manuscript it reads:

> This *cataparatem* I give to the boy; let him bring out the greased  
> lump of lead, and the skein of thread.

In another old manuscript:

> This *catafloratem* the boy, at the same time, brings out …  
> the rough lump of lead and the skein of thread.

In another copy:

> This *cataporatem* the boy brings out at the same time: the greased  
> lump of lead …

Others read:

> This *catapiratem* the boy should bring out at the same time, the hook,  
> a little piece of lead, *rodus* (“unrefined bronze”), and the thread’s *metaxa*.

*Rodus* is the same as *raudus* or *rudus*. Festus, under *rodus*, says: “The common people used the word *rodus* not only for unfinished bronze, as Lucilius does when he says:

> A little piece of lead, unrefined bronze, and the *metaxa* of thread.

In place of *metaxam*, some write *mataxam*, as Grialius also published it. The Italians call a ball or skein of thread *matassa*, something gathered and wound together; Isidore discusses it below, in chapter 29. In Lucilius’s verse some understand *mataxam* as a small cord [Col. 1029B] or thread.

### Note 4

“*Retes … conopeum*.” It would be better to have *retis* in the nominative case, which Priscian recognizes. *Conopeum* is so called because the Greeks call gnats κώνωπες (*kōnōpes*), not from the Egyptian city Canopus, as Isidore suggests.

## Chapter VI

### Note 1

“On account, of course, of the strength of the work.” Grialius interprets this as referring to an ironworker. But it really seems to belong to the explanation of the word *faber*: a *faber* is every craftsman who makes something from any harder and stronger material, such as a goldsmith or a carpenter. Among the earlier authors, the name *faber* was no more proper to an ironworker than to other craftsmen. Those who made something from wax, gypsum, or a similar material were called *plastae*.

### Note 3

“It also has a medicinal use.” This half-verse may perhaps have been formed accidentally.

### Note 5

“*Fabrica*.” Properly, this is the workshop of any craftsman. Isidore uses it for the workshop of an ironworker, just as above he uses *faber* for an ironworker.

### Note 6

“*Favilta*.” Barth, Book XLII of his *Adversaria*, chapter 17, observes that Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 10, used *favilla* for any fine powder, and that a poet should by no means be bound by the decisions of grammarians, who define *favillae* as sparks left behind by fire, as Servius does, especially in his note on Aeneid III. Concerning our Isidore he adds:

> Isidore transcribed those very words of Servius in Book XIX, chapter 6, of the *Etymologies*, unless someone inserted them from Servius’s commentary into the Virgilian glosses, as the scholiasts of a later age are accustomed to copy Isidore word for word. In this matter even very learned men plainly wrong him when they accuse him of plagiarism, although he himself drew upon earlier materials in remarkable ways.

Thus, while many think that Isidore was expanded from earlier sources, Barth suspects that many passages from Isidore’s commentaries entered the books of earlier authors. One thing is certain: Isidore should not be accused of plagiarism, even when it is clear that he benefited from the commentaries of earlier authors. He himself testifies to this in his preface.

### Note 7

“But charcoal, which lacks flame.” This is no longer Servius’s comment on the cited passage of Book XI, verse 788. Some hold that *carbo* derives from the Greek κάρφος (*karphos*), “a dry fragment.” It should be observed that a piece of wood burned by fire is also called *carbo*, “charcoal.”

## Chapter VII

### Note 1

“*Tudes*.” Grialius printed *tudis* in the text and *tudes* in the note, the latter being preferable; for the form is *tudes, tuditis*. Festus: “*Tudites* are hammers, so called from *tundere*, ‘to pound.’”

### Note 2

“*Multorum magnis*.” Barth, Book XXVII of his *Adversaria*, chapter 2, thinks that the second verse of Lucilius may be an anapaest following a hexameter, for Lucilius’s satires were not written exclusively in hexameters. In a certain old book he found it written as follows:

> He pounds with many great blows.

Some report it as:

> He pounds with the great blows of many.

Others attempt to complete the hexameter by adding something.

### Note 4

“*Limum lene est*.” *Limus* as an adjective means “oblique” or “transverse”; *limus* as a noun is the softer mud that is usually carried along by water. Isidore may perhaps be speaking of this. I showed in my commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 9, verse 51, that the funerary inscription of Sergius—or Servius—of Pola, or, as Grialius writes, of Sertius, is apocryphal and was fabricated only in the fifteenth century.

## Chapter VIII

### Note 1

“*Structores*.” In *Various Works on Dedication under the Adze*, p. 270, and note 328, it is said that *structores* should be corrected to *instructores* in Isidore; but Grialius had printed *structores* long before.

### Note 2

“*Machiones*.” Barth, Book XI of his *Adversaria*, chapter 27, asserts that in old manuscripts of Isidore he found *mationes* instead of *machiones*, as the common editions give it. He himself thinks that *machinones* should be read and interprets it as referring to those who climbed any sort of machines. Becman, p. 637, says that Isidore means the Gallic *massones*, or masons, who were formerly called *machinones* from *machina*, and later *machiones*, with the Spanish and French pronunciation in which a thick *ch* has the value of *s*.

## Chapter X

### Note 1

“*Instaurare*.” Varro and Festus also derive it from *instar*, “likeness” or “model.” [Col. 1030B]

### Note 3

“*Albus, tiburtinus, columbinus, fluviatilis, spongia, rubrus*.” Grialius punctuates it as follows: “white, Tiburtine dove-colored, river-derived”; other printed editions do the same, except that they have *fluvialis* instead of *fluviatilis*. It would seem better to read: “white, Tiburtine, dove-colored, river-derived, or *fluvialis*,” following Palladius, Book I, title 10:

> We shall also burn lime from hard white stone, or Tiburtine stone, or river dove-colored stone, or red stone, or sponge stone, etc.

Yet it is clear from what follows that Isidore distinguishes not only Tiburtine stone from dove-colored stone, but both of them from river stone.

### Note 5

“*Vapore*.” That is, “by fire”; Prudentius and many others use *vapor* for fire.

### Note 6

“*Mortalitate et mollitie*.” Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 22, in the more recent corrected editions, has *mortalitate materiae*, “by the perishability of the material.” But Isidore seems to have read something else.

### Note 7

“*Arenatius*.” Perhaps *arenaceus*, for Pliny uses this adjective.

### Note 8

“*Piperinus conchleatius*.” As far as I know, these are not recorded by others. In place of *conchteatius*, perhaps *cochleatus* should be read; but elsewhere also, in Isidore’s manuscripts, *conchlea* is found for *cochlea*.

### Note 11

“*Spongia*.” In the text Grialius wrote *sfungia*, and in the note *sphungia*. I restored *spongia*, as in Book XII, chapter 6, no. 60.

### Note 14

“*Domorum, fictilium operum*.” In some copies these words are presented as follows:

> Of houses and earthen works for walls and foundations, which are fitted to roofs with baked bricks, curved tiles, and flat tiles.

In others the punctuation is:

> Of houses. Earthen works for walls and foundations are fitted, with baked bricks, curved tiles, and flat tiles, to roofs.

### Note 20

“*Gratissimus*.” That is, “stone.” Or read *gratissimum*.

## Chapter XIV

### Note 1

“*Lithostrota sunt elaborata arte picturae*.” Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1215, asserts that Isidore confuses the ancient *camerae*, in which there were plaster crowns, with the *camerae* of later times, that is, true coffered ceilings, in which there was no gypsum. But he does not explain why, in true coffered ceilings, coffers could not have been formed with gypsum. Learned discussions of ancient painting, sculpture, modeling, engraving, and related subjects have been collected in Gronovius’s *Treasury of Greek Antiquities* and Graevius’s *Roman Antiquities*, to say nothing of the authors whom Fabricius mentions in his *Bibliography*.

## Chapter XVII

### Note 3

“*Sinopis*, etc.” From Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 6.

### Note 4

“*Pontica*.” The red pigment itself was called *Pontic sinopis*.

### Note 5
