“*Syricum*.” Salmasius, p. 1157 of his *Plinian Exercises*, says that Isidore is wrongly speculating in claiming that *Syricum* was so called from the Syrian Phoenicians. He himself thinks that it was called *Syricum* from the island of Syros, just as Pherecydes is called Syrus from the same island. Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 7 from the middle onward, and Book XXXV, chapter 6 from the middle onward, discusses the color *Syricum*. Hardouin criticizes those who, against the manuscripts, read *Scyricum* in Pliny.

It should be noted that Isidore says, “He writes the headings of books in *Syricum*.” On this ancient custom, one should consult those who have written on diplomatics and on the art of identifying manuscripts. [Col. 1031A]

### Note 6

“*Saepe fit aut sinopide*.” It would be clearer to read: “It is often made from sinopis mixed with sandyx.”

### Note 7

“*Minium*.” Concerning the river Minius, see Book XIII, chapter 21, no. 32.

### Note 8

“*A dracone*.” Perhaps because the Egyptians called the dragon *Kneh*. Others investigate a Hebrew origin. There are several kinds of *cinnabaris*: one is mineral, another artificial, made from sulfur and quicksilver. See Matthioli’s note on Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 59. Another kind of cinnabar exudes from trees in India like gum, after the bark has first been cut. Many believe that the story of a kind of cinnabar produced from a dragon and an elephant (*barro*) is fabulous. There is a learned dissertation on the origin of the word *cinnabaris* by Johann Philipp Casel, who admirably illuminates this passage of Isidore.

### Note 13

“*Exusta rubrica*.” Perhaps the reading should be: “Ochre is also made from burned red pigment.” Grialius prefers the opposite arrangement.

### Note 14

“*Vestoriani*.” Hardouin likewise insists that *vestorianum* should be read in Pliny.

### Note 15

“*Rubeaque*.” In Grialius and in other printed editions and manuscripts one reads *rubeaque*; I restored *rubiaque*, for that is how it is written, although in manuscripts *i* is sometimes changed into *e*.

[Col. 1031B]

### Note 19

“*Usta*.” Vitruvius discusses *usta* in much the same way in Book VII, chapter 11.

### Note 21

“*Est enim*.” Isidore often uses *enim*, “for,” in place of *autem*, “however,” a usage also found in other authors.

### Note 22

“*Annulare*.” Grialius had punctuated it as follows: “*Annulare*, which they call white, is that with which …”

### Note 23

“*Chalcanthum*.” In an old undated edition it reads:

> *Chalcanthum* is so called because it is the *thymum* of lime, that is, its flower; hence among the Latins it is also called the flower of bronze.

This variant reading was also recorded by Vulcanius. In Vatican Codex 623, discussed in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 93, no. 34, the same explanation is given for the word *chalcanthum*.

## Chapter XVIII

### Note 2

“*Prava*.” Properly, *pravus* means “distorted” or “not straight”; hence it is used for “vicious” and “wicked.”

### Note 3

“*Martellus, machina*.” Concerning *martellus*, see chapter 7, no. 2; concerning *machina*, chapter 8, no. 2, of this book. In my old edition the passage is arranged as follows:

> A *martellus* is called a medium-sized hammer by diminutive formation. *Machines* are so called from the machines on which they stand because of the height of the walls.

## Chapter XIX

### Note 2

In Papias, Ugutio, John of Genoa, and the old glossaries—which for the most part draw from Isidore—in place of *sarcitector* one also finds *sartitector* or *sartatector*, as though derived from *sarta tecta*, “repaired and roofed,” or, as it was called in a later age, *sartatectum*.

### Note 3

“*Ellychnium*.” Book XVII, chapter 6, no. 25, reports this same matter; there I printed *ellychnium* instead of *lychnum*, as others have it, or *lycnium*, as Grialius has it here.

### Note 4

“*Materia*.” From *materia* the Spaniards retain the word *madera* for “wood,” as, I think, I said elsewhere.

### Note 6

“*Tholus … cuplae … luctantes*.” A round building was also called a *tholus*; concerning this, see Rosweyd in his *Onomasticon*. Papias and John of Genoa repeat almost the same account of *cupla*. In Latin, *luctantes* are usually called *cantherii* or *capreoli*.

[Col. 1031D]

### Note 7

“*Scindulae … epigri*.” Those who write *scandulae* derive the word from *scandere*, “to climb.” Stewechius, in his note on Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, Book II, chapter 23, prefers the spelling *scindula* and the etymology given by Isidore. In Augustine, Palladius, and Seneca the Philosopher, some read *epiuri*, others *epigri*, and others still read it differently. In Augustine’s words cited by Grialius, *epigri* are distinguished from *clavi*, just as wooden nails are distinguished from iron nails. Gataker, Book II of his *Miscellaneous Adversaria*, chapter 19, thinks that both words, *epigri* and *epiuri*, are genuine. Bochart’s *Canaan*, Book I, chapter 38, should be consulted for an explanation of this matter. See also Isidore’s Glossary with notes.

### Note 9

“*A stridore*.” Lucretius, Book II, verse 410:

> The harsh horror of the shrieking saw.

Hyginus and other authors of the later period likewise use the verb *exsulo* actively.

### Note 11

“*Securis … dolabra … dextralis*.” In the *Various Works on Dedication under the Adze*, with Mazochius’s notes, pp. 185 and following, there is a fuller discussion of the etymology of *securis* and of this passage of Isidore, which I reproduce here.

When Isidore says that the *securis* is sharp on one side and digging on the other, he may be describing the axe of his own age; or rather, the words “digging on the other side” should be excluded. Isidore likewise seems to be speaking of his own age when he identifies the *dolabra* and the *securis* with Hesychius and the glossaries.

The passage could be arranged as follows:

> As though a half-axe; for it is sharp on one side. This also occurs in …

And:

> This is also a *dolabra*, because it has two blades: it is sharp on one side and digging on the other. For a simple *securis* is *dextralis* (“right-handed”), because it is suited to the right hand.

The *dolabra*, however, should be thought to derive not from *labra*, “blades” or “lips,” but from *dolus*, “guile.” These observations are drawn largely from the cited work.

It is indeed a plausible conjecture that scribes added to *securis* the words “digging on the other side,” since this is proper to the *dolabra*. But I do not agree that the passage should continue, “For a simple *securis* is *dextralis*.” Barth, Book I of his *Adversaria*, chapter 4, says: “*Dextrales* are axes that can be wielded with one hand,” as Isidore explains them; and this word still survives among the Spaniards, whose language is exceptionally conservative in retaining Latin. [Col. 1032B]

Grialius printed *reservavit* in the text, along with others; in the note he prefers *servavit*.

### Note 12

“*Ab hastulis*.” Some correct this to *ab assulis*, but *ab astulis* or *ab hastulis* is sound. See Book XVII, chapter 6, no. 26.

### Note 15

“*Scobina*, so called because by rubbing it produces *scoben* (sawdust). *Cantherium* … *Galla* … *Guvia* …” In the printed editions the passage is corrupt: “*Scophina*, so called because by adhering it makes a *scophem*.” Salmasius corrected the passage, p. 1077 of his *Plinian Exercises*, and Mariettus indicated the correction, as I said in my note to Prudentius, Book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 439, “the file wearing away.”

In Vatican Codex 623, discussed in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 93, after *faciat* there is: “*Canterium, Gubia*.” Immediately afterward: “Here begins Book XXVII, according to some.”

## Chapter XX

### Note 1

“*Ordisse*.” Perhaps Isidore wrote *ordiri*, that is, “to show how to begin and to color.”

## Chapter XXI

### Note 1

“*Camisia vocatur*.” The same name passed into the vernacular languages. See Ferrarius, *On Clothing*, Book III, chapter 5, Ducange, and the following chapter, no. 29.

### Note 3

“*Pileum*.” It is also called *pileus*. In place of *galeriam*, perhaps *galerium* or *galeram* should be read; for *galera* was used in antiquity for *galerus*. See chapter 30 of this book, no. 5.

## Chapter XXII

### Note 1

“*Tegmen*.” By syncope it is derived from *tegumen* or *tegimen*; critics prefer the latter spelling, while *tegumen* has the appearance of greater antiquity. *Indumentum* is indeed derived from *induere*, “to put on”; but the word *intus*, “within,” which Isidore adds, indicates a special property of the word, not its etymology.

For the clothing of the ancients, one should consult Lazarus Baïf, Octavius Ferrarius, Albert Rubens, and others who have also written about particular kinds of clothing, such as Donius, Manutius, Theophilus Raynaudus, and so forth.

### Note 2

“*Vestimentum*.” What I have just said about *indumentum* should equally be understood of *vestimentum*: *vestimentum* derives from *vestitus*, “clothing,” not from *vestigium*, “footprint.”

### Note 7

“*Pectoralis*.” Ammianus, Book XIV, chapter 9, or 30: “A *pectoralis* tunic.”

### Note 8

“*Manuleata*.” Grialius printed *manicleata* in the text, [Col. 1032D] but in the note preferred *manuleata*, as Brissonius also emends it in Book I of *On the Persian Kingdom*, no. 64. Other ancient authors likewise show some variation in this word, but the more common spelling is *manuleata*, *manulea*. Compare Ducange.

### Note 9

“*Clavis*.” The *clavi* that Isidore calls *clavi* are called *virgulae*, “little stripes,” by Alcuin; *lineae*, “lines,” by Amalarius; *zonae*, “bands,” by John the Deacon; and *tramites*, “paths,” by Rabanus, as Montfaucon observes in volume III, part I, Book I, chapter 6, of his *Antiquities*, where he discusses the *latus clavus*. From manuscript glosses in which the author Placidus is cited—perhaps Placidus Lutatius—he produces: “*Clavus*, a purple-trimmed garment.”

When Isidore says that the *dalmatica* is a priestly tunic, he suggests that it was a garment especially proper to bishops. The Arabic-Latin glosses say: “A *dalmata*, a white priestly garment with purple *clavi*.” Ducange collects much more concerning the *dalmatica* in his Glossary.

### Note 13

“*Bombycinum dicitur*.” See the note to Book XI, chapter 5, no. 8.

[Col. 1033A]

### Note 14

“*Holoporphyra*.” Salmasius, in his work on Trebellius Pollio, p. 208, corrects *oloporphyra* or *holoporphyra* to *olovera*. He says:

> Isidore, who is not a poor authority in many passages, interprets *olovera* as “entirely purple”; the common editions print *oloporphyra*, while the manuscripts we have seen have *olophara*, *olofera*, and *oloferia*. There is no doubt that *olofera* is *olovera*; thus *fasculum* appears for *vasculum* in Isidore’s glosses.

I discussed this scribal corruption, in which *f* frequently appears for *v* in manuscripts, in my note to Sedulius, Book I, verse 1967, concerning the prose. Salmasius explains *olovera* as deriving from *verus*, “true,” in a mixture of Greek and Latin, as with *epitogium*, etc. He observes that others incorrectly write *oloberum* from *berus*.

### Note 15

“*Byssum*.” Sirmond, volume I of his works, p. 977, discusses *byssus*. Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 1:

> Throughout the world, first place belongs to linen, which is not consumed by fire. Next is women’s *byssine* cloth, produced around Elis in Achaea, chiefly for their luxuries.

### Note 18

“*Segmentata*.” Salmasius, in his work on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 224, verse 40, explains it as follows:

> To weave upward: the woof, or threads, were below, and consequently the garment was woven in the upper parts; thus the woof was always drawn and pushed upward with the comb. They called this “weaving upward” and “weaving in height.”

Mariana, in his note to Book I of *Against the Jews*, chapter 38, thinks that the *tunica recta* was Christ’s seamless tunic, of which John’s Gospel says that it was woven “from above throughout.” Perhaps the *tunica recta* was begun either from the upper part—that is, from above—or from the lower part, that is, upward.

A *segmentata* garment is checkered and distinguished by inset designs. Symmachus, Book IV, letter 42: “A *segmentata* garment.”

[Col. 1033B]

### Note 20

“*Citrosa*.” In Naevius, some explain a *citrosa* garment as one fragrant with the scent of citron. See Macrobius, Book III of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 19. In Isidore, *concrispa* would better be *concrispata*, “made curly.”

### Note 22

“*Acu textilis*.” Gibert Cuperus, *Observations*, Book II, chapter 12, emends this to *acu textili*, that is, “with the needle of the weavers,” for, as he says, *acus* by itself means the needle with which embroiderers adorned garments.

I do not agree. Here *textilis* means the same as *texta*, “woven,” as in other authors; and *acu texta* is the same as *acu ornata*, “adorned with needlework.” Garments are not only sewn with a needle, but also woven or ornamented with a needle; and this was the art of the Phrygians, to weave, adorn, and decorate garments with a needle. [Col. 1033C]

### Note 24

“*Pannucia*” is the spelling, not *pannutia* or *panutia*, as in Grialius. Some interpret *Baucis pannucia* as “wrinkled” or “withered.” But Petronius, in the *Satyricon*, chapter 14, clearly speaks of a *pannucia* garment, that is, one sewn from pieces of cloth.

In place of *colobium*, *colobus* occurs in the Theodosian Code. *Lebitonarium* is also called *lebiton*, *lebeton*, or *levitico*. See the examples in Rosweyd’s *Onomasticon*.

### Note 25

“*Lumbare*.” Ducange discusses *lumbare* and *renale* at length in his Glossary.

### Note 27

“*Licinum*.” In Vegetius, Book II of *Veterinary Medicine*, chapters 22 and 28, *licinium* is a *licium*, “thread,” smeared with medicine for healing wounds. I find nothing concerning *licinum* in another sense.

[Col. 1033D]

### Note 28

“*Armilausa*.” Concerning *armilausae*, I shall quote the words of Conrad Samuel Schurzfleisch, *Philosophical Philological Disputation* 85, nos. 14 and 15:

> The garments of the *circumcelliones* differed from the *rhenones*. In shape and appearance they resembled the tunics of the Spaniards, which they called *armilausae*. Concerning these garments write the scholiast on Juvenal, Paulinus of Nola, Isidore, and others. In Isidore’s copies *armelausa* is usually read, but since most other writers use *armilausa*, and since *i* is easily changed into *e* in manuscripts, I restored *armilausa*, to which Isidore himself points, as though it were *armiclausa*. Perhaps the Spanish name *almilla* derives from this word *armilausa*.

Ducange has more on *armilausa*.

### Note 29

“*Camisas*.” Concerning *camisa* or *camisia*, see the preceding chapter, no. 1; concerning *cama*, Book XX, chapter 11. We Spaniards still say *cama* for “bed.”

### Note 30

“*Tubraci*, because from *bracae*.” Salmasius, in his work on Lampridius, p. 128, verse 15, reads: “*Tubruci*, because they extend from the *bracae* as far as the shin,” and he interprets *bracae* as being used by Isidore for leg-coverings, as also by the interpreter of Juvenal, namely for coverings of the legs or feet.

## Chapter XXIII

### Note 1

“*Gallis lenae*.” In Vatican Codex 623, discussed in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 93, no. 34, there is a variant: “For the Gauls, linen … for the Spaniards, tight-fitting” (*Galli linea* … *Hispanis stringens*). Some read *lumae* instead of *lenae*. See Isidore’s Glossary with notes, under *Luma*.

### Note 2

“And *sarabara*.” In the Vulgate: “And their *sarabala* would not have been changed.” Others write *saraballa* instead of *sarabara*. Tertullian used the feminine gender. Concerning this word, see the onomastic index of Zaccaria and Pollux, vol. II, p. 1335.

I also made several observations in my commentary on Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 143, drawing on the very learned bishop Simone de Magistris. Bottarius, volume III of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 58, thinks that Daniel’s word *sarabara* should be understood as referring to head-coverings, such as Isidore says are seen depicted on the heads of magi, and such as the ancient painting he illustrates shows on the heads of the three youths. [Col. 1034B]

### Note 3

“*Lenae saga*.” In Isidore’s Glossary there is: “*Luma*, a square *sagum*.” Hence Salmasius, in his work on Trebellius Pollio, p. 199, verse 15, says that in Isidore at this passage one should not read *lenae*, or, as others have it, *linnae*, but *lumae*. Salmasius reads it this way in Pollio as well, and derives *lumum, lumi*, or *luma, lumae*, from the Greek λῶμα (*lōma*). Consult Bochart, Book I of *Canaan*, chapter 42, and Ducange’s Dictionary.

### Note 4

“*Rhenones*.” Others derive *rhenones* from ῥινός (*rhinós*), “hide.” Concerning the word *reptos*, compare letter 40 among the Bonifatian letters:

> My devotion sent to Your Reverence a silver cup gilded inside, and two *repta*.

And letter 77:

> We sent you small gifts, namely one *reptem ruptilem* (“woven coverlet”; reading uncertain).

### Note 5

“*Vestis Sarda*.” What is read in Vulcanius and others—“a Germanic garment”—is plainly an error, for above he says that the Sardinians have *mastrucae*. Prudentius also attributes *mastrucae* to the Getae. The more common spelling is *mastruca*, but *mastruga* also occurs in other authors.

[Col. 1034C]

### Note 6

“*Linamentis*.” Brissonius, Book I of *On the Persian Kingdom*, no. 64, corrects *lineamentis* or *linamentis* to *velamentis*, “coverings,” on the basis of Justin, Book I, chapter 2, section 3. Brissonius’s annotator conjectures *velamentis*. A *liniamentum* from *linum*, “flax,” is one thing; *lineamentum* or *liniamentum* from *linea*, “line,” is another.

### Note 7. *Cirros*

Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 762, asserts that *cirros* does not mean curly hair, as some commentators explain, but that among the Greeks *cirrus* is hair gathered into a knot at the crown, while among the Germans it means hair twisted into a knot. In Latin, as the same Salmasius says, *cirrus* is a knot of hair. Most others say that *cirros* means hair naturally curly or twisted.

*Grani* were hair flowing loose and spread out; this word is believed to be Gothic. The First Council of Braga, held in 561, chapter 11:

> It was likewise decreed that lectors in church, adorned in secular dress, should not sing the psalms, nor let down *grani* according to pagan custom.

Others think that *grani* is the part of the beard below the nose, that is, the moustache. Compare Ducange, under *Grani*. Cinnabar perhaps indicates the red color of Gothic clothing [Col. 1034D], or the fact that the Goths marked their faces with red pigment. See Sirmond, vol. I, p. 880.

It may be asked what people are meant by the *Picti*. Virgil called the Geloni *Picti*, *Georgics* II, verse 115; Servius interprets this as “bearing marks,” just as the Agathyrsi are called painted by the same Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 146. Isidore perhaps means the northern Britons, concerning whom Claudian writes, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, verse 54:

> That man—the light Moors, and the Picts, not falsely so called.

### Note 8. “Among men the hair is shorn; among women it is abundant”

Poets are especially accustomed to praise women for the abundance of their hair, while conversely they say that women without hair are ugly. Salmasius published a work on the hair of men and the coiffure of women.

## Chapter XXIV

### Note 3. “Whose likeness, etc.”

This indicates that in Isidore’s time, at least in Spain, there was no use of the toga [Col. 1035A]. Many statues of men wearing the toga can still be seen at Rome and elsewhere. The toga was not very unlike the *stola*, as the latter is described by Isidore in the following chapter. An *instita*, or sufficiently long band sewn beneath the toga, seems to have produced the *stola*, or to have extended it so that it reached down to the ankles.

In the earliest times the toga was common to both sexes. Later it became the distinctive garment of men, except that prostitutes were compelled to wear it.

### Note 6. *Toga candida*

Isidore suggests that the color of the toga was white, and that, when chalk was added, it became whiter still. This is confirmed by Manutius the younger, *Questions by Letter* III, chapter 1.

### Note 8. *Trabea*

Gutberlethus, *On the Salii*, chapter 10, using Isidore and Servius, refutes Lipsius, who, in his commentary on book III of Tacitus’ *Annals*, teaches that the *trabea* was the distinctive garment of knights, not of kings, generals, and augurs.

Servius, commenting on *Aeneid* VII, verse 612, reports from Suetonius that there were three kinds of *trabea*:

> One was sacred to the gods and consisted entirely of purple. Another belonged to kings; it was purple, but had some white in it. The third was augural, made of purple and scarlet.

### Note 9. Sallustius: “The toga”

The words of Sallust are not found elsewhere. They suggest, by metonymy, that the emperor exchanged war for peace.

### Note 13. *Sagum*

Bochart, *Canaan* I, chapter 42, observes that *sagum* derives from *saccus*, not *saccus* from *sagum*; consequently, he seems to deny that *sagum* is a Gallic word.

### Note 15. *Mantum*

The word *manto* is still current among the Spaniards, but it is used for a fuller garment. In glossaries *mandum* is also written for *mantum*. Ducange, and those who enlarged his *Glossary*, discuss *manto* and its etymology at length.

### Note 17. *Casula*

The word was used not only for a hooded garment but also for the hood itself. Abbot Theodemar writes:

> We say that the hood is what we call by another name the *casula*.

It is also used for the *planeta*, or priestly vestment. Rabanus, *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 21—and, following him, Uguccio and John of Genoa—writes:

> *Casula* is commonly called the priest’s *planeta*, because, like a little house, it covers the whole body, and it signifies charity.

Ducange, already cited, offers many other examples.

Bonarroti, in *Vitra*, p. 170, shows that the *planeta* was derived from the *paenula*, and asserts that no mention of it as a sacred vestment is found before the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 634. Yet in that council some read *patena*, not *planeta*. Some conclude that the use of the *planeta* by deacons had already become established in the time of Gregory the Great, on the basis of John the Deacon, who, in book IV, chapter 83 of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, describes a portrait of the deacon Gordianus made at the command of that same Saint Gregory. His clothing, he says, included a chestnut-colored *planeta* beneath a dalmatic. See Bottari, vol. I of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 206.

Isidore perhaps wrote: “The Greeks called them *planetae*.”

### Note 18

Perhaps one should read: “For they called *birrum* *pirrum*.”

The ancient glosses have:

> Βυῤῥὸν, ξανθὸν, καὶ πυῤῥὸν.

That is: “*Byrron*, yellow, and *pyrrhon*, red.”

Isidore’s glosses read:

> *Birrus*: red.

*Birrus* was used for any garment, but sometimes for an expensive one, as in the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 13:

> A monk ought not to be dressed in linen; it is not lawful for him to use an *orarium*, *birri*, or *planetae*.

Some also believe that *birrum* was the distinctive episcopal garment, which is commonly called the *rochet*. Rosweyd discusses the *birrus* at length in his *Onomasticon*, in addition to the other authorities cited by Ducange.

### Note 19. “The skins of melons”

It seems certain that Isidore wrote “the skins of melons.” For, apart from Papias and Uguccio, who nearly copy Isidore, John of Jerusalem, chapter 38 of *On the Institution of Monks*, and Abbot Theodemar in his letter to Charlemagne agree on the same point:

> That covering was therefore called *cie* because in ancient times it was customarily made from the skin of that animal which, because of the roundness of its body, is called *melos*.

This etymology, however, is not very pleasing to critical scholars.

## Chapter XXV

### Note 1. “*Regillum* is thoroughly washed”

In Vatican Codex 623, discussed in the *Isidorian Studies*, chapter 93, section 34, one reads, with Grialius: “*Regillum* is thoroughly washed”; others have *praelatum*. In his explanation of the *peplum*, Isidore agrees with the Greeks. See John Nicholas, chapter 12 of *The Triumph of the Romans*.

### Note 3. *Stola*

An example of the matronly *stola*, as Isidore describes it here, may be seen on an ancient coin of Pietas, veiled in this fashion, in Matthew Brower of Niedeck’s work *On Adorations*, chapter 13.

Ferrarius nevertheless maintains, in *On the Art of Dress* III, chapter 17, that Isidore was mistaken here, since the *stola* is rather a tunic extending to the ankles. This is certainly supported by many ancient writers who speak of the *stola*. Yet the *stola* could have reached to the ankles while also covering the head. See the preceding chapter, section 3.

Some write *recinium*. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 30, writes:

> The most ancient covering was the *ricinium*, which they used doubled, because they threw half of it backward; it was called *recinium* from *reiciendo* (“throwing back”).

For *mavors*, many give *mafors* or *maphors*. Compare Rosweyd in the *Onomasticon*, leaving aside Ducange. Bottari, vol. II of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 165, suspects that the head-covering in which a certain woman is represented in plate 165 is a *mavort*.

### Note 5. “This among the ancients, etc.”

Regarding these words of Isidore, Brissonius, *Selected Antiquities* I, chapter 4, expresses the following opinion:

> Although, because of the lack of other testimony, I would not dare to affirm this as certain, I nevertheless regard it as established that women condemned for adultery changed their clothing and, after laying aside the *stola*, took up the toga.

I do not know whether Cicero’s statement confirms Isidore’s view, *On Divination* II, chapter 69:

> The garment of the beloved woman is her little cloak.

Of Tamar we read in Genesis 38 that, after laying aside the garments of her widowhood, she put on a *theristrum* and, having changed her clothing, sat at the fork of the road, and so forth.

### Note 6. *Theristrum*

The word is explained by Pollux, book VII, chapter 13. Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 4, writes:

> What sort of Hercules was that in Omphale’s *theristrum*?

In manuscript glosses, which I shall publish among the appendices, *theristrum* is called, in the commentary on Genesis 38, a head-band or linen cloth. Ducange gives other examples in his *Glossary*.

In the First Toledo Codex the words of Isaiah are reproduced:

> Concerning this in Isaiah: “Linen cloths, ribbons, and *theristra*.”

### Note 7. *Anaboladium*

On *anaboladium*, or *anabolagium*, or *anabolarium*, see Ducange. In ancient inscriptions *anabolium* is occasionally used for a cloak.

## Chapter XXVI

### Note 1. *Stragulum*

Some critics believe that *stragulum*, *vestis stragula*, or, as the Vulgate says, *stragulata*, was used by ancient writers not for a cloak but only for a bed-covering. Isidore takes the opposite view, and certain passages of the ancients clearly support him.

### Note 2. *Lodices*

In printed editions one finds *ludices*, so that the etymology may be derived from *ludi*. Among the ancients, indeed, *o* and *u* were easily interchanged. But since the correct spelling is *lodices*, that spelling should be retained, even if we believe that its genuine etymology derives from *ludi*.

The word *galmapis*, or *galnapes*, is read in various ways among medieval writers and in glossaries: *galnabis*, *galbanis*, *galnape*, *ganape*, and so forth. Some derive it from *galbanum*; others, more plausibly, from *gausape*, or *gaunape*, which means a *stragulum*, or covering.

### Note 3. *Fulcra*

Properly speaking, these are supports, and the word is usually applied to the supports of beds. Isidore perhaps calls them ornaments because they were generally decorated.

Unless one prefers to understand by *fulcra* the other ornaments of beds, which also support us, including headrests. Papias writes:

> A *reclinatorium* is a support for the head.

Servius calls *fulcra* the sideboards of beds. Properly, a *sponda* is the outer board of a bed to which the cords are attached, by which the mattress is supported. The word is also used for either side of a bed, especially the outside, by which one climbs into it. See Vossius, *Etymology*.

### Note 4. *Pulvillus*

This is a diminutive of *pulvinus*. The following distinction is usually made between *pulvinus* and *pulvinar*: a *pulvinus* belongs to private persons, whereas a *pulvinar* belongs to the gods, or to emperors who wished to be regarded as gods.

I therefore suspected that one should read “from the *pulvinar*,” which is the bed of the gods. But in book XX, chapter 11, section 3, one finds: “A *pulvinar* is the bed of the rich.”

*Culcita* is better written than *culcitra*, as it appeared in Grialius’ text.

### Note 5. *Psila tapeta*

For *sipla* and *siplae*, as they appear in the printed editions, I restored *psila* and *psilae*. The etymology of the word does not compel us to believe that Isidore wrote *sipla*.

### Note 6. *Mantelia*

In ancient times hands were wiped at table with *mantelia*, as may be gathered from Varro. Later the *mappa* was used for wiping hands at table, and *mantelia* were then used only for covering tables. The word *manteles* remains current among the Spaniards.

Grialius printed in the text *quasi manupae*, and in the note *quasi manuppae*. The old copies vary.

For *mapella* some have *mappella*, others *mappulla*. I would prefer *mappulla*, a word used by Saint Jerome.

*Toral* coverings were placed around the bed as decoration, but *toralia* were also called the coverings laid over a bed. *Toralia* were also more valuable tablecloths; for *tori* properly meant the richly covered beds of eminent persons, just as *pulvinaria* were beds richly spread for the gods. See Heumann, in his commentary on Cicero’s *Pro Milone*, chapter 17.

### Note 7. *Sabanum* is Greek

Some believe it to be an old Spanish word; certainly the Spaniards now use it to denote bed linen. Many use *sabanum* for linen, including Palladius, Apicius, Vegetius, Marcellus Empiricus, Gregory the Great, and others whom one may consult in Ducange.

Among the poems of Saint Eugenius of Toledo, book II, poem 41, the title is “To the *sabana*”:

> When you have completed all that the care of bathing requires,  
> Spread bright linens over your limbs.

### Note 8. “In the hall, etc.”

Varro also indicates this in Nonius, chapter 14, section 4. Others assert that the word *aulaea*, αὐλαία, is older than King Attalus.

## Chapter XXVII

### Note 1. “*Lana* from *laniando*”

In the printed editions it was *a laniendo*, which is meaningless. Festus writes:

> *Dilaniare* means to tear apart and, as it were, to pull wool; hence *lacinia*. And a *lanius* is one who tears apart an animal.

### Note 2. *Stupa*

Grialius writes *stuppa*, *stippa*, and *stippatores* with double *p*. Many approve this spelling in *stuppa*, although others disagree; but *stipo* is always pronounced with a single *p*.

### Note 4. “Called *aranea*”

In Grialius one finds *vocati* in certain copies.

### Note 5. “And as it were a thickness”

Papias, following Isidore, writes:

> *Placium* is *stupa*, as though it meant the thickness of silk.

Many relate that the use of silk passed from the Seres to the Persians, and from them to the Greeks and Romans, and that, when silkworm eggs were brought to Constantinople in Justinian’s time, it spread throughout Europe. See Vossius’ *Etymological Dictionary*, under *Sericum*, and the discussion of Giovanni Francesco Giorgetti on the origin of silk, printed after his Italian poem *On the Silkworm*.

## Chapter XXVIII

### Note 1. “For it is a little worm”

It was an ancient opinion among writers that *coccum* was a worm. Some called the matter into question; more recent investigators, after conducting experiments, found worms in the *coccum*.

### Note 4. *Ostrum*

Vitruvius, *On Architecture* VII, chapter 13, states that the juice of the shellfish is properly called *ostrum*, and that it is not of one color but, according to the various regions of the sky, may be black, livid, violet, or red [Col. 1037D].

On the purple color of *ostrum*, see Pollux, *Onomasticon* I, chapter 4, and Seneca, *Natural Questions* I, chapter 3.

### Note 6. *Ferrugo*

It is not entirely clear whether Virgil should be understood as referring to Spanish *ferrugo* or Pontic *ferrugo*. Servius either varied in his interpretation or understood Virgil to refer only to Pontic *ferrugo*.

Others interpret Iberian *ferrugo* as Spanish or Baetican. Virgil himself, as well as most other ancient poets, certainly means the Spaniards when speaking of the Iberians.

### Note 8. *Menum*

On *melinum*, see chapter 17 of this book, section 21.

### Note 9. “Because it is from what has been burned”

It seems that one should read: “which is from *usta*,” or “which is made from *usta*.” On *usta*, see chapter 17 of this book, section 19.

## Chapter XXIX

### Note 1. *Insubuli*

Grialius printed *insubuli* in the text, as did the other printed editions. Therefore, what he indicates in the note—*insula*—should, I believe, be regarded as an error [Col. 1038A].

In Lucretius some read *ensilia*. In John of Genoa and in certain glossaries one finds *insibulus*, *insubulare*, and *insublum*. Guibert, *On the Relics of the Saints* I, chapter 3, section 1, used the word *insubulus*.

### Note 2. *Alibrum*

Some dictionaries have *alabrum* for *alibrum*. But since knowledge of this word evidently passed from Isidore to the authors of the glossaries, *alibrum* should be retained.

### Note 5. “From hairs”

Becmannus, p. 562, supports this etymology and rejects the alternatives proposed by others.

### Note 6. *Mataxa*

It is written both *mataxa* and *metaxa*. Papias believed it to be a little ball-shaped instrument.

### Note 7. *Panuliae*

In Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, chapter 23, the word is read in various ways: *panuelium*, *panucellium*, *pannuelium*, *pannelium*, and so forth.

In Isidore one might read *panuelia* or *panuela*. *Panucellium* is said to be a ball of carded wool prepared for spinning, or a spindle wound with thread, or a shuttle with which standing weavers advance the cloth.

## Chapter XXX

### Note 3. *Tiara*

Brissonius carefully describes the form of the *tiara* in *On the Persian Kingdom* III, p. 24 [Col. 1038B].

### Note 4. “Twisted,” that is, “wound”

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, verse 1085:

> Meanwhile, while the twisted fillet binds the wandering locks.

See the commentary on that passage, where I discussed the *infula* and ribbons.

Countless writers have explained the subject of crowns; Fabricius cites them in chapter 14 of his *Bibliography*. On ancient coins and marble monuments one may see sacrificial victims wearing fillets with hanging ribbons. See the following chapter, section 6.

### Note 5. “From *apiendo*”

Perhaps one should read *ab apendo*, since the ancients used *apere* for “to be suitable.” On the *galerus*, see chapter 21, section 3.

### Note 6. *Cidaris*

It was a *tiara* rather than a *mitra*. In Raynaud’s *On the Cap*, p. 191, Cyrus is seen conspicuous with a diadem around his *tiara*, or *cidaris*.

## Chapter XXXI

### Note 1. *Diadema*

In some old editions this chapter 31 is joined to the preceding chapter 30, and the two are made into one [Col. 1038C].

Rupertus infers from a coin that queens also used the diadem, in his *Historical Orator*, p. 793. In the case of the pontiff, the *infula* was the same as the diadem in the case of the king.

### Note 2. *Nimbus*

One should note the custom, already current in Isidore’s time, of depicting angels adorned with a *nimbus*. Antonius Franciscus Gorius discusses the *nimbus* of the saints in his commentary on “The Mitred Head of Jesus Christ,” besides Benedict XIV and the non-Catholic scholars Johann Behm and Johann Beisk.

Bonarroti, in *The Life of the Ancient Christians*, p. 66, thinks that the use of the *nimbus* in representations of angels began in the sixth century, and in paintings of other saints in the seventh century.

Yet there is a panel older than the sixth century, number 44, which Bottari discusses in vol. I of *Subterranean Rome*, p. 199. In it a *nimbus* is placed around Christ, Saint John the Baptist, and an angel.

Only in Plautus does one read:

> The more I look at her.

### Note 3. “The same, and also a *cappa*”

Salmasius, in his commentary on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 224, verse 28, annotates these words as follows:

> Hence we call *cappae* the little cloaks with which women cover their heads, and *cappellae* and *cappulae* our caps.

The Italians certainly call a *galerus* a *cappello*, and the hood of the Friars a *cappuccio* [Col. 1038D].

### Note 4. *Mitra*, *infula*, and *vitta*

*Mitra*, *infula*, and *vitta* are not rarely confused, although they differ. See Theophilus Raynaud, *On the Cap*.

Properly, the *mitra* is a cap; the *infula* is a band; the ribbons hung down from the *infula*. Nevertheless, some, contrary to Isidore and Servius, think that the *infulae* hung from the ribbons, not the ribbons from the *infulae*. See Gesner, *Thesaurus*, under *Infula*.

It may be questioned how consecrated women, or women devoted to God, could have adopted a *mitra* as a head ornament, since the *mitra* was customarily an ornament of prostitutes. Servius also attests this in his commentary on *Aeneid* IV, verse 216:

> *Mitra*, that is, a curved cap, from which there also hung a covering of beads.

Indeed, those who were accused of effeminacy were also charged with wearing a *mitra*. Much reading shows that *mitrae* properly belonged to prostitutes. Some think that Servius was mistaken. See Nicolaus Mercerus, in his commentary on Alexander ab Alexandro’s *Genial Days* V, and Turnebus, *Adversaria* IV, chapter 14, and XXIX, chapter 25.

I would believe that consecrated women adopted the *mitra* because it was also characteristic of old women, as Scaliger observes in his commentary on Virgil’s *Copa*. Ovid, *Fasti* IV, verse 517:

> … she had imitated an old woman and with a *mitra*  
> had pressed down her hair.

As I suppose, a modest color distinguished the *mitrae* of consecrated women from those of prostitutes; for the *mitrae* of prostitutes were multicolored and decorated. Juvenal, *Satire* 3, verse 66:

> Go to those who delight in the barbarian whore’s painted *mitra*.

Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV, chapter 9:

> Polygnotus was the first to paint women in bright clothing and to cover their heads with multicolored *mitrae*.

### Note 5. *Ricula*

This is a diminutive of *rica*, which was the head-covering of the priestesses of the flamines while they were performing sacred rites.

The form *rigula*, found in certain printed and manuscript copies, is a scribal error; scribes often used *g* for *c* [Col. 1039B].

### Note 6. *Vittae*

On the *vittae*, see the preceding chapter, section 4.

### Note 8. “*Discriminalia* … *cincinni*”

One kind of pin was a dressing pin, another was the golden *discriminalis*, of which Isidore speaks here. Instead of *ab auribus*, Isidore may have written *ab anti*, unless he was referring to the Greek ὦτα, “ears.”

John Voweranus, in his notes on Petronius, Salmasius in his notes on Solinus, Bonannus, Montfaucon, and others discuss the *discericulum*, or hairpin. Grialius had written *cincini* in the text.

### Note 9. *Acus*

Isidore also lists these pins among the *discriminalia*, book XI, chapter 1, section 31.

Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 200, presents instruments of women’s toilette drawn from ancient monuments: golden hairpins, some set with gems; a *viriola* made of tiny emeralds; a golden earring; a *stalagmium*; and so forth.

See also Guasco’s work *On the Female Hairdresser* [Col. 1039C].

### Note 10. “With which precious objects”

Jerome, letter 10:

> From those ears may hang the precious grains of new harvests.

Salmasius discusses this custom at greater length in his *Plinian Exercises*, p. 402. Pliny, at the beginning of book XII, mentions wounds of the ears caused by earrings. Gaspar Bartholinus published a special book on the earrings of the ancients, to which Thomas Bartholinus added a supplement.

### Note 11. “But necklaces for women”

Quintilian, book XI, chapter 1:

> Men are disfigured by necklaces, pearls, and the long dress, which are ornaments of women.

### Note 12. *Monile*

Some wish to derive the word from *moneo*, as though it meant a memorial and pledge.

A necklace in the shape of a serpent is understood in an inscription found in Gruter, p. 70, no. 8, and Donius, class 1, no. 41:

> To the god Aesculapius … a golden torque made from two little dragons.

See Johann Scheffer, *On the Ancient Torques*, section 4, pp. 51 ff., and Bottari, vol. I of *Subterranean Rome*, plates 17 and 19.

### Note 14. “Commonly called a *muraena*”

Jerome, in the passage cited by Grialius, uses the diminutive *muraenula*:

> The gold of her neck, which the common people indeed call a *muraenula*, etc.

Perhaps Isidore also wrote *muraenula* [Col. 1039D].

### Note 16. “Common bracelets … *viriolae*”

Grialius, along with the other editors, printed in the text: “It is common for men and women, etc.” In the note he indicates another reading.

Casaubon, in his commentary on Capitolinus, p. 140, verse 20, adopts Vulcanius’ reading:

> It is common for men and women … they are on the right hand, broad, and are worn before the sleeve, and can be joined there by a single nail.

He explains this of *dextrocheria*, which were worn before the sleeve—that is, at the junction of the hand and arm—and joined by a single nail.

Salmasius, commenting on the same passage of Julius Capitolinus, thinks Isidore should be corrected as follows:

> A *dextrale* is common to men and women, because both sexes have right hands.

He ridicules Isidore’s reasoning and adds that the words following in Vulcanius—“broad, etc.”—are not Isidore’s but belong, as he says, to some inept and foolish monk. None of the old books acknowledge those words, although he consulted many of them and compared them with copies of the *Etymologies*.

Yet perhaps Isidore wrote: “*Dextrales* are common, etc.,” with “it is established” understood, as I have supplied it; or perhaps: “It is common for men and women, etc.”

Although Isidore’s Glossary reads *dextralia, brachialia*, Graevius nevertheless thinks that *dextrae* should be restored, as in the current editions.

For *viriolae*, some read *viriliae*; but *viriolae* is sound. Tertullian, chapter 4 of *On the Pallium*, uses the word *viria*, or, as others read it, *viriola*, a diminutive also used by Pliny.

### Note 17. *Lunulae*

Tertullian, *On the Adornment of Women*, chapter 10:

> Let no one condemn little crescents.

In Plautus some read *lunulam*, others *lunellam*.

### Note 19. *Periscelides*

Horace, *Epistles* I, verse 56:

> He reports the clever wiles of a notorious prostitute, often [telling] of a little dog, often of a *periscelis* snatched from one who weeps for it.

## Chapter XXXII

### Note 1. *Annuli*

In former times *anus* was written for *annus*; hence the spelling varies between *anulus* and *annulus*. Neither should be rejected [Col. 1040B].

### Note 2. “Because a certain vein passes through it, etc.”

See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII, chapter 13, and Gellius X, chapter 10.

John of Spain and Christian Falster wrote about the ring finger and the slight superstitions associated with it. Fabricius lists them, together with many others who either published small works on rings or made observations about them, in chapter 17, section 8 of his *Bibliography*.

### Note 3. “The golden ring, etc.”

Lipsius, *Electa* II, chapter 8, thinks that Isidore’s words are misleading in this matter:

> For, he says, they give a golden ring to freeborn persons and a silver one to freedmen.

He is mistaken: among freeborn persons, only knights and senators had the right to a golden ring. Even the knights, when serving in the army, used an iron ring after the Second Punic War, except for the tribunes.

Dietericus, in his notes on Brissonius’ *Lex Julia on Adultery*, p. 198, admits that most people call Isidore’s reliability into question. He nevertheless says that he will decide nothing, since laws may have varied according to different periods [Col. 1040C].

Certainly Justinian granted the right to the golden ring to all freedmen, whereas previously all freeborn persons already possessed that right. A dissertation by Pietro Burmanni on the right to golden rings was published in 1734 and reprinted in 1740.

As for Isidore’s distinction between jeweled and solid rings, he makes it because solid rings were made of solid material without the gem with which *unguli*, or jeweled rings, were adorned.

Strictly speaking, however, solid rings were so called to distinguish them from open and hollow rings, which were concave inside so that they could contain something.

### Note 4. *Leve*

Grialius writes: “It is smooth and an unencumbered limb.”

I shall not omit Tertullian’s own words, *Apology*, chapter 6:

> When no woman knew gold except on one finger, which her bridegroom had pledged with the ring given before marriage … but now among women, because of gold, no limb is unadorned; because of wine, no kiss is free, etc.

### Note 5. *Ungulus*

Or perhaps *ungulum*. It is believed to have been called *ungulus* for *annulus* in the language of the Orcadians.

Lipsius attempted to emend Pliny’s words about the Samothracian rings. Salmasius refutes him, however, and, after quoting Isidore’s words in his commentary on Aelius Spartianus, p. 5, verse 35, says:

> No one could explain Pliny’s passage better or more briefly.

Pliny’s words, book XXXIII, chapter 1, from the middle, are:

> Slaves too now bind iron with gold; others adorn it with pure gold alone. The origin of this license is revealed by the name itself, since the institution was established in Samothrace.

Lucretius calls these rings, book VI, verse 1042:

> Samothracian iron rings.

### Note 6. “They called it *Thynnam*”

It should rather be said that *Thynia* was a region of Bithynia.

Almost all manuscript copies vary among themselves in the verses, and the conjectures of the critics are diverse. Ludovicus D’Orléans, in his *New Reflections on Tacitus’ Annals*, p. 534, confidently asserts that these are verses of Maecenas written on the death of Horace. Certainly it was a joke of Augustus that Maecenas should play with verse about precious stones.

He thinks one should read:

> Mourning you, my life, I seek neither emeralds  
> nor beryls, my Flaccus, nor, *spiro* [uncertain reading],  
> a white pearl,  
> nor those …

The final two verses can easily be restored to their true reading, although Grialius printed the last one corruptly:

> Nor rings, nor jasper stones.

Grialius expressed the first three in the text as follows:

> With my life mourning, I seek neither emeralds  
> nor beryls for myself, Flaccus, nor gleaming,  
> intensely white pearls.

Janus Guillelmus, *Similarities* I, chapter 5, also inclines to the view that the verses are Maecenas’ and were addressed to Horace. He presents them corrected as follows:

> Mourning you, my life, I seek neither emeralds,  
> nor beryls, Flaccus, nor gleaming  
> pearls, always white, do I seek.

He explains that the verse refers to the Roman custom of wearing especially elegant rings in mourning. He also observes that *candida* stands for *candide*, just as *crebra* stands for *crebro*.

If we assert that the verses are Maecenas’, the title ought to be “Maecenas to Flaccus,” or “On the Death of Flaccus.”

Andreas Schottus, *Human Observations* II, chapter 6, also assigns these little verses to Maecenas and presents four different readings. The first is that of Andrea Alciati, who was earlier both in age and in the praise due to industry:

> Gleaming, my life, I seek neither emeralds,  
> nor beryls for me, Flaccus, nor gleaming  
> nor brilliantly white pearls.

The second differs little from this and belongs to Antonius Covarruvias, who initially read *lugenti*, and in the second verse *mihi mitte*, omitting *Flacce*.

The third is Turnebus’:

> The emeralds mourn you, my life, and the beryl also, Flaccus; nor do I now seek gleaming pearls amid the white ones [the text is corrupt].

The last is Duza’s:

> Mourning you, my life, I seek neither emeralds,  
> nor beryls for me, Flaccus, nor gleaming  
> among white pearls do I seek.

Pliny too praises beryls as gleaming among white pearls [Col. 1041C].

Leaving aside the question of who composed the verses and whether they were written on the death of Flaccus, I printed them as I judged they ought to be restored after comparing the manuscript copies with one another. See also Scaliger, book I of the *Catalecta*, and Salmasius’ commentary on Vopiscus’ *Aurelian*.

## Chapter XXXIII

### Note 1. “The girdle … the *campestre*”

Grialius printed in the text *a cinctu*, and *unde et campestre*, apparently by mistake. Some printed editions have *campestris*. The correct noun is *campestre*, and in the plural *campestria*, as in chapter 22, section 5 [Col. 1041D].

Arntzenius, in his *Miscellanies*, chapter 17, where he illustrates many passages of Arator, at verse 630 of book II, thinks that *et utrisque minima* should be replaced by *et utriusque*, following the Paris edition of 1509. Perhaps *et utrisque minor* would be better; but in Isidore *et utriusque minima* can be tolerated.

He observes, however, following Taubmann’s commentary on Plautus, *Aulularia* III, 6, 92, that *semicinctia* is a garment which girds the front part of a person, from the belt and loins down to the feet.

### Note 2. *Balteus*

The word is used in both forms, *balteus* and *balteum*.

### Note 3. *Lactantes*

Vulpius discusses Catullus’ verse in his notes on poem 63, where he prefers the reading *luctantes* to the *lactantes*, or *lactentes*, of the common text.

I printed Prudentius’ verse in this form, together with Isidore, against Heinsius, who had read:

> This is the name of a gem fastened to a fillet.

Compare my commentary on that passage.

### Note 4. “The *limus* is a girdle”

Sperlingius had concocted some notion about the god Juno from the corrupt reading *lunus est cinctus*. Gisb. Cuperus refutes him in letter 94 to that same Sperlingius, observing that many had long ago corrected it to *limus est cinctus*. Compare book XV, chapter 14, section 2.

### Note 5. *Succinctorium*

Papias interprets *succinctoria* as garments by which only the genitals are covered. Others think that *succinctoria* are the same as *perizomata*, or *campestria*.

Mazochius published a dissertation on the *semicinctium* in volume III of his *Spicilegium*. In note 3, p. 298, he observes that the *succinctorium* was similar to the breeches of boys, which were fastened at the top of the shoulder with straps.

He criticizes Isidore because, although Isidore says that the *brachile*, or *brachiale*, is now not a belt for the arms but for the loins, he derives its etymology from the arms, whereas he should have derived it from *braccae*, breeches.

He likewise concludes that the *succinctorium* was so called because it girded the loins, not because it was drawn beneath the arms, surrounded the armpits, and girded them on both sides.

But if in former times the *redimiculum*, or *succinctorium*, or *brachile*, surrounded and girded the armpits, as Isidore relates, Isidore’s etymology should not be rejected, even though, as time passed, the *succinctorium* became only a belt for the loins.

Certainly Cassian, *On the Institutions of Monks* I, chapter 6, explains *redimiculum*, *succinctorium*, or, as he himself more precisely calls it, *rebrachiatorium*, in the same way. He derives the words *rebrachiatorium* and *succinctorium* from the arms and from the armpits girded on either side.

Likewise, in the *Life of Saint Eligius*, chapter 34:

> With forearms bared and sleeves drawn up.

And in the *Acts of Saint Otto*, p. 599, volume I of the June collection:

> With his sleeves drawn back and his garment girded, he seized the sickle in his right hand.

The Benedictines do not agree about what *bracile*, or *brachile*, means in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 55. Some think it is a belt; others, a girdle for the loins.

On these words one should consult Ducange. Under *bracile* he indicates *demissum*—“lowered”—as a correction to Isidore’s words; but Cassian also used *divisa* in the same way.

The form of the *redimiculum* described by Isidore may be seen in Bonarroti, represented on a nude boy painted on glass, plate 28. Compare also the image of the Good Shepherd in Bottari, volume II of *Subterranean Rome*, plate 101 [Col. 1042B].

### Note 7. *Vitta*

Among the ancients *vitta* was a band for the head. The use of the word in the sense of something with which the breast is bound seems to belong to a later period. From this, I suppose, the Italian word *vita* developed, when it came to mean the stature of the body.

## Chapter XXXIV

### Note 1. “From *calo*, etc.”

See the note on chapter 1 of this book, section 15, and below, section 6 of this chapter [Col. 1042C].

### Note 3. “They used those that had been found”

The use of *utor* with an accusative occurs more than once in Isidore and other writers. A dissertation by Otto Sperlingius on *crepidae* is extant.

### Note 4. “Kings used shoes”

Vulcanius joins these words as follows: “Kings used shoes, and the Caesars—their form.” Grialius has: “Kings used shoes. And the Caesars. Their form.” These last two words are distinguished from the rest as though they were a separate heading. Perhaps something is missing after *eorum*.

Benedictus Balduinus of Amiens, in his work *On the Ancient Shoe*, chapter 8, gives the following unusual observation about the form of Roman shoes:

> So that the form of the ancient shoe may also become better known in this respect, I remember that long ago, when, as a young man, I was working in my father’s shoemaker’s workshop making shoes—and this is how I came to write about shoes—I saw a remarkable shoe made from boiled leather. It certainly served not for putting on the foot but, like a cup, for taking and offering wine. Its form was such that it ended in a curved point, resembling an extended tongue, bent upward toward the nostrils.

> I would dare to assert that the ancient Roman shoe was of this kind.

### Note 8. *Obstrigilli*

In the words of Pliny cited by Grialius, some read *obstrigillis*, against Harduinus.

### Note 10. *Mullei*

Salmasius, in his commentary on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 246, verse 33, seems to approve this explanation by Isidore of the *mullei*, and adds that everything agrees with the Tuscan shoes described by Servius.

But in his note on the dedication of the statue of Regilla by Herodes, he says that the crescents on the shoes were made of ivory, bone, or bronze; that Isidore was misled by the word *σφύριον* (*sphýrion*), which means a little hammer, and accordingly translated *ἐπισφύρια* (*episphyria*)—the crescents—as *malleoli*, little hammers.

He concludes that the *mullei*, that is, red shoes, differed from the senatorial shoes, which were black, only in color. Patricians who had held curule office used the *mullei*.

Cerda adds much else in his commentary on chapter 4 of Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*:

> He puts a clean or reddish shoe on the impure leg.

### Note 11. *Solo*

Vulpius proves from Plautus and Lucretius, in his notes on Catullus, that *solum* may also mean *solea*, the sole. Martial, book IX, epigram 75:

> And to bite the rotten mud and the old sole.

Add Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 666, with my commentary.

“From material”: that is, from wood [Col. 1043A].

### Note 12. “The diminutive *socelli*”

Perhaps the diminutive is *socculi*. On *caligae*, see Negronius, who wrote a learned work on this subject.

### Note 13. Without a sole

Gataker, in *Miscellanea*, Book II, chapter 19, judges Festus to be mistaken in identifying a type of shoe called *cernuus*, and Isidore in supposing, from a verse of Lucilius, that a *soccus* was a shoe without a sole. Vossius expresses the same opinion in his *Etymologicon*. There are various opinions concerning the *folleati*. Grialius printed *foliates* in the text but indicated *folleatos* in the notes. Hofmann, in his *Lexicon*, interprets *folleati calcei* as looser shoes: when the foot presses down and rests upon the ground, they are inflated and swell; when it is lifted, they deflate—whence *follare* and *follicare* were properly used. Salmasius, in his notes on Trebellius Pollio, p. 182, line 17, observes that the ancients also said *caligem* for *caligam*, confirming this from Isidore’s words, *sola caligis*, that is, *sola caligae*. In Isidore’s glossary: *Caliges*, Gallic shoes of soldiers; elsewhere, *Calces Gallicae militum*. Grialius printed *sculponiae* in the text and *sculponeae* in the notes; others likewise give the latter form.

**Same place.** This Apicius is said to have lived under Tiberius; concerning him, see Pliny, Book X, chapter 48. Two other Apicii, devoted to the pursuit of gluttony, are mentioned: one lived around the time of Caesar, the other under Trajan.

## BOOK TWENTY

### Chapter I

**No. 2.** *Stibadium* comes from the Greek στιβάς (*stibas*), meaning “a bed” or “a thing spread out.” The Romans used this word for a semicircular couch, arranged for three couches at round tables. Matters relating to the banquets, dinners, food, and drink of the ancients have been explained in many works and dissertations, especially in Gronovius’s *Thesaurus Antiquitatum Graecarum*, vol. IX, and Graevius’s *Thesaurus Antiquitatum Romanarum*, vol. XII.

**Same place. On feeding.** Grialius printed *ad cibatum* in the text, although in the notes he gives *ad cibitum* at the first occurrence.

### Chapter II

**No. 2.** *Alimonia*, *alimoniam*, and *alimentum* are ordinarily used indiscriminately for the same thing.

**No. 5. On the two necessities: bread and wine.** This is a suitable reason why Jesus Christ wished bread and wine to be used for the sacrament of the Eucharist.

**No. 7. Only porridge.** It would more correctly be *sola puls*; but Isidore often forms nouns of this kind in such a way that the nominative resembles the genitive.

**No. 8. *Satura*.** Grialius printed *satyra* in the text and *satura* in the notes. See Book V, chapter 16. The distinction Isidore explains between *satietas* and *saturitas* is not usually observed.

**No. 10. *Jentaculum*.** I retain the reading accepted by everyone. Why should I believe that Isidore departed from it? The Spaniards indeed say *jantar*, changing *e* into *a*.

**No. 11. *Prandium*.** Trebellius Pollio, in *The Life of Saloninus Gallienus*, chapter 2: “Most people say that *prandium* was so called because it prepares soldiers for war.” Formerly, the food eaten in the morning was called *prandium*; that eaten at midday, *coena*; and that eaten in the evening, *vesperna*. Later, when dinner began to be postponed until evening, the food eaten around midday was called *prandium*, that eaten before midday *jentaculum*, and that eaten after midday *merenda*.

**No. 13. *Annona*.** Some derive *annona* from *annus*, “year.” In Martial, printed editions give *exstructos* instead of *excelsos*. See Rosweyd, in the *Onomasticon*, under “the ninth hour,” and Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 8, line 9, with my commentary; also *Peristephanon*, hymn 6, line 55, where the hour for ending fasts and partial fasts is discussed.

**No. 14. *Communicantes*.** Papias: “Communion is called spiritual food because it is received in common by all who are worthy, for the giving of life to souls.” Compare Du Cange, under *Communio*.

**No. 15. *Panis*.** Volume I of the *Inscriptions of the French Academy*, no. 331, contains much on bread. Vossius reviews various etymologies. Seneca, letter 9: “Then he sprinkled flour with water, subdued it by continuous kneading, and shaped bread, which at first hot ash and a heated potsherd baked thoroughly; later ovens were gradually discovered.” In Festus, at the passage cited by Grialius, some read *iterum coctus*, “baked again,” instead of *parum coctus*, “insufficiently baked”; this is supported by Plautus and Isidore. This bread was also called *dipyrus*, “twice-baked,” *biscoctus*, “dry,” *paximas*, and *paximatium”; concerning it, see Rosweyd, *Onomasticon*, under *Paximates*. In Isidore’s glossary: “*Paximatium*: bread baked under ashes.” Grialius prefers *subcineritius*.

**No. 16. *Spongia*.** Grialius printed in the text: “A sponge-bread kneaded for a long time with water”; in the notes he suggests something else.

**No. 17. *Laganum*.** There is an erudite dissertation by Mazzocchi in volume II of the *Spicilegium Biblicum*, on Exodus 29:22–23, concerning the *torta* of bread, small cakes, and *lagana*. The words of Exodus are: “You shall take the fat of the ram … and one loaf of bread, one cake mixed with oil, and one *laganum* from the basket of unleavened bread that is set before the Lord.” Mazzocchi prefaces this as follows: “No one, so far as I know, has undertaken to elucidate the baking terms of Scripture with greater care, except that Isidore rarely passed them over in his *Etymologies*.” Mazzocchi suspects that the words concerning the *laganum*—“which is first fried in water and afterward in oil”—have been inserted by another hand, because, as Vossius testifies, they are absent from several manuscripts, although many secular descriptions of the *laganum* state that it should first be cooked in water and afterward fried in oil. Some describe the *laganum* in another way.

**No. 18. *Dulcia*.** Prudentius uses the word in nearly this sense, *Psychomachia*, line 429:

> Let these at last be your dishes,  
> bitter instead of the excessive sweets of a past age.

After *asperso sumuntur*, older editions add: “*Crustula* is a diminutive of *crusta*: bread sprinkled with oil, hollow in the middle and twisted. This is a *torta* of bread.” Mazzocchi likewise read the passage in this way and discusses the *torta* at length in the work cited.

**No. 19. From the mill, brought out.** In some glossaries and editions of Papias one finds *de mola gestum*, “carried from the mill,” which should not be accepted.

**No. 21. “It is called baked.”** From Servius, on *Aeneid* XI, line 553: “And baked with oak.” It either means an ancient spear—for anything very old is called “baked”—and so forth.

**No. 25.** *Axungia* comes from “anointing axles,” according to Pliny, Book XXVIII. The Spaniards call it *enjundia*.

**No. 27. *Frumen*, and so forth.** The same is discussed in Book XVII, chapter 3, no. 2. For the etymology of *pulpa*, consult Vossius’s *Etymologicon*. Becmann, together with Casaubon, approves the derivation indicated by Isidore.

**No. 28. In Lucania.** From Varro, Book IV of *The Latin Language*, chapter 24. The Spaniards retain a trace of the name, calling *lucanica* “*longaniza*.”

**No. 29. *Minutalis*.** Apicius gives various examples in Book IV, chapter 3. In Aelfric’s Saxon glossary, *martisia* or *baptitusa* is explained as meat that has been struck or pounded.

**No. 30. *Isicia*.** In Apicius it is written *hysitium*, *esitium*, and *isicium*. Jacobus a Partibus, in his glosses on Alexander of Tralles, Book II, chapter 73: “*Isicia* are made as follows: fish are cooked and afterward placed in vinegar or wine, and a powder of aromatic spices is sprinkled over them.” Varro gives this account of the name in Book IV of *The Latin Language*, chapter 22: “*Insicia*, from the fact that meat is cut up,” and so forth. Hence some write *insicium*; usage, however, has caused the *n* to be lost. Macrobius, Book VII, chapter 8: “*Insicium* was named from cutting up; after the loss of the letter, it acquired the name it now has.”

**No. 31. *Galaticae*.** Perhaps they do not differ from *galatina*, concerning which William Brito writes in Book X of the *Philippiad*: “While *galatina* preserves its vigor for them.” Barthius, commenting on this passage, understands a thick broth which, poured over fish as a seasoning, preserves their flavor and strength in the flesh for a longer time. Nothing now occurs to me concerning *sphaera*, unless perhaps it is *spira*, a kind of pastry discussed by Festus and Cato, chapter 77 of *On Agriculture*.

**No. 32. “Masters of the kitchen from *jus*,” and so forth.** Hence they also called the art of cookery a *codex*. See my notes on Sedulius, in the preface:

> Do not seek here the work of a craftsman of the *Codex*.

Some think that the word *jus* began to be used from *jus coquinae*, “the law of the kitchen,” because equal portions of food were distributed to the diners. See Suidas under δαιτή (*daite*, “banquet”) and δαιτρός (*daitros*, “distributor of portions”). Salmasius, in his notes on Trebellius Pollio, p. 207, line 17, reads: “This the Greeks call *zema*,” and rebukes those who, against the authority of the books, as he says, improperly restore ζωμός (*zomos*, “broth”). From manuscript glossaries he produces: “*Zemae*: pots.” But I do not see in what sense edible broth could be called a pot. It is different if by *zaema* is understood also kitchen broth, or the broth of bakers, as Du Cange demonstrates with several testimonies. Vulcanius did find *zema* in one old manuscript; but other copies vary, as they do in nearly all Greek words occurring in the *Etymologies*, which the scribes did not sufficiently understand. Vulcanius himself judged that ζωμόν should be restored.

**No. 34. *Lac*, and so forth.** Volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 19, contains some relevant observations.

**No. 35. *Quactum*.** You will scarcely find it elsewhere; the Spaniards say *quajo*.

**No. 36. “The honeys were from dew.”** Salmasius, p. 1018 of his *Plinian Exercises*, says of these words: “Isidore, often not a bad authority, while following older writers, gives us *saccharum*—sugar—in place of *manna*.” Salmasius adds that heavenly honey is our manna. In Virgil’s verse, Grialius and other printed and manuscript copies give *hactenus*; I have restored *protinus* from the Lucca manuscript and from the Virgilian text.

**No. 37. περὶ ὑγίας, “concerning health.”** In other copies of Grialius it is *περὶ ὐγεινῶν*, “concerning healthy things.” And immediately afterward, *sicut contrario*, “just as conversely.”

### Chapter III

**No. 2. Wine.** Gataker, chapter 5 of the posthumous *Miscellanea*, observes that *vinum* is a Greek word and is called nearly the same thing among other peoples. He therefore ridicules not only Isidore, who says that the ancients called wine *venenum*, “poison,” and derives the etymology from its filling the veins, and so forth, but also Varro, who derives *vinum* from *vis*, “force.” Concerning the law by which Roman women were forbidden to drink wine, see Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 13; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book X, chapter 23; and others. It is certain that at the rites of Bona Dea, or Fauna Fatua, Roman women used wine. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, chapter 11, records the notable deed of maidservants who challenged men to drink a great quantity of wine, pretending that a festival was being held among them, and so forth. Even today, in many regions, it is considered disgraceful for women to drink wine.

**No. 3. *Merenda*.** On *merenda*, see above, chapter 2. In Grialius’s text there was *purum fit*, evidently by error, as I think.

**No. 5. *Roseum … Amineum*.** Italians call red wine *rosso*. *Amineum* wine was named rather from a region than from its color, as were also the *amineae* vines, discussed in Book XVII, chapter 5, no. 18. More curious, but exceedingly rare, is Andrea Bacci’s book *On the Natural History of Wines, the Wines of Italy, Banquets of the Ancients, Artificial Wines, and Beers*, Rome, at the press of Mutius, 1596.

**No. 8.** Even in our own time, the people of Flanders have, according to ancient custom, offered honorary wine to the emperor when he came among them.

**No. 9. “Whence also acid.”** Some read *unde et acinum*, “whence also *acinum*.” See below, no. 11.

**No. 10. *Lactatum … mulsum*.** Hardouin, at the passage of Pliny cited by Grialius, reads *jactatu* from the manuscripts instead of *lactatu*. A drink made from water and honey is *hydromeli*, or *mulsa aqua*. *Mulsum* absolutely means wine mixed with honey, μελίκρατον (*melikraton*), *oenomeli*.

**No. 11. *Aenomeli … hydromeli*.** In the text Grialius, together with other printed editions, gives *oenomelum*, *hydromelum*; in the notes he indicates *oenomeli*, which is the better ending. As I have just said, *hydromeli* is a drink made from water and honey, and is so called for that reason. On *lorea*, compare Rosweyd, in the *Onomasticon*, under *Posca*, where we read the following from a manuscript glossary of Cambrai: “*Acini* are called the remains of grapes that have been thrown away,” and so forth. *Acinum*, in the neuter, is what grapes are washed with after the wine has been pressed; it is called *acinum*, as if *aquidum*, and is called second wine and is the drink of slaves. In the same glossary, *posca*, or *pusca*, is second wine; but more correctly *posca* is a drink made by tempering a mixture of water and vinegar. It was also simply called *acetum*, “vinegar,” and perhaps Isidore should be understood as referring to this at no. 9, except that he plainly expresses wine mixed with water.

**Nos. 12–13. *Melicratum … faecula*.** *Melicratum* has already been discussed at no. 10. *Faecula* was the same as *halec*; but Horace distinguishes *faecula Coa* from *halec*. It should not be punctuated with Grialius as *faecula, Coa*. Horace calls it *faecula Coa* in order to distinguish it from the common variety, which was also called *halec*. The name *faecula Coa* was derived either because the best was made on the island of Cos, or because it consisted of the sediment of Coan wine.

**No. 14. *Passum … defrutum*.** Ulpian, *Digest*, Book XXXIII, title 6, law 9: “If anyone has bequeathed wine, the bequest will fully include *aenomeli* and *passum*, but it will not include *defrutum*.” Nonius confirms the etymology of *defrutum* from *defervescere*, “to boil down.” Isidore followed Servius, on *Georgics* II, line 93: “*Passum* is so called from *patior*, ‘to undergo,’ because must is boiled down and thereby becomes *passum*.” Hence *defrutum* was so called because it is “defrauded,” as it were, and suffers a fraud. Others think *passum* is more correctly derived from *pando*, “to spread,” than from *patior*, since *patior* is a deponent verb. Compare Vossius, in the *Etymologicon*, and, concerning *defrutum*, Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 9.

**No. 15. *Sapa*.** Varro, Nonius, and Pliny, in the same Book XIV, chapter 9, explain what it is.

**No. 16. *Sicera*.** Methodius, quoted by Photius, manuscript 237, understands by *sicera* every drink capable of causing intoxication. Meibomius, however, in Book III, chapter 3 of his work *On Beer*, wishes wine pressed from grapes to be excluded. Andreas Schottus, following Isidore, Hesychius, and Zonaras, translates Methodius’s words: “*Sicera* is anything outside wine pressed from the vine that intoxicates.” See Fabricius, *Bibliographia*, chapter 19, no. 5.

**No. 17. *Cervisia*.** Hadrianus Junius, *Annotations*, Book II, chapter 12: “It is certain that in our time beer is made from barley, which is first soaked, then roasted and dried again, with wheat flour added, together with the flowers of the willow-like hop and the lees of beer, which serve in place of yeast.” Isidore seems to have recognized nearly this method of preparation. Junius adds further remarks on the difference between ancient *cythus*, or *zythum*—called *celia*, *caelia*, or *ceria* by the Spaniards—and modern *cervisia*. G. G. Kirchmeierus published a dissertation on the ancient Scythian *celia*, *aelia*, and *zythum*; Johannes Henricus Meibomius wrote a treatise on beers and wine.

**No. 18. *Celia*.** Grialius writes *caelia*; *celia* is the more usual form. Isidore took these words concerning *celia* from Orosius, Book V, chapter 7: “Finally, all the Numantines suddenly burst out through two gates, having first fortified themselves with a generous drink—not of wine, for that region is not productive of it, but of the juice of wheat, prepared by an art which they call *celia* from heating.” “For that fiery power is stirred up … is added.” But in Orosius the reading should be *quo fermento*, “with which ferment,” which seems better than *quo fermentato*, “with which fermented [drink].”

**No. 19. *Garum*.** The most highly praised *garum* was made from mackerel in the fish-processing establishments of Carthage Spartaria. See Pliny, Book XXXI, chapters 7 and 8.

**No. 20. *Muria*.** Martial, Book XIII, epigram 103, concerning *muria*, which was far inferior to *garum*:

> I confess, I am the daughter of an Antipolitan tuna;  
> had I been a mackerel, I would not have been sent to you.

**No. 21.** Rosweyd, in the *Onomasticon*, interprets *ptisana* as *posca*, discussed above at no. 11. In this passage *zema* will mean broth, and *op zema* means expressed juice. Servius, on *Aeneid* IV, said that *zema* for “pot” was a vulgar, not a Latin, word. Compare Du Cange.

### Chapter IV

**No. 2. “Why have you made me thus?”** In the Vulgate: “Why have you made me thus?”

**No. 3. Earthen vessels in Samos.** Plautus alluded to this in *Stichus*, Act V, scene 4, line 12:

> Yet we drink from our own little Samian vessel.

**No. 6. *Creta … quae Samia appellatur*.** Perhaps clay called Samian was also produced not far from Rome, although the name originated from the island of Samos. For vessels were likewise called Samian that had not been made from the clay of the island of Samos.

**No. 9. *Discus … quod det escas*.** Montfaucon, *Antiquity Explained*, Book III, chapter 4, volume II, part I, where he discusses *disci*, rejects the etymology “because it gives food” and observes that such etymologies lend little authority to the testimony of ancient writers such as Isidore and Varro. *Discus* is certainly Greek; nor is there any evidence from elsewhere that it was formerly *iscus*.

**No. 10. *Parapsis*.** Sirmond, volume I of his works, column 1889, discusses the explanation of this word, as have many others. It is written *paropsis*, from παρά (*para*, “beside”) and ὄψον (*opson*, “food, relish”), and *parapsis*, from παρά and ἀψίς (*apsis*, “curvature”); hence *absis* also means a food vessel. Concerning *patina*, see chapter 8, no. 2.

**No. 11. *Gavata … scutella*.** Grialius punctuates the passage as follows: “and with open mouths, dishes”; *gabata*, and so forth, which is less satisfactory. Sirmond, in volume I of his works, Book II of Ennodius, poem 22, whose title is “On a *compostile* having seven *gavatae*,” observes from Martial and Fortunatus that *gavata* is a type of dish. He also cites Isidore: “A dish is *gavata*, as though *cavata*, ‘hollowed out,’” and the glosses: “*Paropsis*: *gavata* or *catinus*.” Thus, he says, the word should be read in the same way in both places. *Scutella* is a diminutive of *scutra*, a type of vessel, and perhaps derives its name from *scutum*, “shield.” Thus *capella* comes from *capra*, and *mitella* from *mitra*. The Spaniards call a *scutella* an *escudilla*, and the Italians a *scodella*.

**No. 12. *Apophoreta*.** Isidore calls a food vessel suitable for carrying *apophoreta* an *apophoreta*; I do not know on whose authority. Grialius had printed: “A saltcellar, a vessel suitable for such things.”

**No. 13. “That of the ancients.”** I would prefer “that of Martial,” for the Vatican manuscript contains *illud metrum distichon*, and perhaps *metrum* was produced from an abbreviation of Martial.

**No. 14. *Trisceles*.** Those who write *trisciles* are influenced by the authority of certain manuscripts; but in ancient parchment manuscripts *e* and *i* are very often interchanged.

### Chapter V

**No. 3. *Cratera*.** In Virgil’s verse, *crateras* is from *crater*; in Persius’ verse, the form is from *cratera*, *craterae*, unless we say that the final syllable is lengthened by the caesura, which is unnecessary.

**No. 4. A kind of cup called *amystis*.** So Pollux, Book III, chapter 16. Sidonius uses this word in prose after poem 22, addressed to Pontius Leontius. In Horace, some understand *amystidem* not as a cup but as the drink itself, in the Thracian manner. For *baccea*, medieval writers and glossaries also give *bacca*, *baccharium*, *bacchonica*, *bachoaicha*, *bachia*, and *bachoica*.

### Chapter VI

**No. 1.** Many write *flascae*. The forms *phlascula* and *phlaco* are also found in medieval writers and monuments.

**No. 3.** Among the ancient Latins, *sicula* means a small *sica*, or dagger. Some later writers used *sicula* for *sicla*, *siclo*, or *sigla*, a measure of liquids.

**No. 4. *Situla*.** Grialius’s text had *sicula*; in the notes he correctly gives *situla*.

**No. 5. *Orca*.** I do not conclude from Varro, cited by Grialius, that the word is Spanish. For there were *orcae* in other provinces as well. Horace, Book II of the *Satires*, line 65:

> But it will be fitting to mix it with rich unmixed wine and *muria*,  
> not any other than that in which a Byzantine jar has decayed.

Pliny, Book XV, chapter 19: “Where figs abound, jars are filled in Asia, while casks are filled in the African city of Ruspina.” The Spanish *orza* comes from *orca*.

**No. 6. *Seriola*.** This is a diminutive of *seria*, a word used by Persius and Palladius for an elongated, bulging earthen vessel. Isidore’s statement concerning the direct arrangement of the *orcae* is not supported by the testimony of others. John of Genoa and others, on Isidore’s authority, assert that its etymology derives from Syria.

**No. 7. *Cupae*, and so forth.** Hence also *copa*, a woman who sells wine, and the Spanish word *copa*, a vessel from which water or wine is drunk. *Mulctrum* is also called *mulctrale*, and there is a feminine form *mulctra*, although some maintain that there was a distinction between *mulctra* and *mulctrale*. Ancient Christians often depicted the *mulctrale* on glass, as can be seen in Buonarroti, and on sarcophagi, as in Bottari, volume I of *Subterranean Rome*.

**No. 8. *Labrum*.** The word is used of any large vessel whose rims are spread outward like lips. There were bathing, wine, and water *labra*, and so forth. In Saint Ambrose and others it also means a funerary vessel suitable for containing a corpse. Here Isidore takes it for the font in which infants were washed; perhaps this is what Anastasius the Librarian had in mind when, in his account of Saint Sylvester, he uses *labrum* to indicate the basin of the baptismal font.

**No. 9. *Siphon*.** Mazzocchi, in volume I of the *Spicilegium Biblicum*, on Genesis 13:10, demonstrates that the etymology of *siphon* is purely Hebrew: “Nor is this surprising,” he says, “since the Orientals used it, as Isidore states.” He adds other remarks concerning the use of siphons in the cultivation of gardens and fields.

### Chapter VII

**No. 2. *Alabastrites*.** *Alabastrites* was discussed in Book XVI, chapter 5, no. 7. Vessels for perfumes were similarly made from onyx, and nard-perfume was especially accustomed to being stored in them, as is clear from Catullus, Horace, and Propertius.
