**No. 4. *Lenticula*, and so forth.** This is the reading of the ancient manuscripts, as Vulcanius also acknowledged, although he nevertheless printed a quite different one.

### Chapter VIII

**No. 2. *Patella*.** On *patella*, see chapter 4, no. 10, of this book.

**No. 6. *Mola … rutabulum*.** In Greek, μύλη (*myle*) is a mill, and μύλων (*mylon*) a millhouse or bakery. Grialius preferred *rotabulum*; but other writers spell it *rutabulum*, and there is no evidence that Isidore wrote it otherwise. It is well known that in manuscripts *o* and *u* are frequently confused.

### Chapter IX

**No. 2. “Hence also *arcivum*.”** Perhaps Isidore does not mean *archium*, or *archivum*, which comes from the Greek ἀρχή (*arche*, “beginning, authority”), but *arcivum*, concerning which an old glossary says: “*Arcivus*: restraining, forbidding.” Thus, in Festus, Scaliger reads *arciva avis* for *arcula avis*, namely a bird which at the taking of auspices forbids something to be done.

**No. 3. *Cibutum … arcam*.** In Greek, κιβωτός (*kibotos*) means a chest or box. *Cibutum* is repeated in old glossaries after Isidore.

**No. 4. *Mozicia … modicum*.** Papias: “*Mozica*, as though *modica*; hence *mozus*, with *z* for *d*,” and so forth. From Isidore, John of Genoa gives: “*Mozina*, from *modus*, a type of repository, as though *modina*.” Aelfric’s glossary: “*Mozyta*, or a little chest.” It should be observed that among the ancients *di* was easily changed into *z*, as in *zabulus* for *diabolus*, and *Zanium* for *Dianium*. The form *hozie* for *hodie* belongs here.

**No. 6. *Sitarciae*.** Becmann and others prove that *sitarcia*, or *sitarchia*, has a Greek origin. Properly, *sitarcia* is the provision prepared for a journey; by metonymy, it means the bag in which that provision is contained. Isidore’s statement that *sitarciae* belong to sailors seems capable of confirmation not only by Apuleius but also by other authorities. Jerome, in the preface to his commentary on Matthew, addressed to Eusebius: “I am surprised that, since you are suddenly about to sail to Rome, you wished me to give you this, as it were, a *sitarcia*, by briefly explaining Matthew.” An old scholiast on Juvenal, *Satire* 12, line 61: “Between a *sitarcia* and an axe, consider what is necessary for carrying aboard a ship.” But the word is extended to other things as well.

**No. 8. *Canistrum*.** Varro, Book IV of *The Latin Language*, chapter 25: “*Tryblia* and *canistra*, which people think are Latin, are Greek.”

**No. 10. *Sporta … from *spartum*.** Nonius, chapter 2, no. 833: “*Sportae* are derived either from *spartum*, as though *sparteae*, or from *asportare*, ‘to carry away.’ Vulcanius adds other material which, although absent from the manuscripts, he nevertheless considers sound.”

### Chapter X

**No. 1. “From fire.”** I restore this form from Grialius’s note, for the text had *ab igne*, which amounts to the same thing. Concerning the word *culina*, see the learned remarks of the distinguished Clemens Biagius in *Monumenta Graeca et Latina*, p. 195.

**No. 2. *Lucerna … as Persius … cicindela*.** I have restored *ut Persius*, “as Persius has it.” Grialius, following Servius, took the words as *ut Juvenalis*; but the verse belongs to Persius, and Vulcanius and other older printed editions identify Persius. Servius’ reasoning, adopted by Isidore—that if *lucerna* came from *lux*, “light,” the verse would be metrically impossible because *lu* would be long—proves nothing, since many derivatives change their quantity, such as *arena*, *arista*, and *acerbus*. Concerning the matter itself, Varro, Book IV of *The Latin Language*, chapter 25: “Afterward came the lamp, called from *lux*, ‘light,’ or because the Greeks call it λύχνος (*lychnos*).” For *cicendela*, as it stood in Grialius’s text and in other printed editions, I have written *cicindela*, for that is the name of a certain kind of fly that shines at night.

**No. 3. “Here for you,” and so forth.** Perhaps the verses beginning “Here for you” are not by Martial but by another earlier writer, from whom Martial derived his material.

**No. 4. *Lacunaria*.** No other reference occurs to *lacunaribus* as hanging lights.

**No. 5. *Funalia*, and so forth.** See Book XI, chapter 2, no. 34; Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 38; and Kirchmann, *On Roman Funerals*, Book II, chapter 3. I should not omit mentioning here something I could have mentioned in many other places: how careless the recent Madrid editor was, who committed the following to type: “*Funalia*: candelabra among the ancients, in which cords coated with wax, or with some such fuel for light, were fixed.” The words “they had projecting spikes or hooks” have been omitted. Similar errors occur throughout, and no correction of the misprints is apparent anywhere. Semler, in his note on Isidore’s Glossary under *Scolaces*, corrects the corrupt old editions at this point, apparently forgetting or unaware of Grialius’s edition. He seems, however, to wish to read *scoliae*, not *scoliae*, deriving it from the masculine Greek σκώλιοι (*skolioi*).

**No. 8. *Lucubrum*, and so forth.** Papias and other lexicographers and glossographers give nearly the same account from Isidore. Forcellini says that *lucubrum*, included among barbarous words, means anything made from dry material for kindling a fire.

**No. 10. “For foretelling.”** Grialius and other printed editions have *ad pronuntianda*, “for proclaiming.” But *ad praenuntianda*, “for foretelling,” is correct; the same words are also found in Book XV, chapter 2, no. 37.

### Chapter XI

**No. 1. *Lecticae*.** For more on *lecticae*, see Lipsius, Book I of the *Electa*, chapter 19. The ancients thought that *lecticae* were an invention of the Bithynians, as Vulpius observes in his notes on Catullus, p. 39. The more common spelling in Caesar, Pliny, and others is *storea*, from στὸρεω (*storeo*), “to spread.” Grialius printed *storiatus*, *storia*.

**No. 2. *Cama … grabatum … bajonola*.** On *cama*, see Book XIX, chapter 22, no. 29. The neuter *grabatum* is scarcely found among earlier writers; in Greek it is κράβατος or κράββατος (*krabatos*). Cicero, Martial, and others use the masculine *grabatus* for a low bed on which beggars and two-obol prostitutes slept. Perhaps *grabatus* should be read in Isidore. For *bajonola*, Du Cange thought *bajulona* should be read, as in Uguccione: “*Bajulona*: a bed carried during a journey.” The spelling of this word varies in other glossaries and likewise in Isidore’s manuscripts.

**No. 3. “The *pulvinar*, the bed of the rich … *spingae* … *punicani*.”** The same is discussed in Book XIX, chapter 26, no. 4. Compare the note. Du Cange understands *spingas*, *spingatas*, and *figies* as *sphingas*, and observes that such sphinxes can be seen on seats in the agate of the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, as preserved by Santamantius. Pliny also discusses *Punicani* couches, Book XXXIII, chapter 11. For a similar reason there were also windows called *Punicani*, *Punicani* joinery, and so forth. Some read: “First brought from Carthage,” which, with the *a* omitted, is more Latin.

**No. 4. “The first,” he says, and so forth.** In Vatican manuscript 93, as in other ancient copies, the passage reads: “Concerning this Satyrus says in his *Life*: ‘At first,’ he says, ‘contrary to the custom of emperors, they used couches instead of beds.’”

**No. 5. *Spondae … pluteus*.** A bed had two *spondae*: one external, simply called the bed’s *sponda*; the other internal, placed against the wall and furnished with a *pluteus*, against which wives reclined. The latter was called *pluteus*. The word *sponda* passed into Italian. In dining couches, by contrast, *sponda* denoted the inner side next to the table, while *pluteus* denoted the outer side. See Gesner, *Thesaurus*, under *Pluteus*.

**No. 7. *Feretrum … capulus*.** On *feretrum*, see above, Book XVIII, chapter 9, no. 1. Kirchmann, *On Roman Funerals*, Book II, chapter 3, also rejected the etymology of *capulus* from “because it is over the heads,” and so forth. *Capularis senex* occurs in Caecilius, quoted by Fulgentius, *On Ancient Speech*, no. 23. Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus*, Act III, scene 1, line 33:

> Do I seem to you so much a man of Acheron? So much a corpse-ready old man?

**No. 8. “Hence also *scabelli*.”** It should be “Hence also *scabella*, which …” Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 12, citing Psalm 109:2, says *suppedaneum pedum tuorum*, “the footstool of your feet”; the Vulgate has *scabellum pedum tuorum*. Quintilian, Book I, chapter 4, or section 6: “Let the boy learn what is proper to letters, what is common, what relationship they have with one another; and let him not wonder why *scabellum* is formed from *scamnum*.” Pliny has the adjective *scansilis*; but *scansile* for steps and similar things is assigned to the Middle Ages, concerning which see Du Cange under *scandile*, *scansile*, from Papias and others.

**No. 9. Chairs of teachers.** Joannes Andreas Schmid published a dissertation on the chairs of the ancient teachers at Jena in 1683. Even after the practice of reclining at banquets became customary, men too sometimes dined while seated, especially at funeral banquets, as is observed in an ancient painting in the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, reproduced by Bottari, volume II of *Subterranean Rome*, plate 127. Compare also volume III, plate 141. Aldus Manutius the Younger, in Book I, chapter 4 of *Questions by Letter*, accurately discusses the manner of reclining and eating, and observes that reclining was indeed considered disgraceful in women, but that later, corrupted by the contagion of custom, they began to recline.

**No. 10. *Sella*.** After Lipsius, Scheffer, *On Vehicles*, Book II, chapter 4, teaches that formerly *sellae* were common to both sexes, while *cathedrae* belonged to women, although softer men did not refuse to use *cathedrae*.

### Chapter XII

**No. 1. *Carrum*.** Scheffer, *On Vehicles*, Book II, chapter 27, thinks that *carrum* was a word borrowed from barbarians, perhaps from the Gauls. Concerning Isidore’s etymology he says: “What is the axle of wheels? Is it that around which they turn? But this is not the axle in vehicles. Nor does the fact that they appear to have wheels explain *carri*.” In Book II, chapter 15, he himself asserts that *currus* comes from *currere*, “to run,” where he explains that Isidore meant *currus* to be so called because it runs, as though it had many wheels. Compare my note on Book XVIII, chapter 35, no. 1. In any case, the “axle of wheels” mentioned by Isidore seems to be the axle, that is, the rounded beam around which the wheel turns. Others think *carrum* was named from its four wheels, as though *quadrum* or *quarrum*, as in Stephen of Tournai, letter 229.

**No. 2. *Rheda*.** Quintilian, Book I, chapter 5, or section 9, says that the word is Gallic. It is also written *reda*; but there is no independent evidence that the ancients used *retas* for *rhedae*. *Retae* were trees projecting from the banks of rivers, concerning which see Gellius, Book XI, chapter 17.

**No. 3. *Carpentum … caracutium*.** Scheffer, in his discussion of the *carpentum*, which he thinks was named from Carmenta, believes that Isidore intended simply to describe a ceremonial *carpentum*. He therefore observes that in the 1595 edition *pompaticum* is referred to the *carpentum*, not to the following type of vehicle. I have no doubt, however, that Isidore derives the word *carpentum* only from a ceremonial or procession *carro*, as Vossius also interprets it in his *Etymologicon*. Becmann agrees with Scheffer and believes that Isidore calls *carpentum pompaticum* a type of vehicle; but he suspects that, instead of *quasi carrum pompaticum*, we should read *quasi carrum pendentem*, “as though a hanging wagon.” *Caracutium*, or *carracutium*, is not found among earlier writers; Papias, the Arabic-Latin glossary, and the Saxon glossary took it from Isidore. In Vitruvius, Book X, chapter 14, *capsus* is the part of a *rheda* in which the passengers sit.

**No. 4. *Pilentum*.** Vulcanius and the older printed editions give: “*Pilentum*, or *petoritum*, a vehicle constructed with four wheels.” Scheffer, *On Vehicles*, Book II, chapter 25, thinks it should be punctuated: “*Pilentum*, or *petoritum contextum*, a four-wheeled vehicle.” *Petoritum* was indeed four-wheeled; but most writers report that the *pilentum* had only two wheels. As can be inferred from Grialius’s edition, Isidore assigns four wheels to both the *pilentum* and the *petoritum*. See my commentary on Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*, line 1088, and Pithoeus, *Adversaria Subseciva*, Book I, chapter 5.

**No. 5. *Basterna*.** This was a vehicle for matrons. Rosweyd discusses it at length in the *Onomasticon*, under *Basterna*. Compare also the ancient epigram in Pithoeus’s collection:

> The golden *basterna* encloses chaste matrons.

### Chapter XIII

**No. 1. *Baculus*.** Becmann explains the origin of *baculus* as Hebrew.

**No. 3. *Forfices … forpiceps … forcipes*.** Vossius, in his *Etymologicon*, doubts the Latinity of *forpiceps*. It is nevertheless found in Cassiodorus’s *Orthography*, chapter 4, from the manuscript of Velserus, and in Sidonius, *Epithalamium of Polemius*, poem 15, line 185, according to the best copies. Du Cange lists and transcribes other medieval writers who adopted and explained this Isidorian distinction among *forpex*, *forfex*, and *forceps*; it is enough to refer to him.

**No. 5. *Catenatum*.** Perhaps *catenatum*, or *catenatium*, is the bolt that the Italians call *catenaccio* and the Spaniards *cerrojo*. The Spanish *candado* and Italian *lucchetto* designate an instrument that is locked without a key and opened with a key. In the *Life of Saint Fructuosus*, chapter 19, or elsewhere, no. 18: “They secured the doors of the dwelling with chains and bolts, and with various strong fastenings.” Laurentius Joannes Molin was occupied with explaining this not especially obvious subject and published a dissertation *On the Keys of the Ancients*.

### Chapter XIV

**No. 1. *Occulto*.** In editions of Lucretius the form is *occulte* instead of *occulto*. In Servius, on *Georgics* I, line 46, “and worn down by the furrow,” the reading is:

> The plowshare diminishes imperceptibly in the field.

**No. 2. *Buris*.** It is also called *bura*, *burae*. Grialius printed in the text *in quo vomer inducitur*, “into which the plowshare is inserted,” while in the notes he suggests that Isidore read *includitur*, “in which the plowshare is enclosed.” Both verbs occur in Servius, on *Georgics* I, line 172: “The *dentale* is the piece of wood into which the plowshare is enclosed … for nearly all such plowshares in Italy are of this kind. The *dentale*, however, is the piece of wood into which the plowshare is inserted.”

N. 5. *Falcastrum.* In Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 6: “And he ordered an implement to be given to him, which, from its resemblance to a sickle, is called a *falcastrum*, so that he might cut down thornbushes in a certain place.” It occurs in other writers of the later period.

N. 6. *Rastrum.* It differs from the *rutrum*: the latter served for digging the earth, the former for scraping and smoothing it. [Col. 1051D] See Salmasius, p. 365 of the *Exercitationes Plinianae*.

N. 7. *Quod circa codicem.* Papias: “That which is around the *caudex*, etc.” Aelfric’s Anglo-Saxon Glossary: “*Scudicia*, or a digging spade.” It is also written *scuditia*.

N. 10. *Tribula.* In Spanish it is called *trillo*. Schoetgenius reproduced the figure of this implement, as well as that of the small wagon, which does not differ greatly from the *tribula*, in *Antiquitates triturae*, pp. 34 and 36. Juvencus also uses the word *pala*, book I, verse 378. See what I noted on that passage.

N. 11. *Frumenta cilluntur.* Servius, on book II of the *Georgics*, verse 389: “By which grain is threshed, from *cilleo*.” Isidore uses the verb *cillo, cillis*, which amounts to the same thing.

N. 12. Those grain tokens were such that, when presented, each person received a fixed quantity of grain from the prefect of the grain supply; such tokens were formerly distributed at Rome to poorer people for the purpose of relieving their want. See Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapters 40 and 41, and *Nero*, chapter 11; Juvenal, Martial, and others.

[Col. 1052A] N. 13. *Verennes*, etc. Papias adds that they are implements used by country people. What they were like, others do not explain. Columella, in the passage cited by Grialius, says: “Press the myrtle berries enclosed in a little wooden basket.” From this most people derive *fiscellus*, not *fiscellum*, as Grialius suggests. The usual form is *fiscella*. In Aelfric’s Saxon Glossary: “*Fisclum Eleseocche*, literally, the oil of the sick.”

## CHAPTER XV

N. 1. *Haustra.* Nonius, chapter 1, no. 43, thinks that *haustra* are jars by which water is drawn, attached to the wheels of a machine; Vitruvius, book X, chapter 9, supports this view. Nonius’s words are these: “Properly, *haustra* are called the jars of wheels, from drawing water, just as in Greek ἄντλια [*antlia*].”

N. 2. *Gyrgillus.* The Italians say *girella*, the Spaniards *polea*. John of Genoa assigns this word another meaning as well: “*Gyrgillus*, from *gyrus*, is a woman’s implement, otherwise called *volutorium*, because by turning it in a circle the threads are unwound from it.” Some write *girgillus*.

N. 3. *Telonem.* Pithoeus, *Adversaria*, book II, chapter 16, corrected it to either *tellenonem* or *tollonem*. Some indeed read *tollonem* in Plautus and Columella, but most others disagree. The philosopher Seneca also mentions *tollenon*. In some printed editions two words have been made into one, *Hamalupus*. Salmasius, in Trebellius Pollio, p. 207, line 30, shows that *ama*, or *hama*, is a Greek word for an implement with which a garden is dug, not an implement for extinguishing fire, as others maintain. But the passages cited by Grialius suggest otherwise. Add Juvenal, *Satire* XIV, verses 305–306:

> With the hooks arranged, Licinus orders cohorts  
> of slaves to keep watch at night.

N. 4. *Lupus … Canicula … Harpax.* Livy mentions *lupus* in this sense; I do not know whether anyone besides Isidore mentions *canicula*. Instead of *harpax*, *harpago* would be preferable.

## CHAPTER XVI

N. 1. *Fressa.* It is written *fressus* and *fresus*.

N. 2. *Lupata.* Montfaucon, *Antiquities Explained*, book III, chapter 1, title 4, part I, discusses *lupata* bits, which, as can be gathered from Isidore, were furnished with wolves’ teeth. [Col. 1052C] Others think that the outer edges of the *lupata* terminated beyond the horse’s mouth in the heads of wolves. Montfaucon says that neither interpretation is free from difficulty. Ovid called the *lupata* “wolves.” Compare the preceding chapter, no. 4, and the *Various Readings*.

N. 4. *Antella … Cingulum.* Grialius retained *antella* in the text, and I do not think it should be changed. It could indeed have been said in either form. In the first Gothic–Toletan manuscript, under the word *Antella*, there is the gloss *pectoralia* [“breast ornaments”]. Ebrard of Béthune, in the *Graecismus*, chapter 10:

> *Est antella, quod est in pectore quadrupedantis …*  
> “It is *antella*, that which is on the breast of a four-footed animal …”

> *Dicatur postella, quod est a posteriori*  
> “Let it be called *postella*, that which is at the rear.”

You will also find written *antela, antilena, postelina, postela*, and so forth. For *cingula*, feminine gender, the Spaniards say *cincha*, the Italians *cigna* or *cinghia*. Ovid uses this word.

N. 5. *Sagma … salma.* Horse coverings are often called *saga*, and those who correct this word should not be heeded, although *sagma* is Greek and is not derived from *sagum*. See Casaubon, on Capitolinus, p. 37, line 22. The word *salma* passed into certain vernacular languages. Hence the Spaniards use *ensalma* and *enjalma*. Perhaps the Italian word *soma* derives from *sagma*. Scheffer, *On the History of Vehicles*, book II, chapter 2, thinks that *sagmae* were pack-saddles on which loads were placed, whereas *sellae*, *strata*, or *saga* belonged to the people who sat upon them; *sagmae*, or pack-saddles, were for receiving loads.

Instead of *capulum funis*, or *funus*, as it is read in some places, Gisbert Cuperus, *Observations*, book II, chapter 9, corrected it to *capulus funis*, so that *capulus* would be an adjective. But he offers no adequate reason for this. Let us therefore retain *capulum*, or, with Isidore’s Glossary and Papias, *caplum*. In certain vernacular languages *cable* means a nautical rope.

N. 6. *Stimuli.* *Stimulus* derives from the Greek στίζω [*stizō*], meaning “I prick.”

N. 7. *Strigiles … Character.* Mercurialis reproduced the figure of a *strigilis* in book I, chapter 8, of *The Art of Gymnastics*. *Character* properly means a mark engraved, branded, or inscribed with an iron instrument or by some other method. Georgius Longus discusses the red-hot iron with which cattle and flocks were branded, in *On Signet Rings*, chapter 11; he rightly preferred *ferrum caloratum* [“heated iron”] to *ferrum coloratum* [“colored iron”], the reading of certain editions. Calpurnius, *Eclogue* 5, verses 84ff., describes the manner in which these marks and signs were impressed upon animals. A philological dissertation exists by Sigismund Friedrich Dresigius, *On the Use of Stigmata among the Ancients*, not to mention the well-known work of Théophile Raynaud, *On Sacred and Profane Stigmatism*.

N. 8. *Cautertum*, from καίω [*kaiō*], “I burn.” Marks were often branded with a cautery as identifying signs, so that greedy people would not appropriate the property of others, especially cattle and flocks.
